\section{Avertissement and
Introduction}\label{avertissement-and-introduction}

\subsection{Avertissement}\label{avertissement}

We present here a slightly revised re-edition of the original Séminaire,
whose aim and content are indicated in the Introduction. The revision
consisted essentially in the correction of typographical errors, the
addition (in footnotes) of some supplementary remarks or references, the
present subdivision into three volumes each equipped with a detailed
table of contents and an index of notation, and the adjunction of a
terminological index at the end of Volume 3. In addition, Exposé VI\_B
by J.-E. Bertin has been partially rewritten by him, in particular §§ 5
and 10, so that some references to that Exposé differ from references to
the original Exposé. The reader will find a list of the Séminaire's
Exposés at the beginning of the present volume.

Since the first edition of the present Séminaire appeared, the
\emph{Éléments de Géométrie Algébrique}, Chap. IV, have appeared in
their entirety, which renders certain passages of the Séminaire
unnecessary; we have occasionally indicated in footnotes the relevant
references to EGA IV that allow such passages to be short-circuited.

For another exposition on algebraic groups using systematically the
language of schemes, we point to the book by M. Demazure and P. Gabriel,
\emph{Groupes algébriques} (North-Holland \& Masson et Cie). Unlike the
present Séminaire, this book assumes no knowledge of algebraic geometry,
but contains all the necessary preliminaries from the theory of schemes,
and its reading can therefore serve as an introduction to the study of
our Séminaire. (It also contains themes not covered in the Séminaire,
such as the Dieudonné-style structure theory of commutative affine
algebraic groups, in \emph{loc. cit.} Chap. V.)

Bures-sur-Yvette, March 1970

\subsection{Introduction}\label{introduction}

\textbf{1.} The aim of the present seminar is twofold.

On the one hand, we aim to give convenient foundations for the theory of
group schemes in general. Exposés I to IV will provide for this purpose
the indispensable preliminary exercises in schematic and categorical
syntax. To obtain a language that ``fits'' geometric intuition
effortlessly, and to avoid eventually unbearable circumlocutions, we
always identify a prescheme \(X\) over another \(S\) with the functor
\((Sch)^{\circ}/S \to (Ens)\) that it represents,\footnote{Such a
  viewpoint seems to have been envisaged for the first time eight or
  nine years ago, in connection with the theory of formal groups, by P.
  Cartier, who unfortunately did not take the trouble to make it precise
  and systematic as it deserved.} and it is necessary to give many
definitions in such a way that they apply to arbitrary functors,
representable or not. Moreover, nearly all the functors we shall have to
use will be ``sheaves'' (for the ``faithfully flat quasi-compact
topology''); Exposé IV, which treats groups only incidentally, gives a
sketch of the language of ``localization'' and sheaves, which turns out
to be very convenient for questions of representability of functors as
well. Above all, this Exposé will provide us, for questions of passage
to the quotient, with the most convenient framework for what follows.

Exposé V gives some general results on the existence of quotients, taken
up in Exposé VI\_A in the case of the quotient of an algebraic group
over a field (or more generally, over an Artinian ring) by a
subgroup.\footnote{For a more thorough study of passage to the quotient,
  in particular by reductive groups, see the important study by D.
  Mumford, \emph{Geometric Invariant Theory}, Ergebnisse der Mathematik,
  Bd. 34, Springer, 1965. Let us observe that, on an important point,
  the terminology of this book does not agree with ours: over a field of
  characteristic \(p > 0\), the groups that Mumford calls
  ``reductive''{[}\^{}N.D.E-I-intro-1{]} are the smooth groups of
  multiplicative type in the sense of the seminar (cf.~Exp. IX). One may
  presumably consider that Mumford's acceptation of the word
  ``reductive'', which loses its meaning over a base that is not a
  field, was adopted by him on a provisional basis and as a kind of
  stopgap (and this is also roughly what Mumford explains, for other
  motives, from the second paragraph of his preface!).} The latter
Exposé and Exposé VI\_B which follows it also contain various elementary
results specific to algebraic groups over a field, used routinely
thereafter.

Exposé VII studies certain facts linked to the characteristic of the
base field, and in particular develops with appropriate generality the
correspondence between radicial group schemes of height 1 and restricted
\(p\)-Lie algebras.

Finally, Exposé XVIII contains the generalization, in the theory of
schemes, of Weil's theorem on the ``birational'' definition of algebraic
groups.

On the other hand, we propose to generalize to groups over an arbitrary
base prescheme the Borel--Chevalley structure theory of affine algebraic
groups. It has moreover become apparent in the course of writing up the
seminar notes that the affine hypothesis is unnecessary for many results
of the theory. The most complete results are obtained, evidently, in the
case of ``semisimple group schemes'', or more generally ``reductive''
ones, with which we shall be exclusively concerned from Exposé XIX
onwards. Chevalley himself had already given the construction of the
``Tôhoku'' groups over the ring of integers, a construction that will be
taken up in the present seminar. The principal uniqueness
theorem\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} This refers to Corollary XXIII.5.6, which
  is easily deduced from the uniqueness theorem for split reductive
  groups (cf.~XXIII, Th. 4.1 and Cor. 5.2), given that every semisimple
  \(S\)-group is a ``twisted form'' (for the étale topology) of a
  ``Tôhoku'' group (cf.~XXII, Cor. 2.3).} gives a simple
characterization of the ``twisted'' variants of these Tôhoku groups over
a base prescheme \(S\): they are the affine and smooth groups over \(S\)
whose geometric fibers are connected semisimple groups in the usual
sense.\footnote{This is the essential result of M. Demazure's thesis
  (\emph{Schémas en groupes réductifs}, Bull. Soc. Math. France
  \textbf{93} (1965), 369--413).}

\textbf{2.} As in the case of the theory known over an algebraically
closed field, a crucial role is played by the sub-tori of the group
schemes under consideration. The preliminary study of tori --- and, more
generally, of ``group schemes of multiplicative type'' (both from the
intrinsic viewpoint and from the viewpoint of multiplicative-type
subgroups of a given group) --- therefore takes up a fairly large place
in this seminar (Exposés VIII to XII). Their remarkable rigidity (in
certain respects greater even than that of abelian schemes, or of
semisimple group schemes) makes them very effective working instruments
for the study of certain more general groups.

\textbf{3.} From Exposé XII onwards (with the exception of Exposé XVIII
already mentioned) we shall routinely use the theory of affine algebraic
groups over an algebraically closed field, which the reader will find in
the \emph{Séminaire Chevalley} 1956, in particular in Exposés IV to IX
of that seminar. We shall also use, but to a lesser extent, the later
Exposés of the \emph{Séminaire Chevalley}, devoted to the structure of
semisimple algebraic groups. Indeed, we shall take up Chevalley's theory
directly in the framework of schemes: it will be seen that in this way
(even over a base field) the exposition gains in simplicity and in
precision.

\textbf{4.} The principal object of the present seminar is evidently to
develop techniques that apply to the study of group schemes over an
arbitrary base, i.e.~essentially to the study of families of algebraic
groups. As such, the infinitesimal properties of such families, and in
particular the case of an Artinian base scheme, play an important role.
These properties intervene even for the study

of algebraic groups over a field \(k\), in the case where the latter is
not perfect, in order in particular to apply the technique of descent in
the non-Galois case. Among the new results obtained in this case, let us
mention the existence of maximal tori and Cartan subgroups in any smooth
algebraic group, the rationality of the variety of maximal tori, and
various related results (Exp. XIV\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} In particular,
  Theorems 1.1 and 6.1.}), or the correspondence between the ``forms''
of a semisimple group and the principal homogeneous bundles under a
suitable (in general non-connected) semisimple algebraic group (Exp.
XXIV, 1.16--1.20). In general, one may say that the methods required to
work over a non-perfect base field are essentially those used for
arbitrary base preschemes, and thereby fall outside the framework of
classical algebraic geometry.

\textbf{5.} It has not seemed useful to indicate at the head of the
written-up Exposés the date or dates of the corresponding oral
presentations at the Séminaire. Let us merely say that the order of the
mimeographed Exposés (from I to XXVI) does correspond to the order of
the oral presentations. On the other hand, the writing-up of the final
text is sometimes notably later than the oral presentation, and often
differs from it fairly substantially, the written text being generally
more detailed and more complete (such as Exp. IV and VII\_B), or indeed
substantially more general (such as Exp. XII or VII\_B) than the oral
presentation. Other written Exposés correspond to no oral presentation
(VI\_B, VII\_A, XV, XVI, XVII, and essentially XXVI), and were written
up and inserted into the mimeographed seminar either to provide
convenient references for various other Exposés (this is notably the
case of VI\_B), or because they constitute a natural extension of the
notions and techniques already developed. One should note as a
consequence that the reading of Exposés VII\_A, VII\_B, XV, XVI, XVII is
not necessary for the study of the rest of the seminar, and in
particular for the part of this seminar devoted to reductive group
schemes.

\textbf{6.} From the theory of schemes, we shall mainly use the general
language of schemes, expounded in EGA I; the notions of flat morphism,
étale morphism, smooth morphism, expounded in SGA 1, I to V; and finally
the theory of faithfully flat descent of SGA 1, VIII. We have as far as
possible avoided formulating unnecessary noetherian hypotheses, which
has required us in return to replace the usual hypothesis ``of finite
type'' by the hypothesis ``of finite presentation''. For the notion of
morphism of finite presentation, the reader is referred to EGA IV, 1.4
and 1.6. The results of SGA 1, I to IV, most often stated in the
noetherian context, will be developed in the general case in EGA
IV,\footnote{Since the writing of this introduction, the four parts (§§
  1 to 21) of EGA IV have appeared.} where standard methods for reducing
certain types of statements (involving hypotheses of finite
presentation) to the noetherian case will also be developed in detail
(EGA IV, §§ 8, 9, 11). The reader who does not wish to admit these
results from EGA IV can simplify certain statements or their proofs by
assuming the base prescheme to be locally noetherian. He will, however,
expose himself to difficulties in cases where the proof

proceeds by descent from \texttt{Â} to \(A\), where \texttt{Â} is the
completion of a noetherian local ring \(A\), since this method leads to
the introduction of the (in general non-noetherian) ring
\(\hat{A} \otimes_{A} \hat{A}\).

\textbf{7.} References will be made following the usual decimal system:
the reference 5.7.11 refers to the proposition (or lemma, definition,
etc.) of that name in the same Exposé; in the reference XVII 7.8 the
Roman numeral indicates the number of the Exposé. We shall use the
following abbreviations for our standard references:

\section{Preface to Tome II}\label{preface-to-tome-ii}

\emph{A note from the translator.}

Tome II of the 2011 SMF re-edition of SGA 3 contains Exposés VIII
through XVIII, with no separate front matter, errata sheet, or notation
index of its own --- the editors chose to consolidate the volume-level
apparatus into Tomes I and III only. Reading-order navigation for the
Tome II Exposés can be found in the \href{README.md}{README}; references
to the Avertissement, Introduction, and reference convention all live
with \href{00-i-avertissement-introduction.md}{Tome I's front matter};
and the translation glossary applies uniformly across the three Tomes.
The Tome I errata sheet flags Exposé II only (§ 1.2), and the Tome III
errata sheet does not concern this Tome.

Topically, Tome II spans three threads. Exposés VIII--XII (Grothendieck)
develop the theory of groups of multiplicative type --- diagonalizable
groups (VIII), homomorphisms between groups of multiplicative type (IX),
characterization and classification (X), representability criteria (XI),
and the foundational structure theorems on maximal tori, the Weyl group,
Cartan subgroups, and the reductive center (XII), which together provide
the language used throughout Tome III. Exposés XIII--XV (Grothendieck,
with Serre's appendix in XIV, and Raynaud in XV) develop the theory of
regular elements in algebraic groups and Lie algebras and apply it to
the construction and parametrization of maximal tori, in particular in
smooth group schemes over a non-perfect field. Exposés XVI--XVIII close
the Tome with Raynaud's treatment of groups of zero unipotent rank and
of unipotent algebraic groups and their extensions (XVI--XVII), and
Artin's writing-up of Weil's theorem on the construction of a group from
a rational law (XVIII).

Several of the Exposés in this Tome were inserted into the mimeographed
Séminaire without a corresponding oral presentation, as Grothendieck
notes in §5 of the Introduction: VII\_A and VII\_B from Tome I, and XV,
XVI, XVII from this Tome, may be read as natural extensions of the
techniques developed in the surrounding material rather than as steps in
the main line; the reader heading for the reductive-group material of
Tome III need not pause on them.

The Exposés in this Tome are listed below; for the full reading order
across all three Tomes, see the \href{README.md}{README}.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \href{08-groupes-diagonalisables.md}{Exposé VIII --- Diagonalizable
  groups (Grothendieck)}
\item
  \href{09-groupes-type-multiplicatif-homomorphismes.md}{Exposé IX ---
  Groups of multiplicative type: homomorphisms (Grothendieck)}
\item
  \href{10-caracterisation-classification-groupes-multiplicatif.md}{Exposé
  X --- Characterization and classification of groups of multiplicative
  type (Grothendieck)}
\item
  \href{11-criteres-representabilite.md}{Exposé XI --- Representability
  criteria (Grothendieck)}
\item
  \href{12-tores-maximaux-weyl-cartan-centre-reductif.md}{Exposé XII ---
  Maximal tori, the Weyl group, Cartan subgroups, the reductive center
  (Grothendieck)}
\item
  \href{13-elements-reguliers-groupes-algebres-lie.md}{Exposé XIII ---
  Regular elements: algebraic groups and Lie algebras (Grothendieck)}
\item
  \href{14-elements-reguliers-suite-applications.md}{Exposé XIV ---
  Regular elements: continuation, applications (Grothendieck, app.
  Serre)}

\section{Exposé I. Algebraic structures. Group
cohomology}\label{exposuxe9-i.-algebraic-structures.-group-cohomology}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{Version of 13/10/2024.} This Exposé consists of two parts; the
first gathers a certain number of general definitions and sets up
notations that will often be used in the sequel, while the second treats
group cohomology and culminates in Theorem 5.3.3 (vanishing of the
cohomology of diagonalizable groups).

We choose once and for all a Universe.\footnote{N.D.E.: Cf. SGA 4, Exp.
  I, § 0 and Appendix; see also the discussion in {[}DG70{]}, p.~xxvi.}
All the definitions stated and all the constructions carried out will be
relative to this Universe. We shall systematically allow ourselves the
following abuse of language: in order to define a functor
\(f : C \to C'\), we shall content ourselves with defining the object
\(f(S)\) of \(C'\) for every object \(S\) of \(C\), each time that there
is no ambiguity about the way to define \(f(h)\) for an arrow \(h\) of
\(C\). In practice, we shall say: let \(f : C \to C'\) be the functor
defined by \(f(S) = \cdots\).

\subsection{1. Generalities}\label{generalities}

\subsubsection{1.1.}\label{section}

Let \(C\) be a category. We shall denote by \texttt{Ĉ} the category
\(\operatorname{Hom}(C^{\circ}, (Ens))\) of contravariant functors from
\(C\) to the category \texttt{(Ens)} of sets.\footnote{N.D.E.: One calls
  it the category of presheaves on \(C\), cf.~IV 4.3.1.} There exists a
canonical functor \(h : C \to \hat{C}\) which associates to every
\(X \in Ob(C)\) the functor \texttt{hX} such that

\[
hX(S) = \operatorname{Hom}(S, X).
\]

For every functor \(F \in Ob(\hat{C})\), one defines (cf.~for example
EGA 0\_III, 8.1.4) a bijection

\[
\operatorname{Hom}(hX, F) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(X).
\]

\footnote{N.D.E.: This result is often called the ``Yoneda Lemma''; we
  shall use this terminology in other N.D.E.}

In particular, for every pair \texttt{X,\ Y} of objects of \(C\), the
following canonical map is bijective:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_C(X, Y) ⥲ Hom\_Ĉ(hX, hY);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~the functor \(h\) is fully faithful. It thus defines an isomorphism
of \(C\) onto a full subcategory of \texttt{Ĉ}, and an equivalence of
\(C\) with the full subcategory of \texttt{Ĉ} formed by the
representable functors (i.e.~those isomorphic to a functor of the form
\texttt{hX}). In the sequel, we shall often identify \(X\) and
\texttt{hX}. The following numbers aim to show that this identification
can be made without danger.

\textbf{Remark 1.1.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This remark has been added.}
\emph{We sometimes need the following variant. Let \(D\) be a full
subcategory of \(C\) and let \(X, Y \in Ob(D)\); denote by \(h'_{X}\)
and \(h'_{Y}\) the restrictions to \(D\) of \texttt{hX} and \texttt{hY}.
Then one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_C(X, Y) = Hom\_D(X, Y) = Hom\_D̂(h′\_X, h′\_Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and therefore: to give a morphism \(X \to Y\) ``is the same
thing'' as to give, functorially in \(T\), a map
\(\phi(T) : \operatorname{Hom}(T, X) \to \operatorname{Hom}(T, Y)\), for
every \(T \in Ob(D)\).}

\subsubsection{1.2.}\label{section-1}

\footnote{N.D.E.: The order has been modified, in order to introduce
  fiber products before monomorphisms, cf.~N.D.E. (9).} We shall say
that \(F\) is a \emph{subobject} (or a \emph{subfunctor}) of \(G\) if
\(F(S)\) is a subset of \(G(S)\) for each \(S\).

In \texttt{Ĉ}, ``arbitrary'' inverse limits exist and are computed by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(lim←\_i F\_i)(S) = lim←\_i F\_i(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Likewise, ``arbitrary'' direct limits exist and are
  computed ``argument by argument'', i.e.
  \((\lim\to_{i} F_{i})(S) = \lim\to_{i} F_{i}(S)\); but in general the
  functor \(h\) does not commute with direct limits.} In particular,
fiber products are defined by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(F ×\_G F′)(S) = F(S) ×\_\{G(S)\} F′(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: In particular, the kernel of a pair of morphisms
  \(u, v : F \Rightarrow G\) is the subfunctor \(Ker(u, v)\) of \(F\)
  defined by \(Ker(u, v)(S) = {x \in F(S) | u(x) = v(x)}\).}

We shall choose as final object of \texttt{Ĉ} the functor \(e\) such
that \(e(S) = {\emptyset}\)\footnote{N.D.E.: \({\emptyset}\) (the set of
  subsets of the empty set) denotes the one-element set.}. Every
\(F \in Ob(\hat{C})\) has a unique morphism into \(e\), and one sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F × F′ = F ×\_e F′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The functor \(h\) commutes with inverse limits; in particular, for
\(X \times X'\) to exist (\(X, X' \in Ob(C)\)), resp. for \(C\) to admit
a final object \(e\), it is necessary and sufficient that
\(hX \times hX'\) be representable, resp. that \(e\) be representable,
and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{hX × hX′ ≃ h\_\{X×X′\}    and    he ≃ e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A monomorphism of \texttt{Ĉ} is nothing other than a morphism
\(F \to G\) such that, for every \(S \in Ob(C)\), the corresponding map
of sets \(F(S) \to G(S)\) is injective.\footnote{N.D.E.: If
  \(F(S) \to G(S)\) is injective for every \(S\), it is clear that
  \(F \to G\) is a monomorphism; the converse is seen by considering the
  diagram \(F \times_{G} F \Rightarrow F \to G\). One thus obtains that:
  ``\(F \to G\) is a monomorphism if and only if the diagonal morphism
  \(F \to F \times_{G} F\) is an isomorphism'' (cf.~EGA I, 5.3.8).
  Likewise, it is clear that if \(F(S) \to G(S)\) is surjective for
  every \(S\), then \(F \to G\) is an epimorphism, and the converse is
  seen by considering the amalgamated sum \(G \bigsqcup_{F} G\), cf.~the
  proof of Lemma 4.4.4 in Exp. IV.}

\emph{The functor \(\Gamma\).} For every \(F \in Ob(\hat{C})\), one sets

\[
\Gamma(F) = \operatorname{Hom}(e, F);
\]

an element of \(\Gamma(F)\) is therefore a family
\((\gamma_{S})_{S\in Ob(C)}\), \(\gamma_{S} \in F(S)\), such that for
every arrow \(f : S' \to S''\) of \(C\) one has
\(F(f)(\gamma_{S''}) = \gamma_{S'}\).

One sets \(\Gamma(X) = \Gamma(hX)\) for \(X \in Ob(C)\). If \(C\) has a
final object \(e\), one therefore has an isomorphism
\(\Gamma(X) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(e, X)\).

\subsubsection{1.3.}\label{section-2}

Let \(S \in Ob(C)\). We denote by \(C/S\) the category of objects of
\(C\) over \(S\), i.e.~the category whose objects are the arrows
\(f : T \to S\) of \(C\), with \(\operatorname{Hom}(f, f')\) being the
subset of \(\operatorname{Hom}(T, T')\) formed by those \(u\) such that
\(f = f' \circ u\). If \(C\) has a final object \(e\), then \(C/e\) is
isomorphic to \(C\). The category \(C/S\) has a final object: the
identity arrow \(S \to S\).

If \(f : T \to S\) is an object of \(C/S\), then one can form the
category \((C/S)/f\), which by abuse of language one denotes
\((C/S)/T\), and one has a canonical isomorphism

\[
C/T \simeq (C/S)/T.
\]

This construction also applies to the category \texttt{Ĉ}; one defines
in particular the category \(\hat{C}/hS\). On the other hand, one can
form the category \(\hat{C}_{/S}\).

If \(f : T \to S\) is an object of \(C/S\), then \(\Gamma(f)\) is
identified with the set \(\Gamma(T/S)\) of sections of \(T\) over \(S\),
that is, of arrows \(S \to T\) which are right inverses of \(f\). Note
that \(hf : hT \to hS\) is then an object of \(\hat{C}/hS\), and one
has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(hf) ≃ Γ(hT/hS) ≃ Γ(T/S) ≃ Γ(f).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{1.4.}\label{section-3}

We now propose to define an equivalence of categories \(\hat{C}_{/S}\)
and \(\hat{C}/hS\), that is, to prove that ``to give a functor on the
category of objects of \(C\) over \(S\) is \texttt{the\ same\ thing} as
to give a functor on \(C\) endowed with a morphism into \texttt{hS}''.

\textbf{(i)} \emph{Construction of
\(\alpha S : \hat{C}/hS \to \hat{C}_{/S}\).}

Let first \(H : F \to hS\) be an object of \(\hat{C}/hS\). We must
define a functor \(\alpha S(H)\) on \(C/S\). Let first \(f : T \to S\)
be an object of \(C/S\); we define \(\alpha S(H)(f)\) as the inverse
image of \(f \in hS(T)\) by the map
\(H(T) : F(T) \to hS(T)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: For example, if \(F = hX\)
  then \(H\) corresponds to a morphism \(h : X \to S\) and
  \(H(T) : \operatorname{Hom}_{C}(T, X) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{C}(T, S)\)
  is the map \(g \mapsto h \circ g\), whence
  \(\alpha S(hX) = \operatorname{Hom}_{C/S}(-, X)\).}

Next, let \(u : f \to f'\) be an arrow of \(C/S\); then
\(F(u) : F(T') \to F(T)\) induces a map from \(\alpha S(H)(f')\) into
\(\alpha S(H)(f)\), which we denote \(\alpha S(H)(u)\). One verifies at
once that the maps

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ↦ αS(H)(f)    and    u ↦ αS(H)(u)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

do define a functor on \(C/S\), hence an object \(\alpha S(H)\) of
\(\hat{C}_{/S}\).

Finally, let \(H : F \to hS\) and \(H' : F' \to hS\) be two objects of
\(\hat{C}/hS\) and \(U : H \to H'\) a morphism of \(\hat{C}/hS\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        U}
\NormalTok{   F ──────→ F′}
\NormalTok{    ╲       ╱}
\NormalTok{   H ╲     ╱ H′}
\NormalTok{      ╲   ╱}
\NormalTok{       hS}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then for every \(f : T \to S\), the map \(U(T) : F(T) \to F'(T)\)
induces a map

\[
\alpha S(U)(f) :  \alpha S(H)(f) \to \alpha S(H')(f),
\]

which defines a morphism of functors

\[
\alpha S(U) :  \alpha S(H) \to \alpha S(H').
\]

One verifies easily that the maps

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ↦ αS(H)    and    U ↦ αS(U)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

do define a functor \(\alpha S : \hat{C}/hS \to \hat{C}_{/S}\).

\textbf{(ii) Proposition 1.4.1.} \emph{The functor
\(\alpha S : \hat{C}/hS \to \hat{C}_{/S}\) is an equivalence of
categories.}

We only indicate the principle of the construction of a quasi-inverse
functor \(\beta S : \hat{C}_{/S} \to \hat{C}/hS\). Let \(G\) be a
functor on \(C/S\); for every object \(T\) of \(C\), one sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{βS(G)(T) = sum of the sets G(f) for f ∈ Hom(T, S) = hS(T),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which defines a functor \(\beta S(G)\) on \(C\), equipped with an
obvious projection onto \texttt{hS}.

\subsubsection{1.5.}\label{section-4}

The equivalence \(\alpha S\) commutes with the functors \(\Gamma\). In
other words, if \(H : F \to hS\) is an object of \(\hat{C}/hS\) and
\(\alpha S(H)\) the corresponding object of \(\hat{C}_{/S}\), one has

\[
\Gamma(\alpha S(H)) \simeq \Gamma(H) \simeq \Gamma(F/hS).
\]

The equivalence \(\alpha S\) commutes with the functors \(h\), i.e.~if
\(f : T \to S\) is an object of \(C/S\), then \(hf : hT \to hS\) is an
object of \(\hat{C}/hS\) whose transform by \(\alpha S\) is nothing
other than \(h_{C/S}(f)\), where

\[
h_{C/S} : C/S \to \hat{C}_{/S}
\]

is the canonical functor.\footnote{N.D.E.: Cf. N.D.E. (10).} As a
consequence:

\textbf{Proposition 1.5.1.} \emph{Let \(H : F \to hS\) be an object of
\(\hat{C}/hS\). For \(\alpha S(H) : (C/S)^{\circ} \to (Ens)\) to be
representable, it is necessary and sufficient that
\(F : C^{\circ} \to (Ens)\) be representable; if \(F \simeq hT\), then
\(\alpha S(H)\) is representable by the object \(T \to S\) of \(C/S\).}

The equivalence \(\alpha S\) is transitive in \(S\): if \(f : T \to S\)
is an object of \(C/S\), one has a commutative diagram of equivalences

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                α\_\{S/hT\}                    α\_f}
\NormalTok{   (Ĉ/hS)/hT  ─────────→ (Ĉ\_\{/S\})/h\_T  ─────────→  Ĉ\_\{(C/S)/T\}}
\NormalTok{        ╲                                              ╱}
\NormalTok{      ≃  ╲                                            ╱  ≃}
\NormalTok{          ╲                                          ╱}
\NormalTok{           ────────────→ Ĉ/hT  ──────────────→ Ĉ\_\{/T\}}
\NormalTok{                                  α\_T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\alpha_{S/hT}\) denotes (provisionally) the restriction
(cf.~1.6) of the functor \(\alpha S\) to objects above \texttt{hT}.

\subsubsection{1.6. Base change in a
functor}\label{base-change-in-a-functor}

For every \(S \in Ob(C)\), one has a canonical functor

\[
iS : C/S \to C
\]

defined by \(iS(f) = T\) if \(f\) is the arrow \(T \to S\). If
\(f : T \to S\) is an object of \(C/S\), one denotes by
\(i_{T/S} = i_{f}\) the functor:

\[
i_{T/S} : (C/S)/T \to C/S,
\]

and one has the commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                i\_\{T/S\}       iS}
\NormalTok{   (C/S)/T  ─────────→ C/S  ─────→ C}
\NormalTok{        ╲                          ╱}
\NormalTok{      ≃  ╲                        ╱ iT}
\NormalTok{          ╲                      ╱}
\NormalTok{           C/T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, identifying \((C/S)/T\) with \(C/T\) as we shall do henceforth,

\[
iS \circ i_{T/S} = iT.
\]

In the same way, if one identifies \(C\) and \(C/e\) when \(C\) has a
final object \(e\), then \(i_{S/e} : C/S \to C/e\) is identified with
\texttt{iS}.

For \(X \in Ob(C)\) (resp. \(Y \in Ob(C/S)\)), let \(pS(X)\) (resp.
\(p_{T/S}(Y)\)) denote the object of \(C/S\) (resp. of \(C/T\)), when it
exists, defined by \(X \times S\) (resp. \(Y \times_{S} T\)) equipped
with its second projection:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   X × S                  Y ×\_S T}
\NormalTok{     │                        │}
\NormalTok{   pS(X) ↓     resp.     p\_\{T/S\}(Y) ↓}
\NormalTok{     │                        │}
\NormalTok{     S                        T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The (partially defined) functor \texttt{pS} (resp. \(p_{T/S}\)) is
called the \emph{base change functor}. It is by definition of the
product (resp. of the fiber product) the right adjoint of the functor
\texttt{iS} (resp. \(i_{T/S}\)).\footnote{N.D.E.: I.e. if
  \(g : U \to S\) (resp. \(h : V \to T\)) is an object of \(C/S\) (resp.
  \(C/T\)) then \(iS(g) = U\) and \(i_{T/S}(h)\) is the object
  \(f \circ h : V \to S\) of \(C/S\), and one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{C/S\}(U, X × S) ≃ Hom\_C(U, X)    resp.    Hom\_\{C/T\}(V, X ×\_S T) ≃ Hom\_\{C/S\}(V, X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
} One also denotes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pS(X) = XS    and    p\_\{T/S\}(Y) = YT.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The functor \texttt{iS} defines a functor (restriction)

\[
i*_{S} : \hat{C} \to \hat{C}_{/S};
\]

one denotes \(FS = i*_{S}(F) = F \circ iS\). One has obviously

\[
i*_{T/S} \circ i*_{S} = i*_{T},
\]

that is, for every functor \(F \in Ob(\hat{C})\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(FS)T = FT.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The notation requires a justification, which is the following:

\textbf{Proposition 1.6.1.} \emph{For the functor
\((hX)S : (C/S)^{\circ} \to (Ens)\) to be representable, it is necessary
and sufficient that the product \(X \times S\) exist. One then has}

\[
(hX)S \simeq h_{XS}.
\]

This shows that \texttt{FS} has two interpretations: restriction of the
functor \(F\) to \(C/S\), and functor obtained by base change
\(e \leftarrow S\). This leads to the following notation:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   F        FS          FT}

\NormalTok{   │         │           │}
\NormalTok{   e ←────── S ←──────── T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which renders both of the preceding interpretations. Note that one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(FS) ≃ Hom(hS, F) ≃ F(S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

in particular

\[
\Gamma(XS) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(S, X).
\]

\subsubsection{1.7.0.}\label{section-5}

\footnote{N.D.E.: The following lemma has been added (cf.~SGA 4, I.3.4);
  it is used in the proof of 1.7.1 and will be useful several times in
  the sequel.} Let \(E\) be an object of \texttt{Ĉ}. Consider the
category \texttt{C\_E} of objects of \(C\) above \(E\): its objects are
the pairs \((V, \rho)\) formed by an object \(V\) of \(C\) and a
\texttt{Ĉ}-morphism \(\rho : hV \to E\), i.e.~\(\rho \in E(V)\); a
morphism from \((V, \rho)\) to \((V', \rho')\) is

the datum of a \(C\)-morphism \(f : V \to V'\) such that
\(\rho' \circ f = \rho\) (i.e.~\(E(f)(\rho') = \rho\)). Denote by \(L\)
the functor

\[
\lim\to_{(V,\rho)\in C_{E}} hV,
\]

i.e.~for every \(S \in Ob(C)\), \(L(S) = \lim\to_{(V,\rho)} hV(S)\) is
the set of equivalence classes of triples \((V, \rho, v)\), where
\(v : S \to V\) is a \(C\)-morphism, and where one identifies
\((V, \rho, v)\) with \((V', \rho', f \circ v)\) for every
\(C\)-morphism \(f : V \to V'\) such that \(\rho' \circ f = \rho\).

Then the map \(\phi_{E}(S)\) which to the class of \((V, \rho, v)\)
associates the element \(\rho \circ v\) of \(E(S)\) is well defined, and
defines a morphism of functors

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ\_E :  lim→\_\{(V,ρ)∈C\_E\} hV → E.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma.} \emph{\(\phi_{E}\) is an isomorphism.}

Indeed, let \(S \in Ob(C)\). Every \(x \in E(S)\) is the image under
\(\phi_{E}(S)\) of the triple \((S, x, id_{S})\); this shows that
\(\phi_{E}(S)\) is surjective. On the other hand, let
\(\ell_{1} = (V_{1}, \rho_{1}, v_{1})\) and
\(\ell_{2} = (V_{2}, \rho_{2}, v_{2})\) be two elements of \(L(S)\)
having the same image in \(E(S)\); set
\(\gamma = \rho_{1} \circ v_{1} = \rho_{2} \circ v_{2}\). Then
\(\ell_{1}\) and \(\ell_{2}\) are both equal, in \(L(S)\), to the class
of the triple \((S, \gamma, id_{S})\). This shows that \(\phi_{E}(S)\)
is injective.

\textbf{Corollary.} \emph{For every object \(F\) of \texttt{Ĉ}, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(E, F) = lim←\_\{(V,ρ)∈C\_E\} F(V).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{1.7. Objects Hom, Isom,
etc.}\label{objects-hom-isom-etc.}

Let \(F\) and \(G\) be two objects of \texttt{Ĉ}. We shall define
another object of \texttt{Ĉ} in the following way:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(F, G)(S) = Hom\_\{Ĉ\_\{/S\}\}(FS, GS) ≃ Hom\_\{Ĉ/hS\}(F × hS, G × hS) ≃ Hom\_Ĉ(F × hS, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The object \(\operatorname{Hom}(F, G)\) defined above has the following
properties:

\textbf{(i)} \(\operatorname{Hom}(e, G) \simeq G\).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  And, if \(E\) is a third object of \texttt{Ĉ}, one has
  \texttt{Hom(E,\ F\ ×\ G)\ ≅\ Hom(E,\ F)\ ×\ Hom(E,\ G)}.}

\textbf{(ii)} \emph{The formation of \texttt{Hom} commutes with base
extension:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(FS, GS) ≃ Hom(F, G)\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{(iii)} \emph{\((F, G) \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}(F, G)\) is a
bifunctor, contravariant in \(F\) and covariant in \(G\).}

These three properties are obvious from the definitions.

We shall show that, for every object \(E\) of \texttt{Ĉ}, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(E, Hom(F, G)) ≅ Hom(E × F, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(\phi : E \times F \to G\); we must associate to it a morphism of
\(E\) into \(\operatorname{Hom}(F, G)\). So let \(S' \to S\) be an arrow
of \(C\). One has maps

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E(S) × F(S′) → E(S′) × F(S′) ──φ(S′)──→ G(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Every element \(e\) of \(E(S)\) therefore defines, for every
\(S' \to S\), a map \(F(S') \to G(S')\) functorial in \(S'\), i.e.~an
element \(\theta_{\phi}(e)\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}(F, G)(S)\). One has
thus obtained a map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ ↦ θ\_φ,    Hom(E × F, G) → Hom(E, Hom(F, G)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is ``functorial in \(E\)''.

\textbf{Proposition 1.7.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: Point (b) has been added,
  which will be useful in II.1 and II.3.11. On the other hand, a second,
  more direct, proof of (a) has been sketched.} \emph{Let
\(E, F, G \in Ob(\hat{C})\).}

\emph{(a) The map \(\phi \mapsto \theta_{\phi}\) is a bijection:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(E × F, G) ⥲ Hom(E, Hom(F, G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(b) Moreover, one has an isomorphism of functors:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(E, Hom(F, G)) ≃ Hom(E × F, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(a)} Consider both members as functors in \(E\). The asserted
result is true if \(E = hX\); indeed, in that case it is nothing other
than the definition of the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}(F, G)\). On the
other hand, both members as functors in \(E\) transform direct limits
into inverse limits. Finally, by Lemma 1.7.0, every object \(E\) of
\texttt{Ĉ} is isomorphic to the direct limit of the \texttt{hX}, where
\(X\) runs over the category \texttt{C\_E}. This proves (a).

\footnote{(continuation of the proof of Proposition 1.7.1, sketching a
  direct argument)} Let us sketch a direct proof of (a). To every
\(\theta \in \operatorname{Hom}(E, \operatorname{Hom}(F, G))\), one
associates the element \(\phi_{\theta}\) of
\(\operatorname{Hom}(E \times F, G)\) defined as follows. For every
\(S \in Ob(C)\), one has a map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{θ(S) : E(S) → Hom(F × S, G),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

functorial in \(S\). If \((e, f) \in E(S) \times F(S)\), then \(f\) is a
morphism \(S \to F\), hence \(f \times id_{S}\) is a morphism
\(S \to F \times S\); on the other hand, \(\theta(S)(e)\) is a morphism
\(F \times S \to G\), so by composition one obtains a morphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{θ(S)(e) ∘ (f × id\_S) : S → G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~an element \(\phi_{\theta}(S)(e, f)\) of \(G(S)\). One verifies
easily that the correspondence \(S \mapsto \phi_{\theta}(S)\) is
functorial in \(S\), hence defines a morphism \(\phi_{\theta}\) from
\(E \times F\) to \(G\). We leave to the reader the verification that
the maps \(\theta \mapsto \phi_{\theta}\) and
\(\phi \mapsto \theta_{\phi}\) are mutually inverse bijections.

Let us prove (b). If \(S \in Ob(C)\), one has, by 1.7 (ii) and (a)
applied to \(C/S\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(E, Hom(F, G))(S) ≃ Hom\_S(ES, Hom\_S(FS, GS))}
\NormalTok{                     ≅ Hom\_S(ES ×\_S FS, GS)}
\NormalTok{                     ≅ Hom(E × F × S, G)}
\NormalTok{                     ≅ Hom(E × F, G)(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and these isomorphisms are functorial in \(S\).

\textbf{Corollary 1.7.2.} \emph{One has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(E, Hom(F, G)) ≃ Hom(F, Hom(E, G)),}
\NormalTok{Hom(E, Hom(F, G)) ≃ Hom(F, Hom(E, G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, taking \(E = e\), and taking into account
\(\operatorname{Hom}(e, G) \simeq G\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(Hom(F, G)) ≃ Hom(F, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note that the composition of \texttt{Hom}'s provides functorial
morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(F, G) × Hom(G, H) → Hom(F, H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(F\) and \(G\) are two objects of \texttt{Ĉ}, one denotes by
\(Isom(F, G)\) the subset of \(\operatorname{Hom}(F, G)\) formed by the
isomorphisms of \(F\) onto \(G\). One then defines a subobject
\(Isom(F, G)\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}(F, G)\) by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom(F, G)(S) = Isom(FS, GS).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One then has isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(Isom(F, G)) ≃ Isom(F, G),}
\NormalTok{Isom(F, G) ≃ Isom(G, F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In the particular case where \(F = G\), one sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{End(F) = Hom(F, F),    End(F) = Hom(F, F) ≃ Γ(End(F)),}
\NormalTok{Aut(F) = Isom(F, F),    Aut(F) = Isom(F, F) ≃ Γ(Aut(F)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The formation of the objects \texttt{Hom,\ Isom,\ Aut,\ End} commutes
with base change.

\textbf{Remark 1.7.3.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 1.7.3 has been
  added, for subsequent references.} One can construct an object
isomorphic to \(Isom(F, G)\) in the following manner: one has a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(F, G) × Hom(G, F) → End(F);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

permuting \(F\) and \(G\), one deduces a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(F, G) × Hom(G, F) → End(F) × End(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, the identity morphism of \(F\) is an element of
\(\operatorname{End}(F)\) and therefore defines a morphism
\(e \to \operatorname{End}(F)\). Doing the same with \(G\) and forming
the product, one finds a morphism

\[
e \to \operatorname{End}(F) \times \operatorname{End}(G).
\]

It is then immediate that the fiber product of \(e\) and of
\(\operatorname{Hom}(F, G) \times \operatorname{Hom}(G, F)\) over
\(\operatorname{End}(F) \times \operatorname{End}(G)\) is isomorphic to
\(Isom(F, G)\).

All these definitions apply in particular to the case where
\(F = hX, G = hY\). In the case where \(\operatorname{Hom}(hX, hY)\) is
representable by an object of \(C\), one denotes this object by
\(\operatorname{Hom}(X, Y)\). It has the following property: if
\(Z \times X\) exists, then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(Z, Hom(X, Y)) ≃ Hom(Z × X, Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This property characterizes it when the products exist in \(C\).

One defines similarly (when they happen to exist) objects

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom(X, Y),    End(X),    Aut(X);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

we simply note that, by the construction given above, \(Isom(X, Y)\)
exists whenever fiber products exist in \(C\) and
\texttt{Hom(X,\ Y),\ Hom(Y,\ X),\ End(X)} and \(\operatorname{End}(Y)\)
exist.

All that precedes applies equally to categories of the form \(C/S\). The
corresponding objects will be denoted as explicitly as possible by
appropriate symbols: for example, if \(T\) and \(T'\) are two objects of
\(C\) above \(S\), one will denote by \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(T, T')\)
the object \(\operatorname{Hom}_{C/S}(T/S, T'/S)\).

\subsubsection{1.8. Constant objects}\label{constant-objects}

Let \(C\) be a category in which direct sums and fiber products exist,
and in which direct sums commute with base change (for example, the
category of schemes\footnote{N.D.E.: The former terminology
  ``préschémas/schémas'' has been replaced by the current terminology
  ``schémas/schémas séparés''.}). For every set \(E\) and every object
\(S\) of \(C\), we set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1.8.1)    ES =  the direct sum of a family (S\_i)\_\{i∈E\}}
\NormalTok{                 of objects of C all isomorphic to S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This object is characterized by the formula:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1.8.2)    Hom\_C(ES, T) = Hom(E, Hom\_C(S, T)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(T \in Ob(C)\), where the second \texttt{Hom} is taken in the
category of sets.

The object \texttt{ES} is equipped with a canonical projection onto
\(S\), in such a way that \(E \mapsto ES\) is in fact a functor from
\texttt{(Ens)} to \(C/S\).

\footnote{N.D.E.: In the three paragraphs that follow, the order of the
  sentences has been modified and some clarifications added concerning
  the role of the hypothesis \((\ast)\) below.} If \(S' \to S\) is an
arrow of \(C\), one has, since direct sums commute with base change,

\[
E_{S'} = (ES)_{S'}.
\]

In particular, if \(C\) has a final object \(e\), one has

\[
ES = (Ee)_{S}.
\]

The functor \(E \mapsto ES/S\), from \texttt{(Ens)} to \(C/S\), commutes
with finite products. For this, it suffices to see that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(×)    ES ×\_S FS = (E × F)\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, by the results of 1.7 applied to \(C/S\), one has, for every
\(T \in Ob(C/S)\), natural isomorphisms (all unspecified \texttt{Hom}'s
being taken in \(C/S\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom((E × F)\_S, T) ≅ Hom\_\{(Ens)\}(E × F, Hom(S, T)) ≅}
\NormalTok{        Hom\_\{(Ens)\}(E, Hom\_\{(Ens)\}(F, Hom(S, T))) ≅ Hom\_\{(Ens)\}(E, Hom(FS, T))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(ES ×\_S FS, T) ≅ Hom(ES, Hom(FS, T)) ≅ Hom\_\{(Ens)\}(E, Hom(S, Hom(FS, T))).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now \texttt{Hom(S,\ Hom(FS,\ T))\ ≅\ Hom(FS,\ T)}, hence \((\times)\).

Suppose that, with \(\emptyset\) denoting an initial object of \(C\),
the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   ∅ ────→ S}
\NormalTok{   │         │}
\NormalTok{   ↓         ↓}
\NormalTok{   S ────→ S ⊔ S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\((\ast)\) \emph{is cartesian.}

(This is the case for the category of schemes.)\footnote{N.D.E.:
  \((\ast)\) is not verified if \(C\) is the category whose arrows are
  \(A \to B\) and \(id_{A}, id_{B}\); in this case \(B \bigsqcup B = B\)
  and \texttt{B\ ×\_B\ B\ =\ B\ ≄\ A}.} Then the functor
\(E \mapsto ES\) commutes with finite inverse limits.

Indeed, taking \((\times)\) into account, it suffices to see that
\(E \mapsto ES\) commutes with fiber products. Let \(u : E \to G\) and
\(v : F \to G\) be two maps of sets. Since in \(C\) direct sums commute
with base change, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    FS ×\_\{GS\} ES ≅ ⨆\_\{f∈F\} S\_f ×\_\{GS\} ES ≅ ⨆\_\{f∈F, x∈E\} S\_f ×\_\{GS\} S\_x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(v(f) \neq u(x)\), there exists in \(C/S\) a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S\_f ×\_\{GS\} S\_x → S\_f ×\_\{S\_\{v(f)\} ⊔ S\_\{u(x)\}\} S\_x;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

now by hypothesis \((\ast)\) the right-hand term is \(\emptyset\).
Consequently,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)    S\_f ×\_\{GS\} S\_x ≅ ∅    if v(f) ≠ u(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, if \(v(f) = u(x)\), there exists in \(C/S\) a
morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S → S\_f ×\_\{GS\} S\_x;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since \(S \xrightarrow{id} S\) is the final object of \(C/S\), it
follows that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)    S\_f ×\_\{GS\} S\_x ≅ S    if v(f) = u(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combining (1), (2), and (3) one obtains an isomorphism functorial in
\(S\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{FS ×\_\{GS\} ES ≅ ⨆\_\{F ×\_G E\} S = (F ×\_G E)\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

An object of the form \texttt{ES} will be called a \emph{constant
object}. Note that one has a morphism functorial in \(E\):

\[
E \to \Gamma(ES/S)
\]

which associates to each \(i \in E\) the section of \texttt{ES} over
\(S\) defined by the isomorphism of \(S\) onto \(S_{i}\). Suppose
condition \((\ast)\) is satisfied for every object \(S\) of \(C\); then
the morphism \(E \to \Gamma(ES/S)\) is a monomorphism for every
\texttt{S\ ≄\ ∅}.

If \(C\) is the category of schemes, then \(\Gamma(ES/S)\) is identified
with the locally constant maps from the topological space \(S\) to the
set \(E\), the preceding map associating to each element of \(E\) the
corresponding constant map. Note that, by what was just said,
\texttt{ES} may also be defined as representing the functor which to
every \(S'\) over \(S\) associates the set of locally constant functions
from the topological space \(S'\) to the set \(E\).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Note also that the diagonal morphism
  \(ES \to ES \times_{S} ES = (E \times E)_{S}\) is a closed immersion,
  i.e.~\texttt{ES} is separated over \(S\).}

\subsection{2. Algebraic structures}\label{algebraic-structures}

Given a species of algebraic structure in the category of sets, we
propose to extend it to the category \(C\). Let us first treat one
example: the case of groups.

\subsubsection{2.1. Group structures}\label{group-structures}

We retain the notations of the preceding paragraph.

\textbf{Definition 2.1.1.} \emph{Let \(G \in Ob(\hat{C})\). By a}
\texttt{Ĉ}-group structure \emph{on \(G\), we mean the datum, for every
\(S \in Ob(C)\), of a group structure on the set \(G(S)\), in such a way
that for every arrow \(f : S' \to S''\) of \(C\), the map
\(G(f) : G(S'') \to G(S')\) is a group homomorphism. If \(G\) and \(H\)
are two \texttt{Ĉ}-groups, by a} morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups
\emph{from \(G\) into \(H\) we mean any morphism
\(u \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, H)\) such that for every \(S \in Ob(C)\),
the map of sets \(u(S) : G(S) \to H(S)\) is a group homomorphism.}

One denotes by \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\hat{C}-Gr.}(G, H)\) the set of
morphisms of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups from \(G\) into \(H\), and by
\((\hat{C}-Gr.)\) the category of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups.

\textbf{Examples.} Let \(E \in Ob(\hat{C})\); the object
\(\operatorname{Aut}(E)\) is endowed in an obvious manner with a
\texttt{Ĉ}-group structure. The final object \(e\) has a unique
\texttt{Ĉ}-group structure which makes it a final object of
\((\hat{C}-Gr.)\).

For every \(S \in Ob(C)\), let \(e_{G}(S)\) be the identity element of
\(G(S)\). The family of the \(e_{G}(S)\)

defines an element \(e_{G} \in \Gamma(G) = \operatorname{Hom}(e, G)\)
which is a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups \(e \to G\), and which is
called the \emph{unit section} of \(G\).

Note that to give a \texttt{Ĉ}-group structure on \(G\) amounts to
giving a composition law on \(G\), i.e.~a \texttt{Ĉ}-morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π\_G : G × G → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that, for every \(S \in Ob(C)\), \(\pi_{G}(S)\) endows \(G(S)\)
with a group structure.

In the same way, \(f : G \to H\) is a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups if
and only if the following diagram is commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              π\_G}
\NormalTok{   G × G ─────────→ G}
\NormalTok{     │              │}
\NormalTok{   (f,f)           f}
\NormalTok{     ↓     π\_H      ↓}
\NormalTok{   H × H ─────────→ H}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A subobject \(H\) of \(G\) such that, for every \(S \in Ob(C)\),
\(H(S)\) is a subgroup of \(G(S)\), obviously has a \texttt{Ĉ}-group
structure induced by that of \(G\): it is the only one for which the
monomorphism \(H \to G\) is a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups. The
\texttt{Ĉ}-group \(H\) endowed with this structure is called a
\emph{sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-group of \(G\)}.

If \(G\) and \(H\) are two \texttt{Ĉ}-groups, the product \(G \times H\)
is endowed with an obvious \texttt{Ĉ}-group structure: for every
\(S \in Ob(C)\), one endows \(G(S) \times H(S)\) with the product group
structure of the group structures given on \(G(S)\) and \(H(S)\). The
\texttt{Ĉ}-group \(G \times H\) endowed with this structure will be
called the \emph{product \texttt{Ĉ}-group} of \(G\) and \(H\) (it is
indeed the product in the category of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups).

If \(G\) is a \texttt{Ĉ}-group, then for every \(S \in Ob(C)\),
\texttt{GS} is a \(\hat{C}_{/S}\)-group. If \(G\) and \(H\) are two
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups, one defines the object
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{\hat{C}-Gr.}(G, H)\) of \texttt{Ĉ} by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{Ĉ{-}Gr.\}(G, H)(S) = Hom\_\{Ĉ\_\{/S\}{-}Gr.\}(GS, HS)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(Note: \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\hat{C}-Gr.}\) is not in general a
\texttt{Ĉ}-group, nor a fortiori the \texttt{Hom} object in

the category \((\hat{C}-Gr.)\)).

One defines similarly the objects

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{Ĉ{-}Gr.\}(G, H),    End\_\{Ĉ{-}Gr.\}(G),    Aut\_\{Ĉ{-}Gr.\}(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 2.1.2.} \emph{Let \(G \in Ob(C)\). By a} \(C\)-group
structure \emph{on \(G\), we mean a \texttt{Ĉ}-group structure on
\(hG \in Ob(\hat{C})\). By a} morphism of the \(C\)-group \(G\) into the
\(C\)-group \(H\), \emph{we mean an element
\(u \in \operatorname{Hom}(G, H) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(hG, hH)\)
which defines a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups from \texttt{hG} into
\texttt{hH}.}

One denotes by \texttt{(C-Gr.)} the category of \(C\)-groups. Note that
there exists in \texttt{(Cat)} a cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   (C{-}Gr.) ─────────→ (Ĉ{-}Gr.)}
\NormalTok{      │                  │}
\NormalTok{      ↓        h         ↓}
\NormalTok{      C ─────────────→  Ĉ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

All the preceding definitions and constructions therefore transport at
once to \texttt{(C-Gr.)} whenever the functors they involve (products,
\texttt{Hom} objects, etc.) are representable. They also apply to the
categories \(C/S\). In that case, we shall write
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-Gr.}\) for
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{\hat{C}_{/S}-Gr.}\), etc.

\subsubsection{2.2.}\label{section-6}

More generally, if \texttt{(T)} is a species of structure on \(n\) base
sets defined by finite inverse limits (for example, by commutativities
of diagrams constructed with cartesian products: structures of monoid,
group, set with operators, module over a ring, Lie algebra over a ring,
etc.), the preceding construction permits one to define the notion of
``structure of species \texttt{(T)} on \(n\) objects
\(F_{1}, \cdots, F_{n}\) of \texttt{Ĉ}'':

such a structure will be the datum, for each \(S\) of \(C\), of a
structure of species \texttt{(T)} on the sets
\(F_{1}(S), \cdots, F_{n}(S)\) in such a way that for every arrow
\(S' \to S''\) of \(C\), the family of maps
\((F_{i}(S'')) \to (F_{i}(S'))\) is a polyhomomorphism for the species
of structure \texttt{(T)}. One defines similarly the morphisms of the
species of structure \texttt{(T)}, whence a category
\((\hat{C} \times \hat{C} \cdots \times \hat{C})^{(T)}\). The fully
faithful functor \((h \times h \times \cdots \times h)\) then allows one
to define by inverse image the category
\((C \times C \times \cdots \times C)^{(T)}\), and then, as it commutes
with inverse limits, to transport to it all the properties, notions, and
notations of a functorial kind introduced in \texttt{Ĉ}. Suppose now
that in \(C\) fiber products exist, and let \texttt{(T)} be a species of
algebraic structure defined by the datum of certain morphisms between
cartesian products satisfying axioms consisting of certain
commutativities of diagrams constructed using the preceding arrows. A
structure of species \texttt{(T)} on a family of objects of \(C\) will
therefore be defined by certain morphisms between cartesian products
satisfying certain commutation conditions. It follows that if \(C\) and
\(C'\) are two categories possessing products and \(f : C \to C'\) is a
functor commuting with products, then for every family of objects
\((F_{i})\) of \(C\) endowed with a structure of species \texttt{(T)},
the family \((f(F_{i}))\) of objects of \(C'\) will thereby also be
endowed with a structure of species \texttt{(T)}. Every \(C\)-group will
be transformed into a \(C'\)-group, every pair (\(C\)-ring, \(C\)-module
over this \(C\)-ring) into an analogous pair in \(C'\), etc.

In particular, let \(C\) be a category satisfying the conditions of
1.8;\footnote{N.D.E.: Including the condition \((\ast)\).} the functor
\(E \mapsto ES\) defined in \emph{loc. cit.} commutes with finite
inverse limits; it therefore transforms group into \(S\)-group
(i.e.~\(C/S\)-group), ring into \(S\)-ring, etc.

\textbf{Remark.} It is good to note that the preceding construction
procedure applied to the category \texttt{Ĉ} does give back the notions
already defined there; in other words, it amounts to the same thing to
give on an object of \texttt{Ĉ} a structure of species \texttt{(T)} when
one considers this object as a functor on \(C\), or to give a structure
of species \texttt{(T)} on the representable functor on \texttt{Ĉ}
defined by this object.\footnote{N.D.E.: For example, for group
  structures: let \(G \in Ob(\hat{C})\); if the functor
  \(\hat{C} \to (Ens)\),
  \(F \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\hat{C}}(F, G)\) is endowed with a
  group structure, the same is true of its restriction to \(C\),
  \(X \mapsto G(X)\). Conversely, if \(G\) is a \texttt{Ĉ}-group, then
  the ``multiplication'' morphism \(\pi_{G} : G \times G \to G\) induces
  for every \(F \in Ob(\hat{C})\) a group structure on
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\hat{C}}(F, G)\), functorial in \(F\).}

We shall still treat two particular cases of the preceding construction,
the case of structures with operator groups and the case of modules.

\subsubsection{2.3. Structures with operator
groups}\label{structures-with-operator-groups}

\textbf{Definition 2.3.1.} \emph{Let \(E \in Ob(\hat{C})\) and
\(G \in Ob(\hat{C}-Gr.)\). A structure of} object with
\texttt{Ĉ}-operator group \(G\) (\emph{or of \(G\)-object}) \emph{on
\(E\) is the datum, on \(E(S)\), for every \(S \in Ob(C)\), of a
structure of set with operator group \(G(S)\) in such a way that, for
every arrow \(S' \to S''\) of \(C\), the map of sets
\(E(S'') \to E(S')\) is compatible with the operator homomorphism
\(G(S'') \to G(S')\).}

As usual, it amounts to the same thing to give a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ : G × E → E}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which for each \(S\) endows \(E(S)\) with a structure of set with
operators \(G(S)\). But \texttt{Hom(G\ ×\ E,\ E)\ ≃\ Hom(G,\ End(E))},
so \(\mu\) defines a morphism \(G \to \operatorname{End}(E)\), and it is
immediate that this maps \(G\) into \(\operatorname{Aut}(E)\) and is a
morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups. Consequently: to give on \(E\) a
structure of object with \texttt{Ĉ}-operator group \(G\) is equivalent
to giving a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups

\[
\rho : G \to \operatorname{Aut}(E).
\]

In particular, every element \(g \in G(S)\) defines an automorphism
\(\rho(g)\) of the functor \texttt{ES}, that is, an automorphism of
\(E \times hS\) commuting with the projection \(E \times hS \to hS\),
and in particular an automorphism of the set \(E(S')\) for every
\(S' \to S\).

\textbf{Definition 2.3.2.} \emph{One denotes by \(E^{G}\) the subobject
of \(E\) defined as follows:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E\^{}G(S) = \{x ∈ E(S) | x\_\{S′\} invariant under G(S′) for every S′ → S\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(x_{S'}\) denotes the image of \(x\) by
\(E(S) \to E(S')\).}

Then \(E^{G}\) (\emph{``subobject of invariants of \(G\)''})

is the largest subobject of \(E\) on which \(G\) operates trivially.

\textbf{Definition 2.3.3.} \emph{Let \(F\) be a subobject of \(E\). One
denotes by \(Norm_{G} F\) and \(Centr_{G} F\) the sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-groups
of \(G\) defined by}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the original, replacing the
  inclusion \(\rho(g) FS \subset FS\) by an equality, in order to ensure
  that \(Norm_{G}(F)\) is indeed a group (see \texttt{VI\_B} 6.4 for
  conditions under which the ``transporter'' coincides with the ``strict
  transporter'').}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Norm\_G F)(S) = \{g ∈ G(S) | ρ(g) FS = FS\}}
\NormalTok{              = \{g ∈ G(S) | ρ(g) F(S′) = F(S′), for every S′ → S\},}

\NormalTok{(Centr\_G F)(S) = \{g ∈ G(S) | ρ(g)|FS = identity\}}
\NormalTok{               = \{g ∈ G(S) | ρ(g)|F(S′) = identity, for every S′ → S\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where the vertical bar after \(\rho(g)\) denotes restriction.}

\textbf{Scholium 2.3.3.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: Scholium 2.3.3.1 and Remark
  2.3.3.2 have been added.} \emph{In particular, let
\(x \in \Gamma(E)\), i.e.~(cf.~1.2) a collection of elements
\(x_{S} \in E(S)\), \(S \in Ob(C)\), such that for every arrow
\(f : S' \to S\) one has \(E(f)(x_{S}) = x_{S'}\) (if \(C\) has a final
object \texttt{S\_0} one has \(\Gamma(E) = E(S_{0})\)). Then \(x\)
defines a subfunctor of \(E\), which we shall denote \(\bar{x}\), and
one has} \(Norm_{G} \bar{x} = Centr_{G} \bar{x}\). \emph{We shall denote
by \(Stab_{G}(x)\) and call} stabilizer of \(x\) \emph{this functor; for
every \(S \in Ob(C)\) one therefore has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Stab\_G(x)(S) = \{g ∈ G(S) | ρ(g) x\_S = x\_S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Suppose that fiber products exist in \(C\); if \(G = hG\)} (resp.
\(E = hE\)), \emph{where \(G\) is a \(C\)-group (resp. \(E \in Ob(C)\)),
and if \(C\) has a final object \texttt{S\_0}, so that \(x\) is a
morphism \(S_{0} \to E\), then \(Stab_{G}(x)\) is representable by the
fiber product \(G \times_{E} S_{0}\), where \(G \to E\) is the composite
of \(id_{G} \times x : G = G \times S_{0} \to G \times E\) and of
\(\mu : G \times E \to E\).}

\textbf{Remark 2.3.3.2.}\footnote{N.D.E.: Scholium 2.3.3.1 and Remark
  2.3.3.2 have been added.} \emph{The formation of \(E^{G}\),
\(Norm_{G} F\) and \(Centr_{G} F\) commutes with base change, i.e.~for
every \(S \in Ob(C)\) one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(E\^{}G)\_S = (ES)\^{}\{GS\},    (Norm\_G F)\_S ≃ Norm\_\{GS\} F\_S,    (Centr\_G F)\_S ≃ Centr\_\{GS\} F\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 2.3.4.} \emph{If \(G\) is a \(C\)-group and \(E\) an
object of \texttt{Ĉ}} (resp. \(E\) an object of \(C\)) \emph{a structure
of \(G\)-object on \(E\)} (resp. on \(E\)) \emph{is a structure of
\texttt{hG}-object on \(E\)} (resp. \texttt{hE}).

In view of this definition, all the notions and notations defined above
transport to \(C\) when they involve only representable functors: for
example, if \(Norm_{hG}(hF)\) is representable, then there exists one
and only one subobject of \(G\) that represents it, and which is then a
sub-\(C\)-group of \(G\); one denotes it \(Norm_{G}(F)\), etc.

\textbf{Definition 2.3.5.} \emph{a) One says that the \texttt{Ĉ}-group
\(G\)} operates \emph{on the \texttt{Ĉ}-group \(H\) if \(H\) is endowed
with a structure of \(G\)-object such that, for every \(g \in G(S)\),
the automorphism of \(H(S)\) defined by \(g\) is a group automorphism.}

It amounts to the same thing to say that for every \(g \in G(S)\), the
automorphism \(\rho(g)\) of \texttt{HS}

is an automorphism of \(\hat{C}_{/S}\)-groups, or that the morphism of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups \(G \to \operatorname{Aut}(H)\) maps \(G\) into
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{\hat{C}-Gr.}(H)\).

\emph{b) In the situation above, there exists on the product
\(H \times G\) a unique \texttt{Ĉ}-group structure such that, for every
\(S\), \((H \times G)(S)\) is the semidirect product of the groups
\(H(S)\) and \(G(S)\) relative to the given operation of \(G(S)\) on
\(H(S)\). We shall denote this \texttt{Ĉ}-group \(H \cdot G\) and call
it the} semidirect product \emph{of \(H\) by \(G\). One therefore has by
definition}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(H ⋅ G)(S) = H(S) ⋅ G(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(G\) be a \texttt{Ĉ}-group. For every arrow \(S' \to S\) of \(C\)
and every \(g \in G(S)\), let \(Int(g)\) be the automorphism of
\(G(S')\) defined by \(Int(g) h = g h g^{-1}\). This definition extends
into that of a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Int : G → Aut\_\{Ĉ{-}Gr.\}(G) ⊂ Aut(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Definition 2.3.3 therefore applies, and one has sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-groups of
\(G\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_G(E) and Centr\_G(E)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every subobject \(E\) of \(G\).

\textbf{Definition 2.3.6.} \emph{One calls} center of \(G\) \emph{and
one denotes by \(Centr(G)\) the sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-group \(Centr_{G}(G)\) of
\(G\). One says that \(G\) is} commutative \emph{if \(Centr(G) = G\),
or, what amounts to the same thing, if \(G(S)\) is commutative for every
\(S\).}

\emph{One says that the sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-group \(H\) of \(G\) is}
invariant \emph{in \(G\) (or} normal*) if \(Norm_{G}(H) = G\), or, what
amounts to the same thing, if \(H(S)\) is invariant in \(G(S)\) for
every \(S\).*\footnote{N.D.E.: Moreover, one says that \(H\) is
  \emph{central} in \(G\) if \(Centr_{G}(H) = G\), or, what amounts to
  the same thing, if \(H(S)\) is central in \(G(S)\) for every \(S\).}

\textbf{Definition 2.3.6.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: Definitions 2.3.6.1 and
  2.3.6.2 have been added.} \emph{Let \(f : G \to G'\) be a morphism of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups. One calls} kernel of \(f\), \emph{and one denotes by
\texttt{Ker\ f}, the sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-group of \(G\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Ker f)(S) = \{x ∈ G(S) | f(S)(x) = 1\} = Ker f(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(S \in Ob(C)\); it is an invariant
sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-group.}

\emph{Note that if \(G = hG\) and \(G' = hG'\), if \(C\) has a final
object \texttt{S\_0} and if fiber products exist in \(C\), then
\(Ker(f)\) is representable by \(S_{0} \times_{G'} G\).}

\textbf{Definition 2.3.6.2.}\footnote{N.D.E.: Definitions 2.3.6.1 and
  2.3.6.2 have been added.} \emph{Let \(E \in \hat{C}\) and \(G\) a
\texttt{Ĉ}-group operating on \(E\). One says that the operation of
\(G\) on \(E\) is} faithful \emph{if the kernel of the morphism
\(G \to \operatorname{Aut}(E)\) is trivial, i.e.~if for every
\(S \in Ob(C)\) and \(g \in G(S)\), the condition \(g_{S'} \cdot x = x\)
for every \(S' \to S\) and \(x \in E(S')\) entails \(g = 1\).}

Many definitions and propositions of the elementary theory of groups
transpose easily. Let us simply point out the following, which will be
useful to us:

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.7.} \emph{Let \(f : W \to G\) be a morphism of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups. Set \(H(S) = Ker f(S)\). Let \(u : G \to W\) be a
morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups which is a section of \(f\)}

\emph{(and which is then necessarily a monomorphism). Then \(W\) is
identified with the semidirect product of \(H\) by \(G\) for the
operation of \(G\) on \(H\) defined by \((g, h) \mapsto Int(u(g)) h\)
for \(g \in G(S)\), \(h \in H(S)\), \(S \in Ob(C)\).}

The set of these definitions and propositions transports as usual to
\(C\). One defines in particular the semidirect product of two
\(C\)-groups \(H\) and \(G\) (with \(G\) operating on \(H\)) when the
cartesian product \(H \times G\) exists, and one has the analogue of
Proposition 2.3.7 in the following form:

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.8.} \emph{Let
\(H \xrightarrow{i} W \xrightarrow{f} G\) be a sequence of morphisms of
\(C\)-groups such that for every \(S \in Ob(C)\), \texttt{(H(S),\ i(S))}
is a kernel of \(f(S) : W(S) \to G(S)\). Let \(u : G \to W\) be a
morphism of \(C\)-groups which is a section of \(f\). Then \(W\) is
identified with the semidirect product of \(H\) by \(G\) for the
operation of \(G\) on \(H\) such that if \(S \in Ob(C)\), \(g \in G(S)\)
and \(h \in H(S)\), one has \(Int(u(g)) i(h) = i({}^{g} h)\).}

\subsection{3. The category of O-modules, the category of
G-O-modules}\label{the-category-of-o-modules-the-category-of-g-o-modules}

\textbf{Definition 3.1.} \emph{Let \(O\) and \(F\) be two objects of
\texttt{Ĉ}. One says that \(F\) is a} \texttt{Ĉ}-module \emph{over the
\texttt{Ĉ}-ring \(O\), or in abbreviated form an} \(O\)-module,
\emph{if, for every \(S \in Ob(C)\), one has endowed \(O(S)\) with a
ring structure and \(F(S)\) with a structure of module over this ring in
such a way that, for every arrow \(S' \to S''\) of \(C\),
\(O(S'') \to O(S')\) is a ring homomorphism and \(F(S'') \to F(S')\) is
a homomorphism of abelian groups compatible with this ring
homomorphism.}

If \(O\) is fixed, one defines in the usual way a morphism of the
\(O\)-modules \(F\) and \(F'\), whence the commutative group
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O}(F, F')\), and the category of \(O\)-modules,
denoted \texttt{(O-Mod.)}.

\textbf{Lemma 3.1.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: Statements 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 have
  been added to make explicit that the category \texttt{(O-Mod.)} is
  abelian and verifies the axiom (AB 5), and moreover has enough
  injective objects if the category \(C\) is small. An error in 3.1.2,
  reported in 2016 by Linyuan Liu, has been corrected here.}
\emph{\texttt{(O-Mod.)} is endowed with a structure of abelian category,
defined ``argument by argument''. Moreover, \texttt{(O-Mod.)} verifies
the axiom (AB 5) (cf.~{[}Gr57, 1.5{]}), i.e.~arbitrary direct sums
exist, and if \(M\) is an \(O\)-module, \(N\) a submodule, and
\((F_{i})_{i\in I}\) a directed family of submodules of \(M\), then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⋃\_\{i∈I\} (F\_i ∩ N) = (⋃\_\{i∈I\} F\_i) ∩ N.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, let \(f : F \to F'\) be a morphism of \(O\)-modules. One defines
the \(O\)-modules \texttt{Ker\ f} (resp. \texttt{Im\ f} and
\texttt{Coker\ f}) by setting, for every \(S \in Ob(C)\),
\((Ker f)(S) = Ker f(S)\) (resp. ⋯). Then \texttt{Ker\ f} (resp.
\texttt{Coker\ f}) is a kernel (resp. cokernel) of \(f\), and one has an
isomorphism of \(O\)-modules \(F/ Ker f \xrightarrow{\sim} Im f\). This
proves that \texttt{(O-Mod.)} is an abelian category.

Arbitrary direct sums exist and are defined ``argument by argument''.
Finally, if \(M\) is an \(O\)-module, \(N\) a submodule, and
\((F_{i})_{i\in I}\) a directed family of submodules of \(M\), then the
inclusion

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⋃\_\{i∈I\} (F\_i ∩ N) ⊂ (⋃\_\{i∈I\} F\_i) ∩ N}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an equality: indeed, if \(S \in Ob(C)\) and
\(x \in N(S) \cap \bigcup_{i} F_{i}(S)\), there exists \(i \in I\) such
that \(x \in N(S) \cap F_{i}(S)\).

\textbf{Proposition 3.1.2.}\footnote{N.D.E.: Statements 3.1.1 and 3.1.2
  have been added to make explicit that the category \texttt{(O-Mod.)}
  is abelian and verifies the axiom (AB 5), and moreover has enough
  injective objects if the category \(C\) is small. An error in 3.1.2,
  reported in 2016 by Linyuan Liu, has been corrected here.}
\emph{Suppose the category \(C\) is small, i.e.~that \(Ob(C)\) is a set.
Then \texttt{(O-Mod.)} has a generator, and therefore enough injective
objects.}

\emph{Proof.} For every object \(S\) of \(C\), one defines the
\(O\)-module \texttt{O\_S} as follows. For every object \(S'\),
\(O_{S}(S')\) is a direct sum of copies of \(O(S')\) indexed by
\(\operatorname{Hom}(S', S)\), i.e.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{O\_S(S′) = ⊕\_\{g : S′ → S\} O(S′) g.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For every morphism \(f : S'' \to S'\), denoting \(f*\) the ring
homomorphism \(O(S') \to O(S'')\), the morphism
\(O_{S}(f) : O_{S}(S') \to O_{S}(S'')\) sends each element \texttt{a\ g}
of \(O_{S}(S')\) (where

\(a \in O(S')\) and \(g : S' \to S\)) to the element \(f*(a) g \circ f\)
of \(O_{S}(S'')\). One verifies easily that this does define a functor
in \(O\)-modules.

Since, by hypothesis, \(Ob(C)\) is a set, one can consider the direct
sum \(G = \oplus_{S\in Ob(C)} O_{S}\).

\textbf{Lemma 3.1.2.1.} \emph{Let \(F\) be an \(O\)-module. For every
\(S \in Ob(C)\), every element \(x\) of \(F(S)\) defines a unique
morphism of \(O\)-modules \(\tilde{x} : O_{S} \to F\) such that
\(\tilde{x}(1 id_{S}) = x\).}

\emph{Proof.} Let \(\phi\) be a morphism of \(O\)-modules
\(O_{S} \to F\) such that \(\phi(1 id_{S}) = x\). Let \(g : S' \to S\)
and \(a \in O(S')\). The \(O(S')\)-linearity and the commutativity of
the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              φ}
\NormalTok{   O\_S(S) ────────→ F(S)}
\NormalTok{     │              │}
\NormalTok{   O\_S(g)          F(g)}
\NormalTok{     ↓     φ        ↓}
\NormalTok{   O\_S(S′) ────────→ F(S′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

entail that
\(\phi(ag) = a \phi(1g) = a F(g)(\phi(1 id_{S})) = a F(g)(x)\). So
\(\phi\), if it exists, is determined by the previous equality.
Conversely, if one defines \(\phi\) thus, then for every
\(f : S'' \to S'\) one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ ∘ O\_S(f)(ag) = φ(f*(a) g ∘ f) = f*(a) F(g ∘ f)(x) = F(f)(a F(g)(x)) = F(f) ∘ φ(ag)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              φ}
\NormalTok{   O\_S(S′) ────────→ F(S′)}
\NormalTok{     │              │}
\NormalTok{   O\_S(f)          F(f)}
\NormalTok{     ↓     φ        ↓}
\NormalTok{   O\_S(S″) ────────→ F(S″)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is commutative. This proves the lemma.

Now, let \(F\) be an \(O\)-module. For every \(S \in Ob(C)\), let
\(F_{0}(S)\) be a system of generators of the \(O(S)\)-module \(F(S)\),
and let \texttt{L\_S} be the direct sum indexed by \(F_{0}(S)\) of
copies of \texttt{O\_S}. By the lemma, one obtains a morphism of
\(O\)-modules \(L_{S} \to F\), such that the morphism
\(L_{S}(S) \to F(S)\) is surjective, hence an epimorphism in the
category of \(O(S)\)-modules.

Set \(I = \bigsqcup_{S\in Ob(C)} F_{0}(S)\). Then one obtains a morphism
of \(O\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\^{}\{⊕I\} ──→ ⊕\_\{S∈Ob(C)\} L\_S ──→ F}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is ``argument by argument'' an epimorphism, hence an epimorphism
of \texttt{(O-Mod.)}. This shows that \(G\) is a generator of
\texttt{(O-Mod.)} (cf.~{[}Gr57, 1.9.1{]}). Since \texttt{(O-Mod.)}
verifies (AB 5), it then follows from {[}Gr57, 1.10.1{]} that
\texttt{(O-Mod.)} has enough injective objects.

\textbf{Remark 3.1.3.} \emph{If \texttt{O\_0} is the \texttt{Ĉ}-ring
defined by \(O_{0}(S) = \mathbb{Z}\) (which should not be confused with
the functor associated to the constant object \(\mathbb{Z}\)), then the
category of \texttt{O\_0}-modules is isomorphic to the category of
commutative \texttt{Ĉ}-groups.}

\textbf{Definition 3.1.4.} \emph{Note that, if \(F\) is an \(O\)-module,
then for every \(S \in Ob(C)\), \texttt{FS} is an \texttt{O\_S}-module.
One can therefore define a \texttt{Ĉ}-abelian group
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O}(F, F')\) by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_O(F, F′)(S) = Hom\_\{O\_S\}(FS, F′\_S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One defines similarly the objects}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_O(F, F′),    End\_O(F)    and    Aut\_O(F),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the last being a \texttt{Ĉ}-group for the structure induced by the
composition of automorphisms.}

\textbf{Definition 3.2.} \emph{Let \(O\) be a \texttt{Ĉ}-ring, \(F\) an
\(O\)-module and \(G\) a \texttt{Ĉ}-group. By a} structure of
\(G\)-\(O\)-module \emph{on \(F\) we mean a structure of \(G\)-object
such that for every \(S \in Ob(C)\) and every \(g \in G(S)\), the
automorphism of \(F(S)\) defined by \(g\) is an automorphism of its
\(O(S)\)-module structure.}

It amounts to the same thing to say that the morphism of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups

\[
\rho : G \to \operatorname{Aut}(F)
\]

defined in 2.3 maps \(G\) into the sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-group
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{O}(F)\) of \(\operatorname{Aut}(F)\). To give a
structure of \(G\)-\(O\)-module on the \(O\)-module \(F\) is therefore
to give a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups

\[
\rho : G \to \operatorname{Aut}_{O}(F).
\]

One defines in a natural way the abelian group
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{G-O}(F, F')\), hence the additive category of
\(G\)-\(O\)-modules denoted \texttt{(G-O-Mod.)}.

\textbf{Remark 3.2.1.} \emph{The reader will note that
\texttt{(G-O-Mod.)} may also be defined as the category of
\texttt{O{[}G{]}}-modules, where \texttt{O{[}G{]}} is the algebra of the
\texttt{Ĉ}-group \(G\) over the \texttt{Ĉ}-ring \(O\), whose definition
is clear.\footnote{N.D.E.: The following sentence has been added; this
  will be used in section 5.} Consequently, by 3.1.1 and 3.1.2,
\texttt{(G-O-Mod.)} is an abelian category verifying the axiom (AB 5);
moreover, if \(C\) is small, \texttt{(G-O-Mod.)} has enough injective
objects.}

All the constructions of this paragraph specialize at once to the case
where \(G\) (or \(O\), or both) are representable by objects of \(C\),
which are thereby endowed with the corresponding algebraic structures.

We have treated succinctly the case of the principal algebraic
structures encountered in the rest of this seminar. For the others
(structure of \(O\)-Lie algebra for example), we believe that the reader
will have had enough examples in this paragraph to make the general
mechanism sketched in 2.2 work himself in each particular case.

We shall now apply what we have just done to the category of schemes,
denoted \texttt{(Sch)}, and more generally to the categories \((Sch)/S\)
(also denoted \((Sch/S)\)).

\subsection{4. Algebraic structures in the category of
schemes}\label{algebraic-structures-in-the-category-of-schemes}

We shall allow ourselves, whenever there is no ambiguity, the following
abuses of language: one will designate by \(T\) the object
\(T \xrightarrow{f} S\) of \(C/S\), the datum of \(f\) (``structural
morphism of \(T\)'') being understood, and one will identify \(C\) with
a subcategory of \texttt{Ĉ}. Given the compatibilities stated in the
preceding paragraphs, these identifications can be made without danger.

We shall further simplify the terminology along the following model: a
\texttt{(Sch)}-group will also be called a \emph{group scheme}, a
\((Sch)/S\)-group a \emph{group scheme over \(S\)}, or \emph{\(S\)-group
scheme}, or \emph{\(S\)-group}, or \emph{\(A\)-group} when \(S\) is the
spectrum of the ring \(A\).

\subsubsection{4.1. Constant schemes}\label{constant-schemes}

The category of schemes satisfies the conditions required in 1.8. One
can therefore define constant objects in it; for every set \(E\), one
has a scheme \(E_{\mathbb{Z}}\), and for every scheme \(S\), an
\(S\)-scheme \(ES = (E_{\mathbb{Z}})_{S}\). Recall (cf.~\emph{loc.
cit.}) that for every \(S\)-scheme \(T\),
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(T, ES)\) is the set of locally constant maps

from the topological space \(T\) to \(E\).

The functor \(E \mapsto ES\) commutes with finite inverse limits. In
particular if \(G\) is a group, \texttt{GS} is an \(S\)-group scheme; if
\(O\) is a ring, \texttt{OS} is an \(S\)-ring scheme, etc.

\subsubsection{4.2. Affine S-groups}\label{affine-s-groups}

Let us recall a certain number of things about affine \(S\)-schemes (EGA
II, § 1). One says that the \(S\)-scheme \(T\) is \emph{affine over
\(S\)} if the inverse image of every affine open subset of \(S\) is
affine. The \texttt{OS}-algebra \(f_{*}(O_{T})\), which one denotes
\(A(T)\), is then quasi-coherent (\(f\) denotes the structural morphism
of \(T\)). Conversely, to every quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-algebra
\(A\), one can associate an \(S\)-scheme affine over \(S\), denoted
\(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\). These functors \(T \mapsto A(T)\) and
\(A \mapsto \operatorname{Spec}(A)\) are quasi-inverse equivalences
between the category of \(S\)-schemes affine over \(S\) and the category
opposite to that of quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-algebras.

It follows that to give an algebraic structure on an \(S\)-scheme \(T\)
affine over \(S\) is equivalent to giving the corresponding structure on
\(A(T)\) in the category opposite to that of quasi-coherent
\texttt{OS}-algebras. In particular, if \(G\) is an \(S\)-group affine
over \(S\), \(A(G)\) is endowed with a structure of augmented
\texttt{OS}-bialgebra, that is, one has two morphisms of
\texttt{OS}-algebras

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Δ : A(G) → A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G)    and    ε : A(G) → OS}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

corresponding to the morphisms of \(S\)-schemes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π : G × G → G    and    e\_G : S → G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The maps \(\Delta\) and \(\epsilon\) satisfy the following conditions
(which express that \(G\) is an \(S\)-monoid):\footnote{N.D.E.: And, of
  course, the inversion morphism \(G \to G\) induces a morphism of
  \texttt{OS}-algebras \(\tau : A(G) \to A(G)\) which, together with
  \(\Delta\) and \(\epsilon\), makes \(A(G)\) an \texttt{OS}-Hopf
  algebra.}

\textbf{(HA 1)} \emph{\(\Delta\) is co-associative: the following
diagram is commutative}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G)}
\NormalTok{                        ╱            ╲}
\NormalTok{                Δ      ╱              ╲  id ⊗ Δ}
\NormalTok{                      ╱                ╲}
\NormalTok{                 A(G)                  A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G)}
\NormalTok{                      ╲                ╱}
\NormalTok{                       ╲              ╱  Δ ⊗ id}
\NormalTok{                Δ       ╲            ╱}
\NormalTok{                       A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{(HA 2)} \emph{\(\Delta\) is compatible with \(\epsilon\): the
two following composites are the identity}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
