\NormalTok{        Δ                       id ⊗ ε                ∼}
\NormalTok{A(G) ────→ A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ─────────→ A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} OS ──→ A(G),}

\NormalTok{        Δ                       ε ⊗ id                ∼}
\NormalTok{A(G) ────→ A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ─────────→ OS ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ──→ A(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us take this opportunity to note once more that it follows from the
definition of an \(S\)-group structure that to give such a structure on
an \(S\)-scheme \(G\) affine over \(S\), it is not necessary to verify
anything on \(A(G)\), but simply to endow each \(G(S')\) for \(S'\)
above \(S\) with a group structure functorial in \(S'\).

This remark applies \emph{mutatis mutandis} to morphisms.

\subsubsection{4.3. The groups G\_a and G\_m. The ring
O}\label{the-groups-g_a-and-g_m.-the-ring-o}

\paragraph{4.3.1.}\label{section-7}

Let \(G_{a}\) be the functor from \((Sch)^{\circ}\) to \texttt{(Ens)}
defined by

\[
G_{a}(S) = \Gamma(S, OS)
\]

endowed with the \(\hat{Sch}\)-group structure defined by the additive
group structure of the ring \(\Gamma(S, OS)\). It is representable by an
affine scheme, which we shall denote \(G_{a}\), which is therefore a
group scheme

\[
G_{a} = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}[T].
\]

Indeed,
\texttt{G\_a(S)\ =\ Hom(S,\ G\_a)\ =\ Hom\_\{Alg.\}(ℤ{[}T{]},\ Γ(S,\ OS))\ ≃\ Γ(S,\ OS)}.

For every scheme \(S\), one therefore has an \(S\)-group affine over
\(S\), denoted \(G_{a,S}\), which corresponds to the
\texttt{OS}-bialgebra \texttt{OS{[}T{]}}, with the diagonal map and the
augmentation defined by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Δ(T) = T ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ T,    ε(T) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{4.3.2.}\label{section-8}

Let \(G_{m}\) be the functor from \((Sch)^{\circ}\) to \texttt{(Ens)}
defined by

\[
G_{m}(S) = \Gamma(S, OS)^{\times},
\]

where \(\Gamma(S, OS)^{\times}\) denotes the multiplicative group of
invertible elements of the ring \(\Gamma(S, OS)\), endowed with its
natural \(\hat{Sch}\)-group structure. It is representable by an affine
scheme denoted \(G_{m}\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_m = Spec ℤ[T, T\^{}\{{-}1\}] = Spec ℤ[ℤ],}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\mathbb{Z}[\mathbb{Z}]\) denotes the algebra of the group
\(\mathbb{Z}\) over the ring \(\mathbb{Z}\). Indeed,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_m(S) = Hom\_\{Alg.\}(ℤ[T, T\^{}\{{-}1\}], Γ(S, OS)) ≃ Γ(S, OS)\^{}×.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For every scheme \(S\), one therefore has an \(S\)-group affine over
\(S\) denoted \(G_{m,S}\), which corresponds to the \texttt{OS}-algebra
\(OS[\mathbb{Z}]\), with the diagonal map and augmentation defined by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Δ(x) = x ⊗ x    and    ε(x) = 1,    for x ∈ ℤ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{4.3.3.}\label{section-9}

Let \(O\) be the functor \(G_{a}\) endowed with its \(\hat{Sch}\)-ring
structure. It is represented by the scheme
\(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}[T]\), which we shall denote \(O\) when
considering it as endowed with its ring scheme structure.

For every scheme \(S\),
\texttt{OS\ =\ S\ ×\_\{Spec\ ℤ\}\ Spec\ ℤ{[}T{]}\ =\ Spec(OS{[}T{]})} is
therefore an \(S\)-ring scheme, affine over \(S\). (Note: in EGA II
1.7.13, \texttt{OS} is denoted \texttt{S{[}T{]}}).

\paragraph{4.3.3.1.}\label{section-10}

\footnote{N.D.E.: This paragraph has been added, which will be useful
  later (cf.~II 1.3).} For every object \(X\) of \(\hat{Sch}\),
\(O(X) = \operatorname{Hom}(X, O)\) is endowed with a ring structure,
functorial in \(X\). In particular, if \(X'\) is a scheme and one is
given morphisms \(x : X' \to X\) and \(f : X \to O\) (i.e.
\(f \in O(X)\)), then \(f(x) = f \circ x\) is an element of
\(O(X') = \Gamma(X', O_{X'})\).

\textbf{Definition.} \emph{Let \(\pi : M \to X\) be a morphism of
\(\hat{Sch}\), and let \(OX = O \times X\). One says that \(M\) is an
\texttt{OX}-module if one has given, for every \(X\)-scheme \(X'\), a
structure of \(O(X')\)-module on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(X', M)\),
functorial in \(X'\).}

This amounts to giving a law of \(X\)-abelian group
\(\mu : M \times_{X} M \to M\) and an ``external law''

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{O × M = OX ×\_X M → M,    (f, m) ↦ f ⋅ m}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is an \(X\)-morphism (i.e.~\(\pi(f \cdot m) = \pi(m)\)) and which,
for every \(x \in X(S)\), endows \(M(x) = {m \in M(S) | \pi(m) = x}\)
with a structure of \(O(S)\)-module.

In this case, for every \(Y \in Ob \hat{Sch}_{/X}\) (not necessarily
representable), \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(Y, M) = \Gamma(M_{Y}/Y)\) is an
\(O(Y)\)-module, functorially in \(Y\).

\subsubsection{4.4. Diagonalizable groups}\label{diagonalizable-groups}

\paragraph{4.4.1.}\label{section-11}

The construction of \(G_{m}\) generalizes as follows: let \(M\) be a
commutative group and \(M_{\mathbb{Z}}\) the group scheme associated to
it by the procedure of 4.1. Consider the functor defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D(M)(S) = Hom\_\{groups\}(M, G\_m(S)) ≃ Hom\_\{S{-}Gr.\}(MS, G\_\{m,S\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is a commutative \(\hat{Sch}\)-group representable by a group scheme
that one will denote \(D(M)\); one will therefore have by definition:

\[
D(M) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{(Sch)-Gr.}(M_{\mathbb{Z}}, G_{m}).
\]

Set in fact

\[
D(M) = \operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}[M],
\]

where \(\mathbb{Z}[M]\) is the algebra of the group \(M\) over the ring
\(\mathbb{Z}\); one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D(M)(S) = Hom\_\{Alg.\}(ℤ[M], Γ(S, OS)) ≃ Hom\_\{groups\}(M, Γ(S, OS)\^{}×)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by the very definition of the algebra \(\mathbb{Z}[M]\).

\paragraph{4.4.2.}\label{section-12}

For every scheme \(S\) one therefore has an \(S\)-group scheme affine
over \(S\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D\_S(M) = D(M)\_S = Hom\_\{(Sch){-}Gr.\}(M\_ℤ, G\_m)\_S = Hom\_\{S{-}Gr.\}(MS, G\_\{m,S\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is associated to the \texttt{OS}-bialgebra \texttt{OS{[}M{]}},
endowed with the diagonal map and augmentation defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Δ(x) = x ⊗ x    and    ε(x) = 1,    for x ∈ M.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{4.4.3.}\label{section-13}

If \(f : M \to N\) is a homomorphism of commutative groups, one defines
in an obvious manner a morphism of \(S\)-groups

\[
D_{S}(f) : D_{S}(N) \to D_{S}(M),
\]

whence a functor

\[
D_{S} : M \mapsto D_{S}(M)
\]

from the category of abelian groups to the category of \(S\)-groups
affine over \(S\), which one may also define as the composite of the
functor \(M \mapsto MS\) and of the functor
\(MS \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{S-Gr.}(MS, G_{m,S})\). This functor
commutes with extensions of the base.

An \(S\)-group isomorphic to a group of the form \(D_{S}(M)\) is said to
be \emph{diagonalizable}. Note that the elements of \(M\) are
interpreted as certain characters of \(D_{S}(M)\), that is, certain
elements of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-Gr.}(D_{S}(M), G_{m,S})\). (Confer
VIII 1).

\paragraph{4.4.4.}\label{section-14}

Let us give some examples of diagonalizable groups. One has first

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D(ℤ) = G\_m    and    D(ℤ\^{}r) = (G\_m)\^{}r.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One sets

\[
\mu_{n} = D(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}),
\]

and calls it the \emph{group of \(n\)-th roots of unity}. Indeed, one
has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ\_n(S) = Hom\_\{groups\}(ℤ/nℤ, Γ(S, OS)\^{}×) = \{f ∈ Γ(S, OS) | f\^{}n = 1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The \(S\)-group \(\mu_{n,S}\) corresponds to the \texttt{OS}-algebra
\(OS[T]/(T^{n} - 1)\). Suppose in particular that \(S\) is the spectrum
of a field \(k\) of characteristic \(p = n\). Setting \(T - 1 = s\), one
finds

\[
k[T]/(T^{p} - 1) = k[s]/(s^{p}),
\]

which shows that the underlying topological space of \(\mu_{p,k}\)
reduces to a point, the local ring of this point being the artinian
\(k\)-algebra \(k[s]/(s^{p})\). (In the same vein, let us note that the
\(S\)-schemes \(G_{a,S}, G_{m,S}, OS\) are smooth over \(S\), that
\(D_{S}(M)\) is

flat over \(S\) and that it is formally smooth (resp. smooth) over \(S\)
if and only if no residue characteristic of \(S\) divides the torsion of
\(M\) (resp. and if moreover \(M\) is of finite type), cf.~Exp. VIII,
2.1).

\subsubsection{4.5. Other examples of
groups}\label{other-examples-of-groups}

The preceding procedure applies to the ``classical groups'' (linear
groups \(GL_{n}\), symplectic \(Sp_{n}\), orthogonal \(O_{n}\), etc.).
One defines for example \(GL_{n}\) as representing the functor
\(GL_{n}\) such that:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{GL\_n(S) = GL(n, Γ(S, OS)) = Aut\_\{OS\}(OS\^{}n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One can construct it for example as the open subscheme of
\(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}[T_{ij}]\)
(\(1 \leqslant i, j \leqslant n\)) defined by the function
\(f = det((T_{ij})^{n}_{i,j=1})\), that is,
\(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}[T_{ij}, f^{-1}]\).

\subsubsection{4.6. Functor-modules in the category of
schemes}\label{functor-modules-in-the-category-of-schemes}

We propose to associate to every \texttt{OS}-module on the scheme \(S\)
an \texttt{OS}-module (where \texttt{OS} denotes the functor-ring
introduced in 4.3.3). This can be done in two different ways. Precisely:

\textbf{Definition 4.6.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme. For every
\texttt{OS}-module \(F\) one denotes by \(V(F)\) and \(W(F)\) the
contravariant functors on \((Sch)/S\) defined by:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V(F)(S′) = Hom\_\{O\_\{S′\}\}(F ⊗\_\{OS\} O\_\{S′\}, O\_\{S′\}),}
\NormalTok{W(F)(S′) = Γ(S′, F ⊗\_\{OS\} O\_\{S′\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(where \(F \otimes_{OS} O_{S'}\) denotes the inverse image on
\(S'\) of the \texttt{OS}-module \(F\)).}

Then \(V(F)\) and \(W(F)\) are endowed in an obvious manner with a
structure of \texttt{OS}-modules (recall that
\(OS(S') = \Gamma(S', O_{S'}) = W(OS)(S')\)), in such a way that one has
in fact defined two functors \(V\) and \(W\) from the category of
\texttt{OS}-modules to the category of \texttt{OS}-modules, with \(V\)
contravariant and \(W\) covariant.

We restrict ourselves in the rest of this paragraph to the case where
the \texttt{OS}-modules in question are quasi-coherent, that is, we
consider \(V\) and \(W\) as

functors from the category \texttt{(OS-Mod.q.c.)} of quasi-coherent
\texttt{OS}-modules to the category of \texttt{OS}-modules

\[
V : (OS-Mod.q.c.)^{\circ} \to (OS-Mod.),
W : (OS-Mod.q.c.) \to (OS-Mod.).
\]

\textbf{Remark 4.6.1.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 4.6.1.1 has been
  added, for subsequent references.} \emph{The reader will note that, in
what follows, all the propositions involving only the functor \(W\) are
valid for arbitrary \texttt{OS}-modules, not necessarily
quasi-coherent.}

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.2.} \emph{(i) The functors \(V\) and \(W\)
commute with base extension: if \(S'\) is above \(S\) and if \(F\) is a
quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-module, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V(F ⊗ O\_\{S′\}) ≃ V(F)\_\{S′\}    and    W(F ⊗ O\_\{S′\}) ≃ W(F)\_\{S′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) The functors \(V\) and \(W\) are fully faithful: the
canonical maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{OS\}(F, F′) → Hom\_\{OS\}(V(F′), V(F))}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{OS\}(F, F′) → Hom\_\{OS\}(W(F), W(F′))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are bijective.}

\emph{(iii) The functors \(V\) and \(W\) are additive:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V(F ⊕ F′) ≃ V(F) ×\_S V(F′)    and    W(F ⊕ F′) ≃ W(F) ×\_S W(F′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Parts (i) and (iii) are obvious from the definitions. For (ii), one
takes for \(S'\) open subschemes of \(S\). We leave the proof to the
reader (for \(V\), use EGA II, 1.7.14).

Recall (cf.~3.1.4) that if \(F, F'\) are \texttt{OS}-modules,
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{OS}(F, F')\) denotes the \(S\)-functor (in abelian
groups) which to every \(S' \to S\) associates
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S'}}(F_{S'}, F'_{S'})\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.3.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The isomorphism
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{OS}(W(F), W(F')) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_{OS}(V(F'), V(F))\)
  has been added.} \emph{One has canonical morphisms in
\texttt{(OS-Mod.)}:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                        W(Hom\_\{OS\}(F, F′))}
\NormalTok{                        ╱             ╲}
\NormalTok{                       ↙               ↘}
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{OS\}(W(F), W(F′))           Hom\_\{OS\}(V(F′), V(F))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This follows immediately from 4.6.2 (i) and (ii).

\textbf{Notation 4.6.3.1.} \emph{Let \(F\) be a quasi-coherent
\texttt{OS}-module. One knows (EGA II, 1.7.8) that the \(S\)-functor
\(V(F)\) is representable by an \(S\)-scheme affine over \(S\) which one
denotes \(V(F)\) and calls the} vector fibration\footnote{N.D.E.:
  ``vector bundle'' has been replaced by ``vector fibration''; current
  usage being to call a vector fibration that is locally trivial of rank
  \(r\) a ``vector bundle of rank \(r\)'', i.e.~one whose sheaf of
  sections is locally isomorphic to \(OS^{\oplus r}\).} \emph{defined by
\(F\):}

\[
V(F) = \operatorname{Spec}(S(F)),
\]

\emph{where \(S(F)\) denotes the symmetric algebra of the
\texttt{OS}-module \(F\).\footnote{N.D.E.: Let us point out here the
  articles {[}Ni04{]} (resp. {[}Ni02{]}), which show that if \(S\) is
  noetherian and \(F\) is a coherent \texttt{OS}-module, then \(W(F)\)
  (resp. the \(S\)-group which to every \(T \to S\) associates
  \(\operatorname{Aut}_{OT}(F \otimes OT)\)) is representable if and
  only if \(F\) is locally free.}}

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.4.} \emph{Let \(F\) and \(F'\) be two
quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-modules, \(A\) a quasi-coherent
\texttt{OS}-algebra. One has a functorial isomorphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Spec(A), Hom\_\{OS\}(W(F′), W(F))) ⥲ Hom\_\{OS\}(F′, F ⊗\_\{OS\} A).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, denoting \(X = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\), the first member is
canonically isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{OS}(W(F'), W(F))(X)\),
that is, by definition, to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{OX\}(W(F′)\_X, W(F)\_X) ≃ Hom\_\{OX\}(W(F′ ⊗ O\_X), W(F ⊗ O\_X))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(cf.~4.6.2 (i)), which by 4.6.2 (ii) can also be written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{OX\}(F′ ⊗ O\_X, F ⊗ O\_X) = Hom\_\{OS\}(F′, π\_*(π*(F))),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where one denotes \(\pi : X \to S\) the structural morphism. But, by EGA
II, 1.4.7, one has \(\pi_{*}(\pi*(F)) \simeq F \otimes A\), which
completes the proof.

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.4.1.} \emph{One has a canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(F ⊗ A) ≃ Hom\_S(Spec(A), W(F)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed,\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been detailed in what follows.}
let \(f : S' \to S\) be an \(S\)-scheme and \(X' = X \times_{S} S'\);
one has a cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              f′}
\NormalTok{   X′ ───────→ X}
\NormalTok{   │           │}
\NormalTok{   π′          π}
\NormalTok{   ↓     f     ↓}
\NormalTok{   S′ ───────→ S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and by EGA II, 1.5.2, \(X'\) is affine over \(S'\) and
\(\pi'_{*}(O_{X'}) = f*(A)\). One has therefore

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Spec(A), W(F))(S′) = Hom\_\{S′\}(Spec(f*(A)), W(f*(F)))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and by 4.6.4 applied to \(f*(F)\), \(F' = O_{S'}\) and \(f*(A)\), this
equals

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(S′, f*(F) ⊗ f*(A)) = Γ(S′, f*(F ⊗ A)) = W(F ⊗ A)(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.5.} \emph{If \(F\) and \(F'\) are two
\texttt{OS}-modules locally free of finite type, the morphisms of 4.6.3
are isomorphisms.}

Indeed, for every \(S' \to S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(Hom\_\{OS\}(F, F′))(S′) = Γ(S′, Hom\_\{OS\}(F, F′) ⊗ O\_\{S′\}) = Hom\_\{O\_\{S′\}\}(F ⊗ O\_\{S′\}, F′ ⊗ O\_\{S′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But the second member is indeed isomorphic to
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{OS}(W(F), W(F'))(S')\) and to
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{OS}(V(F'), V(F))(S')\), by 4.6.2 (i) and (ii).

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.5.1.} \emph{Let \(F\) be an \texttt{OS}-module
locally free of finite type. Set
\(F^{\vee} = \operatorname{Hom}_{OS}(F, OS)\). One has canonical
isomorphisms:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(F\^{}∨) ≃ Hom\_\{OS\}(W(F), OS) ≃ V(F),}
\NormalTok{V(F\^{}∨) ≃ Hom\_\{OS\}(V(F), OS) ≃ W(F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has finally the following proposition:

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.6.} \emph{Let \(f : F \to F'\) be a morphism of
\texttt{OS}-modules locally free of finite rank. For
\(W(f) : W(F) \to W(F')\) to be a monomorphism, it is necessary and
sufficient that \(f\) identify \(F\) locally with a direct factor of
\(F'\).}

The direct proposition is essentially contained in EGA 0\_I,
5.5.5.\footnote{N.D.E.: The following sentence has been detailed.}
Conversely, if \(F\) is locally a direct factor of \(F'\), then for
every \(\pi : S' \to S\), \(\pi* F\) is a submodule of \(\pi* F'\)
(because locally a direct factor), so \(W(F)(S') = \Gamma(S', \pi* F)\)
is a submodule of \(W(F')(S') = \Gamma(S', \pi* F')\).

\subsubsection{4.7. The category of
G-OS-modules}\label{the-category-of-g-os-modules}

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group and \(F\) an \texttt{OS}-module; \(W(F)\) is
endowed with a structure of \texttt{OS}-module.

\textbf{Definition 4.7.1.} \emph{By a} structure of
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module on \(F\) \emph{we mean a structure of
\texttt{hG}-\texttt{OS}-module on \(W(F)\) (cf. 3.2). A morphism of
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules is by definition a morphism of the associated
\texttt{hG}-\texttt{OS}-modules. One thus obtains the category
\texttt{(G-OS-Mod.)}, and one denotes \texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)} the full
subcategory formed by the \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules that are
quasi-coherent as \texttt{OS}-modules.}

To give a structure of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module on \(F\) is therefore,
by 3.2, to give a morphism of \(\hat{Sch}_{/S}\)-groups

\[
\rho : hG \to \operatorname{Aut}_{OS}(W(F)).
\]

\textbf{Remark 4.7.1.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This remark has been added,
  taken from {[}DG{]}, II, § 2, 1.1.} \emph{Since by 4.6.2 one has an
anti-isomorphism of \(S\)-functors in groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)    Aut\_\{OS\}(W(F)) ≃ Aut\_\{OS\}(V(F)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one sees that it is equivalent to give a structure of
\texttt{hG}-\texttt{OS}-module on \(W(F)\) or on \(V(F)\).} Indeed, let
\(\rho : hG \to \operatorname{Aut}_{OS}(W(F))\) be as above. For every
\(T \to S\) and \(g \in G(T)\), denote by \(\rho*(g)\) the image of
\(\rho(g)\) by the anti-isomorphism \texttt{(†)}; one has therefore
\(\rho*(gh) = \rho*(h) \circ \rho*(g)\), i.e. \(\rho*\) defines a
structure of \texttt{hG}-\texttt{OS}-module ``on the right'' on
\(V(F)\). Setting \(\rho^{\vee}(g) = \rho*(g^{-1})\), one obtains indeed
a structure of \texttt{hG}-\texttt{OS}-module on \(V(F)\), the datum of
which is equivalent to that of \(\rho\).

\textbf{Remark 4.7.1.1.} One can say that one has constructed the
categories one has just defined by the cartesian squares:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                        ───→ (G{-}OS{-}Mod.) ───→ (hG{-}OS{-}Mod.)}
\NormalTok{   (G{-}OS{-}Mod.q.c.)}
\NormalTok{                                                   │}
\NormalTok{                                                  forget}
\NormalTok{                              W                    ↓}
\NormalTok{   (OS{-}Mod.q.c.) ─────→ (OS{-}Mod.) ──────→ (OS{-}Mod.).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been corrected by suppressing the
  assertion that the category \texttt{(G-OS-Mod.)} is abelian, see
  4.7.2.1 below.} The categories \texttt{(OS-Mod.)} and
\texttt{(OS-Mod.)} are abelian, but one should be careful that in
general the functor \(W\) is neither left nor right exact.

\textbf{Remark 4.7.1.2.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This remark has been added.}
Let \(F\) be a \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module. The subsheaf of invariants
\(F^{G}\) is defined as follows: for every open subset \(U\) of \(S\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F\^{}G(U) = W(F)\^{}G(U) = \{x ∈ F(U) | g ⋅ x\_\{S′\} = x\_\{S′\} for every S′ ──f──→ U, g ∈ G(S′)\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(x_{S'}\) denotes the image of \(x\) in
\(\Gamma(S', f*(F)) = \Gamma(U, f_{*} f*(F))\).

One should be careful that the natural morphism
\(W(F^{G}) \to W(F)^{G}\) is not in general an isomorphism. For example,
if \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) and \(G\) is the constant
group \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} = {1, \tau}\) acting on \(F = OS\) by
\(\tau \cdot 1 = -1\), one has \(F^{G} = 0\) but, if \(R\) is an
\texttt{F\_2}-algebra, \(W(F)^{G}(\operatorname{Spec}(R)) = R\).

\paragraph{4.7.2.}\label{section-15}

We suppose from now until the end of n° 4.7 that \(G\) is affine over
\(S\).\footnote{N.D.E.: Cf. \texttt{VI\_B}, §§ 11.1--11.6 for the
  extension of the results of 4.7.2 to the case where \(G\) is not
  necessarily affine, but where \(G\) and \(F\) are assumed to be flat
  over \(S\).} Then, by virtue of 4.6.4, the datum of a morphism of
\(S\)-functors

\[
\rho : hG \to \operatorname{End}_{OS}(W(F))
\]

is equivalent to that of a morphism of \texttt{OS}-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ : F → F ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To say that \(\rho\) is a morphism of \(\hat{Sch}_{/S}\)-groups is then
equivalent to saying that \(\mu\) satisfies the following axioms:

\textbf{(CM 1)} \emph{the following diagram is commutative}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              μ}
\NormalTok{   F ────────────→ F ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G)}
\NormalTok{   │                   │}
\NormalTok{   μ                  id ⊗ Δ}
\NormalTok{   ↓     μ ⊗ id        ↓}
\NormalTok{   F ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ──→ F ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{(CM 2)} \emph{the following composite is the identity}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        μ                       id ⊗ ε              ∼}
\NormalTok{F ────────→ F ⊗ A(G) ──────────→ F ⊗ OS ────────→ F.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

These axioms (CM 1) and (CM 2) are those of a (right) comodule
structure\footnote{N.D.E.: Left \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules correspond in
  a natural way to right \(A(G)\)-comodules.} over the bialgebra
\(A(G)\).

Set \(A = A(G)\). If \(F\) and \(F'\) are \(A\)-comodules, a morphism of
comodules \(f : F \to F'\) is a morphism of \texttt{OS}-modules such
that the following diagram is

commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              f}
\NormalTok{   F ────────────→ F′}
\NormalTok{   │              │}
\NormalTok{   μ\_F           μ\_\{F′\}}
\NormalTok{   ↓     f ⊗ id   ↓}
\NormalTok{   F ⊗ A ──────→ F′ ⊗ A.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One thus obtains the category \texttt{(A-Comod.)}, and one will denote
by \texttt{(A-Comod.q.c.)} the full subcategory formed by the
\(A\)-comodules that are quasi-coherent as \texttt{OS}-modules. One has
thus obtained:

\textbf{Proposition 4.7.2.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group affine
over \(S\). One has equivalences of categories:}

\[
(G-OS-Mod.) \cong (A(G)-Comod.)
(G-OS-Mod.q.c.) \cong (A(G)-Comod.q.c.)
\]

\footnote{N.D.E.: The following sentence has been added.} \emph{If
moreover \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(\Lambda)\) is affine and if one
denotes \(\Lambda[G] = \Gamma(S, A(G))\), one has an equivalence of
categories}

\[
(A(G)-Comod.q.c.) \cong (\Lambda[G]-Comod.).
\]

\footnote{N.D.E.: The following paragraph has been added, taken from
  {[}Se68, § 1.3{]}.} Suppose moreover that \(A = A(G)\) is a flat
\texttt{OS}-module. Let \(E\) be an \(A\)-comodule and \(F\) a
sub-\texttt{OS}-module of \(E\). Since \(A\) is flat over \texttt{OS},
one can identify \(F \otimes A\) (resp. \(F \otimes A \otimes A\)) with
a sub-\texttt{OS}-module of \(E \otimes A\) (resp.
\(E \otimes A \otimes A\)). Suppose that \(\mu_{E}\) maps \(F\) into
\(F \otimes A\); then its restriction \(\mu_{F} : F \to F \otimes A\)
endows \(F\) with a structure of \(A\)-comodule; one says that \(F\) is
a \emph{subcomodule} of \(E\). By passage to the quotient, \(\mu_{E}\)
defines a morphism of \texttt{OS}-modules \(E/F \to E/F \otimes A\),
which endows \(E/F\) with a structure of \(A\)-comodule. If
\(f : E \to E'\) is a morphism of \(A\)-comodules, \texttt{Ker\ f}
(resp. \texttt{Im\ f}) is a sub-\(A\)-comodule of \(E\) (resp. \(E'\)),
and \(f\) induces an isomorphism of \(A\)-comodules:
\(E/Ker f \xrightarrow{\sim} Im f\). Moreover, if \(E\) and \(E'\) are
quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-modules, so are \texttt{Ker\ f} and
\texttt{Im\ f}. Consequently, \texttt{(A-Comod.)} and
\texttt{(A-Comod.q.c.)} are abelian categories.

\textbf{Corollary 4.7.2.1.} \emph{Suppose that \(G\) is affine and flat
over \(S\). Then the category \texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)} (resp.
\texttt{(G-OS-Mod.)}), equivalent to the category of \(A(G)\)-comodules
quasi-coherent over \texttt{OS} (resp. \(A(G)\)-comodules), is abelian.}

\paragraph{4.7.3.}\label{section-16}

Suppose now that \(G\) is a diagonalizable group, that is, that \(A(G)\)
is the algebra of a commutative group \(M\) over the sheaf of rings
\texttt{OS}. If \(F\) is an \texttt{OS}-module, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F ⊗ A(G) = ⨆\_\{m ∈ M\} F ⊗ m OS.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To give a morphism of \texttt{OS}-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ : F → F ⊗ A(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is therefore equivalent to giving \texttt{OS}-endomorphisms
\((\mu_{m})_{m \in M}\) of \(F\), such that for every section \(x\) of
\(F\) on an open subset of \(S\), \((\mu_{m}(x))\) is a section of the
direct sum \(\bigsqcup_{m \in M} F\) (this means that on every
sufficiently small open subset, there are only finitely many
restrictions of the \(\mu_{m}(x)\) that are nonzero).

For \(\mu\) defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ(x) = ∑\_\{m ∈ M\} μ\_m(x) ⊗ m}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

to satisfy (CM 1) (resp. (CM 2)) it is necessary and sufficient that one
have

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ\_m ∘ μ\_\{m′\} = δ\_\{mm′\} μ\_m,    (resp. ∑\_\{m ∈ M\} μ\_m = Id\_F),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which means that the \(\mu_{m}\) are pairwise orthogonal projectors with
sum the identity. One has thus proved:

\textbf{Proposition 4.7.3.} \emph{If \(G = D_{S}(M)\) is a
diagonalizable \(S\)-group, the category of quasi-coherent
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules (resp. of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules) is
equivalent to the category of quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-modules (resp.
of \texttt{OS}-modules) graded of type \(M\).}

\textbf{Remark.} If \(F\) is endowed with a structure of
\texttt{OS}-algebra preserved by the operations of \(G\), then the
gradation of \(F\) is a gradation of algebra. More precisely:

\textbf{Corollary 4.7.3.1.} \emph{The functor
\(A \mapsto \operatorname{Spec} A\) induces an equivalence between the
category of quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-algebras graded of type \(M\) and
the category opposite to that of \(S\)-schemes affine over \(S\) with
\(S\)-operator group \(G = D_{S}(M)\).}

\textbf{Proposition 4.7.4.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a diagonalizable
\(S\)-group. If \(0 \to F_{1} \to F_{2} \to F_{3} \to 0\) is an exact
sequence of quasi-coherent \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules that splits as a
sequence of \texttt{OS}-modules, then it also splits as a sequence of
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules.}

Indeed, if \(G = D_{S}(M)\), each \(F_{i}\) is graded by the
\((F_{i})_{m}\), and for each \(m \in M\) the sequence

\[
0 \to (F_{1})_{m} \to (F_{2})_{m} \to (F_{3})_{m} \to 0
\]

of \texttt{OS}-modules is split. The preceding proposition then entails
the result.

\subsection{5. Group cohomology}\label{group-cohomology}

\subsubsection{5.1. The standard complex}\label{the-standard-complex}

\footnote{N.D.E.: This complex is often called the ``Hochschild
  complex''; see for example § II.3 of {[}DG70{]}.} Let \(C\) be a
category, \(G\) a \texttt{Ĉ}-group, \(O\) a \texttt{Ĉ}-ring, and \(F\) a
\(G\)-\(O\)-module. One sets, for \(n \geqslant 0\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\^{}n(G, F) = Hom(G\^{}n, F)    and    C\^{}n(G, F) = Hom(G\^{}n, F),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(G^{0}\) is the final object \(e\). Then \(C^{n}(G, F)\) (resp.
\(C^{n}(G, F)\)) is endowed in an obvious manner with a structure of
\(O\)-module (resp. of \(\Gamma(O)\)-module), and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\^{}n(G, F) ≅ Γ(C\^{}n(G, F))    and    C\^{}n(G, F)(S) = C\^{}n(GS, FS).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To give an element of \(C^{n}(G, F)\) is to give for each
\(S \in Ob(C)\) an \(n\)-cochain of \(G(S)\) in \(F(S)\), functorially
in \(S\). The boundary operator

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂ : C\^{}n(G(S), F(S)) → C\^{}\{n+1\}(G(S), F(S)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which, recall, is given by the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂f(g\_1, …, g\_\{n+1\}) = g\_1 f(g\_2, …, g\_\{n+1\})}
\NormalTok{                    + ∑\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{n\} ({-}1)\^{}i f(g\_1, …, g\_i g\_\{i+1\}, …, g\_\{n+1\})}
\NormalTok{                    + ({-}1)\^{}\{n+1\} f(g\_1, …, g\_n),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is functorial in \(S\) and therefore defines a homomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂ : C\^{}n(G, F) → C\^{}\{n+1\}(G, F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \(\partial \circ \partial = 0\). One has thus defined a
complex of abelian groups (and even of \(\Gamma(O)\)-modules) denoted
\(C*(G, F)\). One defines in the same way the complex of \(O\)-modules
\(C*(G, F)\), and one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C*(G, F) = Γ(C*(G, F)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One denotes by \(H^{n}(G, F)\) (resp. \(H^{n}(G, F)\)) the groups (resp.
the \texttt{Ĉ}-groups) of cohomology of the complex \(C*(G, F)\) (resp.
\(C*(G, F)\)).

One has in particular

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}0(G, F) = F\^{}G    and    H\^{}0(G, F) = Γ(F\^{}G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 5.1.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This remark has been added.}
\emph{The ``set-theoretic'' description of \(\partial\) given above is
convenient for verifying that \(\partial \circ \partial = 0\). One can
also define \(\partial\) in terms of the multiplication
\(m : G \times G \to G\) and the action \(\mu : G \times F \to F\) as
follows: for every \(f \in C^{n}(G, F)\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂f = μ ∘ (id\_G × f) + ∑\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{n\} ({-}1)\^{}i f ∘ (id\_\{G\^{}\{i{-}1\}\} × m × id\_\{G\^{}\{n{-}i\}\}) + ({-}1)\^{}\{n+1\} f ∘ pr\_\{[1,n]\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(pr_{[1,n]}\) denotes the projection of
\(G^{n+1} = G^{n} \times G\) onto \(G^{n}\). Similarly, for every
\(S \in Ob(C)\) and \(f \in C^{n}(G, F)(S) = C^{n}(GS, FS)\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂f = μ\_S ∘ (id\_\{GS\} × f) + ∑\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{n\} ({-}1)\^{}i f ∘ (id\_\{GS\^{}\{i{-}1\}\} × m\_S × id\_\{GS\^{}\{n{-}i\}\}) + ({-}1)\^{}\{n+1\} f ∘ pr\_\{[1,n]\_S\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(m_{S}\) and \(\mu_{S}\) are deduced from \(m\) and \(\mu\)
by base change.}

\subsubsection{5.2.}\label{section-17}

\footnote{N.D.E.: The following recollection has been added.} Recall
(cf.~§ 3) that \texttt{(G-O-Mod.)} is endowed with a structure of
abelian category, defined ``argument by argument''; thus,

\[
0 \to F' \to F \to F'' \to 0
\]

is an exact sequence of \(G\)-\(O\)-modules if and only if the sequence
of abelian groups

\[
0 \to F'(S) \to F(S) \to F''(S) \to 0
\]

is exact, for every \(S \in Ob(C)\).

\footnote{N.D.E.: The following sentence has been added.} Suppose \(C\)
small; then, by 3.2.1, \texttt{(G-O-Mod.)} has enough injective objects,
so that the derived functors of the left exact functors \(H^{0}\) and
\(H^{0}\) are defined. We now propose to show that the functors
\(H^{n}\) (resp. \(H^{n}\)) are indeed the derived functors of \(H^{0}\)
(resp. \(H^{0}\)).

\textbf{Definition 5.2.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been
  modified, in order to introduce 5.2.0.1 and 5.2.0.2, which will be
  useful in the proof of Theorem 5.3.1.} \emph{For every \(O\)-module
\(P\), one denotes by \(E(P)\) the object \(\operatorname{Hom}(G, P)\)
of \texttt{Ĉ} endowed with the structure of \(G\)-\(O\)-module defined
as follows: for every \(S \in Ob(C)\) one has
\(\operatorname{Hom}(G, P)(S) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(GS, PS)\), and
one makes \(g \in G(S)\) and \(a \in O(S)\) operate on
\(\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(GS, PS)\) by the formulas}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(g ⋅ φ)(h) = φ(hg)    and    (a ⋅ φ)(h) = a φ(h),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(h \in G(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Moreover, for every
\(\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(GS, PS)\) one sets}

\[
\epsilon(\phi) = \phi(1) \in P(S)
\]

\emph{(where \texttt{1} denotes the unit element of \(G(S)\)).}

This defines a functor \(E : (O-Mod.) \to (G-O-Mod.)\) and a natural
transformation \(\epsilon : E \to Id\), where \texttt{Id} denotes the
identity functor of \texttt{(O-Mod.)}.

\textbf{Remark 5.2.0.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been
  modified, in order to introduce 5.2.0.1 and 5.2.0.2, which will be
  useful in the proof of Theorem 5.3.1.} \emph{In what follows, let us
denote by \texttt{G\_1} and \texttt{G\_2} two copies of \(G\). Then the
morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_1 × E(P) → E(P),    (g\_1, φ) ↦ (g\_2 ↦ φ(g\_2 g\_1))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{corresponds via the isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(G\_1 × E(P), E(P)) ≃ Hom(E(P), Hom(G\_1, Hom(G\_2, P)))}
\NormalTok{                     ≃ Hom(E(P), Hom(G\_2 × G\_1, P))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{to the morphism
\(\phi \mapsto ((g_{2}, g_{1}) \mapsto \phi(g_{2} g_{1}))\), i.e.~to the
morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(G, P) → Hom(G\_2 × G\_1, P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induced by the multiplication \(\mu_{G} : G \times G \to G\),
\((g_{2}, g_{1}) \mapsto g_{2} g_{1}\).}

\textbf{Lemma 5.2.0.2.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been modified,
  in order to introduce 5.2.0.1 and 5.2.0.2, which will be useful in the
  proof of Theorem 5.3.1.} \emph{(i) The functor \(E\) is right adjoint
to the forgetful functor \((G-O-Mod.) \to (O-Mod.)\); more precisely,
\(\epsilon : E \to Id\) induces for every \(M \in (G-O-Mod.)\) and
\(P \in Ob(O-Mod.)\) a bijection}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{G{-}O{-}Mod.\}(M, E(P)) ⥲ Hom\_\{O{-}Mod.\}(M, P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{functorial in \(M\) and \(P\).}

\emph{(ii) Consequently, if \(I\) is an injective object of
\texttt{(O-Mod.)} then \(E(I)\) is an injective object of
\texttt{(G-O-Mod.)}.}

\emph{Proof.} To every \(O\)-morphism \(f : M \to P\), one associates
the element \(\phi_{f}\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{O}(M, E(P))\) defined
as follows. For every \(S \in Ob(C)\) and \(m \in M(S)\),
\(\phi_{f}(m)\) is the element of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(GS, PS)\)
defined by: for every \(g \in G(S')\), \(S' \to S\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ\_f(m)(g) = f(g m) ∈ P(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, for every \(h \in G(S)\), one has
\(\phi_{f}(h m) = h \cdot f(m)\), i.e.~\(\phi_{f}\) is an element of

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{G-O-Mod.}(M, E(P)).
\]

If \(\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{G-O-Mod.}(M, E(P))\) and if one
denotes, for every \(m \in M(S)\), \(f(m) = \phi(m)(1)\), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ\_f(m)(g) = f(g m) = φ(g m)(1) = (g ⋅ φ(m))(1) = φ(m)(g),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~\(\phi_{f} = \phi\). Conversely, it is clear that
\(\phi_{f}(m)(1) = f(m)\). This proves (i), and (ii) follows at once.

\textbf{Definition 5.2.0.3.} \emph{Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-\(O\)-module;
the identity map of \(M\) (considered as an \(O\)-module) corresponds by
adjunction to the morphism of \(G\)-\(O\)-modules}

\[
\mu_{M} : M \to E(M)
\]

\emph{such that for every \(S \in Ob(C)\) and \(m \in M(S)\),
\(\mu_{M}(m)\) is the morphism \(GS \to MS\) defined by: for every
\(S' \to S\) and \(g \in G(S')\),
\(\mu_{M}(m)(g) = g \cdot m_{S'} \in M(S')\).}

Note that \(\mu_{M}\) is a monomorphism. Indeed,
\(\epsilon_{M} : E(M) \to M\) is a morphism of \(O\)-modules such that
\(\epsilon_{M} \circ \mu_{M} = id_{M}\); consequently \(M\) is a direct
factor, as an \(O\)-module, of \(E(M)\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.1.} \emph{Suppose that \(C\) is small, that
finite products exist in it, and that \(G\) is representable. Then, the
functors \(H^{n}(G, -)\) (resp. \(H^{n}(G, -)\)) are the derived
functors of the left exact functor \(H^{0}(G, -)\) (resp.
\(H^{0}(G, -)\)) on the category of \(G\)-\(O\)-modules.}

By virtue of the well-known general results,\footnote{N.D.E.: Cf.
  {[}Gr57{]}, 2.2.1 and 2.3. Moreover, the original has been detailed in
  what follows.} it suffices to verify that the \(H^{n}(G, -)\) (resp.
\(H^{n}(G, -)\)) form an effaceable cohomological functor in degrees
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}.

Let

\[
0 \to F' \to F \to F'' \to 0
\]

be an exact sequence of \(G\)-\(O\)-modules, and let \(S \in Ob(C)\). By
hypothesis, \(G\) is representable by an object \(G \in Ob(C)\), and
finite products exist in \(C\); in particular \(C\) has a final element
\(e\). Hence each \(G^{n} \times hS\) is representable by
\(G^{n} \times S\) (with \(G^{0} = e\)), and the sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 → F′(G\^{}n × S) → F(G\^{}n × S) → F″(G\^{}n × S) → 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is exact. This shows that the sequence of \(O\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 → C\^{}n(hG, F′) → C\^{}n(hG, F) → C\^{}n(hG, F″) → 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is exact. It follows that \(C*(G, -)\), considered as a functor on
\texttt{(G-O-Mod.)} with values in the category of complexes of
\texttt{(O-Mod.)}, is exact. This shows that the

\(H^{n}(G, -)\) indeed form a cohomological functor. Since the functor
\(\Gamma\) is exact, the same is true for the \(H^{n}(G, -)\). It will
now suffice to prove:

\textbf{Lemma 5.2.2.} \emph{For every \(P \in Ob(O-Mod.)\), one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}n(G, Hom(G, P)) = 0    and    H\^{}n(G, Hom(G, P)) = 0, for n \textgreater{} 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It suffices to prove that \(C*(G, \operatorname{Hom}(G, P))\) and
\(C*(G, \operatorname{Hom}(G, P))\) are homotopically trivial in degrees
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}. It suffices even to do this for the second,
the corresponding result for the first being deduced from it by base
change.\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been detailed in what follows.}
Now, one defines for every \(n \geqslant 0\) a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{σ : C\^{}\{n+1\}(G, Hom(G, P)) → C\^{}n(G, Hom(G, P))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

as follows. Let \(f \in C^{n+1}(G, \operatorname{Hom}(G, P))\); for
every \(S \in Ob(C)\) and \(g_{1}, \cdots, g_{n} \in G(S)\),
\(\sigma(f)(g_{1}, \cdots, g_{n})\) is the element of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(GS, PS)\) defined by: for every \(S' \to S\)
and \(x \in G(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{σ(f)(g\_1, …, g\_n)(x) = f(x, g\_1, …, g\_n)(e) ∈ P(S′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(where \(e\) denotes the unit element of \(G(S')\)). Then, \(\sigma\) is
a homotopy operator in degrees \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}. Indeed, for
every \(g_{1}, \cdots, g_{n+1} \in G(S)\) and \(x \in G(S')\) one has,
on the one hand:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂σ(f)(g\_1, …, g\_\{n+1\})(x) = f(x g\_1, g\_2, …, g\_\{n+1\})(e)}
\NormalTok{                          + ∑\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{n\} ({-}1)\^{}i f(x, g\_1, …, g\_i g\_\{i+1\}, …, g\_\{n+1\})(e)}
\NormalTok{                          + ({-}1)\^{}\{n+1\} f(x, g\_1, …, g\_n)(e),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and on the other hand:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{σ(∂f)(g\_1, …, g\_\{n+1\})(x) = (x f(g\_1, g\_2, …, g\_\{n+1\}))(e) {-} f(x g\_1, g\_2, …, g\_\{n+1\})(e)}
\NormalTok{                          + ∑\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{n\} ({-}1)\^{}\{i+1\} f(x, g\_1, …, g\_i g\_\{i+1\}, …, g\_\{n+1\})}
\NormalTok{                          + ({-}1)\^{}\{n+2\} f(x, g\_1, …, g\_n)(e),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∂σ(f) + σ(∂f))(g\_1, …, g\_\{n+1\})(x) = f(g\_1, …, g\_\{n+1\})(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~\(\partial \sigma + \sigma\partial\) is the identity map of
\(C^{n+1}(G, \operatorname{Hom}(G, P))\), for every \(n \geqslant 0\).

\textbf{Remark 5.2.3.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This remark has been added.}
\emph{The hypothesis ``\(C\) small'' is used only to ensure the
existence of the derived functors \(R^{n} H^{0}\) and \(R^{n} H^{0}\).
In any case, the foregoing shows that the functors \(H^{n}(G, -)\)
(resp. \(H^{n}(G, -)\)) form a cohomological functor, effaceable in
degrees \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}, hence they are the (right) satellite
functors of the left exact functor \(H^{0}(G, -)\) (resp.
\(H^{0}(G, -)\)), in the sense of {[}Gr57, 2.2{]}; if
\texttt{(G-O-Mod.)} has enough injective objects (which is the case if
\(C\) is small), they coincide with the derived functors (}loc. cit.*
2.3).*

\subsubsection{5.3. Cohomology of
G-OS-modules}\label{cohomology-of-g-os-modules}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group, and \(F\) a quasi-coherent
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module. One defines the cohomology groups of \(G\)
with values in \(F\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}n(G, F) = H\^{}n(hG, W(F)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(for the notations, cf.~4.6).

Suppose \(G\) is affine over \(S\). Then, in view of Proposition 4.6.4,
this cohomology is computed as follows: \(H^{n}(G, F)\) is the \(n\)-th
homology group of the complex \(C*(G, F)\) whose \(n\)-th term is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\^{}n(G, F) = Γ(S, F ⊗ A(G) ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ A(G))}
\NormalTok{                       └────── n times ──────┘}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(f\) (resp. \(a_{i}\)) is a section of \(F\) (resp. of \(A(G)\)) on
an open subset of \(S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂(f ⊗ a\_1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ a\_n) = μ\_F(f) ⊗ a\_1 ⊗ a\_2 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ a\_n}
\NormalTok{                     + ∑\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{n\} ({-}1)\^{}i f ⊗ a\_1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ Δ a\_i ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ a\_n}
\NormalTok{                     + ({-}1)\^{}\{n+1\} f ⊗ a\_1 ⊗ a\_2 ⋯ ⊗ a\_n ⊗ 1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\Delta : A(G) \to A(G) \otimes A(G)\) and
\(\mu_{F} : F \to F \otimes A(G)\) describe the coalgebra structure of
\(A(G)\) and the comodule structure of \(F\). Note in passing that the
cohomology of \(G\) with values in \(F\) therefore depends only on the
comodule structure of \(F\), and in particular only on the \(S\)-monoid
structure of \(G\).

One has in particular

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}0(G, F) = Γ(S, F\^{}G),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(F^{G}\), the \emph{sheaf of invariants of \(F\)}, is defined as
the sheaf whose sections on the open subset \(U\) of \(S\) are the
sections of \(F\) on \(U\) whose inverse image in any \(S'\) over \(U\)
is invariant under \(G(S')\) (cf.~4.7.1.2).

\textbf{Theorem 5.3.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group affine and flat over \(S\). The functors \(H^{n}(G, -)\) are
the derived functors of \(H^{0}(G, -)\) on the category of
quasi-coherent \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules.}

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been modified to show
  that the category \texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)} is abelian and has enough
  injective objects. One may compare with {[}Ja03{]}, Part I, 3.3-3.4,
  3.9, 4.2 and 4.14-4.16 (where one should be aware that ``\(k\)-group
  scheme'' means ``affine \(k\)-group scheme'', cf.~\emph{loc. cit.},
  2.1).} Since \(G\) is affine and flat over \(S\), by 4.7.2.1, the
category \texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)} is equivalent to the category
\texttt{(A(G)-Comod.q.c.)} of \(A(G)\)-comodules quasi-coherent over
\texttt{OS}, and is therefore abelian. On the other hand, \(A(G)\) being
a flat \texttt{OS}-module, each functor
\(F \mapsto F \otimes_{OS} A(G)^{\otimes n}\) is exact; since moreover
\(S\) is affine, one obtains that \(C*(G, -)\) is an exact functor on
\texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)}.

Denote by \(\Delta\) (resp. \(\eta\)) the comultiplication (resp. the
augmentation) of \(A(G)\). For every quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-module
\(P\), one denotes \(Ind(P) = P \otimes_{OS} A(G)\) endowed with the
structure of \(A(G)\)-comodule defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{id\_P ⊗ Δ : P ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) → P ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

this defines a functor
\texttt{Ind\ :\ (OS-Mod.q.c.)\ →\ (G-OS-Mod.q.c.)}.

It follows from 4.6.4.1, 5.2.0, and 5.2.0.1 that one has an isomorphism
of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    W(Ind(P)) ≃ E(W(P)) = Hom(G, W(P)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Via this identification, the morphism \(\epsilon : E(W(P)) \to W(P)\)
corresponds to the morphism of \texttt{OS}-modules
\(id_{P} \otimes \eta : Ind(P) \to P\).

One has already used that the functor \(W : (OS-Mod.) \to (OS-Mod.)\) is
fully faithful; the same is true, by Definition 4.7.1, of its
restriction to \texttt{(G-OS-Mod.)}, i.e.~if \(M, M'\) are
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules, one has a functorial isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{G{-}OS{-}Mod.\}(M, M′) ≃ Hom\_\{G{-}OS{-}Mod.\}(W(M), W(M′)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consequently, one deduces from Lemma 5.2.0.2 the following:

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.1.1.} \emph{(i) The functor \texttt{Ind} is right
adjoint to the forgetful functor \((G-OS-Mod.q.c.) \to (OS-Mod.q.c.)\).
More precisely, the map \(id_{P} \otimes \eta : Ind(P) \to P\) induces
for every object \(M\) of \texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)} a bijection}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{G{-}OS{-}Mod.\}(M, Ind(P)) ⥲ Hom\_\{OS\}(M, P).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) Consequently, if \(I\) is an injective object of
\texttt{(OS-Mod.q.c.)} then \(Ind(I)\) is an injective object of
\texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)}.}

Let \(F\) be a \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module and \(\mu_{F} : F \to Ind(F)\)
the map defining the structure of \(A(G)\)-comodule. It follows from
5.2.0.3 (or from axioms (CM 1) and (CM 2) of 4.7.2) that \(\mu_{F}\) is
a morphism of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules, and that
\((id_{F} \otimes \eta) \circ \mu_{F} = id_{F}\), hence that \(F\) is a
direct factor of \(Ind(F)\) as \texttt{OS}-module; in particular,
\(\mu_{F}\) is a monomorphism. Since, by \((\ast)\) and 5.2.2,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}n(G, W(Ind(F))) ≃ H\^{}n(G, Hom\_S(G, W(F))) = 0    for n \textgreater{} 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one therefore obtains that \(H^{n}(G, -)\) is effaceable for \(n > 0\).

Finally, \(S\) being affine, \texttt{(OS-Mod.q.c.)} has enough injective
objects. So let \(F \hookrightarrow I\) be a monomorphism of
\texttt{OS}-modules, where \(I\) is an injective object of
\texttt{(OS-Mod.q.c.)}; then, \(A(G)\) being flat over \texttt{OS},
\(Ind(F)\) is a sub-\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module of \(Ind(I)\), whence:

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.1.2.} \emph{The abelian category
\texttt{(G-OS-Mod.q.c.)} has enough injective objects.}

Taking {[}Gr57, 2.2.1 and 2.3{]} into account (already used in the proof
of 5.2.1), this completes the proof of Theorem 5.3.1.

\textbf{Remark 5.3.1.3.} \emph{One can also prove 5.3.1.1 by the
following computation. To every morphism of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules
\(\phi : M \to P \otimes_{OS} A(G)\) one associates the
\texttt{OS}-morphism \((id_{P} \otimes \eta) \circ \phi : M \to P\).
Conversely, to every \texttt{OS}-morphism \(f : M \to P\) one associates
the morphism of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules
\((f \otimes id_{A(G)}) \circ \mu_{M} : M \to P \otimes_{OS} A(G)\). One
sees at once that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(id\_P ⊗ η) ∘ (f ⊗ id\_\{A(G)\}) ∘ μ\_M = (f ⊗ id\_\{OS\}) ∘ (id\_P ⊗ η) ∘ μ\_M = f.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{On the other hand, for every \(\phi\) the following diagram is
commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              φ}
\NormalTok{   M ────────────→ P ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G)}
\NormalTok{   │                   │}
\NormalTok{   μ\_M               id\_P ⊗ Δ}
\NormalTok{   ↓     φ ⊗ id\_\{A(G)\}    ↓}
\NormalTok{   M ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ──→ P ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G) ⊗\_\{OS\} A(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{It follows that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{((id\_P ⊗ η) ∘ φ ⊗ id\_\{A(G)\}) ∘ μ\_M = (id\_P ⊗ η ⊗ id\_\{A(G)\}) ∘ (φ ⊗ id\_\{A(G)\}) ∘ μ\_M}
\NormalTok{                                   = (id\_P ⊗ η ⊗ id\_\{A(G)\}) ∘ (id\_P ⊗ Δ) ∘ φ = φ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{This proves 5.3.1.1 (i) (and (ii) follows).}

Let \(F\) be a \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module; one has seen above that axiom
(CM 2) of 4.7.2 shows that, considered as \texttt{OS}-module, \(F\) is a
direct factor of \(E(F)\). This entails:

\textbf{Proposition 5.3.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme and
\(G\) an \(S\)-group affine and flat; suppose that every exact sequence
\(0 \to F_{1} \to F_{2} \to F_{3} \to 0\) of quasi-coherent
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules that splits as a sequence of
\texttt{OS}-modules also splits as a sequence of
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules.}

\emph{Then, the functors \(H^{n}(G, -)\) are zero for \(n > 0\) (or what
amounts to the same, the functor \(H^{0}(G, -)\) is exact).}

Indeed, by hypothesis, the sequence of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules

\[
0 \to F \to E(F) \to E(F)/F \to 0
\]

is split; \(F\) is therefore a direct factor, as
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module, of \(E(F)\), whose cohomology is zero.

One immediately deduces from this and from Proposition 4.7.4:

\textbf{Theorem 5.3.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme and \(G\) a
diagonalizable \(S\)-group. For every quasi-coherent
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module \(F\), one has \(H^{n}(G, F) = 0\), for
\(n > 0\).}

\textbf{Remark.} \emph{Proposition 5.3.2 remains valid when \(G\) is not
necessarily flat over \(S\); the proof then appeals to relative
cohomology.\footnote{N.D.E.: The editors did not seek to develop this
  remark.}}

\subsection{6. G-equivariant objects and
modules}\label{g-equivariant-objects-and-modules}

\footnote{N.D.E.: This section has been added.} Let \(C\) be a category
having a final object and in which fiber products exist. Let \(G\) be a
\texttt{Ĉ}-group, \(\pi : M \to X\) a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}, and
\(\lambda = \lambda_{X} : G \times X \to X\) an action of \(G\) on
\(X\). In the sequel, one will denote \(Y \times_{f} M\) the fiber
product of \(\pi : M \to X\) and an \(X\)-functor \(f : Y \to X\).

For every \(U \in Ob(C)\) and \(x \in X(U)\), one will denote
\(M_{x} = U \times_{x} M\), i.e.~for every \(\phi : U' \to U\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M\_x(U′) = \{m ∈ M(U′) | π(m) = x\_\{U′\} = φ*(x)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, if \(g \in G(U)\) one will also denote \texttt{gx} the element
\(\lambda(g, x)\) of \(X(U)\).

\textbf{Definition 6.1.} \emph{a) One says that \(M\) is a}
\(G\)-equivariant \(X\)-object \emph{if one has given an action
\(\Lambda : G \times M \to M\) of \(G\) on \(M\) lifting \(\lambda\),
i.e.~such that the square below is commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                   Λ}
\NormalTok{   G × M ─────────────→ M}
\NormalTok{   │                    │}
\NormalTok{   id\_G × π             π}
\NormalTok{   ↓        λ           ↓}
\NormalTok{   G × X ─────────────→ X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{This amounts to giving for every morphism
\((g, x) : U \to G \times X\) maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Λ\_x\^{}U(g) : M\_x(U) → M\_\{gx\}(U),    m ↦ g ⋅ m}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{verifying \(1 \cdot m = m\) and
\(g \cdot (h \cdot m) = (gh) \cdot m\) and functorial in the
\((G \times X)\)-object \(U\). This still amounts to giving morphisms of
\(U\)-objects:}

\[
\Lambda_{x}(g) : M_{x} \to M_{gx}
\]

\emph{verifying \(\Lambda_{x}(1) = id\) and
\(\Lambda_{hx}(g) \circ \Lambda_{x}(h) = \Lambda_{x}(gh)\).}

\emph{b) Let now \(O\) be a \texttt{Ĉ}-ring and let \(OX = O \times X\).
Under the conditions of (a), one says that \(M\) is a} \(G\)-equivariant
\texttt{OX}-module \emph{if it is an \texttt{OX}-module (cf.~Definition
4.3.3.1, valid for any ring functor on a category \(C\)) and if the
action \(\Lambda\) is compatible with the \texttt{OX}-module structure
of \(M\), i.e.~if for every \((g, x) \in G(U) \times X(U)\)
(\(U \in Ob(C)\)), the map \(\Lambda_{x}(g) : M_{x} \to M_{gx}\),
\(m \mapsto g \cdot m\) is a morphism of \texttt{OU}-modules.}

\textbf{Remark 6.2.} \emph{(i) In (a) above, the conditions
\(\Lambda_{x}(1) = id\) and
\(\Lambda_{hx}(g) \circ \Lambda_{x}(h) = \Lambda_{x}(gh)\) evidently
entail that each \(\Lambda_{x}(g)\) is an isomorphism, with inverse
\(\Lambda_{gx}(g^{-1})\). Conversely, if one assumes that each
\(\Lambda_{x}(g)\) is an isomorphism, the condition
\(\Lambda_{hx}(g) \circ \Lambda_{x}(h) = \Lambda_{x}(gh)\) applied to
\(h = 1\) gives \(\Lambda_{x}(1) = id\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(M\) be an \texttt{OX}-module. First, one sees that
giving a morphism \(\Lambda : G \times M \to M\) making the diagram of
6.1 commutative and such that each morphism}

\(\Lambda_{x}(g) : M_{x} \to M_{gx}\), \(m \mapsto g \cdot m\), \emph{is
an isomorphism of \texttt{OU}-modules, is equivalent to giving an
isomorphism of \(O_{G\times X}\)-modules:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{θ : G × M = (G × X) ×\_\{pr\_X\} M ⥲ (G × X) ×\_λ M}
\NormalTok{                (g, x, m) ↦ (g, x, g ⋅ m).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Since one has assumed that each \(\Lambda_{x}(g)\) is an
isomorphism, the equality \(\Lambda_{x}(1) = id\) will be a consequence
of the equality
\(\Lambda_{hx}(g) \circ \Lambda_{x}(h) = \Lambda_{x}(gh)\) applied to
\(h = 1\). One therefore obtains that \(\Lambda\) is an action of \(G\)
on \(M\) (i.e.~\(g \cdot (h \cdot m) = (gh) \cdot m\)) if and only if
the diagram of \((G \times G \times X)\)-isomorphisms below is
commutative (where one denotes \(\mu\) the multiplication of \(G\) and
\(f*(\theta)\) the isomorphism deduced from \(\theta\) by a base change
\(f : G \times G \times X \to G \times X\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              pr*\_\{2,3\}(θ)}
\NormalTok{   (G × G × X) ×\_\{pr\_X ∘ pr\_\{2,3\}\} M  ⥲  (G × G × X) ×\_\{λ ∘ pr\_\{2,3\}\} M}

\NormalTok{       (μ × id\_X)*(θ) ≀                              ≀ (id\_G × λ)*(θ)}

\NormalTok{   (G × G × X) ×\_\{λ ∘ (μ × id\_X)\} M     (G × G × X) ×\_\{λ ∘ (id\_G × λ)\} M.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One sees therefore that giving a \(G\)-equivariant
\texttt{OX}-module structure on \(M\) is equivalent to giving an
isomorphism \(\theta\) of \(O_{G\times X}\)-modules as above, such that
the diagram above is commutative.}

\emph{(iii) All that precedes extends to the case where \(G\) is only a
\texttt{Ĉ}-monoid: in that case, giving an action
\(\Lambda : G \times M \to M\) lifting \(\lambda\) and such that each
\(\Lambda_{x}(g) : M_{x} \to M_{gx}\) is a morphism of
\texttt{OU}-modules is equivalent to giving a morphism \(\theta\) of
\(O_{G\times X}\)-modules as in (ii), such that the diagram above
(without the ∼ under the arrows) is commutative, and such that
\(p_{M} \circ \theta \circ (\epsilon_{G} \times id_{M}) = id_{M}\),
where \(\epsilon_{G}\) denotes the unit section of \(G\) and \(p_{M}\)
the projection onto \(M\).}

\subsubsection{6.3. G-equivariant
morphisms}\label{g-equivariant-morphisms}

Let \(Y\) be a second object of \texttt{Ĉ}, endowed with an action
\(\lambda_{Y} : G \times Y \to Y\) of \(G\), and let \(N\) be a second
\(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module. One says that a
\texttt{Ĉ}-morphism \(f : Y \to X\) (resp. a morphism of
\texttt{OX}-modules \(\phi : M \to N\)) is \emph{\(G\)-equivariant} if
it commutes with the action of \(G\), i.e.~if one has set-theoretically
\(f(g \cdot y) = g \cdot f(y)\) (resp.
\(\phi(g \cdot m) = g \cdot \phi(m)\)), which is equivalent to saying
that \(f \circ \lambda_{Y} = \lambda_{X} \circ (id_{G} \times f)\)
(resp.
\(\phi \circ \Lambda_{M} = \Lambda_{N} \circ (id_{G} \times \phi)\)).

One then obtains at once the following lemma:

\textbf{Lemma 6.3.1.} \emph{Let \(f : Y \to X\) be a \(G\)-equivariant
morphism and \(M\) a \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module. Then the
inverse image \(f*(M) = Y \times_{f} M\) is a \(G\)-equivariant
\texttt{OY}-module.}

On the other hand, \(G\) acts on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\hat{C}}(Y, X)\).
Indeed, let \(T \in Ob(C)\), \(g \in G(T)\) and \(\phi\) a
\(T\)-morphism \(Y_{T} \to X_{T}\); then \(g\) defines automorphisms
\(\lambda_{Y}(g)\) and \(\lambda_{X}(g)\) of \texttt{Y\_T} and
\texttt{X\_T}, and one will denote \(g \cdot \phi\) (or also
\(g \phi g^{-1}\)) the morphism
\(\lambda_{X}(g) \circ \phi \circ \lambda_{Y}(g^{-1})\). This defines an
action of \(G(T)\) on \(\operatorname{Hom}_{T}(Y_{T}, X_{T})\),
functorial in \(T\).

\textbf{Definition 6.3.2.} \emph{If \(\phi : Y \to X\) is an arbitrary
\texttt{Ĉ}-morphism, one can therefore consider its stabilizer
\(Stab_{G}(\phi)\) (cf.~2.3.3.1): for every \(T \in Ob(C)\),
\(Stab_{G}(\phi)(T)\) is the subgroup \(G(T)\) formed by the \(g\) such
that \(g \circ \phi_{T} = \phi_{T} \circ g\), i.e.~such that the
diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              φ\_T}
\NormalTok{   Y\_T ────────────→ X\_T}
\NormalTok{   │                  │}
\NormalTok{   g                  g}
\NormalTok{   ↓     φ\_T          ↓}
\NormalTok{   Y\_T ────────────→ X\_T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{commutes. Then, the morphism \(\phi : Y \to X\) is equivariant
under \(Stab_{G}(\phi)\).}

\subsubsection{6.4. Global sections}\label{global-sections}

Let \(M\) be a \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module. Denote by
\texttt{S\_0} the final object of \(C\), and (cf.~Exp. II, 1.1) by
\(\prod_{X/S_{0}} M\) the ``functor of sections of \(M\) over \(X\)'':
it is the functor which to every \(T \in Ob(C)\) associates

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_X(X\_T, M) = Hom\_\{X\_T\}(X\_T, M\_T) = Γ(M\_T/X\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Recall, on the other hand, that every morphism \(g : Z \to Y\) of
\texttt{Ĉ}-objects above \(X\) induces a morphism of abelian groups
\(M(g) : M(Y) \to M(Z)\), which is compatible with the ring morphism
\(g* : O(Y) \to O(Z)\). In particular, when \(Z = Y\) (with \(g\) then
an \(X\)-endomorphism of \(Y\)), one obtains a morphism of abelian
groups

\[
M(g) : M(Y) \to M(Y)
\]

which is not in general a morphism of \(O(Y)\)-modules, but which
verifies, for every \(m \in M(Y)\) and \(\alpha \in O(Y)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M(g)(α ⋅ m) = g*(α) ⋅ M(g)(m).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This said, one will write simply, in the sequel, \(g*\) instead of
\(M(g)\).

Let \(T \in Ob(C)\) and let \(X_{T} = X \times T\) and \(pr_{X}\) the
projection \(X_{T} \to X\). For every \(\alpha \in O(X_{T})\) and
\(g \in G(T)\), set \(g(\alpha) = (g^{-1})*(\alpha)\): it is the element
of \(O(X_{T})\) defined set-theoretically by: for every \(S \in Ob(C)\)
and \(x \in X(S)\), \(t \in T(S)\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g(α)(x, t) = α(g\^{}\{{-}1\} x, t).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One thus obtains a (left) action of \(G(T)\) by ring automorphisms on
\(O(X_{T})\), functorial in \(T\), and such that \(g(\alpha) = \alpha\)
if \(\alpha\) is the image in \(O(X_{T})\) of an element of \(O(T)\).

Now denote by \(\phi\) the identity morphism of \texttt{X\_T} (cf.~6.3
and the generalization further below to a morphism \(\phi : Y \to X\))
and designate \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(X_{T}, M)\) by \(M(\phi g^{-1})\)
resp. \(M(\phi)\), according as \texttt{X\_T} is regarded as an
\(X\)-object via \(pr_{X} \circ \lambda(g^{-1})_{T}\), resp. \(pr_{X}\).

Then \(\lambda(g^{-1})_{T}\) is an \(X\)-morphism between these two
\(X\)-objects, hence, by the preceding, one obtains a morphism of
abelian groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(g\^{}\{{-}1\})* : M(φ) → M(φ g\^{}\{{-}1\}),    m ↦ m ∘ λ(g\^{}\{{-}1\})\_T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which verifies
\((g^{-1})*(\alpha \cdot m) = (g \alpha) \cdot (g^{-1})*(m)\) for every
\(m \in M(\phi)\) and \(\alpha \in O(X_{T})\). (If \(m\) is a section of
\texttt{M\_T} on \texttt{X\_T} then \((g^{-1})*(m)\) is the section
defined set-theoretically by \((x, t) \mapsto m(g^{-1} x, t)\).) In
particular, \((g^{-1})*\) is a morphism of \(O(T)\)-modules.

By the functoriality of the morphisms of \(O(X_{T})\)-modules
\(\Lambda_{x}(g)\), one obtains a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                 (g\^{}\{{-}1\})*}
\NormalTok{   M(φ) ──────────────→ M(φ g\^{}\{{-}1\})}
\NormalTok{     │                      │}
\NormalTok{   Λ\_φ(g)               Λ\_\{φ g\^{}\{{-}1\}\}(g)}
\NormalTok{     ↓     (g\^{}\{{-}1\})*        ↓}
\NormalTok{   M(g φ) ─────────→ M(g φ g\^{}\{{-}1\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(g \phi g^{-1} = \phi\), since \(\phi\) is the identity map.
Setting \(A(g) = (g^{-1})* \circ \Lambda_{\phi}(g)\), one therefore
obtains a morphism of abelian groups

\[
A(g) : M(\phi) \to M(\phi)
\]

which is ``compatible with the action of \(G(T)\) on \(O(X_{T})\)'',
i.e.~which verifies

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A(g)(α ⋅ m) = (g α) ⋅ A(g)(m).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, if \(h\) is a second element of \(G(T)\), it follows from the
functoriality of \(M\) and of the morphisms \(\Lambda_{x}(g)\) that one
has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                M(φ)}
\NormalTok{                  ╲}
\NormalTok{                 Λ\_φ(g)}
\NormalTok{                    ╲                Λ\_φ(hg)}
\NormalTok{                     ╲}
\NormalTok{            Λ\_φ(h)    ╲                         ╲}
\NormalTok{                       ↓                         ↘}
\NormalTok{                   M(g φ) ────────→ M(hg φ) ───────→ M(φ)}
\NormalTok{                   (g\^{}\{{-}1\})*   Λ\_φ(h)    (hg)\^{}\{{-}1\}*}
                                    
\NormalTok{                       (g\^{}\{{-}1\})*                ((hg)\^{}\{{-}1\})*}
                       
\NormalTok{                   M(φ) ───────→ M(h φ) ─────────→ M(φ)}
\NormalTok{                          Λ\_φ(h)         (h\^{}\{{-}1\})*}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(A(h) \circ A(g) = A(hg)\). Consequently, one has obtained the
following proposition:

\textbf{Proposition 6.4.1.} \emph{For every \(T\), the
\(O(X_{T})\)-module \((\prod_{X/S_{0}} M)(T) = \Gamma(M_{T}/X_{T})\) is
endowed, in a way functorial in \(T\), with an action of \(G(T)\)
``compatible with the action of \(G(T)\) on \(O(X_{T})\)'', i.e.~which
verifies}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A(g)(α ⋅ m) = g(α) ⋅ A(g)(m).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(g(\alpha) = \alpha\) for \(\alpha \in O(T)\), this gives in
particular that \(\prod_{X/S_{0}} M\) is a \(G\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-module.

More generally, let, as in 6.3, \(Y\) be a second \(G\)-equivariant
\texttt{Ĉ}-object, \(\phi : Y \to X\) a \texttt{Ĉ}-morphism and
\(H = Stab_{G}(\phi)\). Then the fiber product
\(M_{\phi} = Y \times_{\phi} M\) is an \(H\)-equivariant
\texttt{OY}-module. One therefore obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 6.4.2.} \emph{The functor \(\prod_{Y/S_{0}} M_{\phi}\)
is a \(Stab_{G}(\phi)\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-module.}

\subsubsection{6.5. G-equivariant
OX-modules}\label{g-equivariant-ox-modules}

Let us apply what precedes in the following situation. Let \(S\) be a
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group scheme acting on an \(S\)-scheme \(X\), and
\(F\) an \texttt{OX}-module (not necessarily quasi-coherent).

\textbf{Definition 6.5.1.} \emph{One says that \(F\) is a}
\(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module \emph{if the \texttt{OX}-module
\(M = W(F)\) is \(G\)-equivariant, i.e.~if one has given, for every
morphism \((g, x) : U \to G \times_{S} X\), isomorphisms of
\texttt{OU}-modules}

\[
\Lambda_{x}(g) : W(x*(F)) \xrightarrow{\sim} W((gx)*(F)),
\]

\emph{functorial in \(U\) and verifying
\(\Lambda_{hx}(g) \circ \Lambda_{x}(h) = \Lambda_{x}(gh)\).} Since the
functor \(W\) is fully faithful (cf.~4.6.1.1 and 4.6.2), one therefore
obtains isomorphisms of \texttt{OU}-modules

\[
\Lambda_{x}(g) : x*(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} (gx)*(F),
\]

where one recalls that \texttt{gx} denotes the morphism
\(\lambda \circ (g, x) : U \to X\). In particular, applying this to the
identity morphism of \(G \times_{S} X\), one obtains an isomorphism of
\(O_{G \times_{S} X}\)-modules

\[
(\star)    \theta : pr*_{X}(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} \lambda*(F)
\]

\emph{such that the diagram \((\star\star)\) of morphisms of sheaves on
\(G \times_{S} G \times_{S} X\) below is commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                     pr*\_\{2,3\}(θ)}
\NormalTok{   pr*\_\{2,3\} ∘ pr*\_X(F) ────────→ pr*\_\{2,3\} ∘ λ*(F)    (id\_G × λ)* ∘ pr*\_X(F)}

\NormalTok{                                  (⋆⋆)                  ≀ (id\_G × λ)*(θ)}

\NormalTok{   (μ × id\_X)* ∘ pr*\_X(F) ──→ (μ × id\_X)* ∘ λ*(F)      (id\_G × λ)* ∘ λ*(F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, if \(E\) is a second \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module, one
says that a morphism of \texttt{OX}-modules \(\phi : E \to F\) is
\emph{\(G\)-equivariant} if the morphism \(W(\phi) : W(E) \to W(F)\) is.
With the above notations, this is equivalent to saying that
\(\theta_{F} \circ pr*_{X}(\phi) = \lambda*(\phi) \circ \theta_{E}\).

\textbf{Remark 6.5.2.} \emph{If \(f : Y \to X\) is a \(G\)-equivariant
morphism, it follows from 6.3.1 that \(f*(F)\) is a \(G\)-equivariant
\texttt{OY}-module.}

\textbf{Remark 6.5.3.} \emph{Suppose moreover \(F\) quasi-coherent. Then
it follows from what precedes that giving a \(G\)-equivariant
\texttt{OX}-module structure on \(M = W(F)\) is equivalent to giving
such a structure on \(V(F)\), which is itself equivalent to giving an
action of \(G\) on the vector fibration \(V(F)\), compatible with the
action on \(X\) and ``linear'' on the fibers.}

Indeed, denote by \(\phi\) the isomorphism
\(\lambda*(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} pr*_{X}(F)\) inverse of \(\theta\). For
every morphism \((g, x) : U \to G \times_{S} X\), one has an isomorphism
of \texttt{OU}-modules
\(\phi_{x}(g) = \Lambda_{x}(g)^{-1} = \Lambda_{gx}(g^{-1})\) from
\((gx)*(F)\) to \(x*(F)\); it induces an isomorphism of
\texttt{OU}-modules

\[
V((gx)*(F)) \xrightarrow{\sim} V(x*(F))
\]

which one will denote \(t \phi_{x}(g)\). One then has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t φ\_\{gx\}(h) ∘ t φ\_x(g) = t (Λ\_\{gx\}(h) ∘ φ\_x(g))\^{}\{{-}1\} = Λ\_x(hg)\^{}\{{-}1\} = t φ\_x(hg).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since, for every \(X\)-scheme \(f : Y \to X\), one has
\(V(F) \times_{f} Y \simeq V(f*(F))\) (cf.~4.6.2), one therefore obtains
that the isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t φ : G ×\_S V(F) = (G ×\_S X) ×\_\{pr\_X\} V(F) = V(pr*\_X(F))}
\NormalTok{                                  ⥲ V(λ*(F)) = (G ×\_S X) ×\_λ V(F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

endows \(V(F)\) with a \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module structure.
Finally, identifying each functor \(V(-)\) with the vector fibration
that represents it, and composing \(t \phi\) with the projection onto
\(V(F)\), one obtains an action of \(G\) on the vector fibration
\(V(F)\), compatible with the action on \(X\) and ``linear'' on the
fibers.

One thus recovers the definition given, for example, in {[}GIT, Chap. 1,
§ 3{]}, up to the fact that in \emph{loc. cit.} Mumford considers a
locally free \texttt{OX}-module of finite rank \(E\), and defines an
action of \(G\) on \(V(E) = W(E^{\vee})\). Indeed, the diagram
\((\star\star)\) above, with \(\theta\) replaced by \(\phi\) and the
direction of the arrows reversed, is exactly the one one finds in
\emph{loc. cit.}, Def. 1.6, and the isomorphism \(t \phi\) above
coincides with the isomorphism \(\Phi\) of \emph{loc. cit.}, p.~31.

\textbf{Remark 6.5.4.} \emph{Consider in particular the case where
\(X = S\), endowed with the trivial action of \(G\). In this case, a
\(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OS}-module \(F\) is the same thing as a
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module (cf.~4.7.1). Moreover, if one denotes \(f\) the
morphism \(G \to S\) (equal here to \(pr_{X}\) and to \(\lambda\)), then
the isomorphism}

\[
(\star)    \theta : f*(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} f*(F)
\]

\emph{is an element of}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{OG\}(f*(F), f*(F)) = Hom\_\{OG\}(W(f*(F)), W(f*(F))) = End\_\{OS\}(W(F))(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which is nothing other than the morphism
\(\rho : G \to \operatorname{End}_{OS}(W(F))\) defining the operation of
\(G\) on \(W(F)\). Moreover, \(\theta\) corresponds by adjunction to the
morphism of \texttt{OS}-modules
\(f_{*}(\theta) \circ \tau : F \to f_{*} f*(F)\), where
\(\tau : F \to f_{*} f*(F)\) is the ``unit'' morphism of the adjunction.
(This will be used in \texttt{VI\_B}, 11.10.bis.)}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{6.6. The functors ∏\emph{\{X/S\} W(F) and
W(p}*(F))}{6.6. The functors ∏\{X/S\} W(F) and W(p*(F))}}\label{the-functors-xs-wf-and-wpf}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group scheme acting on
\(S\)-schemes \(X\) and \(Y\) via the morphisms
\(\lambda : G \times_{S} X \to X\) and \(\mu : G \times_{S} Y \to Y\),
and let \(p : X \to Y\) be a \(G\)-equivariant morphism. Suppose that
the morphisms \(p : X \to Y\) and \(\nu_{Y} : Y \to S\) are
quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and that \(\pi : G \to S\) is flat.

Then the projection \(pr_{Y} : G \times_{S} Y \to Y\) is flat, as is
\(\mu\) (since \(\mu\) is the composite of \(pr_{Y}\) and of the
automorphism \((g, y) \mapsto (g, gy)\)). Finally, for a variable
\(S\)-scheme \(f : T \to\), one will denote by \(p_{T} : X_{T} \to T\)
and \(f_{X} : X_{T} \to X\) the morphisms deduced from \(p\) and \(f\)
by base change.

Let \(F\) be a quasi-coherent and \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module,
and let \(\theta\) be the isomorphism
\(pr*_{X}(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} \lambda*(F)\) of 6.5.1 \((\star)\).
Since \(p\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated,

\(p_{*}(F)\) is quasi-coherent (cf.~EGA I, 9.2.1).

\textbf{Lemma 6.6.1.} \emph{The quasi-coherent \texttt{OY}-module
\(p_{*}(F)\) is \(G\)-equivariant.}

Indeed, one has the two cartesian squares below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                pr\_X            λ}
\NormalTok{   G ×\_S X ─────────→ X ←───────── G ×\_S X}
\NormalTok{       q              │                q}
\NormalTok{                      p                 }
\NormalTok{                pr\_Y            μ}
\NormalTok{   G ×\_S Y ─────────→ Y ←───────── G ×\_S Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(p\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated and \(pr_{Y}\) and
\(\mu\) are flat, it follows from EGA III, 1.4.15 (completed by EGA
IV\_1, 1.7.21) that one has \(q_{*} pr*_{X}(F) = pr*_{Y} p_{*}(F)\) and
\(q_{*} \lambda*(F) = \mu* p_{*}(F)\). Consequently, \(\theta\) induces
an isomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{θ\_Y : pr*\_Y p\_*(F) ⥲ μ* p\_*(F),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one obtains similarly that \(\theta_{Y}\) verifies the ``cocycle
condition'' 6.5.1 \((\star\star)\) (since the morphisms
\(G \times_{S} G \times_{S} Y \to G \times_{S} Y\) involved are flat).
This proves the lemma.

In particular, take \(Y = S\) endowed with the trivial action of \(G\).
Taking Remark 6.5.4 into account, one then obtains that \(p_{*}(F)\) is
a \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module. If moreover \(G\) is affine over \(S\) and
if one denotes \(A(G) = \pi_{*}(O_{G})\), then \(p_{*}(F)\) is therefore
an \(A(G)\)-comodule, by 4.7.2.

On the other hand, by 6.4.1, the functor \(\prod_{X/S} W(F)\), which to
every \(f : T \to S\) associates

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(f\_X*(F))(X\_T) = Γ(X\_T, f\_X*(F)) = Γ(T, p\_\{T*\} f\_X*(F))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module. Moreover, one has a canonical morphism
\(\tau : W(p_{*}(F)) \to \prod_{X/S} W(F)\), which is given for every
\(f : T \to S\) by the canonical morphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(T, f* p\_*(F)) → Γ(T, p\_\{T*\} f\_X*(F))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and which is an isomorphism when restricted to the full subcategory of
schemes \(T\) flat over \(S\), and one verifies without difficulty that
\(\tau\) is a morphism of \(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules. Consequently, one
has obtained the following proposition (for point (ii), compare with
{[}GIT{]}, p.~32).

\textbf{Proposition 6.6.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme acting on an \(S\)-scheme \(X\), and \(F\) a
quasi-coherent and \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module. Suppose that
\(\pi : G \to S\) is flat and that \(p : X \to S\) is quasi-compact and
quasi-separated.}

\emph{(i) Then \(p_{*}(F)\) is a quasi-coherent
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-module. Moreover, the canonical morphism
\(W(p_{*}(F)) \to \prod_{X/S} W(F)\) is a morphism of
\(G\)-\texttt{OS}-modules, and these two functors coincide on the
category of flat \(S\)-schemes.}

\emph{(ii) If moreover \(G\) is affine over \(S\) and if one denotes
\(A(G) = \pi_{*}(O_{G})\), then \(p_{*}(F)\) is endowed with a structure
of \(A(G)\)-comodule.\footnote{N.D.E.: The same is true if \(G\) is
  flat, quasi-compact and quasi-separated over \(S\) and if \(p_{*}(F)\)
  is a flat \texttt{OS}-module, cf.~Exp. \texttt{VI\_B}, 11.6.1 (ii).}}

\subsubsection{6.7. Stabilizers}\label{stabilizers}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group scheme acting on an
\(S\)-scheme \(X\), and let \(F\) be a quasi-coherent \(G\)-equivariant
\texttt{OX}-module. Let \(Y\) be a second \(S\)-scheme endowed with an
action of \(G\) (possibly trivial), let \(\phi : Y \to X\) be an
\(S\)-morphism, not necessarily \(G\)-equivariant, and let
\(Stab_{G}(\phi)\) be the stabilizer in \(G\) of \(\phi\) (cf.~6.3.2).

Let us point out at once (see Exp. \texttt{VI\_B}, § 6) that
\(Stab_{G}(\phi)\) is representable by a closed sub-group scheme \(H\)
of \(G\) if \(X\) is separated over \(S\) and if \(Y\) is essentially
free over \(S\) (cf.~\emph{loc. cit.}, Déf. 6.2.1). Indeed, consider the
morphism \(r : G \times_{S} Y \to X \times_{S} X\) given
set-theoretically by \(r(g, y) = (\phi(y), g \phi(g^{-1} y))\), and let
\(P = G \times_{S} Y\) and \(P'\) the inverse image by \(r\) of the
diagonal \(\Delta_{X/S}\). Then one has (cf.~\emph{loc. cit.}, 6.2.4
(a))

\[
Stab_{G}(\phi) = \prod_{P/G} P'
\]

and therefore, by \emph{loc. cit.}, \(Stab_{G}(\phi)\) is representable
by a closed sub-group scheme \(H\) of \(G\) if \(X\) is separated over
\(S\) and if \(Y\) is essentially free over \(S\); this second condition
being automatically verified if \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, or if
\(Y = S\). Under these hypotheses, \(\phi*(F)\) is then a quasi-coherent
\(H\)-equivariant \texttt{OY}-module (cf.~6.5.2).

Hence, if moreover \(\pi : G \to S\) and \(p : Y \to S\) are
quasi-compact and quasi-separated over \(S\), and \(\pi\) flat, then
\(p_{*} \phi*(F)\) is an \(H\)-\texttt{OS}-module, by 6.6.2. In
particular, one obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 6.7.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme acting on an \(S\)-scheme \(X\), and \(F\) a
quasi-coherent \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OX}-module. Suppose that
\(\pi : G \to S\) is flat and that \(X \to S\) is quasi-compact and
separated. Let \(\tau : S \to X\) be a section of \(X\) over \(S\).}

\emph{(i) The stabilizer \(H = Stab_{G}(\tau)\) is a closed sub-group
scheme of \(G\), and \(\tau*(F)\) is a quasi-coherent
\(H\)-\texttt{OS}-module.}

\emph{(ii) If moreover \(H\) is affine over \(S\) (for example, if \(G\)
is) and if one denotes \(A(H) = \pi_{*}(O_{H})\), then \(\tau*(F)\) is
an \(A(H)\)-comodule.}

\subsubsection{6.8. G-equivariant sheaves on
G}\label{g-equivariant-sheaves-on-g}

To conclude, let us point out two results (6.8.1 and 6.8.6 below) that
will be used in Exposés II and III (cf.~in particular III, 4.25).

\textbf{Proposition 6.8.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\(\pi : G \to S\) an \(S\)-group scheme, \(\epsilon : S \to G\) the unit
section. Consider the action by left translations of \(G\) on itself.
Then the functors \(E \mapsto \pi*(E)\) and \(F \mapsto \epsilon*(F)\)
induce equivalences, quasi-inverse to one another, between the category
of quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-modules and that of quasi-coherent
\(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OG}-modules.}

\emph{Proof.} Denote by \(\mu\) the multiplication of \(G\) and by
\(pr_{2}\) the second projection \(G \times_{S} G \to G\). Since
\(\pi \circ \mu = \pi \circ pr_{2}\), then, for every quasi-coherent
\texttt{OS}-module \(E\), one has a canonical isomorphism
\(\mu* \pi*(E) = pr*_{2} \pi*(E)\), and one verifies easily that this
isomorphism satisfies the ``cocycle condition'' 6.5.1 \((\star\star)\),
i.e.~\(\pi*(E)\) is a \(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OG}-module. Since
\(\epsilon* \pi*(E) = E\), the functor \(E \mapsto \pi*(E)\) is

fully faithful; it remains therefore to see that for every
\(G\)-equivariant \texttt{OG}-module \(F\), one has
\(F \simeq \pi* \epsilon*(F)\). By hypothesis, one has an isomorphism
\(\theta : pr*_{2}(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mu*(F)\); taking the inverse
image of \(\theta\) by the morphism \(\tau : G \to G \times_{S} G\) of
components \((id_{G}, \epsilon \circ \pi)\), one obtains an isomorphism
\(F \xrightarrow{\sim} \pi* \epsilon*(F)\).

\textbf{Remarks 6.8.2.} \emph{(a) Consider the action of
\(G \times_{S} G\) on \(G\) defined by
\((g_{1}, g_{2}) \cdot g = g_{1} g g^{-1}_{2}\); then the stabilizer of
the unit section \(\epsilon : S \to G\) is the diagonal subgroup \(H\)
of \(G \times_{S} G\). Consequently, if \(F\) is a quasi-coherent
\((G \times_{S} G)\)-equivariant \texttt{OG}-module then, by 6.5.2,
\(E = \epsilon*(F)\) is endowed with a structure of
\(H\)-\texttt{OS}-module.}

\emph{(b) One can show that \(F \mapsto \epsilon*(F)\) is an equivalence
of categories, between the category of quasi-coherent
\((G \times_{S} G)\)-equivariant \texttt{OG}-modules and that of
quasi-coherent \(H\)-\texttt{OS}-modules. This is a particular case of
more general ``descent'' results (cf.~Exp. IV, § 2 and SGA 1, VIII), see
for example {[}Th87{]}, 1.2--1.3.}

\textbf{Remark 6.8.3.} \emph{One retains the notations of 6.8.1. For
every quasi-coherent \texttt{OS}-module \(E\), denote by
\(\pi^{G}_{*} \pi*(E)\) the sub-\texttt{OS}-module of
\(\pi_{*} \pi*(E)\) whose sections on every open subset \(V\) of \(S\)
are the \(\gamma \in \Gamma(\pi^{-1}(V), \pi*(E))\) such that
\(g \cdot \gamma_{S'} = \gamma_{S'}\) for every \(S' \to V\) and
\(g \in G(S')\). Then the natural morphism \(E \to \pi^{G}_{*} \pi*(E)\)
is an isomorphism: this is immediate if
\(\pi_{*} \pi*(E) = E \otimes_{OS} \pi_{*}(O_{G})\) (for example if
\(G \to S\) is affine, or if \(G \to S\) is quasi-compact and
quasi-separated and \(E\) flat), and it is verified without difficulty
in the general case.}

\textbf{Remark 6.8.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(H\) an \(S\)-group
