scheme acting on an \(S\)-scheme \(X\), \(F\) an \texttt{OX}-module.
Suppose \(H\) flat over \(S\) and denote by \(W_{P}(F)\) the restriction
of the functor \(W(F)\) to the full subcategory formed by the
\(S\)-schemes that are flat. Since, by 6.5.1, endowing \(F\) with a
structure of \(H\)-equivariant module is equivalent to giving an
isomorphism \(\theta : pr*_{X}(F) \to \lambda*(F)\) of sheaves on
\(G \times_{S} X\), verifying the ``cocycle condition''
\((\star\star)\), one sees that to give an \(H\)-equivariant module
structure on \(F\), it suffices to give such a structure on
\(W_{P}(F)\).}

\textbf{Recollection 6.8.5.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme and
\(Y\) a sub-\(S\)-scheme of \(X\). One denotes by \(N_{Y/X}\) the
conormal sheaf of the immersion \(i : Y \hookrightarrow X\) (cf.~EGA
IV\_4, 16.1.2). If \(S' \to S\) is a flat morphism and if one denotes
\(i' : Y' \hookrightarrow X'\) the immersion deduced from \(i\) by base
change, then by} loc. cit., \emph{16.2.2 (iii), one has
\(N_{Y/X} \otimes_{OY} O_{Y'} = N_{Y'/X'}\).}

\textbf{Proposition 6.8.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(X\) an
\(S\)-group scheme, \(Y\) a sub-\(S\)-group scheme of \(X\). Suppose
\(Y\) flat over \(S\). Then the conormal sheaf \(N_{Y/X}\) is a
\((Y \times_{S} Y)\)-equivariant \texttt{OY}-module.}

Indeed, \(H = Y \times_{S} Y\) is flat over \(S\), so by Remark 6.8.4,
it suffices to endow \(W_{P}(N_{Y/X})\) with an \(H\)-equivariant module
structure. Let \(S'\) be a flat \(S\)-scheme, let
\(Y' \hookrightarrow X'\) be the immersion obtained by base change, and
let \(N' = N_{X/Y} \otimes_{OY} O_{Y'}\). By 6.8.5, one has
\(N' = N_{Y'/X'}\).

Every \(h \in H(S')\) induces an automorphism of \(Y'\), and one
therefore obtains, for every \(y \in Y'(S')\), isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(S′, y*(N′)) ⥲ Γ(S′, y* h*(N′))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which endow \(W_{P}(N)\) with a structure of \(H\)-equivariant module
(cf.~6.1).

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes}

\section{Exposé II. Tangent bundles, Lie
algebras}\label{exposuxe9-ii.-tangent-bundles-lie-algebras}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{Version of 14/10/2024.} We propose in this Exposé to construct
the analogue, in the theory of schemes, of the tangent bundles and Lie
algebras of the classical theory. It will however be useful not to
restrict ourselves to schemes properly speaking, but also to consider
certain functors on the category of schemes which are not necessarily
representable (for example the functors \texttt{Hom}, \texttt{Norm},
etc.). As announced in the preceding Exposé (cf.~I 1.1), we shall
identify a scheme with the functor associated to it.

On the other hand, the constructions presented below go beyond the
framework of the theory of schemes. They are equally valid, for example,
in the theory of analytic spaces with nilpotent elements, modulo a few
modifications of detail.

Before beginning this construction, we must lay down a few general
definitions that complement those of I 1.7.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{1. The functors
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\)}{1. The functors \textbackslash operatorname\{Hom\}\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)}}\label{the-functors-operatornamehom_zsx-y}

Let us resume the notations of I 1.1. We identify the category \(C\)
with a full subcategory of
\(\hat{C} = \operatorname{Hom}(C^{\circ}, (Ens))\) (in particular we
suppress the underlines\footnote{Rendered in this edition by boldface
  characters \texttt{F,\ G,\ V,\ W}, cf.~Exposé I. However, for functors
  such as \texttt{Norm} and \texttt{Centr} (cf.~5.2) the underlines have
  been kept in the original, and they have been added for the functor
  \texttt{Lie}, this to distinguish the functor \(Lie(G/S)\) from the
  \(\Gamma(S, O_{S})\)-Lie algebra \(Lie(G/S) = Lie(G/S)(S)\), used for
  example in Exposé VII\_A.} that allowed us to distinguish graphically
an object of \texttt{Ĉ} from an object of \(C\)).

Consider the following situation: four objects of \texttt{Ĉ}, denoted
\texttt{S,\ X,\ Y,\ Z}, the first being in fact an object of \(C\), with
\(X\) and \(Y\) above \(Z\), and \(Z\) above \(S\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        X                   Y}
\NormalTok{         ╲                 ╱}
\NormalTok{       pX ╲               ╱ pY}
\NormalTok{            ╲           ╱}
\NormalTok{             ╲         ╱}
\NormalTok{                Z}
\NormalTok{                │}
\NormalTok{                ↓}
\NormalTok{                S .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 1.1.} \emph{We define an object of \(\hat{C}/S\),
denoted \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\), by:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)(S′) = Hom\_\{Z\_\{S′\}\}(X\_\{S′\}, Y\_\{S′\}) = Hom\_Z(X ×\_S S′, Y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every object \(S'\) of \(C/S\).} One sees at once that
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\) is nothing other than the subobject
of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, Y)\) formed by the morphisms compatible
with \texttt{pX} and \texttt{pY}, that is to say, the kernel of the pair
of morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(X, Y) ⇒ Hom\_S(X, Z)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined: the first by composition with \texttt{pY}; the second as the
constant morphism whose ``image'' is \texttt{pX}.

On the other hand, one sees as in I 1.7 that, for every object \(T\) of
\texttt{Ĉ} above \(S\), one has a natural bijection:\footnote{One has
  detailed the points (2), (3), (4); in particular, (4) will be used in
  3.11.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   Hom\_S(T, Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)) ≃ Hom\_Z(X ×\_S T, Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, by I 1.7.1, if \texttt{E,\ F} are objects of \texttt{Ĉ} above
\(Z\), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_Z(E, Hom\_Z(F, Y)) ≃ Hom\_Z(E ×\_Z F, Y) ≃ Hom\_Z(F, Hom\_Z(E, Y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Applying this with \(E = X\) and \(F = Z \times_{S} T\), one obtains
natural bijections, for every object \(T\) of \(\hat{C}/S\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)   Hom\_S(T, Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)) ≃ Hom\_Z(X ×\_S T, Y) ≃ ⎰ Hom\_Z(Z ×\_S T, Hom\_Z(X, Y))}
\NormalTok{                                                      ⎱ Hom\_Z(X, Hom\_Z(Z ×\_S T, Y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, these bijections are functorial in \(T\), so one obtains
isomorphisms of \(S\)-functors:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4)   Hom\_S(T, Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)) ⥲ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Hom\_Z(Z ×\_S T, Y))}
\NormalTok{                                ≃ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X ×\_S T, Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us point out two particular cases of the definition. If \(Z = S\),
one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S/S\}(X, Y) = Hom\_S(X, Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, when \(X = Z\), one sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(5)   ∏\_\{Z/S\} Y = Hom\_\{Z/S\}(Z, Y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so that by definition

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∏\_\{Z/S\} Y)(S′) = Hom\_Z(Z ×\_S S′, Y) ≃ Γ(Y\_\{S′\}/Z\_\{S′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The functor \(\prod_{Z/S} : \hat{C}/Z \to \hat{C}/S\) is right adjoint
to the base-change functor from \(S\) to \(Z\): for every \(S\)-functor
\(U\) one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(U, ∏\_\{Z/S\} Y) = Hom\_Z(U ×\_S Z, Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(If \(C = (Sch)\) and if \(Z\) is an \(S\)-scheme, the functor
\(\prod_{Z/S}\) is called \emph{``Weil restriction of
scalars''}.)\footnote{One has added the two preceding sentences.} Let us
note also that one has an isomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(6)   Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y) ≃ Hom\_\{X/S\}(X, Y ×\_Z X) = ∏\_\{X/S\}(Y ×\_Z X),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives in particular, for \(Z = S\), an isomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(7)   Hom\_S(X, Y) ≃ ∏\_\{X/S\} Y\_X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 1.2.} The functor
\(Y \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\) commutes with products in
the following sense: one has a functorial isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)   Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y ×\_Z Y′) ≃ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y) ×\_S Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows that if \(Y\) is a \(Z\)-group, resp. a \(Z\)-ring, etc.,
then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\) is an \(S\)-group, resp. an
\(S\)-ring, etc.

\textbf{Remark 1.3.}\footnote{One has added this remark, useful for
  Corollary 3.11.1.} Moreover, let \(\pi : M \to Y\) be a \(Y\)-functor
of \texttt{O\_Y}-modules (cf.~I, 4.3.3.1). Set
\(H = \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\). Then
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, M)\) is equipped with a natural structure
of \texttt{O\_H}-module; more precisely, for every \(H'\) above \(H\),
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{H}(H', \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, M))\) is
equipped with a natural structure of \(O(H' \times_{S} X)\)-module.

Indeed, denote by \(m : M \times_{Y} M \to M\) and
\(\lambda : O_{Y} \times_{Y} M \to M\) the morphisms defining the
structures of \(Y\)-(abelian) group and of \texttt{O\_Y}-module. Let
\(H'\) be an \(S\)-scheme above \(H = \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\),
i.e.~one has been given a \(Z\)-morphism \(f : X \times_{S} H' \to Y\),
which therefore makes \(X \times_{S} H'\) a \(Y\)-object. Then,

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{H}(H', \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, M))
\]

is the set of \(Z\)-morphisms \(\phi : X \times_{S} H' \to M\) such that
\(\pi \circ \phi = f\), i.e.~of \(Y\)-morphisms
\(X \times_{S} H' \to M\).

If \(\phi, \psi\) are two such morphisms, one defines \(\phi + \psi\) as
the \(Y\)-morphism composite

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ×\_S H′ ──(φ × ψ)──→ M ×\_Y M ──m──→ M}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one verifies that this equips \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, M)\)
with a structure of abelian group above
\(H = \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\).\footnote{Of course, if \(M\) is
  a \(Y\)-group (not necessarily abelian) and if one sets
  \(\phi \cdot \psi = m \circ (\phi \times \psi)\), this makes
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, M)\) a group above
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\).}

Likewise, if \(a\) is an element of \(O(X \times_{S} H')\), i.e.~an
\(S\)-morphism \(a : X \times_{S} H' \to O_{S}\), one defines \(a\phi\)
as the composite \(\lambda \circ (a \times \phi)\), where
\(a \times \phi\) denotes the \(Y\)-morphism from \(X \times_{S} H'\) to
\(O_{Y} \times_{Y} M \simeq O_{S} \times_{S} M\) with components \(a\)
and \(\phi\); one verifies that this equips
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{H}(H', \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, M))\) with a
structure of \(O(X \times_{S} H')\)-module, functorial in the
\(H\)-object \(H'\).

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{2. The schemes
\(I_{S}(M)\)}{2. The schemes I\_\{S\}(M)}}\label{the-schemes-i_sm}

\textbf{Definition 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(M\) a
quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-module. We denote by \(D_{O_{S}}(M)\) the
quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-algebra \(O_{S} \oplus M\) (where \(M\) is
considered as an ideal of square zero). We denote by \(I_{S}(M)\) the
\(S\)-scheme \(\operatorname{Spec} D_{O_{S}}(M)\).}\footnote{Note that
  \(I_{S}(M)\) has the same underlying space as \(S\).}

\emph{In particular we set \(D_{O_{S}} = D_{O_{S}}(O_{S})\),
\(I_{S} = I_{S}(O_{S})\), and we call them respectively the algebra of
dual numbers over \(S\) and the scheme of dual numbers over \(S\).}

Then \(M \mapsto I_{S}(M)\) is a contravariant functor from the category
of quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-modules to that of \(S\)-schemes. In
particular the morphisms \(0 \to M\) and \(M \to 0\) define respectively
the structural morphism \(\rho : I_{S}(M) \to I_{S}(0) = S\) and a
section \(\epsilon_{M}\) of it, which we call the \emph{zero
section}.\footnote{Compare with 3.1.1.}

\textbf{2.1.1.}\footnote{One has detailed the original in what follows,
  and one has added the numbering 2.1.1 to 2.1.3.} Since
\(M \mapsto I_{S}(M)\) is a contravariant functor, every
\(a \in \operatorname{End}_{O_{S}}(M)\) defines an \(S\)-endomorphism
\(a^{*}\) of \(I_{S}(M)\), and one has \(1^{*} = id\),
\((ab)^{*} = b^{*} \circ a^{*}\), \(0^{*} = \epsilon_{M} \circ \rho\)
and \(a^{*} \circ \epsilon_{M} = \epsilon_{M}\). Consequently, the
\(S\)-scheme \(I_{S}(M)\) is equipped with a right action of the
multiplicative monoid of \(\operatorname{End}_{O_{S}}(M)\), which
commutes with the \(S\)-morphisms \(I_{S}(M) \to I_{S}(M')\) arising
from morphisms \(M' \to M\); in particular, the operators \(a^{*}\)
preserve the zero section of \(I_{S}(M)\).

For every \(a \in \operatorname{End}_{O_{S}}(M)\) and \(f : S' \to S\)
and \(m \in I_{S}(M)(S')\), we shall write \(m \cdot a = a^{*}(m)\);
then \(m \cdot 1 = m\), \((m \cdot a) \cdot b = m \cdot (ab)\),
\(m \cdot 0 = \epsilon_{M}(\rho(m))\) and, if \(m = \epsilon_{M}(f)\),
then \(m \cdot a = m\).\footnote{In the sequel, one will be principally
  interested in the case where \(a \in O(S)\), acting by homotheties on
  \(M\). For example, if \(M\) is a free \texttt{O\_S}-module of rank
  \(r\), then, for every \(S' \to S\),
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(S', I_{S}(M))\) is identified with the set of
  \(r\)-tuples \((\epsilon_{1}, \cdots, \epsilon_{r}) \in O(S')\) such
  that \(\epsilon_{i} \epsilon_{j} = 0\) for all \texttt{i,\ j}, and one
  has
  \((\epsilon_{1}, \cdots, \epsilon_{r}) \cdot a = (a \epsilon_{1}, \cdots, a \epsilon_{r})\)
  for every \(a \in O(S)\).}

\textbf{Remark 2.1.2.} \emph{The formation of the \(I_{S}(M)\) commutes
with base extension: one has canonical isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I\_S(M)\_\{S′\} ≃ I\_\{S′\}(M ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_\{S′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To simplify, we shall write \(I_{S'}(M) = I_{S}(M)_{S'}\); more
generally, if \(X\) is an \(S\)-functor (not necessarily representable),
we shall write \(I_{X}(M) = I_{S}(M) \times_{S} X\).

\textbf{2.1.3.}\footnote{One has added this paragraph, which will be
  useful in 3.4.2 and 4.6.2.} By what precedes, the multiplicative
monoid of \(O(S')\) acts on the \(S'\)-scheme \(I_{S'}(M)\),
functorially in \(M\), i.e.~the \(S\)-scheme \(I_{S}(M)\) is equipped
with a structure of object with monoid of operators \texttt{O\_S}, this
structure being functorial in \(M\). One thus has a morphism of
\(S\)-schemes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{λ : I\_S(M) ×\_S O\_S ⟶ I\_S(M),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

verifying obvious conditions. For every \(S\)-functor \(X\), one obtains
by base change a morphism of \(X\)-functors:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{λ\_X : I\_X(M) ×\_S O\_S ⟶ I\_X(M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which makes the \(S\)-functor \(I_{X}(M)\) into an object with monoid of
operators \(O(X)\): every element \(a\) of
\(O(X) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, O_{S})\) defines an
\(X\)-endomorphism
\(a^{*} = \lambda_{X} \circ (id_{I_{X}(M)} \times (a \circ pr_{X}))\) of
\(I_{X}(M)\); explicitly, if \(x \in X(S')\) and
\(m \in I_{S}(M)(S') = I_{S'}(M)(S')\), then \(a(x) = a \circ x\)
belongs to \(O(S')\) and one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(m, x) · a = (m · a(x), x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This operation is functorial in \(M\) and preserves the zero section
\(\epsilon_{M} : X \to I_{X}(M)\), i.e.
\(a^{*} \circ \epsilon_{M} = \epsilon_{M}\) for every \(a \in O(X)\).

Moreover, this operation is ``functorial in \(X\)'' in the following
sense: if \(\pi : Y \to X\) is a morphism of \(S\)-functors and
\(u : O(X) \to O(Y)\) the corresponding ring morphism
(i.e.~\(u(a) = a \circ \pi \in O(Y)\) for every
\(a \in O(X) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, O_{S})\)), then the following
diagram is commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              a\^{}*}
\NormalTok{   I\_X(M) ─────────→ I\_X(M)}
\NormalTok{      ↑                 ↑}
\NormalTok{      π                 π}
\NormalTok{              u(a)\^{}*}
\NormalTok{   I\_Y(M) ─────────→ I\_Y(M) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{2.2.} Let now \(M\) and \(N\) be two quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_S}-modules. The commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                M ⊕ N}
\NormalTok{              ↗   ↑   ↘}
\NormalTok{            ↗     │     ↘}
\NormalTok{          M       │       N}
\NormalTok{            ↘     ↓     ↙}
\NormalTok{              ↘   │   ↙}
\NormalTok{                  0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defines a commutative diagram of \(S\)-schemes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                I\_S(M ⊕ N)}
\NormalTok{              ↗     ↑      ↖}
\NormalTok{            ↗       │        ↖}
\NormalTok{          ↗       ε\_\{M⊕N\}      ↖}
\NormalTok{       I\_S(M)        │        I\_S(N)}
\NormalTok{(∗)       ↖         │         ↗}
\NormalTok{            ↖       │       ↗}
\NormalTok{            ε\_M     │     ε\_N}
\NormalTok{                ↘   │   ↙}
\NormalTok{                    S .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 2.2.} \emph{For every \(S\)-scheme \(X\), the
diagram of functors over \(S\) obtained by applying the functor
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(-, X)\) to diagram (∗) is cartesian:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                Hom\_S(I\_S(M ⊕ N), X)}
\NormalTok{              ↙                      ↘}
\NormalTok{        Hom\_S(I\_S(M), X)        Hom\_S(I\_S(N), X)}
\NormalTok{              ↘                      ↙}
\NormalTok{                Hom\_S(S, X) = X .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It must be verified that for every \(S' \to S\), the diagram of sets
obtained by taking the value of the functors on \(S'\) is cartesian.
Since the formation of \(I_{S}(P)\) commutes with base extension in the
sense explained above, it suffices to do it for \(S' = S\), hence to
verify that the following diagram of sets is cartesian:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                X(I\_S(M ⊕ N))}
\NormalTok{              ↙              ↘}
\NormalTok{        X(I\_S(M))       X(I\_S(N))}
\NormalTok{              ↘     X(ε\_\{M⊕N\})↙}
\NormalTok{              X(ε\_M)  ↓  X(ε\_N)}
\NormalTok{                    X(S) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, if \(x \in X(S)\), it follows from SGA 1, III 5.1\footnote{See also
  the addition 0.1.8 in Exp. III.}, that \(X(\epsilon_{M})^{-1}(x)\) is
isomorphic, functorially in \(M\), to

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}}(x^{*}(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), M),
\]

where \(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}\) denotes the sheaf of relative differentials
of \(X\) with respect to \(S\). Now this latter functor (in \(M\))
evidently transforms a direct sum of \texttt{O\_S}-modules into the
product of the corresponding sets, whence the result.

\textbf{Corollary 2.2.1.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme and \(M\) a
free \texttt{O\_S}-module of finite type. The functor
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S}(M), X)\) is isomorphic (as functor above
\(X\)) to a finite product (above \(X\)) of copies of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S}, X)\).}

\textbf{Nota 2.2.2.} \emph{It follows from the proof of the proposition
that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S}, X)\) is isomorphic as \(X\)-functor
to \(V(\Omega^{1}_{X/S})\) (I 4.6.1), hence representable by the vector
fibration}\footnote{Cf. N.D.E. (33) of Exp. I.}
\emph{\(V(\Omega^{1}_{X/S})\).}

\subsection{3. The tangent bundle, condition
(E)}\label{the-tangent-bundle-condition-e}

In this section, unless otherwise stated, the letters \(M, M', N\),
etc., will always denote free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite type (that
is to say, isomorphic to a finite direct sum of copies of
\texttt{O\_S}).

We shall systematically use the identifications justified in Exposé I;
thus we shall say ``functor above \(S\)'' to designate indifferently a
functor equipped with a morphism into \(S\) (= \(h_{S}\)) or a functor
on the category of objects above \(S\). Likewise we shall say
``group-functor above \(S\)'', etc.

\textbf{Definition 3.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(M\) a free
\texttt{O\_S}-module of finite type. Let \(X\) be a functor above \(S\).
One calls} \textbf{tangent bundle to \(X\) above \(S\) relative to the
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(M\)} \emph{and denotes by \(T_{X/S}(M)\) the
\(S\)-functor}

\[
T_{X/S}(M) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S}(M), X).
\]

\emph{In particular, one calls} \textbf{tangent bundle to \(X\) above
\(S\)} \emph{and denotes by \(T_{X/S}\) the functor}\footnote{When
  \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) and \(X\) is a \(k\)-scheme, one has
  \(T_{X/S}(S') = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(S' \otimes_{k} k[\epsilon], X) = X(S' \otimes_{k} k[\epsilon])\);
  one thus recovers one of the usual definitions of the tangent bundle.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{X/S\} = T\_\{X/S\}(O\_S) = Hom\_S(I\_S, X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then \(M \mapsto T_{X/S}(M)\) is a covariant functor from the category
of free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite type to the category of
\(S\)-functors. In particular the morphisms\footnote{One has corrected
  ``\(0 \to M\) and \(M \to 0\)'' to: ``\(M \to 0\) and \(0 \to M\)''.}
\(M \to 0\) and \(0 \to M\) define respectively an \(S\)-morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π\_M : T\_\{X/S\}(M) ⟶ T\_\{X/S\}(0) ≃ X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and a section \(\tau_{0}\) of it, called the \emph{zero section} (or
\emph{null section}).

\textbf{Remark 3.1.1.}\footnote{One has added the paragraphs 3.1.1 and
  3.1.2.} One should note that the projection
\(\pi_{M} : T_{X/S}(M) \to X\) is induced by the zero section
\(\epsilon_{M} : S \to I_{S}(M)\), while the null section
\(\tau_{0} : X \to T_{X/S}(M)\) is induced by the structural morphism
\(\rho : I_{S}(M) \to S\); i.e., for every point
\(t \in T_{X/S}(M)(S')\) (resp. \(x \in X(S')\)), corresponding to an
\(S\)-morphism \(f : S' \times_{S} I_{S}(M) \to X\) (resp.
\(g : S' \to X\)), one has
\(\pi(t) = f \circ (id_{S'} \times \epsilon_{M})\) (resp.
\(\tau_{0}(x) = g \circ (id_{S'} \times \rho)\)).

It follows from 3.1 that \(M \mapsto T_{X/S}(M)\) is a covariant functor
from the category of free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite type to that
of functors above \(X\). In particular \(O(S)\) is a monoid of operators
of the \(X\)-functor \(T_{X/S}(M)\) which respects ``functoriality in
\(M\)''.

\textbf{Scholie 3.1.2.}\footnote{One has added the paragraphs 3.1.1 and
  3.1.2.} What precedes means, in particular, the following. For every
\(S\)-morphism \(\phi : X' \to X\), set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Σ(X′, M) = Hom\_X(X′, T\_\{X/S\}(M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has an action of the multiplicative monoid
\(\operatorname{End}_{O_{S}}(M)\) on \(\Sigma(X', M)\), denoted
\((\lambda, x) \mapsto \lambda \ast x\), such that
\(\lambda \ast (\mu \ast x) = (\lambda \mu) \ast x\), \(1 \ast x = x\),
and \(0 \ast x = \tau_{0} \circ \phi\), where \(\tau_{0}\) is the null
section \(X \to T_{X/S}(M)\). One has likewise an action of
\(\operatorname{End}_{O_{S}}(M \oplus M)\) on
\(\Sigma(X', M \oplus M)\).\footnote{In fact, one is interested only in
  the action of \(O(S)\) (resp. \(O(S) \times O(S)\)) on
  \(\Sigma(X', M)\) (resp. \(\Sigma(X', M \oplus M)\)), cf.~below and
  the proof of 3.6.}

Moreover, let \(m : M \oplus M \to M\) (resp.
\(\delta : M \to M \oplus M\)) be the addition (resp. the diagonal map)
of \(M\), and denote by
\(m_{X'} : \Sigma(X', M \oplus M) \to \Sigma(X', M)\) and
\(\delta_{X'} : \Sigma(X', M) \to \Sigma(X', M \oplus M)\) the morphisms
induced by \(m\) and \(\delta\). For \(\lambda, \mu \in O(S)\), denote
by \(\ell_{\lambda}\) (resp. \(\ell_{\lambda,\mu}\)) multiplication by
\(\lambda\) in \(M\) (resp. by \((\lambda, \mu)\) in \(M \oplus M\)).
Since \(m \circ \ell_{\lambda,\lambda} = \ell_{\lambda} \circ m\) and
\(m \circ \ell_{\lambda,\mu} \circ \delta = \ell_{\lambda+\mu}\), one
has, for every \(z \in \Sigma(X', M \oplus M)\) and
\(x \in \Sigma(X', M)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)   λ ∗ m(z) = m((λ, λ) ∗ z),    m((λ, μ) ∗ δ(x)) = (λ + μ) ∗ x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 3.2.} \emph{Let
\(u \in X(S) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(S, X) = \Gamma(X/S)\). One calls}
\textbf{tangent space to \(X\) above \(S\) at the point \(u\) relative
to \(M\)}, \emph{and denotes by \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\), the \(S\)-functor
obtained from the \(X\)-functor \(T_{X/S}(M)\) by pullback along the
morphism \(u : S \to X\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   L\^{}u\_\{X/S\}(M) ──────→ T\_\{X/S\}(M)}
\NormalTok{       │                    │}
\NormalTok{       │                    │ π}
\NormalTok{       ↓        u           ↓}
\NormalTok{       S ───────────────→   X .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular \(L^{u}_{X/S}(O_{S})\) is denoted \(L^{u}_{X/S}\).
It is the} \textbf{tangent space to \(X\) above \(S\) at the point
\(u\)}.

\textbf{Remark 3.2.1.}\footnote{One has added this remark.} It follows
from 3.1.1 that, for every \(t : S' \to S\), \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)(S')\) is
the set of \(S\)-morphisms \(f : I_{S'}(M) \to X\) such that
\(f \circ \epsilon_{M} = u \circ t\), where
\(\epsilon_{M} : S' \to I_{S'}(M)\) is the zero section.

Let us note immediately the

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.} \emph{If \(X\) is representable by an
\(S\)-scheme denoted \(\tilde{X}\), then \(T_{X/S}(M)\) and
\(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) are representable. In particular \(T_{X/S}\) and
\(L^{u}_{X/S}\) are representable by vector fibrations on \(\tilde{X}\)
and on \(S\), which are respectively \(V(\Omega^{1}_{\tilde{X}/S})\) and
\(V(u^{*}(\Omega^{1}_{\tilde{X}/S}))\).}

It clearly suffices to prove the proposition for \(T_{X/S}(M)\); the
analogous results for \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) follow by pullback. By
Corollary 2.2.1, it even suffices to do it for \(T_{X/S}\), and in that
case, the proposition is nothing other than the remark noted in 2.2.2.

\textbf{Remark 3.3.1.} From this proposition follows a particularly
simple description of the vector fibration representing \(L^{u}_{X/S}\):
the image of the section \(u\) of \(X\) over \(S\) is locally
closed\footnote{Cf. EGA I, 5.3.11.}, hence defined by a quasi-coherent
ideal \(m\) of a scheme induced on an open subset of \(X\). The quotient
\(m/m^{2}\) can be considered as a quasi-coherent module on \(S\). It is
this module that defines the sought-after vector fibration.

Take for example \(X\) an algebraic scheme over a field \(k\) and \(u\)
a \(k\)-rational point of \(X\). Let \(m\) be the maximal ideal of the
local ring \(O_{X,u}\) and let \(t\) be the \(k\)-vector space dual to
\(m/m^{2}\); it is the Zariski tangent space of \(O_{X,u}\) at the point
\(u\). Then, with the notations of I 4.6.5.1, one has:

\[
L^{u}_{X/k} = V(m/m^{2}) = W(t).
\]

Having closed this parenthesis, let us return to the general situation.
Let us remark first that \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) is a covariant functor from
the category of free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite type to that of
functors above \(S\). In particular \(O(S)\) is a set of operators of
the \(S\)-functor \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) which respects functoriality in
\(M\).\footnote{Cf. 3.1.2.}

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.} \emph{The formation of \(T_{X/S}(M)\) and
\(L_{X/S}(M)\) commutes with base extension: for every \(S\)-scheme
\(S'\), one has isomorphisms functorial in \(M\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{X\_\{S′\}/S′\}(M ⊗ O\_\{S′\}) ⥲ T\_\{X/S\}(M)\_\{S′\},}
\NormalTok{L\^{}\{u′\}\_\{X\_\{S′\}/S′\}(M ⊗ O\_\{S′\}) ⥲ L\^{}u\_\{X/S\}(M)\_\{S′\},   where u′ = u\_\{S′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This results immediately from the fact that \texttt{Hom} commutes with
base extension.

\textbf{Corollary 3.4.1.} \emph{The \(X\)-functor \(T_{X/S}(M)\) (resp.
the \(S\)-functor \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\)) is naturally equipped with a
structure of object with operators \texttt{O\_X} (resp. \texttt{O\_S}),
this structure being functorial in \(M\).}

Let us show this first for \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\). For each \(S'\) above
\(S\), \(O(S')\) acts on \(M \otimes O_{S'}\) hence on
\(L^{u'}_{X_{S'}/S'}(M \otimes O_{S'}) = L^{u}_{X/S}(M)_{S'}\); now one
verifies that this action is functorial in \(S'\). It thus equips
\(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\), as announced, with a structure of functor with
operators \texttt{O\_S}.

For \(T_{X/S}(M)\) it is a little more complicated. For each \(X'\)
above \(X\), set \(T_{X/S}(M)_{X'} = T_{X/S}(M) \times_{X} X'\); one
must equip
\(T_{X/S}(M)_{X'}(X') = \operatorname{Hom}_{X}(X', T_{X/S}(M))\) with a
structure of set with monoid of operators \(O(X')\) in a manner
functorial in \(X'\). For this one constructs the following diagram,
where \(X_{X'}\) denotes \(X \times_{S} X'\) and \(f'\) denotes the
section of \(X_{X'}\) over \(X'\) defined by \(f : X' \to X\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                T\_\{X\_\{X′\}/X′\}(M)}
\NormalTok{              ↙                ↘}
\NormalTok{   T\_\{X/S\}(M) ←─────  T\_\{X/S\}(M)\_\{X′\}}
\NormalTok{       ↓                     ↓}
\NormalTok{                X\_\{X′\}}
\NormalTok{              ↙        ↘ f′}
\NormalTok{            ↙             ↘}
\NormalTok{   X ←────  f               X′}
\NormalTok{              ↘            ↙}
\NormalTok{                  S .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has detailed the original in what follows.} This diagram,
joined with 3.2.1, shows that \(T_{X/S}(M)_{X'}(X')\) is identified with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\^{}\{f′\}\_\{X\_\{X′\}/X′\}(M)(X′) = \{ X′{-}morphisms ψ : I\_\{X′\}(M) → X\_\{X′\} such that ψ ∘ ε\_M = f′ \},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

on which every \(a \in O(X')\) acts via its action on \(I_{X'}(M)\),
i.e., with the notations of 2.1.1, one has:
\(a\psi = \psi \circ a^{*}\), i.e.~for every \(X'' \to X'\) and
\(x \in I_{X'}(M)(X'')\), \((a\psi)(x) = \psi(x \cdot a)\). One then
verifies easily that this construction is functorial in \(X'\).

The isomorphisms of Proposition 3.4 are then, by construction,
isomorphisms for the structures of \(O_{X_{S'}}\)-objects, resp.
\(O_{S'}\)-objects.

\textbf{Remark 3.4.2.}\footnote{One has added Remarks 3.4.2 and 3.4.3.}
The action of \texttt{O\_X} on \(T_{X/S}(M)\) can be seen, more simply,
as follows. For every \(f : X' \to X\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_X(X′, T\_\{X/S\}(M)) = \{ φ ∈ Hom\_S(I\_\{X′\}(M), X) | φ ∘ ε\_M = f \},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one saw in 2.1.3 that \(I_{X'}(M)\), considered as \(S\)-functor, is
equipped with an action of the monoid \(O(X')\) which preserves the zero
section \(\epsilon_{M} : X' \to I_{X'}(M)\). Consequently, if one
denotes by \(a^{*}\) the \(X'\)-endomorphism of \(I_{X'}(M)\) defined by
\(a \in O(X')\), one has: \(a\phi = \phi \circ a^{*}\), i.e., for every
\(S' \to S\) and
\((m, x') \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(S', I_{S}(M) \times_{S} X')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(aφ)(m, x′) = φ(m · a(x′), x′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(note that \(a^{*} \circ \epsilon_{M} = \epsilon_{M}\), whence
\((a\phi) \circ \epsilon_{M} = \phi \circ \epsilon_{M} = f\)).

Likewise, the action of \texttt{O\_S} on \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) can be
described as follows. For every \(t : S' \to S\), \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)(S')\)
is the set of \(S\)-morphisms \(\phi : I_{S'}(M) \to X\) such that
\(\phi \circ \epsilon_{M} = u \circ t\); for such a \(\phi\) and
\(a \in O(S')\), one has: \(a\phi = \phi \circ a^{*}\).

\textbf{Remark 3.4.3.}\footnote{One has added Remarks 3.4.2 and 3.4.3.}
The observations of 3.1.2 hold equally for the action of \texttt{O\_S}
on \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) and that of \texttt{O\_X} on \(T_{X/S}(M)\).

\textbf{Definition 3.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(X\) an
\(S\)-functor. One says that \(X\) satisfies} \textbf{condition (E)}
\emph{relative to \(S\) if, for every \(S'\) above \(S\) and all free
\(O_{S'}\)-modules \(M\) and \(N\) of finite type, the diagram of sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                X(I\_\{S′\}(M ⊕ N))}
\NormalTok{              ↙                  ↘}
\NormalTok{       X(I\_\{S′\}(M))           X(I\_\{S′\}(N))}
\NormalTok{              ↘                  ↙}
\NormalTok{                  X(S′) ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{obtained by applying \(X\) to the diagram (∗) defined in 2.1, is
cartesian.}\footnote{For examples of \(S\)-functors and \(S\)-groups not
  satisfying (E), see 6.2 and 6.3.}

\textbf{3.5.1.}\footnote{One has added what follows.} It comes to the
same thing to say that the functor \(M \mapsto T_{X/S}(M)\) transforms
direct sums of free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite type into products
of \(X\)-functors; in this case, the same holds for the functor
\(M \mapsto L^{u}_{X/S}(M) = S \times_{X} T_{X/S}(M)\), for every
\(u \in \Gamma(X/S)\).

Proposition 2.2 shows that every representable functor satisfies
condition (E).

\emph{Abbreviation:} instead of saying ``X satisfies condition (E) with
respect to \(S\)'', we shall sometimes say ``\(X/S\) satisfies condition
(E)''.

If \(X/S\) satisfies condition (E), the functor \(M \mapsto T_{X/S}(M)\)
commutes with products and therefore transforms groups into groups. In
particular \(T_{X/S}(M)\) is a commutative \(X\)-group. For the same
reason, \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) is a commutative \(S\)-group.

\textbf{Proposition 3.6.} \emph{If \(X/S\) satisfies (E), the abelian
group structure on \(T_{X/S}(M)\) (resp. \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\)) and the
action of \texttt{O\_X} (resp. \texttt{O\_S}) equip \(T_{X/S}(M)\)
(resp. \(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\)) with a structure of \texttt{O\_X}-module
(resp. \texttt{O\_S}-module).}

The action of \texttt{O\_X} (resp. \texttt{O\_S}) is functorial in
\(M\); it therefore respects the abelian group structure that is deduced
by functoriality from that of \(M\).\footnote{One has detailed what
  follows.} Indeed, let us resume the notations of 3.1.2. The structure
of (abelian) \(X\)-group on \(T_{X/S}(M)\) is defined by the composite:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{X/S\}(M) ×\_X T\_\{X/S\}(M) ≃ T\_\{X/S\}(M ⊕ M) ──m──→ T\_\{X/S\}(M),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and on the other hand the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{X/S\}(M) ──δ──→ T\_\{X/S\}(M ⊕ M) ≃ T\_\{X/S\}(M) ×\_X T\_\{X/S\}(M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is the diagonal morphism. Taking into account Remark 3.4.3, one deduces
from the equalities (†) of 3.1.2 that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{λ(x + y) = λx + λy,    (λ + μ)x = λx + μx,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(f : X' \to X\),
\(x, y \in \operatorname{Hom}_{X}(X', T_{X/S}(M))\) and
\(\lambda, \mu \in O(X')\).

\textbf{Remark 3.6.1.} \emph{If \(X\) is representable, in which case it
satisfies (E) and \(T_{X/S}\) and \(L^{u}_{X/S}\) are representable by
vector fibrations, the preceding laws are the same as those deduced from
the vector fibration structures (cf.~I 4.6).}\footnote{I.e., for every
  \(S\)-morphism \(f : X' \to X\), the action of \(O(X')\) on
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(X', T_{X/S}(M))\) corresponds, via the
  identification
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(X', T_{X/S}(M)) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{X'}}(f^{*}(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), M \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{X'})\),
  to the natural action of \(O(X')\) on the right-hand term; this
  follows from the proof of SGA 1, III 5.1 (see also the addition 0.1.8
  in Exp. III).}

\textbf{Proposition 3.4 bis.} \emph{If \(X/S\) satisfies (E), then
\(X_{S'}/S'\) satisfies (E) and the isomorphisms of 3.4 respect the
structures of \(O_{X_{S'}}\)-modules, resp. of \(O_{S'}\)-modules.}

Without comment.

\textbf{Proposition 3.7.} \emph{The functors \(T_{X/S}(M)\) and
\(L^{u}_{X/S}(M)\) are functorial in \(X\), i.e., if \(f : X \to X'\) is
an \(S\)-morphism, one has commutative diagrams:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                T(f)                                       L(f)}
\NormalTok{   T\_\{X/S\}(M) ──────→ T\_\{X′/S\}(M)        L\^{}u\_\{X/S\}(M) ──────→ L\^{}\{f∘u\}\_\{X′/S\}(M)}
\NormalTok{        ↓                  ↓                       ↘             ↙}
\NormalTok{        X  ──────────→     X′  ,                       S .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover,}\footnote{One has added the sentence that follows.}
\emph{if \(f\) is a monomorphism, so are \(T(f)\) and \(L(f)\).}

The existence of \(T(f)\) and \(L(f)\), as well as the last assertion,
follow immediately from the definitions. The commutativity of the
diagrams then follows from the functoriality of these morphisms with
respect to \(M\) and from the fact that \(T_{X/S}(0) = X\).

\textbf{Remark 3.7.1.}\footnote{One has added the hypothesis that \(X\)
  and \(X'\) be representable, and one has detailed what follows.}
Suppose \(X\) and \(X'\) representable and let \(r\) be the rank of the
free \texttt{O\_S}-module \(M\). Then, by 2.2.2, \(T_{X/S}(M)\) is
isomorphic to the product over \(X\) of \(r\) copies of
\(V(\Omega^{1}_{X/S})\), and likewise for \(T_{X'/S}(M)\). Consequently,
the above square is cartesian when \(f\) is an open immersion, more
generally when \(f^{*}(\Omega^{1}_{X'/S}) = \Omega^{1}_{X/S}\), for
example if \(f\) is étale; under these conditions, one has an
isomorphism of \(S\)-functors

\[
L^{u}_{X/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{f\circ u}_{X'/S}(M).
\]

In general, the cartesian square of 3.7 defines a morphism of
\(X\)-functors:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{X/S\}(M) ────────→ T\_\{X′/S\}(M) ×\_\{X′\} X}
\NormalTok{       ↘                  ↙}
\NormalTok{              X .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 3.7 bis.} \emph{Let \(f : X \to X'\) be an
\(S\)-morphism; if \(X\) and \(X'\) satisfy (E) with respect to \(S\),
then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              T(f)                                                L(f)}
\NormalTok{T\_\{X/S\}(M) ─────────→ T\_\{X′/S\}(M)\_X       resp.   L\^{}u\_\{X/S\}(M) ─────────→ L\^{}\{f∘u\}\_\{X′/S\}(M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a morphism of \texttt{O\_X}-modules (resp. of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules).}

This follows from Proposition 3.7 by functoriality in \(M\).

\textbf{Proposition 3.8.} \emph{Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two functors
above \(S\). One has isomorphisms functorial in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3.8.1)   T\_\{X/S\}(M) ×\_S T\_\{Y/S\}(M) ⥲ T\_\{(X×\_S Y)/S\}(M),}
\NormalTok{(3.8.2)   L\^{}u\_\{X/S\}(M) ×\_S L\^{}v\_\{Y/S\}(M) ⥲ L\^{}\{(u,v)\}\_\{(X×\_S Y)/S\}(M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has detailed what follows.} The first isomorphism follows
from 1.2 (∗); the second is deduced from it by the base change
\((u, v) : S \to X \times_{S} Y\).

\textbf{Remark 3.8.0.} Note that (3.8.1) can also be interpreted as an
isomorphism of \(X \times_{S} Y\)-functors

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{X/S\}(M) ×\_X (X ×\_S Y) × T\_\{Y/S\}(M) ×\_Y (X ×\_S Y) ⥲ T\_\{(X×\_S Y)/S\}(M).}
\NormalTok{                            (X×\_S Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 3.8.1.} \emph{If \(X/S\) is equipped with an algebraic
structure defined by finite cartesian products, then \(T_{X/S}(M)\) is
equipped with a structure of the same kind and the projection
\(T_{X/S}(M) \to X\) is a morphism of this kind of structure.}

\textbf{Proposition 3.8 bis.} \emph{If \(X/S\) and \(Y/S\) satisfy (E),
then \((X \times_{S} Y)/S\) satisfies (E) and (3.8.1) (resp. (3.8.2)) is
an isomorphism of \(O_{X\times_{S} Y}\)-modules (resp.
\texttt{O\_S}-modules).}

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{One has added this proof.} Suppose that \(X/S\)
and \(Y/S\) satisfy (E). Then, by 3.5.1 and (3.8.1), so does
\((X \times_{S} Y)/S\). Let us show that (3.8.1) is an isomorphism of
\(O_{X\times_{S} Y}\)-modules.

Let \((x, y) : Z \to X \times_{S} Y\) be an \(S\)-morphism; taking into
account 3.4.2, it suffices to see that the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\{ φ ∈ Hom\_S(I\_Z(M), X) | φ ∘ ε\_M = x \} × \{ ψ ∈ Hom\_S(I\_Z(M), Y) | ψ ∘ ε\_M = y \}}
\NormalTok{   ⟶ \{ θ ∈ Hom\_S(I\_Z(M), X ×\_S Y) | θ ∘ ε\_M = (x, y) \}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which to \((\phi, \psi)\) associates \(\phi \times \psi\) is a morphism
of \(O(Z)\)-modules. But this is clear, because if \(a \in O(Z)\) then
\(a \cdot (\phi, \psi) = (\phi \circ a^{*}, \psi \circ a^{*})\) is sent
to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(φ ∘ a\^{}*) × (ψ ∘ a\^{}*) = (φ × ψ) ∘ a\^{}* = a · (φ × ψ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Likewise, using 3.2.1, one shows that (3.8.2) is an isomorphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules.

\textbf{3.9.0.}\footnote{One has added this paragraph, in order to
  explain the introduction of the notion of \(S\)-\(H\)-functor.} If
\(X\) is an \(S\)-group and if \(e : S \to X\) denotes its unit section,
one writes:

\[
Lie(X/S, M) = L^{e}_{X/S}(M),
\]

i.e., \(Lie(X/S, M)\) is defined by the cartesian square:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                   i}
\NormalTok{   Lie(X/S, M) ────────→ T\_\{X/S\}(M)}
\NormalTok{       │                     │}
\NormalTok{       │                     │ p}
\NormalTok{       ↓        e            ↓}
\NormalTok{       S ─────────────────→  X .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By Corollary 3.8.1, the projection \(p : T_{X/S}(M) \to X\) is a
morphism of \(S\)-groups, and it follows that \(Lie(X/S, M)\) is
equipped with a structure of \(S\)-group, and is isomorphic via \(i\) to
the kernel of \(p\).

If, moreover, \(X/S\) satisfies condition (E), we shall see in
Proposition 3.9 that the \(S\)-group structure on \(Lie(X/S, M)\),
induced by that of \(X\), coincides with the abelian group structure
induced by functoriality in \(M\) (cf. 3.5.1). In fact, this result is
valid under the weaker hypothesis that \(X\) be an \(S\)-functor of
monoids or, more generally, an \(S\)-functor of \(H\)-sets (cf.~the
definition below).

\textbf{Definitions 3.9.0.1.} \emph{a) Let us introduce the following
terminology:}\footnote{This is inspired by the notion of \(H\)-space in
  topology.} \emph{an} \textbf{\(H\)-set} \emph{is a set \(X\) equipped
with a composition law with two-sided unit, denoted \(e_{X}\) or simply
\(e\). If \(f : X \to Y\) is a morphism of \(H\)-sets, its kernel
\texttt{Ker\ f} is \(f^{-1}(e_{Y})\); it is a sub-\(H\)-set of \(X\).}

\emph{b) An} \textbf{\(H\)-object} \emph{in a category \(C\) is defined
in the usual manner: it is therefore an object \(X\) of \(C\), equipped
with a morphism \(X \times X \to X\) such that there exists a section of
\(X\) (above the final object) possessing the properties of a two-sided
unit. Every \(C\)-monoid, in particular every \(C\)-group, is therefore
a \(C\)-\(H\)-object. In particular, an \(H\)-object of the category of
functors above the scheme \(S\) will be called an}
\textbf{\(S\)-\(H\)-functor}.

\emph{c) If \(X\) is an \(S\)-\(H\)-functor (for example, an
\(S\)-group), and if \(e : S \to X\) denotes the unit section of \(X\),
one writes:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(X/S, M) = L\^{}e\_\{X/S\}(M)    and    Lie(X/S) = Lie(X/S, O\_S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us make explicit the following particular case of 3.8.1.\footnote{One
  has added Corollary 3.9.0.2, which will be useful in 4.1.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.9.0.2.} \emph{If \(X\) is an \(S\)-\(H\)-functor
(resp. an \(S\)-group), then \(T_{X/S}(M)\) and \(Lie(X/S, M)\) are also
\(S\)-\(H\)-functors (resp. \(S\)-groups), and one has morphisms of
\(S\)-\(H\)-functors (resp. of \(S\)-groups):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                   i                p}
\NormalTok{   Lie(X/S, M) ────────→ T\_\{X/S\}(M) ⇄ X ,}
\NormalTok{                                     s}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(i\) is an isomorphism of \(Lie(X/S)(M)\) onto
\texttt{Ker\ p} and \(s\) is a section of \(p\).}

\textbf{Proposition 3.9.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-\(H\)-functor
satisfying (E) with respect to \(S\). The \(S\)-\(H\)-functor structure
of \(Lie(X/S, M)\) coming from that of \(X\) coincides with the
\(S\)-group structure defined in 3.5.1.}

It follows from what was said above that \(Lie(X/S, M)\) is an
\(H\)-object in the category of \texttt{O\_S}-modules. The proposition
will then follow from the following lemma:\footnote{Inspired by the
  standard proof showing that the fundamental group of an \(H\)-space is
  abelian.}

\textbf{Lemma 3.10.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category. Let \(G\) be an
\(H\)-object in the category of \(C\)-\(H\)-objects; \(G\) is therefore
a \(C\)-\(H\)-object (whose composition law we shall denote
\(f : G \times G \to G\)) equipped with a morphism of
\(C\)-\(H\)-objects \(h : G \times G \to G\).}\footnote{\(G \times G\)
  is equipped with the law
  \((G \times G) \times (G \times G) \to G \times G\),
  \(((x, z), (y, t)) \mapsto (f(x, y), f(z, t))\).} \emph{Then \(f = h\)
and \(f\) is commutative.}

By taking the values of the functors on a variable argument, one
reduces, in the usual manner, to verifying the lemma when \(C\) is the
category of sets. One thus has a set \(G\) and two maps
\(f, h : G \times G \to G\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(f(x, y), f(z, t)) = f(h(x, z), h(y, t)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has on the other hand two elements of \(G\), namely \(e\) and \(u\),
with \(f(e, x) = f(x, e) = x\), \(h(u, x) = h(x, u) = x\). One sees
first that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(f(u, y), f(x, u)) = f(x, y) = h(f(x, u), f(u, y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, for \(y = e\), resp. \(x = e\), one obtains,
respectively,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x = f(x, e) = h(f(u, e), f(x, u)) = h(u, f(x, u)) = f(x, u),}
\NormalTok{y = f(e, y) = h(f(e, u), f(u, y)) = h(u, f(u, y)) = f(u, y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, on substituting in the original equality,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(y, x) = f(x, y) = h(x, y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This proves the lemma, and thus Proposition 3.9. From 3.9 one then
deduces the following corollaries.

\textbf{Corollary 3.9.1.} \emph{If \(X\) is an \(S\)-\(H\)-functor
satisfying (E) with respect to \(S\), every element of \(X(I_{S}(M))\)
which projects onto the unit element of \(X(S)\) is invertible.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.9.2.} \emph{If \(X\) is an \(S\)-monoid satisfying
(E) with respect to \(S\), an element of \(X(I_{S}(M))\) is invertible
if and only if its image in \(X(S)\) is.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.9.3.} \emph{If \(X\) is an \(S\)-group satisfying
(E) with respect to \(S\), the two \(S\)-group laws on \(Lie(X/S, M)\)
coincide.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.9.4.}\footnote{One has added this corollary, which
  amplifies Remark 4.1.1.2 below.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group
satisfying (E) with respect to \(S\). For \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), let
\(n_{G} : G \to G\) be the morphism of \(S\)-functors defined by
\(g \mapsto g^{n}\). Then the derived morphism
\(L(n_{G}) : Lie(G/S) \to Lie(G/S)\) is ``multiplication by \(n\)'',
i.e.~the map that to every \(x \in Lie(G/S)(S')\) associates
\texttt{n\ x}.}

Let us first remark that \(n_{G}\) is not in general a morphism of
groups, but it preserves the unit section \(e : S \to G\), so the
derived morphism \(L(n_{G})\) indeed sends \(Lie(G/S) = L^{e}_{X/S}\)
into itself. If one denotes by \(i\) the inclusion
\(Lie(G/S) \hookrightarrow T_{G/S}\), then \(L(n_{G})\) is defined by
the equality \(i(L(n_{G})(x)) = i(x)^{n}\), for every \(S' \to S\) and
\(x \in Lie(G/S)(S')\). Now, by 3.9, the two group laws on \(Lie(G/S)\)
(coming from condition (E) and coming from the law of \(G\)) coincide,
i.e.~one has \(i(x)^{n} = i(n x)\), whence \(L(n_{G})(x) = n x\).

Before drawing other consequences of Proposition 3.9, let us prove
another functoriality result:

\textbf{Proposition 3.11.} \emph{In the situation of Section 1, one has
an isomorphism functorial in \(M\)}

\[
T_{\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X,Y)/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, T_{Y/Z}(M)).
\]

Indeed, by definition (cf.~3.1):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) = Hom\_S(I\_S(M), Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By the isomorphism (4) of 1.1, applied to \(T = I_{S}(M)\), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(I\_S(M), Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)) ≃ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Hom\_Z(Z ×\_S I\_S(M), Y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Taking into account the isomorphism
\(Z \times_{S} I_{S}(M) \simeq I_{Z}(M)\), this gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ≃ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Hom\_Z(I\_Z(M), Y)) = Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 3.11.1.} \emph{If \(Y/Z\) satisfies (E), then
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)/S\) satisfies (E) and the isomorphism
of 3.11 respects the \(O\)-module structures above
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\).}\footnote{Setting
  \(H = \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\), this implies in particular
  that \(T_{H/S}(M)\) is equipped with a natural structure of module
  over \(\prod_{X \times_{S} H/H} O_{H}\). This result has seemed
  somewhat surprising to the editors; for this reason one has detailed
  the proof.}

\emph{Proof.} Let \texttt{M,\ N} be two free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of
finite type. If \(Y/Z\) satisfies (E), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{Y/Z\}(M ⊕ N) ≃ T\_\{Y/Z\}(M) ×\_Y T\_\{Y/Z\}(N).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The right-hand term is a subfunctor of
\(T_{Y/Z}(M) \times_{S} T_{Y/Z}(N)\) and via the isomorphism of 1.2 (∗),
one obtains an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M ⊕ N)) ≃}
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M)) ×\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)\} Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(N)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combined with 3.11, this implies:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)/S\}(M ⊕ N) ≃}
\NormalTok{   T\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ×\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)\} T\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)/S\}(N),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\) satisfies (E) with respect to
\(S\). This proves the first assertion of the corollary.

Let us see the second. Denote by \(H = \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\)
and give ourselves an \(S\)-morphism
\(\Delta : H' \to \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\), i.e., a
\(Z\)-morphism \(\delta : H' \times_{S} X \to Y\), which therefore makes
\(H' \times_{S} X\) a \(Y\)-object.

On the one hand, one has a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_H(H′, Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M))) ───→ Hom\_S(H′, Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M)))}

\NormalTok{   Hom\_Y(H′ ×\_S X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M)) ──────────→ Hom\_Z(H′ ×\_S X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M))}

\NormalTok{   \{ ψ ∈ Hom\_Z(I\_\{H′ ×\_S X\}(M), Y) | ψ ∘ ε\_M = δ \} ──→ Hom\_Z(I\_\{H′ ×\_S X\}(M), Y) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 1.3, the action of \(\alpha \in O(H' \times_{S} X)\) on
\(\Psi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{Y}(H' \times_{S} X, T_{Y/Z}(M))\) is
given by: for every \(U \to S\) and
\((h, x) \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(U, H' \times_{S} X)\) (\(U\) being
then above \(Y\) via \(\delta \circ (h, x)\)),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(αΨ)(h, x) = α(h, x) Ψ(h, x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\alpha(h, x) \in O(U)\) acts on \(\Psi(h, x) \in T_{Y/Z}(M)(U)\)
via the structure of \texttt{O\_Y}-module of \(T_{Y/Z}(M)\). By 3.4.2,
this last is given, via the identification

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_Y(H′ ×\_S X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M)) = \{ ψ ∈ Hom\_Z(I\_\{H′ ×\_S X\}(M), Y) | ψ ∘ ε\_M = δ \},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by: for every
\((m, h, x) \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(U, I_{S}(M) \times_{S} H' \times_{S} X)\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   (αψ)(m, h, x) = ψ(m · α(h, x), h, x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, consider the tangent space
\(T_{H/S}(M) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S}(M), H)\); one has a
commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_H(H′, T\_\{H/S\}(M)) ──────────→ Hom\_S(H′, T\_\{H/S\}(M))}

\NormalTok{   \{ Φ ∈ Hom\_S(I\_\{H′\}(M), H) | Φ ∘ ε\_M = Δ \} ────────→ Hom\_S(I\_\{H′\}(M), H)}
\NormalTok{                          (∗)}
\NormalTok{   \{ φ ∈ Hom\_Z(I\_\{H′ ×\_S X\}(M), Y) | φ ∘ ε\_M = δ \} ────→ Hom\_Z(I\_\{H′ ×\_S X\}(M), Y) ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the bijection (∗) is given as follows (cf.~1.1 (2) and I 1.7.1):
for every \(U \to S\) and
\((m, h, x) \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(U, I_{S}(M) \times_{S} H' \times_{S} X)\)
(so that \(U\) is above \(Z\) via \(U \xrightarrow{x} X \to Z\)), one
has \(\Phi(m, h) \in \operatorname{Hom}_{Z}(X \times_{S} U, Y)\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)   φ(m, h, x) = Φ(m, h) ∘ (x × id\_U) ∈ Hom\_Z(U, Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 3.4.2 (where one replaces \(X\) by \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\)
and \(X'\) by \(H'\)), the action of \(a \in O(H')\) on
\(\Phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{H'}(M), H)\) is given by: for every
\(U \to S\) and
\((m, h) \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(U, I_{S}(M) \times_{S} H')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(aΦ)(m, h) = Φ(m · a(h), h).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consequently, if \(\phi\) (resp. \(a\phi\)) is the element of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z}(I_{H' \times_{S} X}(M), Y)\) associated with
\(\Phi\) (resp. \(a\Phi\)), one has, by (†),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   (aφ)(m, h, x) = Φ(m · a(h), h) ∘ (x × id\_U) = φ(m · a(h), h, x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combined with (1), this shows that the isomorphism
\(T_{H/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, T_{Y/Z}(M))\)
of 3.11.1 is an isomorphism of \(O(H)\)-modules; moreover, for every
\(H' \to H\), the structure of \(O(H')\)-module on
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{H}(H', T_{H/S}(M))\) extends, in a manner
functorial in \(H'\), to a structure of \(O(H' \times_{S} X)\)-module.

In particular, for \(Z = S\), one obtains the following corollary.

\textbf{Corollary 3.11.2.} \emph{One has an isomorphism functorial in
\(M\)}

\[
T_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, T_{Y/S}(M)).
\]

\emph{Moreover, if \(Y/S\) satisfies (E), then
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, Y)/S\) satisfies (E) and the preceding
isomorphism respects the \(O\)-module structures above
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, Y)\).}

\footnote{One has added the sentences that follow.} Let \(u : X \to Y\)
be an \(S\)-morphism; one identifies it with the constant morphism
\(u : S \to \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, Y)\) such that \(u(f) = u\) for
every \(f : S' \to S\). One sees at once that the fiber product of \(u\)
and of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, T_{Y/S}(M)) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, Y)\)
is identified with \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Y/S}(X, T_{Y/S}(M))\), where
\(X\) is above \(Y\) via \(u\). Consequently, from the definition of
\(L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M)\) and the preceding corollary
one deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 3.11.3.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) be an
\(S\)-morphism. One has an isomorphism functorial in \(M\) (where in the
right-hand term \(X\) is above \(Y\) via \(u\)):}

\[
L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{Y/S}(X, T_{Y/S}(M)).
\]

\footnote{One has added the sentence that follows.} \emph{It is an
isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules if \(Y/S\) satisfies (E).}

In particular, for \(Y = X\), \(\operatorname{End}_{S}(X)\) is an
\(S\)-functor of monoids, hence a fortiori an \(S\)-\(H\)-functor;
recalling that \(Lie(\operatorname{End}_{S}(X)/S, M)\) denotes
\(L^{e}_{\operatorname{End}_{S}(X)/S}(M)\), where \(e\) is the unit
section (cf.~3.9.0.1), one obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 3.11.4.} \emph{One has an isomorphism functorial in
\(M\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(End\_S(X)/S, M) ⥲ ∏\_\{X/S\} T\_\{X/S\}(M);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has added the sentence that follows.} \emph{it is an
isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules if \(X/S\) satisfies (E).}

\textbf{Remark 3.11.5.}\footnote{One has added this remark.} Suppose
that \(X/S\) satisfies (E). Then
\(\prod_{X/S} T_{X/S}(M) = \operatorname{Hom}_{X/S}(X, T_{X/S}(M))\) is
equipped with a structure of \((\prod_{X/S} O_{X})\)-module, i.e.~for
every \(S' \to S\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{X/S\}(X, T\_\{X/S\}(M))(S′) = \{ ψ ∈ Hom\_X(I\_\{S′\}(M) ×\_S X, X) | ψ ∘ (ε\_M × id\_X) = pr\_X \}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is equipped with a structure of \(O(X \times_{S} S')\)-module,
functorial in \(S'\). This follows, at one's choice, from 3.6 and the
properties of the functor \(\prod_{X/S}\) (cf.~1.2), or from the proof
of 3.11.1.

We shall now interpret geometrically the definition of the tangent
bundle.

\footnote{One has simplified the original in what follows.} Let \(U\) be
an \(S\)-functor; by I 1.7.2, one has isomorphisms functorial in \(M\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{X/S\}(M)(U) = Hom\_S(U, Hom\_S(I\_S(M), X)) ≃ Hom\_S(I\_S(M), Hom\_S(U, X))}
\NormalTok{              ≃ Hom\_\{I\_S(M)\}(U\_\{I\_S(M)\}, X\_\{I\_S(M)\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, the morphism \(M \to 0\) gives a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_S(U, T\_\{X/S\}(M))  ⥲  Hom\_\{I\_S(M)\}(U\_\{I\_S(M)\}, X\_\{I\_S(M)\})}
\NormalTok{            │                              │}
\NormalTok{            │ π\_M                          │ identity}
\NormalTok{            ↓                              ↓}
\NormalTok{   Hom\_S(U, X)  ─────────────────────→  Hom\_S(U, X) ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the second vertical arrow is obtained by the base change
\(\epsilon_{M} : S \to I_{S}(M)\).\footnote{Via the isomorphism
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{I_{S}(M)}(U_{I_{S}(M)}, X_{I_{S}(M)}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(U \times_{S} I_{S}(M), X)\),
  this is equivalent to Remark 3.1.1. Likewise, 3.12 is equivalent to
  the first part of Remark 3.4.2.}

In consequence:

\textbf{Proposition 3.12.} \emph{Let \(h_{0} : U \to X\) be an
\(S\)-morphism. Then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(U, T_{X/S}(M))\) is
identified with the set of \(I_{S}(M)\)-morphisms from \(U_{I_{S}(M)}\)
to \(X_{I_{S}(M)}\) which restrict to \(h_{0}\) on \(U\) (viewed as a
subobject of \(U \times_{S} I_{S}(M)\) via
\(id_{U} \times_{S} \epsilon_{M}\)).}

\footnote{One has detailed the original in what follows.} In particular,
for \(U = X\) and \(h_{0} = id_{X}\), one obtains the

\textbf{Corollary 3.12.1.} \emph{The set \(\Gamma(T_{X/S}(M)/X)\) is
identified with the set of \(I_{S}(M)\)-endomorphisms \(\phi\) of
\(X_{I_{S}(M)}\) which induce the identity on \(X\), i.e.~such that the
following diagram be commutative:}\footnote{When \(M = O_{X}\), these
  are called ``infinitesimal endomorphisms'' of \(X\); see 6.2 at the
  end of this Exposé.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  φ}
\NormalTok{   I\_X(M) ──────────→ I\_X(M)}
\NormalTok{      ↑                   ↑}
\NormalTok{   ε\_M                    ε\_M}
\NormalTok{                id}
\NormalTok{       X ──────────────→  X .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has detailed the original in what follows.} On the other
hand, by 3.11.2,
\(\Gamma(T_{X/S}(M)/X) \simeq Lie(\operatorname{End}_{S}(X)/S, M)(S)\);
if moreover \(X/S\) satisfies (E), then \(\operatorname{End}_{S}(X)/S\)
satisfies (E), so \(Lie(\operatorname{End}_{S}(X)/S, M)\) is an
\texttt{O\_S}-module by 3.6 (and in fact a
\((\prod_{X/S} O_{X})\)-module, by 3.11.5). Applying 3.9, one deduces
the

\textbf{Proposition 3.13.} \emph{If \(X/S\) satisfies (E), the abelian
group \(\Gamma(T_{X/S}(M)/X)\) is identified with the set of
\(I_{S}(M)\)-endomorphisms of \(X_{I_{S}(M)}\) inducing the identity on
\(X\). Consequently, every \(I_{S}(M)\)-endomorphism of \(X_{I_{S}(M)}\)
which induces the identity on \(X\) is an automorphism.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.13.1.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) be an
\(S\)-isomorphism, \(Y/S\) satisfying (E). Every \(I_{S}(M)\)-morphism
from \(X_{I_{S}(M)}\) into \(Y_{I_{S}(M)}\) which extends \(u\) is an
isomorphism.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.13.2.} \emph{If \(Y/S\) satisfies (E), then the
monomorphism \(Isom_{S}(X, Y) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, Y)\)
induces, for every \(u \in Isom_{S}(X, Y)\), an isomorphism}

\[
L^{u}_{Isom_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M).
\]

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{One has added the proof that follows.} One must
see that
\(L^{u}_{Isom_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M)(S') \to L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M)(S')\)
is a bijection, for every \(S' \to S\). By base change (cf.~3.4), it
suffices to do it for \(S' = S\). In this case,
\(L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M)(S)\) (resp.
\(L^{u}_{Isom_{S}(X,Y)/S}(M)(S)\)) is the set of \(I_{S}(M)\)-morphisms
(resp. automorphisms) \(X_{I_{S}(M)} \to Y_{I_{S}(M)}\) which extend
\(u\), and one applies the preceding corollary.

\textbf{Corollary 3.13.3.} \emph{If \(X/S\) satisfies (E), the
monomorphism \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X) \to \operatorname{End}_{S}(X)\)
induces, for every \(u \in \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)\), an isomorphism
\(L^{u}_{\operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{u}_{\operatorname{End}_{S}(X)/S}(M)\).
In particular, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut\_S(X)/S, M) ⥲ Lie(End\_S(X)/S, M) ⥲ ∏\_\{X/S\} T\_\{X/S\}(M),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has added what follows.} \emph{so that
\(Lie(\operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)/S, M)\) is equipped with a structure of
\((\prod_{X/S} O_{X})\)-module.}

\textbf{3.14.} Suppose to conclude that \(X\) is
representable.\footnote{One has added the reminder of 2.2.2, and
  detailed the sequel.} In this case, one saw in 2.2.2 that the
\(X\)-functor \(T_{X/S}\) is representable by \(V(\Omega^{1}_{X/S})\),
whence bijections:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(T\_\{X/S\}/X) ≃ Hom\_X(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}, O\_X) ≃ Dér\_\{O\_S\}(O\_X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is also deduced from what precedes, as follows. By 3.13,
\(\Gamma(T_{X/S}/X)\) is identified with the set of infinitesimal
endomorphisms of \(X\) (i.e.~of \texttt{I\_S}-endomorphisms of
\(X_{I_{S}}\) inducing the identity on \(X\)). Now \(X\) and
\(X_{I_{S}}\) have the same underlying topological space, the
corresponding rings of sheaves being \texttt{O\_X} and
\(D_{O_{X}} = O_{X} \oplus M\), where \(M = O_{X}\) is considered as
ideal of square zero. Denoting by \(\pi : D_{O_{X}} \to O_{X}\) the
morphism of \texttt{O\_X}-algebras that vanishes on \(M\), one deduces
that to give an infinitesimal endomorphism of \(X\) is equivalent to
giving a morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-algebras
\(\phi : O_{X} \to D_{O_{X}}\) such that
\(\pi \circ \phi = id_{O_{X}}\), which is equivalent to giving an
\texttt{O\_S}-derivation of the sheaf of rings \texttt{O\_X}.

Moreover, one sees easily that if
\(D, D' \in D\acute{e}r_{O_{S}}(O_{X})\) and if one denotes by
\(\phi_{D}\) the infinitesimal endomorphism corresponding to \(D\), then

\[
\phi_{D+D'} = \phi_{D} \circ \phi_{D'}.
\]

This shows that the identification

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\{ infinitesimal endomorphisms of X \} ≃ Dér\_\{O\_S\}(O\_X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an isomorphism of abelian groups. Taking into account 3.13 (and
3.11.5), one has therefore constructed an isomorphism of abelian groups
(and even of \(O(X)\)-modules)

\[
\Gamma(T_{X/S}/X) \xrightarrow{\sim} D\acute{e}r_{O_{S}}(O_{X}),
\]

which recovers the classical interpretation of tangent vector fields in
terms of derivations of the structure sheaf.\footnote{Moreover, this
  isomorphism is functorial in \(S\): if \(S' \to S\), setting
  \(X' = X_{S'}\), one has
  \(Lie(\operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)/S)(S') \simeq \Gamma(T_{X'/S'}/X') \simeq D\acute{e}r_{O_{S'}}(O_{X'})\).}
Let us remark in passing that \(\Gamma(T_{X/S}/X)\) is equal to
\(H^{0}(X, g_{X/S})\), where \(g_{X/S}\) is the dual of
\(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}\).

\subsection{4. Tangent space to a group --- Lie
algebras}\label{tangent-space-to-a-group-lie-algebras}

\textbf{4.1.} Let \(G\) be a group-functor above \(S\). By 3.9.0.2,
\(T_{G/S}(M)\) and \(Lie(G/S, M)\) are equipped with structures of
groups above \(S\) and one has morphisms of groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       i                p}
\NormalTok{   Lie(G/S, M) ────────→ T\_\{G/S\}(M) ⇄ G ;}
\NormalTok{                                     s}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by definition \(i\) is an isomorphism of \(Lie(G/S)(M)\) onto the kernel
of \(p\) and \(s\) is a section of \(p\). It then follows from I 2.3.7
that this sequence of morphisms allows one to identify \(T_{G/S}(M)\)
with the semi-direct product of \(G\) by \(Lie(G/S, M)\).

\textbf{Definition 4.1.A.}\footnote{One has added the numbering 4.1.A
  and 4.1.B to highlight these definitions.} \emph{The corresponding
action of \(G\) on \(Lie(G/S, M)\) is denoted}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad : G ⟶ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Lie(G/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and called the} \textbf{adjoint representation} \emph{(relative to
\(M\)) of \(G\); one has therefore by definition, for \(x \in G(S')\)
and \(X \in Lie(G/S, M)(S')\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(x) X = i\^{}\{{-}1\}(s(x) i(X) s(x)\^{}\{{-}1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(G\) is commutative, then \(T_{G/S}(M)\) is also commutative
and \(Ad(x) X = X\).}

\textbf{Definition 4.1.B.}\footnote{One has added the numbering 4.1.A
  and 4.1.B to highlight these definitions.} \emph{If \(G\) and \(H\)
are two group-functors above \(S\) and if \(f : G \to H\) is a morphism
of groups, by functoriality there is deduced a morphism of exact
sequences compatible with the canonical sections:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   1 ─→ Lie(G/S, M) ─→ T\_\{G/S\}(M) ─→ G ─→ 1}
\NormalTok{            │ L(f)         │ T(f)       │ f}
\NormalTok{            ↓              ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{   1 ─→ Lie(H/S, M) ─→ T\_\{H/S\}(M) ─→ H ─→ 1 ;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{\(L(f)\), which we shall also write \(Lie(f)\), is the}
\textbf{derived morphism} \emph{of \(f\).}\footnote{If \(f\) is a
  monomorphism, so are \(L(f)\) and \(T(f)\), cf.~3.7.}

\textbf{Remark 4.1.C.}\footnote{One has added this remark.} \emph{If
\(G/S\) and \(H/S\) satisfy (E), then \(L(f)\) respects the
\texttt{O\_S}-module structures deduced from ``functoriality in \(M\)''
(cf.~3.6).}

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.1.} \emph{Let \(g \in G(S)\). Then
\(Ad(g) : Lie(G/S, M) \to Lie(G/S, M)\) is the derived morphism of
\(Int(g) : G \to G\).}

Indeed \(Ad(g) X = i^{-1}(Int(g) i(X))\), which is nothing other than
\(L(Int(g))(X)\) by the very definition of the derived morphism.

Suppose that \(G/S\) satisfies (E). Then, by Proposition 3.9, the group
structure on \(Lie(G/S, M)\) defined as above is nothing other than the
structure induced by its \texttt{O\_S}-module structure (defined thanks
to (E)). One then deduces from the preceding proposition and the
functoriality of the action of \texttt{O\_S} (cf.~3.6) the corollary:

\textbf{Corollary 4.1.1.1.} \emph{Suppose that \(G/S\) satisfies (E).
Then \texttt{Ad} sends \(G\) into the subgroup}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(Lie(G/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{of \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(Lie(G/S, M))\), i.e., for every
\(g \in G(S')\), \(Ad(g)\) respects the \(O_{S'}\)-module structure of
\(Lie(G'/S', M)\) (where \(G' = G \times_{S} S'\)). In other words,
\texttt{Ad} is a} \textbf{linear representation} \emph{(cf. I, 3.2) of
\(G\) in the \texttt{O\_S}-module \(Lie(G/S, M)\).}

\textbf{Remarks 4.1.1.2.} \emph{a) For \(G/S\) to satisfy (E), it is
necessary and sufficient that for every pair \((M, N)\) of free
\texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite type, the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                Lie(G/S, M ⊕ N)}
\NormalTok{              ↙                ↘}
\NormalTok{        Lie(G/S, M)        Lie(G/S, N)}
\NormalTok{              ↘                ↙}
\NormalTok{                Lie(G/S, 0) = S ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{obtained by applying the functor \(Lie(G/S, -)\) to the diagram
(∗) of 2.1, be cartesian.}

\emph{b) Suppose that \(G/S\) satisfies (E). Then the derived morphism
of the group law \(\pi : G \times_{S} G \to G\) is nothing other than
the addition law in \(Lie(G/S, M)\).} (N.B. \(\pi\) is not a morphism of
groups, but \(\pi(e, e) = e\), so the derived morphism \(L(\pi)\) sends
\(T^{(e,e)}_{(G\times_{S} G)/S}(M) = Lie(G/S, M) \times_{S} Lie(G/S, M)\)
into \(Lie(G/S, M)\), cf.~3.7 and 3.8.) For every \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\),
one shows likewise that if one denotes by \(n_{G} : G \to G\) the
morphism of \(S\)-functors defined by \(g \mapsto g^{n}\), then the
derived morphism \(L(n_{G})\) is multiplication by \(n\) on
\(Lie(G/S)\), cf.~3.9.4.

\textbf{4.1.2.0.}\footnote{One has detailed the original in what
  follows, in order to show the action of \(G\) on the functors
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{G/S}(G, T_{G/S}(M))\) and
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(G, Lie(G/S, M))\).} Consider now the
\(S\)-functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{G/S}(G, T_{G/S}(M))\); for every
\(S' \to S\), one has \(T_{G/S}(M)_{S'} \simeq T_{G_{S'}/S'}(M)\)
(cf.~3.4) and therefore:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{G/S\}(G, T\_\{G/S\}(M))(S′) ≃ Hom\_\{G\_\{S′\}\}(G\_\{S′\}, T\_\{G\_\{S′\}/S′\}(M)) = Γ(T\_\{G\_\{S′\}/S′\}(M)/G\_\{S′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note first that one has an isomorphism, functorial in \(S'\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)   Hom\_\{S′\}(G\_\{S′\}, Lie(G\_\{S′\}/S′, M)) ⥲ Γ(T\_\{G\_\{S′\}/S′\}(M)/G\_\{S′\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which to every \(f : G_{S'} \to Lie(G_{S'}/S', M)\) associates the
section \(s_{f} : G_{S'} \to T_{G_{S'}/S'}(M)\) such that, for every
\(S'' \to S'\) and \(g \in G(S'')\):

\[
s_{f}(g) = i(f(g)) s(g).
\]

Let \(h\) be an automorphism of the functor \(G_{S'}\) above \(S'\), not
necessarily respecting the group structure. To every section \(\tau\) of
\(T_{G_{S'}/S'}(M)\), one can associate \(h(\tau)\) defined by transport
of structure: it is, for example, the only section of
\(T_{G_{S'}/S'}(M)\) making commutative the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              τ}
\NormalTok{   G\_\{S′\} ─────────→ T\_\{G\_\{S′\}/S′\}(M)}
\NormalTok{       │                        │}
\NormalTok{       h                       T(h)}
\NormalTok{       │            h(τ)        │}
\NormalTok{       ↓                        ↓}
\NormalTok{   G\_\{S′\} ─────────→ T\_\{G\_\{S′\}/S′\}(M) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, take for \(h\) the right translation \(t_{x}\) by an
element \(x\) of \(G(S')\), i.e., \(h(g) = t_{x}(g) = g \cdot x\), for
every \(g \in G(S'')\), \(S'' \to S'\). Then one has immediately

\[
t_{x}(s_{f}) = s_{t_{x}(f)}
\]

where \(t_{x}(f)\) denotes the morphism from \(G_{S'}\) into
\(Lie(G_{S'}/S', M)\) defined by

\[
t_{x}(f)(g) = f(g \cdot x^{-1}),
\]

for every \(g \in G(S'')\), \(S'' \to S'\).

It follows that if one makes \(G\) act by right translations on

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{G/S\}(G, T\_\{G/S\}(M))    and    Hom\_S(G, Lie(G/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

in the following way: for every \(S' \to S\), \(x \in G(S')\),
\(\sigma \in \Gamma(T_{G_{S'}/S'}(M)/G_{S'})\) and
\(f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S'}(G_{S'}, Lie(G_{S'}/S', M))\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(σ · x)(g) = σ(g · x\^{}\{{-}1\}) · s(x)    and    (f · x)(g) = f(g · x\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(g \in G(S'')\), \(S'' \to S'\), then the isomorphism (∗)
above respects the actions of \(G\).

In particular, by this isomorphism, the elements of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{G/S}(G, T_{G/S}(M))^{G}(S')\) correspond to the
constant morphisms from \(G_{S'}\) into \(Lie(G_{S'}/S', M)\)
(i.e.~factoring through the projection \(G_{S'} \to S'\)) or also to the
elements of \(Lie(G_{S'}/S', M)(S') = Lie(G/S, M)(S')\).

\emph{Terminology.} The elements of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{G/S}(G, T_{G/S}(M))^{G}(S')\) will be called
``sections of \(T_{G_{S'}/S'}(M)\) invariant under right translation''.

One then obtains the:

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.2.}\footnote{The statements 4.1.2, 4.1.3 and
  4.1.4 are obtained more simply by remarking that the automorphisms of
  \(G\) invariant by right translations are the left
  translations.{[}\^{}N.D.E-II-53{]}} \emph{The map
\(Lie(G/S, M)(S) \to \Gamma(T_{G/S}(M)/G)\) which to
\(X \in Lie(G/S, M)(S)\) associates the section \(x \mapsto X \cdot x\)
is a bijection of \(Lie(G/S, M)(S)\) onto the part of
\(\Gamma(T_{G/S}(M)/G)\) formed by the sections invariant under right
translation.}

Likewise, one makes \(G\) act on the right on
\(\operatorname{End}_{I_{S}(M)/S}(G_{I_{S}(M)})\) as follows: for every
\(S' \to S\), \(x \in G(S')\) and
\(u \in \operatorname{End}_{I_{S}(M)/S}(G_{I_{S}(M)})(S') = \operatorname{End}_{I_{S'}(M)}(G_{I_{S'}(M)})\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u · x)(g) = u(g · x\^{}\{{-}1\}) · x,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(g \in G(S'')\), \(S'' \to I_{S'}(M)\). Then the morphism of
3.12.1

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{G/S}(G, T_{G/S}(M)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{End}_{I_{S}(M)/S}(G_{I_{S}(M)})
\]

respects the actions of \(G\) and therefore induces, for every
\(S' \to S\), a bijection between \(\Gamma(T_{G_{S'}/S'}(M)/G_{S'})\)
and the set of \(I_{S'}(M)\)-endomorphisms \(u\) of \(G_{I_{S'}(M)}\)
which induce the identity on \(G\) and ``commute with right
translations'', i.e.~which verify \(u_{S''} \cdot x = u_{S''}\) for
every \(S'' \to S'\) and \(x \in G(S'')\). One obtains therefore:

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.3.}\footnote{The statements 4.1.2, 4.1.3 and
  4.1.4 are obtained more simply by remarking that the automorphisms of
  \(G\) invariant by right translations are the left
  translations.{[}\^{}N.D.E-II-53{]}} \emph{There exists a bijection
functorial in \(G\) between the set \(Lie(G/S, M)(S)\) and the set of
\(I_{S}(M)\)-endomorphisms of \(G_{I_{S}(M)}\) inducing the identity on
\(G\) and commuting with the right translations of \(G\) (in the sense
indicated above).}

Taking now into account 3.13:

\textbf{Theorem 4.1.4.}\footnote{The statements 4.1.2, 4.1.3 and 4.1.4
  are obtained more simply by remarking that the automorphisms of \(G\)
  invariant by right translations are the left
  translations.{[}\^{}N.D.E-II-53{]}} \emph{Let \(G\) be an
\(S\)-functor of groups; suppose that \(G/S\) satisfies (E). Then the
group \(Lie(G/S, M)(S)\) is identified, functorially in \(G\), with the
group of \(I_{S}(M)\)-automorphisms of \(G_{I_{S}(M)}\) inducing the
identity on \(G\) and commuting with the right translations of \(G\) (in
the sense indicated above).}

One thus recovers (in the case \(M = O_{S}\)) one of the classical
definitions of the Lie algebra of a group.

\textbf{4.2.0.}\footnote{One has added paragraph 4.2.0, whose results
  are used implicitly in 4.2 and 4.7 of the original.} Before going
further, let us establish new corollaries of 3.11. Let \texttt{X,\ Y} be
above \(Z\), with \(Z\) above \(S\), as in Section 1. As one saw in
3.11, the isomorphisms 1.1 (4):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   Hom\_S(I\_S(M), Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Y)) ⥲ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, Hom\_Z(I\_Z(M), Y))}
\NormalTok{                                     ≃ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X ×\_S I\_S(M), Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induce the isomorphism \(\theta\) below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   T\_\{Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X,Y)\}(M) ⥲ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/Z\}(M))}
\NormalTok{                            ≃ Hom\_\{Z/S\}(X ×\_S I\_S(M), Y) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 1.3, if \(Y\) is a \(Z\)-group, so is
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z}(V, Y)\) for every \(V \to Z\) (in particular
for \(V = I_{Z}(M)\)); explicitly, if \(Z'' \to Z' \to Z\) and
\(\phi, \psi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{Z}(V_{Z'}, Y)\), then
\(\phi \cdot \psi\) is defined by
\((\phi \cdot \psi)(v) = \phi(v) \psi(v)\), for every
\(v \in V_{Z'}(Z'')\).

Suppose now that \(X\) and \(Y\) are \(Z\)-groups and let us pose the
following definition.

\textbf{Definition 4.2.0.1.} \emph{Let
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{(Z/S)-gr.}(X, Y)\) be the subfunctor of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Z/S}(X, Y)\) defined by: for every \(S' \to S\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)   Hom\_\{(Z/S){-}gr.\}(X, Y)(S′) = Hom\_\{Z\_\{S′\}{-}gr.\}(X\_\{S′\}, Y\_\{S′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{This definition applies equally when one replaces \(Y\) by the
\(Z\)-group \(T_{Y/Z}(M)\).}

One then sees easily that
\(T_{\operatorname{Hom}_{(Z/S)-gr.}(X,Y)/S}(M)(S')\) corresponds, in the
preceding isomorphisms (2), to the \(Z_{S'}\)-morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ : X\_\{S′\} ×\_\{S′\} I\_\{S′\}(M) ⟶ Y\_\{S′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which are ``multiplicative in \(X\)'', i.e.~which verify
\(\phi(x_{1} x_{2}, m) = \phi(x_{1}, m) \phi(x_{2}, m)\), and these
correspond to the morphisms of \(Z_{S'}\)-groups
\(X_{S'} \to T_{Y/Z}(M)_{S'}\). One has thus obtained:

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.0.2.} \emph{Let \texttt{X,\ Y} be \(Z\)-groups,
with \(Z\) above \(S\). One has isomorphisms of \(S\)-functors,
functorial in \(M\):}

\[
T_{\operatorname{Hom}_{(Z/S)-gr.}(X,Y)}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{(Z/S)-gr.}(X, T_{Y/Z}(M)).
\]

In particular, for \(Z = S\), one obtains the following corollary.
Before stating it, let us remark that if \(Y\) is a commutative
\(S\)-group, so is \(T_{Y/S}(M)\), then
\(H = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X, Y)\) and
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X, T_{Y/S}(M))\), and finally
\(T_{H/S}(M)\).

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.0.3.} \emph{Let \texttt{X,\ Y} be \(S\)-groups.
One has isomorphisms of \(S\)-functors, functorial in \(M\):}

\[
T_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X,Y)/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X, T_{Y/S}(M)).
\]

\emph{If \(Y\) is commutative, these are moreover isomorphisms of
abelian \(S\)-groups.}

\textbf{Definition 4.2.0.4.}\footnote{One has inserted here this
  definition, which in the original appeared in 4.3.} \emph{If \(Y\) is
an \texttt{O\_S}-module, the functor \(T_{Y/S}(M)\) (resp.
\(Lie(Y/S, M)\)) is equipped with an \texttt{O\_S}-module structure
deduced from that of \(Y\). Equipped with this structure, it will be
denoted \(T'_{Y/S}(M)\) (resp. \(Lie'(Y/S, M)\)).}

Consequently, if \texttt{X,\ Y} are \texttt{O\_S}-modules, then
\(T'_{Y/S}(M) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S}(M), Y)\) and
\(H = \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}-mod.}(X, Y)\), then
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}-mod.}(X, T'_{Y/S}(M))\) and \(T'_{H/S}(M)\),
are equipped with an \texttt{O\_S}-module structure, and one obtains
the:

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.0.5.} \emph{If \texttt{X,\ Y} are
\texttt{O\_S}-modules, one has isomorphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules,
functorial in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T′\_\{Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X, T′\_\{Y/S\}(M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 4.2.A.}\footnote{One has detailed the original in
  what follows; in particular, one has added Definition 4.2.A and Remark
  4.2.B.} \emph{Let \texttt{X,\ L} be \(S\)-groups, with \(X\) acting on
\(L\) by group automorphisms (cf.~I 2.3.5). One defines the subfunctor
\(Z^{1}_{S}(X, L)\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, L)\) as follows: for
every \(S' \to S\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Z¹\_S(X, L)(S′) = \{ φ ∈ Hom\_\{S′\}(X\_\{S′\}, L\_\{S′\}) | φ(x\_1 x\_2) = φ(x\_1) (x\_1 · φ(x\_2)),}
