\NormalTok{                                                 for all x\_1, x\_2 ∈ X(S″), S″ → S′ \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{It is called the ``functor of} \textbf{crossed homomorphisms}
\emph{from \(X\) to \(L\)``.}

\textbf{Remark 4.2.B.}\footnote{One has detailed the original in what
  follows; in particular, one has added Definition 4.2.A and Remark
  4.2.B.} \emph{a) If \(L'\) is a second \(S\)-group on which \(X\) acts
by group automorphisms, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Z¹\_S(X, L ×\_S L′) ≃ Z¹\_S(X, L) ×\_S Z¹\_S(X, L′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{b) If \(L\) is a \(G\)-\texttt{O\_S}-module, \(Z^{1}_{S}(X, L)\)
coincides with the kernel of the differential
\(\partial : \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, L) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X^{2}, L)\)
defined in I 5.1; in particular, \(Z^{1}_{S}(X, L)\) is in this case an
\texttt{O\_S}-module.}

\textbf{4.2.} Let \(u : X \to Y\) be a morphism of \(S\)-groups; then
\(L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X,Y)/S}(M)\) is described as
follows. First, one saw in 3.11.3 that one has an isomorphism of
\(S\)-functors, functorial in \(M\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)   L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_S(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Hom\_\{Y/S\}(X, T\_\{Y/S\}(M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, since \(Y\) is an \(S\)-group, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{Y/S\}(M) = Lie(Y/S, M) · Y = Lie(Y/S, M)\_Y;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

there follows an isomorphism of \(S\)-functors, functorial in \(M\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_S(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Hom\_S(X, Lie(Y/S, M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For every \(S' \to S\), let \(u' : X' \to Y'\) denote the morphism
deduced from \(u\) by base change. Consider the \(S\)-functor defined as
follows:\footnote{This is Definition 4.2.0.1 applied to \(Z = Y\) and to
  the \(Y\)-groups \(u : X \to Y\) and \(T_{Y/S}(M)\).} for every
\(S' \to S\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{(Y/S){-}gr.\}(X, Lie(Y/S, M) · Y)(S′) = Hom\_\{Y′{-}gr.\}(X′, (Lie(Y/S, M) · Y)\_\{S′\})}
\NormalTok{                                        = Hom\_\{Y′{-}gr.\}(X′, Lie(Y′/S′, M) · Y′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then one sees easily that the isomorphism (†) induces an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†′)   L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Hom\_\{(Y/S){-}gr.\}(X, Lie(Y/S, M) · Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ──u──→ Y ──Ad──→ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Lie(Y/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defines an action of \(X\) on \(L = Lie(Y/S, M)\) by group
automorphisms.

If \(\Phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_{Y/S}(X, Lie(Y/S, M) \cdot Y)\), then,
for every \(S'' \to S' \to S\) and \(x \in X(S'')\), one can write in a
unique manner

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Φ(S′)(x) = φ(S′)(x) · u′(x),    where φ(S′)(x) ∈ Lie(Y′/S′, M)(S″);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

this determines an element \(\phi\) of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, Lie(Y/S, M))\). Then \(\Phi(S')\) is a
morphism of groups if, and only if, for all \(x_{1}, x_{2} \in X(S'')\)
one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ(S′)(x\_1 x\_2) = φ(S′)(x\_1) ( u(x\_1) φ(S′)(x\_2) u(x\_1)\^{}\{{-}1\} )}
\NormalTok{              = φ(S′)(x\_1) (x\_1 · φ(S′)(x\_2)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e., if and only if \(\phi \in Z^{1}_{S}(X, Lie(Y/S, M))\). One has
thus obtained the:

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) be a morphism of
\(S\)-groups. One has an isomorphism of \(S\)-functors, functorial in
\(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Z¹\_S(X, Lie(Y/S, M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has added the sentences that follow and Proposition 4.2
  bis, implicit in the original.} Suppose further that \(Y/S\) satisfies
(E). Then it follows from 4.2.0.3, exactly as in the proof of 3.11.1,
that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X, Y)/S\) satisfies (E). So one has
(cf.~3.5.1):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M ⊕ N) ≃ L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ×\_S L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(N).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(This also follows from 4.2 and 4.2.B a).) Consequently,
\(L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X,Y)/S}(M)\) is equipped, like
\(Z^{1}_{S}(X, Lie(Y/S, M))\) (cf.~4.2.B b)), with an
\texttt{O\_S}-module structure, deduced from functoriality in \(M\). One
deduces that the isomorphism of 4.2 is, in this case, an isomorphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules:

\textbf{Proposition 4.2 bis.}\footnote{One has added the sentences that
  follow and Proposition 4.2 bis, implicit in the original.} \emph{Let
\(u : X \to Y\) be a morphism of \(S\)-groups; suppose that \(Y/S\)
satisfies (E). One has an isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules,
functorial in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Z¹\_S(X, Lie(Y/S, M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, when \(Y/S\) satisfies (E), one deduces from 3.13.1, exactly
as in the proof of 3.13.2, that for every \(u \in Isom_{S-gr.}(X, Y)\)
one has an isomorphism functorial in \(M\):

\[
(\ast)   L^{u}_{Isom_{S-gr.}(X,Y)/S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} L^{u}_{\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X,Y)/S}(M).
\]

One deduces from this the following two corollaries.

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.1.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) be a morphism of
\(S\)-groups; if \(Y/S\) satisfies (E), one has an isomorphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules, functorial in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\^{}u\_\{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Z¹\_S(X, Lie(Y/S, M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.2.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-group; if \(X/S\)
satisfies (E), one has an isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules,
functorial in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X)/S, M) ⥲ Z¹\_S(X, Lie(X/S, M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has added the sentence that follows.} Moreover, if \(Y\)
is commutative, the adjoint action of \(Y\) on \(L = Lie(X/S, M)\) is
trivial, whence \(Z^{1}_{S}(X, L) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(X, L)\).
Therefore:

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.3.} \emph{Let \(Y\) be a commutative \(S\)-group;
one has an isomorphism of \(S\)-functors, functorial in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(X, Lie(Y/S, M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{4.3.} Consider now the case where \(X\) and \(Y\) are
\texttt{O\_S}-modules. Recall (cf.~4.2.0.4) that one writes
\(T'_{Y/S}(M)\) (resp. \(Lie'(Y/S, M)\)) for the functor \(T_{Y/S}(M)\)
(resp. \(Lie(Y/S, M)\)) equipped with the \texttt{O\_S}-module structure
deduced from that of \(Y\).

When \(Y/S\) satisfies (E), we shall always write \(Lie(Y/S, M)\) for
the functor \(Lie(Y/S, M)\) equipped with the \texttt{O\_S}-module
structure defined for every functor satisfying (E). In this case, we
know (cf.~3.9) that the abelian-group structures of \(Lie(Y/S, M)\) and
\(Lie'(Y/S, M)\) coincide, but the same is not a priori true for those
of module (see a counterexample in §6.3). For every \(S' \to S\) and
\(a \in O(S')\), we shall write \(a \cdot' m\) (resp. \(a \cdot m\)) for
the action of \(a\) on \(m \in Lie'(Y/S, M)(S')\) (resp. on
\(m \in Lie(Y/S, M)(S')\)), and similarly for the action of \(a\) on
\(T'_{Y/S}(M)\) and \(T_{Y/S}(M)\).

One has \(T'_{Y/S}(M) \simeq Lie'(Y/S, M) \oplus Y\) as
\texttt{O\_S}-modules; consequently one obtains, exactly as for
Propositions 4.2 and 4.2 bis, the:

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) be a morphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules. One has an isomorphism of \(S\)-functors,
functorial in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)   L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) ⥲ Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X, Lie′(Y/S, M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has added the sentence that follows.} \emph{If \(Y/S\)
satisfies (E), then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}-mod.}(X, Y)/S\)
satisfies (E) and (∗) is an isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules when
one equips both sides with the \texttt{O\_S}-module structure deduced
from functoriality in \(M\).}\footnote{Note that on the right-hand term,
  this is the structure defined by \((a\phi)(x) = a \cdot \phi(x)\),
  where \(a \cdot \phi(x)\) denotes the action of \(a\) on
  \(\phi(x) \in Lie(Y/S, M)\). This differs from the action
  \((a \cdot' \phi)(x) = a \cdot' \phi(x) = \phi(ax)\), but coincides
  with it if \(Lie(Y/S, M) = Lie'(Y/S, M)\).}

\textbf{Remark 4.3 bis.}\footnote{One has added this remark, which will
  be useful in 4.5.1.} Let \(u : X \to Y\) be a morphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules; denote by \(\tau_{u}\) the map which to every
morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules \(\phi : X \to Lie'(Y/S, M)\)
associates the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u ⊕ φ : X ⟶ T′\_\{Y/S\}(M) = Y ⊕ Lie′(Y/S, M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then the isomorphism of 4.3 fits into the following commutative diagram,
functorial in \(M\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M)  ⥲  Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X, Lie′(Y/S, M))}
\NormalTok{            │                                     │}
\NormalTok{            ↓                                     ↓ τ\_u}
\NormalTok{   T\_\{Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M)    ⥲   Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X, T′\_\{Y/S\}(M)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, when \(Y/S\) satisfies (E), one deduces from 3.13.1, exactly
as in the proof of 3.13.2, that for every
\(u \in Isom_{O_{S}-mod.}(X, Y)\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)   L\^{}u\_\{Isom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M) = L\^{}u\_\{Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X,Y)/S\}(M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.1.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \texttt{O\_S}-module
satisfying (E) with respect to \(S\). One has an isomorphism functorial
in \(M\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X)/S, M) ⥲ Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X, Lie′(X/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which respects the \texttt{O\_S}-module structures deduced from
functoriality in \(M\).}\footnote{Cf. N.D.E. (61). Moreover, one has
  added the sentence that follows, as well as its proof.} \emph{In
particular, \(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(X)/S\) satisfies (E).}

\emph{Proof.} The first assertion follows from (∗) and 4.3; let us prove
the second. As \(X/S\) satisfies (E), one has isomorphisms of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules
\texttt{Lie′(X/S,\ M\ ⊕\ N)\ ≃\ Lie′(X/S,\ M)\ ×\_S\ Lie′(X/S,\ N)}, and
thus:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X)/S, M ⊕ N) ≃}
\NormalTok{   Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X)/S, M) ×\_S Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(X)/S, N).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Taking 4.1.1.2 a) into account, this proves that
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(X)/S\) satisfies (E).

\textbf{4.3.2.} Before continuing in this direction, let us examine more
closely the relations between \(Y\), \(Lie(Y/S)\) and \(Lie'(Y/S)\). Let
us remark first that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   Lie(O\_S/S, M) = Lie′(O\_S/S, M) = W(M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(where \(W(M)\) is defined in I 4.6) and that one therefore has a
canonical isomorphism

\[
(2)   d : O_{S} \xrightarrow{\sim} Lie(O_{S}/S).
\]

Let now \(F\) be an \texttt{O\_S}-module. For every
\(S_{2} \to S_{1} \to S\)\footnote{One has changed \(S' \to S\) to
  \(S_{2} \to S_{1} \to S\), because one must let \texttt{S\_2} and
  \texttt{S\_1} vary (cf. below). Moreover, one has detailed the
  original in what follows.}, one has a dihomomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)   ⎰ F(S\_1) → F(S\_2)}
\NormalTok{       ⎱ O(S\_1) → O(S\_2),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence a morphism of \(O(S_{2})\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S\_1) ⊗\_\{O(S\_1)\} O(S\_2) ⟶ F(S\_2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, setting \(S_{1} = S'\) and \(S_{2} = I_{S'}(M)\), one
deduces morphisms of \(O(S')\)-modules, functorial in \(M\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S′) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} T\_\{O\_S/S\}(M)(S′) ⟶ T′\_\{F/S\}(M)(S′);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

letting \(S'\) vary, one obtains morphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules,
functorial in \(M\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4)   F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} T\_\{O\_S/S\}(M) ⟶ T′\_\{F/S\}(M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

These morphisms are functorial in \(M\), hence compatible with the
projections of the tangent bundles onto their bases; they therefore
define morphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(5)   F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ⟶ Lie′(F/S, M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that one has the commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   0 ─→ F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ─→ F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} T\_\{O\_S/S\}(M) ─→ F ─→ 0}
\NormalTok{                ↓                              ↓                 ↓}
\NormalTok{   0 ─────→ Lie′(F/S, M)   ──────→     T′\_\{F/S\}(M)   ────→ F ─→ 0 .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One may consider the morphisms (5) as morphisms of abelian \(S\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(6)   F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ⟶ Lie(F/S, M);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

tensoring \(F\) with the isomorphism
\(d : O_{S} \xrightarrow{\sim} Lie(O_{S}/S)\), one deduces (for
\(M = O_{S}\)) a morphism of abelian \(S\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(7)   F ⥲ F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S) ⟶ Lie(F/S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

also denoted \(d : F \to Lie(F/S)\).

\textbf{Remark 4.3.3.}\footnote{One found in the original the assertion
  that when \(F/S\) satisfies (E), the morphisms (6) (and hence (7)) are
  morphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules, assertion contradicted by a
  counterexample given in 6.3. One has deleted this assertion, inserted
  here the example just mentioned, and modified Definition 4.4
  accordingly. This is without consequence for the sequel.} When \(F/S\)
satisfies (E), the morphisms (6) and (7) are not necessarily morphisms
of \texttt{O\_S}-modules, when one equips both sides with the module
structures deduced from that of \(M\) thanks to condition (E).

For example, let \(k\) be a field of characteristic \(p > 0\),
\(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), and let \(F\) be the
\texttt{O\_S}-module which to every \(S\)-scheme \(T\) associates
\(F(T) = \Gamma(T, O_{T})\) equipped with the \(O(T)\)-module structure
obtained by making scalars act through the \(p\)-th power, i.e.,
\(r \cdot f = r^{p} f\), for \(r \in O(T)\), \(f \in F(T)\). As
\(S\)-functor of groups, \(F\) is isomorphic to \(G_{a, S}\). Therefore
\(F\) satisfies (E) and \(Lie(F/S)\) is identified with
\(Lie(G_{a, S}/S) \cong O_{S}\). Then, the canonical morphism
\(d : F \to Lie(F/S)\) is, for every \(T \to S\), the identity map
\(F(T) \to O(T)\): it indeed respects the abelian-group structure but
not the \texttt{O\_S}-module structure.

\textbf{Remark 4.3.4.}\footnote{One has added this remark, which will be
  useful in 4.6.2.} One can make the morphisms (4) and (5) explicit as
follows. The morphism
\(\Theta : F \otimes_{O_{S}} T_{O_{S}/S}(M) \to T'_{F/S}(M) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S}(M), F)\)
is defined by: for every \(S' \to S\), \(\alpha \in O(I_{S'}(M))\), and
\(f : S' \to F\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Θ(f ⊗ α) = α · (τ\_0 ∘ f) = α · (f ∘ ρ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\tau_{0}\) is the null section \(F \to T'_{F/S}(M)\) and
\(\rho\) the structural morphism \(I_{S'}(M) \to S'\). Then \(\Theta\)
induces a morphism
\(\theta : F \otimes_{O_{S}} Lie(O_{S}/S, M) \to Lie'(F/S, M)\); this
follows from the ``functoriality in \(M\)'' already mentioned after (4),
and can be seen explicitly as follows. On the one hand, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie′(F/S, M)(S′) = \{ φ ∈ Hom\_S(I\_\{S′\}(M), F) | φ ∘ ε\_M = e \},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(e\) denotes the unit section \(S' \to F\). On the other hand,
\(Lie(O_{S}/S, M)(S') = \Gamma(S', M)\) is the kernel of the
augmentation \(\eta : O(I_{S'}(M)) \to O(S')\), and it is therefore a
question of seeing that if \(f \in F(S')\) and
\(\alpha \in \Gamma(S', M)\), then
\(\alpha \cdot (f \circ \rho) \circ \epsilon_{M} = e\).

Consider the dihomomorphism (3), in the case where \(S_{2} \to S_{1}\)
is the \(S\)-morphism \(\epsilon_{M} : S' \to I_{S'}(M)\); one has then
a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       F(ε\_M)}
\NormalTok{   F(I\_\{S′\}(M)) ─────────────→ F(S′)}
\NormalTok{        │ α                       │ η(α)}
\NormalTok{        ↓        F(ε\_M)           ↓}
\NormalTok{   F(I\_\{S′\}(M)) ─────────────→ F(S′) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For every \(\phi : I_{S'}(M) \to F\), one therefore has
\((\alpha \cdot \phi) \circ \epsilon_{M} = \eta(\alpha) \cdot (\phi \circ \epsilon_{M})\),
whence \((\alpha \cdot \phi) \circ \epsilon_{M} = e\) if
\(\eta(\alpha) = 0\).

In particular, taking \(M = t O_{S}\), one has
\(Lie(O_{S}/S) = t O_{S}\) and the morphism \(F \to Lie'(F/S)\) is given
by \(f \mapsto t \cdot (f \circ \rho)\).

\textbf{Remark 4.3.5.}\footnote{One has added this remark, which will be
  useful in 4.5 and 4.7.} Let \(F\) be an \texttt{O\_S}-module, set
\(E = \operatorname{End}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)\) and denote by \(d_{F}\) and
\(d_{E}\) the morphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules given by 4.3.2 (5):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d\_F : F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ⟶ Lie′(F/S, M),}
\NormalTok{d\_E : E ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ⟶ Lie′(E/S, M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One deduces from 4.3.4 the following commutative diagram of morphisms of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                      d\_E}
\NormalTok{   E ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ──────────────→ Lie′(E/S, M)}
\NormalTok{                                                  ↑ ≃ (∗)}
\NormalTok{                                      d\_F}
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{O\_S\}(F, F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M)) ─→ Hom\_\{O\_S\}(F, Lie′(F/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the right vertical arrow is the isomorphism (∗) of 4.3. Therefore
(loc. cit.), if \(F/S\) satisfies (E), then \(E/S\) satisfies (E) and
(∗) is also an isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules when one equips the
right-hand terms with the \texttt{O\_S}-module structure deduced from
(E).

\textbf{Remark 4.4.0.}\footnote{Taking into account the modifications in
  Definition 4.4 (cf.~N.D.E. (65)), one has inserted here this remark,
  which in the original figured in the proof of 4.4.1.} In 4.3.2, the
morphisms (4) are isomorphisms if and only if the morphisms (5) are.
Moreover, if these conditions are verified, then \(F/S\) satisfies (E).
Indeed, it suffices to verify that
\texttt{Lie′(F/S,\ M\ ⊕\ N)\ ≃\ Lie′(F/S,\ M)\ ×\_S\ Lie′(F/S,\ N)}. Now
one has the commutative diagram below, where by hypothesis the
horizontal arrows are isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M ⊕ N)  ⥲  Lie′(F/S, M ⊕ N)}
\NormalTok{              │ ≀                          │}
\NormalTok{              ↓                            ↓}
\NormalTok{   F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} (Lie(O\_S/S, M) ×\_S Lie(O\_S/S, N))  ⥲  Lie′(F/S, M) ×\_S Lie′(F/S, N);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the second vertical arrow is therefore also an isomorphism, i.e.~\(F/S\)
satisfies (E).

\textbf{Definition 4.4.} \emph{One says that \(F\) is a} \textbf{good
\texttt{O\_S}-module} \emph{if the morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} T\_\{O\_S/S\}(M) ⟶ T\_\{F/S\}(M)}
\NormalTok{or, equivalently,}
\NormalTok{F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ⟶ Lie(F/S, M),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are isomorphisms of abelian \(S\)-groups (so that \(F/S\)
satisfies (E)) and if moreover they respect the \texttt{O\_S}-module
structures deduced from condition (E).}

\textbf{Corollary 4.4.1.}\footnote{The original showed that (i) implies
  (ii) and (iii); one has added the implication (ii) ⇒ (i).} \emph{Let
\(F\) be an \texttt{O\_S}-module. Consider the following conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(F\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module.}

\emph{(ii) \(F/S\) satisfies (E) and \(d : F \to Lie(F/S)\) is an
isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules.}

\emph{(iii) \(Lie(F/S, M) = Lie'(F/S, M)\).}

\emph{Then one has (i) ⇔ (ii) ⇒ (iii).}

\emph{Proof.} (i) ⇒ (ii) follows from the definition. To prove (ii) ⇒
(i), one must show that the morphisms of abelian \(S\)-groups
(functorial in \(M\))

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ⥲ Lie(F/S, M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are isomorphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules. Since \(F/S\) satisfies (E),
both sides transform finite direct sums of copies of \texttt{O\_S} into
finite products of abelian \(S\)-groups. This reduces us to the case
\(M = O_{S}\), which follows from the hypothesis.

Finally, (i) ⇒ (iii) follows from the definition and from the fact that
the isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ⥲ Lie′(F/S, M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

of 4.3.2 (5) are morphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules.

\textbf{Examples 4.4.2.} \emph{For every quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_S}-Module \(E\), the \texttt{O\_S}-modules \(V(E)\) and
\(W(E)\) defined in I 4.6 are good.}

\footnote{One has added what follows.} Indeed, for every
\(f : S' \to S\), the morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V(E)(S′) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} O(I\_\{S′\}(M)) ⟶ T\_\{V(E)/S\}(M)(S′)}
\NormalTok{W(E)(S′) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} O(I\_\{S′\}(M)) ⟶ T\_\{W(E)/S\}(M)(S′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

correspond, respectively, to the morphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{S′\}{-}mod.\}(f\^{}*(E), O\_\{S′\}) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} Γ(S′, D\_\{O\_\{S′\}\}(M))}
\NormalTok{   ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_\{S′\}{-}mod.\}(f\^{}*(E), D\_\{O\_\{S′\}\}(M))}
\NormalTok{Γ(S′, f\^{}*(E)) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} Γ(S′, D\_\{O\_\{S′\}\}(M))}
\NormalTok{   ⟶ Γ(S′, f\^{}*(E) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S′\}\} D\_\{O\_\{S′\}\}(M));}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

these are isomorphisms, since \(D_{O_{S'}}(M)\) is isomorphic, as
\(O_{S'}\)-module, to a finite direct sum of copies of \(O_{S'}\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.} \emph{Let \(F\) be a good
\texttt{O\_S}-module. Then:}

\emph{(i) \(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)/S\) satisfies (E) and one
has a functorial isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)/S, M) ⥲ Hom\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F, Lie(F/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which respects the \texttt{O\_S}-module structures deduced from
condition (E). In particular, one has an isomorphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)/S) ⥲ End\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii)}\footnote{One has added the point (ii), immediate consequence
  of what precedes.} \emph{Moreover,
\(\operatorname{End}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module.}

Indeed, by 4.4.1, \(F/S\) satisfies (E) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   Lie(F/S, M) = Lie′(F/S, M) ≃ F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Assertion (i) then follows from 4.3.1. Set
\(E = \operatorname{End}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)\). By (1) and Remark 4.3.5, one
has the following commutative diagram of morphisms of abelian
\(S\)-groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                              d\_E}
\NormalTok{   End\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F) ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M) ────→ Lie(End\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)/S, M)}
\NormalTok{                                                            ↑ ≃ (∗)}
\NormalTok{                                              d\_F}
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{O\_S\}(F, F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} Lie(O\_S/S, M)) ────→ Hom\_\{O\_S\}(F, Lie(F/S, M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(d_{F}\) and (∗) are isomorphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules;
consequently, so is \(d_{E}\). This proves (ii).

\textbf{Scholie 4.5.1.}\footnote{One has added this scholie, implicit in
  the original, which will be useful in 4.7.1. (Here and in the sequel,
  one writes \(t, t'\), etc. for variables of square zero, the letter
  \(\epsilon\) being reserved for the unit section of groups.)} Set
(cf.~2.1) \(O_{I_{S}} = O_{S} \oplus t O_{S}\) (with \(t^{2} = 0\)), and
let \(F\) be a good \texttt{O\_S}-module. Then, for every \(S' \to S\),
the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S′) ⊕ t F(S′) = F(S′) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} O(I\_\{S′\}) ⟶ F(I\_\{S′\}) = F(S′) ⊕ Lie(F/S)(S′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(which is the identity on \(F(S')\)) induces an isomorphism of
\(O(S')\)-modules \(t F(S') \simeq Lie(F/S)(S')\). Letting \(S'\) vary,
one obtains an isomorphism which one may write \(Lie(F/S) \simeq t F\).

For every \(S' \to S\), one has therefore, by 4.5, a commutative
diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   End\_\{O\_\{S′\}{-}mod.\}(F\_\{S′\}) ⥲ Hom\_\{O\_\{S′\}{-}mod.\}(F\_\{S′\}, t F\_\{S′\}) ⥲ Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)/S)(S′)}
\NormalTok{              │                            │                                       │}
\NormalTok{              ↓                            ↓                                       ↓}
\NormalTok{                       Aut\_\{O\_\{I\_\{S′\}\}{-}mod.\}(F\_\{I\_\{S′\}\})              T\_\{Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)/S\}(S′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one deduces from 4.3 bis that every
\(X \in \operatorname{End}_{O_{S'}-mod.}(F_{S'})\) corresponds to the
element \(id + t X\) of
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{I_{S'}}-mod.}(F_{I_{S'}})\).

\textbf{Definition 4.6.} \emph{One says that the \(S\)-functor of groups
\(G\) is} \textbf{good} \emph{if \(G/S\) satisfies condition (E) and if
\(Lie(G/S)\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module.}

\footnote{One has added the sentence that follows.} Note that if \(F\)
is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module, it is a good \(S\)-group; indeed \(F/S\)
satisfies (E) and \(Lie(F/S) \simeq F\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module.

\textbf{Example 4.6.1.} \emph{If \(G\) is representable, it is good.
Indeed, \(G/S\) satisfies (E) and \(Lie(G/S)\) is of the form \(V(E)\),
hence good, by 4.4.2.}

\textbf{Lemma 4.6.2.}\footnote{One has added this lemma.} \emph{Let
\(G\) be an \(S\)-functor of groups such that \(G/S\) satisfies (E), and
let \(F = Lie(G/S)\). Then \(F\) satisfies (E) and the morphism of
abelian groups \(d : F \to Lie(F/S)\) respects the \texttt{O\_S}-module
structures.}

\emph{Consequently, \(G\) is good if and only if \(F \to Lie(F/S)\) is
bijective.}

\emph{Proof.} Suppose that \(G/S\) satisfies (E). Let \texttt{M,\ N} be
free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite rank. Write \(F(N) = Lie(G/S, N)\)
and \(e\) the unit section of \(G\).

For every \(S' \to S\), one has
\(F(N)(S') = { g \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S'}(N), G) | g \circ \epsilon_{N} = e}\)
and \(Lie(F(N)/S, M)(S') = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(I_{S'}(M), F(N))\) is
identified with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\{ Φ ∈ Hom\_S(I\_\{S′\}(N) ×\_\{S′\} I\_\{S′\}(M), G) |}
\NormalTok{       Φ ∘ (ε\_N × id\_\{I\_\{S′\}(M)\}) = e ∈ G(I\_\{S′\}(M)),}
\NormalTok{       Φ ∘ (id\_\{I\_\{S′\}(N)\} × ε\_M) = e ∈ G(I\_\{S′\}(N)) \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This shows that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   Lie(F(N)/S, M) ≃ Lie(F(M)/S, N).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

As \(G/S\) satisfies (E), one deduces:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(F(N)/S, M\_1 ⊕ M\_2) ≃ Lie(F(M\_1 ⊕ M\_2)/S, N)}
\NormalTok{                       ≃ Lie((F(M\_1) ×\_S F(M\_2))/S, N).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 3.8, the right-hand term is isomorphic to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(F(M\_1)/S, N) ×\_S Lie(F(M\_2)/S, N) ≃ Lie(F(N)/S, M\_1) ×\_S Lie(F(N)/S, M\_2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   Lie(F(N)/S, M\_1 ⊕ M\_2) ≃ Lie(F(N)/S, M\_1) ×\_S Lie(F(N)/S, M\_2),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \(F(N)/S\) satisfies (E), by Remark 4.1.1.2 a).

Let us now show that the morphism of abelian groups
\(d : F(N) \to Lie(F(N)/S)\) respects the \texttt{O\_S}-module
structures. Consider the free \texttt{O\_S}-module \(M = t O_{S}\), so
that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{O(I\_\{S′\}(M)) = O(S′)[t]/(t²) = O(S′) ⊕ t O(S′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(Lie(O_{S}/S) \simeq t O_{S}\). We denote by \(\rho_{t}\) the
structural morphism \(I_{S}(M) \to S\), which corresponds to the
injection
\(u_{t} : O_{S} \hookrightarrow D_{O_{S}}(M) = O_{S} \oplus t O_{S}\).
Recall (cf.~3.4.2) that, for every \(S\)-functor \(X\),
\(F(N)(X) = Lie(G/S, N)(X)\) is the set of \(S\)-morphisms
\(\phi : I_{X}(N) \to G\) such that \(\phi \circ \epsilon_{N} = e\), and
that the action of \(a \in O(X)\) is given by
\(a \cdot \phi = \phi \circ a^{*}\), where \(a^{*}\) is the endomorphism
of \(I_{X}(N)\) associated with \(a\), cf.~2.1.3.

Consequently, by 4.3.4, the morphism
\(d : F(N) \xrightarrow{\sim} F(N) \otimes_{O_{S}} t O_{S} \to Lie(F(N)/S)\)
is given by: for every \(S' \to S\) and
\(f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(S', F(N))\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ↦ f ⊗ t ↦ t · (f ∘ ρ\_t) = f ∘ ρ\_t ∘ t\^{}*,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where, in the last term, \(f \circ \rho_{t} \in F(N)(I_{S'}(M))\) is
considered as an \(S\)-morphism \(\phi : I_{I_{S'}(M)}(N) \to G\) (such
that \(\phi \circ \epsilon_{N} = e\)). It is a question of seeing that
\(d\) is a morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules, i.e., that
\(d(a \cdot f) = u_{t}(a) \cdot d(f)\) for every \(a \in O(S')\).

Considering \(f \in F(N)(S')\) as a morphism \(I_{S'}(N) \to G\), one
has likewise \(a \cdot f = f \circ a^{*}\). On the other hand, by the
functoriality in \(X\) of the action of \(O(X)\) on \(I_{X}(N)\)
(cf.~2.1.3), one has the commutative diagram below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          a\^{}*}
\NormalTok{   I\_\{S′\}(N) ─────────────────→ I\_\{S′\}(N)}
\NormalTok{       ↑                              ↑}
\NormalTok{       ρ\_t                            ρ\_t}
\NormalTok{                       u\_t(a)\^{}*}
\NormalTok{   I\_\{I\_\{S′\}(M)\}(N) ─────────────→ I\_\{I\_\{S′\}(M)\}(N) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d(a · f) = f ∘ a\^{}* ∘ ρ\_t ∘ t\^{}* = f ∘ ρ\_t ∘ u\_t(a)\^{}* ∘ t\^{}* = f ∘ ρ\_t ∘ t\^{}* ∘ u\_t(a)\^{}* = u\_t(a) · d(f)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(the second-to-last equality resulting from the fact that \(O\) is
commutative). This completes the proof of Lemma 4.6.2.

\textbf{Theorem 4.7.} \emph{If \(F\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module, the
\(S\)-group \(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)\) is good.}

\footnote{One has simplified the original, using the additions made in
  4.3.1 and 4.5.} Indeed, by 4.5,
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)/S\) satisfies (E) and
\texttt{Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S-mod.\}(F)/S)\ ≃\ End\_\{O\_S-mod.\}(F)} is a
good \texttt{O\_S}-module.

\textbf{4.7.1.}\footnote{One has added the numbering 4.7.1, 4.7.2,
  4.7.3.} Let now \(G\) be an \(S\)-group and \(F\) a good
\texttt{O\_S}-module. Suppose given a linear representation of \(G\) in
\(F\), that is to say (I 4.7.1), a morphism of \(S\)-groups

\[
\rho : G \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F).
\]

If \(G/S\) satisfies (E), one deduces from 4.1.C and 4.5 a morphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules, denoted \(\rho'\) or \(d\rho\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(G/S) ⟶ Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)/S) ≃ End\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has added the sentence that follows.} Moreover, setting
\(O_{I_{S}} = O_{S} \oplus t O_{S}\) (with \(t^{2} = 0\)), one deduces
from 4.5.1 that, if \(S' \to S\) and
\(X \in Lie(G/S)(S') \subset G(I_{S'})\), then one has in
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{I_{S'}}-mod.}(F_{I_{S'}})\) the following
equality:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)   ρ(X) = id + t ρ′(X),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~for every \(S'' \to I_{S'}\) and \(f \in F(S'')\), one has in
\(F(S'')\) the equality \(\rho(X)(f) = f + t \rho'(X)(f)\).

\textbf{Definition 4.7.2.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a good \(S\)-group. Then
\(Lie(G/S)\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module, and one has a morphism of
\(S\)-groups \texttt{Ad\ :\ G\ →\ Aut\_\{O\_S-mod.\}(Lie(G/S))}. One
deduces from 4.7.1 a morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ad : Lie(G/S) ⟶ End\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(Lie(G/S)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{or, what amounts to the same, an \texttt{O\_S}-bilinear morphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(G/S) ×\_S Lie(G/S) ⟶ Lie(G/S),    (x, y) ↦ [x, y] = ad(x) · y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(where \(x\) and \(y\) denote two arbitrary elements of
\(Lie(G/S)(S') = Lie(G_{S'}/S')(S')\)). If \(G\) is commutative, then
\([x, y] = 0\).}

\textbf{4.7.3.} One can give an equivalent definition of the bracket as
follows: let us remark first that it suffices to do it for
\(x, y \in Lie(G/S)(S)\). Let us remark next that there is a canonical
isomorphism \(I_{S} \times_{S} I_{S} \simeq I_{I_{S}}\); to avoid
confusions, let us denote by \(I\) and \(I'\) two copies of
\texttt{I\_S} and set \(O_{I} = O_{S}[t]\), \(O_{I'} = O_{S}[t']\),
where \(t^{2} = 0 = t'^{2}\). One has then a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   I × I′ ──→ I′}
\NormalTok{     │         │}
\NormalTok{     ↓         ↓}
\NormalTok{     I  ────→  S ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the two arrows starting from \(I \times I'\) identifying it with the
scheme of dual numbers over \(I\) or over \(I'\). There follows a
commutative diagram of groups (where one writes \(L = Lie(G/S)\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                  1            1}
\NormalTok{                                  │            │}
\NormalTok{                                  ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{                                L(I) ──────→ L(S) ─→ 1}
\NormalTok{                                  │            │}
\NormalTok{   1 ─→ L(I′) ─→ G(I × I′) ─→ G(I′) ─→ 1}
\NormalTok{(1)            │            │}
\NormalTok{                                  ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{   1 ─→ L(S) ─→ G(I) ─→ G(S) ─→ 1}
\NormalTok{                                  │            │}
\NormalTok{                                  ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{                                  1            1 .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The ninth piece of the puzzle is nothing other than \(Lie(L/S)(S)\). If
\(G\) is good, this is \(L(S)\) and one has therefore the following
commutative diagram, where the lines and columns are exact sequences of
groups, the five \(L(-)\) are commutative,\footnote{One has detailed the
  original in what follows.} and where, taking into account the
identification \(L(I) = L(S) \oplus t L(S)\) (resp.
\(L(I') = L(S) \oplus t' L(S)\)), the injection
\(L(S) \hookrightarrow L(I)\) (resp. \(L(S) \hookrightarrow L(I')\)) is
given by \(u \mapsto t u\) (resp. \(u \mapsto t' u\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          t}
\NormalTok{   z ∈ L(S) ────────→ L(I) ─────→ L(S) ∋ x}
\NormalTok{       │ t′                          │}
\NormalTok{       ↓                             ↓}
\NormalTok{   L(I′) ────→ G(I × I′) ────→ G(I′)}
\NormalTok{       │                             │}
\NormalTok{       ↓                             ↓}
\NormalTok{   y ∈ L(S) ─────→ G(I) ─────→ G(S) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now in such a diagram, if one takes two elements \(x\) and \(y\) as
marked, and one lifts arbitrarily \(x\) resp. \(y\) to an element
\(\tilde{x} \in L(I)\) resp. \(y' \in L(I')\), the commutator
\(\tilde{x} y' \tilde{x}^{-1} y'^{-1}\) in \(G(I \times I')\) does not
depend on the chosen lifts and is the image of an element \(z\) as
marked. The reader will verify that one has \(z = [x, y]\).\footnote{The
  original indicated in a footnote: ``(∗) The author acknowledges, at
  Gabriel's request, that the exercise is not immediate; this is
  moreover the reason why it is not in the text''. One has given the
  details, taking into account the addition made in 4.7.1; see also
  {[}DG70{]}, § II.4, 4.2.}

Indeed, if one still denotes by \(x\) the image of \(x\) by the
canonical section \(L(S) \to L(I)\) (and likewise for \(y\)), then
\(\tilde{x} = xu\) and \(y' = yv\), with
\(u, v \in L(S) = L(I) \cap L(I')\), and since \(L(I)\) and \(L(I')\)
are commutative one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x̃ y′ x̃\^{}\{{-}1\} y′\^{}\{{-}1\} = x u y v u\^{}\{{-}1\} x\^{}\{{-}1\} v\^{}\{{-}1\} y\^{}\{{-}1\}}
\NormalTok{                     = x u y u\^{}\{{-}1\} v x\^{}\{{-}1\} v\^{}\{{-}1\} y\^{}\{{-}1\}}
\NormalTok{                     = x y x\^{}\{{-}1\} y\^{}\{{-}1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, this element is sent to the unit element of \(G(I)\) and of
\(G(I')\), hence comes from a (unique) \(z\) as indicated. Finally,
considering \(y\) (resp. \(x\)) as an element of \(L_{I'}(I')\) (resp.
of \(L(S) \subset G(I')\)), one has by 4.7.1 (∗):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x y x\^{}\{{-}1\} = Ad(x)(y) = (id + t′ ad(x))(y) = y + t′ [x, y],}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so the element \(x y x^{-1} y^{-1}\) of \(L(I')\) is the image of the
element \(z = [x, y]\) of \(L(S)\).

On this construction the following two properties appear:

\emph{(i) the bracket is ``functorial in \(G\)'':} precisely,
\(G \mapsto Lie(G/S)\) is a functor from the category of good
\(S\)-groups to the category of good \texttt{O\_S}-modules equipped with
an \texttt{O\_S}-bilinear composition law.

\emph{(ii) One has \([x, y] + [y, x] = 0\):} indeed the diagram is
symmetric with respect to the first diagonal.\footnote{I.e. \(x\) and
  \(y\) play symmetric roles: the image in \(G(I \times I')\) of
  \texttt{{[}y,\ x{]}} equals the commutator
  \(y' \tilde{x} y'^{-1} \tilde{x}^{-1}\), which is the inverse of
  \(\tilde{x} y' \tilde{x}^{-1} y'^{-1} = [x, y]\). On the other hand
  (cf.~4.10 below), one does not know whether one necessarily has
  \([x, x] = 0\): if one considers \(x\) as an element
  \(\tilde{x} \in L(I)\) (resp. \(x' \in L(I')\)) it is not a priori
  clear that \(\tilde{x}\) and \(x'\) commute. . .}

\textbf{Proposition 4.8.} \emph{Let \(F\) be a good
\texttt{O\_S}-module. Via the identification}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)/S) = End\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(g) · Y = g ∘ Y ∘ g\^{}\{{-}1\}    and    [X, Y] = X ∘ Y − Y ∘ X,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(S' \to S\),
\(g \in \operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S'}-mod.}(F_{S'})\), and
\texttt{X,\ Y\ ∈\ Lie(Aut\_\{O\_S-mod.\}(F)/S)(S′)\ =\ End\_\{O\_\{S′\}-mod.\}(F\_\{S′\})}.}

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{One has detailed and simplified the original in
  what follows.} By base change, one reduces to \(S' = S\), which
permits one to lighten the notation. Set \(I = I_{S}\) and
\(O_{I} = O_{S}[t]\) (with \(t^{2} = 0\)). Recall (cf.~4.5.1) that the
inclusion
\texttt{i\ :\ End\_\{O\_S-mod.\}(F)\ ↪\ Aut\_\{O\_I-mod.\}(F\_I)} sends
\(Y\) to \(id + t Y\). Then, by definition of \(Ad(g)\) (cf.~4.1.A), one
has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{id + t Ad(g)(Y) = g ∘ (id + t Y) ∘ g\^{}\{{-}1\} = id + t (g ∘ Y ∘ g\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(Ad(g)(Y) = g \circ Y \circ g^{-1}\).

Let \(I'\) be a second copy of \texttt{I\_S}, set \(O_{I'} = O_{S}[t']\)
(with \(t'^{2} = 0\)). Apply the results of 4.7.3 to
\(G = \operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)\) and
\texttt{L\ =\ Lie(G/S)\ =\ Aut\_\{O\_S-mod.\}(F)}. One identifies \(X\)
with its image under the canonical section
\(L(S) \hookrightarrow L(I)\); its image in \(G(I \times I')\) is then
\(id + t' X\), whose inverse is \(id - t' X\). Likewise, \(Y\) lifts to
\(id + t Y\), whose inverse is \(id - t Y\). Then, the commutator

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(id + t′ X) ∘ (id + t Y) ∘ (id − t′ X) ∘ (id − t Y) = id + t t′ (X ∘ Y − Y ∘ X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is the image in \(G(I \times I')\) of the element
\(Z = X \circ Y - Y \circ X\) of \(L(S)\) (indeed, \(Z\) is sent to
\(t Z \in L(I)\), then to \(id + t' t Z \in G(I \times I')\)). By 4.7.3,
this shows that \([X, Y] = X \circ Y - Y \circ X\).

\textbf{Corollary 4.8.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a good \(S\)-group and
\(x, y, z \in Lie(G/S)(S')\). One has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[x, [y, z]] + [y, [z, x]] + [z, [x, y]] = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{One has detailed the original in what follows.} Indeed, since
\(G\) is good, \(Lie(G/S)\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module and
therefore, by 4.7, \(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(Lie(G/S))\) is a
good \(S\)-group. Then, the morphism of \(S\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad : G ⟶ Aut\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(Lie(G/S))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

gives, by the functoriality 4.7.3 (i): \(ad[x, y] = [ad x, ad y]\).
Combined with 4.8, this gives:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ad[x, y] = [ad x, ad y] = ad x ∘ ad y − ad y ∘ ad x,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which, applied to an element \(z\), gives the Jacobi relation.

\textbf{Corollary 4.8.2.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a good \(S\)-group acting
linearly on a good \texttt{O\_S}-module \(F\) (i.e.~let \(F\) be a
\(G\)-\texttt{O\_S}-module, with \(G\) and \(F\) good). Then the linear
map \texttt{ρ′\ :\ Lie(G/S)\ →\ End\_\{O\_S-mod.\}(F)} is a
representation, i.e.~one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ρ′([x, y]) = ρ′(x) ∘ ρ′(y) − ρ′(y) ∘ ρ′(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Scholie 4.9.} \emph{To every good \(S\)-group (for example
representable), one has associated a good \texttt{O\_S}-module
\(Lie(G/S)\) functorially equipped with a bilinear map satisfying}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[x, y] + [y, x] = 0,    [x, [y, z]] + [y, [z, x]] + [z, [x, y]] = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{We shall call \(Lie(G/S)\) equipped with this structure the ``Lie
algebra'' of \(G\) over \(S\) (the quotation marks being justified by
the fact that one does not know whether \(Lie(G/S)\) is, strictly
speaking, an \texttt{O\_S}-Lie algebra}\footnote{Because one does not
  know whether \([x, x] = 0\), see 4.10 which follows.}\emph{). To every
linear representation of \(G\) in a good \texttt{O\_S}-module \(F\) is
associated a representation of its ``Lie algebra''. In particular, to
the adjoint representation of \(G\) is associated the adjoint
representation of its ``Lie algebra''.}

\textbf{Definition 4.10.} \emph{A group-functor \(G\) above \(S\) is
said to be} \textbf{very good} \emph{if it is good and if \(Lie(G/S)\)
is an \texttt{O\_S}-Lie algebra (i.e.~if one has identically
\([x, x] = 0\)).}

\textbf{Examples 4.10.1.} \emph{The following \(S\)-groups are very
good: \(\operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F)\) for every good
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(F\) (cf.~4.7 and 4.8), every representable group
(see below), every good \(S\)-group admitting a monomorphism into a very
good \(S\)-group, for example every good subgroup-functor of a
representable group, or every good \(S\)-group admitting a faithful
linear representation in a good \texttt{O\_S}-module, for example every
good \(S\)-group such that \texttt{Ad} is a monomorphism . . .}

\textbf{4.11.} Suppose now that \(G\) is a group scheme over \(S\). By
4.1.4, \(Lie(G/S)(S)\) is identified with the group of infinitesimal
automorphisms of \(G/S\) right-invariant, that is to say, by 3.14, with
the group of derivations of \texttt{O\_G} over \texttt{O\_S} invariant
by right translation. Moreover this identification respects the module
structure and is an\footnote{One has corrected a sign error in the
  original, cf.~{[}DG70{]}, § II.4, 4.4 and 4.6.} anti-isomorphism of
Lie algebras, as one sees by reasoning as in 4.7.3: set
\(O_{I} = O_{S}[t]\) and \(O_{I'} = O_{S}[t']\) and let \(x \in L(I)\)
and \(y \in L(I')\). The left translation \(\lambda_{x}\) (resp.
\(\lambda_{y}\)) is an \(S\)-automorphism of \(G_{I\times I'}\) which
induces the identity on \(G_{I'}\) (resp. \texttt{G\_I}) and which
corresponds to an \texttt{O\_S}-automorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u = id + t d\_x    resp.    v = id + t′ d\_y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

of \(O_{G_{I\times I'}} = O_{G}[t, t']/(t^{2}, t'^{2})\), where
\(d_{x}, d_{y}\) are \texttt{O\_S}-derivations of \texttt{O\_G}
invariant by right translation. Since the correspondence between
\(S\)-automorphisms of \(G_{I\times I'}\) and
\texttt{O\_S}-automorphisms of \(O_{G_{I\times I'}}\) is contravariant,
\(\lambda_{x} \lambda_{y} \lambda^{-1}_{x} \lambda^{-1}_{y}\)
corresponds to
\(v^{-1} u^{-1} v u = id + t t' (d_{y} d_{x} - d_{x} d_{y})\). One
deduces, by 4.7.3, that the map \(x \mapsto -d_{x}\) is an isomorphism
of Lie algebras (for more details, see {[}DG70{]}, § II.4, 4.4 and 4.6).
What precedes is valid for \(Lie(G/S)(S') = Lie(G_{S'}/S')(S')\) for
every \(S' \to S\). One thus recovers the classical
definition:\footnote{One has detailed the original in what follows; in
  particular, one has added, for later references, the numbering 4.11.1
  to 4.11.8.}

\textbf{Scholie 4.11.1.} \emph{Via the isomorphism \(x \mapsto -d_{x}\),
\(Lie(G/S)\) is identified with the functor that to every \(S'\) above
\(S\) associates the \(O(S')\)-Lie algebra of derivations of \(G_{S'}\)
with respect to \(S'\) invariant by right translation.}

Since one knows already, by 4.6.1, that every representable group is
good, it follows from what precedes:

\textbf{Corollary 4.11.2.} \emph{Every representable group is very
good.}

Let \(\epsilon : S \to G\) be the unit section of \(G\). Set
\(\omega^{1}_{G/S} = \epsilon^{*}(\Omega^{1}_{G/S})\) and recall
(cf.~3.3) that \(Lie(G/S)\) is representable by the vector fibration
\(V(\omega^{1}_{G/S})\).

\textbf{Scholie 4.11.3.} \emph{One has therefore associated functorially
to every \(S\)-group scheme \(G\) a vector fibration
\(Lie(G/S) = V(\omega^{1}_{G/S})\) over \(S\), which represents the
functor \(Lie(G/S)\), hence is equipped with a structure of \(S\)-scheme
of \texttt{O\_S}-Lie algebras. Moreover (cf.~3.4 and 3.8), this
construction commutes with base extension and finite products.}

\textbf{Remarks 4.11.4.}\footnote{One has detailed what follows, taking
  into account the additions made in Exp. I, § 6.8.} Denote by \(\pi\)
the morphism \(G \to S\).

\emph{a)} The \texttt{O\_G}-module \(\Omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is evidently
\((G \times_{S} G)\)-equivariant (cf.~I, § 6) and therefore, by I 6.8.1,
one has \(\Omega^{1}_{G/S} \simeq \pi^{*}(\omega^{1}_{G/S})\). It
follows for example that \(\Omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is locally free (resp.
locally free of finite type) if \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is, which is in
particular the case if \(S\) is the spectrum of a field (resp. if \(S\)
is the spectrum of a field and \(G\) locally of finite type over \(S\)).

\emph{b)} Moreover, by I 6.8.2, \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is equipped with a
canonical structure of \(G\)-\texttt{O\_S}-module, which induces on
\(V(\omega^{1}_{G/S}) = Lie(G/S)\) the adjoint action.\footnote{For this
  reason, the linear action of \(G\) on \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) could be
  called the ``pre-adjoint action''; in fact, by abuse of language, one
  will still speak of ``the adjoint action'' on \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\).
  Let us point out here a slightly more general construction, which will
  be used in Exp. III (cf.~in particular III 0.8). Suppose given, for
  every \(Y \to S\), an \texttt{O\_Y}-module \(N(Y)\), and for every
  \(S\)-morphism \(\phi : Z \to Y\), a morphism of \texttt{O\_Z}-modules
  \(N(\phi) : \phi^{*} N(Y) \to N(Z)\), which is functorial in \(\phi\)
  (this is the case, for example, if \(J\) is a quasi-coherent ideal of
  \texttt{O\_S} and if one sets \(N(Y) = J O_{Y}\), cf.~Exp. III); then
  the action of \(G\) on \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) induces a (generalized)
  ``adjoint action'' of \(G\) on the \(S\)-functor of abelian groups
  that to every \(f : Y \to S\) associates
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y}}(f^{*}(\omega^{1}_{G/S}), N(Y))\).}

\emph{c)} On the other hand (cf.~EGA I, 5.3.11 and 5.4.6), \(\epsilon\)
is an immersion, and is a closed immersion if \(G\) is separated over
\(S\). Therefore \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is identified with \(I/I^{2}\),
where \(I\) is the quasi-coherent ideal defining \(\epsilon(S)\) in an
open subset \(U\) of \(G\) in which \(\epsilon(S)\) is closed (if
\(G \to S\) is separated, one may take \(U = G\), and if
\(G = \operatorname{Spec} A(G)\) is affine over \(S\), \(I\) is nothing
other than the augmentation ideal of \(A(G)\), i.e.~the kernel of
\(\epsilon^{\natural} : A(G) \to O_{S}\), cf.~I 4.2).\footnote{One has
  added the preceding description of \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\), which will be
  useful later (for example, in VII\_A, 5.5).}

\textbf{Remark 4.11.5.} One can deduce from the isomorphism
\(\Omega^{1}_{G/S} \simeq \pi^{*}(\omega^{1}_{G/S})\) that the
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is identified with the sheaf
\(\pi_{*}(\Omega^{1}_{G/S})^{G}\) of ``differentials of \(G\) with
respect to \(S\) invariant on the right'', that is to say, with the
sheaf whose sections on an open subset \(U\) of \(S\) are the sections
of \(\Omega^{1}_{G/S}\) on \(\pi^{-1}(U)\) invariant by right
translation (cf.~I, 6.8.3, compare also with VII\_A, 2.4).\footnote{This
  description of \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) in terms of invariant
  differentials will not be used in the sequel.}

\textbf{Notation 4.11.6.} \emph{One denotes by \(Lie(G/S)\) the sheaf of
sections of the vector fibration \(Lie(G/S) \to S\); it is the
\texttt{O\_S}-module
\((\omega^{1}_{G/S})^{\vee} = \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}}(\omega^{1}_{G/S}, O_{S})\)
dual to \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) (cf.~EGA II 1.7.9). It is equipped with a
structure of \texttt{O\_S}-Lie algebra.}

\emph{Since this construction does not commute with base extension (in
general), the Lie algebra structure on this module does not allow one to
reconstruct the structure of \(S\)-scheme of \texttt{O\_S}-Lie algebras
on \(Lie(G/S)\).}\footnote{Because
  \(Lie(G/S) \cong (\omega^{1}_{G/S})^{\vee}\) does not necessarily
  determine \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\). For example, if
  \(S = \mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}\) (\(k\) a field) and if \(G\) is the
  \(S\)-group whose fiber at \(s = 0\) is \(G_{a,k}\) and the other
  fibers are the unit group, then \(Lie(G/S) = 0\) but
  \(Lie(G_{s}/k)(k) = k\).}

However one has:

\textbf{Lemma 4.11.7.} \emph{Suppose \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) locally free
of finite type (which is the case in particular if \(G\) is smooth over
\(S\) (cf.~EGA IV\_4, 17.2.4), or if \(S\) is the spectrum of a field
and \(G\) locally of finite type over \(S\)). Then
\(Lie(G/S)^{\vee} \cong (\omega^{1}_{G/S})^{\vee\vee} \cong \omega^{1}_{G/S}\)
and therefore}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(G/S) = V(ω¹\_\{G/S\}) = V(Lie(G/S)\^{}∨) = W(Lie(G/S))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(the last equality following from I 4.6.5.1).}

Finally, let \(G \to H\) be a monomorphism of group-functors. Then
\(Lie(G/S) \to Lie(H/S)\) is also a monomorphism (cf. 3.7). Since every
vector monomorphism of vector fibrations is a closed
immersion\footnote{Let \(f : M \to N\) be a morphism of
  \texttt{O\_S}-modules and \(P = Coker(f)\). If \(V(N) \to V(M)\) is a
  monomorphism, the surjective morphism \(Sym(N) \to Sym(P)\) factors
  through \texttt{O\_S}, so \(P = 0\).} one obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 4.11.8.} \emph{Let \(G \hookrightarrow H\) be a
monomorphism of \(S\)-group schemes.}

\emph{(i) \(Lie(G/S) \to Lie(H/S)\) is a closed immersion and therefore
\(\omega^{1}_{H/S} \to \omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is an epimorphism.}

\emph{(ii) If \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) is locally free of finite type, then
the corresponding morphism \(Lie(G/S) \to Lie(H/S)\) is an isomorphism
of \(Lie(G/S)\) onto a sub-module of \(Lie(H/S)\) locally direct
factor.}

\subsection{5. Computation of some Lie
algebras}\label{computation-of-some-lie-algebras}

\subsubsection{5.1. Examples of Lie algebras: diagonalizable
groups}\label{examples-of-lie-algebras-diagonalizable-groups}

Let \(G = D_{S}(M)\) be a diagonalizable group over \(S\) (I 4.4). Since
the formation of \(Lie(G/S)\) commutes with base extension, it suffices
to make the construction for \(G = D(M)\). One has then:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G(I\_S) = Hom\_\{gr.\}(M, Γ(I\_S, O\_\{I\_S\})\^{}×) = Hom\_\{gr.\}(M, Γ(S, D\_\{O\_S\})\^{}×).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now one has a split exact sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 ⟶ Γ(S, O\_S) ⟶ Γ(S, D\_\{O\_S\})\^{}× ⟶ Γ(S, O\_S)\^{}× ⟶ 1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives that \(Lie(G)(S)\) is identified with
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{gr.}(M, O(S))\) equipped with its obvious
\(O(S)\)-module structure. One thus obtains, after base change:

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.} \emph{One has isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(M\_S, O\_S) ⥲ Lie(D\_S(M)/S)    and    Hom\_\{gr.\}(M̃\_S, O\_S) ⥲ Lie(D\_S(M)/S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(where, in the second isomorphism, \(\tilde{M}_{S}\) denotes the
constant sheaf of groups on \(S\) defined by \(M\), and
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{gr.}\) the sheaf of homomorphisms of sheaves of
groups).}

\textbf{Corollary 5.1.1.} \emph{If \(M\) is free of finite type (or, as
we shall say later, if \(D_{S}(M)\) is a split torus), then (see I,
4.6.5 for the definition of \(W\))}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(Lie(D\_S(M)/S)) ⥲ Lie(D\_S(M)/S),}
\NormalTok{M\^{}∨ ⊗\_ℤ O\_S    ⥲ Lie(D\_S(M)/S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(M^{\vee}\) denotes the dual of the abelian group \(M\). In
particular}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{O\_S ⥲ Lie(G\_\{m,S\}/S)    and    O\_S ⥲ Lie(G\_\{m,S\}/S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{5.2. Normalizers and
centralizers}\label{normalizers-and-centralizers}

Let us first prove a few lemmas. Recall (cf.~I 3.1.1) that a sequence
\(0 \to F' \to F \to F'' \to 0\) of \texttt{O\_S}-modules is said to be
exact if for every \(S' \to S\) the sequence
\(0 \to F'(S') \to F(S') \to F''(S') \to 0\) of \(O(S')\)-modules is
exact.

Likewise, a sequence \(1 \to G' \to G \to G'' \to 1\) of \(S\)-groups is
said to be exact if for every \(S' \to S\) the sequence of groups
\(1 \to G'(S') \to G(S') \to G''(S') \to 1\) is exact.

\textbf{Lemma 5.2.1.}\footnote{One has detailed the statement of the
  lemma (and its proof); this will be useful in 5.3.1.} \emph{Let
\(1 \to G' \to G \to G'' \to 1\) be an exact sequence of \(S\)-groups.}

\emph{(i) The sequences
\(1 \to T_{G'/S}(M) \to T_{G/S}(M) \to T_{G''/S}(M) \to 1\) and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 ⟶ Lie(G′/S, M) ⟶ Lie(G/S, M) ⟶ Lie(G″/S, M) ⟶ 1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are then exact.}

\emph{(ii) Let \(1 \to H' \to H \to H'' \to 1\) be a second sequence of
groups; it is exact if and only if the sequence below is exact:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 ⟶ G′ ×\_S H′ ⟶ G ×\_S H ⟶ G″ ×\_S H″ ⟶ 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) If two of the \(S\)-groups \(G', G, G''\) satisfy (E), the
third also satisfies (E).}

\emph{(iv) If \(0 \to F' \to F \to F'' \to 0\) is an exact sequence of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules and if two of the modules \(F', F, F''\) are good,
the third is also.}

\emph{(v) If two of the \(S\)-groups \(G', G, G''\) are good, the third
is also.}

\footnote{One has added the proof of points (iii) and (v).} The first
part of (i) is immediate, and the second part follows. Likewise, (ii) is
immediate. Let us prove (iii). To abbreviate, write
\(L(M) = Lie(G, M)\), \(L'(M) = Lie(G', M)\), etc. Then one has the
following commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   1 ─→ L′(M ⊕ N) ─→ L(M ⊕ N) ─→ L″(M ⊕ N) ─→ 1}
\NormalTok{              │              │             │}
\NormalTok{              ↓              ↓             ↓}
\NormalTok{   1 ─→ L′(M) ×\_S L′(N) ─→ L(M) ×\_S L(N) ─→ L″(M) ×\_S L″(N) ─→ 1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

in which the first (resp. the second) row is exact by (i) (resp. (i) and
(ii)). Assertion (iii) follows.

Let us prove (iv). One has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   0 ─→ F′ ⊗\_\{O\_S\} T\_\{O\_S/S\}(M) ─→ F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} T\_\{O\_S/S\}(M) ─→ F″ ⊗\_\{O\_S\} T\_\{O\_S/S\}(M) ─→ 0}
\NormalTok{              │                          │                           │}
\NormalTok{              ↓                          ↓                           ↓}
\NormalTok{   0 ─────→ T\_\{F′/S\}(M) ─────────→ T\_\{F/S\}(M) ─────────→ T\_\{F″/S\}(M) ─────→ 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

with exact rows (the first, because \(T_{O_{S}/S}(M)\) is a free
\texttt{O\_S}-module hence flat, the second by (i)). It follows that if
two of the modules \(F', F, F''\) are good, the third is also. Finally,
(v) follows from (iii) and (iv).

\textbf{Lemma 5.2.2.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group, \texttt{E,\ H}
two \(G\)-objects, \(F\) a \(G\)-\texttt{O\_S}-module.}

\emph{(i) The canonical homomorphism
\(E^{G} \times_{S} H^{G} \to (E \times_{S} H)^{G}\) is an isomorphism.}

\emph{(ii) If \(F\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module, so is \(F^{G}\).}

\footnote{One has detailed the original in what follows.} The first
assertion is immediate; let us prove the second. For every \(S' \to S\),
one has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   F\^{}G(I\_\{S′\}(M)) ─────────────→ F(I\_\{S′\}(M))}
\NormalTok{              ↑ φ                       ↑ ≃ φ\_1}
\NormalTok{   F\^{}G(S′) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} O(I\_\{S′\}(M)) ─→ F(S′) ⊗\_\{O(S′)\} O(I\_\{S′\}(M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one must show that \(\phi\) is bijective; now it is evidently
injective; let us show that it is surjective. Let
\((t_{0}, \cdots, t_{n})\) be a basis of the free \(O(S')\)-module
\(O(I_{S'}(M))\) and let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u = Σ\_\{i=0\}\^{}n f\_i ⊗ t\_i}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be an element of \(F(S') \otimes_{O(S')} O(I_{S'}(M))\) such that
\(\phi_{1}(u)\) belongs to \(F^{G}(I_{S'}(M))\). Let us show that the
\(f_{i}\) belong to \(F^{G}(S')\).

Let \(S'' \to S'\); one can consider \(S''\) as above \(I_{S'}(M)\) via
the zero section \(\epsilon_{M}\). Then, for every \(g \in G(S'')\), one
has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u\_\{S″\} = g · u\_\{S″\} = Σ\_\{i=0\}\^{}n g · (f\_i)\_\{S″\} ⊗ (t\_i)\_\{S″\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since the \((t_{i})_{S''}\) form a basis of
\(O(I_{S''}(M)) \simeq O(I_{S'}(M)) \otimes_{O(S')} O(S'')\) over
\(O(S'')\), it follows that \(g \cdot (f_{i})_{S''} = (f_{i})_{S''}\),
whence \(f_{i} \in F^{G}(S')\) for every \(i\).

\emph{Notations.}\footnote{One has detailed these notations.} If \(E\)
is an \(S\)-group and \(F\) a sub-\(S\)-group of \(E\), one denotes by
\(E/F\) the \(S\)-functor that to every \(S' \to S\) associates the set
\(E(S')/F(S')\) of classes \(\bar{x} = x F(S')\), \(x \in E(S')\). If
\(E\) is a commutative \(S\)-group then \(E/F\) is a commutative
\(S\)-group.

Let now \(G\) be an \(S\)-group and \(K\) a sub-\(S\)-group of \(G\);
set \(E = Lie(G/S, M)\) and \(F = Lie(K/S, M)\). The adjoint action of
\(K\) on \(E\) stabilizes \(F\), hence induces an action of \(K\) on the
\(S\)-functor \(E/F\). Then, for every \(S' \to S\), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(E/F)\^{}K(S′) = \{ x̄ ∈ E(S′)/F(S′) | for every f : S″ → S′ and k ∈ K(S″),}
\NormalTok{                                   f\^{}*(x̄\^{}\{{-}1\}) Ad(k)(f\^{}*(x̄)) ∈ F(S″) \},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(f^{*}(\bar{x})\) denotes the image of \(\bar{x}\) in \(E(S'')\).

\textbf{Theorem 5.2.3.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group, \(K\) a
sub-\(S\)-group of \(G\). Write (I 2.3.3)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N = Norm\_G(K),    Z = Centr\_G(K).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Make \(K\) act on \(Lie(G/S, M)\) through the adjoint
representation of \(G\).}

\emph{(i) If the group law of \(Lie(G/S, M)\) is commutative}\footnote{Condition
  automatically verified if \(G\) satisfies (E) (cf.~3.9), for example
  if \(G\) is representable.} \footnote{For an example where the
  \(S\)-group \(Lie(G/S)\) is not commutative, see 6.3.}\emph{, then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(N/S, M) / Lie(K/S, M) = ( Lie(G/S, M) / Lie(K/S, M) )\^{}K.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) If the group law of \(Lie(G/S, M)\) is
commutative}\footnote{Condition automatically verified if \(G\)
  satisfies (E) (cf.~3.9), for example if \(G\) is representable.}\emph{,
then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Z/S, M) = Lie(G/S, M)\^{}K.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) If \(G\) satisfies (E) (resp. if \(G\) and \(K\) satisfy
(E)), then \(Z\) satisfies (E) (resp. \(N\) satisfies (E)).}

\emph{(iv) Suppose \(G\) is good; then \(Z\) is good; if moreover \(G\)
is very good, then \(Z\) is very good.}

\emph{(v) Suppose \(G\) and \(K\) are good; then \(N\) is good; if
moreover \(G\) is very good, then \(N\) is very good.}

To prove (i) and (ii)\footnote{One has detailed the proof, adding in
  particular Lemma 5.2.3.0, implicit in the original.} we shall use the
following lemma, which follows from the diagram of exact sequences
considered in 4.1.B (with \(G\) and \(H\) interchanged).

\textbf{Lemma 5.2.3.0.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group, \(H\) a
sub-\(S\)-group of \(G\), and \(M\) a free \texttt{O\_S}-module of
finite type. Then \(T_{H/S}(M)\) and \(Lie(G/S, M)\) are
sub-\(S\)-groups of \(T_{G/S}(M)\) and one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{H/S\}(M) ∩\_T Lie(G/S, M) = Lie(H/S, M),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where one has set
\texttt{T\_\{H/S\}(M)\ ∩\_T\ Lie(G/S,\ M)\ :=def\ T\_\{H/S\}(M)\ ×\_\{T\_\{G/S\}(M)\}\ Lie(G/S,\ M)}.}

Since the functors considered in (i) and (ii) commute with base
extension, it suffices to show the equalities of \(S\)-points.

Set \(H = N\) (resp. \(= Z\)) and let \(\alpha = \pm 1\). By the
preceding lemma and the definition of \(N\) and \(Z\) (cf.~I 2.3.3), one
has: \(Lie(H/S, M)(S) =\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\{ X ∈ Lie(G/S, M)(S) ⊂ G(I\_S(M)) |}
\NormalTok{       for every f : S′ → I\_S(M) and u ∈ K(S′),}
\NormalTok{            f\^{}*(X\^{}α) · u · f\^{}*(X\^{}\{{-}α\}) · u\^{}\{{-}1\} ∈ K(S′),}
\NormalTok{       resp. f\^{}*(X) · u · f\^{}*(X\^{}\{{-}1\}) · u\^{}\{{-}1\} = 1   (∗) \},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(f^{*}(X)\) denotes the image of \(X\) in \(G(S')\).

To simplify the writing, let us write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = Lie(G/S, M),    k = Lie(K/S, M),    n = Lie(N/S, M),    z = Lie(Z/S, M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(X \in Lie(H/S, M)(S)\), the equalities (∗) are valid for every
\(f : S' \to S\), since \(f = \rho \circ \epsilon_{M} \circ f\) factors
through \(I_{S}(M)\) (where \(\rho : I_{S}(M) \to S\) is the structural
morphism and \(\epsilon_{M} : S \to I_{S}(M)\) the zero section). One
deduces that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n(S)/k(S) ⊂ (g/k)\^{}K(S)    and    z(S) ⊂ g\^{}K(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To prove the reverse inclusions, suppose henceforth \(g = Lie(G/S, M)\)
commutative; then \(g^{K}\) and \((g/k)^{K}\) are commutative
\(S\)-groups. Let \(X \in g(S)\) and \(\bar{X}\) its image in
\((g/k)(S)\), suppose that \(\bar{X} \in (g/k)^{K}(S)\) (resp.
\(X \in g^{K}(S)\)) and let us show that \(X \in n(S)\) (resp.
\(X \in z(S)\)).

Let \(f : S' \to I_{S}(M)\); let us show that the preceding condition
(∗) is verified for every \(u \in K(S')\). Consider the cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                p}
\NormalTok{   I\_\{S′\}(M) ──────→ I\_S(M)}
\NormalTok{       │ ρ′            │ ρ}
\NormalTok{       ↓     ρ ∘ f     ↓}
\NormalTok{       S′ ──────→     S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and let \(h\) be the section of \(\rho'\) defined by \(f\). It suffices
to show that, for every \(v \in K(I_{S'}(M))\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗∗)   p\^{}*(X\^{}α) · v · p\^{}*(X\^{}\{{-}α\}) · v\^{}\{{-}1\} ∈ K(I\_\{S′\}(M)),}
\NormalTok{       resp. p\^{}*(X) · v · p\^{}*(X\^{}\{{-}1\}) · v\^{}\{{-}1\} = 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, taking \(v = \rho'^{*}(u)\) and applying \(h^{*}\) to (∗∗), one
obtains (∗), since \(\rho' \circ h = id_{S'}\) and \(p \circ h = f\).

Let us now show (∗∗); for simplicity, we shall write \(X\) instead of
\(p^{*}(X)\). Every \(v \in K(I_{S'}(M))\) is written in a unique manner
\(Y \cdot k\) where \(Y \in Lie(K/S, M)(S')\) and \(k \in K(S')\). The
expression \(X^{\alpha} \cdot u \cdot X^{-\alpha} \cdot u^{-1}\) then
becomes
\(X^{\alpha} \cdot Y \cdot (k \cdot X^{-\alpha} \cdot k^{-1}) \cdot Y^{-1}\)
which, since \(Lie(G/S, M)\) is commutative, is written
\(X^{\alpha} Ad(k)(X^{-\alpha})\). Now this is a priori in
\(Lie(G/S, M)(S')\); taking into account Lemma 5.2.3.0, the condition
(∗∗) for \(X\) therefore becomes: for every \(k \in K(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⎰ Ad(k)(X) = X,                                if H = Z;}
\NormalTok{⎱ X\^{}α Ad(k)(X\^{}\{{-}α\}) ∈ Lie(K/S, M)(S′),         if H = N.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

When \(H = Z\), this condition is indeed a consequence of the hypothesis
\(X \in g^{K}(S)\). When \(H = N\), the condition is also written:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗′)   Ad(k)(X) = X    and    Ad(k)(X\^{}\{{-}1\}) = X\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

now the second condition of (∗′) is a consequence of the first, since
the action of \(K\) on \(g/k\) respects the group structure of this
latter. Therefore, when \(H = N\), the condition (∗∗) for \(X\) is
indeed a consequence of the hypothesis \(\bar{X} \in (g/k)^{K}(S)\).
This proves (i) and (ii).

To prove (iii)--(v), let us write \(g(M) = Lie(G/S, M)\) and define
similarly \(k(M)\), \(z(M)\) and \(n(M)\). If \(G/S\) satisfies (E),
then \(g(M \oplus N) \simeq g(M) \times_{S} g(N)\) and therefore, by
5.2.2 (i),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g(M ⊕ N)\^{}K ≃ g(M)\^{}K ×\_S g(N)\^{}K,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(z(M \oplus N) \simeq z(M) \times_{S} z(N)\), so \(Z\) satisfies
(E). If moreover \(K/S\) satisfies (E), one obtains successively
isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(g/k)(M ⊕ N) ≃ (g/k)(M) ×\_S (g/k)(N),}
\NormalTok{(g/k)\^{}K(M ⊕ N) ≃ (g/k)(M)\^{}K ×\_S (g/k)(N)\^{}K,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

then a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   0 ─→ k(M ⊕ N) ─→ n(M ⊕ N) ─→ (n/k)(M ⊕ N) ─→ 0}
\NormalTok{            ≀ │              │                ≀ │}
\NormalTok{              ↓              ↓                  ↓}
\NormalTok{   0 ─→ k(M) ×\_S k(N) ─→ n(M) ×\_S n(N) ─→ (n/k)(M) ×\_S (n/k)(N) ─→ 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

from which it follows that
\(n(M \oplus N) \simeq n(M) \times_{S} n(N)\), so \(N\) satisfies (E).

Henceforth, write \(g = g(O_{S}) = Lie(G/S)\) and define similarly
\texttt{k,\ z,\ n}. If \(G\) is good, \(g\) is a good
\texttt{O\_S}-module so, by 5.2.2 (ii), \(z \simeq g^{K}\) is also, so
\(Z\) (which satisfies (E) by (iii)) is good. If moreover \(K\) is good,
then \(k\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module so, by 5.2.1 (iv) and 5.2.2
(ii), so are \(g/k\) and \((g/k)^{K}\). Taking into account the exact
sequence

\[
0 \longrightarrow k \longrightarrow n \longrightarrow (g/k)^{K} \longrightarrow 0,
\]

one obtains, by 5.2.1 (iv) again, that \(n\) is good. Finally, if in
addition to the preceding conditions, \(G\) is very good, i.e., if one
has identically \([x, x] = 0\) for every \(x \in g\), it is clear that
\(Z\) and \(N\) are very good. This proves (iii), (iv) and (v).

\textbf{Corollary 5.2.3.1.} \emph{One has
\texttt{Lie(Centr(G)/S)\ =\ Lie(G/S)\^{}G} if the group law of
\(Lie(G/S)\) is commutative.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.2.3.2.} \emph{If the group law of \(Lie(G/S)\) is
commutative and if \(K\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\), then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{( Lie(G/S) / Lie(K/S) )\^{}K = Lie(G/S) / Lie(K/S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{5.3. Linear
representations}\label{linear-representations}

Let \(G\) be a good \(S\)-group acting linearly on a good
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(F\) via

\[
\rho : G \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S}-mod.}(F).
\]

One has defined (4.7.1 and 4.8.2) a corresponding linear representation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ρ′ : Lie(G/S) ⟶ End\_\{O\_S{-}mod.\}(F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The sub-\(S\)-groups \(Norm_{G}(E)\) and \(Centr_{G}(E)\) are defined
for every part \(E\) of \(F\), for example for every
sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module \(E\) of \(F\).

\textbf{Definition 5.3.0.} \emph{One will pose analogously: for every
\(S' \to S\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)(S′) = \{ X ∈ Lie(G/S)(S′) | ρ′(X) E\_\{S′\} ⊂ E\_\{S′\} \};}
\NormalTok{Centr\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)(S′) = \{ X ∈ Lie(G/S)(S′) | ρ′(X) E\_\{S′\} = 0 \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(Note that this construction can be made for any linear
representation of an \texttt{O\_S}-``Lie algebra'' (in the sense of 4.9)
and that the two subobjects constructed are sub-\texttt{O\_S}-modules
stable under the bracket.)}

\textbf{Theorem 5.3.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a good \(S\)-group acting
linearly on a good \texttt{O\_S}-module \(F\) and let \(E\) be a
sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module of \(F\).}

\emph{(i) One has \texttt{Lie(Centr\_G(E)/S)\ =\ Centr\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)}
and \(Centr_{G}(E)\) is a good \(S\)-group; it is very good if \(G\)
is.}

\emph{(ii) Suppose that \(E\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module.
Then}\footnote{One has corrected the original, which stated the equality
  that follows without hypotheses on \(E\); see 6.5.1 for
  counterexamples.}
\emph{\texttt{Lie(Norm\_G(E)/S)\ =\ Norm\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)} and
\(Norm_{G}(E)\) is a good \(S\)-group; it is very good if \(G\) is.}

The proof is left to the reader.

\textbf{5.3.2.} Let \(G\) be a good \(S\)-group; what precedes applies
in particular to the case where one takes for \(\rho\) the adjoint
representation of \(G\). Let \(E\) be a good\footnote{One has added this
  hypothesis; cf.~6.5.1.} sub-module of \(Lie(G/S)\); to it one
therefore associates two subgroups of \(G\), its centralizer and its
normalizer. By 5.3.1, their Lie algebras are respectively the
centralizer and the normalizer of \(E\) in \(Lie(G/S)\) computed as
usual by means of the bracket:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)(S′) = \{ X ∈ Lie(G/S)(S′) | [X, E\_\{S′\}] = 0 \},}
\NormalTok{Norm\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)(S′)  = \{ X ∈ Lie(G/S)(S′) | [X, E\_\{S′\}] ⊂ E\_\{S′\} \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{5.3.3.} Let \(K\) be a sub-\(S\)-group of \(G\), then
\(Lie(K/S)\) is a sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module of \(Lie(G/S)\); suppose that
\(Lie(K/S)\) is a good \texttt{O\_S}-module\footnote{One has added this
  hypothesis; cf.~6.5.1.} (which is the case if \(K\) is a good
\(S\)-group). One evidently has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr\_G(K) ⊂ Centr\_G(Lie(K/S)),}
\NormalTok{Norm\_G(K) ⊂ Norm\_G(Lie(K/S)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, by 5.3.1,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Centr\_G(K)/S) ⊂ Centr\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(Lie(K/S)),}
\NormalTok{Lie(Norm\_G(K)/S) ⊂ Norm\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(Lie(K/S)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but none of these four inclusions is a priori an equality; we shall see
by the sequel many examples.

It follows in particular from these inclusions that if \(K\) is a normal
subgroup of \(G\), then \(Lie(K/S)\) is an ideal of \(Lie(G/S)\).

\subsection{6. Miscellaneous remarks}\label{miscellaneous-remarks}

\textbf{6.1.} One can define the bracket of two infinitesimal
automorphisms for an \(S\)-functor \(X\) which is not necessarily a
group. It suffices to apply the results of this Exposé to the group
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)\). To arrive at an agreeable formalism, one
is led to suppose \(X\) good, i.e.~to suppose that the
\texttt{O\_X}-module \(T_{X/S}\) is good (if \(X\) is an \(S\)-group,
this definition evidently coincides with Definition 4.6).

\textbf{6.2.} There exist functors possessing infinitesimal
endomorphisms that are not automorphisms, hence a fortiori not
satisfying condition (E).\footnote{One has detailed the original in what
  follows. In particular, the correct definition of the ``free abelian
  monoid on a pointed set'' was pointed out to us by O. Gabber.} For
every pointed set \((E, x_{0})\), let \(MA(E)\) be the free abelian
monoid generated by \(E\) and let \(MAP(E, x_{0})\) be the abelian
monoid obtained by quotienting \(MA(E)\) by the equivalence relation
generated by the relation \(m \sim x_{0} + m\). Then
\((E, x_{0}) \mapsto MAP(E, x_{0})\) is the left adjoint of the
forgetful functor from the category of abelian monoids to that of
pointed sets; one will say that \(MAP(E, x_{0})\) is the ``free abelian
monoid on the pointed set \((E, x_{0})\)''.

Take then for \(X\) the functor that to every scheme \(S\) associates
the free abelian monoid on the set \(O(S)\), pointed by the zero
element. Every morphism
\(f : S \to I_{\mathbb{Z}} = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}[\epsilon])\)
corresponds to an element of square zero \(u_{f}\) of \(O(S)\), and
hence defines an endomorphism of \(X(S)\) by \(x \mapsto x + u_{f}\)
(sum in \(MAP(O(S), 0)\)). One thus obtains an endomorphism \(\phi\) of
\(X_{I_{\mathbb{Z}}} = X \times_{\mathbb{Z}} I_{\mathbb{Z}}\), defined
as follows. For every \(f \in I_{\mathbb{Z}}(S)\) and \(x \in X(S)\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ((x, f)) = (x + u\_f, f).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(f_{0} : S \to I_{\mathbb{Z}}\) is the composite of the structural
morphism \(S \to \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) and the zero section
of \(I_{\mathbb{Z}}\), the corresponding element is \(u_{f_{0}} = 0\),
and so \(\phi((x, f_{0})) = (x, f_{0})\), since \(x + 0 = x\) in
\(MAP(O(S), 0)\). This shows that \(\phi\) induces the identity on
\(X\); it is therefore an infinitesimal endomorphism of \(X\) which is
evidently not an automorphism.

\textbf{6.3.} There exist modules that are not good. On the one hand,
one can modify the preceding counterexample slightly:\footnote{One has
  added what follows.} take for \(F(S)\) the free \(O(S)\)-module with
basis the elements of \(O(S)\); then \(F\) does not satisfy condition
(E) with respect to \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\); moreover, let
\(G\) be the \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group defined by \(G(S) = GL_{n}(R(S))\),
where \(n \geqslant 2\) and \(R(S)\) is the \(O(S)\)-algebra of the
abelian group \(O(S)\); then the \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group
\(Lie(G/\mathbb{Z})\) is not commutative.

\footnote{In what follows, one has detailed example a) and added example
  b).} On the other hand, one can give the following counterexamples.
Let \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), with \(k\) a field of characteristic
\(p > 0\).

\emph{a)} Let \(F\) be the \texttt{O\_S}-module which to every
\(S\)-scheme \(T\) associates \(F(T) = \Gamma(T, O_{T})\) equipped with
the \(O(T)\)-module structure obtained by making scalars act through the
\(p\)-th power, that is to say, \(r \cdot f = r^{p} f\), for
\(r \in O(T)\), \(f \in F(T)\). As \(S\)-functor of groups, \(F\) is
isomorphic to \(G_{a, S}\). Therefore \(F/S\) satisfies (E) and
\(Lie(F/S)\) is identified with \(Lie(G_{a, S}/S) \cong O_{S}\). Then,
the canonical morphism \(F \to Lie(F/S)\) is,

for every \(T \to S\), the identity map \(F(T) \to O(T)\): it respects
the abelian-group structure but not the module structure. Therefore
\(F\) is not good (cf.~4.4.1).

\emph{b)} Let \(\alpha_{p,k}\) be the \(k\)-functor of groups which to
every \(S\)-scheme \(T\) associates

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\_\{p,k\}(T) = \{ x ∈ O(T) | x\^{}p = 0 \};}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

it is represented by \(\operatorname{Spec}(k[X]/(X^{p}))\) so it is a
very good \(S\)-group; it is also equipped with an \texttt{O\_S}-module
structure, but it is not a good \texttt{O\_S}-module, because the
canonical morphism \(\alpha_{p,k} \to Lie(\alpha_{p,k}/k) = G_{a,k}\) is
not bijective.

\textbf{6.4.} Let \(G\) be a group-functor on \(S\). One has by
definition the following implications

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G/S satisfies (E)) ⇐ (G is good) ⇐ (G is very good).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{And \(G\) is very good if it is representable (4.11). For
  representability criteria, see for example {[}MO67{]}. On the other
  hand, for the automorphisms of an affine algebraic group (over an
  algebraically closed field of characteristic 0), let us cite
  {[}HM69{]}.} It would be interesting to prove or counter-exemplify the
implications in the reverse direction.

\textbf{6.5.}\footnote{One has added this paragraph.} Let \texttt{Nil}
be the \(\mathbb{Z}\)-functor of groups defined as follows: for every
scheme \(S\), \(Nil(S)\) is the ideal of \(O(S)\) formed by the
nilpotent elements, i.e.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Nil(S) = \{ x ∈ O(S) | there exists n ∈ ℕ such that x\^{}n = 0 \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(\texttt{Nil} is very good but is not representable.) Let \(Nil^{2}\),
\(O_{r\acute{e}d}\) and \(F\) be the \(\mathbb{Z}\)-functors of groups
that to every scheme \(S\) associate, respectively, the ideal
\(Nil(S)^{2}\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{O\_\{réd\}(S) = O(S) / Nil(S),    F(S) = O(S) / Nil(S)².}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One sees easily that \(Lie(O_{r\acute{e}d}/\mathbb{Z}) = 0\), so the
\(O_{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module \(O_{r\acute{e}d}\) is not good (although it
is a good \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group). If \texttt{M,\ N} are
\(\mathbb{Z}\)-modules free of finite rank, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Nil²(I\_S(M ⊕ N)) ≃ Nil²(S) ⊕ Nil(S) ⊗\_ℤ M ⊕ Nil(S) ⊗\_ℤ N}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and therefore

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(I\_S(M ⊕ N)) ≃ F(S) ⊕ O\_\{réd\}(S) ⊗\_ℤ M ⊕ O\_\{réd\}(S) ⊗\_ℤ N.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One deduces, on the one hand, that the \(\mathbb{Z}\)-functor of groups
\(F\) satisfies condition (E) and, on the other hand, that
\(Lie(F/\mathbb{Z}) = O_{r\acute{e}d}\); since this latter is not a good
\(O_{\mathbb{Z}}\)-module, this shows that \(F\) is an example of a
\(\mathbb{Z}\)-group that satisfies (E) but is not good.

\textbf{6.5.1.} Let us also give the counterexamples mentioned in
5.3.1--5.3.3. Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(F\) the good \texttt{O\_S}-module
\(O^{\oplus 2}_{S}\) equipped with the natural action of the good
\(S\)-group \(G = GL_{2,S}\), and \(E\) the sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module of
\(F\) formed by the pairs \((x_{1}, x_{2})\) such that \(x_{2}\) is
nilpotent. Set \(N = Norm_{G}(E)\). Then \(Lie(N/S) = Lie(G/S)\) while,
for every \(S' \to S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)(S′) = \{ ⎡a b⎤ | a, b, c, x ∈ O(S′), x nilpotent \},}
