\NormalTok{                          ⎣x c⎦}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \texttt{Lie(Norm\_G(E)/S)\ ≠\ Norm\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(E)}.

By considering the semi-direct product \(G_{1} = F \cdot G\), one
obtains an analogous counterexample where \(E\) is a
sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module of \(Lie(G_{1}/S)\); moreover, with the
notations introduced above, \(E = Lie(K/S)\) where \(K\) is the subgroup
\(O_{S} \oplus Nil^{2}\) of \(F\) (i.e., for every \(S' \to S\),
\(K(S')\) is formed by the pairs \((x_{1}, x_{2})\) such that
\(x_{2} \in Nil(S')^{2}\)).

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-1}

\section{Exposé III. Infinitesimal
extensions}\label{exposuxe9-iii.-infinitesimal-extensions}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-0{]} In this Exposé, we place ourselves in the
following general situation. We have a scheme \(S\) and a coherent
nilpotent ideal \(I\) on \(S\). We denote by \(S_{n}\) the closed
subscheme of \(S\) defined by the ideal \(I^{n+1}\) (\(n \geq 0\)). In
particular \(S_{0}\) is defined by \(I\). Since \(I\) is nilpotent,
\(S_{n}\) is equal to \(S\) for \(n\) large enough, and the \texttt{Sᵢ}
have the same underlying topological space. A typical example of this
situation is the following: \(S\) is the spectrum of a local Artinian
ring \(A\), \(I\) is the ideal defined by the radical of \(A\), so that
\(S_{0}\) is the spectrum of the residue field of \(A\).

In the preceding situation, one is given a certain number of data above
\(S_{0}\), and one looks above \(S\) for data which lift them, that is
to say, which give them back by base change from \(S\) to \(S_{0}\).
This is done step by step, by way of the \(S_{n}\). At each step, we
propose to define the obstructions encountered, and to classify, when
they exist, the solutions obtained.

The passage from \(S_{n}\) to \(S_{n+1}\) can be generalized as follows:
one has a scheme \(S\), two ideals \(I\) and \(J\) with \(I \supset J\),
and \(I \cdot J = 0\) (in the preceding case \(S\), \(I\) and \(J\) are
respectively \(S_{n+1}\), \(I/I^{n+2}\), \(I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}\)). We denote
by \(S_{0}\) (resp. \texttt{S\_J}) the closed subscheme of \(S\) defined
by \(I\) (resp. \(J\)), and we pose a problem of extension from
\texttt{S\_J} to \(S\).

In (SGA 1, III), problems of extension of morphisms of schemes and of
extension of schemes were treated. We pose here the problems of
extension of morphisms of groups, of extension of group structures, and
of extension of subgroups.

We have gathered in a § 0 the results of (SGA 1, III) which will be
useful to us, in order to put them in the most convenient form for our
purpose, and to spare the reader from having to refer constantly to (SGA
1, III).{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-1{]} § 1 collects some computations of group
cohomology which will be useful in what follows and which have nothing
to do with scheme theory. §§ 2 and 3 treat respectively of the extension
of group morphisms and the extension of group structures. In § 4, we
have briefly recalled the proof of a result stated in (TDTE IV)
concerning the extension of subschemes, and applied this result to the
problem of extension of subgroups. For the rest of the Seminar, only the
result of § 2, concerning the extension of morphisms of groups, will be
indispensable.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-2{]}

The idea of reducing infinitesimal extension problems to the usual
computations of cohomology in extensions of groups was suggested by J.
Giraud at the oral exposé (whose computations were notably more
complicated and less transparent). Unfortunately, it seems that this
method only applies well to the first two problems studied, and we have
been unable to escape rather painful computations in the case of
extensions of subgroups.

To simplify the language, we shall call a \(Y\)-functor, resp.
\(Y\)-scheme, etc., a functor, resp. scheme, etc., equipped with a
morphism into the functor \(Y\), thus extending the definitions of
Exposé I (which concerned only the case of a representable \(Y\)).

\subsection{0. Reminders from SGA 1 III and various
remarks}\label{reminders-from-sga-1-iii-and-various-remarks}

Let us first state a general definition.

\textbf{Definition 0.1.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category, \(X\) an object
of \texttt{Ĉ}, \(G\) a \texttt{Ĉ}-group acting on \(X\). We say that
\(X\) is \textbf{formally principal homogeneous}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-3{]}
under \(G\) if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:}

\emph{(i) for each object \(S\) of \(C\), the set \(X(S)\) is empty or
principal homogeneous under \(G(S)\);}

\emph{(ii) the morphism of functors \(G \times X \to X \times X\)
defined set-theoretically by \((g, x) \mapsto (gx, x)\) is an
isomorphism.}

This being so, we shall put the results of (SGA 1, III, §
5){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-4{]} in the form which will be most useful to us. We
shall employ the following general notations throughout this section. We
have a scheme \(S\) and on \(S\) two quasi-coherent ideals \(I\) and
\(J\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I ⊃ J   and   I · J = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular we shall therefore have \(J^{2} = 0\). We shall denote by
\(S_{0}\) (resp. \texttt{S\_J}) the closed subscheme of \(S\) defined by
the ideal \(I\) (resp. \(J\)). For every \(S\)-functor \(X\), we shall
systematically denote by \(X_{0}\) and \texttt{X\_J} the functors
obtained by base change from \(S\) to \(S_{0}\) and \texttt{S\_J}. Same
notation for a morphism.

\textbf{Definition 0.1.1.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-5{]} \emph{Let \(X\) be an
\(S\)-functor. Define a functor \(X^{+}\) above \(S\) by the formula:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, X⁺) = Hom\_\{S\_J\}(Y\_J, X\_J) = Hom\_S(Y\_J, X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for a variable \(S\)-scheme \(Y\).} In the notations of (Exp. II,
1), one has

\[
X^{+} \simeq \prod_{S_{J}/S} X_{J} .
\]

The identity morphism of \texttt{X\_J} defines by construction an
\(S\)-morphism

\[
p_{X} : X \to X^{+} .
\]

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-6{]} Explicitly, for every \(S\)-scheme \(Y\), the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_X(Y) : Hom\_S(Y, X) → Hom\_S(Y, X⁺) = Hom\_S(Y\_J, X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is the map induced by the morphism \(Y_{J} \to Y\).

\textbf{Remark 0.1.2.} \emph{Let us now observe that if \(X\) is an
\(S\)-group functor, then \texttt{X\_J} is an \texttt{S\_J}-group
functor; then the formula defining \(X^{+}\) endows it with a structure
of \(S\)-group functor, and the description of \(p_{X}\) above shows
that \(p_{X} : X \to X^{+}\) is a morphism of \(S\)-group functors.}

\textbf{Remark 0.1.3.} \emph{On the other hand, for every \(S\)-group
functor \(Y\), one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Y, X⁺) = Hom\_\{S\_J{-}gr.\}(Y\_J, X\_J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Indeed, let \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X^{+})\),
corresponding to \(f_{J} \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S_{J}}(Y_{J}, X_{J})\);
the condition that \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Y, X^{+})\) is
that, for every \(T \to S\) and \(y, y' \in Y(T)\), one has
\(f(y \cdot y') = f(y) \cdot f(y')\), and this is equivalent to}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_J(y\_J) · f\_J(y\_J′) = f\_J((y · y′)\_J);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{since \((y \cdot y')_{J} = y_{J} \cdot y_{J}'\) (because
\(Y(T) \to Y(T_{J}) = Y_{J}(T_{J})\) is a morphism of groups), this is
the condition for \(f_{J}\) to be a morphism of groups. Applying this to
\(Y = X\), we recover that \(p_{X}\), which corresponds to
\(id_{X_{J}}\), is a morphism of \(S\)-group functors.}

Let us now return to the general case, but assume that \(X\) is an
\(S\)-scheme. Since an \(S\)-morphism of a variable \(S\)-scheme \(Y\)
into \(X^{+}\) is by definition an \texttt{S\_J}-morphism \(g_{J}\) of
\texttt{Y\_J} into \texttt{X\_J}, we shall define an \(X^{+}\)-functor
in abelian groups \texttt{L\_X} as follows.

\textbf{Scholie 0.1.4.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-7{]} \emph{If \(\pi : Y \to S\)
is a morphism of schemes and \(M\) an \texttt{O\_S}-module, we denote by
\(M \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{Y}\) the inverse image \(\pi*(M)\). If \(J\) is
an ideal of \texttt{O\_S}, we denote by \(J \cdot O_{Y}\) the ideal of
\texttt{O\_Y} image of the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π*(J) = J ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y → O\_Y .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note that, for every morphism of \(S\)-schemes \(f : Z \to Y\), one has
an epimorphism of \texttt{O\_Z}-modules:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f*(J · O\_Y) → J · O\_Z ,                              (0.1.4)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

as follows from the commutative diagram below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_Z   ─────►   J ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Z}
\NormalTok{            │                                │}
\NormalTok{            ▼                                ▼}
\NormalTok{f*(J · O\_Y) = (J · O\_Y) ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_Z   ───►   J · O\_Z .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 0.1.5.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-8{]} \emph{Let \(X\) be an
\(S\)-scheme. For every \(X^{+}\)-scheme \(Y\), given by a morphism
\(g_{J} : Y_{J} \to X_{J}\), we set:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, L\_X) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(\Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) denotes the module of relative
differentials of \(X_{0}\) with respect to \(S_{0}\) (cf. SGA 1, I.1 or
EGA IV₄, 16.3), and where \(J \cdot O_{Y}\) is regarded as an
\(O_{Y_{0}}\)-module thanks to the fact that it is annihilated by
\(I\).}

Then \texttt{L\_X} is an \(X^{+}\)-functor in abelian
groups.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-9{]} Indeed, for every \(X^{+}\)-morphism
\(f : Z \to Y\), the functor \(f_{0}*\) and the morphism
\(f_{0}*(J \cdot O_{Y}) \to J \cdot O_{Z}\) of (0.1.4) induce a natural
morphism of abelian groups \(L_{X}(f)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Y)}
\NormalTok{        → Hom\_\{O\_\{Z₀\}\}(f₀* g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), f₀*(J · O\_Y))}
\NormalTok{        → Hom\_\{O\_\{Z₀\}\}(f₀* g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Z).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us finally note that \(L_{X}(f)\) is described locally as follows.
Note first that \(Y\) and \texttt{Y\_J} have the same underlying
topological space, and similarly for \(V\) and \texttt{V\_J} if \(V\) is
an open subset of \(Y\). Let then \(U = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\) be an
affine open of \(X\) above an affine open
\(\operatorname{Spec}(\Lambda)\) of \(S\),
\(V = \operatorname{Spec}(B)\) an affine open of \(Y\) such that
\(g_{J}(V_{J}) \subset U\), and \(W = \operatorname{Spec}(C)\) an affine
open of \(f^{-1}(V)\). Let \(J\) and \(I\) be the ideals of \(\Lambda\)
corresponding to \(J\) and \(I\). Then \(f\) (resp. \(g_{J}\)) induces a
morphism of \(\Lambda\)-algebras \(\theta : B \to C\) (resp.
\(\phi : A \to B/JB\)), and one obviously has \(\theta(JB) \subset JC\).
On the other hand,
\(m \in \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{0}}}(g_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), J \cdot O_{Y})\)
induces an element \(D\) of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{V₀\}\}(g₀*(Ω¹\_\{U/S\}), J · O\_V) = Hom\_\{B/IB\}(Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗\_A B/IB, JB) = Der\_Λ(A, JB),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the image of \(L_{X}(f)(m)\) in

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{W₀\}\}(f₀* g₀*(Ω¹\_\{U/S\}), J · O\_Z) = Hom\_\{C/IC\}(Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗\_A C/IC, JC) = Der\_Λ(A, JC)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is none other than \(\theta \circ D\).

\textbf{Remark 0.1.6.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-10{]} \emph{Let \(f : X \to W\)
be an \(S\)-morphism. It induces an \(S\)-morphism
\(f^{+} : X^{+} \to W^{+}\) defined as follows: if \(g\) is an element
of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X^{+})\), corresponding to an
\(S\)-morphism \(g_{J} : Y_{J} \to X\), then \(f^{+}(g)\) is the element
\(f \circ g_{J}\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, W^{+})\). It is clear
that the following diagram is commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        f}
\NormalTok{   X ─────► W}
\NormalTok{   │         │}
\NormalTok{p\_X│         │p\_W}
\NormalTok{   ▼   f⁺    ▼}
\NormalTok{   X⁺ ────► W⁺ .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Reminders 0.1.7.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-11{]} \emph{In this paragraph,
given an \(S\)-scheme \(X\), we ``recall'' certain functorial properties
of the module of differentials \(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}\) and of the first
infinitesimal neighborhood of the diagonal \(\Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\),
properties which follow easily from (EGA IV₄, §§ 16.1--16.4), but which
do not figure there explicitly.}

\textbf{a)} Let us begin by recalling the following facts (cf.~EGA II,
§§ 1.2--1.5). Let \(g : Y \to X\) be a morphism of schemes,
\(\pi : X' \to X\) an affine \(X\)-scheme, \(B\) the quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_X}-algebra \(\pi_{*}(O_{X'})\); then the \(Y\)-scheme
\(Y \times_{X} X'\) is affine and corresponds to the quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_Y}-algebra \(g*(B)\), and one has a commutative diagram of
bijections:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_X(Y, X′)            ──∼──►    Hom\_Y(Y, Y ×\_X X′)}
\NormalTok{    │                                       │}
\NormalTok{    ≀                                       ≀}
\NormalTok{    ▼                                       ▼}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_X{-}alg.\}(B, g\_*(O\_Y))   ──∼──►   Hom\_\{O\_Y{-}alg.\}(g*(B), O\_Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, these bijections are functorial in the pair \((X, X')\), i.e.,
if \(W'\) is an affine \(W\)-scheme, corresponding to the quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_W}-algebra \(A\), if one has a commutative diagram of
morphisms of schemes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{            X′ ──f′──► W′}
\NormalTok{          ↗ g′         │}
\NormalTok{         /             │}
\NormalTok{        ↗              │}
\NormalTok{      Y ──g──► X ──f──► W ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and if we denote by \(\phi : A \to f_{*}(B)\) and
\(\phi\sharp : f*(A) \to B\) (resp. \(\theta : B \to g_{*}(O_{Y})\) and
\(\theta\sharp : g*(B) \to O_{Y}\)) the algebra morphisms associated to
\(f'\) (resp. to a variable \(X\)-morphism \(g' : Y \to X'\)), then one
has the following commutative diagram (where \(Y\) is viewed as a
\(W\)-scheme via \(f \circ g\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                         g′ ↦ f′ ∘ g′}
\NormalTok{Hom\_X(Y, X′) ──────────────────────► Hom\_W(Y, W′)}
\NormalTok{                                          │}
\NormalTok{                                          ≃}
\NormalTok{                                          ▼}
\NormalTok{                                Hom\_\{O\_W{-}alg.\}(A, f\_* g\_*(O\_Y))}
\NormalTok{                                          │}
\NormalTok{                                          ≃}
\NormalTok{       θ ↦ θ ∘ φ♯                         ▼}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_X{-}alg.\}(B, g\_*(O\_Y)) ──────► Hom\_\{O\_X{-}alg.\}(f*(A), g\_*(O\_Y))}
\NormalTok{       │                                  │}
\NormalTok{       ≀                                  ≀}
\NormalTok{       ▼   ψ ↦ ψ ∘ g*(φ♯)                 ▼}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_Y{-}alg.\}(g*(B), O\_Y) ──────► Hom\_\{O\_Y{-}alg.\}(g* f*(A), O\_Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{b)} Let now \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme. Let \(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}\)
be the module of differentials of \(X\) over \(S\), and
\(\Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\) the first infinitesimal neighborhood of the
diagonal immersion \(\delta_{X} : X \to X \times_{S} X\); it is a
subscheme of \(X \times_{S} X\), of which the diagonal \(\Delta_{X/S}\)
is a closed subscheme. We denote by \(pr^{i}_{X}\) (\(i = 1, 2\)) the
two projections \(X \times_{S} X \to X\), and by \(\pi_{X}\) the
restriction of \(pr^{1}_{X}\) to \(\Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\).

On the one hand, every morphism \(f : X \to W\) of \(S\)-schemes induces
an \(S\)-morphism
\(\Delta^{(1)} f : \Delta^{(1)}_{X/S} \to \Delta^{(1)}_{W/S}\) such that
the following diagram is commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       δ\_X            pr\_X}
\NormalTok{   X ─────► Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\} ─────► X ×\_S X ─────► X}
\NormalTok{   │              │               │           │}
\NormalTok{ f │       Δ⁽¹⁾f │            f×f│         f │}
\NormalTok{   ▼       δ\_W   ▼                ▼   pr\_W   ▼}
\NormalTok{   W ─────► Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{W/S\} ─────► W ×\_S W ─────► W .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, \(\Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\) is, via the projection
\(\pi_{X}\), an affine \(X\)-scheme, spectrum of the augmented
quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_X}-algebra

\[
P^{1}_{X/S} = O_{X} \oplus \Omega^{1}_{X/S},
\]

where \(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}\) is an ideal of square zero; the augmentation
is the morphism of \texttt{O\_X}-algebras
\(\epsilon_{X} : P^{1}_{X/S} \to O_{X}\) which vanishes on
\(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}\) and which corresponds to the closed immersion
\(\delta_{X} : X \hookrightarrow \Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\). Then, every
morphism of \(S\)-schemes \(f : X \to W\) induces a morphism of
augmented \texttt{O\_X}-algebras

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f*(P¹\_\{W/S\}) = O\_X ⊕ f*(Ω¹\_\{W/S\}) → P¹\_\{X/S\} = O\_X ⊕ Ω¹\_\{X/S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, equivalently, a morphism of \texttt{O\_X}-modules

\[
f_{X/W/S} : f*(\Omega^{1}_{W/S}) \to \Omega^{1}_{X/S},
\]

cf.~(EGA IV₄, 16.4.3.6) (and (16.4.18.2) for the notation
\(f_{X/W/S}\)).

Since \(\pi_{X} : \Delta^{(1)}_{X/S} \to X\) is affine, then, by a),
\(\Delta^{(1)} f\) is entirely determined by \(f_{X/W/S}\) and, for
every \(X\)-scheme \(g : Y \to X\), the set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_X(Y, Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\}) ≃ Hom\_\{O\_Y{-}alg.\}(O\_Y ⊕ g*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}), O\_Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is identified with a subset of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y}}(g*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), O_{Y})\), namely the
subset

\[
\tilde{\operatorname{Hom}}_{O_{Y}}(g*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), O_{Y})
\]

formed by the \texttt{O\_Y}-morphisms
\(\psi : g*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}) \to O_{Y}\) such that \(Im(\psi)\) is an
ideal of \texttt{O\_Y} of square zero.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-12{]}

Consequently, applying a) to the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              Δ⁽¹⁾ f}
\NormalTok{   Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\} ────► Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{W/S\}}
\NormalTok{       ↗}
\NormalTok{    g′│}
\NormalTok{       │}
\NormalTok{    Y ──g──► X ──f──► W}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and taking into account that \(\Delta^{(1)} f\) is the restriction to
\(\Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\) of \(f \times f\), one obtains the following
commutative diagram, functorial in the \(X\)-scheme
\texttt{Y\ ──g──►\ X}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              (g, g′) ↦ (f∘g, f∘g′)}
\NormalTok{Hom\_X(Y, X ×\_S X) ──────────────────────────────► Hom\_W(Y, Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{W/S\})}
\NormalTok{       ↑                                                  ↑}
\NormalTok{       │                                                  │}
\NormalTok{       │                              g′ ↦ Δ⁽¹⁾f ∘ g′}
\NormalTok{Hom\_X(Y, Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\}) ────────────────────────► Hom\_W(Y, Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{W/S\})       (0.1.7 (∗))}
\NormalTok{       │                                                  │}
\NormalTok{       ≃                                                  ≃}
\NormalTok{       ▼            ψ ↦ ψ ∘ g*(f\_\{X/W/S\})                  ▼}
\NormalTok{Hom̃\_\{O\_Y\}(g*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}), O\_Y) ──────────────► Hom̃\_\{O\_Y\}(g* f*(Ω¹\_\{W/S\}), O\_Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 0.1.7.1.} \emph{Let us end this paragraph with the
following remark, which will be useful later (cf.~0.1.10). If we denote
by \(\tilde{L}_{X}\) the \(X\)-functor which to every \(X\)-scheme
\(g : Y \to X\) associates
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y}}(g*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), O_{Y})\), and
\(\tilde{L}_{f} : \tilde{L}_{X} \to \tilde{L}_{W}\) the morphism of
functors defined above (which to every \(\psi \in \tilde{L}_{X}(Y)\)
associates \(\psi \circ g*(f_{X/W/S})\)), what precedes shows that we
have a commutative diagram of functors:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ×̃ X L̃\_X  ◄──∼──  Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\}  ─────► X ×\_S X}
\NormalTok{    │                   │                 │}
\NormalTok{f ×̃\_f│                Δ⁽¹⁾f│           f×f│}
\NormalTok{    ▼                   ▼                 ▼}
\NormalTok{W ×̃ W L̃\_W  ◄──∼──  Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{W/S\}  ─────► W ×\_S W.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Theorem 0.1.8.} \emph{(SGA 1, III 5.1){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-13{]} Let
\(Y\), \(X\) be two \(S\)-schemes, \(J\) a quasi-coherent ideal of
\texttt{O\_Y} of square zero, \texttt{Y\_J} the closed subscheme of
\(Y\) defined by \(J\), and \(g_{J} : Y_{J} \to X\) an \(S\)-morphism.}

\emph{a) The set \(P(g_{J})\) of \(S\)-morphisms \(g : Y \to X\) which
extend \(g_{J}\) is either empty, or principal homogeneous under the
abelian group}

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{J}}}(g_{J}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), J).
\]

\emph{b) If \(i : Y_{0} \hookrightarrow Y_{J}\) is the closed immersion
defined by a quasi-coherent ideal \(I \supset J\) such that
\(I \cdot J = 0\), and if \(g_{0} = g_{J} \circ i\), the preceding
abelian group is isomorphic to}

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{0}}}(g_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), J).
\]

\emph{Proof.} (b) follows at once from (a). Indeed, \(J\), being
annihilated by \(I\), can be considered as an \(O_{Y_{0}}\)-module,
whence, by adjunction:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\}(g\_J*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}), J) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(i* g\_J*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}), J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To prove (a), we may assume \(P(g_{J}) \neq \emptyset\), i.e.~that there
exists an \(S\)-morphism \(g : Y \to X\) extending \(g_{J}\). Let us
denote by \(j\) the immersion \(Y_{J} \hookrightarrow Y\). Then
\(P(g_{J})\) is the set of \(S\)-morphisms \(g' : Y \to X\) such that
\(g' \circ j = g_{J}\). The datum of such a \(g'\) is equivalent to the
datum of an \(S\)-morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : Y → X ×\_S X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \(pr_{1} \circ h = g\) and \(h_{J} = \delta \circ g_{J}\),
where \(h_{J} = h \circ j\) and \(\delta\) is the diagonal immersion
\(X \hookrightarrow X \times_{S} X\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                h\_J = δ ∘ g\_J}
\NormalTok{   X ×\_S X  ◄──────────────── Y\_J}
\NormalTok{    │  ▲ h                    │}
\NormalTok{pr₁│   ╲                    j │}
\NormalTok{    ▼    ╲                     ▼}
\NormalTok{    X  ◄─g───                  Y .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(h_{J}\) factors through \(\delta\) and \(Y\) is in the first
infinitesimal neighborhood of the immersion \(j : Y_{J} \to Y\) (since
\(J^{2} = 0\)), then, by functoriality (cf.~EGA IV₄, 16.2.2 (i)), the
\(h\)'s sought factor uniquely through \(\Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\)
(cf.~0.1.7). Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y′ = Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\} ×\_X Y    and    Y\_J′ = Y′ ×\_Y Y\_J = Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\} ×\_X Y\_J .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then the \(h\)'s sought are in bijection with the sections \(u\) of
\(Y' \to Y\) which extend the section
\(u_{J} = (\delta \circ g_{J}, id)\) of \(Y_{J}' \to Y_{J}\). On the
other hand, \(Y'\) (resp. \(Y_{J}'\)) is an affine scheme over \(Y\)
(resp. \texttt{Y\_J}), corresponding to the quasi-coherent algebra

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = O\_Y ⊕ g*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}),    resp.    A\_J = A ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y\_J\} = O\_\{Y\_J\} ⊕ g\_J*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us denote by \(\epsilon : A \to O_{Y}\) the canonical augmentation
of \(A\) (i.e.~the morphism of \texttt{O\_Y}-algebras \(A \to O_{Y}\)
which vanishes on \(g*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S})\)), and likewise define
\(\epsilon_{J} : A_{J} \to O_{Y_{J}}\). Then,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(Y′/Y) ≃ Hom\_\{O\_Y{-}alg.\}(A, O\_Y),    Γ(Y\_J′/Y\_J) ≃ Hom\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}{-}alg.\}(A\_J, O\_\{Y\_J\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and, via these isomorphisms, the section \(u = (\delta \circ g, id)\)
(resp. \(u_{J}\)) corresponds to \(\epsilon\) (resp. \(\epsilon_{J}\)).
Consequently, \(P(g_{J})\) is in bijection with the set of algebra
morphisms \(A \to O_{Y}\) which reduce to \(\epsilon_{J}\), and via this
bijection, \(g\) corresponds to \(\epsilon\).

Set \(M = g*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S})\). Then
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y}-alg.}(A, O_{Y})\) is identified with the set
of \texttt{O\_Y}-morphisms \(\psi : M \to O_{Y}\) such that \(Im(\psi)\)
is an ideal of square zero, and we are interested in those which induce
the null morphism \(M \to O_{Y_{J}} = O_{Y}/J\), i.e.~which send \(M\)
into \(J\). Conversely, since \(J^{2} = 0\), every
\texttt{O\_Y}-morphism \(\phi : M \to J\) comes from a (unique) algebra
morphism \(A \to O_{Y}\), reducing to \(\epsilon_{J}\). Finally, we have
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y}}(g*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), J) = \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{J}}}(g_{J}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), J)\)
since \(J^{2} = 0\) (cf.~the proof of (b) already seen). One thus
obtains a bijection

\[
P(g_{J}) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{J}}}(g_{J}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), J)
\]

by which \(g\) corresponds to the null morphism.

For every
\(m \in \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{J}}}(g_{J}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}), J)\),
denote by \(m \cdot g\) the element of \(P(g_{J})\) associated to \(g\)
and \(m\) by the preceding bijection. We have already seen that
\(0 \cdot g = g\); it remains to see that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{m′ · (m · g) = (m + m′) · g.                            (0.1.8 (∗))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is verified locally.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-14{]} Indeed, the two
preceding morphisms \(Y \to X\) induce the same continuous map as \(g\)
between the underlying topological spaces; it therefore suffices to
verify that for every affine open \(U = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\) of
\(X\) above an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}(\Lambda)\) of \(S\),
and every affine open \(V = \operatorname{Spec}(B)\) of \(g^{-1}(U)\),
they induce the same morphism of \(\Lambda\)-algebras \(A \to B\).

Let \(J = \Gamma(V, J)\) and let \(\phi, \psi\) and \(\eta\) be the
morphisms \(A \to B\) induced by \(g\), \(m \cdot g\) and
\(m' \cdot (m \cdot g)\) respectively; they coincide modulo \(J\). One
can uniquely write \(\psi = \phi + D\) (resp. \(\eta = \psi + D'\)),
where \(D\) (resp. \(D'\)) is an element of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Der\_φ(A, J) = \{δ ∈ Hom\_Λ(A, J) | δ(ab) = φ(a) δ(b) + φ(b) δ(a)\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(resp. \(\operatorname{Der}_{\psi}(A, J)\)). But
\(\operatorname{Der}_{\phi}(A, J) = \operatorname{Der}_{\psi}(A, J)\)
since \(J^{2} = 0\), and both are identified with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{B/J\}(Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗\_A B/J, J),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and via this identification \(D\) corresponds to \(m\) and \(D'\) to
\(m'\). Then \(\eta = \phi + D + D'\) and \(D + D'\) corresponds to
\(m + m'\), whence the equality (∗).

\textbf{Corollary 0.1.9.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-15{]} \emph{Let \(X\) be an
\(S\)-scheme; resume the notations of 0.1.5. Then \(X\) is endowed with
a (left) action of the \(X^{+}\)-abelian group \texttt{L\_X}, which
makes \(X\) into a formally principal homogeneous object under
\texttt{L\_X} above \(X^{+}\), i.e.~one has an isomorphism of
\(X^{+}\)-functors:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X × X ──∼──► X × X}
\NormalTok{       X⁺          X⁺}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(defined set-theoretically by \((m, x) \mapsto (x, m \cdot x)\)).}

\emph{Proof.} Let \(i_{0}\) be the immersion
\(X_{0} \hookrightarrow X\). Note first that, since
\(X_{0} = X \times_{S} S_{0}\), one has
\(i_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}) \simeq \Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) (cf.~EGA
IV, 16.4.5).

Let \(Y\) be an \(X^{+}\)-scheme, given by an \(S\)-morphism
\(g_{J} : Y_{J} \to X\), and let \(g_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) be the
morphism obtained by base change. By 0.1.8, if
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(Y, X)\) is non-empty, it is a principal
homogeneous set under the group

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀* i₀*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}), J · O\_Y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is identified with
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{0}}}(g_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}), J \cdot O_{Y}) = L_{X}(Y)\).
One therefore has a bijection

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X(Y) × Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, X)  ──∼──►  Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, X ×\_\{X⁺\} X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

given by \((m, g) \mapsto (g, m \cdot g)\). Let us show that this is
``functorial in \(Y\)''.

Let \(f : Z \to Y\) be a morphism of \(S\)-schemes. It is a question of
showing that the diagram below is commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X(Y) × Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, X) ──∼──► Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, X ×\_\{X⁺\} X)}
\NormalTok{   │                                       │}
\NormalTok{L\_X(f) × f                             f × f}
\NormalTok{   ▼                                       ▼}
\NormalTok{L\_X(Z) × Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Z, X) ──∼──► Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Z, X ×\_\{X⁺\} X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(Y, X) = \emptyset\), there is nothing to
show. It therefore suffices to see that, for every \(S\)-morphism
\(g : Y \to X\) extending \(g_{J}\) and every \(m \in L_{X}(Y)\), one
has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(m · g) ∘ f = L\_X(f)(m) · (g ∘ f).                       (0.1.9 (∗))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

These two \(S\)-morphisms \(Z \to X\) coincide on \texttt{Z\_J} with
\(g_{J} \circ f_{J}\); in particular, they induce the same continuous
map as \(g \circ f\) between the underlying topological spaces.
Consequently, it suffices to see that, if \(z \in Z\), \(y = f(z)\),
\(x = g(y)\), and if \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) denote respectively the local
rings \(O_{X,x}\), \(O_{Y,y}\), \(O_{Z,z}\), then the morphisms
\(A \to C\) induced by \((m \cdot g) \circ f\) and
\(L_{X}(f)(m) \cdot (g \circ f)\) coincide. Denote by \(s\) the image of
\(x\) in \(S\), \(\Lambda = O_{S,s}\), \(J\) and \(I\) the ideals of
\(\Lambda\) corresponding to \(J\) and \(I\), and let
\(\phi, \psi : A \to B\) and \(\theta : B \to C\) be the morphisms of
\(\Lambda\)-algebras induced by \(g\), \(m \cdot g\), and \(f\). Then
\(m\) induces an element \(D\) of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{B/IB\}(Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗\_A B/IB, JB) = Der\_Λ(A, JB)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one has \(\psi = \phi + D\); hence \((m \cdot g) \circ f\)
corresponds to
\(\theta \circ \psi = \theta \circ \phi + \theta \circ D\). Now, we have
seen in 0.1.5 that \(\theta \circ D\) is the image of \(L_{X}(f)(m)\) in

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{C/IC\}(Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗\_A C/IC, JC) = Der\_Λ(A, JC);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

consequently, \(\theta \circ \phi + \theta \circ D\) is the image of
\(L_{X}(f)(m) \cdot (g \circ f)\). This proves the equality (0.1.9 (∗)).

\textbf{Corollary 0.1.10.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-16{]} \emph{a) \texttt{L\_X}
depends functorially on \(X\): for every \(S\)-morphism \(f : X \to W\),
there exists an \(S\)-morphism \(L_{f} : L_{X} \to L_{W}\) which is a
morphism of abelian groups ``above \(f^{+}\)'', i.e., the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        L\_f}
\NormalTok{   L\_X ────► L\_W}
\NormalTok{   │           │}
\NormalTok{   ▼   f⁺      ▼}
\NormalTok{   X⁺ ──────► W⁺}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is commutative, and for every \(Y \to X^{+}\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_f(Y) : Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, L\_X) → Hom\_\{W⁺\}(Y, L\_W)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(where \(Y\) is above \(W^{+}\) via \(f^{+}\)) is a morphism of
abelian groups.}

\emph{b) Moreover, the following diagram is commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X × X ─∼─► X ×\_\{X⁺\} X}
\NormalTok{   │              │}
\NormalTok{L\_f × f        f × f}
\NormalTok{   ▼              ▼}
\NormalTok{L\_W × W ─∼─► W ×\_\{W⁺\} W .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} a) \(L_{f}\) is induced by the morphism of
\(O_{X_{0}}\)-modules
\(f_{X_{0}/W_{0}/S_{0}} : f_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{W_{0}/S_{0}}) \to \Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\)
(cf.~0.1.7 b)): for every \(X^{+}\)-scheme \(Y\), given by an
\(S\)-morphism \(g_{J} : Y_{J} \to X\), one has a commutative diagram,
functorial in \(Y\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          L\_f(Y)}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Y) ───► Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀* f₀*(Ω¹\_\{W₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Y)}
\NormalTok{       │                                                       │}
\NormalTok{       ▼                                                       ▼}
\NormalTok{     \{g\_J\}                                                \{f\_J ∘ g\_J\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(L_{f}(Y)\) is the map
\(\psi \mapsto \psi \circ g_{0}*(f_{X_{0}/W_{0}/S_{0}})\), which is
indeed a morphism of abelian groups.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-17{]}

Let us prove (b). Let \(Y\) be an \(X^{+}\)-scheme; if
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(Y, X) = \emptyset\) there is nothing to
show. So let \(g \in \operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(Y, X)\); it must be seen
that for every \(m \in L_{X}(Y)\), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ∘ (m · g) = L\_f(Y)(m) · (f ∘ g).                       (0.1.10 (∗))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, \(g\) being fixed,
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(Y, X \times_{X^{+}} X)\) is a subset of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X}(Y, \Delta^{(1)}_{X/S})\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X(Y) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Y) = Hom\_\{O\_Y\}(g*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}), J · O\_Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

a subset of \(\tilde{L}_{X}(Y)\) (cf.~0.1.7); finally, \(L_{f}(Y)\) is
the restriction to \(L_{X}(Y)\) of the map \(\tilde{L}_{f}(Y)\).
Moreover, the bijection

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X(Y) ──∼──► Hom\_X(Y, X ×\_\{X⁺\} X),    m ↦ (g, m · g)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is (the inverse of) the restriction to
\(L_{X}(Y) \subset \tilde{L}_{X}(Y)\) of the bijection
\texttt{Hom\_X(Y,\ Δ⁽¹⁾\_\{X/S\})\ ──∼──►\ \{g\}\ ×\ L̃\_X(Y)} considered
in 0.1.7.1. Consequently, the equality (0.1.10 (∗)) results from (0.1.7
(∗)); indeed, if we denote by \(g'\) the \(X\)-morphism
\(Y \to \Delta^{(1)}_{X/S}\) defined by \((g, m \cdot g)\), then the
element of \(\tilde{L}_{W}(Y)\) corresponding to
\((f \circ g, f \circ g')\) is \(\tilde{L}_{f}(Y)(m) = L_{f}(Y)(m)\),
i.e., one indeed has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_f(m) · (f ∘ g) = f ∘ (m · g).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 0.1.11.} \emph{Let \(X\), \(X'\) be two \(S\)-schemes. One
has a commutative diagram:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X ×\_S L\_\{X′\} ──∼──► L\_\{X ×\_S X′\}}
\NormalTok{       │                  │}
\NormalTok{       ▼                  ▼}
\NormalTok{X⁺ ×\_S X′⁺  ──∼──► (X ×\_S X′)⁺ .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-18{]} \emph{Proof.} First, for every \(S\)-scheme
\(Y\), \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X^{+} \times_{S} X'^{+})\) equals
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X^{+}) \times \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X'^{+})\)
and this is isomorphic to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y\_J, X) × Hom\_S(Y\_J, X′) = Hom\_S(Y, (X ×\_S X′)⁺);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

this proves that
\(X^{+} \times_{S} X'^{+} \simeq (X \times_{S} X')^{+}\).

Next, let \(Y\) be a scheme above \(X^{+} \times_{S} X'^{+}\) via a
morphism \(h : Y_{J} \to X \times_{S} X'\); set \(f = p \circ h\) and
\(g = q \circ h\), where we have denoted by \texttt{p,\ q} the
projections of \(X \times_{S} X'\) to \(X\) and \(X'\). Since
\(\Omega^{1}_{(X_{0} \times_{S_{0}} X'_{0})/S_{0}} \cong p_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}) \oplus q_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{X'_{0}/S_{0}})\)
(cf.~EGA IV₄, 16.4.23), one obtains a natural isomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(f₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Y) × Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X′₀/S₀\}), J · O\_Y)}
\NormalTok{    ≃ Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(h₀*(Ω¹\_\{(X₀ ×\_\{S₀\} X′₀)/S₀\}), J · O\_Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e., \(L_{X}(Y) \times L_{X'}(Y) \simeq L_{X \times_{S} X'}(Y)\).

\textbf{Remark 0.1.12.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-19{]} \emph{Let \(C\) be a
category stable under fibered products, \(S\) an object of \(C\),
\(T_{1}\), \(T_{2}\) two objects above \(S\) and, for \(i = 1, 2\),
\(L_{i}\) and \(X_{i}\) two objects above \(T_{i}\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_1 ──► T\_1 ◄── X\_1        L\_2 ──► T\_2 ◄── X\_2}
\NormalTok{              ╲                    ╱}
\NormalTok{                ╲                ╱}
\NormalTok{                  ▼            ▼}
\NormalTok{                       S                  .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then one has a natural isomorphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(L\_1 ×\_\{T\_1\} X\_1) ×\_S (L\_2 ×\_\{T\_2\} X\_2) ≃ (L\_1 ×\_S L\_2) ×\_\{T\_1 ×\_S T\_2\} (X\_1 ×\_S X\_2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consequently, from the preceding lemma one deduces the:

\textbf{Corollary 0.1.13.} \emph{Let \texttt{X\_1}, \texttt{X\_2} be two
\(S\)-schemes. One has a commutative diagram of isomorphisms:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        L\_\{X\_1 ×\_S X\_2\} ×\_\{(X\_1 ×\_S X\_2)⁺\} (X\_1 ×\_S X\_2)}
\NormalTok{              │                                ╲}
\NormalTok{   (0.1.11) ≃ ▼                                  ≃}
\NormalTok{        (L\_\{X\_1\} ×\_S L\_\{X\_2\}) ×\_\{(X\_1⁺ ×\_S X\_2⁺)\} (X\_1 ×\_S X\_2)}
\NormalTok{                              ──∼──►}
\NormalTok{        (L\_\{X\_1\} ×\_\{X\_1⁺\} X\_1) ×\_S (L\_\{X\_2\} ×\_\{X\_2⁺\} X\_2) .}
\NormalTok{                                                (0.1.12)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We can now state:

\textbf{Proposition 0.2.} \emph{For every \(S\)-scheme \(X\), one can
define a (left) action of the \(X^{+}\)-abelian group \texttt{L\_X} on
the \(X^{+}\)-object \(X\), such that:}

\emph{(i) this action makes \(X\) into a formally principal homogeneous
object under \texttt{L\_X} above \(X^{+}\), i.e.~the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X × X ──► X × X}
\NormalTok{       X⁺          X⁺}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an isomorphism of \(X^{+}\)-functors;}

\emph{(ii) this action is functorial in the \(S\)-scheme \(X\), i.e.,
for every \(S\)-morphism \(f : X \to W\), the following diagram is
commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X ×\_\{X⁺\} X ─────► X}
\NormalTok{     │              │}
\NormalTok{ L\_f × f          f │}
\NormalTok{     ▼              ▼}
\NormalTok{L\_W ×\_\{W⁺\} W ─────► W ;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) this action ``commutes with fibered product'', i.e.~for all
\(S\)-schemes \texttt{X\_1} and \texttt{X\_2}, the following diagram is
commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_\{X\_1 ×\_S X\_2\} ×\_\{(X\_1 ×\_S X\_2)⁺\} (X\_1 ×\_S X\_2)  ──►  X\_1 ×\_S X\_2}
\NormalTok{        │                                                    ▲}
\NormalTok{        ≃                                                    │}
\NormalTok{        ▼                                                    │}
\NormalTok{(L\_\{X\_1\} ×\_S L\_\{X\_2\}) ×\_\{(X\_1⁺ ×\_S X\_2⁺)\} (X\_1 ×\_S X\_2) ──∼──► (L\_\{X\_1\} ×\_\{X\_1⁺\} X\_1) ×\_S (L\_\{X\_2\} ×\_\{X\_2⁺\} X\_2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-20{]} (i) and (ii) follow respectively
from Corollaries 0.1.9 and 0.1.10. To prove (iii), denote
\(P(X) = L_{X} \times_{X^{+}} X\), for every \(S\)-scheme \(X\). Then,
by (ii) applied to the projections
\(p_{i} : X_{1} \times_{S} X_{2} \to X_{i}\), one obtains commutative
squares

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(X\_1 ×\_S X\_2)  ─────►  X\_1 ×\_S X\_2}
\NormalTok{       │                     │}
\NormalTok{  L\_\{p\_i\} × p\_i             p\_i}
\NormalTok{       ▼                     ▼}
\NormalTok{   P(X\_i)         ─────►   X\_i}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for \(i = 1, 2\), and hence a commutative square:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(X\_1 ×\_S X\_2)         ─────►   X\_1 ×\_S X\_2}
\NormalTok{       │                                ║}
\NormalTok{       ▼                                ▼}
\NormalTok{P(X\_1) ×\_S P(X\_2)      ─────►   X\_1 ×\_S X\_2 .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combining this with Corollary 0.1.13, one obtains that the vertical
arrow is an isomorphism, and that one has the commutative diagram
announced in (iii).

\textbf{Remark 0.3.} \emph{Suppose the \(X^{+}\)-scheme \(Y\) flat over
\(S\) (cf.~SGA 1, IV). Then one can write}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, L\_X) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(g₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 0.4.} \emph{Denote by \(\pi_{0} : X_{0} \to S_{0}\) the
structural morphism and suppose there exists an \(O_{S_{0}}\)-module
\(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) such that
\(\Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}} \simeq \pi_{0}*(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}})\)
(the case will arise in particular when \(X_{0}\) is an \(S_{0}\)-group,
cf.~II, 4.11). If one defines a functor \(L'_{X}\) above \(S\) by the
formula}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, L′\_X) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J · O\_Y),     (0.4.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one then has
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(Y, L_{X}) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, L'_{X})\)
for every \(X^{+}\)-scheme \(Y\), that is to say}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_X = L′\_X × X⁺ .}
\NormalTok{              S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-21{]} Then, since
\(L_{X} \times_{X^{+}} X = L'_{X} \times_{S} X\), the action of
\texttt{L\_X} on \(X\) induces an action of \(L'_{X}\) on \(X\), and
this action respects the morphism \(p_{X} : X \to X^{+}\); indeed, if
\(Y\) is an \(S\)-scheme, \(h : Y \to X\) an \(S\)-morphism and \(m\) an
element of \(L'_{X}(Y)\), then \(h\) and \(m \cdot h\) have the same
restriction to \texttt{Y\_J}, i.e.~\(p_{X}(m \cdot h) = p_{X}(h)\).

\textbf{Remark 0.5.} \emph{Keep the hypotheses and notations of 0.4 and
suppose moreover that \(Y\) is an \(S\)-scheme flat over \(S\). Then we
have}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{X⁺\}(Y, L\_X) = Hom\_S(Y, L′\_X) = Hom\_\{S₀\}(Y₀, L⁰\_X),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where the \(S_{0}\)-functor in abelian groups \(L^{0}_{X}\) is
defined by the following identity (with respect to the variable
\(S_{0}\)-scheme \(T\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L⁰\_X) = Hom\_\{O\_T\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T).    (0.5.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In the notations of (II, 1), we have therefore shown that the
functors \(L'_{X}\) and \(\prod_{S_{0}/S} L^{0}_{X}\) have the same
restriction to the full subcategory of \((Sch)/S\) whose objects are the
\(S\)-schemes \(Y\) flat over \(S\).}

\textbf{Remark 0.6.} \emph{Keep the hypotheses and notations of
0.5{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-22{]} and suppose moreover that there exists a
section \(\epsilon_{0}\) of \(\pi_{0} : X_{0} \to S_{0}\); one then has
\(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}} \simeq \epsilon_{0}*(\Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}})\).}

First, one has (independently of the preceding hypothesis):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L⁰\_X) = Γ(T, Hom\_\{O\_T\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now suppose that \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) admits a finite
presentation (cf.~EGA 0\_I, 5.2.5), which will in particular be the case
if \(X_{0}\) is locally of finite presentation over \(S_{0}\) (cf.~EGA
IV₄, 16.4.22). Then, if \(T\) is flat over \(S_{0}\), it follows from
(EGA 0\_I, 6.7.6) that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_T\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T) ≃ Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L⁰\_X) = Γ(T, Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Introducing the notation \(W(\cdot)\) of (I, 4.6.1), we have therefore
proved that for every \(S_{0}\)-scheme \(T\) flat over \(S_{0}\), one
has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L⁰\_X) = Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, W(Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J))).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In summary, if \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) admits a finite
presentation, and if one restricts to the category of \(S\)-schemes flat
over \(S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L′\_X = ∏\_\{S₀/S\} W(Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J)),                  (0.6.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S_{0}}}(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}, J)\) is a
quasi-coherent \(O_{S_{0}}\)-module, by EGA I, 9.1.1.

Note finally that if \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) is moreover locally
free (of finite rank), for example if \(X_{0}\) is smooth over \(S_{0}\)
(in which case it is automatically locally of finite presentation over
\(S_{0}\)), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J) ≃ Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J ,           (0.6.2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where, by abuse of language (\(X_{0}\) not being necessarily an
\(S_{0}\)-group), we denote by \(Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})\) the dual of the
\(O_{S_{0}}\)-module \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\).{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-23{]}

Proposition 0.2 (and its proof) has two important
corollaries.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-24{]}

\textbf{Corollary 0.7.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme.}

\emph{a) Every \(S\)-endomorphism of \(X\) inducing the identity on
\texttt{X\_J} is an automorphism.}

\emph{b) One has an exact sequence of groups:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► Hom\_\{O\_\{X₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J · O\_X) ──i──► Aut\_S(X) ──► Aut\_\{S\_J\}(X\_J) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{c) Moreover, if one makes \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)\) act on the
first group by transport of structure, one has, for all
\(u \in \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)\) and
\(m \in \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{X_{0}}}(\Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}, J \cdot O_{X})\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i(u · m) = u · i(m) · u⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} By 0.2 (i), \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(X, X)\) is a
principal homogeneous set under
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(X, L_{X})\), since it is certainly
non-empty: it contains a marked point, namely the identity automorphism
of \(X\).{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-25{]} Consequently, the map
\(m \mapsto m \cdot id_{X}\) induces a bijection

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{X₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J · O\_X) = L\_X(X) ──∼──► Hom\_\{X⁺\}(X, X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(m \in L_{X}(X)\) and let \(f = m' \cdot id_{X}\) be an element of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(X, X)\). Applying 0.2 (ii) to \(f\), one
obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ∘ (m · id\_X) = L\_f(X)(m) · f = L\_f(X)(m) · (m′ · id\_X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, since \(f\) is an \(X^{+}\)-endomorphism of \(X\),
one has \(f_{J} = id_{X_{J}}\) and therefore \(f_{0} = id_{X_{0}}\);
since \(L_{f}\) depends only on \(f_{0}\) (cf.~N.D.E. (17) in 0.1.10),
one therefore has \(L_{f}(X)(m) = m\). Consequently, the equality above
rewrites as:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(m′ · id\_X) ∘ (m · id\_X) = m · (m′ · id\_X) = (m + m′) · id\_X .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This shows that the bijection \(m \mapsto m \cdot id_{X}\) transforms
the group law of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(X, L_{X})\) into the
composition law of \(X^{+}\)-endomorphisms of \(X\).

It follows first that every element of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(X, X)\) is invertible, which is the first
assertion of the statement, and then that one has an exact sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► Hom\_\{X⁺\}(X, L\_X) ──i──► Aut\_S(X) ──► Aut\_\{S\_J\}(X\_J) ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is the second.

Let us now note that the morphism \(i\) defined above is functorial in
\(X\) for isomorphisms, because it is defined in structural terms from
the action of \texttt{L\_X} on \(X\) above \(X^{+}\), itself functorial
in \(X\) by assertion (ii) of Proposition 0.2.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-26{]}
Hence every automorphism \(u\) of \(X\) above \(S\) induces by transport
of structure isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : Hom\_\{X⁺\}(X, L\_X) ──∼──► Hom\_\{X⁺\}(X, L\_X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \texttt{f\ :\ Aut\_S(X)\ ──∼──►\ Aut\_S(X)} such that the following
diagram is commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{            i}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{X⁺\}(X, L\_X) ────► Aut\_S(X)}
\NormalTok{      │                    │}
\NormalTok{      h                    f}
\NormalTok{      ▼     i              ▼}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{X⁺\}(X, L\_X) ────► Aut\_S(X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~such that \(f \circ i = i \circ h\). On the other hand, \(f\) is
given by the commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        a}
\NormalTok{   X ─────► X}
\NormalTok{   │         │}
\NormalTok{ u │         │ u}
\NormalTok{   ▼  f(a)   ▼}
\NormalTok{   X ─────► X ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, \(f(a) = u \circ a \circ u^{-1}\) for every
\(a \in \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)\). Writing \(i(h(m)) = f(i(m))\), one
finds the desired formula.

\textbf{Corollary 0.7.bis.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme such that
\texttt{X\_J} is an \texttt{S\_J}-monoid. Then \texttt{L\_X} is endowed
with a structure of \(S\)-monoid, one has a split exact sequence of
\(S\)-monoids:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                i           p}
\NormalTok{1 ──► L′\_X ────► L\_X ⇄ ──► X⁺ ──► 1}
\NormalTok{                     s}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and the monoid law induced on \(L'_{X}\) coincides with its
abelian group structure. In particular, if \texttt{X\_J} is an
\texttt{S\_J}-group, then \texttt{L\_X} is an \(S\)-group and is the
semidirect product of \(X^{+}\) and \(L'_{X}\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, since \texttt{X\_J} is an \texttt{S\_J}-monoid,
then \(X^{+} = \prod_{S_{J}/S} X_{J}\) is an \(S\)-monoid (indeed, one
has \(X^{+}(Y) = X_{J}(Y_{J})\) for every \(Y \to S\)). For every
\(S\)-scheme \(Y\), denote by \(\tilde{Y}_{J}\) the \texttt{Y\_J}-affine
scheme corresponding to the quasi-coherent \(O_{Y_{J}}\)-algebra
\(O_{Y_{J}} \oplus J \cdot O_{Y}\) (i.e.~the graded algebra associated
to the filtration \(O_{Y} \supset J \cdot O_{Y}\)). Then \(L_{X}(Y)\) is
identified with \(X_{J}(\tilde{Y}_{J})\) and \(L'_{X}(Y)\) with the
kernel of the morphism \(p : X_{J}(\tilde{Y}_{J}) \to X_{J}(Y_{J})\)
induced by the ``zero section'' \(Y_{J} \to \tilde{Y}_{J}\) (i.e.~by the
morphism of \(O_{Y_{J}}\)-algebras \(O_{\tilde{Y}_{J}} \to O_{Y_{J}}\)
vanishing on the ideal \(J \cdot O_{Y}\)). One has therefore, for every
\(Y \to S\), a split exact sequence of monoids, functorial in \(Y\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       i              p}
\NormalTok{1 ──► L′\_X(Y) ──────► L\_X(Y) ⇄ ──► X⁺(Y) ──► 1 .}
\NormalTok{                            s}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It remains to see that the monoid law induced on \(L'_{X}\) coincides
with its abelian group structure. Denote by \texttt{µ} the monoid law of
\texttt{L\_X} and \(e\) its unit section; one must show that for all
\(m, m' \in L'_{X}(Y)\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{µ(m · e, m′ · e) = (m + m′) · e .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This can be seen in either of the following ways. On the one hand, one
can revisit the proof of equality (0.1.10 (∗)) by replacing the morphism
\(f : X \to W\) appearing there with the morphism
\texttt{µ\ :\ L\_X\ ×\_S\ L\_X\ →\ L\_X}. Identifying
\(X^{+}(Y) = X_{J}(Y_{J})\) with its image by \(s\) in
\(L_{X}(Y) = X_{J}(\tilde{Y}_{J})\), one obtains that, for all
\(g, g' \in X_{J}(Y_{J})\) and \(m, m' \in L'_{X}(Y)\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{µ(m · g, m′ · g′) = L\_µ\^{}\{(g, g′)\}(m, m′) · µ(g, g′),                      (⋆)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \texttt{L\_µ\^{}\{(g,\ g′)\}} denotes the morphism derived from
\texttt{µ} at the point \((g, g')\) (i.e.~\(\tilde{Y}_{J}\) is above
\(L_{X} \times_{S} L_{X}\) via \((g, g')\)). In particular, one has
\texttt{µ(m\ ·\ e,\ m′\ ·\ e)\ =\ L\_µ\^{}\{(e,\ e)\}(m,\ m′)\ ·\ e};
now
\texttt{L\_µ\^{}\{(e,\ e)\}(m,\ m′)\ =\ L\_\{ℓ\_e\}(m′)\ +\ L\_\{r\_e\}(m)},
where \(\ell_{e}\) (resp. \(r_{e}\)) denotes left (resp. right)
translation by \(e\), which is the identity map of \texttt{X\_J}, whence
\texttt{L\_µ\^{}\{(e,\ e)\}(m,\ m′)\ =\ m\ +\ m′}.

Alternatively, one can proceed as follows (cf.~the proof of {[}DG70{]},
§ II.4, Th. 3.5). By Lemma 0.1.11, the formation of \(X^{+}\) and of
\texttt{L\_X} ``commutes with products'', and hence the same holds for
\(L'_{X}\); it follows that the morphism
\texttt{µ′\ :\ L′\_X\ ×\ L′\_X\ →\ L′\_X} induced by \texttt{µ} is a
homomorphism for the abelian-group structure. One then deduces from
Lemma 3.10 of Exp. II that \texttt{µ′} coincides with the abelian-group
law.

\textbf{0.8.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-27{]} Let now \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme
such that \texttt{X\_J} is an \texttt{S\_J}-group. Suppose there exists
an \(S\)-morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P : X × X ──► X}
\NormalTok{        S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that the morphism obtained by base change

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P\_J : X\_J × X\_J ──► X\_J}
\NormalTok{            S\_J}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is the group law of \texttt{X\_J}. (An important particular case of the
preceding situation will be the case where \(X\) is an \(S\)-group and
one takes for \(P\) its group law.) From this one deduces a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_P : L\_X × L\_X ≃ L\_\{X ×\_S X\} ──► L\_X}
\NormalTok{              S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which, in fact, does not depend on \(P\), because it is computed by
means of the group law \texttt{P\_J} of \texttt{X\_J}, as we shall now
see.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-28{]} Indeed, by (ii) and (iii) of 0.2, for every
\(Y \to S\) and \(x, x' \in X(Y)\), \(m, m' \in L'_{X}(Y)\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(m · x, m′ · x′) = L\_P\^{}\{(x, x′)\}(m, m′) · (x, x′) = L\_P\^{}\{(x, x′)\}(m, m′) · µ(g, g′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(g\) (resp. \(g'\)) is the image of \(x\) (resp. \(x'\)) in
\(X^{+}(Y)\). Moreover (cf.~the proof of 0.10), \(L^{(x, x')}_{P}\)
equals \texttt{L\_µ\^{}\{(g,\ g′)\}} and, by 0.7.bis (⋆), this is the
element of \(L'_{X}(Y)\) defined by the following equality in
\(L_{X}(Y)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_µ\^{}\{(g, g′)\}(m, m′) · µ(g, g′) = µ(m · g, m′ · g′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, if we denote by \(\times\) (instead of \texttt{µ}) the group
law of \texttt{L\_X} and \texttt{Ad} the ``adjoint action'' of \(X^{+}\)
on \(L'_{X}\) (which factors through \(X_{0}\) and is induced by the
adjoint action of \(X_{0}\) on \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\)), one
obtains that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L\_µ\^{}\{(g, g′)\}(m, m′) × g × g′ = m × g × m′ × g′ = (m × Ad(g)(m′)) × g × g′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence finally \(L^{(x, x')}_{P}(m, m') = m \times Ad(g)(m')\). We
therefore obtain:

\textbf{Proposition 0.8.} \emph{Let \(P : X \times_{S} X \to X\) be an
\(S\)-morphism such that \texttt{P\_J} endows \texttt{X\_J} with a
structure of \texttt{S\_J}-group. Denote by \(\times\) the group law of
\(L'_{X}\) and by \((m, x) \mapsto m \cdot x\) the morphism
\(L'_{X} \times_{S} X \to X\) defining the action of \(L'_{X}\) on
\(X\), and let \(Ad : X^{+} \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(L'_{X})\) be
the ``adjoint action'' of \(X^{+}\) on \(L'_{X}\) (which is induced by
the adjoint action of \(X_{0}\) on \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\)). Then,
for every \(S' \to S\) and \(x, x' \in X(S')\),
\(m, m' \in L'_{X}(S')\), one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(m · x, m′ · x′) = (m × Ad(p\_X(x))(m′)) · P(x, x′).        (0.8.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(X\) is an \(S\)-group, we shall denote by \(\ast\) its law,
\(e\) its unit section, and \(i\) the \(S\)-morphism defined by:}

\[
i(m) = m \cdot e ,
\]

\emph{for every \(S' \to S\) and \(m \in L'_{X}(S')\).}

\textbf{Corollary 0.9.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-group. Then
\(X^{+}\) is naturally endowed with a structure of \(S\)-group, and
\(p_{X}\) is a morphism of \(S\)-groups. Moreover, the \(S\)-morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i : L′\_X ──► X,    m ↦ m · e}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an isomorphism of \(S\)-groups from \(L'_{X}\) onto
\(Ker(p_{X})\), and one has, for all \(S' \to S\), \(x' \in X(S')\),
\(m \in L'_{X}(S')\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{m · x′ = (m · e) ∗ x′ = i(m) ∗ x′ .                  (0.9.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The first two assertions have already been proved in 0.1.2. Since \(X\)
is formally principal homogeneous over \(X^{+}\) under
\(L_{X} = L'_{X} \times_{S} X^{+}\), the morphism \(i\) is indeed an
isomorphism of \(S\)-functors from \(L'_{X}\) onto the kernel of
\(p_{X}\). The fact that \(i\) is a morphism of groups and the formula
(0.9.1) follow from formula (0.8.1) applied respectively to
\(x = x' = e\), and to \(x = e\), \(m' = 1\).

\textbf{Corollary 0.10.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-group. With the
preceding notations, for every \(S' \to S\) and all \(x \in X(S')\) and
\(m' \in L'_{X}(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x ∗ i(m′) ∗ x⁻¹ = i(Ad(p\_X(x))(m′)) .                 (0.10.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This follows from the equality \(i(m') \ast x^{-1} = m' \cdot x^{-1}\)
and from (0.8.1) applied to \(m = 1\) and \(x' = x^{-1}\).

When \(X\) is an \(S\)-group, we have therefore explicitly determined
the kernel of \(X \to X^{+}\) and the action of the inner automorphisms
of \(X\) on this kernel. We shall now see that one can do the same for
certain \(S\)-group functors not necessarily representable. One case
will be useful to us, namely that of the \texttt{Aut} functors (I, 1.7).
Let us state at once:

\textbf{Proposition 0.11.} \emph{Let \(E\) be an \(S\)-scheme. Denote
\(X = \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(E)\). The kernel of the morphism of
\(S\)-group functors}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_X : X ──► X⁺}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is canonically identified with the \(S\)-functor in commutative
groups \(L'_{X}\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, L′\_X) = Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J · O\_\{E ×\_S Y\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(Y\) denotes a variable \(S\)-scheme.}

Indeed, if \(Y\) is a variable \(S\)-scheme, one has
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X) = \operatorname{Aut}_{Y}(E \times_{S} Y)\),
and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, X⁺) = Hom\_S(Y\_J, X) = Aut\_\{Y\_J\}(E ×\_S Y\_J) = Aut\_\{Y\_J\}((E ×\_S Y) ×\_Y Y\_J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Applying 0.7 b) to the \(Y\)-scheme \(E \times_{S} Y\), one obtains an
isomorphism of groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, L′\_X) ≃ Ker(Hom\_S(Y, X) ──► Hom\_S(Y, X⁺)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

an isomorphism that one verifies easily to be functorial in the
\(S\)-scheme \(Y\). One thus obtains an isomorphism of \(S\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L′\_X ≃ Ker(X ──► X⁺),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which completes the proof of Proposition 0.11.

\textbf{Corollary 0.12.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-29{]} \emph{We keep the
notations of 0.11: \(E\) is an \(S\)-scheme and
\(X = \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(E)\). One has a natural action \(f\) of
\(X\) on \(L'_{X}\) defined as follows. For every \(S\)-scheme \(Y\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, X) = Aut\_Y(E ×\_S Y)}
\NormalTok{and    Hom\_S(Y, L′\_X) = Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀ / Y₀\}, J · O\_\{E ×\_S Y\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(N. B.
\(\Omega^{1}_{E_{0}/S_{0}} \otimes_{S_{0}} O_{Y_{0}} \simeq \Omega^{1}_{E_{0} \times_{S_{0}} Y_{0} / Y_{0}}\),
cf. EGA IV₄, 16.4.5); the first group acts on the second by transport of
structure and this action is indeed functorial in \(Y\). One then has
the formula:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x · i(m) · x⁻¹ = i(f(x) m),                              (0.12.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(Y \to S\) and all
\(x \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X)\),
\(m \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, L'_{X})\).}

Indeed, this follows from 0.7 c) applied to the \(Y\)-scheme
\(E \times_{S} Y\).

\textbf{Reminder 0.13.} \emph{The direct image of a quasi-coherent
module by a morphism of finite presentation is quasi-coherent. Under the
same conditions, the formation of the direct image commutes with flat
base change: in the situation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ◄────g′──── T′ = T ×\_S S′}
\NormalTok{│                  │}
\NormalTok{f                  f′}
\NormalTok{▼      g           ▼}
\NormalTok{S ◄──────────── S′ ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{if one supposes \(f\) (and therefore \(f'\)) of finite
presentation and \(g\) (and therefore \(g'\)) flat, one has for every
quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_T}-module \(F\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_*(F) ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_\{S′\} = f′\_*(F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_\{S′\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where, more elegantly,}

\[
g*(f_{*}(F)) = f'_{*}(g'*(F)).
\]

These two facts hold more generally for a quasi-compact and
quasi-separated morphism \(f\), cf.~(EGA I, 9.2.1) and (EGA III₁,
1.4.15) in the quasi-compact separated case (taking into account EGA
III₂, Err\_III 25) and (EGA IV₁, 1.7.4 and 1.7.21).

\textbf{Remark 0.14.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-30{]} \emph{Resume the notations
of 0.11: let \(E\) be an \(S\)-scheme, \(X = \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(E)\)
and \(L'_{X}\) the \(S\)-functor in commutative groups defined by:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L′\_X(Y) = Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J · O\_\{E ×\_S Y\})}
\NormalTok{         = Hom\_\{O\_\{E ×\_S Y\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E/S\} ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y, J · O\_\{E ×\_S Y\})}
\NormalTok{         = Γ(E ×\_S Y, Hom\_\{O\_\{E ×\_S Y\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E/S\} ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y, J · O\_\{E ×\_S Y\})).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Suppose \(Y\) flat over \(S\); then one has isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J · O\_\{E ×\_S Y\} ←─∼─ (J · O\_E) ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y ─∼→ (J · O\_E) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\} .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Suppose moreover \(E\) of finite presentation over \(S\); then
\(\Omega^{1}_{E/S}\) is an \texttt{O\_E}-module of finite presentation
(cf.~EGA IV₄, 16.4.22), and hence, by (EGA 0\_I, 6.7.6),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{E ×\_S Y\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E/S\} ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y, (J · O\_E) ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y) ≃ Hom\_\{O\_E\}(Ω¹\_\{E/S\}, J · O\_E) ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_Y .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Denote by \(\pi : E \to S\) and \(g : Y \to S\) the structural
morphisms; applying 0.13 to the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E ◄────g′──── E ×\_S Y}
\NormalTok{│                 │}
\NormalTok{π                 π′}
\NormalTok{▼      g          ▼}
\NormalTok{S ◄────────────── Y ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and to the \texttt{O\_E}-module
\(F = \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{E}}(\Omega^{1}_{E/S}, J \cdot O_{E})\), one
obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(E ×\_S Y, g′*F) = Γ(Y, π′\_* g′* F) = Γ(Y, g* π\_* F) = W(π\_* F)(Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We have therefore shown that, if \(E\) is of finite presentation over
\(S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L′\_X = W(π\_* Hom\_\{O\_E\}(Ω¹\_\{E/S\}, J · O\_E))                        (0.14.1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

on the category of \(S\)-schemes flat over \(S\). Note moreover that the
module of which we take the \(W\) is quasi-coherent, by (EGA I, 9.1.1
and 9.2.1).

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-31{]} Denote by \(L_{0}\) the \(S_{0}\)-functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(π\_\{0*\} Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀/S₀\}, J · O\_E)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, returning to the definition of \(L'_{X}(Y)\) and taking into
account the isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J · O\_\{E ×\_S Y\} ≃ (J · O\_E) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one obtains, by arguing as above, that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L′\_X(Y) = L₀(Y₀) = L₀(Y ×\_S S₀) = ∏\_\{S₀/S\} L₀(Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Hence, on the category of \(S\)-schemes flat over \(S\), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L′\_X = ∏\_\{S₀/S\} W(π\_\{0*\} Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀/S₀\}, J · O\_E)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is not obvious that the action of \(X\) on \(L'_{X}\) defined in 0.12
comes from an action of \(X_{0} = \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}}(E_{0})\) on
\(L_{0}\); this is however the case when, moreover, \(E\) is flat over
\(S\).

Indeed, in this case one has canonical isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J · O\_E ≃ J ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_E ≃ J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{E₀\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L₀ ≃ W(π\_\{0*\} Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀/S₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{E₀\})),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L′\_X = ∏\_\{S₀/S\} W(π\_\{0*\} Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀/S₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{E₀\})).        (0.14.2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, for every \(S_{0}\)-scheme \(T\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L₀(T) ≃ Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀ ×\_\{S₀\} T\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀ ×\_\{S₀\} T / T\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{E₀ ×\_\{S₀\} T\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S_{0}}(T, X_{0}) = \operatorname{Aut}_{T}(E_{0} \times_{S_{0}} T)\)
acts by transport of structure on \(L_{0}(T)\), functorially in \(T\);
finally, for every \(S\)-scheme \(Y\) flat over \(S\), the action by
transport of structure of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(Y, X) = \operatorname{Aut}_{Y}(E \times_{S} Y)\)
on \(L'_{X}(Y) = L_{0}(Y_{0})\) factors through
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{Y_{0}}(E_{0} \times_{S_{0}} Y_{0})\).

Let us finally extract from (SGA 1, III) the following two propositions.

\textbf{Proposition 0.15.} \emph{(SGA 1, III, 6.8){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-32{]}
For every \texttt{S\_J}-scheme \(Y\) smooth over \texttt{S\_J} and
affine, there exists an \(S\)-scheme \(X\) smooth over \(S\) such that
\(X \times_{S} S_{J} \simeq Y\), and such an \(X\) is unique up to
(non-unique) isomorphism.}

\textbf{Proposition 0.16.} \emph{(SGA 1, III, 5.5){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-33{]}
Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme smooth over \(S\). For every affine
\(S\)-scheme \(Y\), the canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_X(Y) : Hom\_S(Y, X) ──► Hom\_S(Y, X⁺) = Hom\_\{S\_J\}(Y\_J, X\_J)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is surjective.}

\textbf{Corollary 0.17.} \emph{Let \(E\) be an \(S\)-scheme smooth over
\(S\) and affine; denote \(X = \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(E)\). For every
affine \(S\)-scheme \(Y\), the canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Aut\_Y(E ×\_S Y) = Hom\_S(Y, X) ──► Hom\_S(Y, X⁺) = Aut\_\{Y\_J\}(E\_J ×\_\{S\_J\} Y\_J)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is surjective.}

Indeed, \(Y \times_{S} E\) is affine over \(Y\), itself affine, so
affine. Applying 0.16, one deduces that every \texttt{S\_J}-morphism
\(Y_{J} \times_{S_{J}} E_{J} \to E_{J}\) extends to an \(S\)-morphism
\(Y \times_{S} E \to E\). {[}\^{}N.D.E-III-34{]} In other words, every
\texttt{Y\_J}-endomorphism of \(Y_{J} \times_{S_{J}} E_{J}\) lifts to a
\(Y\)-endomorphism of \(Y \times_{S} E\). Then, 0.7 a) shows that every
\texttt{Y\_J}-automorphism of \(Y_{J} \times_{S_{J}} E_{J}\) lifts to a
\(Y\)-automorphism of \(Y \times_{S} E\), which is the announced
property.

\subsection{1. Extensions and
cohomology}\label{extensions-and-cohomology}

\subsubsection{1.1.}\label{section-18}

Let \(C\) be a category stable under fibered
products.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-35{]} Let \(S\) be an object of \(C\), \(G\)
an (representable) \(S\)-group, and \(F\) an \(S\)-functor in
commutative groups on which \(G\) acts. We defined in (I, 5.1) the
cohomology groups \(H^{n}(G, F)\). Recall that these are the homology
groups of a complex denoted \(C\ast(G, F)\) where, denoting
\((G/S)^{n} = G \times_{S} \cdot \cdot \cdot \times_{S} G\) (\(n\)
factors),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Cⁿ(G, F) = Hom\_S((G/S)ⁿ, F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(G\), and hence the \((G/S)^{n}\), are representable, one has
also

\[
C^{n}(G, F) = F((G/S)^{n});
\]

from this, and from the definition of the boundary operator, one sees
that the complex \(C\ast(G, F)\) depends only on the restriction of
\(F\) to the full subcategory of \(C/S\) whose objects are the cartesian
powers of \(G\) over \(S\). Consequently, one has the:

\textbf{Lemma 1.1.1.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category stable under fibered
products,{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-35{]} \(S\) an object of \(C\), \(G\) a
representable \(S\)-group. Denote by \(C(G)\) the full subcategory of
\(C/S\) whose objects are the cartesian powers of \(G\) over \(S\). Let
\(F\) and \(F'\) be two \(S\)-functors in commutative groups on which
\(G\) acts. If \(F\) and \(F'\) have the same restriction to \(C(G)\),
one has a canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H∗(G, F) ──∼──► H∗(G, F′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{1.1.2. Cohomology and restriction of
scalars.}\label{cohomology-and-restriction-of-scalars.}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-36{]} Let us state another comparison result. Let now
\(T \to S\) be a morphism in \(C\). If \(F\) is a \(T\)-functor in
commutative groups, then the functor obtained by ``restriction of
scalars'' (cf.~Exp. II, 1)

\[
F_{1} = \prod_{T/S} F
\]

is an \(S\)-functor in commutative groups and one has a morphism of
\(S\)-group functors

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u : ∏\_\{T/S\} Aut\_\{T{-}gr.\}(F) ──► Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(F₁) .[\^{}N.D.E{-}III{-}37]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let now \(G\) be an \(S\)-group functor and let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_T ──► Aut\_\{T{-}gr.\}(F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be an action of \texttt{G\_T} on \(F\). By definition of the functor
\(\prod_{T/S}\), one deduces a morphism of \(S\)-group functors

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ──► ∏\_\{T/S\} Aut\_\{T{-}gr.\}(F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, by composition with \(u\), an action of \(G\) on
\(F_{1} = \prod_{T/S} F\).{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-38{]}

\textbf{Lemma 1.1.2.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, one has a
canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H∗(G, ∏\_\{T/S\} F) ≃ H∗(G\_T, F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, by the definition of cohomology, the standard complexes are
canonically isomorphic.

\subsubsection{1.2. Lifting of group
morphisms.}\label{lifting-of-group-morphisms.}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-39{]} Following the general principles, we lay down the
following definition:

\textbf{Definition 1.2.1.} \emph{Let
\texttt{1\ →\ M\ ──u──►\ E\ ──v──►\ G} be a sequence of morphisms of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups. We say that it is \textbf{exact} if the following
equivalent conditions are verified:}

\emph{(i) for every \(S \in Ob C\), the following sequence of ordinary
groups is exact:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1  ──►  M(S) ──u(S)──► E(S) ──v(S)──► G(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) for every object \(H\) of \texttt{Ĉ}, the following sequence
of ordinary groups is exact:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1  ──►  Hom(H, M) ──u(H)──► Hom(H, E) ──v(H)──► Hom(H, G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Taking in particular \(H = G\) in (ii), one sees that the set of
sections of \(v\) (not respecting \emph{a priori} the group structures)
is empty or principal homogeneous under \(\operatorname{Hom}(G, M)\).
Suppose it is non-empty; so let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s : G ──► E}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be a section of \(v\). Then for every \(S \in Ob C\) and every
\(x \in G(S)\), the element \(s(x)\) of \(E(S)\) defines an inner
automorphism of \texttt{E\_S} which normalizes \texttt{M\_S} (more
correctly, the image of \texttt{M\_S} by \(u_{S}\)), hence an
automorphism of \texttt{M\_S}.

\textbf{Scholie 1.2.1.1.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-40{]} \emph{If \(M\) is
commutative, one sees ``set-theoretically'' that this automorphism does
not depend on the chosen section, but only on \(x\), and depends
multiplicatively on it. In summary, to every exact sequence}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(E)     1  ──►  M  ──u──►  E  ──v──►  G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that \(M\) is commutative and that \(v\) admits a section, is
associated a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ──► Aut\_\{Ĉ{-}gr.\}(M)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which is called the \textbf{action of \(G\) on \(M\) defined by
the extension \texttt{(E)}}.}

\textbf{Definition 1.2.1.2.} \emph{We saw in (I, 2.3.7) that \(v\)
admits a section which is a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups if and only if
the extension \texttt{(E)} is isomorphic (``as an extension'') to the
semidirect product of \(M\) by \(G\) relative to the preceding action.
Such a section of \(v\) will be called a \textbf{section of the
extension \texttt{(E)}}, or simply a \textbf{section of \texttt{(E)}}.}

\emph{If \(s\) is a section of \texttt{(E)} and if
\(m \in \Gamma(M) \simeq Ker(\Gamma(E) \to \Gamma(G))\) (for the
definition of \(\Gamma\), see I, 1.2), then the morphism \(G \to E\)
defined by{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-41{]}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x ↦ u(m) s(x) u(m)⁻¹}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is also a section of \texttt{(E)}, said to be \textbf{deduced from
\(s\) by the inner automorphism defined by \(m\)} (or by \(u(m)\)).}

\textbf{Lemma 1.2.2.} \emph{Let
\texttt{(E)\ :\ 1\ →\ M\ ──u──►\ E\ ──v──►\ G} be an exact sequence of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups such that \(M\) is commutative and \(v\) admits a
section. Let \(G\) act on \(M\) in the manner defined by \texttt{(E)}.}

\emph{(i) The extension \texttt{(E)} canonically defines a class
\(c(E) \in H^{2}(G, M)\) whose vanishing is necessary and sufficient for
the existence of a section of \texttt{(E)}.}

\emph{(ii) If \(c(E) = 0\), the set of sections of \texttt{(E)} is
principal homogeneous under the group \(Z^{1}(G, M)\), and the set of
sections of \texttt{(E)} modulo the action of the inner automorphisms
defined by the elements of \(\Gamma(M)\) is principal homogeneous under
the group \(H^{1}(G, M)\).}

\emph{(iii){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-42{]} Let \(s\) be a section of
\texttt{(E)}; the set of conjugates of \(s\) by the inner automorphisms
defined by \(\Gamma(M)\) is in bijection with
\(\Gamma(M)/H^{0}(G, M)\).}

\emph{Proof.} It proceeds exactly as in the case of ordinary groups, the
fact that one starts from a section of \(v\) ensuring the functoriality
of the set-theoretic computations. Let us briefly indicate the principal
steps.

\textbf{a)} To each section \(s\) of \(v\), one associates the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ds : G × G ──► M,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined set-theoretically by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u(Ds(x, y)) = s(xy) s(y)⁻¹ s(x)⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One shows that \texttt{Ds} is a 2-cocycle by the following
computation.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-43{]} By the definition of the differential
of the standard complex (I, 5.1), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∂² Ds)(x, y, z) = (s(x) Ds(y, z) s(x)⁻¹) · Ds(x, y)⁻¹ · Ds(xy, z)⁻¹ · Ds(x, yz);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

it suffices to substitute the definition of \texttt{Ds} into this
formula to find (without using any commutativity)
\(Ds \in Z^{2}(G, M)\).

\textbf{b)} If \(s\) and \(s'\) are two sections of \(v\), there exists
\(f : G \to M\) such that \(s(x) = f(x) s'(x)\). One then has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ds′(x, y) = f⁻¹(xy) Ds(x, y) s(x) f(y) s(x)⁻¹ f(x),}
\NormalTok{          = Ds(x, y) · f⁻¹(xy) · (s(x) f(y) s(x)⁻¹) · f(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.

\[
Ds' = Ds \cdot \partial^{1} f.
\]

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-44{]} This shows that the class of \texttt{Ds} in
\(H^{2}(G, M)\) does not depend on the chosen section \(s\) of \(v\); it
is the class \(c(E)\) of the extension \texttt{(E)}.

\textbf{c)} Let \(s\) and \(s'\) be two sections of \(v\) and let
\(m \in \Gamma(M)\). Then, the equality \(s(x) = m^{-1} s'(x) m\) (for
every \(x \in G(S)\), \(S \in Ob C\)) is equivalent to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s(x) = m⁻¹ s′(x) m s′(x)⁻¹ s′(x),   i.e.   s = ∂⁰ m · s′ .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, the stabilizer of \(s\) in \(\Gamma(M)\) is the subgroup
of \(m \in \Gamma(M)\) such that \(\partial^{0} m = e_{M}\), i.e.~the
subgroup \(H^{0}(G, M)\). This already proves (iii).

\textbf{d)} The reasoning is now habitual.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-45{]} Let
\(s_{0}\) be an arbitrary section of \(v\); there exists a section
\(s\), necessarily of the form \(s = f \cdot s_{0}\), which is a
morphism of groups, i.e.~which satisfies \(Ds = 0\), if and only if
\((Ds_{0})^{-1} = \partial^{1} f\), i.e., if and only if the class
\(c(E)\) is zero. This proves (i).

In this case, the set of sections of \texttt{(E)} consists of the
sections \(s' = h \cdot s\), where \(h : G \to M\) satisfies
\(\partial^{1} h = 0\), i.e.~\(h \in Z^{1}(G, M)\). Moreover, by point
c), two such sections \(h_{1} \cdot s\) and \(h_{2} \cdot s\) are
conjugate under \(\Gamma(M)\) if and only if \(h_{1}\) and \(h_{2}\)
have the same image in \(H^{1}(G, M)\). This proves (ii).

Let still

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(E)     1  ──►  M  ──u──►  E  ──v──►  G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be an exact sequence of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups with \(M\) commutative. Let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : H ──► G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups. Consider \(E_{f} = H \times_{G} E\);
it is a \texttt{Ĉ}-group and the projection \(v_{f} : E_{f} \to H\) is a
morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups. Likewise for \(e_{f} : E_{f} \to E\). On
the other hand, if one sends \(M\) into \(E\) via \(u\) and into \(H\)
via the unit morphism, one defines a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups
\(u_{f} : M \to E_{f}\). We have thus constructed a commutative diagram
of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(E)     1  ──►  M  ──u──►  E   ──v──►  G}
\NormalTok{                ║          ▲           ▲}
\NormalTok{                id        e\_f          f}
\NormalTok{                           │           │}
\NormalTok{                          u\_f          v\_f}
\NormalTok{(E\_f)   1  ──►  M  ─────►  E\_f  ─────► H .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has immediately:

\textbf{Lemma 1.2.3.} \emph{(i) The sequence \((E_{f})\) is exact.}
