\emph{(ii) The map \(s \mapsto e_{f} \circ s = f'\) realizes a bijective
correspondence between the morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s : H ──► E\_f}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that \(v_{f} \circ s = id\) (that is, the sections of
\(v_{f}\)) and the morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f′ : H ──► E}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that \(v \circ f' = f\) (that is, the morphisms \(f'\)
``lifting'' \(f\)).}

\emph{(iii) In the preceding correspondence, sections of \((E_{f})\) and
morphisms of groups \(f'\) lifting \(f\) correspond.}

Applying Lemma 1.2.2 to the extension \((E_{f})\) and taking into
account 1.2.3, one obtains the following proposition (which formally
contains 1.2.2):

\textbf{Proposition 1.2.4.} \emph{Let
\texttt{(E)\ :\ 1\ →\ M\ →\ E\ ──v──►\ G} be an exact sequence of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups with \(M\) commutative. Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : H ──► G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups; suppose it lifts to a morphism
(not necessarily of groups) \(f' : H \to E\). Let \(H\) act on \(M\) by
the composite morphism (multiplicative and independent of the choice of
\(f'\)),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ──f′──► E ──int──► Aut\_\{Ĉ{-}gr.\}(M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) The morphism \(f\) canonically defines a class
\(c(f) \in H^{2}(H, M)\) whose vanishing is necessary and sufficient for
the existence of a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f′ : H ──► E}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{lifting \(f\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(c(f) = 0\), the set of morphisms of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups
\(f'\) lifting \(f\), modulo the action of the inner automorphisms
defined by elements of \(\Gamma(M)\) (i.e.~by elements \(m\) of
\(\Gamma(E)\) such that \(v(m) = e\)), is principal homogeneous under
\(H^{1}(H, M)\).}

\emph{(iii) If \(f' : H \to E\) is a morphism of groups lifting \(f\),
the set of transforms of \(f'\) by the inner automorphisms defined by
the elements of \(\Gamma(M)\) is isomorphic to
\(\Gamma(M)/\Gamma(M^{H}) = \Gamma(M)/H^{0}(H, M)\).}

\subsubsection{1.3. Extensions of group
laws.}\label{extensions-of-group-laws.}

Consider the following situation: one has a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)     p : X ──► Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and a commutative \texttt{Ĉ}-group \(M\) acting on \(X\), such that
\(X\) is formally principal homogeneous above \(Y\) under \texttt{M\_Y}.

If \(g : Y \to Z\) is an arbitrary morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}, then
\(g \circ p : X \to Z\) is invariant under \(M\): for each
\(S \in Ob C\), \((g \circ p)(S)\) is invariant under the action of
\(M(S)\) acting on \(X(S)\). Conversely, we shall assume the following
condition verified for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\).

\((+)_{n}\) : Every morphism from \(X^{n}\) to \(M\), invariant under
the action of \(M^{n}\) on \(X^{n}\), factors uniquely through
\(p^{n} : X^{n} \to Y^{n}\) (where the powers \(n\) denote cartesian
powers).

\textbf{Lemma 1.3.1.} \emph{(i) If \(h\) is a morphism from \(Y\) to
\(M\), the automorphism \(u_{h}\) of \(X\) defined set-theoretically by
\(x \mapsto h(p(x)) \cdot x\) preserves the fibers of \(p\) and commutes
with the actions of \(M\) on \(X\),{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-46{]} i.e. for all
\(S \in Ob C\) and \(x \in X(S)\), \(m \in M(S)\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p(h(p(x)) · x) = p(x),     m · (h(p(x)) · x) = h(p(m · x)) · (m · x) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) This construction realizes a bijective correspondence between
morphisms from \(Y\) to \(M\) and automorphisms of \(X\) preserving the
fibers of \(p\) and commuting with the actions of \(M\).}

The first part is clear, since \(p(m \cdot x) = p(x)\) and \(M\) is
commutative.

Conversely, an automorphism \(u\) of \(X\) preserving the fibers of
\(p\) is written set-theoretically \(x \mapsto g(x) \cdot x\), where
\(g\) is some morphism from \(X\) to \(M\). If \(u\) commutes with the
actions of \(M\), the morphism \(g\) is invariant under
\(M\){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-47{]} and one concludes by condition \((+)_{1}\).

We now suppose given in addition a group law on \(Y\) and an action of
\(Y\) on \(M\), that is, a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(‡)     f : Y ──► Aut\_\{Ĉ{-}gr.\}(M).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 1.3.2.} \emph{A composition law on \(X\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P : X × X ──► X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is said to be \textbf{admissible} if it verifies the following two
conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(P\) lifts the group law of \(Y\), i.e.~the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{            P}
\NormalTok{X × X ─────────► X}
\NormalTok{(p,p)│           │ p}
\NormalTok{     ▼           ▼}
\NormalTok{Y × Y ─────────► Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is commutative.}

\emph{(ii) For every \(S \in Ob C\) and all \(x, y \in X(S)\),
\(m, n \in M(S)\), one has the following relation:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(++)     P(m · x, n · y) = m · f(p(x))(n) · P(x, y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 1.3.3.} \emph{For a group law \(\ast\) on \(X\) to
be admissible, it is necessary and sufficient that the following four
conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i) \(p : X \to Y\) is a morphism of groups.}

\emph{(ii) The morphism \(i : M \to X\) defined by
\(i(m) = m \cdot e_{X}\) is an isomorphism of groups from \(M\) onto
\(Ker(p)\), that is to say: one has set-theoretically
\((m \cdot e_{X}) \ast (n \cdot e_{X}) = (mn) \cdot e_{X}\).}

\emph{(iii) One has \(m \cdot x = (m \cdot e_{X}) \ast x = i(m) \ast x\)
for each \(m \in M(S)\), \(x \in X(S)\).}

\emph{(iv) The inner automorphisms of \(X\) act on \(Ker(p)\) by the
set-theoretic formula}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x ∗ i(m) ∗ x⁻¹ = i(f(p(x)) m).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The proof is immediate.

\textbf{Lemma 1.3.4.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-48{]} \emph{Let \(h\) be a
morphism \(Y \to M\) and \(u_{h}\) the automorphism
\(x \mapsto h(p(x)) \cdot x\) of \(X\) (cf.~1.3.1). Let \(P\) be an
admissible composition law (resp. an admissible group law) on \(X\) and
let \(P'\) be the composition law on \(X\) deduced from \(P\) by means
of \(u_{h}\), i.e. \(P'(x, y) = u^{-1}_{h}(P(u_{h}(x), u_{h}(y)))\).
Then:}

\emph{(i) \(P'\) is an admissible composition law (resp. an admissible
group law).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(x, y \in X(S)\) (\(S \in Ob C\)), setting
\(v = p(x)\) and \(w = p(y)\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P′(x, y) = (h(vw)⁻¹ · h(v) · f(v)(h(w))) · P(x, y) = (∂¹ h)(p(x), p(y)) · P(x, y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} One has \(u^{-1}_{h} = u_{h^{\vee}}\), where
\(h^{\vee} : Y \to M\) is defined by \(h^{\vee}(y) = h(y)^{-1}\). By
1.3.2 (i) and (ii), one has
\(P(h(v) \cdot x, h(w) \cdot y) = h(v) \cdot f(v)(h(w)) \cdot P(x, y)\)
and \(p(P(x, y)) = vw\), whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P′(x, y) = (h(vw)⁻¹ · h(v) · f(v)(h(w))) · P(x, y) = (∂¹ h)(p(x), p(y)) · P(x, y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is then immediate that \(P'\) verifies conditions (i) and (ii) of
1.3.2.

\textbf{Definition 1.3.5.} \emph{Two admissible composition laws deduced
from one another by the procedure of 1.3.4 are said to be
\textbf{equivalent}.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-49{]}}

\textbf{Proposition 1.3.6.} \emph{Suppose there exists an admissible
composition law on \(X\). Then:}

\emph{(i) There exists a class \(c \in H^{3}(Y, M)\) (canonically
determined), whose vanishing is necessary and sufficient for the
existence of an admissible \textbf{associative} composition law on
\(X\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(c = 0\), the set of admissible and associative
composition laws (resp. of equivalence classes of admissible and
associative composition laws) on \(X\) is principal homogeneous under
\(Z^{2}(Y, M)\) (resp. \(H^{2}(Y, M)\)).}

The proof proceeds in several steps.

\textbf{a)} Let \(P\) be an admissible composition law on \(X\). Since
\(P\) lifts the composition law of \(Y\) which is associative, there
exists a unique morphism \(a : X^{3} \to M\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)     P(x, P(y, z)) = a(x, y, z) · P(P(x, y), z).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By applying conditions 1.3.2 (i) and (ii), one sees at once that \(a\)
is invariant under the action of \(M^{3}\) on
\(X^{3}\),{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-50{]} whence, by applying hypothesis
\((+)_{3}\), the following result:

\textbf{(1)} There exists a unique morphism \(DP : Y^{3} \to M\) such
that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(x, P(y, z)) = DP(p(x), p(y), p(z)) · P(P(x, y), z),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(P\) is associative if and only if \(DP = 0\).

\textbf{b)} Compute step by step \(P(P(P(x, y), z), t)\) by means of the
preceding formula. Setting \(p(x) = u\), \(p(y) = v\), \(p(z) = w\),
\(p(t) = h\), one obtains{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-51{]} the following pentagonal
diagram, where an arrow \texttt{a\ ──m──►\ b} means that
\(b = m \cdot a\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       P(x, P(y, P(z, t)))}
\NormalTok{       DP(u,v,wh) ↙                      ↘ f(u)(DP(v,w,h))}
\NormalTok{                ↙                          ↘}
\NormalTok{P(P(x, y), P(z, t))                    P(x, P(P(y, z), t))}
\NormalTok{       │                                       │}
\NormalTok{   DP(uv,w,h)                             DP(u,vw,h)}
\NormalTok{       ▼            DP(u,v,w)                  ▼}
\NormalTok{P(P(P(x, y), z), t) ◄──────────────── P(P(x, P(y, z)), t)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{DP(u, v, w) · DP(u, vw, h) · f(u)(DP(v, w, h)) · DP(u, v, wh)⁻¹ · DP(uv, w, h)⁻¹ = e\_M}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e., \(\partial^{3} DP(u, v, w, h) = e_{M}\). As moreover the first
member of the preceding formula can be written, by means of \(P\) and
\(a\), as the expression in \((x, y, z, t)\) of a certain morphism
\(X^{4} \to M\), it follows from the uniqueness hypothesis in
\((+)_{4}\) that \(\partial^{3} DP\) and \(e_{M}\), which factor through
the same morphism, are equal, hence

\textbf{(2)} \texttt{DP} is a cocycle, i.e.~one has
\(DP \in Z^{3}(Y, M)\).

\textbf{c)} If \(P\) and \(P'\) are two admissible composition laws on
\(X\), there exists a unique morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{b : X² ──► M}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \(P'(x, y) = b(x, y) \cdot P(x, y)\). Applying 1.3.2 (ii) to
\(P\) and \(P'\), one sees that \(b\) is invariant under \(M^{2}\),
whence, by \((+)_{2}\):

\textbf{(3)} For every pair of admissible composition laws \((P, P')\),
there exists a unique \(d(P, P') : Y^{2} \to M\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P′(x, y) = d(P, P′)(p(x), p(y)) · P(x, y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the set of admissible composition laws becomes in this way principal
homogeneous under \(\operatorname{Hom}(Y^{2}, M) = C^{2}(Y, M)\).

\textbf{d)} Under the preceding conditions, one has the formula:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4)     DP′ − DP = ∂² d(P, P′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{e)} \(P\) and \(P'\) are equivalent if and only if there exists
a morphism \(h \in C^{1}(Y, M) = \operatorname{Hom}(Y, M)\) such that
\(d(P, P') = \partial^{1} h\); this follows from the definition of
equivalence and from 1.3.4 (ii).

\textbf{f)} It now only remains to conclude: one seeks a \(P'\) that is
associative, i.e.~such that \(DP' = e_{M}\). Now \texttt{DP} is a
cocycle whose class in \(H^{3}(Y, M)\) does not depend on the chosen
admissible composition law \(P\) (by (3) and (4)). This class is the
desired obstruction \(c\). One will be able to choose a \(P'\) answering
the conditions if and only if \(c = 0\); indeed, choosing an arbitrary
\(P\), one will have to solve, by (1):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 = DP′ = DP + ∂² d(P, P′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is possible by (3) and (4) if and only if \(c = 0\). The set of
associative \(P'\) is principal homogeneous under \(Z^{2}(Y, M)\), again
by (3) and (4). The set of associative \(P'\) up to equivalence is
principal homogeneous under \(H^{2}(Y, M)\) by (e).

\subsection{2. Infinitesimal extensions of a morphism of group
schemes}\label{infinitesimal-extensions-of-a-morphism-of-group-schemes}

Resume the notations of § 0. Let \(Y\) and \(X\) be two \(S\)-group
functors. Let \(M\) be the kernel of the morphism of groups
\(p_{X} : X \to X^{+}\). One thus has an exact sequence of \(S\)-group
functors

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 ──► M ──► X ──p\_X──► X⁺ .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By definition of \(X^{+}\), one has isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, X⁺)       ──∼──► Hom\_\{S\_J\}(Y\_J, X\_J)}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Y, X⁺) ──∼──► Hom\_\{S\_J{-}gr.\}(Y\_J, X\_J),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, p\_X) : Hom\_S(Y, X) ──► Hom\_S(Y, X⁺)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

associates to an \(S\)-morphism \(f : Y \to X\) the \(S\)-morphism
\(f^{+} : Y \to X^{+}\) corresponding by the preceding isomorphisms to
the \texttt{S\_J}-morphism \(f_{J} : Y_{J} \to X_{J}\) obtained by base
change from \(f\). If \(M\) is commutative, one can apply to this
situation Proposition 1.2.4.

\subsubsection{2.0.}\label{section-19}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-52{]} In what follows, we shall be interested in the
following case: \(Y\) is flat over \(S\), and \(X\) is an \(S\)-group
functor of one of the following two species:

\textbf{a)} \(X\) is an \(S\)-group scheme,

\textbf{b)} \(X = \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(E)\) where \(E\) is an
\(S\)-scheme, of finite presentation over \(S\).

Denote by \((Flat)/S\) the category of \(S\)-schemes flat over \(S\). In
case (a) (resp. (b)), the \(S\)-group functor \(M = Ker(X \to X^{+})\),
its restriction \(L\) to \((Flat)/S\), and the actions of the inner
automorphisms of \(X\) on \(M\), have been computed in 0.9, 0.5, and
0.10 (resp. 0.11, 0.14, and 0.12). That is to say, in case (a), let
\(L_{0}\) be the \(S_{0}\)-functor in commutative groups defined by: for
every \(S_{0}\)-scheme \(T_{0}\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T₀, L₀) = Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

on which \(X_{0}\) acts via its adjoint representation in
\(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\); then \(L = \prod_{S_{0}/S} L_{0}\),
i.e.~for every \(S\)-scheme \(T\), one has
\(L(T) = L_{0}(T \times_{S} S_{0})\).

In case (b), denote by \(\pi\) the structural morphism \(E \to S\); then
\(L\) is the functor in abelian groups on \((Flat)/S\) defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(T, L) = Γ(T, π\_*(Hom\_\{O\_E\}(Ω¹\_\{E/S\}, J · O\_E)) ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_T),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

on which \(X\), considered as a functor on \((Flat)/S\), acts as we saw
in 0.12.

Then, one has an exact sequence of functors in groups on \((Flat)/S\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(E)     1 ──► L ──► X ──► X⁺ .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, \(Y\) being supposed flat over \(S\), the groups
\(H^{i}(Y, M)\) depend, by 1.1.1, only on the restriction \(L\) of \(M\)
to \((Flat)/S\). Since \(L = \prod_{S_{0}/S} L_{0}\) in case (a), then
by 1.1.2, one has in this case isomorphisms
\(H^{i}(Y, L) \simeq H^{i}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\).

Then, taking the preceding into account, one deduces from Proposition
1.2.4 the:{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-53{]}

\textbf{Theorem 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(I\) and \(J\) two
quasi-coherent ideals such that \(I \supset J\) and \(I \cdot J = 0\),
defining the closed subschemes \(S_{0}\) and \texttt{S\_J}, and let:}

\emph{--- \(X\) an \(S\)-group functor of type (a) or (b), and
\(L_{0}\), \(L\) as above;}

\emph{--- \(Y\) an \(S\)-group scheme flat over \(S\) and
\(f_{J} : Y_{J} \to X_{J}\) a morphism of \texttt{S\_J}-groups.}

\emph{Then:}

\emph{(i) For \(f_{J}\) to lift to a morphism of \(S\)-groups
\(Y \to X\), it is necessary and sufficient that the following two
conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i₁) \(f_{J}\) lifts to a morphism of \(S\)-functors \(Y \to X\)
(by 1.2.4, this defines an action of \(Y\) on \(L\), which does not
depend on the chosen lift; moreover, in case (a), the action thus
obtained of \(Y_{0}\) on \(L_{0}\) comes from the morphism
\(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) and from ``the adjoint action'' of \(X_{0}\)
on \(L_{0}\));}

\emph{(i₂) A certain obstruction \(c(f_{J})\), defined canonically by
\(f_{J}\), vanishes, where \(c(f_{J})\) is a class in \(H^{2}(Y, L)\)
(\(\simeq H^{2}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\) in case (a)).}

\emph{(ii) If the conditions of (i) are satisfied, the set \(E\) of
morphisms of \(S\)-group functors \(Y \to X\) extending \(f_{J}\) is
principal homogeneous under \(Z^{1}(Y, L)\)
(\(\simeq Z^{1}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\) in case (a)), and \(E\) modulo the
action of the inner automorphisms of \(X\) defined by the sections of
\(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit section of \texttt{X\_J} over
\texttt{S\_J}, is principal homogeneous under \(H^{1}(Y, L)\)
(\(\simeq H^{1}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\) in case (a)).}

\emph{(iii) If \(f : Y \to X\) is a morphism of \(S\)-group functors
extending \(f_{J}\), the set of morphisms \(Y \to X\) transforms of
\(f\) by the inner automorphisms defined by the sections of \(X\) over
\(S\) inducing the unit section of \texttt{X\_J} over \texttt{S\_J} is
isomorphic to \(\Gamma(L)/H^{0}(Y, L)\)
(\(\simeq \Gamma(L_{0})/H^{0}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\) in case (a)).}

\textbf{Remark 2.1.1.}{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-54{]} \emph{If
\(f, f' : Y \to X\) are morphisms of \(S\)-group functors extending
\(f_{J}\), one therefore obtains a cocycle \(d(f, f') \in Z^{1}(Y, L)\)
(\(\simeq Z^{1}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\) in case (a)), such that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)     f′ = d(f, f′) · f .[\^{}N.D.E{-}III{-}55]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{We shall denote by \(\bar{d}(f, f')\) the image of \(d(f, f')\) in
\(H^{1}(Y, L)\) (\(\simeq H^{1}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\) in case (a)).}

\textbf{Remark 2.2.} \emph{We keep the preceding notations; in
particular, \(Y\) is flat over \(S\). In case (b), \(L\) is, by
(0.14.1), the restriction to \((Flat)/S\) of the functor}

\[
W(\pi_{*}(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{E}}(\Omega^{1}_{E/S}, J \cdot O_{E}))),
\]

\emph{where \(\pi : E \to S\) is the structural morphism. In case (a),
suppose moreover that \(X\) is locally of finite presentation over
\(S\); then by (0.6.1), \(L\) is the restriction to \((Flat)/S\) of the
functor}

\[
\prod_{S_{0}/S} W(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S_{0}}}(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}, J)).
\]

In both cases, the module of which we take the \(W\) is quasi-coherent,
by (EGA I, 9.1.1). Suppose moreover \(Y\) affine over
\(S\).{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-56{]} Then, by (I, 5.3), one obtains:

\textbf{a)}
\(H^{i}(Y, L) = H^{i}(Y_{0}, L_{0}) = H^{i}(Y_{0}, \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S_{0}}}(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}, J))\),

\textbf{b)}
\(H^{i}(Y, L) = H^{i}(Y, \pi_{*}(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{E}}(\Omega^{1}_{E/S}, J \cdot O_{E})))\).

\textbf{Remark 2.3.} \emph{1) By 0.16 and 0.17, condition \((i_{1})\) is
automatically verified when \(Y\) is an affine scheme and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)     \{  in case (a), X is smooth over S;}
\NormalTok{           in case (b), E is smooth and affine over S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{2) Moreover, under these conditions (\(Y\) always being supposed
flat over \(S\), cf.~2.0), one can write in case (a), by 2.2 a) and
(0.6.2),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hⁱ(Y, L) = Hⁱ(Y₀, L₀) = Hⁱ(Y₀, Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-57{]} and in case (b), by (0.14.2), 1.1.2 and (I,
5.3),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hⁱ(Y, L) = Hⁱ(Y₀, π\_\{0*\} Hom\_\{O\_\{E₀\}\}(Ω¹\_\{E₀/S₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{E₀\})).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us now state a certain number of corollaries concerning the case
where \(Y\) is an \(S\)-diagonalizable group (I, 4.4); one knows then
(loc. cit. 5.3.3) that if \(S\) is affine, \(H^{n}(Y, F) = 0\) for
\(n > 0\) and every quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-module \(F\). First, a
particular case:

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(S_{0}\) a
closed subscheme defined by a nilpotent ideal. Let \(Y\) be a
diagonalizable \(S\)-group and let:}

\emph{a) \(X\) an \(S\)-group locally of finite presentation over
\(S\),}

\emph{b) \(X = \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(E)\) where \(E\) is an
\(S\)-scheme locally of finite presentation.}

\emph{Let \(f : Y \to X\) be a morphism of \(S\)-groups such that the
morphism \(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) obtained by base change is the unit
morphism. Then \(f\) is the unit morphism.}

Indeed, the question is local on \(S\) and (in (b)) on \(E\). We may
therefore suppose \(S\) affine and (in (b)) \(E\) of finite presentation
over \(S\). Now introducing the closed subschemes \(S_{n}\) of \(S\)
defined by the powers of the ideal defining \(S_{0}\), one is reduced to
the case where \(S_{0}\) is defined by an ideal of square zero, and in
that case the asserted statement follows from the theorem, via 2.2.

In the case where one does not necessarily suppose that \(f_{0}\) is the
unit morphism, one has:

\textbf{Corollary 2.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) and \(S_{0}\) be as in 2.4.
Suppose moreover \(S\) affine. Let \(Y\) be a diagonalizable
\(S\)-group, \(X\) an \(S\)-group functor, and
\(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) a morphism of \(S_{0}\)-group functors.}

\emph{(i){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-58{]}}

\emph{(ii) Suppose that one of the following two properties holds:}

\emph{(a) \(X\) is an \(S\)-group smooth over \(S\);}

\emph{(b) \(X = \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(E)\) where \(E\) is smooth and
affine over \(S\).}

\emph{Then \(f_{0}\) extends to a morphism of \(S\)-groups \(Y \to X\);
two such extensions are conjugate by an inner automorphism of \(X\)
defined by a section of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit section of
\(X_{0}\) over \(S_{0}\).}

Introduce the \(S_{n}\) as above.{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-59{]} For (ii), note
first that a scheme smooth over \(S\) is necessarily locally of finite
presentation over \(S\); hence, in case (b), \(E\) being smooth and
affine over \(S\) is necessarily of finite presentation over \(S\),
i.e.~we are indeed under hypothesis (b) of 2.0.

Then, under the hypotheses of (ii), condition \((i_{1})\) of 2.1 is
automatically verified by 0.16 and 0.17; moreover every section of
\(X_{S_{n}}\) over \(S_{n}\) lifts to a section of \(X_{S_{n+1}}\) over
\(S_{n+1}\), by the definition of ``smooth over \(S\)'' in case (a), and
by 0.17 in case (b). Consequently, if \(f\) and \(f'\) are two lifts of
\(f_{0}\), one can suppose step by step that \(f_{n} = f_{n}'\) by
lifting the inner automorphism whose existence is asserted by part (ii)
of the theorem, which completes the proof.

By reasoning likewise, taking into account Remark 2.3, one obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 2.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(I\) a nilpotent
ideal defining the closed subscheme \(S_{0}\), \(Y\) an \(S\)-group flat
over \(S\) and affine, \(X\) an \(S\)-group smooth over \(S\).}

\emph{(i) If, for every \(n \geq 0\), one has
\(H^{2}(Y_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}) = 0\),
every morphism of \(S_{0}\)-groups \(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) lifts to
a morphism of \(S\)-groups \(f : Y \to X\).}

\emph{(ii) If, for every \(n \geq 0\), one has
\(H^{1}(Y_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}) = 0\),
two such lifts are conjugate by an inner automorphism of \(X\) defined
by a section of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit section of \(X_{0}\)
over \(S_{0}\).}

Now one has the following lemma:

\textbf{Lemma 2.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme, \(G\) an affine
\(S\)-group, \(F\) a quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-module, \(L\) a
locally free \texttt{O\_S}-module. Suppose one has an action of \(G\) on
\(F\) in the sense of Exposé I, which defines an action of \(G\) on
\(F \otimes_{O_{S}} L\){[}\^{}N.D.E-III-60{]}. Denote by \(\Lambda\) the
ring of \(S\), \(L\) the \(\Lambda\)-module defining \(L\) (which is
therefore a projective module). One has a canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H*(G, F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} L) ≃ H*(G, F) ⊗\_Λ L.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-61{]} Indeed, denote by \(A\) the \texttt{O\_S}-algebra
\(A(G)\) and consider the complex \(C\) of quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_S}-modules:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► F ──► F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} A ──► F ⊗\_\{O\_S\} A ⊗\_\{O\_S\} A ──► · · ·}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By (I, 5.3), \(H*(G, F)\) (resp. \(H*(G, F \otimes_{O_{S}} L)\)) is the
cohomology of the complex \(\Gamma(S, C)\) (resp.
\(\Gamma(S, C \otimes_{O_{S}} L)\)). Now, since \(S\) is affine, one has
(cf.~EGA I, 1.3.12)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(S, C ⊗\_\{O\_S\} L) ≃ Γ(S, C) ⊗\_Λ L.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(L\) is a projective \(\Lambda\)-module (hence flat), one has
also
\(H*(\Gamma(S, C) \otimes_{\Lambda} L) \simeq H*(\Gamma(S, C)) \otimes_{\Lambda} L\),
whence the announced result.

By using the lemma, one transforms 2.6 into:

\textbf{Corollary 2.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme, \(I\) a
nilpotent ideal on \(S\) defining the closed subscheme \(S_{0}\).
Suppose the \(I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}\) locally free on \(S_{0}\). Let \(Y\) be
an \(S\)-group flat over \(S\) and affine, \(X\) an \(S\)-group smooth
over \(S\), and \(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) a morphism of \(S\)-groups.}

\emph{(i) If \(H^{2}(Y_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\), \(f_{0}\) lifts to
a morphism of \(S\)-groups \(Y \to X\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(H^{1}(Y_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\), two such lifts are
conjugate by an inner automorphism of \(X\) defined by a section of
\(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit section of \(X_{0}\) over \(S_{0}\).}

In particular, taking \(Y = X\):

\textbf{Corollary 2.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) and \(S_{0}\) be as above. Let
\(X\) be an \(S\)-group smooth over \(S\) and affine.}

\emph{(i) If \(H^{1}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\), every endomorphism
of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the identity on \(X_{0}\) is the inner
automorphism defined by a section of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit
section of \(X_{0}\) over \(S_{0}\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\), every
\(S_{0}\)-automorphism of \(X_{0}\) extends to an \(S\)-automorphism of
\(X\).{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-62{]}}

\textbf{Remark 2.10.} \emph{The assertions concerning \(H^{1}\) have
converses by the theorem. Let us signal as an example the following: if
\(S = IS_{0}\) is the scheme of dual numbers over \(S_{0}\) (II, 2.1)
and if \(X\) is a flat \(S\)-group such that every automorphism of \(X\)
over \(S\) inducing the identity on \(S_{0}\) is the inner automorphism
defined by a section of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit section of
\(X_{0}\) over \(S_{0}\), then
\(H^{1}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\).{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-63{]}}

\textbf{Corollary 2.11.} \emph{Let \(S\), \(I\) and \(J\) be as in 2.1.
Let \(Y\) be an \(S\)-group scheme flat over \(S\), \(X\) an \(S\)-group
scheme, \(f : Y \to X\) a morphism of \(S\)-groups. The set of morphisms
from \(Y\) to \(X\) deduced from \(f\) by conjugation by elements
\(x \in X(S)\) inducing the unit of \(X(S_{J})\) is isomorphic to the
quotient}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E = Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J) / Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J)\^{}\{ad(Y₀)\} ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where the second group consists of the \(O_{S_{0}}\)-morphisms
\(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}} \to J\) which by every base change
\(S' \to S_{0}\) give morphisms
\(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}} \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{S'} \to J \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{S'}\)
invariant under the action of \(Y_{0}(S')\) on the first factor.}

By 2.1 (iii), one knows that the set sought is isomorphic to
\(\Gamma(L_{0})/H^{0}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\). Now
\(\Gamma(L_{0}) = \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S_{0}}}(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}, J)\)
and \(H^{0}(Y_{0}, L_{0})\) is evidently none other than
\(\Gamma(L_{0})^{ad(Y_{0})}\) in the sense of the preceding statement.

\textbf{Corollary 2.12.} \emph{Under the conditions of 2.11, suppose
moreover \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) locally free of finite rank. Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E ≃ Γ(S₀, Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J) / H⁰(Y₀, Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{[}\^{}N.D.E-III-64{]} Indeed, if \(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) is
locally free of finite rank, one has
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S_{0}}}(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}, J) \simeq Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} J\).

\textbf{Corollary 2.13.} \emph{Suppose moreover \(Y_{0}\)
diagonalizable. Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E ≃ Γ(S₀, Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J) / Γ(S₀, Lie(X₀/S₀)\^{}\{ad(Y₀)\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})^{ad(Y_{0})}\) can be constructed as the
factor of the decomposition of (I, 4.7.3) corresponding to the null
character of \(Y_{0}\).}

Indeed, if \(Y_{0} \simeq D_{S_{0}}(M)\), one has by loc. cit. a
decomposition into direct sum:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(X₀/S₀) = Lie(X₀/S₀)₀ ⊕ ⨁\_\{m ∈ M, m ≠ 0\} Lie(X₀/S₀)\_m .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By tensoring with \(J\), one finds an analogous decomposition for
\(Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} J\), whence the relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H⁰(Y₀, Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗ J) ≃ Γ(S₀, Lie(X₀/S₀)₀ ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 2.14.} \emph{Suppose moreover \(S_{0}\) affine. Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E ≃ Γ(S₀, [Lie(X₀/S₀) / Lie(X₀/S₀)\^{}\{ad(Y₀)\}] ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{3. Infinitesimal extensions of a group
scheme}\label{infinitesimal-extensions-of-a-group-scheme}

Still in the notation of n° 0 (\(S\), \(I\), \(J\), etc.), let us give
ourselves an \(S\)-scheme \(X\) and suppose \texttt{X\_J} endowed with a
group structure. We propose to find the \(S\)-group structures on \(X\)
inducing on \texttt{X\_J} the given structure.

From now on, we assume \(X\) flat over \(S\). Let \(C\) be the category
of \(S\)-schemes flat over \(S\). We have therefore \(X \in Ob C\). We
shall denote by \(Y\), resp. \(M\), the functor on \(C\) defined by
\(X^{+}\), resp. \(L'_{X}\). The canonical morphism
\(p_{X} : X \to X^{+}\) defines a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}

\[
p : X \longrightarrow Y
\]

and the action of \(L'_{X}\) on \(X\) in \((Sch)/S\) defines an action
of \(M\) on \(X\) in \texttt{Ĉ}. One verifies at once that \(X\) thus
becomes formally principal homogeneous under \texttt{M\_Y} above \(Y\)
(cf.~0.2 (i) and 0.4).

The action of \(X^{+}\) on \(L'_{X}\) defined in 0.8 (denoted
\texttt{Ad} in loc. cit.) defines an action denoted \(f\) of \(Y\) on
\(M\). One knows, on the other hand (0.5), that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_Ĉ(Z, M) ≃ Hom\_\{S₀\}(Z₀, L₀),     Z ∈ Ob C,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(L_{0}\) is the functor defined in 0.5.

\textbf{Lemma 3.1.} \emph{(i) Condition \((+)_{n}\) of 1.3 is satisfied
for every positive integer \(n\).}

\emph{(ii) If one makes the \(S_{0}\)-group \(X_{0}\) act on the
\(S_{0}\)-functor \(L_{0}\) through its adjoint representation, one has
a canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H*(X₀, L₀) ≃ H*(Y, M),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(the first cohomology being computed in \((Sch)/S_{0}\), the
second in \(C\)).}

Both parts of the lemma follow from the relation:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_Ĉ(Y, M) ≃ Hom\_\{(Sch)/S₀\}(X⁺ ×\_S S₀, L₀)}
\NormalTok{            ≃ Hom\_\{S₀\}(X₀, L₀)}
\NormalTok{            ≃ Hom\_Ĉ(X, M),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which arises at once from the definition of \(M\) as a
\(\prod_{S_{0}/S}\). This relation being more generally satisfied on
replacing \(X\), \(Y\) by \(X_{n}\), \(Y_{n}\), one deduces that every
morphism \(X_{n} \to M\) factors in a unique manner through \(Y_{n}\),
which entails \((+)_{n}\). One also deduces from it the relation
\(C*(Y, M) = C*(X_{0}, L_{0})\), which entails (ii).

We may therefore apply the constructions of 1.3. In particular:

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.} \emph{Let \(P : X \times_{S} X \to X\) be a
morphism. In order for \(P\) to induce the group law of \texttt{X\_J},
it is necessary and sufficient that \(P\) be an admissible composition
law (cf.~1.3.2) on \(X\).}

Indeed, in order for \(P\) to induce the group law of \texttt{X\_J}, it
is necessary and sufficient that \(P\) lift the group law of \(X^{+}\),
or equivalently that of \(Y\). It therefore only remains to show that
every morphism \(P\) lifting the group law of \texttt{X\_J} satisfies
the identity \texttt{(++)} of 1.3.2 (ii), and this is exactly what was
seen in 0.8.

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(S_{0}\) a
closed subscheme defined by a nilpotent ideal. Let \(X\) be a flat
\(S\)-scheme, quasi-compact or locally of finite presentation over
\(S\). Let \(P : X \times_{S} X \to X\) be a composition law on \(X\).
In order for \(P\) to be a group law, it is necessary and sufficient
that the two following conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i) \(P\) is associative.}

\emph{(ii) \(P\) induces on \(X_{0} = X \times_{X} S_{0}\) a group law.}

These conditions are obviously necessary. Let us show that they are
sufficient. Suppose first that \(X \to S\) has a section. Since
\(X(S')\) is then non-empty for each \(S' \to S\), it
suffices\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the original by suppressing
  the inadequate reference to an exercise of Bourbaki on semigroups
  (cf.~{[}BAlg{]}, § I.2, Exercises 9--13) and by indicating the role of
  left and right translations; see the following N.D.E.} to show that,
for every \(x \in X(S')\), the left and right translations by \(x\) are
isomorphisms of \(X_{S'}\).\footnote{N.D.E.: Let \(E\) be a non-empty
  set equipped with an associative composition law, such that every left
  translation \(\ell_{x}\) is bijective; fix \(x_{0} \in E\). There
  exists a unique \(e \in E\) such that \(x_{0} \cdot e = x_{0}\); then
  \(x_{0} \cdot e \cdot x = x_{0} \cdot x\) entails \(e \cdot x = x\),
  for every \(x \in E\). On the other hand, for every \(x\) there exists
  a unique \(x'\) such that \(x \cdot x' = e\). Suppose moreover that
  there exists \(b \in E\) such that the right translation \(r_{b}\) is
  injective. Then, for every \(x\), the equality
  \(x \cdot e \cdot b = x \cdot b\) gives \(x \cdot e = x\) (i.e.~\(e\)
  is a neutral element), and \(x \cdot x' \cdot x = x = x \cdot e\)
  entails \(x' \cdot x = e\), i.e.~\(x'\) is the inverse of \(x\) from
  the left and the right, hence \(E\) is a group. Note that the
  hypothesis ``\(r_{b}\) injective'' is necessary: on every set \(E\)
  one can define a composition law by \(x \cdot y = y\), for all
  \(x, y \in E\); then every left translation is the identity (whence
  the associativity of the law), but for every \(y\) one has
  \(r_{y}(E) = {y}\), hence \(E\) is not a group if \(|E| > 1\).}

One may evidently suppose \(S' = S\); the translation in question \(t\)
induces on \(X_{0}\) a translation \(t_{0}\) of \(X_{0}\), which is
therefore an automorphism since \(X_{0}\) is a group. One concludes by
flatness (SGA 1 III 4.2).\footnote{N.D.E.: Since \(X\) and \(X_{0}\)
  have the same underlying topological space and \(t_{0}\) is an
  automorphism, \(t\) is a homeomorphism, hence an affine morphism,
  cf.~Exp. VI\_B, 2.9.1 or EGA IV₄, 18.12.7.1. It thus suffices to see
  that if \(J\) is a nilpotent ideal of a ring \(\Lambda\), and
  \(\phi : A \to B\) a morphism of \(\Lambda\)-algebras, with \(B\) flat
  over \(\Lambda\), such that \(\phi \otimes_{\Lambda} (\Lambda/J)\) is
  bijective, then \(\phi\) is bijective. By the ``nilpotent Nakayama
  lemma'', \(\phi\) is surjective; moreover, \(B\) being flat over
  \(\Lambda\), one also has
  \(Ker(\phi) \otimes_{\Lambda} (\Lambda/J) = 0\), whence
  \(Ker(\phi) = 0\), hence \(\phi\) is bijective.}

No longer supposing now that \(X\) has a section over \(S\), suppose
that there exists an \(S' \to S\) such that \(X_{S'}\) has a section
over \(S'\). Then \(X_{S'}\) is an \(S'\)-group according to what we
have just seen; consider its unit section \(e'\). The inverse image of
\(e'\) by \(pr_{i} : S' \times_{S} S' \to S'\) (\(i = 1, 2\)) is the
unit section of \(X_{S''}\) for the group law inverse image of
\(P_{S'}\) by \(pr_{i}\). But since \(P\) is ``defined over \(S\)'',
these two group laws coincide, and therefore so do their unit sections.
One has therefore \(pr_{1}*(e') = pr_{2}*(e')\).

If \(S' \to S\) is a descent morphism (cf.~Exp. IV n° 2), there will
exist a section of \(X\) giving \(e'\) by base extension, and we shall
be done. Since \texttt{X\_X} has a section over \(X\) (the diagonal
section), one sees that it now suffices to prove that \(X \to S\) is a
descent morphism. Now it is flat and surjective, and quasi-compact or
locally of finite presentation, hence covering for (fpqc), hence a
descent morphism (Exp. IV, n° 6).

\textbf{Remark.} \emph{In fact the hypothesis \(X \to S\) quasi-compact
or locally of finite presentation is superfluous, by virtue of the
following result which the reader will prove as an exercise on Exposé
IV:}

\emph{Under the conditions of the text on \(S\) and \(S_{0}\), if
\(X \to S\) is a flat morphism and \(X_{0} \to S_{0}\) a morphism
covering for (fpqc), then \(X \to S\) is a descent morphism.}

\textbf{Lemma 3.4.} \emph{In order for two admissible composition laws
on \(X\) to be equivalent (cf.~1.3.5), it is necessary and sufficient
that they be deduced from one another by an automorphism of \(X\) over
\(S\) inducing the identity on \texttt{X\_J}.}

Indeed, the morphisms constructed in 1.3.1 are exactly those of the
preceding statement (by 0.7).\footnote{N.D.E.: Indeed, by the proof of
  0.7, the \(S\)-endomorphisms of \(X\) inducing the identity on
  \texttt{X\_J} are the automorphisms \(m \cdot id_{X}\), for \(m\)
  ranging over \(M(X) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(X, M)\) (for every
  \(S' \to S\) and \(x \in X(S')\), one has
  \((m \cdot id_{X})(x) = m(x) \cdot x\)). Now, by the proof of 3.1,
  each \(m : X \to M\) factors in a unique manner through a morphism
  \(h\) from \(Y = X^{+}\) to \(M\), and therefore \(m \cdot id_{X}\) is
  the automorphism \(u_{h}\) introduced in 1.3.1. The lemma then follows
  from the definition of equivalence, cf.~1.3.4 and 1.3.5.}

Taking all the preceding results into account, Proposition 1.3.6 gives:

\textbf{Theorem 3.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(I\) and \(J\) two
ideals on \(S\) such that \(I \supset J\), \(I \cdot J = 0\), \(S_{0}\)
and \texttt{S\_J} the closed subschemes of \(S\) which they define. Let
\(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme flat over \(S\) (and locally of finite
presentation or quasi-compact over \(S\)), \(X_{0}\) and \texttt{X\_J}
the schemes obtained by base change. Suppose \texttt{X\_J} endowed with
an \texttt{S\_J}-group structure and denote by \(L_{0}\) the
\(S_{0}\)-functor in commutative groups defined by the formula}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L₀) = Hom\_\{O\_T\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{on which \(X_{0}\) acts through its adjoint representation.}

\emph{(i) For there to exist an \(S\)-group structure on \(X\) inducing
the given structure on \texttt{X\_J}, it is necessary and sufficient
that the following conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i₁) There exists a morphism of \(S\)-schemes
\(X \times_{S} X \to X\) inducing the group law of \texttt{X\_J}.}

\emph{(i₂) A certain obstruction class belonging to
\(H^{3}(X_{0}, L_{0})\) (defined canonically by the data of \(X\) and
the group law of \texttt{X\_J}) is zero.}

\emph{(ii) If the conditions of (i) are satisfied, the set \(E\) of
group laws on \(X\) inducing the given law of \texttt{X\_J} is a
principal homogeneous set under \(Z^{2}(X_{0}, L_{0})\), and \(E\)
modulo the \(S\)-automorphisms of \(X\) inducing the identity on
\texttt{X\_J}, is a principal homogeneous set under
\(H^{2}(X_{0}, L_{0})\).}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added what follows.} Indeed, every morphism of
\(S\)-schemes \(f : X \times_{S} X \to X\) inducing the group law of
\texttt{X\_J} is, by 3.2, an admissible composition law on \(X\); then,
by 1.3.6 (i), the existence of an associative admissible composition law
\(P : X \times_{S} X \to X\) is equivalent to the vanishing of a certain
class \(c(f) \in H^{3}(X_{0}, L_{0})\), and in this case, by 3.3, \(P\)
is a group law. This proves (i), and (ii) then follows from 3.3 and
1.3.6 (ii).

\textbf{Remark 3.5.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this remark,
  analogue of 4.5.1, to introduce the notation \(\delta(\mu, \mu')\) (or
  \(\delta(X, X')\)), used in 4.38; consequently, we have also added in
  3.5 (ii) above the part concerning \(E\) itself.} \emph{If \(\mu\),
\(\mu'\) are group laws on \(X\) inducing the given law of
\texttt{X\_J}, one therefore obtains a cocycle
\(\delta(\mu, \mu') \in Z^{2}(X_{0}, L_{0})\), the sign convention
chosen being that \(\mu' = \delta(\mu, \mu') \cdot \mu\), that is, for
every \(S' \to S\) and \(x, y \in X(S')\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ′(x, y) = δ(μ, μ′)(x₀, y₀) · μ(x, y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have conformed to the sign conventions of the
  original, in order to have in 4.38 (5) the equality
  \(\partial^{1}\bar{d}(X, X') = \bar{\delta}(X, X')\) (see also N.D.E.
  (54)).}

We shall denote by \(\bar{\delta}(\mu, \mu')\) the image of
\(\delta(\mu, \mu')\) in \(H^{2}(X_{0}, L_{0})\). Finally, if \(X\)
endowed with the group law \(\mu\) (resp. \(\mu'\)) is designated simply
by \(X\) (resp. \(X'\)), one will write \(\delta(X, X')\) instead of
\(\delta(\mu, \mu')\), and likewise for \(\bar{\delta}(X, X')\).

\textbf{Remark 3.6.} \emph{Let \texttt{X\_J} be an \texttt{S\_J}-scheme
smooth over \texttt{S\_J} and affine. By 0.15, there exists up to
isomorphism a unique \(S\)-scheme \(X\), smooth over \(S\), reducing to
\texttt{X\_J}. If \texttt{X\_J} is endowed with an \texttt{S\_J}-group
structure, it follows from 0.16 that condition (i₁) is automatically
satisfied. Moreover, by 0.6 the definition of \(L_{0}\) simplifies and
one obtains:}

\textbf{Corollary 3.7.} \emph{Let \(S\), \(I\) and \(J\) be as in 3.1.
Let \texttt{X\_J} be an \texttt{S\_J}-group smooth over \texttt{S\_J}
and affine.}

\emph{(i) The set of \(S\)-groups smooth over \(S\) and reducing to
\texttt{X\_J}, up to isomorphism (inducing the identity on
\texttt{X\_J}), is empty or principal homogeneous under the group}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H²(X₀, Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) There exists an \(S\)-group smooth over \(S\) reducing to
\texttt{X\_J} if and only if a certain obstruction in}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H³(X₀, Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is zero.}

One deduces as usual the following corollaries:

\textbf{Corollary 3.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(S_{0}\) a
closed subscheme defined by a nilpotent ideal \(I\). Let \(X_{0}\) be an
\(S_{0}\)-group smooth over \(S\) and affine.}

\emph{(i) If
\(H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}) = 0\)
for every \(n \geq 0\), two \(S\)-groups smooth over \(S\) reducing to
\(X_{0}\) are isomorphic (by an isomorphism inducing the identity on
\(X_{0}\)).}

\emph{(ii) If
\(H^{3}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}) = 0\)
for every \(n \geq 0\), there exists an \(S\)-group smooth over \(S\),
reducing to \(X_{0}\).}

\textbf{Corollary 3.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme and
\(S_{0}\) a closed subscheme defined by a nilpotent ideal \(I\). Suppose
the \(I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}\) locally free on \(S_{0}\). Let \(X_{0}\) be an
\(S_{0}\)-group smooth and affine over \(S_{0}\).}

\emph{(i) If \(H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\), two \(S\)-groups
smooth over \(S\) reducing to \(X_{0}\) are isomorphic.}

\emph{(ii) If \(H^{3}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\), there exists an
\(S\)-group smooth over \(S\) reducing to \(X_{0}\).}

\textbf{Corollary 3.10.} \emph{Let \(S_{0}\) be a scheme and
\(S = IS_{0}\) the scheme of dual numbers over \(S_{0}\). Let \(X_{0}\)
be an \(S_{0}\)-group smooth over \(S_{0}\). In order for every
\(S\)-group \(Y\), smooth over \(S\), such that \(Y_{0}\) be
\(S_{0}\)-isomorphic to \(X_{0}\), to be \(S\)-isomorphic to
\(X = X_{0} \times_{S_{0}} S\), it is necessary and sufficient that
\(H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = 0\).\footnote{N.D.E.: This is used in
  XXIV, 1.13.}}

Indeed, by virtue of 3.5 the set of classes, up to an \(S\)-group
isomorphism ``inducing the identity on \(X_{0}\)'', of such groups
\(Y\), is in bijection with \(H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}))\); hence
the set of classes, up to an arbitrary \(S\)-group isomorphism, is in
bijection with

\[
H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}))/\Gamma_{0},
\]

where

\[
\Gamma_{0} = \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(X_{0})
\]

(which acts in the evident manner on the \(H^{2}\)). The conclusion
follows at once.\footnote{N.D.E.: Indeed,
  \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(X_{0})\) acts by group automorphisms
  on the abelian group \(H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}))\), hence the
  orbit of \texttt{0} is the singleton \texttt{\{0\}}; consequently the
  quotient set is a singleton if and only if
  \(H^{2}(X_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})) = {0}\).}

\subsection{4. Infinitesimal extensions of closed
subgroups}\label{infinitesimal-extensions-of-closed-subgroups}

Let us first state a result valid in an arbitrary abelian category.

\textbf{Lemma 4.1.} \emph{Let \(0 \to A' \to^{i} A \to^{p} A'' \to 0\)
be an exact sequence, \(\phi : A' \to Q\) a morphism and
\(\pi : A'' \to P\) an epimorphism with kernel \(C\). Let \(E\) be the
set (up to isomorphism) of quadruples \((B, f, g, h)\) such that the
sequence}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► Q ──f──► B ──g──► P ──► 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be exact and the diagram below commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► A′ ──i──► A ──p──► A′′ ──► 0}
\NormalTok{       │        │         │}
\NormalTok{       φ        h         π}
\NormalTok{       ↓        ↓         ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► Q ──f──► B ──g──► P  ──► 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) For \(E\) to be non-empty, it is necessary and sufficient that
the image in \(Ext^{1}(C, Q)\) of the element \(A\) of
\(Ext^{1}(A'', A')\) be zero.}

\emph{(ii) Under these conditions, \(E\) is a principal homogeneous set
under the abelian group \(\operatorname{Hom}(C, Q)\).}

Introduce the amalgamated sum \(B' = A \sqcup_{A'} Q\). One then has a
commutative diagram with exact rows:\footnote{N.D.E.: One has
  \(Coker(j) = B' \sqcup_{Q} 0 = A \sqcup_{A'} 0 = A''\), and one sees
  that \(Ker(j) \simeq Ker(i) = 0\) by reasoning ``as if \(C\) were a
  category of modules''; for a proof solely in terms of arrows, see for
  example {[}Fr64{]}, Th. 2.5.4 (∗).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► A′ ──i──► A ──p──► A′′ ──► 0}
\NormalTok{       │       j│         ║}
\NormalTok{       φ        ↓         ║}
\NormalTok{0 ──►  Q  ───► B′ ──────► A′′ ──► 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and it is clear that the category of solutions of the problem posed is
canonically isomorphic to the category of solutions of the corresponding
problem for the sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► Q ──► B′ ──► A′′ ──► 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the morphisms \(id_{Q}\) and \(\pi : A'' \to P\).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  In what follows, we have replaced \(A\) by \(B'\) and detailed the end
  of the argument.} In this case, the set \(E\) is in bijection with the
set of subobjects \(N\) of \(B'\) such that \(B' \to A''\) induces an
isomorphism of \(N\) with the kernel \(C\) of \(A'' \to P\), that is to
say, the set of morphisms \(e : C \to B'\) lifting the canonical
morphism \(C \to A''\). The abelian group
\(G = \operatorname{Hom}(C, Q)\) acts on \(E\) by \(g \cdot e = g + e\)
(addition in \(\operatorname{Hom}(C, B')\)), and if \(E \neq \emptyset\)
this makes \(E\) into a principal homogeneous set under \(G\).

One deduces from this:

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have rewritten the
  statement to be exactly in the setting of the application made of it
  in 4.3; moreover, we have detailed the proof, following the
  indications given by M. Demazure.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\texttt{S\_J} the closed subscheme defined by a quasi-coherent ideal
\(J\) of square zero, \(X\) an \(S\)-scheme, \(F\) an
\texttt{O\_X}-module, \(X_{J} = X \times_{S} S_{J}\),
\(F_{J} = F \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S_{J}}\), and \(G_{J} = F_{J} / H_{J}\) a
quotient module of \texttt{F\_J}. Suppose given a morphism of
\(O_{X_{J}}\)-modules}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} G\_J ⟶ Q.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Let \(E\) be the sheaf of sets on \(X\) defined as follows: for
every open \(U\) of \(X\), \(E(U)\) is the set of quotient modules \(G\)
of \(F|_{U}\), such that \(G/JG = G_{J}|_{U}\) and there exists an
isomorphism}

\[
h : JG \xrightarrow{\sim} Q|_{U}
\]

\emph{making the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                      f|\_U}
\NormalTok{J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} (G\_J|\_U) ────► Q|\_U}
\NormalTok{       │                    ↗}
\NormalTok{       can.                h ≃}
\NormalTok{       ↓                  /}
\NormalTok{       JG ──────────────}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{commutative (\(h\) is then unique, since
\(J \otimes_{O_{S_{J}}} (G_{J}|_{U}) \to JG\) is an epimorphism). Then
\(E\) is a sheaf formally principal homogeneous under the sheaf in
commutative groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = Hom\_\{O\_X\}(H\_J, Q) = Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(H\_J, Q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} If \(E(U) = \emptyset\) there is nothing to prove; one may
therefore suppose that \(E(U)\) contains an element \(\tilde{G}\). Then,
in the diagram below, \(h\) is an isomorphism and all the arrows are
epimorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                          f|\_U}
\NormalTok{J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} (F\_J|\_U) ─► J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} (G\_J|\_U) ─────► Q|\_U}
\NormalTok{        │                          │                      ↗}
\NormalTok{        can.                       can.                 h ≃}
\NormalTok{        ↓                          ↓                    /}
\NormalTok{        JF|\_U  ──────────────►   JG̃   ──────────────────}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Therefore, the morphism
\(J \otimes_{O_{S_{J}}} (F_{J}|_{U}) \to Q|_{U}\) induces an epimorphism
(necessarily unique) \(\phi : JF|_{U} \to Q|_{U}\), and if \(G\) is an
\texttt{O\_U}-module such that \(G/JG = G_{J}|_{U}\) and one has a
commutative diagram with exact rows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► JF|\_U ─────► F|\_U ─────► F\_J|\_U ──► 0}
\NormalTok{        │           │            │}
\NormalTok{        φ           │            π}
\NormalTok{        ↓     p\_J   ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► Q|\_U ─────► G ──────►  G\_J|\_U ──► 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(where \(p_{J}\) is the projection \(G \to G/JG = G_{J}|_{U}\), so that
\(Q|_{U} = Ker(p_{J}) = JG\)), then one can identify \(G\) with a
quotient module of \(F|_{U}\). Consequently, by 4.1 (ii), the set
\(E(U)\) is principal homogeneous under the abelian group

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_X\}(H\_J, Q)(U) = Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(H\_J, Q)(U).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.} \emph{(TDTE IV 5.1) Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\texttt{S\_J} the closed subscheme defined by a quasi-coherent ideal
\(J\) of square zero, \(X\) an \(S\)-scheme, \(F\) a quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_X}-module, \(X_{J} = X \times_{S} S_{J}\),
\(F_{J} = F \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S_{J}}\). Let \(G_{J} = F_{J} / H_{J}\)
be a quasi-coherent quotient module of \texttt{F\_J}, flat over
\texttt{S\_J}.}

\emph{For every open \(U\) of \(X\), let \(E(U)\) be the set of
quasi-coherent\footnote{N.D.E.: To lighten the statement, we have added
  here the hypothesis that \(G\) be quasi-coherent, and deferred to the
  proof the remark that this hypothesis is automatically satisfied; we
  have detailed the proof accordingly.} quotient modules \(G\) of
\(F|_{U}\), flat over \(S\), and such that \(G/JG \simeq G_{J}|_{U}\).
Then the \(E(U)\) form a sheaf of sets \(E\) on \(X\), which is formally
principal homogeneous under the sheaf in commutative groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(H\_J, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} G\_J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Denote by \(\pi : X \to S\) the structural morphism. Let
\(U\) be an open of \(X\) and \(G\) an \texttt{O\_U}-module flat over
\(S\) and such that \(G/JG \simeq G_{J}|_{U}\). Then, for every
\(x \in U\), \(G_{x}\) is a flat module over the local ring \(O_{S,s}\)
(where \(s = \pi(x)\)), and therefore the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J\_s ⊗\_\{O\_\{S,s\}\} (G/JG)\_x = J\_s ⊗\_\{O\_\{S,s\}\} G̅\_x ⟶ (JG)\_x}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective; one has therefore an exact sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ J ⊗\_\{O\_S\} (G\_J|\_U) ⟶ G ⟶ G\_J|\_U ⟶ 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since \(J \otimes_{O_{S}} (G_{J}|_{U})\) and \(G_{J}|_{U}\) are
quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_U}-modules, so is \(G\) (cf.~EGA III, 1.4.17).

Conversely, since one has supposed \texttt{G\_J} flat over
\texttt{S\_J}, if \(G\) is a quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_U}-module such
that \(G/JG \simeq G_{J}\) and such that the morphism
\(J \otimes_{O_{S_{J}}} G_{J} \to JG\) is bijective, then \(G\) is flat
over \(S\), by the ``fundamental criterion of flatness'' (cf.~SGA 1 IV,
5.5\footnote{N.D.E.: See also {[}BAC{]}, § III.5, th. 1.}).

Consequently, the set \(E(U)\) considered here coincides with the set
considered in 4.2, taking for \(f\) the identity morphism of
\(J \otimes_{O_{S_{J}}} G_{J}\), and the conclusion follows therefore
from 4.2. QED.

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed what follows and added Corollary
  4.3.1. Recall that ``pseudo-torsor'' is synonymous with ``formally
  principal homogeneous''.} Let us preserve the preceding notation. Let
\texttt{Y\_J} be a closed subscheme of \texttt{X\_J}, defined by a
quasi-coherent ideal \(I_{Y_{J}}\). We assume \texttt{Y\_J} flat over
\texttt{S\_J}. Then, applying 4.3 to \(F = O_{X}\) and
\(G_{J} = O_{Y_{J}} = O_{X_{J}}/I_{Y_{J}}\), one obtains the following
corollary.

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.1.} \emph{Let \(S, S_{J}, J, X, X_{J}, Y_{J}\) and
\(I_{Y_{J}}\) be as above; one assumes \texttt{Y\_J} flat over
\texttt{S\_J}. Denote by \texttt{A\_J} the sheaf in commutative groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(I\_\{Y\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{on \texttt{X\_J} and \(A = i_{*}(A_{J})\), where \(i\) is the
immersion \(X_{J} \hookrightarrow X\).}

\emph{For every open \(U\) of \(X\), let \(E(U)\) be the set of closed
subschemes \(Y\) of \(U\), flat over \(S\), such that
\(Y \times_{S} S_{J} = Y_{J} \cap U\). Then \(E\) is an
\(A\)-pseudo-torsor.}

\emph{If moreover a \(Y\) exists locally (that is, if every \(x \in X\)
has an open neighborhood \(U\) such that \(E(U) \neq \emptyset\)), then
\(E\) is an \(A\)-torsor.} Now one knows (see for example EGA IV₄,
16.5.15) that the \(A\)-torsors on \(X\) are parametrized by the group
\(H^{1}(X, A) = H^{1}(X_{J}, A_{J})\), and that \(E\) has a global
section (i.e.~\(E(X) \neq \emptyset\)) if and only if the cohomology
class corresponding to \(E\) is zero. One thus obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 4.4.} \emph{Let \(S, S_{J}, J, X, X_{J}, Y_{J}\) and
\(I_{Y_{J}}\) be as above; one assumes \texttt{Y\_J} flat over
\texttt{S\_J}. Let \(E\) be the set of closed subschemes \(Y\) of \(X\),
flat over \(S\), such that \(Y \times_{S} S_{J} = Y_{J}\).}

\emph{(i) The set \(E\) is empty or principal homogeneous under the
abelian group}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H⁰(X, A) = H⁰(X\_J, A\_J) = Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(I\_\{Y\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) For \(E\) to be non-empty, it is necessary and sufficient
that the two following conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(a) There exists locally on \(X\) a solution of the problem.}

\emph{(b) A certain obstruction is zero, lying in}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(X\_J, Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(I\_\{Y\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\})).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Complement 4.4.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this
  complement, useful to prove point (ii) of Proposition 4.8.} \emph{Let
us keep the notation of 4.4 and suppose that \(E\) contains an element
\(Y\). Denote by \texttt{I\_Y} the ideal of \texttt{O\_X} defining
\(Y\), and \(I_{Y_{J}}\) its image in \(O_{X_{J}}\). Then, as was seen
in the proof of 4.2, one has a commutative diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{X\_J\} ──► JO\_X}
\NormalTok{         │                  │}
\NormalTok{         ↓                  ↓}
\NormalTok{J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\} ──≃─► JO\_Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{hence an epimorphism of \texttt{O\_X}-modules
\(\phi : JO_{X} \to J \otimes_{O_{S_{J}}} O_{Y_{J}}\); denote by \(K\)
its kernel.} Then, for every element \(Y'\) of \(E\), the morphism
\(O_{X} \to O_{Y'}\) factors through \(O_{X}/K\) (which is the
amalgamated sum \(B'\) of the proof of Lemma 4.1) and, denoting by
\(I_{Y'}\) the ideal of \(Y'\) in \texttt{O\_X}, one has a commutative
diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       0          0}
\NormalTok{                       │          │}
\NormalTok{                       ↓          ↓}
\NormalTok{                  I\_\{Y′\}/K  ──≃──► I\_\{Y\_J\}}
\NormalTok{                       │            │}
\NormalTok{                       ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► (JO\_X)/K ──► O\_X/K ──► O\_\{X\_J\} ──► 0}
\NormalTok{        │            │ ≀         │}
\NormalTok{        ↓            ↓           ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\} ──► O\_\{Y′\} ──► O\_\{Y\_J\} ──► 0}
\NormalTok{                       │            │}
\NormalTok{                       ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{                       0            0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Therefore, replacing \(X\) by the closed subscheme defined by \(K\), one
reduces to \(K = 0\). Then, the datum of \(Y'\) is equivalent to that of
the sub-\texttt{O\_X}-module \(I_{Y'}\) of \texttt{O\_X}, sending
bijectively onto \(I_{Y_{J}}\) by the projection
\(p : O_{X} \to O_{X_{J}}\); denote by
\(f' : I_{Y_{J}} \xrightarrow{\sim} I_{Y'}\) (resp.
\(f : I_{Y_{J}} \xrightarrow{\sim} I_{Y}\)) the inverse isomorphism.
Then \(f' - f\) is an element of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(I\_\{Y\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\}) = Hom\_\{O\_\{X\_J\}\}(I\_\{Y\_J\}, JO\_Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which we shall denote \(d(Y', Y)\). (Note that
\(d(Y, Y') = -d(Y', Y)\).)

For our fixed \(Y\) and variable \(Y'\), consider the morphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I\_\{Y′\} ⟶ O\_X ⟶ O\_Y = O\_X/I\_Y;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since the composition with \(O_{Y} \to O_{Y_{J}}\) is zero, one knows
that it takes values in \(JO_{Y} = J \otimes_{O_{S_{J}}} O_{Y_{J}}\).
More precisely, if \(V\) is an open of \(X\), \(x'\) a section of
\(I_{Y'}\) on \(V\) and \(x_{J}\) its image in \(\Gamma(V, I_{Y_{J}})\),
then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x′ = f′(x\_J) = f(x\_J) + (f′ − f)(x\_J) = f(x\_J) + d(Y′, Y)(x\_J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consequently: the morphism \(I_{Y'} \to JO_{Y}\) is given by
\(d(Y', Y)\).

\textbf{4.5.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the numbering 4.5.0 to
  mark the return to the original.} Let us keep the notation of 4.3.1
and 4.4 and carry out a certain number of transformations:
\(I_{Y_{J}}/I^{2}_{Y_{J}}\) is a quasi-coherent \(O_{X_{J}}\)-module
annihilated by \(I_{Y_{J}}\), hence is the direct image of a
quasi-coherent \(O_{Y_{J}}\)-module denoted \(N_{Y_{J}/X_{J}}\), called
the \emph{conormal sheaf} to \texttt{Y\_J} in \texttt{X\_J}.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have corrected the following sentence.} Since
\(J \otimes_{O_{S_{J}}} O_{Y_{J}}\) is annihilated by \(I_{Y_{J}}\), the
sheaf in commutative groups \texttt{A\_J} of 4.3.1 identifies with:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\}(I\_\{Y\_J\}/I\_\{Y\_J\}², J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\}) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, for every \(i \geq 0\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hⁱ(X\_J, A\_J) = Hⁱ(Y\_J, Hom\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\})).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed what follows.} One can then suppress
the hypothesis ``\(Y\) closed'', as follows. Let us first note that
every open \texttt{U\_J} of \texttt{X\_J} comes by base change from the
open subscheme \(U\) of \(X\) having the same underlying topological
space as \texttt{U\_J}. Let now \texttt{Y\_J} be a closed subscheme of
\texttt{U\_J}, flat over \texttt{S\_J}, and \(I_{Y_{J}}\) the
quasi-coherent ideal of \(O_{U_{J}}\) defining \texttt{Y\_J}. If
\texttt{Y\_J} lifts to a subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\), then \(Y\), having
the same underlying topological space as \texttt{Y\_J}, is a closed
subscheme of \(U\); consequently, the obstruction to lifting
\texttt{Y\_J} to a subscheme, flat over \(S\), of \(X\) or of \(U\) is
``the same'', it resides in

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(Y\_J, Hom\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\})).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, let us return to the notation of n° 0: let \(I\) be a
quasi-coherent ideal of \texttt{O\_S} such that \(J \subset I\) and
\(IJ = 0\), and let \(S_{0}\) be the closed subscheme of \texttt{S\_J}
defined by \(I\). For every \(S\)-scheme \(Z\), one denotes
\(Z_{J} = Z \times_{S} S_{J}\) and \(Z_{0} = Z \times_{S} S_{0}\). Then,
since \(J\) is annihilated by \(I\), one has, with the notation of 4.4:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\} = J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_J\}\} O\_\{Y\_J\}) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

etc. One thus obtains:

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(S_{0}\) and
\texttt{S\_J} the closed subschemes defined by the quasi-coherent ideals
\(I\) and \(J\), such that \(I \supset J\) and \(I \cdot J = 0\). Let
\(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme and \texttt{Y\_J} a subscheme of \texttt{X\_J},
flat over \texttt{S\_J}. Let \(A_{0}\) be the \(O_{Y_{0}}\)-module
defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A₀ = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) For there to exist a subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\), reducing to
\texttt{Y\_J}, flat over \(S\), it is necessary and sufficient that the
following conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(a) Such a \(Y\) exists locally on \(X\).}

\emph{(b) A certain obstruction in \(R^{1}\Gamma(Y_{0}, A_{0})\) is
zero.\footnote{N.D.E.: Here, we have denoted
  \(R^{1}\Gamma(Y_{0}, A_{0})\) the ``coherent'' cohomology group
  \(H^{1}(Y_{0}, A_{0})\) of the \(O_{Y_{0}}\)-module \(A_{0}\), in
  order to distinguish it from the ``Hochschild'' cohomology groups
  \(H^{i}(Y_{0}, M_{0})\) (\(Y_{0}\) an \(S_{0}\)-group, \(M_{0}\) an
  \(O_{S_{0}}\)-module) which will be considered starting from 4.16.}}

\emph{(ii) Under these conditions, the set of \(Y\) satisfying the
required conditions is principal homogeneous under the commutative group
\(\Gamma(Y_{0}, A_{0})\).}

\textbf{Remark 4.5.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have placed here this remark,
  which replaces Remark 4.7 of the original.} \emph{It follows from 4.5
(ii) that for every pair \((Y, Y')\) of subschemes\footnote{N.D.E.: We
  have corrected ``closed subschemes'' to ``subschemes''.} of \(X\),
flat over \(S\) and reducing to \texttt{Y\_J}, one has a ``deviation''}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d(Y′, Y) ∈ Γ(Y₀, A₀) = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\});}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the sign convention adopted in 4.4.1 being that \(d(Y', Y)\)
corresponds to the morphism of \texttt{O\_X}-modules}

\[
I_{Y'} \hookrightarrow O_{X} \longrightarrow O_{Y}
\]

\emph{(which takes values in
\(JO_{Y} \simeq J \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{Y_{0}}\) and factors through
\(I_{Y_{J}'} = I_{Y_{J}}\) and then through \(N_{Y_{J}/X_{J}}\)).}

\textbf{Remark 4.6.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have kept, for the record,
  Remark 4.6 of the original, in which the definition of ``locally
  complete intersection'' does not appear. We have added next the
  ``good'' definition, drawn from SGA 6, VII 1.4 (which replaces that of
  EGA IV₄, 16.9.2), and the proof of the three results stated in the
  remark.} \emph{If \(X\) is flat over \(S\) and if \texttt{Y\_J} is
locally complete intersection in \texttt{X\_J}, then condition (a) is
always satisfied and every \(Y\) flat over \(S\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J}
is then locally complete intersection in \(X\). If moreover \(Y_{0}\) is
affine, condition (b) is also satisfied.}

\textbf{Definition 4.6.1.} \emph{(cf.~SGA 6, VII 1.1) Let \(B\) be a
commutative ring, \(f : E \to B\) a \(B\)-linear morphism, where \(E\)
is a free \(B\)-module of finite rank \(d\), and \(I\) the ideal
\(f(E)\) (if one chooses a basis of \(E\), \(f\) is given by a
\(d\)-tuple \((f_{1}, ..., f_{d})\) of elements of \(B\), and \(I\) is
the ideal generated by the \texttt{fᵢ}). The} \textbf{Koszul complex}
\emph{\(K\bullet(f)\) is the graded \(B\)-module \(\bigwedge\bullet E\),
equipped with the differential (of degree \(-1\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x₁ ∧ ··· ∧ xᵢ ↦ Σⱼ₌₁ⁱ (−1)ʲ⁻¹ f(xⱼ) x₁ ∧ ··· ∧ x̂ⱼ ∧ ··· ∧ xᵢ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore an augmented chain complex (\(B/I\) being in degree
\(-1\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{··· ⟶ ⋀² E ⟶ E ──f──► B ⟶ B/I ⟶ 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which by definition is exact in degree \texttt{0}, since \(I = f(E)\).
One says that \(f\) is \textbf{regular} if \(K\bullet(f)\) is acyclic in
degrees \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}, that is, if the augmented complex
above is a resolution of \(C = B/I\).

In this case, the proof of SGA 6, VII 1.2 b) shows that the
\(C\)-modules \(I^{n}/I^{n+1}\) (\(n \in \mathbb{N}\)) are free,
\(I/I^{2}\) being of rank \(d\).

\textbf{Definition 4.6.2.} \emph{(cf.~SGA 6, VII 1.4) Let \(X\) be a
scheme, \(Y\) a subscheme, \(U\) an open of \(X\) such that \(Y\) is a
closed subscheme of \(U\), defined by the quasi-coherent ideal
\texttt{I\_Y}.}

\emph{One says that \(Y\) is} \textbf{locally complete intersection}
\emph{in \(X\) if \(Y \hookrightarrow X\) is a regular immersion in the
sense of SGA 6, VII 1.4, that is, if for every \(y \in Y\) there exists
an affine open neighborhood \(V\) of \(y\) in \(U\), a finite free
\texttt{O\_V}-module \(E\), and a regular morphism \(f : E \to O_{V}\)
of image \(I_{Y}|_{V}\), i.e.~such that \(K\bullet(f)\) be a resolution
of \(O_{Y \cap V}\).}

This implies that the immersion \(Y \hookrightarrow X\) is locally of
finite presentation, and, by 4.6.1, that the conormal sheaf
\(N_{Y/X} = I_{Y}/I^{2}_{Y}\) is a finite locally free
\texttt{O\_Y}-module.

\textbf{Lemma 4.6.3.}\footnote{N.D.E.: In order to prove the results
  stated in Remark 4.6, we have added Lemmas 4.6.3, 4.6.4 and
  Proposition 4.6.5, as well as Remark 4.6.6.} \emph{Let \(A\) be a
ring, \(J\) an ideal of \(A\) of square zero, \(\bar{A} = A/J\), \(B\) a
flat \(A\)-algebra, \(E\) a free \(B\)-module of finite rank,
\(f : E \to B\) a morphism of \(B\)-modules. One supposes that the
morphism
\(\bar{g} : \bar{E} = E \otimes_{A} \bar{A} \to \bar{B} = B \otimes_{A} \bar{A}\)
induced by \(f\) is regular and that \(\bar{B}/\bar{g}(\bar{E})\) is
flat over \texttt{Ā}.}

\emph{Then \(f\) is regular and \(B/f(E)\) is flat over \(A\).}

\emph{Proof.} Set \(C = B/f(E)\) and
\(\bar{C} = C \otimes_{A} \bar{A} = \bar{B}/\bar{g}(\bar{E})\). First,
the \(\bigwedge^{i}_{B}(E)\) are free \(B\)-modules, hence flat
\(A\)-modules, since \(B\) is flat over \(A\). As
\(\bigwedge\bullet_{B} E \otimes_{A} \bar{A} \simeq \bigwedge\bullet_{\bar{B}} \bar{E}\),
one obtains therefore an exact sequence of complexes:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ J ⊗\_A ⋀•\_B E ⟶ ⋀•\_B E ⟶ ⋀•\_B̄ Ē ⟶ 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, since \(J^{2} = 0\), one has
\(J \otimes_{A} M = J \otimes_{A} \bar{A} \otimes_{A} M\) for every
\(A\)-module \(M\). Denoting by dashed arrows the augmentation
morphisms, and by \(d\) the rank of \(E\), one therefore obtains the
bicomplex that follows, where the rows are exact:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                 0              0              0}
\NormalTok{                 ↓              ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► J ⊗\_A ⋀ᵈ\_B̄ Ē ──► ⋀ᵈ\_B E ──► ⋀ᵈ\_B̄ Ē ──► 0}
\NormalTok{                 ↓              ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{                ⋮              ⋮              ⋮}
\NormalTok{                 ↓              ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► J ⊗\_A Ē  ──────► E   ──────► Ē  ─────► 0}
\NormalTok{        │id⊗ḡ           │f             │ḡ}
\NormalTok{        ↓               ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► J ⊗\_A B̄  ──────► B   ──────► B̄  ─────► 0}
\NormalTok{        ⤍              ⤍              ⤍}
\NormalTok{        J ⊗\_A C̄  ──────► C   ──────► C̄  ─────► 0}
\NormalTok{        ↓               ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{        0               0              0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, the right and left columns are exact, since
\(K\bullet(\bar{g})\) is a resolution of \(\bar{C}\) and the latter is
flat over \texttt{Ā}. Hence, considering the long exact homology
sequence associated with the exact sequence of unaugmented complexes,
one obtains that \(K\bullet(f)\) is acyclic in degrees
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}, and that one has in degree \texttt{0} an
exact sequence:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ J ⊗\_A C̄ ⟶ C ⟶ C̄ ⟶ 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Hence \(C\) is flat over \(A\), by the ``fundamental criterion of
flatness'' (cf.~{[}BAC{]}, § III.5, th. 1).

\textbf{Lemma 4.6.4.}\footnote{N.D.E.: In order to prove the results
  stated in Remark 4.6, we have added Lemmas 4.6.3, 4.6.4 and
  Proposition 4.6.5, as well as Remark 4.6.6.} \emph{Let \(A\) be a
commutative ring, \(J\) a nilpotent ideal, \(N \subset M\) two
\(A\)-modules such that \(M/N\) is flat over \(A\). If
\(x_{1}, ..., x_{n}\) are elements of \(N\) whose images generate the
image \(\bar{N}\) of \(N\) in \(M/JM\), then they generate \(N\).}

Indeed, denote by \(N'\) the submodule of \(N\) generated by the
\texttt{xᵢ}, and \(Q = N/N'\). Then the morphism
\(N' \otimes (A/J) \to \bar{N}\) is surjective. On the other hand, since
\(M/N\) is flat over \(A\), the morphism \(N \otimes (A/J) \to \bar{N}\)
is bijective. One thus obtains that \(Q \otimes (A/J) = 0\), whence
\(Q = 0\) by the ``nilpotent Nakayama lemma'' (one has
\(Q = JQ = J^{2}Q = \cdot\cdot\cdot = 0\)).

One can now prove:

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.5.}\footnote{N.D.E.: In order to prove the
  results stated in Remark 4.6, we have added Lemmas 4.6.3, 4.6.4 and
  Proposition 4.6.5, as well as Remark 4.6.6.} \emph{Let
\texttt{S,\ I,\ J} and \(X, Y_{J}\) be as in 4.5. Suppose moreover \(X\)
flat over \(S\) and \texttt{Y\_J} locally complete intersection in
\texttt{X\_J}.}

\emph{a) Then condition (a) of 4.5 (i) is satisfied; moreover, every
\(Y\) flat over \(S\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J} is locally complete
intersection in \(X\).}

\emph{b) If moreover \(Y_{0}\) is affine, condition (b) of loc. cit. is
likewise satisfied.}

\emph{Proof.} The first assertion of (a) follows from Lemma 4.6.3; the
second then results from Lemma 4.6.4. On the other hand, the hypothesis
entails (cf.~4.6.2) that \(N_{Y_{J}/X_{J}}\) is a finite locally free
\(O_{Y_{J}}\)-module, hence the \(O_{Y_{0}}\)-module

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A₀ = Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is quasi-coherent (cf.~EGA I, 1.3.12), whence
\(R^{1}\Gamma(Y_{0}, A_{0}) = 0\) if \(Y_{0}\) is affine.

\textbf{Remark 4.6.6.}\footnote{N.D.E.: In order to prove the results
  stated in Remark 4.6, we have added Lemmas 4.6.3, 4.6.4 and
  Proposition 4.6.5, as well as Remark 4.6.6.} \emph{Let us conclude
this paragraph by the following example, which shows that, under the
hypotheses of Lemma 4.6.3, if \((\bar{g}_{1}, \bar{g}_{2})\) is a
regular sequence generating the ideal \(\bar{I} = \bar{g}(\bar{E})\), it
does not necessarily lift to a regular sequence in \(B\).}

\emph{Let \(k\) be a field, \(\bar{A} = k[X, Y]\), denote by
\(k\epsilon\) the \texttt{Ā}-module \(\bar{A}/(X, Y)\) (i.e.
\(P \cdot \epsilon = P(0, 0)\epsilon\) for every \(P \in \bar{A}\)), and
let \(A = \bar{A} \oplus k\epsilon\), where \(J = k\epsilon\) is an
ideal of square zero. One has \(A/J = \bar{A}\).}

\emph{The algebra \(B = A \otimes_{k} k[Z, T]\) is free over \(A\),
hence flat; one has \(\bar{B} = k[X, Y, Z, T]\). Set
\(\bar{g}_{1} = XZ - YT\) and \(\bar{g}_{2} = XZ - 1\). Since the
polynomial \(\bar{g}_{1}\) is irreducible, \(\bar{B}/(\bar{g}_{1})\) is
integral, and therefore \((\bar{g}_{1}, \bar{g}_{2})\) is a regular
sequence in \(\bar{B}\), generating the ideal
\(\bar{I} = (XZ - 1, YT - 1)\). Hence}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C̄ = B̄/Ī = k[X, Y, X⁻¹, Y⁻¹] = Ā[X⁻¹, Y⁻¹]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a flat \texttt{Ā}-algebra (and also a flat \(A\)-algebra). But
every lift in \(B\) of \(\bar{g}_{1}\) is of the form
\(XY - ZT + \lambda \epsilon\), where \(\lambda \in k[Z, T]\), hence
annihilates \(\epsilon\).}

\textbf{4.7.} One has suppressed here Remark 4.7, placed in 4.5.1.

\textbf{Remark 4.8.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have inserted here this
  remark, used in the following proposition; it appeared in 4.10 of the
  original.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(S'\) a closed subscheme,
\(X\) an \(S\)-scheme, \(Y\) a sub-\(S\)-scheme of \(X\), and
\(X' = X \times_{S} S'\), \(Y' = Y \times_{S} S'\). Then, one has a
surjective morphism of \(O_{Y'}\)-modules}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y′\} ──surj──► N\_\{Y′/X′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, up to replacing \(X\) by a certain open, one may suppose that
\(Y\) is closed, defined by an ideal \texttt{I\_Y} of \texttt{O\_X};
then the image of \texttt{I\_Y} in \(O_{X'}\) is the ideal \(I_{Y'}\)
defining \(Y'\), and one has a surjective morphism of \(O_{Y'}\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π : (I\_Y/I\_Y²) ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y′\} ──surj──► I\_\{Y′\}/I\_\{Y′\}².}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Suppose moreover that \(O_{Y} = O_{X}/I_{Y}\) is flat over
\texttt{O\_S}; then the natural morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I\_Y ⊗\_\{O\_X\} O\_\{X′\} ⟶ I\_\{Y′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective (cf.~EGA IV₂, 2.1.8). One then has the following
commutative diagram with exact rows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I\_Y² ⊗\_\{O\_X\} O\_\{X′\} ──► I\_Y ⊗\_\{O\_X\} O\_\{X′\} ──► (I\_Y/I\_Y²) ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y′\} ──► 0}
\NormalTok{       │                       │ ≀                       │ π surj.}
\NormalTok{       surj.                   ↓                         ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ──► I\_\{Y′\}² ──────────► I\_\{Y′\} ──────────► I\_\{Y′\}/I\_\{Y′\}² ────────────► 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence one deduces, by the snake lemma:\footnote{N.D.E.: In the
  original, this was indicated in Remark 4.10, under the additional
  hypothesis that \(Y'\) was locally complete intersection in \(X'\).
  This hypothesis figured also, consequently, in statements 4.12--4.14;
  it seems in fact superfluous, and we have suppressed it from the
  above-mentioned statements.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y′\} ⥲ N\_\{Y′/X′\}     if Y is flat over S.        (4.8.0)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 4.8.} \emph{Let \(S, S_{0}, S_{J}\) and
\texttt{I,\ J} be as in 4.5.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have suppressed the
  hypothesis that \(I\) be nilpotent, which appears superfluous (cf.~the
  proof).} Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme, \(Y\) a subscheme of \(X\), and
\(i\) the immersion \(Y \hookrightarrow X\).}

\emph{(i) For every \(S\)-morphism \(f : T \to X\) such that
\(f_{J} : T_{J} \to X_{J}\) factors through \texttt{Y\_J}, one can
define an obstruction}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    c(X, Y, f) ∈ Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{whose vanishing is equivalent to the existence of a factorization
of \(f\) through \(Y\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(Y'\) be a second subscheme of \(X\). Suppose that
\(Y_{J}' = Y_{J}\) and that \(Y, Y'\) are flat over \(S\). One then has
isomorphisms (cf.~4.8.0):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{JO\_Y ≃ J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\} ≃ JO\_\{Y′\}    and    N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y\_J\} ⥲ N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{whence an isomorphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u : Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, JO\_Y) ⥲ Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}, JO\_\{Y′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Denoting by \(i' : Y' \to X\) the canonical immersion and
\(d(Y, Y')\) the deviation of 4.5.1, one has:\footnote{N.D.E.: See also
  4.27 further on.}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗∗)    c(X, Y, i′) = u(d(Y, Y′)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) The canonical morphism
\texttt{N\_\{Y/X\}\ ──D──►\ i*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\})} (cf.~SGA 1 II, formula
4.3)\footnote{N.D.E.: See also EGA IV₄, 16.4.21. Recall that if \(U\) is
  an affine open of \(X\) such that \(Y \cap U\) is defined by the ideal
  \(I\) of \(A = O_{X}(U)\), if one denotes by \(d\) the differential
  \(A \to \Gamma(U, \Omega^{1}_{X/S})\), and if \(x \in I\), then
  \(D(x + I^{2})\) is the element \(d(x) \otimes 1\) of
  \(\Gamma(U, \Omega^{1}_{X/S}) \otimes_{A} (A/I)\).} induces a
morphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D₀ : N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\} ⟶ Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{X₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and hence, for every \(S\)-morphism \(f : T \to X\) as in (i), a
morphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
