\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{v\_\{f₀\} : Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*(Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), JO\_T) → Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_T),}
\NormalTok{                                       a ↦ a ∘ f₀*(D₀)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where above the first group is
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(T, L_{X})\), cf.~0.1.5. For
\(a \in \operatorname{Hom}_{X^{+}}(T, L_{X})\), one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗∗∗)    c(X, Y, a · f) − c(X, Y, f) = v\_\{f₀\}(a),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(a \cdot f\) denotes the composite morphism
\texttt{T\ ──\{a×f\}──►\ L\_X\ ×\_\{X⁺\}\ X\ →\ X}.}

We shall prove part (i) of the proposition, leaving the reader to (not)
verify assertions (ii) and (iii); this verification is done by reduction
to the affine case, then by comparison of explicit
definitions.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have done these verifications below.}

Let us therefore prove (i). The morphism \(f : T \to X\) defines a
morphism of sheaves of rings
\(\phi : O_{X} \to f_{*}(O_{T})\).\footnote{N.D.E.: On the one hand, we
  have suppressed the hypothesis that \(I\) be nilpotent, i.e.~that
  \(X_{0}\) have the same underlying topological space as \(X\); on the
  other hand, we have detailed the following sentence.} Let \(U\) be an
open subscheme of \(X\) in which \(Y\) is closed; since \(T\) (resp.
\texttt{Y\_J}) has the same underlying space as \texttt{T\_J} (resp.
\(Y\)), the continuous map underlying \(f\) sends \(T\) into \(U\), and
since \(U\) is an open of \(X\), \(\phi\) induces a morphism of sheaves
of rings \(O_{U} = O_{X}|_{U} \to f_{*}(O_{T})\), i.e.~\(f\) factors
through \(U\).

Therefore, one may restrict to the case where \(Y\) is closed, hence
defined by a sheaf of ideals \texttt{I\_Y}. For \(f\) to factor through
\(Y\), it is necessary and sufficient that the composite map
\(I_{Y} \to O_{X} \to f_{*}(O_{T})\) be zero. Since \(f_{J}\) factors
through \texttt{Y\_J}, the composite map
\(I_{Y_{J}} \to O_{X_{J}} \to f_{*}(O_{T_{J}})\) is zero. Considering
the commutative diagram, where the first row is exact:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ──► f\_*(JO\_T) ──────► f\_*(O\_T) ─────► f\_*(O\_\{T\_J\})}
\NormalTok{            ↖              ↑                 ↑}
\NormalTok{              ↖           φ                 φ\_J}
\NormalTok{                ↖          │                  │}
\NormalTok{                  ↖       O\_X ────────────► O\_\{X\_J\}}
\NormalTok{              φ      ↖    ↑                   ↑}
\NormalTok{                       ↖  I\_Y ────────────► I\_\{Y\_J\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one deduces that \(\phi\) sends \texttt{I\_Y} into
\(f_{*}(JO_{T})\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed what follows.}
Since \(J^{2} = 0\), it follows that \(f_{*}(JO_{T})\), viewed as
\texttt{O\_X}-module via \(\phi\), is annihilated by \texttt{I\_Y};
consequently, \(\phi\) induces a morphism of \texttt{O\_X}-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : i\_*(N\_\{Y/X\}) = I\_Y/I\_Y² ⟶ f\_*(JO\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, one has cartesian squares:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T₀ ──f₀──► X₀ ◄──i₀── Y₀}
\NormalTok{│τ\_\{T₀\}    │τ\_\{X₀\}    │τ\_\{Y₀\}}
\NormalTok{↓          ↓          ↓}
\NormalTok{T ──f───► X ◄──i──── Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(iT_{0}\) etc. are the closed immersions deduced by base change
from \(S_{0} \hookrightarrow S\). Since \texttt{JO\_T} is a
quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_T}-module annihilated by \(I\), one has an
isomorphism

\[
JO_{T} \simeq (\tau_{T_{0}})_{*}\tau_{T_{0}}*(JO_{T}),
\]

whence
\(f_{*}(JO_{T}) \simeq (\tau_{X_{0}})_{*}(f_{0})_{*}\tau_{T_{0}}*(JO_{T})\).
Therefore \(h\) corresponds, by adjunction, to a morphism of
\(O_{T_{0}}\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h₀ : f₀*τ\_\{X₀\}* i\_*(N\_\{Y/X\}) ⟶ i\_\{T₀\}*(JO\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now,
\(\tau_{X_{0}}* i_{*}(N_{Y/X}) \simeq (i_{0})_{*}\tau_{Y_{0}}*(N_{Y/X}) = N_{Y/X} \otimes_{O_{Y}} O_{Y_{0}}\).
Hence, returning to the abuse of notation
\(i_{T_{0}}*(JO_{T}) = JO_{T}\) constantly used, \(h_{0}\) identifies
with a morphism of \(O_{T_{0}}\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h₀ : f₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}) ⟶ JO\_T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is the obstruction \(c(X, Y, f)\) sought. This proves (i).

When \(f\) is the immersion \(i' : Y' \hookrightarrow X\), one sees that
\(c(X, Y, i')\) comes from the morphism
\(I_{Y} \hookrightarrow O_{X} \to O_{Y'}\) hence corresponds, by 4.4.1
and 4.5.1, to the class \(d(Y, Y')\). This proves (ii).

Let us prove (iii). First, \(D : N_{Y/X} \to i_{*}(\Omega^{1}_{X/S})\)
induces a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D₀ : τ\_\{Y₀\}*(N\_\{Y/X\}) ⟶ τ\_\{Y₀\}* i\_*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\}) = i\_0* τ\_\{X₀\}*(Ω¹\_\{X/S\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and, since \(X_{0} = X \times_{S} S_{0}\), one has
\(\tau_{X_{0}}*(\Omega^{1}_{X/S}) \simeq \Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) (cf.
EGA IV₄, 16.4.5). One thus obtains the announced morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D₀ : N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\} ⟶ Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{X₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, we shall verify equality \((\ast\ast\ast)\) after the remark
below.

\textbf{Remark 4.9.} \emph{The obstruction \(c(X, Y, f)\) is computed
locally on \(T\). Let \(U = \operatorname{Spec}(C)\) be an affine open
of \(T\) above an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) of \(X\),
itself above an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}(\Lambda)\) of \(S\);
let \(J \subset I \subset \Lambda\) (resp. \(I_{Y} \subset A\)) be the
ideals corresponding to \(J \subset I\) (resp. to \texttt{I\_Y}), let
\(B = A/I_{Y}\) and let \(\phi : A \to C\) be the morphism of
\(\Lambda\)-algebras corresponding to \(f : T \to X\); since
\(f(T_{J}) \subset Y_{J}\) one has \(\phi(I_{Y}) \subset JC\) and
therefore \(\phi\) induces a morphism of \(\Lambda\)-algebras
\(B \to C/JC \to C_{0} = C/IC\). Then the obstruction \(c = c(X, Y, f)\)
is computed by the following commutative diagram:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I\_Y ────────────► A ─────φ─────► C}
\NormalTok{                                  ↑}
\NormalTok{                                  │c}
\NormalTok{I\_Y/I\_Y² ──► I\_Y/I\_Y² ⊗\_B C₀ ────► JC,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{that is, it is defined, above the open \(U\), as the unique
element of}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{C₀\}(I\_Y/I\_Y² ⊗\_B C₀, JC) = Hom\_\{B₀\}(I\_Y/I\_Y² ⊗\_B B₀, JC)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that, with the evident notation, one has
\(c(x \otimes_{B} 1) = \phi(x)\), for every \(x \in I_{Y}\).}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added what follows.} One can now complete the
proof of 4.8 (iii). The equality \((\ast\ast\ast)\) is verified locally
on \(T\), so one is reduced to the affine situation described above. Let
us denote by \(d_{A/\Lambda}\) the differential
\(A \to \Omega^{1}_{A/\Lambda}\). Then \(a\) corresponds, above \(U\),
to an element \(a_{U}\) of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{C₀\}(Ω¹\_\{A₀/Λ₀\} ⊗\_\{A₀\} C₀, JC) ≃ Hom\_\{B₀\}(Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗\_A B₀, JC) ≃ Hom\_A(Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\}, JC).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, on the one hand, \(v_{f_{0}}(a)\) corresponds above \(U\) to the
element \(a_{U} \circ \bar{D}_{0}\), where \(\bar{D}_{0}\) is the
morphism of \(B\)-modules\footnote{N.D.E.: Cf. N.D.E. (93).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I\_Y/I\_Y² ⟶ Ω¹\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗\_A B₀,    x + I\_Y² ↦ d\_\{A/Λ\}(x) ⊗ 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand (cf.~the proofs of 0.1.8 and 0.1.9), the morphism of
\(\Lambda\)-algebras \(\phi' : A \to C\) corresponding to \(a \cdot f\)
differs from \(\phi\) by the \(\Lambda\)-derivation \(A \to JC\)
associated with \(a_{U}\), i.e. one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ′ = φ + a\_U ∘ d\_\{A/Λ\} = φ + a\_U ∘ (d\_\{A/Λ\} ⊗ 1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consequently, denoting \(c' = c(X, Y, a \cdot f)\), one has for every
\(x \in I_{Y}\), denoting by \(\bar{x}\) its image in
\(I_{Y}/I^{2}_{Y}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(c′ − c)(x̄ ⊗ 1) = a\_U(d\_\{A/Λ\}(x) ⊗ 1) = (a\_U ∘ D̄₀)(x̄) = v\_\{f₀\}(a)(x̄).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This shows that \(c' - c = v_{f_{0}}(a)\).

\textbf{4.10.} One has suppressed Remark 4.10 of the original, made
obsolete by the addition of Remark 4.8.0.

\textbf{4.11.} We now propose to study the following situation. Let
\(S, S_{J}\) and \(S_{0}\) be as in 4.8; one has three \(S\)-schemes
\(X, X', T\), a subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\) (resp. \(Y'\) of \(X'\)), and
morphisms \(f : T \to X'\) and \(g : X' \to X\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                  Y′         Y}
\NormalTok{                                  ⊂          ⊂}
\NormalTok{                                  ↓i′        ↓i}
\NormalTok{T ──────f────► X′ ──────g────► X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One supposes that by reduction modulo \(J\), this diagram completes into
a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                    Y\_J′ ──┄──► Y\_J}
\NormalTok{                                    ⊂            ⊂}
\NormalTok{                                  ↗ i\_J′         ↓i\_J}
\NormalTok{                                ↗}
\NormalTok{T\_J ──────f\_J────► X\_J′ ──────g\_J────► X\_J.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore by 4.8 obstructions:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c(X, Y, g ∘ i′) ∈ Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀′\}\}(i\_0′*g\_0*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_\{Y′\}),}
\NormalTok{c(X′, Y′, f) ∈ Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*(N\_\{Y′/X′\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y′\}\} O\_\{Y₀′\}), JO\_T),}
\NormalTok{c(X, Y, g ∘ f) ∈ Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*g₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_T),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whose relations one seeks to compute.\footnote{N.D.E.: From 4.17 on, we
  shall apply this to the case where \(X\) is an \(S\)-group,
  \(g : X \times_{S} X \to X\) the multiplication, \(Y\) a subscheme of
  \(X\) such that \texttt{Y\_J} is a subgroup of \texttt{X\_J},
  \(Y' = Y \times_{S} Y\), and to the two morphisms \(Y^{3} \to X^{2}\)
  which send \((y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3})\) to \((y_{1}y_{2}, y_{3})\), resp.
  \((y_{1}, y_{2}y_{3})\). In this case, the comparison of the above
  obstructions will show that the obstruction to \(Y\) being a subgroup
  of \(X\) resides in a certain cohomology group (Hochschild)
  \(H^{2}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\).}

\textbf{Lemma 4.12.} \emph{Suppose \(Y'\) flat over \(S\), so that
\(J \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{Y_{0}'} = JO_{Y'}\).}

\emph{(i) One has a natural morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{b\_\{f₀\} : Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀′\}\}(i\_0′*g\_0*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_\{Y′\}) ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*g₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) One has also a natural morphism, functorial in
\(T\),\footnote{N.D.E.: We have suppressed the hypothesis ``\(Y_{0}'\)
  locally complete intersection in \(X_{0}'\)'', superfluous by 4.8.0;
  on the other hand, we have added that \(a_{g_{0}}(f_{0})\) is
  ``functorial in \(T\)'', this playing a crucial role in the proof of
  4.17.}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a\_\{g₀\}(f₀) : Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*(N\_\{Y′/X′\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀′\}), JO\_T) ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*g₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed the proof, to make
  visible the ``functoriality in \(T\)'' of \(a_{g_{0}}\).} Let us first
note that, \(X, X', Y, Y'\) being fixed, to give a \(T\) as above is
equivalent to giving a morphism
\((f, f_{J}) : T \to X' \times_{X'^{+}} Y'^{+}\). Set
\(Z = X' \times_{X'^{+}} Y'^{+}\) and denote by \(M\) and \(M'\) the
\(Z\)-functors defined by: for every \(f : T \to Z\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M(T) = Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*g₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀\}), JO\_T)}
\NormalTok{M′(T) = Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*(N\_\{Y′/X′\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀′\}), JO\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: The situation will simplify from 4.16 on: one will
  restrict to schemes flat over \(S\), \(Y\) will be a flat \(S\)-group
  and \(Y' = Y \times_{S} Y\); one will then obtain \(S_{0}\)-functors
  \(N_{0}\) and \(N_{0}'\).}

One has in any case a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f₀*(J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀′\}) ──── J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\}}
\NormalTok{        │                              │}
\NormalTok{        ↓                              ↓}
\NormalTok{f₀*(JO\_\{Y′\})       ─┄┄┄┄─►          JO\_T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since \(Y'\) is flat over \(S\), the left arrow is an isomorphism,
hence one obtains a morphism of \(O_{T_{0}}\)-modules
\(f_{0}*(JO_{Y'}) \to JO_{T}\). The latter induces a morphism of abelian
groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*g₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀\}), f₀*(JO\_\{Y′\})) ⟶ M(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and, composing with the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M(Y′) ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*g₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀\}), f₀*(JO\_\{Y′\})),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induced by \(f_{0}*\), one obtains the morphism
\(b_{f_{0}} : M(Y') \to M(T)\).

Likewise, one has in any case a diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_0*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}) ─┄┄┄┄┄─► N\_\{Y′/X′\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y′\}\} O\_\{Y₀′\}}
\NormalTok{              │                                    │}
\NormalTok{              ↓                                    ↓}
\NormalTok{g\_0*(N\_\{Y₀/X₀\})  ────────────────────► N\_\{Y₀′/X₀′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since \(Y'\) is flat over \(S\), the second vertical arrow is an
isomorphism by 4.8.0. One thus obtains an \(O_{Y_{0}'}\)-morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i\_0′*g\_0*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\}) ⟶ N\_\{Y′/X′\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y′\}\} O\_\{Y₀′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which induces a morphism \(a_{g_{0}}(id_{Y'}) : M'(Y') \to M(Y')\) and,
for every \(f : T \to Z\), a morphism \(a_{g_{0}}(f) : M'(T) \to M(T)\)
such that one has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M′(Y′) ──\{a\_\{g₀\}(id\_\{Y₀′\})\}──► M(Y′)}
\NormalTok{  │                              │}
\NormalTok{  b′\_\{f₀\}                        b\_\{f₀\}}
\NormalTok{  ↓                              ↓}
\NormalTok{M′(T)  ──\{a\_\{g₀\}(f₀)\}──────► M(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(where \(b'_{f_{0}}\) is defined like \(b_{f_{0}}\)). QED.

\textbf{Remark 4.12.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this remark, used
  in the proof of 4.17.} \emph{Denote by \(M_{0}\) and \(M_{0}'\) the
\(Y_{0}'\)-functors defined by: for every \(f : T_{0} \to Y_{0}'\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M₀(T) = Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*g₀*(N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀\}), J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\})}
\NormalTok{M₀′(T) = Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(f₀*(N\_\{Y′/X′\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀′\}), J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Note immediately that \(Z_{0} = Y_{0}'\) and that on the category
of \(Z\)-schemes \(T\) which are flat over \(S\), \(M\) and \(M'\)
coincide, respectively, with the functors \(\prod_{S_{0}/S} M_{0}\) and
\(\prod_{S_{0}/S} M_{0}'\). In this case, \(b_{f_{0}}\) is simply the
morphism}

\[
f_{0}* : M_{0}(Y_{0}') \longrightarrow M(T_{0})
\]

\emph{induced by \(f_{0}\), and for every morphism \(u : U \to T\),
setting \(h = f \circ u\), one has a commutative diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M₀′(T₀) ──\{a\_\{g₀\}(f₀)\}──► M₀(T₀)}
\NormalTok{   │                          │}
\NormalTok{   u₀*                        u₀*}
\NormalTok{   ↓                          ↓}
\NormalTok{M₀′(U₀) ──\{a\_\{g₀\}(h₀)\}──► M₀(U₀)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{i.e.~\(a_{g_{0}}\) becomes a morphism of functors
\(\prod_{S_{0}/S} M_{0}' \to \prod_{S_{0}/S} M_{0}\).}

\textbf{Proposition 4.13.} \emph{Suppose \(Y'\) flat over \(S\). One has
then the formula:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c(X, Y, g ∘ f) = a\_\{g₀\}(c(X′, Y′, f)) + b\_\{f₀\}(c(X, Y, g ∘ i′)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since the definition of the different obstructions and of the morphisms
\(a_{g_{0}}\) and \(b_{f_{0}}\) is local, one easily sees that it
suffices to verify the given formula when the different schemes in play
are affine. Let us thus denote \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(\Lambda)\),
\(S_{J} = \operatorname{Spec}(\Lambda/J)\),
\(S_{0} = \operatorname{Spec}(\Lambda/I)\),
\(T = \operatorname{Spec}(C)\), \(X = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\),
\(Y = \operatorname{Spec}(A/I_{Y}) = \operatorname{Spec}(B)\),
\(X' = \operatorname{Spec}(A')\),
\(Y' = \operatorname{Spec}(A'/I_{Y'}) = \operatorname{Spec}(B')\).

One has therefore a diagram of rings and ideals\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  kept the notation of the original, denoting \(f : A' \to C\) and
  \(g : A \to A'\) the morphisms of rings corresponding to
  \(f : T \to X'\) and \(g : X' \to X\). This explains the formula
  \(c(X, Y, g \circ f)(\bar{x} \otimes 1) = f(g(x))\), for
  \(x \in I_{Y}\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                B′         B}
\NormalTok{                                ↑          ↑}
\NormalTok{                                π′         π}
\NormalTok{                                │          │}
\NormalTok{                C ◄──f── A′ ◄──g── A}
\NormalTok{                                ↑          ↑}
\NormalTok{                                │          │}
\NormalTok{                            I\_\{Y′\}      I\_Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us study the different terms of the formula to be proved. In what
follows, if \(x \in I_{Y}\) (resp. \(u \in I_{Y'}\)), we denote by
\(\bar{x}\) (resp. \texttt{ū}) its image in \(I_{Y}/I^{2}_{Y}\) (resp.
\(I_{Y'}/I^{2}_{Y'}\)); on the other hand, if \(m\) belongs to a
\(\Lambda\)-module \(M\), we denote by \(\bar{m}_{0}\) its image in
\(M_{0} = M/IM\).

One has seen that \(c = c(X, Y, g \circ f)\) is the unique
\(C_{0}\)-morphism \(I_{Y}/I^{2}_{Y} \otimes_{B} C_{0} \to JC\) such
that \(c(\bar{x} \otimes 1) = f(g(x))\), for every \(x \in I_{Y}\).

Fix \(x \in I_{Y}\); one has \(g(x) \in I_{Y'} + JA'\) since
\(g_{J}(Y_{J}') \subset Y_{J}\). Write
\(g(x) = x' + \Sigma \lambda_{i} a'_{i}\), with \(x' \in I_{Y'}\),
\(\lambda_{i} \in J\), \(a'_{i} \in A'\). One therefore has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    c(X, Y, g ∘ f)(x̄ ⊗ 1) = f(g(x)) = f(x′) + Σ λᵢ f(a′ᵢ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now consider \(a_{g_{0}}(c(X', Y', f))\). According to the definitions
laid down, it is defined by the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                       f}
\NormalTok{                          I\_\{Y′\} ─────────────► C}
\NormalTok{                                                ↑}
\NormalTok{                                                │c(X′,Y′,f)}
\NormalTok{                                  ≃            │}
\NormalTok{I\_\{Y₀′\}/I\_\{Y₀′\}² ⊗\_\{B₀′\} C₀ ◄── I\_\{Y′\}/I\_\{Y′\}² ⊗\_\{B′\} C₀ ────► JC}
\NormalTok{        ↑                                                ↗}
\NormalTok{        │g₀                                            ↗}
\NormalTok{        │                                            ↗ a\_\{g₀\}(c(X′,Y′,f))}
\NormalTok{I\_\{Y₀\}/I\_\{Y₀\}² ⊗\_\{B₀\} C₀ ◄── I\_Y/I\_Y² ⊗\_B C₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore \(a_{g_{0}}(c(X', Y', f))(\bar{x} \otimes 1) = f(u)\),
where \(u\) is an element of \(I_{Y'}\) whose image \texttt{ū} in
\(I_{Y_{0}'}/I^{2}_{Y_{0}'}\) satisfies
\(\bar{u}_{0} \otimes 1 = \bar{g}_{0}(\bar{x}_{0}) \otimes 1 = \bar{g}_{0}(\bar{x}_{0}) \otimes 1\).
One can therefore take \(u = x'\) and one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)    a\_\{g₀\}(c(X′, Y′, f))(x̄ ⊗ 1) = f(x′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consider finally \(b_{f_{0}}(c(X, Y, g \circ i'))\). By hypothesis, the
morphism of \(\Lambda_{0}\)-algebras \(f_{0} : A_{0}' \to C_{0}\)
factors through \(B_{0}'\), and therefore, since
\(J \otimes_{\Lambda_{0}} B_{0}' \xrightarrow{\sim} JB'\) (\(B'\) being
flat over \(\Lambda\)), one obtains a morphism of \(B_{0}'\)-modules
\(\psi : JB' \to JC\) such that one has a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{J ⊗\_\{Λ₀\} A₀′ ──\{id⊗π′\}──► J ⊗\_\{Λ₀\} B₀′ ──\{id⊗f₀\}──► J ⊗\_\{Λ₀\} C₀}
\NormalTok{       │                          │ ≀}
\NormalTok{       ↓                          ↓}
\NormalTok{   JA′  ──────π′──────►       JB′ ──ψ─►       JC.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Denote \(\phi : JB' \otimes_{B_{0}'} C_{0} \to JC\) the morphism of
\(C_{0}\)-modules deduced from \(\psi\); then one has, for every
\(a' \in A'\), \(\lambda \in J\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)    φ(λπ′(a′) ⊗ 1) = λf(a′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, \(b_{f_{0}}(c(X, Y, g \circ i'))\) is defined by the commutative
diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              π′ ∘ g}
\NormalTok{              I\_Y  ──────────────────────► B′}
\NormalTok{                                            ↑}
\NormalTok{                                            │c(X,Y,g∘i′)}
\NormalTok{                                            │}
\NormalTok{              I\_Y/I\_Y² ⊗\_B B₀′ ────────► JB′}
\NormalTok{                          │                    │}
\NormalTok{                          ↓                    ↓}
\NormalTok{              I\_Y/I\_Y² ⊗\_B C₀ ────────► JB′ ⊗\_\{B₀′\} C₀}
\NormalTok{                              ↘                      ↘ φ}
\NormalTok{                                ↘                      ↘}
\NormalTok{                                  ↘ b\_\{f₀\}(c(X,Y,g∘i′))   ↘}
\NormalTok{                                    ↘                       ↘}
\NormalTok{                                                               JC.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)    b\_\{f₀\}(c(X, Y, g ∘ i′))(x̄ ⊗ 1) = φ(Σ λᵢ π′(a′ᵢ) ⊗ 1) = Σ λᵢ f(a′ᵢ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the last equality following from \texttt{(†)} above. The comparison of
the three explicit results (1), (2), (3) gives the formula sought.

\textbf{Corollary 4.14.} \emph{Let \(Y, Y'\) be two flat subschemes of
\(X\), reducing to \texttt{Y\_J}; suppose \(Y_{0}\) locally complete
intersection in \(X_{0}\). If \(f : T \to X\) is an \(S\)-morphism such
that \(f_{J}\) factors through \(Y_{J} \to X_{J}\), one has the formula}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c(X, Y, f) − c(X, Y′, f) = b\_\{f₀\}(d(Y, Y′)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, applying the preceding formula to the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                 Y′           Y}
\NormalTok{                                 ⊂            ⊂}
\NormalTok{                                 ↓i′          ↓i}
\NormalTok{                       T ─f──► X ──id──► X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one finds \(c(X, Y, f) - c(X, Y', f) = b_{f_{0}}(c(X, Y, i'))\).
Moreover, by 4.8 (ii), one has \(c(X, Y, i') = d(Y, Y')\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.15.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-group smooth over
\(S\) and \(Y\) a sub-\(S\)-group flat and locally of finite
presentation over \(S\). Then \(Y\) is locally complete intersection
(cf.~4.6.2) in \(X\).}

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added in the statement the
  hypothesis that \(Y\) be locally of finite presentation over \(S\),
  and have given the following proof, more direct than the one sketched
  in the original. To be complete, let us also detail the latter. As in
  the proof given above, one reduces first to the case where
  \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(k\) being an algebraically closed
  field. By EGA IV₄, 16.9.10 and 19.3.2, it suffices to see that, for
  every \(y \in Y\), the completion of the local ring \(O_{Y,y}\) is the
  quotient of a complete noetherian local ring by a regular sequence. By
  loc. cit., 19.3.3, the set of \(y \in Y\) satisfying this property is
  an open \(U\) of \(Y\); since \(Y\) is of finite type over \(k\), it
  suffices to show that \(U\) contains every closed point. Since \(Y\)
  is a \(k\)-group it suffices, by a translation argument, to show that
  the property is true for the completion of \(O_{Y,e}\), that is, for
  the ``formal group'' \texttt{Ŷ} corresponding to \(Y\) (cf.~Exp.
  VII\_B). Now, since \(X\) is smooth, the affine algebra \(A(\hat{X})\)
  is an algebra of formal power series \(k[[X_{1}, ..., X_{n}]]\), and
  one concludes with the help of the Dieudonné structure theorem which
  shows that \(A(\hat{Y})\) is isomorphic to a quotient
  \(k[[X_{1}, ..., X_{r+s}]]/(X^{p^{n_{1}}}_{1}, ..., X^{p^{n_{r}}}_{r})\),
  where \(p\) is the characteristic exponent of \(k\) and
  \(r + s \leq n\), cf.~VII\_B, Remark 5.5.2 (b).} We shall show that
the immersion \(Y \to X\) is regular in the sense of EGA IV₄, 16.9.2,
which implies that it is also regular in the sense of 4.6.2, by EGA IV₄,
19.5.1 (moreover, by loc. cit., the two definitions are equivalent if
\(S\) is locally noetherian). Therefore, in what follows, we take
``regular immersion'' in the sense of EGA IV₄, 16.9.2. Since \(X\) and
\(Y\) are flat and locally of finite presentation over \(S\), then, by
EGA IV₄, 19.2.4, it suffices to show that, for every \(s \in S\),
\(Y_{s} \to X_{s}\) is a regular immersion. By EGA IV₄, 19.1.5 (ii), one
is reduced to verifying the assertion on the geometric fibers of \(S\),
that is, when \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field
\(k\).

Then, by VI\_A, 3.2, the quotient \(X/Y\) exists and is smooth, the
morphism \(\pi : X \to X/Y\) is flat, and one has a cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y ──f──► X}
\NormalTok{│        │}
\NormalTok{i        π}
\NormalTok{↓        ↓}
\NormalTok{e ────► X/Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(where \(e\) is the image in \(X/Y\) of the unit point of \(X\)).
Therefore, by flat base change (cf.~EGA IV₄, 19.1.5 (ii)), it suffices
to see that \(i\) is a regular immersion, which is immediate since the
noetherian local ring \(O_{X/Y, e}\) is smooth, hence its maximal ideal
is generated by a regular sequence.

\textbf{4.16.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have reorganized 4.16 by regrouping
  there, on the one hand, the hypotheses stated at the end of 4.15 and,
  on the other hand, the definition of the obstruction \texttt{DY}.} Let
\(X\) be an \(S\)-group smooth over \(S\), denote
\(\mu : X \times_{S} X \to X\) its group law. Suppose given a
sub-\texttt{S\_J}-group \texttt{Y\_J} of \texttt{X\_J}, flat and locally
of finite presentation over \texttt{S\_J}. By 4.15, \texttt{Y\_J} is
locally complete intersection in \(X\).

Hence, by 4.6.5, every flat \(S\)-scheme\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  corrected the original by adding ``flat''.} \(Y\) lifting
\texttt{Y\_J} is locally complete intersection in \(X\). For such a
\(Y\) one has, by 4.8.0,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4.16.1)    N\_\{Y/X\} ⊗\_\{O\_Y\} O\_\{Y₀\} = N\_\{Y₀/X₀\} = N\_\{Y\_J/X\_J\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{Y\_J\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, denote by \(\epsilon_{0} : S_{0} \to Y_{0}\) the unit
section of \(Y_{0}\) and \(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\) the quasi-coherent
\(O_{S_{0}}\)-module:

\[
n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} = \epsilon_{0}*(N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}).
\]

Since \(Y_{0}\) and \(X_{0}\) are \(S_{0}\)-groups, one sees easily that
\(N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\) is invariant under the (say left) translations of
\(Y_{0}\), hence\footnote{N.D.E.: See 4.25 further on.} is the inverse
image by \(Y_{0} \to S_{0}\) of \(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\), i.e.~one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4.16.2)    N\_\{Y₀/X₀\} = n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Taking (4.16.1) and (4.16.2) into account, one deduces on the one hand
from 4.5 that the set of sub-\(S\)-schemes \(Y\) of \(X\), flat over
\(S\), lifting \texttt{Y\_J}, is empty or principal homogeneous under

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4.16.3)    Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀\}\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one deduces on the other hand from 4.8 (i) that, for every such
\(Y\) and every \(S\)-morphism \(f : T \to X\) such that
\(f_{J} : T_{J} \to X_{J}\) factors through \texttt{Y\_J}, the
obstruction \(c(X, Y, f)\) to \(f\) factoring through \(Y\) is an
element of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\}, JO\_T);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

if moreover \(T\) is flat over \(S\), this last group equals

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_\{T₀\}\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\}, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_\{T₀\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This leads to introducing the group functor \(N_{0}\) below:

\textbf{Definition 4.16.1.} \emph{Let \(N_{0}\) be the \(S_{0}\)-functor
in commutative groups defined by: for every \(Z \in Ob (Sch)/S_{0}\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    Hom\_\{S₀\}(Z, N₀) = Hom\_\{O\_Z\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_Z, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_Z).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then, the set of sub-\(S\)-schemes \(Y\) of \(X\), flat over
\(S\), lifting \texttt{Y\_J}, is empty or principal homogeneous under}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(Y₀, N₀) = C¹(Y₀, N₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{For each such \(Y\), consider the following diagram:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                Y ×\_S Y          Y}
\NormalTok{                  ⊂              ⊂}
\NormalTok{                (i,i)            i}
\NormalTok{                  ↓     μ        ↓}
\NormalTok{                X ×\_S X ────► X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and denote \(DY = c(X, Y, \mu \circ (i, i))\) the obstruction to
\(\mu \circ (i, i)\) factoring through \(Y\), i.e.~to \(Y\) being stable
under the group law of \(X\); by what precedes, \texttt{DY} is an
element of}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N₀(Y₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀) = C²(Y₀, N₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 4.17.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have modified 4.17 and 4.18
  taking into account the additions made in 4.16.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an
\(S\)-group smooth over \(S\) and \texttt{Y\_J} a
sub-\texttt{S\_J}-group of \texttt{X\_J}, flat and locally of finite
presentation over \texttt{S\_J}. For each subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\), flat
over \(S\) and lifting \texttt{Y\_J}, consider the obstruction defined
in 4.16.1:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{DY ∈ Hom\_\{S₀\}(Y₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀, N₀) = C²(Y₀, N₀)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) For \(Y\) to be a sub-\(S\)-group of \(X\), it is necessary
and sufficient that \(DY = 0\).}

\emph{(ii) If one makes \(Y_{0}\) act on \(N_{0}\) by functoriality from
the inner automorphisms of \(Y_{0}\), then
\(DY \in Z^{2}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\).}

\emph{(iii) If \(Y\) and \(Y'\) are two subschemes of \(X\), flat over
\(S\), lifting \texttt{Y\_J} (so that the deviation
\(d(Y, Y') \in C^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) is defined, cf.~4.5.1), one has
\(DY' - DY = \partial^{1}d(Y, Y')\).\footnote{N.D.E.: In the original,
  one finds \(DY' - DY = -\partial d(Y, Y')\), but their \(\partial\) is
  the opposite of the differential \(\partial^{1}\) defined in I, 5.1.}}

Let us successively prove these various assertions.

\textbf{4.18.} \emph{Proof of 4.17 (i).} By definition, one has
\(DY = 0\) if and only if \(Y\) is stable under the group law of \(X\).
Hence \(DY = 0\) if \(Y\) is a subgroup of \(X\). Conversely, if
\(DY = 0\), \(Y\) is equipped with the induced law \(\mu_{Y}\), which is
associative and reduces modulo \(J\) to the group law on \texttt{X\_J};
since \(Y\) is flat and locally of finite presentation over \(S\), it
follows from 3.3 that \(\mu_{Y}\) is a group law.

\textbf{4.19.} \emph{Proof of 4.17 (ii).} This is done by comparing the
two values of \(u = c(X, Y, \mu^{2} \circ (i, i, i))\) computed in the
two following diagrams \((D_{j})\), \(j = 1, 2\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                Y ×\_S Y ×\_S Y     Y ×\_S Y     Y}
\NormalTok{                       ⊂              ⊂        ⊂}
\NormalTok{(D\_j)              (i,i,i)        (i,i)         i}
\NormalTok{                       │  f\_j           μ        ↓}
\NormalTok{                       ↓                ↓        │}
\NormalTok{                X ×\_S X ×\_S X ────► X ×\_S X ──► X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(f_{1} = (1, \pi)\), \(f_{2} = (\pi, 1)\), and where one denotes
by \(\mu^{2}\) the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{μ ∘ f₁ = μ ∘ f₂ : X ×\_S X ×\_S X ⟶ X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have slightly modified the notations, and detailed
  the beginning of the argument.}

Set \(\mu_{Y} = \mu \circ (i, i)\), \(f_{j,Y} = f_{j} \circ (i, i, i)\)
and \(\mu_{2,Y} = \mu^{2} \circ (i, i, i)\). For \(j = 1, 2\), denote by
\(a_{j}\) and \(b_{j}\) the morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a\_j = a\_\{μ₀\}((f\_\{j,Y\})₀)    and    b\_j = b\_\{(f\_\{j,Y\})₀\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

associated with the pair of morphisms \((f_{j,Y}, \mu)\) by Lemma 4.12;
one has therefore:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)   Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀³\}\}((f\_\{j,Y\})₀*(N\_\{Y₀×Y₀/X₀×X₀\}), JO\_\{Y₀³\}) ──\{a\_j\}──► Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀³\}\}((μ\_\{2,Y\})₀*(N\_\{Y₀/X₀\}), JO\_\{Y₀³\})}

\NormalTok{      Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀²\}\}((μ\_Y)₀*(N\_\{Y₀/X₀\}), JO\_\{Y₀²\}) ──\{b\_j\}──► Hom\_\{O\_\{Y₀³\}\}((μ\_\{2,Y\})₀*(N\_\{Y₀/X₀\}), JO\_\{Y₀³\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since
\(N_{Y_{0}\times Y_{0}/X_{0}\times X_{0}} \simeq pr_{1}* N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \oplus pr_{2}* N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\)
(since \(X_{0}\) and \(Y_{0}\) are flat over \(S_{0}\)), and
\(N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \simeq n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{Y_{0}}\),
then:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(f\_\{j,Y\})₀*(N\_\{Y₀×Y₀/X₀×X₀\}) ≃ (n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊕ n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}) ⊗ O\_\{Y₀³\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and, likewise,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(μ\_\{2,Y\})₀*(N\_\{Y₀/X₀\}) ≃ n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀³\}    and    (μ\_Y)₀*(N\_\{Y₀/X₀\}) ≃ n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀²\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, since \(Y^{2}_{0}\) and \(Y^{3}_{0}\) are flat over \(S_{0}\),
then \texttt{(†)} rewrites in the following form:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(‡)  ⎧ a\_j : Hom\_\{S₀\}(Y₀³, N₀ ⊕ N₀) → Hom\_\{S₀\}(Y₀³, N₀)}
\NormalTok{     ⎩ b\_j : Hom\_\{S₀\}(Y₀², N₀) → Hom\_\{S₀\}(Y₀³, N₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Applying 4.13 twice to \(c(X, Y, \mu_{2,Y}) = u\), one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a₁(c(X², Y², f₁)) + b₁(c(X, Y, μ\_Y)) = u = a₂(c(X², Y², f₂)) + b₂(c(X, Y, μ\_Y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, \(c(X, Y, \mu_{Y}) = DY\) and, since \(f_{1} = (1, \mu)\) and
\(f_{2} = (\mu, 1)\), one has, with evident notations:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c(X², Y², f₁) = (0, DY)    and    c(X², Y², f₂) = (DY, 0).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Hence, one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u = a₁((0, DY)) + b₁(DY) = a₂((DY, 0)) + b₂(DY).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The first thing one notes is that \(b_{j}\) is nothing other than
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S_{0}}((f_{j,Y})_{0}, N_{0})\), that is to say,
the morphism deduced from \((f_{j,Y})_{0}\) by functoriality.

The identity above therefore becomes:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a₁((0, DY)) − Hom((μ, 1), N₀)(DY) + Hom((1, μ), N₀)(DY) − a₂((DY, 0)) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One recognizes the two middle terms: they are the parts
``\(DY(xy, z)\)'' and ``\(DY(x, yz)\)'' of the 2-coboundary formula. It
only remains, then, to identify the two other terms.

We must first compute the map \(a_{j}\). Now it comes, by inverse image
by \((f_{j,Y})_{0}\), from the morphism of \(O_{Y^{2}_{0}}\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P : n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗ O\_\{Y₀²\} ⟶ (n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊕ n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}) ⊗ O\_\{Y₀²\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induced by the product in \(Y_{0}\). Now this morphism is described in
the following way: consider the vector bundle
\(V = V(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}})\); \(P\) gives by duality a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V(P) : V ×\_\{S₀\} V ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀ ⟶ V ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀ ×\_\{S₀\} Y₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is expressed set-theoretically by\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  replaced \texttt{a,\ b} by \texttt{ab,\ b} to make visible that
  \(V(P)\) comes by inverse image on \(Y^{2}_{0}\) from the
  multiplication morphism
  \(V_{Y_{0}} \times_{S_{0}} V_{Y_{0}} \to V_{Y_{0}}\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V(P)(u, v, a, b) = (u + Ad(a)v, ab, b).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is proved exactly like the corresponding fact on Lie algebras, that
is, on the module \(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\). One first notes that
\(V\) is endowed by functoriality in \(Y_{0}\) with a group structure in
the category of vector bundles on \(S_{0}\); by virtue of the lemma
already used for Lie algebras (Exposé II, 3.10), this structure
coincides with the group structure underlying its \texttt{O\_S}-module
structure. One then sees that
\(V(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{Y_{0}}) = V(N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}})\)
is also endowed with a structure of \(S_{0}\)-group which is none other
than the semi-direct product of that of \(V\) by that of \(Y_{0}\). It
only remains to identify the operations of \(Y_{0}\) on \(V\) to
establish the desired formula.

Let us now compute the two remaining terms. Consider first
\(a_{1}((0, DY))\). One computes it by the diagram (where \(n\) denotes
\(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n ⊗ O\_\{Y₀²\} ──P──► (n + n) ⊗ O\_\{Y₀²\}}
\NormalTok{    │                      │}
\NormalTok{    (f₁,Y)₀*               (f₁,Y)₀*}
\NormalTok{    ↓                      ↓}
\NormalTok{n ⊗ O\_\{Y₀³\}        (n + n) ⊗ O\_\{Y₀³\}}
\NormalTok{       ↘                     │}
\NormalTok{         ↘                   (0, DY)}
\NormalTok{           ↘ a₁((0,DY))      ↓}
\NormalTok{             ↘             J ⊗ O\_\{Y₀³\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Considering now the vector bundles defined by these different modules as
so many schemes over \(S_{0}\) and taking points with values in
anything, one has, denoting \((u, x, y, z)\) a point of
\(V(J) \times Y^{3}_{0}\);

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Ad(x)DY\_\{y,z\}(u), x, yz) ◄──────── (0 + DY\_\{y,z\}(u), x, yz)}
\NormalTok{              ↑                                  ↑}
\NormalTok{              │                                  │}
\NormalTok{              │                            (0 + DY\_\{y,z\}(u), x, y, z)}
\NormalTok{              │                                  ↑}
\NormalTok{              │                                  │}
\NormalTok{(Ad(x)DY\_\{y,z\}(u), x, y, z) ◄──────── (u, x, y, z).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has thus obtained \(a_{1}((0, DY))(x, y, z) = Ad(x)DY(y, z)\), which
is indeed the first term of the coboundary. One would have likewise
\(a_{2}((DY, 0))(x, y, z) = DY(x, y)\), whence\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  changed the signs to make them compatible with I 5.1.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 = Ad(x)DY(y, z) − DY(xy, z) + DY(x, yz) − DY(x, y) = (∂²DY)(x, y, z).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{4.20.} \emph{Proof of 4.17 (iii).}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  detailed the original in what follows.} This is done by comparing the
two values of \(v = c(X, Y, \mu \circ (i', i'))\) computed in the two
following diagrams

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                      Y′       Y}
\NormalTok{                                       ⊂        ⊂}
\NormalTok{(∗)                                    i′       i}
\NormalTok{                                       │  μ∘(i′,i′)    │}
\NormalTok{            Y′ ×\_S Y′ ────────────────► X       X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                      Y ×\_S Y    Y}
\NormalTok{                                          ⊂        ⊂}
\NormalTok{(†)                                    (i,i)       i}
\NormalTok{                          (i′,i′)         μ        ↓}
\NormalTok{            Y′ ×\_S Y′ ──────────► X ×\_S X ──────► X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Denote \(f = \mu \circ (i', i')\); then \((\ast)\) gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    v = DY′ + f₀*(c(X, Y, i′)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now \(Y_{0}' = Y_{0}\) and \(f_{0}\) is the multiplication
\(Y^{2}_{0} \to Y_{0}\); one deduces from this that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)    f₀*(c(X, Y, i′))(x₀, y₀) = c(X, Y, i′)(x₀y₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set \(c = c(X, Y, i')\); via the identification
\(N_{0}' \simeq N_{0} \oplus N_{0}\),
\(c(X \times_{S} X, Y \times_{S} Y, (i', i'))\) identifies with the pair
\((c, c)\). Then, denoting \(h = (i', i')\), \texttt{(†)} gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)    v = h₀*(DY) + a\_\{μ₀\}(c, c).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now \(h_{0}\) is the identity map of \(Y^{2}_{0}\), whence
\(h_{0}*(DY) = DY\). Finally, by the computation of \(a_{\mu_{0}}\) done
previously, one has for every \(S' \to S\) and
\(x_{0}, y_{0} \in Y_{0}(S_{0}')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4)    a\_\{μ₀\}(c, c)(x₀, y₀) = c(x₀) + Ad(x₀)(c(y₀)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One thus obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(DY′ − DY)(x₀, y₀) = Ad(x₀)c(X, Y, i′)(y₀) − c(X, Y, i′)(x₀y₀) + c(X, Y, i′)(x₀)}
\NormalTok{                    = (∂¹c(X, Y, i′))(x₀, y₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(c(X, Y, i') = d(Y, Y')\) (cf.~4.8 (ii)), this shows that
\(DY' - DY = \partial^{1}d(Y, Y')\).

\textbf{Theorem 4.21.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(I\) and \(J\) two
ideals\footnote{N.D.E.: We have suppressed the hypothesis that \(I\) be
  nilpotent, which appears superfluous.} on \(S\) such that
\(I \supset J\) and \(I \cdot J = 0\). Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-group
smooth over \(S\) and \texttt{Y\_J} a sub-\texttt{S\_J}-group of
\texttt{X\_J}, flat and locally of finite presentation over
\texttt{S\_J}. Consider the \(S_{0}\)-functor in commutative groups
\(N_{0}\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, N₀) = Hom\_\{O\_T\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T),    T ∈ Ob (Sch)/S₀,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{on which \(Y_{0}\) acts via the inner automorphisms of \(X_{0}\).}

\emph{(i) For there to exist a sub-\(S\)-group of \(X\), flat over
\(S\), which reduces to \texttt{Y\_J}, it is necessary and sufficient
that the two following conditions be verified:}

\emph{(i₁) There exists a subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\), flat over \(S\),
lifting \texttt{Y\_J} (condition automatically satisfied if \(Y_{0}\) is
affine, cf.~4.6.5).}

\emph{(i₂) A certain canonical obstruction, element of
\(H^{2}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\), is zero.}

\emph{(ii) If the conditions of (i) are satisfied, the set of
sub-\(S\)-groups \(Y\) of \(X\), flat over \(S\) and reducing to
\texttt{Y\_J} is a principal homogeneous set under the group
\(Z^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\).\footnote{N.D.E.: The question of whether the
  preceding set, modulo conjugation by the \(x \in X(S)\) inducing the
  unit of \(X(S_{J})\), is principal homogeneous under
  \(H^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\), occupies n°s 4.23 to 4.36.}}

Indeed, condition (i₁) is necessary. Suppose it satisfied and let \(Y\)
be flat over \(S\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J}. We must seek a \(Y'\) flat
over \(S\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J} as well such that
\(DY' = 0\),\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected \(\partial DY'\) to
  \(DY'\).} cf.~4.17 (i). By 4.17 (iii), this amounts to seeking a
\(d(Y', Y) \in C^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) such that
\(DY = \partial^{1}d(Y', Y)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: Cf. N.D.E. (110).}

Let \(c \in H^{2}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) be the image class of \texttt{DY},
which is a cocycle by 4.17 (ii). It does not depend on the choice of
\(Y\) by 4.17 (iii), and its vanishing is necessary and sufficient for
the existence of a \(d(Y', Y)\) satisfying the preceding equation. This
proves (i).

If one has now chosen \(Y\) such that \(DY = 0\), the equation to solve
becomes \(\partial^{1}d(Y', Y) = 0\), which proves (ii).

\textbf{Remark 4.22.} \emph{Let us keep the notation of 4.21. By 4.15,
\(Y_{0}\) is locally complete intersection in \(X_{0}\), hence
\(N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\) is a finite locally free \(O_{Y_{0}}\)-module, and
consequently \(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} = \epsilon_{0}*(N_{Y_{0}/X_{0}})\) is a
finite locally free \(O_{S_{0}}\)-module. Hence, denoting
\(n^{\vee}_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} = \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{Y_{0}}}(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}, O_{Y_{0}})\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_T\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T) ≃ n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}\^{}∨ ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(T \to S_{0}\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed what
  precedes; this shows that the following isomorphism is valid without
  flatness hypothesis; on the other hand, since 4.16, we have restricted
  ourselves to \(S\)-schemes \(f : T \to S\) flat over \(S\) to ensure
  that the group
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{T}}(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{T_{0}}, JO_{T})\),
  in which the obstruction \(c(X, Y, f)\) resides, coincides with
  \(N_{0}(T_{0})\) (cf.~the end of 4.16).} Consequently, the
\(S_{0}\)-functor \(N_{0}\) is isomorphic to the functor}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}\^{}∨ ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J) ≃ W(Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}, J)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{It results in isomorphisms:\footnote{N.D.E.: With the notation of
  I 5.3, assuming \(Y_{0}\) affine over \(S_{0}\).}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H²(Y₀, N₀) ≃ H²(Y₀, Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}, J)) ≃ H²(Y₀, n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}\^{}∨ ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J),}
\NormalTok{Z¹(Y₀, N₀) ≃ Z¹(Y₀, Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}, J)) ≃ Z¹(Y₀, n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}\^{}∨ ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{4.23.} Still under the hypotheses of 4.21, we are now going to
study how the set of \(Y\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J} behaves with respect to
conjugation by sections of \(X\). If \(x\) is a section of \(X\) over
\(S\) inducing the unit section of \texttt{X\_J}, the inner automorphism
\(Int(x)\) defined by \(x\) transforms flat subgroups of \(X\) lifting
\texttt{Y\_J} into flat subgroups of \(X\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J}. Now,
under the conditions of 4.21 (ii), the set of these subgroups is
principal homogeneous under \(Z^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\); we shall see that
there then exists a subgroup \(\Gamma\) of
\(B^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced
  \(Z^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) by \(B^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\), since the proof
  shows that \(\Gamma\) is a subgroup of \(B^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\),
  cf.~4.27--4.29.} such that two subgroups of \(X\), flat over \(S\),
and lifting \texttt{Y\_J}, are conjugate (by \(x \in X(S)\) inducing the
unit of \(X(S_{J})\)) if and only if their ``difference'' in
\(Z^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) is an element of \(\Gamma\). In the best cases,
we shall show that \(\Gamma\) equals \(B^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\), hence that
the set of flat subgroups of \(X\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J}, modulo
conjugation by \(x \in X(S)\) inducing the unit of \(X(S_{J})\), is
empty or principal homogeneous under \(H^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) (cf.~4.29
and 4.36).

\textbf{4.24.} We keep the notation of 4.21. Let \(Y\) be a flat
subgroup of \(X\), reducing to \texttt{Y\_J}. Recall that we introduced
in 0.5 the functor \(L^{X}_{0}\) (resp. \(L^{Y}_{0}\)) defined by the
identity with respect to the variable \(S_{0}\)-scheme \(T\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L₀\^{}X) = Hom\_\{O\_T\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T, J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} O\_T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(resp. similarly on replacing \(X\) by \(Y\)), as well as the functor
\(L'_{X} = \prod_{S_{0}/S} L^{X}_{0}\).

Now one has:

\textbf{Lemma 4.25.} \emph{There exists a canonical exact sequence of
\(Y_{0}\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    n\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ──d──► ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ──► ω¹\_\{Y₀/S₀\} ──► 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{possessing the following properties:}

\emph{(i) By inverse image on \(Y_{0}\), \(d\) gives the morphism
\(\bar{D}_{0}\) of 4.8 (iii).}

\emph{(ii) If \(X_{0}\) and \(Y_{0}\) are smooth over \(S_{0}\), then
\(d\) is injective. Since the two \(\omega^{1}\) are then locally free
of finite type, so is \(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\) and the sequence is locally
split.}

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed the proof, taking into
  account the additions made in Exp. I, § 6.8.} Denote by \(\pi_{0}\)
the morphism \(Y_{0} \to S_{0}\). By SGA 1 II, formula (4.3) (see also
EGA IV₄, 16.4.21), one has a canonical exact sequence of
\(O_{Y_{0}}\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)    N\_\{Y₀/X₀\} ──D̄₀──► Ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ⊗\_\{O\_\{X₀\}\} O\_\{Y₀\} ──► Ω¹\_\{Y₀/S₀\} ──► 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since this sequence is formed of
\((Y_{0} \times_{S} Y_{0})\)-equivariant modules and morphisms, its
inverse image \texttt{(+)} by \(\epsilon_{0}*\) is an exact sequence of
\(Y_{0}\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules, and \texttt{(†)} is the inverse image
of \texttt{(+)} by \(\pi_{0}*\) (cf.~Exp. I, § 6.8). This proves (i).

Suppose moreover \(X_{0}\) and \(Y_{0}\) smooth over \(S_{0}\). Then, by
SGA 1 II 4.10 (see also EGA IV₄, 17.2.3 (i) and 17.2.5), \(D\) is
injective and the sequence \texttt{(†)} is formed of
\(O_{Y_{0}}\)-modules locally free of finite type (hence is locally
split). By the equivalence of categories I, 6.8.1, \(d\) is also
injective, and therefore the sequence \texttt{(+)} has the indicated
properties.

\textbf{4.26.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed the original, to make
  visible that one has an exact sequence of
  \(Y_{0}\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules.} For every \(S_{0}\)-scheme
\(f : T \to S_{0}\), \texttt{(+)} gives an exact sequence of
\(Y_{0}(T)\)-\(O(T)\)-modules

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_T\}(f*(ω¹\_\{Y₀/S₀\}), f*(J)) ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_T\}(f*(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}), f*(J)) ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_T\}(f*(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}), f*(J)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence one has an exact sequence of \(Y_{0}\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4.26.1)    0 ⟶ L₀\^{}Y ⟶ L₀\^{}X ──d──► N₀.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

From this one deduces an exact sequence of complexes of abelian groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C*(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C*(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ──d*──► C*(Y₀, N₀),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and in particular, a commutative diagram with exact rows

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ──d⁰──► C⁰(Y₀, N₀)}
\NormalTok{        │ ∂              │ ∂                │ ∂}
\NormalTok{        ↓                ↓                  ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C¹(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C¹(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ──d¹──► C¹(Y₀, N₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note that \(C^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{Y}_{0})\) (resp.
\(C^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})\)) is none other than
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S_{0}}(S_{0}, L^{Y}_{0}) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(S, L'_{Y})\)
(resp. ···), i.e.~(cf.~0.9) the group of sections of \(Y\) (resp. \(X\))
over \(S\) inducing the unit section of \texttt{X\_J}. Note also that
\(d^{1}\) is none other than the morphism \(v_{i_{Y_{0}}}\) of 4.8
(iii), where \(i_{Y_{0}} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) is the canonical
immersion.\footnote{N.D.E.: This results from the definition of
  \(d : n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \to \Omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) (cf. 4.25) and
  from that of \(v_{i_{Y_{0}}}\) (cf.~4.8).}

\textbf{Lemma 4.27.} \emph{Under the conditions of 4.21 for
\texttt{S,\ I,\ J} and \(X\), let \(Y\) be a subgroup of \(X\), flat
over \(S\) and lifting \texttt{Y\_J}. Denote \(i : Y \hookrightarrow X\)
the canonical immersion.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added point (i) below,
  which will be useful in 4.35.1 and then in 4.38 (4) and (5).}}

\emph{(i) Let \(i' : Y \to X\) be a morphism of \(S\)-schemes lifting
\(i_{0}\) (so that \(i'\) is also an immersion), let \(Y' = i'(Y)\) and
let \(d(i, i')\) be the element of \(C^{1}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})\) such that
\(i' = d(i, i') \cdot i\) (cf. 1.2.4). Then the deviation
\(d(Y, Y') \in C^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) (cf.~4.5.1) is given by the
formula:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d(Y, Y′) = d¹(d(i, i′)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) Let \(x \in C^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})\) be a section of \(X\)
over \(S\) inducing the unit section of \texttt{X\_J} over
\texttt{S\_J}. Then the deviation
\(d(Y, Int(x)Y) \in C^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) (cf.~4.5.1) is given by the
formula:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{−d(Y, Int(x)Y) = d¹∂x = ∂ d⁰x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, \(Y'\) is the image of \(Y\) by the composite
morphism:\footnote{N.D.E.: Recall that
  \(L'_{X} = \prod_{S_{0}/S} L^{X}_{0}\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y ──\{(d(i,i′), i)\}──► L′\_X ×\_S X ⟶ X,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is denoted \(d(i, i') \cdot i\) in 4.8 (iii); by loc. cit. and the
equality \(v_{i_{0}} = d^{1}\), one has therefore:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c(X, Y′, d(i, i′) · i) − c(X, Y′, i) = v\_\{i₀\}(d(i, i′)) = d¹(d(i, i′)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \(d(i, i') \cdot i = i'\) factors through \(Y'\) by definition,
hence the first term is zero; moreover, by 4.8 (ii), one has
\(c(X, Y', i) = d(Y', Y) = -d(Y, Y')\). Hence
\(d(Y, Y') = d^{1}(d(i, i'))\), which proves (i).

Let now \(x\) be as in (ii). By the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xyx⁻¹ = xyx⁻¹y⁻¹y = (x − Ad(y)x)y = (−∂x)(y) · y,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one sees that \(Y'\) is the image of \(Y\) by the immersion
\(i' = (-\partial x) \cdot i_{Y}\). Hence, by (i) one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{−d(Y, Int(x)Y) = d¹∂x = ∂ d⁰x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 4.28.} \emph{For two subgroups \(Y\) and \(Y'\) of
\(G\), flat over \(S\) and lifting \texttt{Y\_J}, to be conjugate by a
section of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit section of \texttt{X\_J},
it is necessary and sufficient that
\(d(Y, Y') \in \partial d^{0} C^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0}) \subset \partial C^{0}(Y_{0}, N_{0}) = B^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\).}

\textbf{Corollary 4.29.} \emph{If \(d^{0}\) is surjective, \(Y\) and
\(Y'\) as above are conjugate by a section of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing
the unit section of \texttt{X\_J} if and only if
\(d(Y, Y') \in B^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\).}

\textbf{Corollary 4.30.} \emph{Let \(Y\) be as in 4.27; the set of
conjugates of \(Y\) by sections of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit
section of \texttt{X\_J} is isomorphic to:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d¹∂(C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X)) = C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) / Ker d¹∂.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note now that \(C^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})/Ker d^{1}\partial\) is computed
solely with the help of the left square of the commutative diagram of
4.26. It follows in particular that one can also compute it in any
diagram of the same type having the same left square. Consider in
particular the functor \(L^{X}_{0}/L^{Y}_{0}\) above \(S_{0}\) defined
by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L₀\^{}X/L₀\^{}Y) = Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L₀\^{}X) / Hom\_\{S₀\}(T, L₀\^{}Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ⟶ C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X/L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ 0}
\NormalTok{        │ ∂              │ ∂                  │ ∂}
\NormalTok{        ↓                ↓                    ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C¹(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C¹(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ⟶ C¹(Y₀, L₀\^{}X/L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence by the preceding remark:

\textbf{Corollary 4.31.} \emph{Let \(Y\) be as in 4.27; the set of
conjugates of \(Y\) by sections of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit
section of \texttt{X\_J} is isomorphic to}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E = ∂(C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X/L₀\^{}Y)) = C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X/L₀\^{}Y) / H⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X/L₀\^{}Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 4.32.} \emph{Suppose moreover \(S_{0}\) affine and
\(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\) finite locally free.\footnote{N.D.E.: We
  have corrected \(Lie(Y_{0}/S_{0})\) to \(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\).}
If one denotes
\(F_{0} = [Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})/Lie(Y_{0}/S_{0})] \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} J\),
one has \(E = \Gamma(S_{0}, F_{0})/H^{0}(Y_{0}, F_{0})\).}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed the original in what follows.}
Indeed, since \(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\) is finite locally free, as is
\(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) (since \(X\) is supposed smooth over
\(S\)), one has, by 0.6:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L₀\^{}Y = W(Lie(Y₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J)    and    L₀\^{}X = W(Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, by 4.25, one has an exact sequence of
\(Y_{0}\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ K ⟶ ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\} ──φ──► ω¹\_\{Y₀/S₀\} ⟶ 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(where \(K = Ker(\phi)\)). Since \(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\) and
\(\omega^{1}_{X_{0}/S_{0}}\) are finite locally free, one has a locally
split exact sequence:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ Lie(Y₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J ⟶ Lie(X₀/S₀) ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J ⟶ F₀ ⟶ 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows that one has an exact sequence of
\(Y_{0}\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules:

\[
0 \longrightarrow L^{Y}_{0} \longrightarrow L^{X}_{0} \longrightarrow W(F_{0}).
\]

By the reasoning that served us to prove 4.31, we can compute \(E\) as
the image of the composite map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C⁰(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ──π──► C⁰(Y₀, W(F₀)) ──∂──► C¹(Y₀, W(F₀)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now the map \(\pi\) above is the map
\(\Gamma(S_{0}, Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} J) \to \Gamma(S_{0}, F_{0})\).
Hence, \(S_{0}\) being affine, \(\pi\) is surjective and one finds
indeed the announced result.

\textbf{Corollary 4.33.} \emph{Let \texttt{S,\ I,\ J} and \(X\) be as in
4.21, and let \(Y\) be a diagonalizable subgroup of \(X\). Suppose
\(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\) finite locally free and \(S_{0}\)
affine.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the hypothesis on
  \(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\) and replaced the hypothesis ``\(S\)
  affine'' by ``\(S_{0}\) affine''.} The set of subgroups of \(X\)
conjugate to \(Y\) by a section of \(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit
section of \texttt{X\_J} is isomorphic to}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E = Γ(S₀, [Lie(X₀/S₀) / Lie(X₀/S₀)\^{}\{ad(Y₀)\}] ⊗\_\{Γ(S₀, O\_\{S₀\})\} Γ(S₀, J))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added what follows, cf.~4.34.} that is,
isomorphic to \(L^{X}_{0}(Y_{0})/H^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})\).}

Indeed, one writes by I 4.7.3 (cf.~2.13):

\[
Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) = Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})^{ad(Y_{0})} \oplus R.
\]

Since \(Y_{0}\) is commutative one has
\(Lie(Y_{0}/S_{0}) \subset Lie(X_{0}/S_{0})^{ad(Y_{0})}\), hence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F₀ = [Lie(X₀/S₀)\^{}\{ad(Y₀)\} / Lie(Y₀/S₀)] ⊗ J ⊕ R ⊗ J,}
\NormalTok{F₀\^{}\{ad(Y₀)\} = [Lie(X₀/S₀)\^{}\{ad(Y₀)\} / Lie(Y₀/S₀)] ⊗ J.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 4.32, one has therefore \(E \simeq \Gamma(S_{0}, R \otimes J)\).
Returning to the definition of \(R\), one is done.

\textbf{Corollary 4.34.} \emph{Let \texttt{S,\ I,\ J} and \(X\) be as in
4.21, and let \(Y\) be a diagonalizable subgroup of \(X\). Suppose
\(\omega^{1}_{Y_{0}/S_{0}}\) finite locally free and \(S_{0}\)
affine.\footnote{N.D.E.: Cf. N.D.E. (129).} If \(x \in X(S)\) induces
the unit section of \texttt{X\_J} and normalizes \(Y\), then it
centralizes \(Y\).}

This results immediately from comparison of the preceding corollary and
2.14. Indeed, 4.33 shows that the elements of
\(C^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})\) which globally preserve \(Y\) are the
elements of \(H^{0}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})\), and one has seen in 2.14 that
these are precisely those which act trivially on the canonical immersion
\(Y \to X\).

\textbf{4.35.} Let us return to the general situation of 4.21 and
suppose \texttt{Y\_J} smooth over \texttt{S\_J}. Then, by 4.25 (ii), one
has an exact sequence of \(Y_{0}\)-\(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules:

\[
(\ast)    0 \longrightarrow Lie(Y_{0}/S_{0}) \longrightarrow Lie(X_{0}/S_{0}) \longrightarrow n^{\vee}_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \longrightarrow 0
\]

and they are finite locally free \(O_{S_{0}}\)-modules.

On the other hand, by SGA 1, II 4.10, every subscheme \(Y\) of \(X\)
lifting \texttt{Y\_J} and flat over \(S\) will be smooth over
\(S\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added what follows and Proposition
  4.35.1, implicit in the original, cf.~4.38 (5).} Suppose moreover
\(S_{0}\) and \texttt{Y\_J} affine. Then, since
\(n^{\vee}_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}\) is a locally free \(O_{S_{0}}\)-module, the
sequence \((\ast)\) remains exact when one applies
\(\otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} J\) to it, and then takes the inverse image on
\(Y^{n}_{0}\), and as the \(Y^{n}_{0}\) are affine, one therefore
obtains an exact sequence of complexes of abelian groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C*(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C*(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ──d*──► C*(Y₀, N₀) ⟶ 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and in particular, a commutative diagram with exact rows

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C¹(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C¹(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ──d¹──► C¹(Y₀, N₀) ⟶ 0}
\NormalTok{        │ ∂                │ ∂                │ ∂}
\NormalTok{        ↓                  ↓                  ↓}
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ C²(Y₀, L₀\^{}Y) ⟶ C²(Y₀, L₀\^{}X) ──d²──► C²(Y₀, N₀) ⟶ 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let now \(Y, Y'\) be two subgroups of \(X\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J} and
flat, hence smooth, over \(S\). As \texttt{Y\_J} is affine, then, by
0.15, \(Y\) and \(Y'\) are isomorphic as schemes extending
\texttt{Y\_J}, i.e.~there exists an isomorphism of \(S\)-schemes

\[
f : Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y'
\]

inducing the identity on \texttt{Y\_J}. On the one hand, by 1.2.4, \(f\)
defines an element \(a\) of \(C^{1}(Y_{0}, L^{X}_{0})\) such that
\(f(y) = a(y_{0})y\), for every \(y \in Y(S')\), \(S' \to S\), and by
4.27 (i), one has

\[
d^{1}(a) = d(Y, Y').
\]

Moreover, since \(Y, Y'\) are subgroups of \(X\), the above element
belongs to \(Z^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\) (cf.~4.21). Then \(\partial a\) is an
element of \(Z^{2}(Y_{0}, L^{Y}_{0})\) whose image \(\bar{\partial}a\)
in \(H^{2}(Y_{0}, L^{Y}_{0})\) depends only on the class
\(\bar{d}(Y, Y') \in H^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0})\); this being the definition of
the connecting map
\(\partial^{1} : H^{1}(Y_{0}, N_{0}) \to H^{2}(Y_{0}, L^{Y}_{0})\), one
has therefore:

\[
\partial^{1}(\bar{d}(Y, Y')) = \bar{\partial}a.
\]

On the other hand, let us transport by \(f\) the group structure of
\(Y'\) and let \(Y_{1}\) be the group obtained (which thus has \(Y\) as
underlying scheme), that is, the group law \(\mu_{1}\) of \(Y_{1}\) is
defined by: for every \(S' \to S\) and \(x, y \in Y(S')\),

\[
\mu_{1}(x, y) = f^{-1}(f(x)f(y)).
\]

By 3.5.1, \(Y_{1}\) defines a cocycle
\(\delta(Y, Y_{1}) \in Z^{2}(Y_{0}, Lie(Y_{0}/S_{0}))\) such that, for
every \(S' \to S\) and \(x, y \in Y(S')\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{δ(Y, Y₁)(x₀, y₀) xy = μ₁(x, y) = f⁻¹(f(x)f(y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set \(b = \delta(Y, Y_{1})\). For every \(S' \to S\) and
\(x, y \in Y(S')\), one has \((b(x_{0}, y_{0})xy)_{0} = x_{0}y_{0}\) and
therefore one obtains that \(f(b(x_{0}, y_{0})xy)\) equals, on the one
hand, \(a(x_{0}y_{0})b(x_{0}, y_{0})xy\) and, on the other hand,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(x)f(y) = a(x₀)x a(y₀)y = a(x₀) Ad(x₀)(a(y₀)) xy.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Comparing the two expressions, one obtains that \(b(x_{0}, y_{0})\)
equals

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(x₀y₀)⁻¹ a(x₀) Ad(x₀)(a(y₀)) = Ad(x₀)(a(y₀)) − a(x₀y₀) + a(x₀) = (∂a)(x₀, y₀),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.~\(\delta(Y, Y_{1}) = \partial a\). We have thus obtained:

\textbf{Proposition 4.35.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added what follows
  and Proposition 4.35.1, implicit in the original, cf.~4.38 (5).}
\emph{Under the hypotheses of 4.21, suppose moreover \(S_{0}\) affine
and \texttt{Y\_J} smooth over \texttt{S\_J} and affine. Let \(Y, Y'\) be
two subgroups of \(X\) lifting \texttt{Y\_J} and flat (hence smooth)
over \(S\), let \(f : Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y'\) be an isomorphism of
\(S\)-schemes inducing the identity on \texttt{Y\_J}, denote by
\(Y_{1}\) the group obtained by transporting via \(f\) the group
structure of \(Y'\). Then one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∂¹(d̄(Y, Y′)) = δ(Y, Y₁).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 4.36.} \emph{Under the hypotheses of 4.21, suppose
moreover \texttt{Y\_J} smooth over \texttt{S\_J} and \(S_{0}\) affine.
The set of sub-\(S\)-groups \(Y\) of \(X\) flat (or smooth) over \(S\),
reducing to \texttt{Y\_J}, modulo conjugation by sections of \(X\) over
\(S\) inducing the unit section of \texttt{X\_J}, is either empty, or a
principal homogeneous set under the group}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(Y₀, [Lie(X₀/S₀)/Lie(Y₀/S₀)] ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} J).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It suffices for us to verify that Corollary 4.29 applies, that is, that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d⁰ : Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(ω¹\_\{X₀/S₀\}, J) ⟶ Hom\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\}(n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}, J)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is surjective. Now this follows from the fact that the sequence
\texttt{(+)} of 4.25 (ii) is split, \(S_{0}\) being affine.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  This also follows from the proof of 4.32.}

Let us finally state a corollary common to 4.21 and 4.36, which will in
fact be the only form under which we shall use in what follows the
general results of this section.\footnote{N.D.E.: For example, 4.37 is
  used in Exposé IX to prove statements 3.2 bis and 3.6 bis.}

\textbf{Corollary 4.37.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(S_{0}\) the
closed subscheme defined by a nilpotent ideal \(I\). Let \(X\) be an
\(S\)-group smooth over \(S\), and \(Y_{0}\) a sub-\(S_{0}\)-group of
\(X_{0}\), flat over \(S_{0}\).}

\emph{(i) If \(S_{0}\) is affine, \(Y_{0}\) smooth over \(S_{0}\), and
if}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(Y₀, [Lie(X₀/S₀)/Lie(Y₀/S₀)] ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} Iⁿ⁺¹/Iⁿ⁺²) = 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(n \geq 0\), two sub-\(S\)-groups of \(X\), flat (or
smooth) over \(S\), reducing to \(Y_{0}\), are conjugate by a section of
\(X\) over \(S\) inducing the unit section of \(X_{0}\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(Y_{0}\) is affine and of finite presentation and
if\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S_{0}}}(n_{Y_{0}/X_{0}}, I^{n+1}/I^{n+2})\)
  by \(n^{\vee}_{Y_{0}/X_{0}} \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} I^{n+1}/I^{n+2}\), in
  accordance with Remark 4.22.}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H²(Y₀, n\_\{Y₀/X₀\}\^{}∨ ⊗\_\{O\_\{S₀\}\} Iⁿ⁺¹/Iⁿ⁺²) = 0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(n \geq 0\), there exists a sub-\(S\)-group of \(X\),
flat over \(S\), reducing to \(Y_{0}\).}

\textbf{4.38.} It remains to relate the three constructions which we
have made in this Exposé. To avoid inessential complications, we shall
place ourselves in the following situation: \(S_{0}\) is the spectrum of
a field \(k\), \(S\) is the spectrum of the dual numbers \(D(k)\), \(G\)
is an \(S\)-group smooth over \(S\), \(K\) a sub-\(S\)-group, smooth
over \(S\) and affine.

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have slightly modified the original in what
  follows. In particular, we have replaced \(X\) by \(G\) and \(Y\) by
  \(K\), and we have denoted \(g_{0}\) and \(k_{0}\) their Lie algebras.
  On the other hand, we have written explicitly \(H^{i}(K_{0}, \cdot)\)
  instead of the abbreviation \(H^{i}(\cdot)\) of the original.} Denote
\(g_{0} = Lie G_{0}\) (which here equals
\(\Gamma(S_{0}, Lie G_{0}) = Lie(G_{0}/S_{0})(S_{0})\)) and
\(k_{0} = Lie K_{0}\). One has an exact sequence of \(k\)-vector
spaces\footnote{N.D.E.: Equipped with the adjoint action of \(K_{0}\).}:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ k₀ ──i──► g₀ ──d──► n\_\{K₀/G₀\}\^{}∨ ⟶ 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

giving rise to an exact cohomology sequence:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 ⟶ H⁰(K₀, k₀) ──i⁰──► H⁰(K₀, g₀) ──d⁰──► H⁰(K₀, g₀/k₀)}
\NormalTok{   ──∂⁰──► H¹(K₀, k₀) ──i¹──► H¹(K₀, g₀) ──d¹──► H¹(K₀, n\_\{K₀/G₀\}\^{}∨) ──∂¹──► H²(K₀, k₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now these various groups all have a geometric meaning.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\item
  \(H^{0}(K_{0}, k_{0}) = Lie Centr(K_{0})\)\footnote{N.D.E.: Since the
    formation of centralizers and normalizers commutes with base change
    (cf.~I 2.3.3.1), we have written \(Centr(K_{0})\) instead of
    \(Centr(K)_{0}\) in the original, and similarly
    \(Centr_{G_{0}}(K_{0})\) and \(Norm_{G_{0}}(K_{0})\) instead of
    \(Centr_{G}(K)_{0}\) and \(Norm_{G}(K)_{0}\).} by II 5.2.3.
\item
  \(H^{0}(K_{0}, g_{0}) = Lie Centr_{G_{0}}(K_{0})\)\footnote{N.D.E.:
    Since the formation of centralizers and normalizers commutes with
    base change (cf.~I 2.3.3.1), we have written \(Centr(K_{0})\)
    instead of \(Centr(K)_{0}\) in the original, and similarly
    \(Centr_{G_{0}}(K_{0})\) and \(Norm_{G_{0}}(K_{0})\) instead of
    \(Centr_{G}(K)_{0}\) and \(Norm_{G}(K)_{0}\).} (idem).
\item
  \(H^{0}(K_{0}, g_{0}/k_{0}) = Lie Norm_{G_{0}}(K_{0})/k_{0}\)\footnote{N.D.E.:
    Since the formation of centralizers and normalizers commutes with
    base change (cf.~I 2.3.3.1), we have written \(Centr(K_{0})\)
    instead of \(Centr(K)_{0}\) in the original, and similarly
    \(Centr_{G_{0}}(K_{0})\) and \(Norm_{G_{0}}(K_{0})\) instead of
    \(Centr_{G}(K)_{0}\) and \(Norm_{G}(K)_{0}\).} (idem).
\item
  \(H^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0}) = Lie \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(K_{0}) / Im(k_{0})\),
  where \(Im(k_{0})\) denotes the image of \(k_{0}\) by the morphism
  \(Lie(Int_{0})\) deduced from
  \(Int_{0} : K_{0} \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(K_{0})\). Indeed,
  it follows from 2.1 (ii), applied to \(Y = X = K\) and
  \(f_{0} = id_{K_{0}}\), that \(Z^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\) is the group of
  infinitesimal automorphisms of the \(S_{0}\)-group \(K_{0}\), and that
  \(H^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\) is obtained by quotienting by inner
  infinitesimal automorphisms, i.e.~by the image of \(k_{0}\). Moreover,
  by II 4.2.2, one also has
  \(Z^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0}) = Lie \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(K_{0})\)\footnote{N.D.E.:
    And this is the Lie algebra \(\operatorname{Der}_{k}(k_{0})\) of
    derivations of \(k_{0}\); hence \(H^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\) is the
    quotient of \(\operatorname{Der}_{k}(k_{0})\) by inner derivations
    (i.e.~by the image of
    \(ad : k_{0} \to \operatorname{Der}_{k}(k_{0})\)).}.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\item
  \(H^{1}(K_{0}, g_{0})\) is, by 2.1 (ii), the group of deviations
  between homomorphisms \(K \to G\) extending the canonical immersion
  \(i_{0} : K_{0} \to G_{0}\), modulo the deviations obtained by the
  action of the inner automorphisms of \(G\) defined by elements of
  \(G(S)\) giving the unit of \(G(S_{0})\) (that is, elements of
  \(g_{0}\)).
\item
  \(H^{1}(K_{0}, n^{\vee}_{K_{0}/G_{0}})\) is, by 4.36, the group of
  deviations between subgroups \(K'\) of \(G\) extending \(K_{0}\) and
  flat over \(S\) (hence smooth over \(S\), cf.~SGA 1, II 4.10), modulo
  the deviations obtained by the action of the inner automorphisms of
  \(G\) constructed as previously.
\item
  \(H^{2}(K_{0}, k_{0})\) is, by 3.5 (ii), the group of deviations
  between group structures on \(K\) extending that of \(K_{0}\), modulo
  the \(S\)-automorphisms of \(K\) inducing the identity on \(K_{0}\).
\end{enumerate}

We now propose to show how one can make explicit the six morphisms of
the preceding exact sequence in the geometric interpretation we have
just given.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(i^{0}\) and \(d^{0}\) are nothing other than the morphisms obtained
  by passage to the Lie algebra (then by passage to the quotient for
  \(d^{0}\)), starting from the canonical monomorphisms:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr(K₀) ⟶ Centr\_\{G₀\}(K₀) ⟶ Norm\_\{G₀\}(K₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This indeed results immediately from the definition of the
identifications (a), (b), and (c).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  One constructs \(\partial^{0}\) as follows. Let
  \(\bar{x} \in Lie Norm_{G_{0}}(K_{0})/k_{0}\). Lift it to
  \texttt{x\ ∈\ Lie\ Norm\_\{G₀\}(K₀)\ ⊂\ Norm\_G(K)(S)}. Then
  \(Int(x)\) defines an automorphism of \(K\) inducing the identity on
  \(K_{0}\), hence an element of
  \(Lie \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(K_{0})\). Denote \(Int(\bar{x})\)
  the image of this element in
  \(Lie \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(K_{0})/Im(k_{0})\). Then one has:
\end{enumerate}

\[
(\ast)    \partial^{0}(\bar{x}) = -Int(\bar{x}) = Int(\bar{x}^{-1}).
\]

Indeed, let us compute the element of
\(Lie \operatorname{Aut}_{S_{0}-gr.}(K_{0})\) defined by \(Int(x)\). It
will correspond by definition to an element \(a\) of
\(Z^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x y x⁻¹ = a(y₀) y,    for every y ∈ K(S′), S′ → S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But this can also be written
\(a(y_{0}) = xyx^{-1}y^{-1} = x - Ad(y)x = -\partial(x)(y_{0})\), whence
\(a = -\partial(x)\).

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the following sentence.} On the other
hand, the image of \(x \in Lie Norm_{G_{0}}(K_{0}) \subset g_{0}\) by
\(\partial\) is an element of \(Z^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\), whose image
\(\bar{\partial}(x)\) in \(H^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\) depends only on
\(\bar{x}\), and by definition of the connecting map \(\partial^{0}\),
one has

\[
\partial^{0}(\bar{x}) = \bar{\partial}(x);
\]

combined with the equality \(a = -\partial(x)\), this proves \((\ast)\).

3)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed the original in what follows, and
  in \((\ast\ast)\) we have corrected \(u \circ i\) to \(i \circ u\).}
Denote \(i : K \to G\) the canonical immersion. Let \texttt{ū} be an
element of \(H^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\), image of a

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u ∈ Lie Aut\_\{S₀{-}gr.\}(K₀) ⊂ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(K).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗∗)    i¹(ū) = d̄(i, i ∘ u),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\bar{d}(i, i \circ u)\) is the class defined in 2.1.1.

Indeed, \(u\) is the image of an element \(v \in Z^{1}(K_{0}, k_{0})\)
such that \(u(y) = v(y_{0})y\), and \(i^{1}(\bar{u})\) is the image in
\(H^{1}(K_{0}, g_{0})\) of the cocycle
\(i \circ v \in Z^{1}(K_{0}, g_{0})\).

Now, since \(i\) is a morphism of groups, the equality
\(u(y) = v(y_{0})y\) entails \(iu(y) = iv(y_{0})i(y)\). It follows that
\(i \circ v = d(i, i \circ u)\), whence \((\ast\ast)\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(i' : K \to G\) be a morphism of groups lifting \(i_{0}\), let
  \(d(i, i')\) be the class defined in 2.1.1, and let
  \(d(K, i'(K)) \in C^{1}(K_{0}, n_{K_{0}/X_{0}})\) be the deviation
  defined in 4.5.1; by 4.21, \(d(K, i'(K))\) belongs to
  \(Z^{1}(K_{0}, n_{K_{0}/X_{0}})\). Denote \(\bar{d}(K, i'(K))\) its
  image in \(H^{1}(K_{0}, n_{K_{0}/X_{0}})\). Then, by 4.27 (i), one
  has:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)    d¹(d̄(i, i′)) = d̄(K, i′(K)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Finally, let \(K'\) be a subgroup of \(G\) lifting \(K_{0}\) and flat,
  hence smooth, over \(S\). We have supposed that \(K_{0}\) is affine.
  Then one knows that \(K\) and \(K'\) are isomorphic as schemes
  extending \(K_{0}\) (cf.~0.15), hence there exists an isomorphism of
  \(S\)-schemes
\end{enumerate}

\[
f : K \xrightarrow{\sim} K'
\]

inducing the identity on \(K_{0}\). Let us transport by \(f\) the group
structure of \(K'\) and let \(K_{1}\) be the group obtained (which thus
has \(K\) as underlying scheme), that is, the group law \(\mu_{1}\) of
\(K_{1}\) is defined by: for every \(S' \to S\) and \(x, y \in K(S')\),

\[
\mu_{1}(x, y) = f^{-1}(f(x)f(y)).
\]

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have modified the original in what follows, taking
  into account the additions made in 3.5.1 and 4.35.1.} By 3.5.1,
\(K_{1}\) defines a cocycle \(\delta(K, K_{1}) \in Z^{2}(K_{0}, k_{0})\)
such that, for every \(S' \to S\) and \(x, y \in K(S')\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{δ(K, K₁)(x₀, y₀) xy = μ₁(x, y) = f⁻¹(f(x)f(y)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, by 4.35.1, one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(‡)    ∂¹(d̄(K, K′)) = δ̄(K, K₁).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Bibliography}\label{bibliography-3}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Additional references cited in this Exposé.}

{[}BAlg{]} N. Bourbaki, \emph{Algèbre}, Chap. I--III, Hermann, 1970.

{[}BAC{]} N. Bourbaki, \emph{Algèbre commutative}, Chap. I--IV, Masson,
1985.

\& North-Holland, 1970.

\section{Exposé IV. Topologies and
sheaves}\label{exposuxe9-iv.-topologies-and-sheaves}

\emph{by M. Demazure}\footnote{This text develops the substance of two
  oral expositions of A. Grothendieck, completing the latter on several
  important points which had been passed over in silence or scarcely
  touched on.}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Version of 13/10/2024.}

This Exposé is intended to acquaint the reader with the essentials of
the language of topologies and sheaves (without cohomology),
particularly convenient in questions of passage to the quotient (among
others).

The first three sections develop the language of passage to the
quotient. The fourth, which is the central part, is the exposition of
the theory of sheaves, oriented principally towards the application to
questions of quotients; the fifth is an application to passage to the
quotient in groups and to principal homogeneous fibered objects. The
last section concerns more specifically the category of schemes, and
defines various useful topologies on this category.

The reader will profitably refer to {[}AS{]}, {[}MA{]}, {[}D{]}, and SGA
4; {[}D{]} in particular as regards the applications of topologies to
the theory of descent, and SGA 4 for questions of universes
(particularly mistreated in this Exposé).

\subsection{1. Universal effective
epimorphisms}\label{universal-effective-epimorphisms}

In what follows in this Exposé, we suppose fixed a category \(C\).

\textbf{Definition 1.1.} \emph{A morphism \(u : T \to S\) is called an}
epimorphism \emph{if, for every object \(X\), the corresponding map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X(S) = Hom(S, X) ⟶ X(T) = Hom(T, X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is injective.}\footnote{N.D.E.: that is, if \(u\) is
  right-cancellable.} \emph{One says that \(u\) is a} universal
epimorphism \emph{if for every morphism \(S' \to S\), the fiber product
