\(T' = T \times_{S} S'\) exists, and \(u' : T' \to S'\) is an
epimorphism.}

\textbf{Definition 1.2.} \emph{A diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A —u→ B ⇉\_\{v₁,v₂\} C}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{of maps of sets is said to be} exact \emph{if \(u\) is injective
and if its image is formed by the elements \(b\) of \(B\) such that
\(v_{1}(b) = v_{2}(b)\). A diagram of the same type in \(C\) is said to
be} exact \emph{if for every object \(X\) of \(C\), the corresponding
diagram of sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A(X) → B(X) ⇉ C(X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is exact; one then also says that \(u\) makes \(A\) into a} kernel
\emph{of the pair of arrows \((v_{1}, v_{2})\). Dually, a diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C ⇉\_\{v₁,v₂\} B —u→ A}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{in \(C\) is said to be exact if it is exact as a diagram in the
opposite category \(C^{\circ}\), i.e.~if for every object \(X\) of
\(C\), the corresponding diagram of sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X(A) → X(B) ⇉ X(C)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is exact.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This implies, in particular, that
  \(u\) be an epimorphism.} \emph{One also says that \(u\) makes \(A\)
into a} cokernel \emph{of the pair of arrows \((v_{1}, v_{2})\).}

\textbf{Definition 1.3.} \emph{A morphism \(u : T \to S\) is called an}
effective epimorphism \emph{if the fiber square \(T \times_{S} T\)
exists, and if the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ×\_S T ⇉\_\{pr₁,pr₂\} T —u→ S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is exact, i.e.~if \(u\) makes \(S\) into a cokernel of
\((pr_{1}, pr_{2})\). One says that \(u\) is a} universal effective
epimorphism \emph{if for every morphism \(S' \to S\), the fiber product
\(T' = T \times_{S} S'\) exists, and the morphism \(u' : T' \to S'\) is
an effective epimorphism.}

One evidently has the implications:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{universal effective epimorphism  ⟹  effective epimorphism}
\NormalTok{            ⇓                                ⇓}
\NormalTok{universal epimorphism            ⟹  epimorphism,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but in general no other implication holds.\footnote{N.D.E.: For example,
  if \(C = (Sch)\) is the category of schemes, one sees easily that
  every universal epimorphism is surjective. Let
  \(T = \coprod_{p prime} \operatorname{Spec}(F_{p})\) and
  \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(Z)\); then the morphism \(u : T \to S\) is
  an epimorphism that is not universal. On the other hand, one sees that
  \(T \times_{S} T\) is identified with \(T\), so that the two
  projections \texttt{T\ ×\_S\ T\ ⇉\ T} coincide; since \(id_{T}\) does
  not descend to a morphism \(S \to T\), this shows that \(u\) is not an
  effective epimorphism.}

\textbf{Definition 1.4.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 1.4.0 has been
  added for later references.} \emph{We ``recall'' that a morphism
\(u : T \to S\) is said to be} squarable \emph{if for every morphism
\(S' \to S\), the fiber product \(T \times_{S} S'\) exists.}

\textbf{Lemma 1.4.} \emph{Consider morphisms
\(U \xrightarrow{v} T \xrightarrow{u} S\). Then}

\emph{a) \texttt{u,\ v} epimorphisms \(\Longrightarrow uv\) epimorphism
\(\Longrightarrow u\) epimorphism,}

\emph{b) \texttt{u,\ v} universal epimorphisms \(\Longrightarrow uv\)
universal epimorphism, and \(u\) squarable \(\Longrightarrow u\)
universal epimorphism.}

Lemma 1.4 is trivial from the definitions. From it we conclude:

\textbf{Corollary 1.5.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) and \(u' : X' \to Y'\)
be universal epimorphisms, such that \(Y \times Y'\) exists; then
\(X \times X'\) exists and \(u \times u' : X \times X' \to Y \times Y'\)
is a universal epimorphism.}

Let us also note:

\textbf{Definition 1.6.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 1.6.0 has been
  added for later references.} \emph{One says that an object \(S\) of
\(C\) is} squarable \emph{if its product with every object of \(C\)
exists. (If \(C\) has a final object \(e\), this is equivalent to saying
that the morphism \(S \to e\) is squarable, cf.~1.4.0.)}

\textbf{Lemma 1.6.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) be a morphism in \(C/S\);
for it to be an epimorphism (resp. universal epimorphism, resp.
effective epimorphism, resp. universal effective epimorphism), it
suffices that the corresponding morphism in \(C\) be such, and this is
also necessary if one supposes that \(S\) is a squarable object of
\(C\).}

Immediate proof left to the reader. One uses the hypothesis ``\(S\)
squarable'' in order to interpret the \(C\)-morphisms from an object
\(Y\) of \(C/S\) into an object \(Z\) of \(C\) as the \(C/S\)-morphisms
from \(Y\) into \(Z \times S\).

\textbf{Lemma 1.7.} \emph{With the notation of 1.4: \texttt{u,\ v}
effective epimorphisms and \(v\) universal epimorphism
\(\Longrightarrow uv\) effective epimorphism.}

To see this, one considers the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S ⇇ T ⇇ T ×\_S T}
\NormalTok{  ↑   ↑v   ↑v×\_S v}
\NormalTok{    U ⇇ U ×\_S U}
\NormalTok{        ↖}
\NormalTok{       U ×\_T U}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One notes that by hypothesis, row 1 and column 1 are exact, and that by
virtue of 1.5 and 1.6, \(v \times_{S} v\) is an epimorphism (\(v\) being
a universal epimorphism). The conclusion follows by an evident
diagram-chase: if an element of \(X(U)\) has the same images in
\(X(U \times_{S} U)\), it has \emph{a fortiori} the same images in
\(X(U \times_{T} U)\), hence comes from an element of \(X(T)\) since
column 1 is exact. As row 1 is exact, it suffices to verify that the
element under consideration has the same images in
\(X(T \times_{S} T)\), and since \(v \times_{S} v\) is an epimorphism,
it suffices to verify that the images in \(X(U \times_{S} U)\) are the
same, which is indeed the case.

\textbf{Proposition 1.8.} \emph{Consider morphisms
\(U \xrightarrow{v} T \xrightarrow{u} S\). Then \texttt{u,\ v} universal
effective epimorphisms \(\Longrightarrow uv\) universal effective
epimorphism, and \(u\) squarable \(\Longrightarrow u\) universal
effective epimorphism.}

The first implication follows at once from 1.7. For the second, one
looks at the diagram (of ``bisimplicial'' type):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S ⇇ T ⇇ T ×\_S T}
\NormalTok{↑uv  ↑   ↑}
\NormalTok{U ⇇ U ×\_S T ⇇ U ×\_S T ×\_S T}
\NormalTok{↑    ↑           ↑}
\NormalTok{U ×\_S U ⇇ U ×\_S U ×\_S T ⇇ U ×\_S U ×\_S T ×\_S T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Columns 1, 2, 3 are exact by virtue of the hypothesis ``\texttt{uv}
universal effective epimorphism'', row 2 is exact, since
\(U \times_{S} T \to U\) is an effective epimorphism (because it has a
section over \(U\)), and the same holds for row 3 (same reason). An
evident diagram-chase then shows that row 1 is exact, i.e.~\(u\) is an
effective epimorphism. As the hypotheses made are invariant under any
change of base \(S' \to S\), it follows that \(u\) is in fact a
universal effective epimorphism.

\textbf{Corollary 1.9.} \emph{Let \(u : X \to Y\) and \(u' : X' \to Y'\)
be universal effective epimorphisms, such that \(Y \times Y'\) exists;
then \(X \times X'\) exists and
\(u \times u' : X \times X' \to Y \times Y'\) is a universal effective
epimorphism.}

Proof as for 1.5 by the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y′ ⇇ X′}
\NormalTok{↑    ↑u′}
\NormalTok{X ⇇ X × Y′ ⇇ X × X′}
\NormalTok{↑u             ↘ u×u′}
\NormalTok{Y ⇇ Y × Y′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 1.10.} \emph{Consider a squarable morphism
\(u : T \to S\), and a change-of-base morphism \(S' \to S\) which is a
universal effective epimorphism. For \(u\) to be a universal effective
epimorphism, it is necessary and sufficient that
\(u' : T' = T \times_{S} S' \to S'\) be one:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ⇇v′ T′}
\NormalTok{↓u    ↓u′}
\NormalTok{S ⇇v  S′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Only the ``it suffices'' requires a proof. Now if \(u'\) is a universal
effective epimorphism, so is \(vu'\) by 1.8, and since \(vu' = uv'\),
one concludes by 1.8 that \(u\) is a universal effective epimorphism.

\textbf{Remark 1.11.} \emph{The same reasoning shows that in 1.10 one
can replace ``universal effective epimorphism'' by ``universal
epimorphism'' or ``universal and effective epimorphism'', or simply by
``epimorphism'' (and in this last case, the hypothesis ``\(u\)
squarable'' is evidently unnecessary).}

In the proof of 1.8 we used the following result, which deserves to be
made explicit:

\textbf{Proposition 1.12.} \emph{Let \(u : T \to S\) be a morphism that
admits a section. Then \(u\) is an epimorphism, and if
\(T \times_{S} T\) exists, it is an effective epimorphism, and a
universal effective epimorphism if moreover \(u\) is squarable.}

The first assertion is contained in 1.4 a), and the third will follow at
once from the second, which it will therefore suffice to establish. In
fact we have a stronger conclusion: for every functor
\(F : C^{\circ} \to (Ens)\) (not necessarily representable), the diagram
of sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S) → F(T) ⇉ F(T ×\_S T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is exact. This may be considered as a particular case of the formalism
of Čech cohomology (in dimension 0!), which we content ourselves with
recalling here. Suppose simply that \(T \times_{S} T\) exists; one then
sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ȟ⁰(T/S, F) = Ker(F(T) ⇉ F(T ×\_S T)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One may evidently regard \(\check{H}^{0}(T/S, F)\) as a contravariant
functor in the argument \(T\) varying in \(C/S\), every \(S\)-morphism
\(T' \to T\) defining a map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    Ȟ⁰(T/S, F) → Ȟ⁰(T′/S, F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Fix \(T\) and \(T'\) in \(C/S\). A well-known calculation shows that if
there exists an \(S\)-morphism from \(T'\) into \(T\), the corresponding
map (+) is in fact independent of the choice of this
morphism,\footnote{N.D.E.: This is the following argument, communicated
  by M. Demazure. Let \(f, g : T' \to T\), and let
  \(\phi : T' \to T \times_{S} T\) be the morphism with components \(f\)
  and \(g\), whence \(p_{1} \circ \phi = f\) and
  \(p_{2} \circ \phi = g\). Then
  \(F(\phi) : F(T \times_{S} T) \to F(T')\) satisfies
  \(F(\phi) \circ F(p_{1}) = F(f)\) and
  \(F(\phi) \circ F(p_{2}) = F(g)\). Now, for every
  \(x \in \check{H}^{0}(T/S, F)\), one has
  \(F(p_{1})(x) = F(p_{2})(x)\). Hence, applying \(F(\phi)\) to both
  sides, one obtains \(F(f)(x) = F(g)(x)\), which shows that \(f\) and
  \(g\) induce the same morphism.} so that \(\check{H}^{0}(T/S, F)\) may
be regarded as a functor on the category associated to the set
\(Ob C/S\) preordered by the relation of ``domination'' (\(T'\)
dominates \(T\) if there exists an \(S\)-morphism from \(T'\) into
\(T\)). In particular, if \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic in this latter
category, i.e.~if each dominates the other, then (+) is an isomorphism
of sets. This applies in particular to the case where \(T'\) is the
final object of \(C/S\), i.e.~essentially \(S\) itself; in any case
\(T\) dominates \(T' = S\), and the converse is true precisely if
\(T/S\) has a section. This establishes 1.12 in the strengthened form
announced.

\textbf{Remark 1.13.} \emph{For various applications, the notions
introduced in the present Exposé, and the results stated, must be
developed more generally relative to a family of morphisms
\(u_{i} : T_{i} \to S\) with the same target (instead of a single
morphism \(u : T \to S\)). Thus, such a family will be said to be}
epimorphic \emph{if for every object \(X\) of \(C\), the corresponding
map}

\[
X(S) \to \prod_{i} X(T_{i})
\]

\emph{is injective, and one introduces in the same way the notion of an}
effective epimorphic \emph{family and the ``universal'' variants of
these notions. We shall admit, if need be, in what follows, that the
results of the present Exposé extend to this more general situation.}

\textbf{Remark 1.14.} \emph{Every morphism that is at once a
monomorphism and an effective epimorphism is an isomorphism.}

Indeed, in the notation of 1.3, the fact that \(T \to S\) be a
monomorphism entails that the two morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pr₁, pr₂ : T ×\_S T ⇉ T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are equal (and are isomorphisms). Now a diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C ⇉\_\{v,v\} B —u→ A}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is exact only if \(u\) is an isomorphism, as follows immediately from
the definition.\footnote{N.D.E.: One will note that a monomorphism which
  is an epimorphism is not necessarily an isomorphism. For example, in
  \(C = (Sch)\), the morphism
  \texttt{Spec(F\_p)\ ∐\ Spec(Z{[}1/p{]})\ →\ Spec(Z)} is a monomorphism
  and a surjective epimorphism, but is not an isomorphism.}

\subsection{2. Descent morphisms}\label{descent-morphisms}

Let us recall the following definitions:

\textbf{Definition 2.1.} \emph{Let \(f : S' \to S\) be a morphism such
that \(S'' = S' \times_{S} S'\) exists, and let \(u' : X' \to S'\) be an
object over \(S'\). One calls} gluing datum \emph{on \(X'/S'\), relative
to \(f\), an \(S''\)-isomorphism}

\[
c : X''_{1} \xrightarrow{\sim} X''_{2}
\]

\emph{where \(X''_{i}\) (\(i = 1, 2\)) denotes the inverse image
(supposed to exist) of \(X'/S'\) under the projection
\(pr_{i} : S'' \to S'\). One says that the gluing datum \(c\) is a}
descent datum \emph{if it satisfies the ``cocycle condition''}

\[
pr*_{3},_{1}(c) = pr*_{3},_{2}(c) pr*_{2},_{1}(c)
\]

\emph{where \(pr_{i},_{j}\) (\(1 \leq j < i \leq 3\)) are the canonical
projections from \(S''' = S' \times_{S} S' \times_{S} S'\) into \(S''\)
(N.B. one now supposes that \(S'''\) also exists), where
\(pr*_{i},_{j}(c)\) is the inverse image of \(c\), considered as an
\(S'''\)-morphism from \(X'''_{j}\) into \(X'''_{i}\), and where for
every integer \(k\) between 1 and 3, \(X'''_{k}\) denotes the inverse
image (supposed to exist) of \(X'/S'\) under the projection of index
\(k\), \(q_{k} : S''' \to S'\).}

In the second part of the definition, we have therefore used
identifications and abuses of writing in current use,\footnote{N.D.E.:
  for example, one has identified, on the one hand,
  \(pr*_{2},_{1}(X''_{1}) = pr*_{3},_{1}(X''_{1})\) and, on the other
  hand, \(pr*_{2},_{1}(X''_{2}) = pr*_{3},_{2}(X''_{2})\).} which
experience proves to be harmless, but which it is evidently fitting to
avoid in a rigorous exposition of the theory of descent (which must
precisely justify to a certain extent these common abuses of language).
Such a formal exposition ({[}D{]}) has been written by Giraud (with the
aim of justifying and making precise SGA 1, VII, which was never
written). For a detailed exposition of the results of faithfully flat
descent of which constant use will be made in the present Séminaire, one
may consult SGA 1, VIII.

Let \(f : S' \to S\) still be a morphism such that
\(S'' = S' \times_{S} S'\) exists, and let \(X\) be an object over \(S\)
such that \(X' = X \times_{S} S'\) and \(X'' = X \times_{S} S''\) exist;
then the inverse images of \(X'\) under \texttt{prᵢ} (\(i = 1, 2\))
exist and are canonically isomorphic, and consequently \(X'/S'\) is
endowed with a canonical gluing datum relative to \(f\). When \(S'''\)
and \(X''' = X \times_{S} S'''\) exist, this is even a descent datum. If
\(Y\) is another object over \(S\), satisfying the same conditions as
\(X/S\), then for every \(S\)-morphism \(X \to Y\), the corresponding
\(S'\)-morphism \(X' \to Y'\) is ``compatible with the canonical gluing
data'' on \(X', Y'\). If in particular \(S' \to S\) is a squarable
morphism, then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ⟼ X′ = X ×\_S S′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a functor from the category \(C/S\) into the ``category of objects
over \(S'\) equipped with a descent datum relative to \(f\)'' --- a
category whose definition is left to the reader, and which is a full
subcategory of the ``category of objects over \(S'\) equipped with a
gluing datum relative to \(f\)''.

This being so:

\textbf{Definition 2.2.} \emph{One says that a morphism \(f : S' \to S\)
is a} descent morphism \emph{(resp. an} effective descent morphism*) if
\(f\) is squarable (i.e.~for every \(X \to S\), the fiber product
\(X \times_{S} S'\) exists), and if the preceding functor
\texttt{X\ ⟼\ X′\ =\ X\ ×\_S\ S′} from the category \(C/S\) of objects
over \(S\), into the category of objects over \(S'\) equipped with a
descent datum relative to \(f\), is fully faithful (resp. an equivalence
of categories).*

One notes that the first of these two notions can be expressed using
only the notion of gluing datum (hence without involving the triple
fiber product \(S'''\)), \(f\) being a descent morphism if \(f\) is
squarable and \texttt{X\ ⟼\ X′} is a fully faithful functor from the
category \(C/S\) into the category of objects over \(S'\) equipped with
a gluing datum relative to \(f\). When one makes this definition
explicit, one finds that it means that for two objects \texttt{X,\ Y}
over \(S\), the following diagram of sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(×)    Hom\_S(X, Y) → Hom\_\{S′\}(X′, Y′) ⇉\_\{p₁, p₂\} Hom\_\{S″\}(X″, Y″)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is exact, where \(p_{i}(u')\) denotes the inverse image of
\(u' \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S'}(X', Y')\) under the projection
\(pr_{i} : S'' \to S'\), for \(i = 1, 2\); indeed, the kernel of the
pair \((p_{1}, p_{2})\) is by definition none other than the set of
\(S'\)-morphisms \(X' \to Y'\) compatible with the canonical gluing
data.

Note that, by definition of the inverse images \(Y', Y''\), one has
canonical bijections

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S′\}(X′, Y′) ≃ Hom\_S(X′, Y)    and    Hom\_\{S″\}(X″, Y″) ≃ Hom\_S(X″, Y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so that the exactness of the diagram (×) is equivalent to that of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(××)    Hom\_S(X, Y) → Hom\_S(X′, Y) ⇉ Hom\_S(X″, Y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

obtained by applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(-, Y)\) to the diagram in
\(C/S\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(×××)   X″ ⇉ X′ → X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is deduced from

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S″ ⇉ S′ → S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by the base change \(X \to S\). This proves, taking account of 1.6, the
first part of the following proposition:

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.} \emph{Let \(f : S' \to S\) be a morphism. If
it is a universal effective epimorphism, it is a descent morphism, and
the converse is true if \(S\) is a squarable object of \(C\) (i.e.~its
product with every object of \(C\) exists).}

It remains to prove that if \(f\) is a descent morphism, it is a
universal effective epimorphism, that is, that for every morphism
\(X \to S\), the diagram (×××) is exact, i.e.~for every object \(Z\) of
\(C\), the transform of this diagram by \(\operatorname{Hom}(-, Z)\) is
an exact diagram of sets. Now by hypothesis \(Z \times S\) exists; let
\(Y\) be the object of \(C/S\) that it defines; then the transform of
(×××) by \(\operatorname{Hom}(-, Z)\) is isomorphic to the transform by
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(-, Y)\), and this last is exact by the
hypothesis on \(f\).

One may therefore apply to universal effective epimorphisms the results
on descent morphisms, such as the following:

\textbf{Proposition 2.4.} \emph{Let \(f : S' \to S\) be a descent
morphism (for example a universal effective epimorphism). Then:}

\emph{a) For every \(S\)-morphism \(u : X \to Y\), \(u\) is an
isomorphism (resp. a monomorphism) if and only if \(u' : X' \to Y'\)
is.}

\emph{b) Let \texttt{X,\ Y} be two subobjects of \(S\), \(X'\) and
\(Y'\) the subobjects of \(S'\) inverse images of the preceding ones.
For \(X\) to be contained in \(Y\) (resp. to be equal to \(Y\)), it is
necessary and sufficient that the same hold for \(X', Y'\).}

For (a), it follows from the definition that if \(u'\) is an isomorphism
in the category of objects with gluing datum, then \(u\) is an
isomorphism; now one notes at once that every isomorphism of objects
over \(S'\) compatible with gluing data is an isomorphism of objects
with gluing datum, i.e.~its inverse is also compatible with the gluing
data. For b), one is reduced to proving that if \(X'\) is contained in
\(Y'\), i.e.~if there exists an \(S'\)-morphism \(X' \to Y'\), then the
same holds for \texttt{X,\ Y} over \(S\). Now since \(Y' \to S'\), and
hence also \(Y'' \to S''\), is a monomorphism, one sees that
\(X' \to Y'\) is automatically compatible with the gluing data, hence
comes from an \(S\)-morphism \(X \to Y\). Note that the proof holds more
generally when one has two objects \texttt{X,\ Y} over \(S\), with
\(Y \to S\) a monomorphism, and one asks whether the morphism
\(X \to S\) factors through \(Y\): it suffices that \(X' \to S'\) factor
through \(Y'\).

\textbf{Corollary 2.5.} \emph{Let \(f : S' \to S\) be a universal
effective epimorphism and \(g : S \to T\) a morphism such that
\(S \times_{T} S\) exists. Suppose that \(S'' = S' \times_{S} S'\) is
also a fiber product of \(S'\) with itself over \(T\),
i.e.~\(S' \times_{S} S' \xrightarrow{\sim} S' \times_{T} S'\). Then
\(g : S \to T\) is a monomorphism (and conversely, of course).}

Indeed, consider the cartesian diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S′ ×\_S S′ ⥲ S′ ×\_T S′}
\NormalTok{    ↓             ↓ f}
\NormalTok{    S    →    S ×\_T S,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the second horizontal arrow is the diagonal morphism. By virtue of
1.9 the second vertical arrow \(f\) is a universal effective
epimorphism, by hypothesis the first horizontal arrow is an isomorphism,
hence by virtue of 2.4 a) or b) at one's choice,\footnote{N.D.E.:
  applied to \(f : S' \times_{T} S' \to S \times_{T} S = Y\).} the same
holds for \(S \to S \times_{T} S\), which means precisely that
\(g : S \to T\) is a monomorphism.

\textbf{Remark 2.6.} \emph{The notions introduced in 2.1, in terms of
morphisms between certain inverse limits, become explicit in an obvious
way in terms of the contravariant functors defined by the objects
\(S, S', X'\) under consideration: subject to the existence of the fiber
products envisaged in 2.1, there is a one-to-one correspondence between
gluing data (resp. descent data) on \(X'/S'\) relative to \(S' \to S\),
and gluing data (resp. descent data) for the corresponding objects in
\(\hat{C} = \operatorname{Hom}(C^{\circ}, (Ens))\). This allows one, if
one wishes, to extend these notions to the case where one makes no
hypothesis of existence of fiber products in \(C\).}

\textbf{Remark 2.7.} \emph{The notions introduced in this number
generalize to the case of families of morphisms. They can on the other
hand be presented in a more intrinsic manner using the notion of sieve
(4.1). For these questions, the reader is referred to {[}D{]}.}

\subsection{3. Universal effective equivalence
relations}\label{universal-effective-equivalence-relations}

\subsubsection{3.1. Equivalence relations:
definitions}\label{equivalence-relations-definitions}

\textbf{Definition 3.1.1.} \emph{One calls a} \(C\)-equivalence relation
\emph{in \(X \in Ob C\) a representable subfunctor \(R\) of the functor
\(X \times X\), such that for every \(S \in Ob C\), \(R(S)\) is the
graph of an equivalence relation in \(X(S)\).}

This definition applies in particular to the category \texttt{Ĉ}. If one
considers \(X\) as an object of \texttt{Ĉ}, one then sees that a
\texttt{Ĉ}-equivalence relation in \(X\) is nothing other than a
subfunctor \(R\) of \(X \times X\) such that \(R(S)\) is the graph of an
equivalence relation in \(X(S)\) for every object \(S\) of
\(C\).\footnote{N.D.E.: The condition is evidently necessary.
  Conversely, if for every \(S \in Ob C\), \(R(S)\) is the graph of an
  equivalence relation, then this equivalence relation extends to
  \(R(F)\) for every \(F \in Ob \hat{C}\), by declaring that two
  morphisms \(\phi, \psi : F \to R\) are equivalent if, for every
  \(S \in Ob C\) and \(x \in F(S)\), \(\phi(x)\) and \(\psi(x)\) are
  equivalent in \(X(S)\).}

If \(R\) is a \(C\)-equivalence relation in \(X\), one denotes by
\texttt{pᵢ} the morphism from \(R\) into \(X\) induced by the projection
\(pr_{i} : X \times X \to X\). One thus has a diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p₁, p₂ : R ⇉ X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 3.1.2.} \emph{A morphism \(u : X \to Z\) is said to
be} compatible \emph{with \(R\) if \(up_{1} = up_{2}\). An object of
\(C\) that is a cokernel of the pair \((p_{1}, p_{2})\) is also called
a} quotient object \emph{of \(X\) by \(R\) and denoted \(X/R\).}

One thus has an exact diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⇉\_\{p₁, p₂\} X —p→ X/R}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(X/R\) represents the covariant functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_C(X/R, Z) = \{morphisms from X into Z compatible with R\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since quotient objects have been chosen in \(C\), the quotient \(X/R\)
is unique (when it exists).

These definitions generalize at once to the case of a
\texttt{Ĉ}-equivalence relation in \(X\), but one will notice that the
identification of objects of \(C\) with their images in \texttt{Ĉ} does
not commute with the formation of quotients, that is, the quotient
\(X/R\) of \(X\) by \(R\) in \(C\) is not \emph{a priori} a quotient of
\(X\) by \(R\) in \texttt{Ĉ}. One should therefore guard against rashly
identifying \(C\) with its image in \texttt{Ĉ} in questions involving
passages to the quotient.\footnote{N.D.E.: Let us illustrate this by
  giving an outline of the sequel of this Exposé. Let \(G\) be a
  \(C\)-group, \(H\) a sub-\(C\)-group, \(R\) the equivalence relation
  in \(G\) defined by \(G \times H \to G \times G\),
  \texttt{(g,\ h)\ ⟼\ (g,\ gh)} (cf.~3.2). The functor \(Q\) defined by
  \(Q(S) = G(S)/H(S)\) is a quotient in \texttt{Ĉ} (according to 4.4.9
  applied to the least fine topology, cf.~4.4.2), but it is not in
  general the quotient that one wishes. For example, for \(C = (Sch)\),
  one has an exact sequence of (affine) group schemes:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 ⟶ μ₂ ⟶ G\_m —p→ G\_m ⟶ 1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  which identifies \(G_{m}\) with the quotient \(G_{m}/\mu_{2}\).
  Moreover, since \(p\) is a finite and locally free morphism, then
  \(G_{m}\) is the sheaf-quotient of \(G_{m}\) by \(\mu_{2}\) in the
  larger category of sheaves for the (fppf) topology, cf.~4.6.6 (ii) and
  6.3.2. By contrast, the quotient \(Q\) in \texttt{Ĉ} is not isomorphic
  to \(G_{m}\) since, for example, \(Q(Z) = {1}\) while
  \(G_{m}(Z) = {\pm 1}\). Hence \(Q\) is not an (fppf) sheaf, and
  \emph{a fortiori} \(Q\) is not representable.}

In what follows, we shall say simply \emph{equivalence relation} for
\emph{\texttt{Ĉ}-equivalence relation}; we shall specify, when
appropriate, whether we are dealing with \(C\)-equivalence
relations.\footnote{N.D.E.: Note that, even for a \texttt{Ĉ}-equivalence
  relation in \(X\), one is interested in the existence of a quotient in
  \(C\).}

\textbf{Definition 3.1.3.} \emph{If \(X\) is an object of \(C\) over
\(S\), one calls an} equivalence relation in \(X\) over \(S\) \emph{an
equivalence relation \(R\) in \(X\) such that the structural morphism
\(X \to S\) is compatible with \(R\).}

The canonical monomorphism \(R \to X \times X\) then factors through the
monomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ×\_S X ⟶ X × X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and defines an equivalence relation in the object \(X \to S\) of
\(C/S\). When the quotient \(X/R\) exists, it is endowed with a
canonical morphism into \(S\) and the corresponding object of \(C/S\) is
a quotient of \(X \in Ob C/S\) by the preceding equivalence relation.

Conversely, if \(S\) is a squarable object of \(C\) and if \(Y \to S\)
is a quotient of \(X\) by this equivalence relation (in \(C/S\)), then
\(Y\) is a quotient of \(X\) by \(R\) in \(C\). In any case, we shall
never have to consider quotients in \(C/S\) that are not already
quotients in \(C\).

\textbf{Definition 3.1.4.} \emph{If \(X\) (resp. \(X'\)) is an object of
\(C\) equipped with an equivalence relation \(R\) (resp. \(R'\)), a
morphism}

\[
u : X \to X'
\]

\emph{is said to be} compatible with \(R\) and \(R'\) \emph{if the
following equivalent conditions are satisfied:}

\emph{(i) for every \(S \in Ob C\), two points of \(X(S)\) congruent
modulo \(R(S)\) are transformed by \(u\) into two points of \(X'(S)\)
congruent modulo \(R'(S)\);}

\emph{(ii) there exists a morphism \(R \to R'\) (necessarily unique)
making commutative the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R   →   R′}
\NormalTok{↓        ↓}
\NormalTok{X × X → X′ × X′.}
\NormalTok{        (u × u)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By the universal property of \(X/R\), there then exists (when the
quotients \(X/R\) and \(X'/R'\) exist) a unique morphism \(v\) making
commutative the diagram

\[
X   \xrightarrow{p}  X/R
\downarrow u         \downarrow v
X'  \xrightarrow{p'} X'/R'.
\]

\textbf{Definition 3.1.5.} \emph{A subobject (= a representable
subfunctor) \(Y\) of \(X\) is said to be} stable under the equivalence
relation \(R\) \emph{if the following equivalent conditions are
satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(S \in Ob C\), the subset \(Y(S)\) of \(X(S)\) is
stable under \(R(S)\).}

\emph{(ii) The two subobjects of \(R\) inverse images of \(Y\) under
\(p_{1}\) and \(p_{2}\) are identical.}

An important particular case of stable subobject of \(X\) is the
following: the quotient \(X/R\) exists and \(Y\) is the inverse image on
\(X\) of a subobject of \(X/R\).

\textbf{Definition 3.1.6.} \emph{Let \(R\) be an equivalence relation in
\(X\) and \(X' \to X\) a morphism. The equivalence relation \(R'\) in
\(X'\) obtained by the cartesian diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R′      →    R}
\NormalTok{↓             ↓}
\NormalTok{X′ × X′ →  X × X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is said to be the equivalence relation in \(X'\)} inverse image
\emph{of the equivalence relation \(R\) in \(X\). In particular, if
\(X'\) is a subobject of \(X\), one says it is the equivalence relation}
induced in \(X'\) by \(R\), \emph{and one denotes it \(R_{X'}\).}

The morphism \(X' \to X\) is compatible with \(R'\) and \(R\); one thus
has, when the quotients exist, a morphism \(X'/R' \to X/R\) (3.1.4). If
\(X'\) is a subobject of \(X\), we shall see later that in certain cases
one can prove that \(X'/R' \to X/R\) is a monomorphism, hence identifies
\(X'/R'\) with a subobject of \(X/R\). When this is so, the inverse
image of this subobject in \(X\) will be a subobject of \(X\) containing
\(X'\) and stable under \(R\): the \emph{saturation} of \(X'\) for the
equivalence relation \(R\).

\textbf{Proposition 3.1.7.} \emph{If the subobject \(Y\) of \(X\) is
stable under \(R\), one has two cartesian squares, for \(i = 1, 2\):}

\[
R_{Y}   \to  R
\downarrow p_{i}     \downarrow p_{i}
Y     \to  X.
\]

Immediate proof.

\subsubsection{3.2. Equivalence relation defined by a group acting
freely}\label{equivalence-relation-defined-by-a-group-acting-freely}

\textbf{Definition 3.2.1.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and
\(H\) a \(C\)-group acting on \(X\) (that is, equipped with a morphism
of \texttt{Ĉ}-groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ⟶ Aut(X)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One says that \(H\) acts} freely \emph{on \(X\) if the following
equivalent conditions are satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(S \in Ob C\), the group \(H(S)\) acts freely on
\(X(S)\);}

\emph{(ii) The morphism of functors}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H × X ⟶ X × X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined set-theoretically by \texttt{(h,\ x)\ ⟼\ (hx,\ x)} is a
monomorphism.}

(In the preceding definition, one supposed that the group \(H\) acted
``on the left'' on \(X\). One evidently has an analogous notion in the
case where the group acts ``on the right'', that is, when one is given a
morphism of groups from the group \(H^{\circ}\) opposite to \(H\) into
\(\operatorname{Aut}(X)\)).

If \(H\) acts freely on \(X\), the image of \(H \times X\) under the
morphism of (ii) is an equivalence relation in \(X\) called the
\emph{equivalence relation defined by the action of \(H\) on \(X\)}.
When the quotient of \(X\) by this equivalence relation exists, it is
denoted \(H\backslash X\)

(\(X/H\) when \(H\) acts on the right). It represents the following
covariant functor: if \(Z\) is an object of \(C\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(H\textbackslash{}backslash X, Z) = \{morphisms from X into Z invariant under H\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the morphism \(f : X \to Z\) is said to be \emph{invariant under
\(H\)} if for every \(S \in Ob C\), the corresponding morphism
\(X(S) \to Z(S)\) is invariant under the group \(H(S)\).

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.2.} \emph{Under the conditions of 3.2.1, let \(Y\) be
a subobject of \(X\). The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(Y\) is stable under the equivalence relation defined by
\(H\) (3.1.5);}

\emph{(ii) For every \(S \in Ob C\), the subset \(Y(S)\) of \(X(S)\) is
stable under \(H(S)\);}

\emph{(iii) There exists a morphism \(f\), necessarily unique, making
commutative the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H × Y  —f→  Y}
\NormalTok{↓             ↓}
\NormalTok{H × X   →   X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Under these conditions, \(f\) defines a morphism of
\texttt{Ĉ}-groups}

\[
H \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(Y)
\]

\emph{and the equivalence relation defined in \(Y\) by this action of
\(H\) is none other than the equivalence relation induced in \(Y\) by
the equivalence relation defined in \(X\) by the action of \(H\).}

Immediate proof. One evidently has an analogous statement for a ``right
action''. The action of \(H\) on \(Y\) defined above will be called the
\emph{action induced in \(Y\) by the given action of \(H\) on \(X\)}.

Let us now consider the following situation: \(H\) and \(G\) are two
\(C\)-groups and one is given a morphism of groups

\[
u : H \longrightarrow G.
\]

Then \(H\) acts on \(G\) by translations (one sets set-theoretically
\(hg = u(h)g\)) and acts freely there if and only if \(u\) is a
monomorphism. The quotient of \(G\) by this action of \(H\) is denoted,
when it exists, \(H\backslash G\). One defines similarly a right action
of \(H\) on \(G\) and a quotient \(G/H\). These quotients are functorial
with respect to the groups in question; more precisely, one has the
following lemma, stated for right quotients:

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.3.} \emph{Let \(u : H \to G\) and \(u' : H' \to G'\)
be two monomorphisms of \(C\)-groups. Suppose given a morphism of
\(C\)-groups}

\[
f : G \longrightarrow G'.
\]

\emph{The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(f\) is compatible with the equivalence relations defined in
\(G\) and \(G'\) by \(H\) and \(H'\).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(S \in Ob C\), one has
\(f u(H(S)) \subset u'(H'(S))\).}

\emph{(iii) There exists a morphism \(g : H \to H'\), necessarily unique
and multiplicative, such that the following diagram is commutative}

\[
H  \xrightarrow{g}  H'
\downarrow u        \downarrow u'
G  \xrightarrow{f}  G'.
\]

\emph{Under these conditions, if the quotients \(G/H\) and \(G'/H'\)
exist, there exists a unique morphism \(\bar{f}\) making commutative the
diagram}

\[
G   \xrightarrow{f}   G'
\downarrow p          \downarrow p'
G/H \xrightarrow{\bar{f}}  G'/H'.
\]

The first part is proved by reduction to the set-theoretic case. The
second follows at once from (i).

One could translate to the present situation the notions introduced
above for general equivalence relations. Let us simply signal the
following lemma, whose proof is immediate by reduction to the
set-theoretic case:

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.4.} \emph{Let \(u : H \to G\) be a monomorphism of
\(C\)-groups and \(G'\) a sub-\(C\)-group of \(G\). For the subobject
\(G'\) of \(G\) to be stable under the equivalence relation defined by
\(H\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(u\) factor through the
canonical monomorphism \(G' \to G\), and under this condition the action
of \(H\) on \(G'\) induced by the action of \(H\) on \(G\) defined by
\(u\) is none other than the action deduced from the monomorphism
\(H \to G'\) that factors \(u\).}

\subsubsection{3.3. Universal effective equivalence
relations}\label{universal-effective-equivalence-relations-1}

\textbf{Definition 3.3.1.} \emph{Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a morphism. One
calls the} equivalence relation defined by \(f\) in \(X\), \emph{and
denotes by \(R(f)\), the \texttt{Ĉ}-equivalence relation in \(X\) image
of the canonical monomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ×\_Y X → X × X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 3.3.2.} \emph{Let \(R\) be an equivalence relation in
\(X\). One says that \(R\) is} effective \emph{if}

\emph{(i) \(R\) is representable (i.e.~is a \(C\)-equivalence
relation);}

\emph{(ii) the quotient \(Y = X/R\) exists in \(C\);}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  ``in \(C\)'' has been added.}

\emph{(iii) the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⇉\_\{p₁, p₂\} X —p→ Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{makes \(R\) the fiber square of \(X\) over \(Y\), that is, \(R\)
is the equivalence relation defined by \(p\).}

\textbf{Scholie 3.3.2.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 3.3.2.1 (resp.
  3.3.3.1) has been added for later references. On the other hand,
  Remark 3.3.3.2 has been added.} \emph{If \(R\) is an effective
equivalence relation in \(X\), then \(p\) is an effective epimorphism
(1.3). If \(f : X \to Y\) is an effective epimorphism, then \(R(f)\) is
an effective equivalence relation in \(X\) a quotient of which is \(Y\).
There is therefore a ``Galois'' one-to-one correspondence between
effective equivalence relations in \(X\) and effective quotients of
\(X\) (i.e.~equivalence classes of effective epimorphisms with source
\(X\)).}

\textbf{Definition 3.3.3.} \emph{One says that the equivalence relation
\(R\) in \(X\) is} universally effective \emph{if the quotient
\(Y = X/R\) exists, and if, for every \(Y' \to Y\), the fiber products
\(X' = X \times_{Y} Y'\) and \(R' = R \times_{Y} Y'\) exist and \(R'\)
is a fiber square of \(X'\) over \(Y'\). It amounts to the same to say
that \(R\) is effective and that \(p : X \to X/R\) is a universal
effective epimorphism.}

\textbf{Scholie 3.3.3.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 3.3.2.1 (resp.
  3.3.3.1) has been added for later references. On the other hand,
  Remark 3.3.3.2 has been added.} \emph{There is therefore, as above, a
one-to-one correspondence between universal effective equivalence
relations in \(X\) and universal effective quotients of \(X\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.3.3.2.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 3.3.2.1 (resp.
  3.3.3.1) has been added for later references. On the other hand,
  Remark 3.3.3.2 has been added.} \emph{Suppose that \(C\) is the
category of \(S\)-schemes and let \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) denote the affine
space of dimension 1 over \(S\). Let \(R \subset X \times_{S} X\) be a
universal effective equivalence relation and \(p : X \to Y\) the
quotient. Then, for every open \(U\) of \(Y\),
\(O(U) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(U, \mathbb{A}^{1}_{S})\) is the set of
elements \(\phi\) of
\(O(p^{-1}(U)) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(p^{-1}(U), \mathbb{A}^{1}_{S})\)
such that \(\phi \circ pr_{1} = \phi \circ pr_{2}\). In particular, if
\(R\) is given by the action of a group \(H\) acting freely on the right
on \(X\) (cf.~3.2.1), then \(O(U)\) is the set of
\(\phi \in O(p^{-1}(U))\) such that \(\phi(xh) = \phi(x)\), for every
\(S' \to S\) and \(x \in X(S')\), \(h \in H(S')\).}

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.4.} \emph{Let \(R\) be a universal effective
equivalence relation in \(X\). Let \(f : X \to Z\) be a morphism
compatible with \(R\), hence factoring through \(g : X/R \to Z\). The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(g\) is a monomorphism;}

\emph{(ii) \(R\) is the equivalence relation defined by \(f\).}

Indeed, (i) trivially entails (ii); the converse is none other than 2.5.

\textbf{Definition 3.3.5.} \emph{Let \(H\) be a \(C\)-group acting
freely on \(X\). One says that \(H\) acts} effectively, \emph{or that
the action of \(H\) on \(X\) is} effective \emph{(resp.} universally
effective*), if the equivalence relation defined in \(X\) by the action
of \(H\) is effective (resp. universally effective).*

\subsubsection{3.4. (M)-effectivity}\label{m-effectivity}

In practice, it is most often difficult to characterize universal
effective epimorphisms. One often disposes, nevertheless, of a certain
number of morphisms of this type, for example in scheme theory, of
faithfully flat quasi-compact morphisms. This leads to the developments
below.

\textbf{3.4.1.} Let us first state a certain number of conditions
bearing on a family \texttt{(M)} of morphisms of \(C\):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\item
  \texttt{(M)} is stable under extension of the base, i.e., every
  \(u : T \to S\) element of \texttt{(M)} is squarable (cf.~1.4.0) and
  for every \(S' \to S\), \(u' : T \times_{S} S' \to S'\) is an element
  of \texttt{(M)}.
\item
  The composite of two elements of \texttt{(M)} is in \texttt{(M)}.
\item
  Every isomorphism is an element of \texttt{(M)}.
\item
  Every element of \texttt{(M)} is an effective epimorphism.
\end{enumerate}

Note that (a) and (b) entail:

(a′) The cartesian product of two elements of \texttt{(M)} is in
\texttt{(M)}: let \(u : X \to Y\) and \(u' : X' \to Y'\) be two
\(S\)-morphisms, elements of \texttt{(M)}. If \(Y \times_{S} Y'\)
exists, then \(X \times_{S} X'\) exists and \(u \times_{S} u'\) is an
element of \texttt{(M)}.

This follows from the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y′    ⇇    X′}
\NormalTok{↑           ↑u′}
\NormalTok{X  ⇇  X ×\_S Y′  ⇇  X ×\_S X′}
\NormalTok{↑u                   ↘ u×\_S u′}
\NormalTok{Y  ⇇  Y ×\_S Y′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Likewise (a) and (d) entail:

(d′) Every element of \texttt{(M)} is a universal effective epimorphism.

\textbf{3.4.2.} The family \((M_{0})\) of universal effective
epimorphisms satisfies the conditions (a) through (d) of 3.4.1. Indeed,
(a), (c) and (d) are satisfied by definition, (b) follows from 1.8. In
what follows, we shall suppose given a family \texttt{(M)} of morphisms
of \(C\) satisfying these conditions: our results will therefore apply
in particular to the family \((M_{0})\).

\textbf{Definition 3.4.3.} \emph{One says that the equivalence relation
\(R\) in \(X\) is of} type \texttt{(M)} \emph{if it is representable and
if \(p_{1} \in (M)\) (which by (b) and (c) entails that
\(p_{2} \in (M)\)).}

\emph{One says that \(R\) is} \texttt{(M)}-effective \emph{if it is
effective and if the canonical morphism \(X \to X/R\) is an element of
\texttt{(M)}.}

\emph{One says that the quotient \(Y\) of \(X\) is}
\texttt{(M)}-effective \emph{if the canonical morphism \(X \to Y\) is an
element of \texttt{(M)}.}

The following consequences result from this definition:\footnote{N.D.E.:
  The numbering 3.4.3.1 has been added for later references, and the
  proof of point (i) has been detailed.}

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.3.1.} \emph{(i) An \texttt{(M)}-effective
equivalence relation is of type \texttt{(M)} and universally effective.}

\emph{(ii) An \texttt{(M)}-effective quotient is universally effective
(cf.~3.3.3).}

\emph{(iii) The maps \texttt{R\ ⟼\ X/R} and \texttt{p\ ⟼\ R(p)} realize
a one-to-one correspondence between \texttt{(M)}-effective equivalence
relations in \(X\) and \texttt{(M)}-effective quotients of \(X\).}

\emph{(iv) \((M_{0})\)-effective is equivalent to universally
effective.}

Let us prove point (i). Since \(R\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective, one has a
cartesian square

\[
R   \xrightarrow{p_{2}}  X
\downarrow p_{1}          \downarrow p
X   \xrightarrow{p}   X/R,
\]

and \(p \in (M)\). Then, by 3.4.1 (a), \(p_{1}\) and \(p_{2}\) belong to
\texttt{(M)}, hence \(R\) is of type \texttt{(M)}.

Set \(Y = X/R\) and let \(Y' \to Y\) be an arbitrary morphism. By 3.4.1
(a), the fiber products \(X' = X \times_{Y} Y'\) and
\(R' = R \times_{Y} Y'\) exist and the morphisms \(X' \to Y'\) and
\(p'_{i} : R' \to X'\) belong to \texttt{(M)}. Finally, since
\(R = X \times_{Y} X\), one obtains, by associativity of the fiber
product:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R′ = X ×\_Y X ×\_Y Y′ = X′ ×\_\{Y′\} X′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This shows that \(R'\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective; hence in particular,
\(R\) is universally effective. This proves (i), and also (iv). Points
(ii) and (iii) follow from this, taking account of Definition 3.3.2.

\textbf{3.4.4.} Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-group whose structural morphism is
an element of \texttt{(M)}. Then if \(H\) acts freely on the
\(S\)-object \(X\), it defines an equivalence relation of type
\texttt{(M)}. Indeed, by (a) the fiber product \(H \times_{S} X\) exists
and \(pr_{2} : H \times_{S} X \to X\) is an element of \texttt{(M)}. One
says that the action of \(H\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective if the
equivalence relation defined in \(X\) by this action is
\texttt{(M)}-effective.

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.5 ((M)-effectivity and base change).} \emph{Let
\(R\) be an \texttt{(M)}-effective equivalence relation in \(X\) over
\(S\). Set \(Y = X/R\). Let \(S' \to S\) be a change of base such that
\(Y' = Y \times_{S} S'\) exists. Then \(X' = X \times_{S} S'\) exists,
\(R' = R \times_{S} S'\) is an \texttt{(M)}-effective equivalence
relation in \(X'\) over \(S'\) and \(X'/R' \simeq (X/R)'\).}

Indeed, the canonical morphisms \(X \to Y\) and \(R \to Y\) are elements
of \texttt{(M)}, hence by (a′) \(X'\) and \(R'\) are representable. By
associativity of the product, \(R'\) is the equivalence relation defined
in \(X'\) by the canonical morphism \(X' \to Y'\) which is an element of
\texttt{(M)}, whence the conclusion.

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.6 ((M)-effectivity and cartesian products).}
\emph{Let \(R\) (resp. \(R'\)) be an \texttt{(M)}-effective equivalence
relation in \(X\) (resp. \(X'\)) over \(S\). If
\((X/R) \times_{S} (X'/R')\) exists, then \(X \times_{S} X'\) exists,
\(R \times_{S} R'\) is an \texttt{(M)}-effective equivalence relation in
\(X \times_{S} X'\) over \(S\) and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X ×\_S X′)/(R ×\_S R′) ≃ (X/R) ×\_S (X′/R′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set \(Y = X/R\), \(Y' = X'/R'\). By (a′), the fiber product
\(X \times_{S} X'\) exists and the canonical morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{q : X ×\_S X′ → Y ×\_S Y′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an element of \texttt{(M)}. Now the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X ×\_S X′) ×\_\{(Y ×\_S Y′)\} (X ×\_S X′) ≃ (X ×\_Y X) ×\_S (X′ ×\_\{Y′\} X′)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(all products without subscript are taken over \(S\)) shows that
\(R \times_{S} R'\) is the equivalence relation defined by \(q\) in
\(X \times_{S} X'\), which completes the proof.

\textbf{3.4.7.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This paragraph has been added.} Suppose
that \(C\) has a final object \(e\) and let \(f : G \to G'\) be a
morphism of \(C\)-groups, such that \(f \in (M)\). Then, by 3.4.1 (a),
the kernel \(Ker(f)\) is representable by \(e \times_{G'} G\), and the
morphism \(Ker(f) \to e\) belongs to \texttt{(M)}.

On the other hand, the equivalence relation defined by \(f\) is the same
as that defined by the action of \(Ker(f)\) (say, on the right) on
\(G\), i.e., it is the image of the morphism
\(G \times Ker(f) \to G \times G\), defined set-theoretically by
\texttt{(g,\ h)\ ⟼\ (g,\ gh)}. Consequently, one deduces from 3.3.2.1
the following corollary:

\textbf{Corollary 3.4.7.1.} \emph{Suppose that \(C\) has a final object
\(e\) and let \(f : G \to G'\) be a morphism of \(C\)-groups, such that
\(f \in (M)\). Then the action of \(Ker(f)\) on \(G\) is
\texttt{(M)}-effective and \(G'\) is the quotient \(G/Ker(f)\).}

\subsubsection{3.5. Construction of quotients by
descent}\label{construction-of-quotients-by-descent}

It frequently happens that one does not know how to construct a quotient
directly, but that one does know how to do so after a suitable change of
base. The present number gives a criterion useful in this situation.

We have seen in §2.1 the definition of a descent datum on an object
\(X'\) over \(S'\) relative to a morphism \(S' \to S\).

\textbf{Definition 3.5.1.} \emph{One says that a descent datum on \(X'\)
relative to \(S' \to S\) is} effective \emph{if \(X'\) equipped with
this descent datum is isomorphic to the inverse image on \(S'\) of an
object \(X\) over \(S\), equipped with its canonical descent datum.}

If \(S' \to S\) is a descent morphism (2.2), then the \(X\) of the
definition is unique up to unique isomorphism. To say that \(S' \to S\)
is an effective descent morphism (2.2), is to say that it is a descent
morphism and that every descent datum relative to this morphism is
effective.

Consider now an equivalence relation \(R\) in an object \(X\) over
\(S\). Let \(X'\) (resp. \(X''\), resp. \(X'''\)) be the inverse images
of \(X\) on \(S'\), \(S'' = S' \times_{S} S'\) and
\(S''' = S' \times_{S} S' \times_{S} S'\) and let \(R', R'', R'''\) be
the equivalence relations deduced from \(R\) by inverse image. Suppose
that the equivalence relation \(R'\) in \(X'\) is
\texttt{(M)}-effective, and consider the quotient \(Y' = X'/R'\), which
is an object over \(S'\). Its two inverse images on \(S''\) are
isomorphic to \(X''/R''\) by 3.4.5. The \(S'\)-object \(Y'\) is
therefore endowed with a canonical gluing datum. Using likewise the
uniqueness of \(X'''/R'''\), one sees that this is even a descent datum.
(Remark: it has been implicitly supposed in this proof that all the
fiber products written existed, which is the case in particular if
\(S' \to S\) is squarable, for example a descent morphism).

\textbf{Proposition 3.5.2.} \emph{Let \(R\) be an equivalence relation
in the object \(X\) over \(S\). Let \(S' \to S\) be a universal
effective epimorphism. Suppose that every \(S\)-morphism whose inverse
image on \(S'\) is in \texttt{(M)} is itself in \texttt{(M)}. The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(R\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective in \(X\);}

\emph{(ii) \(R'\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective in \(X'\) and the canonical
descent datum on \(X'/R'\) is effective.}

\emph{If this is so, the ``descended'' object of \(X'/R'\) is
canonically isomorphic to \(X/R\).}

The fact that (i) entails (ii) is none other than the translation, in
the language of descent, of 3.4.4. If one shows the converse, the last
assertion of the proposition will be a consequence of the fact that a
universal effective epimorphism is a descent morphism (2.3), hence that
the ``descended object'' is unique (up to unique isomorphism).

So let us prove (ii) ⇒ (i). Let \(Y'\) be the quotient \(X'/R'\) and
\(Y\) the descended object. As the canonical morphism
\(p' : X' \to X'/R' = Y'\) is by construction compatible with the
descent data (its inverse images on \(S''\) coincide with the canonical
morphism \(X'' \to X''/R''\)), it comes by inverse image on \(S'\) from
an \(S\)-morphism \(p : X \to Y\). Since \(p'\) is an element of
\texttt{(M)}, it follows from the hypothesis made on the morphism
\(S' \to S\) that \(p\) is also an element of \texttt{(M)}. As \(p'\) is
compatible with the equivalence relation \(R'\), \(p\) is compatible
with \(R\), again because a universal effective epimorphism is a descent
morphism. One thus has a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⟶ X ×\_Y X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To prove that \(R\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective and that \(Y\) is
isomorphic to \(X/R\), it suffices to prove that this morphism is an
isomorphism. Now it becomes one by extension of the base from \(S\) to
\(S'\), since \(R'\) is effective; it is therefore an isomorphism for
the same reason as before (2.4).

Note that the hypothesis of the text is satisfied if one takes for
\texttt{(M)} the family \((M_{0})\) of universal effective epimorphisms
and if \(C\) has fiber products (1.10). One deduces the

\textbf{Corollary 3.5.3.} \emph{Suppose that \(C\) has fiber products
(over \(S\) would suffice). Let \(R\) be an equivalence relation in
\(X\) over \(S\) and \(S' \to S\) a universal effective epimorphism. The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(R\) is universally effective in \(X\),}

\emph{(ii) \(R'\) is universally effective in \(X'\) and the canonical
descent datum on \(X'/R'\) is effective.}

\emph{If this is so, the ``descended'' object of \(X'/R'\) is
canonically isomorphic to \(X/R\).}

\subsection{4. Topologies and sheaves}\label{topologies-and-sheaves}

The notion of sieve, and the presentation of the notion of topology
(4.2.1) adopted here (more intrinsic and in many respects more
convenient than the one by covering families of {[}MA{]}), are due to J.
Giraud {[}AS{]}.

\subsubsection{4.1. Sieves}\label{sieves}

\textbf{Definition 4.1.1.} \emph{One calls a} sieve \emph{of the
category \(C\) a subfunctor \(C\) of the final functor
\(e : C^{\circ} \to (Ens)\).}

To every sieve \(C\) of \(C\) one associates the set \(E(C)\) of objects
\(X\) of \(C\) such that \(C(X) \neq \emptyset\), that is, such that the
structural morphism \(X \to e\) factors through \(C\). One thus has the
equivalences

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)   X ∈ E(C) ⟺ C(X) = e(X) = \{∅\}.}
\NormalTok{      X ∉ E(C) ⟺ C(X) = ∅.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The set \(E = E(C)\) enjoys the following property:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(++)   If X ∈ E and if Hom(Y, X) ≠ ∅, then Y ∈ E.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(Note that if one equips the set \texttt{Ob\ C} with its natural
preorder structure (\(Y\) dominating \(X\) if there exists an arrow from
\(Y\) into \(X\)), the sets \(E\) satisfying (++) are the subsets of
\texttt{Ob\ C} that contain every dominator\footnote{N.D.E.: Here,
  ``dominator'' is taken in the sense of the preorder relation mentioned
  above, i.e., \(Y\) dominates \(X\) if there exists an arrow
  \(Y \to X\). On the other hand, if \texttt{X,\ Y} are two subobjects
  of an object \(Z\), one says (cf.~2.4) that \(Y\) contains \(X\) if
  \(X \subset Y\). To avoid any ambiguity between these two
  terminologies, ``majorant'' has been replaced in the sequel by
  ``dominating'' in the first case, and by ``containing'', in the
  second.} of one of their elements.)

Conversely, if \(E\) is a subset of \texttt{Ob\ C} enjoying property
(++), then \(E\) is written in a unique way in the form \(E(C)\) and
\(C\) is defined by the formulas (+). There is therefore a one-to-one
correspondence between sieves of \(C\) and subsets of \texttt{Ob\ C}
satisfying condition (++). By abuse of language, we shall sometimes say
that the set \(E(C)\) is a sieve of \(C\).

\footnote{N.D.E.: The sentence that follows has been detailed.} Let
\(C\) and \(C'\) be two sieves of \(C\); since they are two subfunctors
of the final functor \(e\), it amounts to the same to say that \(C\)
dominates \(C'\) (for the relation of domination in \(Ob \hat{C}\)), or
that \(C\) is a subfunctor of \(C'\), or yet that
\(E(C) \subset E(C')\); one then says that \(C\) is \emph{finer} than
\(C'\). One sees that this gives an order structure on the set of sieves
of \(C\). Furthermore, one has \(E(C) \cap E(C') = E(C \times C')\) and
therefore the set of sieves of \(C\) is filtered for the order relation
``being finer''.

Every subset \(E\) of \(Ob \hat{C}\), for example a subset of
\texttt{Ob\ C}, defines a sieve \(C(E)\): the set of \(X \in Ob C\) such
that \(F(X) \neq \emptyset\) for at least one \(F \in E\) satisfies
condition (++) and defines the sought sieve.

This sieve can also be defined as the image of the family of morphisms
\({F \to e, F \in E}\) in the sense of the following definition:

\textbf{Definition 4.1.2.} \emph{Let \({F_{i} \to F}\) be a family of
morphisms of \texttt{Ĉ} with the same target \(F\). One calls} image
\emph{of this family the subfunctor of \(F\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S ⟼ ⋃ᵢ Im Fᵢ(S) ⊂ F(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.3.} \emph{The formation of the image commutes
with base extension: in the preceding notation, denote by \(I\) the
image of the family \({F_{i} \to F}\); for every}

\emph{morphism \(G \to F\) of \texttt{Ĉ}, the image of the family of
morphisms \({F_{i} \times_{F} G \to G}\) is the subfunctor
\(I \times_{F} G\) of \(G\).}

\textbf{Definition 4.1.4.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 4.1.4.0 has
  been added in order to highlight this definition.} \emph{Let \(C\) be
a sieve of \(C\). If \(E\) is a subset of \texttt{Ob\ C} such that
\(C(E) = C\), one says that \(E\) is a} base \emph{of \(C\). Every sieve
\(C\) has a base, for example the set \(E(C)\).}

We propose to describe the set \(\operatorname{Hom}(C, F)\), where \(C\)
is a sieve of \(C\) and \(F\) an object of \texttt{Ĉ}, using a base
\({S_{i}}\) of \(C\). For each pair \((i, j)\), one has a diagram in
\texttt{Ĉ}:

\[
S_{i} \times S_{j} \to S_{i}
\downarrow           \downarrow
S_{j}      \to  e,
\]

whence a diagram of sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ(F) = Hom(e, F) —σ→ ∏ᵢ Hom(Sᵢ, F) ⇉\_\{τ₁, τ₂\} ∏\_\{i,j\} Hom(Sᵢ × Sⱼ, F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \(\tau_{1}\sigma = \tau_{2}\sigma\). One thus has a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(e, F) ⟶ Ker(∏ᵢ Hom(Sᵢ, F) ⇉ ∏\_\{i,j\} Hom(Sᵢ × Sⱼ, F)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One verifies immediately:

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.4.} \emph{One has an isomorphism, functorial in
\(F\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(C, F) ⥲ Ker(∏ᵢ Hom(Sᵢ, F) ⇉ ∏\_\{i,j\} Hom(Sᵢ × Sⱼ, F)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(e, F) → Ker(∏ᵢ Hom(Sᵢ, F) ⇉ ∏\_\{i,j\} Hom(Sᵢ × Sⱼ, F))}
\NormalTok{                        ↑ ≀}
\NormalTok{Hom(e, F) →            Hom(C, F),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where the last line is induced by the canonical morphism
\(C \to e\), is commutative.}

\textbf{Corollary 4.1.5.} \emph{Suppose that the fiber products
\(S_{i} \times S_{j}\) are representable, for example}

\emph{that the \texttt{Sᵢ} are squarable. One then has, for every
\(F \in Ob \hat{C}\), an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(C, F) ⥲ Ker(∏ᵢ F(Sᵢ) ⇉ ∏\_\{i,j\} F(Sᵢ × Sⱼ)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 4.1.6.} \emph{Let \(R\) be a sieve of \(C\); denote by
\(\bar{R}\) the full subcategory of \(C\) whose set of objects is
\(E(R)\) and by}

\[
i_{R} : \bar{R} \longrightarrow C
\]

\emph{the inclusion functor. One has an isomorphism, functorial in
\(F \in Ob \hat{C}\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(R, F) ⥲ Γ(F ∘ i\_R)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(e, F)  →  Hom(R, F)}
\NormalTok{   ↕ ≀          ↕ ≀}
\NormalTok{   Γ(F)    →  Γ(F ∘ i\_R),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where the second line is induced by the functor \(i_{R}\), is
commutative.}

\textbf{Definition 4.1.7.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category. One calls a}
sieve of the object \(S\) of \(C\) \emph{a sieve of the category
\(C/S\).}

A sieve of \(S\) is therefore a sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-object of \(S\). To it
corresponds canonically a subset of \(Ob C/S\) containing the source of
every arrow whose target it contains. By abuse of language, such a set
will also be called a sieve of \(S\).

\subsubsection{4.2. Topologies:
definitions}\label{topologies-definitions}

\textbf{Definition 4.2.1.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category. One calls a}
topology \emph{on \(C\) the datum, for each \(S\) of \(C\), of a set
\(J(S)\) of sieves of \(S\), called} covering sieves \emph{or}
refinements \emph{of \(S\),}

\emph{the datum satisfying the following axioms:}

\emph{(T 1) For every refinement \(R\) of \(S\) and every morphism
\(T \to S\), the sieve \(R \times_{S} T\) of \(T\) is covering
(``stability under base change'').}

\emph{(T 2) If \texttt{R,\ C} are two sieves of \(S\), if \(R\) is
covering, and if for every \(T \in Ob C\) and every morphism
\(T \to R\), the sieve \(C \times_{S} T\) of \(T\) is covering, then
\(C\) is a refinement of \(S\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: that is: if \(C\) is
  covering ``locally with respect to the covering sieve \(R\)'', then
  \(C\) is covering.}

\emph{(T 3) If \(C \supset R\) are two sieves of \(S\) and if \(R\) is
covering, then \(C\) is covering.}

\emph{(T 4) For every \(S\), \(S\) is a refinement of \(S\).}

One can reformulate these axioms in the following way. Suppose given a
topology \texttt{S\ ⟼\ J(S)} on \(C\) and, for every object \(F\) of
\texttt{Ĉ}, denote by \(J(F)\) the set of subfunctors \(R\) of \(F\)
such that for every morphism \(T \to F\) of \texttt{Ĉ} where \(T\) is
representable, \(R \times_{F} T\), which is a sieve of \(T\), is
covering. By virtue of (T 1), this notation is compatible with the
preceding one. One will also say that \(R \in J(F)\) is a
\emph{refinement} of \(F\). One verifies immediately that the preceding
axioms entail the following properties:

(T′ 0) If \(F \supset G\) are two objects of \texttt{Ĉ}, and if for
every \(S \in Ob C\) and every morphism \(S \to F\),
\(G \times_{F} S \in J(S)\), then \(G \in J(F)\).

(T′ 1) If \(G \in J(F)\), and if \(H \to F\) is a morphism of
\texttt{Ĉ}, then \(G \times_{F} H \in J(H)\).

(T′ 2) If \(F \supset G \supset H\) are three objects of \texttt{Ĉ}, if
\(G \in J(F)\) and \(H \in J(G)\), then \(H \in J(F)\).

(T′ 3) If \(F \supset G \supset H\) are three objects of \texttt{Ĉ} and
if \(H \in J(F)\), then \(G \in J(F)\).

(T′ 4) For every \(F \in Ob \hat{C}\), \(F \in J(F)\).

Conversely, if one gives oneself, for every \(F \in Ob \hat{C}\), a set
\(J(F)\) of subobjects of \(F\) satisfying the properties (T′ 0) through
(T′ 4), the map \texttt{S\ ⟼\ J(S)} defines a topology on \(C\) and the
two preceding constructions are inverse to each other.

From (T′ 1), (T′ 2) and (T′ 3)\footnote{N.D.E.: (T′ 1) and (T′ 2)
  suffice: \(G \cap H = G \times_{F} H\) belongs to \(J(H)\), by (T′ 1),
  hence to \(J(F)\), by (T′ 2).} results the following property:

(T′ 5) If \(G\) and \(H\) are two subobjects of \(F\) and if
\(G, H \in J(F)\), then \(G \cap H \in J(F)\).

The set \(J(F)\), ordered by the relation \(\supset\), is therefore
filtered; this remark will be useful later.

\textbf{4.2.2.} One says that the topology defined by \(J\) is
\emph{finer} than the topology defined by \(J'\) if for every
\(S \in Ob C\), \(J(S) \supset J'(S)\) (it amounts to the same to say
that for every \(F \in Ob \hat{C}\), \(J(F) \supset J'(F)\)).

Every set of topologies on \(C\) has a greatest lower bound: let \(I\)
be an indexing set, and for each \(i \in I\), let \texttt{S\ ⟼\ Jᵢ(S)}
be a topology on \(C\). Set \(J(S) = \bigcap_{i\in I} J_{i}(S)\); it is
immediate that one has thus defined a topology on \(C\), and that this
is indeed the greatest lower bound of the given set.

In particular, let us give ourselves, for each \(S \in Ob C\), a set
\(E(S)\) of sieves of \(S\). One calls the \emph{topology generated by
these sets} the least fine topology for which the elements of \(E(S)\)
are refinements of \(S\) for every \(S\).

\textbf{Definition 4.2.3.} \emph{Let \({F_{i} \to F}\) be a family of
morphisms of \texttt{Ĉ}. Let \(G \subset F\) be the image (4.1.2) of
this family. The family is said to be} covering \emph{if \(G \in J(F)\).
A morphism is said to be covering if the family reduced to this morphism
is covering.}

This definition applies in particular to an inclusion: a sieve \(C\) of
\(S\) is covering if and only if the canonical morphism \(C \to S\) is
covering.

The axioms (T′ 0) through (T′ 5) entail for covering families the
following properties:

(C 0) Let \({F_{i} \to F}\) be a family of morphisms of \texttt{Ĉ}. If
for every representable base change \(S \to F\), the family
\({F_{i} \times_{F} S \to S}\) is covering, then so is the initial
family.

(C 1) For every covering family \({F_{i} \to F}\) and every morphism
\(G \to F\), the family \({F_{i} \times_{F} G \to G}\) is covering
(``stability under base change'').

(C 2) If \({F_{i} \to F}\) is a covering family and if, for each \(i\),
\({F_{ij} \to F_{i}}\) is a covering family, then the composite family
\({F_{ij} \to F}\) is covering (``stability under composition'').

(C 3) If \({G_{j} \to F}\) is a covering family, and if
\({F_{i} \to F}\) is a family of morphisms with target \(F\) such that
for each \(j\) there exists an \(i\) such that \(G_{j} \to F\) factors
through \(F_{i} \to F\), then \({F_{i} \to F}\) is covering
(``saturation'').

(C 4) Every family reduced to an isomorphism is covering.

Note that (C 2) and (C 3) also entail:

(C 5) If \({F_{i} \to F}\) is a family of morphisms with target \(F\)
such that there exists a covering family \({G_{j} \to F}\) such that for
every \(j\) the family \({F_{i} \times_{F} G_{j} \to G_{j}}\) is
covering, then the family \({F_{i} \to F}\) is covering (``a locally
covering family is covering'').

\textbf{4.2.4.} Conversely, let \(C\) be a category having fiber
products and let us give ourselves, for each \(S \in Ob C\), a set of
families of morphisms of \(C\) with target \(S\), said to be
\emph{covering families}, the datum satisfying axioms (C 1) through (C
4) (hence also (C 5) which is a consequence). For every \(S \in Ob C\),
let \(J(S)\) be the set

of sieves of \(S\) having a covering base (or, what amounts to the same
by (C 3), all of whose bases are covering). Then \texttt{S\ ⟼\ J(S)}
defines a topology on \(C\). The two preceding constructions are inverse
to each other.

In fact, in applications, it is impractical to consider all covering
families, since one sometimes has fairly simple descriptions of a
``sufficient'' number of such families. This leads to posing the
following definitions.

\textbf{Definition 4.2.5.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This definition has been
  placed here (placed in the original after 4.2.5), since it will be
  used in 6.2.1 in a slightly more general setting than that of 4.2.5.}
\emph{Let \(C\) be a category. Suppose given, for each \(S \in Ob C\), a
set \(P(S)\) of families of morphisms of \(C\) with target \(S\). One
calls the} topology generated by \(P\) \emph{the least fine topology for
which the given families are covering.}

\textbf{Definition 4.2.5.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category. One calls a}
pretopology \emph{on \(C\) the datum for each \(S \in Ob C\) of a set
\(R(S)\) of families of morphisms \({S_{i} \to S}\) with target \(S\),
said to be} covering for the pretopology under consideration,
\emph{satisfying the following axioms:}

\emph{(P 1) For every family \({S_{i} \to S} \in R(S)\) and every
morphism \(T \to S\), the fiber products \(S_{i} \times_{S} T\) exist
and \({S_{i} \times_{S} T \to T} \in R(T)\).}

\emph{(P 2) If \({S_{i} \to S} \in R(S)\) and if for each \(i\),
\({T_{ij} \to S_{i}} \in R(S_{i})\), then the composite family
\({T_{ij} \to S}\) belongs to \(R(S)\).}

\emph{(P 3) Every family reduced to an isomorphism is covering.}

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.6.} \emph{For every \(S\), let \(J(S)\) be the
set of sieves of \(S\) covering for the topology generated by the
pretopology \(R\). Let \(J_{R}(S)\) be the part of \(J(S)\) formed by
the sieves defined by the families of \(R(S)\). Then \(J_{R}(S)\) is
cofinal in \(J(S)\): every refinement of \(S\) contains a sieve defined
by a family of \(R(S)\).}

For every \(S\), let \(J'(S)\) be the set of sieves of \(S\) containing
a sieve of \(J_{R}(S)\). One evidently has \(J'(S) \subset J(S)\). To
show that \(J(S) = J'(S)\), it suffices to show that the \(J'(S)\) make
a topology on \(C\), that is, that they satisfy axioms (T 1) through (T
4). Now (T 1), (T 3), (T 4) are evidently satisfied. It remains to
verify (T 2).\footnote{N.D.E.: in what follows, typographical errors of
  the original have been corrected.}

So let \(U\) be an element of \(J'(S)\) and \(C\) a sieve of \(S\); one
supposes that for every \(T \to U\), the sieve \(C \times_{S} T\) is in
\(J'(T)\) and one must prove that \(C \in J'(S)\). By definition of
\(J'\), \(U\) contains a refinement \(U'\) defined by a family
\({S_{i} \to S} \in R(S)\). Since one has verified (T 3), it suffices to
prove that \(U' \cap C \in J'(S)\), so one may suppose that \(U = U'\).
By hypothesis, for every \(i\), \(C \times_{S} S_{i} \in J'(S_{i})\);
there therefore exists, for each \(i\), a covering family
\({T_{ij} \to S_{i}} \in R(S_{i})\) such that \(T_{ij} \to S_{i}\)
factors through \(C \times_{S} S_{i} \to S_{i}\). The morphism
\(T_{ij} \to S\) therefore factors through \(C \to S\), which shows that
\(C\) contains the sieve defined by the composite family
\({T_{ij} \to S}\), and one has finished by (P 2).

The axioms (P 1) through (P 3) are those of {[}MA{]}. Given the
practical interest of pretopologies, we shall interpret each important
result with the aid of a pretopology defining the given topology.

\textbf{Remark 4.2.7.} \emph{One can introduce a somewhat more general
notion: one gives, for each \(S\), a set of covering families satisfying
(P 1), (P 3) and Proposition 4.2.6. This presents itself in particular
when the given families satisfy (P 1), (P 3) and (C 5). The reader may
consult {[}D{]}.}

\textbf{Definition 4.2.8.} \emph{Let \(C\) be equipped with a topology,
and let \(S\) be an object of \(C\). Let \(P(S')\) be a relation
involving an argument \(S' \in Ob C/S\). Suppose that
\(\operatorname{Hom}(S'', S') \neq \emptyset\) entails
\(P(S') \Rightarrow P(S'')\). One says that \(P\) is true} locally on
\(S\) \emph{for the topology under consideration, if the following
equivalent conditions are satisfied:}

\emph{(i) The set of \(S' \to S\) such that \(P(S')\) is true is a
refinement of \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) There exists a refinement of \(S\) such that \(P(S')\) is
true for every \(S'\) of this refinement.}

\emph{(iii) (If the given topology is defined by a pretopology). There
exists a covering family for this pretopology such that \(P(S')\) is
true for every \(S'\) of this family.}

\textbf{Example 4.2.9.} \emph{Let \(f : X \to Y\) be an \(S\)-morphism.
One will say that \(f\) is} locally an isomorphism \emph{if there exists
a covering family \({S_{i} \to S}\) such that for every \(i\),
\(f \times_{S} S_{i}\)}

\emph{is an isomorphism. It amounts to the same to require that there
exist a refinement \(R\) of \(S\) such that for every \(T \to R\),
\(X(T) \to Y(T)\) is an isomorphism.}

One will see in the sequel many other examples of ``local'' language.

\subsubsection{4.3. Presheaves, sheaves, sheaf associated to a
presheaf}\label{presheaves-sheaves-sheaf-associated-to-a-presheaf}

\textbf{Definition 4.3.1.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category. One calls a}
presheaf of sets \emph{on \(C\) any contravariant functor from \(C\)
into the category of sets. The category
\(\hat{C} = \operatorname{Hom}(C^{\circ}, (Ens))\) is called the}
category of presheaves \emph{on \(C\). If \(C\) is equipped with a
topology, one says that the presheaf \(P\) is} separated \emph{(resp.}
is a sheaf*) if for every \(S \in Ob C\) and every \(R \in J(S)\), the
canonical map*

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    P(S) = Hom(S, P) ⟶ Hom(R, P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is injective (resp. bijective). One calls} category of sheaves,
\emph{and denotes by \(\tilde{C}\), the full subcategory of \texttt{Ĉ}
whose objects are the sheaves.}\footnote{N.D.E.: One will note that if
  \(Q\) is a subpresheaf of a separated presheaf \(P\), then \(Q\) is
  separated. Indeed, for every sieve \(R\) of \(S\), the composite map
  \(Q(S) \hookrightarrow P(S) \hookrightarrow P(R)\) is injective and
  factors through \(Q(S) \to Q(R)\).}

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.2.} \emph{Let \(P\) be a separated presheaf
(resp. a sheaf). For every functor \(H \in Ob \hat{C}\) and every
\(R \in J(H)\), the canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    Hom(H, P) ⟶ Hom(R, P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is injective (resp. bijective).}

Indeed, let \(P\) be a separated presheaf, \(H\) a presheaf,
\(R \in J(H)\), and \(u, v : H \to P\) such that \(uj = vj\). For every
\(f : S \to H\), \(S \in Ob C\), \(R \times_{H} S\) is a refinement of
\(S\) and \(uf j_{S} = vf j_{S}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ×\_H S —j\_S→ S}
\NormalTok{   ↓f\_R         ↓f}
\NormalTok{   R    —j→   H   ⇉\_\{u, v\} P.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(P\) is separated, one deduces \(uf = vf\). This being true for
every representable \(S\), one has \(u = v\).

Suppose now that \(P\) is a sheaf. Let \(g : R \to P\); let us show that
it factors through \(H\). For every \(f : S \to H\), \(S \in Ob C\),
\(g \circ f_{R} : R \times_{H} S \to P\) factors

in a unique way through \(S\), hence defines a morphism \(h : S \to P\),
which is evidently functorial in \(f\), by uniqueness:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ×\_H S —f\_R→ R —g→ P}
\NormalTok{   ↓j\_S          ↓j   ↗h}
\NormalTok{   S      —f→   H.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has thus defined for every \(S\) a map from \(H(S)\) into \(P(S)\)
functorial in \(S\), hence a morphism from \(H\) into \(P\) that answers
the required conditions.

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.2.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: This corollary has been
  added.} \emph{Let \texttt{R,\ F} be two sheaves. If \(R\) is a
refinement of \(F\), then \(R = F\).}

Indeed, suppose that \(R\) is a refinement of \(F\) and denote by \(j\)
the inclusion \(R \hookrightarrow F\). By 4.3.2, one has
\(\operatorname{Hom}(F, R) = \operatorname{End}(R)\), hence there exists
\(\pi : F \to R\) such that \(\pi \circ j = id_{R}\). One has likewise
\(\operatorname{End}(F) = \operatorname{Hom}(R, F)\), and the equality
\(j \circ \pi \circ j = j\) entails \(j \circ \pi = id_{F}\), hence
\(j\) is an isomorphism.

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.3 ({[}AS{]}, 1.3).} \emph{Let \(C\) be a
category. Let \(P\) be a presheaf on \(C\); for every \(S \in Ob C\),
denote by \(J(S)\) the set of sieves \(R\) of \(S\) such that for every
\(T \to S\), the map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    Hom(T, P) ⟶ Hom(R ×\_S T, P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is injective (resp. bijective). Then the \(J(S)\) define a
topology on \(C\), i.e.~satisfy axioms (T 1) through (T 4).}

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.4.} \emph{Let, for every \(S \in Ob C\), \(K(S)\)
be a family of sieves satisfying (T 1). Let \(P\) be a presheaf on
\(C\). For it to be separated (resp. a sheaf) for the topology generated
by the \(K(S)\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every
\(S \in Ob C\) and every \(R \in K(S)\), the canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    Hom(S, P) ⟶ Hom(R, P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be injective (resp. bijective).}

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.5.} \emph{Let, for each \(S \in Ob C\), \(R(S)\)
be a set of families of morphisms of \(C\) with target \(S\), satisfying
(P 1) (for example defining a pretopology). Let \(P\) be a presheaf on
\(C\). For \(P\) to be separated (resp. a sheaf) for the topology
generated by \(R\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every
\(S \in Ob C\) and every family \({S_{i} \to S} \in R(S)\), the map}

\[
P(S) \longrightarrow \prod_{i} P(S_{i})
\]

\emph{be injective, (resp. the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(S) ⟶ ∏ᵢ P(Sᵢ) ⇉ ∏\_\{i,j\} P(Sᵢ ×\_S Sⱼ)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be exact).}

\textbf{Definition 4.3.6.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category. One calls the}
canonical topology \emph{on \(C\) the finest topology for which all
representable functors are sheaves.}

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.7.} \emph{For a sieve \(R\) of \(S\) to be a
refinement for the canonical topology, it is necessary and sufficient
that for every morphism \(T \to S\) of \(C\) and every \(X \in Ob C\),
the canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(T, X) ⟶ Hom(R ×\_S T, X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be bijective.}

\textbf{Definition 4.3.8.} \emph{A sieve covering for the canonical
topology will be called a} universal effective epimorphic sieve.

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.9.} \emph{A universal effective epimorphic family
defines a universal effective epimorphic sieve. Conversely, every
squarable family defining a universal effective epimorphic sieve is
universal effective epimorphic.}

Let us return to the case where \(C\) is equipped with an arbitrary
topology and pass to the construction of the sheaf associated to a
presheaf \(P\). Let \(S\) be an object of \(C\). If \(R \supset R'\) are

two refinements of \(S\), one has a diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(S, P) ⟶ Hom(R, P)}
\NormalTok{                 ↘}
\NormalTok{              Hom(R′, P).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The ordered set \(J(S)\) is filtered, as has already been remarked.
Since \(S\) is an element of \(J(S)\), one has an evident morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(S, P) ⟶ lim→\_\{R ∈ J(S)\} Hom(R, P).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 4.3.10.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The numbering 4.3.10.0
  has been added for later references. On the other hand, it follows
  from the definition that if \(Q \to P\) is a monomorphism, the same
  holds for \(LP \to LQ\); hence \(L\) ``preserves monomorphisms'' (see
  also 4.3.16 for a more general result: \(L\) ``commutes with finite
  inverse limits'').} \emph{One sets
\(\check{H}^{0}(S, P) = \lim\to_{R \in J(S)} \operatorname{Hom}(R, P)\).
One verifies that \(\check{H}^{0}(S, P)\) depends functorially on \(S\),
hence defines a functor \texttt{LP} by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(++)   Hom(S, LP) = Ȟ⁰(S, P) = lim→\_\{R ∈ J(S)\} Hom(R, P).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has by construction morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ℓ\_P : P ⟶ LP}
\NormalTok{z\_R : Hom(R, P) → Hom(S, LP).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 4.3.10.} \emph{(i) For every refinement \(R\) of \(S\) and
every \(u : R \to P\), the diagram}

\[
P  \xrightarrow{\ell_{P}}  LP
\uparrow u           \uparrow z_{R}(u)
R  \xrightarrow{i_{R}}  S
\]

\emph{is commutative.}

\emph{(ii) For every morphism \(v : S \to LP\), there exists a
refinement \(R\) of \(S\) and a morphism \(u : R \to P\) with
\(v = z_{R}(u)\).}

\emph{(iii) Let \(Q\) be a functor and \(u, v : Q \to P\) such that
\(\ell_{P} u = \ell_{P} v\). Then the kernel of the pair \((u, v)\) is a
refinement of \(Q\).}

\emph{(iv) Let \(u : R \to P\) and \(u' : R' \to P\); for
\(z_{R}(u) = z_{R'}(u')\), it is necessary and sufficient that there
exist a refinement \(R'' \subset R \cap R'\) of \(S\) such that \(u\)
and \(u'\) coincide on \(R''\).}

\emph{Proof.} (i): One must verify that \(z_{R}(u) i_{R} = \ell_{P} u\).
For this, it suffices to verify that the composites of these two
morphisms with every morphism \(g : T \to R\), where \(T\) is
representable, are equal. Now consider \(f = i_{R} g\) and the fiber
product \(R' = R \times_{S} T\):\footnote{N.D.E.: Denote by \(p\) the
  projection \(R' \to R\). Since \(i_{R}\) is a monomorphism, one has
  \(p = g i_{R'}\). Let \(g'\) be the section of \(i_{R'}\) defined by
  \(g\); then \(p g' = g\) and therefore \(p g' i_{R'} = g i_{R'} = p\);
