  this entails \(g' i_{R'} = id_{R'}\) and therefore
  \(i_{R'} : R' \to T\) is an isomorphism, with inverse \(g'\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P  —ℓ\_P→  LP}
\NormalTok{↑u           ↑z\_R(u)}
\NormalTok{R  —i\_R→  S}
\NormalTok{↑p           ↑f}
\NormalTok{R′  —∼→   T (via i\_\{R′\}, g)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By definition of \(\ell_{P}\), \(\ell_{P} u g = z_{R}(u) f\) (this is
the particular case of what one is trying to prove in which \(i_{R}\) is
an isomorphism), and now \(z_{R}(u) f = z_{R}(u) i_{R} g\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  and (iv) merely translate the definition of
  \(\operatorname{Hom}(S, LP)\) as a direct limit.
\end{enumerate}

(iii): If \(K\) denotes the kernel of the pair \((u, v)\), then for each
morphism \(f : S \to Q\) where \(S\) is representable,
\(K \times_{Q} S\) is a subfunctor of the kernel of the pair of arrows
\(uf, vf : S \to P\). One is therefore reduced, by (T′ 0), to proving
the assertion in the case where \(Q = S\) is representable. But in this
case, it follows from (ii) and (iv) that \(K\) contains a refinement of
\(S\) hence is a refinement of \(S\).

One verifies finally that \texttt{P\ ⟼\ LP} defines a functor

\[
L : \hat{C} \longrightarrow \hat{C}
\]

and \texttt{P\ ⟼\ ℓ\_P} a morphism of functors

\[
\ell : Id_{\hat{C}} \longrightarrow L.
\]

Let us now state the essential result:

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.11.} \emph{(i) If \(P\) is any presheaf,
\texttt{LP} is separated and \(\ell_{P} : P \to LP\) is covering
(4.2.3).}

\emph{(ii) If \(P\) is a sheaf, \(P \to LP\) is an isomorphism.}

\emph{(iii) For every presheaf \(P\) and every separated presheaf (resp.
sheaf) \(F\), the map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(ℓ\_P, F) : Hom(LP, F) → Hom(P, F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is injective (resp. bijective).}

\emph{(iv) If \(P\) is separated, \(\ell_{P} : P \to LP\) is a covering
monomorphism (hence \(P\) is a refinement of \texttt{LP}), and
\texttt{LP} is a sheaf.}

\emph{Proof.} (i) First, \(P \to LP\) is covering; indeed, for every
morphism \(v : S \to LP\), there exists, by 4.3.10 (i) and (ii), a
refinement \(R\) of \(S\) such that one has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P  —ℓ\_P→  LP}
\NormalTok{↑v′          ↑v}
\NormalTok{P ×\_\{LP\} S  ←  S}
\NormalTok{↑                  ↑i\_R}
\NormalTok{R}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence \(P \times_{LP} S \to S\) is covering. It follows, by (C 0), that
\(P \to LP\) is covering.

If on the other hand two morphisms \(v_{1}, v_{2} : S \to LP\) induce
the same morphism on a refinement \(R\) of \(S\), let us show that they
are equal. There exist refinements \texttt{Rᵢ}, \(i = 1, 2\), and
morphisms \(u_{i} : R_{i} \to P\) such that
\(z_{R_{i}}(u_{i}) = v_{i}\). Taking \(R\) small enough, one may suppose
\(R_{1} = R_{2} = R\). It then follows from the commutative diagram of
4.3.10

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  that \(\ell_{P} u_{1} = \ell_{P} u_{2}\). By loc. cit. (iii),
  \(u_{1}\) and \(u_{2}\) therefore coincide on a refinement of \(R\),
  hence a refinement of \(S\), which entails that
  \(z_{R}(u_{1}) = z_{R}(u_{2})\), by loc. cit. (iv).
\item
  is clear, for if \(P\) is a sheaf,
  \(\operatorname{Hom}(S, P) \to \operatorname{Hom}(R, P)\) is already
  an isomorphism for every refinement \(R\) of \(S\).
\item
  Let \(u\) and \(v\) be two morphisms \(LP \to F\) such that
  \(u\ell_{P} = v\ell_{P}\). To show that \(u = v\), it suffices to see
  that \(uf = vf\) for every \(f : S \to LP\) where \(S\) is
  representable. Now there exists a refinement \(R\) of \(S\) and a
  morphism \(g : R \to P\) with \(f = z_{R}(g)\). Then \texttt{uf} and
  \texttt{vf} coincide on \(R\) with \(u\ell_{P} g = v\ell_{P} g\),
  hence coincide on \(R\). If \(F\) is separated, one therefore has
  \(uf = vf\). Suppose now that \(F\) is a sheaf; one then has the
  commutative diagram
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P  —ℓ\_P→  LP}
\NormalTok{↘             ↓}
\NormalTok{   F   →    LF}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which shows that \(\operatorname{Hom}(\ell_{P}, F)\) is surjective.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Let us show that if \(P\) is separated, \(P \to LP\) is a
  monomorphism. For this, it suffices to see that for every pair of
  morphisms \(u, v : S \to P\) (where \(S\) is representable) such that
  \(\ell_{P} u = \ell_{P} v\) one has \(u = v\). Now loc. cit. (iii)
  shows that \(u\) and \(v\) coincide on a refinement of \(S\), hence
  coincide because \(P\) is separated. This shows that \(P \to LP\) is a
  monomorphism; as it is covering by (i), one obtains that \(P\) is a
  refinement of \texttt{LP}.
\end{enumerate}

Let us finally show that \texttt{LP} is a sheaf. As we already know by
(i) that it is a separated presheaf, it suffices to see that for every
\(S \in Ob C\), every refinement \(R\) of \(S\) and every morphism
\(h : R \to LP\), there exists a morphism \(u : S \to LP\) with
\(u i_{R} = h\). Now \(R' = P \times_{LP} R\) is a refinement of \(R\),
since \(P\) is a refinement of \texttt{LP}, hence \(R'\) is

a refinement of \(S\). Set \(u = z_{R'}(h')\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P  —ℓ\_P→  LP}
\NormalTok{↑h′           ↑u (via h)}
\NormalTok{R′  —j→   R   —i\_R→  S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has \(u i_{R'} = \ell_{P} h' = hj\), whence \(u i_{R} j = hj\).
Since \(R'\) is a refinement of \(R\) and since \texttt{LP} is
separated, 4.3.2 shows that \(u i_{R} = h\).

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.12.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The statement of the
  corollary and its proof have been detailed.} \emph{Let \(F\) be a
sheaf and \(R\) a sub-\texttt{Ĉ}-object of \(F\). Then \(R\) is a
separated presheaf, \(\ell_{R} : R \to LR\) is a covering monomorphism,
and one has a commutative diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R  —i→  F}
\NormalTok{↘         ↗ j}
\NormalTok{   LR.}
\NormalTok{↑ℓ\_R}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Consequently, \(R\) is a refinement of \(F\) if and only if \(j\)
is an isomorphism.}

We have already noted that \(R\) is separated and that \(j\) is a
monomorphism, cf.~N.D.E. (24) and (26). By 4.3.11 (iv), \(\ell_{R}\) is
a covering monomorphism. Therefore, if \(j\) is an isomorphism, \(R\) is
a refinement of \(F\). Conversely, if \(i\) is covering, so is \(j\),
hence it is an isomorphism by 4.3.2.1.

\textbf{Remark 4.3.13.} \emph{If \(J'(S)\) is a cofinal subset of
\(J(S)\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(S, LP) = lim→\_\{R ∈ J′(S)\} Hom(R, P).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular, let \texttt{S\ ⟼\ R(S)} be a pretopology generating
the given topology. The functor \(L\) can be described using the
covering families that are elements of \(R(S)\). Making the formula
above explicit, one recovers the construction of {[}MA{]}.}

Denote by \(i\) the inclusion functor \(\tilde{C} \to \hat{C}\). From
Proposition 4.3.11 results the following theorem:

\textbf{Theorem 4.3.14.} \emph{There exists a unique functor
\(a : \hat{C} \to \tilde{C}\) such that the following diagram is
commutative}

\[
\hat{C}  \xrightarrow{L}  \hat{C}
\downarrow a         \downarrow L
\tilde{C}  \xrightarrow{i}  \hat{C},
\]

\emph{i.e., for every presheaf \(P\), \(L(L(P))\) is a sheaf. The
functors \(i\) and \(a\) are adjoint to one another: for every presheaf
\(P\) and every sheaf \(F\) one has an isomorphism, functorial in \(P\)
and \(F\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_Ĉ(P, i(F)) ≃ Hom\_C̃(a(P), F),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{that is,}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(P, F) ≃ Hom(a(P), F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 4.3.15.} \emph{The sheaf \(a(P)\) is said to be}
associated \emph{to the presheaf \(P\).}

\textbf{Remark 4.3.16.} \emph{As the functor \(L\) is constructed using
inverse limits and filtered direct limits, it commutes with finite
inverse limits.}\footnote{N.D.E.: In particular, if \(K\) is the kernel
  of a pair of morphisms of presheaves \texttt{u,\ v\ :\ Q\ ⇉\ P}, then
  \texttt{LK} is the kernel of \texttt{Lu,\ Lv\ :\ LQ\ ⇉\ LP} (this will
  be used in 4.4.5).}

\emph{Moreover, if one identifies \(L(P \times P)\) with
\(LP \times LP\), the morphism \(\ell_{P\times P}\) is identified with
\(\ell_{P} \times \ell_{P}\). It follows for example that if \(P\) is a
presheaf of groups, \texttt{LP} is also canonically equipped with a
structure of presheaf of groups and the canonical morphism \(P \to LP\)
is a morphism of groups. The same holds for the functor \(a\), which
shows that if \(P\) is a presheaf of groups and \(F\) a sheaf of groups,
one has an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{Ĉ{-}gr.\}(P, i(F)) ≃ Hom\_\{C̃{-}gr.\}(a(P), F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{See {[}D{]} for more details.}

\textbf{4.3.17.} If \(V\) is any category, one calls a \emph{presheaf on
\(C\) with values in \(V\)} a contravariant functor from \(C\) into
\(V\). To define sheaves with values in \(V\), we must first recall the
definition of the inverse limit of a functor. If \(R\) and \(V\) are two
categories, and

\[
F : R^{\circ} \longrightarrow V
\]

a contravariant functor from \(R\) to \(V\), one denotes by
\(\lim\leftarrow F\) the object of \(\hat{V}\) defined as follows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{lim← F(X) = Hom\_V̂(X, lim← F) = lim←\_\{U ∈ Ob R\} Hom\_V(F(U), X) = Hom(c\_X, F),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(X\) is a variable object of \(V\), where \(c_{X}\) denotes the
contravariant functor from \(R\) to \(V\) that sends each object of
\(R\) to \(X\) and each arrow of \(R\) to \(id_{X}\), and where the last
Hom is taken in the category \(\operatorname{Hom}(R^{\circ}, V)\). If
\(R\) has a final object \(e_{R}\), one has
\(\lim\leftarrow F = F(e_{R})\). If \(V\) is the category of sets, the
functor \(\lim\leftarrow\) is identified with the functor \(\Gamma\).

If \(S\) is an object of \(C\) and \(R\) a sieve of \(S\), denote by
\(\bar{R}\) the full subcategory of \(C/S\) whose set of objects is
\(E(R)\) and \(i_{R} : \bar{R} \to C/S\) the canonical functor. If \(P\)
is a presheaf on \(C\) with values in \(V\), it defines by restriction a
functor \(P_{S} : (C/S)^{\circ} \to V\). The functor \(i_{R}\) induces a
morphism of \(\hat{V}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(S) = P\_S(S) = lim← P\_S ⟶ lim←(P\_S ∘ i\_R).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One denotes by \(\lim\leftarrow_{R} P\) the object
\(\lim\leftarrow(P_{S} \circ i_{R})\) of \(\hat{V}\). By virtue of
4.1.6, Definition 4.3.1 generalizes to the

\textbf{Definition 4.3.18.} \emph{The presheaf \(P\) on \(C\) with
values in \(V\) is said to be} separated \emph{(resp.} a sheaf*), if for
every \(S \in Ob C\) and every \(R \in J(S)\), the canonical morphism of
\(\hat{V}\)*

\[
P(S) \longrightarrow \lim\leftarrow_{R} P
\]

\emph{is a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism).}

In the case where \(V\) is the category \texttt{(Gr.)} of groups (or any
other category of sets equipped with algebraic structures defined by
finite inverse limits), one can see (cf.~{[}D{]}) that there is
equivalence between the following notions: a presheaf on \(C\) with
values in \texttt{(Gr.)} whose underlying presheaf of sets is a sheaf,
and a group in the category of sheaves of sets. Taking account of these
identifications, we shall always consider sheaves with values in a
category of sets equipped with algebraic structures defined by finite
inverse limits

as sheaves of sets, equipped in the category \(\tilde{C}\) with the
corresponding algebraic structure.

\subsubsection{4.4. Exactness properties of the category of
sheaves}\label{exactness-properties-of-the-category-of-sheaves}

\textbf{Theorem 4.4.1.} \emph{(i) Arbitrary inverse limits exist in
\(\tilde{C}\); ``they are computed in \texttt{Ĉ}'', i.e.~the inclusion
functor \(i : \tilde{C} \to \hat{C}\) commutes with inverse limits: if
\((X_{\alpha})\) is an inverse system of sheaves, the presheaf}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{lim← i(X\_α) : S ⟼ lim← X\_α(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a sheaf and one has \texttt{i(lim←\ X\_α)\ =\ lim←\ i(X\_α)}.}

\emph{(ii) Arbitrary direct limits exist in \(\tilde{C}\): if
\((X_{\alpha})\) is a direct system of sheaves, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{lim→ X\_α = a(lim→ i(X\_α))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(\lim\to i(X_{\alpha})\) is the presheaf direct limit of
the \(i(X_{\alpha})\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{lim→ i(X\_α) : S ⟼ lim→ X\_α(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) The functor \(a : \hat{C} \to \tilde{C}\) commutes with
arbitrary direct limits and with finite inverse limits.}

Assertions (i) and (ii) follow formally from the adjunction formula
(4.3.14), and\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been modified here.} the
first assertion of (iii) follows from (ii). Finally, the second
assertion of (iii) has already been pointed out in 4.3.16.

\textbf{Scholie 4.4.2.} \emph{This theorem allows one to use the
following method to prove in \(\tilde{C}\) an assertion bearing
simultaneously on arbitrary direct limits and finite inverse limits (for
example: ``every epimorphism is universally effective'', cf.~below). One
begins by proving the corresponding assertion in the category of sets,
then one extends it ``argument by argument'' to the category}

\emph{of presheaves. Next, one uses the preceding theorem to pass from
the category of presheaves to the category of sheaves. One will see in
the sequel many examples of this method (4.4.3, 4.4.6, 4.4.9, etc.).}

Let us finally remark that the assertions relative to the category of
presheaves are formally corollaries of the assertions relative to the
category of sheaves. It suffices in fact to take as topology the least
fine topology (``chaotic''), that is, the topology defined by
\(J(S) = {S}\) for every \(S \in Ob C\); every functor is indeed a sheaf
for this topology.

\textbf{Proposition 4.4.3.} \emph{Let \(F = {F_{i} \to F}\) be a family
of morphisms of sheaves. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(F\) is an epimorphic family.}

\emph{(ii) \(F\) is a universal effective epimorphic family (1.13).}

\emph{(iii) \(F\) is covering (4.2.3).}

\emph{(iv) The sheaf image of \(F\) (that is, the sheaf associated to
the presheaf image of \(F\) (4.1.2)) is \(F\).}

The equivalence of (iii) and (iv) follows from 4.3.12. The other
equivalences will follow from the following lemmas.

\textbf{Lemma 4.4.4.} \emph{Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a monomorphism of
sheaves which is an epimorphism. Then \(f\) is an isomorphism.}

The lemma is first clear in the category of sets. Let us prove it next
in the category of presheaves. Consider the presheaf

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V : S ⟼ Y(S) ∐\_\{X(S)\} Y(S);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

it is the amalgamated sum of \(Y\) and \(Y\) under \(X\) in the category
of presheaves.\footnote{N.D.E.: The continuation of the proof has been
  slightly modified.} Denote by \(i_{1}\) and \(i_{2}\) the two
``coordinate'' morphisms \(Y \to V\). If \(X \to Y\) is an epimorphism
in the category of presheaves, then \(i_{1} = i_{2}\). In this case, for
each \(S\), the map \(X(S) \to Y(S)\) is surjective; as it is also
injective, it is a bijection, and therefore \(X \to Y\) is an
isomorphism.

Let us place ourselves finally in the category \(\tilde{C}\) of sheaves.
By 4.4.1 (ii), the amalgamated sum in \(\tilde{C}\) of the sheaves \(Y\)
and \(Y\) under \(X\) is the sheaf \(Z\) associated to the presheaf
\(V\). Consider the diagram of morphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X —f→ Y ⇉\_\{i₁, i₂\} V —τ→ Z = a(V).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has \(i_{1} f = i_{2} f\), whence \(\tau i_{1} f = \tau i_{2} f\),
and therefore \(\tau i_{1} = \tau i_{2}\), since \(f\) is an epimorphism
in \(\tilde{C}\). By point (iii) of the lemma below, the presheaf \(V\)
is separated, hence \(\tau\) is a monomorphism (4.3.11 (iv)). Therefore
\(i_{1} = i_{2}\), and we have seen above that this

entails that \(f : X \to Y\) is an isomorphism. This proves Lemma 4.4.4,
once one has verified that \(V\) is separated.

\footnote{N.D.E.: Point (i) of Lemma 4.4.5 has been corrected, and the
  proof of the three points detailed.} Let \(R_{\emptyset}\) be the
presheaf that to every \(S \in Ob C\) associates the empty set; it is an
initial object of \texttt{Ĉ}.

\textbf{Lemma 4.4.5.} \emph{(i) Suppose that
\(R_{\emptyset} \notin J(S)\), for every \(S \in Ob C\). If \((X_{i})\)
is a family of separated presheaves, the direct sum presheaf
\(\coprod_{i} X_{i}\) is separated.}\footnote{N.D.E.: In general, the
  direct sum of two sheaves \texttt{F,\ G} is not a sheaf. Indeed, let
  \(S_{1}, S_{2} \in Ob C\); suppose that the direct sum
  \(S = S_{1} \coprod S_{2}\) exists in \(C\) and that the fiber product
  \(S_{1} \times_{S} S_{2}\) is an initial object \(\emptyset\) of \(C\)
  (cf.~I, 1.8). Let \(R\) be the sieve of \(S\) with base
  \({S_{1}, S_{2}}\); then \((F \coprod G)(R)\) is the disjoint union of
  \(F(S) \coprod G(S)\) and of \(F(S_{i}) \times G(S_{j})\) for
  \(i \neq j\), hence \(F \coprod G\) is not a sheaf in general. On the
  other hand, if \(C\) is the category with a single object \(S\) and
  \(id_{S}\) as sole morphism, equipped with the topology defined by
  \(J(S) = {R_{\emptyset}, S}\), then the only separated presheaves are
  \(R_{\emptyset}\) and \(X = h_{S}\) (which is a sheaf), and
  \(X \coprod X\) is not separated.}

\emph{(ii) Consider an equivalence relation in the category of
presheaves:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ⇉\_\{u, v\} Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and let \(w : Y \to Z\) be the quotient. If \(X\) is a sheaf and
\(Y\) separated, then \(Z\) is separated.}

\emph{(iii) Consider an amalgamated sum in the category of presheaves,
where \(u\) and \(u'\) are monomorphisms:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X  —u→   Y}
\NormalTok{↓u′         ↘}
\NormalTok{Y′    →    V.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(Y\) and \(Y'\) are separated, and \(X\) a sheaf, then \(V\)
is separated.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Set \(X = \coprod_{i} X_{i}\). Let \(S \in Ob C\) and
  \(\tau : R \hookrightarrow S\) a refinement of \(S\), and let
  \(x_{1}, x_{2}\) be two elements of \(X(S)\) such that
  \(x_{1} \circ \tau = x_{2} \circ \tau\); there exist indices
  \texttt{i,\ j} such that \(x_{1} \in X_{i}(S)\) and
  \(x_{2} \in X_{j}(S)\). Since \(R \neq R_{\emptyset}\), there exists a
  morphism \(\phi : T \to R\), with \(T \in Ob C\). Then,
  \(x_{1} \circ \tau \circ \phi = x_{2} \circ \tau \circ \phi\), and
  since \(X(T)\) is the disjoint union of the \(X_{k}(T)\), this entails
  \(i = j\). Then, since \texttt{Xᵢ} is separated and a subobject of
  \(X\), the map \(X_{i}(S) \to X_{i}(R) \to X(R)\) is injective, and
  therefore \(x_{1} = x_{2}\). This proves that \(X\) is separated.
\end{enumerate}

Let us prove (iii). Consider the morphisms \(i : Y \to V\) and
\(j : Y' \to V\), and let \(K\) be the kernel of:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y × Y′ ⇉\_\{p, q\} V,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(p = i \circ pr_{1}\) and \(q = j \circ pr_{2}\).

Let \(S \in Ob(C)\). Since \(u\) and \(u'\) are monomorphisms, one can
identify \(X(S)\) with its image in \(Y(S)\) (resp. \(Y'(S)\)); denote
by \(Z(S)\) (resp. \(Z'(S)\)) the complement. Then

\(V(S)\) is identified with the disjoint union of \(Z(S)\), \(Z'(S)\)
and \(X(S)\), and one easily sees that the maps \(i(S) : Y(S) \to V(S)\)
and \(j(S) : Y'(S) \to V(S)\) are injective, and that the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u × u′)(S) : X(S) ⟶ K(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective. Consequently, \(i\) and \(j\) are monomorphisms, and
\(u \times u' : X \to K\) is an isomorphism.

Set \(U = Y \coprod Y'\), and let \(\tau : R \hookrightarrow S\) be a
refinement of \(S\); one has a commutative diagram:

\[
U(S)  \xrightarrow{U(\tau)}  U(R)
\downarrow                  \downarrow
V(S)  \xrightarrow{V(\tau)}  V(R).
\]

Let \(v_{1}, v_{2} \in V(S)\) whose images in \(V(R)\) coincide. By the
definition of \(V\), \(v_{1}, v_{2}\) lift to elements \(y_{1}, y_{2}\)
of \(U(S)\); denote by \(z_{1}, z_{2}\) their images in \(U(R)\). Then
\(z_{1}, z_{2}\) have the same image in \(V(R)\).

Since \(i : Y \to V\) and \(j : Y' \to V\) are monomorphisms, the maps
\(Y(R) \to V(R)\) and \(Y'(R) \to V(R)\) are injective. Therefore, since
\(Y\) and \(Y'\) are separated, if \(y_{1}\) and \(y_{2}\) both belong
to \(Y(S)\) or to \(Y'(S)\), then \(y_{1} = y_{2}\). Otherwise, one may
suppose that \(y_{1} \in Y(S)\) and \(y_{2} \in Y'(S)\), whence
\(z_{1} \in Y(R)\) and \(z_{2} \in Y'(R)\). But then, since
\(i \circ z_{1} = j \circ z_{2}\), the morphism
\(z_{1} \boxtimes z_{2} : R \to Y \times Y'\) factors through \(K = X\).
Moreover, since \(X(R) = X(S)\) (because \(X\) is a sheaf), there exists
\(x \in X(S)\) such that \(u(x) \circ \tau = z_{1} = y_{1} \circ \tau\)
and \(u'(x) \circ \tau = z_{2} = y_{2} \circ \tau\), whence, since \(Y\)
and \(Y'\) are separated, \(u(x) = y_{1}\) and \(u'(x) = y_{2}\), and
therefore \(v_{1} = v_{2}\). This proves that \(V\) is separated.

Let us prove (ii). Let us first remark that the morphism of presheaves

\[
X \xrightarrow{u\boxtimes v} K,
\]

where \(K\) denotes the kernel of the pair of morphisms
\(w \circ pr_{i} : Y \times Y \to Z\), is an isomorphism. Indeed, for
every \(T \in Ob C\), \(X(T)\) is an equivalence relation in \(Y(T)\),
so that the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X(T) —u⊠v→ Y(T) × Y(T) ⇉\_\{w∘pr₁, w∘pr₂\} Z(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is exact in the category of sets.

Let now \(S \in Ob C\) and \(g_{1}, g_{2} : S \to Z\) be two morphisms
that coincide on a refinement \(\tau : R \hookrightarrow S\) of \(S\).
Since \(S \in Ob C\), one has \(Z(S) = Y(S)/X(S)\),

by construction of \(Z\), and therefore there exist morphisms
\(f_{1}, f_{2} : S \to Y\) such that \(w f_{i} = g_{i}\).

Then, \(w f_{1} \tau = w f_{2} \tau\) and therefore, by what precedes,
there exists a morphism \(\phi : R \to X\) such that
\(u \phi = f_{1} \tau\) and \(v \phi = f_{2} \tau\). Since \(X\) is a
sheaf, there exists \(\psi : S \to X\) such that \(\phi = \psi \tau\),
and therefore one has in \(Y(R)\) the equalities:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u ψ τ = f₁ τ ,    v ψ τ = f₂ τ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(Y(S) \to Y(R)\) is injective (\(Y\) being separated), this
entails \(u \psi = f_{1}\) and \(v \psi = f_{2}\), whence it follows
that \(g_{1} = g_{2}\). This proves that \(Z\) is separated.

\textbf{Lemma 4.4.6.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The statement of the lemma and
  its proof have been detailed.} \emph{(i) Let
\({F_{i} \xrightarrow{f_{i}} F}\) be a family of morphisms of
presheaves, and let \(G \subset F\) be the presheaf image. Then the
following diagram in \texttt{Ĉ} is exact:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∐ᵢ Fᵢ ×\_G ∐ⱼ Fⱼ ⇉\_\{pr₁, pr₂\} ∐ᵢ Fᵢ ⟶ G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{i.e., for every presheaf \(H\), the following diagram of sets is
exact:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    Hom(G, H) ⟶ ∏ᵢ Hom(Fᵢ, H) ⇉\_\{p, q\} ∏\_\{i,j\} Hom(Fᵢ ×\_G Fⱼ, H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) Every covering family of morphisms of sheaves is universally
effective epimorphic.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(H\) be a presheaf. The map \(f*\) which to a morphism
  \(\phi : G \to H\) associates the family of morphisms
  \(\phi \circ f_{i} : F_{i} \to H\) is injective, since for every
  \(S \in Ob C\), \(\phi(S)\) is determined by the
  \((\phi \circ f_{i})(S)\), since the family
  \(f_{i}(S) : F_{i}(S) \to G(S)\) is surjective. It is clear that the
  image of \(f*\) is contained in \(Ker(p, q)\). Conversely, let
  \(\phi_{i} : F_{i} \to H\) be a family of morphisms such that, for
  every \texttt{i,\ j}, the diagram below is commutative:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Fᵢ ×\_G Fⱼ → Fⱼ}
\NormalTok{↓             ↓ φⱼ}
\NormalTok{Fᵢ   —φᵢ→  H.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, for every \(S\), the map \(\coprod_{i} F_{i}(S) \to H(S)\) factors
uniquely as a map \(\phi(S) : G(S) \to H(S)\), and this defines a
morphism \(\phi : G \to H\) such that \(f*(\phi) = (\phi_{i})\). This
proves the exactness of the sequence (∗), and point (i).

Let us prove (ii). Since the notion of covering family is stable under
base extension, it suffices to show that every covering family is
effective epimorphic. So let \({F_{i} \to F}\) be a covering family of
morphisms of sheaves, and let \(G\) be the presheaf image of this
family. Since the family is covering, so is the monomorphism
\(G \hookrightarrow F\), hence, by 4.3.12, one has \(a(G) = F\).

On the other hand, since \(G \hookrightarrow F\) is a monomorphism, the
fiber products \(F_{i} \times_{G} F_{j}\) and \(F_{i} \times_{F} F_{j}\)
are the same. Hence, by (i), the following diagram of sets is exact, for
every presheaf \(H\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗∗)   Hom(G, H) ⟶ ∏ᵢ Hom(Fᵢ, H) ⇉\_\{p, q\} ∏\_\{i,j\} Hom(Fᵢ ×\_F Fⱼ, H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If moreover \(H\) is a sheaf, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(G, H) = Hom(a(G), H) = Hom(F, H),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and then (∗∗) shows that \({F_{i} \to F}\) is indeed an effective
epimorphic family in the category \(\tilde{C}\) of sheaves.

\textbf{Lemma 4.4.7.} \emph{Every family of morphisms of sheaves
\({F_{i} \to F}\) factors as a covering family \({F_{i} \to G}\) and a
monomorphism \(G \to F\).}

It suffices in fact to take for \(G\) the sheaf image of the given
family.

\emph{Proof of Proposition 4.4.3:} one has seen in 4.4.6 that (iii) ⇒
(ii), and one evidently has (ii) ⇒ (i). Let finally \({F_{i} \to F}\) be
an epimorphic family; by Lemma 4.4.7, it factors as a covering family
followed by a monomorphism. But the latter, being dominated\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Recall (cf.~N.D.E. (17)) that one says that a morphism \(g : G \to H\)
  is \emph{dominated} by a family of morphisms \(F_{i} \to H\) if this
  family factors through \(g\).} by an epimorphic family, is an
epimorphism, hence an isomorphism by 4.4.4.

\textbf{Remark 4.4.8.}\footnote{N.D.E.: In order to be in accord with
  later references, the numbering of the original, which contained two
  nos. 4.4.7, has been corrected.} \emph{As the presheaf image of the
family \(F\) is separated, the construction of the associated sheaf
shows that the conditions of Proposition 4.4.3 are also equivalent to
the following:}

\emph{(v) For every \(S \in Ob C\), every \(f \in F(S)\) is locally in
the image of \(F\), that is:}

\emph{(vi) For every \(S \in Ob C\) and every \(f \in F(S)\), the set of
\(S' \to S\) such that the image of \(f\) in \(F(S')\) is in the image
of one of the \(F_{i}(S')\) is a refinement of \(S\).}

\emph{(vii) (If the topology is defined by a pretopology \(R\)). For
every \(S \in Ob C\) and every \(f \in F(S)\), there exists a family
\({S_{j} \to S} \in R(S)\) such that for every \(j\) the image
\texttt{fⱼ} of \(f\) in \(F(S_{j})\) is in the image of one of the
\(F_{i}(S_{j})\).}

\textbf{Remark 4.4.8.bis.} \emph{If the sheaf \(F\) is representable,
the preceding conditions are also equivalent to:}

\emph{(viii) The set of \(T \to F\) (\(T \in Ob C\)), such that there
exist an \(i\) and a commutative diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Fᵢ → F}
\NormalTok{↑   ↗}
\NormalTok{T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a refinement of \(F\).}

Indeed, if (viii) is satisfied, the presheaf image of the \texttt{Fᵢ} is
dominated by\footnote{N.D.E.: ``contains'' has been replaced by: ``is
  dominated by'', cf.~N.D.E. (17).} a refinement of \(F\), which entails
that the family is covering. Conversely, one applies (vi) to
\(id_{F} \in F(F)\).

This condition is expressed in pictorial language in the following way:
\emph{locally on \(F\), there exists an \(i\) such that \(F_{i} \to F\)
has a section}. In particular, a morphism

\(G \to F\), where \(G\) is a sheaf and \(F\) a representable sheaf,
will be covering if and only if it has \emph{locally (on \(F\)) a
section}.

\footnote{N.D.E.: Lemmas 4.4.8.1 and 4.4.8.2 have been added.} The
following lemmas will be useful in VI\_B, 8.1 and 8.2.

\textbf{Lemma 4.4.8.1.} \emph{Let \(Q \subset P\) be presheaves of
groups on \(C\), \(Q\) being normal in \(P\). Suppose that \(P\) is
separated, and that \(Q\) is a sheaf. Then the presheaf of groups
\(P/Q\) is separated. Consequently, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(P/Q) = L(P/Q) = lim→\_\{R ∈ J(S)\} (P/Q)(R).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It suffices to show the first assertion, since the second follows from
it, by 4.3.11 (iv) and (ii). Let \(S \in Ob C\) and \(R\) a sieve of
\(S\), and let \(y \in P(S)/Q(S)\) whose image in \((P/Q)(R)\) is the
identity. One must show that \(y = 1\). Now, by hypothesis, the morphism
\(P(S) \to P(R)\) (resp. \(Q(S) \to Q(R)\)) is injective (resp. an
isomorphism), and in the commutative diagram below, the top row is
exact:

\[
1 \to Q(S) \to P(S) \to P(S)/Q(S) \to 1
    \downarrow \wr    \downarrow        \downarrow
1 \to Q(R) \to P(R) \to (P/Q)(R).
\]

The result will follow from this, if one shows that the bottom row is
exact. Let \(f : R \to P\) whose image in \((P/Q)(R)\) is the identity,
and let \(\phi : T \to R\) with \(T \in Ob C\). Then \(f \circ \phi\) is
the identity of \((P/Q)(T) = P(T)/Q(T)\),
i.e.~\(f \circ \phi \in Q(T)\). Therefore, \texttt{φ\ ⟼\ f\ ∘\ φ} is a
functorial map \(R(T) \to Q(T)\), hence defines a morphism of functors
\(\pi : R \to Q\) such that \(\pi(id_{R}) = f\), whence \(f \in Q(R)\).
This proves the exactness of the bottom row, and the lemma is proved.

\textbf{Lemma 4.4.8.2.} \emph{Let \(H \subset G\) be presheaves of
groups on \(C\).}

\emph{(i) If \(H\) is normal in \(G\), then \(L(H)\) is normal in
\(L(G)\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(H\) is central in \(G\), then \(L(H)\) is central in
\(L(G)\).}

Let \(S \in Ob C\); it must be shown (cf.~I 2.3.6) that \(L(H)(S)\) is
normal (resp. central) in \(L(G)(S)\). Let \(h \in L(H)(S)\) and
\(g \in L(G)(S)\); there exist a sieve \(R\) of \(S\) and elements
\(h' \in H(R)\), \(g' \in G(R)\), such that \(h = z_{R}(h')\) and
\(g = z_{R}(g')\) (notation of 4.3.10). Since \(z_{R}\) is a morphism of
groups, one has \(g h g^{-1} h^{-1} = z_{R}(g' h' g'^{-1} h'^{-1})\).

In case (i), one has \(g' h' g'^{-1} h'^{-1} \in H(R)\), whence
\(g h g^{-1} h^{-1} \in LH(S)\); in case (ii),
\(g' h' g'^{-1} h'^{-1} = 1\) and therefore \(g h g^{-1} h^{-1} = 1\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.4.9.} \emph{Every equivalence relation in
\(\tilde{C}\) is universally effective (3.3.3): let \(R\) be a
\(\tilde{C}\)-equivalence relation in the sheaf \(X\); then the sheaf
associated to the separated presheaf}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i(X)/i(R) : S ⟼ X(S)/R(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a universal effective quotient of \(X\) by \(R\).}

Let \(X/R\) be the sheaf quotient of \(X\) by \(R\), which exists by
4.4.1 (ii): \(X/R = a(i(X)/i(R))\). We must show that \(X \to X/R\) is a
universal effective epimorphism, and that the morphism
\(f : R \to X \times_{X/R} X\) is an isomorphism. The first assertion
has already been proved (4.4.3). As for \(f\), it comes by application
of the functor \(a\) from the morphism
\(i(R) \to i(X) \times_{i(X/R)} i(X)\) or, since \(i(X)/i(R)\) is
separated (4.4.5 (ii)) so that \(i(X)/i(R) \to i(X/R)\) is a
monomorphism, from the canonical morphism
\(i(R) \to i(X) \times_{i(X)/i(R)} i(X)\).

One is therefore reduced to proving the same assertion in the category
of presheaves. But \(i(X)/i(R)\) is the presheaf
\texttt{S\ ⟼\ X(S)/R(S)} and one is reduced to proving the analogous
assertion in the category of sets, where it is immediate.

\textbf{Proposition 4.4.10.} \emph{Under the conditions of 4.4.9, let
\(Y\) be a subsheaf of \(X\). Denote by \texttt{R\_Y} the equivalence
relation induced in \(Y\) by \(R\). Then the canonical morphism (3.1.6)}

\[
Y/R_{Y} \longrightarrow X/R
\]

\emph{is a monomorphism: it identifies \(Y/R_{Y}\) with a subsheaf of
\(X/R\), which is the} sheaf image \emph{of the composite morphism}

\[
Y \longrightarrow X \longrightarrow X/R.
\]

The morphism of presheaves

\[
i(Y)/i(R_{Y}) = i(Y)/i(R)_{i(Y)} \longrightarrow i(X)/i(R)
\]

is a monomorphism. Since the functor \(a\) is left exact (4.3.16), it
transforms monomorphisms into monomorphisms, and therefore

\[
Y/R_{Y} \longrightarrow X/R
\]

is a monomorphism. The last assertion follows from the commutative
diagram

\[
Y     \to   X
\downarrow           \downarrow
Y/R_{Y} \to X/R,
\]

and the fact that \(Y \to Y/R_{Y}\) is covering.

By virtue of this proposition, we shall always identify \(Y/R_{Y}\) with
a subsheaf of \(X/R\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.4.11.} \emph{Let \(R\) be a
\(\tilde{C}\)-equivalence relation in the sheaf \(X\). For every
subsheaf \(Y\) of \(X\) stable under \(R\), denote by \(Y'\) the
quotient \(Y/R_{Y}\) considered as a subsheaf of \(X' = X/R\). Then
\(Y = Y' \times_{X'} X\), and the maps \texttt{Y\ ⟼\ Y/R\_Y} and
\texttt{Y′\ ⟼\ Y′\ ×\_\{X′\}\ X} realize a bijective correspondence
between the set of subsheaves \(Y\) of \(X\) stable under \(R\) and the
set of subsheaves \(Y'\) of \(X'\).}

If \(Y'\) is a subsheaf of \(X'\), then \(Y' \times_{X'} X\) is a
subsheaf of \(X\) stable

under \(R\).\footnote{N.D.E.: and one has \((Y' \times_{X'} X)/R = Y'\).}
If \(Y'\) is obtained by passage to the quotient from a subsheaf \(Y\)
of \(X\), then \(Y\) is a subobject of \(Y' \times_{X'} X\). It
therefore suffices to show that if one has two subsheaves \(Y\) and
\(Y_{1}\) of \(X\), stable under \(R\), \(Y_{1}\) containing \(Y\), and
if the quotients \(Y/R_{Y}\) and \(Y_{1}/R_{Y_{1}}\) are identical, then
\(Y = Y_{1}\). One is evidently reduced to proving the same assertion in
the case where \(Y_{1} = X\). Denoting then by \(P\) (resp. \(Q\)) the
presheaf \(i(X)/i(R)\) (resp. \(i(Y)/i(R_{Y})\)), the diagram

\[
X  \to  P
\uparrow       \uparrow
Y  \to  Q
\]

is cartesian. Since one has a commutative diagram

\[
P  \to  a(P)
\uparrow       \uparrow
Q  \to  a(Q),
\]

and since \(Q \hookrightarrow a(Q)\) is covering (4.3.11), the
monomorphism \(Q \hookrightarrow P\) is covering, hence \(Q\) is a
refinement of \(P\). By base change, \(Y\) is a refinement of \(X\).
Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are sheaves, this entails (4.3.12) \(Y = X\).

\textbf{4.4.12.} In particular, if \(Y\) is a subsheaf of \(X\), and if
\(Y' = Y/R_{Y}\), then the preceding correspondence defines a subsheaf
\texttt{Ȳ} of \(X\), stable under \(R\), containing \(Y\) and minimum
for these properties, which one calls the \emph{saturation} of \(Y\) for
the equivalence relation \(R\).

\subsection{Footnotes (chunk-A)}\label{footnotes-chunk-a}

\subsubsection{4.5. The case of a topology coarser than the canonical
topology}\label{the-case-of-a-topology-coarser-than-the-canonical-topology}

By 4.3.6 and 4.3.8, the following conditions are equivalent for a
topology \(T\) on \(C\):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \(T\) is coarser than the canonical topology of \(C\).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item
  Every representable presheaf is a sheaf for \(T\).
\item
  Every covering sieve for \(T\) is universal effective epimorphic.
\end{enumerate}

If \(T\) is defined by a pretopology \(S \mapsto R(S)\), these
conditions are further equivalent to

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Every family belonging to \(R(S)\) is universal effective epimorphic.
\end{enumerate}

In the case where these conditions are satisfied, the canonical functor
\(C \to \hat{C}\) factors through a functor
\(j_{C} = j : C \to \tilde{C}\) (we shall also write
\(j(S) = \tilde{S}\)\footnote{N.D.E.: and we shall also write
  \(h_{S} = \hat{S}\), cf.~the first commutative diagram of 4.5.4.}).

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.1.} \emph{The functor \(j : C \to \tilde{C}\) is
fully faithful and commutes with arbitrary inverse limits. It is in
particular left exact and therefore preserves the algebraic structures
defined by finite inverse limits.}

This follows at once from consideration of the commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        C}
\NormalTok{       ╱ ╲}
\NormalTok{    j ╱   ╲ (canonical)}
\NormalTok{     ↙     ↘}
\NormalTok{    C̃  ─── i ───→  Ĉ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and from 4.4.1 (i).

Before exhibiting other properties of the functor \(j\), we need to
define the topology induced on a category \(C/S\). No longer assuming
the given topology necessarily coarser than the canonical one, this is
done as follows: if \(C\) is a sieve of \(T\) in \(C\) and one has a
morphism \(T \to S\), then \(C\) defines naturally a sieve of \(T\) in
\(C/S\), denoted \(J(T)\) (since the definition of a sieve of \(T\)
depends only on the category \(C/T = (C/S)/T\)). If, for example, \(C\)
is defined by the family \({T_{i} \to T}\), then its image in \(C/S\) is
defined by the same family considered as a family of morphisms of
\(C/S\). This being said, the map \(T \mapsto J(T)\) defines a topology
on \(C/S\) called the \emph{topology induced} by the given topology.
With the definitions of {[}AS{]}, 2.3, it is the coarsest of the
topologies on \(C/S\) for which the canonical functor

\[
i_{S} : C/S \longrightarrow C
\]

is a comorphism\footnote{N.D.E.: i.e., such that for every object
  \(T \to S\) of \(C/S\), every covering sieve \(R'\) of
  \(i_{S}(T \to S) = T\), considered as a sieve of
  \((T \to S) \in Ob C/S\), is covering.}. One will note that the
identifications

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(C/S)/T = C/T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

respect the topologies by definition.

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a representable sheaf on
\(C\) and \(F \to S\) a morphism of \texttt{Ĉ}. In order for
\(S' \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(S', F)\) to be a separated presheaf
(resp. a sheaf) on \(C/S\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(F\) be
a separated presheaf (resp. a sheaf) on \(C\).}

For every functor \(P\), one has (I 1.4.1)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(P, F) = ⨆\_\{f ∈ Hom(P, S)\} Hom\_f(P, F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have expanded the original in what follows.}

Let \(S' \in Ob C\) and \(\eta : C' \to S'\) a covering sieve. As \(S\)
is a sheaf, the map \(f \mapsto f \circ \eta\) establishes a bijection
\(\operatorname{Hom}(S', S) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}(C', S)\).
Consequently, the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_Ĉ(S′, F) ⟶ Hom\_Ĉ(C′, F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

decomposes as a ``disjoint union'' of the maps

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_f(S′, F) ⟶ Hom\_\{f ∘ η\}(C′, F).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The proposition follows.

\textbf{Corollary 4.5.3.} \emph{The topology induced on \(C/S\) by a
topology on \(C\) coarser than the canonical topology of \(C\), is
coarser than the canonical topology of \(C/S\).}

\textbf{Corollary 4.5.4.} \emph{Suppose the given topology on \(C\) is
coarser than the canonical topology. For every \(S \in Ob C\), one has
an equivalence of categories}

\[
\tilde{C}/\tilde{S} \xrightarrow{\sim} \tilde{C}/S.
\]

\emph{The following diagrams are commutative up to isomorphism (all
unlabelled arrows being equivalences):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              (j\_C)/S                (i\_C)/S̃                (a\_C)/Ŝ}
\NormalTok{    C/S ─────────────→  C̃/S̃ ───────────────→  Ĉ/Ŝ ────────────────→  C̃/S̃}
\NormalTok{      ║                  ≀                     ≀                       ≀}
\NormalTok{      ║       j\_\{C/S\}            i\_\{C/S\}                 a\_\{C/S\}}
\NormalTok{    C/S ──────────────→  C̃/S ───────────────→  Ĉ/S ────────────────→  C̃/S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        T̃}
\NormalTok{       ╱ ╲}
\NormalTok{      ╱   ╲}
\NormalTok{   ╱        ↘}
\NormalTok{  C̃/S̃     C̃/S / T̃}
\NormalTok{   ↘ ≃   ↗}
\NormalTok{      ╲ ╱}
\NormalTok{      C̃/T̃ ─→ C̃/T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The commutativity of the first two squares results from the definition
of the equivalence \(\tilde{C}/\tilde{S} \to \tilde{C}/S\). To prove the
commutativity of the last, one must see that the following square is
commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       L′}
\NormalTok{Ĉ/Ŝ ────→  Ĉ/Ŝ}
\NormalTok{  │           │}
\NormalTok{  │           │}
\NormalTok{  ↓    L″     ↓}
\NormalTok{Ĉ/S ────→  Ĉ/S ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(L'\) is the restriction of the functor \texttt{L\_C} to
\(\hat{C}/\hat{S}\) and \(L''\) the functor \(L_{C/S}\); this is easily
seen by going back to the definition of the functors \(L\) (given after
4.3.9). As for the second diagram, this is none other than the
restriction to the sheaf categories of the corresponding diagram on the
categories of presheaves (Exposé I, n° 1), which is commutative.

\textbf{Scholie 4.5.5.} \emph{The various assertions of this number show
that, in the case where the given topology is coarser than the canonical
topology, one may identify \(C\) with a full subcategory of
\(\tilde{C}\), itself a full subcategory of \texttt{Ĉ}, and that under
this identification one may indulge in the usual abuses of language
regarding \(C \to \hat{C}\), justified by the commutativities above. Let
us explicitly remark that the first diagram of 4.5.4 shows that one may
use the functor \(a\) without special precaution.}

We shall see in the next number that the identification of \(C\) with a
full subcategory of \(\tilde{C}\) (contrary to what was the case for
\texttt{Ĉ}) commutes with the formation of certain direct limits, and we
shall then say how to use this fact.

From now on, and unless explicitly stated otherwise, we shall assume the
given topology coarser than the canonical topology and we shall
systematically make the identifications described above.

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.6.} \emph{Let \(F\) and \(G\) be two sheaves
over \(S\) and \(f : F \to G\) an \(S\)-morphism. The following
conditions on \(f\) are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(f\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism, resp. an
isomorphism) in \(\tilde{C}\).}

\emph{(ii) \(f\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism, resp. an
isomorphism) in \(\tilde{C}/S = \tilde{C}/S\).}

For monomorphism and isomorphism, this is evident (it is a question of
presheaves). For epimorphism, it follows from the description of
epimorphisms as covering morphisms (4.4.3) and from the fact that, by
definition of the induced topology, these are the same in \(\tilde{C}\)
and \(\tilde{C}/S\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.7.} \emph{Let \(f : F \to G\) be a morphism of
sheaves. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(f\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism, resp. an
isomorphism).}

\emph{(ii) For each \(S \in Ob C\), \(f_{S} : F_{S} \to G_{S}\) is
locally a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism, resp. an isomorphism),
that is:}

\emph{(iii) For each \(S \in Ob C\), the set of \(T \to S\) such that
\(F_{T} \to G_{T}\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism, resp. an
isomorphism) is a refinement of \(S\).}

\emph{If the given topology is defined by a pretopology \(R\), these
conditions are further equivalent to the following:}

\emph{(iv) For each \(S \in Ob C\), there exists a covering family
\({S_{i} \to S} \in R(S)\) such that for every \(i\),
\(F_{S_{i}} \to G_{S_{i}}\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism,
resp. an isomorphism).}

\emph{If the category \(C\) has a final object \(e\), one may content
oneself with taking \(S = e\) in conditions (ii), (iii), and (iv).}

One obviously has (ii) ⇔ (iii) ⇔ (iv). To prove the equivalence of (i)
and (ii) as well as the supplement concerning the final object, one must
show that (ii) ⇒ (i) and that the notions in question are stable under
base extension. Let us first prove this last point. For monomorphism and
isomorphism, this is evident (it is a question of presheaves). For
epimorphism, it follows from the fact that every epimorphism of sheaves
is universal (4.4.3).

Let us finally show that (ii) entails (i). Suppose first that
\(f_{S} : F_{S} \to G_{S}\) is locally a monomorphism (resp. an
isomorphism). There then exists a covering sieve \(C\) of \(S\) such
that for every \(T \to C\), \(f_{T}\) is a monomorphism (resp. an
isomorphism). As an inverse limit of monomorphisms (resp. isomorphisms)
is one, \(\operatorname{Hom}(C, f)\) will be a monomorphism (resp. an
isomorphism) (cf.~4.1.4). The commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{            Hom(C, f)}
\NormalTok{Hom(C, F) ────────────→ Hom(C, G)}
\NormalTok{   ↑                       ↑}
\NormalTok{   ≀                       ≀}
\NormalTok{            f(S)}
\NormalTok{   F(S) ─────────────→ G(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

then shows that \(f(S)\) is injective (resp. bijective). Suppose finally
that \(f : F \to G\) is locally an epimorphism and let \(H \subset G\)
be its image. For each \(S \to G\), \(H \times_{G} S\) is the image of
\(f \times_{G} S : F \times_{G} S \to S\). To show that \(f\) is an
epimorphism, one must show that \(H\) is a refinement of \(G\), that is,
that \(H \times_{G} S\) is a refinement of \(S\) for each \(S\). But
since this is so after every base change \(T \to S\) of a refinement of
\(S\) (since \(f \times_{G} S\) is locally covering), \(H \times_{G} S\)
is indeed a refinement of \(S\) (Axiom (T 2)).

\textbf{Corollary 4.5.8.} \emph{Let \(F\) and \(G\) be two sheaves over
\(S\) and \(f : F \to G\) an \(S\)-morphism. In order for \(f\) to be a
monomorphism, resp. an epimorphism, resp. an isomorphism, it is
necessary and sufficient that it be so locally on \(S\).}

\textbf{Remark 4.5.9.} \emph{The proof of the proposition shows that it
remains valid, for the part concerning monomorphisms (resp.
isomorphisms), when one only assumes that \(F\) is a separated presheaf
(resp. a sheaf) and \(G\) an arbitrary presheaf (resp. a separated
presheaf).}

Let us provisionally return to the case of an arbitrary topology and lay
down a definition.

\textbf{Definition 4.5.10.} \emph{Let \(G \to F\) be a morphism of
\texttt{Ĉ}. We say that \(G\) is a} relative sheaf above \(F\) \emph{if
for every \(F\)-functor \(H\) and every refinement \(R\) of \(H\), the
canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    Hom\_F(H, G) ⥲ Hom\_F(R, G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is bijective.}

Proposition 4.5.2 immediately generalizes:

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.11.} \emph{If \(F\) is a sheaf, \(G\) is a
relative sheaf above \(F\) if and only if it is a sheaf.}

\textbf{Lemma 4.5.12.} \emph{In the situation \(X \to T \to S\) (where
\texttt{X,\ T,\ S} are three objects of \texttt{Ĉ}), if \(X\) is a
relative sheaf above \(T\), then \(U = \prod_{T/S} X\) is a relative
sheaf above \(S\).}

Indeed, one has for every \(S\)-functor \(Y\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(Y, U) = Hom\_T(T ×\_S Y, X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(C\) is a sieve of \(Y\), then \(T \times_{S} C\) is a sieve of
\(T \times_{S} Y\); one concludes at once.

\textbf{Corollary 4.5.13.} \emph{The presheaves
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{T/S}(X, Y)\), \(Isom_{S}(X, Y)\), etc., are
sheaves when the arguments appearing in them are also.}

Indeed, all these presheaves are constructed by means of fibered
products and presheaves \(\prod_{T/S} X\) (I 1.7 and II 1). It therefore
suffices to verify the result for a presheaf \(\prod_{T/S} X\); in this
case, the assertion follows from 4.5.11 and 4.5.12.

\subsubsection{4.6. Description of the quotient of a sheaf by an
equivalence
relation}\label{description-of-the-quotient-of-a-sheaf-by-an-equivalence-relation}

Recall that we are assuming the topology \(T\) given to be coarser than
the canonical topology.

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.1.} \emph{Let \(R \Rightarrow X\) (with
morphisms \(p_{1}, p_{2}\)) be a \(\tilde{C}\)-equivalence relation in
the sheaf \(X\). Let \(F \in Ob \hat{C}\) be defined as follows: for
each \(S\) of \(C\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S) = \{ sub{-}S{-}sheaves Z of X\_S stable under R × S[\^{}N.D.E{-}IV{-}43], whose quotient by R\_Z is S,}
\NormalTok{         i.e. such that the diagram R\_Z ⇒ Z → S is exact \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then for every sheaf \(Y\), \(\operatorname{Hom}(Y, F)\) is
identified with the set:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\{ sub{-}Y{-}sheaves of X × Y stable under R × Y and whose quotient is Y \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular the sub-sheaf \(R\) of \(X \times X\) corresponds to
an element \(p\) of \(\operatorname{Hom}(X, F)\) and the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⇒ X →\^{}p F}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is exact, hence identifies \(F\) with the sheaf-quotient \(X/R\).}

Indeed, set \(Q = X/R\). For every sheaf \(Y\) and every morphism
\(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(Y, Q)\) corresponding to a section
\(s : Y \hookrightarrow Q \times Y\), consider the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R × Y ⇒ X × Y ──→ Q × Y}
\NormalTok{                    ↑     ↑}
\NormalTok{(∗)                 │     │ s}
\NormalTok{                    │     │}
\NormalTok{                    Z ──→ Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the square is cartesian. It is immediate by 4.4.11 that \(Z\) is a
sub-\(Y\)-sheaf of \(X \times Y\), stable under \(R \times Y\), whose
quotient is \(Y\), and that, conversely, every \(Z\) of this type comes
from a unique section of \(Q \times Y\) over \(Y\). Taking first \(Y\)
representable, one extracts an isomorphism \(Q \simeq F\). Taking next
\(Y\) arbitrary, one extracts the announced form of
\(\operatorname{Hom}(Y, F)\). Considering finally the canonical morphism
\(X \to Q\), one sees at once that it corresponds to the sub-\(X\)-sheaf
\(R\) of \(X \times X\), which completes the proof.

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.2.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an arbitrary subfunctor of
\(F\) such that
\(\operatorname{Hom}(X, G) \subset \operatorname{Hom}(X, F)\) contains
\(R\). Then the canonical morphism \(p : X \to F\) factors through
\(G\).}

Since \(p\) is covering (4.4.9 and 4.4.3), it follows that \(G\) is a
refinement of \(F\). In particular, every sub-sheaf \(G\) of \(F\)
satisfying the preceding condition is equal to \(F\) (4.3.12).

\textbf{4.6.3.} We are now going to interest ourselves in the case where
\(X\) and \(R\) are representable. Let us first introduce some
terminology. Besides the conditions (a) to (d) introduced in 3.4.1, we
shall use other conditions on a family \texttt{(M)} of morphisms of
\(C\), which we state below, recalling the conditions (a) to (c) already
given, for completeness.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\item
  \texttt{(M)} is stable under base extension.
\item
  The composite of two elements of \texttt{(M)} is in \texttt{(M)}.
\item
  Every isomorphism is an element of \texttt{(M)}.
\end{enumerate}

(d\_T) Every element of \texttt{(M)} is covering.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Recall that \(T\) denotes the given topology on \(C\), coarser than
  the canonical topology.}

(e\_T) Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a morphism of \(C\). If there exists a
refinement \(R\) of \(Y\) such that for every \(Y' \to R\),
\(X \times_{Y} Y' \to Y'\) is an element of \texttt{(M)}, then \(f\) is
an element of \texttt{(M)}.

Recall that (a) and (b) entail

(a′) The cartesian product of two elements of \texttt{(M)} is an element
of \texttt{(M)}.

On the other hand, (a) and (d\_T) entail by 4.3.9:

(d′) Every element of \texttt{(M)} is a universal effective epimorphism.

\textbf{4.6.4.} The preceding conditions are verified by the family of
covering morphisms, denoted \texttt{(M\_T)}, when \(C\) has fibered
products. Indeed (cf.~4.2.3), (a) follows from (C 1), (b) from (C 2),
(c) from (C 4), (d\_T) from the definition, (e\_T) from (C 5). The
results we shall establish for a family satisfying these conditions will
apply in particular to the family \texttt{(M\_T)}. In particular, one
may take for \(T\) the canonical topology and for \texttt{(M)} the
family of universal effective epimorphisms.

\textbf{Lemma 4.6.5.} \emph{Let \texttt{(M)} be a family of morphisms
satisfying the properties (a) to (e\_T) above. Let \(R\) be a
\(C\)-equivalence relation in \(X \in Ob C\), of type \texttt{(M)}. Let
\(\tilde{X}\) be the sheaf defined by \(X\), \(\tilde{R}\) the
\(\tilde{C}\)-equivalence relation in \(\tilde{X}\) defined by \(R\) and
\(\tilde{X}/\tilde{R}\) the sheaf-quotient. In order for \(R\) to be
\texttt{(M)}-effective, it is necessary and sufficient that
\(\tilde{X}/\tilde{R}\) be representable. If this is so,
\(\tilde{X}/\tilde{R}\) is represented by the quotient \(X/R\).}

Suppose first that \(R\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective and denote
\(Y = X/R\). The canonical morphism \(p : X \to Y\) is an element of
\texttt{(M)}, hence covering by (d\_T). The corresponding morphism

\[
\tilde{p} : \tilde{X} \longrightarrow \tilde{X}/\tilde{R}
\]

is therefore a universal effective epimorphism of \(\tilde{C}\) (4.4.3),
hence identifies \(\tilde{X}/\tilde{R}\) with the quotient of
\(\tilde{X}\) by the equivalence relation \(R'\) defined in
\(\tilde{X}\) by \(\tilde{p}\). As the canonical functor
\(C \to \tilde{C}\) commutes with fibered products, \(R'\) is none other
than \(\tilde{R}\), since \(R\) is the equivalence relation defined by
\(p\).

Conversely, suppose \(\tilde{X}/\tilde{R}\) representable by an object
\(Y\) of \(C\). Let \(p : X \to Y\) be the morphism deduced from the
canonical morphism \(\tilde{X} \to \tilde{X}/\tilde{R}\); it is a
covering morphism by 4.4.3. It is clear as before that \(R\) is the
equivalence relation defined by \(p\). It only remains to show that
\(p \in (M)\). Now the cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⥲ X ×\_Y X ──→ X}
\NormalTok{           │      │}
\NormalTok{        pr\_2     p}
\NormalTok{           ↓      ↓}
\NormalTok{           X ───→ Y}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

shows that \(p\) becomes \(p_{2}\), which is an element of \texttt{(M)},
after base change by the covering morphism \(p\). One concludes by
(e\_T).

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.5.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this
  corollary.} \emph{Let \texttt{(M)} satisfy the properties (a) to
(e\_T) above and let \(f : G \to G'\) be a morphism of \(C\)-groups,
such that \(f \in (M)\). Suppose \(Ker(f)\) representable (which is the
case if \(C\) has a final object \(e\)). Then the equivalence relation
in \(G\) defined by \(H = Ker(f)\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective and \(G'\)
represents the sheaf-quotient \(\tilde{G}/\tilde{H}\) for the topology
\(T\).}

This follows from 4.6.5 and 3.4.7.1.

We are now in a position to state the main result of this number.

\textbf{Theorem 4.6.6.} \emph{Let \texttt{(M)} be a family of morphisms
verifying the axioms (a) to (e\_T) of 4.6.3. Let \(R\) be a
\(C\)-equivalence relation of type \texttt{(M)} (cf.~3.4.3) in the
object \(X\) of \(C\). Consider the functor \(F \in Ob \hat{C}\) defined
as follows:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S) = \{ sub{-}S{-}sheaves Z of X\_S stable under R × S whose quotient by R\_Z is S \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Let \texttt{F\_0} be the subfunctor of \(F\) defined as follows:
\(F_{0}(S)\) consists of the \(Z \in F(S)\) that are representable, that
is:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F\_0(S) = \{ sub{-}C/S{-}objects Z of X\_S stable under R × S, such that}
\NormalTok{           R\_Z is (M){-}effective and has quotient S (i.e. such that}
\NormalTok{           Z → S belongs to (M) and R\_Z ≃ Z ×\_S Z) \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then:}

\emph{(i) The morphism \(p \in \operatorname{Hom}(X, F) = F(X)\) defined
by the sub-object \(R\) of \(X \times X\) identifies \(F\) with the
sheaf-quotient of \(X\) by \(R\).}

\emph{(ii) The following conditions are equivalent:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{a) \(F\) is representable.}
\item
  \emph{b) \texttt{F\_0} is representable.}
\item
  \emph{c) \(R\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective.}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Under these conditions, \(F = F_{0} = X/R\).}

\emph{(iii) Let \texttt{(N)} be a family of morphisms stable under base
change, such that for every covering family \({S_{i} \to S}\) and every
family \({T_{i} \to S_{i}}\) of morphisms of \texttt{(N)}, every descent
datum on the \(T_{i}\) relative to \({S_{i} \to S}\) is effective.
Suppose \(X\) squarable (cf.~1.6.0) and the morphism
\(R \to X \times X\) an element of \texttt{(N)}. Then \(F_{0} = F\).}

\emph{Proof.} (i) has already been proved (4.6.1).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  We have seen the equivalence of a) and c) as well as the equality
  \(F = X/R\). It remains to prove that b) or c) implies \(F_{0} = F\).
  Let us first remark, as is moreover affirmed in the statement, that
  \texttt{F\_0} is indeed a subfunctor of \(F\); for every
  \(S \in Ob C\) and every \(Z \in F_{0}(S)\), the morphism \(Z \to S\)
  is squarable, hence \(Z \times_{S} S'\) is an element of \(F_{0}(S')\)
  for every \(S' \to S\). As \(R \in F(X)\) belongs to \(F_{0}(X)\),
  4.6.2 shows that b) implies \(F_{0} = F\).
\end{enumerate}

Now suppose c) verified and let \(Q\) be an object of \(C\) representing
\(X/R\). Then the morphism \(X \to Q\) is an element of \texttt{(M)}
and, for every \(S \in Ob C\) and every \(Z \in F(S)\), the diagram (∗)
of 4.6.1 shows that \(Z = S \times_{Q \times S} X \times S\) is
representable, and \(Z \to S\) belongs to \texttt{(M)}, hence
\(Z \in F_{0}(S)\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(S, F)\) correspond to \(Z \in F(S)\).
  We must show that \(f\) factors through \texttt{F\_0}, that is, that
  \(Z\) is representable. This is clear first if \(f\) factors through
  \(X\), by virtue of:
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Lemma 4.6.7.} \emph{Let \(x_{0} \in X(S)\). The image of
\(x_{0}\) in \(F(S)\) corresponds to the sub-sheaf \(Z\) of
\texttt{X\_S} defined by the two cartesian squares}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              id\_\{X\_S\} × x\_0}
\NormalTok{   X\_S ─────────────────→ X\_S ×\_S X\_S ──→ X × X}
\NormalTok{    ↑                          ↑              ↑}
\NormalTok{    │                          │              │}
\NormalTok{    Z ──────────────────→     R\_S ─────────→ R}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This lemma follows at once from the description of the morphism
\(X \to F\).

Let us return to the proof of the theorem. If \(f\) factors through
\(X\), then \(Z\) is representable and, as \(R \to X \times X\) is an
element of \texttt{(N)}, the same holds for \(Z \to X_{S}\).

In general, \(f\) does not necessarily factor through \(X\); but since
\(X \to F\) is covering (4.4.3), there exists by 4.4.8 (vii) a covering
family \({S_{i} \to S}\) and for each \(i\) a morphism \(S_{i} \to X\)
making commutative the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ────→ F}
\NormalTok{↑       ↑}
\NormalTok{│       │ f}
\NormalTok{S\_i ──→ S .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By what precedes, the morphism \(f_{i} : S_{i} \to F\) defined by the
preceding diagram belongs to \(\operatorname{Hom}(S_{i}, F_{0})\) and
corresponds to the sub-sheaf \(Z \times_{S} S_{i}\) of \(X_{S_{i}}\).
The morphism \(Z \times_{S} S_{i} \to X_{S_{i}}\) is an element of
\texttt{(N)} and the family \(X_{S_{i}} \to X_{S}\) covering. It
therefore only remains to establish:

\textbf{Proposition 4.6.8.} \emph{Let \({S_{i} \to S}\) be a covering
family and \(Z\) a sheaf above \(S\). Suppose that for each \(i\), the
\(S_{i}\)-functor \(Z \times_{S} S_{i}\) is representable by an object
\(T_{i}\). Then the family of \(T_{i}\) is equipped with a canonical
descent datum relative to \(S_{i} \to S\). In order for \(Z\) to be
representable, it is necessary and sufficient that this datum be
effective; if this is so, the ``descended'' object represents \(Z\).}

Let us first remark that by 4.4.3, \({S_{i} \to S}\) is a universal
effective epimorphic family in \(\tilde{C}\), hence a descent family in
\(\tilde{C}\) (2.3). If \(Z\) is representable by the object \(T\), then
\(T \times_{S} S_{i}\) (considered as a sheaf) is isomorphic to
\(Z \times_{S} S_{i}\), hence the descent datum on the \(T_{i}\) is
effective and the (unique) descended object is isomorphic to \(Z\).
Conversely, suppose that the canonical descent datum on the \(T_{i}\) is
effective and let \(T\) be the descended object. Since the family
\({S_{i} \to S}\) is a descent family in \(\tilde{C}\), there exists an
\(S\)-morphism \(T \to Z\) which by base extension to each \(S_{i}\)
recovers the canonical morphism \(T_{i} \to Z \times_{S} S_{i}\). This
morphism is locally an isomorphism; as \(T\) and \(Z\) are sheaves, it
follows from 4.5.8 that it is an isomorphism.

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.9.} \emph{Let \(R\) be an \texttt{(M)}-effective
equivalence relation in \(X\). For every sheaf \(F\), the map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(X/R, F) ⟶ Hom(X, F)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{identifies the first set with the part of the second consisting of
the morphisms compatible with \(R\).}

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.10.} \emph{Let \(T '\) be a topology coarser than
\(T\), for which the morphisms of \texttt{(M)} are covering. Under the
conditions of 4.6.6 (iii), \(X/R\) is also the sheaf-quotient of \(X\)
by \(R\) in every intermediate topology between \(T '\) and the
canonical topology.}

\textbf{Remark 4.6.11.} \emph{If in the statement of 4.6.6 (iii), one
furthermore assumes that, under the hypotheses of the text, if one
denotes \(T\) the descended object, the morphism \(T \to S\) is an
element of \texttt{(N)}, then the inclusion morphisms
\(Z \hookrightarrow X_{S}\) are also elements of \texttt{(N)}, as
follows at once from the construction of \(Z\) by descent.}

\textbf{Remark 4.6.12.} \emph{The implications c) ⇒ b) ⇒ a) and c) ⇒
{[}F\_0 = F = X/R{]} have been established without recourse to the
``if'' part of Lemma 4.6.5, which is the only place where condition
(e\_T) is used. They therefore remain valid if \texttt{(M)} satisfies
only conditions (a) to (d\_T). An example of such a family \texttt{(M)}
is that of squarable covering morphisms (compare with 4.6.4). In the
case of the canonical topology, these are none other than the universal
effective epimorphisms. One therefore has:}

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.13.} \emph{Let \(R\) be a universal effective
equivalence relation in \(X\). Then the object \(X/R\) of \(C\) is the
sheaf-quotient of \(X\) by \(R\) for the canonical topology. It
represents the following functor: \((X/R)(S)\) is the set of
sub-\(C/S\)-objects \(Z\) of \texttt{X\_S} stable under \(R \times S\)
and such that the induced equivalence relation is universal effective
and has \(S\) as quotient.}

Similarly, for an arbitrary topology:

\textbf{Corollary 4.6.14.} \emph{Let \texttt{(M)} be the family of
squarable covering morphisms. If \(R\) is an \texttt{(M)}-effective
equivalence relation in \(X\), then the object \(X/R\) of \(C\) is the
sheaf-quotient of \(X\) by \(R\) and represents the functor
\texttt{F\_0} of 4.6.6.}

\textbf{Scholie 4.6.15.} \emph{We can now bring the following precisions
to 4.5.5.} Whereas in questions involving exclusively inverse limits
(fibered products, algebraic structures, etc.), one may, by the results
of Exposé I and 4.5.5, identify \(C\) indifferently with a full
subcategory of \(\tilde{C}\) or of \texttt{Ĉ}, it is not the same in
those that mix inverse and direct limits. In all questions involving
both inverse and direct limits, in particular passages to the quotient
(example: group structure on the quotient of a group by an invariant
subgroup), we shall consider the given category as embedded in the
category of sheaves; thus if \(R\) is a \(C\)-equivalence relation in
the object \(X\) of \(C\), \(X/R\) will denote the sheaf-quotient of
\(X\) by \(R\) (previously denoted \(j(X)/j(R)\)), hence in the case
where this sheaf is representable, the object it represents. The
preceding results show that in the most important cases, a quotient in
\(C\) will also be a quotient in the category of sheaves; in any case,
we forbid ourselves the use of the notation \(X/R\) for a quotient in
\(C\) that does not coincide with the quotient in \(\tilde{C}\) (for
example one that is not universal), thus modifying the definitions of n°
3.

To study a problem of the type above, one therefore places oneself first
in the category of sheaves, where all the usual results are valid
(cf.~n° 4.4), then one specializes the results obtained to the original
category, using the results of the present number and, when one has
them, descent effectivity criteria. We shall see examples of this method
in the following numbers.

\subsubsection{4.7. Use of effectivity criteria: isomorphism
theorem}\label{use-of-effectivity-criteria-isomorphism-theorem}

In this number, we give an example of the use of effectivity criteria.
The data of departure are a topology \(T\) on \(C\) (always coarser than
the canonical topology), a family \texttt{(M)} of morphisms of \(C\)
verifying the axioms (a) to (e\_T) of 4.6.3, and a family \texttt{(N)}
of morphisms of \(C\) liable to verify the following axioms:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{(N)} is stable under base extension.
\end{enumerate}

(f\_T) ``the morphisms of \texttt{(N)} descend by the given topology'';
that is: for every \(S \in Ob C\), every covering family
\({S_{i} \to S}\) and every family \({T_{i} \to S_{i}}\) of morphisms of
\texttt{(N)}, every descent datum on the \(T_{i}\) relative to
\({S_{i} \to S}\) is effective, and if one denotes \(T\) the descended
object, the morphism \(T \to S\) is an element of \texttt{(N)}.

Since every element of \texttt{(M)} is covering (condition 4.6.3
(d\_T)), (f\_T) entails the following axiom:\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  placed the axiom (f\_M) here (which figured before Proposition 4.7.2).}

(f\_M) If \(Y \to X\) is an element of \texttt{(N)} and \(X \to X_{1}\)
an element of \texttt{(M)}, every descent datum on \(Y\) relative to
\(X \to X_{1}\) is effective; if one denotes \texttt{Y\_1} the descended
object, \(Y_{1} \to X_{1}\) is an element of \texttt{(N)}.

Let us at once signal an example of this situation, which will be
treated later: \(C\) is the category of schemes, \(T\) the faithfully
flat quasi-compact topology; \texttt{(M)} the family of faithfully flat
quasi-compact morphisms, \texttt{(N)} the family of closed immersions,
or that of quasi-compact immersions.\footnote{N.D.E.: cf.~§ 6.4, see
  also VI\_A, 5.3.1.}

Let us recall the principal result of 4.6.6 (taking into account
4.6.11):

\textbf{Proposition 4.7.1.} \emph{If \(X\) is a squarable object of
\(C\), \(R\) an equivalence relation of type \texttt{(M)} in \(X\), such
that \(R \to X \times X\) is an element of \texttt{(N)}, with
\texttt{(N)} verifying (a) and (f\_T), then the sheaf-quotient \(X/R\)
is defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X/R)(S) = \{ sub{-}S{-}objects Z of X\_S, stable under R × S, such that Z → X\_S}
\NormalTok{             belongs to (N), Z → S is covering (or an element of (M)),}
\NormalTok{             and R\_Z ≃ Z ×\_S Z \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, one has:

\textbf{Proposition 4.7.2.} \emph{Let \(X \in Ob C\) and \(R\) an
\texttt{(M)}-effective equivalence relation in \(X\). Let \texttt{(N)}
be a family of morphisms verifying (a) and (f\_M).}

\emph{For every sub-object \(Y\) of \(X\), stable under \(R\) and such
that \(Y \to X\) belongs to \texttt{(N)}, the equivalence relation
induced in \(Y\) by \(R\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective and the quotient
\(Y/R_{Y} = Y'\) is a sub-object of \(X' = X/R\) such that \(Y' \to X'\)
belongs to \texttt{(N)}.}

\emph{The map \(Y \mapsto Y'\) is a bijection between the set of
sub-objects \(Y\) of \(X\), stable under \(R\), such that \(Y \to X\)
belongs to \texttt{(N)}, and the set of sub-objects \(Y'\) of \(X'\)
such that \(Y' \to X'\) belongs to \texttt{(N)}. The inverse map is
\(Y' \mapsto Y' \times_{X'} X\).}

\emph{Proof.} As \(R\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective, the morphism
\(X \to X'\) belongs to \texttt{(M)}. Let \(Y'\) be a sub-object of
\(X'\) such that the canonical morphism \(Y' \to X'\) belongs to
\texttt{(N)}. Then, the sub-object \(Y = Y' \times_{X'} X\) of \(X\) is
stable under \(R\), and the morphism \(Y \to X\) (resp. \(Y \to Y'\))
belongs to \texttt{(N)} (resp. \texttt{(M)}) since \texttt{(N)} and
\texttt{(M)} are stable under base change. Let \texttt{R\_Y} denote the
equivalence relation induced in \(Y\) by \(R\). By 4.4.11, the sheaf
quotient \(Y/R_{Y}\) is represented by \(Y'\) and therefore, by 4.6.5,
\texttt{R\_Y} is \texttt{(M)}-effective.

Conversely, let us show that every sub-object \(Y\) of \(X\), stable
under \(R\), such that the structural morphism \(Y \to X\) belongs to
\texttt{(N)}, is obtained in this way. Indeed, if \(Y\) is stable under
\(R\), its two images in \(R = X \times_{X'} X\) are identical and \(Y\)
is equipped with a descent datum relative to \(X \to X'\); the desired
result follows, since the family \texttt{(N)} verifies the axiom (f\_M).

\textbf{Corollary 4.7.3.} \emph{Let \(X \in Ob C\) and \(R\) an
\texttt{(M)}-effective equivalence relation in \(X\); assume moreover
that \(R \to X \times X\) belongs to \texttt{(N)}, where \texttt{(N)}
verifies (a) and (f\_T). Then, for every \(Y\) as in 4.7.2,
\(R_{Y} \to Y \times Y\) also belongs to \texttt{(N)} and therefore, by
4.7.1, one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Y/R\_Y)(S) = \{ sub{-}S{-}objects Z of Y\_S, stable under R\_Y × S, such that Z → Y\_S}
\NormalTok{               belongs to (N) (then Z → X\_S also belongs to it), Z → S is covering,}
\NormalTok{               and R\_Z ≃ Z ×\_S Z \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{5. Passage to the quotient and algebraic
structures}\label{passage-to-the-quotient-and-algebraic-structures}

\subsubsection{5.1. Principal homogeneous
bundles}\label{principal-homogeneous-bundles}

\textbf{Definition 5.1.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have introduced the
  numbering 5.1.0, to refer to it later.} \emph{We recall (III 0.1) that
an object \(X\) with (right) operator group \(H\) is said to be}
formally principal homogeneous\footnote{N.D.E.: One also says
  ``pseudo-torsor'', cf.~EGA IV\_4, 16.5.15. On the other hand, the more
  general notion of formally homogeneous object (not necessarily
  principal homogeneous), is defined in the addendum 6.7.1 at the end of
  this Exposé.} \emph{under \(H\) if the canonical morphism (of
functors)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X × H ⟶ X × X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined by \((x, h) \mapsto (x, xh)\) is an isomorphism. It
amounts to the same thing to say (cf.~loc. cit.) that for every
\(S \in Ob C\), \(X(S)\) is formally principal homogeneous under
\(H(S)\), that is, empty or principal homogeneous under \(H(S)\). In
particular, if \(H\) is made to operate on itself by (right)
translations, \(H\) becomes formally principal homogeneous under
itself.}

\textbf{Definition 5.1.1.} \emph{The object \(X\) with operator group
\(H\) is said to be} trivial \emph{if it is isomorphic (as object with
operator group \(H\)) to \(H\) on which \(H\) operates by translations.}

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.2.} \emph{Let \(X\) be formally principal
homogeneous under \(H\). One has an isomorphism}

\[
\Gamma(X) \xrightarrow{\sim} Isom_{H-obj.}(H, X)
\]

\emph{of principal homogeneous sets under \(\Gamma(H)\).}

To every section \(x\) of \(X\) one associates the morphism from \(H\)
to \(X\) defined setwise by \(h \mapsto xh\). The stated assertion is
immediate, by reduction to the set-theoretic case.

\textbf{Corollary 5.1.3.} \emph{One has an isomorphism of objects with
operators \(H\)}

\[
X \xrightarrow{\sim} Isom_{H-obj.}(H, X).
\]

\textbf{Corollary 5.1.4.} \emph{In order for an object with operator
group to be trivial, it is necessary and sufficient that it be formally
principal homogeneous and possess a section.}

\textbf{Definition 5.1.5.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category equipped with a
topology. We say that the \(S\)-object \(X\) with \(S\)-operator group
\(H\) is a} principal homogeneous bundle under \(H\) \emph{if it is
locally trivial, that is, if the following equivalent conditions are
satisfied:\footnote{N.D.E.: In this case, one also says that \(X\) is an
  \(H\)-torsor.}}

\emph{(i) The set of \(T \to S\) such that (the functor)
\(X \times_{S} T\) is trivial under \(H \times_{S} T\) is a refinement
of \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) There exists a covering family (for a pretopology defining
the given topology) \({S_{i} \to S}\) such that for each \(i\), the
\(S_{i}\)-functor \(X \times_{S} S_{i}\) with \(S_{i}\)-functor-group of
operators \(H \times_{S} S_{i}\) is trivial (= has a section over
\(S_{i}\)).}

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.6.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category equipped with
a topology \(T\). Let \texttt{(M)} be a family of morphisms of \(C\)
verifying the axioms (a) to (e\_T) of 4.6.3. Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-group
such that the structural morphism \(H \to S\) is an element of
\texttt{(M)} and \(P\) an \(S\)-object with \(S\)-operator group \(H\).
The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(P\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(H\)
(Definition 5.1.5).}

\emph{(ii) \(P\) is formally principal homogeneous under \(H\) and the
structural morphism \(P \to S\) is an element of \texttt{(M)}.}

\emph{(iii) There exists a morphism \(S' \to S\) element of \texttt{(M)}
such that by base extension from \(S\) to \(S'\), \(P\) becomes trivial,
that is, \(P \times_{S} S'\) is trivial under \(H \times_{S} S'\).}

\emph{(iv) \(H\) operates freely on \(P\), in an \texttt{(M)}-effective
manner, and the quotient \(P/H\) is isomorphic to \(S\).}

Let us first remark that (ii) and (iv) are equivalent, taking into
account that, in either case, \(P \to S\) is an element of \texttt{(M)},
hence squarable, which ensures the representability of the fibered
products \(H \times_{S} P\) and \(P \times_{S} P\). It is clear that
(ii) entails (iii), as one can take \(P\) itself as \(S'\), the
hypothesis that \(P\) is formally principal homogeneous entailing that
\(P \times_{S} P\) is trivial under \(H \times_{S} P\) (5.1.4), since it
has a section (the diagonal section). It is clear that (iii) entails
(i), since \({S' \to S}\) is a covering family, by axiom (d\_T). It
therefore remains to show that (i) entails (ii). The morphism of sheaves
\(P \times_{S} H \to P \times_{S} P\) is locally an isomorphism, hence
an isomorphism (4.5.8); \(P\) is therefore formally principal
homogeneous. The structural morphism \(P \to S\) is locally isomorphic
to the structural morphism \(H \to S\) which is an element of
\texttt{(M)}. It is therefore itself an element of \texttt{(M)} by
(e\_T).

The equivalence between (i) and (iv) generalizes:

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.7.} \emph{Under the same hypotheses on \(C\) and
\texttt{(M)}, let \(H\) be an \(S\)-group and \(X\) an \(S\)-object on
which \(H\) operates (on the right). Suppose the structural morphism
\(H \to S\) is an element of \texttt{(M)}. The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(H\) operates freely on \(X\) and in an
\texttt{(M)}-effective manner.}

\emph{(ii) There exists an \(S\)-morphism \(p : X \to Y\) compatible
with the equivalence relation defined in \(X\) by the action of \(H\)
and such that the operation of \(H \times_{S} Y\) on \(X\) above \(Y\)
thus deduced makes \(X\) a principal homogeneous bundle under
\texttt{H\_Y} above \(Y\).}

\emph{Under these conditions \(p\) identifies \(Y\) with the quotient
\(X/H\).}

If \(p : X \to Y\) is a morphism compatible with the action of \(H\),
then the operation of \(H \times_{S} Y\) on \(X\) above \(Y\) thus
deduced defines in \(X\) the same equivalence relation as the action of
\(H\), by virtue of the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\_Y ×\_Y X ⥲ H ×\_S X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The proposition follows from this remark and from the equivalence (iv) ⇔
(i) above.

\textbf{Corollary 5.1.7.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this
  particular case as a corollary, which will be used several times in
  the following Exposés.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category having a final
object, stable under fibered products, and equipped with a topology
\(T\) coarser than the canonical topology. Let \(f : G \to H\) be a
morphism of \(C\)-groups, and \(K = Ker(f)\). Assume \(f\) covering for
the topology \(T\).}

\emph{Then \(H\) represents the sheaf quotient \(G/K\), and \(f\) is a
\texttt{K\_H}-torsor. (N.B. One will also say that: ``\(G\) is a
\(K\)-torsor above \(H\)''.)}

Indeed, as \(f\) is covering, it is a universal effective epimorphism
(4.4.3), hence by 3.3.3.1, \(H\) is the quotient of \(G\) by the
equivalence relation \(R(f) = G \times_{H} G\). On the other hand, the
morphism \(G \times K \to G \times_{H} G\), \((g, k) \mapsto (g, gk)\)
is an isomorphism of objects with operator group
\(K_{G} = G \times_{H} K_{H}\) (its inverse being given by
\((g, g') \mapsto (g, g^{-1} g')\)). Hence, on the one hand, \(R(f)\) is
the equivalence relation defined by \(K\); on the other hand, since the
morphism \(f : G \to H\) is covering, \(f\) is a \texttt{K\_H}-torsor,
by 5.1.6 (ii) (or directly by definition 5.1.5 (ii)).

We can now make Theorem 4.6.6 more precise in the case of passage to the
quotient by an operator group:

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.8.} \emph{Under the hypotheses of 5.1.7, let
\texttt{F\_0} denote the functor over \(S\) defined as follows: for each
\(S' \to S\), \(F_{0}(S')\) is the set of representable
sub-\(S'\)-functors \(Z\) of \(X \times_{S} S'\), stable under
\(H \times_{S} S'\) and being principal homogeneous bundles under this
\(S'\)-group for the induced action (3.2.2).}

\emph{(i) The following conditions are equivalent:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{a) The operation of \(H\) on \(X\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective and
  free.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added ``and free''.}}
\item
  \emph{b) \texttt{F\_0} is representable.}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Under these conditions, one has \(F_{0} = X/H\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \texttt{(N)} be a family of morphisms, stable under base
change, such that for every covering family \({S'_{i} \to S'}\) and
every family \({T_{i} \to S'_{i}}\) of morphisms of \texttt{(N)}, every
descent datum on the \(T_{i}\) relative to \({S'_{i} \to S'}\) is
effective. Assume the morphism \(X \times_{S} H \to X \times_{S} X\) is
an element of \texttt{(N)} and \(X\) squarable. Then the element \(p\)
of \(\operatorname{Hom}(X, F_{0})\) corresponding to the sub-object
\(X \times_{S} H\) of \(X \times_{S} X\) identifies \texttt{F\_0} with
the sheaf-quotient \(X/H\).}

\subsubsection{5.2. Group structures and passage to the
quotient}\label{group-structures-and-passage-to-the-quotient}

In this number we interest ourselves in the algebraic structures one can
