place on the quotient \(G/H\) of a group by a subgroup. We shall first
place ourselves in the category of sheaves on \(C\) for an arbitrary
topology. By taking the canonical topology and using 4.5.12, we shall
obtain results for the universal effective passage to the quotient in
\(C\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.1.} \emph{Let \(u : H \to G\) be a monomorphism
of sheaves of groups. There exists on the sheaf-quotient \(G/H\) a
unique structure of object with operator group \(G\) such that the
canonical morphism}

\[
p : G \longrightarrow G/H
\]

\emph{is a morphism of objects with operator group \(G\). This structure
is functorial with respect to the pair \((G, H)\): if one has a
commutative diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ──→ G}
\NormalTok{│      │}
\NormalTok{│      │ f}
\NormalTok{↓      ↓}
\NormalTok{H′ ──→ G′ ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the morphism \(f : G/H \to G'/H'\) (3.2.3) is compatible with the
morphism \(f\) on the operator groups.}

Indeed, the sheaf \(G/H\) is the sheaf associated with the presheaf

\[
i(G)/i(H) : S \mapsto G(S)/H(S);
\]

as the functor \(a\) is left exact, it transforms objects with operator
groups into objects with operator group. As the presheaf \(i(G)/i(H)\)
is equipped with a structure of object with operator groups \(i(G)\),
then \(G/H = a(i(G)/i(H))\) is equipped with a structure of object with
operators \(a(i(G)) = G\). This structure obviously enjoys all the
stated properties.

\textbf{Corollary 5.2.2.} \emph{Let \(u : H \to G\) be a monomorphism of
\(C\)-groups. Suppose that the operation of \(H\) on \(G\) is universal
effective. There exists on the object-quotient \(G/H \in Ob C\) a unique
structure of object with operator group \(G\) such that
\(p : G \to G/H\) is a morphism of objects with operators. This
structure is functorial in the pair \((H, G)\) (with \(H\) operating in
a universal effective manner in \(G\)), in the preceding sense.}

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.3.} \emph{Let \(u : H \to G\) be a monomorphism
of sheaves of groups identifying \(H\) with an invariant sub-sheaf of
groups of \(G\). There exists on the sheaf-quotient \(G/H\) a unique
structure of sheaf of groups such that the canonical morphism
\(p : G \to G/H\) is a morphism of groups. This structure is functorial
in the pair \((H, G)\) (with \(H\) invariant).}

The proof is similar to that of 5.2.1.

\textbf{Corollary 5.2.4.} \emph{Let \(u : H \to G\) be a monomorphism of
\(C\)-groups identifying \(H\) with an invariant subgroup of \(G\).
Suppose that the action of \(H\) on \(G\) is universal effective. There
exists on the object-quotient \(G/H \in Ob C\) a unique group structure}

\emph{such that the canonical morphism \(G \to G/H\) is a morphism of
groups. This structure is functorial with respect to the pair \((H, G)\)
(\(H\) invariant, \(H\) operating in a universal effective manner).}

One can characterize the group structure of \(G/H\) in a more telling
manner:

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.5.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.2.4, let
\(K\) be a \(C\)-group and \(f : G \to K\) a morphism. The following
conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(f\) is a morphism of groups compatible with the equivalence
relation defined by \(H\).}

\emph{(ii) \(f\) is a morphism of groups inducing the trivial morphism
\(H \to K\).}

\emph{(iii) \(f\) factors as a morphism of groups \(G/H \to K\).}

\emph{In particular, one has an isomorphism, functorial in the group
\(K\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{C{-}gr.\}(G/H, K) ⥲ \{f ∈ Hom\_\{C{-}gr.\}(G, K) | f ∘ u = e\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The equivalence of (i) and (ii) is proved set-theoretically. One
obviously has (iii) ⇒ (ii). The equivalence of (iii) and (ii) follows
from the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom(G/H, K) ≃ Hom(i(G)/i(H), K)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and from the definition of the group structure of \(G/H\).

\textbf{Remark 5.2.6.} \emph{In the preceding situation, if the kernel
of \(f\) is exactly \(H\), the morphism \(G/H \to K\) that factors \(f\)
is a monomorphism. This follows at once from 3.3.4.}

In the case of sheaves of groups, one can make 4.4.11 more precise by
means of the

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.7.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a sheaf of groups, \(H\)
an invariant sub-sheaf of groups. For every sub-sheaf of groups \(K\) of
\(G\) containing \(H\), let \(K'\) be the quotient group \(K/H\)
considered as a subgroup of \(G' = G/H\).}

\emph{One has \(K = K' \times_{G'} G\), and the maps \(K \mapsto K/H\)
and \(K' \mapsto K' \times_{G'} G\) realize a bijection between the set
of sub-sheaves of groups of \(G\) containing \(H\) and the set of
sub-sheaves of groups of \(G'\). In this correspondence, the invariant
sub-sheaves of groups of \(G\) and of \(G'\) correspond.}

The first part follows easily from 4.4.11 and 3.2.4. It remains to see
that \(K\) is invariant in \(G\) if and only if \(K'\) is invariant in
\(G'\). If \(K\) is invariant in \(G\), then the presheaf \(i(K)/i(H)\)
is invariant in \(i(G)/i(H)\). The same holds for the associated
sheaves, by virtue of the usual argument. If conversely \(K'\) is
invariant in \(G'\), then the fibered product \(K \times_{G'} G\) is
invariant in \(G\), as one sees immediately.

If now \(L\) is an arbitrary sub-sheaf of groups of \(G\), let
\(\bar{L}\) be the saturation of \(L\) for the equivalence relation
defined by \(H\); we shall also write \(\bar{L} = L \cdot H\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.8.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions,
\(L \cdot H\) is a sub-sheaf of groups of \(G\) containing \(H\) and the
image of \(L\) in \(G/H\) is identified with}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(L · H)/H ≃ L/(H ∩ L).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, let \(L'\) denote the sheaf image of \(L\) in \(G/H\). It is a
sub-sheaf of groups of \(G/H\) corresponding to \(L \cdot H\) in the
correspondence of the preceding proposition. As the morphism
\(L \to L'\) is covering, hence a universal effective epimorphism of
sheaves, it follows from 4.4.9 that \(L'\) is identified with the
quotient of \(L\) by the kernel of \(L \to L'\) which is obviously none
other than \(H \cap L\).

Let us finally consider the following situation: we have a sheaf of
groups \(G\), a sub-sheaf of groups \(K\) and a sub-sheaf of groups
\(H\) of \(K\), invariant in \(K\). Let us first define a (right)
operation of the sheaf of groups \(H\backslash K\) (= \(K/H\)) on
\(G/H\). The group \(K\) operates by right translations on \(G\). As
\(H\) is invariant in \(K\), this operation is compatible with the
equivalence relation defined by the action of \(H\) and therefore
defines an operation of \(K\) on \(G/H\), that is, a morphism from the
opposite group \(K^{\circ}\) to \(K\) into \(\operatorname{Aut}(G/H)\).
As the latter is a sheaf (4.5.13) and this morphism is trivial on \(H\),
it factors through \(K/H\) and defines the sought operation. As the
right and left operations of \(G\) on itself commute, the operations of
\(G\) and \(K/H\) on \(G/H\) commute.

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.9.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions,
\(K/H\) operates freely (on the right) on \(G/H\) and one has a
canonical isomorphism of sheaves with operator group \(G\)}

\[
(G/H)/(K/H) \simeq G/K.
\]

\emph{When \(K\) is invariant in \(G\), in which case \(K/H\) is
invariant in \(G/H\) (5.2.7), this isomorphism respects the group
structures of the two sides.}

One has an isomorphism of presheaves

\[
(i(G)/i(H)) / (i(K)/i(H)) \xrightarrow{\sim} i(G)/i(K),
\]

which respects the structures of objects with operator group \(i(G)\).
The announced result is obtained by applying the functor \(a\) to this
relation.

\textbf{Corollary 5.2.10.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a \(C\)-group, \(K\) a
sub-\(C\)-group of \(G\), \(H\) an invariant sub-\(C\)-group of \(K\).
Let \texttt{(M)} be a family of morphisms of \(C\) verifying the axioms
(a) to (e\_T). Suppose the operation of \(H\) on \(G\) (resp. \(K\)) on
the right is \texttt{(M)}-effective. Then \(K/H\) operates in a natural
manner freely on the right on \(G/H\); this operation commutes with that
of \(G\). The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) The operation of \(K\) on \(G\) is \texttt{(M)}-effective.}

\emph{(ii) The operation of \(K/H\) on \(G/H\) is
\texttt{(M)}-effective.}

\emph{Under these conditions, one has an isomorphism of
objects\footnote{N.D.E.: of \(C\).} with operator group \(G\):}

\[
(G/H)/(K/H) \simeq G/K.
\]

\subsubsection[5.3. Use of effectivity criteria: Noether's
theorem]{\texorpdfstring{5.3. Use of effectivity criteria: Noether's
theorem\footnote{N.D.E.: In fact, the isomorphisms established in 5.2.8
  to 5.2.10 would deserve to be called ``Noether isomorphism theorems''.}}{5.3. Use of effectivity criteria: Noether's theorem}}\label{use-of-effectivity-criteria-noethers-theoremn.d.e-iv-54}

Let \(C\), \(T\) and \texttt{(M)} be as usual. Let \texttt{(N)} be a
family of morphisms verifying the axioms (a) and (f\_M) of 4.7. Putting
together 5.2.7 and 4.7.2, one obtains:

\textbf{Proposition 5.3.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a \(C\)-group. Let \(H\)
be a sub-\(C\)-group of \(G\), invariant and operating in an
\texttt{(M)}-effective manner in \(G\).}

\emph{For every sub-\(C\)-group \(K\) of \(G\) containing \(H\) and such
that the morphism \(K \to G\) belongs to \texttt{(N)}, \(H\) operates in
\(K\) in an \texttt{(M)}-effective manner and the quotient \(K/H = K'\)
is a sub-\(C\)-group of \(G/H = G'\) such that the morphism
\(K' \to G'\) belongs to \texttt{(N)}.}

\emph{The map \(K \mapsto K'\) is a bijection between the set of
sub-\(C\)-groups \(K\) of \(G\), containing \(H\) and such that
\(K \to G\) belongs to \texttt{(N)}, and the set of sub-\(C\)-groups
\(K'\) of \(G'\) such that \(K' \to G'\) belongs to \texttt{(N)}. The
inverse map is \(K' \mapsto K \times_{G'} G\). In this correspondence,
the invariant subgroups of \(G\) and \(G'\) correspond.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.2.} \emph{If \(H \to G\) is an element of
\texttt{(N)}, then \(C\) has a final object \(e\) and the unit section
\(e \to G/H\) is an element of \texttt{(N)}.\footnote{N.D.E.: This
  follows from the proposition applied to \(K = H\).}}

\subsection{6. Topologies in the category of
schemes}\label{topologies-in-the-category-of-schemes}

\subsubsection{6.1. The Zariski topology}\label{the-zariski-topology}

This is the topology generated by the following pretopology: a family of
morphisms \({S_{i} \to S}\) is covering if each morphism is an open
immersion and the union of the images of the \(S_{i}\) is all of \(S\).
It is denoted (Zar).

\textbf{Definition 6.1.1.} \emph{A sheaf for the Zariski topology is
also called} a functor of local nature*: it is a contravariant functor
from \texttt{(Sch)} to \texttt{(Ens)} such that for every scheme \(S\)
and every covering of \(S\) by opens \(S_{i}\), one has an exact
diagram:*

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S) → ∏\_i F(S\_i) ⇒ ∏\_\{i,j\} F(S\_i ∩ S\_j).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, a functor of local nature transforms direct sums into
products. As every representable functor is a sheaf, this topology is
coarser than the canonical topology.

From the terminological point of view, whenever we say ``local'',
``locally'', without precision, it will be with reference to the Zariski
topology, hence in the usual sense.

\subsubsection{6.2. A procedure for constructing
topologies}\label{a-procedure-for-constructing-topologies}

\textbf{Proposition 6.2.1.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category, \(C '\) a
full subcategory, \(P\) a set of families of morphisms of \(C\) with the
same target, stable under base change and under composition
(i.e.~verifying the axioms (P 1) and (P 2) of 4.2.5), \(P'\) a set of
families of morphisms of \(C '\) containing the families reduced to an
identity isomorphism. Equip \(C\) with the topology generated by \(P\)
and \(P'\) (cf.~4.2.5.0) and suppose the three conditions below are
verified:}

\emph{(a) If \({S_{i} \to S} \in P'\) (hence \(S_{i}, S \in Ob C '\))
and if \(T \to S\) is a morphism of \(C '\), then the fibered products
\(S_{i} \times_{S} T\) (in \(C\)) exist and the family
\({S_{i} \times_{S} T \to T}\) belongs to \(P'\) (hence
\(S_{i} \times_{S} T \in Ob C '\)). (Remark: this condition entails that
\(P'\) is stable under base change in \(C '\), but is not equivalent to
it, since it further supposes that the inclusion functor from \(C '\) to
\(C\) commutes with certain fibered products).}

\emph{(b) For every \(S \in Ob C\), there exists \({S_{i} \to S} \in P\)
with \(S_{i} \in Ob C '\) for each \(i\).}

\emph{(c) In the following situation:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              S\_\{ijk\}}
\NormalTok{                │ (P′)}
\NormalTok{                ↓}
\NormalTok{        (P)  S\_\{ij\}}
\NormalTok{   S\_i ←──── │}
\NormalTok{        (P′) │}
\NormalTok{             ↓}
\NormalTok{             S ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(S, S_{i}, S_{ij}, S_{ijk} \in Ob C '\);
\({S_{i} \to S} \in P'\); \({S_{ij} \to S_{i}} \in P\) for each \(i\);
\({S_{ijk} \to S_{ij}} \in P'\) for each \texttt{ij}, there exists a
family \({T_{n} \to S} \in P'\) and for each \(n\) a multi-index
\texttt{(ijk)} and a commutative diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S\_\{ijk\} ←──── T\_n}
\NormalTok{       ╲     ╱}
\NormalTok{        ╲   ╱}
\NormalTok{         ╲ ╱}
\NormalTok{          S .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then, in order for a sieve \(R\) of \(S \in Ob C\) to be covering,
it is necessary and sufficient that there exist a composite family}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ←┄┄┄ S\_\{ij\}}
\NormalTok{        │ (P′)}
\NormalTok{        ↓}
\NormalTok{   S ←─ S\_i}
\NormalTok{        (P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(S_{i}, S_{ij} \in Ob C '\), \({S_{i} \to S} \in P\),
\({S_{ij} \to S_{i}} \in P'\) for each \(i\), and the morphisms
\(S_{ij} \to S\) so obtained factor through \(R\) (in other words, the
sieve generated by this composite family is contained in \(R\)).}

\emph{Proof.} As the families elements of \(P\) and of \(P'\) are
covering, a family composed of such families will be also (C 2), hence a
sieve of the indicated form will be covering, since it contains a
covering sieve.

Conversely, it suffices to see that the sieves of this form do indeed
form a topology, i.e.~it suffices to verify the axioms (T 1) to (T 4) of
4.2.1.

\emph{Axiom (T 4).} Let \(S \in Ob C\). There exists by (b) a family
\({S_{i} \to S} \in P\) with \(S_{i} \in Ob C '\). The families
\({S_{i} \to^{id_{S_{i}}} S_{i}}\) are elements of \(P'\) by hypothesis.
The sieve \(S\) of \(S\) is therefore of the desired form:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S\_i ───→ S}
\NormalTok{ │  (P′) id    id\_S}
\NormalTok{ ↓  (P)    }
\NormalTok{S\_i ───→ S .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Axiom (T 3).} Evident.

\emph{Axiom (T 2).} Let \(R\) be a sieve of \(S\) of the desired form
and let \(C\) be a sieve\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the original
  here.} of \(S\) such that, for every \(T \in Ob C\) and every morphism
\(T \to S\) factoring through \(R\), the sieve \(C \times_{S} T\) of
\(T\) is of the desired form. Then, as \(S_{ij} \to S\) factors through
\(R\), the sieve \(C_{ij} = C \times_{S} S_{ij}\) of \(S_{ij}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        S\_\{ij\} ←─── C\_\{ij\}}
\NormalTok{       ╱  (P′)}
\NormalTok{      ╱}
\NormalTok{    S\_i}
\NormalTok{     │ (P)}
\NormalTok{     ↓}
\NormalTok{     S ←──── C}
\NormalTok{     ↑}
\NormalTok{     R}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is of the desired form; hence, for each \texttt{ij}, one has a diagram
of the form:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S\_\{ijkl\}}
\NormalTok{   │ (P′)}
\NormalTok{   ↓}
\NormalTok{S\_\{ijk\}}
\NormalTok{   │}
\NormalTok{   │ (P)}
\NormalTok{   ↓}
\NormalTok{S\_\{ij\} ←──── C\_\{ij\} .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore proved that there exists a composite family

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S\_\{ijkl\} ──(P′)─→ S\_\{ijk\} ──(P)─→ S\_\{ij\} ──(P′)─→ S\_i ──(P)─→ S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

belonging to \(P \circ P' \circ P \circ P'\), factoring through \(C\),
and where all objects other than \(S\) are in \(C '\). Applying
condition (c) to each family \({S_{ijkl} \to S_{i}}\), one deduces that
for each \(i\) there exists a family \({T_{in} \to S_{i}} \in P'\), such
that \(T_{in} \to S\) factors through one of the \(S_{ijkl}\), hence
through \(C\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{in\} ──→ S\_\{ijkl\}}
\NormalTok{   │ (P′)}
\NormalTok{   ↓}
\NormalTok{   S\_i}
\NormalTok{   │ (P)}
\NormalTok{   ↓}
\NormalTok{   S ←──── C .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The sieve \(C\) of \(S\) is therefore of the desired form, which
completes the verification.

\emph{Axiom (T 1).} Let \(R\) be a sieve of \(S\) of the given form and
let \(T \to S\) be a morphism of \(C\). Let us show that the sieve
\(R \times_{S} T\) of \(T\) is of the desired form.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       S\_\{ij\} ←──────── U\_\{ikj\}}
\NormalTok{          │ (P′)              (P′)}
\NormalTok{          ↓                   ↓}
\NormalTok{   S\_i ←─────────── T\_i ←─(P)── U\_\{ik\}}
\NormalTok{          │                       ╱}
\NormalTok{          │ (P)            (P)   ╱ (P)}
\NormalTok{          ↓                     ╱}
\NormalTok{   R ──→ S ←──────── T ←───────}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(T_{i} = S_{i} \times_{S} T\). The family \({T_{i} \to T}\) belongs
to \(P\) (by (P 1)). Applying (b), one constructs
\({U_{ik} \to T_{i}} \in P\), with the \(U_{ik} \in Ob C '\). By
hypothesis (condition (P 2) on \(P\)), one has \({U_{ik} \to T} \in P\).
By (a), \(U_{ik} \times_{S_{i}} S_{ij} = U_{ikj}\) is an object of
\(C '\) and for each \texttt{ik}, \({U_{ikj} \to U_{ik}} \in P'\). Then,
the commutative diagram below

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ←──────── U\_\{ikj\}}
\NormalTok{              │ (P′)}
\NormalTok{              ↓}
\NormalTok{              U\_\{ik\}}
\NormalTok{              │ (P)}
\NormalTok{              ↓}
\NormalTok{S ←──── T ←── }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

shows that the morphisms \(U_{ijk} \to T\) factor through the sieve
\(T \times_{S} R\) of \(T\), which is therefore of the desired form,
which completes the proof.

\textbf{Corollary 6.2.2.} \emph{If \(S \in Ob C '\) and if \(R\) is a
sieve of \(S\), \(R\) is covering if and only if there exists a family
\({T_{i} \to S} \in P'\), factoring through \(R\).}

Indeed, such a sieve is covering. On the other hand, it suffices to
apply (c) by taking the family \({S_{i} \to S}\) reduced to the identity
isomorphism of \(S\) to deduce from the proposition that a covering
sieve is of the indicated form.

\textbf{Corollary 6.2.3.} \emph{In order for a presheaf \(F\) on \(C\)
to be separated (resp. a sheaf), it is necessary and sufficient that the
morphism}

\[
F(S) \longrightarrow \prod_{i} F(S_{i})
\]

\emph{be injective (resp. that the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S) ⟶ ∏\_i F(S\_i) ⇒ ∏\_\{i,j\} F(S\_i ×\_S S\_j)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be exact) in the two following cases:}

\emph{(i) \({S_{i} \to S} \in P\),}

\emph{(ii) \(S, S_{i} \in Ob C '\); \({S_{i} \to S} \in P'\).}

Indeed, the conditions are necessary, since the families in question are
covering. If \(C\) is the sieve of \(S\) image of a family of morphisms
\({S_{ij} \to^{(P')} S_{i} \to^{(P)} S}\), a straightforward diagram
chase shows that the conditions of the corollary entail that
\(\operatorname{Hom}(S, F) \to^{g} \operatorname{Hom}(C, F)\) is
injective (resp. bijective). But every refinement \(R\) of \(S\)
contains a sieve \(C\) of the above type and one has a commutative
diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                f}
\NormalTok{Hom(S, F) ───────────→ Hom(R, F)}
\NormalTok{       ╲                  ╱}
\NormalTok{        ╲ g           h ╱}
\NormalTok{         ╲             ╱}
\NormalTok{          ↘           ↙}
\NormalTok{           Hom(C, F) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One knows that \(g\) is injective, hence so is \(f\). Therefore \(F\) is
separated. But \(R\) is a refinement of \(C\), hence \(h\) is also
injective. If \(g\) is bijective, then \(f\) is also, hence \(F\) is a
sheaf.

\textbf{Remark 6.2.4.} \emph{The preceding corollary does not follow
from 4.3.5, because \(P'\) is not stable under base extension.}

\textbf{Remark 6.2.5.} \emph{Condition (c) is verified in particular in
the case where}

\emph{(i) \(P'\) is stable under composition.}

\emph{(ii) If \({S_{j} \to S}\) is a family of morphisms of \(C '\),
element of \(P\), there exists a subfamily element of \(P'\).}

\subsubsection{6.3. Application to the category of
schemes}\label{application-to-the-category-of-schemes}

One takes for \(C\) the category of schemes, for \(C '\) the full
subcategory formed by affine schemes, for \(P\) the set of surjective
families of open immersions. One will consider several sets \(P'\):

\(P'_{1}\) : finite surjective families, composed of flat morphisms.

\(P'_{2}\) : finite surjective families, composed of flat morphisms of
finite presentation and quasi-finite.\footnote{N.D.E.: Let \(P''_{2}\)
  denote the set of finite surjective families, composed of flat
  morphisms of \(C '\) of finite presentation. According to Proposition
  6.3.1 below, the topology \texttt{T\_2} generated by \(P\) and
  \(P'_{2}\) coincides with the topology generated by \(P\) and
  \(P''_{2}\). This follows from the results of EGA IV\_4, § 17.16 on
  quasi-sections; see the proof of 6.3.1. Let us cite here the following
  particular case of EGA IV\_4, 17.16.2: let \(S\) be affine and
  \(f : X \to S\) a surjective flat morphism locally of finite
  presentation; then there exists a morphism \(S' \to S\) faithfully
  flat, of finite presentation, quasi-finite, with \(S'\) affine, and an
  \(S\)-morphism \(S' \to X\).}

\(P'_{3}\) : finite surjective families, composed of étale morphisms.

\(P'_{4}\) : finite surjective families, composed of étale and finite
morphisms.

For each of these sets \(P'_{i}\), except \(P'_{4}\), the conditions of
Proposition 6.2.1 are verified ((c) thanks to 6.2.5, since an affine
scheme being quasi-compact, every family of morphisms of \(C '\),
element of \(P\), contains a finite subfamily that is also in \(P\),
hence in \(P'_{i}\) for \(i = 1, 2, 3\)). The topology \(T_{i}\)
generated by \(P\) and \(P'_{i}\) is denoted and called in the following
way:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_1 = (fpqc) = faithfully flat quasi{-}compact topology.}
\NormalTok{T\_2 = (fppf) = faithfully flat (locally) of finite presentation topology.}
\NormalTok{T\_3 = (ét)  = étale topology.}
\NormalTok{T\_4 = (étf) = étale finite topology.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

As \(P'_{1} \supset P'_{2} \supset P'_{3} \supset P'_{4}\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(fpqc) ≥ (fppf) ≥ (ét) ≥ (étf) ≥ (Zar).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 6.3.1.} \emph{(i) In order for the sieve \(R\) of
\(S\) to be covering for \(T_{i}\), \(1 \leq i \leq 3\), it is necessary
and sufficient that there exist a covering \((S_{p})\) of \(S\) by
affine opens and for each \(p\) a family \({S_{pq} \to S_{p}}\) element
of \(P'_{i}\), the \(S_{pq}\) being affine, such that each morphism
\({S_{pq} \to S}\) factors through \(R\).\footnote{N.D.E.: By
  hypothesis, each family \({S_{pq} \to S} \in P'_{i}\) is finite, hence
  \(S'_{p} = \bigsqcup_{q} S_{pq}\) is affine and the family can
  therefore be replaced by the morphism \(S'_{p} \to S_{p}\), which
  still belongs to \(P'_{i}\).}}

\emph{(ii) In order for a presheaf \(F\) on \texttt{(Sch)} to be a sheaf
for (fpqc) (resp. (fppf), (ét), (étf)), it is necessary and sufficient
that}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{a) \(F\) be a sheaf for (Zar), i.e.~a functor of local nature.}
\item
  \emph{b) For every faithfully flat (resp. faithfully flat of finite
  presentation and quasi-finite, resp. surjective étale, resp.
  surjective étale finite) morphism \(T \to S\), where \(T\) and \(S\)
  are affine, one has an exact diagram:}
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S) ⟶ F(T) ⇒ F(T ×\_S T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) The topologies \(T_{i}\), \(i = 1, 2, 3, 4\), are coarser
than the canonical topology.}

\emph{(iv) Every surjective family formed of flat and open morphisms
(resp. flat and locally of finite presentation, resp. étale, resp. étale
and finite) is covering for (fpqc) (resp. (fppf), resp. (ét), resp.
(étf)).}

\emph{(v) Every finite surjective family formed of flat and
quasi-compact morphisms is covering for (fpqc). In particular, every
faithfully flat and quasi-compact morphism is covering for (fpqc).}

\emph{Proof.} (i) follows from 6.2.1, (ii) from 6.2.3, taking into
account the fact that a sheaf for the Zariski topology transforms direct
sums into products. Every representable functor being a sheaf for (Zar)
and verifying condition (b) of (ii) by SGA 1, VIII 5.3, \texttt{T\_1} is
coarser than the canonical topology, which proves (iii).

Let us prove (iv). Let \({S_{i} \to S}\) be a family of morphisms as in
the statement. Considering a covering of \(S\) by affine opens, one
reduces immediately to the case where \(S\) is affine.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have simplified what follows, taking advantage of the fact that
  \(S\) is henceforth assumed affine.}

Let us first treat the case where the morphisms \(S_{i} \to S\) are flat
and open (resp. étale). Let \(S_{ij}\) be a covering of \(S_{i}\) by
affine opens. As the morphisms in question are open, the images
\(T_{ij}\) of the \(S_{ij}\) form an open covering of \(S\). As \(S\) is
affine, hence quasi-compact, it is covered by a finite number of opens
\(T_{ij}\), for \((i, j)\) running through a finite set \(F\). Then
\(S' = \bigsqcup_{F} S_{ij}\) is affine, and the morphism \(S' \to S\)
belongs to \(P'_{1}\), resp. \(P'_{3}\), hence is covering. As it
factors through the given family, the latter is covering.

In the case (étf), each \(S_{i}\) is finite over \(S\) hence is affine;
in the preceding argument, one can then take the covering \({S_{i}}\) of
\(S_{i}\), and one obtains that \(S' \to S\) belongs to \(P'_{4}\).

Let us now consider the case where the morphisms \(f_{i} : S_{i} \to S\)
are flat and locally of finite presentation. For every \(s \in S\),
there exists, by (the proof of) EGA IV\_4, 17.16.2, an affine subscheme
\(X(s)\) of a certain \(S_{i}\), such that \(s \in f_{i}(X(s))\) and
that the morphism \(g_{i} : X(s) \to S\), restriction of \(f_{i}\), is
flat, of finite presentation, and quasi-finite. Then, \(g_{i}(X(s))\) is
an open neighborhood \(U(s)\) of \(s\) (EGA IV\_2, 2.4.6), and, \(S\)
being affine, it is covered by a finite number of such opens
\(U(s_{j})\), \texttt{j\ =\ 1,\ ...,\ n}. Consequently,
\(X' = \bigsqcup_{j} X(s_{j})\) is affine, and the morphism \(X' \to S\)
is surjective, flat, of finite presentation, and quasi-finite, hence
belongs to \(P'_{2}\).\footnote{N.D.E.: This shows that, if one denotes
  \(P''_{2}\) the set of finite surjective families of morphisms of
  \(C '\) flat of finite presentation, the topology generated by \(P\)
  and \(P''_{2}\) equals \texttt{T\_2}. On the other hand, with the
  notations at the start of the proof of (iv), if one takes a covering
  of \(S_{i}\) by affine opens, of finite presentation over \(S\), one
  obtains that \(S' \to S\) belongs to \(P''_{2}\).} This completes the
proof of (iv).

Let us prove (v). Let \({S_{i} \to S}\) be a finite faithfully flat and
quasi-compact family. Let \(T_{j}\) be a covering of \(S\) by affine
opens. The \(S_{ij} = T_{j} \times_{S} S_{i}\) are quasi-compact and
therefore have finite affine open coverings \(T_{ijk}\). Each morphism
\(T_{ijk} \to T_{j}\) is flat, and the family \({T_{ijk} \to T_{j}}\) is
finite and surjective, hence covering for \texttt{T\_1}. The family
\({T_{ijk} \to S}\) is therefore also, by composition. It factors
through the given family which is therefore also:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S\_i ←──── S\_\{ij\} ←──── T\_\{ijk\}}
\NormalTok{                          ╱}
\NormalTok{                         ╱}
\NormalTok{                        ╱}
\NormalTok{S ←──── T\_j ←─────────}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 6.3.2.} \emph{Let \((M_{i})\) be the following family
of morphisms:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{(M\_1) : faithfully flat and quasi-compact morphisms.}
\item
  \emph{(M\_2) : faithfully flat morphisms locally of finite
  presentation.}
\item
  \emph{(M\_3) : surjective étale morphisms.}
\item
  \emph{(M\_4) : surjective étale finite morphisms.\footnote{N.D.E.: We
    have corrected the original by adding the surjectivity hypothesis
    for \texttt{(M\_3)} and \texttt{(M\_4)}, which is automatically
    satisfied in the other cases.}}
\end{itemize}

\emph{The family \((M_{i})\) verifies the axioms (a), (b), (c),
(d\_\{T\_i\}) and (e\_\{T\_i\}) of 4.6.3.}

Indeed, for (a), (b), (c), it is classical (EGA and SGA 1,
passim.).\footnote{N.D.E.: cf.~EGA I, 6.6.4 for ``quasi-compact'', EGA
  II, 6.1.5 for ``finite'', EGA IV\_1, 1.6.2 for ``locally of finite
  presentation'', EGA IV\_2, 2.2.13 for ``faithfully flat'', and EGA
  IV\_4, 17.3.3 for ``étale''.} By 6.3.1, (iv) and (v), \((M_{i})\)
verifies (d\_\{T\_i\}). It remains to see that \((M_{i})\) verifies
(e\_\{T\_i\}); for this, it suffices to see that \((M_{i})\) verifies
(e\_\{T\_1\}), which entails the others. This follows from SGA 1, VIII
(nos 4 and 5).

\textbf{Corollary 6.3.3.} \emph{If \(X\) is a scheme and \(R\) an
equivalence relation in \(X\) of type \((M_{i})\), \(R\) is
\((M_{i})\)-effective if and only if the sheaf-quotient of \(X\) by
\(R\) for \(T_{i}\) is representable and in this case it is represented
by the quotient \(X/R\).}

Indeed, this is 4.6.5.

\subsubsection{6.4. Effectivity
conditions}\label{effectivity-conditions}

We now seek families \texttt{(N)} of morphisms verifying axiom (f\_T) of
4.7. Let us first remark that (f\_\{T\_1\}) entails (f\_\{T\_i\}), so
that we may restrict ourselves to the case of the topology (fpqc).

\textbf{Lemma 6.4.1.} \emph{The following families of morphisms verify
axiom (f\_\{T\_1\}) of 4.7, that is, ``descend by (fpqc)'':}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{(N) : open immersions.}
\item
  \emph{(N′) : closed immersions.}
\item
  \emph{(N″) : quasi-compact immersions.}
\end{itemize}

By virtue of 6.3.1 (ii), it suffices to verify that the given families
descend by the Zariski topology and by a faithfully flat quasi-compact
morphism. The first assertion is clear; let us verify the second. For
(N), this is SGA 1, VIII 4.4; for (N′), this is loc. cit., 1.9. For (N″)
one argues as in loc. cit., 5.5, using the two preceding results.

\textbf{Corollary 6.4.2.} \emph{The same result holds for quasi-compact
open immersions.}

These results allow one to apply to the present situation the general
results of 4.7.1, 4.7.2, 5.1.8, 5.3.1, etc. Let us state one as an
example, the first.

\textbf{Corollary 6.4.3.} \emph{(= 4.7.1 + 4.6.10).} \emph{Let \(X\) be
a scheme and \(R\) an equivalence relation in \(X\). Suppose that
\(R \to X\) is faithfully flat and quasi-compact and that
\(R \to X \times X\) is a closed immersion (resp. open, resp.
quasi-compact, resp. quasi-compact open). Then the sheaf-quotient
\(X/R\) is the same for the topology (fpqc) and for the canonical
topology, and for each scheme \(S\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(X/R)(S) = \{ closed (resp. open, resp. retrocompact[\^{}N.D.E{-}IV{-}63], resp. open retrocompact)}
\NormalTok{             subschemes Z of X\_S, stable under R × S, such that Z → S is}
\NormalTok{             faithfully flat quasi{-}compact and the diagram R\_Z ⇒ Z → S is exact \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{6.5. Principal homogeneous
bundles}\label{principal-homogeneous-bundles-1}

Let us simply indicate the terminology:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   topology     principal homogeneous bundles}
\NormalTok{   (fpqc)       "         "         "             (tout court)}
\NormalTok{   (ét)         "         "         "             quasi{-}isotrivial}
\NormalTok{   (étf)        "         "         "             locally isotrivial}
\NormalTok{   (Zar)        "         "         "             locally trivial.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{6.6. Other topologies}\label{other-topologies}

One sometimes uses other topologies on the category of schemes. Let us
indicate one: the \emph{global étale finite} topology (étfg), generated
by the pretopology whose covering families are the surjective families
formed of étale finite morphisms. It is not finer than the Zariski
topology. The corresponding principal homogeneous bundles are called
``isotrivial''.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                     (canonical)}
\NormalTok{                         │}
\NormalTok{                       (fpqc)}
\NormalTok{                         │}
\NormalTok{                       (fppf)}
\NormalTok{                         │}
\NormalTok{                        (ét)}
\NormalTok{                         │}
\NormalTok{                       (étf)}
\NormalTok{                       ╱    ╲}
\NormalTok{                      ╱      ╲}
\NormalTok{                  (Zar)    (étfg)}
\NormalTok{                      ╲      ╱}
\NormalTok{                       ╲    ╱}
\NormalTok{                    (chaotic)[\^{}N.D.E{-}IV{-}64]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection[6.7. Homogeneous spaces]{\texorpdfstring{6.7. Homogeneous
spaces\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the numbers that follow.}}{6.7. Homogeneous spaces}}\label{homogeneous-spacesn.d.e-iv-65}

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group scheme, \(X\) an \(S\)-scheme with (left)
operator group \(G\), and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Φ : G ×\_S X ⟶ X ×\_S X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the morphism of \(S\)-schemes defined setwise by
\((g, x) \mapsto (gx, x)\). Let us recall (cf.~5.1.0 and III.0.1) that
one says that \(X\) is a \emph{formally principal homogeneous space}
under \(G\) if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  for every \(T \to S\), the set \(X(T)\) is empty or principal
  homogeneous under \(G(T)\),
\item
  \(\Phi\) is an isomorphism of \(S\)-functors,
\item
  \(\Phi\) is an isomorphism of \(S\)-schemes.
\end{enumerate}

(The equivalence (i) ⇔ (ii) is clear, and one has (ii) ⇔ (iii) since
\(C = (Sch/S)\) is a full subcategory of \texttt{Ĉ}.)

The definition of formally homogeneous space (not necessarily principal
homogeneous) is obtained by requiring that \(\Phi\) be an epimorphism in
the category of sheaves for an appropriate topology \(T\). Indeed, the
condition that \(\Phi\) be an epimorphism of \(S\)-functors amounts to
the requirement that, for every \(T \to S\), the set \(X(T)\) be empty
or homogeneous (not necessarily principal homogeneous) under \(G(T)\),
but this condition is too restrictive, as the following simple example
shows. Let \(S = \operatorname{Spec} R\), \(G = G_{m,R}\) and
\(X = G_{m,R}\) on which \(G\) acts via \(t \cdot x = t^{2} x\). Then
the morphism \(\Phi\) is étale, finite, and surjective, hence an
epimorphism in the category of sheaves for the topology (étf) (a
fortiori, an epimorphism of \(S\)-schemes); on the other hand, the
points \texttt{1} and \(-1\) of \(X(R)\) are not conjugate by an element
of \(G(R)\), so that the morphism
\(G(R) \times X(R) \to X(R) \times X(R)\) is not surjective.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Evidently, this difficulty arises from the fact that if \(C '\) is a
  full subcategory of \texttt{Ĉ} containing \(C\), for example, the
  category \(\tilde{C}_{T}\) of sheaves on \(C\) for a topology \(T\)
  coarser than the canonical topology, and if \(f : X \to Y\) is a
  morphism in \(C\), then the implications:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f epimorphism of Ĉ ⇒ f epimorphism of C ′ ⇒ f epimorphism of C}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  are in general strict.} One is therefore led to lay down the following
definition:

\textbf{Definition 6.7.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group, \(X\) an
\(S\)-scheme with operator group \(G\), and \(T\) a topology on
\((Sch/S)\), coarser than the canonical topology. We say that \(X\) is
a} formally homogeneous space under \(G\) (relative to the topology
\(T\)) \emph{if the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:}

\emph{(i) the morphism \(\Phi : G \times_{S} X \to X \times_{S} X\) is
an epimorphism in the category of sheaves for the topology \(T\),}

\emph{(ii) for every \(T \to S\), and \(x, y \in X(T)\), there exists a
morphism \(T' \to T\) covering for the topology \(T\), and
\(g \in G(T')\), such that \(y_{T'} = g \cdot x_{T'}\).}

\textbf{Remark 6.7.2.} \emph{Condition (i) implies, in particular, that
\(\Phi\) is a universal effective epimorphism in \((Sch/S)\)
(cf.~4.4.3). This entails, as one easily sees, that \(\Phi\) is
surjective (cf.~1.3, N.D.E. (3)).}

\textbf{Proposition and Definition 6.7.3.}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  cf.~{[}Ray70{]}, Def. VI.1.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group,
\(X\) an \(S\)-scheme with operator group \(G\), and \(T\) a topology on
\((Sch/S)\), coarser than the canonical topology. The following
conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(X\) verifies the two hypotheses below:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{(1) the morphism \(\Phi : G \times_{S} X \to X \times_{S} X\) is
  covering, i.e.~\(X\) is a \(G\)-formally homogeneous space,}
\item
  \emph{(2) the morphism \(X \to S\) is also covering, i.e.~locally for
  the topology \(T\), it has a section (cf. RefIV.4.4.8bis.bis).}
\end{itemize}

\emph{(ii) ``Locally on \(S\) for the topology \(T\)'', \(X\) is
isomorphic, as a scheme with operator group \(G\), to the sheaf quotient
(for \(T\)) of \(G\) by a sub-group-scheme \(H\), i.e.~there exists a
covering family \({S_{i} \to S}\) such that each \(X \times_{S} S_{i}\)
represents the sheaf quotient of \(G \times_{S} S_{i}\) by a certain
sub-group-scheme \(H_{i}\).}

\emph{Under these conditions, one says that \(X\) is a
\(G\)-}homogeneous space* (relative to the topology \(T\)).*

\emph{Proof.} Suppose (ii) is verified. Set
\(G_{i} = G \times_{S} S_{i}\) and \(X_{i} = X \times_{S} S_{i}\). Then,
\(X_{i}\) has a section over \(S_{i}\), namely the composite of the unit
section \(\epsilon_{i} : S_{i} \to G_{i}\) and the projection
\(\pi_{i} : G_{i} \to X_{i} = G_{i}/H_{i}\). Hence \(X \to S\) is
covering.

On the other hand, \(\pi_{i}\) is covering, hence
\(\pi_{i} \times \pi_{i}\) is also (cf.~4.2.3 (C 1) and (C 2)), and one
has a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                 Φ\_i}
\NormalTok{G\_i ×\_\{S\_i\} X\_i ────→ G\_i ×\_\{S\_i\} X\_i}
\NormalTok{       ↑                       ↑}
\NormalTok{  id × π\_i                   π\_i × π\_i}
\NormalTok{       │                       │}
\NormalTok{                 Ψ\_i}
\NormalTok{G\_i ×\_\{S\_i\} G\_i ────→ G\_i ×\_\{S\_i\} G\_i}
\NormalTok{                  ∼}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\Phi_{i}\) is deduced from \(\Phi\) by the base change
\(S_{i} \to S\) and \(\Psi_{i}\) is the isomorphism defined setwise by
\((g, g') \mapsto (gg', g)\). Then
\((\pi_{i} \times \pi_{i}) \circ \Psi_{i}\) is covering, hence
\(\Phi_{i}\) is also (4.2.3 (C 3)). This shows that \(\Phi\) is
``locally covering'', hence is covering (4.2.3 (C 5)). This proves that
(ii) ⇒ (i).

Conversely, suppose (i) is verified, and suppose moreover that the
structural morphism \(X \to S\) has a section \(\sigma\). By EGA I,
5.3.13, \(\sigma\) is an immersion. Let us define \(H = G \times_{X} S\)
by the diagram below, in which the two squares are cartesian:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ──→ G ──id\_G ⊠ σ──→ G ×\_S X}
\NormalTok{│      │                 │}
\NormalTok{│      π                 Φ}
\NormalTok{↓ σ    ↓    id\_X ⊠ σ     ↓}
\NormalTok{S ──→ X ──────────────→ X ×\_S X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\pi\), \(id_{G} \boxtimes \sigma\) and
\(id_{X} \boxtimes \sigma\) denote the morphisms defined setwise, for
\(T \to S\) and \(g \in G(T)\), \(x \in X(T)\), by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π(g) = g · σ\_T,    (id\_G ⊠ σ)(g) = (g, σ\_T),    (id\_X ⊠ σ)(x) = (x, σ\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then, \(\pi\) is covering, and \(H\) is a sub-group-scheme of \(G\),
representing the stabilizer \(Stab_{G}(\sigma)\) of \(\sigma\) (cf.~I,
2.3.3), i.e., for every \(T \to S\), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H(T) = \{ g ∈ G(T) | g · σ\_T = σ\_T \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us denote \(G/H\) the presheaf \(T \mapsto G(T)/H(T)\), and
\(a(G/H)\) the associated sheaf, for the topology \(T\). By what
precedes, one obtains a commutative diagram of morphisms of presheaves
with operator group \(G\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ──π──→ X}
\NormalTok{ ╲       ↗}
\NormalTok{  ╲     ╱ π̄}
\NormalTok{   ↘   ╱}
\NormalTok{   G/H}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\bar{\pi}\) is a monomorphism. As \(\pi\) is covering,
\(\bar{\pi}\) is also and therefore, by 4.3.12, \(\bar{\pi}\) induces an
isomorphism \(a(G/H) \xrightarrow{\sim} X\). One has therefore proved
that: if \(X\) is a \(G\)-homogeneous space such that \(X \to S\) admits
a section \(\sigma\), then \(X\) represents the sheaf quotient \(G/H\),
where \(H = G \times_{X} S\) is the stabilizer of \(\sigma\).

In the general case, there exists by hypothesis a covering family
\({S_{i} \to S}\) such that each morphism
\(X_{i} = X \times_{S} S_{i} \to S_{i}\) has a section \(\sigma_{i}\).
Set \(G_{i} = G \times_{S} S_{i}\); then the morphism
\(\Phi_{i} : G_{i} \times_{S_{i}} X_{i} \to X_{i} \times_{S_{i}} X_{i}\)
deduced from \(\Phi\) by the base change \(S_{i} \to S\) is again
covering. Hence, by what precedes, \(X_{i} \cong G_{i}/H_{i}\), where
\(H_{i}\) is the stabilizer in \(G_{i}\) of \(\sigma_{i}\). This
completes the proof of the implication (i) ⇒ (ii).

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-2}

\section{Exposé V. Construction of quotient
schemes}\label{exposuxe9-v.-construction-of-quotient-schemes}

\emph{by P. Gabriel}

The aim of this Exposé is to prove the theorems stated in TDTE
III.\footnote{N.D.E.: namely, theorems 5.1, 5.3, 6.1, 6.2 and 7.2 of
  TDTE III. The first two (resp. the next two) correspond to theorem 4.1
  (resp. theorems 7.1 and 8.1) of this Exposé. Theorem 7.2 of TDTE III
  is proved in Exp. VI\_A, 3.2 and 3.3.} If \(X\) and \(T\) are two
objects of a category \(C\), we write \(X(T)\) instead of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{C}(T, X)\). Similarly, if \(\phi : Y \to X\) is an
arrow (resp. an object \(T\)) of \(C\), then \(\phi(T)\) denotes the map
\(g \mapsto \phi \circ g\) from \(Y(T)\) to \(X(T)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        T}
\NormalTok{       / \textbackslash{}}
\NormalTok{      g   φ ∘ g}
\NormalTok{     /     \textbackslash{}}
\NormalTok{    Y ─ φ → X,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(T(\phi)\) denotes the map \(g \mapsto g \circ \phi\) from \(T(X)\)
to \(T(Y)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{    Y ─ φ → X}
\NormalTok{     \textbackslash{}     /}
\NormalTok{      g ∘ φ   g}
\NormalTok{       \textbackslash{}   /}
\NormalTok{        T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, if \(P\) is a scheme, we write \(P\) for the underlying set of
\(P\).

Exceptionally, in the present Exposé we do not follow the convention
stated in IV 4.6.15 on the notation for quotients (loc. cit., top of
page 227 of the original), since we wish to give here a construction of
quotients which also applies to ``pre-equivalence relations''\footnote{N.D.E.:
  that is, groupoids with base \(X\), cf.~the terminology at the end of
  section 1. When \(C\) is the category of schemes, the quotient
  \(p : X \to Y\) of a groupoid \(X\ast\) with base \(X\) exists under
  certain hypotheses (cf.~4.1, 6.1, 7.1); if, moreover, \(X\ast\) is an
  equivalence relation, then \(p\) is, under the same hypotheses,
  faithfully flat and quasi-compact, hence a universal epimorphism,
  cf.~loc. cit.} that are not equivalence relations.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{1.
\(C\)-groupoids}{1. C-groupoids}}\label{c-groupoids}

\textbf{a)} Let \(C\) be a category in which products and fiber products
exist. Recall first that a diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        d₁       p}
\NormalTok{   X₁ ⇉ X₀ → Y}
\NormalTok{        d₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

in \(C\) is said to be \emph{exact} if \(p d_{0} = p d_{1}\) and if, for
every \(T \in C\), \(T(p)\) is a bijection of \(T(Y)\) onto the subset
of \(T(X_{0})\) consisting of arrows \(f : X_{0} \to T\) such that
\(f d_{0} = f d_{1}\). One also says that \((Y, p)\) is the
\emph{cokernel} of \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) and writes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Y, p) = Coker(d₀, d₁).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{b)} Let, for example, \(C\) be the category \texttt{(Esp.An)} of
ringed spaces. In this case, there always exists a cokernel \((Y, p)\),
which can be described as follows: the underlying topological space of
\(Y\) is obtained from \(X_{0}\) by identifying the points \(d_{0}(x)\)
and \(d_{1}(x)\) and endowing \(Y\) with the quotient topology. The
canonical map \(\pi : X_{0} \to Y\) together with \(d_{0}, d_{1}\) then
induces a double arrow of sheaves of rings on \(Y\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       δ₀}
\NormalTok{    π\_∗(O₀) ⇉ π\_∗(d\_\{0∗\} O₁) = π\_∗(d\_\{1∗\} O₁),}
\NormalTok{                       δ₁}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(O_{i}\) is the structure sheaf of \(X_{i}\). We choose for the
sheaf of rings on \(Y\) the subsheaf of \(\pi_{\ast}(O_{0})\) whose
sections \(s\) satisfy \(\delta_{0}(s) = \delta_{1}(s)\). The arrow
\(p\) is defined in the evident way.

Let\footnote{N.D.E.: Lemmas 1.1 and 1.2 have been added; they are used
  several times in sections 5 to 9.} \texttt{X₁\ ⇉\ X₀} be a diagram
(with arrows \(d_{0}, d_{1}\)) in \texttt{(Esp.An)} and let \((Y, p)\)
be its cokernel. We say that an open set \(U\) of \(X_{0}\) is
\emph{saturated} if \(d^{-1}_{0}(U) = d^{-1}_{1}(U)\), which is
equivalent to saying that \(U = p^{-1}(p(U))\). In this case, since
\(Y\) is endowed with the quotient topology, \(p(U)\) is an open subset
of \(Y\).

\textbf{Lemma 1.1.} \emph{Let \(U\) be a saturated open set of \(X\) and
\(V = p(U)\). If we denote by \(U_{1}\) the open set
\(d^{-1}_{0}(U) = d^{-1}_{1}(U)\) of \(X_{1}\), and by
\(\tilde{d}_{0}\), \(\tilde{d}_{1}\), and \(\tilde{p}\) the restrictions
of \(d_{0}, d_{1}\) to \(U_{1}\), and of \(p\) to \(U\), then
\((V, \tilde{p})\) is a cokernel in \texttt{(Esp.An)} of:}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  This is not the case in the category of schemes. Take, for example,
  \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(C)\),
  \(X_{0} = A^{2}_{S} = \operatorname{Spec}(C[x_{1}, x_{2}])\), let
  \(d_{1} : G_{m,S} \times_{S} A^{2}_{S} \to A^{2}_{S}\) be the action
  of \(G_{m,S}\) by homotheties on \(A^{2}_{S}\), let \(d_{0}\) be the
  projection onto the second factor, and \(U = A^{2}_{S} - {m}\), where
  \(m\) is the point \texttt{(0,\ 0)}. Then projective space
  \(P^{1}_{S}\) is the cokernel of \((\tilde{d}_{0}, \tilde{d}_{1})\) in
  \texttt{(Esp.\ An)} and in \texttt{(Sch)}, and the cokernel \(Y\) of
  \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) in \texttt{(Esp.\ An)} is the union of
  \(P^{1}_{S}\) and the point \(y_{0} = {p(m)}\); the only open set
  containing \(y_{0}\) is \(Y\), and one has \(\Gamma(Y, O_{Y}) = C\).
  If \(f : A^{2}_{S} \to T\) is a morphism of \(S\)-schemes such that
  \(f d_{0} = f d_{1}\) and if \(V = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\) is an
  affine open of \(T\) containing the point \(t_{0} = f(y_{0})\), then
  \(f^{-1}(V) = A^{2}\) and the ring morphism \(A \to C[x_{1}, x_{2}]\)
  factors through \(C\); this shows that \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(C)\)
  is the cokernel of \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) in the category \((Sch/S)\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{         d̃₁      p̃}
\NormalTok{   U₁ ⇉ U → V.}
\NormalTok{         d̃₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The verification is straightforward.

\textbf{Lemma 1.2.} \emph{Let \texttt{X₁\ ⇉\ X₀} be a diagram in
\texttt{(Sch)} (with arrows \(d_{0}, d_{1}\)) and let \((Y, p)\) be its
cokernel in \texttt{(Esp.An)}.}

\emph{(i) If \(Y\) is a scheme and \(p\) a morphism of schemes, then
\((Y, p)\) is a cokernel of \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) in \texttt{(Sch)}.}

\emph{(ii) Suppose that every point of \(X_{0}\) possesses a saturated
open neighborhood \(U\) such that, denoting by \(\tilde{d}_{0}\) and
\(\tilde{d}_{1}\) the restrictions of \(d_{0}\) and \(d_{1}\) to
\(d^{-1}_{0}(U) = d^{-1}_{1}(U)\), and by \((Q, q)\) the cokernel of
\((\tilde{d}_{0}, \tilde{d}_{1})\) in \texttt{(Esp.An)}, the space \(Q\)
is a scheme and \(q\) a morphism of schemes. Then \((Y, p)\) is a
cokernel of \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) in \texttt{(Sch)}.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  is proved in § 4.c); since the proof is short, let us repeat it here.
  Let \(f : X_{0} \to Z\) be a morphism of schemes such that
  \(f d_{0} = f d_{1}\). By hypothesis, there is a unique morphism of
  ringed spaces \(r : Y \to Z\) such that \(f = r p\). It remains to
  show that, for every \(y \in Y\), the homomorphism
  \(O_{r(y)} \to O_{y}\) induced by \(r\) is local. This follows from
  the fact that \(p\) is surjective, so that \(y\) is of the form
  \(p(x)\), and from the fact that the homomorphism
  \(O_{f(x)} \to O_{x}\) induced by \(f\) is local.
\item
  follows from (i) and the preceding lemma.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{c)} In this Exposé we study the existence of
\(Coker(d_{0}, d_{1})\) when the double arrow \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) is
inserted in a richer context; more precisely, let
\(X_{2} = X_{1} \times_{d_{1}, d_{0}} X_{1}\) denote the fiber product
of the diagram

\[
                X_{1}
                \downarrow d_{1}
(\ast)             X_{0}
                \uparrow d_{0}
                X_{1},
\]

and let \(d'_{0}\) and \(d'_{2}\) be the two canonical projections of
\(X_{2}\) onto \(X_{1}\); one then has by definition a Cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  d′₀}
\NormalTok{            X₂ ─────→ X₁}
\NormalTok{            │          │}
\NormalTok{        d′₂ │          │ d₁}
\NormalTok{            ↓          ↓}
\NormalTok{            X₁ ─────→ X₀.}
\NormalTok{                  d₀}
\NormalTok{(0)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, let us give ourselves a third arrow
\(d'_{1} : X_{2} \to X_{1}\); we say that
\texttt{(d₀,\ d₁\ :\ X₁\ ⇉\ X₀,\ d′₁)} is a \(C\)-\emph{groupoid} if for
every object \(T\) of \(C\), \(X_{1}(T)\) is the set of arrows of a
groupoid \(X\ast(T)\) whose set of objects is \(X_{0}(T)\), with source
map \(d_{1}(T)\), target map \(d_{0}(T)\), and composition map
\(d'_{1}(T)\) (one identifies, as usual,
\((X_{1} \times_{d_{1}, d_{0}} X_{1})(T)\) with
\(X_{1}(T) \times_{d_{1}(T), d_{0}(T)} X_{1}(T)\); we also recall that a
groupoid is a category in which every arrow is invertible).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Hence, in this case, \(X_{2}(T)\) is the set of pairs
  \((f_{2}, f_{1})\) of composable arrows, that is, such that
  \(d_{0}(f_{1}) = d_{1}(f_{2})\), and \(d'_{0}\), \(d'_{1}\),
  \(d'_{2}\) send \((f_{2}, f_{1})\) to \(f_{2}\),
  \(f_{2} \circ f_{1}\), \(f_{1}\) respectively.}

If \(\phi\) is an arrow of the groupoid \(X\ast(T)\), the map
\(f \mapsto \phi \circ f\) is a bijection from the set of arrows \(f\)
whose target coincides with the source of \(\phi\) onto the set of
arrows having the same target as \(\phi\). One sees easily that this
fact can be translated by saying that the square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  d′₁}
\NormalTok{            X₂ ─────→ X₁}
\NormalTok{            │          │}
\NormalTok{        d′₀ │          │ d₀}
\NormalTok{            ↓          ↓}
\NormalTok{            X₁ ─────→ X₀}
\NormalTok{                  d₀}
\NormalTok{(1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is Cartesian.

Similarly, the map \(g \mapsto g \circ \phi\) is a bijection from the
set of arrows \(g\) of \(X\ast(T)\) having source equal to the target of
\(\phi\) onto the set of arrows having the same source as \(\phi\). This
fact can again be translated by saying that the square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  d′₁}
\NormalTok{            X₂ ─────→ X₁}
\NormalTok{            │          │}
\NormalTok{        d′₂ │          │ d₁}
\NormalTok{            ↓          ↓}
\NormalTok{            X₁ ─────→ X₀}
\NormalTok{                  d₁}
\NormalTok{(2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is Cartesian.

On the other hand, let \(s : X_{0} \to X_{1}\) be the unique arrow of
\(C\) such that, for every \(T\), \(s(T) : X_{0}(T) \to X_{1}(T)\)
associates to every object of \(X\ast(T)\) the identity arrow of that
object.\footnote{N.D.E.: \(T \mapsto s(T)\) defines an element of
  \(\operatorname{Hom}(h_{X_{0}}, h_{X_{1}})\), and the latter equals
  \(\operatorname{Hom}(X_{0}, X_{1})\) by the Yoneda lemma.} The arrow
\(s\) satisfies the equalities

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)        d₁ s = id\_\{X₀\},}
\NormalTok{(3 bis)    d₀ s = id\_\{X₀\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, the associativity of the composition maps \(d'_{1}(T)\)
translates into the commutativity of the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              d′₁ × X₁}
\NormalTok{   X₁ ×\_\{d₁, d₀\} X₁ ×\_\{d₁, d₀\} X₁ ─────────→ X₁ ×\_\{d₁, d₀\} X₁}
\NormalTok{            │                                       │}
\NormalTok{   X₁ × d′₁ │                                       │ d′₁}
\NormalTok{            ↓                                       ↓}
\NormalTok{   X₁ ×\_\{d₁, d₀\} X₁ ──────────d′₁──────────────→ X₁.}
\NormalTok{(4)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Conversely, the conditions (1), (2), and (4) together with the existence
of an arrow \(s\) satisfying (3) imply that \texttt{(X₁\ ⇉\ X₀,\ d′₁)}
is a \(C\)-groupoid. The condition (3) is harmless; it merely ensures
that the map \(d_{1}(T) : X_{1}(T) \to X_{0}(T)\) is surjective for
every \(T \in C\). In what follows we shall mostly make use of the
Cartesian squares (0), (1) and (2), which we summarize in the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  d′₁              d₀}
\NormalTok{            X₂  ────→  X₁  ──────→  X₀}
\NormalTok{                  d′₀}
\NormalTok{        d′₂ │           │ d₁}
\NormalTok{            ↓           ↓}
\NormalTok{            X₁  ────→  X₀}
\NormalTok{                  d₀}
\NormalTok{(0,1,2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In this diagram the two left-hand squares (i.e.~the squares (0) and (2))
are Cartesian; the first row is exact, and \(X_{2}\) is identified with
the fiber product \(X_{1} \times_{d_{0}, d_{0}} X_{1}\).

We use associativity only indirectly, for instance to ensure the
existence of an arrow \(s\) satisfying (3) and (3 bis), or else to
ensure the existence of an arrow

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)   σ : X₁ → X₁    such that    d₀ σ = d₁    and    d₁ σ = d₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(one chooses \(\sigma\) so that \(\sigma(T) : X_{1}(T) \to X_{1}(T)\)
sends every arrow of \(X\ast(T)\) to its inverse).\footnote{N.D.E.: It
  follows from the Yoneda lemma that \(\sigma\) is an involutive
  automorphism of \(X_{1}\); this will be used, for example, in 3.e) and
  in theorem 4.1.}

By abuse of language, we shall sometimes call a \(C\)-\emph{groupoid} a
diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        d′₀, d′₁, d′₂      d₀, d₁}
\NormalTok{   X₂ ⇶ X₁ ⇉ X₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that (0), (1) and (2) are Cartesian, (4) is commutative, and there
exists \(s\) satisfying (3). The object \(X_{2}\) will therefore be
allowed to be ``a'' fiber product of (∗) without being ``the'' fiber
product of (∗).\footnote{N.D.E.: see example 2.a) below.}

\textbf{Terminology.} Instead of \(C\)-groupoid \(X\ast\), we shall also
speak of the \emph{groupoid \(X\ast\) with base \(X_{0}\)}, or of the
\emph{pre-equivalence relation \(X\ast\) in \(X_{0}\)}.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{2. Examples of
\(C\)-groupoids}{2. Examples of C-groupoids}}\label{examples-of-c-groupoids}

\textbf{a)} Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and \(G\) a \(C\)-group
acting on the left on \(X\). We denote by \(d_{0} : G \times X \to X\)
the arrow defining the action of \(G\) on \(X\), by
\(d_{1} : G \times X \to X\) the projection of the product onto the
second factor, by \(\mu : G \times G \to G\) the arrow defining the
\(C\)-group structure of \(G\), and finally by \(pr_{2,3}\) the
projection of \(G \times G \times X = G \times (G \times X)\) onto the
second factor. Then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  pr\_\{2,3\}              d₁}
\NormalTok{   G × G × X      ⇉      G × X         ⇉   X}
\NormalTok{                  μ × X                 d₀}
\NormalTok{                  G × d₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a \(C\)-groupoid.

\textbf{b)} Let \(d_{0}, d_{1} : X_{1} \to X_{0}\) be an
\emph{equivalence pair}, i.e., if
\(d_{0} \boxtimes d_{1} : X_{1} \to X_{0} \times X_{0}\) is the arrow
with components \(d_{0}\) and \(d_{1}\), we suppose that
\((d_{0} \boxtimes d_{1})(T)\) is, for every object \(T\) of \(C\), a
bijection of \(X_{1}(T)\) onto the graph of an equivalence relation on
\(X_{0}(T)\). The set \(X_{1}(T)\) therefore identifies with the set of
pairs \((x, y)\) of elements of \(X_{0}(T)\) such that \(x \sim y\);
similarly, the set \(X_{2}(T) = (X_{1} \times_{d_{1}, d_{0}} X_{1})(T)\)
identifies with the set of triples \((x, y, z)\) of elements of
\(X_{0}(T)\) such that \(x \sim y\) and \(y \sim z\). There is therefore
one and only one arrow \(d'_{1} : X_{2} \to X_{1}\) making the squares
(1) and (2) commute: \(d'_{1}(T)\) must send \((x, y, z) \in X_{2}(T)\)
to \((x, z) \in X_{1}(T)\). For this choice of \(d'_{1}\),
\texttt{(d₀,\ d₁\ :\ X₁\ ⇉\ X₀,\ d′₁)} is a \(C\)-groupoid.

Conversely, consider a \(C\)-groupoid \(X\ast\) such that
\(d_{0} \boxtimes d_{1} : X_{1} \to X_{0} \times X_{0}\) is a
monomorphism. Then \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) is an equivalence pair and
\(X\ast\) can be reconstructed from \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) as explained a
few lines above.\footnote{N.D.E.: In particular, if \(G\) is a
  \(C\)-group acting on the left on an object \(X\) of \(C\) and if
  \(X\ast\) is the \(C\)-groupoid defined in a), then \((d_{0}, d_{1})\)
  is an equivalence pair if and only if \(G\) acts freely on \(X\),
  cf.~Exp. III, 3.2.1.}

\textbf{c)} If \(p : X \to Y\) is any arrow of \(C\) and if \(pr_{1}\)
and \(pr_{2}\) are the two projections of \(X \times_{p, p} X\) onto
\(X\), then \texttt{(pr₁,\ pr₂)\ :\ X\ ×\_\{p,\ p\}\ X\ ⇉\ X} is an
equivalence pair. One says that \(p\) is an \emph{effective epimorphism}
if the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  pr₁           p}
\NormalTok{   X ×\_\{p, p\} X  ⇉  X  ────→  Y}
\NormalTok{                  pr₂}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is exact, that is, if \((Y, p) = Coker(pr_{1}, pr_{2})\).

Let, for example, \(S\) be a Noetherian scheme and let \(C\) be the
category of schemes finite over \(S\). Let us show that an epimorphism
in \(C\) is not necessarily effective: take \(S\) equal to
\(\operatorname{Spec} k[T^{3}, T^{5}]\), where \(k\) is a commutative
field, \(Y\) equal to \(S\), and \(X\) equal to
\(\operatorname{Spec} k[T]\). If \(i\) is the inclusion of
\(B = k[T^{3}, T^{5}]\) into \(A = k[T]\), take \(p\) equal to
\(\operatorname{Spec} i\). In this case \(X \times_{p, p} X\) identifies
with \(\operatorname{Spec}(A \otimes_{B} A)\) and
\(Coker(pr_{1}, pr_{2})\) with \(\operatorname{Spec} B'\), where \(B'\)
is the subring of \(A\) consisting of \(a\) such that
\(a \otimes_{B} 1 = 1 \otimes_{B} a\). Now

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T⁷ ⊗\_B 1 = (T² T⁵) ⊗\_B 1 = T² ⊗\_B T⁵ = T² ⊗\_B (T³ T²) = T⁵ ⊗\_B T² = 1 ⊗\_B T⁷.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

So \(T^{7}\) belongs to \(B'\), does not belong to \(B\), and
\(\operatorname{Spec} B'\) is distinct from \(\operatorname{Spec} B\),
which yields the counterexample.\footnote{N.D.E.: The same argument
  applies for \(B = k[T^{3}, T^{4}]\) and \(T^{5} \otimes_{B} 1\); more
  generally, for \(B = k[T^{n}, T^{n+r}]\) and the element
  \(T^{n+2r} \otimes_{B} 1\), provided that \(n\) does not divide
  \texttt{2r}.}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{3. Some sorites on
\(C\)-groupoids}{3. Some sorites on C-groupoids}}\label{some-sorites-on-c-groupoids}

Here, in no particular order, are some remarks used in what follows:

\textbf{a)} Let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        d′₀, d′₁, d′₂      d₀, d₁}
\NormalTok{   X₂ ⇶ X₁ ⇉ X₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be a \(C\)-groupoid and \(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) an arrow of \(C\).
We shall define a \(C\)-groupoid with base \(Y_{0}\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        e′₀, e′₁, e′₂      e₀, e₁}
\NormalTok{   Y₂ ⇶ Y₁ ⇉ Y₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which we shall call \emph{induced by \(X\ast\) and \(f_{0}\)}. One also
says that \(Y\ast\) is the \emph{inverse image of \(X\ast\) under the
base change \(f_{0}\)}.

We choose for \(Y_{1}\) the fiber product of the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                 f₁}
\NormalTok{   Y₁ ─────────→ X₁}
\NormalTok{   │              │}
\NormalTok{   │              │ d₀ ⊠ d₁}
\NormalTok{   ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{   Y₀ × Y₀ ────→ X₀ × X₀,}
\NormalTok{        f₀ × f₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and for \(e_{0}\) and \(e_{1}\) the arrows obtained by composing the
canonical arrow \(Y_{1} \to Y_{0} \times Y_{0}\) with the first and
second projections of \(Y_{0} \times Y_{0}\). The morphism
\(Y_{1} \to Y_{0} \times Y_{0}\) is then \(e_{0} \boxtimes e_{1}\), and
one has \(f_{0} \circ e_{i} = d_{i} \circ f_{1}\) for \(i = 0, 1\),
where we have written \(f_{1}\) for the projection of \(Y_{1}\) onto
\(X_{1}\).

We set \(Y_{2} = Y_{1} \times_{e_{0}, e_{1}} Y_{1}\), cf.~1.c). One can
say that the pair \((e_{0}, e_{1})\) is defined in such a way that, for
every \(T \in C\) and every pair \((y, x)\) of elements of \(Y_{0}(T)\),
there is a certain one-to-one correspondence
\(\psi \mapsto {}_{y} \psi_{x}\) between the arrows \(\psi\) of
\(X\ast(T)\) with source \(f_{0}(x)\) and target \(f_{0}(y)\) and the
arrows \({}_{y} \psi_{x}\) of \(Y\ast(T)\) with source \(x\) and target
\(y\). One therefore determines \(e'_{1} : Y_{2} \to Y_{1}\) by
defining, for every \(T \in C\), the composition of arrows of
\(Y\ast(T)\) by the formula

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   \_z ψ\_y ∘ \_y φ\_x = \_z (ψ ∘ φ)\_x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is clear that this definition makes each \(Y\ast(T)\) into a
groupoid.

\textbf{b)} Knowing the \(C\)-groupoid \(X\ast\) and the base change
\(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\), one can reconstruct the pair
\texttt{(e₀,\ e₁)\ :\ Y₁\ ⇉\ Y₀} in another way:\footnote{N.D.E.: this
  second viewpoint will be used in 3.f) and in the proof of 6.1.}
construct \(Y_{0} \times_{X_{0}} X_{1}\), \(pr_{1}\) and \(pr_{2}\) so
that the square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       pr₂}
\NormalTok{   Y₀ ×\_\{X₀\} X₁ ─────→ X₁}
\NormalTok{        │              │}
\NormalTok{    pr₁ │              │ d₀}
\NormalTok{        ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{        Y₀ ──────────→ X₀}
\NormalTok{                  f₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is Cartesian. One then verifies without difficulty, by reduction to the
set-theoretic case, that one has the Cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              e₀ ⊠ f₁}
\NormalTok{   Y₁ ─────────────→ Y₀ ×\_\{X₀\} X₁}
\NormalTok{   │                       │}
\NormalTok{e₁ │                       │ d₁ ∘ pr₂}
\NormalTok{   ↓                       ↓}
\NormalTok{   Y₀ ────────────────→ X₀,}
\NormalTok{              f₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(f_{1}\) denotes the canonical projection of
\(Y_{1} = (Y_{0} \times Y_{0}) \times_{(X_{0} \times X_{0})} X_{1}\)
onto \(X_{1}\).

\textbf{c)} We shall give two examples of inverse images of a
\(C\)-groupoid. Take \(Y_{0}\) equal to \(X_{1}\), \(f_{0}\) equal to
\(d_{0}\). For every object \(T\) of \(C\), \(Y_{1}(T)\) then identifies
with the set of diagrams of the form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        φ}
\NormalTok{   b ────→ d}
\NormalTok{   ↑        ↑}
\NormalTok{   f        g}
\NormalTok{   │        │}
\NormalTok{   a        c}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

of \(X\ast(T)\). The source of such a diagram is the arrow \(f\), the
target is the arrow \(g\). These diagrams compose in the evident way.

Now put \(Y'_{0} = X_{1}\), \(f'_{0} = d_{1}\) (we add the
primes\footnote{N.D.E.: ``accents'' in the original.} to avoid any
confusion with the preceding example). In this case, \(Y'_{1}(T)\)
identifies, for every \(T \in C\), with the set of diagrams of the form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   b        d}
\NormalTok{   ↑        ↑}
\NormalTok{   f        g}
\NormalTok{   │   ψ   │}
\NormalTok{   a ────→ c}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

of the groupoid \(X\ast(T)\). The source of such a diagram is \(f\), the
target is \(g\); the composition of these diagrams is evident.

This being so, it is clear that the identity map of \(Y_{0}(T)\) and the
map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        φ                       }
\NormalTok{   b ────→ d           b        d}
\NormalTok{   ↑        ↑          ↑        ↑}
\NormalTok{   f        g    ↦     f        g}
\NormalTok{   │        │          │  g⁻¹φf │}
\NormalTok{   a        c          a ─────→ c}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

from \(Y_{1}(T)\) to \(Y'_{1}(T)\) define an isomorphism of the groupoid
\(Y\ast(T)\) onto \(Y'\ast(T)\). Moreover, this isomorphism depends
functorially on \(T\), so that the \(C\)-groupoids \(Y\ast\) and
\(Y'\ast\) are isomorphic.\footnote{N.D.E.: This will play a crucial
  role in the proof of lemma 6.1.}

\textbf{d)}

\textbf{Proposition 3.1.} \emph{We keep the notations of a) and assume
that \(f_{0}\) is an effective and universal epimorphism. Then
\(Coker(d_{0}, d_{1})\) exists if and only if \(Coker(e_{0}, e_{1})\)
exists.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The original has been modified to make
  explicit the isomorphism below.} \emph{Moreover, in that case,
\(f_{0}\) induces an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Coker(d₀, d₁) ⥲ Coker(e₀, e₁).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us first recall that an epimorphism \(f_{0} : Y_{0} \to X_{0}\) is
said to be \emph{universal} if, for every Cartesian square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Y′ ─────→ Y₀}
\NormalTok{   │         │}
\NormalTok{f′ │         │ f₀}
\NormalTok{   ↓         ↓}
\NormalTok{   X′ ─────→ X₀,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\(f'\) is an epimorphism. This being so, let us denote by
\(C(d_{0}, d_{1})\) the covariant functor from \(C\) to sets which
associates to every \(T \in C\) the kernel of the pair
\texttt{T(d₀),\ T(d₁)\ :\ T(X₀)\ ⇉\ T(X₁)}. We define
\(C(e_{0}, e_{1})\) similarly. For every \(T \in C\), one therefore has
a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                           T(d₁)}
\NormalTok{   C(d₀, d₁)(T) ────→ T(X₀) ⇉ T(X₁)}
\NormalTok{                           T(d₀)}
\NormalTok{        │                  │           │}
\NormalTok{   T(f) │           T(f₀) │           │ T(f₁)}
\NormalTok{        ↓                  ↓           ↓}
\NormalTok{                           T(e₁)}
\NormalTok{   C(e₀, e₁)(T) ────→ T(Y₀) ⇉ T(Y₁),}
\NormalTok{                           T(e₀)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(T(f)\) is the injection induced by the injection \(T(f_{0})\).
If we show that \(T(f)\) is a surjection for every \(T\), we shall have
a functorial isomorphism
\(f : C(d_{0}, d_{1}) \xrightarrow{\sim} C(e_{0}, e_{1})\), so that the
representability of one of these functors will be equivalent to that of
the other; this will prove our proposition.

To prove the surjectivity of \(T(f)\), consider the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          f₁}
\NormalTok{              Y₁ ─────────────→ X₁}
\NormalTok{            ↗  }
\NormalTok{        Δ ↗  e₀ │ e₁          d₀ │ d₁}
\NormalTok{         ↗      ↓                ↓}
\NormalTok{   Y₀ ×\_\{X₀\} Y₀ ─────→ Y₀ ─────→ X₀,}
\NormalTok{                   pr₂      f₀}
\NormalTok{              pr₁}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\Delta\) is the section of \(Y_{1} \to Y_{0} \times Y_{0}\)
defined by the morphism
\(s \circ f_{0} \circ pr_{1} : Y_{0} \times Y_{0} \to X_{1}\), with
\(s : X_{0} \to X_{1}\) the arrow satisfying equalities (3) and (3 bis)
of section 1.

If the arrow \(g : Y_{0} \to T\) is such that
\(g \circ e_{0} = g \circ e_{1}\), then
\(g \circ e_{0} \circ \Delta = g \circ e_{1} \circ \Delta\), so
\(g \circ pr_{1} = g \circ pr_{2}\). Since \(f_{0}\) is an effective
epimorphism, \(g\) factors through \(f_{0}\) and an arrow
\(h : X_{0} \to T\), that is to say \(g = T(f_{0})(h)\). It remains to
show that \(h\) belongs to \(C(d_{0}, d_{1})(T)\), i.e.~satisfies
\(h d_{0} = h d_{1}\); now one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   h d₀ f₁ = h f₀ e₀ = g e₀ = g e₁ = h f₀ e₁ = h d₁ f₁,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence the desired equality, since \(f_{1}\) is an epimorphism (because
\(f_{0}\) is a universal epimorphism).

\textbf{e)} Consider now a scheme \(S\) and choose \(C\) equal to
\((Sch/S)\). The data of a \(C\)-groupoid

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        d′₀, d′₁, d′₂      d₀, d₁}
\NormalTok{   X₂ ⇶ X₁ ⇉ X₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

allows one to define an equivalence relation on the set \(X_{0}\)
underlying the scheme \(X_{0}\): if \(x, y \in X_{0}\), one writes
\(x \sim y\) when there exists \(z \in X_{1}\) such that \(x = d_{1} z\)
and \(y = d_{0} z\). The reflexivity and symmetry of this relation are
evident;\footnote{N.D.E.: Reflexivity follows from the existence of
  \(s : X_{0} \to X_{1}\) which is a section of both \(d_{0}\) and
  \(d_{1}\); symmetry follows from the existence of the involution
  \(\sigma\) of \(X_{1}\) which ``exchanges \(d_{0}\) and \(d_{1}\)'',
  that is, satisfies \(d_{0} \sigma = d_{1}\) and
  \(d_{1} \sigma = d_{0}\), cf.~§ 1, (3), (3 bis) and (†).} let us prove
transitivity: if \(x \sim y\) and \(y \sim z\), there exist
\(u, v \in X_{1}\) with \(x = d_{1} u\), \(y = d_{0} u\),
\(y = d_{1} v\), \(z = d_{0} v\). It follows that \((v, u)\) belongs to
the set-theoretic fiber product \(X_{1} \times_{d_{1}, d_{0}} X_{1}\).
Since the canonical map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   X₁ ×\_\{d₁, d₀\} X₁ ⟶ X₁ ×\_\{d₁, d₀\} X₁}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

from the set underlying the fiber product into the fiber product of the
underlying sets is surjective, \((v, u)\) is the image of some
\(w \in X_{2}\). One then has \(x = d_{1} d'_{1} w\) and
\(z = d_{0} d'_{1} w\), whence \(x \sim z\).

\textbf{f)} We keep the notations of a) and b), \(C\) still being
\((Sch/S)\). If \texttt{x,\ y} are points of \(Y_{0}\), we shall see
that one has \(x \sim y\) if and only if \(f_{0}(x) \sim f_{0}(y)\) (the
inverse image of the equivalence relation defined by a groupoid is the
equivalence relation defined by the inverse image of the groupoid).

Indeed, suppose \(x \sim y\). There exists therefore \(z \in Y_{1}\)
such that \(x = e_{1}(z)\) and \(y = e_{0}(z)\). Since
\(f_{0} \circ e_{i} = d_{i} \circ f_{1}\) for \(i = 0, 1\), one then has
\(f_{0}(x) = d_{1} f_{1}(z)\) and \(f_{0}(y) = d_{0} f_{1}(z)\), whence
\(f_{0}(x) \sim f_{0}(y)\).

Conversely, suppose \(f_{0}(x) \sim f_{0}(y)\) and let \(z \in X_{1}\)
be such that \(f_{0}(y) = d_{1}(z)\) and \(f_{0}(x) = d_{0}(z)\). Using
the construction and notations of b), there is then a point \(t\) of
\(Y_{0} \times_{X_{0}} X_{1}\) such that \(pr_{1}(t) = x\) and
\(pr_{2}(t) = z\). Similarly, since \(f_{0}(y) = d_{1} pr_{2}(t)\),
there is \(s \in Y_{1}\) such that \(y = e_{1}(s)\) and
\((e_{0} \boxtimes f_{1})(s) = t\). One then has
\(e_{0}(s) = pr_{1}(e_{0} \boxtimes f_{1})(s) = pr_{1}(t) = x\). Whence
\(x \sim y\).

\subsection{4. Passage to the quotient by a finite and flat groupoid
(proof of a particular
case)}\label{passage-to-the-quotient-by-a-finite-and-flat-groupoid-proof-of-a-particular-case}

\textbf{Theorem 4.1.} \emph{Consider a \((Sch/S)\)-groupoid}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        d′₀, d′₁, d′₂      d₀, d₁}
\NormalTok{   X₂ ⇶ X₁ ⇉ X₀.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Suppose the following conditions are satisfied:}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Since \(d_{0} = d_{1} \sigma\), where \(\sigma\) is an involutive
  automorphism of \(X_{1}\), these two conditions are symmetric in
  \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{0}\); moreover, one has
  \(d_{0} d^{-1}_{1}(x) = d_{1} d^{-1}_{0}(x)\).}

\emph{a) \(d_{1}\) is finite locally free;}

\emph{b) for every \(x \in X_{0}\), the set \(d_{0} d^{-1}_{1}(x)\) is
contained in an affine open of \(X_{0}\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: One cannot
  omit hypothesis b). Indeed, H. Hironaka has given an example of an
  action of the finite group \(G = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) on a proper
  \(C\)-variety \(X_{0}\) such that the quotient \(X_{0}/G\) is an
  algebraic space which is not a scheme ({[}Hi62{]}, see also
  {[}Mum65{]}, Chap. 4, § 3).}

\emph{Then:}

\emph{(i) There exists a cokernel \((Y, p)\) of \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) in
\((Sch/S)\); moreover, such a \((Y, p)\) is a cokernel of
\((d_{0}, d_{1})\) in the category of all ringed spaces.}

\emph{(ii) \(p\) is integral and open, and \(Y\) is affine if \(X_{0}\)
is affine.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added that \(p\) is open, by taking
  up the analogous proof given in 6.1.}

\emph{(iii) The morphism \(X_{1} \to X_{0} \times_{Y} X_{0}\) with
components \(d_{0}\) and \(d_{1}\) is surjective.}

\emph{(iv) If \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) is an equivalence pair, then
\(X_{1} \to X_{0} \times_{Y} X_{0}\) is an isomorphism}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Note that, in this case, \(X_{1} \to X_{0} \times_{S} X_{0}\) is
  therefore an immersion (EGA I, 5.3.10); see also VI\_B, 9.2.1. On the
  other hand, for the existence of the quotient (in the category of
  schemes or that of algebraic spaces) under the weaker hypothesis that
  \(d_{0}\) and \(d_{1}\) are finite (but not necessarily flat), see
  {[}An73{]}, § 1.1, {[}Fe03{]}, {[}Ko08{]}\ldots{}} \emph{and
\(p : X_{0} \to Y\) is finite locally free.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  made explicit the consequences which follow; see {[}Ray67a{]}, th. 1
  (iii) and the proof given further on, at the end of section 5.}
\emph{Moreover, \((Y, p)\) is a cokernel of \((d_{0}, d_{1})\) in the
category of sheaves for the (fppf) topology and, for every base change
\(Y' \to Y\), \(Y'\) is the cokernel of the groupoid
\(X\ast \times_{Y} Y'\) obtained from \(X\ast\) by the base change
\(X_{0} \times_{Y} Y' \to X_{0}\).}

\emph{In particular, for every base change \(S' \to S\),
\(Y' = Y \times_{S} S'\) is the cokernel of the \(S'\)-groupoid
\(X'\ast = X\ast \times_{S} S'\). So, in this case, ``the formation of
the quotient commutes with base change''.}

It evidently follows from (i) that the topological space underlying
\(Y\) is the quotient of the topological space underlying \(X_{0}\) by
the equivalence relation defined by the \((Sch/S)\)-groupoid \(X\ast\).

We shall first prove this theorem when \(X_{0}\) is affine and \(d_{1}\)
is locally free of constant rank \(n\). We shall see next how to reduce
to this particular case.

In the case in which we have placed ourselves, \(X_{0}\), \(X_{1}\) and
\(X_{2}\) are affine. We can therefore suppose that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   X\_i = Spec A\_i,   d\_j = Spec δ\_j,   d′\_k = Spec δ′\_k,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the \(A_{i}\) being commutative rings and the \(\delta_{j}\),
\(\delta'_{k}\) ring homomorphisms. One can then replace the diagram (0,
1, 2) by the following

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                    δ′₁}
\NormalTok{            A₂ ⇇ A₁ ⇇ A₀}
\NormalTok{                    δ′₀         δ₀}
\NormalTok{   (0,1,2)∗   δ′₂        δ₁}
\NormalTok{                    δ₁}
\NormalTok{            A₁ ⇇ A₀,}
\NormalTok{                    δ₀}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the two left-hand squares are cocartesian.

Let \(B\) denote the subring of \(A_{0}\) consisting of those
\(a \in A_{0}\) such that \(\delta_{0}(a) = \delta_{1}(a)\).

\textbf{a)} Let us show that \(A_{0}\) is integral over \(B\). If \(a\)
belongs to \(A_{0}\), let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   P\_\{δ₁\}(T, δ₀(a)) = Tⁿ − σ₁ T\^{}\{n−1\} + ⋯ + (−1)ⁿ σ\_n}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be the characteristic polynomial of \(\delta_{0}(a)\) when \(A_{1}\) is
regarded as an algebra over \(A_{0}\) via the homomorphism
\(\delta_{1}\) (cf.~Bourbaki, Alg. VIII, § 12 and Alg. comm. II, § 5,
exercise 9). Since the left-hand squares of \((0,1,2)\ast\) are
cocartesian, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   δ₀(P\_\{δ₁\}(T, δ₀(a))) = P\_\{δ′₂\}(T, δ′₀ δ₀(a))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   δ₁(P\_\{δ₁\}(T, δ₀(a))) = P\_\{δ′₂\}(T, δ′₁ δ₀(a)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\delta'_{0} \delta_{0} = \delta'_{1} \delta_{0}\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   δ₀(P\_\{δ₁\}(T, δ₀(a))) = δ₁(P\_\{δ₁\}(T, δ₀(a))),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, \(\delta_{0}(\sigma_{i}) = \delta_{1}(\sigma_{i})\) for every
\(i\). Hamilton--Cayley moreover tells us that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   δ₀(a)ⁿ − δ₁(σ₁) δ₀(a)\^{}\{n−1\} + ⋯ + (−1)ⁿ δ₁(σ\_n) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\delta_{1}(\sigma_{i}) = \delta_{0}(\sigma_{i})\), one also has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   δ₀(a)ⁿ − δ₀(σ₁) δ₀(a)\^{}\{n−1\} + ⋯ + (−1)ⁿ δ₀(σ\_n) = 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   aⁿ − σ₁ a\^{}\{n−1\} + ⋯ + (−1)ⁿ σ\_n = 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since there exists a homomorphism \(\tau : A_{1} \to A_{0}\) such that
\(\tau \delta_{0} = id_{A_{0}}\), hence \(\delta_{0}\) is injective. It
follows that \(A_{0}\) is integral over \(B\).

\textbf{b)} Consider now two prime ideals \(x\) and \(y\) of \(A_{0}\).
We shall show that the equality \(x \cap B = y \cap B\) entails the
existence of a prime ideal \(z\) of \(A_{1}\) such that \(x = d_{0}(z)\)
and \(y = d_{1}(z)\).

Indeed, if the assertion were not true, \(x\) would be distinct from
\(\delta^{-1}_{0}(t)\) for every prime ideal \(t\) of \(A_{1}\) such
that \(\delta^{-1}_{1}(t) = y\). For such a \(t\) one would have
\(\delta^{-1}_{0}(t) \cap B = \delta^{-1}_{1}(t) \cap B = y \cap B = x \cap B\),
whence by Cohen--Seidenberg (cf.~Bourbaki, Alg. comm. V, § 2, cor. 1 of
prop. 1) \(x\) would be contained in no
\(\delta^{-1}_{0}(t)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have expanded on the
  original in what follows; in particular, we have added lemma 4.1.1,
  taken from {[}DG70{]}, III, § 2.4, Lemma 4.3.} Now there are at most
\(n\) prime ideals \(t\) of \(A_{1}\) such that
\(\delta^{-1}_{1}(t) = y\) (cf.~loc. cit., prop. 3), so, by the ``Prime
Avoidance Lemma'' (loc. cit., II, § 1, prop. 3), there would exist
