  \(X\)-derivations of \texttt{∆\_\{X/S\}} correspond, according to
  1.3.1, to the \(S\)-derivations of \(id_{X}\), i.e., to the
  \(p^{-1}(O_{S})\)-derivations of \texttt{O\_X}.}

\subsubsection{1.4.2.}\label{section-71}

Let \(d\) be a differential operator and \(u\) a section of \(X\) over
\(S\). We call \emph{value of \(d\) at \(u\)} the composed
\(S\)-deviation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S ──u→ X ──d→ X (over id\_X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

According to 1.3 and 1.4.1, if \(d\) is a differential operator of order
\(\leqslant m\), then \texttt{du} (resp. \(d\)) is canonically
associated with a morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules
\(d' : u^{-1}(O_{X}) / I^{m+1}_{u} \to O_{S}\) (resp. a morphism of
\texttt{O\_X}-modules \(d'' : P^{m}_{X/S} \to O_{X}\)).

It is clear that one can construct \(d'\) from
\texttt{d\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} as follows: the square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                 u × X}
\NormalTok{   X ≃ S ×\_X X  ──────→  X × X}
\NormalTok{       │                   │}
\NormalTok{       p                   pr₁}
\NormalTok{       │           u       │}
\NormalTok{       ▼                   ▼}
\NormalTok{       S          ───────→ X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is cartesian, which allows us to identify \(X\) with
\(S \times_{X} (X \times X)\), \(u\) with \texttt{S\ ×\_X\ ∆}, hence
\(u^{*}(P^{m}_{X/S})\) with \(u^{-1}(O_{X}) / I^{m+1}_{u}\). One thus
identifies \(u^{*}(d'')\) with a morphism
\(u^{-1}(O_{X}) / I^{m+1}_{u} \to O_{S}\), which is none other than
\(d'\).

\subsubsection{1.5.}\label{section-72}

Set as usual \(I_{S} = \operatorname{Spec} O_{S}[T] / (T^{2})\). Let
\(\tau : S \to I_{S}\) be the zero section and \(\sigma\) the canonical
deviation of \(\tau\) which we defined in 1.2.0, i.e.~the homomorphism
of \texttt{O\_S}-modules which vanishes on the unit section of
\(O_{S}[T]/(T^{2})\) and which sends the class \(t\) of \(T\) modulo
\(T^{2}\) to the unit section of \texttt{O\_S}.

Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-scheme. To every \texttt{I\_S}-automorphism \(u\)
of \(I_{S} \times X\) inducing the identity on \(X\) there is associated
by composition a differential operator \(D_{u}\) of \(X\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ≃ S × X ──σ × X→ I\_S × X ──u→ I\_S × X ──pr₂→ X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

According to II, 3.14, the map \(u \mapsto D_{u}\) is an isomorphism of
the \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-Lie algebra

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Aut X) := Lie(Aut X)(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

onto the \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-Lie algebra of \(p^{-1}(O_{S})\)-derivations
of \texttt{O\_X}. The inverse isomorphism associates with every
derivation \(D\) the automorphism of \(I_{S} \times X\) corresponding to
the automorphism \(a + bt \mapsto a + (Da + b)t\) of
\(O_{X}[T]/(T^{2})\).

\subsection{2. Invariant differential operators on group
schemes}\label{invariant-differential-operators-on-group-schemes}

\subsubsection{2.1.}\label{section-73}

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group scheme; we denote by \(\epsilon\) or
\(\epsilon_{G} : S \to G\) the unit section of \(G\).

\textbf{Definition.} \emph{Let \(U(G)\) be the \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-module
of \(S\)-deviations of \(\epsilon_{G}\) (or \(S\)-deviations of the
origin) (cf.~1.1).}

\emph{If \(d\) and \(e\) are two elements of \(U(G)\), \(d \times e\) is
an \(S\)-deviation of
\(\epsilon \times \epsilon : S \simeq S \times S \to G \times G\). The
image of \(d \times e\) by the multiplication morphism
\(m : G \times G \to G\) (cf.~1.2) will be called the product of \(d\)
and \(e\) and will be denoted \(d \cdot e\).}

\emph{The \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-module \(U(G)\) is thus equipped with a
structure of associative \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-algebra having
\(\epsilon_{G}\) as unit element (1.1). We shall say that \(U(G)\) is
the} infinitesimal algebra \emph{of \(G\).}\footnote{One now says ``the
  algebra of distributions'' (at the origin) of \(G\), cf.~{[}DG70{]}, §
  II.4, 6.1 and {[}Ja03{]}, I 7.7.}

When \(T\) ranges over the schemes above \(S\), the infinitesimal
algebra \(U(G_{T})\) of the \(T\)-group \(G \times T\) obviously varies
contravariantly in \(T\), so that we may speak of the
\emph{infinitesimal algebra functor}.

When \(T\) ranges over the opens of \(S\), one therefore obtains a
presheaf \(T \mapsto U(G_{T})\) of \texttt{O\_S}-algebras; moreover,
according to 1.1.3, this is a sheaf. We shall denote it
\(\mathcal{U}(G)\) and we shall call it the \emph{sheaf of infinitesimal
algebras of \(G\)}.

The algebra \(U(G)\) is also a covariant functor in \(G\). Indeed, if
\(u : G \to H\) is a homomorphism of \(S\)-groups and \(d\) an
\(S\)-deviation of \(\epsilon_{G}\), the image of \(d\) by \(u\) is an
element \(U(u)(d) = ud\) of \(U(H)\). The map \(U(u) : U(G) \to U(H)\)
thus defined is obviously a homomorphism of \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-algebras.
One defines similarly a homomorphism \(\mathcal{U}(u)\) from
\(\mathcal{U}(G)\) to \(\mathcal{U}(H)\).

\subsubsection{2.2.}\label{section-74}

Let \(d\) be an element of \(U(G)\), i.e., an \(S\)-deviation of the
origin of \(G\). Consider the \(S\)-deviation \(d \times G\) of
\(\epsilon \times G : G \simeq S \times G \to G \times G\) obtained from
\(d\) by base change (1.2.2); the image of \(d \times G\) by the
multiplication morphism \(m : G \times G \to G\) is an \(S\)-deviation
of \(m \circ (\epsilon \times id_{G}) = id_{G}\), i.e., an element of
\(Dif_{G/S}\), which we shall denote \(d_{G}\).

The map \(d \mapsto d_{G}\) is obviously \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-linear and
the ``commutative'' diagram below shows that one has
\((e \cdot d)_{G} = d_{G} \cdot e_{G}\):\footnote{We have corrected the
  original, replacing in the diagram \(d \times G \times G\) by
  \(G \times d \times G\), so that the composition on the left side of
  the triangle is \((e \times d) \times G\), and so that the map
  \(d \mapsto d_{G}\) is an anti-isomorphism of \(U(G)\) onto the
  right-invariant differential operators (cf. 2.3, 2.4 below); on the
  other hand, by defining \({}_{G} d\) as the image under \(m\) of
  \(G \times d\), one would obtain similarly an isomorphism of \(U(G)\)
  onto the left-invariant differential operators (cf.~{[}DG70{]}, §
  II.4, Th. 6.5). We have corrected 2.4 and 2.5 accordingly.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                 m × G}
\NormalTok{   G × G × G  ─────────────────────────────→  G × G}
\NormalTok{       △                                       △}
\NormalTok{       │ G × d × G                              │ G × m}
\NormalTok{       │ ε × G × G                              │}

\NormalTok{  G × G                              G × G                     m}
\NormalTok{   △  △                              △  △}
\NormalTok{   │  │ e × G   m                   │  │ d × G   m}
\NormalTok{   │  │ ε × G                       │  │ ε × G}
\NormalTok{   │                                │}
\NormalTok{   │           e\_G                  │           d\_G}
\NormalTok{   G  ─────────────→  G  ─────────────→  G       (over id\_G everywhere).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The commutativity of the two bottom triangles follows from the
definition of \(d_{G}\) and \(e_{G}\); on the other hand, the composed
\(S\)-deviation of \(e \times G\) and \(G \times d \times G\) is
\((e \times d) \times G\) (cf.~1.2.2), its image by \(m \times G\) is
\((e \cdot d) \times G\), and the image of the latter by \(m\) is
therefore equal to \((e \cdot d)_{G}\).

One thus obtains an anti-homomorphism \(U(G) \to Dif_{G/S}\) of
\(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-algebras, called \emph{right translation}.\footnote{It
  would be preferable to call this a \emph{left action}. Indeed, let for
  example \(d\) be an \(S\)-derivation of the origin; according to
  1.2.1, \(d\) is the composition of the \(S\)-derivation
  \((\tau, \partial_{t}) : S \to I_{S}\) and a morphism
  \(x : I_{S} \to G\) such that \(x \circ \tau = \epsilon\)
  (i.e.~\(x \in Lie(G/S)(S)\)), and then \(d_{G}\) is the derivation of
  \texttt{O\_G} which sends a local section \(\phi\) to the section
  \(g \mapsto \partial_{t} \phi(xg)\). Moreover, with this terminology,
  one could say: ``the left action commutes with right translations''.}

If \(\mathcal{D}if_{G/S}\) denotes the sheaf of \(S\)-differential
operators on \(G\) (cf.~1.4) and \(p\) the structural morphism
\(G \to S\), one defines similarly a ``right translation'':
\(\mathcal{U}(G) \to p_{*}(\mathcal{D}if_{G/S})\).

\subsubsection{2.3.}\label{section-75}

We shall now characterize the differential operators of \(G\) over \(S\)
of the form \(d_{G}\). Let \(g : S \to G\) be a section of the
structural morphism of \(G\) and \(g_{G}\) the right translation of
\(G\) by \(g\), i.e., the composed morphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_G : G ≃ G × S ──G × g→ G × G ──m→ G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For every differential operator \(D\) of \(G\) over \(S\), the
composition \(g^{-1}_{G} D g_{G}\) (cf.~1.2) is again an \(S\)-deviation
of \(id_{G}\), i.e., an element of \(Dif_{X/S}\); we shall denote:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D\^{}g = g\_G\^{}\{{-}1\} D g\_G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We shall say that \(D\) is \emph{right-invariant} if, for every base
change \(t : T \to S\) and every section \(g : T \to G \times T\), one
has \((D_{T})^{g} = D_{T}\).

\textbf{Lemma.} \emph{For every differential operator \(D\) of \(G\)
over \(S\), the following assertions are equivalent (where \(m\) is the
multiplication morphism of \(G\)):}

\emph{(i) \(D\) is right-invariant.}

\emph{(ii) The two following deviations of \(m\) are equal:
\(D m = m(D \times G)\).}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  ⇒ (i): since the condition (ii) is stable under base change, it
  suffices to show that (ii) entails the equality \(D^{g} = D\) for
  every section \(g : S \to G\). Let \(h\) be the morphism
  \(G \times g : G \simeq G \times S \to G \times G\), so that
  \(m \circ h\) is the right translation \(g_{G}\). The equality
  \(D^{g} = D\) is equivalent to the equality
  \(g_{G} \circ D = D \circ g_{G}\), and this follows from the
  commutative diagram:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                    m                     h}
\NormalTok{       G  ←──────────  G × G  ←──────────  G}

\NormalTok{   D, id\_G        D × G, id\_\{G × G\}      D, id\_G}

\NormalTok{                    m                     h}
\NormalTok{       G  ←──────────  G × G  ←──────────  G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  ⇒ (ii): take indeed for \(t : T \to S\) the structural morphism
  \(p : G \to S\), for section \(g : T \to G \times T\) the diagonal
  morphism \texttt{∆\ :\ G\ →\ G\ ×\ G}. The right translation
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∆\_\{G × G\} : G × G  ⟶  G × G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is then the morphism from \(G \times G\) into \(G \times G\) with
components \(m\) and \(pr_{2}\). The equality
\texttt{(D\_G)\^{}∆\ =\ D\_G} is then equivalent to the commutativity of
the first square of the following diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  ∆\_\{G × G\}                  pr₁}
\NormalTok{       G × G  ──────────────→  G × G  ──────────→  G}

\NormalTok{   D\_G, id\_\{G × G\}          D\_G, id\_\{G × G\}    D, id\_G}

\NormalTok{                  ∆\_\{G × G\}                  pr₁}
\NormalTok{       G × G  ──────────────→  G × G  ──────────→  G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The equality (ii) thus follows from the fact that
\texttt{m\ =\ pr₁\ ∘\ ∆\_\{G\ ×\ G\}}.

Consider for example an element \(d\) of the infinitesimal algebra
\(U(G)\). The squares of the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          d × G × G                            m × G}
\NormalTok{       G × G  ←────  S × G × G  ──────────────→  G × G × G  ──────────→  G × G}
\NormalTok{                          ε × G × G}

\NormalTok{         m                    S × m                  G × m                  m}

\NormalTok{                          d × G                                m}
\NormalTok{         G  ←────  S × G  ──────────────→  G × G  ──────────→  G}
\NormalTok{                          ε × G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are then commutative. Since one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{m ∘ (d × G) = d\_G    and    (m × G) ∘ (d × G × G) = d\_G × G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one also has \(d_{G} \circ m = m \circ (d_{G} \times G)\). Therefore:
\emph{for every \(S\)-deviation \(d\) of the origin, \(d_{G}\) is a
right-invariant differential operator}.

\subsubsection{2.4. Theorem.}\label{theorem.-1}

\emph{(i) The map \(d \mapsto d_{G}\) is an anti-isomorphism\footnote{We
  have corrected ``isomorphism'' to ``anti-isomorphism'', and added
  assertion (ii), cf.~N.D.E. (17).} of the infinitesimal algebra
\(U(G)\) onto the subalgebra \(Dif^{G}_{G/S}\) of \(Dif_{G/S}\) formed
by the right-invariant differential operators.}

\emph{(ii) Similarly, the map \(d \mapsto {}_{G} d\) is an isomorphism
of \(U(G)\) onto the subalgebra of \(Dif_{G/S}\) formed by the
left-invariant differential operators.}

Let in fact \(D\) be an arbitrary differential operator of \(G\) over
\(S\) and let us denote by \texttt{D\_0} its value at the origin, i.e.,
the composed deviation \(S \xrightarrow{\epsilon} G \xrightarrow{D} G\)
(over \(id_{G}\)). The right-invariant differential operator
\((D_{0})_{G}\) is then obtained by composition:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ≃ S × G ──ε × G→ G × G ──D × G→ G × G ──m→ G (over id\_\{G × G\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(D\) is right-invariant, one has \(D m = m(D \times G)\), whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D = D m(ε × G) = m(D × G)(ε × G) = (D\_0)\_G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, the map \(d \mapsto d_{G}\) is surjective.

Conversely, let \(d\) be an \(S\)-deviation of the origin. One then has
a commutative square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          d × G}
\NormalTok{       G × G  ←──────────  G}
\NormalTok{         △                  △}
\NormalTok{   G × ε │                  │ ε}
\NormalTok{                       d}
\NormalTok{       G × S ≃ G  ←──────  S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence it follows that
\(d = m(G \times \epsilon) d = m(d \times G) \epsilon = (d_{G})_{0}\).
\emph{A fortiori}, the map \(d \mapsto d_{G}\) is injective. This proves
the theorem.

When \(S\) varies, Theorem 2.4 obviously implies that the right
translation \(\mathcal{U}(G) \to p_{*}(\mathcal{D}if_{G/S})\) is an
anti-isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-algebras of \(\mathcal{U}(G)\) onto
the sheaf of \texttt{O\_S}-algebras \(p_{*}(\mathcal{D}if_{G/S})^{G}\),
which to every open \(U\) of \(S\) associates
\(Dif^{G_{U}}_{G_{U} / U}\).

\subsubsection{2.4.1. Remark.}\label{remark.}

Consider the commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       η}
\NormalTok{        G  ←──────────  G × G}
\NormalTok{        △               △    △}
\NormalTok{     p  │   ε        pr₁ │    │ ∆}
\NormalTok{        │       p        │}
\NormalTok{        S  ←──────────  G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\eta\) denotes the morphism
``\((x, y) \mapsto y x^{-1}\)''.\footnote{i.e., \(G\) acts on itself on
  the left by right translations.} The latter induces morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{η\textquotesingle{} : η\^{}\{{-}1\}(O\_G) ⟶ O\_\{G × G\}    and    ∆\^{}\{{-}1\}(η\textquotesingle{}) : p\^{}\{{-}1\} ε\^{}\{{-}1\}(O\_G) ⟶ ∆\^{}\{{-}1\}(O\_\{G × G\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For every integer \(n \geqslant 1\), set
\(p^{n}_{G/S} = \epsilon^{-1}(O_{G}) / I^{n+1}_{\epsilon}\) (cf.~1.3 and
1.4 for the notations).\footnote{In what follows, we have corrected the
  original, which referred to the square formed by the morphisms \(p\),
  \(p\), \(\eta\), and \(pr_{1}\), instead of \(\epsilon\), \(\eta\),
  \texttt{∆} and \(p\).} Since the square formed by the morphisms
\(\epsilon\), \(\eta\), \texttt{∆} and \(p\) is cartesian,
\texttt{∆\^{}\{-1\}(η\textquotesingle{})} induces an isomorphism of
\texttt{O\_G}-modules:

\[
p^{*}(p^{n}_{G/S}) \xrightarrow{\sim} P^{n}_{G/S}.
\]

The differential operators of \(G\) over \(S\) of order \(\leqslant n\)
therefore correspond bijectively to the morphisms of
\texttt{O\_G}-modules \(p^{*}(p^{n}_{G/S}) \longrightarrow O_{G}\),
i.e., to the morphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules

\[
p^{n}_{G/S} \longrightarrow p_{*}(O_{G}).
\]

In this bijection, the right-invariant differential operators correspond
to the composed arrows

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\^{}n\_\{G/S\} ──→ O\_S ──can.→ p\_*(O\_G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One thus recovers the isomorphism of Theorem 2.4.

\subsubsection{2.5.}\label{section-76}

\footnote{In this paragraph, we have modified the order, beginning by
  defining the map \(\alpha : Lie(G) \to U(G)\), and we have corrected
  the original as indicated in N.D.E. (17).} Let \(Lie(G)\) be the Lie
algebra of \(G\);\footnote{In this Exposé, if \(G\) (resp. \(X\)) is an
  \(S\)-group scheme (resp. an \(S\)-scheme), the ``Lie algebra''
  \(Lie(G)\) (resp. \(Lie(\operatorname{Aut} X)\)) denotes, with the
  notations of Exposé II, \(Lie(G/S)(S)\) (resp.
  \(Lie(\operatorname{Aut}_{S}(X)/S)(S)\)); it is a
  \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-Lie algebra, according to II, 4.11 and 3.14.} we
shall define a morphism of \(\Gamma(O_{S})\)-Lie algebras
\(\alpha : Lie(G) \to U(G)\).

Let \(s : S \to I_{S}\) be the zero section of \(I_{S} \to S\) and
\(\sigma\) the deviation of \(s\) defined in 1.2.0. Recall (cf.~II, 4.1)
that \(Lie(G)\) is the set of morphisms \(x : I_{S} \to G\) such that
\(x \circ s = \epsilon_{G}\). Then the composition

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S ──σ→ I\_S ──x→ G (over s)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an \(S\)-deviation of \(\epsilon_{G}\), i.e., an element of \(U(G)\);
with the notations of 1.2 \texttt{(†)}, it is denoted \(\sigma x\).
Moreover, according to 1.2.1, the map \(\alpha : x \mapsto \sigma x\) is
an isomorphism of \(O_{S}(S)\)-modules from \(Lie(G)\) onto the
submodule \(D\acute{e}r(\epsilon_{G})\) of \(U(G)\) formed by the
\(S\)-derivations of \(\epsilon_{G}\). We shall see that \(\alpha\) is a
morphism of Lie algebras.\footnote{See also II, 4.11.} Let

\[
\rho' : U(G) \longrightarrow Dif_{G/S}
\]

be the algebra morphism which to an \(S\)-deviation \(d\) of
\(\epsilon_{G}\) associates the left-invariant differential operator
\({}_{G} d \in Dif_{G/S}\), cf.~2.2, N.D.E. (17).

Let \(\rho : G \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(G)\) be the homomorphism of
group functors which to an \(S\)-morphism \(g : T \to G\) associates the
right translation of \texttt{G\_T} by \(g\), i.e.~the morphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_T ≃ T ×\_T G\_T ──G\_T × g→ G\_T ×\_T G\_T ──m\_T→ G\_T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Recall also (cf.~1.5 and II, 3.14) that
\texttt{Lie(Aut\ G)\ =\ Lie(Aut\_S(G)/S)(S)} is identified with the
infinitesimal automorphisms of \(G\), i.e., with the automorphisms of
\(I_{S} \times G\) inducing the identity on \(G\).

Since \(\rho\) is a monomorphism, the same holds for the morphism
\texttt{Lie(ρ)\ :\ Lie(G/S)\ →\ Lie(Aut\_S(G)/S)} (see, for example,
Exp. II, N.D.E. (50)), hence \texttt{Lie(ρ)\ :\ Lie(G)\ →\ Lie(Aut\ G)}
is injective.

On the other hand, according to 1.5, the map \(\beta\) which to every
infinitesimal automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) associates the differential
operator \(D_{u}\) of \(G\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ≃ S × G ──σ × G→ I\_S × G ──u→ I\_S × G ──pr₂→ G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an isomorphism of \(Lie(\operatorname{Aut} G)\) onto the Lie
subalgebra of \(Dif_{G/S}\) formed by the \(p^{-1}(O_{S})\)-derivations
of \texttt{O\_G}.

For every \(x \in Lie(G)\), one has the commutative square below which
determines the image of \(x\) by \(Lie(\rho)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       Lie(ρ)(x)}
\NormalTok{       I\_S × G  ───────────────→  I\_S × G}

\NormalTok{   x × G                                pr₂}
\NormalTok{                          m}
\NormalTok{       G × G  ──────────────────→  G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Taking this diagram into account, the image of \(Lie(\rho)(x)\) by
\(\beta\) is the composed deviation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ≃ S × G ──σ × G→ I\_S × G ──G × x→ G × G ──m→ G (over s × G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which, according to 2.2 N.D.E. (17), is none other than
\({}_{G}(\sigma x) = \rho'(\alpha(x))\). One thus obtains a commutative
diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       Lie(ρ)}
\NormalTok{       Lie(G)  ─────────────────→  Lie(Aut G)}
\NormalTok{          │                              │}
\NormalTok{        α │                              │ β}
\NormalTok{          │              ρ\textquotesingle{}              │}
\NormalTok{          ▼                              ▼}
\NormalTok{       U(G)  ──────────────────────────→  Dif\_\{G/S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(Lie(\rho)\), \(\beta\) and \(\rho'\) are morphisms of Lie
algebras. Since \(\rho'\) is injective, it follows that \(\alpha\) is
also a morphism of Lie algebras. Consequently, one has obtained:

\textbf{Proposition.} \emph{\(\alpha\) is an isomorphism of
\(O_{S}(S)\)-Lie algebras, from \(Lie(G)\) into the Lie algebra of
\(S\)-derivations of \(\epsilon_{G}\), itself isomorphic via
\(Lie(\rho)\) to the Lie algebra of \(S\)-derivations of \(G\) invariant
under left translation.}\footnote{There are examples of Lie algebras
  \(\mathfrak{g}\) over a ring \(A\), such that the map
  \(\mathfrak{g} \to U(\mathfrak{g})\) is not injective, cf.~{[}BLie{]},
  § I.2, Ex. 9. The above result shows (since \(\alpha\) factors through
  \(Lie(G) \to U(Lie(G)) \to U(G)\)) that this cannot happen for
  ``algebraic'' Lie algebras, i.e., of the form \(Lie(G)\), where \(G\)
  is an \(A\)-group scheme.}

\subsection{3. Coalgebras and Cartier
duality}\label{coalgebras-and-cartier-duality}

\subsubsection{3.1.}\label{section-77}

Let \(S\) be a scheme (or, more generally, a ringed space). An
\emph{\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra}\footnote{One also says ``cogebra'',
  cf.~{[}BAlg{]}, III § 11.1. On the other hand, one will note that in
  this Exposé (as well as in VII\_B), we place ourselves in the category
  of cocommutative coalgebras (i.e., those satisfying condition (i)),
  which is crucial for defining the product and the notion of group
  coalgebra (cf.~3.1.0 and 3.2).} is a pair \texttt{(𝒰,\ ∆\_𝒰)}
consisting of an \texttt{O\_S}-module \(\mathcal{U}\) and a morphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules \texttt{∆\_𝒰\ :\ 𝒰\ →\ 𝒰\ ⊗\_\{O\_S\}\ 𝒰} (called
the \emph{diagonal morphism} or \emph{comultiplication}) such that:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  \texttt{σ\ ∘\ ∆\_𝒰\ =\ ∆\_𝒰}, where
  \(\sigma(a \otimes b) = b \otimes a\).
\item
  The square
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              ∆\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{       𝒰  ──────────────────────→  𝒰 ⊗\_\{O\_S\} 𝒰}

\NormalTok{   ∆\_𝒰                                    id\_𝒰 ⊗ ∆\_𝒰}

\NormalTok{                          ∆\_𝒰 ⊗ id\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{       𝒰 ⊗\_\{O\_S\} 𝒰  ──────────────────→  𝒰 ⊗\_\{O\_S\} 𝒰 ⊗\_\{O\_S\} 𝒰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is commutative.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  There exists a morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules
  \(\epsilon_{\mathcal{U}} : \mathcal{U} \to O_{S}\), called the
  \emph{augmentation}, such that the composed morphisms
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒰 ──∆\_𝒰→ 𝒰 ⊗\_\{O\_S\} 𝒰 ──id\_𝒰 ⊗ ε\_𝒰→ 𝒰 ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_S ≃ 𝒰}
\NormalTok{𝒰 ──∆\_𝒰→ 𝒰 ⊗\_\{O\_S\} 𝒰 ──ε\_𝒰 ⊗ id\_𝒰→ O\_S ⊗\_\{O\_S\} 𝒰 ≃ 𝒰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are the identity morphism of \(\mathcal{U}\).

If \(\epsilon_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\epsilon'_{\mathcal{U}}\) are two
augmentations, one has
\texttt{ε\_𝒰\ =\ (ε\_𝒰\ ⊗\ ε\textquotesingle{}\_𝒰)\ ∘\ ∆\_𝒰\ =\ ε\textquotesingle{}\_𝒰};
the augmentation is therefore uniquely determined by (iii).

If \texttt{(𝒰,\ ∆\_𝒰)} and \texttt{(𝒱,\ ∆\_𝒱)} are two
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebras, a \emph{morphism} from the first into the
second is a morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules
\(f : \mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{V}\) such that the diagrams

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        f                              f}
\NormalTok{   𝒰  ────→  𝒱                    𝒰  ────→  𝒱}
\NormalTok{   │          │                    │          │}
\NormalTok{ ∆\_𝒰         ∆\_𝒱      and        ε\_𝒰        ε\_𝒱}
\NormalTok{   ▼          ▼                    │          │}
\NormalTok{                                   ▼          ▼}
\NormalTok{   𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰  ─f ⊗ f→  𝒱 ⊗ 𝒱                  O\_S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are commutative. Morphisms of coalgebras compose like morphisms of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules, so that we shall be able to speak of the
\emph{category of \texttt{O\_S}-coalgebras}.

\subsubsection{3.1.0.}\label{section-78}

\footnote{We have added the numbering 3.1.0, for later references.} This
category has finite products: the final object is the
\texttt{O\_S}-module \texttt{O\_S}, the comultiplication being the
identity; the product of two coalgebras \texttt{(𝒰,\ ∆\_𝒰)} and
\texttt{(𝒱,\ ∆\_𝒱)} is the tensor product
\(\mathcal{U} \otimes_{O_{S}} \mathcal{V}\), the comultiplication being
the composed morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒰 ⊗ 𝒱 ──∆\_𝒰 ⊗ ∆\_𝒱→ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒱 ⊗ 𝒱 ──id\_𝒰 ⊗ σ ⊗ id\_𝒱→ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒱 ⊗ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒱}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\sigma(a \otimes b) = b \otimes a\); the canonical projections
of \(\mathcal{U} \otimes \mathcal{V}\) onto the factors \(\mathcal{U}\)
and \(\mathcal{V}\) are the morphisms
\(id_{\mathcal{U}} \otimes \epsilon_{\mathcal{V}}\) and
\(\epsilon_{\mathcal{U}} \otimes id_{\mathcal{V}}\),\footnote{The
  following has been added. Let us also recall that, to show that
  \(\mathcal{U} \otimes \mathcal{V}\) is indeed the product of
  \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) in the category of cocommutative
  \texttt{O\_S}-cogebras, one verifies that if one has an arbitrary
  \texttt{O\_S}-cogebra \(\mathcal{E}\) and morphisms of cogebras
  \(f : \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{U}\) and
  \(g : \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{V}\), then every morphism of cogebras
  \(\phi : \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{U} \otimes \mathcal{V}\) such that
  \(pr_{\mathcal{U}} \circ \phi = f\) and
  \(pr_{\mathcal{V}} \circ \phi = g\) is necessarily equal to
  \texttt{(f\ ⊗\ g)\ ∘\ ∆\_ℰ}, and this is a morphism of cogebras if and
  only if it equals \texttt{(g\ ⊗\ f)\ ∘\ ∆\_ℰ}.} and the ``diagonal
morphism'' \(\mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{U} \otimes \mathcal{U}\)
(corresponding to the pair of morphisms
\((id_{\mathcal{U}}, id_{\mathcal{U}})\)) is none other than the
comultiplication \texttt{∆\_𝒰}.

\subsubsection{3.1.1.}\label{section-79}

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a commutative \texttt{O\_S}-algebra, locally free
and of finite type as an \texttt{O\_S}-module. If we set

\[
\mathcal{A}^{*} = \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}-Mod.}(\mathcal{A}, O_{S}),
\]

the canonical morphism \(\phi\) from
\(\mathcal{A}^{*} \otimes_{O_{S}} \mathcal{A}^{*}\) into
\((\mathcal{A} \otimes_{O_{S}} \mathcal{A})^{*}\) is invertible. If
\(m : \mathcal{A} \otimes \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}\) is the morphism
defining the multiplication of \(\mathcal{A}\), one obtains by
composition a diagonal morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∆\_\{𝒜\^{}*\} : 𝒜\^{}* ──m\^{}*→ (𝒜 ⊗ 𝒜)\^{}* ──φ\^{}\{{-}1\}→ 𝒜\^{}* ⊗ 𝒜\^{}*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This diagonal morphism obviously makes \(\mathcal{A}^{*}\) an
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra whose augmentation is the

transpose morphism of the morphism \texttt{O\_S\ →\ 𝒜} defined by the
unit section of \texttt{𝒜}. Moreover,

it is clear that:

\emph{The functor \(\mathcal{A} \mapsto \mathcal{A}^{*}\) is an
anti-equivalence of the category of \texttt{O\_S}-algebras which are
locally free and of finite type as \texttt{O\_S}-modules, onto the
category of \texttt{O\_S}-coalgebras locally free and of finite type as
\texttt{O\_S}-modules.}

\subsubsection{3.1.2.}\label{section-80}

To every \texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra \(\mathcal{U}\) is canonically
associated an \(S\)-functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Spec\^{}* 𝒰 : (Sch/S)° ⟶ (Ens).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note indeed that, for every \(S\)-scheme \(q : T \to S\),
\(q^{*}(\mathcal{U} \otimes_{O_{S}} \mathcal{U})\) is identified with
\(q^{*}(\mathcal{U}) \otimes_{O_{T}} q^{*}(\mathcal{U})\), so that
\texttt{q\^{}*(∆\_𝒰)} makes \(\mathcal{U}_{T} = q^{*}(\mathcal{U})\)
into an \texttt{O\_T}-coalgebra; we can therefore set by definition and
with an obvious abuse of notation:\footnote{For every
  \(x \otimes y \in \Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T}) \otimes_{O(T)} \Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\),
  its image in
  \(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T} \otimes_{O_{T}} \mathcal{U}_{T})\) is
  again denoted \(x \otimes y\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Spec\^{}* 𝒰)(T) = \{ x ∈ Γ(T, 𝒰\_T) | ε\_\{𝒰\_T\}(x) = 1 and ∆\_\{𝒰\_T\}(x) = x ⊗ x \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The sections \(x\) of \(\mathcal{U}_{T}\) obviously correspond to the
morphisms of \texttt{O\_T}-modules \(\xi : O_{T} \to \mathcal{U}_{T}\);
the conditions \(\epsilon(x) = 1\) and \texttt{∆(x)\ =\ x\ ⊗\ x} simply
express that \(\xi\) is a morphism of coalgebras. One therefore also
has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Spec\^{}* 𝒰)(T) = Hom\_\{O\_T{-}coalg.\}(O\_T, 𝒰\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, one has the following proposition:\footnote{We have added
  the numbering 3.1.2.1, for later references. Note moreover that the
  \(S\)-functor \(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}\) is a sheaf for
  the Zariski topology (and even for the (fpqc) topology if
  \(\mathcal{U}\) is a quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-module).}

\textbf{Proposition 3.1.2.1.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a commutative
\texttt{O\_S}-algebra which is locally free of finite type as an
\texttt{O\_S}-module. Then the \(S\)-functor
\(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{A}^{*}\) is represented by
\(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A}\).}

Indeed, for every \(S\)-scheme \(T\), one has canonical isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Spec\^{}* 𝒜\^{}*)(T) = Hom\_\{O\_T{-}coalg.\}(O\_T, 𝒜\_T\^{}*) ≃ Hom\_\{O\_T{-}alg.\}(𝒜\_T, O\_T) ≃ (Spec 𝒜)(T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.2.}\label{section-81}

An \texttt{O\_S}-\emph{coalgebra in groups} (i.e., a group in the
category of \texttt{O\_S}-coalgebras) consists of the data of an
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra \texttt{(𝒰,\ ∆\_𝒰)} and three morphisms of
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebras
\(m_{\mathcal{U}} : \mathcal{U} \otimes \mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{U}\),
\(\eta_{\mathcal{U}} : O_{S} \to \mathcal{U}\) and
\(c_{\mathcal{U}} : \mathcal{U} \to \mathcal{U}\) satisfying the
conditions (ii)\emph{, (iii)} and (vi) below; on the other hand, the
fact that \(m_{\mathcal{U}}\) is a morphism of cogebras translates into
the commutativity of diagrams (iv) and (v)

below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              m\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{       𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰  ────────────────────→  𝒰}

\NormalTok{   ∆\_𝒰 ⊗ ∆\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{       │}
\NormalTok{(iv)   ▼                                  ∆\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{   𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰}

\NormalTok{   id\_𝒰 ⊗ σ ⊗ id\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{                              m\_𝒰 ⊗ m\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{   𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰  ──────────────────→  𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              m\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{       𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰  ────────────────────→  𝒰}
\NormalTok{              ╲                    ╱}
\NormalTok{(v)            ╲                  ╱}
\NormalTok{        ε\_𝒰 ⊗ ε\_𝒰              ε\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{                  ╲          ╱}
\NormalTok{                       O\_S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(ii)* The square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              id\_𝒰 ⊗ m\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{       𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰  ──────────────────→  𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰}

\NormalTok{   m\_𝒰 ⊗ id\_𝒰                                 m\_𝒰}

\NormalTok{                              m\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{       𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰  ────────────────────→  𝒰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is commutative.

(iii)* The two compositions below equal the identity morphism of
\(\mathcal{U}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒰 ≃ 𝒰 ⊗ O\_S ──id\_𝒰 ⊗ η\_𝒰→ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ──m\_𝒰→ 𝒰}
\NormalTok{𝒰 ≃ O\_S ⊗ 𝒰 ──η\_𝒰 ⊗ id\_𝒰→ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ──m\_𝒰→ 𝒰.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  The composed morphism below is equal to
  \(\eta_{\mathcal{U}} \circ \epsilon_{\mathcal{U}}\):
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒰 ──∆\_𝒰→ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ──c\_𝒰 ⊗ id\_𝒰→ 𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰 ──m\_𝒰→ 𝒰.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.2.1.}\label{section-82}

The morphisms \(\eta_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(c_{\mathcal{U}}\) are
uniquely determined by \(m_{\mathcal{U}}\). On the other hand,
conditions (ii)* and (iii)* simply express that \(m_{\mathcal{U}}\)
makes \(\mathcal{U}\) an \texttt{O\_S}-algebra having as unit section
the image by \(\eta_{\mathcal{U}}\) of the unit section of
\texttt{O\_S}. Condition (iv) also expresses that the diagonal morphism
\texttt{∆\_𝒰} is compatible with multiplication; and indeed,
\texttt{∆\_𝒰\ :\ 𝒰\ →\ 𝒰\ ⊗\ 𝒰} must be a homomorphism of group
coalgebras, which also entails the commutativity of the triangle

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       O\_S}
\NormalTok{                  ╱         ╲}
\NormalTok{             η\_𝒰              η\_𝒰 ⊗ η\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{(v)*            ╱               ╲}
\NormalTok{              ╱                   ╲}
\NormalTok{       𝒰  ───────────────────→  𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰.}
\NormalTok{                       ∆\_𝒰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, as in every category, the \emph{antipode}
\(c_{\mathcal{U}}\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathcal{U}\) onto the
``opposite'' group object;\footnote{i.e.~endowed with the multiplication
  \(m'_{\mathcal{U}} = m_{\mathcal{U}} \circ \sigma\).} in particular,
\(c_{\mathcal{U}}\) induces an algebra isomorphism of \(\mathcal{U}\)
onto the opposite algebra \(\mathcal{U}^{\circ}\).

\subsubsection{3.2.2.}\label{section-83}

Since the functor
\(\mathcal{U} \mapsto \operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}\) commutes
with finite products, it transforms a group coalgebra into a group
\(S\)-functor; and indeed, for every \(S\)-scheme \(T\), the elements
\(x \in \Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\) belonging to
\((\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U})(T)\) form a group under the
multiplication of the algebra \(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\); the
inverse of \(x\) is none other than \(c_{\mathcal{U}}(x)\). According to
3.1.2.1, one has:

\textbf{Scholium 3.2.2.1.}\footnote{We have added this scholium,
  implicit in the original.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be an
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra in groups, finite and locally free as an
\texttt{O\_S}-module. Then the group \(S\)-functor
\(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}\) is represented by the
\(S\)-group, finite and locally free,
\(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{U}^{*}\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.2.2.2.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be an
\texttt{O\_S}-Lie algebra and \(\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{L})\) the
enveloping algebra of \(\mathcal{L}\), i.e., the sheaf on \(S\)
associated with the presheaf which to every open \(V\) assigns the
enveloping algebra \(U(\Gamma(V, \mathcal{L}))\) of the Lie algebra
\(\Gamma(V, \mathcal{L})\).}

Every homomorphism from \(\mathcal{L}\) into the Lie algebra underlying
an associative \texttt{O\_S}-algebra factors in one and only one way
through the canonical morphism from \(\mathcal{L}\) into
\(\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{L})\); moreover, this universal property entails,
besides the functoriality of \(\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{L})\) in
\(\mathcal{L}\), that the enveloping algebra of a product of Lie
algebras is identified with the tensor product of the enveloping
algebras.

In particular, the diagonal morphism
\(\delta : \mathcal{L} \to \mathcal{L} \times \mathcal{L}\) induces an
algebra homomorphism
\texttt{∆\ :\ 𝒰(ℒ)\ →\ 𝒰(ℒ\ ×\ ℒ)\ ≃\ 𝒰(ℒ)\ ⊗\ 𝒰(ℒ)}. The zero morphism
\(\mathcal{L} \to 0\) induces a homomorphism
\(\epsilon : \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{L}) \to \mathcal{U}(0) \simeq O_{S}\).
The isomorphism \(x \mapsto -x\) of \(\mathcal{L}\) onto the opposite
Lie algebra \(\mathcal{L}^{\circ}\) induces an anti-isomorphism \(c\) of
the algebra \(\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{L})\). One then verifies easily that
the multiplication \(m\) of the algebra \(\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{L})\)
makes \texttt{(𝒰(ℒ),\ ∆)} an \texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra in groups with
\(\epsilon\) as augmentation and \(c\) as antipode.\footnote{The group
  \(S\)-functor \(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{L})\) is
  not representable in general, but one will see later (5.5) that if
  \(S\) is a scheme of characteristic \(p\), if \(\mathcal{L}\) is
  finite locally free over \texttt{O\_S} and if
  \(\mathcal{U}_{p}(\mathcal{L})\) is its restricted enveloping algebra
  (cf.~5.3), then
  \(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}_{p}(\mathcal{L})\) is
  represented by a finite and locally free \(S\)-group.}

\subsubsection{3.2.3.}\label{section-84}

\footnote{We have expanded this paragraph.} Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be an
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra in groups. We shall see that the group
\(S\)-functor \(G = \operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}\) is \emph{very
good}, in the sense of II, 4.6 and 4.10.

Let \(M\) be a free \texttt{O\_S}-module of rank \(r\), and let
\(T \to S\) be an \(S\)-scheme. Since
\(I_{T}(M) = \operatorname{Spec}(O_{T} \oplus M_{T})\), so that
\(\pi : I_{T}(M) \to T\) is affine, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π\_*(𝒰\_\{I\_T(M)\}) = 𝒰\_T ⊗\_\{O\_T\} π\_*(O\_\{I\_T(M)\}) = 𝒰\_T ⊗\_\{O\_T\} (O\_T ⊕ M\_T),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and so

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    Γ(I\_T(M), 𝒰\_\{I\_T(M)\}) ≃ Γ(T, 𝒰\_T) ⊗\_\{O(T)\} (O(T) ⊕ Γ(T, M\_T)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \((d_{1}, \cdots, d_{r})\) be a basis of \(M\). Then an element
\(u_{0} + \sum_{i} u_{i} d_{i}\) of
\(\Gamma(I_{T}(M), \mathcal{U}_{I_{T}(M)})\) belongs to \(G(I_{T}(M))\)
if and only if one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 = ε(u\_0 + ∑\_i u\_i d\_i) = ε(u\_0) + ∑\_i ε(u\_i) d\_i,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u\_0 + ∑\_i u\_i d\_i) ⊗ (u\_0 + ∑\_i u\_i d\_i) = ∆(u\_0 + ∑\_i u\_i d\_i) = ∆(u\_0) + ∑\_i ∆(u\_i) d\_i,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is to say:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)    \{ ε(u\_0) = 1,  ∆ u\_0 = u\_0 ⊗ u\_0,    (i.e. u\_0 ∈ G(T))}
\NormalTok{       \{ ε(u\_i) = 0,  ∆(u\_i) = u\_i ⊗ u\_0 + u\_0 ⊗ u\_i,  for i = 1, …, r.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, the morphism \(G(I_{T}(M)) \to G(T)\) corresponding to the
zero section of \(I_{T}(M) \to T\) is given by
\(u_{0} + \sum_{i} u_{i} d_{i} \mapsto u_{0}\). From this, combined with
(1) and (2), one deduces that, if \(N\) is a second free
\texttt{O\_S}-module of finite rank, the diagram of sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       G(I\_T(M ⊕ N))          ─────→  G(I\_T(N))}
\NormalTok{           │                              │}
\NormalTok{           ▼                              ▼}
\NormalTok{       G(I\_T(M))               ─────→  G(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is cartesian, i.e.~\(G\) satisfies condition (E) of II, 3.5.

Let us denote by \(Prim \Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\) the
sub-\(O(T)\)-module of \(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\) formed by the
\emph{primitive elements}, i.e., the elements \(u\) which satisfy (with
the abuse of notation signaled in 3.1.2):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∆u = u ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ u,    ε(u) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{Note that the second condition is a consequence of the first,
  since the first entails that
  \texttt{u\ =\ (id\ ⊗\ ε)\ ∆(u)\ =\ u\ +\ ε(u)}, whence
  \(\epsilon(u) = 0\).}

Since \texttt{(Lie\ G)(T)} is the set of elements
\(u_{0} + u d \in G(I_{T})\) above the unit element \(u_{0} = 1\) of
\(G(T)\), one obtains an isomorphism of \(O(T)\)-modules, functorial in
\(T\):\footnote{The structure of \texttt{O\_S}-module on \texttt{Lie\ G}
  is defined in II, Prop. 3.6.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Lie G)(T) ≃ Prim Γ(T, 𝒰\_T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, one deduces from (1) that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Prim Γ(I\_T(M), 𝒰\_\{I\_T(M)\}) ≃ Prim Γ(T, 𝒰\_T) ⊗\_\{O(T)\} O(I\_T(M)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and it follows that the natural morphism of \(O(I_{T}(M))\)-modules:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Lie G)(T) ⊗\_\{O(T)\} O(I\_T(M)) ⟶ (Lie G)(I\_T(M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an isomorphism, i.e.~\texttt{Lie\ G} is a \emph{good
\texttt{O\_S}-module} (cf.~II, Déf. 4.4).

So \(G\) is a good group \(S\)-functor (cf.~II, Déf. 4.6), and according
to II, 4.7.2, \texttt{Lie\ G} is equipped with an \texttt{O\_S}-bilinear
``Lie bracket'' satisfying the Jacobi identity. It remains to show that
\(G\) is very good, i.e., that the ``bracket'' on \texttt{(Lie\ G)(T)}
satisfies \([u, u] = 0\) for every \(u \in (Lie G)(T)\) (cf.~II, 4.10).

Let \texttt{u,\ v} be two elements of \texttt{(Lie\ G)(T)}, i.e., two
primitive elements of \(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\). Set
\(I = \operatorname{Spec} O_{S}[d]/(d^{2})\) and
\(I' = \operatorname{Spec} O_{S}[d']/(d'^{2})\). Since the composition
law of \(G(I \times I')\) is induced by the multiplication of the
algebra \(\mathcal{U}_{I \times I'}\), one has in \(G(I \times I')\) the
equality:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1 + ud)(1 + vd\textquotesingle{})(1 + ud)\^{}\{{-}1\}(1 + vd\textquotesingle{})\^{}\{{-}1\} = (1 + ud)(1 + vd\textquotesingle{})(1 − ud)(1 − vd\textquotesingle{})}
\NormalTok{                                              = 1 + (uv − vu) dd\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

According to the description of the bracket \texttt{{[}u,\ v{]}} given
before Prop. 4.8 of Exp. II, one obtains that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[u, v] = uv − vu,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the right-hand term is the commutator of \(u\) and \(v\) in the
algebra \(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\), whence \([u, u] = 0\). One has
thus obtained the following proposition:\footnote{We have added this
  proposition, which summarizes the preceding discussion.}

\textbf{Proposition.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be an
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra in groups. The group \(S\)-functor
\(G = \operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}\) is very good, and one has an
isomorphism \(Lie G \simeq Prim \mathcal{W}(\mathcal{U})\) of
\texttt{O\_S}-Lie algebras, where \(Prim \mathcal{W}(\mathcal{U})\)
denotes the functor which to every \(T \to S\) associates the
\(O(T)\)-Lie algebra formed by the primitive elements of
\(\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{U})(T) = \Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T})\).}

\subsubsection{3.3.}\label{section-85}

Suppose finally that \(\mathcal{U}\) is a commutative group coalgebra,
i.e., the triangle

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              σ}
\NormalTok{       𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰  ────────────────────→  𝒰 ⊗ 𝒰}
\NormalTok{              ╲                    ╱}
\NormalTok{(i)*           ╲                  ╱}
\NormalTok{              m\_𝒰              m\_𝒰}
\NormalTok{                  ╲          ╱}
\NormalTok{                       𝒰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is commutative, or in other words that \(m_{\mathcal{U}}\) makes
\(\mathcal{U}\) a commutative \texttt{O\_S}-algebra. Conditions (i),
(ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (i)\emph{, (ii)}, (iii)* and (v)* then
also signify that \(\mathcal{U}\) is a cogroup in the category of
commutative \texttt{O\_S}-algebras. Therefore, if moreover
\(\mathcal{U}\) is a quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-module, then the
affine \(S\)-scheme \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{U}\) is a commutative
\(S\)-group scheme.

In this case, since the diagonal morphism \texttt{∆\textquotesingle{}}
of \(O_{S}[T, T^{-1}]\) sends \(T\) to \(T \otimes T\), the morphisms of
\(S\)-groups from \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{U}\) into
\(\mathbb{G}_{m, S}\) (I 4.3.2) correspond bijectively to the morphisms
of unital \texttt{O\_S}-algebras

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ : O\_S[T, T\^{}\{{-}1\}] ⟶ 𝒰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \texttt{(φ\ ⊗\ φ)\ ∘\ ∆\textquotesingle{}\ =\ ∆\_𝒰\ ∘\ φ} (in
this case, \(\epsilon_{\mathcal{U}} \circ \phi\) is the neutral element
of \(\mathbb{G}_{m, S}(S)\), i.e., the augmentation \(\epsilon'\)). Such
a morphism \(\phi\) is determined by the image \(\phi(T)\), which must
be an invertible element \(x\) of \(\mathcal{U}\) satisfying
\texttt{∆\_𝒰\ x\ =\ x\ ⊗\ x} and
\(\epsilon_{\mathcal{U}}(x) = \epsilon'(T) = 1\). One therefore has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Spec 𝒰, 𝔾\_\{m, S\}) ≃ (Spec\^{}* 𝒰)(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since this formula remains valid after any base change, this gives:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Spec\^{}* 𝒰 ≃ Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Spec 𝒰, 𝔾\_\{m, S\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore obtained the

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.0.} \emph{If \(\mathcal{U}\) is an
\texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra in commutative groups, quasi-coherent as an
\texttt{O\_S}-module, then the affine \(S\)-scheme
\(G = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{U}\) is a commutative \(S\)-group
scheme, and one has an isomorphism of group \(S\)-functors}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Spec\^{}* 𝒰 ≃ Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, 𝔾\_\{m, S\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If one supposes moreover that \(\mathcal{U}\) is a locally free
\texttt{O\_S}-module of finite type, then, according to 3.1.2.1, the
group \(S\)-functor \(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U}\) is
represented by \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{U}^{*}\). One thus obtains
the

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.1 (Cartier duality).} \emph{The functor}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒜(G) ↦ 𝒜(G)\^{}* = Hom\_\{O\_S{-}Mod.\}(𝒜(G), O\_S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induces a duality \((\ast)\) of the category of commutative,
finite and locally free \(S\)-group schemes; it associates with \(G\)
the \(S\)-group \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, \mathbb{G}_{m, S})\).}

\subsection{4. ``Frobeniuseries''}\label{frobeniuseries}

Let \(p\) be a fixed prime number and \((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})\) the
category of schemes of characteristic \(p\), i.e., of schemes above the
prime field \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\). Following the general conventions of
this Seminar, we identify \((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})\) with a subcategory of
\((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})^{\wedge}\) by means of the functor \(h\) of I
1.1. We likewise take advantage of the isomorphism from
\(\operatorname{Hom}(h_{X}, F)\) onto \(F(X)\) defined in I 1.1 to
identify these two sets whenever \(X\) is an \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-scheme
and \(F\) an object of \((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})^{\wedge}\).

\textbf{Notations 4.0.}\footnote{We have added the numbering 4.0, for
  later references.} \emph{If \(T\) is an \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-scheme, a
\(T\)-functor is a morphism \(q : F \to T\) of
\((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})^{\wedge}\) having \(T\) as target; for every
\(T\)-scheme \(r : X \to T\), the set of \(T\)-morphisms \(X \to F\),
i.e., of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-morphisms \(s : X \to F\) such that
\(q \circ s = r\), will then be denoted \(q(r)\), \(q(X/T)\), \(F(r)\)
or \(F(X/T)\) (or even \(F(X)\) when no confusion will be possible with
\(\operatorname{Hom}(h_{X}, F)\)).}

\subsubsection{4.1.}\label{section-86}

For every scheme \(S\) of characteristic \(p\), we denote by \(fr(S)\),
or simply \texttt{fr}, the endomorphism of \(S\) which induces the
identity on the underlying topological space of \(S\) and which
associates \(x^{p}\) with a section \(x\) of \texttt{O\_S} on an open
\(U\).

Then the map \(fr : S \mapsto fr(S)\) is an endomorphism of the identity
functor of \((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})\),\footnote{i.e.~for every morphism of
  \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-schemes \(f : Y \to X\), the diagram below is
  commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                   f}
\NormalTok{          Y  ────────→  X}
\NormalTok{   fr(Y)                fr(X)}
\NormalTok{                   f}
\NormalTok{          Y  ────────→  X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
} which implies the following results. Let \(E\) be an
\(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-functor, i.e., an object of
\((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})^{\wedge}\); the map which to every
\(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-scheme \(S\) associates the endomorphism \(E(fr(S))\)
of \(E(S)\) is a functorial endomorphism of \(E\) which we shall denote
\(fr(E)\) or \texttt{fr}; this notation is compatible with the
identification of \((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})\) with a subcategory of
\((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})^{\wedge}\). Moreover, the map \(E \mapsto fr(E)\)
is an endomorphism of the identity functor of
\((Sch/\mathbb{F}_{p})^{\wedge}\) (which we shall again denote
\texttt{fr}).\footnote{One says that \(fr(X)\) is the ``absolute''
  Frobenius morphism of \(X\), to distinguish it from the ``relative''
  Frobenius morphism \(Fr(X/S)\) introduced below.}

For every \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-scheme \(S\) and every \(S\)-functor
\(q : X \to S\), we denote by \(X^{(p/S)}\) or \(X^{(p)}\) the inverse
image of \(X\) by the base change \(fr(S)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  pr\_X}
\NormalTok{       X\^{}\{(p/S)\}  ──────→  X}
\NormalTok{           │                  │ q}
\NormalTok{           ▼                  ▼}
\NormalTok{                fr(S)}
\NormalTok{            S  ──────────→  S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The commutative square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       fr(X)}
\NormalTok{              X  ──────────→  X}
\NormalTok{              │                  │}
\NormalTok{            q │                  │ q}
\NormalTok{              ▼       fr(S)       ▼}
\NormalTok{              S  ──────────→  S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induces an \(S\)-morphism, denoted \(Fr(X/S)\) (or simply \texttt{Fr}),
from \(X\) into \(X^{(p/S)}\) such that
\(fr(X) = pr_{X} \circ Fr(X/S)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              X}
\NormalTok{              │ ╲}
\NormalTok{              │  ╲  Fr(X/S)}
\NormalTok{              │   ╲}
\NormalTok{              │    ╲             fr(X)}
\NormalTok{              │     X\^{}\{(p/S)\}  ──pr\_X→  X}
\NormalTok{              │       │                  │}
\NormalTok{            q │       │ q\^{}\{(p/S)\}        │ q}
\NormalTok{              ▼       ▼       fr(S)       ▼}
\NormalTok{              S       S       ─────→     S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We shall say that \(Fr(X/S)\) is the \emph{Frobenius morphism of \(X\)
relative to \(S\)}; it is clear that the map \(Fr : X \mapsto Fr(X/S)\)
is a functorial homomorphism.

\footnote{We have expanded the original in what follows.} Let
\(r : T \to S\) be an \(S\)-scheme. For every
\(\phi \in X(r) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(T, X)\) (cf. 4.0), one has a
commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  Fr(X/S)              pr\_X}
\NormalTok{       X  ──────────────→  X\^{}\{(p/S)\}  ──────→  X}
\NormalTok{        ╲                         │                  │}
\NormalTok{         ╲ φ                      │ q\^{}\{(p/S)\}        │ q}
\NormalTok{       r  ╲                       │                  │}
\NormalTok{            ╲                     ▼      fr(S)       ▼}
\NormalTok{              T  ──────────────→  S  ──────────→  S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

According to the definition of \(X^{(p/S)}\) as fibered product,
\(pr_{X}\) induces a bijection:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\^{}\{(p/S)\}(r) = Hom\_S(T, X\^{}\{(p/S)\})  ⥲  Hom\_S(T, X) = X(fr(S) ∘ r).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, \(r \circ fr(T) = fr(S) \circ r\), since \texttt{fr}
is an endomorphism of the identity functor. It follows that the map
\(Fr(X/S)(r) : X(r) \to X^{(p/S)}(r)\) can be characterized by the
commutativity of the following square:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  Fr(X/S)(r)}
\NormalTok{       X(r)  ────────────────→  X\^{}\{(p/S)\}(r)}

\NormalTok{(†)   X(fr(T))                       ≀}
                                          
\NormalTok{       X(r ∘ fr(T))           X(fr(S) ∘ r).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For example, if \(X\) is the subscheme of \(S\) defined by a
quasi-coherent ideal \(\mathcal{I}\), then \(X^{(p)}\) is the subscheme
of \(S\) defined by the ideal \(\mathcal{I}^{{p}}\) generated by the
\(p\)-th powers of the sections of \(\mathcal{I}\); moreover,
\(Fr(X/S)\) is then the canonical immersion of
\(\operatorname{Spec}(O_{X} / \mathcal{I})\) into
\(\operatorname{Spec}(O / \mathcal{I}^{{p}})\).

\subsubsection{4.1.1.}\label{section-87}

\footnote{We have expanded the original in what follows.} Let
\(t : T \to S\) be a base change and \(X_{T} = X \times_{q, t} T\).
Consider the inverse image of \texttt{X\_T} by \(fr(T)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       (X\_T)\^{}\{(p/T)\}  ────→  X\_T  ─────→  X}
\NormalTok{                                              │ q}
\NormalTok{                  fr(T)              t}
\NormalTok{              T  ──────→  T  ──→  S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(t \circ fr(T) = fr(S) \circ t\), then \((X_{T})^{(p/T)}\) is
identified with the inverse image of \(X^{(p/S)}\) by \(t\); in other
words, one has a canonical isomorphism:

\[
X^{(p/T)}_{T}  \xrightarrow{\sim}  (X^{(p/S)})_{T}.
\]

It is clear that, in this identification, \(Fr(X_{T} / T)\) is
identified with the inverse image \(Fr(X/S)_{T}\) of \(Fr(X/S)\).

\paragraph{4.1.1.1.}\label{section-88}

In particular, if \(S\) is the spectrum of the prime field
\(\mathbb{F}_{p}\), \(X^{(p/S)}\) is equal to \(X\) and \(Fr(X/S)\) to
\(fr(X)\). Consequently, \(X^{(p/T)}_{T}\) is identified with
\texttt{X\_T} and \(Fr(X_{T} / T)\) with \(fr(X)_{T}\).

For example, if \(E\) is a set and \texttt{E\_T} the constant
\(T\)-scheme of type \(E\), one has \(E^{(p/T)}_{T} \simeq E_{T}\) and
\(Fr(E_{T} / T) \simeq id_{E_{T}}\).

\subsubsection{4.1.2.}\label{section-89}

The functor \(X \mapsto X^{(p/S)}\) obviously commutes with products; it
therefore transforms an \(S\)-group \(G\) into an \(S\)-group
\(G^{(p/S)}\); moreover, since \texttt{Fr} is a functorial homomorphism,
then

\[
Fr(G/S) : G \longrightarrow G^{(p/S)}
\]

is a homomorphism of \(S\)-groups. We shall denote \texttt{Fr\ G} its
kernel.

If \(r : T \to S\) is a scheme above \(S\), it follows from the diagram
\texttt{(†)} of 4.1 that the value of \texttt{Fr\ G} at \(r\) is the
kernel of the homomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G(fr(T)) : G(r) ⟶ G(r ∘ fr(T)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, when \(T\) is the scheme \texttt{I\_R} of dual numbers over an
\(S\)-scheme \(R\), \(fr(I_{R})\) factors as follows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I\_R  ──can.→  R  ──fr(R)→  R  ──s→  I\_R,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(s\) is the zero section. It follows that \((Fr G)(I_{R})\)
contains the kernel \(Lie(G/S)(R)\) of the morphism
\(G(s) : G(I_{R}) \to G(R)\), and that one therefore has:
\(Lie(G/S) = Lie(Fr G / S)\).

\subsubsection{4.1.3.}\label{section-90}

More generally, for every \(S\)-functor \(X\), we define the
\(S\)-functor \(X^{(p^{n})}\) by recursion on \(n\) by means of the
formulas:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\^{}\{(p)\} = X\^{}\{(p/S)\}    and    X\^{}\{(p\^{}n)\} = (X\^{}\{(p\^{}\{n{-}1\})\})\^{}\{(p)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Similarly, \(Fr^{n}(X/S)\) or \(Fr^{n}\) denote the composed functorial
homomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ──Fr(X/S)→ X\^{}\{(p)\} ──Fr(X\^{}\{(p)\}/S)→ X\^{}\{(p²)\} ──→ ··· ──→ X\^{}\{(p\^{}\{n{-}1\})\} ──Fr(X\^{}\{(p\^{}\{n{-}1\})\}/S)→ X\^{}\{(p\^{}n)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One will note that, according to 4.1.1, \(Fr(X^{(p)}/S)\) coincides with
\(Fr(X/S)^{(p)}\), i.e., the following diagram is commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       X\^{}\{(p)\}  ────→  X}

\NormalTok{   Fr(X\^{}\{(p)\}/S)         Fr(X/S)}

\NormalTok{       X\^{}\{(p²)\}  ────→  X\^{}\{(p)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(G\) is a group \(S\)-functor, \(G^{(p^{n})}\) is also one and
\(Fr^{n}(G/S)\) is a homomorphism of group \(S\)-functors.

\textbf{Definition.} \emph{We shall denote by \(Fr^{n} G\) the kernel of
\(Fr^{n}(G/S)\) and we shall say that \(G\) is of height \(\leqslant n\)
if \(Fr^{n}(G/S)\) is zero, i.e., if \(Fr^{n} G = G\).}

\textbf{Lemma.} \emph{The group subfunctor \(Fr^{n} G\) of \(G\) is
characteristic, i.e., for every \(S\)-scheme \(T\), every endomorphism
\(\phi\) of the group \(T\)-functor \texttt{G\_T} induces an
endomorphism of \((Fr^{n} G)_{T}\).}

Indeed, since the construction of \(G^{(p^{n})}\) and of \(Fr^{n}(G/S)\)
commutes with base changes according to 4.1.1, one may suppose
\(T = S\); in this case, the assertion follows from the fact that
\(Fr^{n}(G/S)\) is a functorial homomorphism.

\subsubsection{4.1.4. Examples.}\label{examples.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Consider first an ``abstract'' abelian group \(M\) and the
  diagonalizable group \(G = D_{S}(M)\) of type \(M\) (I 4.4): for every
  \(S\)-scheme \(T\), \(G(T)\) is therefore the abelian group
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{(Ab)}(M, \Gamma(T, O_{T})^{\times})\). Since
  \(G\) is the inverse image of the diagonalizable group \(D(M)\) over
  \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\), \(G^{(p)}\) is identified with \(G\) and
  \(Fr(G/S)(T)\) is identified with the endomorphism \(x \mapsto x^{p}\)
  of \(G(T)\) (4.1.1). In particular, when \(M\) is equal to
  \(\mathbb{Z}\), one has \(D_{S}(M) = \mathbb{G}_{m, S}\), so that:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}
\(Fr \mathbb{G}_{m, S}\) is the \(S\)-group \(\mu_{p, S}\) which to
every \(S\)-scheme \(T\) associates the group of \(p\)-th roots of unity
in \(\Gamma(T, O_{T})^{*}\).
\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Consider now a scheme \(S\) of characteristic \(p\) and a sheaf of
  modules \(\mathcal{E}\) on \(S\). According to I 4.6.2, one has a
  canonical isomorphism
\end{enumerate}

\[
\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{E})^{(p)} \simeq \mathcal{W}(\mathcal{E}^{(p)}),
\]

where \(\mathcal{E}^{(p)}\) is the inverse image of \(\mathcal{E}\) by
\(fr(S)\). For every \(S\)-scheme \(\pi : T \to S\), the map
\(Fr(\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{E}))(\pi)\) is determined, according to 4.1
\texttt{(†)}, by the commutative triangle

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       Γ(T, π\^{}* fr(S)\^{}* ℰ)  ──can.\textasciitilde{}→  Γ(T, fr(T)\^{}* π\^{}* ℰ)}
\NormalTok{              ╲                                    ╱}
\NormalTok{               ╲                                  ╱}
\NormalTok{        Fr(𝒲(ℰ)/S)(π)                          f\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{                  ╲                          ╱}
\NormalTok{                    Γ(T, π\^{}* ℰ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(f'\) is the map induced by \(fr(T)\).

In particular, if \(\mathcal{E}\) is equal to \texttt{O\_S},
\(\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{E})\) is identified with the additive group
\(\mathbb{G}_{a, S}\). In this case, one has
\(\mathcal{E}^{(p)} = \mathcal{E} = O_{S}\) and the Frobenius morphism
\(Fr(\mathbb{G}_{a, S}/S)\) sends \(x \in \Gamma(T, O_{T})\) to
\(x^{p}\). So:

\begin{quote}
\(Fr \mathbb{G}_{a, S}\) is the \(S\)-group \(\alpha_{p, S}\) which to
every \(S\)-scheme \(T\) associates the group:
\({ x \in \Gamma(T, O_{T}) | x^{p} = 0}\).
\end{quote}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  One would see similarly that, for every quasi-coherent
  \texttt{O\_S}-algebra \(\mathcal{A}\),
  \((\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A})^{(p)}\) is identified with the
  spectrum \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A}^{(p)}\) of the inverse
  image of \(\mathcal{A}\) by \(fr(S)\). If \(\pi\) denotes the
  endomorphism \(x \mapsto x^{p}\) of the sheaf of rings \texttt{O\_S},
  one has therefore
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒜\^{}\{(p)\} = 𝒜 ⊗\_π O\_S    [\^{}N.D.E{-}VII\_A{-}44]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(Fr((\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A})/S)\) is induced by the
morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-algebras
\(\mathcal{A} \otimes_{\pi} O_{S} \to \mathcal{A}\) defined by
\(a \otimes_{\pi} x \mapsto a^{p} x\).

For every quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-module \(\mathcal{E}\), finally,
one has canonical isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒱(ℰ)\^{}\{(p)\} ≃ 𝒱(ℰ\^{}\{(p)\})    and    𝒮(ℰ)\^{}\{(p)\} ≃ 𝒮(ℰ\^{}\{(p)\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{E})\) denotes the symmetric algebra of the
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(\mathcal{E}\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be an \texttt{O\_S}-coalgebra (3.1) and \(T\) a
  scheme of characteristic \(p\). If \(\mathcal{U}^{(p/S)}\) or
  \(\mathcal{U}^{(p)}\) denote the inverse image of the coalgebra
  \(\mathcal{U}\) by \(fr(S)\), one has as in b) a canonical
  isomorphism:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Spec\^{}* 𝒰)\^{}\{(p)\} ≃ Spec\^{}* 𝒰\^{}\{(p)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(\mathcal{U}\) is a coalgebra in groups, the value of
\(Fr(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U})\), i.e., of the kernel of the
Frobenius morphism
\(\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U} \to (\operatorname{Spec}^{*} \mathcal{U})^{(p)}\),
for an \(S\)-scheme \(T\) is therefore the set of elements \(\gamma\) of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Spec\^{}* 𝒰)(T) = \{ x ∈ Γ(T, 𝒰\_T) | ε\_\{𝒰\_T\}(x) = 1, ∆\_\{𝒰\_T\} x = x ⊗ x \}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that the image in
\(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T} \otimes_{fr(T)} O_{T})\) of the element
\(\gamma \otimes_{fr(T)} 1\) of
\(\Gamma(T, \mathcal{U}_{T}) \otimes_{fr(T)} O(T)\) is equal to
\texttt{1}.

\subsubsection{4.2.}\label{section-91}

\footnote{For the content of nos 4.2 and 4.3, one may also consult
  {[}DG70{]}, § IV.3, nos 4--6.} We shall now occupy ourselves with a
construction close to the preceding one: let \(S\) be a scheme of
characteristic \(p\), \(X\) an \(S\)-scheme and \(X^{p_{S}}\) the
product in the category \((Sch/S)\) of \(p\) copies of \(X\).

We then denote by \(U_{p}(X)\) the open subscheme of \(X^{p_{S}}\) which
is the union of the products \(U^{p_{S}}\), when \(U\) ranges over the
affine opens of \(X\). A point \(x\) of \(X^{p_{S}}\) therefore belongs
to \(U_{p}(X)\) if and only if the projections \(pr_{i} x\) of \(x\)
onto the factors of \(X^{p_{S}}\) belong to a common affine open of
\(X\). For example, if every finite part of \(X\) is contained in an
affine open, one has \(U_{p}(X) = X^{p_{S}}\).

The symmetric group \(\mathfrak{S}_{p}\) of order \(p\) operates on
\(X^{p_{S}}\) by permutation of factors and leaves stable the open
\(U_{p}(X)\). We shall call the \emph{\(p\)-fold symmetric product of
\(X\)} and we shall denote \(\Sigma^{p} X\) the quotient of
\(X^{p_{S}}\) by \(\mathfrak{S}_{p}\) in the category of ringed spaces.
Let \(q(X)\), or simply \(q\), be the canonical projection
\(X^{p_{S}} \to \Sigma^{p} X\).

Then \(q\) maps \(U_{p}(X)\) onto an open \(V_{p}(X)\) of the symmetric
product, which one may describe as follows (cf.~V 4.1). The structure
sheaf of \(\Sigma^{p} X\) induces on \(V_{p}(X)\) a scheme structure;
the morphism \(q'(X) : U_{p}(X) \to V_{p}(X)\) induced by \(q(X)\) is
affine and even integral; when \(U\) ranges over the affine opens of
\(X\) which project into an affine open \(V\) of \(S\) varying, the
\(\Sigma^{p} U\) form an affine covering of \(V_{p}(X)\); if \(R\)
denotes the affine algebra of \(V\) and \(A\) that of \(U\),
\(\Sigma^{p} U\) has as affine algebra the subalgebra \(\Sigma^{p} A\)
of \(\bigotimes^{p}_{R} A\) formed by the symmetric tensors.

Consider now the diagonal morphism \(\delta\) of \(X\) into
\(U_{p}(X)\). If \(V = \operatorname{Spec} R\) is an affine open of
\(S\) and \(U = \operatorname{Spec} A\) an affine open of \(X\) above
\(V\), the restriction of \(\delta\) to \(U\) is defined by the algebra
morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{η : ⨂\^{}p\_R A ⟶ A,    a\_1 ⊗ ··· ⊗ a\_p ↦ a\_1 a\_2 ··· a\_p.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One therefore has, if \(N\) is the symmetrization operator:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{η(N(a\_1 ⊗ ··· ⊗ a\_p)) = η(∑\_\{σ ∈ 𝔖\_p\} a\_\{σ(1)\} ⊗ ··· ⊗ a\_\{σ(p)\}) = p! a\_1 ··· a\_p = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In other words, \(\eta\) vanishes on the subspace
\(N(\bigotimes^{p}_{R} A)\) of \(\Sigma^{p} A\) formed by the
symmetrized tensors. Moreover, if \(f\) is a symmetric tensor, one has
obviously \(N(f a) = f N(a)\), which shows that
\(N(\bigotimes^{p}_{R} A)\) is an ideal of \(\Sigma^{p} A\). We shall
henceforth denote

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\^{}\{[p/S]\} = Spec(Σ\^{}p A / N(⨂\^{}p\_R A));}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

it is a closed subscheme of \(\Sigma^{p}(U) = V_{p}(U)\). The union of
the \(U^{[p/S]}\), when \(U\) ranges over the affine opens of \(X\)
which project into a varying affine open \(V\) of \(S\), is a closed
subscheme of \(V_{p}(X)\), denoted \(X^{[p/S]}\).

Moreover, if \(i(X)\) denotes the inclusion of \(X^{[p/S]}\) into
\(V_{p}(X)\), we have just seen that \(q'(X) \circ \delta\) factors
through \(X^{[p/S]}\), whence a morphism
\(F^{[p]}(X/S) : X \to X^{[p/S]}\):\footnote{In the original, this
  morphism (resp. the relative Frobenius morphism) was denoted \(F'\)
  (resp. \(F\)).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                   δ(X)}
\NormalTok{       X\^{}\{p\_S\}  ⊃  U\_p(X)  ←──────────  X}

\NormalTok{   q(X)             q\textquotesingle{}(X)            F\^{}\{[p]\}(X/S)}

\NormalTok{                                   i(X)}
\NormalTok{       Σ\^{}p(X)  ⊃  V\_p(X)  ←──────────  X\^{}\{[p/S]\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is clear that \(X^{[p/S]}\) is functorial in \(X\) and that the map
\(F^{[p]} : X \mapsto F^{[p]}(X/S)\) is a functorial homomorphism.

\subsubsection{4.2.1.}\label{section-92}

The schemes \(X^{[p/S]}\) and \(X^{(p/S)}\) are obviously related: let
\(V\) be an affine open of \(S\) with affine ring \(R\) and \(U\) an
affine open of \(X\) above \(V\); let \(A\) be the affine algebra of
\(U\). If \(\pi\) denotes the endomorphism \(x \mapsto x^{p}\) of \(R\),
then \(U^{(p/S)}\) has \(A \otimes_{\pi} R\) as affine algebra. One
verifies moreover that the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a ⊗\_π λ ↦ (λ a ⊗ ··· ⊗ a    mod    N(⨂\^{}p\_R A))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defines a morphism of \(R\)-algebras from \(A \otimes_{\pi} R\) into
\(\Sigma^{p} A / N(\bigotimes^{p}_{R} A)\), and the latter induces a
morphism \(\phi(U) : U^{[p/S]} \to U^{(p/S)}\) such that
\(\phi(U) \circ F^{[p]}(U/S) = Fr(U/S)\).

``Gluing the pieces'', one then obtains a commutative triangle

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              X}
\NormalTok{                       ╱           ╲}
\NormalTok{              F\^{}\{[p]\}(X/S)         Fr(X/S)}
\NormalTok{                  ╱                   ╲}
\NormalTok{                ╱                       ╲}
\NormalTok{              X\^{}\{[p/S]\}  ──────φ(X)────→  X\^{}\{(p/S)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For example, if \(X\) is the subscheme of \(S\) defined by a
quasi-coherent ideal \(\mathcal{I}\), \(F^{[p]}(X/S)\) is identified
with the identity morphism of \(X\), so that \(\phi(X)\) is the
canonical immersion of \(\operatorname{Spec}(O_{S} / \mathcal{I})\) into
\(\operatorname{Spec}(O_{S} / \mathcal{I}^{{p}})\). One thus sees that
\(\phi(X)\) is not an isomorphism in general.

However, when \(M\) is a free \(R\)-module, it is clear that the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M ⊗\_π R ⟶ Σ\^{}p M / N(⨂\^{}p\_R M),    m ⊗\_π λ ↦ (λ m ⊗ ··· ⊗ m    mod    N(⨂\^{}p\_R M))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective; this map therefore remains bijective when \(M\) is
\(R\)-flat, because every flat module is a filtered direct limit of free
modules (Lazard\footnote{D. Lazard, C. R. Acad. Sc. Paris 258, 1964,
  p.~6313--6316.} \footnote{See also: D. Lazard, Bull. Soc. Math. France
  97 (1969), 81--128, or: {[}BAlg{]}, X § 1.6, Th. 1.}). It follows that

\begin{quote}
\(\phi(X) : X^{[p/S]} \to X^{(p/S)}\) is an isomorphism if \(X\) is a
flat \(S\)-scheme.
\end{quote}

\subsubsection{4.3.}\label{section-93}

Consider finally an \(S\)-group scheme \(G\) in abelian groups. Then the
composed morphism \(\mu(G) : U_{p}(G) \hookrightarrow G^{p_{S}} \to G\),
which is defined by the multiplication, factors through \(V_{p}(G)\),
i.e., there exists a morphism \(\nu(G) : V_{p}(G) \to G\) such that
\(\nu(G) \circ q'(G) = \mu(G)\), so that one has the following
commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          μ(G)                δ(G)}
\NormalTok{       G  ←──────────  U\_p(G)  ←──────────  G}
\NormalTok{        ╲                  │                  │}
\NormalTok{         ╲ ν(G)             │                  │ F\^{}\{[p]\}(G/S)}
\NormalTok{          ╲                 │ q\textquotesingle{}(G)            │}
\NormalTok{                            ▼                  ▼}
\NormalTok{                          V\_p(G)  ←──────  G\^{}\{[p/S]\}}
\NormalTok{                                  i(G)}
\NormalTok{        Ver(G/S)                                Fr(G/S)}
\NormalTok{                                          ╲       ╱}
\NormalTok{                                            φ(G)}
\NormalTok{                                              ▼}
\NormalTok{                                          G\^{}\{(p/S)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

When \(G\) is \(S\)-flat, \(\phi(G)\) is an isomorphism and one can
define a morphism (called the \emph{Verschiebung})

\[
Ver(G/S) : G^{(p/S)} \longrightarrow G
\]

by means of the formula
\(Ver(G/S) = \nu(G) \circ i(G) \circ \phi(G)^{-1}\). When \(G\) ranges
over \(S\)-flat group schemes in abelian groups, the map
\(Ver : G \mapsto Ver(G/S)\) is obviously a functorial homomorphism;
consequently, \(Ver(G/S)\) is a group homomorphism. For every
\(S\)-scheme \(T\) finally, the composed map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G(T) ──δ(G)(T)→ U\_p(G)(T) ──μ(G)(T)→ G(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

sends \(x \in G(T)\) to \(p \cdot x\). We may write \(p \cdot id_{G}\)
instead of \(\mu(G) \circ \delta(G)\), thus obtaining the classical
formula:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)                       Ver(G/S) ∘ Fr(G/S) = p · id\_G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Examples 4.3.1.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\alph{enumi})}
\item
  When \(G\) is a constant \(S\)-scheme in abelian groups, we know that
  \(Fr(G/S)\) is identified with the identity morphism of \(G\)
  (cf.~4.1.1.1). One therefore has \(Ver(G/S) = p id_{G}\).
\item
  When \(G\) is the diagonalizable \(S\)-group of type \(M\),
  \(Fr(G/S)\) is equal to \(p id_{G}\) according to 4.1.4 (a); one then
  sees easily that \(Ver(G/S)\) is the identity morphism of \(G\).
\item
  When \(\mathcal{E}\) is a flat \texttt{O\_S}-module and \(G\) is the
  \(S\)-group \(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{E})\), the morphism \(Ver(G/S)\) is
  zero, as is \(p \cdot id_{G}\). One will see in Exposé VII\_B that a
  commutative algebraic group \(G\) over a field \(k\) is ``unipotent''
  if and only if the composed homomorphism
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\^{}\{(p\^{}n)\} ──Ver(G\^{}\{(p\^{}\{n{-}1\})\}/S)→ G\^{}\{(p\^{}\{n{-}1\})\} ──→ ··· ──→ G\^{}\{(p)\} ──Ver(G/S)→ G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is zero for some \(n\) (one has set
\(G^{(p^{n})} = (G^{(p^{n-1})})^{(p)}\), cf.~4.1.3).\footnote{Since this
  does not appear explicitly in VII\_B, one refers to {[}DG70{]}, §
  IV.3, Prop. 4.11.}

\subsubsection{4.3.2.}\label{section-94}

Since the map \(Ver : G \mapsto Ver(G/S)\) is a functorial homomorphism
when \(G\) ranges over \(S\)-flat group schemes in commutative groups,
the square

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          Ver(G/S)}
\NormalTok{       G\^{}\{(p)\}  ──────────────────→  G}

\NormalTok{   Fr(G/S)\^{}\{(p)\}                            Fr(G/S)}
                                
\NormalTok{                       Ver(G\^{}\{(p)\}/S)}
\NormalTok{       G\^{}\{(p²)\}  ──────────────────→  G\^{}\{(p)\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is commutative, where \(Fr(G/S)^{(p)}\) denotes the inverse image of
\(Fr(G/S)\) by the base change \(fr(S)\). According to 4.1.1, one has
\(Fr(G/S)^{(p)} = Fr(G^{(p)}/S)\), so, according to 4.3 \((\ast)\)
applied to \(G^{(p)}\), one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗∗)        Fr(G/S) ∘ Ver(G/S) = Ver(G\^{}\{(p)\}/S) ∘ Fr(G\^{}\{(p)\}/S) = p · id\_\{G\^{}\{(p)\}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{4.3.3.}\label{section-95}

Suppose finally that \(G\) is a commutative, finite and locally free
\(S\)-group; let \(\mathcal{A}\) be the \texttt{O\_S}-affine algebra of
\(G\) and \(\pi\) the endomorphism of the sheaf of rings \texttt{O\_S}
which sends a section \(x\) of \texttt{O\_S} to \(x^{p}\).\footnote{We
  have modified the order, by first introducing the objects appearing in
  the diagram that follows.} We denote by \(\Sigma^{p} \mathcal{A}\) the
subalgebra of \(\bigotimes^{p}_{O_{S}} \mathcal{A}\) formed by the
sections invariant under the action of the symmetric group, by
\(i(\mathcal{A})\) the inclusion of \(\Sigma^{p} \mathcal{A}\) into the
tensor product. Let \texttt{∆\_p(𝒜)\ :\ 𝒜\ →\ ⨂\^{}p\_\{O\_S\}\ 𝒜} be
the morphism obtained by iterating the diagonal morphism of the
coalgebra \(\mathcal{A}\) (it corresponds to the morphism of
multiplication \(U_{p}(G) = G^{p_{S}} \to G\)); according to the
beginning of paragraph 4.3, \texttt{∆\_p(𝒜)} factors through
\(\Sigma^{p} \mathcal{A}\), i.e., it induces a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(𝒜) : 𝒜 ⟶ Σ\^{}p 𝒜}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \texttt{i(𝒜)\ ∘\ a(𝒜)\ =\ ∆\_p(𝒜)}.

On the other hand, let \(S^{p}(\mathcal{A})\) be the degree-\(p\)
component of the symmetric algebra of \(\mathcal{A}\) and
\(q(\mathcal{A}) : \bigotimes^{p}_{O_{S}} \mathcal{A} \to S^{p}(\mathcal{A})\)
the canonical projection. The multiplication
\(m_{p}(\mathcal{A}) : \bigotimes^{p}_{O_{S}} \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}\)
factors through \(S^{p}(\mathcal{A})\), i.e., it induces a map

\[
b(\mathcal{A}) : S^{p}(\mathcal{A}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}
\]

such that \(b(\mathcal{A}) \circ q(\mathcal{A}) = m_{p}(\mathcal{A})\).

Since \(\Sigma^{p} \mathcal{A}\) is the affine algebra of
\(V_{p}(\mathcal{A})\), then, according to the beginning of 4.3 again,
the composed morphism \(i(G) \circ \phi(G)^{-1}\) induces an algebra
homomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{r(𝒜) : Σ\^{}p 𝒜 ⟶ 𝒜 ⊗\_π O\_S;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

this homomorphism vanishes on the sections of the form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∑\_\{σ ∈ 𝔖\_p\} a\_\{σ(1)\} ⊗ ··· ⊗ a\_\{σ(p)\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and sends \(a \otimes \cdot\cdot\cdot \otimes a\) to
\(a \otimes_{\pi} 1\). Similarly, \(j(\mathcal{A})\) is the morphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules
\(a \otimes_{\pi} 1 \mapsto q(a \otimes \cdot\cdot\cdot \otimes a)\).
One thus obtains the commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       ∆\_p(𝒜)                       m\_p(𝒜)}
\NormalTok{       𝒜  ────────────→  ⨂\^{}p\_\{O\_S\} 𝒜  ──────────────→  𝒜}
\NormalTok{        ╲                  ▲     │                       ▲}
\NormalTok{         ╲ a(𝒜)      i(𝒜) │     │ q(𝒜)         b(𝒜) ╱}
\NormalTok{          ╲                │     ▼                     ╱}
\NormalTok{(𝒜)        Σ\^{}p 𝒜                  S\^{}p(𝒜)}
\NormalTok{              ╲                                       ╱}
\NormalTok{               ╲ r(𝒜)                          j(𝒜) ╱}
\NormalTok{                ╲                                  ╱}
\NormalTok{                   𝒜 ⊗\_π O\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The composition \(r(\mathcal{A}) \circ a(\mathcal{A})\) is associated
with the Verschiebung morphism \(Ver(G/S)\), while
\(b(\mathcal{A}) \circ j(\mathcal{A})\) is associated with the Frobenius
morphism \(Fr(G/S)\).

The commutative diagram \((\mathcal{A})\) above is self-dual; let \(D\)
indeed be the functor which to every \texttt{O\_S}-module
\(\mathcal{M}\) associates the dual \texttt{O\_S}-module
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}}(\mathcal{M}, O_{S})\); it is clear that the
image of the diagram \((\mathcal{A})\) by the functor \(D\) is none
other than the diagram \((D\mathcal{A})\), the morphisms
\(Dr(\mathcal{A})\), \(Da(\mathcal{A})\), \(Dj(\mathcal{A})\) and
\(Db(\mathcal{A})\) being identified respectively with
\(j(D\mathcal{A})\), \(b(D\mathcal{A})\), \(r(D\mathcal{A})\) and
\(a(D\mathcal{A})\). According to 3.3.1, one therefore sees that:

\begin{quote}
In the category of commutative, finite and locally free \(S\)-groups,
Cartier duality interchanges the Frobenius morphism and the
Verschiebung.\footnote{See also {[}DG70{]}, § IV.3, 4.9.}
\end{quote}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{5. Restricted \(p\)-Lie
algebras}{5. Restricted p-Lie algebras}}\label{restricted-p-lie-algebras}

Let us first recall some results from the \emph{Séminaire Sophus
Lie}.\footnote{cf.~P. Cartier, Exemples d'hyperalgèbres, Sém. Sophus Lie
  1955/56, Exp. 3 (accessible on the Numdam site:
  http://www.numdam.org).}

\subsubsection{5.1.}\label{section-96}

Let \(p\) be a prime number, \(R\) a commutative ring of characteristic
\(p\) and \(A\) an associative \(R\)-algebra, but not necessarily
commutative. If \(a\) and \(b\) are two elements of \(A\), we set
\([a, b] = ab - ba\) and \(a \cdot b = L_{a}(b) = R_{b}(a)\). One then
has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(ad x\^{}p)(y) = [x\^{}p, y] = (L\_x\^{}p − R\_x\^{}p)(y) = (L\_x − R\_x)\^{}p(y) = (ad x)\^{}p(y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence Jacobson's first formula:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(i)                        ad(x\^{}p) = (ad x)\^{}p.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{p}\) are \(p\) arbitrary elements of \(A\), then,
denoting by \(N\) the symmetrization operator (cf. 4.2), one has the
equalities:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    N(a\_1 ⊗ ··· ⊗ a\_p) = ∑\_σ a\_\{σ(1)\} ··· a\_\{σ(p)\} = ∑\_τ [a\_\{τ(1)\} [a\_\{τ(2)\} [··· [a\_\{τ(p{-}1)\}, a\_p] ···]]]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\sigma\) ranges over the permutations of \(p\) letters and
\(\tau\) over those of \((p - 1)\) letters. Indeed, the last term equals

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∑\_τ ∑\_\{r=0\}\^{}\{p{-}1\} ∑\_\{i\_1 \textless{} ··· \textless{} i\_r\} (−1)\^{}s a\_\{τ(i\_1)\} a\_\{τ(i\_2)\} ··· a\_\{τ(i\_r)\} a\_p a\_\{τ(j\_s)\} ··· a\_\{τ(j\_1)\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
