For every open ideal \(l\) of \(k\), there exists \(n \in \mathbb{N}*\)
such that \(r^{n} \subset l\), whence
\((rA)^{n} \subset lA \subset lA\), and since the multiplication map
\(m^{n-1} : A^{n} \to A\) is continuous, one also has
\((rA)^{n} \subset lA\), i.e., \(rA/lA\) is a nilpotent ideal of
\(A/lA\). Consequently, \(\phi\) lifts in a unique way to a morphism
\(\phi_{l} : B \to A/lA\). By uniqueness, these morphisms form a
projective system, hence give a continuous morphism
\(\Phi : B \to \lim_{l} A/lA = A\). Moreover, \(\Phi\) is unique since
if \(\Phi'\) is a second lifting of \(\phi\), then \(\Phi'\) and
\(\Phi\) coincide modulo \texttt{lA} for every \(l\), hence are equal.

\textbf{Proposition 1.6.E.} \emph{(a) Let \(X\) be a formal variety over
\(k\) and \(A\) its affine algebra. The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(X\) is étale over \(k\).}

\emph{(ii) \(X\) is topologically flat over \(k\) and the diagonal
morphism \texttt{∆\ :\ X\ →\ X\ ×\ X} is a local isomorphism, i.e.,
\texttt{∆\_X} induces an isomorphism
\texttt{O\_\{X×X,\ ∆(x)\}\ ⥲\ O\_\{X,\ x\}} for every point \(x\) of
\(X\).}

\emph{(iii) For every \(x \in X\), of projection \(s\) on \(Spf(k)\),
\(O_{X, x}\) is isomorphic to \(k_{s}[T]/(F)\), where \(F \in k_{s}[T]\)
is a monic separable polynomial (cf.~1.6.A (ii)).}

\emph{(iv) \(X\) is topologically flat over \(k\), and, for every point
\(x \in X\), of projection \(s\) on \(Spf(k)\),
\texttt{O\_\{X,\ x\}\ ⨶\_k\ κ(s)} is a finite separable extension of
\(\kappa(s)\).}

\emph{(v) For every open ideal \(l\) of \(k\), each local component of
\texttt{A\ ⨶\_k\ (k/l)} is a finite étale algebra over the artinian ring
\(k/l\).}

\emph{(b) \(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}\kappa(k)\) is identified with the
category of étale schemes over \(S_{\kappa(k)}\) (cf.~1.6.C), and the
functor \(X \mapsto X_{\kappa}\) induces an equivalence of categories
\(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}k \xrightarrow{\sim} Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}\kappa(k)\)
(cf.~SGA 1, I 6.1).}

\emph{Proof.} (a) Let \(I\) denote the kernel of the multiplication
morphism \texttt{m\ :\ A\ ⨶\_k\ A\ →\ A}. Suppose \(X\) étale over
\(k\), i.e., \(A\) formally étale over \(k\). Then, by EGA 0\_\{IV\},
20.7.4, the Hausdorff completion of \(I/I^{2}\), for the quotient
topology of that of \(I\), is zero, i.e., one has \(I = I^{2}\). Now,
for every \(x \in X\), \(I\) is contained in the maximal ideal
\texttt{m\_\{∆(x)\}} of \texttt{A\ ⨶\_k\ A}, hence the localization
\texttt{I\_\{m\_\{∆(x)\}\}} is contained in the maximal ideal of
\texttt{O\_\{X×X,\ ∆(x)\}}, and so, by Nakayama's lemma 0.3, one has
\texttt{I\_\{m\_\{∆(x)\}\}\ =\ 0}, and hence
\texttt{∆\ :\ X\ →\ X\ ×\ X} is a local isomorphism.

Suppose now that \texttt{∆} is a local isomorphism and that \(k\) is a
field \(\kappa\), and let us show that each \(O_{X, x}\) is a
finite-dimensional étale \(\kappa\)-algebra. Replacing \(X\) by
\(Spf(O_{X, x})\), one may suppose that \(A = O_{X, x}\) is local. One
proceeds then as in the proof of EGA IV\_4, 17.4.1, (b) ⇒ (d'\,'). Let
\(K\) be a finite normal extension of \(\kappa\) containing the residue
field \(\kappa(x)\), and let \texttt{B\ =\ A\ ⨶\_κ\ K\ =\ A\ ⨶\_κ\ K}
(since \([K : \kappa] < \infty\), then \texttt{−⨶\_κ\ K} and
\texttt{−\ ⨶\_κ\ K} coincide) and
\texttt{X\_K\ =\ Spf(B)\ =\ X\ ⨶\_κ\ K}. Then
\texttt{∆\_K\ :\ X\_K\ →\ X\_K\ ⨶\_K\ X\_K} is again a local
isomorphism, so for every \(y \in X_{K}\), the multiplication
\texttt{B\_y\ ⨶\_K\ B\_y\ →\ B\_y} induces an isomorphism
\texttt{(B\_y\ ⨶\_K\ B\_y)\_\{m\_\{∆\_K(y)\}\}\ ⥲\ B\_y}. Now, since the
residue field of \(B_{y}\) is \(K\) (cf.~for example VI\_A, 1.1.1,
N.D.E. (11)), \texttt{C\ =\ B\_y\ ⨶\_K\ B\_y} is already a local ring
(indeed, \texttt{n\ =\ m\_y\ ⨶\_K\ B\_y\ +\ B\_y\ ⨶\_K\ m\_y} consists
of topologically nilpotent elements, hence is contained in the radical
of \(C\), and \texttt{C/n\ =\ K\ ⨶\_K\ K\ =\ K} is a field), hence one
obtains that the multiplication morphism
\texttt{B\_y\ ⨶\_K\ B\_y\ →\ B\_y} is an isomorphism. Taking a
pseudobasis of \(B_{y}\) over \(K\) containing the unit element
\texttt{1}, one deduces that \(B_{y} = K\). Since moreover \(B\) is
finite over \(A\), \texttt{X\_K} is a finite set, hence
\texttt{B\ =\ A\ ⨶\_κ\ K} is the product of a finite number of copies of
\(K\), and this entails that \(A\) is a finite étale \(\kappa\)-algebra.

One thus obtains that, if \(\kappa\) is a field, every profinite
\(\kappa\)-algebra \(A\) étale over \(\kappa\) is the product of finite
separable extensions \(K_{i}\) of \(\kappa\), endowed with the product
topology, hence the formal variety \(Spf(A)\) is the direct sum of the
\(Spf(K_{i}) = \operatorname{Spec}(K_{i})\), and one deduces that
\(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}\kappa\) is identified with the category of étale
\(\kappa\)-schemes.

What precedes shows the implication (ii) ⇒ (iv) (since
\texttt{O\_\{X,\ x\}\ ⨶\_k\ κ(s)} is formally étale over \(\kappa(s)\)),
and entails point (b) of 1.6.E. Indeed, let \(k\) be again an arbitrary
pseudocompact ring. By what precedes, \(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}\kappa(k)\)
is identified with the category of étale schemes over \(S_{\kappa(k)}\).
Let us show that \(X \mapsto X_{\kappa}\) induces an equivalence
\(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}k \xrightarrow{\sim} Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}\kappa(k)\).
Taking 1.6.D into account, it suffices to show that for every
\(s \in Spf(k)\) and every finite separable extension \(K\) of
\(\kappa(s)\), there exists an étale \(k_{s}\)-algebra \(A\) such that
\texttt{A\ ⨶\_k\ κ(s)\ ≃\ K}. Let \(\xi\) be a primitive element of the
extension \(K/\kappa(s)\), \(n\) its degree, and \(F \in k_{s}[T]\) a
monic polynomial of degree \(n\) whose image \(\bar{F}\) in
\(\kappa(s)[T]\) is the minimal polynomial of \(\xi\). Since
\(\bar{F}'\) is invertible in \(\kappa(s)[T]/(\bar{F})\), it follows
from Nakayama's lemma that \(F'\) is invertible in \(k_{s}[T]/(F)\),
hence \(F\) is a separable polynomial and hence, by 1.6.A (ii),
\(A = k_{s}[T]/(F)\) is an étale \(k_{s}\)-algebra such that
\texttt{A\ ⨶\_k\ κ(s)\ ≃\ K}. One thus obtains that every local
profinite étale \(k_{s}\)-algebra is free of finite rank over \(k_{s}\)
(hence a fortiori topologically free over \(k\)), and hence every
profinite étale \(k\)-algebra is topologically free over \(k\).

On the other hand, condition (v) implies condition (d) of 1.6.B, hence
implies (i). One has thus obtained that (i), (iii) and (v) are
equivalent, and imply (ii), which implies (iv). Finally, let \(A\) be a
profinite \(k\)-algebra satisfying (iv); let us show that \(A\) is
formally étale over \(k\). For this, one may suppose \(A\) and \(k\)
local; denote by \(\kappa\) the residue field of \(k\). By hypothesis,
\texttt{K\ =\ A\ ⨶\_k\ κ} is a finite separable extension of \(\kappa\),
say of degree \(n\). By what we have seen above (and taking Lemma 1.6.D
into account), there exists then a \(k\)-algebra \(B\) free of rank
\(n\), formally étale over \(k\), and a continuous morphism
\(\phi : B \to A\) such that \texttt{φ\ ⨶\_k\ κ} is an isomorphism.
Since \(A\) is topologically flat over \(k\), this entails that
\texttt{Coker(φ)\ ⨶\_k\ κ\ =\ 0} and also
\texttt{Ker(φ)\ ⨶\_k\ κ\ =\ 0}; by Nakayama's lemma 0.3, one therefore
has \(Coker(\phi) = 0 = Ker(\phi)\), hence \(\phi\) is an isomorphism
(cf.~the proof of 0.2.B). This completes the proof of 1.6.E.

Let \(X\) be a formal variety over \(k\). For every \(x \in X\), of
projection \(s\) on \(Spf(k)\), the residue field \(\kappa(x)\) is a
finite extension of \(\kappa(s)\) and one denotes by \(\kappa_{e}(x)\)
the separable closure of \(\kappa(s)\) in \(\kappa(x)\).

\textbf{Proposition 1.6.F.} \emph{(i) The inclusion of
\(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}k\) in \(Vaf_{/}k\) has a left adjoint
\(X \mapsto X_{e}\): the variety \(X_{e}\) has the same points as \(X\),
and for every \(x \in X\), of projection \(s\) on \(Spf(k)\), let
\(\xi\) be a primitive element of \(\kappa_{e}(x)\), \(n\) its degree,
\(u\) an arbitrary lifting of \(\xi\) in \(O_{X, x}\), and
\(F \in k[T]\) monic of degree \(n\) annihilating \(u\); one sets
\(O_{X_{e}, x} = k[T]/(F)\). Then for every
\(Y \in Ob Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}k\), the canonical maps below are
bijective:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{Vaf\_/k\}(X, Y) ────⥲────→ Hom\_\{Vaf\_/κ(k)\}(X\_κ, Y\_κ)}
\NormalTok{                                          ↑}
\NormalTok{                                          ≀}
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{Vaf\_/k\}(X\_e, Y) ────⥲───→ Hom\_\{Vaf\_/κ(k)\}((X\_e)\_κ, Y\_κ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the vertical arrow being induced by the inclusions
\(\kappa_{e}(x) \hookrightarrow \kappa(x)\) for every \(x \in X\). This
defines, in particular, a morphism \(p : X \to X_{e}\), and every
morphism of \(k\)-formal varieties \(\phi : X \to Y\), with \(Y\) étale
over \(k\), factors uniquely through \(p\).}

\emph{(ii) The functor \(X \mapsto X_{e}\) commutes with finite
products.}

Indeed, (i) follows from 1.6.E (b) and 1.6.D. Let us prove (ii). Taking
the equivalence of categories 1.6.E (b) into account, one may suppose
that \(k\) is a field. In this case, one sees easily that if \(X\) is a
semi-local \(k\)-formal variety, i.e., one whose affine algebra \(A\) is
semi-local, then the affine algebra of \(X_{e}\) is the largest
subalgebra of \(A\) which is étale over \(k\); let us denote it by
\(A_{e}\). One thus reduces to seeing that if \texttt{K,\ L} are two
finite-degree extensions of \(k\), then the inclusion
\texttt{K\_e\ ⨶\ L\_e\ ⊂\ (K\ ⨶\ L)\_e} is an equality. Let \(p\) be the
characteristic exponent of \(k\) (i.e., \(p = 1\) if \(char(k) = 0\) and
\(p = char(k)\) otherwise), then for every \texttt{x\ ∈\ K\ ⨶\ L}, there
exists \(n \in \mathbb{N}*\) such that
\texttt{x\^{}\{p\^{}n\}\ ∈\ K\_e\ ⨶\ L\_e}, hence every subalgebra \(B\)
of \texttt{K\ ⨶\ L} is radicial over \texttt{K\_e\ ⨶\ L\_e}, and it
follows that \texttt{K\_e\ ⨶\ L\_e\ =\ (K\ ⨶\ L)\_e}.

Note, keeping the preceding notations, that \(O_{X_{e}, x}\) is not
necessarily a subalgebra of \(O_{X, x}\), but this is the case when
\(X\) is topologically flat over \(k\), by the following proposition.

\paragraph{1.6.1.}\label{section-163}

Let \(Y\) be an étale \(k\)-formal variety and \(f : X \to Y\) a
morphism of \(Vaf_{/}k\). Then one has the cartesian square below, where
\(\Gamma_{f}\) is the graph morphism \(X \to X \times Y\), with
components \(id_{X}\) and \(f\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{            Γ\_f}
\NormalTok{       X ───────→ X × Y}
                       
\NormalTok{       f          f ⊠ id\_Y}
                       
\NormalTok{            ∆\_Y       }
\NormalTok{       Y ───────→ Y × Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows that \(\Gamma_{f}\) is a local isomorphism, hence that
\(f = pr_{Y} \circ \Gamma_{f}\) is topologically flat if \(pr_{Y}\) is,
for example if \(X\) is topologically flat over \(k\).

Conversely, since \(Y \to k\) is topologically flat, \(X \to k\) will be
as well if \(f\) is so (cf.~1.3.3). Taking in particular \(f\) to be the
canonical morphism \(p : X \to X_{e}\) of 1.6, one obtains:

\textbf{Proposition 1.6.1.} \emph{Let \(X\) be a formal variety over
\(k\). The morphism \(X \to X_{e}\) is topologically flat if and only if
\(X\) is topologically flat over \(k\).}

\textbf{Remark 1.6.2.}\footnote{We have inserted this remark here, which
  in the original appeared in 2.5.2.} When \(k\) is a perfect field, the
functor \(X \mapsto X_{e}\) is also right adjoint to the inclusion
\(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}k \hookrightarrow Vaf_{/}k\). Indeed, in this case
one has \(O_{X_{e}, x} = \kappa(x)\) for every \(x \in X\), and the
canonical projections \(O_{X, x} \to \kappa(x)\) define a morphism
\(s : X_{e} \to X\), which is a section of \(p : X \to X_{e}\). For
every morphism \(f : X \to Y\) the diagrams below are commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              f}
\NormalTok{   O\_\{Y, f(x)\} ─→ O\_\{X, x\}       X ──────→ Y}
\NormalTok{                                 ↑          ↑}
\NormalTok{                                 s\_X        s\_Y}
\NormalTok{                                       f\_e}
\NormalTok{   κ(f(x)) ────→ κ(x)            X\_e ────→ Y\_e}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence \(s\) is functorial in \(X\), and it follows that
\(X \mapsto X_{e}\) is right adjoint to the inclusion
\(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}k \hookrightarrow Vaf_{/}k\). Hence, being a right
adjoint, \(X \mapsto X_{e}\) commutes with inverse limits when they
exist in \(Vaf^{\acute{e}}t_{/}k\),\footnote{This is the case for finite
  inverse limits.} hence in particular with finite products. (This can
also be verified directly: for every \(k\)-formal variety \(X\), of
affine algebra \(A\), \(X_{e}\) has as affine algebra the quotient of
\(A\) by its radical \(r(A)\), and since \(k\) is perfect, the quotient
of \texttt{O\_\{X,\ x\}\ ⨶\ O\_\{Y,\ y\}} by its radical is the algebra
\texttt{κ(x)\ ⨶\_k\ κ(y)}, since the latter is semi-simple.)

\subsection{2. Generalities on formal
groups}\label{generalities-on-formal-groups}

\subsubsection{2.1.}\label{section-164}

Let \(k\) be a pseudocompact ring and \(G\) a \(k\)-formal group, that
is, a group of the category \(Vaf_{/}k\) of formal varieties over \(k\).
Let \(A\) be the affine algebra of \(G\). The composition law of \(G\)
evidently defines a diagonal morphism, that is, a homomorphism of
profinite \(k\)-algebras \texttt{∆\_A\ :\ A\ →\ A\ ⨶\_k\ A}; this
homomorphism satisfies the following conditions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  the diagram
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       ∆\_A}
\NormalTok{            A ───────────────→ A ⨶\_k A}

\NormalTok{         ∆\_A                   ∆\_A ⨶ id\_A}
                                
\NormalTok{                   id\_A ⨶ ∆\_A}
\NormalTok{            A ⨶\_k A ────────→ A ⨶\_k A ⨶\_k A}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is commutative.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  there exists an augmentation (necessarily unique), that is, a
  homomorphism of profinite \(k\)-algebras \(\epsilon_{A} : A \to k\)
  such that the composite maps
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              ∆\_A          ε\_A ⨶ id\_A}
\NormalTok{         A ───────→ A ⨶\_k A ───────────→ k ⨶\_k A ≃ A}

\NormalTok{   and    A ───────→ A ⨶\_k A ───────────→ A ⨶\_k k ≃ A}
\NormalTok{              ∆\_A          id\_A ⨶ ε\_A}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are the identity maps of \(A\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  there exists an antipodism (necessarily unique), that is, a
  homomorphism of profinite \(k\)-algebras \(c_{A} : A \to A\) such that
  the composite map
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{         ∆\_A         c\_A ⨶ id\_A        m\_A}
\NormalTok{   A ───────→ A ⨶\_k A ─────────────→ A ⨶\_k A ──────→ A}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is equal to \(\eta_{A} \circ \epsilon_{A}\), where \(m_{A}\) denotes the
linear map sending \texttt{a\ ⨶\ b} to \texttt{ab} and \(\eta_{A}\) the
map \(\lambda \mapsto \lambda \cdot 1_{A}\) from \(k\) into \(A\).

Conversely, the data of \texttt{(∆\_A,\ ε\_A,\ c\_A)} satisfying
(i)--(iii) endows \(G\) with a structure of \(k\)-formal
group.\footnote{One will also say that \(A\) is a \emph{cogroup} in the
  category of profinite \(k\)-algebras. On the other hand, we have
  detailed what follows; in particular, we have made explicit what a
  morphism of formal groups \(K \to G\) is, cf.~Proposition 2.3.1.}
Explicitly, for every profinite \(k\)-algebra \(B\), the set
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{c}(A, B)\) of continuous morphisms of
\(k\)-modules \(\phi : A \to B\) is endowed with a group structure,
functorial in \(B\), defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   φ · φ\textquotesingle{} = m\_B ∘ (φ ⨶ φ\textquotesingle{}) ∘ ∆\_A,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the neutral element being \(\eta_{B} \circ \epsilon_{A}\) (where
\(m_{B}\) is the multiplication of \(B\) and \(\eta_{B}\) the map
\(\lambda \mapsto \lambda \cdot 1_{B}\) from \(k\) into \(B\)), and
\(\phi \circ c_{A}\) being the inverse of \(\phi\); and the set
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{Alp/k}(A, B)\) of continuous morphisms of
\(k\)-algebras \(A \to B\) is a subgroup of it (since the algebra \(B\)
is commutative).

\textbf{Definition 2.1.} \emph{A morphism of \(k\)-formal groups
\(\theta : K \to G\) is, by definition, a morphism of \(k\)-formal
varieties which respects the group structures.} If \(B\) (resp. \(A\))
is the affine algebra of \(K\) (resp. \(G\)) and if \(f : A \to B\) is
the morphism corresponding to \(\theta\), this amounts to saying that
\(f\) is compatible with the comultiplications, i.e.,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   (f ⨶ f) ∘ ∆\_A = ∆\_B ∘ f}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(the conditions \(\epsilon_{B} \circ f = \epsilon_{A}\) and
\(c_{B} \circ f = f \circ c_{A}\) being then automatically satisfied).
One will denote by \(Grf_{/}k\) the category of \(k\)-formal groups.

\textbf{Notations.} \emph{In what follows, we shall call augmentation
ideal of \(A\) the ideal \(I_{A} = Ker(\epsilon_{A})\), and we shall
denote by \(\omega_{G/k}\) the pseudocompact \(k\)-module
\(I_{A}/I^{2}_{A}\), that is, the quotient of \texttt{I\_A} by the
closed ideal generated by the products \texttt{xy}, for
\(x, y \in I_{A}\).}

\subsubsection{2.2.}\label{section-165}

Let \(H\) be a group of the category of coalgebras over \(O_{k}\), i.e.,
for every object \(C\) of \(Alf_{/}k\), \(H(C)\) is endowed with a
structure of \(C\)-coalgebra in groups (cf.~VII\_A 3.2; following Manin,
we shall say \emph{bialgebra}\footnote{One also says \emph{bigèbre}
  (cf.~{[}BAlg{]}, III § 11.4); recall (cf.~VII\_A, 3.1, N.D.E. (26))
  that all the ``bialgebras'' considered here are assumed cocommutative
  and equipped with an antipode, i.e., they are in fact cocommutative
  Hopf algebras.} instead of \emph{coalgebra in groups}); moreover, if
\(\phi : C \to D\) is a morphism of \(Alf_{/}k\), the map
\texttt{D\ ⨶\_C\ H(C)\ →\ H(D)} is a homomorphism of \(D\)-bialgebras.

\textbf{Definition 2.2.} \emph{We shall summarize the above properties
by saying that \(H\) is a} bialgebra over \(O_{k}\).

It is clear that the functor \(H \mapsto Spf*(H)\) of 1.3.5 commutes
with finite products. It therefore transforms a bialgebra over \(O_{k}\)
into a \(k\)-group functor, that is, a (covariant) functor from
\(Alf_{/}k\) to the category of groups.

And indeed, for every \(k\)-algebra \(C\) of finite length, the elements
of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Spf*(H)(C) = Spf*(H(C)) = \{x ∈ H(C) | ε(x) = 1 and ∆(x) = x ⊗ x\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

form a group for the multiplication of the algebra \(H(C)\) (cf.~VII\_A
3.2.2). Note moreover that the condition \texttt{∆(x)\ =\ x\ ⊗\ x}
entails the equality \(\epsilon(x) = \epsilon(x)^{2}\), hence also
\(\epsilon(x) = 1\) if \(C\) is local and \(x \neq 0\).\footnote{Since
  \texttt{∆(x)\ =\ x\ ⊗\ x} one has \(x = \epsilon(x)x\), hence
  \(\epsilon(x) = 0\) can occur only if \(x = 0\).}

\paragraph{2.2.1.}\label{section-166}

A bialgebra \(H\) over \(O_{k}\) is said to be \emph{flat} if the
underlying module is flat (cf.~1.2.1).\footnote{We have detailed the
  original in what follows.} If \(H\) is flat then, by 1.3.5,
\(A = \Gamma*(H)\) is a topologically flat profinite \(k\)-algebra, and
\(Spf*(H)\) is isomorphic, as a functor from
\((Alf_{/}k)^{\circ} = Vaf_{/}k\) to \texttt{(Ens)}, to the functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Spf(A) : C ↦ Hom\_\{Vaf\_/k\}(Spf(C), Spf(A)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The group structure of \(Spf*(H)\) thus endows
\(\mathcal{G}(H) = Spf(A)\) with a structure of formal group, which is
described explicitly as follows.

For every object \(C\) of \(Alf_{/}k\), since the \(C\)-module
underlying \(H(C)\) is projective, one deduces from Lemma 1.2.3.A, by
induction on \(n\), natural isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   H(C)*\^{}⨶(n+1) ≃ Hom\_C(H(C), (H(C)*)\^{}⨶ n)}
\NormalTok{               ≃ Hom\_C(H(C), (H(C)\^{}⨶ n)*) ≃ (H(C)\^{}⨶(n+1))*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One deduces from this (for \(n = 1, 2\)) that the \(C\)-algebra
structure of \(H(C)\) endows \(H(C)*\) with a diagonal map satisfying
conditions 2.1 (i)--(iii), all of this functorially in \(C\).

Consequently, \(A = \Gamma*(H) = \lim H(k/l)*\) is endowed with a
structure of cogroup in \(Alp/k\), which defines on \(\mathcal{G}(H)\)
the announced formal group structure.

Conversely, let \(G\) be a topologically flat \(k\)-formal group, of
affine algebra \(A\), and denote by \(H(G)\) the \(O_{k}\)-coalgebra
\(V_{kf}(A)\) (cf.~1.2.3). The diagonal morphism
\texttt{∆\_A\ :\ A\ →\ A\ ⨶\_k\ A} then induces, for every \(k\)-algebra
\(C\) of finite length, a \(C\)-linear map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   V\_kf(A)(C) ⊗\_C V\_kf(A)(C) ─→ V\_kf(A)(C)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which makes the coalgebra \(V_{kf}(A)(C)\) into a \(C\)-bialgebra. One
says that \(H(G)\) is the \emph{covariant bialgebra} of the formal group
\(G\).\footnote{We have added the adjective ``covariant'' to make it
  visible that the functor \(G \mapsto H(G)\) is covariant; this
  terminology is used in {[}Di73{]}, I § 2.14.} Therefore, by
Proposition 1.3.5.D:

\textbf{Proposition 2.2.1.} \emph{(i) The functors \(G \mapsto H(G)\)
and \(H \mapsto \mathcal{G}(H)\) define an equivalence between the
category of topologically flat \(k\)-formal groups and that of flat
\(O_{k}\)-bialgebras.}\footnote{Recall that in this Exposé,
  ``bialgebra'' means ``cocommutative Hopf algebra''.}

\emph{(ii) This equivalence ``commutes with base change'': if
\(k \to K\) is a morphism of pseudocompact rings, then
\texttt{H(G\ ⨶\_k\ K)\ =\ H(G)\ ⨶\_k\ K} and
\texttt{𝒢(H\ ⨶\_k\ K)\ =\ 𝒢(H)\ ⨶\_k\ K}.}

When \(k\) is an artinian ring and \(G\) a topologically flat
\(k\)-formal group, the functor \(H(G)\) is evidently determined by its
value \(H(G) = H(G)(k)\) at \(k\). One will also say that \(H(G)\) is
the (covariant) \emph{bialgebra} of \(G\).\footnote{We have introduced
  here the notation \(H^{cocom}_{flat/k}\), which will be useful below.}
Consequently, denoting by \(H_{k}\) the category of \(k\)-Hopf algebras
and \(H^{cocom}_{flat/k}\) the full subcategory formed by \(k\)-Hopf
algebras flat over \(k\) and cocommutative, one obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 2.2.1.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an artinian ring.}

\emph{(i) The functors \(G \mapsto H(G)\) and
\(H \mapsto \mathcal{G}(H) = Spf* H(G)\) define an equivalence between
the category of topologically flat \(k\)-formal groups and
\(H^{cocom}_{flat/k}\).}

\emph{(ii) This equivalence ``commutes with base change'': if
\(k \to K\) is a morphism of artinian rings, then
\texttt{H(G\ ⨶\_k\ K)\ =\ H(G)\ ⨶\_k\ K} and
\texttt{𝒢(H\ ⨶\_k\ K)\ =\ 𝒢(H)\ ⨶\_k\ K}.}

On the other hand, let us denote \(H^{com}_{flat/k}\) the full
subcategory of \(H_{k}\) formed by the \(k\)-Hopf algebras flat over
\(k\) and commutative, and recall that the functor \(K \mapsto O(K)\) is
an anti-equivalence of the category of affine \(k\)-group schemes onto
\(H^{com}_{flat/k}\).

\paragraph{2.2.2.}\label{section-167}

Let us suppose for simplicity that \(k\) is artinian and let \(G\) be a
topologically flat \(k\)-formal group.\footnote{We have detailed the
  original in what follows, in order to introduce the notations
  \texttt{D\textquotesingle{}(G)} and \(D(K)\), cf.~{[}Ca62{]}, § 14.}
Then \(G\) is commutative if and only if its affine algebra
\(\mathcal{A}(G)\) has a cocommutative comultiplication, which is
equivalent to saying that the bialgebra \(H(G)\) has a commutative
multiplication. In this case, \(H(G)\) is a commutative and
cocommutative Hopf algebra, flat over \(k\); if one sets
\(D'(G) = \operatorname{Spec} H(G)\), then
\texttt{D\textquotesingle{}(G)} is a commutative \(k\)-group scheme,
affine and flat over \(k\). Conversely, if \(T\) is such a \(k\)-group
scheme, its affine algebra \(O(T)\) is a commutative group in the
category of cocommutative \(k\)-coalgebras flat over \(k\) and hence, by
1.3.5.C, one obtains a topologically flat \(k\)-formal group \(D(T)\) by
setting:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   D(T) = Spf* O(T) = Spf(𝒜),    where 𝒜 = O(T)*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

As, by 1.3.5.D, one has canonical isomorphisms \(G = Spf* H(G)\) and
\(H(D(T)) = O(T)\), one obtains canonical isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   D(D\textquotesingle{}(G)) = Spf* O(D\textquotesingle{}(G)) = Spf* H(G) = G,}
\NormalTok{   D\textquotesingle{}(D(T)) = Spec H(D(T)) = Spec O(T) = T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, denoting by \(k\)-Gr. the category of \(k\)-group schemes, one
has, by Corollary 2.2.1, functorial isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{Grf/k\}(G, D(T)) ≃ Hom\_\{H\_k\}(H(G), O(T)) ≃ Hom\_\{k{-}Gr.\}(T, D\textquotesingle{}(G)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One thus obtains:

\textbf{Proposition (Cartier duality) 2.2.2.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an
artinian ring.}

\emph{(i) The functors \(G \mapsto D'(G) = \operatorname{Spec} H(G)\)
and \(T \mapsto D(T) = Spf* O(T)\) induce an anti-equivalence between
the category \(\mathcal{FC}_{k}\) of commutative topologically flat
\(k\)-formal groups and the category \(\mathcal{AC}_{k}\) of commutative
\(k\)-group schemes, affine and flat, i.e., \(G\) and
\texttt{D\textquotesingle{}(G)} (resp. \(T\) and \(D(T)\)) are related
by the equalities:\footnote{If one denotes by \(\mathcal{FC}^{f}_{k}\)
  (resp. \(\mathcal{AC}^{f}_{k}\)) the full subcategory of
  \(\mathcal{FC}_{k}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{AC}_{k}\)) formed by the
  objects \(G\) (resp. \(T\)) such that \(H(G)\) (resp. \(O(T)\)) is a
  finite \(k\)-module (and hence finite locally free), then
  \(\mathcal{FC}^{f}_{k}\) and \(\mathcal{AC}^{f}_{k}\) both have the
  same objects as the category \(\mathcal{C}\) of commutative and
  cocommutative Hopf \(k\)-algebras, finite and flat over \(k\), the
  correspondence \(G \mapsto H(G)\) (resp. \(T \mapsto O(T)\)) being
  covariant (resp. contravariant), and one thus recovers the ``Cartier
  duality'' of the category \(\mathcal{AC}_{k}\), already seen in
  VII\_A, 3.3.1.}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   H(G) = O(D\textquotesingle{}(G))    and    O(T) = H(D(T)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) This anti-equivalence ``commutes with base change'': if
\(k \to K\) is a morphism of artinian rings, then
\texttt{D\textquotesingle{}(G\ ⨶\_k\ K)\ =\ D\textquotesingle{}(G)\ ⨶\_k\ K}
and \texttt{D(T\ ⨶\_k\ K)\ =\ D(T)\ ⨶\_k\ K}.}

\emph{(iii) In particular, if \(k\) is a field, one obtains an
anti-equivalence between the category of commutative \(k\)-formal groups
and that of commutative affine \(k\)-group schemes, which commutes with
extension of the base field.}

\subsubsection{2.3.}\label{section-168}

Let us now consider an arbitrary \(k\)-formal group\footnote{That is,
  not necessarily topologically flat over \(k\).} \(G\), of affine
algebra \(A\). Let us still denote by \(H(G)\) the \(O_{k}\)-module
\(V_{kf}(A)\) dual to \(A\) and let \(\varphi_{G}\) denote the
functorial homomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   ϕ\_G : H(G) ⨶\_k H(G) ─→ H(G × G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induced by the natural map (0.3.6), for every object \(C\) of
\(Alf_{/}k\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   (A ⨶\_k C)† ⊗\_C (A ⨶\_k C)† ─→ ((A ⨶\_k C) ⨶\_C (A ⨶\_k C))†.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(m : G \times G \to G\) is the multiplication of \(G\), the
composite map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  ϕ\_G              H(m)}
\NormalTok{   H(G) ⨶\_k H(G) ────→ H(G × G) ────────→ H(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

makes \(H(G)\) into an algebra over \(O_{k}\); for every
\(C \in Alf_{/}k\), the unit element of
\texttt{H(G)(C)\ =\ (A\ ⨶\_k\ C)†} is the augmentation of
\texttt{A\ ⨶\_k\ C} (cf.~2.1).\footnote{We have modified the order of
  the sentences in what follows.} If \(G\) is not topologically flat
over \(k\), \(\varphi_{G}\) is not necessarily an isomorphism, and hence
the morphism \(\delta_{G} : H(G) \to H(G \times G)\) induced by the
diagonal morphism ``\(x \mapsto (x, x)\)'' from \(G\) into
\(G \times G\) does not necessarily factor through
\texttt{H(G)\ ⨶\_k\ H(G)}, i.e., \(H(G)\) is not necessarily an
\(O_{k}\)-bialgebra.

For this reason we shall simply say, in the general case, that \(H(G)\)
is the ``\emph{covariant algebra}'' of the formal group \(G\).

Of course, when \(G\) is topologically flat over \(k\), \(\varphi_{G}\)
is an isomorphism, and one recovers the structure of \(O_{k}\)-bialgebra
on \(H(G)\) defined in 2.2.1.

\paragraph{2.3.1. Proposition.}\label{proposition.-5}

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.1.} \emph{Let \(K\) and \(G\) be two
\(k\)-formal groups, of affine algebras \(B\) and \(A\). Assume \(K\)
topologically flat over \(k\). Then there exists a canonical bijection
from \(\operatorname{Hom}_{Grf/k}(K, G)\) onto the set of homomorphisms
of unital \(O_{k}\)-algebras \(h : H(K) \to H(G)\) such that the
diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          h ⨶ h}
\NormalTok{        H(K) ⨶\_k H(K) ──────────→ H(G) ⨶\_k H(G)}
\NormalTok{              ↑                              \textbackslash{}}
\NormalTok{                                              \textbackslash{} ϕ\_G}
\NormalTok{                                               \textbackslash{}}
\NormalTok{   (∗)   ∆\_\{H(K)\}                                H(G × G)}
\NormalTok{                                               /}
\NormalTok{                                              /}
\NormalTok{                                             / δ\_G}
\NormalTok{              h}
\NormalTok{        H(K) ────────────────────→ H(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is commutative.}

Since \(K\) is topologically flat, \(H(K)\) is endowed with a structure
of bialgebra (cf.~2.2) and \texttt{∆\_\{H(K)\}} is its diagonal
morphism; in other words, with the notations of 2.3, one has
\texttt{∆\_\{H(K)\}\ =\ ϕ\_K⁻¹\ ∘\ δ\_K}. When \(G\) is also
topologically flat over \(k\), our proposition follows from the
equivalence of categories established in 2.2.1.

In the general case, one may suppose \(k\) artinian and argue on the
algebras \texttt{H(K)\ =\ B†} and \texttt{H(G)\ =\ A†}. Let
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{c}(A, B)\) be the set of continuous \(k\)-linear
maps from \(A\) into \(B\) and \texttt{Hom\_k(B†,\ A†)} the set of
\(k\)-linear maps from \texttt{B†} into \texttt{A†}.

By 0.3.6.A, one knows that if \texttt{M,\ P} are pseudocompact
\(k\)-modules and \(P\) is projective, the canonical map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_c(M, P) ─→ Hom\_k(P†, M†),    f ↦ ᵗf}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(where \texttt{ᵗf} denotes the transpose of \(f\)) is bijective. (One
will apply this to \texttt{M\ =\ A\ ⨶\ A} and \(P = B\), or \(M = A\)
and \texttt{P\ =\ B\ ⨶\ B}.)

Let \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}_{c}(A, B)\). Consider the diagrams below,
where the squares (0) are commutative, and where the two unnamed
vertical arrows are \texttt{ᵗ(f\ ⨶\ f)}.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                m\_A          ∆\_A}
\NormalTok{   A ⨶ A ────────→ A ────────→ A ⨶ A}

\NormalTok{  f ⨶ f    (1)    f    (2)    f ⨶ f}

\NormalTok{                m\_B          ∆\_B}
\NormalTok{   B ⨶ B ────────→ B ────────→ B ⨶ B}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       ᵗm\_A=δ\_G                ᵗ∆\_A=ϕ\_G}
\NormalTok{   A† ⊗ A† ─→ (A ⨶ A)† ←────── A† ────── (A ⨶ A)† ←── A† ⊗ A†}
\NormalTok{       ↑                ↑                 ↑                 ↑}
                                                            
\NormalTok{   ᵗf⊗ᵗf  (0)             (1\textquotesingle{})    ᵗf    (2\textquotesingle{})               ᵗf⊗ᵗf}
                                                            
\NormalTok{   B† ⊗ B† ─→ (B ⨶ B)† ←────── B† ────── (B ⨶ B)† ←── B† ⊗ B†}
\NormalTok{                       ᵗm\_B=δ\_K                ᵗ∆\_B=ϕ\_K}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(f : A \to B\) corresponds to a morphism of formal groups
\(K \to G\), then squares (1) and (2) are commutative, and
\(\epsilon_{B} \circ f = \epsilon_{A}\); consequently, squares (1') and
(2') are commutative and \texttt{ᵗf} sends the unit of
\texttt{B†\ =\ H(K)} to that of \texttt{A†\ =\ H(G)}, i.e., \texttt{ᵗf}
is a morphism of unital \(k\)-algebras \(H(K) \to H(G)\) such that the
diagram \((\ast)\) of the proposition is commutative.

Conversely, if \texttt{ᵗf} satisfies these conditions, then
\(\epsilon_{B} \circ f = \epsilon_{A}\) and the squares (1') and (2')
are commutative. Since, for \texttt{M\ =\ A\ ⨶\ A} and \(P = B\) (resp.
\(M = A\) and \texttt{P\ =\ B\ ⨶\ B}), the map \(g \mapsto {}^{t}g\) is
injective, one deduces that squares (1) and (2) are commutative, hence
\(f\) is compatible with the multiplications and the diagonal morphisms
of \(A\) and \(B\). It remains to see that \(f(1_{A}) = 1_{B}\). But it
follows from what precedes that \(\epsilon_{B} f(1) = 1\),
\texttt{∆\_B\ f(1)\ =\ f(1)\ ⨶\ f(1)} and \(f(1) \cdot f(1) = f(1)\).
The first two conditions entail, by 2.1 (iii), that \(f(1)\) admits
\(c_{B} f(1)\) as inverse in \(B\); consequently
\(f(1) \cdot f(1) = f(1)\) entails \(f(1) = 1\). So \(f : A \to B\) is a
morphism of \(Alp/k\), compatible with the comultiplications of \(A\)
and \(B\).

\paragraph{2.3.2.}\label{section-169}

Let us suppose now, for simplicity, that the ring \(k\) is artinian.
When \(G\) is topologically flat over \(k\), the algebra
\(H(G) = H(G)(k)\) may be characterized by a universal property (due to
Cartier). Recall (cf.~1.2.1) that if \(U\) is a \(k\)-module, one
denotes by \(W(U)\) the functor which to every \(k\)-algebra \(C\) of
finite length associates the \(C\)-module
\(U \otimes_{k} C\).\footnote{We have added the preceding sentence, and
  in what follows we have denoted \(W(U)\times\) instead of \(U_{m}\).
  Recall on the other hand (cf.~1.2.1) that one calls ``\(k\)-functor''
  a covariant functor \(Alf_{/}k \to (Ens)\).} If \(U\) is a
\(k\)-algebra (associative, with unit element), so is
\(U \otimes_{k} C\); we shall denote by \(W(U)\times\) the \(k\)-group
functor which to every \(C \in Ob Alf_{/}k\) associates the
multiplicative group of the invertible elements of the algebra
\(U \otimes_{k} C\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   W(U)×(C) = (U ⊗\_k C)×.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, let us identify \(G\) with the \(k\)-group functor
\texttt{C\ ↦\ Hom\_\{Vaf\_/k\}(Spf(C),\ G)} and denote by
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{k-Gr.}(G, W(U)\times)\) the set of homomorphisms
of \(k\)-group functors from \(G\) into \(W(U)\times\). One has the

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.2.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an artinian ring. For
every formal group \(G\) topologically flat over \(k\) and for every
\(k\)-algebra \(U\), there is a canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_\{k{-}Gr.\}(G, W(U)×) ⥲ Hom\_\{k{-}Alg.\}(H(G), U).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us denote by \(A\) the affine algebra of \(G\); by hypothesis it is
a projective object of \(PC(k)\), and \texttt{H(G)\ =\ A†}. For every
object \(P\) of \(PC(k)\), let us denote by \texttt{U\ ⨶\_k\ P} the
projective limit of the \(k\)-modules \(U \otimes_{k} (P/N)\), where
\(N\) ranges over the open submodules of \(P\). One has linear maps

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   U ⊗\_k (P/N) ─→ Hom\_k((P/N)*, U)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

sending \(u \otimes x\) to the \(k\)-linear map \(f \mapsto f(x) u\),
and forming a filtered projective system. One obtains therefore, by
passage to the projective limit, a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       ψ\_P}
\NormalTok{(1)    U ⨶\_k P ─────────────→ Hom\_k(P†, U) .}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

When \(P = k\), \(\psi_{k}\) is evidently an isomorphism; moreover, the
two sides of (1), considered as functors in \(P\), commute with infinite
products (every product being a filtered projective limit of finite
products). One obtains therefore that (1) is an isomorphism when \(P\)
is a product of copies of \(k\), then when \(P\) is a projective object
of \(PC(k)\) (the two sides of (1) commuting with finite direct sums).

Let us now denote by \(\operatorname{Hom}_{F}(G, W(U))\) the set of
morphisms of \(k\)-functors from \(G\) into \(W(U)\). Since
\texttt{G\ =\ Spf(A)\ =\ lim\ Spf(A/l)}, where \(l\) ranges over the
open ideals of \(A\), one has canonical isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_F(G, W(U)) = lim Hom\_F(Spf(A/l), W(U)) = lim U ⊗\_k (A/l) = U ⨶\_k A.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By what precedes, one obtains therefore a canonical isomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                              ψ\_A}
\NormalTok{(2)   Hom\_F(G, W(U)) = U ⨶\_k A ──────────────→ Hom\_k(H(G), U).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For every \(k\)-algebra \(C\) of finite length, the multiplication makes
\(U \otimes_{k} C\) into a monoid with unit, and every morphism of
monoids with unit \(G(C) \to U \otimes_{k} C\) is necessarily a morphism
of groups \(G(C) \to (U \otimes_{k} C)\times\). Consequently, one
obtains that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{k-Gr.}(G, W(U)\times)\) is the part
of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{F}(G, W(U))\) formed by the morphisms of
\(k\)-functors into monoids with unit element.

It remains to see that these morphisms correspond to the \(k\)-linear
maps from \(H(G)\) into \(U\) which preserve multiplication and the unit
elements.\footnote{The original indicated: ``(this) follows from the
  functorial character of \(\psi_{A}\)''. We have detailed this in what
  follows.} To simplify the writing, \texttt{H(G)\ =\ A†} will be
denoted \(H\) and one will write \texttt{⨶} instead of \texttt{⨶\_k}.
Let \texttt{∆\_A,\ m\_A} and \(\epsilon_{A}\) (resp.
\texttt{∆\_H,\ m\_H} and \(\epsilon_{H}\)) denote the comultiplication,
multiplication and augmentation of \(A\) (resp. \(H\)). Let
\(\theta \in \operatorname{Hom}_{F}(G, W(U))\), denote by \(\gamma\) its
image in \texttt{U\ ⨶\ A} and \(\phi : H \to U\) the associated
\(k\)-linear map. Then \(\theta\) sends the unit section \(s \in G(k)\)
onto an element \(u\) of \(U\), and since \(s\) corresponds to the
augmentation \(\epsilon : A \to k\), which is the unit element
\texttt{1\_H} of \(H\), one sees that \(\theta(s) = 1_{U}\) if and only
if \(\phi(1_{H}) = 1_{U}\).

Moreover, the morphism \(\theta \circ m_{G} : G \times G \to W(U)\)
corresponds to the element \texttt{(id\_U\ ⨶\ ∆\_A)(γ)}, and this
corresponds, by duality, to the map
\(\phi \circ m_{H} : H \otimes H \to U\).

On the other hand, the morphism
\(\theta \circ pr_{1} : G \times G \to W(U)\) corresponds to the element
\texttt{γ\ ⨶\ 1\_A} of \texttt{U\ ⨶\ A\ ⨶\ A}, which corresponds by
duality to \(\phi \circ (id_{H} \otimes \epsilon) : H \otimes H \to U\).
Similarly, \(\theta \circ pr_{2}\) corresponds to the element
\texttt{τ(γ\ ⨶\ 1\_A)} of \texttt{U\ ⨶\ A\ ⨶\ A} (where
\texttt{τ(u\ ⨶\ a\ ⨶\ b)\ =\ u\ ⨶\ b\ ⨶\ a}), which corresponds by
duality to \(\phi \circ (\epsilon \otimes id_{H}) : H \otimes H \to U\).
Finally, the multiplication map \texttt{μ\ =\ m\_\{U\ ⨶\ A\ ⨶\ A\}}
below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   (U ⨶ A ⨶ A) × (U ⨶ A ⨶ A),  (u ⨶ a₁ ⨶ a₂, u\textquotesingle{} ⨶ a₃ ⨶ a₄) ↦ uu\textquotesingle{} ⨶ a₁a₃ ⨶ a₂a₄}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

can be seen as the composite of the endomorphism \(\sigma_{23}\) of
\texttt{(U\ ⊗\ U)\ ⨶\ A\^{}\{⨶\ 4\}} which ``exchanges the factors
\(a_{2}\) and \(a_{3}\)'', and the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                m\_U ⨶ m\_A ⨶ m\_A}
\NormalTok{   (U ⊗ U) ⨶ A\^{}\{⨶ 2\} ⨶ A\^{}\{⨶ 2\} ──────────────────→ U ⨶ A ⨶ A.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One deduces that the map
\(\mu \circ (\phi \circ pr_{1}, \phi \circ pr_{2}) : G \times G \to W(U)\)
corresponds to the composite map \(\beta\) below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                                  β}
\NormalTok{                H ⊗ H ─────────────────→ U}
\NormalTok{                  ↑                       ↑}
\NormalTok{   id\_H ∘ σ\_\{23\} ∘ id\_H                   m\_U}
                                          
\NormalTok{   H ⊗ H ⊗ H ⊗ H            U ⊗ U}
                                          
\NormalTok{   (id\_H ⊗ ε\_H) ⊗ (ε\_H ⊗ id\_H)   φ ⊗ φ}
                                          
\NormalTok{                H ⊗ H ────────────────────.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, \(\theta\) is compatible with the laws of \(G\) and of
\(W(U)\times\) if and only if \(\theta \circ m_{G}\) equals
\(\mu \circ (\phi \circ pr_{1}, \phi \circ pr_{2})\) which is
equivalent, by what precedes, to \(\phi \circ m_{H} = \beta\). Now it is
clear that \((\phi \circ m_{H})(x \otimes y) = \phi(xy)\), and one sees
easily that \(\beta(x \otimes y) = \phi(x) \phi(y)\).

\subsubsection{2.4.}\label{section-170}

Let us now return to an arbitrary pseudocompact ring \(k\) in order to
apply to formal groups the results of 1.4--1.5 on passage to the
quotient by a topologically flat equivalence relation.\footnote{We have
  detailed the original in what follows.}

Let \(u : H \to G\) be a monomorphism of \(k\)-formal groups,
\(\mu : G \times G \to G\) the ``multiplication'' morphism of \(G\), and
\(\lambda\) the composite morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  id\_G × u           μ}
\NormalTok{   λ :   G × H ────────────→ G × G ──────→ G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(u\) is a monomorphism, the couple

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              pr\_1}
\NormalTok{              ────→}
\NormalTok{   G × H              G}
\NormalTok{              ────→}
\NormalTok{               λ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an equivalence couple in \(Vaf_{/}k\) (cf.~V, 2.b)). Recall
(cf.~1.2.C) that the cokernel \(G/H\) of this couple is defined as
follows.

Let \(O(G)\) and \(O(H)\) be the affine algebras of \(G\) and \(H\),
\texttt{∆\ :\ O(G)\ →\ O(G)\ ⨶\_k\ O(G)} the diagonal morphism of
\(O(G)\), and \(I\) the kernel of the morphism
\(u^{\natural} : O(G) \to O(H)\). (One knows, by Proposition 1.3, that
\(u^{\natural}\) induces an isomorphism
\(O(G)/I \xrightarrow{\sim} O(H)\).) Then the affine algebra \(O(G/H)\)
of \(G/H\) is the kernel of the couple of morphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                    τ\_1}
\NormalTok{                    ───→}
\NormalTok{        O(G)                O(G) ⨶\_k O(H),}
\NormalTok{                    ───→}
\NormalTok{              (id ⨶ u\^{}♮)∆}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \texttt{τ\_1(x)\ =\ x\ ⨶\ 1}, i.e.,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   O(G/H) = \{x ∈ O(G) | ∆(x) − x ⨶ 1 ∈ O(G) ⨶ I\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If, moreover, \(H\) is topologically flat over \(k\), then \(pr_{1}\) is
topologically flat and one deduces from Theorem 1.4 the following
theorem.

\textbf{Theorem 2.4.} \emph{Let \(u : H \to G\) be a monomorphism of
\(k\)-formal groups. Assume \(H\) topologically flat over \(k\). Then
the projection \(p : G \to G/H\) is surjective and topologically flat,
one has an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)                G × H ⥲ G ×\_\{G/H\} G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and \(G/H\) represents the quotient-sheaf for the flat topology.}

\emph{Consequently, \(G/H\) is endowed with a canonical structure of
object with group of operators \(G\), such that \(p : G \to G/H\) is a
morphism of objects with operators. If moreover \(u\) identifies \(H\)
with an invariant subgroup of \(G\), then \(G/H\) is endowed with a
canonical structure of \(k\)-formal group, such that \(p : G \to G/H\)
is a morphism of \(k\)-formal groups, and \(H\) is the kernel of \(p\).}

Indeed, the first assertion follows from 1.4; the other two from IV,
Corollaries 5.2.2 and 5.2.4.

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.}\footnote{We have made this corollary explicit,
  since it is used, for example, in 5.2.1/5.2.3.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a
\(k\)-formal group, \(H\) a formal subgroup of \(G\), \(A\) (resp.
\(A/J\), \(B\)) the affine algebra of \(G\) (resp. \(H\), \(G/H\)),
\texttt{I\_A} the augmentation ideal of \(A\), and
\(I_{B} = B \cap I_{A}\). Assume \(H\) topologically flat over \(k\).
Then \(J\) equals \texttt{AI\_B}, the closed ideal generated by
\texttt{I\_B}.}

Indeed, the projection \(B \to B/I_{B}\) corresponds to the ``unit
section'' \(e : Spf(k) \to G/H\) of \(G/H\). By \((\ast)\), \(H\) is
identified with the fiber product \(Spf(k) \times_{G/H} G\), and hence
its affine algebra \(A/J\) is identified with
\texttt{(B/I\_B)\ ⨶\_B\ A\ ≃\ A/AI\_B}.

\paragraph{2.4.A.}\label{a.}

Let \texttt{G,\ Q} be topologically flat \(k\)-formal groups; assume
that there exist homomorphisms \(\sigma : Q \to G\) and
\(\pi : G \to Q\) such that \(\pi \circ \sigma = id_{Q}\). In
particular, \(\sigma\) is a monomorphism, so \(Q\) is a formal subgroup
of \(G\) (cf.~Remark 1.3). Let \(N = Ker(\pi)\) and \(\sigma'\) the
inclusion \(N \hookrightarrow G\). Then \(G\) is the semi-direct product
of \(N\) by \(Q\) (cf.~I, 2.3.8), i.e., for every \(B \in Ob Alf_{/}k\),
identifying \(N(B)\) and \(Q(B)\) with their images in \(G(B)\) via
\(\sigma'\) and \(\sigma\), \(N(B)\) is an invariant subgroup of
\(G(B)\) and the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    μ : N(B) × Q(B) ─→ G(B),    (x, q) ↦ xq}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective. Then the morphism of \(k\)-formal varieties

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)    θ : G(B) ─→ N(B),    g ↦ g · σπ(g⁻¹)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a retraction of \(\sigma'\), the inverse of \(\mu\) is the map

\[
(3)    g \mapsto (\theta(g), \pi(g))
\]

and \(\theta \circ \sigma' : N \to G/Q\) is an isomorphism of
\(k\)-formal varieties. In particular, \(N\) is topologically flat over
\(k\), by 1.4 (ii). Denote by \(\alpha\) (resp. \(\beta\)) the map from
\(Q \times N\) (resp. \(G \times N = N \times Q \times N\)) to \(N\)
defined setwise by \(\alpha(q, y) = qyq^{-1}\) (resp.
\(\beta(x, q, y) = x \alpha(q, y)\)). Then one has the following
commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              id × θ          θ × id}
\NormalTok{   G × G ───────────→ G × N ──────────→ N × N}
                                       
\NormalTok{   m\_G                  β                m\_N}
                                       
\NormalTok{              θ}
\NormalTok{   G ────────────────→ N.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This may be expressed as follows in terms of the affine algebras \(A\),
\(A_{0}\) and \(A'\) of \(G\), \(Q\) and \(N\) (cf.~5.1.3 below). Let
\(\rho' : A \to A'\), \(\rho : A \to A_{0}\) and \(\tau : A_{0} \to A\)
be the homomorphisms of \(k\)-bialgebras corresponding to \(\sigma'\),
\(\sigma\) and \(\pi\), and let \(I = Ker(\rho)\). Then, by the
preceding Corollary, \(A'\) is identified with \(A/A\tau(J_{0})\), where
\(J_{0}\) denotes the augmentation ideal of \(A_{0}\).

On the other hand, let \(B\) be the affine algebra of \(G/Q\); it is the
kernel of the couple of morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  τ\_1}
\NormalTok{                  ────→}
\NormalTok{     A                       A ⨶\_k A₀,}
\NormalTok{                  ────→}
\NormalTok{            (id ⨶ ρ)∆\_A}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

i.e.,
\texttt{B\ =\ \{x\ ∈\ A\ \textbar{}\ ∆\_A(x)\ −\ x\ ⨶\ 1\ ∈\ A\ ⨶\ I\}}.
Denote by \(\gamma\) the continuous morphism of \(k\)-algebras
\(\theta^{\natural} : A' \to A\); it is a section of \(\rho'\) and an
isomorphism of profinite \(k\)-algebras from \(A'\) onto \(B\). On the
other hand, \(\tau = \pi^{\natural}\) identifies \(A_{0}\) with a
sub-bialgebra of \(A\), which is none other than the affine algebra of
the quotient \texttt{N\ \textbackslash{}\ G}. One deduces from (1) and
(3) that one has an isomorphism of profinite \(k\)-algebras

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    A\textquotesingle{} ⨶\_k A₀ ⥲ A,    a\textquotesingle{} ⨶ a₀ ↦ γ(a\textquotesingle{}) τ(a₀),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whose inverse is the map
\texttt{a\ ↦\ (ρ\textquotesingle{}\ ⨶\ ρ)∆\_A(a)}.

Finally, let us identify \(A'\) with its image in \(A\) via \(\gamma\),
so that the projection \(A \to A'\) is then \(\gamma \rho'\). Denoting
by \texttt{∆\_\{A\textquotesingle{}\}} the comultiplication of \(A'\),
one deduces from (4) that
\texttt{∆\_A(A\textquotesingle{})\ ⊂\ A\ ⨶\ A\textquotesingle{}} and
that the following diagram is commutative:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              ∆\_A}
\NormalTok{        A\textquotesingle{} ────────→ A ⨶ A\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{                          γρ\textquotesingle{} ⨶ id}
                          
\NormalTok{              ∆\_\{A\textquotesingle{}\}}
\NormalTok{        A\textquotesingle{} ────────→ A\textquotesingle{} ⨶ A\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(one also has therefore \(\gamma \rho' \circ c_{A} = c_{A'}\), where
\(c_{A}\) (resp. \(c_{A'}\)) is the antipode of \(A\) (resp. \(A'\))).
On the other hand, denoting by \(m_{A}\) the multiplication of \(A\),
one deduces from (2) that, for every \(a \in A\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   γρ\textquotesingle{}(a) = (m\_A ∘ (id ⊗ τρ c\_A) ∘ ∆\_A)(a).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{2.4.B.}\label{b.}

Let us suppose, for simplicity, \(k\) artinian. Then what precedes is
expressed more simply in terms of the covariant bialgebras of
\texttt{G,\ Q,\ N}. Indeed, since \(G = N \times Q\) as \(k\)-formal
varieties, then \texttt{H(G)\ =\ H(N)\ ⨶\_k\ H(Q)} as \(k\)-coalgebras.
Moreover, since the multiplication of \(G\) is given by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   (x, q) · (x\textquotesingle{}, q\textquotesingle{}) = (x α(q, x\textquotesingle{}), qq\textquotesingle{}),    where α(q, x\textquotesingle{}) = qx\textquotesingle{}q⁻¹,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the multiplication of \(H(G)\) is given as follows: for every
\(x \in H(N), q \in H(Q)\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   (x ⊗ q) · (x\textquotesingle{} ⊗ q\textquotesingle{}) = x φ(q, x\textquotesingle{}) ⊗ qq\textquotesingle{},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \texttt{φ\ :\ H(Q)\ ⨶\_k\ H(N)} is the morphism of
\(k\)-coalgebras induced by \(\alpha\). Since \(\alpha\) is the
composite morphism below (where \(\delta_{G}\) (resp. \(m_{G}\)) is the
diagonal morphism (resp. multiplication) of \(G\), \(c_{Q}\) the
inversion morphism of \(Q\), and
\texttt{v(q\ ⨶\ q\textquotesingle{}\ ⨶\ x)\ =\ q\ ⨶\ x\ ⨶\ q\textquotesingle{}}):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              v ∘ (δ\_G × id)              id × id × c\_Q             m\_G}
\NormalTok{   Q × N ────────────────────→ Q × N × Q ─────────────────→ Q × N × Q ──────→ G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one obtains, denoting still by \(c_{Q}\) the antipode of \(H(Q)\), that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(⋆)    φ(q ⊗ x\textquotesingle{}) = Σ\_i q\_i x\textquotesingle{} c\_Q(q\textquotesingle{}\_i)    if ∆\_\{H(Q)\}(q) = Σ\_i q\_i ⊗ q\textquotesingle{}\_i.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, if \(M\) is an abstract group and if \(H(Q)\) is the
group algebra \texttt{kM} (i.e., \(Q = Spf* kM\) is the constant
\(k\)-formal group \(M_{k}\)), then for every \(\gamma \in M\) and
\(x' \in H(N)\) one has
\(\phi(\gamma \otimes x') = \gamma x' \gamma^{-1}\), and this defines an
action of \(M\) on \(H(N)\) by Hopf algebra automorphisms.

\paragraph{2.4.1. Proposition.}\label{proposition.-6}

\textbf{Proposition 2.4.1.} \emph{Let \(f : G \to K\) be a morphism of
\(k\)-formal groups. If \(H = Ker(f)\) is topologically flat over \(k\),
the homomorphism \(f' : G/H \to K\) induced by \(f\) is a monomorphism.}

This is a consequence of the results of Exposé IV;\footnote{cf.~IV,
  5.2.6.} we nonetheless give a direct proof. Let \(T\) be a formal
variety of finite length over \(k\) and \(t\) an element of \((G/H)(T)\)
such that \(f' \circ t\) is the unit element of \(K(T)\). We must show
that \(t\) is the unit element of \((G/H)(T)\). Denote by \(p\) the
projection \(G \to G/H\) and by \(X\) the fiber product
\(T \times_{G/H} G\).

By 2.4, \(p\) is surjective and topologically flat, hence so is the
morphism \(pr_{1} : X \to T\), hence \(pr_{1}\) is an epimorphism by
Proposition 1.3.1, hence it suffices to show that \(t \circ pr_{1}\) is
the unit element of \((G/H)(X)\). Denote by \(pr_{2}\) the projection
\(X \to G\); one has \(t \circ pr_{1} = p \circ pr_{2}\), whence the
equality
\(1 = f' \circ t \circ pr_{1} = f' \circ p \circ pr_{2} = f \circ pr_{2}\).
Then the exact sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              f}
\NormalTok{   1 ─────→ H ──────→ G ──────→ K}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

shows that \(pr_{2}\) factors through \(H\), hence \(p \circ pr_{2}\) is
the zero morphism. Since \(p \circ pr_{2} = t \circ pr_{1}\), this
proves the proposition.

One deduces from the proposition the following corollary. Let
\(O(G), O(K)\) and \(O(G/H)\) denote the affine algebras of \(G\), \(K\)
and \(G/H\); one has seen (2.4) that \(p\) induces an injection of
\(O(G/H)\) into \(O(G)\). Moreover, by Proposition 1.3, since
\(f' : G/H \to K\) is a monomorphism, the morphism \(O(K) \to O(G/H)\)
is surjective, whence:

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.1.} \emph{Let \(f : G \to K\) be a morphism of
\(k\)-formal groups and \(H = Ker(f)\). If \(H\) is topologically flat
over \(k\), then \(O(G/H)\) is the image of \(O(K)\) in \(O(G)\).}

\paragraph{2.4.2.}\label{section-171}

Let us keep the preceding notations and assume \(H\) and \(G\)
topologically flat over \(k\). Then \(G\) is topologically flat over
\(k\) and over \(G/H\), hence, by 1.3.3, \(G/H\) is topologically flat
over \(k\). Consequently, by 2.4, the canonical projection \(q\) from
\(K\) onto \(Coker(f')\) is topologically flat and \(f'\) is an
isomorphism from \(G/H\) onto \(Ker(q)\). It is clear on the other hand
that one has \(Coker(f) = Coker(f')\). Hence, under the hypothesis that
\(G\) and \(H = Ker(f)\) are topologically flat over \(k\), one has
obtained an isomorphism between \(Ker(q)\), the image of \(f\), and
\(G/Ker(f)\), the coimage of \(f\). This entails the theorem below.

\textbf{Theorem 2.4.2.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field. The commutative
\(k\)-formal groups form an abelian category.}

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.2.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field. The commutative
affine \(k\)-group schemes form an abelian category.}\footnote{See also
  the remarks following VI\_A, 5.4.3.}

This follows from the theorem and the equivalence of categories 2.2.2.

\subsubsection{2.5.}\label{section-172}

A \(k\)-formal group is said to be \emph{étale} if the underlying formal
variety is étale (cf.~1.6); these formal groups have a very simple
structure. Indeed, suppose \(k\) local; let \(\kappa\) be the residue
field of \(k\), \(\kappa_{s}\) a separable closure of \(\kappa\), and
\(\Gamma\) the topological Galois group of \(\kappa_{s}\) over
\(\kappa\). Let us call a \emph{\(\Gamma\)-set} the datum of a set \(E\)
and a continuous operation of \(\Gamma\) on \(E\) (i.e., the isotropy
group of every element \(x \in E\) is an open subgroup of \(\Gamma\)).

For every \(k\)-formal variety \(X\), one sets:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   X(κ\_s) = lim X(ℓ),}
\NormalTok{            ──→}
\NormalTok{              ℓ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\ell\) ranges over the finite extensions of \(\kappa\) contained
in \(\kappa_{s}\).\footnote{Note that if
  \([\kappa_{s} : \kappa] = \infty\), \(\kappa_{s}\) is not a profinite
  \(\kappa\)-algebra, so the preceding notation is an abuse of notation.
  On the other hand, we have detailed the original in what follows.}
Then \(\Gamma\) operates continuously on each \(X(\ell)\), hence also on
\(X(\kappa_{s})\). Moreover, let \texttt{X\_κ\ =\ X\ ⨶\_k\ κ}
(cf.~1.6.C); for every \(\ell\) one has \(X(\ell) = X_{\kappa}(\ell)\),
whence \(X(\kappa_{s}) = X_{\kappa}(\kappa_{s})\).

Suppose now \(X\) étale over \(k\); then \(X_{\kappa}\) is the
\(\kappa\)-formal variety direct sum of the
\(\operatorname{Spec} \kappa(x)\), for \(x \in X\), and if one denotes
by \(X'_{\kappa}\) the \(\kappa\)-scheme direct sum of the
\(\operatorname{Spec} \kappa(x)\), one sees that
\(X_{\kappa}(\kappa_{s})\) is none other than
\texttt{X\textquotesingle{}\_κ(κ\_s)\ =\ Hom\_\{(Sch/κ)\}(Spec\ κ\_s,\ X\textquotesingle{}\_κ)}.

Let us denote \(\mathcal{C} = (Sch^{\acute{e}}t_{/}\kappa)\) the full
subcategory of \((Sch_{/}\kappa)\) formed by the étale
\(\kappa\)-schemes. One knows that the functor
\(X' \mapsto X'(\kappa_{s})\) is an equivalence of \(\mathcal{C}\) onto
the category \(\mathcal{C}'\) of \(\Gamma\)-sets (cf.~SGA 1, V §§ 7--8
or {[}DG70{]}, § I.4 6.4); it therefore induces an equivalence between
the category of \(\mathcal{C}\)-groups and that of
\(\mathcal{C}'\)-groups; now one sees at once that a
\(\mathcal{C}'\)-group is the same thing as an abstract group \(G\)
endowed with a continuous operation of \(\Gamma\) by group automorphisms
(one will then say that \(G\) is a \emph{\(\Gamma\)-group}).

Taking into account the equivalences
\texttt{Vaf\^{}ét\_/k\ ⥲\ Vaf\^{}ét\_/κ\ ⥲\ (Sch\^{}ét\_/κ)} of 1.6.E,
one therefore obtains:

\textbf{Proposition 2.5.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a local pseudocompact ring,
\(\kappa\) its residue field, \(\kappa_{s}\) a separable closure of
\(\kappa\), and \(\Gamma = \operatorname{Gal}(\kappa_{s}/\kappa)\).}

\emph{(i) The functor \(X \mapsto X(\kappa_{s})\) is an equivalence of
the category of étale \(k\)-formal varieties onto that of
\(\Gamma\)-sets.}

\emph{(ii) It induces an equivalence of the category of étale
\(k\)-formal groups onto that of \(\Gamma\)-groups.}

\textbf{Remark 2.5.A.}\footnote{We have added this remark.} Let \(k\) be
a field, \(k_{s}\) a separable closure of \(k\), \(G\) an étale
\(k\)-formal group and \(M\) the abstract group \(G(k_{s})\). Let us
denote by \(X\) a set of representatives of the orbits of
\(\Gamma = \operatorname{Gal}(k_{s}/k)\) in \(M\), and for every
\(x \in X\) let \(\Gamma_{x}\) be its stabilizer, which is a subgroup of
\(\Gamma\) of finite index, and \(L_{x} = k^{\Gamma_{x}}_{s}\), which is
an extension of \(k\) of degree \([\Gamma : \Gamma_{x}]\) (see, for
example, {[}BAlg{]}, V § 10.10). Then, by the equivalence of categories
above, the affine algebra \(\mathcal{A}(G)\) of \(G\) is the product of
the \(L_{x}\), endowed with the product topology, and hence the
\(L_{x}\) are precisely the simple quotients \(\mathcal{A}(G)/m\), where
\(m\) is a maximal open ideal of \(\mathcal{A}(G)\). Since these
correspond by duality to the subcoalgebras of \(H(G)\), one obtains that
\(H(G)\) is pointed (i.e., \(\dim_{k}(C) = 1\) for every simple
subcoalgebra \(C\)) if and only if \(L_{x} = k\) for every \(x\), and in
this case \(\mathcal{A}(G)\) is the topological algebra \(k^{M}\), hence
\(H(G)\) is the group algebra \texttt{kM}, and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   M = \{x ∈ H(G) | ε(x) = 1 and ∆(x) = x ⊗ x\} = G(k).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{2.5.1.}\label{section-173}

Let us now suppose \(k\) an arbitrary pseudocompact ring. Since the
functor \(X \mapsto X_{e}\) of 1.6.F commutes with finite products, it
transforms every formal group \(G\) into an étale formal group
\(G_{e}\), and since the morphism \(p : X \to X_{e}\) of loc. cit. is
functorial in \(X\), then \(p : G \to G_{e}\) is in this case a morphism
of formal groups.

Consider the kernel \(Ker(p)\);\footnote{We have detailed the original
  in what follows.} it is the fiber product of the diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       G}
\NormalTok{                          p}
\NormalTok{                  ε       }
                          
\NormalTok{       Spf(k) ──────→ G\_e}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\epsilon\) is the unit section of \(G_{e}\). Since \(p\) induces
a bijection on the underlying sets, one deduces (cf. 1.2, N.D.E. (41))
that \(Ker(p)\) has as underlying set the image of \(Spf(k)\) under
\(\epsilon\) and that for every point \(s\) of \(Spf(k)\), the local
algebra of \(Ker(p)\) at the point \(\epsilon(s)\) is
\texttt{O\_\{G,\ ε(s)\}\ ⨶\_\{O\_\{G\_e,\ ε(s)\}\}\ k\_s}. Moreover, at
each point \(\epsilon(s)\), the residue field of \(O_{G, \epsilon(s)}\)
is \(\kappa(s)\), and hence \(O_{G_{e}, \epsilon(s)} = k_{s}\), whence
\(O_{Ker(p), \epsilon(s)} = O_{G, \epsilon(s)}\). For these reasons we
shall say that \(Ker(p)\) is the \emph{infinitesimal neighborhood of the
origin} of \(G\) and we shall write \(Ker(p) = G^{0}\), thereby
obtaining an exact sequence:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       incl.        p}
\NormalTok{   1 ──────→ G⁰ ─────────────→ G ──────→ G\_e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In what follows, we shall say that \(G\) is \emph{infinitesimal} if
\(G = G^{0}\).\footnote{We have added the following sentence.} This is
equivalent to saying that for every \(s \in Spf(k)\), or also for every
continuous morphism \(k \to \kappa\), where \(\kappa\) is a field
endowed with the discrete topology, the unit element is the unique
element of \(G(\kappa(s))\) resp. of \(G(\kappa)\).

Suppose furthermore that \(G\) is topologically flat over
\(k\).\footnote{We have detailed what follows.} Then, by 1.6.1, the
morphism \(p : G \to G_{e}\) is topologically flat, and since it is
bijective, it is therefore an effective epimorphism by Proposition
1.3.1. Consequently, \(G_{e}\) is identified with the quotient
\(G/G^{0}\). One has therefore obtained:

\textbf{Corollary 2.5.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a formal group
topologically flat over \(k\). Then \(G_{e}\) is identified with the
quotient \(G/G^{0}\); i.e., one has an exact sequence of formal groups:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                              incl.       p}
\NormalTok{   1 ──────→ G⁰ ─────────────→ G ──────→ G\_e ──────→ 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{2.5.2.}\label{section-174}

Suppose \(k\) is a perfect field. In this case, one has seen (cf.~1.6.2)
that the morphism \(p : X \mapsto X_{e}\) admits a section
\(s : X_{e} \to X\) which depends functorially on \(X\); this section is
therefore a morphism of formal groups when \(X\) is a formal group. One
obtains thus:

\textbf{Proposition 2.5.2.} \emph{When \(k\) is a perfect field, every
\(k\)-formal group \(G\) is canonically isomorphic to the semi-direct
product of an infinitesimal group \(G^{0}\) and an étale group \(G_{e}\)
operating on \(G^{0}\).}\footnote{The same argument shows also that, for
  an arbitrary field \(k\), if all the residue fields of \(G\) equal
  \(k\), then \(G_{e}\) is the constant \(k\)-group \((M)_{k}\), where
  \(M = G(k) = Spf* H(G)\), and \(H(G)\) is the semi-direct product of
  \(H(G^{0})\) by the group algebra \texttt{kM}, cf.~the addition 2.9
  further below.}

\emph{If, moreover, \(G\) is commutative, then \(G\) is the product of
\(G^{0}\) and of \(G_{e}\). By 2.2.2, this canonical decomposition of
commutative \(k\)-formal groups corresponds to an analogous
decomposition of affine commutative \(k\)-group schemes; see paragraph
2.5.3 below.}

\textbf{Remark 2.5.2.A.}\footnote{We have added this remark.} The exact
sequence \(1 \to G^{0} \to G \to G_{e} \to 1\) is not necessarily split
when \(k\) is not perfect: let us give the following example, taken from
{[}DG70{]}, § III.6, 8.6. Let \(k\) be a non-perfect field of
characteristic \(p > 0\). Let \(\lambda \in k - k^{p}\), let
\(L_{\lambda}\) be the abelian \(p\)-Lie algebra with basis \((x, y)\),
the \emph{symbolic \(p\)-th power} (cf.~VII\_A, 5.2) being given by
\(x^{(p)} = x\) and \(y^{(p)} = \lambda x\), let
\(U_{p}(L_{\lambda}) = k[x, y]/(x^{p} - x, y^{p} - \lambda x)\) be the
restricted enveloping algebra of \(L_{\lambda}\) (cf. VII\_A, 5.3), and
let \(G_{\lambda}\) be the commutative \(k\)-formal group with affine
algebra \(U_{p}(L_{\lambda})\). Then \(G_{\lambda}\) is a non-split
extension of the étale constant \(k\)-group
\((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})_{k}\) by the infinitesimal \(k\)-group
\(\alpha_{p,k} = Spf k[x]/(x^{p} - x)\), i.e., one has a non-split exact
sequence of commutative \(k\)-formal groups:\footnote{\(\alpha_{p,k}\),
  \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})_{k}\) and \(G_{\lambda}\) are also
  \(k\)-algebraic groups, finite and flat over \(k\), cf.~N.D.E. (84) in
  2.2.2.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   0 ─────→ α\_\{p,k\} ─────→ G\_λ ─────→ (ℤ/pℤ)\_k ─────→ 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It corresponds by duality to a non-split exact sequence of commutative
\(k\)-algebraic groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   0 ─────→ μ\_\{p,k\} ─────→ D\textquotesingle{}(G\_λ) ─────→ α\_\{p,k\} ─────→ 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\mu_{p,k} = \operatorname{Spec} k[t]/(t^{p} - 1)\) (and one
obtains thus all extensions of \(\alpha_{p,k}\) by \(\mu_{p,k}\),
cf.~{[}DG70{]}, § III.6, 8.6).

\paragraph{2.5.3.}\label{section-175}

Let \(k\) be a field.

\textbf{Definition 2.5.3.A.} \emph{One says that a commutative
\(k\)-group scheme is} unipotent \emph{if it is isomorphic to
\(\operatorname{Spec} H(G)\), where \(G\) is an infinitesimal
commutative \(k\)-formal group.}\footnote{This coincides with the
  ``usual'' notion of unipotent \(k\)-group scheme, cf.~the addition 2.8
  at the end of Section 2.}

On the other hand, following Exp. IX, Definition 1.1, one says that a
\(k\)-group scheme \(H\) is \emph{of multiplicative type} if there
exists a scheme \(S\), faithfully flat and quasi-compact over
\(\operatorname{Spec} k\), such that \texttt{H\_S} is a diagonalizable
\(S\)-group, i.e., is isomorphic to \(D_{S}(M)\) for some ``abstract''
abelian group \(M\).\footnote{The original indicated: ``let us say that
  a commutative \(k\)-group scheme is of multiplicative type if it is
  isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Spec} H(G)\), where \(G\) is an étale
  commutative \(k\)-formal group.'' We have given here the ``usual''
  definition, drawn from Exp. IX, 1.1, and we have shown its equivalence
  with the preceding condition; see also {[}DG70{]}, § IV.1, Th. 2.2.}
By (fpqc) descent, this implies that \(H\) is affine and commutative. On
the other hand, since one may replace \(S\) by the residue field of one
of its points, one sees that \(H\) is of multiplicative type if and only
if there exists an extension \(K\) of \(k\) such that \texttt{H\_K} is a
diagonalizable \(K\)-group.

\textbf{Proposition 2.5.3.B.} \emph{Let \(T\) be an affine commutative
\(k\)-group scheme and let \(k_{s}\) be a separable closure of \(k\).}

\emph{(i) For \(T\) to be of multiplicative type, it is necessary and
sufficient that its dual \(D(T)\) be an étale commutative \(k\)-formal
group.}

\emph{(ii) Consequently, \(T\) is of multiplicative type if and only if
\texttt{T\ ⨶\_k\ k\_s} is diagonalizable.}

\emph{Proof.} Let \(A\) denote the affine algebra of \(D(T)\) and
\(A_{0}\) its local component at the neutral element; then \(D(T)\) is
étale over \(k\) if and only if \(A_{0} = k\). If \(K\) is an extension
of \(k\), then the algebra \texttt{A₀\ ⨶\_k\ K} is local (since it is a
projective limit of local artinian rings), so it coincides with the
local component \texttt{(A\ ⨶\_k\ K)₀}; moreover, since the formation of
\(D(T)\) commutes with base change (cf.~2.2.2), one also has
\texttt{A\ ⨶\_k\ K\ ≃\ D(T\_K)}.

Suppose \(T\) of multiplicative type; then there exists an extension
\(K\) of \(k\) such that \texttt{O(T)\ ⨶\_k\ K} is isomorphic, as a
\(K\)-Hopf algebra, to the group algebra \texttt{KM}, for some abelian
group \(M\). Then \texttt{A\ ⨶\_k\ K} is isomorphic to the algebra
\(K^{M}\), endowed with the product topology, hence one has
\texttt{K\ =\ (A\ ⨶\_k\ K)₀\ =\ A₀\ ⨶\_k\ K} and this entails that
\(A_{0} = k\), so \(D(T)\) is étale.

Conversely, suppose \(D(T)\) étale. Then
\texttt{D(T)\ ⨶\_k\ k\_s\ =\ D(T\_\{k\_s\})} is a \(k_{s}\)-constant
group \(M\), so its covariant bigèbre is the group algebra \(k_{s} M\)
(cf.~Remark 2.5.A), so \texttt{O(T)\ ⨶\_k\ k\_s\ =\ k\_s\ M}, which
proves that \(T\) is of multiplicative type, and split by the extension
\(k \to k_{s}\). The proposition follows.

By 2.2.2, 2.5.1, and 2.5, one obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 2.5.3.C.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field and \(G\) an
affine commutative \(k\)-group scheme.}

\emph{(i) \(G\) contains a subgroup of multiplicative type \(G_{m}\)
such that \(G/G_{m}\) is unipotent.}

\emph{(ii) When \(k\) is perfect, there exists furthermore a canonical
retraction of \(G\) onto \(G_{m}\), so that \(G\) is the product of a
unipotent group and a group of multiplicative type.}

\emph{(iii)}\footnote{We have added point (iii), a consequence of
  Proposition 2.5.} \emph{Let \(k_{s}\) be a separable closure of \(k\)
and \(\Gamma = \operatorname{Gal}(k_{s}/k)\). The category of
\(k\)-group schemes of multiplicative type is anti-equivalent to the
category of continuous \(\Gamma\)-modules.}

\subsubsection{2.6.}\label{section-176}

We shall now study infinitesimal formal groups, to which the following
paragraphs are devoted. In this study, Lie algebras play a primordial
role.

Suppose first that the base ring \(k\) is artinian and let \(G\) be a
formal group over \(k\). One can give three different interpretations of
the Lie algebra of \(G\), all of which we shall use:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(D\) be the algebra \(k[d]/(d^{2})\) of dual numbers over \(k\)
  and \(\delta\) the homomorphism from \(D\) to \(k\) which annihilates
  \(d\). For every formal group \(G\) over \(k\), \(Lie(G)\) is the
  kernel of \(G(\delta)\), so that by definition one has an exact
  sequence of groups
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   1 ────→ Lie(G) ────→ G(D) ──G(δ)──→ G(k) ────→ 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(A\) be the affine algebra of \(G\) and
  \(I_{A} = Ker \epsilon_{A}\) its augmentation ideal. The group
  \(G(D)\) has as elements the morphisms of profinite \(k\)-algebras
  \(f : A \to D\). The condition \(G(\delta)(f) = 1\) is equivalent to
  \(\delta \circ f = \epsilon_{A}\). Since
  \(x - \epsilon_{A}(x) \cdot 1_{A} \in I_{A}\) for every \(x \in A\),
  this is equivalent to \(f(I_{A}) \subset k \cdot d\), hence \(Ker(f)\)
  contains \(I^{2}_{A}\) and therefore also \(\bar{I}^{2}_{A}\) (the
  closure), so \(f\) induces a continuous linear map
  \(f' : I_{A} / I^{2}_{A} = \omega_{G/k} \to k\) such that, for every
  \(x \in A\), one has the equality
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   f(x) = ε\_A(x) · 1\_D + f\textquotesingle{}(x̄) · d,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\bar{x}\) designates the image of
\(x - \epsilon_{A}(x) \cdot 1_{A}\) in \(I_{A}/I^{2}_{A}\). One sees
then that the map \(f \mapsto f'\) defines a bijection of \(Lie(G)\)
onto the topological dual \texttt{ω\_\{G/k\}†} of \(\omega_{G/k}\)
(cf.~0.2.2).

This bijection respects the group structures. Indeed, let \(f\) and
\(g\) be two elements of \(Lie(G)\); their product \(f \cdot g\) is the
composite map \texttt{h\ ∘\ ∆\_A}, where \texttt{h\ :\ A\ ⨶\ A\ →\ D} is
such that
\texttt{h(b\ ⨶\ b\textquotesingle{})\ =\ f(b)\ g(b\textquotesingle{})}.
Now if \(a \in I_{A}\) one has, by 2.1 (ii),
\texttt{∆\_A(a)\ −\ a\ ⨶\ 1\ −\ 1\ ⨶\ a\ ∈\ I\_A\ ⨶\ I\_A}, whence
\((f \cdot g)(a) = f(a) + g(a)\) (cf. also II 3.10).

In what follows, we identify \(Lie(G)\) with \texttt{ω\_\{G/k\}†} by
means of the bijection \(f \mapsto f'\) described above. The group
\(Lie(G)\) is thus endowed with a structure of \(k\)-module.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \texttt{A†} and \texttt{D†} be the \(k\)-modules dual to \(A\) and
  \(D\), \texttt{\{1\_D†,\ d†\}} the dual basis of the basis
  \({1_{D}, d}\) of \(D\) over \(k\) (one has \texttt{1\_D†\ =\ δ}).
  Since \(D\) is free of finite rank over \(k\), the canonical map
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Hom\_c(A, D) ─→ Hom\_k(D†, A†),    f ↦ ᵗf}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective. On the other hand, \(f\) is determined by the values
\({}^{t}f(1_{D}*)\) and \({}^{t}f(d*) = x\).

The condition \(G(\delta)(f) = 1\) is equivalent to the equality
\({}^{t}f(1_{D}*) = \epsilon_{A}\). One sees easily on the other hand
that \(f\) is compatible with multiplication if and only if one has
(cf.~2.3):

\[
(\ast)    \delta_{G}(x) = \varphi_{G}(x \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes x).
\]

Finally, it is clear that a continuous linear map \(f : A \to D\) which
is compatible with multiplication and such that
\(\delta \circ f = \epsilon_{A}\) sends the unit element of \(A\) to
that of \(D\).\footnote{Indeed, \(\delta \circ f = \epsilon_{A}\)
  entails \(f(1) = 1 + \lambda d\), with \(\lambda \in k\), and then
  \(f(1) = f(1)^{2} = 1 + 2\lambda d\) gives \(\lambda = 0\).} The map
\(f \mapsto x\) thus permits us to identify \(Lie(G)\) with the set of
``primitive elements'' of \(H(G)\) (i.e., the \(x \in H(G)\) satisfying
relation \((\ast)\)). If \(x\) and \(y\) are two such elements, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   δ\_G(xy) = δ\_G(x) δ\_G(y) = ϕ\_G(x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x)(y ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ y)}
\NormalTok{          = ϕ\_G(xy ⊗ 1 + x ⊗ y + y ⊗ x + 1 ⊗ xy),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence
\(\delta_{G}(xy - yx) = \varphi_{G}((xy - yx) \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes (xy - yx))\).

This shows that the \(k\)-module \(Lie(G)\) is identified with a Lie
subalgebra of \(H(G)\): we shall say that \(Lie(G)\) is the \emph{Lie
algebra} of \(G\).\footnote{Comparing with VII\_A 2.5, one sees that if
  \(K\) is a \(k\)-group scheme of finite type and if \(G\) is the
  formal completion of \(K\) at the origin (i.e., \(\mathcal{A}(G)\) is
  the completion of the local ring \(O_{K,e}\) for the \(m\)-adic
  topology, where \(m\) is the kernel of the augmentation
  \(\epsilon : O_{K,e} \to k\)), then \(H(G)\) is identified with the
  algebra of distributions \(U(K)\), and \(Lie(G)\) with \(Lie(K)\).
  (The condition that \(K\) be of finite type over \(k\) is used to
  ensure that \(m/m^{2}\) is a \(k\)-module of finite length, hence
  discrete, so that its topological dual coincides with its ordinary
  dual.) In particular, when \(G\) is a finite \(k\)-formal group (i.e.,
  such that \(\mathcal{A}(G)\) is a finite \(k\)-module), in which case
  \(G\) may also be considered as the \(k\)-group scheme
  \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{A}(G)\), the two definitions of
  \(Lie(G)\) coincide.}

\paragraph{2.6.1.}\label{section-177}

When \(k\) is an arbitrary pseudocompact ring and \(G\) a formal group
over \(k\), we call \emph{\(O_{k}\)-Lie algebra of \(G\)} the functor
\(Lie(G)\) which associates to every object \(C\) of \(Alf_{/}k\) the
\(C\)-Lie algebra of the \(C\)-formal group
\texttt{G\textquotesingle{}\ =\ G\ ⨶\_k\ C}:\footnote{We have detailed
  the original in what follows.} set
\texttt{A\textquotesingle{}\ =\ A\ ⨶\_k\ C}, since \texttt{I\_A} is a
direct factor of \(A\), then \(I_{A'}\) equals
\texttt{I\_A\ ⨶\_k\ C\ =\ I\_A\ ⨶\_A\ A\textquotesingle{}}, and since
\texttt{ω\_\{G/k\}\ =\ I\_A\ ⨶\_A\ k} and similarly
\texttt{ω\_\{G\textquotesingle{}/C\}\ =\ I\_\{A\textquotesingle{}\}\ ⨶\_\{A\textquotesingle{}\}\ C},
one obtains that
\texttt{ω\_\{G\textquotesingle{}/C\}\ =\ ω\_\{G/k\}\ ⨶\_A\ C} and hence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Lie(G)(C) = Hom\_c(ω\_\{G/k\} ⨶\_A C, C)    i.e.    Lie(G) = V\_kf(ω\_\{G/k\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(with the notations of 1.2.3.B). Therefore, by Proposition 1.2.3.E,
\(Lie(G)\) is flat over \(O_{k}\) if and only if \(\omega_{G/k}\) is a
projective pseudocompact \(k\)-module.

\paragraph{2.6.2.}\label{section-178}

Conversely, every Lie algebra \(L\) over \(O_{k}\) defines a \(k\)-group
functor. Indeed, let us denote by \(U(L)\) the functor which associates
to every object \(C\) of \(Alf_{/}k\) the enveloping algebra \(U(L(C))\)
of the \(C\)-Lie algebra \(L(C)\). By VII\_A, 3.2.2, \(U(L)\) is a
bialgebra over \(O_{k}\) and therefore determines, by 2.2, a \(k\)-group
functor \(Spf* U(L)\) which we shall henceforth denote
\(\mathcal{G}(L)\). Thus, \(\mathcal{G}(L)(C)\) is the group of elements
\(z \in U(L(C))\) of augmentation \texttt{1} and such that
\texttt{∆\_\{U(L(C))\}(z)\ =\ z\ ⊗\ z}.

Moreover, when \(L\) is flat over \(O_{k}\), one has the following
proposition.

\textbf{Proposition 2.6.2.}\footnote{We have highlighted points (i) and
  (ii), and added point (iii), which will be useful in 2.6.3 and 3.3.2.}
\emph{Let \(L\) be a flat \(O_{k}\)-Lie algebra.}

\emph{(i) \(\mathcal{G}(L)\) is a formal group topologically flat over
\(k\), having \(U(L)\) as \(O_{k}\)-bialgebra.}

\emph{(ii) \(\mathcal{G}(L)\) is infinitesimal.}

\emph{(iii) For every object \(C\) of \(Alf_{/}k\),
\(Lie(\mathcal{G}(L))(C)\) is identified with the set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   Prim U(L(C)) = \{x ∈ U(L(C)) | ε(x) = 0 and ∆(x) = x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{of primitive elements of \(U(L(C))\). In particular, one has a
natural morphism of \(O_{k}\)-Lie algebras
\(\tau_{L} : L \to Lie(\mathcal{G}(L))\).}

Indeed, the hypothesis that \(L\) be flat over \(O_{k}\) means that for
every morphism \(C \to D\) of \(Alf_{/}k\), one has
\(L(D) = L(C) \otimes_{C} D\), and that for each local component \(C'\)
of \(C\), \(L(C')\) is a free \(C'\)-module. The first condition entails
that \(U(L(D)) = U(L(C)) \otimes D\) (by the universal property of the
tensor product and that of the functor \(L \mapsto U(L)\)), and the
second condition entails, by the Poincaré--Birkhoff--Witt theorem
(cf.~Bourbaki, \emph{Groupes et algèbres de Lie}, I 2.7), that
\(U(L(C'))\) is a free \(C'\)-module. Therefore the bialgebra \(U(L)\)
is flat over \(O_{k}\).

To prove (ii) and (iii), one may suppose \(k\) artinian. Set then
\(L = L(k)\), \(U = U(L)\), \(U_{0} = k \cdot 1_{U}\) and let \(U^{+}\)
be the two-sided ideal of \(U\) generated by the image of \(L\). Set in
addition, for every \(n \geqslant 1\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   U\_n = \{u ∈ U | ∆\_U(u) − u ⊗ 1 ∈ U\_\{n−1\} ⊗ U⁺\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 1.3.6, it suffices to show that \(U\) is the union of the \(U_{n}\).
Now, if one identifies \(L\) with its canonical image in \(U\), \(L\) is
evidently contained in \texttt{U\_1}. If \(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}\) are
elements of \(L\), one has
\texttt{∆\_U(x\_1\ ⋯\ x\_n)\ =\ (x\_1\ ⊗\ 1\ +\ 1\ ⊗\ x\_1)\ ⋯\ (x\_n\ ⊗\ 1\ +\ 1\ ⊗\ x\_n)},
which shows, by induction on \(n\), that the product
\(x_{1} \cdots x_{n}\) belongs to \(U_{n}\), hence that
\(U = \cup_{n} U_{n}\). This proves (ii).

On the other hand, let \(D = k[d]/(d^{2})\) be the algebra of dual
numbers over \(k\). By hypothesis one has \(L(D) \simeq L \otimes D\),
whence \(U(L(D)) \simeq U \otimes D\), by the universal properties of
the tensor product and of the enveloping algebra. It follows that
\(Lie(\mathcal{G}(L))(k)\) is identified with the set of elements
\(z = 1 + xd\) of \(U \oplus Ud\) (where \(x \in U\)) such that
\(\epsilon(z) = 1\) and \texttt{∆(z)\ =\ z\ ⊗\ z}, which is equivalent
