\NormalTok{1 ⟶ B ⟶ f\_*(E) ⟶ G ⟶ 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(g : H \to G\) is a \(k\)-morphism of \(k\)-algebraic groups, and
  if \(E\) is an extension of \(G\) by \(A\), the fiber product
  \(E \times_{G} H\) is naturally an extension of \(H\) by \(A\),
  denoted \(g^{*}(E)\). One therefore has a commutative diagram:
\end{enumerate}

\[
1 \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow g^{*}(E) \longrightarrow H \longrightarrow 1
     \downarrow 1_{A}          \downarrow      \downarrow g
1 \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow E \longrightarrow G \longrightarrow 1.
\]

Adapting the proofs given in J.-P. Serre, \emph{Groupes algébriques et
corps de classes}, Chap. VII, one endows \(Ext_{alg}(G, A)\) with a
natural abelian group structure, functorial in \(A\) and \(G\).

\textbf{Proposition A.2.1.} \emph{Let \(0 \to A' \to A \to A'' \to 0\)
be an exact sequence in \((Ab)_{G}\). Then:}

\emph{a) One has a canonical exact sequence of abelian groups:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Z¹(G, A) → Z¹(G, A\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) ─d→ Ext\_\{alg\}(G, A\textquotesingle{}) → Ext\_\{alg\}(G, A) → Ext\_\{alg\}(G, A\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{b) If \(A(k) \to A''(k)\) is surjective, one deduces from a) the
exact sequence:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   H¹(G, A) → H¹(G, A\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) ─d→ Ext\_\{alg\}(G, A\textquotesingle{}) → Ext\_\{alg\}(G, A) → Ext\_\{alg\}(G, A\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The exact sequence of a) generalizes the usual exact sequence of
\(\operatorname{Hom}(\cdot, \cdot)\) valid in the framework of
commutative extensions (\emph{loc. cit.}) and is proved in the same way.
Let us simply recall the definition of the coboundary
\(d : Z^{1}(G, A'') \to Ext_{alg}(G, A')\). For this, consider the
extension

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 ⟶ A\textquotesingle{} ⟶ A · G ⟶ A\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} · G ⟶ 1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

deduced in the obvious way from the exact sequence
\(0 \to A' \to A \to A'' \to 0\). If \(u \in Z^{1}(G, A'')\), \(u\)
defines in the usual way a section homomorphism
\(u : G \to A'' \cdot G\). One then has \(d(u) = u^{*}(A \cdot G)\).

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{A.3. Comparison of \(H^{2}(G, A)\) and
\(Ext_{alg}(G, A)\)}{A.3. Comparison of H\^{}\{2\}(G, A) and Ext\_\{alg\}(G, A)}}\label{a.3.-comparison-of-h2g-a-and-ext_algg-a}

It is well known, in the case of abstract groups, that there exists a
functorial isomorphism between the abelian groups \(H^{2}(G, A)\) and
\(Ext(G, A)\). Likewise in the present case, if \(A\) is an element of
\((Ab)_{G}\), to every 2-cocycle \(u \in Z^{2}(G, A)\) one can associate
a structure of algebraic group on the prescheme \(A \times_{k} G\) which
makes it an element of \(Ext_{alg}(G, A)\). Moreover this extension is
trivial if and only if \(u \in B^{2}(G, A)\) (cf.~Exp. III 1.2.2). Let
us recall that the composition law on \(A \times G\) is defined by the
formula:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(a, g)(a\textquotesingle{}, g\textquotesingle{}) = (a + \{\}\^{}g a\textquotesingle{} + u(g, g\textquotesingle{}), gg\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is clear that the extensions of \(G\) by \(A\) thus obtained are not
arbitrary, since they possess a section. But conversely, if
\(E \in Ext_{alg}(G, A)\) possesses a section \(s\), \(E\) is isomorphic
to the extension of \(G\) by \(A\) associated with the 2-cocycle \(u\)
such that:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u(g, g\textquotesingle{}) = s(g) s(g\textquotesingle{}) s(gg\textquotesingle{})\^{}\{−1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One finally obtains the following proposition:

\textbf{Proposition A.3.1.} \emph{There exists a functorial isomorphism
between the bifunctors with values in abelian groups:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G, A) ↦ H²(G, A)   and   (G, A) ↦ Ext\_s(G, A),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(Ext_{s}(G, A)\) denotes the subgroup of
\(Ext_{alg}(G, A)\) formed by the classes of extensions of \(G\) by
\(A\) that possess a section.}

\subsection{B. Appendix II. Reminders and complements on radicial
groups}\label{b.-appendix-ii.-reminders-and-complements-on-radicial-groups}

Let \(p\) be a prime number \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 1} and let \(S\) be
an \(F_{p}\)-prescheme.

\subsubsection{B.1. The Frobenius
morphism}\label{b.1.-the-frobenius-morphism}

For every \(S\)-prescheme \(X\) and every integer \(n > 0\), denote by
\(P_{n} : X \to X\) the \(F_{p}\)-endomorphism corresponding to raising
to the \(p^{n}\)-th power in \texttt{O\_X}, and denote by \(X^{(n)}\)
the \(S\)-prescheme inverse image of \(X\) under the morphism
\(P_{n} : S \to S\). There then exists a unique \(S\)-morphism
\(F_{n} : X \to X^{(n)}\) making the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ────────→ X}
\NormalTok{ ↘         ↗}
\NormalTok{  ↘  F\_n  ↗}
\NormalTok{   X\^{}\{(n)\}}
\NormalTok{    ↓}
\NormalTok{    ↓P\_n}
\NormalTok{    ↓}
\NormalTok{    S ────→ S}
\NormalTok{        P\_n}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

commutative.

It is clear that \(F_{n}\) is identified with the ``\(n\)-th iterate''
of \(F_{1} = F\), called the Frobenius morphism of \(X/S\).

If \(G\) is an \(S\)-prescheme in groups, \(G^{(n)}\) is an
\(S\)-prescheme in groups and \(F_{n} : G \to G^{(n)}\) is an
\(S\)-morphism of groups. Its kernel \(F_{n}(G)\) is a characteristic
sub-prescheme in groups of \(G\) (i.e.~stable under the functor
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr}(G)\)), and radicial over \(S\). If \(G\) is
an \(S\)-prescheme in groups that is radicial, one says that \(G\) is

of height \(\leqslant h\) if \(F_{h}(G) = G\).

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{B.2. Groups and \(p\)-Lie
algebras}{B.2. Groups and p-Lie algebras}}\label{b.2.-groups-and-p-lie-algebras}

If \(G\) is an \(S\)-prescheme in groups, \(Lie(G)\) (Exp. II) is
naturally a restricted \(p\)-Lie algebra (Exp. VII\_A §§ 5 and 6). In
particular one has the following result (cf.~Exp. VII\_A):

\textbf{Proposition B.2.1.} \emph{i)
\(Lie(\alpha_{p})_{S} = Lie(G_{a})_{S}\)\footnote{N.D.E.: the definition
  of \(\alpha_{p}\), already given at the start of this Exposé, has been
  deleted here.} is a sheaf of \texttt{O\_S}-modules, free over
\texttt{O\_S} of rank 1, generated by an element \(X\) such that
\(X^{(p)} = 0\).}

\emph{ii) \(Lie(\mu_{p})_{S} = Lie(G_{m})_{S}\) is a sheaf of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules, free over \texttt{O\_S} of rank 1, possessing a
canonical basis \(X\) such that \(X^{(p)} = X\).}

Let us now recall the fundamental result proved in Exp. VII\_A § 7:

\textbf{Theorem B.2.2.} \emph{Suppose \(S\) affine with ring \(A\). Then
the functor}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ⟼ Lie G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{establishes an equivalence of categories between, on the one hand,
the category of \(S\)-preschemes in groups \(G\) of finite presentation
and flat over \(S\), of height 1, whose Lie algebra is locally free over
\texttt{O\_S},}

\emph{and, on the other hand, the category of restricted \(p\)-\(A\)-Lie
algebras locally free of finite rank.}

\emph{Moreover, if \(G\) is as above and if \(H\) is an \(S\)-prescheme
in groups of finite presentation, the canonical morphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr\}(G, H) ⟶ Hom\_\{p{-}A{-}Lie\}(Lie G(S), Lie H(S))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an isomorphism.}

\subsubsection{B.3. Radicial groups and smooth
groups}\label{b.3.-radicial-groups-and-smooth-groups}

We now suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\) of
characteristic \(p\).

Let us recall that in Exp. VI\_A § 5, it was shown that if \(G\) is a
\(k\)-algebraic group, \(H\) an algebraic subgroup of \(G\), then the
sheaf \(G/H\) (sheaf for the fpqc topology) is representable. Recall
then (VII\_A 8.3):

\textbf{Proposition B.3.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a \(k\)-algebraic group.
Then there exists an integer \(m\) such that for every
\(n \geqslant m\), the algebraic group \(G / F_{n}(G)\) is smooth over
\(k\).}

\textbf{Proposition B.3.2.} \emph{Consider an exact sequence of
\(k\)-algebraic groups:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → G\textquotesingle{} → G ─u→ G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} → 1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and the following assertions:}

\emph{i) The morphism \(u\) is smooth.}

\emph{ii) \(G'\) is smooth over \(k\).}

\emph{iii) For every integer \(n > 0\), one has the exact sequence:}

\[
1 \longrightarrow F_{n}(G') \longrightarrow F_{n}(G) \longrightarrow F_{n}(G'') \longrightarrow 1.
\]

\emph{iv) The morphism \(F G \to F G''\) is an epimorphism.}

\emph{v) The morphism \((Lie G)(k) \to (Lie G'')(k)\) is surjective.}

\emph{Then one has the following implications:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i) ⇔ ii) ⇒ iii) ⇒ iv) ⇔ v).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, if \(G\) is smooth, the five assertions are equivalent.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\roman{enumi})}
\item
  ⇔ ii) by Exp. VI\_B 9.2 vii).
\item
  ⇒ iii). If \(G'\) is smooth, \(F_{n} : G' \to G'^{(n)}\) is an
  epimorphism and iii) follows from the snake lemma diagram.
\item
  ⇒ iv) is clear.
\item
  ⇔ v) by Theorem B.2.2.
\item
  ⇒ ii) when \(G\) is smooth. Indeed
  \texttt{G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is then smooth, and v)
  entails that one has
  \texttt{dim\ G\textquotesingle{}\ =\ dim\_k(Lie\ G\textquotesingle{})(k)},
  hence \(G'\) is smooth.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{C. Appendix III. Remarks and complements concerning Exposés
XV, XVI,
XVII}\label{c.-appendix-iii.-remarks-and-complements-concerning-exposuxe9s-xv-xvi-xvii}

\subsubsection{C.1.}\label{c.1.}

It may be that propositions 1.2 and 1.2 bis of XV remain true if one
removes the hypothesis that \(H'\) is smooth over \(S'\). This is in
particular the case if \(G\) is finite, flat, and commutative.

\subsubsection{C.2. Complement to XV
4.8}\label{c.2.-complement-to-xv-4.8}

The following proposition, as well as Theorems C.3.1 and C.4.1 below,
will appear in a paper in preparation by M. Raynaud on group schemes
over a discrete valuation ring.\footnote{N.D.E.: comments to be added
  here, including references to VI\_B\ldots{}}

\textbf{Proposition C.2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a
discrete valuation ring, \(t\) its generic point, \(G\) an
\(S\)-prescheme in groups of finite type and flat,
\(\tilde{G} = \operatorname{Spec} \Gamma(G, O_{G})\),
\(u : G \to \tilde{G}\) the canonical morphism. Then:}

\emph{(1) \(\tilde{G}\) is naturally an \(S\)-group scheme and \(u\) is
a homomorphism.}

\emph{(2) \(Ker(u)\) is flat over \(S\) and \((\tilde{G}, u)\) is an
fpqc quotient of \(G\) by \(Ker(u)\), so that \(\tilde{G}\) is the
largest affine quotient of \(G\).}

\emph{(3) If \(G_{t}\) is affine, \(Ker(u)\) is an étale group over
\(S\), equal to the trivial group if and only if \(G\) is separated over
\(S\). In particular, an \(S\)-group scheme \(G\), flat, of finite type,
separated, with affine generic fiber, is affine.}

\subsubsection{C.3.}\label{c.3.}

In the statement of XV 6.6, the hypothesis that \(H\) is equal to its
connected normalizer is unnecessary for the set of points \(s\) of \(S\)
such that \(H_{s}\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G_{s}\) to be an open
set. Indeed, taking up the proof given in paragraph c) preceding Lemma
6.9, and denoting by \(N\) the schematic closure of \(N_{t}\) in \(G\).
Then \(N\) is a closed subscheme in groups of \(G\), flat over \(S\),
majorizing \(H\) and contained in \(N\). It then follows from the
theorem below

that \(G/N\) is representable. Since \(G_{s} / N_{s}\) is proper and
connected, one finishes as in \emph{loc. cit.}

\textbf{Theorem C.3.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: See Theorem 4C in: S.
  Anantharaman, \emph{Schémas en groupes, espaces homogènes et espaces
  algébriques sur une base de dimension 1}, Bull. Soc. Math. France,
  Mém. 33 (1976), 5-79.} \emph{Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a henselian
discrete valuation ring, \(G\) an \(S\)-prescheme in groups locally of
finite type, \(H\) a closed sub-prescheme in groups of \(G\), flat over
\(S\). Then \(G/H\) is representable.}

\subsubsection{C.4. Complement to (XVI
1.1)}\label{c.4.-complement-to-xvi-1.1}

The following theorem refines (VIII 7.9).

\textbf{Theorem C.4.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be the spectrum of a discrete
valuation ring of residue characteristic \(p > 0\), and let \(G\) be a
commutative, smooth \(S\)-group scheme of finite type and separated over
\(S\). Then the following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \({}_{p} G\) is finite over \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(S\)-prescheme \(S'\) and for every
\(S'\)-prescheme in groups \(H'\), of finite presentation over \(S'\),
separated over \(S'\), every \(S'\)-monomorphism \(u : G_{S'} \to H'\)
is an immersion.}

\subsubsection{C.5.}\label{c.5.}

The example (XVII 6.4 a)) provides an example of a smooth group over a
field \(k\), whose unipotent radical is not defined over \(k\). The
following proposition gives a general method for obtaining such groups:

\textbf{Proposition C.5.1.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field, \(K\) a finite
radicial extension of \(k\) of degree \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 1}, \(H\)
a connected, smooth \(K\)-algebraic group of dimension \(r\),
\(G = \prod_{K/k} H/K\), which is a \(k\)-algebraic group, smooth,
connected, of dimension \(r[K : k]\). Let \(u : G_{K} \to H\) be the
canonical homomorphism, and \(R = Ker(u)\). Then:}

\emph{i) The morphism \(u\) is an epimorphism and \(R\) is a smooth,
unipotent, connected algebraic group.}

\emph{ii) If \(U\) is a smooth algebraic subgroup of \(G\) such that
\texttt{U\_K} majorizes \(R\), then \(U = G\).}

\textbf{Corollary.} \emph{Keep the notations of the preceding
proposition.}

\emph{a) If \(H\) is not unipotent, the unipotent radical of
\(G_{\bar{k}}\) is not defined over \(k\).}

\emph{b) If \(H\) is a non-zero abelian variety, \(G\) is not an
extension of an abelian variety by a smooth linear group.}

\emph{c) If \(H\) is not solvable, the solvable radical of
\(G_{\bar{k}}\) is not defined over \(k\), and \(G\) does not possess a
Borel subgroup defined over \(k\).}

Let us first show how the corollary follows from the proposition.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\item
  Let \(U\) be a unipotent radical of \(G\). Then \texttt{U\_K} is the
  unipotent radical of \texttt{G\_K}, hence majorizes \(R\), since \(R\)
  is smooth unipotent connected by i), hence \(U = G\) by ii). Now
  \texttt{G\_K} admits \(H\) as a quotient, and \(H\) is not unipotent
  by hypothesis, hence \(G\) is not unipotent, whence a contradiction.
\item
  If \(G\) is an extension of an abelian variety by a linear group
  \(L\), smooth over \(k\), necessarily \texttt{L\_K} majorizes \(R\),
  hence \(L = G\). Now \(G\) cannot be a linear group since
  \texttt{G\_K} possesses a quotient that is a non-zero abelian variety.
\item
  Let \(S\) (resp. \(B\)) be a solvable radical of \(G\) (resp. a Borel
  subgroup of \(G\)); then \texttt{S\_K} (resp. \texttt{B\_K}) majorizes
  \(R\), hence \(S = G\) (resp. \(B = G\)). But then \(G\) is solvable,
  which contradicts the fact that \texttt{G\_K} possesses a quotient
  that is not solvable.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Proof of Proposition C.5.1.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Let us begin by describing the morphism \(u\). The data of a
  \(K\)-scheme
\end{enumerate}

\[
f : S \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)
\]

allows one to construct the diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Spec(K) ←─h──── T ──jT──→ X}
\NormalTok{   ↓ j           ↓ s}
\NormalTok{   ↓             ↓}
\NormalTok{Spec(k) ←──g──── S          (where g = j ∘ f)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(T = \operatorname{Spec}(K) \times_{\operatorname{Spec}(k)} S\),
\(h\) and \texttt{jT} are the two projections, and \(s\) is the section
of \(T\) over \(S\) such that \(h \circ s = f\). The map

\[
u(S) : G_{K}(S) \longrightarrow H(S)
\]

is simply the composite map:

\[
G_{K}(S) \xrightarrow{\sim} H(T) \to H(S),
\]

where the last arrow is defined by the section \(s\).

Take in particular for \(S\) the spectrum of an algebraic closure
\(\bar{k}\) of \(k\) and for \(f\) the unique \(k\)-morphism
\(K \to \bar{k}\), so that \(T\) is a local Artinian scheme. To prove i)
it suffices to do so after extension \(K \to \bar{k}\) of the base
field. Now it is clear that \(G_{S} = \prod_{T/S} H_{T} / T\) represents
the Greenberg functor of \texttt{H\_T} relative to \(S\) (M. J.
Greenberg, \emph{Schemata over local rings}, Ann. of Maths. 73, 1961,
p.~624-648). The description made above then shows that, by means of
this last identification, \(u_{S}\) is the canonical transition
morphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Green(H\_T) ⟶ H\_S = H\_T ×\_T S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Assertion i) then follows from the fact that \(H\) is smooth over \(K\)
and from (M. J. Greenberg, \emph{Schemata over local rings II}, Ann. of
Maths. 78, 1963, p.~256-266).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  To establish ii) we may suppose \(k\) separably closed. Let \(U\) be a
  smooth algebraic subgroup of \(G\) such that \(U_{K} \supset R\), and
  let us show that \(U = G\).
\end{enumerate}

Since \(G\) is connected, we may suppose \(U\) connected. Let \(V\) be
the smooth connected algebraic subgroup \(u(U_{K})\) of \(H\), and
\(V' = \prod_{K/k} V/K\), which is a smooth connected algebraic subgroup
of \(G\). The group \(V'_{K}\) is an algebraic subgroup of
\texttt{G\_K}, and the canonical morphism \(V'_{K} \to V\) is simply the
restriction of \(u\) to \(V'_{K}\). By hypothesis, \texttt{U\_K}
majorizes \(R\), \emph{a fortiori} \texttt{U\_K} majorizes
\(Ker(V'_{K} \to V)\); on the other hand, by construction, the image of
\texttt{U\_K} in \(H\) is equal to \(V\). One deduces that \texttt{U\_K}
majorizes \(V'_{K}\), hence \(U\) majorizes \(V'\). On the other hand,
the canonical isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G(k) ↪ G(K) ─u(K)→ H(K)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

evidently sends \(U(k)\) into \(V(K) = V'(k)\); that is to say, \(U(k)\)
is contained in \texttt{V\textquotesingle{}(k)}. Since \(U\) is smooth
and \(k\) is separably closed, this entails \(U \subset V'\), whence
\(U = V'\). One then has the equalities:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{([K : k] − 1) dim V = dim Ker(V\textquotesingle{}\_K → V) = dim R = ([K : k] − 1) dim H.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(K \neq k\), one concludes that \(\dim V = \dim H\), whence
\(V = H\) and finally \(U = V' = G\).

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-6}

\section{Exposé XVIII. Weil's theorem on the construction of a group
from a rational
law}\label{exposuxe9-xviii.-weils-theorem-on-the-construction-of-a-group-from-a-rational-law}

\emph{by Michael Artin}

\subsection{0. Introduction}\label{introduction-3}

This Exposé is devoted to the well-known theorem of Weil {[}1{]} which
gives the construction of a group variety from a birational law. It
seems that the generalization of this result to the case where the base
is the spectrum of a discrete valuation ring was already known to
several people; one may consult, for example, {[}2{]}. Here we shall
prove the theorem for a flat group of finite presentation over an
arbitrary base prescheme \(S\). Since the hypotheses must be made with
somewhat more care, the statement is not in the form given by Weil; but
when \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, one sees that the form given here
is essentially equivalent to Weil's. We use the following suggestion of
Grothendieck: given a ``group germ'' \(X\) over a prescheme \(S\), one
is to construct the group as the quotient of \(X \times_{S} X\) by a
suitable equivalence relation.

\subsection{1. ``Recollections'' on rational
maps}\label{recollections-on-rational-maps}

Let \(X/S\) be a relative prescheme and \(U \subseteq X\) an open
subset. We say that \(U\) is \emph{schematically dense in \(X\)
relatively to \(S\)}, or that \(U \hookrightarrow X\) is
\emph{relatively schematically dense}, if for every base change
\(S' \to S\) the open subset \(U \times_{S} S'\) is schematically dense
in \(X \times_{S} S'\). For the definition and properties of this notion
we refer to Exp. IX, § 4.\footnote{cf.~also EGA IV₃, 11.9 and 11.10
  (notably 11.10.8), where one says ``universally schematically dense
  relatively to \(S\)''.}

\textbf{Proposition 1.1.} \emph{(i) A finite intersection, as well as a
union of a non-empty family of opens that are schematically dense
relatively to \(S\), is schematically dense relatively to \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(U \subseteq X\) is schematically dense relatively to
\(S\) and if \(S \to T\) is a morphism, then \(U_{T} \subseteq X_{T}\)
is schematically dense relatively to \(T\).}

\emph{(iii) Let \(U \subseteq V \subseteq X\) be open immersions. For
\(U\) to be schematically dense in \(X\) relatively to \(S\), it is
necessary and sufficient that it be so in \(V\) and that \(V\) be so in
\(X\).}

\emph{(iv) If \(U \subseteq X\) and \(V \subseteq Y\) are relatively
schematically dense, then \(U \times_{S} V\) is schematically dense in
\(X \times_{S} Y\) relatively to \(S\).}

In Exp. IX one finds the following criterion:

\textbf{Proposition 1.2.} \emph{Let \(X/S\) be locally of finite
presentation and flat, and let \(U\) be an open subset of \(X\). If for
each \(s \in S\) the fiber \(U_{s}\) is schematically dense in
\(X_{s}\), then \(U\) is schematically dense in \(X\) relatively to
\(S\).}

In particular:

\textbf{Corollary 1.3.} \emph{If \(X/S\) is locally of finite
presentation and flat, and if each fiber \(X_{s}\) is ``without embedded
component'', then \(U\) is schematically dense in \(X\) relatively to
\(S\) if and only if for each \(s \in S\), \(U_{s}\) is dense in
\(X_{s}\) in the topological sense.}

One easily deduces from the definition the following:

\textbf{Proposition 1.4.} \emph{Let \(U \subseteq X\) be schematically
dense relatively to \(S\), and let \(f, g : X \to Y\) be two morphisms
of functors over \(S\), where \(Y\) satisfies one of the following
conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(Y\) is a prescheme over \(S\) and each fiber \(Y_{s}\) is
separated.}

\emph{(ii) \(Y\) is a presheaf\footnote{N.D.E.: to be made precise for
  which topology: a priori (fpqc).} on \(S\) such that the diagonal
morphism \(Y \to Y \times_{S} Y\) is representable by a closed
immersion.\footnote{N.D.E.: We recall here the definition of a closed
  immersion. A morphism of \(S\)-functors \(F \to G\) is
  \emph{relatively representable} if for every \(S\)-morphism
  \(T \to G\), where \(T\) is an \(S\)-prescheme, the \(T\)-functor
  \(F_{T} = F \times_{S} T\) is representable by a \(T\)-prescheme. A
  morphism of \(S\)-functors \(F \to G\) is an \emph{open} (resp.
  \emph{closed}) \emph{immersion} if it is relatively representable and
  if for every \(S\)-morphism \(T \to G\), where \(T\) is an
  \(S\)-prescheme, the \(T\)-morphism \(F_{T} \to T\) is an open (resp.
  closed) immersion.}}

\emph{Then if \(f = g\) on \(U\), one has \(f = g\).}

\emph{Proof.} In case (i), the standard argument following IX 4.1 shows
that \(f\) and \(g\) are equal on each fiber, so that the subprescheme
\(Ker(f, g)\) of \(X\) is set-theoretically equal to \(X\), hence
closed; and since it majorizes \(U\), it is equal to \(X\),
i.e.~\(f = g\). Case (ii) is proved as in \emph{loc. cit.}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  To be made precise\ldots{}}

\textbf{Definition 1.5.}\footnote{cf.~EGA IV₄, 20.5, where one says
  ``pseudo-morphism of \(X\) into \(Y\) relatively to \(S\)'', in order
  not to conflict with EGA I, 7.12.} \emph{Let \(X\) be a prescheme over
\(S\) and \(Y\) a presheaf over \(S\). By a} rational map
\(f : X \dashrightarrow Y\) over \(S\) \emph{we mean an equivalence
class of morphisms \(f : U \to Y\) over \(S\), where \(U\) is an open of
\(X\) that is schematically dense relatively to \(S\), and where one
sets \((f : U \to Y) \sim (f' : U' \to Y)\) if and only if there exists
an open \(U'' \subseteq U' \cap U\), schematically dense relatively to
\(S\), such that \(f = f'\) on
\texttt{U\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}.}

This definition is made in such a way that one may define in the obvious
way the rational map \(f \times_{S} S'\) for any base change
\(S' \to S\).

If \(U\) is an open of \(X\), we say that the rational map \(f\) is
\emph{defined on \(U\)} if there exists a morphism representing \(f\)
whose set of definition contains \(U\).

\textbf{Definition 1.5.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: The number 1.5.1 has been
  added.} \emph{If \(Y\) satisfies one of the conditions (i), (ii) of
1.4, it is clear that there exists a largest open \(U\) of \(X\) on
which \(f\) is defined, and this \(U\) is schematically dense relatively
to \(S\). It is called the} domain of definition of \(f\) over \(S\),
\emph{and is denoted \(Dom(f)\).}

This notion does not commute with base change in general, but one has:

\textbf{Proposition 1.6.} \emph{Let \(X\) be an \(S\)-prescheme and
\(Y\) an \(S\)-functor satisfying one of the hypotheses (i), (ii) of
1.4. Let \(f : X \dashrightarrow Y\) be a rational map over \(S\), let
\(S' \to S\) be a flat morphism locally of finite presentation, and set
\(f' = f \times_{S} S'\). Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Dom(f\textquotesingle{}) = Dom(f) ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Set \(U = Dom(f)\). It is clear that \(V' = Dom(f')\)
contains \(U \times_{S} S'\). Let \(V\) be the image of \(V'\), which is
an open of \(X\) because \(X' \to X\) is open. We must show that
\(V = U\), that is, we must find a morphism \(V \to Y\) that represents
\(f\). Set \(S'' = S' \times_{S} S'\), and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} = X ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{},   U\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} = U ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{},   V\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} = V\textquotesingle{} ×\_V V\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then \texttt{U\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is schematically
dense in \texttt{X\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} relatively to
\texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}, hence
\texttt{U\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is schematically dense in
\texttt{V\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} relatively to \(S\),
since \(U'' \subseteq V'' \subseteq X''\). The restriction of
\(f' : V' \to Y'\) to \(U'\) is deduced from \(f : U \to Y\) by base
change. The two morphisms \(V'' \to Y\) deduced from \(g\) by base
change are equal on \texttt{U\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}},
hence are equal. Now since \(V' \to V\) is flat and locally of finite
presentation, it is fppf-covering (Exp. IV 6.3), and one finds the
morphism \(V \to Y\) by descent.

We shall make frequent use of the following triviality:

\textbf{Proposition 1.7.} \emph{Let \(X/S\) be faithfully flat, locally
of finite presentation, and let \(U \subseteq X\) be a relatively
schematically dense open. Then there exists a base change \(S' \to S\)
which is fppf-covering, and a section \(x \in X(S')\) which is contained
in \(U(S')\).}

Indeed, \(U/S\) is fppf-covering. One takes \(S' = U\) and the
\(S\)-graph of the inclusion of \(U\) in \(X\) as the section.

\subsection{2. Local determination of a group
morphism}\label{local-determination-of-a-group-morphism}

Let \(G\) and \(H\) be groups and let \(U \subseteq G\) be a subset such
that \(U \cdot U = G\). Then if \(f\) and \(g\) are homomorphisms from
\(G\) to \(H\) such that \(f = g\) on \(U\), one has \(f = g\).
Similarly:

\textbf{Proposition 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a site (cf.~Exp.
IV\footnote{N.D.E.: i.e.~a category equipped with a topology, cf.~IV, §
  4.2.}), \(G\) a sheaf of groups on \(S\), and \(U \subseteq G\) a
subsheaf of sets such that the morphism \(U \times U \to G\) induced by
multiplication is an epimorphism. Then if \(f\) and \(g\) are
homomorphisms from \(G\) to a sheaf of groups \(H\) that are equal on
\(U\), one has \(f = g\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.2.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group prescheme
locally of finite presentation and flat, let \(U \subseteq G\) be an
open that is relatively schematically dense, and let \(H\) be a sheaf of
groups on \(S\) for the fppf topology. Then every homomorphism
\(f : G \to H\) is determined by its restriction to \(U\).}

Indeed, since \(G\) is flat over \(S\), the composition law on \(G\) is
a flat morphism (VI\_B.9.2.xi), and it follows that
\(U \times_{S} U \to G\) is faithfully flat and locally of finite
presentation, hence fppf-covering, hence an epimorphism.

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a group prescheme locally
of finite presentation and flat over \(S\), \(U \subseteq G\) a
relatively schematically dense open, and \(H\) a sheaf of groups for the
fppf topology. Write \(m_{G}\) for the multiplication of \(G\) and
\(m_{H}\) for that of \(H\).}

\emph{Let \(f : U \to H\) be an \(S\)-morphism and assume that there
exists a relatively schematically dense open \(V\) of
\(m^{-1}_{G}(U) \cap U \times_{S} U\) such that the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{            (f × f)|V}
\NormalTok{       V ───────────────→ H ×\_S H}
\NormalTok{       │                     │}
\NormalTok{  m\_G  │                     │ m\_H}
\NormalTok{       ▼          f          ▼}
\NormalTok{       U ───────────────────→ H}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is commutative. Then there exists a morphism of \(S\)-groups
\(\bar{f} : G \to H\) (necessarily unique) extending \(f\), in each of
the following situations:}

\emph{(i) \(H\) is representable.}

\emph{(ii) The diagonal morphism \(H \to H \times_{S} H\) is
representable by a closed immersion.\footnote{N.D.E.: See the note at
  1.4.}}

\emph{(iii) For each section \(a \in U(S)\), the open
\(pr_{2}((a \times_{S} U) \cap V)\) is relatively schematically dense in
\(U\)\footnote{Or in \(G\), which amounts to the same by virtue of 1.1
  (iv).}, and this statement remains true after every base change
\(S' \to S\).}

\emph{Proof.} Note first that \(V\) is relatively schematically dense in
\(G \times_{S} G\). Indeed, \(V\) is relatively schematically dense in

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{m\_G⁻¹(U) ∩ (U ×\_S G) ∩ (G ×\_S U),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the three factors are deduced from \(U \subseteq G\) by an obvious
base change \(G \times_{S} G \to G\), which implies the assertion by
1.1.

To construct a morphism \(\bar{f} : G \to H\), it suffices, since
\(U \times_{S} U \to G\) is fppf-covering, to find a morphism from
\(U \times_{S} U\) to \(H\) such that the two morphisms induced on
\((U \times_{S} U) \times_{G} (U \times_{S} U)\) are the same.

We take \(m_{H} \circ (f \times f) : U \times_{S} U \to H\). We must
verify that whenever we have sections \(a, b, c, d \in U(S')\),
\(S' \to S\) arbitrary, such that \(ab = cd\), we also have
\(f(a)f(b) = f(c)f(d)\). By hypothesis, this is true if \((a, b)\) and
\((c, d)\) are contained in \(V(S')\), since in that case
\(f(a)f(b) = f(ab)\) and \(f(c)f(d) = f(cd)\). Therefore it is true
whenever \((a, b, c, d) \in (V \times_{G} V)(S')\).

I claim that \(V \times_{G} V\) is an open of
\((U \times_{S} U) \times_{G} (U \times_{S} U)\) schematically dense
relatively to \(S\). This will complete the proof in cases (i) and (ii)
by 1.4, the facts that the morphism \(\bar{f}\) so constructed extends
\(f\) and that \(\bar{f}\) is a homomorphism being evident, again by
1.4.

Indeed, we write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V ×\_G V = (V ×\_G (G ×\_S G)) ∩ ((G ×\_S G) ×\_G V).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By symmetry and 1.1, it suffices to verify that
\(V \times_{G} (G \times_{S} G)\) is relatively schematically dense in
\((G \times_{S} G) \times_{G} (G \times_{S} G)\). But this last
prescheme is \(S\)-isomorphic to \(G \times_{S} G \times_{S} G\), the
morphism being given by \((a, b, c, d) \mapsto (a, b, c)\). Thus what
must be shown is that \(V \times_{S} G\) is schematically dense in
\(G \times_{S} G \times_{S} G\) relatively to \(S\), which is a
consequence of the fact that \(V\) is relatively schematically dense in
\(G \times_{S} G\).

It remains to treat case (iii). To prove \(f(a)f(b) = f(c)f(d)\), it is
permitted to make an fppf-covering base change. Suppose we have a
section \(x \in G(S')\), \(S' \to S\) fppf-covering, such that
\((b, x)\), \texttt{(a,\ bx)}, \((d, x)\), \texttt{(c,\ dx)} are all in
\(V\). Then one will have

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(a)f(b)f(x) = f(a)f(bx) = f(abx) = f(cdx) = f(c)f(dx) = f(c)f(d)f(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence the desired equality.

\footnote{N.D.E.: The beginning of the following sentence has been
  added.} To find such an \(x\), set, for every \(z \in U(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V\_z = pr₂((z ×\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\} U\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}) ∩ V\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then the hypotheses on \(x\) say that \(x \in W\), where

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W = V\_b(S\textquotesingle{}) ∩ V\_d(S\textquotesingle{}) ∩ b⁻¹ V\_a(S\textquotesingle{}) ∩ d⁻¹ V\_c(S\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By (iii), \(W\) is relatively schematically dense in \(G\). Hence the
existence of a section \(x\) after an fppf-covering extension follows
from Proposition 1.7.

Let us verify that the morphism so constructed is multiplicative. Let
\(a, b \in G(S')\), \(S' \to S\) arbitrary, and write \(S_{0} = S\).
Choose an fppf-covering base change \(S' \to S\) and a section
\(x \in G(S')\) such that \(x \in U(S')\) and \(ax^{-1} \in U(S')\),
that is, \(x \in (a^{-1}U)^{-1}(S')\). Choose moreover another
fppf-covering extension \(S'' \to S'\) and a section \(y \in G(S'')\)
such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y, by⁻¹, aby⁻¹    belong to U(S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{by⁻¹ ∈ V\_x,   xby⁻¹ ∈ V\_\{ax⁻¹\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then by the definition of \(\bar{f}\), one has on
\texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f̄(a) = f(ax⁻¹)f(x),   f̄(b) = f(by⁻¹)f(y),   f̄(ab) = f(aby⁻¹)f(y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover,

\[
\bar{f}(a)\bar{f}(b) = f(ax^{-1})f(x)f(by^{-1})f(y) = f(ax^{-1})f(xby^{-1})f(y)
        = f(aby^{-1})f(y) = \bar{f}(ab),
\]

whence multiplicativity.

The fact that \(\bar{f}\) extends \(f\) is now easy. Let
\(a \in U(S')\), write \(S_{0} = S\), and choose \(S' \to S\)
fppf-covering and sections \(x, y \in G(S')\) such that \((x, y)\),
\texttt{(ax,\ y)}, \texttt{(a,\ xy)} are in \(V(S')\). Then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f̄(xy) = f(x)f(y) = f(xy),    f̄(axy) = f(ax)f(y) = f(axy).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Hence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f̄(a) = f̄(axy)f̄((xy)⁻¹) = f̄(axy)f̄(xy)⁻¹ = f(axy)f(xy)⁻¹ = f(a).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 2.3.1.} \emph{In many cases hypothesis (iii) is true, for
it will even be true if one replaces \(U\) by a smaller open \(U^{0}\),
still relatively schematically dense in \(G\). For example one has:}

\textbf{Proposition 2.4.} \emph{The situation being as in 2.3, suppose
that each geometric fiber of \(G/S\) is irreducible. Let
\(U^{0} = pr_{1} V\) and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V⁰ = V ∩ m\_G⁻¹(U⁰) ∩ (U⁰ ×\_S U⁰).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(U^{0} \subseteq U\) is an open relatively schematically
dense of \(G\) and the objects \(U^{0}\), \(f|U^{0}\) and \(V^{0}\)
satisfy hypothesis (iii).}

\emph{Proof.} \(U^{0}\) is open because \(G \times_{S} G \to G\) is flat
and locally of finite presentation. All the other verifications are
trivial save hypothesis (iii).

Let \(a \in U(S')\), write \(S_{0} = S\). To verify that
\(pr_{2}((a \times_{S} U^{0}) \cap V^{0})\) is relatively schematically
dense in \(U^{0}\), it suffices to do so fiber by fiber by Corollary
1.3, that is, it suffices to treat the case where \(S\) is the spectrum
of a field, and in that case it suffices to show that \(U^{0}\) is
non-empty, because \(G\) is irreducible and ``without embedded
components'' (cf.~VI\_A, 1.1.1). Now

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pr₂((a ×\_S U⁰) ∩ V⁰) = pr₂((a ×\_S U⁰) ∩ V) ∩ pr₂((a ×\_S U⁰) ∩ m\_G⁻¹(U⁰))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the second term of the right-hand side is dense in \(G\). Hence it
suffices to show that \(pr_{2}((a \times_{S} U^{0}) \cap V)\) is dense
in \(G\), that is, non-empty, which is clear because
\(a \in U^{0} = pr_{1} V\).

\subsection{3. Construction of a group from a rational
law}\label{construction-of-a-group-from-a-rational-law}

\subsubsection{3.0.}\label{section-215}

We are given a prescheme \(X/S\) and a rational map
\(X \times_{S} X \dashrightarrow X\) over \(S\), and we seek a group
\(G/S\) and a birational map relatively to \(S\)\footnote{N.D.E.: To
  make explicit the notion of birational map (relatively to \(S\)),
  perhaps in an addition 1.5.2?}

\[
X \dashrightarrow G
\]

that commutes with the composition laws. We treat only the case where
\(X/S\) satisfies the following hypothesis:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(♦)   X/S is faithfully flat, of finite presentation, and}
\NormalTok{      with separated fibers "without embedded components".}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(Note that the latter two hypotheses are properties that hold for a
group prescheme.\footnote{N.D.E.: cf.~VI\_A, to be made precise\ldots{}})

We shall often suppress the symbol \(S\) in fiber products.

Let \(X/S\) be a prescheme with the properties \texttt{(♦)} above, and
let \(W\) be a subprescheme of finite presentation of
\(X \times X \times X\) having the following property:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)   The three morphisms W → X × X given by the projections of X³ onto X²}
\NormalTok{      are open immersions, schematically dense relatively to S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Notations.} We shall use the following terminology. Given
sections \(a, b, c \in X(S')\), \(S' \to S\) arbitrary, such that
\((a, b, c) \in W(S')\), we write:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{c = ab,    b = a⁻¹c,    a = cb⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 3.0.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have introduced the
  numbering 3.0.1 and 3.0.2.} \emph{We say, given a section
\((a, b) \in X^{2}(S')\), that \texttt{ab}} is defined \emph{if and only
if there exists a section \(c \in X(S')\) such that
\((a, b, c) \in W(S')\), i.e.~if and only if \((a, b)\) lies in
\(pr_{12} W(S')\). Similarly, to say that \(a^{-1}b\) or \(ab^{-1}\) is
defined has the analogous meaning, and one extends this terminology to
products of several factors as well.}

\textbf{Remark 3.0.2.} \emph{Let us note immediately the following fact:
by (i), \(W\) defines a rational map \(X^{2} \dashrightarrow X\) over
\(S\) (the one given by \((a, b) \mapsto ab\)). It may well happen that
this rational map has a domain of definition larger than \(pr_{12} W\).
Nevertheless, we say that \texttt{ab} is defined only if
\((a, b) \in pr_{12} W(S')\).}

\textbf{Definition 3.1.} \emph{A} group germ \emph{is a prescheme
\(X/S\) having the properties \texttt{(♦)} above together with a
subprescheme \(W\) of finite presentation of \(X \times X \times X\)
having the following properties:}

\emph{(i) \(W\) satisfies the property \((\ast)\) above.}

\emph{(ii) For each section \(a \in X(S)\), the sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pr\_i((a × X × X) ∩ W),    i = 2, 3,}
\NormalTok{pr\_i((X × a × X) ∩ W),    i = 3, 1,}
\NormalTok{pr\_i((X × X × a) ∩ W),    i = 1, 2,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are schematically dense in \(X\) relatively to \(S\), and this
statement remains true after every base change \(S' \to S\). (Hypothesis
(i) implies that these sets are opens of \(X\).) Intuitively, this says
that ``\texttt{ax} is defined for \(x\) sufficiently general'', etc.}

\emph{(iii) The law is associative, i.e.~if \((a, b, c) \in X^{3}(S')\),
\(S' \to S\) arbitrary, is such that \texttt{(ab)c} and \(a(bc)\) are
defined, one has \((ab)c = a(bc)\).}

\textbf{Remarks.} \emph{(a) In (i), the condition that \(W\) be
schematically dense in \(X^{2}\) relatively to \(S\) may be replaced by
the condition that for each \(s \in S\) the fiber \(W_{s}\) be dense in
\(X^{2}_{s}\) in the topological sense, thanks to the hypotheses on
\(X\) and to 1.2.}

\emph{(b) Condition (iii) is equivalent to the following: let \(V_{1}\)
(resp. \(V_{2}\)) be the open of \(X^{3}\) where the rational map
\((a, b, c) \mapsto a(bc)\) (resp. \((a, b, c) \mapsto (ab)c\)) is
defined\footnote{In the sense explained in 3.0.1; one could also replace
  these opens by the domains of definition (cf.~1.5) of the rational
  maps in question.}. Then there exists an open
\(V \subseteq V_{1} \cap V_{2}\) which is schematically dense in
\(X^{3}\) relatively to \(S\) on which the two preceding maps coincide.
This is a consequence of 1.4 because, of course, \(V_{1}\) and \(V_{2}\)
are schematically dense in \(X^{3}\) relatively to \(S\).}

\emph{(c) Hypothesis (ii) will serve below to ensure that \(X\) will be
a subobject of the group prescheme that it defines. In many cases one
may deduce (ii) from (i), provided that one replaces \(X\) by an open
\(X^{0}\) relatively schematically dense, and \(W\) by a relatively
schematically dense open of \(W \cap X^{03}\). In fact one has:}

\textbf{Proposition 3.2.} \emph{Suppose that each geometric fiber of
\(X/S\) is irreducible, and let \(W\) be a subprescheme of \(X^{3}\)
satisfying condition (i) of 3.1. Then there exists an open \(X^{0}\) of
\(X\) relatively schematically dense and an open \(W^{0}\) of
\(W \cap (X^{0} \times X^{0})\) relatively schematically dense such that
the pair \((X^{0}, W^{0})\) satisfies conditions (i) and (ii). If (iii)
is satisfied for \((X, W)\), it is satisfied for \((X^{0}, W^{0})\).}

\emph{Proof.} Set \(X^{0} = \bigcap^{3}_{i=1} pr_{i} W\). Each
\(pr_{i} W\) is open in \(X\) because \(W \to X^{2}\) is an open
immersion and the projections \(X^{2} \to X\) are flat and of finite
presentation. Moreover, \(pr_{i} W\) is relatively schematically dense
in \(X\) because \(W\) is so in \(X^{2}\) and the projections
\(X^{2} \to X\) are surjective (it suffices to check density in the
topological sense). Take \(W^{0} = W \cap X^{03}\).

To verify that (i) holds, note that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W⁰ = (W ∩ (X⁰ × X⁰ × X)) ∩ (W ∩ (X × X⁰ × X⁰)) ∩ (W ∩ (X⁰ × X × X⁰)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now
\(W \cap (X^{0} \times X^{0} \times X) \simeq pr_{12} W \cap (X^{0} \times X^{0})\),
hence is relatively schematically dense in \(W\). Similarly, the other
terms of the right-hand side are relatively schematically dense in
\(W\), and consequently \(W^{0}\) is relatively schematically dense in
\(W\). Hence \(pr_{ij} W^{0}\) is relatively schematically dense in
\(pr_{ij} W\), hence in \(X \times X\), hence in \(X^{0} \times X^{0}\).

To verify condition (ii), let \(a \in X^{0}(S')\) and write
\(S_{0} = S\). We must show that, for example,
\(pr_{2}((a \times X^{0} \times X^{0}) \cap W^{0})\) is schematically
dense in \(X^{0}\) relatively to \(S\). By 1.3, it suffices to verify
this fiber by fiber, that is, it suffices to treat the case where \(S\)
is the spectrum of a field, and in that case it suffices to verify that
the open is non-empty, because the fibers of \(X/S\) are irreducible and
``without embedded components''. Since
\(pr_{2}((a \times X \times X) \cap W)\) is non-empty (as \(a\) is a
section of \(X^{0}\)), this open is dense in \(X\). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pr₂((a × X × X) ∩ W) = pr₂((a × X) ∩ pr₁₂ W).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Hence,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pr₂((a × X) ∩ pr₁₂ W) ∩ X⁰ = pr₂((a × X⁰) ∩ pr₁₂ W) = pr₂((a × X⁰ × X) ∩ W)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is dense in \(X\), hence in \(X^{0}\).

Similarly, \(pr_{3}((a \times X \times X^{0}) \cap W)\) is dense in
\(X\), hence in \(pr_{3}((a \times X \times X) \cap W)\),
i.e.~\((a \times X \times X^{0}) \cap W\) is dense in
\((a \times X \times X) \cap W\), i.e.
\(pr_{2}((a \times X \times X^{0}) \cap W)\) is dense in
\(pr_{2}((a \times X \times X) \cap W)\), hence dense in \(X\), hence
dense in \(X^{0}\).

Now since

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pr₂((a × X⁰ × X⁰) ∩ W⁰) = pr₂((a × X⁰ × X⁰) ∩ W)}
\NormalTok{                       = pr₂((a × X⁰ × X) ∩ W) ∩ pr₂((a × X × X⁰) ∩ W),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

it is indeed dense in \(X^{0}\), as was to be shown. The other
assertions of (ii) follow by symmetry, and the fact that condition (iii)
is preserved is trivial.\footnote{N.D.E.: The following sentence has
  been added.} Proposition 3.2 is proved.

\subsubsection{3.2.1.}\label{section-216}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the numbering 3.2.1, as well as 3.2.2.}

Let us now fix a group germ \((X, W)\) over \(S\). We must make some
preliminary remarks on the situation, which we have gathered together
below. We shall use these rules often without explicit mention in the
sequel.

Let \(a \in X(S')\), and write \(S_{0} = S\). Then one obtains a
(bi)rational map \(\phi\) over \(S\) from \(X\) to itself by associating
to a section \(x\) the section \texttt{ax} if it is defined. By 3.1
(ii), the domain of definition of \(\phi\) contains the relatively
schematically dense open \(pr_{2}((a \times X \times X) \cap W)\), and
\(\phi\) defines an isomorphism of this open onto the open (where
\(a^{-1}x\) is defined) \(pr_{3}((a \times X \times X) \cap W)\). This
remark is generalized in the obvious way in Rule 1.

\textbf{Rule 1.} \emph{Let \(P = P(x, t_{1}, \cdots, t_{n})\) be a
``product'' of the symbols \(x, t_{1}, \cdots, t_{n}\) obtained
recursively as follows: \(P_{0} = x\); \(P_{i+1}\) is one of the
following expressions:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P\_i t,   t P\_i,   P\_i⁻¹ t,   t P\_i⁻¹,   P\_i t⁻¹,   t⁻¹ P\_i,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(t\) is one of the \(t_{j}\); \(P_{r} = P\). Let
\(a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n} \in X(S')\). Then there exists a relatively
schematically dense open \(U\) of \(X_{S'}\) such that the product
\(P(x, a_{1}, \cdots, a_{n})\) is defined (in the sense of Remark 3.0.2)
for a section \(x \in X(S'')\) if and only if \(x \in U(S'')\), and the
map \(x \mapsto P(x, (a))\) gives an isomorphism of \(U\) onto another
relatively schematically dense open, denoted \(P(U, (a))\), of
\(X_{S'}\).}

\textbf{Rule 2.} \emph{Let \(a, b \in X(S')\). Then:}

\emph{If \texttt{ab} is defined, so is \(a^{-1}(ab)\), and
\(a^{-1}(ab) = b\).}

\emph{If \(a^{-1}b\) is defined, so is \(a(a^{-1}b)\), and
\(a(a^{-1}b) = b\).}

\emph{If \(ba^{-1}\) is defined, so is \((ba^{-1})a\), and
\((ba^{-1})a = b\).}

\textbf{Rule 3.} \emph{Let \(a, b, b' \in X(S')\). If \(ab = ab'\), if
\(ba = b'a\), if \(a^{-1}b = a^{-1}b'\) or if \(ba^{-1} = b'a^{-1}\),
then \(b = b'\). Here it is implicit that the equality relation implies
that both sides are defined.}

\textbf{Rule 4.} \emph{Let \(a, b, c \in X(S')\). Then whenever both
sides are defined, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a((ba)⁻¹ c) = b⁻¹ c.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Similarly:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(c(ab)⁻¹) a = cb⁻¹,    a⁻¹(ab⁻¹) c = b⁻¹ c,    (c(b⁻¹ a)⁻¹) a = cb⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Rule 5.} \emph{All the following associativity laws are true,
whenever both sides are defined:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(a⁻¹b)c = a⁻¹(bc),    (ab⁻¹)c = a(b⁻¹c),    (ab)c⁻¹ = a(bc⁻¹),}
\NormalTok{(ab)⁻¹c = b⁻¹(a⁻¹c),  (a⁻¹b)c⁻¹ = a⁻¹(bc⁻¹), (ab⁻¹)c⁻¹ = a(cb)⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.2.2. Verification of the
rules.}\label{verification-of-the-rules.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  is by an obvious induction on the length \(r\) of \(P\), the case
  \(r = 1\) being a direct consequence of 3.1 (ii).
\item
  Trivial from the definition.
\item
  Indeed, by Rule 2, for example in the first case, one has
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{b = a⁻¹(ab) = a⁻¹(ab\textquotesingle{}) = b\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Let us verify, for example, the first relation. On the right-hand side
  left multiplication by \(b\) is defined and gives \(c\), by Rule 2.
  Suppose it is also defined on the left-hand side. Then one will have
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{b(a((ba)⁻¹ c)) = (ba)((ba)⁻¹ c) = c.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed \texttt{(ba)} is defined by hypothesis because it figures in the
expression. Hence the middle member is defined and equal to \(c\) by
Rule 2, and equal to the left-hand member by associativity (cf.~3.1
(iii)). Hence Rule 3 implies that the desired equality is true if this
multiplication by \(b\) is defined.

Now fix \(a\) and \(b\). Then Rule 1 implies that \(b(a((ba)^{-1} c))\)
is well defined for \(c\) ``in'' an open \(U\) of \(X\) relatively
schematically dense; hence on this relatively schematically dense open
the two rational maps \(c \mapsto b^{-1} c\) and
\(c \mapsto a((ba)^{-1} c)\) are equal. By 1.4, they are equal on every
common domain of definition, whence the desired result.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\tightlist
\item
  The same kind of argument as the preceding. For example one verifies
  \((ab^{-1})c^{-1} = a(cb)^{-1}\) as follows. If right multiplication
  by \(c\) is defined on the right-hand side, one has equality by Rule
  4. Since it suffices to verify such a formula on a relatively
  schematically dense open, one reduces to the case where this
  multiplication is well defined.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{3.2.3.}\label{section-217}

Consider now the relation \(R\) on \(X \times X\) obtained by setting,
for \(a, b, a', b' \in X(S')\), \((a, b) \sim (a', b') mod R(S')\) if
and only if there exists \(S' \to S\) fppf-covering and a section
\(x \in X(S')\) such that \texttt{(xa)b} and
\texttt{(xa\textquotesingle{})b\textquotesingle{}} are defined and
equal. Then \(R\) is an equivalence relation.

Indeed, this relation is evidently symmetric. By Rule 1, the product
\texttt{(xa)b} is defined if \(x\) is ``in'' a suitable relatively
schematically dense open. Hence 1.7 asserts that there exists
\(S' \to S\) fppf-covering and an \(x \in X(S')\) such that
\texttt{(xa)b} is defined. The relation is therefore reflexive, and
transitivity is a consequence of the following lemma:

\textbf{Lemma 3.3.} \emph{Let
\texttt{x,\ y,\ a,\ b,\ a\textquotesingle{},\ b\textquotesingle{}} be
sections of \(X(S')\) such that \texttt{(xa)b},
\texttt{(xa\textquotesingle{})b\textquotesingle{}}, \texttt{(ya)b},
\texttt{(ya\textquotesingle{})b\textquotesingle{}} are defined. If
\((xa)b = (xa')b'\) then \((ya)b = (ya')b'\).}

Indeed, the lemma says that one may test \((a, b) \sim (a', b')\) with
any \(x \in X(S')\), \(S' \to S\) fppf-covering, such that both products
are defined. Given \(a, b, a', b', a'', b'' \in X(S)\), one may, by Rule
1, 1.1 and 1.7, find an fppf-covering extension \(S' \to S\) and a
section \(x \in X(S')\) such that the three products in question are
defined, whence transitivity.

\emph{Proof of the lemma.} Let us write formally to begin with:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(za)b = ((zx⁻¹)x) a b = ((zx⁻¹)(xa)) b = (zx⁻¹)((xa)b),}
\NormalTok{(za\textquotesingle{})b\textquotesingle{} = ((zx⁻¹)x) a\textquotesingle{} b\textquotesingle{} = ((zx⁻¹)(xa\textquotesingle{})) b\textquotesingle{} = (zx⁻¹)((xa\textquotesingle{})b\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One verifies that these equalities are indeed true if the members are
defined, by the appropriate rules\footnote{N.D.E.: to be made
  precise\ldots{}}. It follows that \((za)b = (za')b'\) if all these
expressions are defined. Moreover, by Rule 1 and the hypotheses already
made, these expressions are well defined if \(z \in X(S'')\) is in
\(V(S'')\), where \(V\) is a certain open of \(X\) relatively
schematically dense (we have taken \(S_{0} = S\)). Hence the two
rational maps from \(X\) to itself given by \(z \mapsto (za)b\) and
\(z \mapsto (za')b'\) are equal, whence \((ya)b = (ya')b'\).

\textbf{Lemma 3.4.} \emph{Consider the rational map
\(\phi : X^{3} \dashrightarrow X\) over \(S\) defined by
\((a, b, c) \mapsto c^{-1}(ab)\). Let \(U\) be the domain of definition
of \(\phi\) and consider the graph \(\Gamma\) of the morphism
\(f : U \to X\) induced by \(\phi\), which is a subscheme of \(X^{4}\).
Then a section \((a, b, c, d) \in X^{4}(S)\) is in \(\Gamma(S)\) if and
only if \((a, b) \sim (c, d)\).}

\emph{Proof.} Note first that the rational map \(\phi\) is the same as
the one given by the formula \((a, b, c) \mapsto (xc)^{-1}((xa)b)\) for
an arbitrary section \(x \in X(S)\). This is the same as saying that one
has \(c^{-1}(ab) = (xc)^{-1}((xa)b)\) whenever both sides are defined.
We leave the verification to the reader.

We show then that the map \(\phi\) is defined at a section
\((a, b, c) \in X^{3}(S)\) if and only if there exists \(d\) with
\((a, b) \sim (c, d)\), and that one then has \(d = \phi(a, b, c)\).
Indeed, suppose that \((a, b) \sim (c, d)\). To verify that \(\phi\) is
defined, it is permitted to make an fppf-covering base change
(Proposition 1.6), and one may therefore assume that there exists a
section \(x \in X(S')\) such that \texttt{(xa)b} and \texttt{(xc)d} are
defined and equal. It follows (Rule 2) that \((xc)^{-1}((xa)b)\) is
defined and equal to \(d\).

Conversely, suppose \(\phi\) is defined at the section \((a, b, c)\) and
let \(d = \phi(a, b, c)\). Choose \(S' \to S\) fppf-covering and a
section \(x \in X(S')\) such that \texttt{(xa)b} and \texttt{(xc)d} are
defined. We want to show that they are equal. For this, it suffices to
show that the two rational maps over \(S\) from \(X\) to itself, given
by \(b \mapsto (xa)b\) and \(b \mapsto (xc)\phi(a, b, c)\), are the
same, which follows from the remark of the first paragraph.

\textbf{Proposition 3.5.} \emph{The equivalence relation
\(R \Rightarrow X^{2}\) is representable, and it is a flat relation of
finite presentation, that is, the projections of \(R\) onto \(X^{2}\)
are flat morphisms of finite presentation.}

\emph{Proof.} We may suppose \(S\) affine. Since \((X, W)\) is of finite
presentation over \(S\), we may descend the whole situation to an \(S\)
of finite type over \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathbb{Z}\), hence
noetherian. We may therefore suppose \(S\) noetherian. Then it is
trivial that the graph \(\Gamma\) of (3.4) is of finite presentation
over \(X^{2}\). The projection \(pr_{12}|\Gamma\) is flat because
\(\Gamma \xrightarrow{\sim} pr_{123} \Gamma\), which is an open of
\(X^{3}\), and the projection \(pr_{12} : X^{3} \to X^{2}\) is flat
because \(X\) is flat over \(S\).

I claim that \(\Gamma\) represents \(R\). Note that there is something
to prove, because the domain of definition of a rational map does not in
general commute with base change. Let \(S'' \to S\). What is clear, by
(3.4) applied to \texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}, is that
\(R(S'') \supset \Gamma(S'')\), because \(\phi \times_{S} S''\) is
certainly defined on \(U \times_{S} S''\). Let then
\((a, b, c, d) \in R(S'')\). We must show that
\((a, b, c, d) \in \Gamma(S'')\). The verification of this is done
locally for, say, the étale topology. We may therefore suppose
\texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} strictly local, i.e.~the
spectrum of a henselian ring with separably closed residue field.
Moreover, by applying (1.6) and the usual passage-to-the-limit standard
arguments, we reduce to the case \(S\) strictly local and \(S'' \to S\)
local. Suppose we have a section \(x \in X(S)\) such that over
\texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} the products
\texttt{(xa)b} and \texttt{(xc)d} are defined. This will imply that
\((xc)^{-1}((xa)b)\) is defined, and equal to \(d\). Now there exists an
open \(V\) of \(X^{3}\) relatively sch. dense such that
\((xc)^{-1}((xa)b)\) is defined if and only if \((a, b, c) \in V(S'')\),
and one has \(V \subseteq U\). Hence \((a, b, c, d) \in \Gamma(S'')\) if
such an \(x\) exists. By (1.6) it is permitted to make a base change
\(S' \to S\) fppf-covering to find such an \(x\). Since \(S\) is
strictly local, one can\footnote{combining Exp. VI\_A, 1.1.1 and EGA
  IV₄, 17.16.2.} find an \(S' \to S\) faithfully flat, local, and finite
and a section \(x \in X(S')\) which ``passes through'' an arbitrary
closed point of the closed fiber of \(X/S\). Now to say that
\texttt{(xa)b} and \texttt{(xc)d} are defined means that over
\texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}, \(x\) lies in a certain
relatively sch. dense open, which is verified on the closed fiber of
\(X_{S''}\). Hence it works.

Let now \(G\) be the quotient of \(X^{2}\) by \(R\) as a sheaf for the
fppf topology. We shall define a composition law on \(G\) as follows.
Let \((g, g') \in G(S')\) be represented by a section
\texttt{((a,\ b),\ (c,\ d))} of \(X^{2} \times X^{2}(S'')\),
\(S'' \to S'\) fppf-covering. Suppose moreover that \(X\) admits a
section \(x\) over \texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} such
that \(a(b(cx))\) and \(x^{-1}d\) are defined, which is permitted by
Rule 1 and (1.7), and we call \texttt{gg\textquotesingle{}} the class in
\(G(S')\) represented by the section \((a(b(cx)), x^{-1}d)\) of
\(X^{2}(S'')\).

Let us verify that \texttt{gg\textquotesingle{}} does not depend on the
choice of the section \(x\) and the representative
\texttt{((a,\ b),\ (c,\ d))}. Indeed, let \((a', b') \sim (a, b)\),
\((c', d') \sim (c, d)\), and \(x'\) be such that
\texttt{a\textquotesingle{}(b\textquotesingle{}(c\textquotesingle{}x\textquotesingle{}))}
and \(x'^{-1}d'\) are defined. We may suppose that all are sections over
\texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}. We must show that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(a(b(cx)), x⁻¹d) ∼ (a\textquotesingle{}(b\textquotesingle{}(c\textquotesingle{}x\textquotesingle{})), x\textquotesingle{}⁻¹d\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, that for a suitable section \(z \in X(S''')\), \(S''' \to S''\)
suitably fppf-covering,

\[
(z(a(b(cx))))(x^{-1}d) = (z(a'(b'(c'x'))))(x'^{-1}d').
\]

Whenever all the products are defined, one has

\[
(z(a(b(cx))))(x^{-1}d) = ((za)(b(cx)))(x^{-1}d) =
                    = (((za)b)(cx))(x^{-1}d) = ((((za)b)c)x)(x^{-1}d) =
                    = (((za)b)c)(x(x^{-1}d)) = (((za)b)c)d,
\]

and the same identities are true with the primes. Now by Rule 1 and
(1.7) there exists such a \(z\). One must therefore show that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(((za)b)c)d = (((za\textquotesingle{})b\textquotesingle{})c\textquotesingle{})d\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \((za)b = (za')b'\) because \((a, b) \sim (a', b')\) (3.3) and one
has the desired equality because \((c, d) \sim (c', d')\).

Consider the natural morphism \(i : X \to G\) defined as follows. For
\(a \in X(S')\), one chooses \(S'' \to S'\) fppf-covering and a section
\(b \in X(S'')\) such that \(ab^{-1}\) is defined, and one sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i(a) = class in G of (ab⁻¹, b).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One easily verifies that this class, which is a priori in \(G(S'')\),
does not depend on the choice of \(b\) and so gives a well-determined
element of \(G(S')\).

The reader will give himself the pleasure of verifying the following:

\textbf{Proposition 3.6.} \emph{The morphism \(i\) commutes with the
composition laws of \(X\) and of \(G\), i.e.~if \(a, b \in X(S')\) are
sections such that \texttt{ab} is defined, one has
\(i(a)i(b) = i(ab)\).}

The goal of this section is the following theorem:

\textbf{Theorem 3.7.}\footnote{N.D.E.: If \(X\) is smooth, separated
  over \(S\), faithfully flat of finite presentation over \(S\), then
  \(G/S\) is representable by an \(S\)-group scheme smooth and of finite
  type over \(S\). This is Theorem 6.6.1 of the book \emph{Néron models}
  of Bosch--Lütkebohmert--Raynaud, Springer (1990).} \emph{Let
\((X, W)\) be a group germ over \(S\), with \(X/S\) faithfully flat, of
finite presentation, and with separated fibers without embedded
component. Then with the notations above one has}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is a sheaf of groups.}

\emph{(ii) \(i : X \to G\) is representable by an open immersion.}

\emph{(iii) \(G\) is representable locally on \(S\) for the fppf
topology.}

\emph{(iv) If \(G/S\) is representable, then it is a flat group of
finite presentation, and \(i : X \to G\) is schematically dense
relatively to \(S\).}

Note that \(G\) is evidently characterized by properties (i), \ldots,
(iv); one may therefore forget the explicit construction of \(G\).

The proof proceeds in several stages:

\textbf{Lemma 3.8.} \emph{(i) Let \(c\) be a section of \(X(S)\); then
the morphism from the prescheme \(c \times X\) (which is
\(S\)-isomorphic to \(X\)) into \(G\) given by
\(c \times X \hookrightarrow X \times X \to G\) is a monomorphism.}

\emph{(ii) Let \({c_{i}}\), \(i \in I\), be sections of \(X(S)\), let
\(Z = \sqcup_{i} c_{i} \times X\), and call \(R^{0} \Rightarrow Z\) the
equivalence relation induced on \(Z\) by the obvious morphism
\(Z \to X^{2}\). Then \(R^{0}\) is a ``gluing'' of the
\(c_{i} \times X \simeq X\).}

\emph{Proof.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  For two sections \((c, a)\) and \texttt{(c,\ a\textquotesingle{})} of
  \((c \times X)(S')\) to have the same image in \(G\), one must have
  \((c, a) \sim (c, a')\), that is, \((xc)a \sim (xc)a'\) for a suitable
  \(x \in X(S'')\), \(S'' \to S'\) fppf-covering, whence \(a = a'\) by
  Rule 3.
\item
  Let \(c_{i}\), \(c_{j}\) be two sections and consider the birational
  map \(\psi_{ji}\) of \(X\) to itself over \(S\) given by the formula
  \(x \mapsto c^{-1}_{j}(c_{i} x)\). This is the same map as the one
  given by \(x \mapsto (yc_{j})^{-1}((yc_{i})x)\), for \(y \in X(S)\),
  as one easily sees. Moreover, one verifies that \(\phi_{ji}\) is
  defined at \(b \in X(S')\) if and only if there exists \(b'\) such
  that \((c_{i}, b) \sim (c_{j}, b')\), and then \(b' = \phi_{ji}(b)\).
  Let \(U_{ji}\) be the domain of definition over \(S\) of
  \(\phi_{ji}\). It remains to show that this domain of definition is
  universal, i.e.~that if \(b \in X(S'')\), \(S'' \to S\) arbitrary, and
  if \(\phi_{ji}\) is defined at \(b\), then \(b \in U_{ji}(S'')\). It
  comes to the same to show that if \(b, b' \in X(S'')\) are such that
  \((c_{i}, b) \sim (c_{j}, b')\), then \(b \in U_{ji}(S'')\). We leave
  the verification of this fact, which is analogous to that of (3.5), to
  the reader.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Lemma 3.9.} \emph{Suppose that \({c_{i}}\), \(i \in I\), are
sections of \(X(S)\) such that \(\sqcup_{i} c_{i} \times X \to G\) is
surjective as a morphism of sheaves. Then \(G\) is representable and
flat, of finite presentation over \(S\), and the structural morphism
\(X^{2} \to G\) is flat and of finite presentation.}

\emph{Proof.} The fact that \(G\) is representable is an immediate
consequence of (3.8), and it follows that
\(\sqcup_{i} c_{i} \times X \to G\) is an open covering. To show that
\(X^{2} \to G\) is flat, it suffices to do so locally, hence to show
that the rational map \(X^{2} \dashrightarrow c_{i} \times X\) induces a
flat morphism on its domain of definition. Now this rational map is
given by \((a, b) \mapsto (c_{i}, ((xc_{i})^{-1}(xa))b)\), \(x\) an
arbitrary section, and if it is defined at \((a, b) \in X^{2}(S')\), one
can find \(S'' \to S'\) fppf-covering and a section \(x \in X(S'')\)
such that \(((xc_{i})^{-1}(xa))b\) is defined. One sees easily that this
is therefore a flat morphism.

It similarly follows that it is locally of finite presentation, hence
fppf-covering. Now by construction, the relation \(R\) is effective.
Hence by (3.5), the morphism \(X^{2} \to G\) becomes of finite
presentation after the base change \(G \leftarrow X^{2}\), which is
fppf-covering; hence \(X^{2} \to G\) is of finite presentation. Let us
show that \(G \to S\) is flat and of finite presentation. It is flat and
locally of finite presentation since \(G\) is covered by the
\(c_{i} \times X \simeq X\). Now \(X^{2}/S\) is quasi-compact, and
\(X^{2} \to G\) is surjective. This shows that \(G/S\) is quasi-compact.
To show that \(G \to S\) is quasi-separated, note that one has the
following cartesian diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              α}
\NormalTok{       R ─────────→ X² ×\_S X²}
\NormalTok{       │                │}
\NormalTok{     γ │                │ β}
\NormalTok{       ▼      Δ         ▼}
\NormalTok{       G ──────────→ G ×\_S G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has \(\gamma\) surjective and \(\alpha, \beta\) quasi-compact, hence
\(\beta \alpha\) is quasi-compact, hence \(\Delta\) is
quasi-compact.\footnote{N.D.E.: Another way to conclude here is by
  faithfully flat descent (EGA IV₂, 2.7.1), since \(\beta\) is
  fppf-covering.}

\textbf{Lemma 3.10.} \emph{Let \({c_{i}}\), \(i \in I\), be sections of
\(X(S)\). For \(\sqcup_{i} c_{i} \times X \to G\) to be surjective as a
morphism of fppf-sheaves, it suffices that the following condition be
satisfied:}

\emph{For each \(S' \to S\) and \((a, b) \in X^{2}(S')\), there exist an
open covering \({S'_{\nu}}\), \(\nu \in N\), of \(S'\) and a function
\(N \to I\) (\(\nu \mapsto i(\nu)\)) such that \((c^{-1}_{i(\nu)} a)b\)
is defined on \(S'_{\nu}\).}

\emph{Proof.} Let \(S'' \to S\) be arbitrary, and \(g \in G(S'')\).
Choose \(S' \to S''\) fppf-covering and a section
\((a, b) \in X^{2}(S')\) representing \(g\). Take the open covering
\({S'_{\nu}}\) of \(S'\) that exists by the hypothesis of the lemma.
Then on each \(S'_{\nu}\) one has
\((a, b) \sim (c_{i(\nu)}, (c^{-1}_{i(\nu)} a)b)\), hence \(g\) is
represented by a section of \([c_{i(\nu)} \times X](S')\) on
\(S'_{\nu}\), which proves surjectivity, because the family of morphisms
\({S'_{\nu} \to S''}\) is fppf-covering.

\textbf{Lemma 3.11.} \emph{Let \(Y/S\) be a prescheme of finite
presentation, and let \({a_{i}}\), \(i \in I\), be sections of \(Y(S)\).
Let \(s_{0}, s_{1}\) be points of \(S\) such that \(s_{0}\) is a
specialization of \(s_{1}\), and \(Y_{j}\) the fiber of \(Y/S\) at the
point \(s_{j}\). Let \(C_{j}\) be the closure in \(Y_{j}\) of the set of
points \({a_{i}(s) \cap Y_{j}}\). Then one has
\(\dim C_{1} \geqslant \dim C_{0}\).}

\emph{Proof.} It suffices to make the verification after a base change
\(S' \to S\) with chosen points \(s'_{0}\) and \(s'_{1}\) such that
\(s'_{j} \mapsto s_{j}\) and \(s'_{0}\) is a specialization of
\(s'_{1}\). One is

therefore (EGA II 7.1.4) reduced to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum
of a valuation ring \(A\), \(s_{0}\) the closed point of \(S\), and
\(s_{1}\) the generic point of \(S\). Now let \(V\) be the closure of
\(C_{1}\) in \(Y\). It is clear that \(C_{0} \subseteq V\), and so the
lemma is a consequence of the ``well-known'' fact that an irreducible
closed subprescheme \(V\) of a prescheme \(Y/S\) of finite presentation
satisfies \(\dim V \times_{S} s_{1} \geqslant \dim V \times_{S} s_{0}\)
if \(S\) is the spectrum of a valuation ring and if
\(V \times_{S} s_{1} \neq \emptyset\) (EGA IV 13.1.6).

\textbf{Lemma 3.12.} \emph{Suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of a local
ring with closed point \(s_{0}\), and let \({c_{i}}\), \(i \in I\), be
sections such that the closure \(C_{0}\) of the set
\({c_{i}(s) \cap X_{0}}\) in the closed fiber \(X_{0}\) is of dimension
equal to \(\dim X_{0} = n\). Then the condition of Lemma 3.9 is
satisfied.}

\emph{Proof.} Note first that the fibers of \(X/S\) all have the same
dimension \(n\), which results from EGA IV 12.1.1 (i) and from the fact
that \(X\) has a rational composition law. Lemma (3.11) therefore
implies that for each morphism \(S_{1} \to S\) with \(S_{1}\) the
spectrum of a field, the dimension of the closure of the set
\({c_{i} \times_{S} S_{1}}\) in \(X_{S_{1}}\) is equal to \(n\). Let us
verify the condition of (3.10). Let \((a, b) \in X^{2}(S')\). For
\((c^{-1}_{i} a)b\) to be defined, it is necessary and sufficient that
\(c_{i}\) be contained in a certain open \(U \subseteq X_{S'}\) which is
sch. dense relatively to \(S'\) (Rule 1). We must show that this is true
for a suitable \(i\), locally on \(S'\). It therefore suffices to treat
the case where \(S'\) is the spectrum of a local ring, and then the fact
that \(c_{i} \in U(S')\) is verified on the closed fiber. We are thus
reduced to the case \(S' = \operatorname{Spec} k\), \(k\) a field. Now
with the notations above, take \(S' = S_{1}\).

One has \(\dim C_{1} = \dim X_{S_{1}}\), and \(U\) is relatively sch.
dense in \(X_{S_{1}}\). Hence \(U \cap C_{1} \neq \emptyset\), whence
\(U \cap {c_{p} \times_{S} S_{1}} \neq \emptyset\), and we are done.

The proof of the theorem is now easy. Note first the following
consequence of the finiteness of Lemma (3.9): if \({A_{i}}\) is an
inductive system of rings over \(S\), if \(\tilde{A} = \lim A_{i}\), and
if the hypotheses of (3.9) are satisfied for
\(S = \operatorname{Spec} \tilde{A}\), then one may descend the object
that represents the quotient \(G\) of \(R \Rightarrow X^{2}\) to one of
\(S_{i} = \operatorname{Spec} A_{i}\) with the finiteness and flatness
properties stated in (3.9). This is the usual passage to the limit (EGA
IV 8 and 11). It follows that for the proof of (iii) and (iv) of (3.7),
one may restrict to the case \(S = \operatorname{Spec} A\), with \(A\) a
strictly local ring. Let then \(x_{0}\) be a closed point of the closed
fiber \(X_{0}\) of \(X/S\). There exists\footnote{cf.~note at the bottom
  of page 15, Exp. VII.} an extension \(A'\) of \(A\), local, free and
finite, and a section of \(X' = X \times_{S} S'\) passing through the
unique point \(x'_{0}\) of \(X'\) above \(x_{0}\). Note that
\(X'_{0} \to X_{0}\) is radicial since \(S\) is strictly local, hence
the residue field of \(A\) separably closed. It follows that there
exists an inductive system \({A_{i}}\) of local rings, flat and finite
over \(S\), such that, setting \(\tilde{A} = \lim A_{i}\) and
\(\tilde{X} = X \times_{S} \operatorname{Spec} \tilde{A}\),
\(\tilde{X}\) has a set of sections which induces a dense set on the
closed fiber \(\tilde{X}_{0}\). For each closed point \(x_{0}\) of
\(X_{0}\) one takes an extension \(A(x_{0})\) such that the
corresponding base change of \(X\) admits a section ``passing through
\(x_{0}\)'', and one takes as inductive system the system of finite
tensor products of the \(A(x_{0})\). Note that \texttt{Ã} is local,
being a limit of local rings. Hence by (3.12) and (3.10) one has the
quotient \(G\)

over \(\operatorname{Spec} \tilde{A}\), hence over one of
\(\operatorname{Spec} A_{i}\) by the remarks above, hence locally for
the fppf topology.

In fact it follows from the constructions that locally for the fppf
topology one can find a finite set of sections \({c_{i}}\)
(\(i = 1, \cdots, r\)) such that \(G\) is covered by the
\(c_{i} \times X\). (ii) and (iv) follow easily from this fact, and we
leave the verification of (i) to the reader.

\textbf{Corollary 3.13.} \emph{The sheaf of groups \(G\) determined by a
group germ \((X, W)\) over \(S\) is representable in each of the
following situations:}

\emph{(i) \(S\) is artinian.}

\emph{(ii) For each local scheme \(S' \to S\) at a closed point \(s\) of
\(S\), \(X_{S'}\) has a set of sections that induces on the closed fiber
a set whose closure is of dimension \(\dim X_{s}\).}

\emph{(iii) \(S\) is strictly local, and \(X/S\) is smooth.}

\emph{(iv) There exists \(S' \to S\) fppf-covering such that \(G_{S'}\)
is representable and affine over \(S\).}

Indeed, (ii) is a consequence of (3.10) and (3.12), (iii) follows
directly from (ii) and ``Hensel's lemma'', (iv) from the descent of
affine schemes, and (i) from the descent of group schemes, which is
possible here because one knows that every finite subset of a group over
a field is contained in an affine open (Exp. VI).
