Séminaire is devoted to the study of reductive groups. Its principal aim
is the generalization of Chevalley's classical results (\emph{Bible} and
\emph{Tôhoku})\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: See the bibliographical
  references at the end of this Exposé. In particular, a re-edition of
  the \emph{Séminaire Chevalley 1956--58}, cited {[}Bible{]}, revised by
  P. Cartier, was published in 2005, cf.~{[}Ch05{]}.} to arbitrary base
schemes, the two central results being the uniqueness theorem (Exp.
XXIII, Th. 4.1 and Cor. 5.1 to 5.10) and the existence theorem (Exp.
XXV, Th. 1.1) for ``pinned'' reductive group schemes corresponding to
prescribed ``root data''. The proofs employed are inspired by
Chevalley's, the technique of schemes permitting one to lend them
increased efficiency.

The results of the first volume of the \emph{Bible} (Exp. 1 to 13) will
be used systematically. By contrast, we shall prove directly over an
arbitrary scheme the results of the second volume (in particular the
isomorphism theorem); a knowledge of the proofs over an algebraically
closed field is therefore not absolutely indispensable.

In the proof of these two fundamental results, we shall use only the
most elementary results from the theory of groups of multiplicative
type, contained essentially in Exp. VIII and IX; we shall, on the other
hand, make essential use of the results of Exposé XVIII.\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  More precisely, Proposition XVIII 2.3 (extension of a ``generic
  homomorphism'' between groups) is used in XXII 4.1.11 and then in Exp.
  XXIII (proof of the uniqueness theorem), and also in Exp. XXIV;
  Theorem XVIII 3.7 (construction of a group from a group germ) is used
  only in Exp. XXV.} The reader specifically interested in the existence
and uniqueness theorems may, on a first reading, skip Exposés X to XVII.

\subsection{1. Reminders on groups over an algebraically closed
field}\label{reminders-on-groups-over-an-algebraically-closed-field}

\textbf{1.1.} In this number, \(k\) will always denote an algebraically
closed field. As announced above, the only results from \emph{Bible}
used in what follows are found in volume 1 (Exposés 1 to 13). All the
results of \emph{Bible} (\emph{loc. cit.}) concerning semisimple groups
are valid more generally for reductive groups (definition below) and
their proof is identical, with the following innocuous modifications:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Exp. 9, § 4, Definition 3: see 1.6.1 below.
\item
  Exp. 12, § 4, Theorem 2, e): suppress ``finite''.
\item
  Exp. 13, § 3, Theorem 2: replace ``rank'' by ``semisimple rank''.
\item
  Exp. 13, § 4, Corollary 2 to Theorem 3: replace ``rank'' by
  ``reductive rank''.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{1.2.} Let \(G\) be a smooth affine connected \(k\)-group. The
\emph{radical} of \(G\) (\emph{Bible}, § 9.4, Prop. 2)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  The reference 9-06 (= Exp. 9, p.~6) has been replaced by § 9.4 (= Exp.
  9, § 4), which applies equally well to {[}Bible{]} and to {[}Ch05{]}.
  When the numbering of {[}Ch05{]} differs from {[}Bible{]}, which is
  the case in Exp. 6, both references will be indicated explicitly.} is
the reduced subgroup associated with the neutral component of the
intersection of the Borel subgroups of \(G\); it is also the largest
smooth connected solvable invariant subgroup of \(G\); we shall denote
it \(rad(G)\).

The \emph{unipotent radical} of \(G\) is the unipotent part of the
radical of \(G\); it is also the largest smooth connected unipotent
invariant subgroup of \(G\); we shall denote it \(rad_{u}(G)\).

\textbf{1.3.} Let \(G\) be a smooth affine connected \(k\)-group, and
\(Q\) a torus of \(G\). Then the centralizer \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) of \(Q\)
in \(G\) is a closed subgroup of \(G\) (Exp. VIII, 6.7), smooth (Exp.
XI, 2.4), and connected (cf.~\emph{Bible}, § 6.6, Th. 6 a) or
{[}Ch05{]}, § 6.7, Th. 7 a)).

One has the fundamental relation:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad\_u(Centr\_G(Q)) = rad\_u(G) ∩ Centr\_G(Q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

First,\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following has been detailed.}
\(U = rad_{u}(G) \cap Centr_{G}(Q)\) is an invariant unipotent subgroup
of \(Centr_{G}(Q)\); let us show that it is smooth and connected. If we
make \(Q\) operate on \(rad_{u}(G)\) by inner automorphisms, \(U\) is
none other than the scheme of invariants of this operation. But this
scheme is smooth and connected, by Lemma 1.4 below.

Consequently, \(U\) is a closed subgroup of \(rad_{u}(Centr_{G}(Q))\).
On the other hand, by \emph{Bible}, Exp. 12, § 3, Cor. to Th. 1, one has
\texttt{rad\_u(Centr\_G(Q))(k)\ ⊂\ rad\_u(G)(k)}. The equality (1.3.1)
follows.

Let us signal a particular case of the foregoing result: if \(G\) is a
smooth affine connected \(k\)-group and if \(T\) is a maximal torus of
\(G\), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr\_G(T) = T · (Centr\_G(T) ∩ rad\_u(G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed (cf.~\emph{Bible}, § 6.6, Th. 6 c) or {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.7, Th. 7
c)), \(Centr_{G}(T)\) is a solvable group, hence the semi-direct product
of its maximal torus \(T\) and its unipotent radical.

By the density theorem (cf.~\emph{Bible}, § 6.5, Th. 5 a) or {[}Ch05{]},
§ 6.6, Th. 6 a)), the union of the \(Centr_{G}(T)\), as \(T\) runs
through the set of maximal tori of \(G\), contains a dense open subset
of \(G\); it therefore follows from (1.3.2):

\textbf{Corollary 1.3.3.} \emph{If \(G\) is a smooth affine connected
\(k\)-group, then the union of the \(T \cdot rad_{u}(G)\), where \(T\)
runs through the set of maximal tori of \(G\), contains a dense open
subset of \(G\).}

\textbf{Notations 1.4.0.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: These notations,
  which figured in 2.3 of the original, have been inserted here; on the
  other hand, the statement and proof of 1.4 have been detailed.}
\emph{We shall systematically use the following notation: if \(S\) is a
scheme and \(s\) a point of \(S\), we denote by \(\bar{s}\) the spectrum
of an algebraic closure \(\kappa\bar{s}\) of \(\kappa(s)\).}

\textbf{Lemma 1.4.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: These notations, which
  figured in 2.3 of the original, have been inserted here; on the other
  hand, the statement and proof of 1.4 have been detailed.} \emph{Let
\(S\) be a scheme, \(Q\) an \(S\)-torus operating on an \(S\)-group
scheme \(H\), separated and smooth over \(S\).}

\emph{(i) The functor of invariants \(H^{Q}\) is representable by a
closed subscheme of \(H\), smooth over \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) If moreover \(H\) is affine over \(S\), and has connected
fibers, then \(H^{Q}\) does too.}

\emph{Proof.} First, by VIII 6.5 (d),\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: See also
  the additions made in VI\_B, 6.2.4 (d) and 6.5.5 (a).} since \(H\) is
separated over \(S\) and \(Q\) essentially free over \(S\), \(H^{Q}\) is
representable by a closed subscheme of \(H\). In particular, if \(H\) is
affine over \(S\), then so is \(H^{Q}\).

Consider now the semi-direct product \(G = H \cdot Q\); it is smooth and
separated over \(S\). Then, the centralizer \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is
representable by a closed subscheme of \(G\), of finite presentation
over \(G\), by Exp. XI 6.11 (a),\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: See also the
  additions made in VI\_B, 6.2.4 (d) and 6.5.5 (a).} and it is smooth
over \(S\) by Exp. XI 2.4.

Since \(Centr_{G}(Q) = H^{Q} \cdot Q\), it follows that \(H^{Q}\) is
smooth over \(S\). (Indeed, using the section
\(\sigma : H^{Q} \to Centr_{G}(Q)\) deduced from the unit section
\(\epsilon_{Q}\) of \(Q\), one sees at once that \(H^{Q}\) is formally
smooth over \(S\); and since moreover \(\epsilon_{Q}\) is of finite
presentation, \(H^{Q}\) is locally of finite presentation over \(S\).)
This proves (i).

Finally, suppose \(H\) affine over \(S\) and with connected fibers. Then
each geometric fiber \(G_{\bar{s}}\) of \(G\) is a smooth affine
connected \(\kappa\bar{s}\)-group, hence, by the first assertion of 1.3,
so is

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr\_\{G\_s̄\}(Q\_s̄) = (Centr\_G(Q))\_s̄ = (H\^{}Q)\_s̄ · Q\_s̄,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and this entails that \((H^{Q})_{\bar{s}}\) is connected.

\textbf{1.5.} We recall that the \emph{reductive rank} of the smooth
affine \(k\)-group \(G\) is the common dimension of the maximal tori of
\(G\). We shall denote it \(rgred(G/k)\) or \(rgred(G)\). In order that
\(rgred(G/k) = 0\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(G\) be
unipotent (i.e.~that \(G = rad_{u}(G)\)), by \emph{Bible}, § 6.4, Cor. 1
to Th. 4 or {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.5, Cor. 1 to Th. 5.

If \(H\) is an invariant subgroup of the smooth affine \(k\)-group
\(G\), then the quotient \(G/H\) is affine and smooth (Exp. VI\_B, 11.17
and VI\_A, 3.3.2 (iii)). Moreover (\emph{Bible}, § 7.3, Th. 3, a) and
c)), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rgred(G) = rgred(G/H) + rgred(H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 1.6.1.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: 1.6 has been
  transformed into 1.6.1 to 1.6.3. Note that in this Séminaire every
  reductive (resp. semisimple, cf.~1.8) \(k\)-group is, by definition,
  connected.} \emph{One says that the \(k\)-group \(G\) is} reductive
\emph{if it is smooth, affine, and connected, and if \(rad(G)\) is a
torus, i.e.~if \(rad_{u}(G) = {e}\).}

\textbf{Lemma 1.6.2.} \emph{Let \(G\) be a reductive \(k\)-group.}

\emph{(i) If \(Q\) is a torus of \(G\), then \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is
reductive.}

\emph{(ii) In particular, if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), then
\(Centr_{G}(T) = T\).}

\emph{(iii) The center of \(G\) is contained in every maximal torus,
hence is diagonalizable.}

\emph{(iv) The radical of \(G\) is the (unique) maximal torus of
\(Centr(G)\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, (i) follows from (1.3.1), (ii) from (1.3.2), and
(iii) follows from (ii). Finally, the maximal torus of \(Centr(G)\)
(i.e.~the neutral component \(Centr(G)^{0}\)) is a smooth connected
solvable subgroup, invariant in \(G\), hence contained in \(rad(G)\);
conversely, \(rad(G)\) is an invariant torus in \(G\), hence central
(\emph{Bible}, § 4.3, Cor. to Prop. 2), whence (iv).

\textbf{Remark 1.6.3.} \emph{If \(G\) is reductive and if
\(\dim(G) \neq rgred(G)\), then \(\dim(G) - rgred(G) \geqslant 2\).
Indeed, this difference is always even (cf.~1.10 below).}

\textbf{1.7.} Let \(G\) be a smooth affine connected \(k\)-group and
\(H\) a smooth connected invariant subgroup. Then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad(H) = (rad(G) ∩ H)⁰\_red   and   rad\_u(H) = (rad\_u(G) ∩ H)⁰\_red,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

as one sees at once. In particular, if \(G\) is reductive, so is \(H\).

Let \(f : G \to G'\) be a surjective morphism of smooth affine connected
\(k\)-groups. Then

\[
f(rad_{u}(G)) = rad_{u}(G').
\]

In particular, if \(G\) is reductive, so is \(G'\).

Let us prove (1.7.2). First, \(f\) sends \(rad_{u}(G)\) into
\(rad_{u}(G')\). Introducing \(H = (f^{-1}(rad_{u}(G')))^{0}_{red}\),
which contains \(rad_{u}(G)\), one has \(rad_{u}(H) = rad_{u}(G)\) and
one is reduced to the case where \(G = H\), i.e.~where \(G'\) is
unipotent. Since the union of the \(T \cdot rad_{u}(G)\) (as \(T\) runs
through the set of maximal tori of \(G\)) is dense in \(G\), the union
of the \(f(T) f(rad_{u}(G))\) is dense in \(G'\); but \(f(T)\) consists
of semisimple elements, so \(f(T) = {e}\), \(G'\) being unipotent; this
shows that \(f(rad_{u}(G))\) is dense in \(G'\). Therefore, by
\emph{Bible}, § 5.4, Lemma 4 or {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.1, Lemma 1,\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  The following has been detailed.} \(f(rad_{u}(G))\) is an open
subgroup of \(G'\); the latter being connected, it follows that
\(f(rad_{u}(G)) = G'\). (N.B.: one can prove under the same hypotheses
that \(f(rad(G)) = rad(G')\).)

\textbf{1.8.} One says that the \(k\)-group \(G\) is \emph{semisimple}
if it is smooth, affine, and connected and if \(rad(G) = {e}\), i.e.~if
\(G\) is reductive and \(Centr(G)\) is finite. If \(G\) is an arbitrary
smooth affine connected \(k\)-group, then \(G / rad(G)\) is semisimple
(\emph{Bible}, § 9.4, Prop. 2), and \(G / rad_{u}(G)\) is reductive. One
calls the \emph{semisimple rank of \(G\)} and denotes by \(rgss(G/k)\)
or \(rgss(G)\) the reductive rank of \(G / rad(G)\).

If \(G\) is reductive, one therefore has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rgred(G) = rgss(G) + dim(rad(G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(G\) is a smooth affine connected \(k\)-group and if \(Q\) is a
central subtorus of \(G\), then \(G/Q\) is semisimple if and only if
\(G\) is reductive and \(Q = rad(G)\). Indeed, if \(G/Q\) is semisimple,
\(Q \supset rad(G)\), so \(rad(G)\) is a torus, so \(G\) is reductive,
so \(rad(G)\) is the maximal torus of \(Centr(G)\), so \(rad(G) = Q\).
If \(G\) is reductive and if \(Q\) is a central subgroup then (\(G/Q\)
is reductive and) \(rgss(G) = rgss(G/Q)\).

\textbf{1.9.} If \(K\) is an algebraically closed extension of \(k\) and
if \(G\) is a smooth affine connected \(k\)-group, then \(G\) is
reductive (resp. semisimple) if and only if \texttt{G\_K} is, and one
has

\[
rgred(G/k) = rgred(G_{K}/K),
rgss(G/k) = rgss(G_{K}/K).
\]

\textbf{1.10.} Let \(G\) be a smooth connected \(k\)-group and let \(T\)
be a torus of \(G\).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following sentence has
  been added.} Denote by \(g\) the \(k\)-Lie algebra of \(G\),
i.e.~\(g = Lie(G) = Lie(G/k)(k)\); likewise denote \(t = Lie(T)\). Then
\(g\) decomposes under the action of \(T\) (via \(T \to G\) and the
adjoint operation of \(G\)) as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = g₀ ⊕ ∐\_\{α ∈ R\} g\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the \(\alpha \in R\) are non-trivial characters of \(T\) and the
\(g_{\alpha}\) are \(\neq 0\). The characters \(\alpha \in R\) are
called the \emph{roots} of \(G\) with respect to \(T\). By Exp. II,
5.2.3 (i), one has

\[
g_{0} = Lie(Centr_{G}(T)).
\]

In particular,\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following has been detailed.}
since \(Centr_{G}(T)\) is connected (1.3 in the case where \(G\) is
affine, and Exp. XII 6.6 b) in the general case), \(T\) is its own
centralizer if and only if \(g_{0} = Lie(T)\).

This condition entails that \(T\) is maximal and that
\(Centr(G) \subset T\), hence by Exp. XII 8.8 d) one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr(G) = Ker(T → GL(g)) = ⋂\_\{α ∈ R\} Ker(α);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

moreover \(Centr(G)\) is then affine, hence \(G \to G/Centr(G)\) is
affine; since the latter group is affine (Exp. XII 6.1),\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  See also the addition VI\_B, 6.2.6.} so is \(G\).

When \(G\) is reductive and \(T\) maximal, the roots in the preceding
sense coincide with the roots in the sense of \emph{Bible}, § 12.2, Def.
1; the latter are indeed roots in the sense of this number
(\emph{Bible}, § 13.2, Th. 1, c)) and there are \(\dim(G) - \dim(T)\) of
them (\emph{Bible}, § 13.4, Cor. 2 to Th. 3). Moreover, if \(\alpha\) is
a root, so is \(-\alpha\) (\emph{Bible}, § 12.2, Cor. to Prop. 1). (As
usual, one writes the group structure of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{k-gr.}(T, G_{m,k})\) indifferently additively or
multiplicatively.) It follows that, for \(G\) reductive,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim(G) − rgred(G) = Card(R)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is always even.

The semisimple rank of the reductive group \(G\) is the rank of the
subset \(R\) of the \(Q\)-vector space
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{k-gr.}(T, G_{m,k}) \otimes Q\) (\emph{Bible}, §
13.3, Th. 2).

\textbf{Lemma 1.11.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field,
\(G\) a smooth affine connected \(k\)-group, \(T\) a torus of \(G\),
\(W(T) = Norm_{G}(T) / Centr_{G}(T)\) the Weyl group of \(G\) with
respect to \(T\). The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is reductive, \(T\) is maximal, \(rgss(G) = 1\).}

\emph{(ii) \(G\) is reductive, \(T\) is maximal, \(G \neq T\); there
exists a subtorus \(Q\) of \(T\), of codimension \texttt{1} in \(T\),
central in \(G\).}

\emph{(iii) \(G\) is not solvable and
\(\dim(G) - \dim(T) \leqslant 2\).}

\emph{(iv) \(W(T) \neq {e}\) and \(\dim(G) - \dim(T) \leqslant 2\).}

\emph{(v) \(W(T) = (Z/2Z)_{k}\) and \(\dim(G) - \dim(T) = 2\).}

\emph{Moreover, under these conditions, there are exactly two roots of
\(G\) with respect to \(T\); they are opposite. Under the conditions of
(ii), \(Q = rad(G)\).}

\emph{Proof.} One has obviously (v) ⇒ (iv). One has (iv) ⇒ (iii) by
\emph{Bible}, § 6.1, Cor. 3 to Th. 1 or {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.2, Cor. 3 to Th.
2. Let us prove (iii) ⇒ (ii): let \(U\) be the unipotent radical of
\(G\); one knows that \(G/U\) is reductive and is not a torus (otherwise
\(G\) would be solvable); one therefore has, by (1.10.4),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim(G/U) − rgred(G/U) = Card(R) ⩾ 2;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rgred(G) = rgred(G/U) + rgred(U) = rgred(G/U),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim(G) − dim(U) − rgred(G) = dim(G/U) − rgred(G/U)}
\NormalTok{                           ⩾ 2 ⩾ dim(G) − dim(T) ⩾ dim(G) − rgred(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This gives \(\dim(U) = 0\), hence \(G\) is reductive,
\(rgred(G) = \dim(T)\), hence \(T\) is maximal,
\(\dim(G) - \dim(T) = 2\). By \emph{Bible}, § 10.4, Prop. 8, there
exists a singular torus \(Q\) of codimension \texttt{1} in \(T\); then
\(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is reductive (1.6.2 (i)), non-solvable (definition of a
singular torus), hence \texttt{dim(Centr\_G(Q))\ −\ rgred(G)\ ⩾\ 2},
which proves that \(G = Centr_{G}(Q)\) and \(Q\) is central in \(G\).

Let us prove (ii) ⇒ (i). One knows that \(G/Q\) is reductive (1.7) and
that \(rgred(G/Q) = 1\), hence \(rgss(G/Q) = 0\) or \texttt{1}. The
first case is impossible, for it would entail \(rgss(G) = 0\), hence
\(G = T\);

one therefore has \(rgred(G/Q) = rgss(G/Q) = 1\), which proves that
\(G/Q\) is semisimple; hence \(Q\) is the radical of \(G\) and
\(rgss(G) = 1\).

Let us finally prove (i) ⇒ (v). If \(Q\) is the radical of \(G\), one
has \(\dim(T) - \dim(Q) = 1\) and \(Q\) is central in \(G\), hence
\(G = Centr_{G}(Q)\), which proves that \(Q\) is a singular torus; by
\emph{Bible}, § 11.3, Th. 2, one has \(W_{G}(T) = (Z/2Z)_{k}\); by
\emph{Bible}, § 12.1, Lemma 1, one has \(\dim(G) - \dim(T) = 2\). There
are therefore at most two roots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\); but
there are at least two, opposite to each other (1.10).

\textbf{Proposition 1.12.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed
field, \(G\) a smooth connected \(k\)-group, \(T\) a torus of \(G\),
\(R\) the set of roots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = g₀ ⊕ ∐\_\{α ∈ R\} g\_α,    with g\_α ≠ 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the decomposition of \(g\) under \(Ad(T)\). For each
\(\alpha \in R\), let \(T_{\alpha}\) be the maximal torus of
\(Ker(\alpha)\)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: i.e., the connected component of
  \(Ker(\alpha)\).} and \(Z_{\alpha} = Centr_{G}(T_{\alpha})\). The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is affine, reductive; \(T\) is maximal.}

\emph{(ii) \(g_{0} = t\), each \(Z_{\alpha}\) (\(\alpha \in R\)) is
reductive.}

\emph{(iii) \(g_{0} = t\), each \(g_{\alpha}\) (\(\alpha \in R\)) is of
dimension \texttt{1}; and if \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) and \(q \in Q\) are
such that \(\beta = q \alpha\), then \(q = \pm 1\); for each
\(\alpha \in R\), there exists \(w_{\alpha} \in G(k)\) which normalizes
\(T\), centralizes \(T_{\alpha}\), but does not centralize \(T\).}

\emph{Moreover, under these conditions, each \(Z_{\alpha}\) is of
semisimple rank \texttt{1} and one has
\(Lie(Z_{\alpha}) = t \oplus g_{\alpha} \oplus g_{-\alpha}\).}

\emph{Proof.} If \(G\) is affine and reductive and if \(T\) is maximal,
each \(Z_{\alpha}\) is affine and reductive (1.6.2 (i)), with maximal
torus \(T\); moreover, \(T\) is its own centralizer (1.6.2 (ii)), hence
\(g_{0} = t\), which proves (i) ⇒ (ii).

On the other hand \(g_{0} = t\) entails that \(T\) is maximal and \(G\)
affine (cf.~1.10), hence each \(Z_{\alpha}\) is affine, smooth, and
connected, by 1.3. In any case, one has, by Exp. II, 5.2.2,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Z\_α) = g\^{}\{T\_α\} = g₀ ⊕ ∐\_\{β ∈ R ∩ Qα\} g\_β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One therefore has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Z\_α) ⊃ t ⊕ g\_α ⊕ g\_\{−α\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which entails \(Z_{\alpha} \neq T\). Since \(T_{\alpha}\) is a subtorus
of codimension \texttt{1} in \(T\), central in \(Z_{\alpha}\), one
obtains by 1.11, applied to \(Z_{\alpha}\), the equivalence (ii) ⇔ (iii)
and the supplements.

It remains to prove (ii) ⇒ (i); one already knows that (ii) entails that
\(T\) is maximal and \(G\) affine. Let \(U\) be its unipotent radical;
it is invariant in \(G\), its Lie algebra is invariant under \(Ad(T)\).
One therefore has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(U) = (Lie(U) ∩ g₀) ⊕ ∐\_\{α ∈ R\} (Lie(U) ∩ g\_α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By (1.3.1), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U ∩ T = U ∩ Centr\_G(T) = rad\_u(Centr\_G(T)) = rad\_u(T) = \{e\},}
\NormalTok{U ∩ Z\_α = U ∩ Centr\_G(T\_α) = rad\_u(Centr\_G(T\_α)) = rad\_u(Z\_α) = \{e\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One therefore has\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: Note that if \(U\), \(L\) are
  two subgroup schemes of \(G\), one has
  \texttt{Lie(U)\ ∩\ Lie(L)\ =\ Lie(U\ ∩\ L)}.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(U) ∩ g₀ = Lie(U) ∩ t = Lie(U ∩ T) = 0,}
\NormalTok{Lie(U) ∩ g\_α ⊂ Lie(U) ∩ Lie(Z\_α) = Lie(U ∩ Z\_α) = 0;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(Lie(U) = 0\) and \(U = {e}\), i.e.~\(G\) is reductive.

\textbf{Corollary 1.13.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed
field, \(G\) a smooth connected \(k\)-group, \(T\) a torus of \(G\),
\(R\) the set of roots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = g₀ ⊕ ∐\_\{α ∈ R\} g\_α}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{as above. For each \(\alpha \in R\), let \(T_{\alpha}\) be the
maximal torus of \(Ker(\alpha)\) and
\(Z_{\alpha} = Centr_{G}(T_{\alpha})\). The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is affine, semisimple; \(T\) is maximal.}

\emph{(ii) \(g_{0} = t\), each \(Z_{\alpha}\) is reductive, and
\(\bigcap_{\alpha \in R} Ker(\alpha)\) is finite.}

\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following sentence has been added.} This
follows from the equalities \(rad(G) = Centr(G)^{0}\) and
\(Centr(G) = \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} Ker(\alpha)\), established in 1.6.2
(iv) and (1.10.3).

\subsection{2. Reductive group schemes. Definitions and first
properties}\label{reductive-group-schemes.-definitions-and-first-properties}

\textbf{Scholie 2.1.} \emph{If \(G\) is a group scheme over \(S\), the
following properties are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is affine and smooth over \(S\), with connected fibers.}

\emph{(ii) \(G\) is affine and flat over \(S\), of finite presentation
over \(S\), with geometrically integral fibers.}

\emph{These properties are stable under base change and local for
(fpqc).}

\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following has been added.} Indeed, suppose
(i) is satisfied. Since \(G\) is affine and smooth over \(S\), it is of
finite presentation over \(S\); and since its fibers are smooth and
connected, they are geometrically integral, by VI\_A, 2.4.

Conversely, if (ii) is satisfied, the fibers of \(G\) are connected and
geometrically reduced, hence smooth (VI\_A, 1.3.1); then \(G\) is smooth
over \(S\), by EGA IV₄, 17.5.2.

Of course, these properties are stable under base change: cf.~EGA II,
1.5.1 for ``affine'', IV₁, 1.6.2 (iii) for ``of finite presentation'',
IV₂, 2.1.4 for ``flat'', and IV₂, 4.6.5 (i) for ``with geometrically
integral fibers''.

On the other hand, these properties are clearly local for the Zariski
topology, so it suffices to verify that if \(S' \to S\) is a faithfully
flat quasi-compact morphism and if \(G_{S'} \to S'\) has the indicated
properties, then so does \(G \to S\). This follows from EGA IV₂, 2.5.1
for ``flat'', 2.7.1 (vi) and (xiii) for ``of finite presentation'' and
``affine'', and 4.6.5 (i) for ``with geometrically integral fibers''
(and also EGA IV₄, 17.7.3 (ii) for ``smooth'').

\textbf{2.2.} Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group scheme satisfying the
preceding conditions, and \(Q\) a torus (cf.~IX, Def. 1.3) of
\(G\).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following has been detailed.} Then,
by XI, 6.11 a) and XI, 2.4, \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is representable by a
closed subgroup scheme of \(G\) (hence affine over \(S\)), of finite
presentation and smooth over \(S\); moreover, since each geometric fiber
\(G_{\bar{s}}\) of \(G\) is a smooth affine connected
\(\kappa\bar{s}\)-group, then, by the first assertion of 1.3, so is

\[
Centr_{G_{\bar{s}}}(Q_{\bar{s}}) = (Centr_{G}(Q))_{\bar{s}}.
\]

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group
scheme smooth and affine over \(S\), with connected fibers, \(T\) a
torus of \(G\). The set of \(s \in S\) such that \(G_{s}\) is a
reductive \(s\)-group, of semisimple rank \texttt{1} and with maximal
torus \(T_{s}\), is an open subset \(U\) of \(S\).}

\emph{Proof.} Since \(G\) and \(T\) are flat over \(S\), the function

\[
s \mapsto \dim(G_{s}/s) - \dim(T_{s}/s)
\]

is locally constant; let \(U_{1}\) be the open subset of points of \(S\)
where it equals \texttt{2}.

\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following has been detailed. Note, on the
  other hand, that section 6 is independent of the rest of this Exposé.}
By 6.3, the Weyl group

\[
W_{G}(T) = Norm_{G}(T) / Centr_{G}(T)
\]

is representable by an \(S\)-group scheme étale and separated over
\(S\), and the function

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s ↦ number of points of W\_G(T)\_s}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is lower semicontinuous. Let \(U_{2}\) be the set of points of \(S\)
where this function is \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 1}; it is open. By 1.11,
the set of \(s\) such that \(G_{s}\) is reductive, of semisimple rank
\texttt{1}, with maximal torus \(T_{s}\), is \(U = U_{1} \cap U_{2}\);
moreover, for every \(s \in U\), \(W_{G}(T)_{s}\) has exactly two
points.

Consequently (cf.~SGA 1, I 10.9 and EGA IV₃, 15.5.1 and IV₄, 18.12.4),
\(W_{G}(T)_{U}\) is étale and finite over \(U\).

\textbf{Remark 2.4.} \emph{The group \(W_{G}(T)_{U}\) is isomorphic to
\((Z/2Z)_{U}\).}

Indeed, by what precedes, it is étale and finite over \(U\); since the
functor of automorphisms of \((Z/2Z)_{U}\) is the trivial group, it
suffices to verify the assertion locally; but the assertion is immediate
if the algebra \(A\) defining \(W_{G}(T)_{U}\) is a free
\texttt{O\_U}-module.\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The hypothesis entails
  that \(A\) is locally free of rank \texttt{2}, and since the
  augmentation ideal \(I\) is a direct factor of \(A\), then, replacing
  \(U\) by a sufficiently small affine open subset
  \(\operatorname{Spec}(R)\), one may assume that \(I = \Gamma(U, I)\)
  is a free \(R\)-module of rank \texttt{1}. If \(x\) is a generator of
  \(I\), one then has \(x^{2} = a x\) for a certain \(a \in R\), and the
  hypothesis that \(A = \Gamma(U, A)\) be étale entails that \(a\) is
  invertible in \(R\), and one then sees easily that \(A\) is the affine
  algebra of the constant \(R\)-group \(Z/2Z\) (compare with the first
  lines of {[}TO70{]}).}

\textbf{Notations and reminders 2.5.0.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: This
  paragraph of notations and reminders has been added.} \emph{Let \(S\)
be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group scheme, \(\epsilon : S \to G\) the
unit section of \(G\). One has seen in II, § 4.11 that the functor
\(Lie(G/S)\) is representable by the vector fibration
\(V(\omega^{1}_{G/S})\) (where
\(\omega^{1}_{G/S} = \epsilon*(\Omega^{1}_{G/S})\)), and one denotes}

\[
g = Lie(G/S) = (\omega^{1}_{G/S})^{V}
\]

\emph{the sheaf of sections of this vector fibration. Suppose moreover
that \(G\) is smooth over \(S\); then \(\omega^{1}_{G/S}\) and hence
\(Lie(G/S)\) are locally free \texttt{O\_S}-modules of finite type, and
one has (cf.~I 4.6.5.1):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(G/S) = W(Lie(G/S)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{i.e.~for every \(S\)-scheme \(S'\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(G/S)(S′) = Γ(S′, Lie(G/S) ⊗ O\_\{S′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{By II 4.1.1.1, the adjoint action of \(G\) endows
\(Lie(G/S) = W(Lie(G/S))\) with a \(G\)-\texttt{O\_S}-module structure,
hence \(Lie(G/S)\) is a \(G\)-\texttt{O\_S}-module (cf.~I 4.7.1). If
moreover \(G\) is affine over \(S\), this amounts to saying, by I 4.7.2,
that \(Lie(G/S)\) is an \(A(G)\)-comodule.}

\emph{If \(T\) is a torus over \(S\) (IX Def. 1.3), one says that \(T\)
is} split \emph{(``trivial'' in the original) if it is isomorphic to
\(G^{r}_{m,S}\) for some integer \(r \geqslant 0\), and one says that
\(T\) is} trivialized \emph{if one has fixed such an isomorphism or,
more generally, an isomorphism \(T \simeq D_{S}(M)\), where \(M\) is a
free abelian group of rank \(r\).}

\emph{Let us finally recall (XII Def. 1.3) that a torus \(T\) of \(G\)
is called} maximal \emph{if, for every \(s \in S\), \(T_{\bar{s}}\) is a
maximal torus of \(G_{\bar{s}}\).}

\textbf{Theorem 2.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group
scheme affine and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected
fibers, and \(s_{0}\) a point of \(S\). Suppose \(G\) flat over \(S\) at
\(\epsilon(s_{0})\) and the geometric fiber \(G_{\bar{s}_{0}}\) (reduced
and) reductive (resp. semisimple). Then there exists an open subset
\(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s_{0}\) and an étale surjective morphism
\(S' \to U\) such that:}

\emph{(i) \texttt{G\_U} is smooth over \(S\), with geometrically
reductive (resp. semisimple) fibers, of constant reductive rank and
semisimple rank.}

\emph{(ii) \(G_{S'}\) possesses a split\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  ``Split'' has been added.} maximal torus \(T\), and the Weyl group
(cf.~6.3)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W\_\{G\_\{S′\}\}(T) = Norm\_\{G\_\{S′\}\}(T) / Centr\_\{G\_\{S′\}\}(T) = Norm\_\{G\_\{S′\}\}(T) / T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is finite over \(S'\).}

\emph{Proof.}\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The proof has been detailed.}
Denote by \(\pi : G \to S\) the structure morphism and
\(\epsilon : S \to G\) the unit section. Since \(G\) is flat over \(S\)
at \(\epsilon(s_{0})\) and \(G_{\bar{s}_{0}}\) reduced (hence smooth
over \(\bar{s}_{0}\), cf.~VI\_A 1.3.1), \(G\) is smooth over \(S\) at
the point \(\epsilon(s_{0})\) (EGA IV₄, 17.5.1), i.e.~there exists an
open neighborhood \(V\) of \(\epsilon(s_{0})\) such that \(\pi|V\) is
smooth. Then, \(S' = \epsilon^{-1}(V)\) is an open subset of \(S\), and
\(G_{S'}\) is smooth over \(S'\) at the points of \(\epsilon(S')\).
Since \(G\) has connected fibers, \(G_{S'}\) is smooth over \(S'\), by
VI\_B, 3.10. So, replacing \(S\) by \(S'\), one may assume \(G\) smooth
over \(S\).

By Exp. XI, Th. 4.1, the functor of subgroups of multiplicative type of
\(G\) is representable by an \(S\)-scheme \(\mathcal{M}\), smooth and
separated over \(S\). Denote by \(r_{0}\) the rank of
\(G_{\bar{s}_{0}}\) and consider the open subscheme
\(\mathcal{M}_{r_{0}}\) of \(\mathcal{M}\), which represents the functor
of subtori of rank \(r_{0}\) of \(G\) (IX 1.4). Smoothness entails that
\(\mathcal{M}_{r_{0}}\) admits a rational point over a finite separable
extension of \(\kappa(s_{0})\) (cf.~EGA IV₄, 17.15.10 (iii)). Thus there
exists \(S' \to S\) étale equipped with a point \(s'_{0}\) mapping to
\(s_{0}\) such that \(G_{s'_{0}}\) admits a torus of rank \(r_{0}\).
Therefore, replacing \(S\) by \(S'\), one may assume that \(G_{s_{0}}\)
admits a torus of rank \(r_{0}\).

By ``Hensel's lemma'' (cf.~XI, 1.10), the smoothness of
\(\mathcal{M}_{r_{0}}\) permits one to lift this torus to an
\(S'\)-torus \(T\) of \(G\), where \(S' \to S\) is étale equipped with a
point \(s'_{0}\) mapping to \(s_{0}\). By Exp. X, 4.5 (see also
6.1\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: which is independent of the rest of this
  Exposé.}), there exists an étale morphism \(f : S'' \to S'\) splitting
\(T\) and such that \(f^{-1}(s'_{0}) \neq \emptyset\). Since an étale
morphism is open and the assertions of (i) are local for the étale
topology, one may therefore assume that \(G\) possesses a split torus
\(T\),\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: In all this volume, ``trivial torus'' has
  been replaced by ``split torus''.} maximal at \(s_{0}\). Write
therefore \(T = D_{S}(M)\) and let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = ∐\_\{m ∈ M\} g\_m}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be the decomposition of \(g = Lie(G/S)\) under \(Ad(T)\) (Exp. I,
4.7.3).

Put \(t = Lie(T)\) and, for every \(m \in M\), denote
\(g_{m}(s_{0}) = g_{m} \otimes_{O_{S}} \kappa(s_{0})\).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  The preceding sentence has been added.} Let \(R\) be the set of
\(m \in M\), \(m \neq 0\), such that \(g_{m}(s_{0}) \neq 0\).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  Note that, \(g\) being a finite locally free \texttt{O\_S}-module,
  \(R\) is a finite set.} Since \(G_{\bar{s}_{0}}\) is reductive, one
has \(g_{0}(s_{0}) = t(s_{0})\), hence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g(s₀) = t(s₀) ⊕ ∐\_\{α ∈ R\} g\^{}α(s₀).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since the modules in question are locally free, one may, by shrinking
\(S\) if necessary, assume the \(g_{\alpha}\) free and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = t ⊕ ∐\_\{α ∈ R\} g\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One recalls, cf.~Exp. XII, 1.12, that a group of multiplicative type
possesses a unique maximal torus (this is moreover essentially trivial
by descent, the diagonalizable case being evident). Let then
\(T_{\alpha}\) be the maximal torus of the kernel of \(\alpha\) and
\(Z_{\alpha} = Centr_{G}(T_{\alpha})\).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The
  following sentence has been detailed.} By 2.2, \(Z_{\alpha}\) is
affine and smooth over \(S\), with connected fibers, and by 1.12, its
fiber \((Z_{\alpha})_{\bar{s}_{0}}\) is reductive, of semisimple rank
\texttt{1}, with maximal torus \(T_{\bar{s}_{0}}\). By 2.3, there
therefore exists an open subset \(U_{\alpha}\) of \(S\), containing
\(s_{0}\), such that \(Z_{\alpha}|U_{\alpha}\) has reductive fibers.

Set \(U = \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} U_{\alpha}\). By 1.12, for every
\(s \in U\), \(G_{\bar{s}}\) is reductive, with maximal torus
\(T_{\bar{s}}\) and the set of roots of \(G_{\bar{s}}\) with respect to
\(T_{\bar{s}}\) is identified with \(R\), so that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rgred(G\_s̄) = dim(T) = rg(M),     rgss(G\_s̄) = rg(R)   (cf. 1.10).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore proved (i) and the first assertion of (ii); it remains
to prove that the Weyl group \(W_{G_{U}}(T_{U})\) is finite over \(U\),
i.e.~``that it has the same number of points in each geometric fiber''
(cf.~SGA 1, I 10.9 and EGA IV₃, 15.5.1 and IV₄, 8.12.4).

For this, it suffices to remark that the geometric fiber of this group
at \(s \in U\) is determined by the situation \(R \subset M\), as the
constant group associated with the ``abstract Weyl group of this root
system'', and in particular is independent of the point \(s\),
cf.~\emph{Bible}, § 11.3, Th. 2 (see also Exp. XXII, no. 3).

\textbf{Corollary 2.6.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group affine and
smooth over \(S\), with connected fibers. The set of points \(s \in S\)
such that \(G_{\bar{s}}\) is reductive (resp. semisimple) is an open
subset \(U\) of \(S\), and the functions}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s ↦ rgred(G\_s̄/s̄),     s ↦ rgss(G\_s̄/s̄)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are locally constant on \(U\).}

\textbf{Definition 2.7.} \emph{An \(S\)-group (= \(S\)-group scheme)
\(G\) is called} reductive \emph{(resp.} semisimple*) if it is affine
and smooth over \(S\), with geometrically connected fibers, and
reductive (resp. semisimple).*

The property of being reductive (resp. semisimple) for an \(S\)-group
\(G\) is stable under base change and local for the (fpqc) topology.

\textbf{2.8.} Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group. For every torus
(resp. maximal torus) \(Q\) of \(G\), \(Z(Q) = Centr_{G}(Q)\) is
reductive (resp. equals \(Q\)). This follows at once from 2.2 and 1.6.
Applying 2.5 to \(Centr_{G}(Q)\), one deduces from it that \(Q\) is
contained (locally for the étale topology) in a maximal torus.

\textbf{Remark 2.9.} \emph{Using as usual the technique of EGA IV₃, § 8,
the finite-presentation hypotheses, and Theorem 2.5, one sees that if
\(G\) is a reductive group over \(S\), there exists an open covering of
\(S\), say \({U_{i}}\), such that each \(G_{U_{i}}\) comes by base
change from a reductive group over a noetherian ring (in fact, a
finitely generated algebra over \(Z\)). Likewise, if \(G\) possesses a
split maximal torus \(T\), one may further assume that \(T_{U_{i}}\)
comes from a split maximal torus of the preceding group, \ldots.}

\subsection{3. Roots and root systems of reductive group
schemes}\label{roots-and-root-systems-of-reductive-group-schemes}

\textbf{3.1.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(T\) an \(S\)-torus operating
linearly on a locally free \texttt{O\_S}-module of finite type \(F\)
(cf. I, § 4.7). For every character \(\alpha\) of \(T\)
(i.e.~\(\alpha \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, G_{m,S})\)), one
defines a subfunctor of \(W(F)\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(F)\^{}α(S′) = \{ x ∈ W(F)(S′) | t·x = α(t) x for all t ∈ T(S″), S″ → S′ \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: This statement has been made
  into a lemma, in order to put it in evidence.} \emph{Then
\(W(F)^{\alpha} = W(F^{\alpha})\), where \(F^{\alpha}\) is a submodule
of \(F\), locally a direct summand in \(F\), hence also locally free.}

Indeed, the assertion is local for the (fpqc) topology, and one may
assume \(T = D_{S}(M)\), where \(M\) is a (free) abelian group of finite
type. Then \(\alpha\) is identified with a locally constant function
from \(S\) to \(M\) (Exp. VIII 1.3), and shrinking \(S\) if necessary,
one may assume that this function is constant. One is then reduced to
Exp. I, 4.7.3.

\textbf{Definition 3.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme smooth and with connected fibers,\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  The original added the hypothesis that \(G\) be of finite presentation
  over \(S\), which does not seem to be used in what follows. In any
  case, \(G\) being smooth over \(S\) and with connected fibers, it is
  quasi-compact and separated over \(S\) (VI\_B, 5.5), hence of finite
  presentation over \(S\).} \(T\) a torus of \(G\). Denote
\(g = Lie(G/S)\) and let \(T\) operate on \(g\) through the adjoint
representation of \(G\).}

\emph{One says that the character \(\alpha\) of \(T\) is a} root
\emph{of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) if the following equivalent
conditions are satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(s \in S\), \(\alpha_{\bar{s}}\) is a root of
\(G_{\bar{s}}\) with respect to \(T_{\bar{s}}\) (1.10).}

\emph{(ii) \(\alpha\) is non-trivial on each fiber and
\(g^{\alpha}(s) \neq 0\) for every \(s \in S\).}

\textbf{Lemma 3.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(T\) an \(S\)-torus,
\(\alpha\) a character of \(T\). The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(\alpha\) is non-trivial on each fiber, that is to say: for
every \(s \in S\), \(\alpha_{\bar{s}}\) is distinct from the unit
character of \(T_{\bar{s}}\).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(S' \to S\), \(S' \neq \emptyset\),
\(\alpha_{S'}\) is distinct from the unit character of \(T_{S'}\).}

\emph{(iii) The morphism \(\alpha\) is faithfully flat.}

\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The original has been simplified; it invoked
  Exp. IX, 5.2. Let us note, however, that \emph{loc. cit.}, 5.3 shows
  that if \(S\) is connected, then the conditions of the lemma are
  verified as soon as (i) is verified at one point \(s\) of \(S\).} It
is clear that (ii) ⇒ (i), and one sees easily that (iii) ⇒ (i). One has
(i) ⇒ (ii), for if \(s' \in S'\) lies over \(s\) and if \(\alpha_{s'}\)
is the unit character, then so is \(\alpha_{s}\). Finally, to prove (i)
⇒ (iii), one reduces to the case where \(T\) is diagonalizable and
concludes by Exp. VIII 3.2 a).

\textbf{3.4.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following has been modified,
  in order to recall the hypotheses of 3.2 and to add that \(T\) is a
  maximal torus.} Let \(G\) be a reductive \(S\)-group scheme, \(T\) a
maximal torus of \(G\). Let \(\alpha\) be a root of \(G\) with respect
to \(T\). Then, by 2.5.0 and 1.12, \(g^{\alpha}\) is a locally free
\texttt{O\_S}-module of rank one. Moreover, by 1.10, \(-\alpha\) is also
a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\). In particular, if \(G\) is of
semisimple rank \texttt{1}, one has by 1.11 and 1.12:

\textbf{Lemma 3.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a reductive
\(S\)-group of semisimple rank \texttt{1}, \(T\) a maximal torus of
\(G\). If \(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), then
\(-\alpha\) is also one, and one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = t ⊕ g\^{}α ⊕ g\^{}\{−α\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(g^{\alpha}\) and \(g^{-\alpha}\) are locally free of rank
\texttt{1}.}

\textbf{Definition 3.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a reductive
\(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(R\) a set of roots of
\(G\) with respect to \(T\). One says that \(R\) is a} root system
\emph{of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) if the following equivalent
conditions are satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(s \in S\), \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha_{\bar{s}}\) is
a bijection of \(R\) onto the set of roots of \(G_{\bar{s}}\) with
respect to \(T_{\bar{s}}\).}

\emph{(ii) The elements of \(R\) are distinct on each fiber (i.e.~if
\(\alpha, \alpha' \in R\), \(\alpha \neq \alpha'\), then
\(\alpha - \alpha'\) (= \(\alpha \alpha'^{-1}\)) is non-trivial on each
fiber), and for every \(s \in S\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim(G\_s/κ(s)) − dim(T\_s/κ(s)) = Card(R).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) One has \(g = t \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R} g^{\alpha}\).}

The equivalence of these various conditions is trivial.

\textbf{Lemma 3.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a reductive
\(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(R\) a root system of
\(G\) with respect to \(T\). Every root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\)
is locally on \(S\) equal to an element of \(R\).}

\emph{Proof.} Visible on condition (iii).

Put \(\mathcal{M} = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, G_{m,S})\); it is a
twisted constant \(S\)-group scheme (Exp. X 5.6). If \(G\) admits a root
system \(R\) with respect to \(T\), then the inclusion
\(R \hookrightarrow \mathcal{M}(S)\) defines a morphism
\(R_{S} \to \mathcal{M}\), where \texttt{R\_S} is the constant
\(S\)-scheme defined by \(R\); thanks to condition (ii), one sees easily
that this morphism is an open and closed immersion whose image is none
other than \(\bigcup_{\alpha \in R} \alpha(S)\) (each \(\alpha \in R\)
being considered as a section \(S \to \mathcal{M}\)).

Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be the functor of roots of \(G\) with respect to
\(T\): by definition, \(\mathcal{R}(S')\) is the set of roots of
\(G_{S'}\) with respect to \(T_{S'}\) for every \(S' \to S\); if
\(S' = \emptyset\), one sets \(\mathcal{R}(\emptyset) = {e}\), and if
\(S' \neq \emptyset\) then the inclusion
\(R \hookrightarrow \mathcal{M}(S')\) identifies \(R\) with a root
system of \(G_{S'}\) with respect to \(T_{S'}\), and therefore, by 3.7,
one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝓡(S′) = Hom\_\{loc. const.\}(S′, R),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which shows that \(\mathcal{R}\) is representable by \texttt{R\_S}.

If one now no longer supposes necessarily that \(G\) possesses a root
system relative to \(T\), \(\mathcal{R}\) is in any case a subsheaf of
\(\mathcal{M}\) for (fpqc). Locally for this topology, \(G\) possesses a
root system with respect to \(T\) (take for example \(T\) split and use
the proof of Th. 2.5). By Exp. IV 4.6.8 and the theory of descent of
open (resp. closed) subschemes,\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: see SGA 1, VIII
  4.4 or EGA IV₂, 2.7.1.} one obtains:

\textbf{Proposition 3.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). The functor \(\mathcal{R}\)
of roots of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) is representable by a twisted
constant finite \(S\)-scheme (Exp. X 5.1) which is an open and closed
subscheme of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, G_{m,S})\).}

\emph{For \(R \subset \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, G_{m,S})\) to be a
root system of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), it is necessary and
sufficient that the morphism
\(R_{S} \to \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, G_{m,S})\) defined by the
preceding inclusion induce an isomorphism
\(R_{S} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{R}\).}

\textbf{3.9.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group,
\(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) a root of \(G\) with respect
to \(T\) (i.e.~a section of \(\mathcal{R}\)). Consider the kernel
\(Ker(\alpha)\) of \(\alpha\), its unique maximal torus \(T_{\alpha}\),
and the centralizer of the latter,
\(Z_{\alpha} = Centr_{G}(T_{\alpha})\). It is an \(S\)-group closed in
\(G\), reductive (2.8) of semisimple rank \texttt{1} (1.12). Moreover,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(Z\_α/S) = t ⊕ g\^{}α ⊕ g\^{}\{−α\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \({\alpha, -\alpha}\) is a root system of \(Z_{\alpha}\) with respect
to \(T\).

\textbf{3.10.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group,
\(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) a root of \(G\) with respect
to \(T\). If \(q \in Q\) and if \(q \alpha\) is a root of \(G\) with
respect to \(T\), then \(q = 1\) or \(q = -1\). This follows at once
from 1.12.

\subsection{4. Roots and vector group
schemes}\label{roots-and-vector-group-schemes}

\textbf{4.1.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(F\) a locally free
\texttt{O\_S}-module of finite type. The \(S\)-scheme \(W(F)\) is smooth
over \(S\). Its Lie algebra is canonically isomorphic to \(F\). Indeed,
one has a canonical isomorphism

\[
W(F) \xrightarrow{\sim} Lie(W(F)/S) = W(Lie(W(F)/S))
\]

(Exp. II, 4.4.1 and 4.4.2). We shall always identify \(F\) and
\(Lie(W(F)/S)\).

\textbf{Lemma 4.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(V\) a vector
fibration over \(S\), smooth over \(S\). Then there exists a unique
isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\[
\exp : W(Lie(V/S)) \xrightarrow{\sim} V
\]

\emph{inducing the identity on the Lie algebras.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  We have kept the original proof; one can also detail it as follows.
  Let \(F\) be a quasi-coherent \texttt{O\_S}-module, \(V = V(F)\).
  Denote by \(\pi\) the projection \(V \to S\) and \(\epsilon\) the zero
  section \(S \to V\). Then \(\Omega^{1}_{V/S} = \pi* F\), whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    ω¹\_\{V/S\} = ε* Ω¹\_\{V/S\} ≃ ε* π* F ≃ F,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  and therefore \(Lie(V/S) = (\omega^{1}_{V/S})^{V} \simeq F^{V}\). If
  one supposes \(V\) smooth over \(S\) then, by (1), \(F\) is locally
  free of finite type, and therefore

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)    V = V(F) ≃ W(Fⱽ) ≃ W(Lie(V/S)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  Now, if \(U\) is an \(S\)-scheme equipped with a section
  \(\tau : S \to U\), and if one is given an isomorphism
  \(\phi : V \xrightarrow{\sim} U\) of ``pointed'' \(S\)-schemes,
  i.e.~such that \(\phi \circ \epsilon = \tau\) (for example if \(U\) is
  an \(S\)-group), then \(\phi\) induces an isomorphism
  \(d\phi : F^{V} \xrightarrow{\sim} Lie(U/S)\), whence an isomorphism
  \(\psi : W(F^{V}) \xrightarrow{\sim} W(Lie(U/S))\) making the
  appropriate diagram commute, which permits one to identify \(U\) with
  \(W(Lie(U/S))\). Since the functor \(W\) is fully faithful, there
  exists a unique isomorphism
  \(\exp : W(Lie(U/S)) \xrightarrow{\sim} U\) such that
  \(Lie(\psi^{-1} \circ \exp) = id\). In fact, one can see directly that
  \(Lie(\psi) = id\), so that \(\exp = \psi\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, \(V = V(F)\) for some quasi-coherent
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(F\). Since \(V\) is smooth over \(S\), then
\(F \simeq \omega^{1}_{V/S}\) is locally free of finite type, and
therefore

\[
Lie(V/S) = V(\omega^{1}_{V/S}) \simeq W(Lie(V/S)).
\]

Moreover, by Exp. II \emph{loc. cit.}, one has a canonical isomorphism

\[
V \xrightarrow{\sim} Lie(V/S) \simeq W(Lie(V/S))
\]

and one has at once the uniqueness of \texttt{exp}, since \(W\) is fully
faithful.

\textbf{4.3. Notations.} If \(V\) is a vector bundle over \(S\), one
will denote by \(V\times\) the open subset of \(V\) obtained by removing
the zero section. Write the group law of \(V\) in multiplicative
notation. The action of \texttt{O\_S} on \(V\) defining the module
structure will then be written exponentially

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{O\_S × V → V,    (x, v) ↦ v\^{}x.}
\NormalTok{       S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has \((v v')^{x} = v^{x} v'^{x}\), \(v^{x+x'} = v^{x} v^{x'}\),
\(v^{x x'} = (v^{x})^{x'}\). In particular, if one restricts the
operator law to \(G_{m,S}\), then \(V\times\) is stable and is therefore
endowed with a structure of object with group of operators \(G_{m,S}\).
We shall again write this law as \((z, v) \mapsto v^{z}\).

\textbf{Definition 4.4.1.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: For later
  references, 4.4 has been transformed into 4.4.1 and 4.4.2.} \emph{Let
\(L\) be an invertible module on \(S\) and \(W(L)\) the associated
vector bundle. Then \(W(L)\times\) is a principal homogeneous bundle
(locally trivial) under \(G_{m,S}\). One denotes
\(\Gamma(S, L)\times = W(L)\times(S)\).}

\textbf{Scholie 4.4.2.} \emph{There is a bijective correspondence
between the isomorphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules \(O_{S} \simeq L\),
the isomorphisms of \texttt{O\_S}-modules
\(O_{S} \simeq W(L)\),\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: Here, one identifies the
  vector bundle \(W(L)\) with the functor in \texttt{O\_S}-modules that
  it represents.} and the sections \(S \to W(L)\times\).}

\emph{This correspondence is effected by
\(f \mapsto W(f) \mapsto W(f)(1)\). It is compatible with extension of
the base. One may therefore consider \(W(L)\times\) as the ``scheme of
trivializations of \(W(L)\)''.}

\textbf{4.5.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(T\) a torus over \(S\), \(P\) an
\(S\)-group with group of operators \(G_{m,S}\) (for example a vector
bundle), \(\alpha\) a character of \(T\). One denotes
\(T \cdot_{\alpha} P\) the semi-direct product of \(P\) by \(T\), where
\(T\) operates on \(P\) by the composite morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T {-}{-}α{-}{-}\textgreater{} G\_\{m,S\} {-}{-}{-}{-}\textgreater{} Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(P).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 4.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme, \(T\) a subgroup of \(G\), \(\alpha\) a character of
\(T\), \(L\) an \texttt{O\_S}-module. Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p : W(L) → G          [\^{}N.D.E{-}XIX{-}35]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be a morphism of \(S\)-group functors. One says that \(p\) is}
normalized by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\) \emph{if it satisfies the
following equivalent conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(p\) is a morphism of objects with group of operators \(T\),
if one makes \(T\) operate on \(W(L)\) by \(\alpha\) and on \(G\) by
inner automorphisms. In other words, for every \(S' \to S\) and all
\(t \in T(S')\) and \(x \in W(L)(S') = \Gamma(S', L \otimes O_{S'})\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(t) p(x) = p(α(t) x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) The morphism \(T \cdot_{\alpha} W(L) \to G\) defined by the
product in \(G\) (i.e.~by \((t, x) \mapsto t \cdot p(x)\)) is a morphism
of groups.}

\textbf{Lemma 4.7.} \emph{Under the conditions of 4.6, suppose moreover
that \(G\) is smooth and has connected fibers,\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  cf.~N.D.E. (28).} \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), \(L\) is
invertible. If \(p\) is a monomorphism and \(\alpha\) non-zero on each
fiber, then \(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed \(Lie(p) : L \to g\) is a monomorphism which
factors through \(g^{\alpha}\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.8.} \emph{Under the conditions of 4.7, suppose
that \(G\) is reductive, and that \(p\) is a monomorphism. Then
\(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) and \(Lie(p)\)
induces an isomorphism}

\[
Lie(p) : L \xrightarrow{\sim} g^{\alpha}.
\]

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, by virtue of 4.7 and the fact that \(g^{\alpha}\)
is invertible, it suffices to prove that \(\alpha\) is non-zero on each
fiber. Let then \(s \in S\) be such that \(\alpha_{s} = 0\) (=
\texttt{1} in multiplicative notation). If \(X\) is a non-zero section
of \(L \otimes_{S} \kappa(s)\), then \(p(X)\) is a unipotent element
\(\neq e\) of \(G(\bar{s})\) which centralizes \(T_{\bar{s}}\), which is
impossible, since the latter is its own centralizer.

\textbf{Corollary 4.9.} \emph{Under the conditions of 4.8, there exists
a monomorphism of groups with operators \(T\) (i.e. normalized by \(T\)
with multiplier \(\alpha\))}

\[
W(g^{\alpha}) \to G
\]

\emph{which induces on the Lie algebras the canonical morphism
\(g^{\alpha} \to g\).}

We shall see shortly that 4.9 is verified in fact whenever \(G\) is a
reductive group and \(\alpha\) a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\),
and that such a morphism is unique.

\textbf{Reminder 4.10.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed
field, \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\),
\(\alpha\) a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\). There exists a
monomorphism}

\[
p : G_{a,k} \to G
\]

\emph{normalized by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\).}

See \emph{Bible}, § 13.1, Th. 1.

\textbf{4.11.} Let us conclude this section with a technical result that
will be useful to us. Let \(S\) be a scheme, and \(L\) an invertible
\texttt{O\_S}-module. Let \(q\) be an integer \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}
such that \(x \mapsto x^{q}\) is an endomorphism of the \(S\)-group
\(G_{a,S}\). (If \(S \neq \emptyset\), one has \(q = 1\), or
\(q = p^{n}\), \(p\) being a prime number that is zero on \(S\); this
follows at once from the elementary fact: the gcd of the binomial
coefficients \texttt{(q\ choose\ i)}, for \(i \neq 0, q\), is \(p\) if
\(q = p^{n}\), \(p\) prime, and \texttt{1} in the contrary case.) The
morphism defined by the \(q\)-th power

\[
L \to L^{\otimes q}
\]

is a morphism of sheaves of abelian groups. It defines by base change a
morphism of \(S\)-group schemes:

\[
W(L) \to W(L^{\otimes q}).
\]

In particular, if \(L'\) is another invertible module and if one has a
morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules

\[
h : L^{\otimes q} \to L',
\]

one deduces from it a morphism of \(S\)-group schemes:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(L) → W(L′),    x ↦ h(x\^{}q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

These notations laid down, one has:

\textbf{Proposition 4.12.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(T\) (resp.
\(T'\)) an \(S\)-torus, \(L\) (resp. \(L'\)) an invertible
\texttt{O\_S}-module, \(\alpha\) (resp. \(\alpha'\)) a character of
\(T\) (resp. \(T'\)).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: ``consider the semi-direct
  product \(T \cdot_{\alpha} W(L)\), resp.
  \(T' \cdot_{\alpha'} W(L')\)'' has been removed. On the other hand,
  the hypothesis in (b) that \(g\) be a morphism of groups, combined
  with (⋆), amounts to saying that the morphism
  \((t, x) \mapsto (f(t), g(x))\) is a morphism of groups from
  \(T \cdot_{\alpha} W(L)\) to \(T' \cdot_{\alpha'} W(L')\).} Let
\(f : T \to T'\) be a morphism of groups and \(g : W(L) \to W(L')\) a
morphism of \(S\)-schemes (not necessarily a morphism of \(S\)-groups)
satisfying the following condition:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(⋆)    g(α(t) x) = α′(f(t)) g(x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for all \(x \in W(L)(S')\), \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Let
\(s_{0} \in S\) be such that \(\alpha_{s_{0}} \neq 0\).}

\emph{a) Suppose that \(g\) sends the zero section to the zero section
and that for every integer \(n > 0\), one has
\((\alpha' \circ f)_{s_{0}} \neq n \alpha_{s_{0}}\). Then \(g = 0\) in a
neighborhood of \(s_{0}\).}

\emph{b) Suppose that \(g\) is a morphism of groups such that
\(g_{s_{0}} \neq 0\). Then there exist an open subset \(U\) of \(S\)
containing \(s_{0}\) and an integer \(q > 0\) such that
\(x \mapsto x^{q}\) is an endomorphism of \(G_{a,U}\) and
\((\alpha' \circ f)_{U} = q \alpha_{U}\).}

\emph{c) Suppose that \((\alpha' \circ f)_{s_{0}} = q \alpha_{s_{0}}\),
where \(q\) is an integer \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} such that
\(x \mapsto x^{q}\) is an endomorphism of \(G_{a,S}\). Then there exist
an open subset \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s_{0}\) and a unique morphism
of \texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\[
h : L^{\otimes q}|U \to L'|U
\]

\emph{such that \(g_{U}\) is the composite morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(L)\_U {-}{-}x↦x\^{}q{-}{-}\textgreater{} W(L\^{}\{⊗q\})\_U {-}{-}W(h){-}{-}\textgreater{} (L′)\_U.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Let us prove (a). Since the conclusion is local on \(S\),
one may assume that

\(W(L) = W(L') = G_{a,S}\) and therefore that \(g\) is expressed as a
polynomial

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g(X) = ∑\_\{n ⩾ 0\} a\_n X\^{}n,    a\_n ∈ Γ(S, O\_S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The condition (⋆) linking \(f\) and \(g\) is written as an identity in
\(\Gamma(S', O_{S'})[X]\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∑\_\{n ⩾ 0\} a\_n α′(f(t)) X\^{}n = ∑\_\{n ⩾ 0\} a\_n α(t)\^{}n X\^{}n,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, for every \(n \geqslant 0\), every \(S' \to S\) and every
\(t \in T(S')\),

\[
a_{n} (\alpha'(f(t)) - \alpha(t)^{n}) = 0.
\]

For each \(n \geqslant 0\), let \(S_{n}\) be the set of \(s \in S\) such
that \((\alpha' \circ f)_{s} = n \alpha_{s}\). One knows (Exp. IX 5.3)
that the \(S_{n}\) are open and closed, and that
\((\alpha' \circ f)_{S_{n}} = n \alpha_{S_{n}}\). Moreover, since
\(\alpha_{s_{0}} \neq 0\), one may, shrinking \(S\) if necessary, assume
that \(\alpha\) is non-zero on each fiber (same reference), which
entails that the \(S_{n}\) are disjoint. Shrinking \(S\) if necessary,
one may therefore assume that one is in one of the two following cases:
there exists an \(n\) such that \(S = S_{n}\), or all the \(S_{n}\) are
empty.

Let \(m \geqslant 0\) be such that \(S_{m} = \emptyset\); I claim that
then \(a_{m} = 0\); indeed \(\alpha' \circ f\) and \(m \alpha\) are
distinct on each fiber of \(S\), and one has:

\textbf{Lemma 4.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(T\) an \(S\)-torus,
\(\alpha\) and \(\alpha'\) two characters of \(T\) distinct on each
fiber; there exists a family \({S_{i} \to S}\) covering for (fpqc), and
for each \(i\) a \(t_{i} \in T(S_{i})\), such that
\(\alpha(t_{i}) - \alpha'(t_{i}) = 1\).}

\emph{Proof.} The lemma is trivial, by reduction to the diagonalizable
case, then to the case \(T = G_{m,S}\).

Let us resume the proof of Proposition 4.12; we have just proved (a). In
cases (b) and (c), there exists an \(n\) such that \(S = S_{n}\) (with
\(n = q\) in (c)). By the preceding result, one has therefore
\(a_{m} = 0\) for \(m \neq n\), which proves that \(g\) is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g(X) = a\_n X\^{}n,    a\_n ∈ Γ(S, O\_S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This proves (c) at once. In case (b), one knows that
\(a_{n}(s_{0}) \neq 0\), one may therefore assume \(a_{n}\) invertible
on \(S\), which entails that \(x \mapsto x^{n}\) is an endomorphism of
\(G_{a,S}\) (by virtue of the hypothesis of (b)) and completes the
proof.

\subsection{5. An instructive example}\label{an-instructive-example}

\textbf{5.1.} Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field of
characteristic \texttt{0}. Put \(A = k[t]\), the polynomial ring in one
variable over \(k\), and \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\). Consider the
following Lie algebra \(g\) over \texttt{O\_S}: as a module, it is free
of dimension \texttt{3}, with basis \texttt{\{X,\ Y,\ H\}}; the
multiplication table is

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[X, Y] = 2t H,    [H, X] = X,   [H, Y] = −Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For \(s \in S\), \(s \neq s_{0}\) (the point defined by \(t = 0\)), the
fiber \(g(s) = g \otimes_{A} \kappa(s)\) is isomorphic to the Lie
algebra of the group \(PGL_{2, \kappa(s)}\). For \(s = s_{0}\), it is a
solvable Lie algebra.

\textbf{5.2.} Let \(G_{1}\) be the group scheme of automorphisms of
\(g\): for every \(S' \to S\), \(G_{1}(S')\) is the group of
automorphisms of the \(O_{S'}\)-Lie algebra
\(g \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'}\). It is a closed subscheme of the group
\(GL(g)\) of automorphisms of the \texttt{O\_S}-module \(g\). Let
\(S' \to S\) and \(u \in M_{3}(\Gamma(S', O_{S'}))\) considered as an
endomorphism of the \texttt{O\_S}-module \(g \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u(X) = a X + b Y + e H,}
\NormalTok{u(Y) = b′ X + a′ Y + e′ H,}
\NormalTok{u(H) = c X + c′ Y + d H.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One sees at once that \(u\) is a section of \(G_{1}\) if and only if
\(det(u)\) is invertible and one has the relations:\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  The equality \([u(X), u(Y)] = 2 t u(H)\) (resp.
  \([u(H), u(X)] = u(X)\), resp. \([u(H), u(Y)] = -u(Y)\)) gives the
  relations (4), (4′), and (5) (resp. (1)--(3), resp. (1′)--(3′)).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)  a(d − 1) = e c,            (1′)  a′(d − 1) = e′ c′,}
\NormalTok{(2)  b(d + 1) = e c′,           (2′)  b′(d + 1) = e′ c,}
\NormalTok{(3)  e = 2t(b c − a c′),        (3′)  e′ = 2t(b′ c′ − a′ c),}
\NormalTok{(4)  2t c = e b′ − a e′,        (4′)  2t c′ = b e′ − e a′,}
\NormalTok{                       (5)  2t(a a′ − b b′) = 2t d.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 5.3.} \emph{The relations (1), (1′), (2), (2′) imply}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{det(u) = a a′ (2 − d) + b b′ (d + 2),}
\NormalTok{a a′ − b b′ = d · det(u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, the first assertion is obtained at once by
inserting the relations (1), (1′), (2), (2′) into the expansion of
\(det(u)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{det(u) = a a′ d + b e′ c + b′ c′ e − a′ e c − a e′ c′ − b b′ d}
\NormalTok{       = a a′ d + b b′ (d + 1) + b b′ (d + 1) − a a′ (d − 1) − b b′ d − a a′ (d − 1)}
\NormalTok{       = a a′ (d − d + 1 − d + 1) + b b′ (d + 1 + d + 1 − d)}
\NormalTok{       = a a′ (2 − d) + b b′ (d + 2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Multiplying this relation by \(d\), one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d · det(u) = a a′ (2d − d²) + b b′ (d² + 2d).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But the relation (1) × (1′) = (2) × (2′) gives at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a a′ (d − 1)² = b b′ (d + 1)².}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combining the two preceding relations, one finds at once the second
sought formula.

\textbf{5.4.} Consider then \(G = G_{1} \cap SL(g)\). It is the closed
subgroup of \(G_{1}\) defined by the equation \(det(u) = 1\). It is
therefore an affine group over \(S\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.5.} \emph{The group \(G\) is smooth over \(S\).}

To prove the proposition, we shall need the following lemmas.

\textbf{Lemma 5.6.} \emph{Let \(U\) be the open subset of
\(\operatorname{End}_{A}(g) \simeq W(M_{3}(O_{S}))\) defined by the
condition ``the product \texttt{a\ d} is invertible'', i.e.~the open
subset \(\operatorname{End}_{A}(g)_{f}\), where \(f\) is the function
defined by \(f(u) = a d\). Then \(U \cap G\) is the closed subscheme of
\(U\) defined by the six equations:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1),  (2),  (2′),  (3),  (3′)   and   (D) : a a′ − b b′ = d.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} It is first clear that these six relations are verified by
every ``point'' of \(G\) (Lemma 5.3), in particular by every ``point''
of \(U \cap G\). Conversely, it must be shown that if \(u \in U(S')\)
(for every \(S' \to S\)), and if \(u\) verifies the six conditions of
the statement, then \(det(u) = 1\) and \(u\) also verifies (1′), (4),
(4′) and (5).

One has first (D) ⇒ (5). By (2) and (2′), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{b b′ (d + 1) = b c e′ = b′ c′ e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But by (3) and (3′), writing \(2t(b c - a c')(b' c' - a' c)\) in two
ways:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(b c − a c′) e′ = (b′ c′ − a′ c) e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combining with the preceding relation, this gives \(a c' e' = a' c e\).
But by (1), \(a' c e = a' a (d - 1)\), which proves
\(a (a' (d - 1) - e' c') = 0\) and entails (1′), since \(a\) is supposed
invertible.

Thus, (1), (2), (2′) and (1′) are verified, hence by Lemma 5.3 and (D)
one has \(d(det(u) - 1) = 0\). Since \(d\) is supposed invertible, this
entails \(det(u) = 1\).

Let us prove (4) and (4′). Let us do it for example for (4′), the other
calculation being deduced from it by symmetry.

By (3), (3′) and (D), one has at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a′ e + b e′ = −2t(a a′ − b b′) c′ = −2t d c′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combining (1′) and (2), one has also\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The sign
  has been corrected.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a′ e + b e′ = −d(b e′ − e a′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which completes the proof of (4′), \(d\) being supposed invertible.

\textbf{Lemma 5.7.} \emph{\(G\) is smooth over \(S\) along the unit
section.}

\emph{Proof.} By 5.6 and SGA 1, II 4.10, it suffices to prove that the
differentials of the functions

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(d − 1) − e c,    b(d + 1) − e c′,    b′(d + 1) − e′ c,}
\NormalTok{e − 2t(b c − a c′),    e′ − 2t(b′ c′ − a′ c),    a a′ − b b′ − d,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

at the points of the unit section of \(G\) are linearly independent. But
denoting by a capital letter the differential of the corresponding
lower-case, these are\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: \(A + A' + B\) has been
  corrected to \(A + A' - D\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D,    2B,    2B′,    E + 2t C′,    E′ + 2t C,    A + A′ − D,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which are indeed linearly independent modulo every \((t - \lambda)\),
\(\lambda \in k\).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: ``\((t - a)\), \(a \in A\)''
  has been corrected to ``\((t - \lambda)\), \(\lambda \in k\)''.}

\textbf{Lemma 5.8.} \emph{For \(s \in S\), \(s \neq s_{0}\), the fiber
\(G_{s}\) is connected and semisimple.}

\emph{Proof.} \footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following sentence has been
  slightly modified.} Indeed, since \(s \neq s_{0}\), \(g(s)\) is
isomorphic to the Lie algebra of \(PGL_{2, \kappa(s)}\) and, on the
other hand, one has \(G_{s} = (G_{1})_{s}\); but it is known that the
group of automorphisms of the Lie algebra of \(PGL_{2}\) over a field of
characteristic \texttt{0} is \(PGL_{2}\) itself, which is connected and
semisimple.

\textbf{Lemma 5.9.} \emph{The fiber \(G_{s_{0}}\) is solvable and has
two connected components which are of the following form:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              ⎛ a   0   0 ⎞                          ⎛ 0    b   0 ⎞}
\NormalTok{G⁰\_\{s₀\} =     ⎜ 0  a⁻¹  0 ⎟      and     G⁻\_\{s₀\} =   ⎜ b⁻¹  0   0 ⎟ .}
\NormalTok{              ⎝ c   c′  1 ⎠                          ⎝ c    c′ −1 ⎠}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one has \(e = e' = 0\), since \(t = 0\) at
\(s_{0}\). One then solves immediately the equations (1), (1′), \ldots{}
(5) and (D).

\textbf{Lemma 5.10.} \emph{The matrix}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{      ⎛ 0   1   0 ⎞}
\NormalTok{w =   ⎜ 1   0   0 ⎟}
\NormalTok{      ⎝ 0   0  −1 ⎠}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a section of \(G\) over \(S\), such that
\(w(s_{0}) \in G^{-}_{s_{0}}\).}

Let us now prove 5.5.\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The following sentence has
  been modified, by adding the reference to VI\_B, 3.10.} Denote by
\(G^{0}\) the union of the neutral components of the fibers of \(G\)
(that is to say the complement of \(G^{-}_{s_{0}}\)); since \(G\) is
smooth over \(S\) along the unit section (5.7), \(G^{0}\) is an open
subgroup of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), by VI\_B, 3.10. Since, by
translation, \(G\) is evidently smooth at the points of \(w(S)\), \(G\)
is smooth over \(S\).

\textbf{5.11.} Consider the morphism \(G_{m,S} \to G^{0}\) defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        ⎛ z   0   0 ⎞}
\NormalTok{z ↦     ⎜ 0  1/z  0 ⎟ .}
\NormalTok{        ⎝ 0   0   1 ⎠}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is a monomorphism that defines a torus \(T\) of \(G^{0}\). I claim
that one has

\[
T = Centr_{G}(T) = Centr_{G^{0}}(T).
\]

It suffices indeed to verify the first equality. Since these are smooth
subgroups of \(G\) over \(S\), it suffices to verify that they have the
same geometric points. For the fibers at points \(s \neq s_{0}\), this
follows from the fact that \(PGL_{2, \kappa(s)}\) is reductive and that
\(T_{s}\) is a maximal torus of it for reasons of dimensions (cf.~1.11).
On the fiber at \(s_{0}\), the computation is done immediately. It
follows in particular that \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\) and of
\(G^{0}\).

\textbf{5.12.} The section \(w\) of \(G\) defined in 5.9 normalizes
\(T\). It follows at once (cf.~2.4) that the Weyl group of \(G\) is
isomorphic to \((Z/2Z)_{S}\), and in particular finite over \(S\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W\_G(T) = Norm\_G(T) / T = (Z/2Z)\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, \(W_{G^{0}}(T)\) is not finite over \(S\): it ``lacks
a point'' above \(s_{0}\).

\textbf{5.13.} The open immersion \(G^{0} \to G\) is not a closed
immersion (since \(G^{0}\) is dense in \(G\)); it is however an affine
morphism (and therefore \(G^{0}\) is affine over \(S\)). Indeed, since
\(G^{0}_{s_{0}}\) is closed in \(G_{s_{0}}\), which is closed in \(G\),
the complement \(U\) of \(G^{0}_{s_{0}}\) in \(G\) is open; \(G^{0}\)
and \(U\) form an open covering of \(G\) and it suffices to verify that
the immersions \(G^{0} \to G^{0}\) and \(G^{0} \cap U \to U\) are
affine; for the first this is trivial, for the second, one notes that
\(U \cap G^{0}\) is defined in \(U\) by the equation \(b \neq 0\).

We have therefore constructed an affine smooth \(S\)-group, with
connected fibers, \(G^{0}\), possessing a maximal torus \(T\) which is
its own centralizer and whose Weyl group \(W_{G^{0}}(T)\) is not finite
(compare with Theorem 2.5).

\subsection{6. Local existence of maximal tori. The Weyl
group}\label{local-existence-of-maximal-tori.-the-weyl-group}

In the course of the proof of 2.5, we used a result from Exp. XI on the
local existence for the étale topology of maximal tori; the proof of
Exp. XI uses a fine representability result (XI 4.1). In the particular
case which occupies us, one may give another proof, based on the ideas
of Exp. XII no. 7, and of a much more elementary nature.

\textbf{Proposition 6.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a smooth,
affine \(S\)-group scheme with connected fibers over \(S\), \(s_{0}\) a
point of \(S\) such that the maximal tori of the geometric fiber
\(G_{\bar{s}_{0}}\) are their own centralizer. There exists an étale
morphism \(S' \to S\) covering \(s_{0}\), and a split maximal torus
\(T\) of \(G_{S'}\).}

\emph{Proof.} First, one may assume \(S\) affine.\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}:
  The preceding sentence as well as the reference to EGA IV in what
  follows have been added.} Since \(G\) is of finite presentation over
\(S\), one may assume \(S\) noetherian, then local, then henselian with
separably closed residue field (cf.~EGA IV, 8.12, § 8.8, and § 18.8).
Set therefore \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\), \(A\) henselian with
separably closed residue field \(k = \kappa(s_{0})\). Choose a maximal
torus \(T_{0}\) of \(G_{0} (= G_{k})\) (one exists, for example because
the scheme of maximal tori of \(G_{0}\) is smooth over \(k\), Exp. XII,
7.1 c)); since \(k\) is separably closed, \(T_{0}\) is split (cf.~X 1.4)
and is therefore given by a monomorphism of groups

\[
f_{0} : G^{r}_{m,k} \to G_{0}.
\]

Let \(m\) be an integer \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 1} prime to the
characteristic of \(k\). By Exp. VIII 6.7, for every \(h > 0\),
\(Centr_{G_{0}}({}_{m^{h}}T_{0})\) is representable by a closed
subscheme of \(G_{0}\). Since the \({}_{m^{h}}T_{0}\) are schematically
dense in \(T_{0}\) (cf.~Exp. IX 4.10) and \(G_{0}\) is noetherian, there
exists an \(h\) such that

\[
Centr_{G_{0}}({}_{m^{h}}T_{0}) = Centr_{G_{0}}(T_{0}) = T_{0}.
\]

Put \(n = m^{h}\); since \(n\) is invertible on \(S\),
\({}_{n} G_{m,S}\) is isomorphic to \((Z/nZ)_{S}\); \(f_{0}\) therefore
defines a monomorphism of groups

\[
u_{0} : (Z/nZ)^{r}_{k} \to G_{0}
\]

such that \(Centr_{G}(u_{0}) = T_{0}\). Now the \(S\)-functor

\[
\mathcal{P} = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}((Z/nZ)^{r}_{S}, G)
\]

is representable by an \(S\)-scheme of finite type (as a closed
subscheme of \(r\) copies of
\({}_{n} G = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}((Z/nZ)_{S}, G) = Ker(G --n--> G)\)).
But \(\mathcal{P}\) is smooth over \(S\) (Exp. IX 3.6), hence
\(u_{0} \in \mathcal{P}(k)\) lifts to a section \(u \in \mathcal{P}(S)\)
(Hensel's lemma, Exp. XI 1.11):

\[
u : (Z/nZ)^{r}_{S} \to G.
\]

Consider \(H = Centr_{G}(u)\); it is a closed subgroup scheme of \(G\),
by Exp. VIII 6.5 e), and one has \(H_{0} = T_{0}\) by
hypothesis.\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}: The reference VIII 6.5 e) has been
  added in what precedes, and the following sentence has been detailed.}
Moreover, \(H\) is smooth over \(S\): indeed, let
\(S' = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\) be an affine scheme over \(S\),
\(u' : ({}_{n} G_{m,S'})^{r} \to G_{S'}\) the morphism deduced from
\(u\) by base change, \(S'_{J} = \operatorname{Spec}(A/J)\), where \(J\)
is an ideal of square zero, and let \(x \in H(S'_{J})\); since \(G\) is
smooth, \(x\) lifts to an element \(g\) of \(G(S')\); then
\(v = int(g)(u')\) verifies \(v_{J} = u'_{J}\) and therefore, by IX 3.2,
there exists an element \(g'\) of \(G(S')\) such that \(g'_{J} = e\) and
\(int(g')(v) = u'\); then \(h = g' g\) belongs to \(H(S')\) and verifies
\(h_{J} = x\).

Let then \(H^{0}\) be the neutral component of \(H\); it is a subgroup
scheme of \(G\), smooth and with connected fibers, whose special fiber
is a torus. By Exp. X 8.1, it is a torus, necessarily split (Exp. X
4.6). Put \(H^{0} = T\) and let \(C = Centr_{G}(T)\), which is a closed
subgroup of \(G\) (Exp. VIII 6.5 e)), smooth (Exp. XI 2.4). Consider
\(C^{0}\) (in fact \(C^{0} = C\), but we do not need to know it); then
\(C^{0} \supset T\) and these are two smooth groups with connected
fibers. They coincide at \(s_{0}\), hence in a neighborhood. Shrinking
\(S\) if necessary, one may therefore assume \(C^{0} = T\), hence
\emph{a fortiori} \(T\) maximal.

\textbf{Remark 6.2.} \emph{The proof shows in particular that the
reductive rank of \(G_{\bar{s}}\) is constant in a neighborhood of
\(s = s_{0}\).}

\textbf{Proposition 6.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), \(Q\) a
subtorus of \(G\).}

\emph{(i) \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) and \(Norm_{G}(Q)\) are representable by
closed subgroup schemes, smooth (and therefore of finite presentation)
over \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is an open and closed subscheme of
\(Norm_{G}(Q)\). The quotient \(W_{G}(Q) = Norm_{G}(Q) / Centr_{G}(Q)\)
is representable by an open subgroup scheme of
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(Q)\); it is therefore an \(S\)-group scheme
quasi-finite, étale and separated over \(S\).}

\emph{(iii) For every \(s \in S\), put}

\[
w(s) = Norm_{G(\bar{s})}(Q(\bar{s})) / Centr_{G(\bar{s})}(Q(\bar{s})).
\]

\emph{Then \(s \mapsto w(s)\) is lower semicontinuous, and is constant
in a neighborhood of \(s\) if and only if \(W_{G}(Q)\) is finite over
\(S\) in a neighborhood of \(s\).}

\emph{Proof.} By Exp. XI 6.11, \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) and \(Norm_{G}(Q)\) are
representable by closed subschemes of finite presentation of \(G\).
These are smooth by Exp. XI 2.4 and 2.4 bis, which proves (i).
Assertions (ii) and (iii) are then proved as in Exp. XI 5.9 and 5.10,
whose proof uses in fact only (i) and not the fine theorems Exp. XI 4.1
and 4.2.

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-8}

\section{Exposé XX. Reductive groups of semisimple rank
1}\label{exposuxe9-xx.-reductive-groups-of-semisimple-rank-1}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{1. Elementary systems. The groups
\(U_{\alpha}\) and
\(U_{-\alpha}\)}{1. Elementary systems. The groups U\_\{\textbackslash alpha\} and U\_\{-\textbackslash alpha\}}}\label{elementary-systems.-the-groups-u_alpha-and-u_-alpha}

\textbf{Recollection 1.1.} \emph{Let \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\),
where \(k\) is an algebraically closed field, and let \(G\) be a
reductive \(S\)-group of semisimple rank 1, \(T\) a maximal torus
(necessarily split) of \(G\). One then has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = t ⊕ g\_α ⊕ g\_\{−α\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\) are the roots of \(G\) with
respect to \(T\). Moreover, there exist two group monomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α : G\_\{a, S\} → G    and    p\_\{−α\} : G\_\{a, S\} → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t p\_α(x) t⁻¹ = p\_α(α(t) x)    and    t p\_\{−α\}(x) t⁻¹ = p\_\{−α\}(α(t)⁻¹ x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(S' \to S\) and all \(t \in T(S')\),
\(x \in G_{a}(S')\), and such that the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_\{a, S\} ×\_S T ×\_S G\_\{a, S\} → G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined by \((y, t, x) \mapsto p_{-\alpha}(y) t p_{\alpha}(x)\),
is radicial and dominant (}Bible\emph{, § 13.4, cor. 2 to th. 3).}

Since the tangent map at the identity is bijective, this morphism is
also separable, hence birational; by Zariski's ``Main Theorem'' (EGA
III₁, 4.4.9), it is therefore an open immersion.

\textbf{Lemma 1.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group
scheme, \(T\) a torus of \(G\), \(Q\) a subtorus of \(T\), \(\alpha\) a
character of \(T\) inducing on \(Q\) a non-trivial character on each
fiber. Let \(p_{\alpha} : G_{a, S} \to G\) (resp.
\(p_{-\alpha} : G_{a, S} \to G\)) be a group morphism normalized by
\(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\) (resp. \(-\alpha\)). Suppose that the
morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u : G\_\{a, S\} ×\_S T ×\_S G\_\{a, S\} → G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined set-theoretically by
\(u(y, t, x) = p_{-\alpha}(y) t p_{\alpha}(x)\), is an open immersion.
Let finally \(q\) be an integer \(\geqslant 0\) and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p : G\_\{a, S\} → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{a group morphism such that for every \(S' \to S\) and all
\(t \in Q(S')\), \(x \in G_{a}(S')\) one has}

\[
int(t)(p(x)) = p(\alpha(t)^{q} x).
\]

\emph{Then there exists a unique \(\nu \in G_{a}(S)\) such that
\(p(x) = p_{\alpha}(\nu x^{q})\).}

Indeed, let \(\Omega\) be the image of \(u\) and \(U = p^{-1}(\Omega)\).
This is an open subset of \(G_{a, S}\) containing the zero section. For
every section \(t\) of \(Q\), the automorphism of \(G_{a, S}\) defined
by multiplication by \(\alpha(t)\) leaves \(U\) globally fixed. We have
\(U = G_{a, S}\); indeed, it suffices to check this when \(S\) is the
spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\); then
\(\alpha : Q(k) \to k*\) is surjective, which proves at once that
\(U(k) \supset k*\), hence \(U = G_{a, k}\). There therefore exist three
morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
