\NormalTok{a : G\_\{a, S\} → G\_\{a, S\},   b : G\_\{a, S\} → T,   c : G\_\{a, S\} → G\_\{a, S\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p(x) = p\_\{−α\}(a(x)) b(x) p\_α(c(x)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The condition on \(p\) translates to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(α(t) x) = α(t)\^{}\{−q\} a(x),}
\NormalTok{b(α(t) x) = b(x),}
\NormalTok{c(α(t) x) = α(t)\^{}q c(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For the same reason as before, one therefore has for every \(S' \to S\)
and every \(z \in G_{m}(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(z x) = z\^{}\{−q\} a(x),   b(z x) = b(x),   c(z x) = z\^{}q c(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{z\^{}q a(z) = a(1),   b(z) = b(1),   c(z) = z\^{}q c(1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(G_{m, S}\) is schematically dense in \(G_{a, S}\), one has at
once for every \(x \in G_{a}(S')\), \(S' \to S\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\^{}q a(x) = a(1) = a(0) = 0,    hence a = 0,}
\NormalTok{c(x) = x\^{}q c(1) = ν x\^{}q,       for some ν ∈ G\_a(S),}
\NormalTok{b(x) = b(1) = b(0) = e,        hence b = e,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which completes the proof.

\textbf{Definition 1.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme. By an
\(S\)-}elementary system* one means a triple \((G, T, \alpha)\) where*

\emph{(i) \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group of semisimple rank 1 (Exp.
XIX 2.7),}

\emph{(ii) \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\),}

\emph{(iii) \(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) (Exp.
XIX 3.2).}

One thus has a direct sum decomposition (Exp. XIX 3.5)\footnote{N.D.E.:
  of \texttt{O\_S}-modules.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = t ⊕ g\_α ⊕ g\_\{−α\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\(g_{\alpha}\) and \(g_{-\alpha}\) being locally free of rank one.

\textbf{1.4.} If \((G, T, \alpha)\) is an \(S\)-elementary system, then
\((G_{S'}, T_{S'}, \alpha_{S'})\) is an \(S'\)-elementary system for
every \(S' \to S\). If \((G, T, \alpha)\) is an \(S\)-elementary system,
then \((G, T, -\alpha)\) is also one.

If \(S\) is a scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(T\) a maximal
torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), then
(Exp. XIX 3.9), \((Z_{\alpha}, T, \alpha)\) is an \(S\)-elementary
system.

Let \((G, T, \alpha)\) be an \(S\)-elementary system. The invertible
module \(g_{\alpha}\) is canonically endowed with a \(T\)-module
structure. One therefore has also a \(T\)-module structure on the vector
bundle \(W(g_{\alpha})\). On the other hand, the inner automorphisms of
\(T\) define on \(G\) a structure of group with group of operators
\(T\).

\textbf{Theorem 1.5.} \emph{Let \((G, T, \alpha)\) be an
\(S\)-elementary system.}

\emph{(i) There exists a unique morphism of groups with group of
operators \(T\)}

\[
\exp : W(g_{\alpha}) \to G
\]

\emph{which induces on the Lie algebras the canonical morphism
\(g_{\alpha} \to g\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: We shall see later (Cor. 5.9)
  that \texttt{exp} is an isomorphism of \(W(g_{\alpha})\) onto a closed
  subgroup of \(G\).}

\emph{In other words, \texttt{exp} is the unique morphism satisfying the
following conditions: for every \(S' \to S\) and every \(t \in T(S')\),
\(X, X' \in W(g_{\alpha})(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{exp(X + X′) = exp(X) exp(X′),}
\NormalTok{int(t)(exp(X)) = exp(α(t) X),}
\NormalTok{Lie(exp)(X) = X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) If one defines analogously (in the \(S\)-elementary system
\((G, T, -\alpha)\))}

\[
\exp : W(g_{-\alpha}) \to G,
\]

\emph{then the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_\{−α\}) ×\_S T ×\_S W(g\_α) → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined set-theoretically by
\((Y, t, X) \mapsto \exp(Y) \cdot t \cdot \exp(X)\) is an open
immersion.}

Suppose we have proved the existence of the desired \texttt{exp}
morphisms, and let us prove the other assertions of the theorem. We
first prove (ii). Since both sides are of finite presentation and flat
over \(S\), it suffices to do so when \(S\) is the spectrum of an
algebraically closed field (SGA 1, I 5.7 and VIII 5.5). Let then
\(S = \operatorname{Spec} k\). Let
\(X \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\),
\(Y \in \Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})^{\times}\). It suffices to prove that the
morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_\{a, k\} ×\_k T ×\_k G\_\{a, k\} → G,   (y, t, x) ↦ exp(yY) t exp(xX)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is an open immersion. Now by 1.1 and 1.2, there exist \(a, b \in k\)
such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{exp(yY) = p\_\{−α\}(a y)    and    exp(xX) = p\_α(b x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\exp : W(g_{-\alpha}) \to G\) induces a monomorphism on Lie
algebras, one has \(a \neq 0\); likewise \(b \neq 0\), and one is
reduced to 1.1.

The uniqueness of the morphism \texttt{exp} may be proved locally on
\(S\); one then reduces to the case where \(g_{\alpha}\) and
\(g_{-\alpha}\) are free, and one has only to apply 1.2 (with \(Q = T\)
and \(q = 1\)).

It remains then to prove the existence of the desired morphism
\texttt{exp}. Let us first remark that, by virtue of the theory of
faithfully flat descent and the uniqueness assertion just proved, it
suffices to demonstrate this existence locally on \(S\) for the (fpqc)
topology. By the usual arguments using finite presentation, one reduces
to the case where \(S\) is noetherian, then to the case where it is
noetherian local. By virtue of the preceding remark, one can therefore
content oneself with proving the existence of the desired morphism
\texttt{exp} when \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\), with \(A\) a complete
noetherian local ring with algebraically closed residue field \(k\). Let
then \(p_{0} : G_{a, k} \to G_{k}\) be a monomorphism of \(k\)-groups
normalized by \(T_{k}\) with multiplier
\(\alpha_{0} = \alpha \otimes_{A} k\) (one exists by 1.1). One knows
(1.1 and 1.2) that the corresponding morphism
\(T_{k} \cdot_{\alpha_{0}} G_{a, k} \to G_{k}\) is an immersion, hence
in particular a monomorphism. Let us provisionally admit the following
two lemmas:

\textbf{Lemma 1.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group of
finite presentation, \(T\) an \(S\)-torus, \(\alpha\) a character
non-trivial on each fiber of \(T\), \(s_{0}\) a point of \(S\). Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : T ·\_α G\_\{a, S\} → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be an \(S\)-group morphism such that \(f_{s_{0}}\) is a
monomorphism and the restriction of \(f\) to \(T\) is a monomorphism.
There exists an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(s_{0}\) such that \(f|U\)
is a monomorphism.}

\textbf{Lemma 1.7.} \emph{Let \(A\) be a complete noetherian local ring
with algebraically closed residue field \(k\), \((G, T, \alpha)\) an
\(A\)-elementary system, \(p_{0} : G_{a, k} \to G_{k}\) a morphism of
\(k\)-groups normalized by \(T_{k}\) with multiplier
\(\alpha \otimes_{A} k\). There exists a group morphism
\(p : G_{a, A} \to G\) normalized by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\).}

Let \(p\) be the morphism whose existence is asserted by 1.7. Let
\(f : T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, S} \to G\) be the corresponding morphism.
It satisfies the hypotheses of 1.6, hence is a monomorphism; in
particular \(p\) is a monomorphism. One then concludes by Exp. XIX 4.9.

\emph{Proof of 1.6.} Denote by
\(\epsilon : S \to T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, S}\) the unit section. Since
\(f\) is unramified at \(\epsilon(s_{0})\), it is so at \(\epsilon(s)\)
for all \(s\) in an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(s_{0}\); \(f|U\) is
therefore unramified (Exp. X 3.5)\footnote{N.D.E.: see also VI\_B, 2.5.},
hence its kernel \(Ker(f)_{U}\) is unramified over \(U\). To prove that
\(f|U\) is a monomorphism, it suffices therefore\footnote{N.D.E.: by EGA
  IV₄, 17.9.1.} to prove that \(Ker(f)_{U}\) is radicial over \(U\),
which is a set-theoretic question. One is thus reduced to proving:

\textbf{Lemma 1.8.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field;
let \(N\) be an invariant subgroup of \(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k}\)
(\(\alpha\) a non-trivial character of the torus \(T\)), étale over
\(k\) and such that \(N \cap T = {e}\). Then \(N = {e}\).}

One has \(int(t')(t, x) = (t, \alpha(t') x)\). If \((t, x)\) is a point
of \(N\), with \(x \neq 0\), then \texttt{(t,\ z\ x)} is also a point of
\(N\) for \(z \in k*\), and \((t, x)\) is not isolated; hence \(N\) is
not quasi-finite. One therefore has set-theoretically \(N \subset T\),
and we are done.

\emph{Proof of 1.7.} Let \(m\) be the radical of \(A\), and
\(S_{n} = \operatorname{Spec}(A/m^{n+1})\), \(n \geqslant 0\). We first
show, by induction on \(n\), that \(p_{0}\) can be extended for each
\(n\) to a morphism of \(S_{n}\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_n : G\_\{a, S\_n\} → G\_\{S\_n\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

normalized by \(T_{S_{n}}\) with multiplier \(\alpha_{S_{n}}\), the
\(p_{n}\) further satisfying the condition
\(p_{n+1} \times_{S_{n+1}} S_{n} = p_{n}\).

Let \(H = T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, S}\). The morphism
\(H_{S_{n}} \to G_{S_{n}}\) defined by \(p_{n}\) is denoted \(f_{n}\).
Let us admit the following lemma:

\textbf{Lemma 1.9.} \emph{If \((G, T, \alpha)\) is a \(k\)-elementary
system, \(k\) algebraically closed, and if \(p : G_{a, k} \to G\) is a
monomorphism normalized by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H²(T ·\_α G\_\{a, k\}, g) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(One lets \(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k}\) act on \(g\) through the
morphism \(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k} \to G\) defined by \(p\), and the
adjoint representation of \(G\)).}

Then, by virtue of Exp. III 2.8, \(f_{n}\) extends to a morphism of
\(S_{n+1}\)-groups

\[
f'_{n+1} : H_{S_{n+1}} \to G_{S_{n+1}}.
\]

Now \(f'_{n+1}\) and the canonical immersion of \(T_{S_{n+1}}\) into
\(G_{S_{n+1}}\) have the same restriction to \(T_{S_{n}}\). By Exp. III
2.5, there exists an element \(g \in G(S_{n+1})\) such that
\(g \times_{S_{n+1}} S_{n} = e\) and such that
\(f_{n+1} = int(g) \circ f'_{n+1}\) restricts to \(T_{n+1}\) along the
canonical immersion of \(T_{n+1}\). Let \(p_{n+1}\) be the restriction
of \(f_{n+1}\) to \(G_{a, S_{n+1}}\). It is a morphism normalized by
\(T_{S_{n+1}}\) with multiplier \(\alpha_{S_{n+1}}\), which extends
\(p_{n}\).

One has thus constructed a coherent system \((f_{n})\) and one must now
algebraize it. Now one has:

\textbf{Lemma 1.10.} \emph{Let \(A\) be a complete noetherian local
ring, \(m\) its maximal ideal, \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\),
\(S_{n} = \operatorname{Spec}(A/m^{n+1})\), \(T\) an \(S\)-torus,
\(\alpha\) a non-zero character of \(T\), \(X\) an affine \(S\)-scheme
on which \(T\) acts. Let \(T\) act on \(G_{a, S}\) via \(\alpha\). Let
\(q\) be an integer \(\geqslant 0\), and let \((f_{n})_{n \geqslant 0}\)
be a coherent system of morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_n : G\_\{a, S\_n\}\^{}q → X\_\{S\_n\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{of objects with operators \(T_{S_{n}}\). There exists a unique
morphism of objects with operators \(T\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : G\_\{a, S\}\^{}q → X}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which induces the \(f_{n}\) (compare with Exp. IX 7.1).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.11.} \emph{If \(X\) is a group with group of
operators \(T\) and if the \(f_{n}\) are group morphisms, then \(f\) is
one too.}

It suffices to apply the uniqueness assertion of the lemma to the two
morphisms \(G^{2q}_{a, S} \to X\) deduced from \(f\) in the usual way.

\emph{Proof of 1.10.} Suppose \(T\) split, which is moreover the case in
the application of 1.10 to the proof of 1.5. One knows (Exp. I 4.7.3.1)
that \(X \mapsto A(X)\) realizes an equivalence between the category of
affine \(S\)-schemes equipped with a \(T\)-operation and the opposite
category of \(S\)-graded algebras of type
\(M = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, G_{m, S})\).

One therefore has gradings

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B = A(X) = ⨁\_\{m ∈ M\} B\_m    and    C = A(G\_\{a, S\}\^{}q) = ⨁\_\{m ∈ M\} C\_m.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One sees at once that each \(C_{m}\) is free of finite type over \(A\).
(Indeed, one has \(C_{m} = 0\) if \(m\) is not a multiple of \(\alpha\),
and if \(m = d \alpha\), \(C_{m}\) is isomorphic to the \(A\)-module of
homogeneous polynomials of degree \(d\), in \(q\) variables.) Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B̂\_m = lim\_n B\_m ⊗\_A (A/m\^{}\{n+1\}),}
\NormalTok{Ĉ\_m = lim\_n C\_m ⊗\_A (A/m\^{}\{n+1\}),}
\NormalTok{B̂ = ⨁\_\{m ∈ M\} B̂\_m,    Ĉ = ⨁\_\{m ∈ M\} Ĉ\_m.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One then has canonical morphisms of \(M\)-graded algebras

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_B : B → B̂    and    g\_C : C → Ĉ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows from the remark made above that \(g_{C}\) is an isomorphism.
To give a coherent system \((f_{n})\) as in the statement is equivalent
to giving a morphism of graded \(A\)-algebras

\[
\hat{F} : \hat{B} \to \hat{C}.
\]

To find a morphism \(f\) as in the statement is equivalent to finding a
morphism of graded \(A\)-algebras \(F : B \to C\) rendering commutative
the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B  ──F──→  C}
\NormalTok{│           │}
\NormalTok{g\_B         g\_C}
\NormalTok{↓           ↓}
\NormalTok{B̂  ──F̂──→  Ĉ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(g_{C}\) is an isomorphism, the existence and uniqueness of \(F\)
are immediate. This proves 1.10.

To complete the proof of 1.5, it remains only to prove 1.9.

\textbf{1.12. Proof of 1.9.} One has
\(g = t \oplus g_{\alpha} \oplus g_{-\alpha}\). As explained in 1.9,
consider \(g\) as a \((T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k})\)-module. It is clear
that \(t \oplus g_{\alpha}\) is a submodule of \(g\), the quotient being
isomorphic to \(g_{-\alpha}\) as a \(k\)-vector space and even as a
\(T\)-module. It is clear that \(G_{a, k}\) acts trivially on this
quotient, which is of dimension 1 (for every group morphism from
\(G_{a, k}\) to \(G_{m, k}\) is trivial). Similarly \(g_{\alpha}\) is a
submodule of \(t \oplus g_{\alpha}\), the quotient being isomorphic to
\(t\) as a \(T\)-module, \(G_{a, k}\) acting trivially on it. To
summarize:

\textbf{Lemma 1.13.} \emph{Under the conditions of 1.9, \(g\) admits a
composition series as \((T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k})\)-module whose
successive quotients are}

\[
g_{-\alpha}, t, g_{\alpha},
\]

\emph{viewed as \((T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k})\)-modules via the
projection \(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k} \to T\).}

One is therefore reduced to computing the cohomology of
\(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k}\) acting via the projection
\(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k} \to T\) and the character \(\beta\) of \(T\)
(here \(\beta = 0\), \(\alpha\), or \(-\alpha\)) on \(W(k)\).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have added the sentence that follows.} Let
\(k[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}]\) denote the algebra of polynomials over \(k\)
in \(n\) variables and \(k_{q}[x_{1}, \cdots, x_{n}]\) the subspace of
homogeneous polynomials of degree \(q\).

\textbf{Lemma 1.14.} \emph{With the preceding notations, one has
\(H^{n}(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k}, k) = H^{n}(C^{*}_{\alpha, \beta})\),
where the complex \(C^{*}_{\alpha, \beta}\) is defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\^{}n\_\{α, β\} = \{ k\_q[x\_1, …, x\_n]   if β = q α, with q ∈ ℕ*;}
\NormalTok{             \{ 0                  otherwise,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{δf(x\_1, x\_2, …, x\_\{n+1\}) = f(x\_2, …, x\_\{n+1\})}
\NormalTok{                         + Σ\_\{i=1\}\^{}n (−1)\^{}i f(x\_1, …, x\_i x\_\{i+1\}, …, x\_\{n+1\})}
\NormalTok{                         + (−1)\^{}\{n+1\} f(x\_1, …, x\_n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, the functor \(M \mapsto H^{0}(T, M)\) is exact on the category
of \(T\)-modules (and the \(H^{q}(T, -)\) vanish), by Exp. I 5.3.2. It
follows, as in the usual case of group cohomology, that
\(H^{n}(T \cdot_{\alpha} G_{a, k}, k)\) can be computed as the \(n\)-th
cohomology group of the complex of cochains of \(G_{a, k}\) in \(k\),
invariant under \(T\), i.e. satisfying

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(α(t) x\_1, …, α(t) x\_n) = β(t) f(x\_1, …, x\_n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This indeed gives the announced complex.

To prove 1.9, it therefore suffices to prove that
\(H^{2}(C^{*}_{\alpha, \beta}) = 0\) for \(\beta = 0, \alpha, -\alpha\),
which is done at once.

\textbf{Remark 1.15.} \emph{One can explicitly compute the groups
\(H^{n}(C^{*}_{\alpha, \beta})\) for \(\beta = q \alpha\) (see M.
Lazard,} Lois de groupes et analyseurs*, Annales E.N.S., 1955). In
particular, one finds \(H^{n}(C^{*}_{\alpha, q \alpha}) = 0\) for
\(n > q\).*

\textbf{Notations 1.16.} \emph{The image of the canonical immersion}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_\{−α\}) ×\_S T ×\_S W(g\_α) → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{will be denoted \(\Omega\). It is an open subset of \(G\)
containing the unit section. The image of}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_\{−α\}),   resp. W(g\_α),   resp. W(g\_\{−α\}) ×\_S T,   resp. T ×\_S W(g\_α)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{will be denoted}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced \(P_{-\alpha}\)
  and \(P_{\alpha}\) by \(U_{-\alpha}\) and \(U_{\alpha}\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_\{−α\},   resp. U\_α,   resp. U\_\{−α\} · T,   resp. T · U\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(U_{\alpha}\) (resp. \(U_{-\alpha}\)) is a subgroup of \(G\)
canonically endowed with a vector bundle structure, and one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(t)(x) = x\^{}\{α(t)\}    (resp. x\^{}\{−α(t)\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(S' \to S\), \(t \in T(S')\), \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\)
(resp. \(x \in U_{-\alpha}(S')\)).}

One has canonical isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T · U\_α ≅ T ·\_α U\_α    and    T · U\_\{−α\} ≅ T ·\_\{−α\} U\_\{−α\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The open set \(\Omega\) is stable under \(int(T)\): one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(t′)(y · t · x) = y\^{}\{−α(t′)\} · t · x\^{}\{α(t′)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 1.17.} \emph{One has
\(Lie(U_{\alpha} / S) = g_{\alpha}\) and
\(Lie(U_{-\alpha} / S) = g_{-\alpha}\). The isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_α)  ──exp──→  U\_α    and    W(g\_\{−α\})  ──exp──→  U\_\{−α\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are those of Exp. XIX 4.2.}

\textbf{Corollary 1.18.} \emph{The open set \(\Omega\) is relatively
schematically dense in \(G\) (cf.~XVIII, § 1).}

Clear by Exp. XVIII, 1.3.\footnote{N.D.E.: see also EGA IV₃, 11.10.10.}

\textbf{Corollary 1.19.} \emph{The center of \(G\) is
\(Centr(G) = Ker(\alpha)\). It is therefore a closed subgroup of \(G\),
of multiplicative type and of finite type.}

The second assertion follows from the first by Exp. IX 2.7. Let us
therefore prove the first. The inner automorphism defined by a section
of \(Ker(\alpha)\) acts trivially on \(\Omega\) (last formula of 1.16),
hence on \(G\) by 1.18. Conversely, if \(g \in G(S)\) centralizes \(G\),
then it centralizes \(T\) and \(U_{\alpha}\), hence is a section of
\(T\) (Exp. XIX 2.8) annihilating \(\alpha\); since this also holds
after any base change, one indeed has \(Centr(G) = Ker(\alpha)\).

\textbf{Corollary 1.20.} \emph{For there to exist a monomorphism
\(p_{\alpha} : G_{a, S} \to G\) normalized by \(T\) with multiplier
\(\alpha\), it is necessary and sufficient that the \texttt{O\_S}-module
\(g_{\alpha}\) be free. More precisely, one has a bijection given by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\_α ↦ (x ↦ exp(x X\_α))    and    p\_α ↦ Lie(p\_α)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{between \(\Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\) and the set of
monomorphisms \(p_{\alpha}\) as above (which is also the set of
isomorphisms of vector group schemes
\(G_{a, S} \xrightarrow{\sim} U_{\alpha}\)).}\footnote{N.D.E.: Indeed,
  on the one hand, \(Lie(G_{a, S}) = O_{S}\) and \(Lie(p_{\alpha})\) is
  an element of
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}}(O_{S}, g_{\alpha}) = \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})\).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.21.} \emph{The subgroups \(U_{\alpha}\) and
\(U_{-\alpha}\) of \(G\) commute on no fiber.}

Indeed, if \((U_{\alpha})_{s}\) and \((U_{-\alpha})_{s}\) commute, then
\(\Omega_{s}\) is a subgroup of \(G_{s}\), hence
\(\Omega_{s} = G_{s}\)\footnote{N.D.E.: by 1.18.} and \(G_{s}\) is
solvable, which contradicts the hypothesis that \(G_{s}\) is reductive
of semisimple rank 1.

\subsection{2. Structure of elementary
systems}\label{structure-of-elementary-systems}

\textbf{Theorem 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \((G, T, \alpha)\) an
\(S\)-elementary system. There exists a morphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_α ⊗\_\{O\_S\} g\_\{−α\} → O\_S,   (X, Y) ↦ ⟨X, Y⟩,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and a morphism of \(S\)-groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α* : G\_\{m, S\} → T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that for every \(S' \to S\) and all
\(X \in \Gamma(S', g_{\alpha} \otimes O_{S'})\),
\(Y \in \Gamma(S', g_{-\alpha} \otimes O_{S'})\) one has the
equivalence:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{exp(X) · exp(Y) ∈ Ω(S′) ⇐⇒ 1 + ⟨X, Y⟩ ∈ G\_m(S′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and under these conditions one has the formula:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(F)    exp(X) · exp(Y) = exp( Y / (1 + ⟨X, Y⟩) ) · α*(1 + ⟨X, Y⟩) · exp( X / (1 + ⟨X, Y⟩) ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, the morphisms \((X, Y) \mapsto \langle X, Y\rangle\) and
\(\alpha*\) are uniquely determined, the former is an isomorphism, hence
puts the modules \(g_{\alpha}\) and \(g_{-\alpha}\) in duality, and one
has} \(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\) \emph{(squaring in \(G_{m, S}\)).}

In view of the uniqueness assertions of the theorem, it suffices to do
the proof locally on \(S\). One can therefore assume \(g_{\alpha}\) and
\(g_{-\alpha}\) free on \(S\). Take then
\(X \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\),
\(Y \in \Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})^{\times}\) and set
\(p_{\alpha}(x) = \exp(x X)\), \(p_{-\alpha}(y) = \exp(y Y)\), for
\(x, y \in G_{a}(S')\), \(S' \to S\). By 1.5 and 1.21, it suffices to
prove:

\textbf{Proposition 2.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group, \(T\) a torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) a character of \(T\)
non-trivial on each fiber, \(p_{\alpha} : G_{a, S} \to G\) (resp.
\(p_{-\alpha} : G_{a, S} \to G\)) a group monomorphism normalized by
\(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\) (resp. \(-\alpha\)). Suppose that:}

\emph{(i) The morphism
\(G_{a, S} \times_{S} T \times_{S} G_{a, S} \to G\) defined by
\((y, t, x) \mapsto p_{-\alpha}(y) t p_{\alpha}(x)\) is an open
immersion. Denote its image by \(\Omega\).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(s \in S\), \((p_{\alpha})_{s}(G_{a, \kappa(s)})\)
and \((p_{-\alpha})_{s}(G_{a, \kappa(s)})\) do not commute.}

\emph{Then there exist \(a \in G_{a}(S)\) and
\(\alpha* \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G_{m, S}, T)\), uniquely
determined, having the following properties: for every \(S' \to S\) and
all \(x, y \in G_{a}(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_\{−α\}(y) ∈ Ω(S′) ⇐⇒ 1 + a x y ∈ G\_m(S′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and, under this condition, one has the formula}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_\{−α\}(y) = p\_\{−α\}( y / (1 + a x y) ) · α*(1 + a x y) · p\_α( x / (1 + a x y) ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, \(a\) is invertible (i.e.~\(a \in G_{m}(S)\)) and
\(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\).}

\emph{Proof:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\Alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  Consider the morphism
\end{enumerate}

\[
G^{2}_{a, S} \to G
\]

defined by \((x, y) \mapsto p_{\alpha}(x) p_{-\alpha}(y)\). Let \(U\) be
the inverse image of \(\Omega\) under this morphism. It is an open
subset of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) containing \(0 \times_{S} G_{a, S}\) and
\(G_{a, S} \times_{S} 0\). There therefore exist uniquely determined
\(S\)-scheme morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A : U → G\_\{a, S\},   C : U → G\_\{a, S\},   B : U → T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

satisfying the set-theoretic relation:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(u) p\_\{−α\}(v) = p\_\{−α\}(A(u, v)) B(u, v) p\_α(C(u, v)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has immediately the relations

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A(0, v) = v,   A(u, 0) = 0,   C(u, 0) = u,   C(0, v) = 0,}
\NormalTok{B(u, 0) = B(0, v) = e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(S'\) be a separated \(S\)-scheme and let \(t \in T(S')\) be a
point of \(T\). Since \(\Omega_{S'}\) is stable under \(int(t)\), then,
by the last formula of 1.16, \(U_{S'}\) is stable under the automorphism
\((x, y) \mapsto (\alpha(t) x, \alpha(t)^{-1} y)\) of \(G^{2}_{a, S'}\),
and one has the relations:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A(α(t) u, α(t)⁻¹ v) = α(t)⁻¹ A(u, v),}
\NormalTok{C(α(t) u, α(t)⁻¹ v) = α(t) C(u, v),}
\NormalTok{B(α(t) u, α(t)⁻¹ v) = B(u, v).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\alpha\) is faithfully flat, one deduces that for every
\(S' \to S\) and every \(z \in G_{m}(S')\), \(U_{S'}\) is stable under
the transformation \((x, y) \mapsto (z x, z^{-1} y)\) and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A(z u, z⁻¹ v) = z⁻¹ A(u, v),}
\NormalTok{C(z u, z⁻¹ v) = z C(u, v),}
\NormalTok{B(z u, z⁻¹ v) = B(u, v).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Suppose first that \(v\) is invertible; setting \(z = v\), one deduces
that if \((u, v)\) is a section of \(U\), then \texttt{(u\ v,\ 1)} is
also one, and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A(u v, 1) = v⁻¹ A(u, v),    B(u v, 1) = B(u, v).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let then \(V\) be the open set of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) defined by\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have added the condition ``\((1, u v) \in U(S')\)''.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u, v) ∈ V(S′) ⇐⇒ (u, v), (u v, 1) and (1, u v) belong to U(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(U\) is an open set of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) containing
\(0 \times_{S} G_{a, S}\) and \(G_{a, S} \times_{S} 0\), then \(V\) is a
neighborhood of the zero section of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) and we have just
seen that the morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u, v) ↦ A(u, v) and (u, v) ↦ v A(u v, 1)}
\NormalTok{resp. (u, v) ↦ B(u, v) and (u, v) ↦ B(u v, 1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

coincide on \(V \cap (G_{a, S} \times_{S} G_{m, S})\). Since
\(G_{a, S} \times_{S} G_{m, S}\) is schematically dense in
\(G^{2}_{a, S}\), these morphisms therefore coincide on \(V\).

One knows that \(A(0, 1) = 1\); it follows that there exists an open set
\texttt{W\_1} of \(G_{a, S}\) containing the zero section such that for
every section \(x\) of \texttt{W\_1}, \(A(x, 1)\) is invertible; setting
\(A(x, 1)^{-1} = F(x)\), one obtains that if
\((u, v) \in V(S')\)\footnote{N.D.E.: here and in what follows, we have
  replaced \(U(S')\) by \(V(S')\).} and \(u v \in W_{1}(S')\),
\(S' \to S\), then \(A(u, v) = v A(u v, 1) = v F(u v)^{-1}\). Arguing
similarly for \(C\), one obtains that there exists an open set
\texttt{W\_2} of \(G_{a, S}\) containing the zero section, and an
element \(E\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have denoted by \(E\) the element
  denoted \(G\) in the original, since \(G\) already denotes the
  \(S\)-group under consideration.} of \(O(W_{2})^{\times}\), such that
\(C(u, v) = u C(1, u v) = u E(u v)^{-1}\), if \((u, v) \in V(S')\) and
\(u v \in W_{2}(S')\). Consequently, setting \(W = W_{1} \cap W_{2}\),
one obtains:

There exists an open set \(W\) of \(G_{a, S}\) containing the zero
section, and \(S\)-morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F : W → G\_\{m, S\},   F(0) = 1,}
\NormalTok{H : W → T,         H(0) = e,}
\NormalTok{E : W → G\_\{m, S\},   E(0) = 1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that if \((u, v) \in V(S')\) and \(u v \in W(S')\), \(S' \to S\),
one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    p\_α(u) p\_\{−α\}(v) = p\_\{−α\}(v F(u v)⁻¹) H(u v) p\_α(u E(u v)⁻¹).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\Alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Let us now use the associativity of \(G\) to write
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(u) p\_\{−α\}(v) p\_\{−α\}(w) = p\_α(u) p\_\{−α\}(v + w).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

There exists an open set \(L\) of \(G^{3}_{a, S}\), containing the unit
section, such that \((u, v, w) \in L(S')\) is equivalent to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u, v) ∈ V(S′),   (u E(u v)⁻¹, w) ∈ V(S′),   (u, v + w) ∈ V(S′),}
\NormalTok{u v ∈ W(S′),     u w E(u v)⁻¹ ∈ W(S′),       u(v + w) ∈ W(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using then the formula (+), one writes at once for
\((u, v, w) \in L(S')\) the relations:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   E(u v + u w) = E(u w E(u v)⁻¹) E(u v),}
\NormalTok{(2)   H(u v + u w) = H(u w E(u v)⁻¹) H(u v),}
\NormalTok{(3)   (v + w) F(u v + u w)⁻¹ = α(H(u v)⁻¹) w F(u w E(u v)⁻¹)⁻¹ + v F(u v)⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is immediate from the definition of \(L\) that
\((1, 0, 0) \in L(S)\). Consider therefore

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L ∩\_T (1 ×\_S G\_\{a, S\} ×\_S G\_\{a, S\}) = 1 ×\_S M;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\(M\) is an open set of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\), containing the section
\texttt{(0,\ 0)}, and for \((v, w) \in M(S')\), one has
\(v, w E(v)^{-1}, v + w \in W(S')\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1′)   E(v + w) = E(w E(v)⁻¹) E(v),}
\NormalTok{(2′)   H(v + w) = H(w E(v)⁻¹) H(v),}
\NormalTok{(3′)   (v + w) F(v + w)⁻¹ = α(H(v))⁻¹ w F(w E(v)⁻¹)⁻¹ + v F(v)⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consider finally the morphism from \(M\) to \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) defined
set-theoretically by \((v, w) \mapsto (v, w E(v)^{-1})\).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have corrected what follows.} It preserves the section
\texttt{(0,\ 0)} and induces an isomorphism of \(M\) onto an open set
\(N\) of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) containing the zero section (the inverse
isomorphism being given by \((x, y) \mapsto (x, y E(x))\)).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  that is, we have made the ``change of variables'' \(x = v\),
  \(y = w E(v)^{-1}\), i.e.~\(v = x\), \(w = y E(x)\).} One has thus
proved the following assertion:

There exists an open set \(N\) of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\), containing the zero
section, such that if \((x, y) \in N(S')\), then \texttt{x,\ y} and
\(x + y E(x)\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected \texttt{y\ E(x)} to
  \(x + y E(x)\).} belong to \(W(S')\) and:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1″)   E(x + y E(x)) = E(x) E(y),}
\NormalTok{(2″)   H(x + y E(x)) = H(x) H(y),}
\NormalTok{(3″)   (x + y E(x)) F(x + y E(x))⁻¹ = x F(x)⁻¹ + α(H(x))⁻¹ y E(x) F(y)⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\Alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  Arguing similarly with left associativity, one demonstrates the
  following assertion:\footnote{N.D.E.: that is, one writes the
    equalities resulting from
    \(p_{\alpha}(t) p_{\alpha}(u) p_{-\alpha}(v) = p_{\alpha}(t + u) p_{-\alpha}(v)\)
    and sets \(v = 1\) and \(x = u\), \(t = y F(u)\)
    (i.e.~\(y = t F(u)^{-1}\)).}
\end{enumerate}

There exists an open set \(N'\) of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\), containing the zero
section, such that if \((x, y) \in N'(S')\), then \texttt{x,\ y} and
\(x + y F(x)\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected \texttt{y\ F(x)} to
  \(x + y F(x)\).} belong to \(W(S')\), and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4″)   F(x + y F(x)) = F(x) F(y),}
\NormalTok{(5″)   H(x + y F(x)) = H(x) H(y),}
\NormalTok{(6″)   (x + y F(x)) E(x + y F(x))⁻¹ = x E(x)⁻¹ + α(H(x))⁻¹ y F(x) E(y)⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We are therefore led to solve the ``functional equation'' (1″).

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(W\) an open set of
\(G_{a, S}\) containing the unit section, \(F : W \to G_{m, S}\) an
\(S\)-morphism. Suppose that \(F(0) = 1\) and that there exists an open
set \(N\) of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) containing the zero section such that for
\((x, y) \in N(S')\), \texttt{x,\ y}, and \(x + y F(x)\)\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have corrected \texttt{y\ F(x)} to \(x + y F(x)\).} belong to
\(W(S')\) and that one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)    F(x + y F(x)) = F(x) F(y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) If \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\), there exists
\(a \in k\) such that \(F(x) = 1 + a x\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(a = F'(0) \in \Gamma(S, O_{S})\) is invertible, then
\(F(x) = 1 + a x\).}

By the hypotheses, we can differentiate the given equation at \(x = 0\)
(resp. at \(y = 0\)) and we find that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    F′(y) (1 + y F′(0)) = F′(0) F(y)    for (0, y) ∈ N(S′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

resp.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F′(x) F(x) = F(x) F′(0)    for (x, 0) ∈ N(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(F\) takes its values in \(G_{m}\), the second relation gives us

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗′)   F′(x) = F′(0)    for (x, 0) ∈ N(S′);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, by the first,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F′(0)(1 + y F′(0)) = F′(0) F(y)    for (y, 0), (0, y) ∈ N(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(a = F'(0)\) is invertible, this gives us

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(y) = 1 + a y,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for \(y\) a section of an open set of \(W\) containing the unit section,
hence schematically dense in \(W\), which proves (ii). This also proves
(i) when \(F'(0) \neq 0\).

If \(F'(0) = 0\), then, by (∗′), \(F'(x) = 0\) when \(x\) is ``near 0'',
hence \(F' = 0\) by schematic density. If \(k\) is of characteristic 0,
\(F\) is a rational fraction with zero derivative, hence constant and
equal to \(F(0) = 1\).

If \(k\) is of characteristic \(p\), and if \(F\) is not
constant,\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected what follows.} there exists
an integer \(n > 0\) and a rational fraction \(F_{1} \in k(X)\) such
that \(F'_{1}(X) \neq 0\) and

\[
F(X) = F_{1}(X^{p^{n}}) = F_{1}(X)^{p^{n}}.
\]

Substituting in the functional equation, one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†\_1)   F\_1(x + y F\_1(x)\^{}\{p\^{}n\}) = F\_1(x) F\_1(y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Differentiating at \(x = 0\), one finds

\[
(\ast_{1})   F'_{1}(y) = F'_{1}(0) F_{1}(y),
\]

and differentiating (†\_1) at \(y = 0\), one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗′\_1)  F′\_1(x) F\_1(x)\^{}\{p\^{}n\} = F\_1(x) F′\_1(0).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since, by hypothesis, \(F'_{1}(X)\) is an invertible element of
\(k(X)\), one deduces from these two equalities that

\[
F_{1}(X)^{p^{n}} = 1,
\]

hence \texttt{F\_1} is a constant, contradicting the initial hypothesis.
This shows that \(F\) is constant, and equal to \(1 = F(0)\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\Alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Suppose \(S\) is the spectrum of a field. If \(F'(0) = 0\), then
  \(F = 1\). Formula (5″) then gives us \(H(x + y) = H(x) H(y)\), which
  shows that \(H\) extends to a group morphism \(G_{a, S} \to T\) (Exp.
  XVIII 2.3), which is necessarily constant of value \(e\). On the other
  hand, by Lemma 2.3, one will also have \(E(x) = 1 + b x\) for some
  \(b \in k\). But then (6″) gives, for \((x, y) \in N(S')\),
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(x + y) E(x + y)⁻¹ = x E(x)⁻¹ + y E(y)⁻¹,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence,\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the sentence that follows. One can
  also see by a direct calculation that the preceding equality entails
  \(0 = x y b (2 + (x + y) b)\), hence \(0 = b(2 + (x + y) b)\), and
  finally \(b = 0\).} by Exp. XVIII 2.3 again, \(x \mapsto x E(x)^{-1}\)
extends to a morphism of \(k\)-groups \(G_{a, k} \to G_{a, k}\), hence
\(x/(1 + b x) = c x\) for some \(c \in k\), whence \(b = 0\) (and
\(c = 1\)).

This shows that \texttt{F,\ H,\ E} are constant of value
\texttt{(1,\ e,\ 1)} in a neighborhood of the unit section, hence
everywhere, which by (+) shows that \(U_{\alpha}\) and \(U_{-\alpha}\)
commute, contrary to hypothesis (ii).

If \(S\) is now arbitrary, one has therefore proved that \(F'(0)\) is
non-zero on no fiber, hence is invertible. The same evidently holds for
\(E'(0)\), which by Lemma 2.3 shows that there exist
\(a, b \in G_{m}(S)\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(♦\_1)   F(x) = 1 + a x,    E(x) = 1 + b x,    for x ∈ W(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\Alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\tightlist
\item
  The rest is now easy. Substituting the preceding results into (3″),
  one finds
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y α(H(x)) (1 + a y) = y (1 + a x + a y(1 + b x)) (1 + a x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This formula is valid for every section \((x, y)\) of \(N\). But since
\(G_{a, S} \times_{S} G_{m, S}\) is schematically dense in
\(G^{2}_{a, S}\), one deduces

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1 + a y) α(H(x)) = (1 + a x + a y(1 + b x)) (1 + a x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Setting \(y = 0\), this gives \(\alpha(H(x)) = (1 + a x)^{2}\).
Substituting this into the preceding equality, one finds\footnote{N.D.E.:
  In the three preceding equalities, we have corrected the original by
  replacing the factor \((1 + b x)\) on the right by \(1 + a x\).
  Substituting the third equality into the second and taking into
  account that \(1 + a x\) is invertible, one obtains the equality
  \(a^{2} x y = a b x y\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a² x y = a b x y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(G_{m, S}\) is schematically dense in \(G_{a, S}\), one deduces
\(a^{2} = a b\), whence, since \(a\) is invertible,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(♦\_2)   a = b    and    α(H(x)) = (1 + a x)².}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(a\) is invertible, \(x \mapsto 1 + a x\) is an automorphism of
\(G_{a, S}\); one can therefore find an open set \(W'\) of \(G_{a, S}\)
containing the section \texttt{1} and a morphism

\[
P : W' \to T
\]

such that \(P(1 + a x) = H(x)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: that is, we have made
  the change of variables \(x' = 1 + a x\), i.e.~\(x = (x' - 1)/a\).}

Substituting in the relation (2′), one finds at once for
\((x, y) \in N(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(1 + a x + a y) = P((1 + a x + a y) / (1 + a x)) P(1 + a x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which proves that there exists an open neighborhood of \texttt{1} in
\(G_{m, S}\) such that one has for \(x\) and \(y\) in this neighborhood
\(P(x) P(y) = P(x y)\). By Exp. XVIII 2.3, there exists a group morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(♦\_3)   α* : G\_\{m, S\} → T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

extending \(P\). Since \(\alpha(H(x)) = (1 + a x)^{2}\) near the section
\texttt{0}, one has \(\alpha(\alpha*(z)) = z^{2}\) near the section
\texttt{1}, hence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(♦\_4)   α ∘ α* = 2.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

F)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have slightly modified what follows, since an
  open set \(V\) was already introduced in A).} Assembling the results
(+) and (♦\_1 --- ♦\_4), one sees that there exist \(a \in G_{m}(S)\)
and \(\alpha* \in \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G_{m, S}, T)\) such that
\(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\) and that, if \((u, v) \in V(S')\) and
\(u v \in W(S')\), then \(1 + a u v\) is invertible and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(u) p\_\{−α\}(v) = p\_\{−α\}( v / (1 + a u v) ) · α*(1 + a u v) · p\_α( u / (1 + a u v) ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consider the open set \(V'\) of \(G^{2}_{a, S}\) defined by
``\(1 + a u v\) invertible'', i.e.~\(V' = (G^{2}_{a, S})_{f}\) where
\(f(u, v) = 1 + a u v\). The two sides of the preceding formula define
morphisms from \(V'\) to \(G\) which coincide in a neighborhood of the
section \texttt{0}, hence coincide on \(V'\). The preceding formula is
therefore valid for every section \((u, v)\) of \(V'\). In particular,
it follows that \(V' \subset U\), where \(U\) is the open set introduced
at the beginning of A).

Let us prove that \(U = V'\). Returning to the notations of A), one has
a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A : U → G\_\{a, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which, on \(V'\), is defined by \(A(u, v) = v (1 + a u v)^{-1}\). To
show that \(U = V'\), which is a set-theoretic question, one is reduced
to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\), hence to the
obvious assertion: the domain of definition of the rational map
\(G^{2}_{a, k} \to G_{a, k}\) defined by the rational fraction
\(Y / (1 + a X Y)\) is the open set defined by the function
\(1 + a X Y\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\Alph{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{6}
\tightlist
\item
  One has thus proved the existence of \(a\) and \(\alpha*\), as well as
  the two additional properties announced. It remains to prove
  uniqueness. Let then \(a'\) and \(\alpha*'\) also satisfy the required
  conditions. If \(u, v \in G_{a}(S')^{2}\), one has at once:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 + a u v invertible ⇒ 1 + a′ u v invertible and v / (1 + a u v) = v / (1 + a′ u v);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one therefore has for every section \(u\) of \(G_{a}(S')\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 + a u invertible ⇒ 1 + a u = 1 + a′ u,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which proves at once \(a = a'\).

With the same notations, one then has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 + a u invertible ⇒ α*(1 + a u) = α*′(1 + a u),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence also \(\alpha* = \alpha*'\).

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.} \emph{Let \(\exp(Y) t \exp(X)\) and
\(\exp(Y') t' \exp(X')\) be two elements of \(\Omega(S')\). Then their
product is in \(\Omega(S')\) if and only if
\(u = 1 + \langle X, Y'\rangle\) is invertible, and one has then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(F′)    exp(Y) t exp(X) · exp(Y′) t′ exp(X′) =}
\NormalTok{             exp(Y + u⁻¹ α(t)⁻¹ Y′) · t t′ α*(u) · exp(u⁻¹ α(t′)⁻¹ X + X′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 2.5.} \emph{One can also write formula (F) of Theorem 2.1
without invoking the morphisms \texttt{exp}. Indeed, transporting
through these morphisms the duality
\(g_{\alpha} \otimes g_{-\alpha} \to O_{S}\), one obtains a canonical
pairing of vector bundles:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_α ×\_S U\_\{−α\} → G\_\{a, S\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which we shall still denote
\((x, y) \mapsto \langle x, y\rangle\). One therefore has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⟨exp X, exp Y⟩ = ⟨X, Y⟩.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(y \in U_{-\alpha}(S')\) and if
\(1 + \langle x, y\rangle \in G_{m}(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(F)    x · y = y\^{}\{(1 + ⟨x, y⟩)⁻¹\} · α*(1 + ⟨x, y⟩) · x\^{}\{(1 + ⟨x, y⟩)⁻¹\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 2.6.} \emph{The pairing}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_α) ×\_S W(g\_\{−α\}) → G\_\{a, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defines a pairing of principal \(G_{m, S}\)-bundles}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_α)\^{}× ×\_S W(g\_\{−α\})\^{}× → G\_\{m, S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{This pairing will be denoted
\((X, Y) \mapsto \langle X, Y\rangle\), or more simply
\((X, Y) \mapsto X Y\).}

For every section \(X \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\), there
therefore exists a unique section \(X^{-1}\) of
\(\Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})^{\times}\) such that \(X X^{-1} = 1\). One has
\((z X)^{-1} = z^{-1} X^{-1}\). The morphism

\[
s : W(g_{\alpha})^{\times} \to W(g_{-\alpha})^{\times}
\]

thus defined is therefore an isomorphism of schemes, compatible with the
isomorphism \(s : z \mapsto z^{-1}\) on the operator groups.

\textbf{Definition 2.6.1.} \emph{One says that \(X\) and
\(s(X) = X^{-1}\) are} paired.

Apply Corollary 2.4 to \(Y = 0 = X'\) and \(Y' = a X^{-1}\),
\(a \in O_{S}(S)\). Then \(u = 1 + a\) and
\(u^{-1} Y' = u^{-1}(u - 1) X^{-1} = (1 - u^{-1}) X^{-1}\), whence:

\textbf{Corollary 2.7.} \emph{Let
\(X \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\) and
\(u \in \Gamma(S, O_{S})^{\times}\). One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α*(u) = exp((u⁻¹ − 1) X⁻¹) exp(X) exp((u − 1) X⁻¹) exp(−u⁻¹ X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 2.8.} \emph{The morphism \(\alpha*\) is called the}
coroot \emph{associated with the root \(\alpha\).}

\textbf{Remark 2.9.} \emph{If \((G, T, \alpha)\) is an \(S\)-elementary
system, \((G, T, -\alpha)\) is also one. By Theorem 2.1 one therefore
has a duality between \(g_{-\alpha}\) and \(g_{\alpha}\), and a coroot
\((-\alpha)*\). Taking the inverse of formula (F), one proves at once}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⟨X, Y⟩ = ⟨Y, X⟩,    (−α)* = −α*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us now pass to the Lie algebra of \(G\). The root \(\alpha\) and the
coroot \(\alpha*\) define the linear forms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{O\_S  ──α*──→  t  ──α──→  O\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One will denote \(H_{\alpha} = \alpha*(1)\). One calls \(\alpha\) the
\emph{infinitesimal root} associated with \(\alpha\), and \(H_{\alpha}\)
the corresponding \emph{infinitesimal coroot}.

\textbf{Lemma 2.10.} \emph{Let \(S' \to S\) and
\(X, X' \in W(g_{\alpha})(S')\), \(H \in W(t)(S')\),
\(Y, Y' \in W(g_{-\alpha})(S')\), \(t \in T(S')\). One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   Ad(t) H = H,    Ad(t) X = α(t) X,    Ad(t) Y = α(t)⁻¹ Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   \{ Ad(exp(X)) H = H − α(H) X,    Ad(exp(X)) X′ = X′,}
\NormalTok{      \{ Ad(exp(X)) Y = Y + ⟨X, Y⟩ H\_α − ⟨X, Y⟩ X.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2′)  \{ Ad(exp(Y)) H = H + α(H) Y,    Ad(exp(Y)) Y′ = Y′,}
\NormalTok{      \{ Ad(exp(Y)) X = X + ⟨X, Y⟩ H\_\{−α\} − ⟨X, Y⟩ Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(3)   [H, X] = α(H) X,    [H, Y] = −α(H) Y,    [X, Y] = ⟨X, Y⟩ H\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\[
(4)   H_{-\alpha} = -H_{\alpha}.
\]

\[
(5)   \alpha(H_{\alpha}) = 2.
\]

The proof of these various formulas is either trivial or an immediate
consequence of formula (F) of 2.1.

\textbf{Corollary 2.11.} \emph{Suppose \(H_{\alpha}\) is non-zero on
every fiber (which is in particular the case if \texttt{2} is invertible
on \(S\), by (5)). Then
\(X_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\) and
\(X_{-\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})^{\times}\) are paired if and
only if \([X_{\alpha}, X_{-\alpha}] = H_{\alpha}\).}

\textbf{2.12.} Let \((G, T, \alpha)\) be an \(S\)-elementary system. We
know (1.19) that the center of \(G\) is \(Centr(G) = Ker(\alpha)\), a
group of multiplicative type and of finite type. If \(Q\) is a subgroup
of multiplicative type of \(Centr(G)\), the quotient \(G/Q\) is affine
over \(S\) (Exp. IX 2.5), smooth over \(S\) (Exp. VI\_B 9.2) with
connected reductive fibers of semisimple rank 1 (Exp. XIX 1.8).

Set \(G' = G/Q\); this is a reductive \(S\)-group of semisimple rank 1;
\(T' = T/Q\) is a maximal torus of it. The open set
\(U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U_{\alpha}\) of \(G\) is stable under \(Q\),
and one sees at once that the quotient is isomorphic to
\(U_{-\alpha} \times_{S} (T/Q) \times_{S} U_{\alpha}\). If one denotes
by \(\alpha'\) the character of \(T'\) induced by \(\alpha\), it follows
that the morphism derived from the canonical morphism \(G \to G'\)
induces isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_α  ──∼──→  g′\_\{α′\}    and    g\_\{−α\}  ──∼──→  g′\_\{−α′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, \(\alpha'\) is a root of \(G'\) with respect to \(T'\).
Hence, denoting by \(\alpha/Q\) the character \(T/Q \to G_{m, S}\)
induced by \(\alpha\), one has:

\textbf{Lemma 2.13.} \emph{If \(Q\) is a subgroup of multiplicative type
of \(Ker(\alpha)\), then}

\[
(G/Q, T/Q, \alpha/Q)
\]

\emph{is an elementary system.}

\textbf{Lemma 2.14.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, the following
diagrams are commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_α)  ──exp──→  G  ←──exp──  W(g\_\{−α\})}
\NormalTok{   │                │                │}
\NormalTok{   can ≀            can              can ≀}
\NormalTok{   ↓                ↓                ↓}
\NormalTok{W(g′\_\{α′\})  ──exp──→  G′  ←──exp──  W(g′\_\{−α′\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_α ⊗ g\_\{−α\}  ──∼──→  O\_S}
\NormalTok{     │                  │}
\NormalTok{     can ≀              id}
\NormalTok{     ↓                  ↓}
\NormalTok{g′\_\{α′\} ⊗ g′\_\{−α′\}  ──∼──→  O\_S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              T}
\NormalTok{        α*  ↗  ↘ α}
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}        G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{        ↓ can   ↑}
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}  ⤴  ⤵  G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{       α′*  ↘  ↗ α′}
\NormalTok{              T′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{3. The Weyl group}\label{the-weyl-group-1}

\textbf{Notations 3.0.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the numbering
  3.0, for later references.} If \((G, T, \alpha)\) is an
\(S\)-elementary system, one will denote

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N = Norm\_G(T),    W = Norm\_G(T) / T,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(cf.~Exp. XIX 6.3); \(N\) is a closed subgroup of \(G\), smooth over
\(S\). One will denote by \(N^{\times}  = N - T\) the open subscheme of
\(N\) induced on the complement of \(T\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  replaced \(Q\) by the more suggestive notation \(N^{\times}\).} Let
\(R\) be the (unique) maximal torus of \(Ker(\alpha)\), and \(T'\) the
image of \(\alpha* : G_{m, S} \to T\), which is a subtorus of dimension
1 of \(T\).

The morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T′ ×\_S R → T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induced by the product in \(T\) is surjective (hence faithfully flat);
indeed, one is reduced to checking this on the geometric fibers, and
this follows at once from the formula \(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\).

\textbf{Theorem 3.1.} \emph{With the preceding notations:}

\emph{(i) \(W\) is isomorphic to the constant group
\((\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})_{S}\).}

\emph{(ii) \(N^{\times}\) is a principal homogeneous bundle locally
trivial under \(T\), on the left by the law \((t, q) \mapsto t q\)
(resp. on the right by the law \((q, t) \mapsto q t\)).}

\emph{(iii) One has the formula}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w) t = t · α*(α(t)⁻¹)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for \(w \in N^{\times}(S')\), \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\). In
the decomposition \(T_{S'} = T'_{S'} \cdot R_{S'}\), \(int(w)\) induces
the identity on \(R_{S'}\) and the symmetry on \(T'_{S'}\). One has the
relations}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α ∘ int(w) = α⁻¹,    int(w) ∘ α* = (α*)⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iv) For \(X \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\), \(S' \to S\), set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X) = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(w_{\alpha}(X) \in N^{\times}(S')\) and the morphism
\(w_{\alpha} : W(g_{\alpha})^{\times} \to N^{\times}\) thus defined
satisfies}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(z X) = α*(z) w\_α(X) = w\_α(X) α*(z)⁻¹,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for \(z \in G_{m}(S')\), \(X \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\),
\(S' \to S\).}

\emph{(v)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the first formula of the
  original.} For \(X, Y \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\), \(S' \to S\),
one has, with the notations of 2.6,}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X) w\_α(Y) = α∨(−X Y⁻¹).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular,}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X)² = α*(−1) ∈ ₂T(S) ∩ Centr(G)(S),}
\NormalTok{w\_α(X)⁻¹ = w\_α(−X) = α*(−1) w\_α(X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(vi) If one defines analogously, for
\(Y \in W(g_{-\alpha})^{\times}(S')\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_\{−α\}(Y) = exp(Y) exp(−Y⁻¹) exp(Y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has (in addition to formulas analogous to the preceding)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_\{−α\}(X⁻¹) = w\_α(X)⁻¹ = w\_α(−X),}
\NormalTok{w\_α(X) w\_\{−α\}(Y) = α*(X Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} (i) has already been seen in Exp. XIX 2.4; it follows at
once that \(N^{\times}\) is indeed a principal homogeneous bundle under
\(T\) for the laws defined in (ii); the fact that it is locally trivial
(for the Zariski topology) follows notably from (iv).

Let us prove (iii); if \(w \in N^{\times}(S)\), it is clear that
\(\alpha \circ int(w)\) is a root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\), hence
is locally equal to \(\alpha\) or \(-\alpha\); since on each fiber it is
\(-\alpha\) (\emph{Bible}, 12-05, proof of the corollary to prop. 1),
one has \(\alpha \circ int(w) = -\alpha\). By transport of structure,
one deduces

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{−α* = int(w)⁻¹ ∘ α* = int(w) ∘ α*,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since \(int(w)^{2} = int(w^{2})\) and \(w^{2}\) is a section of \(T\).
Therefore \(int(w)\) induces the symmetry on \(T'\); since \(R\) is
central, \(int(w)\) induces the identity on \(R\). The formula of (iii)
defines a morphism \(T \to T\) which satisfies the same properties,
hence coincides with \(int(w)\).

Let us prove (iv). One has successively

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X) t w\_α(X)⁻¹ = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(X) t exp(−X) exp(X⁻¹) exp(−X)}
\NormalTok{                  = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(X − α(t) X) exp(α(t)⁻¹ X⁻¹) exp(−α(t) X) t.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By application of formula (F), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{exp(−X⁻¹) exp((1 − α(t)) X) = exp((α(t)⁻¹ − 1) X) α*(α(t)⁻¹) exp(−α(t)⁻¹ X⁻¹).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Substituting in the preceding relation, one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α(X)) t = exp(α(t)⁻¹ X) α*(α(t)⁻¹) exp(−α(t) X) t}
\NormalTok{              = exp(a X) α*(α(t)⁻¹) t,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a = α(t)⁻¹ − (α ∘ α*)(α(t)⁻¹) α(t),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but \(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\), which gives at once \(a = 0\) and
\(w_{\alpha}(X) \in N^{\times}(S')\).

Let us prove the second assertion of (iv). One has\footnote{N.D.E.: The
  first equality follows from 1.5 (i) which, combined with the equality
  \(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\), gives the formulas

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)   α*(z) exp(X) α*(z)⁻¹ = exp(z² X),    α*(z) exp(X⁻¹) α*(z)⁻¹ = exp(z⁻² X),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  the third equality follows from formula (F), and the fourth from (†),
  again. Finally, an analogous calculation shows that
  \(w_{\alpha}(X) \alpha*(z^{-1}) = w_{\alpha}(z X)\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α*(z) w\_α(X) = exp(z² X) exp(−z⁻² X⁻¹) exp(z² X) α*(z)}
\NormalTok{             = exp(z X) exp((z² − z) X) exp(−z⁻² X⁻¹) exp(z² X) α*(z)}
\NormalTok{             = exp(z X) exp(−z⁻¹ X⁻¹) α*(z)⁻¹ exp((z³ − z²) X) exp(z² X) α*(z)}
\NormalTok{             = exp(z X) exp(−z⁻¹ X⁻¹) exp(z X) = w\_α(z X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us prove (v). By virtue of the preceding result, the first formula
of (v) follows at once from the second; let us prove the second:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X)² = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(2 X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(X)}
\NormalTok{        = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(X⁻¹) α*(−1) exp(−2 X) exp(X)}
\NormalTok{        = exp(X) α*(−1) exp(−X) = α*(−1),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since \(\alpha(\alpha*(-1)) = (-1)^{2} = 1\), which proves that
\(\alpha*(-1) \in Centr(G)(S)\).

Let us prove (vi). The first assertion is a particular case of the
second; let us prove the second. Both sides of this formula define
morphisms
\(W(g_{\alpha})^{\times} \times_{S} W(g_{-\alpha})^{\times} \to G\). To
prove that they coincide, it suffices to do so on a non-empty open set
on each fiber (Exp. XVIII 1.4); it therefore suffices to verify the
relation when \(1 + X Y\) is invertible. One then has successively:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X) w\_\{−α\}(Y) = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(X) exp(Y) exp(−Y⁻¹) exp(Y)}
\NormalTok{                 = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹) exp(Y / (1 + X Y)) α*(1 + X Y) exp(X / (1 + X Y)) exp(−Y⁻¹) exp(Y)}
\NormalTok{                 = exp(X) exp(−X⁻¹ / (1 + X Y)) α*(1 + X Y) exp(−Y⁻¹ / (1 + X Y)) exp(Y)}
\NormalTok{                 = exp(−X⁻² Y⁻¹) α*(X Y / (1 + X Y)) exp(X + Y⁻¹) α*(1 + X Y) exp(−Y⁻¹ / (1 + X Y)) exp(Y)}
\NormalTok{                 = exp(−X⁻² Y⁻¹) α*(X Y) exp((Y⁻¹ + X) / (1 + X Y)²) exp(−Y⁻¹ / (1 + X Y)) exp(Y)}
\NormalTok{                 = α*(X Y) exp(−Y) exp(Y) = α*(X Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 3.2.} \emph{Let \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), \(n \neq 0\).
For every \(w \in G(S)\), the following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(w \in N^{\times}(S)\),}

\emph{(ii) one has \(int(w) \circ n \alpha* = -n \alpha*\) (recall that
\((n \alpha*)(z) = \alpha*(z)^{n}\)).}

One has (i) ⇒ (ii) (assertion (iii) of Theorem 3.1); conversely, one may
suppose that \(N^{\times}\) admits a section, and one is reduced to
proving:

\textbf{Lemma 3.3.} \emph{One has \(Centr_{G}(n \alpha*) = T\) for
\(n \neq 0\).}

Indeed, the image \(T'\) of \(n \alpha*\) is a subtorus of \(G\). It
follows (Exp. XIX 2.8) that \(Centr_{G}(n \alpha*)\) is a reductive
subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\). Since on each fiber one has
\(Centr_{G_{s}}(n \alpha*_{s}) \neq G_{s}\), then
\(Centr_{G_{s}}(n \alpha*_{s}) = T_{s}\) (Exp. XIX 1.6.3)\footnote{N.D.E.:
  The hypothesis \(Centr_{G_{s}}(n \alpha*_{s}) \neq G_{s}\) entails
  that
  \texttt{dim\ Centr\_\{G\_s\}(n\ α*\_s)\ −\ dim\ T\_s\ \textless{}\ 2},
  but this difference is even, by \emph{loc. cit.}}, hence
\(Centr_{G}(n \alpha*) = T\), since these are smooth subgroups of \(G\).

\textbf{Remark 3.4.} \emph{The construction of \(w_{\alpha}\) and the
fact that \(w_{\alpha}(X)\) normalizes \(T\) rely only on formula (F).
In particular, if \(G\) is an \(S\)-group satisfying the conditions of
2.2, \(Norm_{G}(T)\) differs from \(T\) on each fiber. It follows that
if \(G\) is an affine \(S\)-group with connected fibers satisfying the
conditions of 2.2, it is reductive of semisimple rank 1. Indeed, it is
smooth in a neighborhood of the unit section, hence smooth, and one can
apply the criterion of Exp. XIX 1.11.}

\textbf{3.5.} Before stating the following theorem, let us make a few
remarks. We identify as usual \(g_{-\alpha}\) with
\((g_{\alpha})^{\otimes-1}\). Similarly, we shall identify
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}}(g_{-\alpha}, g_{\alpha})\) with
\((g_{\alpha})^{\otimes 2}\) and hence

\[
Isom_{O_{S}-mod.}(W(g_{-\alpha}), W(g_{\alpha})) \cong W((g_{\alpha})^{\otimes 2})^{\times}.
\]

If \(w \in N^{\times}(S)\), then \(Ad(w)\) permutes \(g_{\alpha}\) and
\(g_{-\alpha}\) (3.1, (iii)), hence defines an isomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a\_α(w) : g\_\{−α\} ──∼──→ g\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which we shall therefore identify with a section
\(a_{\alpha}(w) \in \Gamma(S, (g_{\alpha})^{\otimes 2})^{\times}\). This
construction is compatible with base change and therefore defines a
morphism

\[
a_{\alpha} : N^{\times} \to W((g_{\alpha})^{\otimes 2})^{\times},
\]

such that \(a_{\alpha}(w) Y = Ad(w) Y\) for all
\(w \in N^{\times}(S')\), \(Y \in \Gamma(S', g_{-\alpha})^{\times}\),
\(S' \to S\).

\textbf{Theorem 3.6.} \emph{(i) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w) exp(Y) = exp(a\_α(w) Y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(S' \to S\) and all \(w \in N^{\times}(S')\),
\(Y \in W(g_{-\alpha})(S')\).}

\emph{(ii) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a\_α(t w) = α(t) a\_α(w),    a\_α(w t) = α(t)⁻¹ a\_α(w).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) If one defines analogously
\(a_{-\alpha} : N^{\times} \to W((g_{-\alpha})^{\otimes 2})^{\times}\),
one has}

\[
a_{-\alpha}(w) = a_{\alpha}(w)^{-1}.
\]

\footnote{N.D.E.: that is, \(a_{-\alpha}(w)\) and \(a_{\alpha}(w)\) are
  paired, cf.~2.6.1.}

\emph{(iv) For every \(X \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\), \(S' \to S\),
one has}

\[
a_{\alpha}(w_{\alpha}(X)) = -X^{2}.
\]

Assertion (i) is trivial, by the characterization of the morphisms
\texttt{exp} given in 1.5. Assertion (ii) is immediate, as is (iii). Let
us prove (iv): let \(X \in \Gamma(S', g_{\alpha})^{\times}\),
\(Z \in \Gamma(S', g_{\alpha})\); by definition\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  detailed what follows.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a\_α(w\_α(X))⁻¹(Z) = Ad(w\_α(X))(Z) = Ad(exp(X)) Ad(exp(−X⁻¹)) Ad(exp(X))(Z).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Applying formulas (2′) and (2) of Lemma 2.10, as well as the equalities
\(H_{-\alpha} = -H_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha(H_{\alpha}) = 2\) (\emph{loc.
cit.} (4) and (5)) and \(\langle X, X^{-1}\rangle = 1\) (2.6), one
obtains that the right-hand side equals successively:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(exp(X)) Ad(exp(−X⁻¹))(Z) = Ad(exp(X))(Z + ⟨X⁻¹, Z⟩ (H\_α − X⁻¹))}
\NormalTok{                            = Z + ⟨X⁻¹, Z⟩ (H\_α − 2 X − X⁻¹ − H\_α + X)}
\NormalTok{                            = Z − ⟨X⁻¹, Z⟩ X − ⟨X⁻¹, Z⟩ X⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \(Z = \langle X^{-1}, Z\rangle X\) and
\(\langle X^{-1}, Z\rangle X^{-1} = X^{-2} Z\), hence this shows that
\(a_{\alpha}(w_{\alpha}(X))^{-1} = -X^{-2}\), whence
\(a_{\alpha}(w_{\alpha}(X)) = -X^{2}\).

\textbf{Corollary 3.7.} \emph{One has in particular}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α(X)) exp(X) = exp(−X⁻¹),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{whence (by the definition of \(w_{\alpha}(X)\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X) exp(X) w\_α(X)⁻¹ = exp(−X) w\_α(X) exp(−X),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{or, by an immediate calculation,}

\[
(w_{\alpha}(X) \exp(X))^{3} = e.
\]

\textbf{Corollary 3.8.} \emph{Let
\(X \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\) and \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\),
\(n \neq 0\). Then \(w_{\alpha}(X)\) is the unique section
\(w \in G(S)\) satisfying}

\emph{(i) \(int(w) \circ n \alpha* = -n \alpha*\).}

\emph{(ii) \((w \exp(X))^{3} = e\).}

One knows that \(w_{\alpha}(X)\) does satisfy these conditions.
Conversely, let \(w \in G(S)\) satisfy (i) and (ii). By 3.2 and 3.1
(ii), one knows that there exists \(t \in T(S)\) such that
\(w = w_{\alpha}(X) t\). Set \(u = \exp(X)\). One then has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w u w⁻¹ = w\_α(X) t exp(X) t⁻¹ w\_α(X)⁻¹ = exp(−α(t) X⁻¹),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and on the other hand

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u⁻¹ w u⁻¹ = exp(−X) w\_α(X) t exp(−X)}
\NormalTok{          = exp(−X) w\_α(X) exp(−X) exp(X − α(t) X) t}
\NormalTok{          = exp(−X⁻¹) exp(X − α(t) X) t = exp(−X⁻¹) t exp(H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now \((w u)^{3} = e \Leftrightarrow w u w^{-1} = u^{-1} w u^{-1}\);
comparing the two decompositions of this element on
\(U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U_{\alpha}\), one extracts \(t = e\).

\textbf{Remark 3.9.} \emph{One can summarize a number of results of this
number by the following diagram of principal homogeneous (left) bundles}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(g\_α)\^{}×  ──w\_α──→  N\^{}×  ──a\_α──→  W((g\_α)\^{}\{⊗2\})\^{}×}
\NormalTok{   ↓                  ↓                   ↓}
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Note that \(a_{\alpha}\) is faithfully flat (\(\alpha\) being so)
and that \(w_{\alpha}\) is a monomorphism if and only if \(\alpha*\) is
a monomorphism. We leave the reader the task of writing the
corresponding diagrams for the right principal bundle structures, as
well as the analogous diagrams for the root \(-\alpha\), and of studying
the relations between these various diagrams.}

\textbf{Lemma 3.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(q\) an integer
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} such that \(x \mapsto x^{q}\) defines an
endomorphism of \(G_{a, S}\), \((G, T, \alpha)\) and
\((G', T', \alpha')\) two \(S\)-elementary systems, \(f : G \to G'\) an
\(S\)-group morphism. Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : (g\_α)\^{}\{⊗q\} ──∼──→ g′\_\{α′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be an isomorphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h\^{}∨ : (g\_\{−α\})\^{}\{⊗q\} ──∼──→ g′\_\{−α′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the contragredient isomorphism. For every \(S' \to S\) and every
\(X \in W(g_{\alpha})(S')\), suppose:}

\[
f(\exp(X)) = \exp(h(X^{q})).
\]

\emph{Then the following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(f(\alpha*(z)) = \alpha'*(z)^{q}\).}

\emph{(ii) \(f(w_{\alpha}(Z)) = w_{\alpha'}(h(Z^{q}))\).}

\emph{(iii) \(f(\exp(Y)) = \exp(h^{\vee}(Y^{q}))\).}

\emph{(Each condition is to be read: for every \(S' \to S\) and every
\(z \in G_{m}(S')\), \(Z \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\),
\(Y \in W(g_{-\alpha})(S')\), one has \ldots).}

Indeed, (i) ⇒ (ii) by 3.8, (ii) ⇒ (iii) by 3.7, (iii) ⇒ (i) by 2.7.

\textbf{Proposition 3.11.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\(q \in \mathbb{Z}\), \(q > 0\), such that \(x \mapsto x^{q}\) defines
an endomorphism of \(G_{a, S}\), \((G, T, \alpha)\) and
\((G', T', \alpha')\) two \(S\)-elementary systems, \(f : G \to G'\) an
\(S\)-group morphism. The following conditions on \(f\) are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) The restriction of \(f\) to \(T\) factors through a morphism
\(f_{T} : T \to T'\) making the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{   │                f\_T          │}
\NormalTok{   q                              q}
\NormalTok{   ↓                ↓             ↓}
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}  ──α′*──→  T′  ──α′──→  G\_\{m, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{commutative.}

\emph{(ii) There exists an (unique) isomorphism of
\texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\[
h : (g_{\alpha})^{\otimes q} \to g'_{\alpha'}
\]

\emph{such that \(f(\exp(X)) = \exp(h(X^{q}))\),
\(f(\exp(Y)) = \exp(h^{\vee}(Y^{q}))\) for all
\(X \in W(g_{\alpha})(S')\), \(Y \in W(g_{-\alpha})(S')\), \(S' \to S\)
(it follows that \(f\) also satisfies the equivalent conditions of
3.10).}

One has (ii) ⇒ (i). Indeed, by 3.10, condition (ii) entails
\(f \circ \alpha* = q \alpha'*\), hence, by 3.3, \(f|T\) factors through
\(T'\). It remains to prove \(\alpha'(f(t)) = \alpha(t)^{q}\), which
follows at once from the fact that \(f\) induces a morphism of groups
\(T \cdot U_{\alpha} \to T' \cdot U_{\alpha'}\).

Let us prove (i) ⇒ (ii). Let \(X \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})\),
\(Y \in \Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})\). Set \(p^{+}(x) = f(\exp(x X))\) and
\(p^{-}(y) = f(\exp(y Y))\); these are group morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\^{}+, p\^{}− : G\_\{a, S\} → G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(α′*(z))\^{}q (p\^{}+(x)) = int(f\_T(α*(z))) (f(exp(x X)))}
\NormalTok{                       = f(int(α*(z))(exp(x X)))}
\NormalTok{                       = f(exp(z² x X)) = p\^{}+(z² x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Applying Lemma 1.2 (with \(Q = \alpha'*(G_{m, S})\)), one deduces that
there exists a section \(X' \in \Gamma(S, g'_{\alpha'})\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(exp(x X)) = p\^{}+(x) = exp(x\^{}q X′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Similarly, there exists a section \(Y' \in \Gamma(S, g'_{-\alpha'})\)
such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(exp(y Y)) = exp(y\^{}q Y′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Writing now that \(f\) is a group morphism, hence that it respects
formula (F), one obtains at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\^{}q Y\^{}q = (X Y)\^{}q = X′ Y′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One concludes easily that \(X^{q} \mapsto X'\) and \(Y^{q} \mapsto Y'\)
define isomorphisms \(h\) and \(h^{\vee}\) as announced.

\textbf{Proposition 3.12.} \emph{Let \((G, T, \alpha)\) be an
\(S\)-elementary system, \(w \in N^{\times}(S)\); set}

\[
\Omega_{0} = \Omega \cap int(w^{-1})(\Omega).
\]

\emph{Let \(d\) be the function on \(\Omega\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d(exp(Y) · t · exp(X)) = α(t)⁻¹ + X Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(\Omega_{0} = \Omega_{d}\), and one has for
\(\exp(Y) \cdot t \cdot \exp(X) \in \Omega_{0}(S')\) the following
formula (set \(z = d(\exp(Y) \cdot t \cdot \exp(X))\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(⋆)    int(w)(exp(Y) · t · exp(X)) = exp(z⁻¹ a\_α(w)⁻¹ X) · t α*(z) · exp(z⁻¹ a\_α(w) Y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, one has \(d \circ int(w) = d^{-1}\).}

Indeed, one has at once\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the original
  by swapping \(a_{\alpha}(w)\) and \(a_{\alpha}(w)^{-1}\), and we have
  detailed the proof of the equality \(d \circ int(w) = d^{-1}\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w)(exp(Y) · t · exp(X)) = exp(a\_α(w) Y) · t α*(α(t)⁻¹) · exp(a\_α(w)⁻¹ X)}
\NormalTok{                            = exp(a\_α(w) Y) · exp(α(t) a\_α(w)⁻¹ X) · t α*(α(t)⁻¹).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 2.1, this is a section of \(\Omega\) if and only if
\(1 + \alpha(t) X Y\) is invertible, which proves indeed the equality
\(\Omega_{0} = \Omega_{d}\); applying then formula (F) of \emph{loc.
cit.}, one deduces by an immediate calculation the announced formula
(⋆). Finally, it follows from (⋆) that one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(d ∘ int(w))(exp(Y) · t · exp(X)) = α(t α*(z))⁻¹ + z⁻² X Y = z⁻² (α(t)⁻¹ + X Y) = z⁻¹,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence the last assertion.

\emph{N.B.} One notes that the function \(d\) is independent of the
choice of \(w\).

\subsection{4. The isomorphism theorem}\label{the-isomorphism-theorem}

\textbf{Theorem 4.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(q \in \mathbb{Z}\),
\(q > 0\), such that \(x \mapsto x^{q}\) is an endomorphism of
\(G_{a, S}\), \((G, T, \alpha)\) and \((G', T', \alpha')\) two
\(S\)-elementary systems. Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : (g\_α)\^{}\{⊗q\} → g′\_\{α′\}    and    h\^{}∨ : (g\_\{−α\})\^{}\{⊗q\} → g′\_\{−α′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be two isomorphisms contragredient to each other. Let
\(f_{T} : T \to T'\) be an \(S\)-group morphism making the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}  ──q──→  G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{   │                  │}
\NormalTok{   α*                 α′*}
\NormalTok{   ↓     f\_T          ↓}
\NormalTok{   T   ──────→        T′}
\NormalTok{   │                  │}
\NormalTok{   α                  α′}
\NormalTok{   ↓                  ↓}
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}  ──q──→  G\_\{m, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{commutative.}

\emph{There exists a unique morphism of \(S\)-groups \(f : G \to G'\)
which extends \(f_{T}\) and satisfies}

\[
f(\exp(X)) = \exp(h(X^{q}))
\]

\emph{for every \(X \in W(g_{\alpha})(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Moreover,
this morphism also satisfies}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(exp(Y)) = exp(h\^{}∨(Y\^{}q))    and    f(w\_α(Z)) = w\_α(h(Z\^{}q)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(S' \to S\) and all \(Y \in \Gamma(S', g_{-\alpha})\),
\(Z \in \Gamma(S', g_{\alpha})^{\times}\).}

If \(f : G \to G'\) extends \(f_{T}\), then
\(f \circ \alpha* = (\alpha'*)^{q}\). If moreover \(f\) satisfies the
second condition, then it satisfies the two others as well by 3.10. It
follows that \(f\) is determined on \(\Omega\) by the relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(exp(Y) t exp(X)) = exp(h\^{}∨(Y\^{}q)) f\_T(t) exp(h(X\^{}q)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\Omega\) is schematically dense in \(G\), this already proves
the uniqueness of \(f\). To prove its existence, it suffices, by virtue
of Exp. XVIII 2.3, to prove that the preceding formula defines a
``generically multiplicative'' morphism from \(\Omega\) to \(G'\). Now,
by 2.4, this amounts to verifying that \(\alpha' \circ f = \alpha^{q}\),
which follows from the fact that \(f\) extends \(f_{T}\).

\textbf{Scholie 4.2.} \emph{One can also interpret 4.1 as follows:
consider the category \(E\) of \(S\)-elementary systems and the category
\(D\) of tuples}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\},  L),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(T\) is a torus, \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha*\) are group
morphisms such that \(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\), and \(L\) is an
invertible \texttt{O\_S}-module (the reader will specify the morphisms
of the two categories under consideration). One defines a functor
\(E \to D\) by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G, T, α) ↦ (G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\},  g\_α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{The preceding theorem says that this functor is fully faithful. It
is in fact an equivalence of categories, as one will see in the next
number. One already has:}

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.} \emph{If \(q = 1\) and if \(f_{T}\) is an
isomorphism, then \(f\) is an isomorphism.}

\textbf{Corollary 4.4.} \emph{If \(q = 1\) and if \(f_{T}\) is
faithfully flat with kernel \(Q\) (cf.~Exp. IX 2.7), then \(f\) is
faithfully flat (quasi-compact) with kernel \(Q\), hence identifies
\(G'\) with \(G/Q\).}

Indeed, if \(f_{T}\) is faithfully flat with kernel \(Q\), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Q = Ker(f\_T) ⊂ Ker(f\_T ∘ α′) = Ker(α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Introducing the \(S\)-elementary system \((G/Q, T/Q, \alpha/Q)\) of
2.13, one is reduced by 2.14 to proving that \(f/Q\) induces an
isomorphism of \(G/Q\) onto \(G'\), which follows at once from 4.3.

\subsection{5. Examples of elementary systems,
applications}\label{examples-of-elementary-systems-applications}

\textbf{5.1.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(L\) an invertible
\texttt{O\_S}-module. Consider the group \texttt{GL} over \(S\) defined
by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{GL(S′) = \{ ( a  b )  | a, d ∈ G\_a(S′), b ∈ W(L)(S′), c ∈ W(L⁻¹)(S′), a d − b c ∈ G\_m(S′) \}}
\NormalTok{         ( c  d )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

equipped with the usual matrix multiplication law. It is locally
isomorphic to \(GL_{2, S}\). It is therefore an \(S\)-group scheme,
affine and smooth over \(S\), with connected fibers.

\emph{Remark.} Let \(L'\) and \(L''\) be two invertible sheaves on
\(S\), such that \(L = L' \otimes L''^{-1}\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  corrected \(L'' \otimes L'^{-1}\) to \(L' \otimes L''^{-1}\) and we
  have detailed the sentence that follows.} Then one has an isomorphism
of \(S\)-groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{GL  ──∼──→  GL(L′ ⊕ L″)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined as follows: if \(x\) (resp. \(y\)) is a section of \(L'\) (resp.
\(L''\)) on an open set \(V\) of \(S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{( a  b ) ( x )   ( a x + b y )}
\NormalTok{( c  d ) ( y ) = ( c x + d y ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{5.2.} One will denote by \texttt{SL} the closed subgroup of
\texttt{GL} defined by the relation \(a d - b c = 1\). It is also an
\(S\)-group scheme, affine and smooth over \(S\), with connected fibers
(isomorphic to \(SL(L' \oplus L'')\) by the preceding isomorphism).

Likewise, consider the morphism \(G_{m, S} \to GL\) defined by
\(z \mapsto (z 0 / 0 z)\). It is a central monomorphism; by passage to
the quotient, one deduces a group \texttt{PL}, smooth and affine over
\(S\), with connected fibers (cf.~Exp. VIII 5.7).

One can see that, by passage to the quotient from the isomorphism of the
preceding remark, \texttt{PL} is identified with the group of
automorphisms of the projective bundle \(P(L' \oplus L'')\) (cf.~EGA, II
4.2.7). One will denote by \(i\) and \(p\) the canonical morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{SL  ──i──→  GL  ──p──→  PL;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\(i\) is a closed immersion, \(p\) is faithfully flat and affine.

\textbf{5.3.} Consider the group morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_G : G²\_\{m, S\} → GL,    t\_G(z, z′) = ( z   0 ),}
\NormalTok{                                       ( 0   z′ )}
\NormalTok{t\_S : G\_\{m, S\} → SL,     t\_S(z) = ( z    0 ),}
\NormalTok{                                  ( 0   z⁻¹ )}
\NormalTok{t\_P : G\_\{m, S\} → PL,     t\_P(z) = p(t\_G(z, 1)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

These are group monomorphisms, which define in each group a (split)
torus of relative codimension 2. For every \(s \in S\), let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X ∈ Γ(s, L ⊗ s)\^{}×;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

then the section \(( 0  X / -X^{-1}  0)\) of \(GL_{s}\) normalizes
\(t_{G}(G^{2}_{m, s})\) and does not centralize it; one concludes from
Exp. XIX 1.6 that \texttt{GL} is reductive, of semisimple rank 1, with
maximal torus \(t_{G}(G^{2}_{m, S})\).

One argues similarly for \texttt{SL} and \texttt{PL}, and one sees that
\texttt{SL} (resp. \texttt{PL}) is reductive, of semisimple rank 1, with
maximal torus \(t_{S}(G_{m, S})\) (resp. \(t_{P}(G_{m, S})\)).

\textbf{5.4.} Reasoning as usual, one determines at once the Lie algebra
of these various groups and the adjoint action of the chosen maximal
torus. Let us do it for \texttt{GL}; this is immediate by Exp. II 4.8:
\(Lie(GL/S)\) is the Lie algebra of the matrices below:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(GL/S) = \{ ( a  b )  | a and d sections of O\_S, b section of L, c section of L⁻¹ \}}
\NormalTok{            ( c  d )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

with the usual bracket; one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(t\_G(z, z′)) ( a  b ) = ( a        z z′⁻¹ b ).}
\NormalTok{               ( c  d )   ( z′ z⁻¹ c    d   )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Denote \(Lie(GL/S) = g\). Let
\(\alpha_{G} : t_{G}(G^{2}_{m, S}) \to G_{m, S}\) be the character
defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\_G(t\_G(z, z′)) = z z′⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One sees at once from the preceding relation that \(\alpha_{G}\) is a
root of \texttt{GL} with respect to \(t_{G}(G^{2}_{m, S})\) and that the
morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u : L → g    (resp. u⁻ : L⁻¹ → g)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined by \(u(X) = ( 0  X / 0  0)\) (resp.
\(u^{-}(X) = ( 0  0 / X  0)\)) is an isomorphism of \(L\) onto
\(g_{\alpha_{G}}\) (resp. of \(L^{-1}\) onto \(g_{-\alpha_{G}}\)).

One has thus proved that \((G, t_{G}(G^{2}_{m, S}), \alpha_{G})\) is an
\(S\)-elementary system.

Setting likewise

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\_S(t\_S(z)) = z²,    α\_P(t\_P(z)) = z,}
