\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one proves that \((SL, t_{S}(G_{m, S}), \alpha_{S})\) and
\((PL, t_{P}(G_{m, S}), \alpha_{P})\) are elementary systems, and one
defines isomorphisms of \(L\) (resp. \(L^{-1}\)) with the corresponding
direct summands of the Lie algebras of \texttt{SL} and \texttt{PL}.

\textbf{5.5.} Set \(\exp ( 0  X / 0  0) = ( 1  X / 0  1)\). One has thus
defined a morphism

\[
W(g_{\alpha_{G}}) \to GL
\]

which induces on the Lie algebras the canonical morphism, hence is the
unique morphism of this type (1.5). Similarly, one sets
\(\exp ( 0  0 / Y  0) = ( 1  0 / Y  1)\). Carrying out the explicit
calculation of formula (F), one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⟨ ( 0  X / 0  0 ), ( 0  0 / Y  0 ) ⟩ = X Y,    α*\_G(z) = ( z   0  ) = t\_G(z, z⁻¹).}
\NormalTok{                                                          ( 0   z⁻¹)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed what follows.}

The open set \(N^{\times} = N^{\times}_{G}\) (defined before 3.1) is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N\^{}×\_G(S′) = \{ ( 0  P ) | P ∈ W(g\_α)\^{}×(S′), Q ∈ W(g\_\{−α\})\^{}×(S′) \},}
\NormalTok{             ( Q  0 )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the morphism \(w_{\alpha_{G}}\) (cf.~3.1 (iv)) is given, for every
\(X \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\), by

\[
w_{\alpha_{G}}(X) = (  0     X);
             ( -X^{-1}  0)
\]

the morphism \(a_{\alpha_{G}}\) (cf.~3.5) is given by:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{if w = ( 0  P ) ∈ N\^{}×\_G(S′), then a\_\{α\_G\}(w) = P Q⁻¹ ∈ W((g\_α)\^{}\{⊗2\})\^{}×(S′),}
\NormalTok{       ( Q  0 )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, for every \(Y \in W(g_{-\alpha})^{\times}(S')\), one has
\(a_{\alpha_{G}}(w)(Y) = P Q^{-1} Y \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\).

\textbf{5.6.} We leave the reader the task of carrying out the same
computations in \texttt{SL} and \texttt{PL}. One finds the same duality
formula and the coroots

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α*\_S(z) = t\_S(z),    α*\_P(z) = t\_P(z²).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Denote by \(p_{T}\) the morphism induced by \(p : GL \to PL\) on
\(t_{S}(G_{m, S})\), i.e.

\[
p_{T}(t_{S}(z)) = t_{P}(z^{2}).
\]

One therefore has the commutative diagram:\footnote{N.D.E.: where
  \(t_{S}\) and \(t_{P}\) are isomorphisms.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                          G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{                       id ╱   ╲ 2}
\NormalTok{                        ╱       ╲}
\NormalTok{                  α*\_S ╱           ╲ α*\_P}
\NormalTok{                     ╱               ╲}
\NormalTok{            t\_S(G\_\{m, S\})  ──p\_T──→  t\_P(G\_\{m, S\})}
\NormalTok{              ↑                          ↑}
\NormalTok{            t\_S                          t\_P}
\NormalTok{              │                          │}
\NormalTok{         G\_\{m, S\}                  G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{                       α\_S ╲   ╱ α\_P}
\NormalTok{                            ╲ ╱}
\NormalTok{                         G\_\{m, S\}.}
\NormalTok{                        ╱   2  ╲}
\NormalTok{                       id        }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One recognizes in the central part the commutative diagram of
4.1\footnote{N.D.E.: with \(q = 1\).} relative to the canonical morphism
\(p \circ i : SL \to PL\), which induces a morphism of the preceding
\(S\)-elementary systems.

\textbf{5.7.} Let now \((G, T, \alpha)\) be any \(S\)-elementary system.
Consider the commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                 G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{              id ↙    ↘ 2}
\NormalTok{            ↙        α*       ↘}
\NormalTok{          ↙                       ↘}
\NormalTok{       ↙                              ↘}
\NormalTok{   G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{       ↘                              ↗}
\NormalTok{         ↘                       ↗}
\NormalTok{            ↘        α       ↗}
\NormalTok{             2 ↘   ↗ id}
\NormalTok{                 G\_\{m, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combining the two preceding diagrams, one obtains a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                       G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{                    α*\_S ↙  α*  ↘ α*\_P}
\NormalTok{                       ↙           ↘}
\NormalTok{                    ↙                 ↘}
\NormalTok{            ↙    α* ∘ t\_S⁻¹       t\_P ∘ α    ↘}
\NormalTok{   t\_S(G\_\{m, S\})  ────→  T  ────→  t\_P(G\_\{m, S\})}
\NormalTok{            ↘                                ↗}
\NormalTok{                ↘                       ↗}
\NormalTok{                    ↘     α       ↗}
\NormalTok{                    α\_S ↘    ↗ α\_P}
\NormalTok{                          G\_\{m, S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using 4.1, one therefore has:

\textbf{Proposition 5.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\((G, T, \alpha)\) an \(S\)-elementary system. Set \(L = g_{\alpha}\)
(and hence \(L^{-1} = g_{-\alpha}\)).}

\emph{(i) There exists a unique group morphism \(f : SL \to G\)
satisfying the following equivalent conditions:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(a)   f( z   0  ) = α*(z),    f( 1  X ) = exp(X);}
\NormalTok{     ( 0   z⁻¹)              ( 0  1 )}

\NormalTok{(b)   f( 1  X ) = exp(X),     f( 1  0 ) = exp(Y);}
\NormalTok{     ( 0  1 )                ( Y  1 )}

\NormalTok{(c)   f( 1  X ) = exp(X),     f(  0     X ) = w\_α(X).}
\NormalTok{     ( 0  1 )                ( −X⁻¹  0 )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) There exists a unique group morphism \(g : G \to PL\)
satisfying}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g(t) = ( α(t)  0 ),    g(exp(X)) = p( 1  X ).}
\NormalTok{       ( 0    1 )                    ( 0  1 )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g(exp(Y)) = p( 1  0 ),    g(w\_α(X)) = p(  0     X ).}
\NormalTok{              ( Y  1 )                  ( −X⁻¹  0 )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{The morphism \(g\) is faithfully flat quasi-compact with kernel
\(Ker(\alpha) = Centr(G)\), and \(g \circ f\) is the canonical morphism
\(SL \to PL\).}

Note that conditions (b) of (i) give an explicit description of the
duality between \(g_{\alpha}\) and \(g_{-\alpha}\).

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.} \emph{Let \((G, T, \alpha)\) be an
\(S\)-elementary system. The subgroups \(T \cdot U_{\alpha}\),
\(T \cdot U_{-\alpha}\), \(U_{\alpha}\) and \(U_{-\alpha}\) are closed.}

Since \(U_{\alpha}\) is a closed subgroup scheme of
\(T \cdot U_{\alpha}\), it suffices to make the verification for the
latter. By Noether's theorem (Exp. IV 5.3.1 and 6.4.1), it suffices to
prove that \((T \cdot U_{\alpha})/Ker(\alpha)\) is a closed subgroup of
\(G/Ker(\alpha)\). By virtue of 5.8, one is therefore reduced to proving
that the subgroup of \texttt{PL} (or of \texttt{GL}, which amounts to
the same by a new application of Noether's theorem) defined by \(c = 0\)
is closed, which is trivial.

Consequently, the morphisms \texttt{exp} of Theorem 1.5 (i) are closed
immersions.

\emph{N.B.} The corollary also follows from the fact that
\(T \cdot U_{\alpha}\) and \(T \cdot U_{-\alpha}\) are ``Borel
subgroups'' of \(G\) (cf.~Exp. XII 7.10).

\textbf{5.10.} Let \(L\) be an invertible \texttt{O\_S}-module and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

a diagram of groups\footnote{N.D.E.: \(T\) being a torus.} such that
\(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\). Let \(R\) be the maximal torus of
\(Ker(\alpha)\) and \(K = \alpha*^{-1}(R)\). Then \(K\) is a subgroup of
multiplicative type of \(G_{m, S}\); by virtue of
\(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\), it is even a subgroup of \(\mu_{2, S}\).
In particular the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{K → SL,    z ↦ ( z   0  )}
\NormalTok{                ( 0   z⁻¹)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is central. One has therefore a central group monomorphism:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{K → R × SL,    z ↦ (α*(z), ( z   0  )).}
\NormalTok{                            ( 0   z⁻¹)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Consider the group \(G = (R \times SL)/K\) obtained by passage to the
quotient. It is an affine and smooth group over \(S\), with connected
fibers. It is immediate that the sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → K → R × t\_S(G\_\{m, S\})  ──u──→  T → 1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(u(x, t_{S}(z)) = x \alpha*(z)\) is exact. The image of
\(R \times t_{S}(G_{m, S})\) in \(G\) is therefore a torus \(T'\)
isomorphic to \(T\). One then shows without difficulty that if
\(\alpha'\) is the character of \(T'\) deduced from \(\alpha\) by the
preceding isomorphism, \((G, T', \alpha')\) is an \(S\)-elementary
system, that \(g'_{\alpha'}\) is isomorphic to \(L\), and that
\(\alpha'*\) is obtained from \(\alpha*\) by the isomorphism
\(T \xrightarrow{\sim} T'\). One has therefore constructed an
\(S\)-elementary system \((G, T', \alpha')\) such that the corresponding
object

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G\_\{m, S\}  ──α′*──→  T′  ──α′──→  G\_\{m, S\},  g′\_\{α′\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

of the category \(D\) defined in 4.2 is isomorphic to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\},  L).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has therefore proved the

\textbf{Theorem 5.11.} \emph{In the notations of 4.2, the functor}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G, T, α) ↦ (G\_\{m, S\}  ──α*──→  T  ──α──→  G\_\{m, S\},  g\_α)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an equivalence of categories between \(E\) and \(D\).}

\subsection{6. Generators and relations for an elementary
system}\label{generators-and-relations-for-an-elementary-system}

\textbf{6.1.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \((G, T, \alpha)\) an
\(S\)-elementary system. Let \(X \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S)\) and
\(u = \exp(X)\); one has seen in 3.8 that the element
\(w = w_{\alpha}(X)\) satisfies in particular the relation

\[
(w u)^{3} = e.
\]

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the sentence that follows.}

One denotes by \(s_{\alpha}\) the automorphism of \(T\) induced by
\(int(w)\); according to Theorem 3.1 (iii), for every \(S' \to S\) and
\(t \in T(S')\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_α(t) = int(w)(t) = t · α*(α(t)⁻¹).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Theorem 6.2.} \emph{Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-sheaf of groups for
(fppf). Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T : T → H,    f\_α : U\_α → H}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be group morphisms and \(h \in H(S)\) a section of \(H\). For
there to exist a (necessarily unique) group morphism}

\[
f : G \to H
\]

\emph{extending \(f_{T}\) and \(f_{\alpha}\) and satisfying
\(f(w) = h\), it is necessary and sufficient that the following
conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(S' \to S\), every \(t \in T(S')\) and every
\(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   f\_T(t) f\_α(x) f\_T(t)⁻¹ = f\_α(t x t⁻¹) = f\_α(x\^{}\{α(t)\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(in other words, \(f_{T}\) and \(f_{\alpha}\) extend to a group
morphism from the semidirect product \(T \cdot U_{\alpha}\) into
\(H\)).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(S' \to S\) and every \(t \in T(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   h f\_T(t) h⁻¹ = f\_T(s\_α(t)) = f\_T(t · α*(α(t)⁻¹)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) One has the two relations in \(H(S)\):}

\[
(3)   h^{2} = f_{T}(\alpha*(-1)),
(4)   (h f_{\alpha}(u))^{3} = e.
\]

\emph{Proof.} Denote additively \(U_{\alpha}\) and \(U_{-\alpha}\) and
multiplicatively their vector structure. If \(f\) satisfies the
conditions of the statement, one necessarily has for every
\(y \in U_{-\alpha}(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(y) = f(w⁻¹ w y w⁻¹ w) = h f\_α(w⁻¹ y w) h⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let then \(f_{-\alpha} : U_{-\alpha} \to H\) be the morphism defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗\_1)    f\_\{−α\}(y) = h f\_α(w⁻¹ y w) h⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is a group morphism. On the other hand, \(f\) is determined on the
big cell \(\Omega\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(y t x) = f\_\{−α\}(y) f\_T(t) f\_α(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This shows the uniqueness of \(f\); since the conditions of the
statement are manifestly necessary, let us show that they are
sufficient.

One has by (4)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h f\_α(u) h⁻¹ h² = f\_α(−u) h⁻¹ f\_α(−u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, by (3) and (1), \(h^{2} = f_{T}(\alpha*(-1))\) commutes with
\(f_{\alpha}(-u)\), which gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h f\_α(u) h⁻¹ = f\_α(−u) h f\_α(−u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But, by definition,
\(h f_{\alpha}(u) h^{-1} = f_{-\alpha}(w u w^{-1})\); by 3.7, since
\(u = \exp(X)\) and \(w = w_{\alpha}(X)\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗\_2)    w u w⁻¹ = −ũ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \texttt{ũ} denotes the element paired with \(u\). One obtains
therefore:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗\_3)    f\_\{−α\}(−ũ) = f\_α(−u) h f\_α(−u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let now \(t\) be a section of \(T\) over a variable \(S' \to S\). Apply
\(int(f_{T}(t))\) to the preceding formula. One obtains on the left-hand
side\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected what follows.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T(t) f\_\{−α\}(−ũ) f\_T(t)⁻¹ = f\_T(t) h f\_α(u) h⁻¹ f\_T(t)⁻¹}
\NormalTok{                           = h (h⁻¹ f\_T(t) h) f\_α(u) (h⁻¹ f\_T(t)⁻¹ h) h⁻¹}
\NormalTok{                           = h f\_T(s\_α(t)) f\_α(u) f\_T(s\_α(t))⁻¹ h⁻¹ = h f\_α(α(s\_α(t)) u) h⁻¹}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by (2) and (1); then since
\(s_{\alpha}(t) = t \cdot \alpha*(\alpha(t)^{-1})\) and
\(\alpha \circ \alpha* = 2\), this equals

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h f\_α(α(t)⁻¹ u) h⁻¹.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, by (∗\_1) and (∗\_2) one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h f\_α(α(t)⁻¹ u) h⁻¹ = f\_\{−α\}(α(t)⁻¹ w u w⁻¹) = f\_\{−α\}(−α(t)⁻¹ ũ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The right-hand side of (∗\_3) gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(−α(t) u) · f\_T(t) h f\_T(t)⁻¹ h⁻¹ · h · f\_α(−α(t) u)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since
\(h f_{T}(t)^{-1} h^{-1} = f_{T}(s_{\alpha}(t^{-1})) = f_{T}(t \cdot \alpha*(\alpha(t)))\),
this equals

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(−α(t) u) · f\_T(α*(α(t))) · h · f\_α(−α(t) u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Comparing the two expressions obtained, one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_\{−α\}(−α(t)⁻¹ ũ) = f\_α(−α(t) u) · f\_T(α*(α(t))) · h · f\_α(−α(t) u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\alpha : T \to G_{m, S}\) is faithfully flat and \(H\) is a
separated presheaf, one can replace \(-\alpha(t)^{-1}\) by an arbitrary
section of \(G_{m, S}\), and one obtains the

\textbf{Lemma 6.2.1.} \emph{For every \(z \in G_{m}(S')\), \(S' \to S\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_\{−α\}(z ũ) = f\_α(z⁻¹ u) · f\_T(α*(−z⁻¹)) · h · f\_α(z⁻¹ u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let now \(x, y \in G_{a}(S')\), \(S' \to S\); suppose \(y\) and
\((1 + x y)\) invertible. Applying the lemma first to \(z = y\), one
obtains\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed the calculations that follow.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(x u) f\_\{−α\}(y ũ) = f\_α((x + y⁻¹) u) · f\_T(α*(−y⁻¹)) · h · f\_α(y⁻¹ u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now \(x + y^{-1} = y^{-1}(1 + x y)\). Applying the lemma to
\(z = y / (1 + x y)\), one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α((x + y⁻¹) u) = f\_\{−α\}( y/(1 + x y) · ũ ) f\_α(−(x + y⁻¹) u) · h · f\_T(α*(−y / (1 + x y))).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Substituting in the preceding equality, one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(x u) f\_\{−α\}(y ũ) = f\_\{−α\}( y / (1 + x y) · ũ ) f\_α(−(x + y⁻¹) u) · h⁻¹ · f\_T(α*(1 + x y)⁻¹) · h · f\_α(y⁻¹ u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(h^{-1} f_{T}(t) h = f_{T}(s_{\alpha}(t))\) by (2) (note that
\(s^{2}_{\alpha} = id\)) and since
\(s_{\alpha} \circ \alpha* = -\alpha*\) (cf.~6.2.1), this equals

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_\{−α\}( y / (1 + x y) · ũ ) f\_α(−(x + y⁻¹) u) · f\_T(α*(1 + x y)) · f\_α(y⁻¹ u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, since for all \(x' \in U_{\alpha}(S')\) and \(z \in G_{m}(S')\)
one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(x′) f\_T(α*(z)) = f\_T(α*(z)) f\_α(z⁻² x′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(x u) f\_\{−α\}(y ũ) = f\_\{−α\}( y / (1 + x y) · ũ ) · f\_T(α*(1 + x y)) · f\_α( −y⁻¹ (1 + x y)⁻¹ / (1 + x y)² + y⁻¹ · u )}
\NormalTok{                     = f\_\{−α\}( y / (1 + x y) · ũ ) · f\_T(α*(1 + x y)) · f\_α( x / (1 + x y) · u ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has thus proved:

\textbf{Lemma 6.2.2.} \emph{Let \(S' \to S\). If
\(a \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(b \in U^{\times}_{-\alpha}(S')\), and
\(1 + a b \in G_{m}(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(a) f\_\{−α\}(b) = f\_\{−α\}( b / (1 + a b) ) f\_T(α*(1 + a b)) f\_α( a / (1 + a b) ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By schematic density, this formula remains valid when
\(b \in U_{-\alpha}(S')\), \(1 + a b\) being always invertible. Consider
then the morphism

\[
f : \Omega \to H
\]

defined by \(f(y t x) = f_{-\alpha}(y) f_{T}(t) f_{\alpha}(x)\).

It follows at once from 6.2.2, from condition 6.2 (i), and from formula
(F′) of 2.4 that if \(g, g' \in \Omega(S')\) and
\(g g' \in \Omega(S')\), one has \(f(g g') = f(g) f(g')\). By Exp. XVIII
2.3 (iii) and 2.4\footnote{N.D.E.: Note that each geometric fiber of
  \(G\) is connected, for example by 1.1.}, there therefore exists a
group morphism \(G \to H\) extending \(f\). Denote it also by \(f\); it
answers the question; it suffices to prove, indeed, that
\(f(w_{\alpha}) = h\). Now
\(w_{\alpha} = u \cdot (-\tilde{u}) \cdot u\), whence, by
(∗\_3):\footnote{N.D.E.: We have simplified the original by invoking
  (∗\_3).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(w\_α) = f\_α(u) f\_\{−α\}(−ũ) f\_α(u) = h.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 6.3.} \emph{We shall complete these results in Exp. XXIII
3.5.}

\section{Exposé XXI. Root data}\label{exposuxe9-xxi.-root-data}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Version of 13/10/2024.} This Exposé collects, in the
absence of a suitable reference,\footnote{N.D.E.: For the results on
  root systems (§§ 1--5), one may consult {[}BLie{]}, Chap. VI.} some
known results on root data (= ``abstract'' root systems), most of which
will be used in what follows.

\textbf{Notations.} --- We denote by \(Q_{+}\) the set of positive (or
zero) rational numbers; one has \(\mathbb{Z} \cap Q_{+} = \mathbb{N}\).
Let \(V\) be a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector space; if \(A\) (resp. \(B\)) is a
subset of \(\mathbb{Q}\) (resp. \(V\)), we denote by \(A \cdot B\) the
image of \(A \otimes B\) under the morphism
\(\mathbb{Q} \otimes V \to V\), in other words the set of linear
combinations of elements of \(B\) with coefficients in \(A\). We write
\(-B = {-1} \cdot B\). We denote by \(E - F\) the set of elements of
\(E\) that do not belong to \(F\).

\subsection{1. Generalities}\label{generalities-1}

\subsubsection{1.1. Definitions, first
properties}\label{definitions-first-properties}

\textbf{Definition 1.1.1.} \emph{Let \(M\) and \(M*\) be two free
\(\mathbb{Z}\)-modules of finite type in duality. Write
\(V = M \otimes \mathbb{Q}\), \(V* = M* \otimes \mathbb{Q}\); these are
two \(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector spaces in duality. We identify \(M\) (resp.
\(M*\)) with a subset of \(V\) (resp. \(V*\)). The canonical bilinear
form on \(M* \times M\) (resp. \(V* \times V\)) is denoted \(( ,)\).}

\emph{Let \(R\) be a finite subset of \(M\). Suppose we are given a map
\(\alpha \mapsto \alpha*\) of \(R\) into \(M*\); the set of \(\alpha*\),
for \(\alpha \in R\), is denoted \(R*\). To each \(\alpha \in R\) we
associate the endomorphism \(s_{\alpha}\) (resp. \(s*_{\alpha}\)) of
\(M\) and \(V\) (resp. \(M*\) and \(V*\)) given by the formulas:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    s\_α(x) = x − (α*, x)α,    i.e.   s\_α = id − α* ⊗ α;}
\NormalTok{(1*)   s*\_α(u) = u − (u, α)α*,   i.e.   s*\_α = id − α ⊗ α*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One says that the pair \((R, R*)\) (more precisely the pair
\((R, R \to M*)\)) is a} root datum \emph{in \((M, M*)\), or that
\((M, M*, R, R*)\) is a} root datum, \emph{if the following axioms are
satisfied:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(DR I)   For each α ∈ R, one has    (α*, α) = 2.}
\NormalTok{(DR II)  For each α ∈ R, one has    s\_α(R) ⊂ R,    s*\_α(R*) ⊂ R*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One says that \(R\) is the} root system \emph{of the root datum
\(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\). The elements of \(R\) (resp. \(R*\))
are called the} roots \emph{(resp.} coroots*) of the root datum.*

\textbf{Remark 1.1.2.} \emph{Axiom (DR I) is equivalent to any of the
following properties:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)   s\_α s\_α = id,        (2*)  s*\_α s*\_α = id,}
\NormalTok{(3)   s\_α(α) = −α,         (3*)  s*\_α(α*) = −α*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 1.1.3.} \emph{Axioms (DR I) and (DR II) entail}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R = −R,   R* = −R*,   0 ∉ R,   0 ∉ R*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 1.1.4.} \emph{The map \(R \to R*\) is a bijection. More
generally, if \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) and \((\alpha*, x) = (\beta*, x)\)
for all \(x \in R\), then \(\alpha = \beta\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one then has
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha) = \alpha - 2\beta\),
\(s_{\alpha}(\beta) = \beta - 2\alpha\). One deduces at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_β s\_α(α) = 2β − α = α + 2(β − α),    s\_β s\_α(β − α) = s\_β(β − α) = β − α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence
\((s_{\beta} s_{\alpha})^{n}(\alpha) = \alpha + 2n(\beta - \alpha) \in R\)
by (DR II). Since \(R\) is finite, one has \(\beta - \alpha = 0\).

\textbf{Corollary 1.1.5.} \emph{The inverse map \(R* \to R\) defines a
root datum}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ℛ* = (M*, M, R*, R)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{called the} dual \emph{of \(\mathcal{R}\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: Note
  that \((\alpha*)* = \alpha\).}

\textbf{Definition 1.1.6.} \emph{We denote by \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) the
subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(R\). We denote by \(V(R)\) the vector
subspace of \(V\) generated by \(R\), that is to say
\(\Gamma_{0}(R) \otimes \mathbb{Q}\). Applying these definitions to
\(\mathcal{R}*\), one constructs similarly \(\Gamma_{0}(R*)\) and
\(V(R*)\).}

\emph{One calls} reductive rank \emph{of \(\mathcal{R}\) the number}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rgred(ℛ) = rank(M) = dim(V) = dim(V*) = rank(M*) = rgred(ℛ*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One calls} semisimple rank \emph{of \(\mathcal{R}\) the number}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rgss(ℛ) = rank(R) = rank(Γ₀(R)) = dim(V(R)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One thus has \(rgss(\mathcal{R}) \leqslant rgred(\mathcal{R})\).}

\emph{We shall see below that
\(rgss(\mathcal{R}) = rgss(\mathcal{R}*)\), that is to say that \(V(R)\)
and \(V(R*)\) have the same dimension.}

\textbf{Definition 1.1.7.} \emph{One says that \(\mathcal{R}\) is}
semisimple \emph{(resp.} trivial*) if
\(rgss(\mathcal{R}) = rgred(\mathcal{R})\) (resp.
\(rgss(\mathcal{R}) = 0\)). For \(\mathcal{R}\) to be trivial it is
therefore necessary and sufficient that \(R\) be empty. The trivial root
datum of reductive rank zero is denoted
\(0 = ({0}, {0}, \emptyset, \emptyset)\).*

\textbf{Definition 1.1.8.} \emph{We denote by \(W(\mathcal{R})\) the
group of transformations of \(M\) generated by the \(s_{\alpha}\),
\(\alpha \in R\). We call it the} Weyl group \emph{of \(\mathcal{R}\).
We write}

\[
W*(\mathcal{R}) = W(\mathcal{R}*).
\]

\emph{Then \(W(\mathcal{R})\) operates on \(R\), \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\),
\(V(R)\), \(M\) and \(V\). If \(w \in W(\mathcal{R})\) and \(x \in M\)
(resp. \(x \in V\)), one has \(wx - x \in \Gamma_{0}(R)\) (resp.
\(wx - x \in V(R)\)); this is immediate from formula (1). Likewise for
\(W*(\mathcal{R})\).}

\textbf{Lemma 1.1.9.} \emph{For all \(\alpha \in R\), \(x \in V\),
\(u \in V*\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(4)    (s*\_α(u), s\_α(x)) = (u, x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, taking the scalar product of (1) and (1*), one
finds that the left-hand side equals
\((u, x) + (u, \alpha)(\alpha*, x)((\alpha*, \alpha) - 2) = (u, x)\).

\textbf{Remark 1.1.10.} \emph{If one assumes \(0 \notin R\) and
\(0 \notin R*\), then 1.1.9 is equivalent to (DR I).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.1.11.} \emph{Denote by \(h \mapsto h^{\vee}\) the
isomorphism of \(GL(M)\) onto \(GL(M*)\) that associates to \(h\) its
contragredient. Then formula (4) is also written}

\[
(5)    (s_{\alpha})^{\vee} = s*_{\alpha}.
\]

\textbf{Corollary 1.1.12.} \emph{The preceding isomorphism induces an
isomorphism of \(W(\mathcal{R})\) onto \(W*(\mathcal{R})\).}

\textbf{Scholie 1.1.13.} \emph{By virtue of the preceding result, we
shall identify \(W\) and \(W*\), and we shall regard \(W\) as a group of
transformations of \(R\), \(R*\), \(M\), \(M*\), \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\),
\(\Gamma_{0}(R*)\), \(V\), \(V*\), \(V(R)\), \(V(R*)\). We shall write
\(s_{\alpha}\) for \(s*_{\alpha}\).}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{1.2. The map
\(p\)}{1.2. The map p}}\label{the-map-p}

\textbf{Lemma 1.2.1.} \emph{Let \(p : M \to M*\) (resp. \(V \to V*\)) be
the linear map defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(6)    p(x) = Σ\_\{u ∈ R*\} (u, x) u.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Write \(\ell(x) = (p(x), x)\). One has the following properties:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(7)    ℓ(x) ⩾ 0,    ℓ(α) \textgreater{} 0    for α ∈ R.}

\NormalTok{(8)    ℓ(w x) = ℓ(x),    for w ∈ W.}

\NormalTok{(9)    (p(x), y) = (p(y), x),    for x, y ∈ V.}

\NormalTok{(10)   ℓ(α) α* = 2 p(α),    for α ∈ R.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} The first three relations are immediate.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  (8) follows from (4), (2) and (DR II).} Let us prove the last. By (1),
for \(u \in V*\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u, α)² α* = (u, α) u − (u, α) s\_α(u)}
\NormalTok{           = (u, α) u + (u, s\_α(α)) s\_α(u)}
\NormalTok{           = (u, α) u + (s\_α(u), α) s\_α(u)    (since s\_α² = id).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(s_{\alpha}\) is a permutation of \(R*\) (by (DR II)), it remains
only to sum over \(u \in R*\) to conclude.

\textbf{Scholie 1.2.2.} \emph{Relation (10) says that
\(\alpha \mapsto \ell(\alpha) \alpha*\) is the restriction to \(R\) of a
linear map from \(M\) into \(M*\). In particular, one has}

\[
(-\alpha)* = -\alpha*.
\]

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.3.} \emph{The map \(p\) induces an isomorphism of
\(V(R)\) onto \(V(R)*\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, \(p\) sends \(V(R)\) into \(V(R*)\). We thus have

\[
\dim(V(R)) \geqslant \dim(V(R*)).
\]

Applying this inequality to the dual root datum, we deduce

\[
\dim(V(R)) = \dim(V(R*)),
\]

so \(p\), being surjective, is also bijective.

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.4.} \emph{One has \(\dim(V(R)) = \dim(V(R*))\),
hence}

\[
rgss(\mathcal{R}) = rgss(\mathcal{R}*).
\]

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.5.} \emph{The bilinear form \((u, x)\) is
nondegenerate on \(V(R*) \times V(R)\), and so puts these
\(\mathbb{Q}\)-vector spaces in duality.}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, if \((u, x) = 0\) for all \(u \in R*\), then
\(p(x) = 0\).

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.6.} \emph{The symmetric bilinear form
\texttt{(p(x),\ y)} is positive nondegenerate on \(V(R)\).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.7.} \emph{\(W\) operates faithfully on \(R\) (and
hence on the other sets of 1.1.13).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, let \(u \in V*\). Let \(w \in W\); suppose that
\(w(\alpha) = \alpha\) for all \(\alpha \in R\), and let us prove that
\(w(u) = u\). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(w(u) − u, α) = (w(u), α) − (u, α) = (u, w⁻¹(α)) − (u, α) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \(w(u) - u \in V(R*)\). If it is orthogonal to all the roots, it is
zero by 1.2.5.

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.8.} \emph{The group \(W\) is finite.}

\textbf{Proposition 1.2.9.} \emph{The operations of \(W\) respect the
correspondence between roots and coroots. In other words, for
\(\alpha \in R\) and \(w \in W\), one has}

\[
w(\alpha*) = w(\alpha)*.
\]

\emph{Proof.} It suffices to verify this for \(w = s_{\beta}\),
\(\beta \in R\), that is to say to verify the formula

\[
s_{\beta}(\alpha*) = s_{\beta}(\alpha)*.
\]

Now \(\ell(s_{\beta}(\alpha)) \cdot s_{\beta}(\alpha)* / 2\) equals:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p(s\_β(α)) = Σ\_\{u ∈ R*\} (u, s\_β(α)) u = Σ\_\{u ∈ R*\} (s\_β(u), α) u = Σ\_\{u ∈ R*\} (u, α) s\_β(u) = s\_β(p(α));}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since \(\ell(s_{\beta}(\alpha)) = \ell(\alpha)\), one obtains
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha)* = s_{\beta}(2 p(\alpha) / \ell(\alpha)) = s_{\beta}(\alpha*)\).

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.10.} \emph{If \(\alpha \in R\) and \(w \in W\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w s\_α w⁻¹ = s\_\{w(α)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed,
\(w s_{\alpha} w^{-1}(x) = x - (\alpha*, w^{-1}(x)) w(\alpha) = x - (w(\alpha*), x) w(\alpha)\),
and this last term equals, by 1.2.9:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x − (w(α)*, x) w(α) = s\_\{w(α)\}(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 1.2.11.} \emph{Let \(R' \subset R\). For
\((M, M*, R', R'*)\) to be a root datum, it is necessary and sufficient
that \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\) imply \(s_{\alpha}(\beta) \in R'\).}

\subsection{2. Relations between two
roots}\label{relations-between-two-roots}

\subsubsection{2.1. Proportional roots}\label{proportional-roots}

\textbf{Proposition 2.1.1.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two
roots. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) There exists \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\) such that
\(\alpha = k \beta\).}

\emph{(ii) \(s_{\alpha} = s_{\beta}\).}

\emph{Moreover, under these conditions one has
\(\alpha* = k^{-1} \beta*\), and \(k\) is equal to one of the numbers
\texttt{1}, \(-1\), \texttt{2}, \(-2\), \texttt{1/2}, \(-1/2\).}

\emph{Proof.} Suppose first (i). One has first

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α* = ℓ(α)⁻¹ · 2 p(α) = k⁻² ℓ(β)⁻¹ · 2 k p(β) = k⁻¹ β*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This entails at once \(s_{\alpha} = s_{\beta}\). Conversely, if
\(s_{\alpha} = s_{\beta}\), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α = s\_α(−α) = s\_β(−α) = (β*, α) β − α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(2 \alpha = (\beta*, \alpha) \beta\), with
\((\beta*, \alpha) \in \mathbb{Z}\), so (ii) entails (i). Finally, if
\(\alpha = k \beta\), then \(\alpha* = k^{-1} \beta*\), whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(α*, β) = 2 k⁻¹,    (β*, α) = 2 k,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \texttt{2k} and \(2k^{-1}\) are integers and we are done.

\textbf{Application 2.1.2.} \emph{The root data \(\mathcal{R}\) with
\(rgss(\mathcal{R}) = 1\) are of one of the following two types:}

\emph{(i)} Type \(A_{1}\): \emph{there exists \(\alpha \in M\) such that
the roots are \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\). The coroots are then
\(\alpha*\) and \(-\alpha*\).}

\emph{(ii)} Type \(A_{1}'\): \emph{there exists \(\alpha \in M\) such
that the roots are \(\alpha\), \(-\alpha\), \(2\alpha\), \(-2\alpha\).
The coroots are then \(\alpha*\), \(-\alpha*\), \(\alpha*/2\),
\(-\alpha*/2\).}

\textbf{Definition 2.1.3.} \emph{One says that \(\alpha \in R\) is}
indivisible \emph{if \(\alpha/2 \notin R\). One says that
\(\mathcal{R}\) is} reduced \emph{if every root is indivisible.}

\emph{For \(\mathcal{R}\) to be reduced it is necessary and sufficient
that \(\mathcal{R}*\) be so. If \(\alpha\) is indivisible and if
\(w \in W\), then \(w(\alpha)\) is indivisible.}

\textbf{Definition 2.1.4.} \emph{Let \(\alpha \in R\). If \(\alpha\) is
indivisible, set \(ind(\alpha) = \alpha\). Otherwise, set
\(ind(\alpha) = \alpha/2\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.1.5.} \emph{If \(\alpha \in R\) is indivisible and
if \(k \alpha \in R\), where \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\), then
\(k \in \mathbb{Z}\).}

\textbf{Proposition 2.1.6.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum.
Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ind(ℛ) = (M, M*, ind(R), ind(R)*)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a reduced root datum, and one has}

\[
W(ind(\mathcal{R})) = W(\mathcal{R}).
\]

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, \(ind(\mathcal{R})\) is a root datum by 1.2.11,
since the Weyl group permutes indivisible roots. The second assertion
follows from 2.1.1.

\textbf{Remark 2.1.7.} \emph{If \(\mathcal{R}\) is not reduced, one has
\(ind(R)* \neq ind(R*)\) and so
\(ind(\mathcal{R}*) \neq ind(\mathcal{R})*\).}

\subsubsection{2.2. Orthogonal roots}\label{orthogonal-roots}

\textbf{Lemma 2.2.1.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two roots.
One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(11)    ℓ(α) (α*, β) = ℓ(β) (β*, α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} This follows at once from 1.2.1, formulas (9) and (10).

\textbf{Corollary 2.2.2.} \emph{Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\). The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \((\alpha*, \beta) = 0\), (i bis) \((\beta*, \alpha) = 0\),}

\emph{(ii) \((p(\alpha), \beta) = 0\),}

\emph{(iii) \(s_{\alpha}(\beta) = \beta\), (iii bis)
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha) = \alpha\),}

\emph{(iv) \(s_{\alpha}(\beta*) = \beta*\), (iv bis)
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha*) = \alpha*\),}

\emph{(v) \(s_{\alpha} \neq s_{\beta}\) and \(s_{\alpha}\) and
\(s_{\beta}\) commute.}

\emph{Proof.} All the equivalences are immediate, except those involving
(v). Let us show that (i) (and (i bis)) entail (v). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_α s\_β(x) = x − (β*, x) β − (α*, x) α + (β*, x) (α*, β) α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \((\alpha*, \beta) = 0\), then \((\beta*, \alpha) = 0\) and
\(s_{\alpha} s_{\beta}(x) = s_{\beta} s_{\alpha}(x)\).

Suppose conversely (v). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_α = s\_β s\_α s\_β = s\_\{s\_β(α)\}    (by 1.2.10).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 2.1, there exists \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\) such that
\(\alpha = k s_{\beta}(\alpha) = k \alpha - k (\beta*, \alpha) \beta\).
Since \(s_{\alpha} \neq s_{\beta}\), \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) are not
proportional by 2.1.1, hence \((\beta*, \alpha) = 0\).

\textbf{Definition 2.2.3.} \emph{Two roots satisfying the equivalent
conditions of 2.2.2 are called} orthogonal.

\textbf{Remark 2.2.4.} \emph{The roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are
orthogonal if and only if the coroots \(\alpha*\) and \(\beta*\) are
orthogonal.}

\textbf{Lemma 2.2.5.} \emph{If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two
orthogonal roots, then \(\alpha + \beta \in R\) if and only if
\(\alpha - \beta \in R\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed,
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha + \beta) = s_{\beta}(\alpha) + s_{\beta}(\beta) = \alpha - \beta\).

\textbf{Lemma 2.2.6.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two
non-orthogonal roots. If one defines \(\ell(\gamma*)\) for a coroot
\(\gamma*\) as \(\ell\) of the root \(\gamma*\) of \(\mathcal{R}*\), one
has the relation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(12)    ℓ(α) ℓ(α*) = ℓ(β) ℓ(β*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, multiplying formula (11) by the corresponding
formula for \(\mathcal{R}*\), and using the equality
\((\gamma*)* = \gamma\) for all \(\gamma \in R\), one finds:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(β*, α) (α*, β) ℓ(α) ℓ(α*) = (β*, α) (α*, β) ℓ(β) ℓ(β*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{2.3. General case}\label{general-case-1}

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.1.} \emph{If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are any
two roots, one has}

\[
(13)    0 \leqslant (\alpha*, \beta)(\beta*, \alpha) \leqslant 4.
\]

\emph{If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are neither proportional nor
orthogonal, one has}

\[
1 \leqslant (\alpha*, \beta)(\beta*, \alpha) \leqslant 3.
\]

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one has
\(4 (p(\alpha), \beta)^{2} = \ell(\alpha) \ell(\beta) (\alpha*, \beta)(\beta*, \alpha)\).
On the other hand, by 1.2.6 the symmetric bilinear form
\texttt{(p(x),\ y)} is positive nondegenerate on \(V(R)\), whence
\((p(x), y)^{2} \leqslant \ell(x) \ell(y)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: with
  equality if and only if \(x\) and \(y\) are proportional.}

\textbf{Corollary 2.3.2.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two
non-orthogonal roots. If \(\ell(\alpha) = \ell(\beta)\), there exists
\(w \in W\) such that \(w(\alpha) = \beta\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, if \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are proportional, then
since \(\ell(\alpha) = \ell(\beta)\), one has \(\alpha = \beta\) or
\(\alpha = -\beta\); in this case one takes \(w = 1\) or
\(w = s_{\alpha}\). If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are neither proportional
nor orthogonal, then by formula (11) and 2.3.1:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(β*, α) = (α*, β) = ±1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \((\beta*, \alpha) = (\alpha*, \beta) = 1\), one takes
\(w = s_{\beta} s_{\alpha} s_{\beta}\). If
\((\beta*, \alpha) = (\alpha*, \beta) = -1\), one takes
\(w = s_{\alpha} s_{\beta}\).

\textbf{Corollary 2.3.3.} \emph{If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two
roots, if \(\alpha \neq \beta\) and \((\beta*, \alpha) > 0\) (resp. if
\(\alpha \neq -\beta\) and \((\beta*, \alpha) < 0\)), then
\(\alpha - \beta\) (resp. \(\alpha + \beta\)) is a root.}

\emph{Proof.} The second case is deduced from the first by changing
\(\beta\) into \(-\beta\). If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are proportional
and \((\beta*, \alpha) > 0\), then \(\beta = \alpha\),
\(2\beta = \alpha\), or \(\beta = 2\alpha\). The first case is excluded.
In the others, one has respectively \(\alpha - \beta = \beta \in R\) or
\(\alpha - \beta = -\alpha \in R\). If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not
proportional, \((\alpha*, \beta)\) and \((\beta*, \alpha)\) are two
strictly positive integers whose product is at most \texttt{3}. One of
them is therefore equal to \texttt{1}. If \((\beta*, \alpha) = 1\), one
has \(\alpha - \beta = s_{\beta}(\alpha) \in R\); if
\((\alpha*, \beta) = 1\), one has
\(\alpha - \beta = -s_{\alpha}(\beta) \in R\).

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.4.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two
non-proportional roots. If \(\beta - \alpha\) is not a root, then
\(\beta + k \alpha \in R\) for \(k = -(\alpha*, \beta)\), but not for
\(k = -(\alpha*, \beta) + 1\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed,
\(\beta - (\alpha*, \beta) \alpha = s_{\alpha}(\beta) \in R\), but
\(\beta + (-(\alpha*, \beta) + 1) \alpha = s_{\alpha}(\beta - \alpha) \notin R\).

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.5.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two
non-proportional roots. The set of integers \(k\) such that
\(\beta + k \alpha \in R\) is an interval \texttt{{[}p,\ q{]}}
(\(p \leqslant 0\), \(q \geqslant 0\)), and one has
\(p + q = -(\alpha*, \beta)\).}

\emph{Proof.} For the first assertion it suffices, for example, to prove
that if \(\beta + k \alpha \in R\), \(k\) integer
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}, then \(\beta + (k - 1) \alpha \in R\). If
\(k = 1\), this is trivial. If \(k \geqslant 2\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(α*, β + k α) = (α*, β) + 2k ⩾ −3 + 4 \textgreater{} 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one concludes by 2.3.3. Let then \texttt{{[}p,\ q{]}} be the
interval in question. Applying 2.3.4 to \(\beta + p \alpha\), one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{q − p = −(α*, β + p α) = −(α*, β) − 2p.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected \(+ 2p\) to \(- 2p\).}

\textbf{Remark 2.3.6.} \emph{The previous formula contains the
qualitative statements 2.2.5 and 2.3.3.}

\textbf{Complements 2.3.7.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added these
  complements, useful for the proof of 3.1.5.} \emph{By 1.2.1 (9) and
1.2.6, the bilinear form on \(V(R)\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⟨x, y⟩ = (p(x), y)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is symmetric and positive definite. By 1.2.1 (10), for any
\(\alpha \in R\) and \(y \in V(R)\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⟨α, y⟩ = (ℓ(α)/2) (α*, y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(\ell(\alpha) = \langle \alpha, \alpha\rangle\).
Consequently, one deduces from 2.3.3 the following corollary.}

\textbf{Corollary.} \emph{Let \(\alpha \neq \beta\) in \(R\). If
\(\alpha - \beta \notin R\), then
\(\langle \alpha, \beta\rangle \leqslant 0\).}

\subsection{3. Simple roots, positive
roots}\label{simple-roots-positive-roots}

\subsubsection{3.1. Systems of simple
roots}\label{systems-of-simple-roots}

\textbf{Lemma 3.1.1.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha_{i}\),
\(i = 1, \cdots, n\), be roots. Assume \(\alpha\) is distinct from the
\(\alpha_{i}\). If one has a relation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α = Σᵢ qᵢ αᵢ,    qᵢ ∈ Q₊,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{there exists an index \(i\) such that \(q_{i} \neq 0\),
\((\alpha*, \alpha_{i}) > 0\), and \(\alpha - \alpha_{i} \in R\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one writes
\(2 = (\alpha*, \alpha) = \Sigma_{i} q_{i} (\alpha*, \alpha_{i})\),
which proves the first two assertions. The third then follows from
2.3.3.

\textbf{Proposition 3.1.2.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha_{i}\),
\(i = 1, \cdots, n\), be roots. If}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α = Σᵢ mᵢ αᵢ,    mᵢ ∈ ℕ₊,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{there exists a sequence \(\beta_{1}, \cdots, \beta_{m}\) of roots
taken from the \(\alpha_{i}\) (not necessarily pairwise distinct) such
that if one denotes}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{γ\_p = Σ\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{p\} βᵢ,    p = 1, …, m,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has \(\gamma_{p} \in R\) and \(\gamma_{m} = \alpha\).}

\emph{Proof.} We argue by induction on the integer
\(\Sigma m_{i} = m'\). If \(\alpha\) equals one of the \(\alpha_{i}\),
say \(\alpha_{i_{0}}\) (which is automatic if \(m' = 1\)), one takes
\(m = 1\), \(\beta_{1} = \alpha_{i_{0}}\). Otherwise, one applies the
previous lemma and there exists an index \(i\) such that
\(m_{i} \neq 0\) and \(\alpha - \alpha_{i}\) is a root. One then has
\((m_{i} - 1) \in \mathbb{N}\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α − αᵢ = (mᵢ − 1) αᵢ + Σ\_\{j ≠ i\} mⱼ αⱼ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It remains only to apply the induction hypothesis to
\(\alpha - \alpha_{i}\).

\textbf{Corollary 3.1.3.} \emph{Let \(R' \subset R\). The following
conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) If \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\) and \(\alpha + \beta \in R\), then
\(\alpha + \beta \in R'\).}

\emph{(ii) \((\mathbb{N} \cdot R') \cap R \subset R'\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one has clearly (ii) ⇒ (i). The converse follows
at once from the proposition.

\textbf{Definition 3.1.4.} \emph{A set of roots satisfying the
conditions of 3.1.3 is called} closed.

\textbf{Proposition 3.1.5.} \emph{Let \(\Delta \subset R\) be a set of
roots. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) The elements of \(\Delta\) are indivisible, linearly
independent, and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⊂ (Q₊ · Δ) ∪ (−Q₊ · Δ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) The elements of \(\Delta\) are linearly independent and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⊂ (ℕ · Δ) ∪ (−ℕ · Δ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) Every root is written in a unique way as a linear
combination of the elements of \(\Delta\), with integer coefficients all
of the same sign.}

\footnote{N.D.E.: In what follows, we have modified the order and
  detailed the proof of the implication (iii) ⇒ (i).} One has obviously
(ii) ⇒ (iii). Denote by \(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\) the
(distinct) elements of \(\Delta\).

\emph{Proof of} (i) ⇒ (ii). Let \(\alpha \in R\). One has thus a unique
expression

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ε α = Σᵢ qᵢ αᵢ    qᵢ ∈ Q₊, ε = ±1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us show that the \texttt{qᵢ} are integers. This is certainly true if
all but one of them are zero (cf.~2.1.5). Otherwise, \(\alpha\) is
distinct from the \(\alpha_{i}\) and, applying 3.1.1, one finds
\(i_{0}\) such that \(\alpha' = \epsilon \alpha - \alpha_{i_{0}} \in R\)
and \(q_{i_{0}} \neq 0\). This gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\textquotesingle{} = (q\_\{i₀\} − 1) α\_\{i₀\} + Σ\_\{i ≠ i₀\} qᵢ αᵢ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since at least one of the \texttt{qᵢ}, \(i \neq i_{0}\), is nonzero, (i)
entails \(q_{i_{0}} - 1 \geqslant 0\). One repeats the operation for
\(\alpha'\) and after finitely many steps one has shown that the
\texttt{qᵢ} are integers.

\emph{Proof of} (iii) ⇒ (i). Let us show that
\(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\) are linearly independent
over \(\mathbb{Q}\). In the contrary case, one would have an equality

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x = Σ\_\{i ∈ I\} aᵢ αᵢ = Σ\_\{j ∈ J\} bⱼ αⱼ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(I\), \(J\) are two disjoint subsets of \({1, \cdots, n}\), at
least one of them, say \(I\), being nonempty, and
\(a_{i}, b_{j} \in \mathbb{N}*\). By Corollary 2.3.7, one has
\(\langle \alpha_{i}, \alpha_{j}\rangle \leqslant 0\) if \(i \in I\) and
\(j \in J\), whence \(\langle x, x\rangle \leqslant 0\) and so
\(x = 0\). Let \(i_{0} \in I\); then the equalities

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\_\{i₀\} = α\_\{i₀\} + Σ\_\{i ∈ I\} aᵢ αᵢ = α\_\{i₀\} + Σ\_\{j ∈ J\} bⱼ αⱼ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

entail (by (iii)) \(a_{i} = 0 = b_{j}\) for all \(i\), \(j\), a
contradiction. This shows that the elements of \(\Delta\) are linearly
independent over \(\mathbb{Q}\); let us show they are also indivisible.

So let \(\beta \in \Delta\) be divisible. One has \(\beta/2 \in R\),
whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{β/2 = ε Σ\_\{α ∈ Δ\} m\_α α,    m\_α ∈ ℕ, ε = ±1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so also \(\beta = 2 \epsilon \Sigma_{\alpha} m_{\alpha} \alpha\), whence
by uniqueness \(m_{\alpha} = 0\) if \(\alpha \neq \beta\) and
\(2 \epsilon m_{\beta} = 1\), a contradiction.

\textbf{Definition 3.1.6.} \emph{A set \(\Delta\) of roots satisfying
the conditions of 3.1.5 is called a} system of simple roots, \emph{or a}
base of \(\mathcal{R}\).

\emph{If \(w \in W\) and if \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots, then
\(w(\Delta)\) is a system of simple roots.}

\textbf{Remark 3.1.7.} \emph{This definition involves only \(R\) and not
\(\mathcal{R}\), and in fact involves only \(ind(R)\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.1.8.} \emph{If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots,
\(\Delta\) is a basis of the free abelian group \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\). One
has thus \(Card(\Delta) = rgss(\mathcal{R})\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.1.9.} \emph{The conditions of 3.1.5 are then evidently
equivalent to:}

\emph{(i′) The elements of \(\Delta\) are indivisible, of number
\(\leqslant rgss(\mathcal{R})\), and
\(R \subset (Q_{+} \cdot \Delta) \cup (-Q_{+} \cdot \Delta)\).}

\emph{(ii′) \(Card(\Delta) \leqslant rgss(\mathcal{R})\) and
\(R \subset (\mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta) \cup (-\mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta)\).}

\textbf{Corollary 3.1.10.} \emph{If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple
roots, then \(ind(\Delta*)\) is a system of simple coroots (i.e. a
system of simple roots of \(\mathcal{R}*\)).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, if
\(\beta = \Sigma_{\alpha \in \Delta} a_{\alpha} \alpha\)
(\(a_{\alpha} \in \mathbb{N}\)), then
\(p(\beta) = \Sigma_{\alpha \in \Delta} a_{\alpha} p(\alpha)\), whence,
by 1.2.1 (10):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{β* = Σ\_\{α ∈ Δ\} a\_α (ℓ(α)/ℓ(β)) α*,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which shows that \(ind(\Delta*)\) satisfies (i′).

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the following sentence, and in 3.1.11 we
  have replaced \(4 a_{\alpha} \ell(\alpha)\) by
  \(2 a_{\alpha} \ell(\alpha)\).} By 2.1.1, if \(\alpha*\) is not
indivisible, then \(\alpha* = 2 u*\), where \(u* \in ind(\Delta*)\) (and
\(u = 2\alpha\)). One deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 3.1.11.} \emph{If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple
roots and if \(\beta = \Sigma_{\alpha \in \Delta} a_{\alpha} \alpha\)
(\(a_{\alpha} \in \mathbb{Z}\)) is the expression of \(\beta\) along
\(\Delta\), then \(2 a_{\alpha} \ell(\alpha)\) is divisible by
\(\ell(\beta)\) (and even by \(2 \ell(\beta)\) if \(\alpha*\) is
indivisible).}

Before continuing to state the properties of systems of simple roots,
let us show that such systems exist.

\subsubsection{3.2. Systems of positive
roots}\label{systems-of-positive-roots}

\textbf{Definition 3.2.1.} \emph{A subset \(R_{+} \subset R\) is called
a} system of positive roots \emph{of \(R\) (or of \(\mathcal{R}\),
cf.~Remark 3.2.2) if it satisfies the following conditions:}

\emph{(P 1) \(R_{+} \cap -R_{+} = \emptyset\).}

\emph{(P 2) \(R_{+} \cup -R_{+} = R\).}

\emph{(P 3) \((Q_{+} \cdot R_{+}) \cap R \subset R_{+}\).}

\emph{In particular, such a set is closed. We shall see later (3.3.8)
that in fact a closed subset satisfying (P 1) and (P 2) also satisfies
(P 3), and hence is a system of positive roots. If \(w \in W\) and if
\(R_{+}\) is a system of positive roots, then \(w(R_{+})\) is a system
of positive roots.}

\textbf{Remark 3.2.2.} \emph{This definition involves only \(R\). One
will also say that \(R_{+}\) is a system of positive roots of
\(\mathcal{R}\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.2.3.} \emph{From (P 1) and (P 2), one obtains at once}

\[
Card(R_{+}) = Card(R)/2.
\]

\emph{It follows that if \(R_{+}\) and \(R'_{+}\) are two systems of
positive roots with \(R_{+} \subset R'_{+}\), then \(R_{+} = R'_{+}\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.2.4.} \emph{If \(R_{+}\) is a system of positive roots,
\(R*_{+}\) is a system of positive coroots (i.e.~a system of positive
roots of \(\mathcal{R}*\)).}

\emph{This follows at once from 1.1.4 and 1.2.2.}

\textbf{Definition 3.2.5.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple
roots. Set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(Δ) = (Q₊ · Δ) ∩ R = (ℕ₊ · Δ) ∩ R.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 3.2.6.} \emph{If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple
roots, \(P(\Delta)\) is a system of positive roots. If \(\Delta\) is a
system of simple roots and \(R_{+}\) is a system of positive roots, one
has the equivalence:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Δ ⊂ R₊  ⟺  R₊ = P(Δ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} The first assertion is immediate. If
\(\Delta \subset R_{+}\), then \(P(\Delta) \subset R_{+}\) by (P 3), so
\(P(\Delta) = R_{+}\) by 3.2.3. The rest is trivial.

\textbf{Remark 3.2.7.} \emph{Systems of positive roots exist: let
\(\geqslant\) be a structure of totally ordered vector space on
\(V(R)\). The set of roots \(\geqslant 0\) for this order relation is a
system of positive roots.}

\textbf{Theorem 3.2.8.} \emph{Let \(R_{+}\) be a system of positive
roots. There exists a unique system of simple roots
\(\mathcal{S}(R_{+})\) such that \(\mathcal{S}(R_{+}) \subset R_{+}\),
i.e.~such that \(R_{+} = P(\mathcal{S}(R_{+}))\).}

\emph{Proof.} Uniqueness follows at once from:

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.9.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots.
Then for \(\alpha \in P(\Delta)\) to belong to \(\Delta\), it is
necessary and sufficient that \(\alpha\) not be a sum of two elements of
\(P(\Delta)\).}

\emph{Proof.} This lemma follows at once from the definitions and from
3.1.2.

Let us now prove the existence of \(\mathcal{S}(R_{+})\). Consider the
set of subsets \(T\) of \(R_{+}\) such that \(T = ind(T)\) and
\((Q_{+} \cdot T) \supset R_{+}\). This set is nonempty, since it
contains \(ind(R_{+})\). Let \(\Delta\) be a minimal element of this set
for the inclusion relation. We show that \(\Delta\) is a system of
simple roots, that is to say, by 3.1.5 (i), that \(\Delta\) is a free
subset of \(M \otimes \mathbb{Q}\).

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.10.} \emph{If \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\) and
\(q \alpha + q' \beta \in R\), where \(q, q' \in \mathbb{Q}\), then
\(q q' \geqslant 0\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, if \(q q' < 0\), one can write (possibly
exchanging \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\))

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a α − b β ∈ R₊,    a, b ∈ Q*₊,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so by hypothesis there exists a relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a α − b β = Σ\_\{γ ∈ Δ\} c(γ) γ,    c(γ) ∈ Q₊.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(a \leqslant c(\alpha)\), it is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{−β = ((c(α) − a)/b) α + Σ\_\{γ ≠ α\} (c(γ)/b) γ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then this element belongs to \((Q_{+} \cdot \Delta) \cap R\), which is
contained in \(R_{+}\) by (P 3). But then
\(\beta \in R_{+} \cap -R_{+}\), which contradicts (P 1).

If, on the contrary, \(a > c(\alpha)\), one writes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(a − c(α)) α = b β + Σ\_\{γ ≠ α\} c(γ) γ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which proves \(\Delta \subset Q_{+} \cdot (\Delta - {\alpha})\),
contrary to the minimal character of \(\Delta\).

Recall (cf.~2.3.7) that the bilinear form on \(V(R)\) defined by
\(\langle x, y\rangle = (p(x), y)\) is a Euclidean inner product;
moreover, for \(\alpha \in R\) one has
\(\langle \alpha, y\rangle = \ell(\alpha) (\alpha*, y) / 2\), so that
\(\langle \alpha, y\rangle\) and \((\alpha*, y)\) have the same sign.

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.11.} \emph{If \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\), then
\((\beta*, \alpha) \leqslant 0\) and so
\(\langle \beta, \alpha\rangle \leqslant 0\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed,
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha) = \alpha - (\beta*, \alpha) \beta \in R\), whence
\((\beta*, \alpha) \leqslant 0\) by 3.2.10.

Let us now prove that \(\Delta\) is free. In the contrary case, 3.2.11
entails, as in the proof of 3.1.5, the existence of a non-trivial
relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Σ\_\{α ∈ Δ\} m(α) α = 0,    m(α) ∈ ℕ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence
\(-\alpha_{0} = (m(\alpha_{0}) - 1) \alpha_{0} + \Sigma_{\alpha \neq \alpha_{0}} m(\alpha) \alpha\),
if \(m(\alpha_{0}) \geqslant 1\). Then, by (P 3), \(\alpha_{0}\) belongs
to \(R_{+} \cap -R_{+}\), contradicting (P 1).

This shows that \(\Delta\) is a base of \(\mathcal{R}\) and completes
the proof of Theorem 3.2.8.

\textbf{Corollary 3.2.12.} \emph{Let \(R_{+}\) be a system of positive
roots, \(\Delta\) a base of \(\mathcal{R}\), and \(w \in W\). One has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Δ ⊂ R₊  ⟺  R₊ = P(Δ)  ⟺  Δ = 𝒮(R₊)}

\NormalTok{P(ind(Δ*)) = P(Δ)*,    𝒮(R*₊) = ind(𝒮(R₊)*);}

\NormalTok{𝒮(w(R₊)) = w(𝒮(R₊)),    P(w(Δ)) = w(P(Δ)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 3.2.13.} \emph{If one has chosen a system of simple
roots \(\Delta\), the elements of \(P(\Delta)\) will be called}
positive. \emph{If one has chosen a system of positive roots \(R_{+}\),
the elements of \(\mathcal{S}(R_{+})\) will be called} simple.

\textbf{Corollary 3.2.14.} \emph{Let \(R_{+}\) be a system of positive
roots. Let \(\alpha \in R_{+}\). The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(\alpha\) is simple
(i.e.~\(\alpha \in \mathcal{S}(R_{+})\)).}

\emph{(ii) \(\alpha\) is not a sum of two elements of \(R_{+}\).}

\emph{(iii) \(R_{+} - {\alpha}\) is closed (cf.~3.1.4).}

\emph{Proof.} The equivalence of (i) and (ii) follows at once from
3.2.9. The equivalence of (ii) and (iii) is immediate.

\textbf{Definition 3.2.15.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple
roots. The sum of the coefficients of the decomposition of a root
\(\alpha\) along \(\Delta\) is called the} order of \(\alpha\)
\emph{relative to \(\Delta\) and is denoted \(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha)\).}

\emph{One has the equivalences:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α ∈ P(Δ)  ⟺  ord\_Δ(α) \textgreater{} 0,    α ∈ Δ  ⟺  ord\_Δ(α) = 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.16.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots
and \(\alpha \in P(\Delta)\). There exists a sequence
\(\alpha_{i} \in \Delta\), \(i = 1, \cdots, m\), such that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α₁ + α₂ + ⋯ + α\_p ∈ P(Δ)    for p = 1, …, m,}
\NormalTok{α₁ + α₂ + ⋯ + α\_m = α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, for every such sequence \(\alpha_{i}\), one has
\(m = ord_{\Delta}(\alpha)\).}

\emph{Proof.} Trivial by 3.1.2.

\subsubsection{3.3. Characterization and conjugacy of systems of
positive
roots}\label{characterization-and-conjugacy-of-systems-of-positive-roots}

\textbf{Lemma 3.3.1.} \emph{If \(\alpha \in P(\Delta)\),
\(\beta \in \Delta\), and if \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not
proportional, then \(s_{\beta}(\alpha) \in P(\Delta)\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed,
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha) = \alpha - (\beta*, \alpha) \beta\). Since at least
one simple root other than \(\beta\) appears in the decomposition of
\(\alpha\) with a nonzero (hence strictly positive) coefficient, it also
appears in the decomposition of \(s_{\beta}(\alpha)\) with the same
coefficient, so \(s_{\beta}(\alpha)\) is also positive.

\textbf{Corollary 3.3.2.} \emph{If \(\beta \in \Delta\), the symmetry
\(s_{\beta}\) interchanges the elements of \(P(\Delta)\) not
proportional to \(\beta\).}

\textbf{Lemma 3.3.3.} \emph{If \(\alpha \in P(\Delta) - \Delta\),
\(\alpha\) indivisible, there exists \(\beta \in \Delta\) such that
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha) \in P(\Delta)\) and
\(ord_{\Delta}(s_{\beta}(\alpha)) < ord_{\Delta}(\alpha)\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, by 3.1.1 there exists \(\beta \in \Delta\) such
that \((\beta*, \alpha) > 0\). Since \(\alpha \notin \Delta\) and is
indivisible, \(\alpha\) cannot be proportional to \(\beta\). Hence
\(s_{\beta}(\alpha) \in P(\Delta)\), by 3.3.1, and one has
\texttt{ord\_Δ(s\_β(α))\ =\ ord\_Δ(α)\ −\ (β*,\ α)\ \textless{}\ ord\_Δ(α)}.

\textbf{Corollary 3.3.4.} \emph{If \(\alpha \in P(\Delta)\) is
indivisible, there exists a sequence \(\beta_{p} \in \Delta\),
\(p = 1, \cdots, q\), such that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\_p = s\_\{β\_p\} ⋯ s\_\{β\_1\}(α) ∈ P(Δ)    for p = 1, …, q,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and \(\alpha_{q} \in \Delta\).}

\emph{Proof.} This follows from 3.3.3 by induction on
\(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha)\).

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.5.} \emph{The Weyl group is generated by the
\(s_{\alpha}\), for \(\alpha \in \Delta\). Every indivisible root is
conjugate to a simple root by an element of the Weyl group.}

\emph{Proof.} The second assertion follows at once from 3.3.4. The first
follows from it by 1.2.10 and 2.1.1.

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.6.} \emph{Let \(R_{+}\) be a system of positive
roots. Let \(P' \subset R\) satisfy (P 2) and be closed. Then there
exists \(w \in W\) such that \(w(R_{+}) \subset P'\).}

Let us state the corollaries at once.

\textbf{Corollary 3.3.7.} \emph{The Weyl group operates transitively on
the set of systems of positive roots (resp. of systems of simple
roots).}

\textbf{Corollary 3.3.8.} \emph{For a subset of \(R\) to be a system of
positive roots, it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy (P 1) and
(P 2) and be closed.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.3.9.} \emph{If one endows \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) with a
structure of ordered group such that every root is
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} or \texttt{\textless{}\ 0}, the set of
positive roots for this order structure is a system of positive roots.}

\emph{Proof of 3.3.6.} One can find \(w \in W\) such that
\(Card(w(R_{+}) \cap P')\) is maximal, hence by replacing \(R_{+}\) by
\(w(R_{+})\) one may assume that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(∗)    Card(R₊ ∩ P\textquotesingle{}) ⩾ Card(R₊ ∩ s\_α(P\textquotesingle{}))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for all \(\alpha \in \mathcal{S}(R_{+}) = \Delta\). Let us show that
\(R_{+} \subset P'\). Otherwise, \(P'\) being closed, there exists
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), \(\alpha \notin P'\). But \(P'\) satisfying (P
2), one has then \(-\alpha \in P'\) (so \(-2\alpha \in P'\) if
\(2\alpha\) is a root). For every \(\beta \in R_{+} \cap P'\), one has
\(\beta \neq \alpha\); if \(2\alpha\) is not a root, then
\(s_{\alpha}(\beta) \in R_{+}\) (by 3.3.1), so

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_α(R₊ ∩ P\textquotesingle{}) ⊂ R₊ ∩ s\_α(P\textquotesingle{});}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but \(R_{+} \cap s_{\alpha}(P')\) also contains
\(\alpha = s_{\alpha}(-\alpha)\), contradicting inequality (∗). If
\(2\alpha\) is a root, one argues similarly.

To study sets of roots satisfying (P 2) and closed, one is therefore
reduced to the case where they contain a set of positive roots.

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.10.} \emph{Let \(R_{+}\) be a system of positive
roots and \(P'\) a closed subset of \(R\) containing \(R_{+}\). If one
denotes \(\Delta = \mathcal{S}(R_{+})\) and
\(\Delta' = \Delta \cap -P'\), then \(P'\) is the union of \(R_{+}\) and
the set of roots that are linear combinations with negative coefficients
of the elements of \(\Delta'\).}

\emph{Proof.} We prove the assertion by induction on the order of a root
\(\gamma \in P' - R_{+}\). If \(ord_{\Delta}(\gamma) = -1\), then
\(-\gamma \in \Delta\) and \(\gamma \in -\Delta'\). If
\(ord_{\Delta}(\gamma) < -1\), there exists, by 3.1.2,
\(\beta \in \Delta\) such that \(-\gamma - \beta \in R\); then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 \textless{} ord\_Δ(−γ − β) = ord\_Δ(−γ) − 1 \textless{} ord\_Δ(−γ)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the first inequality shows that \(-\gamma - \beta \in R_{+}\).
Hence, since \(R_{+} \cap -R_{+} = \emptyset\) and \(\gamma + \beta\) is
a sum of two roots of \(P'\), it is an element of \(P' - R_{+}\) with
\(ord_{\Delta}(\gamma + \beta) > ord_{\Delta}(\gamma)\). So, by the
induction hypothesis, \(\gamma + \beta\) is a linear combination with
negative coefficients of the elements of \(\Delta'\). Since
\(\gamma = (\gamma + \beta) - \beta\), it suffices to verify that
\(\beta \in -P'\). Now \(\gamma \in P'\) and
\(-(\gamma + \beta) \in R_{+} \subset P'\), so
\(-\beta = \gamma - (\gamma + \beta)\) belongs to \(P'\).

\textbf{Definition 3.3.10.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have inserted this
  definition here.} \emph{One says that a subset \(R'\) of \(R\) is}
symmetric \emph{if \(-R' = R'\).}

\textbf{Scholie 3.3.11.} \emph{Let \(P'\) be a set of roots satisfying
(P 2) and closed. There exists a system of simple roots \(\Delta\) and a
subset \(\Delta'\) of \(\Delta\) such that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P\textquotesingle{} = R ∩ (ℕ · Δ ∪ −ℕ · Δ\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If one denotes
\(R_{\Delta'} = (\mathbb{Z} \cdot \Delta') \cap R\), which is a closed
and symmetric subset of \(R\), then \(P'\) is the disjoint union of
\(R_{\Delta'}\) and of the closed part of \(P(\Delta)\) formed by the
\(\alpha \in P(\Delta) - \mathbb{N} \cdot \Delta'\), i.e.~the positive
roots which in the decomposition along \(\Delta\) ``contain at least one
root of \(\Delta - \Delta'\)''.}

\subsubsection{3.4. Closed and symmetric sets of
roots}\label{closed-and-symmetric-sets-of-roots}

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.1.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\)
be a root datum and \(R'\) a closed and symmetric subset of \(R\).
Then:}

\emph{(i) \(\mathcal{R}' = (M, M*, R', R'*)\) is a root datum;}

\emph{(ii) for every system of positive roots \(R_{+}\) of \(R\),
\(R'_{+} = R_{+} \cap R'\) is a system of positive roots of \(R'\);}

\emph{(iii) the Weyl group \(W(\mathcal{R}')\) of \(\mathcal{R}'\) is
the subgroup of \(W(\mathcal{R})\) generated by the \(s_{\alpha}\), for
\(\alpha \in R'\).}

\emph{Proof.} The first assertion is trivial by 1.2.11, the second
follows from 3.3.8, the third is evident.

\textbf{Corollary 3.4.2.} \emph{Let \(w \in W(\mathcal{R}')\). The order
of \(w\) is the smallest integer \(n > 0\) such that
\(w^{n}(\alpha') = \alpha'\) for every \(\alpha' \in R'\).}

\emph{Proof.} It suffices to apply 1.2.7 to the root datum
\(\mathcal{R}'\).

\textbf{Corollary 3.4.3.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two
non-proportional roots. Let \(n\) be the smallest integer
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} such that
\((s_{\alpha} s_{\beta})^{n}(\alpha) = \alpha\) and
\((s_{\alpha} s_{\beta})^{n}(\beta) = \beta\). Then the subgroup
\(W_{\alpha,\beta}\) of \(W\) generated by \(s_{\alpha}\) and
\(s_{\beta}\) is defined by the relations:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_α² = 1,    s\_β² = 1,    (s\_α s\_β)ⁿ = 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Taking 3.4.2 into account, it suffices to verify:

\textbf{Lemma 3.4.4.} \emph{Let \(G\) be the group generated by two
elements \(x\) and \(y\) subject to the relations \(x^{2} = y^{2} = 1\).
Every normal subgroup of \(G\) containing neither \(x\) nor \(y\) is
generated (as a normal subgroup) by an element of the form \((xy)^{n}\),
where \(n > 0\).}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the original in what follows.}
\emph{Proof.} Indeed, every element of \(G\) is written \((xy)^{n}\), or
\((yx)^{n} = (xy)^{-n}\), or:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(a)    x (yx)\^{}\{2n\}    or    y (xy)\^{}\{2n+1\}}

\NormalTok{(b)    y (xy)\^{}\{2n\}    or    x (yx)\^{}\{2n+1\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Now the elements of type (a) (resp. (b)) are
conjugate to \(x\) (resp. to \(y\)).

\textbf{Remark 3.4.5.} \emph{One computes the integer \(n\) immediately:
if one sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(α*, β) = p,    (β*, α) = q,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the original in what
  follows.}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(s\_α s\_β)(α) = (pq − 1) α − q β,    (s\_α s\_β)(β) = p α − β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{The integer \(n\) is therefore the order of the matrix}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{⎛pq − 1   p⎞}
\NormalTok{⎝  −q   −1⎠.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(pq = 0\), then \(p = q = 0\), by 2.2.2, whence \(n = 2\).
Otherwise, by 2.3.1, \texttt{pq} equals \texttt{1}, \texttt{2}, or
\texttt{3}, and one finds, respectively, \(n = 3\), \texttt{4}, or
\texttt{6}.}

\emph{N.B. By writing that the order of the previous matrix is finite,
one recovers inequality (13) of 2.3.1.}

\textbf{Definition 3.4.6.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple
roots and \(\Delta' \subset \Delta\). We write}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R\_\{Δ\textquotesingle{}\} = R ∩ (ℚ · Δ\textquotesingle{}) = R ∩ (ℤ · Δ\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 3.4.7.} \emph{\(R_{\Delta'}\) is closed and symmetric,
\(\Delta'\) is a system of simple roots of the root datum
\((M, M*, R_{\Delta'}, R*_{\Delta'})\), whose Weyl group is the subgroup
\(W_{\Delta'}\) of \(W\) generated by the \(s_{\alpha}\), for
\(\alpha \in \Delta'\). One has \(\Delta \cap R_{\Delta'} = \Delta'\).}

\emph{Proof.} Trivial.

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.8.} \emph{Let \(R' \subset R\). The following
conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) There exists a vector subspace \(V'\) of \(V\) (or of
\(V(R)\)) such that \(R' = R \cap V'\).}

\emph{(ii) There exists a system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\) and
a subset \(\Delta'\) of \(\Delta\) such that \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\).}

\emph{More precisely, under these conditions, every system of simple
roots \(\Delta'\) of \((M, M*, R', R'*)\) is contained in a system of
simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\), and one has \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\).}

\emph{Proof.} One has obviously (ii) ⇒ (i). Suppose (i) verified: then
\(R'\) is closed and symmetric, so \((M, M*, R', R'*)\) is a root datum.
Let \(\Delta'\) be a system of simple roots of this datum and
\(R'_{+} = P(\Delta')\). If \(V' = V\), then \(\Delta'\) is a system of
simple roots of \(\mathcal{R}\) and we are done. Otherwise, there exists
\(x \in V*\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(x, V\textquotesingle{}) = \{0\},    (x, α) ≠ 0    for all α ∈ R − R\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Put \(R_{+}(x) = {\alpha \in R | (x, \alpha) > 0}\) and
\(R_{+} = R_{+}(x) \cup R'_{+}\). For every \(\alpha \in R\), one has
the equivalences

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(x, α) \textgreater{} 0  ⟺  α ∈ R₊(x),}
\NormalTok{(x, α) \textless{} 0  ⟺  α ∈ −R₊(x),}
\NormalTok{(x, α) = 0  ⟺  α ∈ R\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows at once from 3.3.8 that \(R_{+}\) is a system of positive
roots of \(R\). Put \(\Delta = \mathcal{S}(R_{+})\). It evidently
suffices to prove \(\Delta' \subset \Delta\). Otherwise let
\(\alpha \in \Delta' - \Delta\). Then, by 3.2.14, there exist
\(\beta, \gamma \in R_{+}\) such that \(\alpha = \beta + \gamma\). If
\(\beta, \gamma \in R_{+}(x)\), one has \(\alpha \in R_{+}(x)\), which
is absurd since \((x, \Delta') = 0\). If \(\beta\) or \(\gamma\), say
\(\beta\), belongs to \(R'_{+}\), then, since \(R'\) is symmetric and
closed, \(\gamma = \alpha - \beta\) belongs to
\(R_{+} \cap R' = R'_{+}\); but then \(\alpha\) is not simple in
\(R'_{+}\).

\textbf{Lemma 3.4.9.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, let
\(\alpha \in P(\Delta) - R'\). For every \(w \in W_{\Delta'}\), one has
\(w(\alpha) \in P(\Delta) - R'\).}

\emph{Proof.} It indeed suffices to verify this for \(w = s_{\beta}\),
\(\beta \in \Delta'\), in which case it follows from 3.3.1 and from the
fact that \(s_{\beta}(R') = R'\).

\textbf{Lemma 3.4.10.} \emph{Let \(w \in W\). Under the conditions of
3.4.8, the following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(w \in W_{\Delta'}\).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(m \in M\), \(w(m) - m \in V'\).}

\emph{(iii) For every \(\alpha \in R\), \(w(\alpha) - \alpha \in V'\).}

\emph{Proof.} One has obviously (i) ⇒ (ii) ⇒ (iii). Let us prove (iii) ⇒
(i). Let then \(w \in W\) be such that \(w(\alpha) - \alpha \in V'\) for
all \(\alpha \in R\). Write
\(w = s_{\alpha_{n}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{1}}\), with
\(\alpha_{i} \in \Delta\), and let us prove by induction on \(n\) that
each \(\alpha_{i} \in \Delta'\). One may assume that
\(w' = s_{\alpha_{n-1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{1}} \in W_{\Delta'}\). One has
then, for all \(\alpha \in R\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w(α) − α = w\textquotesingle{}(α) − α − (α*\_n, w\textquotesingle{}(α)) α\_n.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Taking \(\alpha = w'^{-1}(\alpha_{n})\), one finds
\(2 \alpha_{n} \in V'\), whence \(\alpha_{n} \in \Delta'\), so
\(w = s_{\alpha_{n}} w'\) belongs to \(W_{\Delta'}\).

\subsubsection{3.5. Miscellaneous
remarks}\label{miscellaneous-remarks-1}

\textbf{Proposition 3.5.1.} \emph{Let \(R_{+}\) be a system of positive
roots. Denote}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ρ\_\{R₊\} = (1/2) Σ\_\{α ∈ ind(R₊)\} α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \((\beta*, \rho_{R_{+}}) = 1\) for every
\(\beta \in \mathcal{S}(R_{+})\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one can write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{2 ρ\_\{R₊\} = β + Σ\_\{α ∈ ind(R₊), α ≠ β\} α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \(s_{\beta}(2 \rho_{R_{+}}) = 2 \rho_{R_{+}} - 2\beta\), by 3.3.2.

\textbf{Corollary 3.5.2.} \emph{Put
\(\rho*_{R_{+}} = (1/2) \Sigma_{\alpha* \in ind(R*_{+})} \alpha*\).
Then:}

\emph{(i) \((\rho*_{R_{+}}, \alpha) > 0\) for every \(\alpha \in R_{+}\)
(i.e.~\(\rho*_{R_{+}} \in \mathcal{C}(R_{+})\), cf. 3.6.8).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(\alpha \in R\), one has
\(ord_{\mathcal{S}(R_{+})}(\alpha) = (\rho*_{R_{+}}, \alpha)\).}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Indeed, by 3.1.5, it suffices to verify the formula for
  \(\alpha \in \Delta\). Now, by 3.5.1 applied to \(\mathcal{R}*\), one
  has in this case
  \((\rho*_{R_{+}}, \alpha) = 1 = ord_{\mathcal{S}(R_{+})}(\alpha)\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.5.3.} \emph{If \(w \in W\), one has
\(\rho_{w(R_{+})} = w(\rho_{R_{+}})\) and
\(\rho*_{w(R_{+})} = w(\rho*_{R_{+}})\).}

\textbf{Proposition 3.5.4.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) be two
non-proportional roots, with \(\alpha\) indivisible. There exists a
system of simple roots containing \(\alpha\) and a root \(\beta\) such
that \(\gamma = a \alpha + b \beta\), with \(a, b \in \mathbb{N}\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, let us construct a basis of the vector space
\(V(R)\) containing \(\alpha_{1} = \alpha\), \(\alpha_{2} = \gamma\).
Consider the lexicographic order with respect to this basis. Denoting by
\(R_{+}\) the set of roots \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}, it is clear that
\(R_{+}\) is a system of positive roots and\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  modified the original, to take into account the case where \(2\alpha\)
  could be a root.} that the smallest element of \(R_{+}\) not
proportional to \(\alpha\) is simple. This element is of the form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{β = p α + q γ,    0 \textless{} q ⩽ 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One thus has \(\gamma = q^{-1} \beta - q^{-1} p \alpha\), and since
\(q > 0\), one has \(q^{-1} \in \mathbb{N}*\) and
\(-q^{-1} p \in \mathbb{N}\).

Let us finally make two remarks about the group \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\).

\textbf{Proposition 3.5.5.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an abelian group and
\(f : R \to G\) a map satisfying the following two conditions:}

\emph{(i) If \(\alpha \in R\), \(f(-\alpha) = -f(\alpha)\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta \in R\),
\(f(\alpha + \beta) = f(\alpha) + f(\beta)\).}

\emph{Then there exists a unique group homomorphism
\(\bar{f} : \Gamma_{0}(R) \to G\) such that
\(\bar{f}(\alpha) = f(\alpha)\) for \(\alpha \in R\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, if \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots of
\(R\), and if \(\beta \in R\) is written
\(\Sigma_{\alpha \in \Delta} a(\alpha) \alpha\), it follows at once from
3.2.16 that
\(f(\beta) = \Sigma_{\alpha \in \Delta} a(\alpha) f(\alpha)\). Now
\(\Delta\) is a basis of \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\).

\textbf{Proposition 3.5.6.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple
roots. There exists on \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) a structure of totally ordered
group such that the roots \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} are the elements of
\(P(\Delta)\) and \(\alpha \mapsto ord_{\Delta}(\alpha)\) is an
increasing function.}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, let \(\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\)
(\(n = rgss(\mathcal{R})\)) be the elements of \(\Delta\). For
\(x \in \Gamma_{0}(R)\), one has a decomposition

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x = Σᵢ mᵢ(x) αᵢ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It suffices to take the lexicographic order with respect to the
functions \(\Sigma m_{i}\), \(m_{n}\), \(m_{n-1}\), \ldots, \(m_{2}\).

\textbf{Remark 3.5.7.} \emph{The first roots are in order:}

\[
\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{n};
\]

\emph{one then has (if these are roots)
\(2 \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{1} + \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{1} + \alpha_{3}, \cdots\).}

\subsubsection{3.6. Weyl chambers}\label{weyl-chambers}

\textbf{Lemma 3.6.1.} \emph{Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional
\(\mathbb{R}\)-vector space.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced
  \(\mathbb{Q}\) by \(\mathbb{R}\).} Let \texttt{fᵢ} be independent
linear forms. Set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C = \{x ∈ V | fᵢ(x) \textgreater{} 0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(C\) is a maximal convex subset of
\(X = V - \bigcup_{i} f^{-1}_{i}(0)\).}

\emph{Proof.} Trivial.

\textbf{Definition 3.6.2.} \emph{A subset \(C\) of \(V\) describable by
the procedure of 3.6.1 will be called (here) a} chamber \emph{of \(V\).}

\textbf{Definition 3.6.3.} \emph{One says that the hyperplane \(H\) of
\(V\) is a} wall \emph{of \(C\) if \(H \cap (\bar{C} - C)\) contains a
nonempty open subset of \(H\).}

\textbf{Remark 3.6.4.} \emph{For a convex subset, the closure is
described without appeal to the topology of \(V\): it is the set of
endpoints of all open segments contained in the given subset.}

\textbf{Lemma 3.6.5.} \emph{Under the conditions of 3.6.1, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C̄ = \{x ∈ V | fᵢ(x) ⩾ 0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{The walls of \(C\) are the hyperplanes \(f^{-1}_{i}(0)\).}

\emph{Proof.} The first assertion is clear. The second then follows from
the fact that \(\bar{C} - C \subset \bigcup_{i} f^{-1}_{i}(0)\) and that
the \(f^{-1}_{i}(0)\) are obviously walls of \(C\).

\textbf{Proposition 3.6.6.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a chamber of \(V\). If
\texttt{Hᵢ}, \(i = 1, 2, \cdots, n\), are the distinct walls of \(C\),
then for every system of linear forms \({u_{i}}\) such that
\(H_{i} = u^{-1}_{i}(0)\), there exist \(\epsilon_{i} \in {-1, +1}\)
such that \(C\) is defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C = \{x ∈ V | εᵢ uᵢ(x) \textgreater{} 0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{For every wall \(H\) of \(C\), one has \(H \cap C = \emptyset\)
and \(H \cap \bar{C} = C_{H}\), where \texttt{C\_H} is a chamber in
\(H\). The walls of \(C_{H_{i}}\) are the \(H_{j} \cap H_{i}\), for
\(j \neq i\).}

\emph{Proof.} This follows trivially from the lemma.

\textbf{Definition 3.6.7.} \emph{The \(C_{H_{i}}\) are the} faces
\emph{of \(C\).}

Let now \(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\) be a root datum. We put
\(V*_{\mathbb{R}} = M* \otimes \mathbb{R}\).

\textbf{Definition 3.6.8.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the definition
  of the hyperplanes \(H_{\alpha}\).} \emph{For every \(\alpha \in R\),
set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\_α = \{x ∈ V*\_ℝ | (x, α) = 0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{We denote
\(X = V*_{\mathbb{R}} - \bigcup_{\alpha \in R} H_{\alpha}\). For every
\(x \in X\), set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R₊(x) = \{α ∈ R | (x, α) \textgreater{} 0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{For every system of positive roots \(R_{+}\), denote}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒞(R₊) = \{x ∈ V*\_ℝ | (x, α) \textgreater{} 0 for all α ∈ R₊\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 3.6.9.} \emph{(i) For every \(x \in X\),
\(R_{+}(x)\) is a system of positive roots. For every system of positive
roots \(R_{+}\), \(\mathcal{C}(R_{+})\) is a chamber in
\(V*_{\mathbb{R}}\). The \(\mathcal{C}(R_{+})\) are the maximal convex
subsets of \(X\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots. One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{𝒞(P(Δ)) = \{x ∈ V*\_ℝ | (x, α) \textgreater{} 0    for all α ∈ Δ\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{The walls of \(\mathcal{C}(P(\Delta))\) are the hyperplanes
\(H_{\alpha} = \alpha^{-1}(0)\), for \(\alpha \in \Delta\); its faces
are the}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\_α = \{x ∈ V*\_ℝ | (x, α) = 0, (x, β) \textgreater{} 0 for β ∈ Δ, β ≠ α\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) One has the equivalence}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R₊(x) = R₊  ⟺  x ∈ 𝒞(R₊).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} It is first clear that \(R_{+}(x)\) is a system of
positive roots. Since \(x \in \mathcal{C}(R_{+}(x))\), the union of the
\(\mathcal{C}(R_{+}(x))\) is \(X\). Property (iii) is immediate; it
follows that the \(\mathcal{C}(R_{+})\) form a partition of \(X\). The
first assertion of (ii) is evident. It follows at once that
\(\mathcal{C}(R_{+})\) is a chamber in \(V\), which proves the rest of
(i). Putting \(C = \mathcal{C}(P(\Delta))\), it remains only to remark
that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C̄ ∩ (V*\_ℝ − ⋃\_\{α ∈ R\} α⁻¹(0)) = C̄ ∩ (V*\_ℝ − ⋃\_\{α ∈ Δ\} α⁻¹(0))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

to complete the proof of (ii) by 3.6.1.

\textbf{Definition 3.6.10.} \emph{The \(\mathcal{C}(R_{+})\) are called
