the} Weyl chambers \emph{of the root datum. On the other hand, for every
Weyl chamber \(C\), one sets \(R_{+}(C) = R_{+}(x)\) for any
\(x \in C\).}

\textbf{Corollary 3.6.11.} \emph{The maps
\(R_{+} \mapsto \mathcal{C}(R_{+})\) and \(C \mapsto R_{+}(C)\) realize
a bijective correspondence between systems of positive roots and Weyl
chambers.}

This correspondence is invariant under the Weyl group:

\textbf{Lemma 3.6.12.} \emph{If \(w \in W(\mathcal{R})\), one has
\(\mathcal{C}(w(R_{+})) = w(\mathcal{C}(R_{+}))\).}

\textbf{Corollary 3.6.13.} \emph{The correspondences
\(\Delta \leftrightarrow R_{+} \leftrightarrow C\) are isomorphisms of
homogeneous spaces under \(W(\mathcal{R})\).}

We shall see later that these homogeneous spaces are principal (5.5).

\textbf{Remark 3.6.14.} \emph{If \(C\) is a Weyl chamber, then \(-C\) is
also one, called the} opposite \emph{of \(C\). There exists therefore a
\(w_{0} \in W\) (and in fact a unique one, cf.~5.5) such that
\(w_{0}(C) = -C\); one calls it the} symmetry \emph{of the root datum
with respect to the Weyl chamber \(C\) (or with respect to \(R_{+}(C)\)
or \(\mathcal{S}(R_{+}(C))\)\ldots).}

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.}\footnote{The following numbers 4.1 to 4.4 are
  used in the proof of 5.1. There exist nowadays simpler proofs of 5.1
  (see {[}BLie{]}, § V.3, Th. 1). \emph{N.D.E.: we have specified the
  reference and placed here this Note, which in the original appeared in
  4.2.}} \emph{Let \(n\) be the order of \(s_{\alpha} s_{\beta}\). Set
\(u_{0} = 0\) and, for \(p \in \mathbb{N}\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u\_\{2p+1\} = u\_\{2p\} + (s\_α s\_β)\^{}p(α);}
\NormalTok{u\_\{2p+2\} = u\_\{2p+1\} + (s\_α s\_β)\^{}p s\_α(β).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then:}\footnote{N.D.E.: Let \(\rho\) be the half-sum of the
  positive roots (cf.~3.5.1); if one sets, as in 4.2 below,
  \(w_{0} = 1\), \(w_{1} = s_{\alpha}\),
  \(w_{2} = s_{\beta} s_{\alpha}\),
  \(w_{3} = s_{\alpha} s_{\beta} s_{\alpha}\), etc., then \(u_{k}\) is
  nothing other than \(\rho - w_{k-1}(\rho)\), which proves (i) since
  \(w_{2n} = id\).}

\emph{(i) \(u_{k+2n} = u_{k}\), for every \(k \in \mathbb{N}\).}

\emph{(ii) \(u_{0} = 0\), \(u_{1} = \alpha\), \(u_{2n-1} = \beta\),
\(u_{2n} = 0\).}

\emph{(iii) If \(1 < k < 2n - 1\), one has
\(u_{k} = a_{k} \alpha + b_{k} \beta\), with
\(a_{k}, b_{k} \in \mathbb{N}*\).}

\emph{Proof.} Assertion (i) follows from
\((s_{\alpha} s_{\beta})^{n} = 1\) and \(u_{2n} = 0\).

Let us prove (ii) and (iii). Direct computation gives, in the four
cases, the following sequences of values:\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  corrected the original, to be in agreement with the convention
  \(\ell(\alpha) \leqslant \ell(\beta)\) of 4.0.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(A₁ × A₁)    0, α, β + α, β, 0.}

\NormalTok{(A₂)         0, α, β + 2α, 2β + 2α, 2β + α, β, 0.}

\NormalTok{(B₂)         0, α, β + 3α, 2β + 4α, 3β + 4α, 3β + 3α, 2β + α, β, 0.}

\NormalTok{(G₂)         0, α, β + 4α, 2β + 6α, 4β + 9α, 5β + 10α, 6β + 10α, 6β + 9α, 5β + 6α,}
\NormalTok{                                                                  4β + 4α, 2β + α, β, 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 4.2.} \emph{Set \(w_{2p} = (s_{\beta} s_{\alpha})^{p}\),
\(w_{2p+1} = s_{\alpha} (s_{\beta} s_{\alpha})^{p}\), so that
\(w_{0}, \cdots, w_{2n-1}\) are the distinct elements of \(W\). Let
\(u_{0}, \cdots, u_{2n-1}\) be the elements of \(V\) defined in 4.1. For
every \(x \in V*\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x − w\_k(x) = n\_k α* + m\_k β*,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{with \(n_{k}, m_{k} \in \mathbb{Q}\) and
\(n_{k} + m_{k} = (x, u_{k})\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: Taking into account
  N.D.E. (17), this follows immediately from 3.5.1 and 1.1.9: one has
  \(n_{k} + m_{k} = (x - w_{k}(x), \rho) = (x, \rho - w_{k-1}(\rho)) = (x, u_{k})\).}

\emph{Proof.} The proof is by induction on \(k\). If \(k = 0\), the
formula is trivially verified. Let us carry out, for example, the
passage from \(w_{2p}\) to \(w_{2p+1}\). One has
\(w_{2p+1} = s_{\alpha} w_{2p}\), whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x − w\_\{2p+1\}(x) = x − w\_\{2p\}(x) + w\_\{2p\}(x) − s\_α w\_\{2p\}(x) = n\_\{2p\} α* + m\_\{2p\} β* + (w\_\{2p\}(x), α) α*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

So

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n\_\{2p+1\} + m\_\{2p+1\} = n\_\{2p\} + m\_\{2p\} + ((s\_β s\_α)\^{}p(x), α)}
\NormalTok{                    = (x, u\_\{2p\}) + (x, (s\_α s\_β)\^{}p(α)) = (x, u\_\{2p+1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the
  statement.} \emph{Let \(x \in V*\). For every \(w \in W\), set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x − w(x) = a\_w α* + b\_w β*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \((x, \alpha) \geqslant 0\) and \((x, \beta) \geqslant 0\),
then \(a_{w} + b_{w} \geqslant 0\). If moreover \((x, \alpha) > 0\)
(resp. \((x, \beta) > 0\)), then \(a_{w} + b_{w} > 0\) for
\(w \neq 1, s_{\beta}\) (resp. for \(w \neq 1, s_{\alpha}\)).}

\emph{Proof.} This follows at once from 4.1 and 4.2.

\textbf{Corollary 4.4.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be any root datum and
\(\Delta\) a system of simple roots. Let \(\gamma\) be a positive root
and \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) two simple roots; let \(W_{\alpha,\beta}\) be
the subgroup of \(W\) generated by \(s_{\alpha}\) and \(s_{\beta}\). If}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ord\_Δ(s\_α(γ)) \textless{} ord\_Δ(γ),    ord\_Δ(s\_β(γ)) ⩽ ord\_Δ(γ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{then, for every \(w \in W_{\alpha,\beta}\), one has
\(ord_{\Delta}(w(\gamma)) \leqslant ord_{\Delta}(\gamma)\); moreover
\(ord_{\Delta}(w(\gamma)) < ord_{\Delta}(\gamma)\) if \(w \neq 1\),
\(w \neq s_{\beta}\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, consider the dual root datum \(\mathcal{R}*\),
then the datum \((M*, M, R'*, R')\), where \(R'\) is the set of roots
which are rational linear combinations of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).
Applying 4.3 to this datum, one finds the announced
corollary.\footnote{N.D.E.: Indeed, the hypotheses are equivalent to
  saying that \((\gamma, \alpha*) > 0\) and
  \((\gamma, \beta*) \geqslant 0\); then \(\gamma - w(\gamma)\) belongs
  to \(\mathbb{N} \alpha + \mathbb{N} \beta\) for every
  \(w \in W_{\alpha,\beta}\), and is \(\neq 0\) if
  \(w \notin {1, s_{\beta}}\).}

\subsection{5. The Weyl group: generators and
relations}\label{the-weyl-group-generators-and-relations}

Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum. Since the Weyl group is the same
for this datum and for the corresponding reduced datum, one may assume
\(\mathcal{R}\) reduced to study the Weyl group.

Let \(\Delta = {\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}}\) be a system of simple
roots (\(n = rgss(\mathcal{R})\)). Let \(n_{ij}\) be the order of the
element \(s_{\alpha_{i}} s_{\alpha_{j}}\) of \(W\). In particular, one
has \(n_{ii} = 1\), and we saw in 3.4.2 and 3.4.3 that the subgroup
\(W_{ij}\) of \(W\) generated by \(s_{\alpha_{i}}\) and
\(s_{\alpha_{j}}\) was defined by the relations:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_\{α\_i\}² = s\_\{α\_j\}² = (s\_\{α\_i\} s\_\{α\_j\})\^{}\{n\_\{ij\}\} = 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Theorem 5.1.} \emph{The group \(W\) is the group generated by
the elements \(s_{\alpha_{i}}\), \(i = 1, 2, \cdots, n\), subject to the
relations \((s_{\alpha_{i}} s_{\alpha_{j}})^{n_{ij}} = 1\).}

\emph{Proof.} We have already seen that the theorem is true when
\(n = 2\); we shall use this remark in the course of the proof.
Introduce the group \(\tilde{W}\) generated by elements \(T_{i}\),
\(i = 1, 2, \cdots, n\), subject to the relations
\((T_{i} T_{j})^{n_{ij}} = 1\). One has in particular \(n_{ii} = 1\),
whence \(T^{2}_{i} = 1\). Let \(p : \tilde{W} \to W\) be the group
morphism that sends \(T_{i}\) to \(s_{\alpha_{i}}\). One knows that
\(p\) is surjective; we shall show it is injective.

\textbf{Lemma 5.2.} \emph{One can define in a unique manner for each
\(\alpha \in P(\Delta)\) an element \(T_{\alpha} \in \tilde{W}\) such
that one has the following properties:}

\emph{(i) \(p(T_{\alpha}) = s_{\alpha}\),}

\emph{(ii) \(T_{\alpha_{i}} = T_{i}\),}

\emph{(iii) if \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) are two positive roots such that
\(s_{\alpha_{i}}(\alpha) = \beta\), then
\(T_{i} T_{\alpha} T_{i} = T_{\beta}\).}

\emph{Proof.} Remark first that it follows from 1.2.10 and 3.3.6 that
(i) is a consequence of (ii) and (iii), and that (ii) and (iii)
completely determine the \(T_{\alpha}\). We shall make the construction
by induction on \(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha)\). If
\(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha) = 1\), then \(\alpha \in \Delta\) and one sets
\(T_{\alpha} = T_{i}\) if \(\alpha = \alpha_{i}\). Consider the
hypothesis:

(H\_p) \emph{there exist \(T_{\alpha}\), for \(\alpha \in P(\Delta)\),
\(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha) \leqslant p\), satisfying (ii) and condition
(iii) whenever \(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha) \leqslant p\),
\(ord_{\Delta}(\beta) \leqslant p\).}

This is verified for \(p = 1\): indeed, if \(\alpha\) and
\(s_{\alpha_{i}}(\alpha) = \beta\) are simple, \(\alpha_{i}\) and
\(\alpha\) are orthogonal, so if one denotes
\(\alpha_{j} = \alpha = \beta\), one has \(n_{ij} = 2\), whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_i T\_j T\_i = T\_j.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Suppose \(p > 1\) and \((H_{p-1})\) verified.

\emph{A) Construction of the \(T_{\alpha}\) for
\(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha) \leqslant p\).} It evidently suffices to do this
for \(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha) = p\). There then exists
\(\alpha_{i} \in \Delta\) such that
\(s_{\alpha_{i}}(\alpha) \in P(\Delta)\) and
\(ord_{\Delta}(s_{\alpha_{i}}(\alpha)) < p\) (3.3.3). One then sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(⋆)    T\_α = T\_i T\_\{s\_\{α\_i\}(α)\} T\_i.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us verify that \(T_{\alpha}\) depends only on \(\alpha\). Let
\(\alpha_{j} \in \Delta\) be such that
\(s_{\alpha_{j}}(\alpha) \in P(\Delta)\) and
\(ord_{\Delta}(s_{\alpha_{j}}(\alpha)) < p\). Let us prove that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+)    T\_i T\_\{s\_\{α\_i\}(α)\} T\_i = T\_j T\_\{s\_\{α\_j\}(α)\} T\_j.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us distinguish two cases.

\emph{(1)} Suppose \(\alpha\) is a linear combination of \(\alpha_{i}\)
and \(\alpha_{j}\). Then the same is true of \(s_{\alpha_{i}}(\alpha)\)
and \(s_{\alpha_{j}}(\alpha)\), and by \((H_{p-1})\),
\(T_{s_{\alpha_{i}}(\alpha)}\) and \(T_{s_{\alpha_{j}}(\alpha)}\) are
written as words in \(T_{i}\) and \(T_{j}\). Since the projection of (+)
in \(W\) is verified, and since the theorem is true for \(n = 2\), so
\(p\) is injective on the subgroup of \(\tilde{W}\) generated by
\(T_{i}\) and \(T_{j}\), (+) is indeed verified.

\emph{(2)} Suppose \(\alpha\) is not a linear combination of
\(\alpha_{i}\) and \(\alpha_{j}\). Then if
\(w \in W_{\alpha_{i}, \alpha_{j}}\), the \(w(\alpha)\) will all be
positive (cf.~3.4.9). The relation to be verified is also written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(++)    (T\_i T\_j)\^{}\{n\_\{ij\} − 1\} T\_\{s\_\{α\_i\}(α)\} (T\_j T\_i)\^{}\{n\_\{ij\} − 1\} = T\_\{s\_\{α\_j\}(α)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now it follows from 4.4 that the \(w(\alpha)\) are all of order \(< p\)
for \(w \in W_{\alpha_{i}, \alpha_{j}}\), \(w \neq 1\). One can
therefore apply hypothesis \((H_{p-1})\) \(2(n_{ij} - 1)\) times, and we
are done.

\emph{B) Verification of \((H_{p})\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed
  the original in what follows.} One must verify that if
\(\alpha_{j} \in \Delta\) and if \(\beta = s_{\alpha_{j}}(\alpha)\)
satisfies \(ord_{\Delta}(\beta) \leqslant p\), then
\(T_{j} T_{\alpha} T_{j} = T_{\beta}\). If \(ord_{\Delta}(\beta) < p\),
this follows from what precedes (since \(T^{2}_{j} = 1\)), so one may
suppose \(ord_{\Delta}(\beta) = p = ord_{\Delta}(\alpha)\). In this
case, \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha_{j}\) are orthogonal, so
\(\beta = \alpha\), and it is a matter of seeing that one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)    T\_j T\_α T\_j = T\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By \((\star)\) above, one has
\(T_{\alpha} = T_{i} T_{s_{\alpha_{i}}(\alpha)} T_{i}\), so it remains
only to verify the following equality:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(+++)    T\_j T\_i T\_\{s\_\{α\_i\}(α)\} T\_i T\_j = T\_α = T\_i T\_\{s\_\{α\_i\}(α)\} T\_i.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Write \(m = n_{ij}\) and \(s_{i} = s_{\alpha_{i}}\),
\(s_{j} = s_{\alpha_{j}}\). One has
\(T_{j} T_{i} = (T_{i} T_{j})^{m-1}\) and, by 4.4, one has
\(ord_{\Delta}(w(\alpha)) < p\) for every \(w \in W_{ij}\) distinct from
\(1 = (s_{i} s_{j})^{m}\) and from
\(s_{j} = s_{i} (s_{i} s_{j})^{m-1}\). One deduces, by the induction
hypothesis, that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_j (T\_i T\_j)\^{}\{m−2\} T\_\{s\_i(α)\} (T\_j T\_i)\^{}\{m−2\} T\_j = T\_\{s\_j (s\_i s\_j)\^{}\{m−2\} s\_i(α)\} = T\_\{s\_i s\_j(α)\} = T\_\{s\_i(α)\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(the last equality since \(s_{j}(\alpha) = \alpha\)), whence finally

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(T\_i T\_j)\^{}\{m−1\} T\_\{s\_i(α)\} (T\_j T\_i)\^{}\{m−1\} = T\_i T\_\{s\_i(α)\} T\_i}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which proves (+++).

\textbf{Lemma 5.3.} \emph{Let \(h \in \tilde{W}\). Write it}

\[
h = T_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots T_{\alpha_{m}}
\]

\emph{with the \(\alpha_{i} \in \Delta\), not necessarily distinct, in
such a way that \(m\) is minimal. Then}

\[
p(h)(\alpha_{m}) \in -P(\Delta).
\]

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, since
\(p(T_{\alpha_{m}})(\alpha_{m}) = s_{\alpha_{m}}(\alpha_{m}) = -\alpha_{m}\),
if \(p(h)(\alpha_{m})\) were positive, there would exist an index \(k\),
\(1 \leqslant k \leqslant m - 1\), such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u = s\_\{α\_\{k+1\}\} ⋯ s\_\{α\_m\}(α\_m) = −s\_\{α\_\{k+1\}\} ⋯ s\_\{α\_\{m−1\}\}(α\_m) ∈ −P(Δ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(s_{\alpha_{k}}(u) \in P(\Delta)\). But then one has necessarily
\(u = -\alpha_{k}\) (3.3.1), whence

\[
s_{\alpha_{k+1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{m-1}}(\alpha_{m}) = \alpha_{k},
\]

which entails by (iii)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_\{α\_k\} T\_\{α\_\{k+1\}\} ⋯ T\_\{α\_\{m−1\}\} T\_\{α\_m\} = T\_\{α\_\{k+1\}\} ⋯ T\_\{α\_\{m−1\}\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and this contradicts the minimal character of \(m\).

Let now \(h \in \tilde{W}\) be such that
\(p(h)(P(\Delta)) \subset P(\Delta)\). By Lemma 5.3, one has
\(p(h) = 1\), which proves Theorem 5.1 and moreover the

\textbf{Corollary 5.4.} \emph{If \(R_{+}\) is a system of positive roots
and if \(w \in W\) is such that \(w(R_{+}) = R_{+}\), then \(w = 1\).}

\textbf{Corollary 5.5.} \emph{The Weyl group operates freely and
transitively on the set of systems of positive roots (resp. of systems
of simple roots, resp. of Weyl chambers).}

Let us now choose a system of simple roots \(\Delta\). Put
\(R^{+} = P(\Delta)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have written \(R^{+}\) here
  instead of \(R_{+}\), in order to be able to write
  \(R^{+}_{\alpha,\beta} = R_{\alpha,\beta} \cap R^{+}\).}

For every pair of simple roots
\((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\), denote by
\(R_{\alpha,\beta}\) the set of roots that are linear combinations of
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Write
\(R^{+}_{\alpha,\beta} = R^{+} \cap R_{\alpha,\beta}\) and let
\(W_{\alpha,\beta}\) be the Weyl group of \(R_{\alpha,\beta}\), that is
to say, the subgroup of \(W\) generated by \(s_{\alpha}\) and
\(s_{\beta}\).

\textbf{Theorem 5.6 (Tits).} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two
simple roots and let \(w \in W\) be such that \(w(\alpha) = \beta\).
There exists a sequence of simple roots
\(\alpha_{0}, \cdots, \alpha_{m}\) and a sequence
\(w_{0}, \cdots, w_{m-1}\) of elements of \(W\) satisfying the following
conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(\alpha_{0} = \alpha\), \(\alpha_{m} = \beta\).}

\emph{(ii) \(w = w_{m-1} w_{m-2} \cdots w_{0}\).}

\emph{(iii) \(w_{i}(\alpha_{i}) = \alpha_{i+1}\), for
\(0 \leqslant i \leqslant m - 1\).}

\emph{(iv) For every \(i\), \(0 \leqslant i \leqslant m - 1\), such that
\(\alpha_{i} \neq \alpha_{i+1}\), one has
\(w_{i} \in W_{\alpha_{i}, \alpha_{i+1}}\).}

\emph{(v) For every \(i\), \(0 \leqslant i \leqslant m - 1\), such that
\(\alpha_{i} = \alpha_{i+1}\), there exists a simple root \(\beta_{i}\)
such that \(w_{i} \in W_{\alpha_{i}, \beta_{i}}\).}

\emph{Proof.} Set\footnote{N.D.E.: In what follows, we have detailed the
  original, and we have corrected equality (1).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M(w) = Card(R⁺ ∩ w⁻¹(−R⁺)) = Card(\{α ∈ R⁺ | w(α) ∈ −R⁺\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(M(w) = 0\), then \(w(R^{+}) = R^{+}\), so \(w = 1\) by 5.4 and the
theorem is trivial (\(m = 0\); assertions (iii) to (v) are empty). We
argue by induction on \(M(w)\). If \(M(w) > 0\), there exists
\(\beta_{0} \in \Delta\) such that \(w(\beta_{0}) \in -R^{+}\). Set
\(\alpha_{0} = \alpha\). Consider the set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = w⁻¹(R⁺) ∩ R\_\{α\_0, β\_0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is a system of positive roots of \(R_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}}\).
There thus exists \(w_{0} \in W_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}}\) such that

\[
w^{-1}_{0}(R^{+}_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}}) = A.
\]

Put \(w' = w w^{-1}_{0}\). By 3.4.9, one has at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R⁺ − R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\} = w\_0(R⁺ − R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)    (R⁺ − R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\}) ∩ w⁻¹(−R⁺) = w\_0((R⁺ − R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\}) ∩ w\textquotesingle{}⁻¹(−R⁺)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2)    β\_0 ∈ R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\} ∩ w⁻¹(−R⁺),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and, since
\(w_{0}(R_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}}) = R_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}}\), one
has \(w_{0}(-A) = R_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}} \cap w'^{-1}(-R^{+})\),
whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(2′)    R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\} ∩ w\textquotesingle{}⁻¹(−R⁺) = R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\} ∩ w\_0(−A) = R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\} ∩ −R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\} = ∅.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows from (1), (2), (2′) that \(M(w') < M(w)\).

Set \(\alpha_{1} = w_{0}(\alpha_{0})\); let us show that
\(\alpha_{1} \in \Delta\), that is to say
\(\alpha_{0} \in w^{-1}_{0}(\Delta)\). One knows that
\(w(\alpha_{0}) \in \Delta\), so \(\alpha_{0} \in w^{-1}(\Delta)\),
hence also
\(\alpha_{0} \in w^{-1}(\Delta) \cap R_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}}\); so
\(\alpha_{0}\) is a simple root of
\(A = w^{-1}(R^{+}) \cap R_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}} = w^{-1}_{0}(R^{+}_{\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}})\),
hence belongs to

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_0⁻¹(Δ ∩ R⁺\_\{α\_0, β\_0\}) = w\_0⁻¹(\{α\_0, β\_0\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(see 3.4.8). So \(\alpha_{1} = w_{0}(\alpha_{0})\) equals \(\alpha_{0}\)
or \(\beta_{0}\). If \(\alpha_{1} \neq \alpha_{0}\), one has
\(\alpha_{1} = \beta_{0}\) and \(w_{0} \in W_{\alpha_{0}, \alpha_{1}}\).

Finally, one has \(\beta = w'(\alpha_{1})\), with \(M(w') < M(w)\), and
one concludes by induction.

\subsection{6. Morphisms of root data}\label{morphisms-of-root-data}

\subsubsection{6.1. Definition}\label{definition}

Let \(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\) and
\(\mathcal{R}' = (M', M'*, R', R'*)\) be two root data. Let
\(f : M' \to M\) be a linear map and \({}^{t}f : M* \to M'*\) the
transposed map.

\textbf{Definition 6.1.1.} \emph{One says that \(f\) is a} morphism
\emph{from \(\mathcal{R}'\) to \(\mathcal{R}\) and writes
\(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\), if \(f\) induces a bijection of
\(R'\) onto \(R\) and \texttt{ᵗf} a bijection of \(R*\) onto \(R'*\).}

Then \texttt{ᵗf} is a morphism of the dual root data:

\[
{}^{t}f : \mathcal{R}* \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}'*.
\]

One sees easily that if \(f\) is a morphism from \(\mathcal{R}'\) to
\(\mathcal{R}\), and if one writes \(\alpha = f(\alpha')\) for
\(\alpha' \in R'\), one has \(\alpha'* = {}^{t}f(\alpha*)\). Indeed, one
sees immediately that if one writes \(p\) and \(p'\) for the maps of
1.2.1 respective to \(\mathcal{R}\) and \(\mathcal{R}'\), one has
\(p' = {}^{t}f \circ p \circ f\), and the assertion sought follows at
once. We leave to the reader the task of proving the statements that
follow, which are almost all trivial.

\textbf{Proposition 6.1.2.} \emph{Let
\(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) be a morphism of root data. If
\(\alpha' \in R'\) and \(\alpha = f(\alpha')\), then
\(\alpha'* = {}^{t}f(\alpha*)\). Moreover, \(f\) induces isomorphisms:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R\textquotesingle{} ⥲ R,    Γ₀(R\textquotesingle{}) ⥲ Γ₀(R),    V(R\textquotesingle{}) ⥲ V(R),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and \texttt{ᵗf} induces isomorphisms:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R* ⥲ R\textquotesingle{}*,    Γ₀(R*) ⥲ Γ₀(R\textquotesingle{}*),    V(R*) ⥲ V(R\textquotesingle{}*),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the last being the transpose of the corresponding morphism induced
by \(f\). The map \(s_{\alpha'} \mapsto s_{f(\alpha')}\) extends to an
isomorphism \(W(\mathcal{R}') \xrightarrow{\sim} W(\mathcal{R})\)
compatible with the operations of these two groups on the sets of
1.1.13.}

\textbf{Proposition 6.1.3.} \emph{The maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Δ\textquotesingle{} ↦ f(Δ\textquotesingle{}),    R\textquotesingle{}₊ ↦ f(R\textquotesingle{}₊),    C\textquotesingle{} ↦ (ᵗf ⊗ ℝ)⁻¹(C\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{define bijective correspondences between systems of simple roots,
systems of positive roots, and Weyl chambers for \(\mathcal{R}'\) and
\(\mathcal{R}\). These correspondences are compatible with the action of
the Weyl groups and with the correspondences}

\[
\mathcal{S}(R_{+}) \leftrightarrow R_{+} \leftrightarrow \mathcal{C}(R_{+}).
\]

\textbf{Lemma 6.1.4.} \emph{Morphisms compose. For the morphism
\(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) to be an isomorphism, it is
necessary and sufficient that \(f : M' \to M\) be bijective.}

\subsubsection{6.2. Isogenies}\label{isogenies}

\textbf{Definition 6.2.1.} \emph{A morphism
\(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) of root data is called an} isogeny
\emph{if \(f : M' \to M\) is injective with finite cokernel.}

\emph{If \(f\) is an isogeny, then \texttt{ᵗf} is an isogeny.}

\textbf{Definition 6.2.2.} \emph{Let
\(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) be an isogeny. Set
\(K(f) = Coker(M' \to^{f} M)\).}

\textbf{Lemma 6.2.3.} \emph{One has a natural pairing}

\[
K(f) \times K({}^{t}f) \to \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z},
\]

\emph{which puts these two finite groups in duality.}

\emph{Proof.} This is classical.

\textbf{Lemma 6.2.4.} \emph{If \(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) is a
morphism, then \(rgss(\mathcal{R}') = rgss(\mathcal{R})\). If moreover
\(f\) is an isogeny, one has also
\(rgred(\mathcal{R}') = rgred(\mathcal{R})\).}

\emph{Proof.} Trivial.

\textbf{Lemma 6.2.5.} \emph{Every morphism of semisimple root data is an
isogeny.}

\emph{Proof.} This follows at once from the fact that \(f\) must induce
an isomorphism of \(V' = V(R')\) onto \(V = V(R)\).

If \(\mathcal{R}'\) and \(\mathcal{R}\) are semisimple, every isogeny
\(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) defines a commutative diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ₀(R\textquotesingle{}) ⥲ Γ₀(R)}
\NormalTok{  ⊂        ⊂}
\NormalTok{  ↓        ↓}
\NormalTok{  M\textquotesingle{}   →   M.}
\NormalTok{       f}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(M = \Gamma_{0}(R)\), then \(f\) is necessarily an isomorphism.

\textbf{Definition 6.2.6.} \emph{A root datum is called} adjoint
\emph{(resp.} simply connected*) if \(M = \Gamma_{0}(R)\), resp.
\(M* = \Gamma_{0}(R*)\).*

An adjoint or simply connected root datum is therefore semisimple. On
the other hand, \(\mathcal{R}\) is adjoint (resp. simply connected) if
and only if \(\mathcal{R}*\) is simply connected (resp. adjoint). By
virtue of the preceding result, one has:

\textbf{Proposition 6.2.7.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a semisimple
root datum. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(\mathcal{R}\) is adjoint (resp. simply connected).}

\emph{(ii) Every isogeny \(\mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) (resp.
\(\mathcal{R} \to \mathcal{R}'\)) is an isomorphism.}

\textbf{Proposition 6.2.8.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be an adjoint
(resp. simply connected) root datum. Every indivisible root (resp.
coroot) is an indivisible element of \(M\) (resp. \(M*\)).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, every indivisible root is part of a basis of
\(\Gamma_{0}(R)\), by 3.3.5.

\subsubsection{6.3. Radical and coradical}\label{radical-and-coradical}

Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum. Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N = \{x ∈ M | (α*, x) = 0 for all α* ∈ R*\};}
\NormalTok{N* = M*/(V(R*) ∩ M*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 6.3.1.} \emph{Consider the canonical morphisms:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N ⟶ M,    M* ⟶ N*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{They are transposes of each other and \(N*\) is identified with
the dual of \(N\).}

\emph{Proof.} This is immediate, taking 1.2.5 into account.

\textbf{Definition 6.3.2.} \emph{One calls} coradical \emph{of
\(\mathcal{R}\) and denotes by \(corad(\mathcal{R})\) the trivial root
datum}

\[
corad(\mathcal{R}) = (N, N*, \emptyset, \emptyset).
\]

\emph{If one sets \(\mathcal{R}_{0} = (M, M*, \emptyset, \emptyset)\)
(this is a trivial root datum), one has therefore a morphism}

\[
corad(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}_{0}.
\]

\textbf{Definition 6.3.3.} \emph{One calls} radical \emph{of
\(\mathcal{R}\) and denotes by \(rad(\mathcal{R})\) the trivial root
datum:}

\[
rad(\mathcal{R}) = corad(\mathcal{R}*)*.
\]

\footnote{N.D.E.: That is, if one denotes
  \(P = {y \in M* | (y, \alpha) = 0 for all \alpha \in R}\) and
  \(P* = M/(V(R) \cap M)\), one has
  \(rad(\mathcal{R}) = (P*, P, \emptyset, \emptyset)\).}

One thus has a diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       corad(ℛ) ──────→ rad(ℛ)}
\NormalTok{            ↘            ↙}
\NormalTok{               ℛ\_0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whose transpose is the corresponding diagram for \(\mathcal{R}*\).

\textbf{Lemma 6.3.4.} \emph{The canonical morphism
\(u : corad(\mathcal{R}) \to rad(\mathcal{R})\) is an isogeny.}

\textbf{Definition 6.3.5.} \emph{Set
\(N(\mathcal{R}) = K(u) = M / ((V(R) \cap M) + \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} Ker(\alpha*))\).
One then has a canonical pairing}

\[
N(\mathcal{R}) \times N(\mathcal{R}*) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}.
\]

\textbf{Lemma 6.3.6.} \emph{One has
\texttt{rgred(rad(ℛ))\ =\ rgred(corad(ℛ))\ =\ rgred(ℛ)\ −\ rgss(ℛ)}, and
the following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(\mathcal{R}\) is semisimple,}

\emph{(ii) \(rad(\mathcal{R}) = 0\),}

\emph{(iii) \(corad(\mathcal{R}) = 0\).}

\subsubsection{6.4. Products of root data}\label{products-of-root-data}

\textbf{Definition 6.4.1.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\)
and \(\mathcal{R}' = (M', M'*, R', R'*)\) be two root data. One calls}
product root datum \emph{of \(\mathcal{R}\) and \(\mathcal{R}'\) and
denotes by \(\mathcal{R}'' = \mathcal{R} \times \mathcal{R}'\) the root
datum \((M'', M''*, R'', R''*)\) where}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} = M × M\textquotesingle{},                 M\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}* = M* × M\textquotesingle{}*,}
\NormalTok{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} = (R × 0) ∪ (0 × R\textquotesingle{}),     R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}* = (R* × 0) ∪ (0 × R\textquotesingle{}*),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha*\) being the obvious map.}

\textbf{Proposition 6.4.2.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, one
has canonical isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Γ₀(R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) ≃ Γ₀(R) × Γ₀(R\textquotesingle{}),    V(R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) ≃ V(R) × V(R\textquotesingle{}),}
\NormalTok{W(ℛ\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) ≃ W(ℛ) × W(ℛ\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{etc., and the equalities}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rgred(ℛ\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) = rgred(ℛ) + rgred(ℛ\textquotesingle{}),    rgss(ℛ\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) = rgss(ℛ) + rgss(ℛ\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One also has a canonical isomorphism of root data}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(ℛ × ℛ\textquotesingle{})* ≃ ℛ* × ℛ\textquotesingle{}*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The preceding definitions extend at once to a product of several
factors. One has at once:

\textbf{Proposition 6.4.3.} \emph{Let
\(\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R}_{1} \times \mathcal{R}_{2} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{R}_{n}\)
be a product of root data. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(\mathcal{R}\) is semisimple (resp. simply connected, resp.
adjoint, resp. reduced).}

\emph{(ii) Each \(\mathcal{R}_{i}\) is semisimple (resp. simply
connected, resp. adjoint, resp. reduced).}

Let us consider the following special case: let \(\mathcal{R}_{0}\) be a
trivial root datum and \(\mathcal{R}_{1}\) a semisimple root datum. One
then has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       ℛ\_0 × ℛ\_1}
\NormalTok{        ↗      ↘}
\NormalTok{      ↗          ↘}
\NormalTok{   ℛ\_1   ──id──→  ℛ\_1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 6.4.4.} \emph{One has canonical isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{corad(ℛ\_0 × ℛ\_1) ⥲ rad(ℛ\_0 × ℛ\_1)}
\NormalTok{        ↘             ↙}
\NormalTok{        ≃           ≃}
\NormalTok{           ℛ\_0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular, \(N(\mathcal{R}_{0} \times \mathcal{R}_{1}) = 0\).}

We shall see later that if conversely \(N(\mathcal{R}) = 0\), then the
root datum \(\mathcal{R}\) is a product of a semisimple datum by a
trivial datum.

\subsubsection{6.5. Induced and coinduced root
data}\label{induced-and-coinduced-root-data}

Let \(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\) be a root datum. Let
\(N \subset M\) be a subgroup containing the roots, i.e.~such that

\[
\Gamma_{0}(R) \subset N \subset M.
\]

The canonical linear map \(i_{N} : N \to M\) gives by transposition a
linear map

\[
{}^{t}i_{N} : M* \longrightarrow N*.
\]

Set \(R_{N} = R\) and \(R*_{N} = {}^{t}i_{N}(R*)\).

\textbf{Lemma 6.5.1.} \emph{\(\mathcal{R}_{N} = (N, N*, R_{N}, R*_{N})\)
is a root datum, and \(i_{N}\) a morphism.}

\emph{Proof.} Let us first show that \({}^{t}i_{N}\) induces an
isomorphism of \(R*\) onto \(R*_{N}\). If \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) and
\({}^{t}i_{N}(\alpha*) = {}^{t}i_{N}(\beta*)\), one has
\((\alpha*, x) = (\beta*, x)\) for all \(x \in N\), in particular for
\(x \in R\), which gives \(\alpha = \beta\) by 1.1.4. The rest follows
without difficulty.

\textbf{Definition 6.5.2.} \emph{\(\mathcal{R}_{N}\) is called the} root
datum induced by \(\mathcal{R}\) on \(N\).

\textbf{Lemma 6.5.3.} \emph{Let \(f : \mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\) be
a morphism. Set \(N = f(M') \subset M\). Then \(f\) factors uniquely
through \(i_{N}\).}

In particular, isogenies \(\mathcal{R}' \to \mathcal{R}\), up to
isomorphism, correspond bijectively to the subgroups of finite index of
\(M/\Gamma_{0}(R)\), which makes 6.2.7 more precise.

Let now \(N*\) be a subgroup of \(M*\) containing \(R*\). One defines
the root datum \emph{coinduced} by \(\mathcal{R}\) on \(N*\) by

\[
\mathcal{R}^{N*} = (\mathcal{R}*_{N*})*,
\]

and one has a canonical morphism:

\[
p_{N*} : \mathcal{R} \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}^{N*}.
\]

\textbf{Lemma 6.5.4.} \emph{Let
\(f : \mathcal{R}' \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}\) be a morphism. There
exist subgroups \(N \subset M\) and \(N'* \subset M'*\) such that \(f\)
factors as}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{        f}
\NormalTok{ℛ\textquotesingle{} ────────────→ ℛ}
\NormalTok{↓                ↑}
\NormalTok{p\_\{N\textquotesingle{}*\}          i\_N}
\NormalTok{↓     f\_0        ↑}
\NormalTok{ℛ\textquotesingle{}\^{}\{N\textquotesingle{}*\} ──⥲──→ ℛ\_N,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(f_{0}\) is an isomorphism.}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one takes \(N = f(M')\) as in 6.5.3. The morphism
\(M' \to N\) obtained is surjective, so its transpose is injective. One
takes the image of the latter as \(N'*\).

Let us now treat certain special cases. If one takes
\(N = \Gamma_{0}(R)\), one writes \(\mathcal{R}_{N} = ad(\mathcal{R})\).
If one takes \(N = V(R) \cap M\), one writes
\(\mathcal{R}_{N} = ss(\mathcal{R})\). One thus has a diagram:

\[
ad(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow ss(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}.
\]

Set \(d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R}) = ss(\mathcal{R}*)*\) and
\(sc(\mathcal{R}) = ad(\mathcal{R}*)*\); by duality, one obtains a
diagram:

\[
\mathcal{R} \longrightarrow d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow sc(\mathcal{R}).
\]

\textbf{Proposition 6.5.5.} \emph{(i) In the first row of the diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ad(ℛ) ⟶ ss(ℛ) ⟶ dér(ℛ) ⟶ sc(ℛ)}
\NormalTok{            ↘         ↗}
\NormalTok{              ℛ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the four data are semisimple and the three morphisms are
isogenies.}

\emph{(ii) \(ad(\mathcal{R})\) is an adjoint datum, and \(\mathcal{R}\)
is adjoint if and only if \(ad(\mathcal{R}) \to \mathcal{R}\) is an
isomorphism.}

\emph{(iii) \(sc(\mathcal{R})\) is a simply connected datum, and
\(\mathcal{R}\) is simply connected if and only if
\(\mathcal{R} \to sc(\mathcal{R})\) is an isomorphism.}

\emph{(iv) The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(a) \(\mathcal{R}\) is semisimple,}

\emph{(b) \(ss(\mathcal{R}) \to \mathcal{R}\) is an isomorphism,}

\emph{(c) \(\mathcal{R} \to d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R})\) is an
isomorphism.}

Let us pause briefly on the morphism
\(ss(\mathcal{R}) \to d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R})\). Referring to the
construction of \(ss(\mathcal{R})\) and \(d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R})\), it
is easy to prove the

\textbf{Lemma 6.5.6.} \emph{Let
\(h : ss(\mathcal{R}) \to d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R})\) be the canonical
isogeny. One has \(K(h) \simeq N(\mathcal{R})\).}

\textbf{6.5.7.} Consider other special cases of induced data. Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N = \{x ∈ M | (α*, x) = 0 for α ∈ R\} × Γ₀(R);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one knows that the sum is direct by 1.2.5. It follows that the root
datum \(\mathcal{R}_{N}\) is identified with the product
\(ad(\mathcal{R}) \times corad(\mathcal{R})\).

One can do the same by replacing \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) by \(V(R) \cap M\),
then dualize these two constructions. One thus obtains a diagram of root
data:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ad(ℛ) → ss(ℛ) → dér(ℛ) → sc(ℛ)}
\NormalTok{  ↓       ↓        ↓        ↓}
\NormalTok{ad(ℛ) × corad(ℛ) → ss(ℛ) × corad(ℛ) → ℛ → dér(ℛ) × rad(ℛ) → sc(ℛ) × rad(ℛ)}
\NormalTok{  ↓       ↓        ↓        ↓}
\NormalTok{ad(ℛ) → ss(ℛ) → dér(ℛ) → sc(ℛ);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is commutative, as one verifies at once. This diagram is self-dual
in an obvious sense. The horizontal morphisms are isogenies. The
composites of the vertical arrows are the identity.

\textbf{Lemma 6.5.8.} \emph{Let \(h_{1}\) and \(h_{2}\) be the canonical
isogenies:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ss(ℛ) × corad(ℛ) ──h\_1──→ ℛ ──h\_2──→ dér(ℛ) × rad(ℛ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One has \(K(h_{1}) \simeq K(h_{2}) \simeq N(\mathcal{R})\).}

\emph{Proof.} This is trivial from the definitions.

\textbf{Corollary 6.5.9.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum. The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(N(\mathcal{R}) = 0\),
i.e.~\(corad(\mathcal{R}) \to rad(\mathcal{R})\) is an isomorphism.}

\emph{(ii) \(h : ss(\mathcal{R}) \to d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R})\) is an
isomorphism.}

\emph{(iii)
\(h_{1} : ss(\mathcal{R}) \times corad(\mathcal{R}) \to \mathcal{R}\) is
an isomorphism.}

\emph{(iv)
\(h_{2} : \mathcal{R} \to d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R}) \times rad(\mathcal{R})\)
is an isomorphism.}

\emph{(v) \(\mathcal{R}\) is the product of a semisimple datum and a
trivial datum.}

Let us also state a trivial consequence of the preceding remarks:

\textbf{Corollary 6.5.10.} \emph{For every root datum \(\mathcal{R}\),
there exist isogenies}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ad(ℛ) × ℛ\_0 ⟶ ℛ ⟶ sc(ℛ) × ℛ\_0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(\mathcal{R}_{0}\) is ``the'' trivial root datum of rank
\(rgred(\mathcal{R}) - rgss(\mathcal{R})\).}

Let us finally note a result that may be useful:

\textbf{Lemma 6.5.11.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum,
\(\Delta\) a system of simple roots, \(\Delta'\) a subset of \(\Delta\);
consider the root datum (cf.~3.4.7)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ℛ\_\{Δ\textquotesingle{}\} = (M, M*, R\_\{Δ\textquotesingle{}\}, R*\_\{Δ\textquotesingle{}\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) If \(\mathcal{R}\) is simply connected, then
\(d\acute{e}r(\mathcal{R}_{\Delta'})\) is simply connected.}

\emph{(ii) If \(\mathcal{R}\) is adjoint, then
\(ss(\mathcal{R}_{\Delta'})\) is adjoint.}

\emph{Proof.} The two assertions are evidently equivalent by duality.
The second reduces to verifying the formula:

\[
M \cap V(R_{\Delta'}) = \Gamma_{0}(R_{\Delta'});
\]

now, if \(M = \Gamma_{0}(R)\), the two sides are equal to the subgroup
of \(M\) generated by \(\Delta'\).

\subsubsection{6.6. Weights}\label{weights}

\textbf{Definition 6.6.1.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum.
Set\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced \(\Gamma(\mathcal{R})\) by
  \(\Lambda(\mathcal{R})\), to avoid any risk of confusion with
  \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\).}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Λ(ℛ) = \{x ∈ V(R) | (α*, x) ∈ ℤ for all α* ∈ R*\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{The elements of \(\Lambda(\mathcal{R})\) are called the} weights
\emph{of \(\mathcal{R}\). The weights of \(\mathcal{R}*\) are called
the} coweights \emph{of \(\mathcal{R}\).}

One has \(\Gamma_{0}(R) \subset \Lambda(\mathcal{R})\) and
\(\Lambda(\mathcal{R})\) is stable under \(W(\mathcal{R})\).

\textbf{Lemma 6.6.2.} \emph{The bilinear map
\(V* \times V \to \mathbb{Q}\) induces a duality}

\[
\Gamma_{0}(R*) \times \Lambda(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}.
\]

\emph{Proof.} Trivial.

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.3.} \emph{Let
\(\Delta* = (\alpha*_{1}, \cdots, \alpha*_{n})\) be a system of simple
coroots. Let \(p_{i}\), \(i = 1, 2, \cdots, n\), be the elements of
\(V(R)\) defined by}

\[
(\alpha*_{i}, p_{j}) = \delta_{ij},
\]

\emph{(whence \(s_{\alpha_{i}}(p_{i}) = p_{i} - \alpha_{i}\) and
\(s_{\alpha_{i}}(p_{j}) = p_{j}\) for \(i \neq j\)).}\footnote{Warning:
  if the datum is not reduced, the \(\alpha_{i}\) do not form a system
  of simple roots.} \emph{Then \(\Lambda(\mathcal{R})\) is the free
abelian group generated by the \(p_{i}\).}

The \(p_{i}\) are called the \emph{fundamental weights} corresponding to
the system of simple coroots \(\Delta*\).

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.4.} \emph{For every \(\alpha* \in \Delta*\), one
has therefore \((\alpha*, \Sigma_{i} p_{i}) = 1\), hence
\(\Sigma_{i} p_{i} = \rho_{R_{+}}\) (cf.~3.5.1), where
\(R_{+} = P(ind(\Delta))\).}

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.5.} \emph{For every \(x \in V(R)\), one has
\(x = \Sigma_{i} (\alpha*_{i}, x) p_{i}\).}

Remark that \(R* \subset \Gamma_{0}(R*)\) and
\(R \subset \Lambda(\mathcal{R})\), so
\((\Lambda(\mathcal{R}), \Gamma_{0}(R*), R, R*)\) is a root datum.

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.6.} \emph{The canonical morphism
\(\Gamma_{0}(R*) \to M*\) is the transpose of the morphism
\(x \mapsto \Sigma_{i} (\alpha*_{i}, x) p_{i}\), which defines a
morphism of root data, and one has a commutative diagram:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              sc(ℛ)}
\NormalTok{            ↗   ≀}
\NormalTok{       ℛ}
\NormalTok{            ↘}
\NormalTok{              (Λ(ℛ), Γ₀(R*), R, R*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One thus has an explicit description of \(sc(\mathcal{R})\) in terms of
the weights of \(\mathcal{R}\). Similarly, one finds a commutative
diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       ad(ℛ)}
\NormalTok{        ≀  ↘}
\NormalTok{              ℛ}
\NormalTok{            ↗}
\NormalTok{       (Γ₀(R), Λ(ℛ*), R, R*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.7.} \emph{For \(\mathcal{R}\) to be simply
connected, it is necessary and sufficient that
\(M = \Lambda(\mathcal{R})\).}

\textbf{Remark 6.6.8.} \emph{One has
\(\Lambda(\mathcal{R}) \cap M = V(R) \cap M\). For \(\mathcal{R}\) to be
semisimple, it is therefore necessary and sufficient that
\(M \subset \Lambda(\mathcal{R})\).}

From the results of 6.5 there also follows:

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.9.} \emph{For \(\mathcal{R}\) to be the product of
a simply connected datum by a trivial datum, it is necessary and
sufficient that \(M \supset \Lambda(\mathcal{R})\).}

Consider now the canonical isogeny

\[
f : ad(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow sc(\mathcal{R}),
\]

and set \(Z(\mathcal{R}) = K(f)\). One has
\(Z(\mathcal{R}) \simeq Z(sc \mathcal{R}) \simeq Z(ad \mathcal{R})\).

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.10.} \emph{One has a canonical isomorphism
\(Z(\mathcal{R}) = \Lambda(\mathcal{R})/\Gamma_{0}(R)\). More precisely,
one has an exact sequence of \(W(\mathcal{R})\)-modules:}

\[
0 \longrightarrow \Gamma_{0}(R) \longrightarrow \Lambda(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow Z(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow 0.
\]

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.11.} \emph{One has a canonical pairing}

\[
Z(\mathcal{R}*) \times Z(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}
\]

\emph{which puts these groups in duality.}

\textbf{Remark 6.6.12.} \emph{One has
\(Z(\mathcal{R} \times \mathcal{R}') \simeq Z(\mathcal{R}) \times Z(\mathcal{R}')\).
Consider in particular simply connected data \(\mathcal{R}_{i}\),
\(i = 1, 2, \cdots, n\), and a trivial datum \(\mathcal{R}_{0}\). Set
\(\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R}_{0} \times \mathcal{R}_{1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{R}_{n}\).
Let \(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\),
\(\mathcal{R}_{0} = (M_{0}, M*_{0}, \emptyset, \emptyset)\). One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M/Γ₀(R) ≃ M\_0 × Z(ℛ\_1) × ⋯ × Z(ℛ\_n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{6.7. Automorphisms}\label{automorphisms}

An automorphism of \(\mathcal{R}\) is, by 6.1.4, an automorphism of
\(M\), say \(u\), such that \(u(R) = R\) and \({}^{t}u(R*) = R*\). In
particular, every element \(w\) of \(W(\mathcal{R})\) defines an
automorphism of \(\mathcal{R}\).

\textbf{Lemma 6.7.1.} \emph{\(W(\mathcal{R})\) is a normal subgroup of
\(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R})\). More precisely, if
\(u \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R})\) and \(\alpha \in R\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u s\_α u⁻¹ = s\_\{u(α)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} The proof is the same as that of 1.2.10.

\textbf{Proposition 6.7.2.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple
roots. Set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E\_Δ(ℛ) = \{u ∈ Aut(ℛ) | u(Δ) = Δ\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R})\) is the semidirect product
of \(W(\mathcal{R})\) by \(E_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R})\).}

\emph{Proof.} This follows at once from the fact that \(W(\mathcal{R})\)
operates simply transitively on the systems of simple roots, and from
the fact that if \(\Delta\) is a system of simple roots of
\(\mathcal{R}\), then \(u(\Delta)\) is a system of simple roots for
every automorphism \(u\) of \(\mathcal{R}\).

We shall see later a simpler description of \(E_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R})\)
in the case of reduced and irreducible root data.\footnote{N.D.E.: when
  \(\mathcal{R}\) is simply connected or adjoint, see 7.4.5.}

\textbf{Definition 6.7.3.} \emph{One denotes by
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{s}(\mathcal{R})\)\footnote{N.D.E.: The exponent
  \(s\) is meant to suggest ``semisimple''.} the set of
\(u \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R})\) such that the following
diagram is commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       u}
\NormalTok{ℛ ────────→ ℛ}
\NormalTok{  ↘       ↙}
\NormalTok{   rad(ℛ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One writes
\(E^{s}_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R}) = E_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R}) \cap \operatorname{Aut}_{s}(\mathcal{R})\).}

\textbf{Remark 6.7.4.} \emph{If
\(u \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R})\), one has therefore
\(u \in \operatorname{Aut}_{s}(\mathcal{R})\) if and only if
\((u - id)(M) \subset V(R)\). In particular
\(W(\mathcal{R}) \subset \operatorname{Aut}_{s}(\mathcal{R})\). It
follows at once:}

\textbf{Proposition 6.7.5.} \emph{The group
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{s}(\mathcal{R})\) is the semidirect product of
\(W(\mathcal{R})\) by \(E^{s}_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R})\), for every system
of simple roots \(\Delta\).}

To every automorphism of \(\mathcal{R}\) is associated by functoriality
an automorphism of \(ad(\mathcal{R})\). One thus has a canonical
morphism

\[
\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(ad(\mathcal{R})).
\]

\textbf{Lemma 6.7.6.} \emph{The morphism
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{s}(\mathcal{R}) \to \operatorname{Aut}(ad(\mathcal{R}))\)
is injective.}

\emph{Proof.} Let \(u\) be an automorphism of \(M\) such that
\((u - id)(M) \subset V(R)\) and \({}^{t}u(\alpha*) = \alpha*\) for
\(\alpha* \in R*\). For every \(x \in M\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(α*, u(x) − x) = (ᵗu(α*) − α*, x) = 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \(u(x) - x = 0\), by 1.2.5.

\textbf{Lemma 6.7.7.} \emph{The group
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{s}(\mathcal{R})\) is finite.}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, it suffices for us to prove that
\(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R})\) is finite if \(\mathcal{R}\) is
adjoint. Since \(M\) is then generated by \(R\), every automorphism of
\(\mathcal{R}\) is determined by the permutation of \(R\) that it
defines.

\textbf{Remark 6.7.8.} \emph{One sees at once that
\(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal{R})\) (resp. \(E_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R})\))
is finite if and only if
\(rgred(\mathcal{R}) - rgss(\mathcal{R}) \leqslant 1\).}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{6.8. \(p\)-morphisms of reduced root
data}{6.8. p-morphisms of reduced root data}}\label{p-morphisms-of-reduced-root-data}

In this number, \(p\) is an integer \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} fixed
once and for all.

\textbf{Definition 6.8.1.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R} = (M, M*, R, R*)\)
and \(\mathcal{R}' = (M', M'*, R', R'*)\) be two reduced root data. One
says that a group morphism}

\[
f : M' \longrightarrow M
\]

\emph{is a} \(p\)-morphism \emph{from \(\mathcal{R}'\) to
\(\mathcal{R}\), if the following conditions are satisfied: there exist
a bijection}

\[
u : R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'
\]

\emph{and a map \(q : R \to {p^{n}, n \in \mathbb{N}}\) such that:}

\emph{(i) \(f(u(\alpha)) = q(\alpha) \alpha\) for every
\(\alpha \in R\).}

\emph{(ii) \({}^{t}f(\alpha'*) = q(\alpha) u(\alpha)*\) for every
\(\alpha \in R\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: Note that these two conditions
  entail
  \(q(\alpha) (u(\alpha)*, u(\beta)) = q(\beta) (\alpha*, \beta)\), for
  all \(\alpha, \beta \in R\).}

\textbf{Corollary 6.8.2.} \emph{A \texttt{1}-morphism is nothing other
than a morphism.}

\textbf{Corollary 6.8.3.} \emph{The transpose of a \(p\)-morphism is a
\(p\)-morphism.}

\textbf{Lemma 6.8.4.} \emph{If \(w \in W(\mathcal{R})\),
\(\alpha \in R\), one has \(q(w(\alpha)) = q(\alpha)\). The map
\(s_{\alpha} \mapsto s_{u(\alpha)}\) extends to an isomorphism
\(u : W(\mathcal{R}) \to W(\mathcal{R}')\) such that}

\[
u(w(\alpha)) = u(w)(u(\alpha)).
\]

\emph{Proof.} It suffices to prove that for \(\alpha, \beta \in R\), one
has \(u(s_{\alpha}(\beta)) = s_{u(\alpha)} u(\beta)\) and
\(q(s_{\alpha}(\beta)) = q(\beta)\). Now one has successively:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(s\_\{u(α)\} u(β)) = f(u(β)) − (u(α)*, u(β)) f(u(α))}
\NormalTok{                = q(β) β − q(β) q(α)⁻¹ (α*, β) q(α) α}
\NormalTok{                = q(β) (β − (α*, β) α) = q(β) s\_α(β).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(\gamma = u^{-1}(s_{u(\alpha)} u(\beta))\), one has therefore
\(q(\gamma) \gamma = f(u(\gamma)) = q(\beta) s_{\alpha}(\beta)\). The
two roots \(\gamma\) and \(s_{\alpha}(\beta)\) are therefore
proportional (over \(\mathbb{Q}\)), so equal or opposite, but
\(q(\gamma)\) and \(q(\beta)\) are positive. One thus has
\(q(\gamma) = q(\beta)\) and \(\gamma = s_{\alpha}(\beta)\).

\textbf{Definition 6.8.5.} \emph{The \(q(\alpha)\) are called the}
radical exponents \emph{of \(f\).}

\textbf{Example 6.8.6.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a reduced root
datum and \(q = p^{n}\) (\(n \in \mathbb{N}\)). Then the multiplication
by \(q : M \to M\), \(x \mapsto q x\) is a \(p\)-morphism whose radical
exponents are all equal to \(q\) (and \(u = id\)); one denotes it}

\[
q : \mathcal{R} \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}.
\]

\textbf{Proposition 6.8.7.} \emph{In the notation of 6.8.1, \(u\)
realizes an isomorphism of the set of systems of simple roots (resp. of
positive roots) of \(R\) onto the corresponding set for \(R'\).}

\emph{Proof.} This follows at once from 3.1.5 (resp. 3.2.1).

\subsection{7. Structure}\label{structure}

\subsubsection{7.1. Decomposition of a root
datum}\label{decomposition-of-a-root-datum}

\textbf{Proposition 7.1.1.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum,
\(\Delta\) a system of simple roots.}

\emph{(i) Let \(R'\) and \texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}
be two closed and symmetric sets of roots forming a partition of \(R\).
If one denotes \(\Delta' = \Delta \cap R'\),
\(\Delta'' = \Delta \cap R''\), then \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\),
\(R'' = R_{\Delta''}\), and every root of \(\Delta'\) is orthogonal to
every root of \(\Delta''\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(\Delta'\) and \(\Delta''\) be two subsets of \(\Delta\)
forming a partition of \(\Delta\) and orthogonal. Then
\(R' = R_{\Delta'}\) and \(R'' = R_{\Delta''}\) form a partition of
\(R\).}

\emph{Proof.} Let us first prove (i).

\textbf{Lemma 7.1.2.} \emph{Under the conditions of (i), if \(\alpha\),
\(\beta\), and \(\alpha + \beta\) are roots, they all three belong to
\(R'\) or all three to \texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}.}

\emph{Proof.} Suppose for example \(\alpha + \beta \in R'\). Then one
cannot have \(\alpha, \beta \in R''\), since
\texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is closed; suppose
therefore \(\alpha \in R'\). Then \(-\alpha \in R'\) and
\(\beta = (\beta + \alpha) - \alpha \in R'\).

Let us now show that \(R' = R_{\Delta'}\) by induction on the order of a
positive root \(\alpha \in R' \cap P(\Delta)\). If
\(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha) = 1\), then
\(\alpha \in R' \cap \Delta = \Delta'\). If
\(ord_{\Delta}(\alpha) > 1\), there exists \(\beta \in \Delta\) such
that \(\alpha - \beta \in R\). By the lemma, one has
\(\beta \in \Delta'\), \(\alpha - \beta \in R'\), so
\(\alpha - \beta \in R_{\Delta'}\) by induction, and finally
\(\alpha = (\alpha - \beta) + \beta \in R_{\Delta'}\).

Let us finally show that \(\Delta'\) and \(\Delta''\) are orthogonal. If
\(\alpha \in \Delta'\) and \(\beta \in \Delta''\), then
\((\beta*, \alpha) \leqslant 0\). If \((\beta*, \alpha) \neq 0\), then
\(\beta + \alpha\) is a root, contrary to the lemma.

Let us prove (ii). If \(\Delta'\) or \(\Delta''\) is empty, this is
immediate. Otherwise, if \(R_{\Delta'}\) and \(R_{\Delta''}\) do not
form a partition of \(R\), there exists a root \(\alpha\) of the form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α = Σ\_i m\textquotesingle{}\_i α\textquotesingle{}\_i + Σ\_j m\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_j α\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_j,    m\textquotesingle{}\_i ∈ ℤ₊, m\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_j ∈ ℤ₊,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where one denotes by \(\alpha'_{i}\) (resp. \(\alpha''_{j}\)) elements
of \(\Delta'\) (resp. \(\Delta''\)). Applying 3.1.2, one deduces a
relation of the form (possibly inverting \(\Delta'\) and \(\Delta''\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{δ = γ + β,    γ ∈ R\_\{Δ\textquotesingle{}\},    β ∈ Δ\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{},    δ ∈ R.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But since \((\beta*, \gamma) = 0\), \(\gamma - \beta\) is also a root by
2.2.5, which is impossible.

\textbf{Proposition 7.1.3.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum.
The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) There exists no non-trivial partition of \(R\) into two closed
and symmetric subsets.}

\emph{(ii) For some (resp. every) system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of
\(R\), there exists no partition of \(\Delta\) into two non-empty
orthogonal subsets.}

\emph{(iii) The natural representation of \(W(\mathcal{R})\) in \(V(R)\)
is irreducible.}

\emph{(iv) For every pair \((\alpha, \beta)\) of roots, there exists a
sequence of roots
\(\alpha_{0}, \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}\), with
\(\alpha = \alpha_{0}\), \(\alpha_{n} = \beta\), such that the roots
\(\alpha_{i}\) and \(\alpha_{i+1}\) (\(i = 0, \cdots, n - 1\)) are
non-orthogonal.}

\emph{Proof.} One has (i) ⇔ (ii) by 7.1.1. One has obviously (iv) ⇒
(ii). Conversely, if (ii) is verified for \(\Delta\), condition (iv) is
verified for \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\). Now for every root, there
exists a simple root not orthogonal to it (3.1.1 for example). On the
other hand (iii) ⇒ (i): in effect, under the conditions of 7.1.1,
\(V(R')\) is stable under \(W(\mathcal{R})\). It remains to prove (i) ⇒
(iii).

So let \(H\) be a vector subspace of \(V(R)\), stable under
\(W(\mathcal{R})\). For every \(\alpha \in R\), the equation
\(s_{\alpha}(H) = H\) gives at once \(\alpha \in H\), or
\(\alpha* \in H^{\perp}\) (orthogonal of \(H\) in \(V(R*)\), which is in
duality with \(V(R)\)). If one sets
\(R' = {\alpha \in R | \alpha \in H}\) and
\(R'' = {\alpha \in R | \alpha* \in H^{\perp}}\), one has realized a
partition of \(R\) into two closed and symmetric subsets.

\textbf{Definition 7.1.4.} \emph{A root datum (resp. a root system)
satisfying the equivalent conditions of 7.1.3 and of semisimple rank
\(\neq 0\) is called} irreducible.

\textbf{Corollary 7.1.5.} \emph{For every root datum \(\mathcal{R}\),
there exists a unique partition (up to order) of \(R\) into closed,
symmetric, and irreducible subsets.}

\textbf{Corollary 7.1.6.} \emph{Every adjoint (resp. simply connected)
root datum is a product of irreducible adjoint (resp. simply connected)
root data.}

\emph{Proof.} It suffices to see this in the adjoint case. The assertion
then follows from the fact that under the conditions of 7.1.1, one has

\[
\Gamma_{0}(R) = \Gamma_{0}(R') \times \Gamma_{0}(R'').
\]

\textbf{Corollary 7.1.7.} \emph{For every root datum (resp. reduced root
datum) \(\mathcal{R}\), there exists an isogeny
\(\mathcal{R} \to \mathcal{R}'\), where \(\mathcal{R}'\) is a product of
a trivial root datum and of irreducible simply connected root data
(resp. and reduced).}

\subsubsection{7.2. Properties of irreducible root
data}\label{properties-of-irreducible-root-data}

\textbf{Definition 7.2.1.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be an irreducible
root datum. For every \(\alpha \in R\), set}

\[
long(\alpha) = \ell(\alpha)/\ell(\alpha_{0}),
\]

\emph{where \(\alpha_{0} \in R\) is such that \(\ell(\alpha_{0})\) is
minimal; one says that \(long(\alpha)\) is the} length \emph{of
\(\alpha\).}

\textbf{Lemma 7.2.2.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be an irreducible root
datum. The Weyl group operates transitively on the set of roots of the
same length.}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\). Since the
representation of \(W\) on \(V(R)\) is irreducible, \(\alpha\) cannot be
orthogonal to all the \(w(\beta)\), \(w \in W\). There exists therefore
\(w \in W\) with \(w(\beta)\) non-orthogonal to \(\alpha\). Now
\(\ell(w(\beta)) = \ell(\beta)\), and one concludes by 2.3.2.

\textbf{Lemma 7.2.3.} \emph{If \(\mathcal{R}\) is irreducible and
reduced, then \(long(R)\) is \texttt{\{1\}}, \texttt{\{1,\ 2\}}, or
\texttt{\{1,\ 3\}}.}

\emph{Proof.} By virtue of the remark used above, for every
\(\alpha, \beta \in R\), there always exists \(w \in W\) such that
\(w(\beta)\) is not orthogonal to \(\beta\). One thus has
\(\ell(\alpha)/\ell(\beta) = 1, 2, 3, 1/2\), or \texttt{1/3} (by 2.3.1).
One has therefore \(long(\alpha) = 1, 2\), or \texttt{3}, but if
\(long(\alpha) = 2\), \(long(\beta) = 3\), then
\(\ell(\alpha)/\ell(\beta) = 2/3\), which is impossible.

\textbf{Remark 7.2.4.} \emph{Reasoning similarly, one proves the
following result: if \(\mathcal{R}\) is irreducible and not reduced with
\(rgss(\mathcal{R}) > 1\), one has \(long(R) = {1, 2, 4}\). If one sets
\(long^{-1}(i) = R_{i}\), then \(ind(R) = R_{1} \cup R_{2}\),
\(R_{4} = 2 R_{1}\), and two non-proportional roots of \texttt{R\_1} are
orthogonal. Conversely, if \(R\) is an irreducible and reduced system
such that \(long(R) = {1, 2}\), set \(long^{-1}(i) = R_{i}\) and suppose
that two non-proportional roots of \texttt{R\_1} are orthogonal; then
\(R \cup 2 R_{1}\) is irreducible, not reduced, and
\(ind(R \cup 2 R_{1}) = R\).}

\textbf{Lemma 7.2.5.} \emph{If \(\mathcal{R}\) is an irreducible root
datum, \(\mathcal{R}*\) also is, and the product
\(long(\alpha) long(\alpha*)\) is constant as \(\alpha\) runs over
\(R\).}

\emph{Proof.} This follows at once from 7.1.3 (iv) and 2.2.6.

\textbf{Definition 7.2.6.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be any root datum.
One calls} length \emph{of \(\alpha \in R\) and denotes by
\(long(\alpha)\) the length of \(\alpha\) in its irreducible component.}

\textbf{Lemma 7.2.7.} \emph{There exists a unique group homomorphism
\(u : \Gamma_{0}(R) \to \Gamma_{0}(R*)\) such that
\(u(\alpha) = long(\alpha) \alpha*\) for \(\alpha \in R\).}

\emph{Proof.} By 3.5.5, it suffices to verify that if
\(\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta \in R\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{long(α) α* + long(β) β* = long(α + β) (α + β)*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), and \(\alpha + \beta\) are in the same
irreducible component of \(R\) by 7.1.2, and one is reduced to 1.2.2.

\textbf{Remark 7.2.8.} \emph{Let \(u\) be as in 7.2.7. For
\(\alpha, \beta \in R\), one has
\((u(\alpha), \beta) = (u(\beta), \alpha)\). Indeed, this amounts to
seeing that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{long(α) (α*, β) = long(β) (β*, α),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which is obviously verified if \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are
orthogonal. If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not orthogonal, then they
are in the same irreducible component of \(R\), and one is reduced to
1.2.1, formula (9).}

\textbf{Remark 7.2.9.} \emph{The symmetric bilinear form
\texttt{(u(x),\ y)} is positive nondegenerate on \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, let \(R_{i}\) be the irreducible components of
\(R\). One has

\[
\Gamma_{0}(R) = \prod_{i} \Gamma_{0}(R_{i}),
\]

and the bilinear form \texttt{(u(x),\ y)} is the product of the forms

\[
2^{-1} \ell(\alpha_{i})^{-1} (p(x), y)
\]

on the \(\Gamma_{0}(R_{i})\), where \(\ell(\alpha_{i})\) is the minimum
of \(\ell(\alpha)\) for \(\alpha \in R_{i}\). Now these various
symmetric bilinear forms are positive nondegenerate (1.2.6).

\subsubsection{7.3. Cartan matrix}\label{cartan-matrix}

Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum. If \(\Delta\) is a system of simple
roots, one calls \emph{Cartan matrix} of \(\mathcal{R}\) relative to
\(\Delta\) the square matrix on the index set \(\Delta\) defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a\_\{α,β\} = (α*, β),    for α, β ∈ Δ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us first remark that if \(\Delta'\) is another system of simple
roots and \(w\) an element of \(W(\mathcal{R})\) such that
\(w(\Delta) = \Delta'\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(w(α)*, w(β)) = (α*, β),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so the Cartan matrix of \(\mathcal{R}\) relative to \(\Delta'\) is
obtained from that relative to \(\Delta\) by the isomorphism
\(\Delta \to \Delta'\) on the index set defined by \(w\). It follows
that, up to isomorphism on the index set, the Cartan matrix depends only
on \(\mathcal{R}\).

\textbf{Proposition 7.3.1.} \emph{The Cartan matrix has the following
properties:}

\emph{(i) \(a_{\alpha,\alpha} = 2\), \(a_{\alpha,\beta} \leqslant 0\)
for \(\alpha \neq \beta\).}

\emph{(ii) \(a_{\alpha,\beta} = 0\) entails \(a_{\beta,\alpha} = 0\).}

\emph{(iii) There exist strictly positive integers \(m_{\alpha}\)
(\(= long(\alpha)\)) such that the matrix}

\[
(m_{\alpha} a_{\alpha,\beta})
\]

\emph{is symmetric, positive, and nondegenerate.}

\emph{(iv) The diagonal minors of the matrix
\((a_{\alpha,\beta})_{\alpha, \beta \in \Delta}\), i.e.~the
determinants}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{det(a\_\{α,β\})\_\{α, β ∈ Δ\textquotesingle{}\}    for Δ\textquotesingle{} ⊂ Δ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are strictly positive.}

\emph{(v) One has
\(s_{\alpha}(\beta) = \beta - a_{\alpha,\beta} \alpha\) and
\(s_{\alpha}(\beta*) = \beta* - a_{\beta,\alpha} \alpha*\).}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, (v) is a definition, (i) follows from 3.2.11, (ii)
from 2.2.2, (iii) from 7.2.9, (iv) follows at once from (iii) by the
relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{det(m\_α a\_\{α,β\})\_\{α, β ∈ Δ\textquotesingle{}\} = (∏\_\{α ∈ Δ\textquotesingle{}\} m\_α) det(a\_\{α,β\})\_\{α, β ∈ Δ\textquotesingle{}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 7.3.2.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) and
\(\mathcal{R}'\) be two simply connected (resp. adjoint) reduced root
data, \(\Delta\) (resp. \(\Delta'\)) a system of simple roots of
\(\mathcal{R}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{R}'\)), and \(u : \Delta \to \Delta'\)
an isomorphism such that if one denotes by \((a_{\alpha,\beta})\) and
\((a'_{\alpha',\beta'})\) the Cartan matrices of \(\mathcal{R}\) and
\(\mathcal{R}'\) relative to \(\Delta\) and \(\Delta'\), one has:}

\[
a'_{u(\alpha), u(\beta)} = a_{\alpha,\beta}.
\]

\emph{Then there exists a unique isomorphism of \(\mathcal{R}\) onto
\(\mathcal{R}'\) that induces \(u\) on \(\Delta\).}

\emph{Proof.} It evidently suffices to make the proof in the adjoint
case. Then \(M = \Gamma_{0}(R)\) and \(M' = \Gamma_{0}(R')\) are the
free abelian groups generated by \(\Delta\) and \(\Delta'\). There
exists therefore a unique isomorphism of groups of \(M\) onto \(M'\)
that induces \(u\) on \(\Delta\). Denote it also \(u\). Let us show that
\(u(R) \subset R'\). Every root \(\alpha\) of \(R\) is written
\(s_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{n}}(\alpha_{n+1})\) with
\(\alpha_{i} \in \Delta\). One has obviously

\[
u(\alpha) = s_{u(\alpha_{1})} \cdots s_{u(\alpha_{n})}(u(\alpha_{n+1})),
\]

by virtue of the hypothesis on \(u\) and the relations (v) of 7.3.1.

It remains to prove that \({}^{t}u(R'*) \subset R*\), which follows from
the fact that the elements of \(M*\) (resp. \(M'*\)) are determined by
the duality with \(R\) or \(\Delta\) (resp. \(R'\) or \(\Delta'\)), by
1.2.5.

\textbf{Corollary 7.3.3.} \emph{A reduced simply connected or adjoint
root datum is determined up to isomorphism by its Cartan matrix.}

\textbf{Corollary 7.3.4.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a reduced simply
connected (resp. adjoint) root datum, and \(\Delta\) a system of simple
roots. The group \(E_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R})\) is identified with the
group of automorphisms of the set \(\Delta\) that leave the Cartan
matrix invariant.}

\textbf{Remark 7.3.5.} \emph{The question of the existence of a root
datum corresponding to a given Cartan matrix satisfying (i), (ii), and
(iv) (for example) is not easily resolved directly, without using the
classification.}

\subsubsection{7.4. Dynkin diagrams}\label{dynkin-diagrams}

\textbf{Definition 7.4.1.} \emph{One calls a} Dynkin diagram structure
\emph{(the word ``schéma'' having been banished for obvious reasons) on
a finite set \(\Delta\) the data of a set of pairs of distinct elements
of \(\Delta\), called} linked pairs, \emph{and of a map from \(\Delta\)
to the set \texttt{\{1,\ 2,\ 3\}}. The notion of isomorphism of such
structures is obvious.}

\textbf{Definition 7.4.2.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a root datum and
\(\Delta\) a system of simple roots. One calls} Dynkin diagram \emph{of
\(\mathcal{R}\) relative to \(\Delta\) the set \(\Delta\), two simple
roots being linked if and only if they are non-orthogonal, with each
root being assigned its length.}

\textbf{Proposition 7.4.3.} \emph{Dynkin diagram and Cartan matrix
determine each other biuniquely.}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, the equivalence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α and β are not linked  ⟺  a\_\{α,β\} = 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{long(α) a\_\{α,β\} = long(β) a\_\{β,α\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(with \(\inf long(\alpha) = 1\) in each connected component of the
diagram) determine the \(a_{\alpha,\beta}\) as a function of the
linkages and lengths, and conversely (the details of the verification
are left to the reader).

\textbf{Corollary 7.4.4.} \emph{A reduced simply connected or adjoint
root datum is determined by its Dynkin diagram.}

\textbf{Corollary 7.4.5.} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a reduced simply
connected or adjoint root datum and \(\Delta\) a system of simple roots.
The group \(E_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R})\) is identified with the group of
automorphisms of the Dynkin diagram of \(\mathcal{R}\) relative to
\(\Delta\), that is to say with the group of permutations of \(\Delta\)
preserving lengths and linkages.}

\textbf{Remark 7.4.6.} \emph{One classifies, with the usual
method,\footnote{Cf. Bourbaki, \emph{Groupes et algèbres de Lie}, Chap.
  VI N° 4.2 or \emph{Séminaire Sophus Lie}.}\footnote{N.D.E.: For a
  slightly different proof, see also {[}De80{]}.} the various connected
Dynkin diagrams, and one shows that each effectively corresponds to an
irreducible reduced simply connected root datum. One finds the
well-known types:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 — 1 — 1 — … — 1 — 1 — 1        Aₙ,   n ⩾ 1.}

\NormalTok{2 — 2 — 2 — … — 2 — 2 ⇒ 1        Bₙ,   n ⩾ 2.}

\NormalTok{1 — 1 — 1 — … — 1 — 1 ⇐ 2        Cₙ,   n ⩾ 3.}

\NormalTok{                            1}
\NormalTok{                           ╱}
\NormalTok{1 — 1 — 1 — … — 1 — 1}
\NormalTok{                           ╲}
\NormalTok{                            1                 Dₙ,   n ⩾ 4.}

\NormalTok{         1}
\NormalTok{         |}
\NormalTok{   1 — 1 — 1 — 1 — 1                          Eₙ,   n = 6, 7, 8.}

\NormalTok{   1 — 1 ⇒ 2 — 2                              F₄.}

\NormalTok{       1 ⇛ 3                                  G₂.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 7.4.5, one finds at once the corresponding group
\(E_{\Delta}(\mathcal{R})\); one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E\_Δ(ℛ) = \{e\}      for A₁, Bₙ, Cₙ, E₇, E₈, F₄, G₂.}
\NormalTok{E\_Δ(ℛ) = ℤ/2ℤ    for Aₙ (n ⩾ 2), Dₙ (n ⩾ 5), E₆.}
\NormalTok{E\_Δ(ℛ) = S₃      for D₄.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{7.5. Complements on
\(p\)-morphisms}{7.5. Complements on p-morphisms}}\label{complements-on-p-morphisms}

Let \(f : \mathcal{R} \to \mathcal{R}'\) be a \(p\)-morphism (cf.~6.8).
It is clear from the definitions that the bijection
\(u : R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'\) associated with \(f\) makes systems of
simple roots, systems of positive roots, irreducible components (etc.)
of \(R\) and \(R'\) correspond. Suppose therefore, for simplicity, \(R\)
and \(R'\) irreducible.

\textbf{Lemma 7.5.1.} \emph{If \(R\) and \(R'\) are irreducible, there
exists \(k \in \mathbb{Q}\) such that for every \(\alpha \in R\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{k long(u(α)) = q(α)² long(α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, one has
\(long(\alpha) (\alpha*, \beta) = long(\beta) (\beta*, \alpha)\) and,
similarly,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{long(u(α)) (u(α)*, u(β)) = long(u(β)) (u(β)*, u(α)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One deduces at once that for non-orthogonal \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\),
one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{q(α)² long(α) / long(u(α)) = q(β)² long(β) / long(u(β))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one concludes then by 7.1.3 (iv).

\textbf{Remark 7.5.2.} \emph{It follows from 7.2.2 and 6.8.4 that
\(q(\alpha)\) depends only on \(long(\alpha)\). One then sees easily
that if \(q(\alpha)\) is not constant, then \(q(\alpha) long(\alpha)\)
is constant, which shows that then \(p = 2\) or \texttt{3}. A glance at
the diagrams of the preceding number shows that there are four possible
cases (we denote by the same letter a Dynkin diagram and the
corresponding simply connected reduced root datum):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p = 2,    Bₙ ──f\_1──→ Cₙ,    Cₙ ──f\_2──→ Bₙ    (with C₂ = B₂).}
\NormalTok{p = 2,    F₄ ──g──→ F₄.}
\NormalTok{p = 3,    G₂ ──h──→ G₂.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{The reader will note that \(f_{1} \circ f_{2}\),
\(f_{2} \circ f_{1}\), \(g \circ g\), and \(h \circ h\) are
\(p\)-morphisms of the form described in 6.8.6.}

\textbf{7.5.3.} One sees at once from the preceding description that if
\(\mathcal{R}\) and \(\mathcal{R}'\) are two reduced root data of
semisimple rank \(\leqslant 2\) and if one has a \(p\)-morphism from
\(\mathcal{R}'\) to \(\mathcal{R}\), then \(\mathcal{R}\) and
\(\mathcal{R}'\) are of the same type. More precisely, one has the
following table.

of \(p\). We use for the rank-2 systems the notations of number 4 (we
denote by \(\alpha, \beta\) the simple roots, with
\(\ell(\alpha) \leqslant \ell(\beta)\)).

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-9}

\section{Exposé XXII. Reductive groups: splittings, subgroups, quotient
groups}\label{exposuxe9-xxii.-reductive-groups-splittings-subgroups-quotient-groups}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{Version of 13/10/2024.} This Exposé consists of two parts. The
first (1 through 5.5) gathers the technical results needed for the proof
of the uniqueness and existence theorems. The second (5.6 to the end)
will not be used in that proof; the end of section 5 will be used in
particular in Exposé XXVI on parabolic subgroups; section 6 establishes,
in the scheme-theoretic setting, the classical results on the derived
group of a reductive group.

\subsection{1. Roots and coroots. Split groups and root
data}\label{roots-and-coroots.-split-groups-and-root-data}

\textbf{Theorem 1.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) a root
of \(G\) relative to \(T\).}

\emph{(i) There exists a unique morphism of groups with operator group
\(T\)}

\[
\exp \alpha : W(g\alpha) \to G
\]

\emph{inducing on the Lie algebras the canonical morphism
\(g\alpha \to g\). This morphism is a closed immersion. The
corresponding morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ·α W(gα) → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is also a closed immersion.}

\emph{If \(p\alpha : Ga,S \to G\) is a monomorphism normalized by \(T\)
with multiplier \(\alpha\), there exists a unique
\(X\alpha \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\)\footnote{The set
  \(\Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\) is defined in XIX 4.4.1.} such that
\(p\alpha(x) = \exp \alpha(xX\alpha)\); one has
\(Lie(p\alpha)(1) = X\alpha\), and the two preceding formulas set up a
bijective correspondence between \(\Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\) and the
set of monomorphisms \(Ga,S \to G\) normalized by \(T\) with multiplier
\(\alpha\).}

\emph{(ii) There exists a unique duality (denoted
\((X, Y) \mapsto XY\))}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{gα ⊗\_\{O\_S\} g\_\{{-}α\} ⥲ O\_S,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and a unique morphism of groups}

\[
\alpha* : Gm,S \to T,
\]

\emph{such that formula (F) of Exp. XX 2.1 holds. One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α ∘ α* = 2,     ({-}α)* = {-}α*,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and \(\alpha*\) is given by the formula of Exp. XX 2.7.}

Indeed, a morphism normalized by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\)
factors necessarily through the closed subgroup
\(Z\alpha = Centr_{G}(T\alpha)\) of \(G\) (cf.~Exp. XIX 3.9). Now
\((Z\alpha, T, \alpha)\) is an \(S\)-elementary system (Exp. XX 1.4),
and one is reduced to the results of Exposé XX (1.5, 2.1, and 5.9).

\textbf{Remark 1.2.} \emph{Part (i) of Theorem 1.1 remains valid if one
only assumes that \(\alpha\) is a character of \(T\), non-trivial on
each fiber. Indeed, one then has a decomposition \(S = S' \coprod S''\)
such that \(\alpha|S'\) is a root of \(G_{S'}\) relative to \(T_{S'}\)
and \(g\alpha|S'' = 0\). If \(S = S'\), one is reduced to 1.1; if
\(S = S''\) the result is trivial; the general case follows
immediately.}

\textbf{Notations 1.3.} \emph{As in Exposé XX, we denote by \(U\alpha\)
the image of \(W(g\alpha)\); it is a closed subgroup of \(G\), equipped
canonically with a vector-space structure. We shall call it the} vector
group associated with the root \(\alpha\). \emph{We say that \(\alpha*\)
is the} coroot associated with \(\alpha\). \emph{Sections
\(X\alpha \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\) and
\(X_{-\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})\) are said to be} paired
\emph{if \(X\alpha \cdot X_{-\alpha} = 1\). Then
\(X\alpha \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\) and likewise for
\(X_{-\alpha}\). The corresponding morphisms \(p\alpha\) and
\(p_{-\alpha}\) are contragredient to one another in the sense of XX,
1.5,\footnote{That is, if one denotes by \(\langle , \rangle\) the
  duality between \(g\alpha\) and \(g_{-\alpha}\) and if one identifies
  \(g\alpha\) with \(U\alpha\) via \(p\alpha(x) = \exp(xX\alpha)\), and
  similarly for \(-\alpha\), then
  \(\langle p\alpha(x), p_{-\alpha}(y)\rangle = xy\).} and one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pα(x) p\_\{{-}α\}(y) = p\_\{{-}α\}(y / (1 + xy)) · α*(1 + xy) · pα(x / (1 + xy)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 1.4.} \emph{Under the conditions of 1.1, let
\(w \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\). Then
\(\beta = \alpha \circ int(w)^{-1} : T \to Gm,S\) is a root of \(G\)
relative to \(T\), \(\beta* = int(w) \circ \alpha*\) is the
corresponding coroot, and the following diagram is commutative:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W(gα)  {-}{-}expα{-}{-}\textgreater{}  G}
\NormalTok{  |                |}
\NormalTok{Ad(w)            int(w)}
\NormalTok{  ↓                ↓}
\NormalTok{W(gβ)  {-}{-}expβ{-}{-}\textgreater{}  G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Trivial: transport of structure.

\textbf{Definitions 1.5.} \emph{(a) Under the conditions of 1.1, we
denote by \(s\alpha\) the automorphism of \(T\) defined by}

\[
s\alpha(t) = t \cdot \alpha*(\alpha(t))^{-1}.
\]

\emph{We denote by \(( ,)\) the canonical pairing:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Gm,S, T) × Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T, Gm,S) → Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Gm,S, Gm,S) = ℤ\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(s\alpha\) operates on
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, Gm,S)\), resp.
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Gm,S, T)\), by the following formulas,
where \(\chi\) (resp. \(u\)) denotes an arbitrary section of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, Gm,S)\) (resp. of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Gm,S, T)\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sα(χ) = χ − (α*, χ) α,}
\NormalTok{sα(u) = u − (u, α) α*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One has \(s\alpha \circ s\alpha = id\) and
\(s_{-\alpha} = s\alpha\).}

\emph{(b) If \(X \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\), then the inner
automorphism \(w\alpha(X)\) of \(T\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{wα(X) = expα(X) exp\_\{{-}α\}({-}X⁻¹) expα(X)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(cf.~Exp. XX 3.1) coincides with \(s\alpha\) (loc. cit.). One then
concludes from 1.4:}

\textbf{Corollary 1.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(\alpha\) and
\(\beta\) two roots of \(G\) relative to \(T\). Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sα(β) = β − (α*, β) α}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a root of \(G\) relative to \(T\), and the corresponding coroot
is}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sα(β)* = sα(β*) = β* − (β*, α) α*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 1.7.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions,
\(\alpha* = \beta*\) implies \(\alpha = \beta\).}

Indeed, if \(\alpha* = \beta*\), one has (cf.~XXI.1.4)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sβ(α) = α − 2β,    sα(β) = β − 2α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and from this one deduces immediately

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(sβ sα)ⁿ(α) = α + 2n(β − α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(\beta \neq \alpha\), there exists \(s \in S\) such that
\(\alpha_{s} \neq \beta_{s}\). But then the preceding formula shows that
there exist infinitely many distinct roots of \(G_{s}\) relative to
\(T_{s}\), which is impossible.

\textbf{Definitions 1.8.0.}\footnote{We have added the numbering 1.8.0
  to highlight these definitions.} \emph{If \(u : Gm,S \to T\) is a
morphism of groups, we shall say that \(u\) is a} coroot \emph{of \(G\)
relative to \(T\) if there exists a root \(\alpha\) of \(G\) relative to
\(T\) such that \(\alpha* = u\). Consider the functor \(R*\) of coroots
of \(G\) relative to \(T\) defined as follows:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R*(S′) = the set of coroots of G\_\{S′\} relative to T\_\{S′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(R\) is the functor of roots of \(G\) relative to \(T\) (Exp.
XIX 3.8), one has a canonical morphism \(R \to R*\). By virtue of 1.7
and Exp. XIX 3.8, one has:}

\textbf{Corollary 1.8.} \emph{The canonical morphism \(R \to R*\) is an
isomorphism. In particular, \(R*\) is representable by a finite twisted
constant \(S\)-scheme, which is an open and closed subscheme of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr}(Gm,S, T)\).}

This leads us to the following definition:

\textbf{Definition 1.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(T\) an
\(S\)-torus. We call} twisted root datum \emph{in \(T\) the data:}

\emph{(i) a finite subscheme \(R\) of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, Gm,S)\),}

\emph{(ii) a finite subscheme \(R*\) of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Gm,S, T)\),}

\emph{(iii) an isomorphism \(R \xrightarrow{\sim} R*\) denoted
\(\alpha \mapsto \alpha*\),}

\emph{satisfying the following conditions:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(DR 1)  For every S′ → S and every α ∈ R(S′), one has α ∘ α* = 2.}
\NormalTok{(DR 2)  For every S′ → S and every α, β ∈ R(S′), one has}
\NormalTok{        α − (β*, α) β ∈ R(S′),    α* − (α*, β) β* ∈ R*(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, if for \(\alpha \in R(S')\) (\(S' \neq \emptyset\)) one
has \(2\alpha \notin R(S')\), the root datum is said to be} reduced.

\textbf{Proposition 1.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(R\) (resp.
\(R*\)) the scheme of roots (resp. of coroots) of \(G\) relative to
\(T\). Then \((R, R*)\) is a reduced twisted root datum in \(T\).}

The only thing that remains to be checked is that this twisted root
datum is reduced. This was done in Exp. XIX 3.10.

\subsubsection{1.11.}\label{section-218}

Let \(T = D_{S}(M)\) be a trivialized torus. If we denote by \(M*\) the
abelian group dual to \(M\), we have canonical isomorphisms (cf.~Exp.
VIII 1.5):

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, Gm,S) \xrightarrow{\sim} M_{S},
\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Gm,S, T) \xrightarrow{\sim} M*_{S},
\]

hence isomorphisms of groups:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T, Gm,S) → Hom\_\{loc.const.\}(S, M),}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Gm,S, T) → Hom\_\{loc.const.\}(S, M*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A character of \(T\) (resp. a morphism of groups \(Gm,S \to T\)) will be
called \emph{constant} (relative to the given trivialization) if the
