preceding isomorphism transforms it into a constant map from \(S\) to
\(M\) (resp. \(M*\)).

\subsubsection{1.12.}\label{section-219}

With the same notations, let \((M, M*, R, R*)\) be a root datum (Exp.
XXI). Then \((R_{S}, R*_{S})\) is a twisted root datum in \(T\).
Conversely, if \((R, R*)\) is a twisted root datum in a torus \(T\), a
\emph{splitting} of this root datum is the data of an ordinary root
datum \((M, M*, R, R*)\) together with an isomorphism
\(T \simeq D_{S}(M)\) that transforms \((R, R*)\) into
\((R_{S}, R*_{S})\).

\textbf{Definition 1.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). We call}
splitting \emph{of \(G\) relative to \(T\) the data}

\emph{(i) of an abelian group \(M\) and an isomorphism
\(T \simeq D_{S}(M)\),}

\emph{(ii) of a system of roots \(R\) of \(G\) relative to \(T\) (Exp.
XIX 3.6),}

\emph{satisfying the following two conditions:}

\emph{(D₁) \(S\) is non-empty and the roots \(\alpha \in R\) (resp. the
corresponding coroots) are identified with constant functions from \(S\)
to \(M\) (resp. \(M*\)).}

\emph{(D₂) The \(g\alpha\) (\(\alpha \in R\)) are free
\texttt{O\_S}-modules.}

\emph{We say that \(G\) is} splittable \emph{relative to \(T\) if there
exists a splitting of \(G\) relative to \(T\). By a} splitting of \(G\)
\emph{we mean the data of a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) and a splitting
of \(G\) relative to \(T\). We say that \(G\) is} splittable \emph{if
there exists a splitting of \(G\). By an} \(S\)-split group \emph{we
mean an \(S\)-reductive group equipped with a splitting; we denote it by
a symbol of the form \((G, T, M, R)\), or simply \(G\) when there is no
risk of confusion.}

Condition (D₁) entails that \(R\) (resp. \(R*\)) is canonically
identified with a subset of \(M\) (resp. \(M*\)).

\textbf{Proposition 1.14.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme (non-empty),
\((G, T, M, R)\) an \(S\)-split group. Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R(G, T, M, R) = (M, M*, R, R*)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a reduced root datum (Exp. XXI 1.1 and 2.1.3); it is a
splitting of the twisted root datum of 1.10.}

This is a trivial consequence of 1.10 and Exp. XIX 3.7.

We shall sometimes write, for simplicity, \(R(G, T, M, R) = R(G)\). We
shall systematically use the notations \(V\), \(V(R)\), \(W\), \ldots{}
of Exp. XXI.

\textbf{Remark 1.15.} \emph{(a) If \(S\) is connected non-empty (resp.
if \(\operatorname{Pic}(S) = 0\)), the condition (D₁) (resp. (D₂)) is
automatically satisfied.}

\emph{(b) If \((G, T, M, R)\) is an \(S\)-split group, then for every
\(S' \to S\), \(S' \neq \emptyset\), \((G_{S'}, T_{S'}, M, R)\) is an
\(S'\)-split group, and \(R(G, T, M, R) = R(G_{S'}, T_{S'}, M, R)\).}

\subsubsection{1.16.}\label{section-220}

Let \(T = D_{S}(M)\) be a trivialized torus. The Lie algebra \(t\) of
\(T\) is canonically identified (Exp. II 5.1.1) with

\[
t \simeq M* \otimes O_{S}.
\]

For every morphism of groups \(u : T \to Gm,S\), \(Lie(u)\) is a linear
form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(u) : t → O\_S = Lie(Gm,S/S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, if \(u\) is defined by an element \(\alpha \in M\), then
\(Lie(u)\) is the linear form \(\alpha\) on \(M* \otimes O_{S}\) defined
by \(\alpha\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α(m ⊗ x) = (m, α) x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Symmetrically, for every morphism of groups \(h : Gm,S \to T\),
\(Lie(h)\) is an \texttt{O\_S}-morphism \(O_{S} = Lie(Gm,S/S) \to t\),
canonically defined by the section

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H = Lie(h)(1) ∈ Γ(S, t).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, if \(h\) is defined by an element \(m \in M*\), one has

\[
H = Lie(h)(1) = m \otimes 1.
\]

Comparing the two definitions, one finds in particular

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α(H) = (h, α) · 1 ∈ Γ(S, O\_S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{1.17.}\label{section-221}

These definitions apply in particular to the case where \(T\) is the
maximal torus of a split group. Each root \(\alpha \in R\) defines an
\emph{infinitesimal root}
\(\alpha \in \operatorname{Hom}_{O_{S}}(t, O_{S})\) with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α(m ⊗ x) = (m, α) x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Each coroot \(\alpha* \in R*\) defines an \emph{infinitesimal coroot}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hα ∈ Γ(S, t),    Hα = α* ⊗ 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For \(\alpha, \beta \in R\), one has the relation

\[
\alpha(H\beta) = (\beta*, \alpha) \cdot 1,
\]

and in particular

\[
\alpha(H\alpha) = 2.
\]

In particular, if \texttt{2} is invertible on \(S\), then \(\alpha\) and
\(H\alpha\) are non-zero on each fiber.

\subsection{2. Existence of a splitting. Type of a reductive
group}\label{existence-of-a-splitting.-type-of-a-reductive-group}

\textbf{Proposition 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). Suppose \(T\) is
split. Then \(G\) is locally splittable relative to \(T\): for every
\(s_{0} \in S\), there exists an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(s_{0}\)
such that the \(U\)-group \texttt{G\_U} is splittable relative to
\texttt{T\_U}.}

Indeed, write \(T \simeq D_{S}(M)\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = ⨿\_\{m ∈ M\} g\^{}m.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(R = { m \in M | m \neq 0, g^{m}(s_{0}) \neq 0}\). Shrinking \(S\)
if necessary (replacing it by an open neighborhood of \(s_{0}\)), we may
suppose that the \(g\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\), are free, and that the
\(g^{m}\), \(m \neq 0\), \(m \notin R\), are zero. We then have

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = t ⨿ ⨿\_\{α ∈ R\} gα,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

with the \(g\alpha\) free of rank 1. It follows that \(R\) is a system
of roots of \(G\) relative to \(T\) (Exp. XIX 3.6). The coroots
\(\alpha*\) corresponding to the \(\alpha \in R\) are then identified
with locally constant functions on \(S\) with values in \(M*\).
Shrinking \(S\) further, we may take them constant, and we are done.

Note that the proof gives immediately:

\textbf{Proposition 2.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a non-empty connected
scheme with \(\operatorname{Pic}(S) = 0\), for example
\(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) or a local scheme (in particular the
spectrum of a field). If \(G\) is an \(S\)-reductive group possessing a
split maximal torus \(T\), then \(G\) is splittable relative to \(T\).}

We deduce immediately from 2.1 and the fact that a reductive group
locally possesses maximal tori for the étale topology (Exp. XIX 2.5):

\textbf{Corollary 2.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group (resp. and \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\)). Then
\(G\) is locally splittable (resp. locally splittable relative to \(T\))
for the étale topology on \(S\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field, \(G\) a
\(k\)-reductive group. There exists a finite separable extension \(K/k\)
such that \texttt{G\_K} is splittable.}

\textbf{Remark 2.5.} \emph{Using 2.1 and the remark Exp. XIX 2.9, one
immediately proves the following result: let \(G = (G, T, M, R)\) be an
\(S\)-split group; there exists a cover of \(S\) by open sets
\texttt{Uᵢ} such that each split group \(G_{U_{i}}\) arises by base
change from a split group over a noetherian ring (in fact, a finitely
generated \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra). We will furthermore prove that every
split group over \(S\) already arises from a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-split group
(Exp. XXV).}

\subsubsection{2.6.}\label{section-222}

Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(G\) a \(k\)-reductive
group. One knows (e.g.~by 2.4) that there exist splittings of \(G\). Let
\((G, T, M, R)\) and \((G, T', M', R')\) be two splittings of \(G\); the
root data \(R(G, T, M, R)\) and \(R(G, T', M', R')\) are then
isomorphic.

Indeed, one sees first that one can reduce to the case where \(T = T'\)
(because there exists \(g \in G(k)\) such that \(T' = int(g) T\), and
one verifies easily that if one transports a splitting by an
automorphism of \(G\), one obtains a root datum isomorphic to the
initial datum); but since \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is connected,
the isomorphism
\(D_{k}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} T \xrightarrow{\sim} D_{k}(M')\) arises
from a unique isomorphism \(M \simeq M'\); for the same reason, there is
at most one system of roots of \(G\) relative to \(T\).

\textbf{Definition 2.6.1.}\footnote{We have added the number 2.6.1 for
  later references.} \emph{If \(G\) is a \(k\)-reductive group (\(k\) an
algebraically closed field), we call} type of \(G\) \emph{the
isomorphism class of the root datum defined by an arbitrary splitting of
\(G\); if \(G\) is a torus, of type \(M\) in the sense of Exp. IX 1.4,
then the type of \(G\) as reductive group is given by the trivial root
datum \((M, M*, \emptyset, \emptyset)\).}

By 1.15 (b),\footnote{We have corrected the original, which referred to
  1.17.} the type is invariant under (algebraically closed) extension of
the base field.

\textbf{Definition 2.7.} \emph{If \(G\) is an \(S\)-reductive group and
\(s \in S\), we call} type of \(G\) at \(s\) \emph{the type of the
\(s\)-reductive group \(G_{s}\).}

For every \(S' \to S\) and every \(s' \in S'\) projecting to
\(s \in S\), the type of \(G_{S'}\) at \(s'\) is equal to the type of
\(G\) at \(s\).

If \(G\) is splittable, and if \((G, T, M, R)\) is a splitting of \(G\),
then the type of \(G\) at \(s\) is the isomorphism class of
\(R(G, T, M, R)\) by 1.15 (b).\footnote{We have corrected the original,
  which referred to 1.17.} It then follows immediately from 2.3:

\textbf{Proposition 2.8.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group
(\(S \neq \emptyset\)). The function}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s ↦ type of G at s}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is locally constant on \(S\). In particular, there is a partition
of \(S\) into non-empty open subschemes such that on each of them \(G\)
is of constant type. More precisely, let \(E\) be the set of types of
the fibers of \(G\); for every \(t \in E\), let \(S_{t}\) be the set of
points \(s \in S\) where \(G\) is of type \(t\); then
\((S_{t})_{t \in E}\) is a partition of \(S\) and each \(S_{t}\) is open
and closed (and non-empty).}

\subsection{3. The Weyl group}\label{the-weyl-group-2}

\subsubsection{3.1.}\label{section-223}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal
torus of \(G\). Then

\[
W_{G}(T) = Norm_{G}(T)/T
\]

is a finite étale \(S\)-group (Exp. XIX 2.5). The morphism
\(n \mapsto int(n)\) induces, by passage to the quotient, a canonical
monomorphism (which is in fact an open immersion):

\[
W_{G}(T) \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(T).
\]

\subsubsection{3.2.}\label{section-224}

Suppose now that \(G\) is splittable relative to \(T\). Choose a
splitting, say \((G, T, M, R)\). We then have a canonical isomorphism
(Exp. VIII 1.5)

\[
\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(T) \simeq (\operatorname{Aut}_{gr.}(M))_{S}.
\]

In particular, if \(W\) is the Weyl group of the root datum \(R(G)\)
(Exp. XXI 1.1.8), we have a monomorphism

\[
W_{S} \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(T).
\]

\subsubsection{3.3.}\label{section-225}

For each root \(\alpha \in R\), the symmetry \(s\alpha \in W\) operates
on \(M\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{sα(x) = x − (α*, x) α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

hence on \(T\) (via the preceding morphism) by

\[
s\alpha(t) = t \cdot \alpha*(\alpha(t))^{-1}.
\]

On the other hand, since \(g\alpha\) is assumed free, there exists
\(X \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\). Consider
\(w\alpha(X) \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) (Exp. XX 3.1). One has (loc. cit.)

\[
int(w\alpha(X))(t) = s\alpha(t).
\]

Since \(W\) is generated by the \(s\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\), it
follows from the preceding remarks that if we regard \(W\) and
\(Norm_{G}(T)(S)/T(S)\) as groups of automorphisms of \(T\), we have

\[
W \subset Norm_{G}(T)(S)/T(S) \subset W_{G}(T)(S).
\]

By definition of the constant group \texttt{W\_S} associated with \(W\)
(cf.~I 1.8), we thus have a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W\_S  ──────────→  W\_G(T)}
\NormalTok{   ↘                ↙}
\NormalTok{       Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \((G, T, M, R)\)
an \(S\)-split group, \(W\) the Weyl group of the root datum \(R(G)\).
Then the canonical monomorphism}

\[
W_{S} \to W_{G}(T) = Norm_{G}(T)/T
\]

\emph{is an isomorphism.}

These are both étale groups over \(S\); it therefore suffices to check
that for every \(s \in S\), \(W_{S}(s) \to W_{G}(T)(s)\) is an
isomorphism.\footnote{Indeed, since \texttt{W\_S} and
  \(W_{G}(T) = Norm_{G}(T)/T\) are étale over \(S\), the morphism
  \(f : W_{S} \to W_{G}(T) = Norm_{G}(T)/T\) is étale (EGA IV₄, 17.3.4);
  if furthermore each \(f_{s}\) is an isomorphism, then, by loc. cit.,
  17.9.1, \(f\) is a surjective open immersion, hence an isomorphism.}
The latter assertion follows, for example, from \emph{Bible}, § 11.3,
th. 2.

\textbf{Remark 3.5.} \emph{Using 2.3, the preceding proposition gives a
new proof of the fact that the Weyl group of a maximal torus of an
\(S\)-reductive group \(G\) is finite over \(S\) (Exp. XIX 2.5
(ii)).}\footnote{Indeed, let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\). The fact
  that \(W_{G}(T)\) is finite over \(S\) is local for the (fpqc)
  topology (EGA IV₂, 2.7.1), so a fortiori for the étale topology. By
  2.3, one may therefore suppose that \(G\) is split relative to \(T\),
  in which case the assertion follows from 3.4.}

\subsubsection{3.6.}\label{section-226}

Under the conditions of 3.1, for every \(w \in W_{G}(T)(S)\), we denote
by \(N_{w}\)\footnote{We have replaced \(Q_{w}\) by \(N_{w}\), just as
  in XX 3.0 we had replaced \(Q\) by \(N\times\).} the fiber product of
the following diagram:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N\_w  ────→  Norm\_G(T)}
\NormalTok{ |              |}
\NormalTok{ ↓              ↓ w}
\NormalTok{ S    ────→  W\_G(T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is an open and closed subscheme of \(Norm_{G}(T)\), which is a
principal homogeneous bundle under \(T\) on the left (resp. on the
right) by the law \((t, q) \mapsto tq\) (resp. \((q, t) \mapsto qt\)).
If \(n \in N_{w}(S)\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{N\_\{ww′\} = n · N\_\{w′\},    N\_\{w′w\} = N\_\{w′\} · n.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.7.}\label{section-227}

In particular, if \(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\) relative to \(T\),
\(N_{s\alpha}\) is none other than what was denoted \(N\times\) in Exp.
XX 3.0. If \(g\alpha\) is free on \(S\), one then has
\(N_{s\alpha}(S) \neq \emptyset\).

By 3.4 and condition (D₂) of the splitting, we deduce:

\textbf{Corollary 3.8.} \emph{Under the conditions of 3.4, the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_G(T)(S) → W\_G(T)(S) = Hom\_\{loc.cons.\}(S, W)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is surjective. In particular, for every \(w \in W\), there exists
\(n_{w} \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) such that \(int(n_{w})|T = w\).}

\subsection{4. Homomorphisms of split
groups}\label{homomorphisms-of-split-groups}

\subsubsection{4.1. The ``big cell''}\label{the-big-cell}

\paragraph{4.1.1.}\label{section-228}

Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split \(S\)-reductive group. Choose a system
of positive roots (Exp. XXI 3.2.1) \(R+\) of the root datum \(R(G)\).
Set \(R- = -R+\).

Choose a total ordering on \(R+\) (resp. \(R-\)) and consider the
morphism induced by the product in \(G\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u : ∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} Uα ×\_S T ×\_S ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} Uα → G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is an open immersion. Indeed, since both sides are flat and of
finite presentation over \(S\), it suffices to verify this on each
geometric fiber (SGA 1, I 5.7 and VIII 5.4); one is thus reduced to the
case where \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field; but,
by \emph{Bible}, § 13.4, cor. 2 to th. 3, \(u\) is radicial and
dominant; since the tangent map of \(u\) at the origin is an isomorphism
(definition of a system of roots), \(u\) is birational; but \(G\) being
normal, one may apply Zariski's ``Main Theorem'' (EGA III₁, 4.4.9) and
\(u\) is an open immersion.

Let us show that the image \(\Omega\) of this open immersion is
independent of the ordering chosen on \(R+\) (resp. \(R-\)). Since this
is a question of comparing open subsets of \(G\), one is reduced to
proving that they have the same geometric points, so one may again
assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Then
the assertion is none other than \emph{Bible}, § 13, prop. 1 (c) and th.
1 (a).

We have thus proved:

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.2.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group. Let \(R+\) be a system of positive roots of \(R\). There exists
an open subset \(\Omega_{R+}\) of \(G\) such that for every total
ordering on \(R+\) (resp. \(R-\)), the morphism induced by the product
in \(G\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} Uα ×\_S T ×\_S ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} Uα → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an open immersion with image \(\Omega_{R+}\).}

\textbf{Remark 4.1.3.} \emph{One can translate 4.1.2 as follows: choose,
for every \(\alpha \in R\), an isomorphism of vector groups
\(p\alpha : Ga,S \xrightarrow{\sim} U\alpha\) (cf.~1.19); then the
morphism (set \(N = Card(R+) = Card(R-)\))}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ga,S\^{}N ×\_S T ×\_S Ga,S\^{}N → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined set-theoretically by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{((xα)\_\{α ∈ R−\}, t, (xα)\_\{α ∈ R+\}) ↦ ∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} pα(xα) · t · ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} pα(xα)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an open immersion whose image depends only on \(R+\) (and not
on the choice of the \(p\alpha\) or the orderings on \(R+\) and
\(R-\)).}

\textbf{Notation 4.1.4.} \emph{We write
\(\Omega_{R+} = \prod_{\alpha \in R-} U\alpha \cdot T \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R+} U\alpha\).}\footnote{And
  we call it the ``big cell'' corresponding to \(R+\).}

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.5.} \emph{The scheme \(\Omega_{R+}\) is of
finite presentation over \(S\) (hence retrocompact in \(G\)) and is
universally schematically dense in \(G\) relative to \(S\) (cf.~Exp.
XVIII 1).}

The first assertion is trivial. Then,\footnote{We have expanded the
  original in what follows.} \(\Omega_{R+}\) is flat and of finite
presentation over \(S\), and contains the unit section, hence meets each
fiber of \(G\) in a non-empty open subset, hence in a dense one; the
second assertion follows from Exp. XVIII 1.3.\footnote{See also EGA IV₃,
  11.10.10.}

\textbf{Corollary 4.1.6.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split
\(S\)-reductive group. Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr(G) = ⋂\_\{α ∈ R\} Ker(α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{We have added the following sentence.}

\emph{Consequently, \(Centr(G)\) is representable by a closed
diagonalizable subgroup of \(G\).}

The second assertion follows immediately from the first. To prove the
latter, one may invoke Exp. XII 4.8 and 4.11; one may also proceed
directly as follows.\footnote{We have expanded the original in what
  follows.}

Let \(S' \to S\). If \(t \in T(S')\) and \(\alpha(t) = 1\) for every
\(\alpha \in R\), then \(int(t)\) induces the identity on \(T_{S'}\) and
on each \((U\alpha)_{S'}\), \(\alpha \in R\), hence also on
\((\Omega_{R+})_{S'}\), hence on \(G_{S'}\) by schematic density, whence
\(t \in Centr(G)(S')\).

Conversely, since \(Centr_{G_{S'}}(T_{S'}) = T_{S'}\) (cf.~Exp. XIX
2.8), if \(g \in G(S')\) centralizes \(T_{S'}\) and the
\((U\alpha)_{S'}\), it is a section of \(T_{S'}\) that annihilates the
\(\alpha \in R\).

\textbf{Corollary 4.1.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. Then the center of \(G\) is representable by a
closed subgroup of \(G\), of multiplicative type; it is also ``the
intersection of the maximal tori of \(G\)'' in the following sense: for
every \(S' \to S\), \(Centr(G)(S')\) is the set of \(g \in G(S')\) whose
inverse image in \(G(S'')\), for every \(S'' \to S'\), is contained in
all the \(T(S'')\), where \(T\) runs through the set of maximal tori of
\(G_{S''}\).}

Taking into account 2.3, the first assertion follows from 4.1.6 by
descent.\footnote{Indeed, the representability of the center by a closed
  subscheme of \(G\) is local for the (fpqc) topology (SGA 1, VIII 5.2
  and 5.4), so a fortiori for the étale topology, and the same holds for
  the property ``of multiplicative type''.} Let us prove the second
assertion. Let \(H\) be ``the intersection of the maximal tori of
\(G\)'' in the preceding sense. One obviously has
\(Centr(G) \subset H\).\footnote{We have expanded the original in what
  follows.} Then, by descent, it suffices to prove \(Centr(G) = H\) in
the case where \(G\) is split. Since \(H\) is contained in the
intersection of the maximal tori of \(G\) in the usual sense, this
follows from the following remark: if \((G, T, M, R)\) is a splitting,
\(\alpha \in R\) and \(X \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\), then
\(int(\exp \alpha(X))(T) \cap T = Ker(\alpha)\), as a trivial
computation shows. (Cf. also Exp. XII 8.6 and 8.8 for a more general
statement.)

\textbf{Remark 4.1.8.} \emph{In what follows, we shall systematically
identify, in the split case, \(T\) with \(D_{S}(M)\). Then \(Centr(G)\)
is none other than \(D_{S}(M/\Gamma_{0}(R))\), where \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\)
is the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(R\) (cf.~Exp. XXI 1.1.6). If
\({\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \cdots, \alpha_{n}}\) is a system of simple
roots of \(R\), one immediately has (cf.~Exp. XX 1.19):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr(G) = ⋂ Ker(αᵢ) = ⋂ Centr(Z\_\{αᵢ\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\((G, T, M, R)\) an \(S\)-split group, \(Q\) an \(S\)-torus,
\(\alpha_{0}\) a character of \(Q\), \(L\) an invertible
\texttt{O\_S}-module,}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : Q → T,    p : W(L) → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{morphisms of groups satisfying the set-theoretic relation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p(α₀(q) x) = int(f(q)) · p(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for all \(q \in Q(S')\), \(x \in W(L)(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Suppose
that \(f\) separates the elements of \(R\) in the following sense: if
\(\alpha, \alpha' \in R\) and \(m, m' \in \mathbb{Z}\), then
\(m \alpha \circ f = m' \alpha' \circ f\) implies
\(m \alpha = m' \alpha'\).\footnote{Note that this is equivalent to the
  hypothesis: if \(\alpha, \alpha' \in R\), \(m, m' \in \mathbb{Z}\) and
  if \((m \alpha \circ f)_{s} = (m' \alpha' \circ f)_{s}\) for every
  geometric point \(s\) of \(S\), then \(m \alpha = m' \alpha'\). In
  particular, this separation hypothesis is stable under base change.}
Finally, let \(s \in S\) be such that \((\alpha_{0})_{s} \neq e\) and
\(p_{s} \neq e\).}

\emph{There then exist an open set \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\), an
integer \(q > 0\) such that \(x \mapsto x^{q}\) is an endomorphism of
\texttt{Ga,U}, a root \(\alpha \in R\), and an isomorphism of
\texttt{O\_U}-modules}

\[
h : (L|U)^{\otimes q} \xrightarrow{\sim} g\alpha|U
\]

\emph{such that}

\emph{(i) \((\alpha \circ f)|U = (q \alpha_{0})|U\),}

\emph{(ii) \(p(X) = \exp \alpha(h(X^{q}))\) for every
\(X \in W(L)(S')\), \(S' \to U\).}

\emph{Moreover, once \(U\) is chosen, \(q\), \(\alpha\) and \(h\) are
uniquely determined.}

Shrinking \(S\) if necessary, we may suppose that \(\alpha_{0}\) is
non-zero on every fiber of \(S\). Choose a system of positive roots
\(R+\) of \(R\) and let \(V = p^{-1}(\Omega_{R+})\). This is an open
subset of \(W(L)\) containing the zero section and stable under
multiplication by every \(\alpha_{0}(q)\), \(q \in Q(S')\),
\(S' \to S\). Since \(\alpha_{0}\) is non-trivial on every fiber, it
follows immediately that \(V = W(L)\), hence that \(p\) factors through
\(\Omega_{R+}\). Choose an arbitrary ordering on \(R+\) and \(R-\); all
products will be taken in this ordering. We thus have unique morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{aα : W(L) → Uα,    α ∈ R,}
\NormalTok{b  : W(L) → T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p(x) = ∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} aα(x) · b(x) · ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} aα(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Writing the covariance condition under \(Q\), one obtains immediately

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{aα(α₀(q) x) = α(f(q)) aα(x),    α ∈ R,}
\NormalTok{b(α₀(q) x)  = b(x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for all \(x \in W(L)(S')\), \(q \in Q(S')\), \(S' \to S\). The second
condition gives at once \(b = e\).

Now let \(\alpha \in R\) be such that \((a\alpha)_{s} \neq e\) (we know
such an \(\alpha\) exists, since \(p_{s}\) is supposed \(\neq e\)).
Applying Exp. XIX 4.12 (a), one deduces that there exists an integer
\(n > 0\) such that \((\alpha \circ f)_{s} = (n \alpha_{0})_{s}\).
Shrinking \(S\), one can assume \(\alpha \circ f = n \alpha_{0}\) (Exp.
IX 5.3). But then, for every \(\alpha' \in R\), \(\alpha' \neq \alpha\),
one has \((\alpha' \circ f)_{s} \neq m \alpha_{0}\) for every integer
\(m > 0\), by virtue of the hypothesis made on \(f\) (and the fact that
the only roots proportional to \(\alpha\) are \(\alpha\) and
\(-\alpha\)). Applying again Exp. XIX 4.12 (a), this time to
\(a\alpha'\), one deduces that \(a\alpha'\) is zero in a neighborhood of
\(S\); since \(R\) is finite, one may, shrinking \(S\) again, suppose
the \(a\alpha'\) zero for \(\alpha' \in R\), \(\alpha' \neq \alpha\).
One then has \(p = a\alpha\), and one may apply Exp. XIX 4.12 (b), then
(c), which gives the announced result (the uniqueness assertions are
obvious).

\textbf{Remark 4.1.10.} \emph{The condition imposed on \(f\) in 4.1.9 is
satisfied in particular when \(f\) is surjective (= faithfully flat).}

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.11.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an
\(S\)-split group, \(R+\) a system of positive roots of \(R\),
\(\Omega_{R+}\) the corresponding ``big cell''.}

\emph{(i) Let \(H\) be a separated \(S\)-group functor\footnote{Recall
  (cf.~Exp. IV, 4.3.5) that an \(S\)-prefunctor \(H\) is separated for a
  topology \(T\) if for every \(S' \to S\) and every family of
  \(S\)-morphisms \((S'_{i} \to S')_{i \in I}\) covering for \(T\), the
  map \(H(S') \to \prod_{i} H(S'_{i})\) is injective.} for (fppf). If
\(f, g : G \Rightarrow H\) are two morphisms of groups that coincide on
\(\Omega_{R+}\), then \(f = g\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-sheaf of groups for (fppf) and
\(f : \Omega_{R+} \to H\) an \(S\)-morphism satisfying the following
condition: for every \(S' \to S\) and every \(x, y \in \Omega_{R+}(S')\)
such that \(xy \in \Omega_{R+}(S')\), one has \(f(xy) = f(x) f(y)\).
There then exists a (unique, by (i)) morphism of groups
\(\bar{f} : G \to H\) extending \(f\).}

Indeed, by 4.1.5, (i) (resp. (ii)) follows immediately from Exp. XVIII
2.2 (resp. 2.3 and 2.4).

\textbf{Remark 4.1.12.} \emph{If \(\alpha \in R+\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(†)    Ω\_\{R+\} ∩ Zα = U\_\{{-}α\} · T · Uα.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{We have expanded the original in what follows.} Indeed, for
every \(S' \to S\), if
\(g = \prod_{\beta \in R-} p\beta(x\beta) \cdot t \cdot \prod_{\beta \in R+} p\beta(x\beta)\)
is an element of \(\Omega_{R+}(S')\) and if \(t' \in T\alpha(S'')\),
then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t′ g t′⁻¹ = ∏\_\{β ∈ R−\} pβ(β(t′) xβ) · t · ∏\_\{β ∈ R+\} pβ(β(t′) xβ)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\) are the only two elements of \(R\)
that take the value 1 on \(T\alpha\), we obtain that \(g\) belongs to
\(Z\alpha = Centr(T\alpha)\) if and only if \(x\beta = 0\) for
\(\beta \neq \pm \alpha\).

By (†), one deduces from XX 2.1 that if \(X \in \Gamma(X, g\alpha)\) and
\(Y \in \Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})\), one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{expα(X) exp\_\{{-}α\}(Y) ∈ Ω\_\{R+\}(S) ⇔ 1 + XY invertible.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{4.2. Morphisms of split
groups}\label{morphisms-of-split-groups}

\textbf{Definition 4.2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme (non-empty),
\((G, T, M, R)\) and \((G', T', M', R')\) two \(S\)-split groups. We say
that the morphism of \(S\)-groups \(f : G \to G'\) is} compatible with
the splittings, \emph{or defines a} morphism of split groups, \emph{if
the restriction of \(f\) to \(T\) factors through a morphism
\(f_{T} : T \to T'\) of the form \(f_{T} = D_{S}(h)\), where
\(h : M' \to M\) is a morphism of groups satisfying the following
condition:}

\emph{there exists a bijection
\(d : R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'\)\footnote{We have replaced the notation
  \(u : R \to R'\) by \(d : R \to R'\).} and for each \(\alpha \in R\)
an integer \(q(\alpha) > 0\) such that \(x \mapsto x^{q(\alpha)}\) is an
endomorphism of \texttt{Ga,S} and that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(d(α)) = q(α) α,    ᵗh(α*) = q(α) d(α)*.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 4.2.2.} \emph{It is immediate that \(h\), \(d\),
\(q(\alpha)\) for \(\alpha \in R\), are uniquely determined by \(f\).
One writes \(h = R(f)\). The \(q(\alpha)\) are the} root exponents
\emph{of \(f\) (or of \(h\)).}

Let \(p\) be the prime number (if it exists) that is zero on \(S\); set
\(p = 1\) if there is no prime number zero on \(S\). Then \(R(f)\) is a
\(p\)-morphism of reduced root data in the sense of Exp. XXI 6.8. One
has thus defined a functor \(R\) from the category of \(S\)-split groups
to that of reduced root data (equipped with \(p\)-morphisms).

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.3.} \emph{Under the conditions of 4.2.1, one has
the following properties:}

\emph{(i) For every \(\alpha \in R\), there exists a unique isomorphism
of \texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\[
f\alpha : (g\alpha)^{\otimes q(\alpha)} \xrightarrow{\sim} g'_{d(\alpha)}
\]

\emph{such that}

\[
f(\exp \alpha(X)) = \exp_{d(\alpha)}(f\alpha(X^{q(\alpha)}))
\]

\emph{for every \(X \in W(g\alpha)(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(\alpha \in R\), one has
\(q(-\alpha) = q(\alpha)\) and \(f\alpha\) and \(f_{-\alpha}\) are
contragredient to one another.}

\emph{(iii) For every \(\alpha \in R\), every \(Z \in W(g\alpha)*(S')\),
\(S' \to S\), one has}

\[
f(w\alpha(Z)) = w_{d(\alpha)}(Z^{q(\alpha)}).
\]

By hypothesis the diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Gm,S  {-}{-}α*{-}{-}\textgreater{}   T   {-}{-}α{-}{-}\textgreater{}   Gm,S}
\NormalTok{ |              |              |}
\NormalTok{ q(α)          f\_T            q(α)}
\NormalTok{ ↓              ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{Gm,S  {-}{-}d(α)*{-}\textgreater{} T′ {-}{-}d(α){-}{-}\textgreater{} Gm,S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is commutative. It follows that \(f\) maps \(Ker(\alpha)\) into
\(Ker(d(\alpha))\), hence \(T\alpha\) into \(T'_{d(\alpha)}\), hence
\(Z\alpha\) into \(Z'_{d(\alpha)}\). There is then nothing more to do
than apply Exp. XX 3.10 and 3.11 to the groups \(Z\alpha\) and
\(Z'_{d(\alpha)}\).

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.4.} \emph{The morphism \(f\) induces a morphism
\(f_{N}\) of \(Norm(T)\) into \(Norm_{G'}(T')\), hence a morphism
\(f_{W}\) of \(W_{G}(T)\) into \(W_{G'}(T')\); the latter is an
isomorphism. More precisely, if we denote by
\(d : W(R(G)) = W \to W' = W(R(G'))\) the isomorphism extending
\(s\alpha \mapsto s_{d(\alpha)}\) (Exp. XXI 6.8.4), we have a
commutative diagram of isomorphisms:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W\_G(T)  {-}{-}f\_W{-}{-}\textgreater{}  W\_\{G′\}(T′)}
\NormalTok{   ↑                  ↑}
\NormalTok{   ≀                  ≀}
\NormalTok{   |                  |}
\NormalTok{  W\_S  {-}{-}d\_S{-}{-}\textgreater{}     W′\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This follows immediately from 3.4, Exp. XXI 6.8.4, and (iii) above.

\textbf{Remark 4.2.5.} \emph{With the notations of 4.2.3, the
restriction of \(f\) to \(\Omega_{R+}\) (for a system of positive roots
\(R+\)) is written explicitly: it maps \(\Omega_{R+}\) to
\(\Omega'_{d(R+)}\) (\(d(R+)\) is a system of positive roots of \(R'\)
by Exp. XXI 6.8.7) and is given by the set-theoretic formula:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} expα(Xα) · t · ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} expα(Xα))}
\NormalTok{  = ∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} exp\_\{d(α)\}(fα(Xα\^{}\{q(α)\})) · f\_T(t) · ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} exp\_\{d(α)\}(fα(Xα\^{}\{q(α)\})).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.6.} \emph{(i) \(f\) is surjective (= faithfully
flat in the present case, cf.~VI\_B 3.11) if and only if \(f_{T}\) is.}

\emph{(ii) One has \(Ker(f) \subset \Omega_{R+}\).}

Let us prove (i): if \(f\) is surjective, then \(f_{T}(T) = f(T)\) is a
maximal torus of \(G'\) (indeed \(f(T)\) is a subtorus of a maximal
torus \(T'\) (Exp. IX 6.8); to verify that \(f(T) = T'\), one reduces to
the case of an algebraically closed field, where this is \emph{Bible}, §
7.3, th. 3 (a)).

If \(f_{T}\) is surjective, the preceding formula shows that \(f\)
induces a surjection from \(\Omega = \Omega_{R+}\) onto
\(\Omega' = \Omega'_{d(R+)}\).\footnote{We have expanded the reference
  to Exp. VI in what follows.} Since the fibers of \(G'\) are connected,
it follows (cf.~Exp. VI\_A, 0.5) that \(f\) is surjective.

Let us prove (ii) and for this admit a result to be proved below
(5.7.4): choose for each \(w \in W\) an \(n_{w} \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\)
representing it; then the open sets \(n_{w} \Omega\) (\(w \in W\)) form
a cover of \(G\). It is then enough to prove that
\(Ker(f) \cap n_{w} \Omega \neq \emptyset\) implies \(w = 1\). If
\(x \in \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\) and \(f(n_{w} x) = 1\), then
\(f(x) = f(n_{w})^{-1}\); but \(f(x) \in \Omega'(S')\) and
\(f(n_{w})^{-1} \in Norm_{G'}(T')(S')\). By 4.2.4, one is reduced to
proving:

\textbf{Lemma 4.2.7.} \emph{Under the conditions of 4.1.2, one has
\(\Omega \cap Norm_{G}(T) = T\).}

Let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x = ∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} pα(xα) · t · ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} pα(xα) = v t u ∈ Ω(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(x\) normalizes \(T_{S'}\), one has for every \(t' \in T(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x t′ x⁻¹ = t′′ ∈ T(S′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, \(x t' = t'' x\), which is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{v (t t′) (t′⁻¹ u t′) = (t′′ v t′′⁻¹) (t′′ t) u,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives \(t'^{-1} u t' = u\), hence
\(u \in Centr_{G}(T)(S') = T(S')\), that is \(u = 1\). Similarly
\(v = 1\).

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.8.} \emph{One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ker(f) = ∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} Kα · Ker(f\_T) · ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} Kα,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where for each \(\alpha \in R\), \(K\alpha\) denotes the finite
\(S\)-group}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Kα = Ker(Uα → Uα\^{}\{⊗q(α)\}) ≃ α\_\{q(α), S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To apply this corollary, let us set:

\textbf{Definition 4.2.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two \(S\)-reductive groups. A morphism of \(S\)-groups \(f : G \to G'\)
that is faithfully flat and finite (i.e.~surjective with finite kernel
over \(S\)) is called an} isogeny. \emph{If moreover \(Ker(f)\) is a
central subgroup of \(G\), one says that \(f\) is a} central isogeny.

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.10.} \emph{Let \(f : G \to G'\) be a morphism of
split groups. For \(f\) to be an isogeny (resp. a central isogeny) it is
necessary and sufficient that \(f_{T}\) be an isogeny, i.e.~that
\(R(f)\) be injective with finite cokernel (resp. and that for every
\(\alpha \in R\), one has \(q(\alpha) = 1\)).}

Indeed, by 4.2.8, \(Ker(f)\) is finite over \(S\) if and only if
\(Ker(f_{T})\) is finite over \(S\), and \(Ker(f) \subset T\) if and
only if each \(q(\alpha) = 1\) (\(Ker(f)\) is then central since of
multiplicative type and invariant, cf.~Exp. IX 5.5).

\textbf{Remark 4.2.11.} \emph{(a) One thus sees that \(f : G \to G'\) is
a central isogeny if and only if \(R(f) : R(G') \to R(G)\) is an isogeny
in the sense of Exp. XXI 6.2; moreover one has in this case (with the
notations of loc. cit.):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ker(f) = D\_S(K(R(f))),    K(R(f)) = Coker(R(f)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(b) If \(G\) and \(G'\) are semisimple, every morphism of split
groups \(f : G \to G'\) is an isogeny.}\footnote{Indeed, since \(G\) and
  \(G'\) are semisimple, \(f_{T}\) is surjective with finite kernel, so
  \(f\) is faithfully flat with finite kernel by 4.2.6 (i) and 4.2.8.}

\emph{(c) If \(f : G \to G'\) is faithfully flat and finite and if \(G\)
is reductive (resp. semisimple), then \(G'\) is also. It is indeed of
finite presentation over \(S\) (Exp. V 9.1), affine over \(S\) (EGA II
6.7.1), smooth over \(S\) (Exp. VI 9.2), with connected reductive (resp.
semisimple) geometric fibers by Exp. XIX 1.7.}

Definition 4.2.1 may seem arbitrary. It is justified by the following
proposition (which we state, for simplicity, for semisimple groups).

We say that a morphism \(f : G \to G'\) of \(S\)-reductive groups is
\emph{splittable} if there exist splittings of \(G\) and \(G'\) with
which \(f\) is compatible. One then has:

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.12.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and
\(G'\) two semisimple \(S\)-groups, \(f : G \to G'\) a morphism of
groups. Let \(s \in S\). The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(Ker f_{s}\) is finite (⇔ \(e\) is isolated in
\texttt{Ker\ f(s)}) and \(f_{s}\) is surjective, i.e.~\(f_{s}\) is an
isogeny.}

\emph{(ii) \(f_{s}\) is splittable.}

\emph{(iii) There exists an étale morphism \(S' \to S\) covering \(s\)
such that \(f_{S'} : G_{S'} \to G'_{S'}\) is splittable.}

One has obviously (iii) ⇔ (ii); (ii) ⇒ (i) follows from 4.2.11 (b) (this
is where the hypothesis that \(G\) and \(G'\) are semisimple intervenes
--- the other implications are valid for reductive groups).

Let us now prove (i) ⇒ (iii). One may suppose \(G\) and \(G'\) split in
such a way that \(f\) induces a morphism \(f_{T} : T \to T'\) (2.3 and
Exp. XIX 2.8); shrinking \(S\), one may suppose that
\(f_{T} = D_{S}(h)\), where \(h\) is a morphism of groups \(M' \to M\).
Let \(\alpha \in R\), and consider the composite morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p : W(gα) {-}{-}expα{-}{-}\textgreater{} G {-}{-}f{-}{-}\textgreater{} G′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(Ker(p_{s})\) is finite, \(p_{s} \neq e\). On the other hand
\(f_{T_{s}}\) is surjective; one may therefore apply 4.1.9, and there
exist an open subset \(V_{\alpha}\) of \(S\) containing \(s\), a root
\(\alpha' \in R'\), an integer \(q(\alpha)\) such that
\(x \mapsto x^{q(\alpha)}\) is an endomorphism of \(Ga,V_{\alpha}\), and
an isomorphism of \(O_{V_{\alpha}}\)-modules

\[
f\alpha : (g\alpha)^{\otimes q(\alpha)}|V_{\alpha} \xrightarrow{\sim} g'_{\alpha'}|V_{\alpha}
\]

such that
\(f(\exp \alpha(X\alpha)) = \exp_{d(\alpha)}(f\alpha(X\alpha^{q(\alpha)}))\)
and \(\alpha' \circ f_{T} = h(\alpha') = q(\alpha) \alpha\). One may
replace \(S\) by the intersection of the \(V_{\alpha}\), for
\(\alpha \in R\). Set \(\alpha' = d(\alpha)\). It is clear that
\(d : R \to R'\) is a bijection, because the kernel of \(h\) is finite
(\(f_{T_{s}}\) being surjective). It only remains to prove that
\(f_{T} \circ \alpha* = q(\alpha) \alpha'*\), which is done by a trivial
modification of the argument used in Exp. XX 3.11.

In any case, as one has seen in the course of the demonstration, one has
(i) ⇒ (iii). Therefore:

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(f : G \to G'\)
an isogeny of reductive groups. Then \(f\) is locally splittable for the
étale topology.}

\subsubsection{4.3. Central quotients of reductive
groups}\label{central-quotients-of-reductive-groups}

Let us first consider a particular case.

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\((G, T, M, R)\) an \(S\)-split group, \(N\) a subgroup of \(M\)
containing \(R\), \(Q = D_{S}(M/N) \subset Centr(G)\). Then:}

\emph{(i) \(G' = G/Q\) is an \(S\)-reductive group, and \(T' = T/Q\) is
a maximal torus of it;}

\emph{(ii) if one identifies \(T'\) with \(D_{S}(N)\), then
\(R \subset N\) is a system of roots of \(G'\) relative to \(T'\),
\((G', T', N, R)\) is a splitting of \(G'\), and \(R(G')\) is
canonically identified with the induced root datum (Exp. XXI 6.5)
\(R(G)^{N}\);}

\emph{(iii) the canonical morphism \(G \to G'\) is compatible with the
splittings, with root exponents 1, and gives by functoriality the
canonical morphism (loc. cit.) \(R(G)^{N} \to R(G)\).}

One knows that \(G' = G/Q\) is representable by an affine group scheme
over \(S\) (Exp. VIII 5.7), smooth over \(S\) (Exp. VI\_B 9.2), with
connected reductive geometric fibers (as quotients of reductive groups,
cf.~Exp. XIX 1.7); \(G'\) is therefore an \(S\)-reductive group.

It is clear that \(T' = T/Q \simeq D_{S}(N)\) is a maximal torus of it.
Note next that, choosing a system of positive roots \(R+\) of \(R\), the
open set \(\Omega_{R+}\) of 4.2 is stable under \(Q\) and that one has a
canonical isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω\_\{R+\}/Q ≃ ∏\_\{α ∈ R−\} Uα ×\_S (T/Q) ×\_S ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} Uα,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and that \(\Omega_{R+}/Q\) is an open subset of \(G'\) containing the
unit section (cf.~Exp. IV, 4.7.2 and 6.4.1).

It follows that, if one denotes by \(g'\) the Lie algebra of \(G'\) and
by \texttt{ᾱ} the character of \(T/Q\) induced by \(\alpha\) (or, which
amounts to the same, defined by \(\alpha \in N\) in the identification
\(T/Q = D_{S}(N)\)), the canonical morphism \(g \to g'\) induces for
each \(\alpha \in R\) an isomorphism

\[
g\alpha \xrightarrow{\sim} g'_{\bar{\alpha}}.
\]

One has thus proved that \(R\) is a system of roots of \(G'\) relative
to \(T'\), and one finishes the proof without difficulty.

\textbf{Corollary 4.3.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(Q\) a normal subgroup of multiplicative type of
\(G\). Then \(Q\) is central in \(G\), the quotient \(G/Q\) is
representable by an \(S\)-reductive group, and the canonical morphism
\(G \to G/Q\) is locally splittable for the étale topology (with root
exponents equal to 1).}

The first assertion follows from Exp. IX 5.5; the others are local for
the étale topology and one is reduced to 4.3.1.

\textbf{Definition 4.3.3.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group.
We say that \(G\) is} adjoint \emph{(resp.} simply connected*) if for
every \(s \in S\), the type of \(G\) at \(s\) is given by an adjoint
(resp. simply connected) root datum, i.e.~(Exp. XXI 6.2.6) such that
\(M\) be generated by \(R\) (resp. \(M*\) generated by \(R*\)).*

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.4.} \emph{(i) An adjoint (resp. simply
connected) reductive group is semisimple.}

\emph{(ii) If \(T\) is a maximal torus of the adjoint (resp. simply
connected) reductive group \(G\) and \(\alpha\) is a root of \(G\)
relative to \(T\), then the infinitesimal root \(\alpha\) is non-zero on
every fiber (resp. \(\alpha*\) is a monomorphism and the infinitesimal
coroot \(H\alpha\) is non-zero on every fiber).}

Indeed, (i) is trivial; (ii) is checked on geometric fibers and follows
immediately from Exp. XXI 6.2.8.

\textbf{Proposition 4.3.5.} \emph{(i) For the reductive group \(G\) to
be adjoint, it is necessary and sufficient that \(Centr(G) = {e}_{S}\).}

\emph{(ii) For every reductive group \(G\), the quotient group
\(G/Centr(G)\) is an adjoint reductive group.}

Indeed, one may suppose \(G\) split; then (i) is trivial (since
\(Centr(G) = D_{S}(M/\Gamma_{0}(R))\)), and (ii) follows from 4.3.1.

\textbf{Definition 4.3.6.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group.
We call} adjoint group of \(G\) \emph{and denote by \(ad(G)\) the group
\(G/Centr(G)\). We call} radical of \(G\) \emph{and denote by \(rad(G)\)
the maximal torus (unique by Exp. XII 1.12) of \(Centr(G)\). We call}
semisimple group associated with \(G\) \emph{the quotient \(G/rad(G)\).}

The preceding definitions are compatible with base change. If
\(s \in S\), \(rad(G)_{s}\) is indeed the radical of \(G_{s}\) in the
usual sense (Exp. XIX 1.6).

\paragraph{4.3.7.}\label{section-229}

If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a split group, then \(rad(G) = D_{S}(M/N)\),
where \(N = M \cap V(R)\), so the semisimple group associated with \(G\)
(and similarly the adjoint group of \(G\)) is equipped with a canonical
splitting (4.3.1) and one has a diagram of split groups

\[
G \to ss(G) \to ad(G)
\]

corresponding to the canonical diagram of root data (Exp. XXI 6.5.5)

\[
ad(R(G)) \to ss(R(G)) \to R(G).
\]

\textbf{Remark 4.3.8.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
adjoint (resp. simply connected) group, \(\Delta\) a system of simple
roots of \(R\). Then the family \({\alpha}_{\alpha \in \Delta}\), resp.
\({\alpha*}_{\alpha \in \Delta}\), induces an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ⥲ (Gm,S)\^{}Δ,    resp.    (Gm,S)\^{}Δ ⥲ T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, \(M = \Gamma_{0}(R)\) (resp. \ldots) and \(\Delta\) is a basis
of the free abelian group \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) (Exp. XXI 3.1.8).

\textbf{Remark 4.3.9.} \emph{The radical of a reductive group is a
characteristic subgroup (i.e.~stable under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\)), by its very definition.}

\subsection{5. Subgroups of type (R)}\label{subgroups-of-type-r}

We are especially interested in reductive groups, but some of the
results we shall establish are valid more generally for a wider class of
groups: groups of type (RR).

\subsubsection{5.1. Groups of type (RR)}\label{groups-of-type-rr}

\textbf{Definition 5.1.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme. We say that \(G\) is} of type (RR) \emph{if it
satisfies the following conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\) and has
connected fibers.}

\emph{(ii) \(G\) locally possesses maximal tori for the (fpqc)
topology.}

\emph{(iii) For every \(s \in S\), every maximal torus \(T\) of
\(G_{s}\), and every root of \(G_{s}\) relative to \(T_{s}\) (Exp. XIX
1.10), \(Lie(G_{s})^{\alpha}\) is of rank 1 (as a vector space over
\(\kappa(s)\)).}

\emph{(iv) For every \(s \in S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of
\(G_{s}\), let \(R\) denote the set of roots of \(G_{s}\) relative to
\(T\) and \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) the subgroup of
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{s-gr.}(T, Gm,s)\) generated by \(R\); then the
content\footnote{The content of the root \(\alpha\) is the positive
  generator of the ideal \({f(\alpha), f \in \Gamma_{0}(R)*}\) of
  \(\mathbb{Z}\); it is the largest integer \(c > 0\) such that
  \(\alpha/c \in \Gamma_{0}(R)\).} of every root \(\alpha \in R\) in the
free abelian group \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) (which is therefore a positive
integer) is invertible on \(S\).}

\textbf{Recall 5.1.1.1.}\footnote{We have added this recall.} \emph{Let
us recall that if \(G\) is a smooth connected algebraic group over an
algebraically closed field \(k\), a} Cartan subgroup \emph{of \(G\) is
the centralizer of a maximal torus of \(G\) (XII 1.0), and such a
subgroup is smooth and connected: for this, as well as for other
characterizations of Cartan subgroups, see Bible, § 7.1, Th. 1 in the
affine case and Exp. XII Th. 6.6 in the general case. If \(S\) is an
arbitrary scheme and \(G\) an \(S\)-smooth group of finite type, a}
Cartan subgroup \emph{of \(G\) is an \(S\)-smooth subgroup \(C\) of
\(G\) such that, for every \(s \in S\), \(C_{s}\) is a Cartan subgroup
of \(G_{s}\) (XII Def. 3.1).}

\textbf{Remark 5.1.2.} \emph{(a) By virtue of Exp. XII 7.1 (where the
hypothesis that \(G\) is separated holds here since \(G\) has connected
fibers, cf.~Exp. VI\_B 5.5), (i) and (ii) entail that \(G\) locally
possesses, for the étale topology, maximal tori (resp. Cartan
subgroups), conjugate locally for the étale topology.}

\emph{(b) The Cartan subgroups of \(G\) have connected fibers (Exp. XII
6.6).}

\emph{(c) If \(G\) is affine over \(S\), (i) and (ii) are respectively
equivalent to}

\emph{(i′) \(G\) is smooth over \(S\) with connected fibers.}

\emph{(ii′) The reductive rank of the fibers of \(G\) is locally
constant (Exp. XII 1.7).}

\emph{(d) By Exp. XII 8.8 (c) and (d), \(G\) has a reductive center
\(Z\) and, for every \(s \in S\), with the notations of (iv), one
has\footnote{The original stated ``under the conditions of (iv)'', but
  the last condition of (iv) does not seem to be used here.}
\(Z_{s} = \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} Ker(\alpha)\), whence}

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{s-gr.}((T/Z)_{s}, Gm,s) \simeq \Gamma_{0}(R).
\]

\emph{(e) Condition (iv) holds in particular in the following two
cases:}

\emph{(1) \(S\) is of characteristic 0;}

\emph{(2) every root is an indivisible element of the group generated by
the roots.}

\emph{(f) Being of type (RR) is stable under base change and is local
for the (fpqc) topology.}

From remarks (c) and (e), one immediately deduces:

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.3.} \emph{A reductive group is of type (RR).}

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group of type (RR), \(Q\) a central subgroup of \(G\) of finite
presentation over \(S\) such that the quotient \(G/Q\) is representable
(for instance \(G\) affine over \(S\) and \(Q\) of multiplicative type
(IX 2.3) or else \(S\) artinian (VI\_A 3.3.2)); then \(G/Q\) is an
\(S\)-group of type (RR).}

Indeed, \(G/Q\) is smooth over \(S\) (Exp. VI\_B 9.2), of finite
presentation over \(S\) (Exp. V 9.1) and with connected fibers, so
condition (i) holds. On the other hand, condition (ii) follows from Exp.
XII 7.6; it remains to verify conditions (iii) and (iv).

Let \(G' = G/Q\), \(u : G \to G'\) the canonical morphism, \(T' = u(T)\)
the maximal torus of \(G'\) image of \(T\) (cf.~Exp. XII 7.1 (e)); for
each \(\alpha \in R\), denote again by \(\alpha\) the character of
\(T'\) defined by \(\alpha\) (one has
\(Q \cap T \subset \bigcap_{\alpha \in R} Ker(\alpha)\) according to
5.1.2 (d)). Let us first prove:

\textbf{Lemma 5.1.5.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.1.4, let
\(T = D_{S}(M)\) be a trivialized maximal torus of \(G\), and suppose
that the decomposition of \(g = Lie(G)\) under \(Ad(T)\) is of the form}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = g⁰ ⨿ ⨿\_\{α ∈ R\} gα,    R ⊂ M − \{0\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where for every \(s \in S\), \(g\alpha(s) \neq 0\) for
\(\alpha \in R\) (so \(g\alpha\) is an invertible \texttt{O\_S}-module
for every \(\alpha \in R\) and \(R\) is the set of roots of \(G_{s}\)
relative to \(T_{s}\) for every \(s \in S\)).}

\emph{Then the Lie algebra \(g'\) of \(G'\) decomposes under \(Ad(T')\)
as follows:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g′ = g′⁰ ⨿ ⨿\_\{α ∈ R\} g′\^{}α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and \(Lie(u)\) induces an isomorphism of \(g\alpha\) onto
\(g'^{\alpha}\).}

Indeed, let \(p = Lie(u) : g \to g'\). One immediately has
\(p(g\alpha) \subset g'^{\alpha}\) for every \(\alpha \in R\), and
\(p(g^{0}) \subset g'^{0}\). Since

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ker(p) = Lie(Q) ⊂ Lie(Centr\_G(T)) = g⁰,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\(p\) induces a monomorphism from \(g\alpha\) into \(g'^{\alpha}\), for
every \(\alpha \in R\).

To prove the lemma, it suffices to do so when \(S\) is the spectrum of
an algebraically closed field, and by virtue of the preceding remarks,
it then suffices to prove that \(rg(g') = rg(g'^{0}) + Card(R)\). Now
set \(C = Centr_{G}(T)\), \(C' = Centr_{G'}(T')\); by Exp. XII 7.1 (e),
\(u\) induces a faithfully flat morphism \(C \to C'\) of kernel \(Q\).
One thus has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim C′ + dim Q = dim C.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \(G\), \(G'\), \(C\) and \(C'\) are smooth, so

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim G = rg(g) = rg(g⁰) + Card(R) = dim C + Card(R)}
\NormalTok{              = dim Q + dim C′ + Card(R) = dim Q + rg(g′⁰) + Card(R)}
\NormalTok{rg(g′) = dim G′ = dim G − dim Q}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which entails

\[
rg(g') = rg(g'^{0}) + Card(R),
\]

that is, the desired relation.

Let us return to the proof of 5.1.4; one may suppose that \(S\) is the
spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Let \(T\) be a maximal torus
of \(G\); applying 5.1.5, one immediately has (iii) and (iv) for
\(G/Q\).

To use the preceding proposition, let us introduce a definition:

\textbf{Definition 5.1.6.} \emph{We say that the \(S\)-group scheme
\(G\) is} of type (RA) \emph{if it is of type (RR) and if it further
satisfies the following condition (iv′) (stronger than (iv)):}

\emph{(iv′) For every \(s \in S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of
\(G_{s}\), every root of \(G_{s}\) relative to \(T\) has a content in
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{s-gr.}(T, Gm,s)\) that is invertible on \(S\).}

\textbf{Remarks 5.1.7.} \emph{(a) An \(S\)-reductive adjoint group is of
type (RA).}

\emph{(b) If \(S\) is of characteristic 0, every group of type (RR) is
of type (RA).}

\emph{(c) Being of type (RA) is stable under base change and is local
for the (fpqc) topology.}

Remark (a) above generalizes to:

\textbf{Proposition 5.1.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group of type (RR), \(Z\) its reductive center, suppose the
quotient \(G/Z\) representable (for instance \(G\) affine over \(S\), or
\(S\) artinian); then \(G/Z\) is of type (RA).}

Indeed, this follows immediately from 5.1.4, 5.1.5, and 5.1.2 (d).

\textbf{Remark 5.1.9.} \emph{If \(G\) is of type (RR) and if \(T\) is a
maximal torus of \(G\), one may apply Exp. XIX 6.3. In particular
\(W_{G}(T)\) is étale, quasi-finite and separated over \(S\).}

\subsubsection{5.2. Subgroups of type (R)}\label{subgroups-of-type-r-1}

\textbf{Definition 5.2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a smooth
\(S\)-group scheme of finite presentation with connected
fibers,\footnote{The hypothesis that \(G\) (resp. \(H\)) be of finite
  presentation over \(S\) is automatically verified because \(G\) (resp.
  \(H\)) being smooth over \(S\) with connected fibers, is quasi-compact
  and separated over \(S\) (VI\_B 5.5), so of finite presentation over
  \(S\).} \(H\) a group subscheme of \(G\). We say that \(H\) is} of
type (R) \emph{if:}

\emph{(i) \(H\) is smooth, of finite presentation over \(S\) and with
connected fibers.\footnote{The hypothesis that \(G\) (resp. \(H\)) be of
  finite presentation over \(S\) is automatically verified because \(G\)
  (resp. \(H\)) being smooth over \(S\) with connected fibers, is
  quasi-compact and separated over \(S\) (VI\_B 5.5), so of finite
  presentation over \(S\).}}

\emph{(ii) For every \(s \in S\), \(H_{s}\) contains a Cartan subgroup
of \(G_{s}\).}

\emph{This notion is stable under base change and local for the (fpqc)
topology.}

\textbf{Recall 5.2.2.} \emph{(cf.~Exp. XII 7.9) Under the preceding
conditions:}

\emph{(a) \(H = Norm_{G}(H)^{0}\).}

\emph{(b) If \(G\) locally possesses, for the étale topology, Cartan
subgroups (resp. maximal tori), so does \(H\), and the Cartan subgroups
(resp. maximal tori) of \(H\) are Cartan subgroups (resp. maximal tori)
of \(G\).}

\textbf{Examples 5.2.3.} \emph{(a) Borel subgroups: a} Borel subgroup
\emph{of \(G\) is a subgroup \(H\) of type (R) whose geometric fibers
are Borel subgroups of those of \(G\).}\footnote{This amounts to saying
  that \(H\) is a smooth subgroup of \(G\), each of whose geometric
  fibers \(H_{s}\) is a Borel subgroup of \(G_{s}\) (since every Borel
  subgroup of \(G_{s}\) is connected and contains a Cartan subgroup of
  \(G_{s}\)).}

\emph{(b) Parabolic subgroups: a} parabolic subgroup \emph{of \(G\) is a
subgroup of type (R) whose geometric fibers contain Borel subgroups.}

Other examples are given by the following propositions.

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.4.} \emph{Let \(G\) be as in 5.2.1,
\(K \subset H\) two group subschemes of \(G\), \(H\) assumed to be of
type (R). Then \(K\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(H\) if and only if
it is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\).}

\footnote{We have expanded what follows.} Indeed, let \(s \in S\). Since
\(H\) is of type (R), every maximal torus of \(H_{s}\) is a maximal
torus of \(G_{s}\), and so likewise for Cartan subgroups.

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.5.} \emph{Let \(G\) be as in 5.2.1, \(T\) a
maximal torus of \(G\), \(Q\) a subtorus of \(T\), \(Z = Centr_{G}(Q)\).
If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\), then
\(H \cap Z\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(Z\).}

Let us first recall that \(Z\) is a closed group subscheme of \(G\), of
finite presentation (Exp. XI 6.11), with connected fibers (Exp. XII
6.6), smooth over \(S\) (Exp. XI 2.4), so it satisfies the conditions
imposed in Definition 5.2.1. Similarly, \(H \cap Z\) is of finite
presentation, smooth and has connected fibers (since
\(H \cap Z = Centr_{H}(Q)\)); moreover
\(H \cap Z \supset Centr_{G}(T)\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group of type (RR) (resp. (RA)), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of
\(G\). Then \(H\) is an \(S\)-group of type (RR) (resp. (RA)).}

Indeed, (i) is clear, (ii) follows from 5.2.2 (b), (iii) and (iv) (resp.
(iv′)) are to be verified when \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically
closed field. Then \(H\) contains a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) (and
hence also \(C = Centr_{G}(T)\)),\footnote{By hypothesis, \(H\) contains
  \(Centr_{G}(T')\) for some maximal torus \(T'\) of \(G\); then \(T\)
  and \(T'\) are conjugate in \(H\), so \(H\) also contains
  \(C = Centr_{G}(T)\).} and the assertions to be proved follow
immediately from:

\textbf{Lemma 5.2.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-group
of type (RR), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\) equipped with a
trivialization \(T \simeq D_{S}(M)\), and suppose that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = g⁰ ⨿ ⨿\_\{α ∈ R\} gα}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(the \(g\alpha\) being then invertible \texttt{O\_S}-modules).}

\emph{Let \(H\) be a subgroup of type (R) containing
\(C = Centr_{G}(T)\) (i.e.~containing \(T\)). Then \(h = Lie(H/S)\) is
locally on \(S\) of the form}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g⁰ + ⨿\_\{α ∈ R′\} gα = g\_\{R′\};}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{more precisely, let, for each \(s \in S\),
\(R'(s) = {\alpha \in R | g\alpha(s) \subset h(s)}\). Then \(R'(s)\) is
a locally constant function of \(s\); if \(U\) is an open subset of
\(S\) on which \(R'(s) = R'\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h\_U = g⁰\_U ⨿ ⨿\_\{α ∈ R′\} gα\_U.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, \(h\) is a submodule of \(g\), locally a direct factor,
containing \(g^{0}\) and stable under \(T\).

\subsubsection{5.3. Strict transporter of two subgroups of type (R).
Applications}\label{strict-transporter-of-two-subgroups-of-type-r.-applications}

\textbf{Recall 5.3.0.}\footnote{We have added this recall, which is used
  in the proofs of 5.3.1 and 5.3.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\)
an \(S\)-smooth group, \(g = Lie(G/S)\) and \(h\) a
sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module of \(g\) that is locally a direct factor. The
\texttt{O\_S}-algebra \(A = Sym(\omega^{1}_{G/S})\) is locally free, so
the \(S\)-scheme \(Lie(G/S) = W(g) = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\) is
essentially free in the sense of Exp. VIII, 6.1. Since \(W(h)\) is a
closed subscheme of \(Lie(G/S)\), of finite presentation over
\(Lie(G/S)\), then \(N = Norm_{G}(h)\) is representable by a closed
group subscheme of \(G\), of finite presentation over \(G\), by Exp.
VIII, 6.5 (a). (See also the additions 6.2.3 and 6.2.4 (a) in Exp.
VI\_B.) On the other hand, by Exp. II 5.3.1, one has
\texttt{Lie(N/S)\ =\ Norm\_\{Lie(G/S)\}(h)}.}

\emph{Finally, by Exp. VI\_B 3.10, if \(N\) is smooth over \(S\) at the
points of the unit section, then the group subfunctor \(N^{0}\) (defined
in VI\_B 3.1) is represented by an open group subscheme of \(N\), smooth
over \(S\).}

\textbf{Proposition 5.3.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group of type (RA) (5.1.6), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\),
\(g \supset h\) their Lie algebras.}

\emph{Then \(Norm_{G}(h)\) (which is representable by a closed subscheme
of \(G\) of finite presentation over \(S\) according to 5.3.0) is smooth
over \(S\) at every point of the unit section, and one has}

\[
Norm_{G}(h)^{0} = H.
\]

\footnote{We have expanded the original in what follows.} Proof. Set
\(N = Norm_{G}(h)\) and \(n = Lie(N/S)\). One has \(H \subset N\) and,
by Exp. II 5.3.1, one has for every \(s \in S\)

\[
h(s) \subset n(s) = Norm_{g(s)}(h(s)).
\]

Now, by 5.3.2 below, one has \(h(s) = Norm_{g(s)}(h(s))\), and since
\(H\) is smooth over \(S\), one has
\(\dim_{\kappa(s)} h(s) = \dim H_{s}\) (cf.~{[}DG70{]}, § II.5, Th.
2.1). One thus obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim\_\{κ(s)\} n(s) = dim\_\{κ(s)\} h(s) = dim H\_s ⩽ dim N\_s}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(N^{0}_{s} = H^{0}_{s} = H_{s}\) (\(H\) having connected
fibers). It follows that the group subfunctor \(N^{0}\) (defined in
VI\_B, 3.1) is represented by the smooth \(S\)-group \(H\). This proves
5.3.1, modulo the following lemma:

\textbf{Lemma 5.3.2.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.2.7, if \(G\) is
of type (RA), one has, for every \(s \in S\),}

\[
Norm_{g(s)}(h(s)) = h(s).
\]

Indeed, one is reduced to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a
field, so where \(h = g_{R'}\) for some \(R' \subset R\). But one
already has

\[
Transp_{g}(t, h) = h.
\]

Indeed, if \(H \in t\) and \(X \in g\alpha\), one has
\([H, X] = \alpha(H) X\), where \(\alpha : t \to O_{S}\) is the derived
morphism of \(\alpha\). Now condition (iv′) says precisely that
\(\alpha \neq 0\) for every \(\alpha \in R\).

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group of type (RA), \(H\) and \(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) of
\(G\), \(h\) and \(h'\) their Lie algebras. Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H = H′ ⇔ h = h′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.4.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.2.7, with
\(G\) of type (RA), the maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ↦ Lie(H/S),    h ↦ Norm\_G(h)⁰}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{realize a bijective correspondence between the set of subgroups of
type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\) and the set of Lie subalgebras of
\(g\) containing \(g^{0}\), stable under \(T\), and whose normalizer in
\(G\) is smooth over \(S\) at every point of the unit section.}

\footnote{We have added the following proof.} Indeed, let \(h\) be a Lie
subalgebra of \(g\) having the above properties. By 5.3.0,
\(H = Norm_{G}(h)^{0}\) is a smooth \(S\)-group scheme. Moreover, since
\(C = Centr_{G}(T)\) stabilizes each \(g\alpha\) and has connected
fibers (XII 6.6), one has \(C \subset H\). Therefore \(H\) is a subgroup
of \(G\) of type (R). By Exp. II 5.3.1, one has
\(Lie(H) = Norm_{g}(h)\). Finally, by the proof of 5.3.2, one has
\(Norm_{g}(h) = h\).

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group of type (RR) (5.1.1), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(H\)
and \(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\), both containing \(T\).
Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H = H′ ⇔ h = h′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By virtue of the finite presentation hypotheses, one reduces as usual
(cf.~EGA IV₃, § 8 and Exp. VI\_B § 10) to the case where \(S\) is
noetherian; it suffices then to verify that \(h = h'\) implies
\(H_{S'} = H'_{S'}\) for every \(S'\) spectrum of an artinian quotient
of a local ring of \(S\);\footnote{Indeed, let \(g \in G\), \(s\) its
  image in \(S\), \(m\) the maximal ideal of \(O_{G,g}\), \(n\) that of
  \(O_{S,s}\), and \(I\) (resp. \(I'\)) the kernel of the morphism of
  \(O_{G,g}\) into \(O_{H,g}\) (resp. \(O_{H',g}\)) (the latter being
  the zero ring if \(g \notin H\), resp. \(g \notin H'\)). Since
  \(O_{G,g}\) is noetherian, \(I\) and \(I'\) are closed for the
  \(m\)-adic topology, so a fortiori for the \(n\)-adic topology, so it
  suffices to show that \(I + n^{n} O_{G,g} = I' + n^{n} O_{G,g}\) for
  every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).} one is thus reduced to the case where
\(S\) is artinian, and one may apply 5.1.8. Let \(u : G \to G' = G/Z\)
be the canonical morphism and \(T' = T/Z\) the maximal torus of \(G'\)
corresponding to \(T\). By Exp. XII 7.12, there exist subgroups of type
(R) \(H_{1}\) and \(H'_{1}\) of \(G'\), containing \(T'\), such that
\(H = u^{-1}(H_{1})\) and \(H' = u^{-1}(H'_{1})\). It suffices to prove
that \(H_{1} = H'_{1}\). But by 5.2.7 and 5.1.5, one has

\[
Lie(H_{1}) = Lie(H'_{1}),
\]

and one reduces to 5.3.3.

\textbf{Remark 5.3.6.} \emph{The fact that \(H\) and \(H'\) contain the
same maximal torus is essential for the validity of 5.3.5 when \(G\) is
not of type (RA). Example: maximal tori of \(SL_{2},k\) for \(k\) of
characteristic 2.}\footnote{Indeed, if \(k\) is algebraically closed,
  all the maximal tori of \(G = SL_{2},k\) are conjugate under \(G(k)\),
  and all have for Lie algebra the line \(k \cdot id \subset M_{2}(k)\)
  (which is invariant under the adjoint action).}

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group of type (RR), \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(H\) and
\(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\), both containing \(T\). The
set \(U\) of \(s \in S\) such that \(H_{s} = H'_{s}\) is open and closed
in \(S\) and \(H_{U} = H'_{U}\).}

Indeed, this follows immediately from 5.3.5 and 5.2.7.

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.8.} \emph{The ``functor of subgroups of type (R)
containing \(T\)'', where \(T\) is a given maximal torus in a group
\(G\) of type (RR), is formally unramified (Exp. XI 1.1).}

\textbf{Theorem 5.3.9.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type (RR)
(5.1.1), \(H\) and \(H'\) two subgroups of type (R) (5.2.1). Let
\(Transt_{G}(H, H')\) be the strict transporter of \(H\) into \(H'\)
defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Transt\_G(H, H′)(S′) = \{g ∈ G(S′) | int(g) H\_\{S′\} = H′\_\{S′\}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(Transt_{G}(H, H')\) is representable by a closed subscheme
of \(G\), which is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\).}

The fact that \(Transt_{G}(H, H')\) is representable by a closed
subscheme of \(G\), of finite presentation over \(S\), follows from Exp.
XI 6.11 (a). To prove that it is smooth over \(S\), we must show that if
\(S\) is affine and \(S_{0}\) is the closed subscheme defined by a
nilpotent ideal \(J\), and if \(g_{0} \in G(S_{0})\) and
\(int(g_{0}) H_{0} = H'_{0}\), there exists \(g \in G(S)\) projecting to
\(g_{0}\) and such that \(int(g) H = H'\). Since the question of
smoothness is local for the étale topology, we may suppose that \(H\)
contains a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\).

Then \(T_{0}\) is a maximal torus of \(H_{0}\), hence
\(int(g_{0}) T_{0}\) is a maximal torus of \(H'_{0}\). By Exp. IX 3.6
bis, there exists a torus \(T'\) of \(H'\) such that
\(T'_{0} = int(g_{0}) T_{0}\); by Exp. IX 3.3 bis, there thus exists
\(g \in G(S)\) projecting to \(g_{0}\) and such that \(int(g) T = T'\).
Replacing \(H\) by \texttt{int(g)\ H} if necessary, we may therefore
suppose that \(H\) and \(H'\) contain the same maximal torus \(T\) and
that \(H_{0} = H'_{0}\). But then \(H = H'\) by 5.3.7. QED.

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.10.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type
(RR), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\). Then \(Norm_{G}(H)\) is
representable by a closed group subscheme of \(G\), of finite
presentation and smooth over \(S\).}

Using now the reasoning that, in Exp. XI, served to deduce 5.4 bis from
5.2 bis, one obtains:

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.11.} \emph{Under the hypotheses of 5.3.9, the
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(H\) and \(H'\) are locally conjugate in \(G\) for the étale
topology.}

\emph{(i bis) idem for the (fpqc) topology.}

\emph{(ii) For every \(s \in S\), \(H_{s}\) and \(H'_{s}\) are conjugate
by an element of \(G(s)\).}

\emph{(ii bis) The structural morphism \(Transt_{G}(H, H') \to S\) is
surjective.}

\emph{(iii) \(Transt_{G}(H, H')\) is a principal homogeneous bundle
under the action of the smooth \(S\)-group scheme of finite presentation
\(Norm_{G}(H)\).}

Let us simply remark that the non-trivial assertion (iii) ⇒ (i) is
Hensel's lemma.

Using now Bible, § 6.4, th. 4 (= {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.5 th. 5) and § 9.3, th.
1, one obtains by 5.3.10 and 5.3.11:

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.12.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type
(RR). The Borel subgroups of \(G\) are closed in \(G\), equal to their
normalizer, and conjugate locally for the étale topology.}

\textbf{Definition 5.3.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a smooth
\(S\)-group scheme of finite presentation with connected
fibers.\footnote{Cf. footnote (25).} By a} Killing couple \emph{of \(G\)
we mean a couple \(T \subset B\), where \(T\) is a maximal torus of
\(G\) and \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\).}

Using now the conjugacy of the maximal tori in \(B\) (cf.~5.1.2 (a) and
5.2.6, for example), one has:

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.14.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type
(RR). The Killing couples of \(G\) are conjugate locally for the étale
topology.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.15.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type
(RR). Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\),
\(W_{G}(T) = Norm_{G}(T)/Centr_{G}(T)\) the corresponding Weyl group
(Exp. XIX 6.3). The ``functor of Borel subgroups of \(G\) containing
\(T\)'' is formally principal homogeneous under \(W_{G}(T)\).}

This follows immediately from 5.3.14 and from the fact that if \(B\) is
a Borel subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\), one has

\[
Norm_{G}(T) \cap B = Centr_{G}(T),
\]

cf.~Exp. XIV 4.4.

\textbf{Proposition 5.3.16.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type
(RR), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R), \(N = Norm_{G}(H)\) its normalizer
(5.3.10). Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(H\), \(W_{H}(T)\) and
\(W_{N}(T)\) the corresponding Weyl groups (étale, quasi-finite,
separated by Exp. XIX 6.3). One has the following exact sequence of
sheaves (for the étale topology) (the morphisms are induced by the
morphisms \(Norm_{H}(T) \to Norm_{N}(T) \to N/H\)):}

\[
1 \to W_{H}(T) \to W_{N}(T) \to N/H \to 1.
\]

The only non-trivial point is that the last arrow is an epimorphism. So
let \(n \in N(S')\), \(S' \to S\). The two maximal tori \(T\) and
\texttt{int(n)\ T} of \(H\) are conjugate in \(H\) locally for the étale
topology. There thus exists a covering family \({S'_{i} \to S'}\) and
for each \(i\) an \(h_{i} \in H(S'_{i})\) such that
\(int(h_{i}) T = int(n) T\). Hence \(n h^{-1}_{i} \in Norm_{N}(T)\),
which gives the desired result.

\textbf{Remark 5.3.17.} \emph{One can describe \(W_{N}(T)\) as follows:
suppose we are reduced to the situation of 5.2.7, with \(h = g_{R'}\).
Then \(W_{N}(T)\) equals \(Norm_{W}(R')\), the sheaf of sections of
\(W = W_{G}(T)\) that, acting on \(R\), normalize \(R'\). Indeed, by
5.3.5, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_N(T) = Norm\_G(H) ∩ Norm\_G(T) = Norm\_G(h) ∩ Norm\_G(T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.18.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-group of type
(RR), \(H\) a subgroup of type (R). Suppose that ``the Weyl groups of
\(G\) are finite'', i.e.~that for every \(S' \to S\) and every maximal
torus \(T\) of \(G_{S'}\), the étale \(S'\)-scheme
\(Norm_{G_{S'}}(T)/Centr_{G_{S'}}(T)\) is finite (cf.~Exp. XIX 6.3
(iii)). The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(H\) is closed in \(G\).}

\emph{(ii) \(Norm_{G}(H)/H\) is representable by a finite étale
\(S\)-scheme.}

\emph{(iii) ``The Weyl groups of \(H\) are finite''.}

Indeed, one may suppose that \(H\) possesses a maximal torus \(T\). By
5.3.10, \(N = Norm_{G}(H)\) is closed in \(G\), so \(W_{N}(T)\) is
closed in \(W_{G}(T)\) and hence finite over \(S\). One obviously has
(i) ⇒ (iii), and (iii) ⇒ (ii) by the exact sequence of 5.3.16. Finally,
(ii) ⇒ (i), because if \(N/H\) is finite, it is separated, so \(H\) is
closed in \(N\), hence in \(G\).

\textbf{Remark 5.3.19.} \emph{When \(G\) is reductive, the preceding
conditions on \(H\) seem always satisfied. We prove them below in most
cases.}

\subsubsection{5.4. Subgroups of type (R) of a split reductive group
(generalities)}\label{subgroups-of-type-r-of-a-split-reductive-group-generalities}

\paragraph{5.4.1.}\label{section-230}

If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of the reductive group \(G\), then
\(H\) contains locally, for the étale topology, a maximal torus of \(G\)
(5.2.2). By 2.3, one may, locally for the étale topology, suppose \(G\)
split relative to this torus. Let then \((G, T, M, R)\) be an
\(S\)-split group, \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) containing
\(T\). By 5.3.5, such a subgroup is characterized by its Lie algebra,
which (5.2.7) is locally on \(S\) of the form \(g_{R'}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_\{R′\} = t ⨿ ⨿\_\{α ∈ R′\} gα.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 5.4.2.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group. We shall say that the subset \(R'\) of \(R\) is} of type (R)
\emph{if \(g_{R'}\) is the Lie algebra of a subgroup of type (R) of
\(G\) containing \(T\). This subgroup, uniquely determined by \(R'\), is
denoted \(H_{R'}\).}

\textbf{Lemma 5.4.3.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, one has the
following equivalences:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ∩ Zα = T  ⇔  α ∉ R′,  −α ∉ R′,}
\NormalTok{H ⊃ Uα     ⇔  α ∈ R′,}
\NormalTok{H ∩ Uα = e  ⇔  α ∉ R′,}
\NormalTok{H ⊃ Zα     ⇔  α ∈ R′,  −α ∈ R′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, \(H \cap Z\alpha\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(Z\alpha\), by
5.2.5; but a subgroup of type (R) of \(Z\alpha\) containing \(T\) is
locally equal to one of the following subgroups: \(T\),
\(T \cdot U\alpha\), \(T \cdot U_{-\alpha}\), \(Z\alpha\), by 5.3.5.

\textbf{Lemma 5.4.4.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.4.2, let \(R+\) be
a system of positive roots; choose orderings on \(R' \cap R+\) and
\(R' \cap -R+\). The morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω\_\{R+, R′\} = ∏\_\{α ∈ R′ ∩ −R+\} Uα ×\_S T ×\_S ∏\_\{α ∈ R′ ∩ R+\} Uα → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induced by the product in \(G\) induces an open immersion}

\[
\Omega_{R+, R'} \to H_{R'}.
\]

Indeed, by 5.4.3, this morphism factors through \(H_{R'}\) and thus
induces an immersion \(\Omega_{R+, R'} \to H_{R'}\). One then argues as
in 4.1.1.

\textbf{Proposition 5.4.5.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group. Let \(R'\) and \(R''\) be two subsets of \(R\) of type (R).}

\emph{(i) \(H_{R'} \cap H_{R''}\) is smooth at every point of the unit
section, \(R' \cap R''\) is of type (R), and one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(H\_\{R′\} ∩ H\_\{R′′\})⁰ = H\_\{R′ ∩ R′′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) One has the equivalence}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\_\{R′\} ⊂ H\_\{R′′\}  ⇔  R′ ⊂ R′′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, (ii) follows immediately from (i). To prove (i), it suffices to
show that \(H_{R'} \cap H_{R''}\) is smooth at every point of the unit
section: its neutral component (cf.~Exp. VI\_B 3.10) will then be a
subgroup of type (R) containing \(T\), hence equal to
\(H_{R' \cap R''}\); but
\(\Omega_{R+, R'} \cap \Omega_{R+, R''} = \Omega_{R+, R' \cap R''}\) is
an open subset of \(H_{R'} \cap H_{R''}\) containing the unit section
and smooth over \(S\).

\textbf{Corollary 5.4.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(s\) a point of
\(S\). If \(H\) and \(H'\) are two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\)
containing \(T\) such that \(H_{s} \subset H'_{s}\), there exists an
open subset \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) such that
\(H_{U} \subset H'_{U}\).}

Indeed, one may suppose \(G\) split relative to \(T\). The assertion
then follows immediately from 5.4.5 (ii).

One is led to ask which subsets \(R'\) of \(R\) are of type (R). One may
suppose the group adjoint; one then has to verify that \(g_{R'}\) is a
Lie algebra and that its normalizer is smooth at every point of the unit
section. The most important case is given by:

\textbf{Theorem 5.4.7.} \emph{Every closed subset \(R'\) of \(R\) is of
type (R). (Recall, cf.~Exp. XXI 3.1.4, that \(R' \subset R\) is called}
closed \emph{if \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\), \(\alpha + \beta \in R\)
entail \(\alpha + \beta \in R'\).)}

\textbf{Remark 5.4.8.} \emph{We shall see later (Exp. XXIII 6.6) that if
\(6 \cdot 1_{S} \neq 0\)\footnote{In fact, it suffices (cf.~loc. cit.)
  that 2 and 3 be non-zero on \(S\).} (for example, if \(S\) has residue
characteristic distinct from 2 and 3), the fact that \(g_{R'}\) is a Lie
algebra already entails that \(R'\) is closed, so \(R'\) is of type (R)
if and only if it is closed. Theorem 5.4.7 thus gives all subsets of
type (R) ``independent of the characteristic''.}

Let us first prove:

\textbf{Lemma 5.4.9.} \emph{Choose for each \(\alpha \in R\) an
\(X\alpha \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\). Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\),
with \(\alpha + \beta \neq 0\) and let \(q\) be the largest integer
\(i\) such that \(\alpha + i\beta \in R\). There exist sections
\(M\alpha,\beta,i \in \Gamma(S, O_{S})\), uniquely determined, such
that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(expα(xXα))(Xβ) = Xβ + ∑\_\{i=1\}\^{}\{q\} Mα,β,i x\^{}i X\_\{β+iα\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(x \in Ga(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

Indeed, \(x \mapsto Ad(\exp \alpha(xX\alpha))(X\beta)\) defines a
morphism \(Ga,S \to W(g) \simeq Gm_{a,S}\). There thus exist sections
\(Y_{n} \in \Gamma(S, g)\), uniquely determined, such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(expα(xXα))(Xβ) = ∑\_\{n ⩾ 0\} x\^{}n Y\_n.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Applying the inner automorphism defined by a section \(t\) of \(T\), one
finds immediately

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(t)(Y\_n) = β(t) α(t)\^{}n Y\_n,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which entails \(Y_{n} \in \Gamma(S, g^{\beta+n\alpha})\). Since
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are not proportional, none of the
\(\beta + n\alpha\) is zero; one thus has \(Y_{n} = 0\) for \(n > q\),
\(Y_{n} = M\alpha,\beta,n X_{\beta+n\alpha}\) for
\(0 \leqslant n \leqslant q\), where \(M\alpha,\beta,n \in Ga(S)\) is
uniquely determined. Setting \(x = 0\) in the formula obtained, one
finds \(Y_{0} = X\beta\), which completes the proof.

\textbf{Remark 5.4.10.} \emph{Differentiating the preceding formula at
\(x = 0\), one finds}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[Xα, Xβ] = \{ Nα,β X\_\{α+β\},  where Nα,β = Mα,β,1, if α + β ∈ R,}
\NormalTok{           \{ 0                                  if α + β ∉ R, α + β ≠ 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us now prove 5.4.7. If \(R'\) is a closed subset of \(R\), then
\(g_{R'}\) is a Lie subalgebra of \(g\), by 5.4.10 and Exp. XX 2.10,
formula (3). By 5.4.9 and Exp. XX 2.10, formula (2), \(U\alpha\)
normalizes \(g_{R'}\) for each \(\alpha \in R'\). Choose a system of
positive roots \(R+\) and consider the open set \(\Omega_{R+}\) of
4.1.2; let \(\Omega_{R+, R'}\) be the closed subscheme of
\(\Omega_{R+}\) defined as follows:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω\_\{R+, R′\} = ∏\_\{α ∈ R′ ∩ −R+\} Uα · T · ∏\_\{α ∈ R′ ∩ R+\} Uα.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The canonical immersion \(\Omega_{R+, R'} \to G\) factors through
\(i : \Omega_{R+, R'} \to Norm_{G}(g_{R'})\). Suppose \(G\) adjoint; the
tangent map of \(i\) at the points of the unit section is bijective by
5.3.2; in particular, the morphism \(i\) is étale at every point of the
unit section, hence is a local immersion\footnote{By EGA IV₄, 17.11.2,
  \(i\) is étale at every point of the unit section (and
