  \(Norm_{G}(g_{R'})\) is smooth at every point of the unit section).
  Furthermore, let \(V\) be the largest open subset of
  \(\Omega_{R+, R'}\) on which \(i\) is étale; since \(i\) is a
  monomorphism, \(i_{V}\) is an open immersion (ibid., 17.9.1).} at
every point of the unit section, hence \(Norm_{G}(g_{R'})\) is smooth at
every point of the unit section, as was to be shown.

\subsubsection{5.5. Borel subgroups of a split reductive
group}\label{borel-subgroups-of-a-split-reductive-group}

\textbf{Proposition 5.5.1.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group. For every system of positive roots \(R+\) of \(R\), \(H_{R+}\)
(which exists by 5.4.7) is a Borel subgroup of \(G\) and, for every
ordering on \(R+\), the morphism induced by the product in \(G\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ×\_S ∏\_\{α ∈ R+\} Uα → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a closed immersion with image \(H_{R+}\). One writes
\(B_{R+} = H_{R+}\).}

By definition of the Borel subgroups, the first assertion may be
verified by replacing \(S\) by the spectrum of an algebraically closed
field. Let \(B\) be the Borel subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) and
corresponding to the system of positive roots \(R+\) (Bible, § 10.4,
prop. 9); the Lie algebra of \(B\) is \(g_{R+}\); one therefore has
\(B = H_{R+}\) by 5.3.5.

Let us prove the second assertion: the morphism in the statement induces
an open immersion
\(i : T \times_{S} \prod_{\alpha \in R+} U\alpha \to H_{R+}\) (5.4.4).
Now \(i\) is surjective (Bible, § 15.1, cor. 1 to prop. 1).

\textbf{Corollary 5.5.2.} \emph{Choose an arbitrary ordering on \(R+\)
and for each \(\alpha \in R+\) an
\(X\alpha \in \Gamma(S, g\alpha)\times\). Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R+\).
For each pair \((i, j) \in \mathbb{N}* \times \mathbb{N}*\) such that
\(i\alpha + j\beta \in R\), there exists a unique section}

\[
C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta} \in \Gamma(S, O_{S})
\]

\emph{such that, for all \(x, y \in Ga(S')\), \(S' \to S\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{expα(xXα) expβ(yXβ) expα(xXα)⁻¹ =}
\NormalTok{    expβ(yXβ) ∏\_\{i,j ∈ ℕ*, iα+jβ ∈ R\} exp\_\{iα+jβ\}(C\_\{i,j,α,β\} x\^{}i y\^{}j X\_\{iα+jβ\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(\alpha = \beta\), the assertion is trivial. Suppose therefore
\(\alpha \neq \beta\); then, by virtue of the proposition, there exist
unique morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F₀ : G²\_\{a,S\} → T,    Fγ : G²\_\{a,S\} → Ga,S    (γ ∈ R+)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{exp(xXα) exp(yXβ) exp(xXα)⁻¹ = F₀(x, y) ∏\_\{γ ∈ R+\} exp(Fγ(x, y) Xγ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Let \(int(t)\) act on this formula;
one immediately has the relations

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(1)   F₀(α(t) x, β(t) y) = F₀(x, y),}
\NormalTok{(2)   Fγ(α(t) x, β(t) y) = γ(t) Fγ(x, y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are two linearly independent characters
(over \(\mathbb{Q}\)) of \(T\), one concludes as usual from the first
relation that \(F_{0}\) is constant, so \(F_{0}(x, y) = e\). Write next

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Fγ(x, y) = ∑ aᵢⱼ x\^{}i y\^{}j,    with aᵢⱼ ∈ Γ(S, O\_S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Substituting in relation (2) and identifying the polynomials of the two
sides, one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{aᵢⱼ (α(t)\^{}i β(t)\^{}j − γ(t)) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(\gamma \neq i\alpha + j\beta\), one knows (Exp. XIX 4.13) that
there exists an \(S' \to S\) faithfully flat quasi-compact and a
\(t \in T(S')\) such that
\(\alpha(t)^{i} \beta(t)^{j} - \gamma(t) = 1\). One thus has
\(a_{ij} = 0\) on \(S'\), hence on \(S\). If
\(\gamma = i\alpha + j\beta\), one sets
\(a_{ij} = C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\). Setting \(x = 0\) (resp. \(y = 0\)),
one finds \(C_{0,1,\alpha,\beta} = 1\) (resp.
\(C_{1,0,\alpha,\beta} = 0\)).

\textbf{Remark 5.5.3.} \emph{Differentiating at \(y = 0\) and comparing
with 5.4.9, one finds}

\[
C_{i,1,\alpha,\beta} = M\alpha,\beta,i.
\]

\textbf{Corollary 5.5.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\),
\(\alpha \neq \beta\) two roots of \(G\) relative to \(T\) such that
\(\alpha + \beta\) is non-trivial on every fiber. Order the set of
\(i\alpha + j\beta\) (\(i, j \in \mathbb{N}*\)) in an arbitrary way. For
all \(i, j \in \mathbb{N}*\) such that \(i\alpha + j\beta \in R\), there
exists a unique morphism of \texttt{O\_S}-modules}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{fα,β,i,j : (gα)\^{}\{⊗i\} ⊗ (gβ)\^{}\{⊗j\} → g\^{}\{iα+jβ\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that for every \(S' \to S\) and every
\(X \in W(g\alpha)(S')\), \(Y \in W(g\beta)(S')\) one has (the
\texttt{exp} on the right being taken in the sense of 1.2\footnote{That
  is, if \(g^{i\alpha+j\beta} = 0\) on a connected component of \(S\),
  the corresponding exponential is 1 on this component.}):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{expα(X) expβ(Y) expα(−X) = expβ(Y) ∏\_\{(i,j)\} exp\_\{iα+jβ\}(fα,β,i,j(X\^{}i ⊗ Y\^{}j)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The assertion is local for (fpqc). By § 2, one may therefore suppose
\(G\) split relative to \(T\), and \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) constant in
the splitting. Since \(\alpha + \beta \neq 0\), there exists a system of
positive roots \(R+\) containing \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (Exp. XXI
3.5.4), and one is reduced to 5.5.2.

\textbf{Corollary 5.5.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) \(G\) possesses Borel subgroups locally for the étale
topology. If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), then \(G\) also
possesses Borel subgroups containing \(T\) locally for the étale
topology.}

\emph{(ii) If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), the ``functor of Borel
subgroups of \(G\) containing \(T\)'' is representable by a principal
homogeneous bundle under \(W_{G}(T)\).}

\emph{(iii) If \((G, T, M, R)\) is split, every Borel subgroup \(B\) of
\(G\) containing \(T\) is locally on \(S\) of the form \(B_{R+}\), where
\(R+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\).}

\emph{(iv) If \(T \subset B\) is a Killing couple of \(G\), there exists
a covering family \({S_{i} \to S}\) for the étale topology, and for each
\(i\) a splitting \((G_{S_{i}}, T_{S_{i}}, M_{i}, R_{i})\) and a system
of positive roots \(R_{i+}\) of \(R_{i}\) such that
\(B_{S_{i}} = B_{R_{i+}}\).}

Indeed, (i) follows from 2.3 and 5.5.1, (ii) from (i) and 5.3.15, (iii)
from (ii) and 5.5.1, (iv) from (iii) and 2.3.

\textbf{Lemma 5.5.6.} \emph{Choose on the group \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\)
generated by the roots a structure of totally ordered group such that
the positive roots are the elements of \(R+\) (cf.~Exp. XXI
3.5.6).\footnote{Note that such an ordering is necessarily compatible
  with \(ord_{\Delta}\), where \(\Delta = S(R+)\) (cf. XXI 3.2.15).} Let
\(\alpha_{1} < \cdots < \alpha_{N}\) be the elements of \(R+\). Consider
the isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : T ×\_S U\_\{α₁\} ×\_S ⋯ ×\_S U\_\{αN\} → B\_\{R+\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induced by the product in \(G\). Set for \(i = 1, \cdots, N\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_\{⩾i\} = f(U\_\{αᵢ\} ×\_S ⋯ ×\_S U\_\{αN\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) Each \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is a normal subgroup of \(B_{R+}\).}

\emph{(ii) For \(1 \leqslant i \leqslant N - 1\), \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is
identified with the semi-direct product}

\[
U_{\geqslant i} = U_{\alpha_{i}} \cdot U_{\geqslant i+1}.
\]

\emph{(iii) \(B_{R+}\) is identified with the semi-direct product}

\[
B_{R+} = T \cdot U_{\geqslant 1}.
\]

\emph{(iv) For \(1 \leqslant i \leqslant N - 1\), the inner
automorphisms of \(U_{\geqslant 1}\) act trivially on
\(U_{\geqslant i}/U_{\geqslant i+1}\) (which is identified with
\(U_{\alpha_{i}}\) by (ii)).}

Let us first prove by induction on \(i\) the following assertion:

\begin{quote}
\(U_{\geqslant i}\) is a normal subgroup of \(B_{R+}\), semi-direct
product of \(U_{\alpha_{i}}\) and \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\).
\end{quote}

The assertion is true for \(i = N\); suppose it for \(i + 1\) and let us
prove it for \(i\). One has (as schemes)

\[
U_{\geqslant i} = U_{\alpha_{i}} \cdot U_{\geqslant i+1};
\]

it is clear first that \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is stable under the inner
automorphisms of \(B_{R+}\). This is clear for \(int(t)\),
\(t \in T(S)\); it suffices to verify it for \(int(x)\),
\(x \in U\alpha(S)\), \(\alpha \in R+\). Now \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\) is
supposed normal, so it suffices to see that
\(int(x) U_{\alpha_{i}} \subset U_{\geqslant i}\). By 5.5.2, if
\(y \in U_{\alpha_{i}}(S')\), one has
\(y^{-1} x y x^{-1} \in U_{\geqslant i+1}(S')\), which entails
\(int(x)(y) \in U_{\geqslant i}(S')\).

Let us now prove that \(U_{\geqslant i}\) is a subgroup of \(B_{R+}\).
If \(x, y \in U_{\geqslant i}(S)\), one may write \(x = p x'\),
\(y = q y'\), with \(p, q \in U_{\alpha_{i}}(S)\), and
\(x', y' \in U_{\geqslant i+1}(S)\). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xy = p x′ q y′ = pq(q⁻¹ x′ q) y′ ∈ U\_\{αᵢ\}(S′) U\_\{⩾i+1\}(S′);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

similarly
\(x^{-1} = p^{-1} (p x'^{-1} p^{-1}) \in U_{\alpha_{i}}(S') U_{\geqslant i+1}(S')\).
We have thus proved (i) and (ii), as well as (iv) along the way. As for
(iii), it is a trivial consequence of 5.5.1.

\textbf{Lemma 5.5.7.} \emph{With the preceding notations, choose for
each \(1 \leqslant i \leqslant N\) an
\(X_{i} \in \Gamma(S, g^{\alpha_{i}})\times\) and consider the
isomorphism}

\[
a : G^{N}_{a,S} \to U_{\geqslant 1}
\]

\emph{defined set-theoretically by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(x₁, …, x\_N) = exp\_\{α₁\}(x₁ X₁) ⋯ exp\_\{αN\}(x\_N X\_N).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{There exists a unique family \((Q_{i})\), \(i = 1, \cdots, N\), of
polynomials}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Qᵢ = Qᵢ(x₁, …, x\_N, y₁, …, y\_N)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{with coefficients in \(\Gamma(S, O_{S})\) such that one has
set-theoretically}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(x₁, …, x\_N) a(y₁, …, y\_N) = a(Q₁(x₁, …, y\_N), …, Q\_N(x₁, …, y\_N)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Furthermore, the \texttt{Qᵢ} have coefficients in the subring of
\(\Gamma(S, O_{S})\) generated by the \(C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\) of 5.5.2
(\(\alpha, \beta \in R+\), \(i, j \in \mathbb{N}*\)) and each
\texttt{Qᵢ} is of the form}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Qᵢ(x₁, …, y\_N) = xᵢ + yᵢ + Q′ᵢ(x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁, y₁, …, yᵢ₋₁).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The existence and uniqueness of the \texttt{Qᵢ} follow immediately from
the fact that \(a\) is an isomorphism of schemes. Denoting \(z\),
\(z'\), \(z''\) sections of \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(x₁, …, x\_N) a(y₁, …, y\_N) =}
\NormalTok{  a(x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁, 0, …, 0) exp(xᵢ Xᵢ) z · a(y₁, …, yᵢ₋₁, 0, …, 0) exp(yᵢ Xᵢ) z′;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

using 5.5.6 (i) and (iv), the right-hand side is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁, 0, …, 0) a(y₁, …, yᵢ₋₁, 0, …, 0) exp((xᵢ + yᵢ) Xᵢ) z′′;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives, reusing 5.5.6,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Qᵢ(x₁, …, x\_N, y₁, …, y\_N) = xᵢ + yᵢ + Q′ᵢ(x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁, y₁, …, yᵢ₋₁),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Q′ᵢ(x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁, y₁, …, yᵢ₋₁) = Qᵢ(x₁, …, xᵢ₋₁, 0, …, 0, y₁, …, yᵢ₋₁, 0, …, 0);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, the precise form requested.

Let us prove finally the assertion on the coefficients of the
polynomials \texttt{Qᵢ}. Let \(A\) be the subring of
\(\Gamma(S, O_{S})\) generated by the \(C_{i,j,\alpha,\beta}\)
(\(\alpha, \beta \in R+\), \(i, j \in \mathbb{N}*\)). Let us prove by
descending induction on \(i\) that if \(x_{1} = \cdots = x_{i-1} = 0\)
and \(y_{1} = \cdots = y_{i-1} = 0\), that is, if
\(a(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{N})\) and \(a(y_{1}, \cdots, y_{N})\) are sections
of \(U_{\geqslant i}\), then the polynomials

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Rⱼ(xᵢ, …, x\_N, yᵢ, …, y\_N) = Qⱼ(x₁, …, x\_N, y₁, …, y\_N)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

have coefficients in \(A\). This is trivial for \(i = N\) and also for
\(j < i\) (because \(R_{j} = 0\) for \(j < i\)). Let \(i < N\), suppose
the assertion verified for \(i + 1\), and let us prove it for \(i\) (and
\(j \geqslant i\)). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(0, …, 0, xᵢ, …, x\_N) = exp(xᵢ Xᵢ) a(0, …, 0, xᵢ₊₁, …, x\_N) = exp(xᵢ Xᵢ) Zᵢ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Similarly write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(0, …, yᵢ, …, y\_N) = exp(yᵢ Xᵢ) Tᵢ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(0, …, xᵢ, …, x\_N) a(0, …, yᵢ, …, y\_N) = exp((xᵢ + yᵢ) Xᵢ) int(exp(−yᵢ Xᵢ))(Zᵢ) · Tᵢ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(exp(−yᵢ Xᵢ))(Zᵢ) = int(exp(−yᵢ Yᵢ))(exp(xᵢ₊₁ Xᵢ₊₁) ⋯ exp(x\_N X\_N))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a product of \(N - i - 1\) sections of \(U_{\geqslant i+1}\) whose
coefficients in the decomposition
\(U_{\geqslant i+1} = U_{\alpha_{i+1}} \cdots U_{\alpha N}\) are
polynomials in \texttt{yᵢ} and \(x_{i+1}\), \ldots, \(x_{N}\) with
coefficients in \(A\) (by 5.5.2). Applying the induction hypothesis, one
deduces that the coefficients of

\[
int(\exp(-y_{i} X_{i}))(Z_{i}) \cdot T_{i}
\]

are also polynomials with coefficients in \(A\), which finishes the
proof.

Let us remark that the preceding induction immediately gives a proof of:

\textbf{Lemma 5.5.8.} \emph{With the notations of 5.5.6, let, for each
\(i = 1, \cdots, N\), a morphism of groups}

\[
f_{i} : U_{\alpha_{i}} \to H,
\]

\emph{where \(H\) is an \(S\)-group functor. For the morphism}

\[
f : U_{\geqslant 1} \to H
\]

\emph{defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(exp(x₁ X₁) ⋯ exp(x\_N X\_N)) = f₁(exp(x₁ X₁)) ⋯ f\_N(exp(x\_N X\_N))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{to be a morphism of groups, it is necessary and sufficient that
for every pair \(i < j\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{fⱼ(exp(xⱼ Xⱼ)) fᵢ(exp(xᵢ Xᵢ)) fⱼ(exp(−xⱼ Xⱼ)) = f(exp(xⱼ Xⱼ) exp(xᵢ Xᵢ) exp(−xⱼ Xⱼ)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{5.6. Subgroups of type (R) with solvable
fibers}\label{subgroups-of-type-r-with-solvable-fibers}

\textbf{Proposition 5.6.1.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group, \(R'\) a subset of \(R\) of type (R) (5.4.2), \(H_{R'}\) the
corresponding subgroup of \(G\). The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(H_{R'}\) has solvable geometric fibers.}

\emph{(ii) There exists a system of positive roots \(R+\) such that
\(R' \subset R+\), hence \(H_{R'} \subset B_{R+}\) (cf. 5.4.5).}

\emph{(iii) \(R' \cap -R' = \emptyset\).}

\emph{(iv) For every ordering on \(R'\), the morphism induced by the
product in \(G\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ×\_S ∏\_\{α ∈ R′\} Uα → H\_\{R′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an isomorphism.}

\emph{(v) \(H_{R'} \cap Norm_{G}(T) = T\).}

\emph{(vi) For every subset \(R''\) of \(R\), of type (R), one has
(cf.~5.4.5)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\_\{R′\} ∩ Norm\_G(H\_\{R′′\}) = H\_\{R′ ∩ R′′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We shall prove these equivalences according to the logical scheme

\[
(iii) \Leftrightarrow (ii) \Rightarrow (vi)
              \Rightarrow (iv) \Rightarrow (v)
              \Rightarrow (i) \Leftrightarrow (ii).
\]

One obviously has (ii) ⇒ (iii) and (vi) ⇒ (v) (take
\(R'' = \emptyset\)). By 5.4.6, it suffices to verify (i) ⇒ (ii) on
geometric fibers; now if \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically
closed field, \(H_{R'}\) is contained in a Borel subgroup containing
\(T\), so of the form \(H_{R+}\) (5.5.5 (iii)).

Similarly (iii) ⇒ (i) is verified on geometric fibers; suppose (iii) is
satisfied; if \(H_{R'}\) were not solvable, there would exist a subtorus
\(Q\) of \(T\), of codimension 1 in \(T\), such that
\(Centr_{H_{R'}}(Q)\) is not solvable (Bible, § 10.4, prop. 8); now
\(Centr_{H_{R'}}(Q)\) has Lie algebra \(g_{R''}\), where \(R''\) is the
set of roots of \(R'\) vanishing on \(Q\), so \(R'' = \emptyset\) or
\({\alpha}\) (by virtue of (iii)); hence \(Centr_{H_{R'}}(Q)\), which is
a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\), is \(T\) or \(T \cdot U\alpha\), hence
solvable, contrary to the hypothesis.

Similarly (ii) ⇒ (iv) is verified on geometric fibers (since these are
flat \(S\)-schemes of finite presentation); by Bible, § 13.2, th. 1 d),
the morphism in question is bijective; it induces an isomorphism on the
tangent spaces at the origin, and one concludes as usual (cf.~4.1.1).

One has (iv) ⇒ (v) by 4.2.7. To prove (v) ⇒ (i), one is again reduced to
the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field,
and one concludes by Bible, § 10.3, cor. to prop. 6 and § 9.3, cor. 3 to
th. 1.

It thus remains only to prove the assertion (ii) ⇒ (vi). One may reduce
to the case where \(G\) is adjoint. One then has, by 5.3.3,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_G(H\_\{R′′\}) = Norm\_G(g\_\{R′′\}) ⊂ Transp\_G(t, g\_\{R′′\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{The inclusion follows from \(t \subset g_{R''}\).} By 5.4.5,
it suffices to prove

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(x)    H\_\{R′\}(S) ∩ Transp\_\{G(S)\}(t, g\_\{R′′\}) ⊂ H\_\{R′ ∩ R′′\}(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us first prove a lemma.

\textbf{Lemma 5.6.2.} \emph{In the notations of 5.5.7, let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u = exp(x₁ X₁) ⋯ exp(x\_N X\_N)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(x_{i} \in Ga(S)\). Let \(m\) be an integer,
\(1 \leqslant m \leqslant N\), such that \(x_{i} = 0\) for \(i < m\).}

\emph{(a) If \(H \in \Gamma(S, t)\), the component of \texttt{Ad(u)\ H}
on \(g^{\alpha_{m}}\) is}

\[
-\alpha_{m}(H) x_{m} X_{m}.
\]

\emph{(b) If \(Y \in \Gamma(S, g^{-\alpha_{m}})\), the component of
\texttt{Ad(u)\ Y} on \(t\) is (with the notations of Exp. XX 2.6)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xₘ ⟨Xₘ, Y⟩ H\_\{αₘ\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Denote indeed \(u = g^{\alpha_{m+1}} + \cdots + g^{\alpha N}\). By
5.4.9, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(exp(xᵢ Xᵢ)) u ⊂ u,    for i \textgreater{} m.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By Exp. XX 2.10, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(exp(xᵢ Xᵢ)) H = H − αᵢ(H) xᵢ Xᵢ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This immediately gives, modulo \(u\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(u) H = Ad(exp(xₘ Xₘ)) H = H − αₘ(H) xₘ Xₘ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which entails the first result.

Likewise denote\footnote{We have corrected the original in what follows.}
\(n = g^{\alpha_{1}} + \cdots + g^{\alpha N}\) and
\(u_{1} = \exp(x_{m+1} X_{m+1}) \cdots \exp(x_{N} X_{N})\). For
\(i > m\), one has \(\alpha_{i} > \alpha_{m}\) so, by 5.4.9, one has,
modulo \(n\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(u₁) Y ≡ Y,    whence    Ad(u) Y ≡ Ad(exp(xₘ Xₘ)) Y.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Applying Exp. XX 2.10, one therefore obtains, modulo \(n\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(u) Y − Y ≡ xₘ ⟨Xₘ, Y⟩ H\_\{αₘ\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence the second result.

Let us return to the proof of inclusion (x). Suppose that there exists
\(h \in H_{R'}(S)\), \(h \notin H_{R' \cap R''}(S)\), such that

\[
Ad(h) t \subset g_{R''}.
\]

One may write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h = t exp(x₁ X₁) ⋯ exp(x\_N X\_N).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(h \notin H_{R' \cap R''}(S)\), there exists a smallest \(m\)
such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t exp(x₁ X₁) ⋯ exp(x\_\{m−1\} X\_\{m−1\}) ∈ H\_\{R′ ∩ R′′\}(S)    and    αₘ ∉ R′′,   xₘ ≠ 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then \(h' = \exp(x_{m} X_{m}) \cdots \exp(x_{N} X_{N})\) also satisfies
the conditions imposed on \(h\) above. But by 5.6.2, for every
\(H \in \Gamma(S, t)\) the component of \(Ad(h') H\) on
\(g^{\alpha_{m}}\) is \(-\alpha_{m}(H) x_{m} X_{m}\). By virtue of the
hypothesis on \(h\) and on \(m\), one has therefore
\(\alpha_{m}(H) = 0\) for every \(H \in \Gamma(S, t)\), which is
impossible (because \(G\) is supposed adjoint and \(\alpha_{m}\) is
therefore non-zero on every fiber).

\textbf{Remark 5.6.2. bis.} \emph{Resume the notations of 5.6.2. If
\(Ad(u)\) is the identity on \(t\) and on \(g^{-\alpha_{m}}\), one has
\(x_{m} = 0\). Indeed, one has \(x_{m} \alpha_{m} = 0\) and
\(x_{m} H_{\alpha_{m}} = 0\); if \(\alpha_{m} \notin 2M\), then
\(\alpha_{m}\) is non-zero on every fiber; if \(\alpha_{m} \in 2M\),
then \(\alpha*_{m} \notin 2M*\) and \(H_{\alpha_{m}}\) is non-zero on
every fiber; in each case, this entails \(x_{m} = 0\). It follows that
\(u = e\) if \(Ad(u)\) operates trivially on \(g\).}

\textbf{Remark 5.6.3.} \emph{If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of the
reductive group \(G\), with solvable geometric fibers, then \(H\) is
closed in \(G\) and \(Norm_{G}(H)/H\) is representable by a separated
finite étale \(S\)-scheme.}

This follows from 5.3.18 and, at one's choice, 3.5 or Exp. XIX 2.5 (ii).

\textbf{Corollary 5.6.4.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split
reductive group. If \(R' \subset R\) is closed and
\(R' \cap -R' = \emptyset\), then \(R'\) is contained in a system of
positive roots.}\footnote{This is in fact a statement about root
  systems, completing Exposé XXI (cf.~{[}BLie{]}, VI § 1.7, Prop. 22)
  and proved here by an indirect route.}

Indeed, \(R'\) is of type (R) by 5.4.7, so the result follows from
5.6.1.

\textbf{Corollary 5.6.5.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.6.1, the
product in \(G\) induces an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∏\_\{α ∈ R′\} Uα ⥲ U\_\{R′\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(U_{R'}\) is a closed group subscheme of \(G\), smooth over
\(S\), with connected and unipotent geometric fibers, independent of the
choice of ordering on \(R'\). Moreover, \(H_{R'}\) is the semi-direct
product \(T \cdot U_{R'}\) (\(U_{R'}\) normal).}

Indeed, if \(R' \subset R+\), then \(H_{R'} \cap U_{\geqslant 1}\)
(notations of 5.5.6) is a closed subgroup of \(G\) of finite
presentation, normal in \(H_{R'}\). By 5.6.1 (iv), one has
\(H_{R'} = T \cdot U_{R'}\), which entails the other assertions.

\textbf{Remark 5.6.6.} \emph{In particular, \(U_{R+}\) is the group
\(U_{\geqslant 1}\) of 5.5.6.}

Let us extract some corollaries of the preceding results concerning
groups of type \(U_{R'}\).

\textbf{Corollary 5.6.7.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split
reductive group, \(R'\) and \(R''\) two subsets of \(R\) of type (R),
with \(R' \cap -R' = \emptyset\).}

\emph{(i) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_\{R′\} ∩ Norm\_G(H\_\{R′′\}) = U\_\{R′ ∩ R′′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) Suppose \(R'\) closed. If the conditions \(\alpha \in R'\),
\(\beta \in R''\) and \(\alpha + \beta \in R\) entail
\(\alpha + \beta \in R'\), then \(H_{R''}\) normalizes \(U_{R'}\).}

Indeed, (i) follows immediately from 5.6.5 and 5.6.1 (vi). To prove
(ii), it suffices, by 5.4.4, to show that \(T\) and each \(U\beta\),
\(\beta \in R''\), normalize \(U_{R'}\).\footnote{Indeed, \(G\) having
  connected fibers is separated over \(S\) by VI\_B 5.5, so by XI 6.11
  (see also the addition 6.5.5 in VI\_B), \(Norm_{G}(U_{R'})\) is
  represented by a closed group subscheme \(N\) of \(G\). If \(N\)
  contains \(T\) and the \(U\beta\), for \(\beta \in R''\), it then
  contains the big cell \(\Omega_{R+, R''}\); now this is schematically
  dense in \(H_{R''}\) by 5.4.4 and EGA IV₃, 11.10.10 (the fibers of
  \(H_{R''}\) are integral and \(\Omega_{R+, R''}\) contains a non-empty
  open subset of each fiber). It follows that \(H_{R''} \subset N\),
  hence \(H_{R''}\) normalizes \(U_{R'}\).} For \(T\), this is trivial;
for \(U\beta\), it follows from 5.5.2 and Exp. XXI 3.1.2.\footnote{One
  must see that, under the hypotheses of (ii), if \(\alpha \in R'\) and
  \(\beta \in R''\), then all roots of the form \(i\alpha + j\beta\)
  with \(i, j \in \mathbb{N}*\) belong to \(R'\), and for this we have
  replaced the reference XXI 2.3.5 by XXI 3.1.2. This may also be seen
  directly by inspection of the rank 2 root systems.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.6.8.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group, \(R+\) a system of positive roots, \(\alpha\) a simple root of
\(R+\) (i.e.~an element of \(R+\) such that \(R+ - {\alpha}\) is
closed). Denote}

\[
U_{\hat{\alpha}} = U_{R+ - {\alpha}}.
\]

\emph{Then}

\emph{(i) \(U_{\hat{\alpha}}\) is a normal subgroup of \(B_{R+}\).}

\emph{(ii) \(U_{R+}\) is the semi-direct product of \(U_{\hat{\alpha}}\)
by \(U\alpha\).}

\emph{(iii) \(U_{-\alpha}\) normalizes \(U_{\hat{\alpha}}\).}

\emph{(iv) \(Z\alpha\) normalizes \(U_{\hat{\alpha}}\).}

\emph{If one defines similarly
\(U_{-\hat{\alpha}} = U_{R- - {-\alpha}}\) (where \(R- = -R+\)), one
has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω\_\{R+\} = U\_\{−α̂\} · U\_\{−α\} · T · Uα · U\_\{α̂\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, (ii) follows from 5.6.5, and (i) from 5.6.7 (ii). Similarly,
(iii) follows from 5.5.2 (indeed, if \(\beta \in R+\),
\(\beta \neq \alpha\), no combination \(i(-\alpha) + j\beta\), with
\(i, j > 0\), can be negative because \(\beta\) contains at least one
simple root \(\neq \alpha\)). Then (iv) follows from (i) and (iii),
because \(U_{-\alpha} \cdot T \cdot U\alpha\) is schematically dense in
\(Z\alpha\). Finally, the last assertion follows from (ii) and its
analogue for \(U_{R-}\).

Let us return to the general situation.

\textbf{Proposition 5.6.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) with solvable
geometric fibers.}

\emph{(i) \(D_{S}(H) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(H, Gm,S)\) is
representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-group, whose type at
\(s \in S\) is \(\mathbb{Z}^{rg_{red}(G_{s})}\). The biduality morphism
(Exp. VIII § 1)}

\[
f : H \to D_{S}(D_{S}(H))
\]

\emph{is smooth and surjective.}

\emph{(ii) The kernel \(H_{u}\) of \(f\) is the largest closed normal
group subscheme of \(H\), smooth over \(S\), with connected and
unipotent geometric fibers. We call it the} unipotent part \emph{of
\(H\) and write also \(H_{u} = rad_{u}(H)\).}

\emph{Then \(H_{u}\) is also the sheaf of commutators of \(H\): every
morphism of groups from \(H\) to an \(S\)-presheaf of commutative groups
separated for (fppf) vanishes on \(H_{u}\) and thus factors through
\(H/H_{u} = D_{S}(D_{S}(H))\).}

\emph{(iii) If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(H\), the morphism
\(T \to H\) induces isomorphisms
\(D_{S}(H) \xrightarrow{\sim} D_{S}(T)\) and
\(T \xrightarrow{\sim} D_{S}(D_{S}(H))\). Furthermore, \(H\) is
identified with the semi-direct product of \(H_{u}\) by \(T\).}

\emph{(iv) In the situation of 5.6.1, if \(H = H_{R'}\), then
\(H_{u} = U_{R'}\).}

The assertions of the proposition are local for the étale topology (Exp.
X 5.5). One may therefore reduce to the case of 5.6.1. One then knows
(5.6.5) that \(H_{R'}\) is the semi-direct product of \(U_{R'}\) by
\(T\). Let us show that \(U_{R'}\) is the sheaf of commutators of
\(H_{R'}\): since \(H_{R'}/U_{R'} = T\) is commutative, it suffices to
prove that every morphism of groups \(\phi : H_{R'} \to V\) as in (ii)
vanishes on \(U_{R'}\). It suffices to prove that \(\phi\) vanishes on
each \(U\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R'\). Now if \(t \in T(S')\),
\(X \in W(g\alpha)(S')\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 = φ(t expα(X) t⁻¹ expα(−X)) = φ(expα((α(t) − 1) X)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\alpha : T \to Gm,S\) is faithfully flat, one deduces
immediately that \(\phi\) vanishes on \(U\times_{\alpha}\); but every
section of \(U\alpha\) is locally the sum of two sections of
\(U\times_{\alpha}\). One thus has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(H, V) = Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(H/U\_\{R′\}, V)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(V\) as above. Applying this result to \(V = Gm,S\), one
deduces immediately (i) and (iii), then (iv) and the second assertion of
(ii). It now suffices to prove the first assertion of (ii); the only
non-trivial fact is that every closed normal subgroup \(U\) of \(H\),
smooth over \(S\) with connected unipotent geometric fibers, is a
subgroup of \(H_{u}\). Now one first has:

\textbf{Lemma 5.6.10.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group,
\(T\) a maximal torus, \(U\) a group subscheme of \(G\), smooth over
\(S\), with unipotent geometric fibers, normalized by \(T\). Then
\(U \cap T = e\).}

Indeed, since \(T = Centr_{G}(T)\), one has \(U \cap T = U^{T}\)
(invariants under \(int(T)\)). Applying Exp. XIX 1.4, one deduces that
\(U \cap T\) is smooth over \(S\), but it is also radicial over \(S\):
for every \(s \in S\), \(U(s) \cap T(s)\) consists of elements that are
simultaneously unipotent and semisimple. This proves the lemma.

Let us return to the proof of 5.6.9 (ii). If \(U\) is a normal subgroup
of \(H\) as above, then the semi-direct product \(T \cdot U\) is a
subgroup of type (R) of \(G\), with solvable geometric fibers. One may
therefore suppose it of the form \(H_{R''}\), with \(R'' \subset R'\).
It suffices to prove \(U = U_{R''}\) and one is therefore reduced to the
case where \(H = T \cdot U\); but the quotient \(H/U\) being
commutative, \(U\) is a subsheaf of the sheaf of commutators of \(H\),
which is \(H_{u}\). QED.

Let us remark that we have in fact just proved:

\textbf{Proposition 5.6.11.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). The maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H ↦ H\_u,    U ↦ T · U}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are mutually inverse bijections between the set of subgroups \(H\)
of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\) and having solvable geometric
fibers, and the set of subgroups \(U\) of \(G\), smooth over \(S\),
normalized by \(T\), with connected and unipotent geometric
fibers.}\footnote{We have removed the hypothesis that \(U\) be closed,
  which is automatically verified. Indeed, for such a \(U\), one has
  \(U \cap T = e\) by 5.6.10, so the semi-direct product
  \(H = T \cdot U\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) (cf.~5.2.1), with
  solvable geometric fibers. So, by 5.6.3, \(H\) is closed in \(G\), and
  since \(U\) is closed in \(H\), it is closed in \(G\).}

In particular, when \((G, T, M, R)\) is split, the groups \(H_{R'}\) and
\(U_{R'}\) correspond.

\textbf{Corollary 5.6.12.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \((G, T, M, R)\)
an \(S\)-split group (resp. and \(R+\) a system of positive roots of
\(R\) defining the Borel subgroup \(B\)).}

\emph{Every smooth group subscheme of \(G\) with connected and unipotent
geometric fibers (resp. every smooth group subscheme of \(B_{u}\))
normalized by \(T\) is locally on \(S\) of the form \(U_{R'}\), where
\(R'\) is a subset of \(R\) contained in a system of positive roots
(resp. a subset of \(R+\)) of type (R).}

For the ``resp.'' case, it suffices to note that the geometric fibers of
the given group are unipotent and connected, by Bible, § 13.2, th. 1
(d).

Proposition 5.6.9 has moreover the following corollary:

\textbf{Corollary 5.6.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) with solvable
geometric fibers, \(Tor(H)\) the functor of maximal tori of \(H\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Tor(H)(S′) = \{maximal tori of H\_\{S′\}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(Tor(H)\) is representable by an affine and smooth
\(S\)-scheme, which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(H_{u}\)
for the law \((h, T) \mapsto int(h) T\).}\footnote{This re-proves and
  refines XII 1.10 (for \(G\) reductive).}

Indeed, if \(T\) and \(T'\) are two maximal tori of \(H_{S'}\), there
exists a unique section \(h \in H_{u}(S')\) such that \(int(h) T = T'\).
The uniqueness of \(h\) follows immediately from the equality

\[
Norm_{G}(T) \cap H_{u} = e
\]

(cf.~for example 5.6.1); it therefore suffices to prove the existence of
\(h\) locally for the étale topology. By 5.2.6 and 5.1.2 (a), one may
suppose \(T\) and \(T'\) conjugate by a section of \(H\), whence the
desired conclusion since \(H = H_{u} \cdot T\) by 5.6.9 (iii). It
follows that \(Tor(H)\) is a principal homogeneous sheaf under
\(H_{u}\), which is affine and smooth over \(S\), which immediately
entails the statement.\footnote{By SGA 1, VIII 2.1 and EGA IV₄, 17.7.1.}

\subsubsection{5.7. Bruhat's theorem}\label{bruhats-theorem}

\textbf{Recall 5.7.1.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field,
\(G\) a \(k\)-reductive group, \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\), \(T\) a
maximal torus of \(B\), \(N = Norm_{G}(T)\). Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G(k) = B(k) N(k) B(k);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{this is Bruhat's theorem (Bible, § 13.4, cor. 1 to th. 3); more
precisely, with the notations of 3.6, the sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B(k) N\_w(k) B(k) = B\_u(k) N\_w(k) B\_u(k)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{form, as \(w\) runs through \((N/T)(k)\), a partition of \(G(k)\).
If \(B'\) is another Borel subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\), the sets
\(B'(k) N_{w}(k) B(k)\) also form a partition of \(G(k)\). Indeed, if
\(y \in N(k)\) is such that \(int(y) B = B'\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y B(k) N\_w(k) B(k) = B′(k) N\_\{yw\}(k) B(k).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Definition 5.7.2.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group, \(R-\) a system of positive roots of \(R\), \(B' = B_{R-}\) the
Borel group it defines. For \(w \in W\), one writes (cf.~5.6.5):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R\^{}w\_− = R− ∩ w(R−),    B′u\_w = U\_\{R\^{}w\_−\} = ∏\_\{α ∈ R\^{}w\_−\} Uα.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(n_{w} \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) is a representative of \(w\)
(3.8), one may also write}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B′u\_w = B′u ∩ int(n\_w) B′u.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 5.7.3.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group, \(R+\) a system of positive roots of \(R\), \(R- = -R+\), \(B\)
(resp. \(B'\)) the Borel subgroup of \(G\) defined by \(R+\) (resp.
\(R-\)). Let \(w \in W\), \(N_{w}\) and \(B'u_{w}\) the corresponding
subschemes of \(G\) (3.8 and 5.7.2).}

\emph{(i) The sheaf \(B' \cdot N_{w} \cdot B\), image of the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B′ ×\_S N\_w ×\_S B → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induced by the product in \(G\), is representable by a subscheme
of \(G\) (in fact a closed subscheme of the open set
\(n_{w} \Omega_{R+}\)).}

\emph{(ii) The morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B′u\_w ×\_S N\_w ×\_S B\^{}u → G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induced by the product in \(G\), is an immersion with image the
preceding subscheme.}

Let us first show that the morphism of (ii) is an immersion. By
definition, \(int(n_{w})^{-1}\) induces a closed immersion of
\(B'u_{w}\) into \(B'u\), so the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(u, b) ↦ n\_w⁻¹ u n\_w b}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induces a closed immersion

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B′u\_w ×\_S B → Ω\_\{R+\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This immediately entails that the morphism of (ii) induces a closed
immersion of the first member into the open set \(n_{w} \Omega_{R+}\).
To prove (i), it suffices to see that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B′(S) N\_w(S) B(S) = B′u\_w(S) N\_w(S) B\^{}u(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, if \(\alpha \in R\), one has
\(int(n_{w}) U\alpha(S) = U_{w(\alpha)}(S)\), so if
\(w^{-1}(\alpha) \in R+\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Uα(S) N\_w(S) B(S) = Uα(S) n\_w T(S) B\^{}u(S)}
\NormalTok{                 = n\_w U\_\{w⁻¹(α)\}(S) T(S) B\^{}u(S)}
\NormalTok{                 = n\_w B(S) = N\_w(S) B\^{}u(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This immediately entails, in view of the definition of \(R^{w}_{-}\),
the desired assertion.

\textbf{Theorem 5.7.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) an
\(S\)-split group, \(B\) the Borel subgroup defined by the system of
positive roots \(R+\), \(B'\) the Borel subgroup defined by
\(R- = -R+\).}

\emph{(i) (Bruhat's theorem) The schemes \(B'u_{w} \cdot N_{w} \cdot B\)
form, as \(w\) runs through \(W\), a partition of the underlying set of
\(G\).}

\emph{(ii) For each \(w \in W\), let \(n_{w}\) be a representative of
\(w\) in \(Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) (3.8); then the open sets
\(n_{w} \Omega = n_{w} B'u \cdot T \cdot B^{u}\) form, as \(w\) runs
through \(W\), a cover of \(G\).}

The two assertions are verified on geometric fibers, where one concludes
by 5.7.1 and 5.7.3.

\textbf{Remark 5.7.5.} \emph{(i) entails that if \(S\) is the spectrum
of a field, \(G(S)\) is the disjoint union of the
\(B'u_{w}(S) \cdot T(S) \cdot B^{u}(S)\). The corresponding assertion
for an arbitrary \(S\) (even local or artinian) is obviously false. Note
however that (ii) entails that if \(S\) is local, \(G(S)\) is the union
of the \(n_{w} \Omega(S)\). In fact:}

\textbf{Corollary 5.7.6.} \emph{Let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple
roots of the split group \(G\) over the local scheme \(S\).}

\emph{(i) Then \(G(S)\) is generated by \(T(S)\) and the \(U\alpha(S)\),
\(\alpha \in \Delta \cup -\Delta\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(G\) is simply connected (4.3.3), \(G(S)\) is already
generated by the \(U\alpha(S)\), \(\alpha \in \Delta \cup -\Delta\).}

Indeed, let \(H\) be the subgroup of \(G(S)\) generated by the
\(U\alpha(S)\), \(\alpha \in \Delta \cup -\Delta\). Let us first remark
that \(H\) contains a representative of each \(s\alpha\)
(\(\alpha \in \Delta\)) in \(Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) (Exp. XX 3.1), hence a
representative \(n_{w}\) of each \(w \in W\).

Since every \(\alpha \in R\) is written \(w(\alpha_{0})\) with
\(w \in W\), \(\alpha_{0} \in \Delta\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Uα(S) = int(n\_w) U\_\{α₀\}(S) ⊂ H.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The subgroup generated by \(H\) and \(T(S)\) thus contains \(\Omega(S)\)
and is therefore the whole of \(G(S)\), by the remark made above.

If now \(G\) is simply connected, let us prove that \(H \supset T(S)\).
By Exp. XX 2.7, \(H\) contains \(\alpha*(Gm(S))\) for every
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), and it suffices to apply 4.3.8.

\textbf{Remark 5.7.6.1.} \emph{Instead of taking, for each
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), \(U\alpha(S)\) and \(U_{-\alpha}(S)\), one may
content oneself with taking \(U\alpha(S)\) and a representative
\(w\alpha\) of the symmetry \(s\alpha\), or else \(U\alpha(S)\) and a
section of \(U\times_{-\alpha}\), \ldots.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.7.7.} \emph{If \(G\) is of semisimple rank 1, choose
a \(u\alpha \in U\times_{\alpha}(S)\). Then \(\Omega\) and
\(u\alpha \Omega\) form a cover of \(G\).}

Indeed, if \(u_{-\alpha}\) is the section of \(U_{-\alpha}\) paired with
\(u\alpha\) (cf.~1.3), one has, by 5.7.4 (ii),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G = Ω ∪ u\_\{−α\}⁻¹ uα u\_\{−α\}⁻¹ Ω,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G = u\_\{−α\} G = u\_\{−α\} Ω ∪ uα u\_\{−α\}⁻¹ Ω = Ω ∪ uα Ω.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 5.7.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. Then \(G\) is essentially free over \(S\) (Exp.
VIII 6.1).}\footnote{See also the additions made in VI\_B, 6.2.1 to
  6.2.6 and 6.5.2 to 6.5.5.}

Indeed, the assertion is local for the (fpqc) topology; one may suppose
\(G\) split. Then \(G\) admits a cover by open subsets isomorphic to
\(G^{N}_{a,S} \times_{S} G^{n}_{m,S}\), which are essentially free.

\textbf{Lemma 5.7.9.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.7.4, let
\(\alpha\) be a simple root of \(R+\) and
\(u\alpha \in U\times_{\alpha}(S)\). For every \(v \in U_{-\alpha}(S)\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω · v ⊂ Ω ∪ uα · Ω.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We have to compare two open subsets of \(G\); it suffices to do so when
\(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\). One thus has to prove

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω(k) v ⊂ Ω(k) ∪ uα Ω(k).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω(k) v = B′u(k) T(k) B\^{}u(k) v = U\_\{−α̂\}(k) U\_\{−α\}(k) T(k) Uα(k) U\_\{α̂\}(k) v}
\NormalTok{       ⊂ U\_\{−α̂\}(k) Zα(k) U\_\{α̂\}(k) v.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(One uses the decomposition of 5.6.8.) Applying now 5.6.8 (iii) and
using 5.7.7 for the group \(Z\alpha\), one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω(k) v ⊂ U\_\{−α̂\}(k) Zα(k) v U\_\{α̂\}(k) ⊂ U\_\{−α̂\}(k) Zα(k) U\_\{α̂\}(k)}
\NormalTok{       ⊂ U\_\{−α̂\}(k) U\_\{−α\}(k) T(k) Uα(k) U\_\{α̂\}(k)   ∪   U\_\{−α̂\}(k) uα U\_\{−α\}(k) T(k) Uα(k) U\_\{α̂\}(k).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using again 5.6.8 (iii) (for \(R-\) instead of \(R+\)), one obtains the
result.

\textbf{Proposition 5.7.10.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.7.4, choose
for each simple root \(\alpha\) a \(u\alpha \in U\times_{\alpha}(S)\).
Let \(U_{1}\) be the submonoid of \(B^{u}(S)\) generated by the
\(u\alpha\). The open sets \(u \Omega\), for \(u \in U_{1}\), form a
cover of \(G\).}

Once again, one may suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\);
by virtue of 5.7.6, it suffices to prove that
\(\bigcup_{u \in U_{1}} u \Omega(k)\) is stable under right
multiplication by \(T(k)\), \(U\alpha(k)\), \(U_{-\alpha}(k)\) (for
\(\alpha\) simple). In the first two cases, this is trivial. In the
last, it follows from the lemma.

\textbf{Remark 5.7.11.} \emph{Let us point out a particular case of
5.7.2. If \(w = s\alpha\) is the symmetry with respect to the simple
root \(\alpha\), then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R− ∩ sα(R−) = R− − \{−α\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(Exp. XXI 3.3.1), and, in the notations of 5.6.8, one therefore
has}

\[
B'u_{s\alpha} = U_{-\hat{\alpha}}.
\]

\textbf{Remark 5.7.12.} \emph{In fact, the proof of 5.7.10 immediately
gives the following statement: under the conditions of 5.7.10, let
\(\Gamma\) be a submonoid of \(G(S)\); for the open sets \(g \Omega\)
(\(g \in \Gamma\)) to form a cover of \(G\), it is necessary and
sufficient that for every \(s \in S\) and every simple root \(\alpha\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(uα)\_s B′u(s) ⊂ Γ · B′u(s) · T(s) · B\^{}u(s).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 5.7.13.} \emph{By 5.5.5 (iii), reasoning as in 5.7.1, one
obtains immediately the following variant of 5.7.4: let \((G, T, M, R)\)
be an \(S\)-split group, \(B\) and \(B'\) two Borel subgroups of \(G\)
containing \(T\); for every \(w \in W\), the sheaf
\(B' \cdot N_{w} \cdot B\) is representable by a subscheme of \(G\);
these subschemes form, for \(w \in W\), a partition of the underlying
set of \(G\). One may also give the analogue of 5.7.3 (ii): one must
set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B′u\_w = B′u ∩ int(n\_w) B̃\^{}u}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(\tilde{B}\) is the Borel subgroup ``opposite'' to \(B\)
relative to \(T\) (cf.~5.9.2).}

\textbf{Proposition 5.7.14.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, and}

\[
Ad : G \to GL_{O_{S}}(g)
\]

\emph{its adjoint representation. Then \(Ker(Ad) = Centr(G)\) (in other
words, the canonical homomorphism deduced from \texttt{Ad} by passage to
the quotient:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad : G/Centr(G) = ad(G) → GL\_\{O\_S\}(g)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a monomorphism).}\footnote{It is in fact a closed immersion, by
  Exp. XVI 1.5 (a).}

One may suppose \(G\) split. Choose on \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\) a total
ordering structure compatible with the group structure and let \(R+\) be
the set of positive roots. By virtue of 5.7.4 (ii) and 4.1.6, it
suffices to prove that if \(n_{w}\) is a representative of the element
\(w\) of \(W\), if \(u \in U(S)\), \(t \in T(S)\), \(v \in U_{-}(S)\),
and if \(Ad(n_{w} v t u) = id\), then \(w = e\), \(v = e\), \(u = e\).
For each \(m \in R \cup {0}\), set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_\{\textgreater{}m\} = ⨿\_\{n \textgreater{} m\} g\^{}n,    g\_\{\textless{}m\} = ⨿\_\{n \textless{} m\} g\^{}n.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(X \in \Gamma(S, g^{m})\); write
\(Ad(tu) X = Ad(v^{-1} n^{-1}_{w}) X\). Now

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(t) Ad(u) X − m(t) X ∈ Γ(S, g\_\{\textgreater{}m\}),}
\NormalTok{Ad(v⁻¹ n\_w⁻¹) X − Ad(n\_w⁻¹) X ∈ Γ(S, g\_\{\textless{}w⁻¹(m)\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(w \neq e\), there exists \(\alpha \in R\) such that
\(w^{-1}(\alpha) < \alpha\), and setting \(m = \alpha\), one obtains a
contradiction because

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(tu) X ∈ Γ(S, g\^{}α + g\_\{\textgreater{}α\}) ∩ Γ(S, g\^{}\{w⁻¹(α)\} + g\_\{\textless{}w⁻¹(α)\}) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Hence \(w = e\), and one may choose \(n_{w} = e\); one then has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(v⁻¹) X − X ∈ Γ(S, g\_\{\textless{}m\} ∩ (g\^{}m + g\_\{\textgreater{}m\})) = 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(Ad(v) X = X\) for every \(X \in \Gamma(S, g^{m})\), so
\(Ad(v) = id\). Similarly \(Ad(u) = id\). One concludes by 5.6.2 bis.

\subsubsection{5.8. Schemes associated with a reductive
group}\label{schemes-associated-with-a-reductive-group}

\textbf{Theorem 5.8.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. Let \(H\) be the functor of subgroups of type (R)
of \(G\): for every \(S' \to S\), \(H(S')\) is the set of subgroups of
type (R) of \(G_{S'}\) (cf.~5.2.1). Then \(H\) is representable by a
quasi-projective \(S\)-scheme of finite presentation over \(S\).}

\footnote{We have expanded the original in what follows.} Let
\(G' = G/Centr(G)\) be the adjoint group of \(G\) (4.3.6) and \(u\) the
morphism \(G \to G'\). By Exp. XII 7.12, the map
\(H' \mapsto u^{-1}(H')\) establishes a bijection between the set of
subgroups of type (R) of \(G'\) and of \(G\) (and this remains valid
after any base change). Thus, replacing \(G\) by \(G'\), one may suppose
that \(G\) is adjoint. Consider then the morphism

\[
u : H \to Grass(g)
\]

which associates with each subgroup of type (R) its Lie algebra (which
is a sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module of \(g\) that is locally a direct
factor.\footnote{Cf. Exp. II 4.11.8.}). Then \(u\) is a monomorphism by
5.3.3. It suffices to prove that it is representable by an immersion of
finite presentation, in other words to prove the following assertion:
for every \(S_{1} \to S\), given a sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module locally a
direct factor \(h\) of \(g_{S_{1}}\), the \(S' \to S_{1}\) such that
\(h_{S'}\) is the Lie algebra of a subgroup of type (R) of \(G_{S'}\)
are exactly those that factor through some subscheme \(\Sigma\) of
finite presentation of \(S_{1}\). Replacing \(S_{1}\) by \(S\), we
reduce to \(S_{1} = S\), and we may furthermore suppose \(S\) affine;
then there exists a noetherian affine scheme \(S_{0}\) such that \(G\)
(resp. \(h\)) arises by base change from an adjoint \(S_{0}\)-reductive
group \(G_{0}\) (resp. a sub-\texttt{O\_S}-module locally a direct
factor \(h_{0}\) of \(g_{0} = Lie(G_{0}/S_{0})\)). It suffices to show
that there exists a subscheme \(\Sigma_{0}\) of \(S_{0}\) with the
required properties (because one will then have
\(\Sigma = \Sigma_{0} \times_{S_{0}} S\)). Replacing \(S\) by \(S_{0}\),
one may therefore suppose \(S\) affine and noetherian (note that then
every subscheme of \(S\) is of finite presentation over \(S\)). Finally,
replacing \(S\) by a sufficiently small open set, one may suppose that
\(g\) is free of rank \(n\) and that \(h\) is a direct factor, free of
rank \(r\).

One must first write that \(h_{S'}\) is a Lie subalgebra of \(g_{S'}\),
i.e.~that the morphism induced by the Lie bracket:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ : h ⊗ h {-}{-}[,]{-}{-}\textgreater{} g}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

factors through \(h\). If \((e_{1}, \cdots, e_{n})\) is a basis of \(g\)
such that \((e_{1}, \cdots, e_{r})\) is a basis of \(h\), then \(\phi\)
is given by sections \(a^{ij}_{k}\) of \texttt{O\_S} (where
\(i, j = 1, \cdots, r\) and \(k = 1, \cdots, n\)), and the preceding
condition is equivalent to saying that \(S' \to S\) factors through the
closed subscheme of \(S\) defined by the equations \(a^{ij}_{k} = 0\)
for \(k = r + 1, \cdots, n\) and \(i, j = 1, \cdots, r\). Replace \(S\)
by this closed subscheme.

Then, by 5.3.0, \(N = Norm_{G}(h)\) is a closed group subscheme of \(G\)
of finite presentation over \(G\). One must now write (cf.~5.3.1) that
\(N_{S'}\) is smooth at every point of the unit section, of relative
dimension \(r = rank(h)\), and that the inclusion of \(h_{S'}\) in
\(Lie(N_{S'}/S')\) is an equality.

\footnote{The original next indicated that, denoting \(n_{N/G}\) the
  inverse image of the conormal sheaf \(N_{N/G}\) by the unit section
  \(S \to N\), the condition that
  \(n_{N_{S'}/G_{S'}} \to \omega^{1}_{G_{S'}/S'}\) be universally
  injective is equivalent to the fact that \(S' \to S\) factors through
  some open subscheme of \(S\). We were unable to justify this point, in
  view of the fact that the formation of \(N_{N/G}\) does not commute
  with base change, and we have replaced this argument with the one that
  follows, indicated by O. Gabber.} Since \(N\) is affine over \(S\)
(being closed in \(G\)), the unit section \(\epsilon : S \to N\) is a
closed immersion, so \(\epsilon(S)\) is defined by a quasi-coherent
ideal \(J\) of \(A(N)\). Note that \(n_{S/N} = J/J^{2}\) is identified
with \(\epsilon*(\Omega^{1}_{N/S})\), so its formation commutes with
every base change \(S' \to S\). By the equivalence (c′) ⇔ (a) in EGA
IV₄, 17.12.1 (applied to \(f : N \to S\) and \(j = \epsilon\)),
\(N_{S'} \to S'\) is smooth, of relative dimension \(r\), at every point
of \(\epsilon(S')\) if and only if
\(n_{S'/N'} = n_{S/N} \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'}\) is locally free of rank
\(r\) and the morphism
\(\phi_{n}(S') : Sym^{n}(n_{S'/N'}) \to J^{n}_{S'}/J^{n+1}_{S'}\) is an
isomorphism for every \(n \geqslant 1\). Denote
\(K_{n}(S') = Ker \phi_{n}(S')\). By TDTE I, Lemma 3.6,
\(n_{S/N} \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'}\) is locally free of rank \(r\) if and
only if \(S' \to S\) factors through some subscheme \(Z\) of \(S\).
Replacing \(S\) by \(Z\), we may therefore suppose that
\(n_{S/N} = J/J^{2}\) is locally free of rank \(r\). Then, for every
\(S' \to S\), one has
\((J^{2}/J^{3}) \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'} = J^{2}_{S'}/J^{3}_{S'}\) and
hence \(K_{2}(S') = K_{2}(S) \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'}\). It follows that
\(\phi_{2}(S')\) is an isomorphism if and only if \(S' \to S\) factors
through the closed subscheme \(S_{2}\) of \(S\) defined by the ideal
generated by the image of \(Sym^{2}(n_{S/N})* \otimes K_{2}(S)\) in
\texttt{O\_S}. Then, over \(S_{2}\), \(J^{2}/J^{3}\) is isomorphic to
\(Sym^{2}(n_{S/N})\), hence locally free, and the same argument shows
that \(\phi_{3}(S')\) is an isomorphism if and only if \(S' \to S\)
factors through some closed subscheme \(S_{3}\) of \(S\), etc. One
obtains thus that \(N_{S'} \to S'\) is smooth, of relative dimension
\(r\), at every point of \(\epsilon(S')\) if and only if \(S' \to S\)
factors through the closed subscheme \(Z\) intersection of the
\(S_{n}\). But then, for every \(S' \to Z\), \(Lie(N_{S'}/S')\) is
locally a direct factor of rank \(r\) of \(g_{S'}\), and so the
inclusion \(h_{S'} \subset Lie(N_{S'}/S')\) is an equality. One then
sets \(H = N^{0}\).

Replacing \(S\) by \(Z\), it remains only to express that \(H_{s'}\) is
of the same reductive rank as \(G_{s'}\) at every point \(s' \in S'\),
or, equivalently, that \(H_{s}\) is of the same reductive rank as
\(G_{s}\) at every point \(s\) of the (set-theoretic) image of \(S'\) in
\(S\). Now this condition defines an open subset of \(S\) (Exp. XIX
6.2).

\textbf{Remark.} \emph{In general, the scheme \(H\) is not smooth over
\(S\). It is however smooth if \texttt{6} is invertible on \(S\), or if
there exists a prime number \(p\) such that \(p \cdot 1_{S} = 0\)
(i.e.~if \(S\) is of characteristic \(p > 0\)).}

\textbf{Corollary 5.8.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\). (Recall
(5.3.10) that \(Norm_{G}(H)\) is representable by a closed group
subscheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\).)}

\emph{Then the quotient sheaf \(G/Norm_{G}(H)\) is representable by a
quasi-projective \(S\)-scheme, smooth and of finite presentation over
\(S\) (which is in fact an open subset of \(H\)).}

Indeed, consider the morphism

\[
f : G \to H,
\]

defined set-theoretically by \(f(g) = int(g) H\). By 5.3.9, this
morphism is smooth and of finite presentation, hence open. Let
\(V = f(G)\) equipped with its structure of open subscheme of \(H\). The
morphism \(f : G \to V\) is covering and of kernel \(Norm_{G}(H)\),
which proves that \(G/Norm_{G}(H)\) is representable by \(V\) (cf.~Exp.
IV 4.6.5).

\textbf{Corollary 5.8.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. Consider the functors \(Tor(G)\), \(Bor(G)\),
\(Kil(G)\) defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Tor(G)(S′) = \{maximal tori of G\_\{S′\}\},}
\NormalTok{Bor(G)(S′) = \{Borel subgroups of G\_\{S′\}\},}
\NormalTok{Kil(G)(S′) = \{Killing couples of G\_\{S′\} (cf. 5.3.13)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) \(Tor(G)\), \(Bor(G)\), \(Kil(G)\) are representable by smooth
\(S\)-schemes of finite presentation, with integral geometric fibers,
and respectively affine, projective, affine over \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) The canonical morphism \(Kil(G) \to Tor(G)\) (resp.
\(Kil(G) \to Bor(G)\)) is finite étale surjective (resp. affine smooth
surjective).}

\emph{(iii) Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\) (resp. \(B\) a Borel
subgroup of \(G\), resp. \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\)). The
morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G → Tor(G),    resp. G → Bor(G),    resp. G → Kil(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g ↦ int(g) T,    resp. g ↦ int(g) B,    resp. g ↦ (int(g) B, int(g) T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induces an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G/Norm\_G(T) ⥲ Tor(G),    resp. G/B ⥲ Bor(G),    resp. G/T ⥲ Kil(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One sees first that (iii) follows from the conjugacy theorem for maximal
tori (resp. Borel subgroups, resp. Killing couples) and the fact that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_G(B) = B,    Norm\_G(B) ∩ Norm\_G(T) = T,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

all results previously established (5.1.2, 5.3.12, 5.3.14, 5.6.1).

It follows first that the canonical morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Tor(G) → H,    Bor(G) → H}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are representable, locally for the étale topology, by open immersions
(5.8.2 and 5.1.2, resp. 5.5.5), hence by descent that \(Tor(G)\) and
\(Bor(G)\) are representable by open subsets of \(H\). Similarly
\(Kil(G)\) is locally (for the étale topology) representable by a scheme
affine over the base (Exp. IX 2.3), hence representable by an affine
\(S\)-scheme, by descent of affine schemes.\footnote{Cf. SGA 1, VIII
  2.1.}

The assertions of (ii) follow immediately from 5.5.5 (ii) and 5.6.13. It
already follows that \(Tor(G)\) is affine over \(S\) (EGA II 6.7.1). It
thus remains only to prove the fact that \(Bor(G)\) is projective over
\(S\). We already know that it is quasi-projective; it remains to prove
that it is proper;\footnote{One may suppose \(S\) affine and, since
  \(Bor(G)\) is of finite presentation over \(S\) by (i), reduce to the
  case where \(S\) is noetherian; one is then under the hypotheses of
  EGA IV₃, 15.7.10.} but it has connected fibers, so by EGA IV₃,
15.7.10, one is reduced to proving it on geometric fibers; if \(S\) is
the spectrum of an algebraically closed field, one has \(Bor(G) = G/B\)
by (iii) and one concludes by Bible, § 6.4, th. 4 (or {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.5,
th. 5).

\textbf{Remark 5.8.4.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.8.3, let \(Q\) be
a central subgroup of multiplicative type of \(G\). The obvious
morphisms define isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Tor(G) ≃ Tor(G/Q),    Bor(G) ≃ Bor(G/Q),    Kil(G) ≃ Kil(G/Q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 5.8.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a group subscheme of \(G\), smooth and of
finite presentation over \(S\). The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) For each \(s \in S\), \(P_{s}\) is a parabolic subgroup of
\(G_{s}\) (i.e.~the quotient scheme \(G_{s}/P_{s}\) is proper over
\(s\), or equivalently \(P_{s}\) contains a Borel subgroup of \(G_{s}\),
cf.~Bible, § 6.4, th. 4 or {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.5, th. 5).}

\emph{(ii) The quotient sheaf \(G/P\) is representable by an
\(S\)-scheme that is smooth and projective over \(S\).}

\emph{Moreover, under these conditions, \(P\) is closed in \(G\), with
connected fibers, and one has \(P = Norm_{G}(P)\).}

One obviously has (ii) ⇒ (i). If (i) holds, then
\(P(s) = Norm_{G(s)}(P_{s})\) and \(P_{s}\) is connected (for the first
point, cf.~Bible, § 12.3, lemme 4;\footnote{We have expanded what
  follows.} the second point follows from this, because
\(P' = P^{0}_{s}\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G_{s}\) normalized by
\(P_{s}\), whence \(P'(s) = P(s)\) and thus \(P' = P_{s}\)); it follows
that \(P\) is of type (R), and that \(P\) equals \(Norm_{G}(P)\), hence
is closed in \(G\). By 5.8.2, \(G/P = G/Norm_{G}(P)\) is representable
by a quasi-projective \(S\)-scheme. Its fibers are connected and proper,
hence it is projective by the reasoning of 5.8.3.

\textbf{Remark 5.8.6.} \emph{The statements 5.8.1, 5.8.2, 5.8.5 are
valid for an \(S\)-group of type (RA), or for an \(S\)-group of type
(RR) satisfying 5.1.8.}\footnote{Indeed, the proof of 5.8.1 only uses
  5.3.3 (valid for a group of type (RA)) and XIX 6.2 which, by XII 1.7
  (b), is also valid for groups of type (RR).}

\textbf{Remark 5.8.7.} \emph{Through the inner automorphisms of \(G\),
one has canonical operations:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G → Aut\_S(Tor(G)),    G → Aut\_S(Bor(G)),    G → Aut\_S(Kil(G)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{which, in the situation of 5.8.3 (iii), are identified with the
canonical operations}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G → Aut\_S(G/Norm\_G(T)),    G → Aut\_S(G/B),    G → Aut\_S(G/T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{One concludes in particular that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ker(G → Aut\_S(Tor(G))) = Ker(G → Aut\_S(Bor(G))) = Ker(G → Aut\_S(Kil(G))) = Centr(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is indeed clear that \(Centr(G)\) operates trivially on each of the
three schemes. Conversely, the kernel of
\(G \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S}(Kil(G))\) is ``the intersection of the
maximal tori of \(G\)'' in the sense of 4.1.7, hence equals \(Centr(G)\)
(loc. cit.). For \(Bor(G)\), one notes that ``the intersection of the
Borel subgroups of \(G\)'' is also ``the intersection of its maximal
tori'' (see the following section). For \(Tor(G)\), one uses Exp. XII
4.11.

\subsubsection{5.9. Properties peculiar to Borel
subgroups}\label{properties-peculiar-to-borel-subgroups}

Most of these properties will be generalized in Exp. XXVI to parabolic
subgroups.

\textbf{Definition 5.9.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(B\) and \(B'\) two Borel subgroups of \(G\). We
say that \(B\) and \(B'\) are in} general position \emph{(or that \(B'\)
is in general position relative to \(B\)) if \(B \cap B'\) is a torus
(necessarily maximal) of \(G\).}

\emph{If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\) contained in \(B\) and
\(B'\), we say that \(B\) and \(B'\) are} opposite \emph{(relative to
\(T\)) if \(B \cap B' = T\).}

\textbf{Proposition 5.9.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\), \(T\) a maximal
torus of \(B\). There exists a unique Borel subgroup \(B'\) of \(G\),
opposite to \(B\) relative to \(T\).}

\emph{If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a splitting of \(G\) relative to \(T\) and
if \(B = B_{R+}\) (5.5.1), then \(B' = B_{-R+}\).}

By faithfully flat descent, it suffices to prove the proposition in the
split case, when \(B = B_{R+}\) (5.5.5 (iv)). Then \(B_{-R+}\) is indeed
opposite to \(B\) (4.1.2); let us show that it is the only Borel
subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) that is opposite to \(B\). If \(B'\)
is a Borel subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\), then \(B'\) is locally on
\(S\) of the form \(B_{R'+}\), where \(R'+\) is another system of
positive roots of \(R\) (5.5.5 (iii)). If \(R'+ \neq -R+\), there exists
\(\alpha \in R'+ \cap R+\), so that
\(U\alpha \subset B_{R+} \cap B_{R'+}\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.9.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\).}

\emph{(i) If \(B'\) is a Borel subgroup of \(G\), the following
conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(a) \(B'\) is in general position relative to \(B\) (5.9.1).}

\emph{(b) \(B'u \cap B^{u} = e\).}

\emph{(b′) \(B'u \cap B = e\).}

\emph{(c) The product in \(G\) induces an open immersion
\(B'u \times_{S} B \to G\).}

\emph{(c′) The canonical morphism \(B'u \to G/B\) is an open immersion.}

\emph{(ii) The functor \(Opp(B)\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S′ ↦ \{Borel subgroups of G\_\{S′\} in general position relative to B\_\{S′\}\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is representable by an open subscheme of \(Bor(G)\) (5.8.3). The
morphism}

\[
Opp(B) \to Tor(B)
\]

\emph{defined by \(B' \mapsto B \cap B'\) is an isomorphism. In
particular (5.6.13) the inner automorphisms of \(B^{u}\) equip
\(Opp(B)\) with a structure of principal homogeneous bundle under
\(B^{u}\).}

Let us first examine (i). One has (a) ⇒ (c): indeed, (c) is local for
the étale topology; by 5.5.5 (iv), one reduces to the case where \(G\)
is split relative to \(B \cap B'\) and \(B\) of the form \(B_{R+}\); by
5.9.2, one then has \(B'u = U_{-R+}\) and one is reduced to 4.1.2.

One trivially has (c′) ⇔ (c) ⇒ (b′) ⇒ (b). It therefore remains to prove
(b) ⇒ (a). Let us first prove (ii): the second assertion is a formal
consequence of 5.9.2, the third follows immediately from this by 5.6.13;
let us prove the first; it is local for the étale topology and one may
therefore suppose that \(B\) possesses a maximal torus \(T\); let
\(B'_{0}\) be opposite to \(B\) relative to \(T\) (5.9.2).

By what precedes, the morphism \(B^{u} \to Bor(G)\) induced by the
canonical morphism \(G \to G/B'_{0} \to Bor(G)\) (5.8.3) induces an
isomorphism \(B^{u} \xrightarrow{\sim} Opp(B)\). One thus has a
commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B\^{}u    ────→  G/B′\_0}
\NormalTok{ ≀              ≀}
\NormalTok{ ↓              ↓}
\NormalTok{Opp(B) ────→  Bor(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now the morphism \(B^{u} \to G/B'_{0}\) is an open immersion (by (i) (a)
⇒ (c′)), which finishes the proof of (ii). Let us immediately note the
corollary:

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.4.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group
and \(B\) and \(B'\) two Borel subgroups of \(G\). If \(s \in S\) is
such that \(B_{s}\) and \(B'_{s}\) are in general position, there exists
an open subset \(V\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) such that \texttt{B\_V}
and \(B'_{V}\) are in general position.}

It only remains to prove (b) ⇒ (a). By virtue of the preceding
corollary, it suffices to do so when \(S\) is the spectrum of an
algebraically closed field \(k\). One may suppose \(G\) split relative
to a maximal torus \(T\) of \(B\). Let \(B'_{0}\) be the Borel subgroup
opposite to \(B\). Since the Borel subgroups of \(G\) are conjugate
under \(G(k)\), there exists \(g \in G(k)\) such that
\(int(g) B'_{0} = B'\). By Bruhat's theorem (5.7.4), one may write
\(g = b n b'\), with \(b \in B(k)\), \(b' \in B'_{0}(k)\),
\(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(k)\). One thus has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B′ = int(b) int(n) B′\_0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(B' \cap B = int(b) (int(n) B'_{0} \cap B)\). If \(n \notin T(k)\),
\(int(n) B'u_{0} \cap B^{u} \neq e\) (cf.~proof of 5.9.2); it follows
that (b) entails \(B' \cap B = int(b)(B'_{0} \cap B) = int(b) T\). QED.

\textbf{Proposition 5.9.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\), \(B^{u}\) its
unipotent part. There exists a sequence of subgroups of \(B\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U₀ = B\^{}u ⊃ U₁ ⊃ ⋯ ⊃ U\_n ⊃ ⋯}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{possessing the following properties:}

\emph{(i) Each \(U_{i}\) is smooth, with connected fibers,
characteristic in \(B\); the inner automorphisms of \(B^{u}\) act
trivially on the (sheaf) quotients \(U_{i}/U_{i+1}\).}

\emph{(ii) For each \(i \geqslant 0\), there exists a locally free
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(E_{i}\) and an isomorphism of \(S\)-sheaves of
groups}

\[
U_{i}/U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\sim} W(E_{i}).
\]

\emph{(iii) For every \(s \in S\), \((U_{n})_{s} = e\) for
\(n \geqslant \dim(B^{u}_{s})\).}

Suppose first that there exists a splitting \((G, T, M, R)\) of \(G\)
and a system of positive roots \(R+\) of \(R\) such that \(B = B_{R+}\).
We denote by \(\Delta\) the set of simple roots of \(R+\); for each
\(\alpha \in R+\), we write \(ord(\alpha)\) for the sum of the
coefficients of \(\alpha\) in the basis \(\Delta\) of \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\);
it is the \emph{order} of \(\alpha\) relative to \(R+\). One has
\(ord(\alpha) \leqslant Card(R+)\). For every \(i > 0\), let \(R^{(i)}\)
be the set of roots of order \(> i\); it is a closed set of positive
roots, so one may construct (5.6.5)

\[
U_{i} = U_{R^{(i)}}.
\]

If \(\alpha \in R+\) and \(\beta \in R^{(i)}\), then
\(\alpha + \beta \in R^{(i+1)}\). It follows, by 5.5.2, that each
\(U_{i}\) is a normal subgroup of \(B\) and that the inner automorphisms
of \(B^{u}\) operate trivially on \(U_{i}/U_{i+1}\). This group is
moreover identified with

\[
\prod_{ord(\alpha) = i + 1} U\alpha
\]

and is thus equipped with a vector-space structure.

If \(B\) is of the form \(B_{R'}\) for another splitting
\((G, T', M', R')\) of \(G\), let us show that the groups \(U'_{i}\)
constructed as above using the new splitting coincide with the \(U_{i}\)
and that the vector-space structures on the successive quotients also
coincide. By 5.6.13, there exists \(b \in B^{u}(S)\) such that
\(T' = int(b) T\); the assertion to be proved is local on \(S\) and one
may therefore suppose that the isomorphism \(T \xrightarrow{\sim} T'\)
induced by \(int(b)\) arises by duality from an isomorphism of root data

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : (M′, M′*, R′, R′*) ⥲ (M, M*, R, R*).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is clear that the roots of \(R'+\) are the
\(\alpha \circ int(b) = h(\alpha)\), \(\alpha \in R+\), and that the
simple roots of \(R'+\) are the \(\alpha \circ int(b) = h(\alpha)\),
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), hence \(ord(h(\alpha)) = ord(\alpha)\) for
\(\alpha \in R+\). On the other hand, it is clear by transport of
structure that the vector groups \(U'_{h(\alpha)}\) are none other than
the \(int(b) U\alpha\). One thus has \(int(b) U_{i} = U'_{i}\); but
\(U_{i}\) being invariant, this gives \(U_{i} = U'_{i}\).

Similarly the isomorphism of vector groups

\[
int(b) : U_{i}/U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\sim} U'_{i}/U'_{i+1}
\]

is the identity, by virtue of what has already been proved.

Let us now treat the general case. There exists a covering family for
the étale topology \({S_{i} \to S}\) and for each \(i\) a splitting
\((G_{i}, T_{i}, M_{i}, R_{i})\) and a system of positive roots
\(R_{i+}\) of \(R_{i}\) such that \(B \times_{S} S_{i} = B_{R_{i+}}\)
(5.5.5, (iii)). For each \(i\), one thus has a family

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B\_\{S\_i\} = U\_\{i,0\} ⊃ U\_\{i,1\} ⊃ ⋯ ⊃ U\_\{i,j\} ⊃ ⋯}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and vector-space structures on the \(U_{i,j}/U_{i,j+1}\). By descent, it
suffices to prove that for every pair \((i, i')\) and every \(j\), one
has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_\{i,j\} ×\_\{S\_i\} S\_\{ii′\} = U\_\{i′,j\} ×\_\{S\_\{i′\}\} S\_\{ii′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(one writes \(S_{ii'} = S_{i} \times_{S} S_{i'}\)) and that the
vector-space structures on the quotients

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(U\_\{i,j\}/U\_\{i,j+1\}) ×\_\{S\_i\} S\_\{ii′\}    and    (U\_\{i′,j\}/U\_\{i′,j+1\}) ×\_\{S\_i\} S\_\{ii′\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

coincide. Now if \(S_{ii'} = \emptyset\), this is trivial; if
\(S_{ii'} \neq \emptyset\), then one is in the situation studied above:
\(B \times_{S} S_{ii'}\) is defined by the system of positive roots
\(R_{i+}\) (resp. \(R_{i'+}\)) in the splitting
\((G_{S_{ii'}}, T_{i} \times_{S_{i}} S_{ii'}, M_{i}, R_{i})\) (resp. in
the splitting
\((G_{S_{ii'}}, T_{i'} \times_{S_{i'}} S_{ii'}, M_{i'}, R_{i'})\)).

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.6.} \emph{If \(S\) is affine,
\(H^{1}(S, B^{u}) = e\), i.e.~every principal bundle under \(B^{u}\)
possesses a section.}

Indeed, \(S\) decomposes as a direct sum of subschemes on each of which
\(B^{u}\) is of constant relative dimension. One may therefore, by 5.9.5
(iii), suppose that there exists an \(n\) such that \(U_{n} = e\).
Since, by TDTE I, B.1.1,\footnote{This is the corollary on page 18 of
  TDTE I.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, U\_i/U\_\{i+1\}) = H¹(S, W(E\_i)) = 0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one has \(H^{1}(S, B^{u}) = 0\).

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.7.} \emph{If \(S\) is affine, \(B\) possesses
maximal tori. If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(B\), one has
\(H^{1}(S, T) = H^{1}(S, B)\).}

The first assertion follows immediately from 5.9.6 and 5.6.13; the
second follows in standard fashion.\footnote{Indeed, one has an exact
  sequence
  \(H^{1}(S, B^{u}) \to H^{1}(S, B) \xrightarrow{\pi} H^{1}(S, B/B^{u}) = H^{1}(S, T)\),
  see {[}Se64{]}, I § 5.5, Prop. 38 or {[}Gi71{]}, III Prop. 3.3.1. Now
  \(H^{1}(S, T) \to H^{1}(S, B)\) is a section of \(\pi\), so \(\pi\) is
  surjective; on the other hand \(H^{1}(S, B^{u}) = 0\) by 5.9.6.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.8.} \emph{If \(G\) is an \(S\)-reductive group,
the canonical morphism (cf.~5.8.3)}

\[
Kil(G) \to Bor(G)
\]

\emph{possesses sections over every affine open subset.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.9.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.9.5, suppose
\(S\) affine; then there exists a locally free \texttt{O\_S}-module
\(E\) such that \(B^{u}\) is, as a scheme, \(S\)-isomorphic to
\(W(E)\).}

Let us show by induction on \(i\) that \(B^{u}/U_{i}\) is
\(S\)-isomorphic to \(W(E_{0} \oplus \cdots \oplus E_{i-1})\). This is
clear for \(i = 0\); suppose \(i \geqslant 1\). Then \(B^{u}/U_{i}\) is
a principal homogeneous bundle of base \(X = B^{u}/U_{i-1}\) under the
group \((U_{i-1}/U_{i})_{X}\). Since \(B^{u}/U_{i-1}\) is affine, by the
induction hypothesis, and since \(U_{i-1}/U_{i} = W(E_{i-1})\), this
bundle is trivial. One thus has (at least) an isomorphism of
\(S\)-schemes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B\^{}u/U\_i ⥲ (B\^{}u/U\_\{i−1\}) ×\_S W(E\_\{i−1\}) = W(E₀ ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ E\_\{i−1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One concludes immediately by condition (iii) of 5.9.5.

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme,
\({s_{i}}\) its closed points, \(B\) a Borel subgroup of the
\(S\)-reductive group \(G\). The canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B\^{}u(S) → ∏\_i B\^{}u(Spec κ(s\_i))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is surjective.}

Indeed, if \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\), \(\kappa(s_{i}) = A/p_{i}\)
and if \(E\) is given by the \(A\)-module \(E\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B\^{}u(S) = E ⊗ A,    B\^{}u(Spec κ(s\_i)) = E ⊗\_A (A/p\_i).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The assertion then follows immediately from the fact that
\(A \to \prod_{i} A/p_{i}\) is surjective.

\subsubsection{5.10. Subgroups of type (R) with reductive
fibers}\label{subgroups-of-type-r-with-reductive-fibers}

\textbf{Proposition 5.10.1.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an
\(S\)-split group, \(R'\) a subset of \(R\) of type (R) (5.4.2),
\(H_{R'}\) the corresponding subgroup of \(G\). The following conditions
are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(H_{R'}\) is reductive (i.e.~has reductive geometric
fibers).}

\emph{(ii) One has \(R' = -R'\), i.e.~\(R'\) is symmetric.}

\emph{Moreover, under these conditions, \((H_{R'}, T, M, R')\) is a
splitting of \(H_{R'}\); for every system of positive roots \(R+\) of
\(R\), \(R'+ = R' \cap R+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R'\) and}

\[
B_{R+} \cap H_{R'} = H_{R'+}
\]

\emph{is a Borel subgroup of \(H_{R'}\), whose unipotent part is}

\[
U_{R+} \cap H_{R'} = U_{R'+}.
\]

One has obviously (i) ⇒ (ii) (it suffices to check it fiber by fiber and
\(R'\) is a system of roots of \(H_{R'}\) relative to \(T\)). To prove
(ii) ⇒ (i), one remarks by 5.4.3 that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\_\{R′\} ∩ Zα = Centr\_\{H\_\{R′\}\}(Tα) = Zα}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(\alpha \in R'\) and one applies the criterion of Exp. XIX
1.12.

If \(R+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\), then
\(R'+ = R+ \cap R'\) is obviously a closed subset of \(R'\) such that
\(R'+ \cup -R'+ = R'\) and \(R'+ \cap -R'+ = \emptyset\), hence a system
of positive roots of \(R'\). The other two assertions follow
respectively from 5.6.1 (vi) and 5.6.7 (i).

\textbf{Corollary 5.10.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) an \(S\)-reductive subgroup such that for
every \(s \in S\), \(G_{s}\) and \(H_{s}\) have the same reductive rank.
Then \(H\) is closed in \(G\), \(Norm_{G}(H)\) is smooth over \(S\),
\(Norm_{G}(H)/H\) is representable by a finite étale \(S\)-scheme.}

\emph{If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(H\) and \(B\) a Borel subgroup of
\(G\) containing \(T\), then \(B \cap H\) is a Borel subgroup of \(H\),
whose unipotent part is \((B \cap H)_{u} = B^{u} \cap H\).}

The first assertions follow immediately from 5.3.10 and 5.3.18, via the
fact that the Weyl groups of \(G\) and \(H\) are finite (Exp. XIX 2.5).
The other assertions are local for the étale topology and reduce to the
case studied in 5.10.1.

\textbf{Proposition 5.10.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(a) If \(Q\) is a torus of \(G\), \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is a subgroup
of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive fibers. If \(Q \subset Q'\) are two
tori of \(G\), then \(Centr_{G}(Q) \supset Centr_{G}(Q')\).}

\emph{(b) If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive
fibers, then \(rad(H)\) (4.3.6) is a torus of \(G\). If \(H \subset H'\)
are two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive fibers, then
\(rad(H) \supset rad(H')\).}

\emph{(c) If \(Q\) is a torus of \(G\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad(Centr\_G(Q)) ⊃ Q    and    Centr\_G(rad(Centr\_G(Q))) = Centr\_G(Q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(d) If \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive
fibers, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Centr\_G(rad(H)) ⊃ H    and    rad(Centr\_G(rad(H))) = rad(H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, (a) follows immediately from Exp. XIX 2.8. To prove (b), it
suffices to note that \(rad(H') \subset H\), because \(H\) contains
(locally for (fpqc)) a maximal torus of \(G\), hence of \(H'\). The
first assertion of (c) (resp. (d)) is trivial, the second follows by the
usual reasoning.

This proposition leads to the following definition:

\textbf{Definition 5.10.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) a reductive subgroup of type (R) of \(G\),
and \(Q\) a subtorus of \(G\).}\footnote{We have modified the original,
  introducing the terminology ``C-critical torus'' instead of ``critical
  torus'', in order to avoid confusions in later references (cf.~Exp.
  XXVI, 3.9). We have also expanded the statement of 5.10.5 and added
  Remark 5.10.5.1.}

\emph{1) We say that \(H\) is a} critical subgroup \emph{if it is the
centralizer of its radical.}

\emph{2) We say that \(Q\) is a} C-critical torus \emph{if it is the
radical of its centralizer.}

It then follows from Proposition 5.10.3:

\textbf{Corollary 5.10.5.} \emph{(i) For every subtorus \(Q\) of \(G\),
\(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is critical.}

\emph{(ii) For every subgroup of type (R) with reductive fibers \(H\) of
\(G\), \(rad(H)\) is a C-critical torus of \(G\).}

\emph{(iii) The maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Q ↦ Centr\_G(Q),    H ↦ rad(H)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are mutually inverse bijections between the set of C-critical tori
of \(G\) and the set of its critical reductive subgroups of type (R).}

\emph{(iv) If \(Q\) is a torus of \(G\), \(rad(Centr_{G}(Q))\) is the
smallest C-critical torus of \(G\) containing \(Q\).}

\emph{(v) If \(H\) is a reductive subgroup of type (R) of \(G\),
\(Centr_{G}(rad(H))\) is the smallest critical reductive subgroup of
type (R) of \(G\) containing \(H\).}

\textbf{Remark 5.10.5.1.}\footnote{We have modified the original,
  introducing the terminology ``C-critical torus'' instead of ``critical
  torus'', in order to avoid confusions in later references (cf.~Exp.
  XXVI, 3.9). We have also expanded the statement of 5.10.5 and added
  Remark 5.10.5.1.} \emph{(1) A torus \(T\) of \(G\) is a critical
subgroup of \(G\) if and only if it is a maximal torus.}

\emph{(2) In what follows, ``critical torus'' means ``C-critical
torus''.}

\textbf{Proposition 5.10.6.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an
\(S\)-split group, \(R'\) a subset of \(R\). The following conditions
are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(R'\) is of type (R), \(H_{R'}\) is reductive and critical.}

\emph{(ii) There exists a system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\) and
a subset \(\Delta'\) of \(\Delta\) such that \(R'\) is the set of
elements of \(R\) that are linear combinations of elements of
\(\Delta'\).}

\emph{(iii) \(R'\) is closed, symmetric, and every system of simple
roots of \(R'\) is the intersection with \(R'\) of a system of simple
roots of \(R\).}

Indeed, by Exp. XXI 3.4.8, (ii) and (iii) are equivalent and are also
equivalent to the fact that \(R'\) is the intersection of \(R\) with a
\(\mathbb{Q}\)-subspace of \(M \otimes \mathbb{Q}\). Now this last
condition is entailed by (i): if \(H_{R'} = Centr_{G}(Q)\), then \(R'\)
is the set of elements of \(R\) that vanish on \(Q\) (Exp. II 5.2.3
(ii)). Finally, this condition entails (i), because \(rad(H_{R'})\) is
the maximal torus of \(\bigcap_{\alpha \in R'} Ker(\alpha)\), hence
\(Centr_{G}(rad(H_{R'}))\) is none other than \(H_{R''}\) where \(R''\)
is the intersection of \(R\) with the subspace generated by \(R'\).

\paragraph{5.10.7.}\label{section-231}

Let us summarize some of the preceding results: let \((G, T, M, R)\) be
an \(S\)-split group, and let \(\Delta\) be a system of simple roots of
\(R\) and \(R+\) the corresponding system of positive roots; choose a
subset \(\Delta'\) of \(\Delta\), denote \(R'\) the set of elements of
\(R\) that are linear combinations of elements of \(\Delta'\) and set
\(R'+ = R' \cap R+\). Let \(T_{\Delta'}\) be the maximal torus of
\(\bigcap_{\alpha \in \Delta'} Ker(\alpha)\) and
