\(Z_{\Delta'} = Centr_{G}(T_{\Delta'})\).

Then \(Z_{\Delta'}\) is a reductive subgroup of \(G\), with radical
\(T_{\Delta'}\); \((Z_{\Delta'}, T, M, R')\) is an \(S\)-split group;
\(B_{R+} \cap Z_{\Delta'}\) is the Borel subgroup of \(Z_{\Delta'}\)
defined by the system of positive roots \(R'+\) (or by the system of
simple roots \(\Delta'\)) and its unipotent part is
\(U_{R+} \cap Z_{\Delta'} = U_{R'+}\).

\textbf{Remark 5.10.8.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.10.4, let \(Q\)
be a critical torus of \(G\), \(L = Centr_{G}(Q)\) its centralizer.
Since \(Q = rad(L)\), then \(Q\) is a characteristic subgroup of \(L\);
it follows immediately that}

\[
Norm_{G}(L) = Norm_{G}(Q),
\]

\emph{hence also}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_G(L)/L = Norm\_G(Q)/Centr\_G(Q) = W\_G(Q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 5.10.2, one deduces:

\textbf{Proposition 5.10.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(Q\) a critical torus of \(G\). The Weyl group
\(W_{G}(Q)\) is (étale) finite over \(S\).}

\textbf{Remark 5.10.10.} \emph{Under the conditions of 5.10.7, one may
make explicit}

\[
W_{G}(T_{\Delta'}) = Norm_{G}(Z_{\Delta'})/Z_{\Delta'}.
\]

\emph{It is the constant group associated with the quotient
\(W_{1}/W_{2}\), where \(W_{1}\) is the subgroup of \(W\) formed by the
elements that normalize the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(\Delta'\),
and \(W_{2}\) is the subgroup of \(W\) generated by the \(s\alpha\),
\(\alpha \in \Delta'\).}

\subsubsection{5.11. Subgroups of type (RC)}\label{subgroups-of-type-rc}

\textbf{Definition 5.11.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. A group subscheme \(H\) of \(G\) is called} of
type (RC) \emph{if it is of type (R), i.e.~(5.2.1) satisfies the
following two conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(H\) is smooth over \(S\), with connected fibers;}

\emph{(ii) for every \(s \in S\), \(H_{s}\) contains a maximal torus of
\(G_{s}\);}

\emph{and if it further satisfies the following condition:}

\emph{(iii) for every \(s \in S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of
\(H_{s}\), the set of roots of \(H_{s}\) relative to \(T\) is a closed
subset of the set of all roots of \(G_{s}\) relative to \(T\).}

\textbf{Remark 5.11.2.} \emph{As we have already noted in 5.4.8,
condition (iii) is a consequence of the others when \texttt{6} is
invertible on \(S\).}\footnote{I.e. when every residue characteristic of
  \(S\) is \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 3}.}

\textbf{Lemma 5.11.3.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be an \(S\)-split
group and \(R'\) a closed subset of \(R\). Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R₁ = \{α ∈ R′ | −α ∈ R′\}    and    R₂ = \{α ∈ R′ | −α ∉ R′\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\) are closed. Consider the groups
\(H_{R'}\), \(H_{R_{1}}\) and \(U_{R_{2}}\) (5.4.7 and 5.6.5), which are
smooth with connected fibers.}

\emph{(i) The group \(U_{R_{2}}\) is normal in \(H_{R'}\) and \(H_{R'}\)
is the semi-direct product of \(U_{R_{2}}\) by \(H_{R_{1}}\).}

\emph{(ii) \(H_{R_{1}}\) is reductive, \(U_{R_{2}}\) has connected and
unipotent geometric fibers; every normal subgroup of \(H_{R'}\), smooth
over \(S\) and with connected and unipotent geometric fibers, is
contained in \(U_{R_{2}}\), and every reductive subgroup of \(H_{R'}\)
containing \(T\) is contained in \(H_{R_{1}}\).}

\emph{(iii) One has \(U_{R_{2}} \cap Norm_{G}(H_{R_{1}}) = e\).}

One first has (iii) by 5.6.7 (i). The first assertion of (i) follows
from 5.6.7 (ii). Since \(U_{R_{2}} \cap H_{R_{1}} = e\) by (iii), the
semi-direct product \(H_{R_{1}} \cdot U_{R_{2}}\) is a subgroup of
\(H_{R'}\); but these are two subgroups of type (R) of \(G\), containing
\(T\), and they have the same Lie algebra \(g_{R'}\); they thus coincide
by 5.3.5, finishing the proof of (i).

Let us now prove (ii); the first two assertions are simply 5.10.1 and
5.6.5. Let \(U\) be a group subscheme of \(H_{R'}\), smooth and of
finite presentation, normal (hence normalized by \(T\)), with connected
and unipotent geometric fibers; by 5.6.12, one has, locally on \(S\),
\(U = U_{R''}\), where \(R''\) is a subset of \(R'\) such that
\(R'' \cap -R'' = \emptyset\). If \(U \not\subset U_{R_{2}}\), then
\(R'' \not\subset R_{2}\), so there exists \(\alpha \in R''\) such that
\(-\alpha \in R'\). Then \(Z\alpha \subset H_{R'}\) (5.4.3), so
\(Z\alpha\) normalizes \(U\). But \(U\) contains \(U\alpha\) and
\(Z\alpha\) possesses a section \(w\) such that
\(int(w) U\alpha = U_{-\alpha}\); this entails \(-\alpha \in R''\),
contradicting the hypothesis \(R'' \cap -R'' = \emptyset\).

Finally, if \(L\) is a reductive subgroup of \(H_{R'}\) containing
\(T\), one has locally on \(S\), \(L = H_{R'''}\), with \(R'''\)
symmetric contained in \(R'\), hence contained in \(R_{1}\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.11.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) a group subscheme of \(G\) of type (RC).}

\emph{(i) \(H\) is closed in \(G\), \(Norm_{G}(H)/H\) is representable
by a finite étale \(S\)-group scheme.}

\emph{(ii) \(H\) possesses a largest normal group subscheme that is
smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected and
unipotent geometric fibers; we call it the} unipotent radical \emph{of
\(H\) and denote it \(rad_{u}(H)\). The quotient sheaf \(H/rad_{u}(H)\)
is representable by an \(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(iii) If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(H\), \(H\) possesses a
reductive subgroup \(L\) containing \(T\) of type (RC) possessing the
two following properties:}

\emph{(a) Every reductive subgroup of \(H\) containing \(T\) is
contained in \(L\).}

\emph{(b) \(H\) is the semi-direct product \(H = L \cdot rad_{u}(H)\),
i.e.~the canonical morphism \(L \to H/rad_{u}(H)\) is an isomorphism.}

\emph{Furthermore, \(L\) is the unique reductive subgroup of \(H\)
containing \(T\) and satisfying one or the other of the two preceding
conditions. Finally, one has the following equalities:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_H(L) = L,    Norm\_H(T) = Norm\_L(T),    W\_H(T) = W\_L(T),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{in particular \(W_{H}(T)\) is finite over \(S\).}

\emph{Proof.} Let us first note that (i) is local for the étale
topology. Therefore, by Corollary 5.3.18, (i) is a consequence of the
last assertion of (iii).

The assertions of (ii) are local for the étale topology. One may
therefore suppose to be in the situation of 5.11.3, where one concludes
immediately by (i) and (ii).

By virtue of the uniqueness assertions contained in it, (iii) is also
local for the étale topology and one may again reduce to the situation
of 5.11.3, where properties (a) and (b) have been verified. The
uniqueness of an \(L\) satisfying (a) is trivial; the uniqueness of an
\(L\) satisfying (b) is obvious, given (a). The equality
\(Norm_{H}(L) = L\) is none other than 5.11.3 (iii); if a section of
\(H\) normalizes \(T\), then it normalizes \(L\), by uniqueness of
\(L\), hence is a section of \(L\) by what was just demonstrated, which
proves the second equality; the third is then trivial.

\textbf{Proposition 5.11.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \texttt{Hc} the functor of subgroups of type (RC)
of \(G\), which is a subfunctor of the functor \(H\) of 5.8.1.}

\emph{(i) \texttt{Hc} is representable by an open subscheme of \(H\),
smooth, quasi-projective, and of finite presentation over \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) There exists a finite étale \(S\)-scheme \(C\ell_{c}\) and a
morphism}

\[
c\ell : Hc \to C\ell_{c},
\]

\emph{smooth, quasi-projective, of finite presentation, surjective, with
connected geometric fibers, possessing the following property:}

\emph{For every \(S' \to S\) and every \(H, H' \in Hc(S')\),
\(c\ell(H) = c\ell(H')\) if and only if \(H\) and \(H'\) are conjugate
in \(G\) locally for the étale topology (or, equivalently by 5.3.11, if
for every \(s \in S\), \(H_{s}\) and \(H'_{s}\) are conjugate by an
element of \(G(s)\)).}

\emph{(iii) \(C\ell_{c}\) and \(c\ell\) are determined (up to unique
isomorphism) by the preceding conditions.}

\emph{(iv) If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a splitting of \(G\), let \(E\) be the
set of conjugacy classes modulo \(W\) of closed subsets of \(R\); then
there exists an isomorphism \(C\ell_{c} \xrightarrow{\sim} E_{S}\) such
that, for every closed subset \(R'\) of \(R\), \(c\ell(H_{R'})\)
corresponds to the canonical image of \(R'\) in
\texttt{E\_S(S)\ =\ Hom\_\{loc.const.\}(S,\ E)}.}

It is first clear that \texttt{Hc} is a sheaf for the étale topology and
that (ii) entails that \(C\ell_{c}\) is none other than the quotient
sheaf of \texttt{Hc} by the equivalence relation defined by conjugation.

This entails first (iii), as well as the fact that it suffices to verify
(i) and (ii) locally for the étale topology. One thus reduces to the
situation of (iv); let us first construct a morphism

\[
f : Hc \to E_{S}.
\]

It suffices to construct an application \(Hc(S) \to E_{S}(S)\)
functorial in \(S\); so let \(H\) be a subgroup of type (RC) of \(G\);
since \(H\) locally for the étale topology possesses maximal tori, and
since the maximal tori of \(G\) are conjugate locally for the étale
topology, there exists a covering family \({S_{i} \to S}\) and for each
\(i\) a \(g_{i} \in G(S_{i})\) and a closed subset \(R_{i}\) of \(R\)
such that
\(int(g_{i})(H \times_{S} S_{i}) = H_{R_{i}} \times_{S} S_{i}\); each
\(R_{i}\) defines a section \(\eta_{i}\) of \(E_{S_{i}}\), i.e.~an
element of \(E_{S}(S_{i})\); it now suffices to prove that the family
\((\eta_{i})\) arises from a section \(\eta = f(H)\) of \texttt{E\_S}
over \(S\), and that the latter depends only on \(H\).

For this, one is reduced to proving that \(H_{R'}\) and \(H_{R''}\) are
conjugate locally for the étale topology if and only if \(R'\) and
\(R''\) are conjugate by an element of the Weyl group \(W\), which is
trivial.

For every \(\eta \in E\), there exists an \(H_{0} \in Hc(S)\) such that
\(f(H_{0}) = \eta\): it suffices to take \(H_{0} = H_{R'}\) where \(R'\)
is a closed subset of \(R\) whose image in \(E\) is \(\eta\). If
\(H \in H_{0}(S')\), \(S' \to S\), \(H\) is conjugate to \(H_{0}\)
locally for the étale topology if and only if \(f(H) = \eta\) (as one
sees immediately by the preceding argument), which shows that
\(f^{-1}(\eta)\) is identified with the quotient \(G/Norm_{G}(H_{0})\),
which by 5.8.2 is an open subset of \(H\), smooth, quasi-projective of
finite presentation over \(S\), with connected and non-empty fibers.
Since \texttt{E\_S} is the sum of the open subschemes images of the
sections corresponding to the \(\eta \in E\), \texttt{Hc} is identified
with the sum of the \(f^{-1}(\eta)\), \(\eta \in E\), which proves (i)
and (ii). Finally, (iv) holds by construction.

\textbf{Corollary 5.11.6.} \emph{If \(u \in C\ell_{c}(S')\),
\(S' \to S\), \(c\ell^{-1}(u)\) is an \(S'\)-scheme that is smooth,
quasi-projective, of finite presentation, with non-empty connected
fibers; it is an open subset of \texttt{Hc} and a ``homogeneous'' scheme
under \(G_{S'}\) (by inner automorphisms). In particular, if
\(H \in c\ell^{-1}(u)(S')\), the morphism \(G_{S'} \to (Hc)_{S'}\)
defined by \(g \mapsto int(g) H\) identifies \(G_{S'}/Norm_{G_{S'}}(H)\)
with \(c\ell^{-1}(u)\).}

\textbf{Examples 5.11.7.} \emph{In particular, one has two canonical
sections \(u_{t}\), \(u_{b}\) of \(C\ell_{c}\) corresponding
respectively to maximal tori (\(R' = \emptyset\)) and to Borel subgroups
(\(R' =\) system of positive roots). The \(S\)-schemes
\(c\ell^{-1}(u_{t})\) and \(c\ell^{-1}(u_{b})\) are none other than the
\(S\)-schemes \(Tor(G)\) and \(Bor(G)\) introduced in 5.8.3. We will see
other examples in Exp. XXVI.}

\textbf{Remark 5.11.8.} \emph{One may construct an \(S\)-scheme
\(C\ell\), of finite presentation and unramified, and a morphism
\(H \to C\ell\) smooth and surjective, with connected geometric fibers,
enjoying properties analogous to 5.11.5 (ii) and (iii).}

\subsection{6. The derived group}\label{the-derived-group}

\subsubsection{6.1. Preliminaries}\label{preliminaries}

In this section, we fix a scheme \(S\), an \(S\)-split group
\((G, T, M, R)\), a system of positive roots \(R+\) of \(R\), and write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B = B\_\{R+\},    B\_{-} = B\_\{R−\},    U = B\^{}u,    U\_{-} = (B\_{-})\^{}u,}
\NormalTok{Ω = Ω\_\{R+\} = U\_{-} · T · U.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{6.1.1.}\label{section-232}

We denote by \(T'\) the subtorus of \(T\) ``image of the family
\(\alpha*\), \(\alpha \in R\)''; in other words, \(T'\) is the image of
the morphism of groups

\[
G^{R}_{m,S} \to T
\]

defined by
\((z_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in R} \mapsto \prod_{\alpha \in R} \alpha*(z_{\alpha})\).
One sees immediately that if \(\Delta\) denotes the set of simple roots
of \(R+\), the morphism

\[
G^{\Delta}_{m,S} \to T'
\]

defined in the same way is surjective with finite kernel. If we identify
\(T\) with \(D_{S}(M)\), then \(T'\) is identified with \(D_{S}(M/N)\),
where

\[
N = M \cap V(R*)^{\perp}
\]

(we denote by \(V(R*)^{\perp}\) the orthogonal of \(V(R*)\) in the
duality between \(V\) and \(V*\)).

\textbf{Lemma 6.1.2.} \emph{The morphism defined by the product in
\(T\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad(G) ×\_S T′ → T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an isogeny (cf.~4.2.9).}

Indeed, the canonical morphism \(rad(T) \to T/T'\) arises by duality
from the morphism of commutative groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M ∩ V(R*)\^{}⊥ → M/(M ∩ V(R)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which one sees immediately to be injective with finite cokernel
(cf.~Exp. XXI 6.3).

\textbf{Definition 6.1.3.} \emph{One writes
\(\Omega' = U_{-} \cdot T' \cdot U\); it is a closed subscheme of
\(\Omega = U_{-} \cdot T \cdot U\).}

\textbf{Lemma 6.1.4.} \emph{Let \(\alpha\) be a simple root and
\(w_{\alpha} \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) lifting \(s_{\alpha}\). One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) Ω′ ∩ Ω ⊂ Ω′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It suffices for us to prove that if \(g \in \Omega'(S)\) and
\(int(w_{\alpha}) g \in \Omega(S)\), then
\(int(w_{\alpha}) g \in \Omega'(S)\). By 5.6.8, write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = a · exp\_\{{-}α\}(Y) · t · expα(X) · b,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

with \(a \in U_{-\hat{\alpha}}(S)\), \(Y \in \Gamma(S, g^{-\alpha})\),
\(t \in T'(S)\), \(X \in \Gamma(S, g^{\alpha})\),
\(b \in U_{\hat{\alpha}}(S)\). One then has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) g = int(w\_α) a · int(w\_α)(exp\_\{{-}α\}(Y) t expα(X)) · int(w\_α) b.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By virtue of 5.6.8 (iv), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) a ∈ U\_\{{-}α̂\}(S),    int(w\_α) b ∈ U\_\{α̂\}(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows that one has the following equivalences (setting
\(h = \exp_{-\alpha}(Y) t \exp \alpha(X)\)):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) g ∈ Ω(S)   ⇔   int(w\_α) h ∈ Ω(S)}
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) g ∈ Ω′(S)  ⇔   int(w\_α) h ∈ Ω′(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One is therefore reduced to the case where \(g = h\). Since one has
(4.1.12)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Zα ∩ Ω = U\_\{{-}α\} · T · Uα,    Zα ∩ Ω′ = U\_\{{-}α\} · T′ · Uα,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one is reduced to proving the following assertion:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) h ∈ (U\_\{{-}α\} · T · Uα)(S)  ⇒  int(w\_α) h ∈ (U\_\{{-}α\} · T′ · Uα)(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now this latter follows immediately from Exp. XX 3.12, which shows that
the component on \(T\) of \(int(w_{\alpha}) h\) is of the form
\(t \cdot \alpha*(z) \in T'(S)\).

\textbf{Lemma 6.1.5.} \emph{For every \(w \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\), there
exists an open subset \(V_{w}\) of \(G\) containing the unit section,
such that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w) Ω′ ∩ V\_w ⊂ Ω′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Choose, for each simple root \(\alpha\), an
\(n_{\alpha} \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) lifting \(s_{\alpha}\). For every
point \(s \in S\), there exist an open subset \(V\) of \(S\) containing
\(s\), a \(t \in T(V)\) and over \(V\) a relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w = n\_\{α₁\} ⋯ n\_\{α\_p\} t,    with the αᵢ simple.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One may obviously content oneself with making the demonstration for
\(V = S\); it is done by induction on \(p\). If \(p = 0\), then
\(w \in T(S)\) and one takes \(V_{w} = G\); suppose therefore
\(w = n_{\alpha} \cdot w'\), \(w'\) satisfying the conclusion of the
lemma; there thus exists an open subset \(V_{w'}\) of \(G\), containing
the unit section, such that
\(int(w') \Omega' \cap V_{w'} \subset \Omega'\). One may then write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w) Ω′ ∩ (int(n\_α) V\_\{w′\} ∩ Ω) = int(n\_α)(int(w′) Ω′ ∩ V\_\{w′\}) ∩ Ω}
\NormalTok{                                  ⊂ int(n\_α) Ω′ ∩ Ω ⊂ Ω′,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by 6.1.4. One then takes \(V_{w} = int(n_{\alpha}) V_{w'} \cap \Omega\)
and we are done.

\textbf{Lemma 6.1.6.} \emph{There exists an open subset \(V_{0}\) of
\(G\), containing the unit section, such that for every \(S' \to S\),
one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U(S′) U\_{-}(S′) ∩ V₀(S′) ⊂ Ω′(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(n_{0}\) be an element of \(Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) lifting the symmetry
\(w_{0}\) of the Weyl group,\footnote{The symmetry \(w_{0}\) is defined
  in XXI 3.6.14.} that is, such that \(int(n_{0}) U = U_{-}\) (cf.~Exp.
XXI 3.6.14); then \(n^{2}_{0} \in T(S)\). Let us show that the open set
\(V_{0} = V_{n_{0}}\) of 6.1.5 answers the question. Indeed

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U(S′) U\_{-}(S′) = int(n₀)(int(n₀)⁻¹ U(S′) · int(n₀)⁻¹ U\_{-}(S′))}
\NormalTok{              = int(n₀)(U\_{-}(S′) · U(S′)) ⊂ int(n₀) Ω′(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U(S′) U\_{-}(S′) ∩ V₀(S′) ⊂ int(n₀) Ω′(S′) ∩ V₀(S′) ⊂ Ω′(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 6.1.7.} \emph{Consider the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : Ω = U\_{-} · T · U → T/T′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{composite of the second projection and the canonical morphism of
\(T\) into \(T/T'\). Then \(f\) is ``generically multiplicative'': there
exists an open subset \(V\) of \(\Omega \times_{S} \Omega\), containing
the unit section (and hence relatively schematically dense, Exp. XVIII
1.3) such that for every \(S' \to S\) and every \((x, y) \in V(S')\),
one has \(xy \in \Omega(S')\) and \(f(xy) = f(x) f(y)\).}

Let \(x\) and \(y\) be two sections of \(\Omega\) over \(S'\). Write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x = u t v,    y = u′ t′ v′,    with u, u′ ∈ U\_{-}(S′), t, t′ ∈ T(S′), v, v′ ∈ U(S′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(V_{0}\) be the open set of 6.1.6 and \(V\) the open subset of
\(\Omega \times_{S} \Omega\) defined by ``\(v u' \in V_{0}(S')\)'' (it
is the inverse image of \(V_{0}\) by the morphism
\(\Omega \times_{S} \Omega\) written set-theoretically
\((x, y) \mapsto v u'\)). Then \(V\) answers the question. Indeed, for
\((x, y) \in V(S')\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xy = (u t v)(u′ t′ v′) = (u t)(v u′)(t′ v′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \(v u' \in \Omega'(S')\), whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{xy ∈ U\_{-}(S′) · t · Ω′(S′) · t′ · U(S′) ⊂ U\_{-}(S′) · tt′ T′(S′) · U(S′),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which shows that \(xy \in \Omega(S')\) and that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(xy) = f(tt′) = f(t) f(t′) = f(x) f(y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 6.1.8.} \emph{There exists a morphism of groups}

\[
f : G \to T/T'
\]

\emph{inducing on \(T\) the canonical projection. The kernel \(Ker(f)\)
of \(f\) is a closed group subscheme of \(G\) smooth over \(S\) and with
connected fibers. Every morphism of groups from \(G\) to a presheaf of
commutative groups on \(S\), separated for (fppf), vanishes on
\(Ker(f)\).}

The first assertion follows immediately from 4.1.11. One has immediately
\(Ker(f) \cap \Omega = \Omega'\), which proves that \(Ker(f)\) is smooth
over \(S\) at every point of the unit section.\footnote{We have added
  ``at every point of the unit section'' as well as the reference to
  VI\_B 3.10 at the end of the proof. Furthermore, in the next sentence
  we have replaced ``prescheme'' with ``presheaf''.} By 5.6.9 (ii),
every morphism \(\phi\) from \(G\) to a presheaf of commutative groups
separated for (fppf) vanishes on \(U\) and \texttt{U\_-}. By Exp. XX
2.7, \(\phi\) therefore vanishes also on \(T'\), hence on \(\Omega'\).
Taking the notations of 5.7.10, one sees that the monoid \(U_{1}\) is
contained in \(Ker(f)(S)\), which shows that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ker(f) = ⋃\_\{u ∈ U₁\} u Ω′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows on the one hand that every \(\phi\) as above vanishes on
\(Ker(f)\), and on the other hand that \(Ker(f)\) has connected fibers,
hence is smooth over \(S\) by Exp. VI\_B 3.10.

\subsubsection{6.2. Derived group of a reductive
group}\label{derived-group-of-a-reductive-group}

\textbf{Theorem 6.2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) \(D_{S}(G) = \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, Gm,S)\) is
representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-group, whose type at
\(s \in S\) is \(\mathbb{Z}^{rg_{red}(G_{s}) - rg_{ss}(G_{s})}\).}

\emph{(ii) Write \(corad(G) = D_{S}(D_{S}(G))\), which is therefore an
\(S\)-torus. The biduality morphism (cf.~Exp. VIII § 1)}

\[
f_{0} : G \to corad(G)
\]

\emph{is smooth and surjective.}

\emph{(iii) The composite morphism}

\[
rad(G) \to G \to corad(G)
\]

\emph{is an isogeny (cf.~4.2.9).}

\emph{(iv) The kernel of \(f_{0}\), denoted}

\[
d\acute{e}r(G) = Ker(f_{0})
\]

\emph{is a closed group subscheme of \(G\), semisimple over \(S\),
called the} derived group \emph{of \(G\). If \(G\) is semisimple, one
has \(d\acute{e}r(G) = G\).}

\emph{(v) Every morphism of groups from \(G\) to an \(S\)-presheaf of
commutative groups, separated for (fppf), vanishes on \(d\acute{e}r(G)\)
and thus factors through \(f_{0}\).}

\emph{Proof.} All assertions of the theorem are local for the étale
topology; one may thus reduce to the case where \(G\) is split over
\(S\). Consider then the morphism \(f\) of 6.1.8. By the last assertion
of 6.1.8, one immediately has an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, Gm,S) ⥲ Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T/T′, Gm,S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which proves (i), then (ii) and gives a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ─────f₀──→ corad(G)}
\NormalTok{ ↘            ≀}
\NormalTok{   f         ↓}
\NormalTok{    ↘  →  T/T′.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One then has (v) by 6.1.8, and (iii) by 6.1.2. One also has
\(Ker(f) = Ker(f_{0})\), which by 6.1.8 entails that \(d\acute{e}r(G)\)
is smooth over \(S\) and has connected fibers; it remains to verify that
its fibers are semisimple; now they are reductive by Exp. XIX 1.7, as
invariant subgroups of reductive groups. By (iii),
\(rad(G) \cap d\acute{e}r(G)\) is finite, which indeed entails that the
fibers of \(d\acute{e}r(G)\) are semisimple.

\textbf{Remark 6.2.2.} \emph{(a) By construction, in the case where
\(G\) is split, \(d\acute{e}r(G)\) is the (fppf) subsheaf of \(G\)
generated by the \(U\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\). (It even suffices to
take the \(U\alpha\), \(\alpha \in \Delta \cup -\Delta\), where
\(\Delta\) is a basis of \(R\).)}

\emph{(b)}\footnote{In what follows, we have expanded the original, and
  suppressed the assertion that ``\(d\acute{e}r(G)\) is the separated
  (fppf) presheaf of commutators of \(G\)''.} \emph{Let \(C\) be the
presheaf of commutators of \(G\), i.e.~the \(S\)-group functor that
associates with every \(S' \to S\) the group of commutators of \(G(S')\)
(i.e.~the subgroup of \(G(S')\) generated by the elements
\(xyx^{-1}y^{-1}\), for \(x, y \in G(S')\)), and let \(\tilde{C}\) be
the associated (fppf) sheaf. Since the quotient
\(G/d\acute{e}r(G) = T/T'\) is commutative, then \(d\acute{e}r(G)\)
contains \(C\) and hence \(\tilde{C}\) (cf.~Exp. IV 4.3.12).}

\emph{On the other hand, the quotient presheaf \(G/\tilde{C}\) is
separated (Exp. IV 4.4.8.1), and therefore by (v) one has
\(d\acute{e}r(G) \subset \tilde{C}\), whence
\(d\acute{e}r(G) = \tilde{C}\), i.e.~\(d\acute{e}r(G)\) is the (fppf)
sheaf of commutators of \(G\).}

\emph{Let us finally note that \(C\), being a subpresheaf of \(G\), is
separated, but is not equal to \(d\acute{e}r(G)\) in general: for
example, \(d\acute{e}r(SL_{2}) = SL_{2}\) but
\(SL_{2}(F_{2}) \simeq S_{3}\) is not equal to its derived group.}

\emph{(c) When \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field
\(k\), \(d\acute{e}r(G)(k)\) is the group of commutators of \(G(k)\)
(Exp. VI\_B 7.10).}

\paragraph{6.2.3.}\label{section-233}

Consider now the two exact sequences

\[
1 \to rad(G) \to G \to ss(G) \to 1,
1 \to d\acute{e}r(G) \to G \to corad(G) \to 1.
\]

Since \(rad(G)\) is central in \(G\), the product in \(G\) defines a
morphism of groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u : rad(G) ×\_S dér(G) → G}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is covering by virtue of 6.2.1 (iii), hence surjective and flat
(Exp. VI\_B 9.2 (xi)).\footnote{Indeed, \(G\) is the (fppf) quotient of
  \(rad(G) \times_{S} d\acute{e}r(G)\) by \(Ker(u)\), which is a group
  of multiplicative type, hence flat over \(S\). Therefore, by VI\_B 9.2
  (xi), the morphism \(u\) is flat.} Its kernel is isomorphic to
\(rad(G) \cap d\acute{e}r(G)\), which is also the kernel of
\(rad(G) \to corad(G)\), hence is a finite subgroup of multiplicative
type of \(rad(G)\).

One reasons similarly for the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G → corad(G) ×\_S ss(G),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whose kernel is \(d\acute{e}r(G) \cap rad(G)\). One thus has:

\textbf{Proposition 6.2.4.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group.
The morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad(G) ×\_S dér(G) → G,    G → corad(G) ×\_S ss(G),    rad(G) → corad(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are central isogenies, and their kernels are isomorphic.}

\textbf{Corollary 6.2.5.} \emph{The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is the product of a semisimple group and a torus.}

\emph{(ii) \(rad(G) \times_{S} d\acute{e}r(G) \xrightarrow{\sim} G\).}

\emph{(iii) \(G \xrightarrow{\sim} corad(G) \times_{S} ss(G)\).}

\emph{(iv) \(rad(G) \cap d\acute{e}r(G) = e\).}

\paragraph{6.2.6.}\label{section-234}

Let us return provisionally to the case of a split group. Let us keep
the notations of 6.1. Set \(N = M \cap V(R*)^{\perp}\). One thus has
\(T' = D_{S}(M/N)\). One has seen that \(U_{-} \cdot T' \cdot U\) was an
open neighborhood of the unit section of \(d\acute{e}r(G)\). One thus
has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(dér(G)/S) = t′ ⨿ ⨿\_\{α ∈ R\} g\^{}α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since the characters induced on \(T'\) by the \(\alpha \in R\) are
non-zero and distinct (cf.~Exp. XXI 1.2.5 --- one has moreover already
used this fact in 6.1.2), \(R\) is a system of roots of
\(d\acute{e}r(G)\) relative to \(T'\). It is then immediate (since
\(U\alpha \subset d\acute{e}r(G)\)) that the \texttt{exp} morphisms of
\(d\acute{e}r(G)\) ``are'' those of \(G\) and similarly for the coroots.

It follows:

\textbf{Proposition 6.2.7.} \emph{In the preceding notations,
\((d\acute{e}r(G), T', M/N, R)\) is a split group with root datum
\(d\acute{e}r(R(G))\). The canonical morphism \(d\acute{e}r(G) \to G\)
gives by functoriality the canonical morphism of root data
\(R(G) \to d\acute{e}r(R(G))\) of Exp. XXI 6.5.}

\emph{N. B.} The reader may, as an exercise, construct the diagram of
split groups corresponding to the three left columns of the diagram of
root data of Exp. XXI 6.5.7.

\textbf{Proposition 6.2.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(d\acute{e}r(G)\) its derived group.}

\emph{(i) For every maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\),
\(T \cap d\acute{e}r(G)\) is a maximal torus of \(d\acute{e}r(G)\). For
every maximal torus \(T'\) of \(d\acute{e}r(G)\),
\(Centr_{G}(T') = rad(G) \cdot T'\) is a maximal torus of \(G\). The two
preceding constructions are inverse to one another and set up a
bijective correspondence between maximal tori of \(G\) and of
\(d\acute{e}r(G)\).}

\emph{(ii) For every Borel subgroup \(B\) of \(G\),
\(B \cap d\acute{e}r(G)\) is a Borel subgroup \(B'\) of
\(d\acute{e}r(G)\). One has \(B'u = B^{u}\). For every Borel subgroup
\(B'\) of \(d\acute{e}r(G)\), \(Norm_{G}(B') = rad(G) \cdot B'\) is a
Borel subgroup of \(G\). The preceding applications are inverse to one
another and set up a bijective correspondence between Borel subgroups of
\(G\) and of \(d\acute{e}r(G)\).}

By the local conjugacy theorem for maximal tori and the construction of
the derived group, the only assertion that remains to prove in (i) is
the following: if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T = (T ∩ dér(G)) · rad(G) = Centr\_G(T ∩ dér(G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The first equality is trivial (one reduces to the split case); the
second follows from this immediately, because \(rad(G)\) is central in
\(G\), so \(T = Centr_{G}(T) = Centr_{G}(T \cap d\acute{e}r(G))\). One
reasons similarly for (ii).

\subsubsection{6.3. Subgroups with commutative
quotients}\label{subgroups-with-commutative-quotients}

\paragraph{6.3.1.}\label{section-235}

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group. If \(H\) is a group subsheaf of
\(G\), the following conditions are equivalent:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(H\) contains \(d\acute{e}r(G)\).
\item
  \(H\) is normal and \(G/H\) is commutative.
\end{itemize}

In this case, the canonical morphism \(f_{0} : G \to corad(G)\) sends
\(H\) to a subsheaf \(f_{0}(H)\) of \(corad(G)\); one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G/H ≃ corad(G)/f₀(H),    H/dér(H) ≃ f₀(H),}
\NormalTok{dér(G) = dér(H),    H = f₀⁻¹(f₀(H)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(d\acute{e}r(G)\) is smooth over \(S\) and has connected
fibers,\footnote{We have expanded the original in what follows. In
  particular, we have added the conclusion (implicit in the original)
  that every subgroup of \(G\), smooth with connected fibers and
  containing \(d\acute{e}r(G)\), is closed in \(G\).} by Exp. IV, 5.3.1
and 6.3.1, and Exp. IV\_B 9.2, the map \(H \mapsto f_{0}(H)\)
establishes a bijective correspondence between group subschemes (resp.
closed group subschemes) of \(G\) containing \(d\acute{e}r(G)\), smooth
over \(S\) and with connected fibers, and group subschemes (resp. closed
group subschemes) of \(corad(G)\), smooth over \(S\) and with connected
fibers.

Now, if \(H'\) is a group subscheme of \(corad(G)\), smooth over \(S\)
with connected fibers, then \(H'\) is of finite presentation over \(S\)
(Exp. VI\_B 5.5) and its fibers are tori (since those of \(corad(G)\)
are), so by Exp. X 8.2, \(H'\) is a subtorus of \(corad(G)\), hence is
closed in \(corad(G)\) (Exp. IX 2.6).

Consequently, every subgroup of \(G\), smooth with connected fibers and
containing \(d\acute{e}r(G)\), is closed in \(G\).\footnote{We have
  expanded the original in what follows. In particular, we have added
  the conclusion (implicit in the original) that every subgroup of
  \(G\), smooth with connected fibers and containing \(d\acute{e}r(G)\),
  is closed in \(G\).}

\paragraph{6.3.2.}\label{section-236}

If \(H\) is a closed group subscheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), with
connected fibers, and normal in \(G\), then \(H\) is reductive. If
furthermore \(H \supset d\acute{e}r(G)\), then
\(d\acute{e}r(H) = d\acute{e}r(G)\) and \(f_{0}(H)\) is identified with
\(corad(H)\). One has thus proved:

\textbf{Proposition 6.3.3.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group.
Every group subscheme \(H\) of \(G\), normal in \(G\), with commutative
quotient (i.e.~containing \(d\acute{e}r(G)\)), smooth over \(S\), with
connected fibers,\footnote{We have removed the hypothesis that \(H\) be
  retrocompact in \(G\), which is automatically verified because, by
  VI\_B 5.5, \(G\) and \(H\) are separated and quasi-compact over \(S\),
  so \(H \hookrightarrow G\) is quasi-compact by EGA IV₁, 1.1.2 (v).} is
closed and reductive. One has \(d\acute{e}r(H) = d\acute{e}r(G)\) and
\(f_{0}(H)\) is identified with \(corad(H)\); one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G/H ≃ corad(G)/corad(H),    H = (H ∩ rad(G)) · dér(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Furthermore, \(H \mapsto f_{0}(H)\) defines a bijection between
the set of subgroups \(H\) of \(G\) possessing the preceding properties
and the set of subtori of \(corad(H)\).}

By a further application of Noether's theorem (Exp. IV, 5.3.1 and
6.3.1), one deduces:

\textbf{Proposition 6.3.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). For every
subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) as above, \(T \cap H\) is a maximal torus of
\(G\) and one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G/H ≃ T/(T ∩ H),    H = (T ∩ H) · dér(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Furthermore, \(H \mapsto T \cap H\) is a bijection between the set
of subgroups \(H\) of \(G\) as above and the set of subtori of \(T\)
containing \(T \cap d\acute{e}r(G)\).}

\subsection{Editor's Notes}\label{editors-notes}

\section{Exposé XXIII. Reductive groups: uniqueness of pinned
groups}\label{exposuxe9-xxiii.-reductive-groups-uniqueness-of-pinned-groups}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Version of 13/10/2024.}

The aim of this Exposé is the proof of the uniqueness theorem (Theorem
4.1). This was proved by Chevalley in the case of an algebraically
closed field; the method of reduction to rank two used here is also due
to Chevalley (see \emph{Bible}, Exp. 23 and 24). Along the way, we
obtain an explicit description of reductive groups by generators and
relations (3.5).

\subsection{1. Pinnings}\label{pinnings}

\textbf{Definition 1.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and
\((G, T, M, R)\) an \(S\)-split group (XXII, 1.13). One calls}
pinning{[}\^{}N.D.E-XXIII-butterfly{]} \emph{of this split group the
datum of a system \(\Delta\) of simple roots of \(R\) and, for each
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), a section
\(X_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\).}{[}\^{}N.D.E-XXIII-butterfly-anchor{]}

In other words, a pinning of the reductive group \(G\) over the nonempty
scheme \(S\) is the datum of:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  a maximal torus \(T\),
\item
  an abelian group \(M\) and an isomorphism \(T \simeq D_{S}(M)\),
\item
  a system of roots \(R\) of \(G\) with respect to \(T\),
\item
  a system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\),
\item
  an \(X_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\) for every
  \(\alpha \in \Delta\), that is, of a
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u\_α = exp\_α(X\_α) ∈ U\_α\^{}×(S)    for every α ∈ Δ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

satisfying condition (D 1) of Exp. XXII, 1.13 (indeed condition (D 2) of
\emph{loc. cit.} is automatically satisfied\footnote{N.D.E.: It is
  implied by condition (v), i.e.~the existence of a section
  \(X_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\).}).

Every split group admits a pinning; in particular, every reductive group
is locally pinnable for the étale topology.

\subsubsection{1.2.}\label{section-237}

If \(G\) is a pinned \(S\)-group --- that is, an \(S\)-split group
equipped with a pinning --- it is canonically endowed with the system of
positive roots \(R^{+}\) defined by \(\Delta\), the corresponding Borel
subgroup \(B = B_{R^{+}}\), the opposite Borel subgroup
\(B^{-} = B_{R^{-}}\), the unipotent groups \(U = B_{u}\),
\(U^{-} = (B^{-})_{u}\), the open set \(U^{-} \cdot T \cdot U\), etc.
Likewise, for each \(\alpha \in \Delta\), one has a canonical
isomorphism of vector groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α : G\_\{a, S\} ⥲ U\_α,    x ↦ exp\_α(x X\_α) = u\_α\^{}x,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

normalized by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\), and whose datum is
equivalent to that of \(X_{\alpha}\) (Exp. XXII, 1.1).

By duality, one deduces an
\(X_{-\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{-\alpha})^{\times}\) and an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{{-}α\} : G\_\{a, S\} ⥲ U\_\{{-}α\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is the contragredient of the preceding one (Exp. XXII, 1.3). We
shall set (Exp. XX, 3.1)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α = w\_α(X\_α) = p\_α(1) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1) p\_α(1) = p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1) p\_α(1) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One then has (\emph{loc. cit.} 3.1, 3.7)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α\^{}2 = α\^{}*({-}1),    int(w\_α) t = s\_α(t) = t · α\^{}*(α(t)\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) p\_α(x) = p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) = p\_\{{-}α\}(x)\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_α = {-}X\_\{{-}α\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) p\_\{{-}α\}(x) = p\_α({-}x) = p\_α(x)\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{{-}α\} = {-}X\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We shall use the preceding notation systematically in what follows.

\textbf{Definition 1.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and
\((G, T, M, R, \Delta, (X_{\alpha}))\) and \((G', T', M', \cdots)\) two
pinned \(S\)-groups. One says that the morphism of split groups (Exp.
XXII, 4.2.1)}

\[
f : G \to G'
\]

\emph{is} compatible with the pinnings, \emph{or that it defines a}
morphism of pinned groups, \emph{if the bijection \(d : R \to R'\)
associated with it (cf.~loc. cit.) satisfies \(d(\Delta) = \Delta'\) and
if, for every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(exp\_α(X\_α)) = exp\_\{d(α)\}(X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\}),    i.e.    f(u\_α) = u\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have denoted by \(d\) the bijection
  \(R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'\) (instead of \(u\)), in order to avoid the
  notation \(u'_{u(\alpha)}\).}

\subsubsection{1.4.}\label{section-238}

If we denote by \(q(\alpha)\) the integer of \emph{loc. cit.}, we
therefore have

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(p\_α(x)) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\}(x\^{}\{q(α)\})    for    α ∈ Δ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and consequently

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(p\_\{{-}α\}(x)) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{{-}d(α)\}(x\^{}\{q(α)\}),    f(w\_α) = w\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Recall (Exp. XXII, 4.2) that, for every \(\alpha \in R\) and all
\(z \in G_{m}(S')\), \(t \in T(S')\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(α\^{}*(z)) = d(α)\^{}*(z)\^{}\{q(α)\} = d(α)\^{}*(z\^{}\{q(α)\}),    d(α)(f(t)) = α(t)\^{}\{q(α)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{1.5.}\label{section-239}

We shall call a \emph{pinned root datum} a root datum endowed with a
system of simple roots, and a \emph{\(p\)-morphism of pinned root data}
a \(p\)-morphism of root data (Exp. XXI, 6.8) sending simple roots to
simple roots.

If \(G\) is a pinned \(S\)-group, we denote by \(R(G)\) the
corresponding pinned root datum (this is the root datum of Exp. XXII,
1.14 equipped with \(\Delta\)). Let \(p\) be the integer defined in Exp.
XXII, 4.2.2. One then has:

\textbf{Scholium 1.6.} \emph{The correspondence \(G \mapsto R(G)\)
defines a functor from the category of pinned reductive \(S\)-groups to
that of pinned root data (with \(p\)-morphisms as morphisms).}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{1.7. The pinned groups
\(Z_{\Delta_{1}}\)}{1.7. The pinned groups Z\_\{\textbackslash Delta\_\{1\}\}}}\label{the-pinned-groups-z_delta_1}

Let \(\Delta_{1}\) be a subset of the system of simple roots \(\Delta\)
of the pinned group \(G\). Let \(T_{\Delta_{1}}\) be the maximal torus
of \(\bigcap_{\alpha \in \Delta_{1}} Ker(\alpha)\); set

\[
Z_{\Delta_{1}} = Centr_{G}(T_{\Delta_{1}}).
\]

Set \(R' = \mathbb{Z} \cdot \Delta_{1} \cap R\); one knows (Exp. XXII,
5.10.7) that \(Z_{\Delta_{1}}\) is a reductive \(S\)-group with radical
\(T_{\Delta_{1}}\), that \texttt{(T,\ M,\ R\textquotesingle{})} is a
splitting of it, and \(\Delta_{1}\) a system of simple roots. It follows
that
\((Z_{\Delta_{1}}, T, M, R', \Delta_{1}, (X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta_{1}})\)
is a pinned \(S\)-group. We shall always equip \(Z_{\Delta_{1}}\) with
this pinning. In particular, we shall consider the groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Z\_α = Z\_\{\{α\}\},    Z\_\{αβ\} = Z\_\{\{α, β\}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We denote by \(B_{\Delta_{1}} = B \cap Z_{\Delta_{1}}\); one knows
(\emph{loc. cit.}) that this is the canonical Borel subgroup\footnote{N.D.E.:
  i.e., the Borel subgroup of \(Z_{\Delta_{1}}\) corresponding to
  \(R'_{+} = R' \cap R_{+}\).} of \(Z_{\Delta_{1}}\), and that its
unipotent part is \(U_{\Delta_{1}} = U \cap Z_{\Delta_{1}}\). In
particular,

\[
B_{\alpha} = T \cdot U_{\alpha}.
\]

We shall denote

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_\{αβ\} = U\_\{\{α, β\}\} = U ∩ Z\_\{αβ\} = ∏\_\{γ ∈ R\^{}+\_\{αβ\}\} U\_γ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\) denotes the set of positive roots that
are linear combinations of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

Now let \(f : G \to G'\) be a morphism of pinned \(S\)-groups. If
\(d : R \to R'\) is the corresponding bijection and if \(\Delta_{1}\) is
a subset of \(\Delta\), then \(d(\Delta_{1}) = \Delta'_{1}\) is a subset
of \(\Delta'\), and it is clear that \(f\) sends \(T_{\Delta_{1}}\) into
\(T'_{\Delta'_{1}}\), hence \(Z_{\Delta_{1}}\) into
\(Z'_{\Delta'_{1}}\). The corresponding \(S\)-morphism

\[
f_{\Delta_{1}} : Z_{\Delta_{1}} \to Z'_{d(\Delta'_{1})}
\]

is compatible with the canonical pinnings; it defines a morphism of
pinned root data

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R(f\_\{Δ\_1\}) : R(Z\_\{Δ\_1\}, T, M, …) → R(Z\_\{Δ\textquotesingle{}\_1\}, T\textquotesingle{}, M\textquotesingle{}, …)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the underlying morphisms \(M' \to M\) of \(R(f)\) and
\(R(f_{\Delta_{1}})\) coincide.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{1.8. Study of the group
\(Norm_{G}(T)\)}{1.8. Study of the group Norm\_\{G\}(T)}}\label{study-of-the-group-norm_gt}

For each pair \((\alpha, \beta)\) of simple roots, denote by
\(n_{\alpha \beta}\) the order of the element \(s_{\alpha} s_{\beta}\)
of the Weyl group \(W\). In particular, \(n_{\alpha \alpha} = 1\). One
has therefore \((w_{\alpha} w_{\beta})^{n_{\alpha \beta}} \in T(S)\).

\textbf{Definition 1.8.1.} \emph{For every
\((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\), one sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_\{αβ\} = (w\_α w\_β)\^{}\{n\_\{αβ\}\} ∈ T(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, one sets (Exp. XX, 3.1)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_α = t\_\{αα\} = w\_α\^{}2 = α\^{}*({-}1) ∈ T(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 1.8.2.} \emph{Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-functor in
groups transforming direct sums of schemes into products (for example a
sheaf for the Zariski topology). Let}

\[
f_{T} : T \to H
\]

\emph{be a morphism of groups and \(h_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\)
elements of \(H(S)\). In order that there exist a morphism of groups
(necessarily unique)}

\[
f_{N} : Norm_{G}(T) \to H
\]

\emph{inducing \(f_{T}\) on \(T\) and such that
\(f(w_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\) for \(\alpha \in \Delta\), it is
necessary and sufficient that the following two conditions be
satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T(s\_α(t)) = h\_α f\_T(t) h\_α\^{}\{{-}1\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\)
(i.e.~\(f_{T} \circ s_{\alpha} = int(h_{\alpha}) \circ f_{T}\)).}

\emph{(ii) For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\),}

\[
f_{T}(t_{\alpha \beta}) = (h_{\alpha} h_{\beta})^{n_{\alpha \beta}}.
\]

\emph{Proof.} Indeed, equip \texttt{(Sch)} with the topology
\(\mathcal{T}\) generated by the pretopology whose covering families are
the direct sums; the hypothesis of the statement says that \(H\) is a
\(\mathcal{T}\)-sheaf. Let \(L\) be the free group with generators
\((m_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in R}\) and \texttt{L\_1} the invariant subgroup
generated by the elements \((m_{\alpha} m_{\beta})^{n_{\alpha \beta}}\),
\((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\). Let \(g : L \to W\) be the
morphism defined by \(g(m_{\alpha}) = s_{\alpha}\); one knows (Exp. XXI,
5.1) that \(g\) induces an isomorphism \texttt{ḡ} of \(L/L_{1}\) onto
\(W\). Make \(L\) act on \(T\) through \(g\) (or, equivalently, by
\(m_{\alpha} \cdot t = s_{\alpha}(t)\)). Let \texttt{L\_S} be the
constant group defined by \(L\); consider the semidirect product
\(T \cdot L_{S} = N\) for the preceding operation. One has a morphism of
\(S\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : T · L\_S = N → Norm\_G(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

unique such that \(h(m_{\alpha}) = w_{\alpha}\), \(h(t) = t\) for every
\(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Let \texttt{N\_1} be the invariant
subsheaf of groups of \(N\) generated by the

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_\{αβ\}\^{}\{{-}1\} · (m\_α m\_β)\^{}\{n\_\{αβ\}\},    (α, β) ∈ Δ × Δ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One evidently has \(N_{1} \subset Ker h\); consider the induced morphism

\[
h_{1} : N/N_{1} \to Norm_{G}(T).
\]

Let us prove that \(h_{1}\) is an isomorphism. Since \(h\) induces on
\(T\) the canonical immersion, which is a monomorphism, the canonical
morphism

\[
T \to N/N_{1}
\]

is also a monomorphism, hence induces an isomorphism of \(T\) onto
\(TN_{1}/N_{1}\). For the same reason, \(h_{1}\) induces an isomorphism
of \(TN_{1}/N_{1}\) onto \(T\); to prove that \(h_{1}\) is an
isomorphism, it therefore suffices to verify that the corresponding
morphism

\[
h_{2} : N/TN_{1} \to Norm_{G}(T)/T
\]

is an isomorphism. Now \texttt{TN\_1} is the invariant
\(\mathcal{T}\)-subsheaf of groups of \(N\) generated by \(T\) and the
\((m_{\alpha} m_{\beta})^{n_{\alpha \beta}}\), that is, the
\(\mathcal{T}\)-subsheaf generated by \(T\) and \texttt{L\_1}, that is,
\(T \cdot (L_{1})_{S}\). The morphism \(h_{2}\) is therefore identified
with the morphism

\[
\bar{g} : L_{S}/(L_{1})_{S} \to W_{S}
\]

which is an isomorphism by construction.

The proof of 1.8.2 is now easy; the conditions are evidently necessary.
Let us prove that they are sufficient. Condition (i) shows that there
exists a morphism

\[
u : N \to H
\]

such that \(u(m_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\) for \(\alpha \in \Delta\), and
\(u|_{T} = f_{T}\). Condition (ii) says that \(u\) vanishes on
\texttt{N\_1}, which yields the result at once.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{1.9. Faithfulness of the functor
\(R\)}{1.9. Faithfulness of the functor R}}\label{faithfulness-of-the-functor-r}

\textbf{Proposition 1.9.1.} \emph{The functor \(R\) of 1.6 is faithful:
if}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f, g : G ⇒ G\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are two morphisms of pinned groups such that \(R(f) = R(g)\), then
\(f = g\).}

Indeed, \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\),
\(U_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\) and
\(U_{-\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\); it therefore suffices to apply:

\textbf{Lemma 1.9.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
reductive \(S\)-group, \(H\) an \(S\)-presheaf in groups, separated for
(fppf). Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f, g : G ⇒ H}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be two morphisms of \(S\)-groups. The following conditions are
equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(f = g\).}

\emph{(ii) \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\), on each
\(U_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\), on each
\(U_{-\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\).}

\emph{(iii) \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\), on each
\(U_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\), and
\(f(w_{\alpha}) = g(w_{\alpha})\) for each \(\alpha \in \Delta\).}

Indeed, (i) ⇒ (ii) is trivial, (ii) ⇒ (iii) follows at once from the
definition of \(w_{\alpha}\) (1.2). It remains to prove (iii) ⇒ (i). If
\(\alpha \in R\), there exists a sequence
\({\alpha_{i}} \subset \Delta\) with
\(\alpha = s_{\alpha_{1}} s_{\alpha_{2}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{n}}(\alpha_{n+1})\),
hence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_α = int(w\_\{α\_1\} ⋯ w\_\{α\_n\}) U\_\{α\_\{n+1\}\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which shows that \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on each \(U_{\alpha}\). It
follows that \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(\Omega\), hence coincide
(Exp. XXII, 4.1.11).

\textbf{Remark 1.9.3.} \emph{If \(G\) is semisimple, one may, in (ii)
and (iii), drop the hypothesis that \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\).
Indeed, \(G\) is generated as an (fppf) sheaf by the \(U_{\alpha}\),
\(\alpha \in R\) (Exp. XXII, 6.2.2 (a)).}

\subsection{2. Generators and relations for a pinned
group}\label{generators-and-relations-for-a-pinned-group}

In this section, we fix a pinned \(S\)-group \(G\). If
\(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\), we shall use the notation \(Z_{\alpha}\),
\(Z_{\alpha \beta}\), \(U_{\alpha \beta}\), \(R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\) of
1.7.

\textbf{Theorem 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group, \(H\) an \(S\)-sheaf in groups for (fppf). Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_N : Norm\_G(T) → H,    f\_α : U\_α → H,    α ∈ R,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be morphisms of groups. In order that there exist a morphism of
groups (necessarily unique)}

\[
f : G \to H
\]

\emph{extending \(f_{N}\) and the \(f_{\alpha} (\alpha \in R)\), it is
necessary and sufficient that the following conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\) and every \(\beta \in R\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_N(w\_α)) ∘ f\_β = f\_\{s\_α(β)\} ∘ int(w\_α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), there exists a morphism of
groups}

\[
F_{\alpha} : Z_{\alpha} \to H
\]

\emph{extending \(f_{\alpha}\), \(f_{-\alpha}\) and
\(f_{N}|_{Norm_{Z_{\alpha}}(T)}\).}

\emph{(iii) For every pair \((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\),
there exists a morphism of groups \(U_{\alpha \beta} \to H\) inducing
\(f_{\gamma}\) on \(U_{\gamma}\) for every
\(\gamma \in R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\) (i.e.
\(U_{\gamma} \subset U_{\alpha \beta}\)).}

\subsubsection{2.1.1. Proof}\label{proof}

The conditions of the statement are evidently necessary. Choose on the
other hand a structure of totally ordered group on \(\Gamma_{0}(R)\)
such that the roots \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} are the elements of
\(R^{+}\) (Exp. XXI, 3.5.6); every product indexed by a subset of \(R\)
will be taken relative to this order.

Denote by \(f_{T}\) the restriction of \(f_{N}\) to \(T\), and consider
the morphism

\[
f : \Omega \to H
\]

defined set-theoretically by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(∏\_\{α ∈ R\^{}{-}\} y\_α · t · ∏\_\{α ∈ R\^{}+\} x\_α) = ∏ f\_α(y\_α) · f\_T(t) · ∏ f\_α(x\_α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Any morphism satisfying the conditions of the statement must extend
\(f\); on the other hand any morphism of groups \(f : G \to H\)
extending \(f\) also extends \(f_{N}\): indeed, extending \(f_{\alpha}\)
and \(f_{-\alpha}\), it satisfies
\(f(w_{\alpha}) = F_{\alpha}(w_{\alpha}) = f_{N}(w_{\alpha})\), and it
extends \(f_{T}\) by hypothesis. By Exp. XXII, 4.1.11 (ii), one is
therefore reduced to proving:

\textbf{Proposition 2.1.2.} \emph{The morphism \(f : \Omega \to H\)
defined above is ``generically multiplicative''; more precisely, for
every \(S' \to S\) and all \(x, y \in \Omega(S')\) such that
\(xy \in \Omega(S')\), one has \(f(xy) = f(x) f(y)\).}

\textbf{Lemma 2.1.3.} \emph{Let \(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(S')\), \(S' \to S\),
and let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) be such that
\(int(n) U_{\alpha} = U_{\beta}\) (i.e.~\(n(\alpha) = \beta\)); then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_N(n)) ∘ f\_α = f\_β ∘ int(n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, it suffices to verify the formula for a system of generators of
the sheaf \(Norm_{G}(T)\); it is true for each \(w_{\alpha}\),
\(\alpha \in \Delta\) (by 2.1 (i)), so it suffices to do it for
\(n \in T(S')\). This is trivial by 2.1 (ii) if \(\alpha\) is simple;
otherwise, one takes a \(w \in W\) such that
\(w^{-1}(\alpha) \in \Delta\); writing \(w\) as a product of simple
reflections,\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced ``fundamental
  symmetries'' by ``simple reflections''.} one is reduced to proving
that if the formula is true for \(\alpha\) and for every \(n\), it is
also true for \(w_{\alpha_{0}}(\alpha)\) and \(t \in T(S')\), where
\(\alpha_{0} \in \Delta\). Now, by 2.1 (i),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_N(t)) ∘ f\_\{w\_\{α\_0\}(α)\} = int(f\_N(t w\_\{α\_0\})) ∘ f\_α ∘ int(w\_\{α\_0\}\^{}\{{-}1\})}
\NormalTok{                             = f\_\{w\_\{α\_0\}(α)\} ∘ int(t w\_\{α\_0\}) ∘ int(w\_\{α\_0\}\^{}\{{-}1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Lemma 2.1.4.} \emph{The restriction of \(f\) to \(U\) (resp.
\(U^{-}\)) is a morphism of groups. In particular, this restriction is
independent of the order chosen on the roots.}

It suffices to give the proof for \(U\). By virtue of Exp. XXII, 5.5.8,
it suffices to verify that for every pair \(\alpha < \beta\) of positive
roots, one has for all \(x_{\alpha} \in U_{\alpha}(S')\),
\(x_{\beta} \in U_{\beta}(S')\), \(S' \to S\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_β(x\_β) f\_α(x\_α) f\_β(x\_β\^{}\{{-}1\}) = f(x\_β x\_α x\_β\^{}\{{-}1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By Exp. XXII, 5.5.2, there exist \(x_{\gamma} \in U_{\gamma}(S')\)
(\(\gamma = i\alpha + j\beta \in R\), \(i > 0\),
\(j \geqslant 0\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected \(i, j > 0\) to
  \(i > 0\), \(j \geqslant 0\) (since \(x_{\alpha}\) appears in the
  product on the right).}) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_β x\_α x\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = ∏\_γ x\_γ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and we must therefore verify the relation

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_β(x\_β) f\_α(x\_α) f\_β(x\_β\^{}\{{-}1\}) = ∏\_\{γ = iα + jβ, i \textgreater{} 0, j ⩾ 0\} f\_γ(x\_γ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By Exp. XXI, 3.5.4, there exists \(w \in W\) such that
\(w(\alpha) = \alpha_{0} \in \Delta\),
\(w(\beta) \in A_{\alpha_{0} \beta_{0}}\) (notation of 1.7), where
\(\beta_{0} \in \Delta\). Lifting \(w\) to an \(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\)
(by Exp. XXII, 3.8), it suffices to verify the preceding relation after
conjugation by \(f_{N}(n)\). By 2.1.3, one is therefore reduced to the
case \(\alpha, \beta \in R^{+}_{\alpha_{0} \beta_{0}}\), a case in which
we conclude by condition 2.1 (iii).

\textbf{Lemma 2.1.5.} \emph{Let \(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) be such that
\(int(n) U = U^{-}\) (i.e.~\(n\) is the symmetry of the Weyl
group\footnote{N.D.E.: relative to \(\Delta\).} (Exp. XXI, 3.6.14)). For
every \(u \in U(S')\), \(S' \to S\) (resp. \(u \in U^{-}(S')\),
\(S' \to S\)), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(n u n\^{}\{{-}1\}) = f\_N(n) f(u) f\_N(n\^{}\{{-}1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Immediate by 2.1.3 and 2.1.4.

\textbf{Lemma 2.1.6.} \emph{Let \(u \in B(S')\), \(v \in B^{-}(S')\),
\(g \in \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(v g u) = f(v) f(g) f(u).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, set \(v = v_{1} t_{1}\), \(g = v_{2} t_{2} u_{2}\),
\(u = t_{3} u_{3}\), with \(v_{i} \in U^{-}(S')\), \(t_{i} \in T(S')\),
\(u_{i} \in U(S')\). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(v) f(g) f(u) = f(v\_1) f\_T(t\_1) f(v\_2) f\_T(t\_2) f(u\_2) f\_T(t\_3) f(u\_3),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

on the one hand, and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(v g u) = f(v\_1 t\_1 v\_2 t\_1\^{}\{{-}1\} t\_1 t\_2 t\_3 t\_3\^{}\{{-}1\} u\_2 t\_3 u\_3)}
\NormalTok{         = f(v\_1 · t\_1 v\_2 t\_1\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_T(t\_1 t\_2 t\_3) f(t\_3\^{}\{{-}1\} u\_2 t\_3 · u\_3).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using 2.1.4 to decompose the two extreme terms of this last expression,
one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(v g u) = f(v\_1) f(t\_1 v\_2 t\_1\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_T(t\_1 t\_2 t\_3) f(t\_3\^{}\{{-}1\} u\_2 t\_3) f(u\_3).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One is then reduced to the obvious formulas

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(t\_1 v\_2 t\_1\^{}\{{-}1\}) = f\_T(t\_1) f(v\_2) f\_T(t\_1)\^{}\{{-}1\},    f(t\_3\^{}\{{-}1\} u\_2 t\_3) = f\_T(t\_3)\^{}\{{-}1\} f(u\_2) f\_T(t\_3),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which follow from the definition of \(f\) and from 2.1.3.

\textbf{Lemma 2.1.7.} \emph{Let \(\alpha \in \Delta\) and
\(g \in \Omega(S') \cap int(w_{\alpha})^{-1} \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\).
Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(w\_α g w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\}) = f\_N(w\_α) f(g) f\_N(w\_α)\^{}\{{-}1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, let \(g \in \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Write, by Exp. XXII,
5.6.8,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = a x\_\{{-}α\} t x\_α b,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

with \(a \in U^{-}_{-\hat{\alpha}}(S')\),
\(x_{-\alpha} \in U_{-\alpha}(S')\), \(t \in T(S')\),
\(x_{\alpha} \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(b \in U_{\hat{\alpha}}(S')\). By
2.1.3, 2.1.4 and the fact that \(s_{\alpha}\) permutes the positive
roots \(\neq \alpha\) (cf.~Exp. XXI, 3.3.2), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_α) a ∈ U\_\{{-}α̂\}\^{}{-}(S\textquotesingle{}),    int(w\_α) b ∈ U\_\{α̂\}(S\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the formula to be proved is true for \(g = a\) or \(g = b\). By
2.1.6, one is therefore reduced to proving the asserted formula when
\(g = x_{-\alpha} t x_{\alpha} \in Z_{\alpha}(S')\). But then
``everything happens in \(Z_{\alpha}\)'', and one concludes by condition
(ii) of 2.1.

\textbf{Lemma 2.1.8.} \emph{Let \(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\). For every
\(S' \to S\) and every \(g \in \Omega(S')\) such that
\(int(n) g \in \Omega(S')\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(n g n\^{}\{{-}1\}) = f\_N(n) f(g) f\_N(n)\^{}\{{-}1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is trivial if \(n \in T(S)\) (by 2.1.3). The two sides of the
preceding formula define morphisms of \(\Omega \cap int(n)^{-1} \Omega\)
into \(H\); to verify that they coincide, it suffices to verify that
there exists an open \(V_{n}\) of \(\Omega\) containing the unit section
such that \(int(n) V_{n} \subset \Omega\), and that \(f \circ int(n)\)
and \(int(f_{N}(n)) \circ f\) coincide on \(V_{n}\). By virtue of the
structure of \(Norm_{G}(T)\), it suffices to prove that if the preceding
assertion is true for an \(n' \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) and if
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), it is true for \(n = n' w_{\alpha}\). Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V\_n = Ω ∩ int(w\_α)\^{}\{{-}1\} V\_\{n\textquotesingle{}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has \(int(n) V_{n} \subset int(n') V_{n'} \subset \Omega\). If
\(g \in V_{n}(S')\), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(n) g = int(n\textquotesingle{}) int(w\_α) g.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now \(int(w_{\alpha}) g \in V_{n'}(S')\), hence by hypothesis

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(int(n\textquotesingle{}) int(w\_α) g) = int(f\_N(n\textquotesingle{})) f(int(w\_α) g);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since \(int(w_{\alpha}) g \in \Omega(S')\), one may apply 2.1.7, which
gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(int(w\_α) g) = int(f\_N(w\_α)) f(g),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one concludes at once.

Let us now prove 2.1.2. Let \(x, x' \in \Omega(S')\); write as usual

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x = v t u,    x\textquotesingle{} = v\textquotesingle{} t\textquotesingle{} u\textquotesingle{},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x x\textquotesingle{} = v t (u v\textquotesingle{}) t\textquotesingle{} u\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 2.1.6 and the relation \(U^{-}(S') \Omega(S') U(S') = \Omega(S')\),
one is reduced to proving that if \(u v' \in \Omega(S')\), then
\(f(u v') = f(u) f(v')\). Let \(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(S')\) be as in 2.1.5
(ii). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(u) = f\_N(n)\^{}\{{-}1\} f(n u n\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_N(n),    f(v\textquotesingle{}) = f\_N(n)\^{}\{{-}1\} f(n v\textquotesingle{} n\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_N(n),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by \emph{loc. cit.}, whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(u) f(v\textquotesingle{}) = f\_N(n)\^{}\{{-}1\} f(n u n\^{}\{{-}1\}) f(n v\textquotesingle{} n\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_N(n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

But \(n u n^{-1} \in U^{-}(S')\), \(n v' n^{-1} \in U(S')\), so that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(n u n\^{}\{{-}1\}) f(n v\textquotesingle{} n\^{}\{{-}1\}) = f((n u n\^{}\{{-}1\})(n v\textquotesingle{} n\^{}\{{-}1\})) = f(n u v\textquotesingle{} n\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(u) f(v\textquotesingle{}) = f\_N(n)\^{}\{{-}1\} f(n u v\textquotesingle{} n\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_N(n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(u v' \in \Omega(S')\), one may apply 2.1.8 and one is done.

\textbf{Remark 2.2.} \emph{Instead of giving oneself \(f_{N}\), one may
give oneself a morphism of groups \(f_{T} : T \to H\) and sections
\(h_{\alpha} \in H(S) (\alpha \in \Delta)\) satisfying the conditions of
1.8.2. One must then replace condition (ii) of the theorem by:}

\emph{(ii') There exists a morphism of groups
\(F_{\alpha} : Z_{\alpha} \to H\) extending}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α,    f\_\{{-}α\},    f\_T    and satisfying    F\_α(w\_α) = h\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We shall now give the preceding theorem a more explicit form. Keep the
preceding notation.

\textbf{Theorem 2.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group. Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-sheaf in groups for (fppf),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T : T → H,    f\_α : U\_α → H,    α ∈ Δ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{morphisms of groups, and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h\_α ∈ H(S),    (α ∈ Δ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{sections of \(H\). In order that there exist a morphism of groups}

\[
f : G \to H
\]

\emph{(necessarily unique) inducing \(f_{T}\) and the
\(f_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\) and satisfying
\(f(w_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\) for every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), it is
necessary and sufficient that the following conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(S' \to S\), every \(t \in T(S')\), every
\(\alpha \in \Delta\) and every \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T(t) f\_α(x) f\_T(t)\^{}\{{-}1\} = f\_α(int(t) x).            (1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), every \(S' \to S\), every
\(t \in T(S')\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h\_α f\_T(t) h\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = f\_T(s\_α(t)) = f\_T(t · α\^{}* α(t)\^{}\{{-}1\}).            (2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\),}

\[
(h_{\alpha} h_{\beta})^{n_{\alpha \beta}} = f_{T}(t_{\alpha \beta}).            (3)
\]

\emph{(iv) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), (recall that we write
\(u_{\alpha} = \exp_{\alpha}(X_{\alpha})\))}

\[
(h_{\alpha} f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha}))^{3} = e.            (4)
\]

\emph{(v) For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\),
\(\alpha \neq \beta\), there exists a morphism of groups}

\[
f_{\alpha \beta} : U_{\alpha \beta} \to H
\]

\emph{satisfying the two following conditions:}

\emph{a) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_\{αβ\}|\_\{U\_α\} = f\_α,    f\_\{αβ\}|\_\{U\_β\} = f\_β,            (5)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{b) For every \(\gamma \in R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\),
\(\gamma \neq \alpha\) (resp. \(\gamma \neq \beta\)), and every
\(x \in U_{\gamma}(S')\), \(S' \to S\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(h\_α) f\_\{αβ\}(x) = f\_\{αβ\}(int(w\_α) x),                                       (6)}
\NormalTok{(resp. int(h\_β) f\_\{αβ\}(x) = f\_\{αβ\}(int(w\_α) x)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} The uniqueness is clear by 1.9.2. Let us prove existence.

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.1.} \emph{There exists a morphism of groups}

\[
f_{N} : Norm_{G}(T) \to H
\]

\emph{extending \(f_{T}\) and satisfying
\(f_{N}(w_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\).}

This is precisely what is asserted by 1.8.2, taking into account
conditions (2) and (3).

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.2.} \emph{There exists a morphism of groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F\_α : Z\_α → H,    α ∈ Δ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{extending \(f_{T}\), \(f_{\alpha}\) and satisfying
\(F_{\alpha}(w_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\), hence extending
\(f_{N}|_{Norm_{Z_{\alpha}}(T)}\).}

This is clear from Exp. XX, 6.2 and conditions (1), (3) and (4).

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.3.} \emph{For every
\((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\), \(\alpha \neq \beta\),
every \(n \in Norm_{Z_{\alpha \beta}}(T)(S)\) such that
\(n(\alpha) = \alpha\) (resp. \(n(\alpha) = \beta\)), i.e.
\(int(n) U_{\alpha} = U_{\alpha}\) (resp.
\(int(n) U_{\alpha} = U_{\beta}\)), every \(S' \to S\) and every
\(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_N(n)) f\_α(x) = f\_α(int(n) x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(resp.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_N(n)) f\_α(x) = f\_β(int(n) x)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, there exist a \(t \in T(S)\) and a sequence
\({\alpha_{i}} \subset {\alpha, \beta}\) such that
\(n = t w_{\alpha_{k}} \cdots w_{\alpha_{1}}\). The condition is
satisfied for \(n = t\) by condition (1). One may therefore suppose
\(n = w_{\alpha_{k}} \cdots w_{\alpha_{1}}\). We proceed by induction on
\(k\), i.e.~we suppose the assertion proved for every \(n\) which can be
written as a product of fewer than \(k - 1\) simple reflections (and
satisfies the hypotheses of the lemma). Consider the roots

\[
\gamma_{i} = s_{\alpha_{i}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{1}}(\alpha).
\]

If all the \(\gamma_{i}\) are positive, i.e.~belong to
\(R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\), one may apply condition (v) of 2.3; using the
notation of 2.3 (v), one concludes at once by induction that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_N(w\_\{α\_i\} ⋯ w\_\{α\_1\})) f\_α(x) = f\_\{αβ\}(int(w\_\{α\_i\} ⋯ w\_\{α\_1\}) x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which for \(i = k\) is the desired property. If not all the
\(\gamma_{i}\) are positive, there exists an index \(j < k\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{γ\_j ∈ R\^{}+,    γ\_\{j+1\} ∉ R\^{}+.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\gamma_{j+1} = s_{\alpha_{j}}(\gamma_{j})\), it follows at once
that \(\gamma_{j} = \alpha_{j}\), by Exp. XXI, 3.3.2, hence that
\(\gamma_{j}\) is \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\), and one may decompose \(n\)
as

\[
n = n' \cdot n'',
n' = w_{\alpha_{k}} \cdots w_{\alpha_{j+1}},
n'' = w_{\alpha_{j}} \cdots w_{\alpha_{1}},
\]

\(n'\) and \texttt{n\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} satisfying the
hypotheses of the lemma and being a product of fewer than \(k - 1\)
reflections, hence satisfying by the induction hypothesis the conclusion
of the lemma.

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.4.} \emph{Let \(\alpha \in R\). If
\(n, n' \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) and \(\beta, \beta' \in \Delta\) satisfy
\(n(\alpha) = \beta\) and \(n'(\alpha) = \beta'\), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_T(n)\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_β(n x n\^{}\{{-}1\}) = int(f\_T(n\textquotesingle{})\^{}\{{-}1\}) f\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(n\textquotesingle{} x n\textquotesingle{}\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

It suffices to verify that if \(n(\alpha) = \beta\),
\(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\), then
\(int(f_{T}(n)) \circ f_{\alpha} = f_{\beta} \circ int(n)\). Now, by
Tits's lemma (Exp. XXI, 5.6), there exists a sequence of simple roots
\(\alpha_{0} = \alpha, \alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{m} = \beta\), and a
sequence of elements \(w_{i} \in W\), \(i = 0, 1, \cdots, m - 1\), with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n = w\_\{m{-}1\} ⋯ w\_0,}
\NormalTok{w\_i(α\_i) = α\_\{i+1\},    i = 0, 1, …, m {-} 1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the following condition being moreover satisfied: for every
\(i = 0, 1, \cdots, m - 1\), there exists a simple root \(\beta_{i}\)
such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_i ∈ W\_\{α\_i β\_i\},    α\_\{i+1\} = α\_i    or    β\_i.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One is then reduced by induction to the case treated in the preceding
lemma.

\textbf{Lemma 2.3.5.} \emph{There exists a family of morphisms of groups
\(f'_{\gamma} : U_{\gamma} \to H\), \(\gamma \in R\), satisfying}

\emph{(i) For \(\alpha \in \Delta\), \(f'_{\alpha} = f_{\alpha}\) and
\(f'_{-\alpha} = F_{\alpha}|_{U_{-\alpha}}\), where \(F_{\alpha}\) is
defined in 2.3.2.}

\emph{(ii) For \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\) and
\(\gamma \in R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\),
\(f'_{\gamma} = f_{\alpha \beta}|_{U_{\gamma}}\).}

\emph{(iii) For every \(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) and
\(\alpha, \beta \in R\) such that \(n(\alpha) = \beta\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_N(n)) f\textquotesingle{}\_α(x) = f\textquotesingle{}\_β(int(n) x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

For every root \(\alpha \in R\), there exists an
\(n \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) such that \(n(\alpha) \in \Delta\). Then define
\(f'_{\alpha}(x)\) as the expression of 2.3.4. This is independent of
the choice of \(n\), and \(f'_{\alpha}\) is indeed a morphism of groups.
Property (iii) is satisfied by construction. The first assertion of (i)
is clear (take \(n = e\)), the second too (take \(n = w_{\alpha}\) and
apply 2.3.2); if \(\gamma \in R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\)
(\(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\)), there exists
\(n \in Norm_{Z_{\alpha \beta}}(T)(S)\) such that \(n(t) = \alpha\) or
\(\beta\); one then applies (iii) and conditions (5) and (6) and has
proved (ii).

\subsubsection{2.3.6.}\label{section-240}

Let us now prove the theorem by showing that the conditions of 2.1 are
satisfied, for the morphisms \(f_{N}\) and \(f'_{\alpha}\),
\(\alpha \in R\).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  2.1 (i) follows from 2.3.5 (iii),
\item
  2.1 (ii) follows from 2.3.5 (i) and 2.3.2,
\item
  2.1 (iii) follows from 2.3.5 (ii) and from the fact that
  \(f_{\alpha \beta}\) is a morphism of groups.
\end{itemize}

An obvious corollary is:

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group of semisimple rank \(\geqslant 1\), \(H\) an (fppf)
\(S\)-sheaf in groups. For each
\((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\), let}

\[
F_{\alpha \beta} : Z_{\alpha \beta} \to H
\]

\emph{be a morphism of groups. In order that there exist a morphism of
groups}

\[
f : G \to H
\]

\emph{inducing the \(F_{\alpha \beta}\), it is necessary and sufficient
that for every \((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\),}

\[
F_{\alpha \beta}|_{Z_{\alpha}} = F_{\alpha \alpha}.
\]

The condition is evidently necessary. Suppose it satisfied. Set
\(f_{T} = F_{\alpha \alpha}|_{T}\) (which does not depend on \(\alpha\),
since
\(F_{\alpha \alpha}|_{T} = F_{\alpha \beta}|_{T} = F_{\beta \beta}|_{T}\)).
Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α = F\_\{αα\}|\_\{U\_α\},    h\_α = F\_\{αα\}(w\_α),    f\_\{αβ\} = F\_\{αβ\}|\_\{U\_\{αβ\}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The conditions of 2.3 are evidently satisfied: (1), (2), (4) ``are
verified'' in \(Z_{\alpha}\), (3), (5) and (6) in \(Z_{\alpha \beta}\).
There therefore exists a morphism \(f : G \to H\) extending \(f_{T}\),
the \(f_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\) and satisfying
\(f(w_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\); it coincides with \(F_{\alpha \beta}\)
on generators of \(Z_{\alpha \beta}\), hence satisfies
\(f|_{Z_{\alpha \beta}} = F_{\alpha \beta}\).

One also has the following technical corollary.

\textbf{Corollary 2.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two pinned \(S\)-groups of semisimple rank 2, \(q\) an integer
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} such that \(x \mapsto x^{q}\) is an
endomorphism of \(G_{a, S}\), \(h : R(G') \to R(G)\) a \(q\)-morphism of
pinned root data. Choose for each \(\alpha \in R^{+}\) an
\(X_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\) and an
\(X'_{d(\alpha)} \in \Gamma(S, g'_{d(\alpha)})^{\times}\) (extending the
canonical choices for \(\alpha \in \Delta\)). Suppose the following
conditions are realized:}

\emph{(i) If \(\Delta = {\alpha, \beta}\), then
\(D_{S}(h)(t_{\alpha \beta}) = t'_{d(\alpha) d(\beta)}\).}

\emph{(ii) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\) and every
\(\beta \in R^{+}\), \(\beta \neq \alpha\) (whence
\(s_{\alpha}(\beta) \in R^{+}\)), if \(z \in G_{m}(S)\) is defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_β = z X\_\{s\_α(β)\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has also}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(β)\} = z\^{}\{q(β)\} X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(s\_α(β))\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) There exists a morphism of groups \(f : U \to U'\) such that
for every \(\alpha \in R^{+}\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f(exp(x X\_α)) = exp(x\^{}\{q(α)\} X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(x \in G_{a}(S')\), `S' → S.}

\emph{Then there exists a morphism of pinned groups \(g : G \to G'\)
such that \(R(g) = h\).}

Indeed, one defines \(f_{\alpha} : U_{\alpha} \to G'\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(exp(x X\_α)) = exp(x\^{}\{q(α)\} X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\});}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one sets \(f_{T} = D_{S}(h)\), \(h_{\alpha} = w'_{d(\alpha)}\). The
conditions of 2.3 are satisfied (note that
\(q(s_{\alpha}(\beta)) = q(\beta)\) (Exp. XXI, 6.8.4) and that one
always has \(D_{S}(h)(t_{\alpha}) = t'_{d(\alpha)}\)), and one concludes
at once.

\textbf{Remark 2.6.} \emph{One may make condition (v) of 2.3 more
precise as follows. One must first verify:}

\emph{(a) For every word in \(w_{\alpha}\) and \(w_{\beta}\) such that
the corresponding word transforms \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\) into
\(\alpha\) or \(\beta\), the relation of type 2.3.3 corresponding is
satisfied. In fact the proof of 2.3.3 shows that it suffices to verify
it for the words in \(w_{\alpha}\) and \(w_{\beta}\) that are minimal
(in the sense that any nontrivial initial sub-word does not satisfy the
imposed conditions).}

\emph{If condition (a) is satisfied, one may now define for each
\(\gamma \in R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\) an \(f_{\gamma} : U_{\gamma} \to H\)
as in 2.3.5; one must then write:}

\emph{(b) The morphism defined by the \(f_{\gamma}\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_\{αβ\} = ∏\_\{γ ∈ R\^{}+\_\{αβ\}\} U\_γ → H}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a morphism of groups. By Exp. XXII, 5.5.8, (b) is entailed by:}

\emph{(b') The preceding morphism respects the commutation relations
between \(U_{\gamma}\) and \(U_{\delta}\) for
\(\gamma, \delta \in R^{+}_{\alpha \beta}\), \(\gamma > \delta\)
(i.e.~the relations in \(C_{i, j, \gamma, \delta}\) of Exp. XII,
5.5.2).}

It is clear that conversely the set of conditions (a) and (b') is
equivalent to (v).

One may even reduce the preceding conditions to conditions bearing only
on the elements \(h_{\alpha}\), \(h_{\beta}\),
\(f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha})\), \(f_{\beta}(u_{\beta})\) of \(H\). A
condition of type (a) will be written for example, if
\(s_{\alpha} s_{\beta} s_{\alpha}(\beta) = \alpha\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(h\_α h\_β h\_α) f\_β(x) = f\_α(int(w\_α w\_β w\_α) x);            (1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(S' \to S\). In particular, for
\(x = u_{\beta}\), one has
\(int(w_{\alpha} w_{\beta} w_{\alpha}) u_{\beta} = u^{z}_{\alpha}\) for
a certain section \(z\) of \(G_{m}(S)\), and the preceding relation will
give

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(h\_α h\_β h\_α) f\_β(u\_β) = f\_α(u\_α)\^{}z.            (1\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us show that, conversely, taking into account conditions (i) to (iv)
of 2.3, (1') entails (1). If \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\), make
\(int(t)\) act on (1'); taking into account conditions (i) and (ii), one
obtains (1) for \(x = int(t) u_{\beta} = u^{\beta(t)}_{\beta}\). It
suffices to remark now that \(\beta : T \to G_{m, S}\) is faithfully
flat, hence that condition (1) is certainly true for
\(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')^{\times}\), \(S' \to S\). Since it is additive in
\(x\), and every section of \(U_{\alpha}\) can be locally written as a
sum of two sections of \(U^{\times}_{\alpha}\), one concludes that (1')
+ (i) + (ii) ⇒ (1).

One reasons similarly with conditions of type (b). It is then necessary
to use the fact that if \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\) are two distinct
(hence linearly independent over \(\mathbb{Q}\)) positive roots, the
morphism \(T \to G^{2}_{m, S}\) of components \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\)
is faithfully flat. We leave the details of this transposition to the
reader.

\subsection{3. Groups of semisimple rank
2}\label{groups-of-semisimple-rank-2}

\subsubsection{3.1. Generalities}\label{generalities-2}

\textbf{Lemma 3.1.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) two roots of \(G\), with
\(\alpha + \beta \neq 0\).}

\emph{(i) If \(\alpha + \beta \notin R\), then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{exp(X\_α) exp(X\_β) = exp(X\_β) exp(X\_α)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for all \(X_{\alpha} \in W(g_{\alpha})(S')\),
\(X_{\beta} \in W(g_{\beta})(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(\alpha + \beta\) and \(\alpha - \beta\) are not roots,
then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(z\_α) exp(X\_β) w\_α(z\_α)\^{}\{{-}1\} = exp(X\_β)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for all \(X_{\beta} \in W(g_{\beta})(S')\),
\(z_{\alpha} \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\), \(S' \to S\), and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(z\_α) w\_β(z\_β) = w\_β(z\_β) w\_α(z\_α)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for all \(z_{\alpha} \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\) and
\(z_{\beta} \in W(g_{\beta})^{\times}(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

\emph{(iii) Let \(X_{\alpha} \in W(g_{\alpha})^{\times}(S')\),
\(X_{\beta} \in W(g_{\beta})^{\times}(S')\), and
\(w \in Norm_{G}(T)(S')\) such that \(w(\alpha) = \beta\); define
\(z \in G_{m}(S')\) by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w) X\_α = z X\_β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w) exp(x X\_α) = exp(x z X\_β),}
\NormalTok{int(w) exp(y X\_α\^{}\{{-}1\}) = exp(y z\^{}\{{-}1\} X\_β\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\NormalTok{int(w) w\_α(X\_α) = β\^{}*(z) w\_β(X\_β).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular, if \(z = \pm 1\), then}

\[
int(w) w_{\alpha}(X_{\alpha}) = w_{\beta}(X_{\beta})^{z}.
\]

\emph{(iv) If one sets \(t_{\alpha} = \alpha^{*}(-1)\),
\(t_{\beta} = \beta^{*}(-1)\), then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
