\NormalTok{s\_α(t\_β) = t\_β t\_α\^{}\{(β\^{}*, α)\},    β(t\_α) = ({-}1)\^{}\{(α\^{}*, β)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} (i) follows at once from Exp. XXII, 5.5.2; (ii) from Exp.
XX, 3.1 and from (i) applied to \((\beta, \alpha)\),
\((\beta, -\alpha)\), \((-\beta, \alpha)\), \((-\beta, -\alpha)\); (iii)
is evident from the definitions. For the last assertion of (iii), note
that \(\beta^{*}(-1) = w_{\beta}(X_{\beta})^{-2}\). Finally, (iv) is
trivial.

\textbf{Proposition 3.1.2 (Groups of type \(A_{1} \times A_{1}\)).}
\emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group of type
\(A_{1} \times A_{1}\), and denote
\(\Delta = R^{+} = {\alpha, \beta}\).}

\emph{(i) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_\{αβ\} = (w\_α w\_β)\^{}2 = t\_α t\_β = (w\_β w\_α)\^{}2 = t\_\{βα\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_β = X\_β,    Ad(w\_β) X\_α = X\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) \(U_{\alpha}\) and \(U_{\beta}\) commute (i.e.~\(U\) is
commutative).}

Indeed, by assertion (ii) of the lemma,
\(w_{\alpha} w_{\beta} = w_{\beta} w_{\alpha}\), whence
\((w_{\alpha} w_{\beta})^{2} = w^{2}_{\alpha} w^{2}_{\beta} = t_{\alpha} t_{\beta}\),
which is (i). By assertion (ii) of the lemma, one has also (ii);
finally, (iii) is assertion (i) of the lemma.

\subsubsection{3.1.3.}\label{section-241}

Let us make condition (v) of 2.3 explicit here. Using the method exposed
in 2.6, one obtains the two following groups of conditions, setting
\(v_{\alpha} = f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha})\) for \(\alpha \in \Delta\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(A)   h\_α v\_β h\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = v\_β,           (B)   v\_α v\_β = v\_β v\_α.}
\NormalTok{      h\_β v\_α h\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = v\_α}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{3.2. Groups of type
\texttt{A\_2}}{3.2. Groups of type A\_2}}\label{groups-of-type-a_2}

\textbf{Proposition 3.2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group of type \texttt{A\_2}, and denote
\(\Delta = {\alpha, \beta}\),
\(R^{+} = {\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta}\).}

\emph{(i) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_\{αβ\} = (w\_α w\_β)\^{}3 = e = (w\_β w\_α)\^{}3 = t\_\{βα\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) Set \(Ad(w_{\beta}) X_{\alpha} = X_{\alpha + \beta}\). Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_β = {-}X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = X\_β,    Ad(w\_β) X\_\{α + β\} = {-}X\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) Set
\(p_{\alpha + \beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{\alpha + \beta}) = int(w_{\beta}) p_{\alpha}(x)\).
Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.2.2.}\label{section-242}

The proof occupies Nos. 3.2.2 to 3.2.7. First,
\((\beta^{*}, \alpha) = (\alpha^{*}, \beta) = -1\), whence
\(\alpha(t_{\beta}) = \beta(t_{\alpha}) = -1\).

Set \(Ad(w_{\beta}) X_{\alpha} = X_{\alpha + \beta}\); one has at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{α + β\} = α(t\_β) X\_α = {-}X\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_β = z X\_\{α + β\},    z ∈ G\_m(S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = β(t\_α) z\^{}\{{-}1\} X\_β = {-}z\^{}\{{-}1\} X\_β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We know (Exp. XXII, 5.5.2) that there exists a unique section
\(A \in G_{a}(S)\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(A x y).            (+)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To prove (ii) and (iii), it therefore remains to show that
\(A = -z = 1\).

\subsubsection{3.2.3.}\label{section-243}

Make \(int(w_{\beta})\) act on the preceding formula (+); one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{{-}β\}({-}y) p\_\{α + β\}(x) = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}y) p\_α({-}A x y).            (++)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.2.4.}\label{section-244}

By definition of \(p_{\alpha + \beta}\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_β p\_α(x) w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{α + β\}(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(1) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1) p\_β(1) p\_α(x) p\_β({-}1) p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_β({-}1) = p\_\{α + β\}(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(p_{\beta}\) and \(p_{\alpha + \beta}\) commute,
\(\alpha + 2\beta\) not being a root, this is also written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(1) p\_α(x) p\_β({-}1) = p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using now (+) in the left member and (++) in the right, one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_β(1) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_β({-}1) = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_α(A x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\alpha + 2\beta\) (resp. \(\alpha - \beta\)) is not a root, the
left (resp. right) member is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(A x)    resp. p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_α(A x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the right-hand term equals
\(p_{\alpha}(A x) p_{\alpha + \beta}(x)\), since \(2\alpha + \beta\) is
not a root. Therefore

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) = p\_α(A x) p\_\{α + β\}(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives (by XXII 4.1.3) \(A = 1\).

\subsubsection{3.2.5.}\label{section-245}

Now make \(int(w_{\alpha})\) act on formula (+); using the fact that
\(A = 1\), one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(z y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) = p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) p\_\{α + β\}(z y) p\_β({-}z\^{}\{{-}1\} x y).            (+++)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.2.6.}\label{section-246}

Write now, as a moment ago,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α p\_β(y) w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{α + β\}(z y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, since \(p_{\alpha}\) and \(p_{\alpha + \beta}\) commute,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(1) p\_β(y) p\_α({-}1) = p\_\{{-}α\}(1) p\_\{α + β\}(z y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using now (+) and (+++), this is also written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}y) = p\_\{α + β\}(z y) p\_β({-}z\^{}\{{-}1\} y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since \(p_{\beta}\) and \(p_{\alpha + \beta}\) commute, this gives
\(z = -1\).

\subsubsection{3.2.7.}\label{section-247}

We have therefore proved (ii) and (iii). Let us prove (i). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α w\_β w\_α = w\_α w\_β w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} w\_α\^{}2 = w\_\{α + β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} t\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_β w\_α w\_β w\_α w\_β = w\_β w\_\{α + β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} t\_α w\_β = w\_β w\_\{α + β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} · s\_β(t\_α) · t\_β}
\NormalTok{                    = w\_α · t\_α t\_β · t\_β = w\_α t\_α = w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(w\_α w\_β)\^{}3 = (w\_β w\_α)\^{}3 = e,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which completes the proof.

\textbf{Remark 3.2.8.} \emph{Condition (v) of 2.3 translates here as
(setting \(v_{\alpha} = f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha})\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(A)   int(h\_α h\_β h\_α) v\_β = vβ → h\_α v\_β h\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = h\_β v\_α h\_β\^{}\{{-}1\}      (B)}
\NormalTok{      int(h\_β h\_α h\_β) v\_α = vα                                                  v\_β v\_α = v\_α v\_β · h\_β v\_α h\_β\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\NormalTok{                                                                                 v\_β · h\_β v\_α h\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = h\_β v\_α h\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} · v\_β,}
\NormalTok{                                                                                 v\_α · h\_β v\_α h\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = h\_β v\_α h\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} · v\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Setting \(v_{\alpha + \beta} = int(h_{\beta}) v_{\alpha}\), the three
last conditions are also written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(B)   v\_β v\_α = v\_α v\_β v\_\{α + β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_α v\_\{α + β\} = v\_\{α + β\} v\_α,}
\NormalTok{      v\_β v\_\{α + β\} = v\_\{α + β\} v\_β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{3.3. Groups of type
\texttt{B\_2}}{3.3. Groups of type B\_2}}\label{groups-of-type-b_2}

\textbf{Proposition 3.3.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group of type \texttt{B\_2}, and denote
\(\Delta = {\alpha, \beta}\),
\(R^{+} = {\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta}\).}

\emph{(i) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_\{αβ\} = (w\_α w\_β)\^{}4 = t\_α = (w\_β w\_α)\^{}4 = t\_\{βα\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) If one sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_α = X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\_α) X\_β = X\_\{2α + β\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = {-}X\_\{α + β\},}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{2α + β\} = X\_β,}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{α + β\} = {-}X\_α,}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{2α + β\} = X\_\{2α + β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) Set}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(x) = exp(x X\_\{α + β\}) = int(w\_β) p\_α(x),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α + β\}(x) = exp(x X\_\{2α + β\}) = int(w\_α) p\_β(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(x\^{}2 y),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_\{2α + β\}(2 x y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.3.2.}\label{section-248}

The proof occupies Nos. 3.3.2 to 3.3.6. One has
\((\beta^{*}, \alpha) = -1\), \((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = -2\), whence
\(\alpha(t_{\beta}) = -1\), \(\beta(t_{\alpha}) = 1\).

Note in passing that \(\beta(t_{\alpha}) = \alpha(t_{\alpha}) = 1\),
which shows that \(t_{\alpha}\) is a section of \(Centr(G)\). Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_α = X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\_α) X\_β = X\_\{2α + β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{α + β\} = α(t\_β) X\_α = {-}X\_α,}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{2α + β\} = β(t\_α) X\_β = X\_β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \((2\alpha + \beta) + \beta\) and \((2\alpha + \beta) - \beta\)
are not roots,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{2α + β\} = X\_\{2α + β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

There exists a scalar \(k \in G_{m}(S)\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = k X\_\{α + β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand, by Exp. XXII, 5.5.2, there exist sections
\(A, B, C \in G_{a}(S)\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(A x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2 y),       (1)}
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_\{2α + β\}(C x y).               (2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is therefore necessary, in (ii) and (iii), to prove that
\(A = B = 1\), \(C = 2\), \(k = -1\).

\subsubsection{3.3.3.}\label{section-249}

Make \(int(w_{\alpha})\) act on formula (2). One finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) = p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{α + β\}(A k x y) p\_β(B x\^{}2 y).       (3)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transforming (2) likewise, one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(k y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) = p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) p\_\{α + β\}(k y) p\_β(C x y).       (4)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transforming (1) by \(int(w_{\beta})\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{{-}β\}({-}y) p\_\{α + β\}(x) = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}y) p\_α({-}A x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2 y).       (5)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.3.4.}\label{section-250}

Write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_β p\_α(x) w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{α + β\}(x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(\alpha + 2\beta\) is not a root, this gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(1) p\_α(x) p\_β({-}1) = p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using (1) in the left member and (5) in the right, one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_β(1) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2) p\_β({-}1) =}
\NormalTok{    p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_α(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}({-}B x\^{}2) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(p_{\beta}\) commutes with \(p_{\alpha + \beta}\) and
\(p_{2\alpha + \beta}\) on the one hand, and \(p_{-\beta}\) commutes
with \(p_{\alpha}\) and \(p_{2\alpha + \beta}\) on the other hand, this
is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2) = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_α(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}({-}B x\^{}2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transforming the right member by (2), one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2) = p\_α(A x) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{2α + β\}((A C {-} B) x\^{}2),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = 1,    C = 2 B.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.3.5.}\label{section-251}

Write now

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α p\_β(y) w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{2α + β\}(y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(3\alpha + \beta\) is not a root, this gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(1) p\_β(y) p\_α({-}1) = p\_\{{-}α\}(1) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using (1) in the left member, (3) in the right, one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}A y) p\_\{2α + β\}(B y) = p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{α + β\}(A k y) p\_β(B y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(p_{\alpha + \beta}\), \(p_{2\alpha + \beta}\) and \(p_{\beta}\)
commute, this gives at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B = 1,    {-}A = A k,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence finally

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = 1,    B = 1,    C = 2,    k = {-}1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.3.6.}\label{section-252}

We have therefore proved (ii) and (iii). Let us prove (i). Taking into
account the equality
\(s_{\beta}(t_{\alpha}) = t_{\alpha} t^{(\alpha^{*}, \beta)}_{\beta} = t_{\alpha}\)
(since \((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = 2\)),\footnote{In the source: ``since
  \((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = 2\)''. The correct expression
  \((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = -2\) was used in the previous section; here
  Demazure exploits the resulting formula
  \(s_{\beta}(t_{\alpha}) = t_{\alpha} t^{-2}_{\beta} = t_{\alpha}\)
  (using \(t^{2}_{\beta} = e\), which holds in \texttt{B\_2}).} one has
successively:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α w\_β w\_α = w\_α w\_β w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} t\_α = w\_\{2α + β\} t\_α,}
\NormalTok{w\_β w\_α w\_β w\_α w\_β = w\_β w\_\{2α + β\} w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} · s\_β(t\_α) · t\_β = w\_\{2α + β\} t\_α t\_β,}
\NormalTok{w\_α w\_β w\_α w\_β w\_α w\_β w\_α = w\_α w\_\{2α + β\} w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} · s\_α(t\_α t\_β) · t\_α = w\_β · t\_α · t\_β t\_α · t\_α}
\NormalTok{                            = w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} t\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\[
(w_{\beta} w_{\alpha})^{4} = t_{\alpha},
\]

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(w\_α w\_β)\^{}4 = s\_β(t\_α) = t\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which completes the proof.

\textbf{Remark 3.3.7.} \emph{Condition (v) of 2.3 translates here as
follows, setting \(v_{\alpha + \beta} = int(h_{\beta}) v_{\alpha}\) and
\(v_{2\alpha + \beta} = int(h_{\alpha}) v_{\beta}\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(A)   int(h\_α h\_β h\_α) v\_β = v\_β,        (B)   v\_β v\_α = v\_α v\_β v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{2α + β\},}
\NormalTok{      int(h\_β h\_α h\_β) v\_α = v\_α,              v\_\{α + β\} v\_α = v\_α v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{2α + β\}\^{}2,}
\NormalTok{                                               v\_\{α + β\} v\_β = v\_β v\_\{α + β\},}
\NormalTok{                                               v\_\{2α + β\} v\_α = v\_α v\_\{2α + β\},}
\NormalTok{                                               v\_\{2α + β\} v\_β = v\_β v\_\{2α + β\},}
\NormalTok{                                               v\_\{2α + β\} v\_\{α + β\} = v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{2α + β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{3.4. Groups of type
\texttt{G\_2}}{3.4. Groups of type G\_2}}\label{groups-of-type-g_2}

\textbf{Proposition 3.4.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group of type \texttt{G\_2}, and denote
\(\Delta = {\alpha, \beta}\),
\(R^{+} = {\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + 2\beta}\).}

\emph{(i) One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_\{αβ\} = (w\_α w\_β)\^{}6 = e = (w\_β w\_α)\^{}6 = t\_\{βα\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) If one sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_α = X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = X\_\{2α + β\},}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_β = {-}X\_\{3α + β\},    Ad(w\_β) X\_\{3α + β\} = X\_\{3α + 2β\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{2α + β\} = {-}X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\_α) X\_\{3α + β\} = X\_β,}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{3α + 2β\} = X\_\{3α + 2β\},    Ad(w\_β) X\_\{α + β\} = {-}X\_α,}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{2α + β\} = X\_\{2α + β\},    Ad(w\_β) X\_\{3α + 2β\} = {-}X\_\{3α + β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) If one sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(x) = exp(x X\_\{α + β\}) = int(w\_β) p\_α(x),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α + β\}(x) = exp(x X\_\{2α + β\}) = int(w\_α w\_β) p\_α(x),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + β\}(x) = exp(x X\_\{3α + β\}) = int(w\_α) p\_β({-}x),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + 2β\}(x) = exp(x X\_\{3α + 2β\}) = int(w\_β w\_α) p\_β({-}x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(x\^{}2 y) p\_\{3α + β\}(x\^{}3 y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(x\^{}3 y\^{}2),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_\{2α + β\}(2 x y) p\_\{3α + β\}(3 x\^{}2 y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(3 x y\^{}2),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + β\}(3 x y),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + β\}(y) p\_β(x) = p\_β(x) p\_\{3α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}x y),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x) = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(3 x y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.4.2.}\label{section-253}

The proof occupies Nos. 3.4.2 to 3.4.9. One has
\((\beta^{*}, \alpha) = -1\), \((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = -3\), whence
\(\beta(t_{\alpha}) = \alpha(t_{\beta}) = -1\). Define
\(X_{\alpha + \beta}\), \(X_{2\alpha + \beta}\), \(X_{3\alpha + \beta}\)
and \(X_{3\alpha + 2\beta}\) as in (ii). One has at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{α + β\} = α(t\_β) X\_α = {-}X\_α,}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{2α + β\} = α(t\_α) β(t\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = {-}X\_\{α + β\},}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{3α + β\} = {-}β(t\_α) X\_β = X\_β,}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{3α + 2β\} = α(t\_β)\^{}3 β(t\_β) X\_\{3α + β\} = {-}X\_\{3α + β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Finally, since \((3\alpha + 2\beta) \pm \alpha\) and
\((2\alpha + \beta) \pm \beta\) are not roots,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{3α + 2β\} = X\_\{3α + 2β\},    Ad(w\_β) X\_\{2α + β\} = X\_\{2α + β\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which completes the proof of (ii).

\subsubsection{3.4.3.}\label{section-254}

By virtue of Exp. XXII, 5.5.2, there exist scalars\footnote{N.D.E.: We
  introduce here absolute constants \(A, B, \cdots, J\). These constants
  will be determined in the pages that follow; their values are
  \(A = B = C = D = 1\), \(E = 2\), \(J = -1\), \(F = G = H = 3\),
  cf.~3.4.8.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, J ∈ G\_a(S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(A x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2 y) p\_\{3α + β\}(C x\^{}3 y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(D x\^{}3 y\^{}2),   (1)}
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_\{2α + β\}(E x y) p\_\{3α + β\}(F x\^{}2 y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(G x y\^{}2),           (2)}
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + β\}(H x y),                                                  (3)}
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + β\}(y) p\_β(x) = p\_β(x) p\_\{3α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(J x y).                                                 (4)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.4.4.}\label{section-255}

Make \(int(w_{\beta})\) act on (1), (3) and (4):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{{-}β\}({-}y) p\_\{α + β\}(x) =}
\NormalTok{    p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}y) p\_α({-}A x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2 y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(C x\^{}3 y) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}D x\^{}3 y\^{}2),       (5)}
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x) = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(H x y),                                    (6)}
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + 2β\}(y) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}x) = p\_\{{-}β\}({-}x) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(y) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}J x y).                                       (7)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Making \(int(w_{\alpha})\) act on (1), one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) =}
\NormalTok{    p\_\{{-}α\}({-}x) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{2α + β\}(A x y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}B x\^{}2 y) p\_β(C x\^{}3 y) p\_\{3α + β\}(D x\^{}3 y\^{}2).        (8)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.4.5.}\label{section-256}

Write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_β p\_α(x) w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{α + β\}(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, \(\alpha + 2\beta\) not being a root,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(1) p\_α(x) p\_α({-}1) = p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1).            (9)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transforming the left member of (9) by (1), then (4), one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(1) p\_α(x) p\_β({-}1)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_α(x) p\_β(1) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + β\}(C x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(D x\^{}3) p\_β({-}1)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_α(x) p\_β(1) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2) p\_β({-}1) p\_\{3α + β\}(C x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((D {-} C J) x\^{}3)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + β\}(C x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((D {-} C J) x\^{}3).            (10)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transforming the right member of (9) by (5), then (7):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_α(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}({-}B x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}C x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}D x\^{}3) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_α(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}({-}B x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}C x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + β\}((C J {-} D) x\^{}3).            (11)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Using now (2), this right member becomes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(A x) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{2α + β\}(A E x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + β\}(A\^{}2 F x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(A G x\^{}3) ×}
\NormalTok{    p\_\{2α + β\}({-}B x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}C x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + β\}((C J {-} D) x\^{}3)}
\NormalTok{= p\_α(A x) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{2α + β\}((A E {-} B) x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + β\}((A\^{}2 F + C J {-} D) x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((A G {-} C) x\^{}3). (12)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

So (9) rewrites:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(A x) p\_\{2α + β\}(B x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + β\}(C x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((D {-} C J) x\^{}3) =}
\NormalTok{   p\_α(A x) p\_\{α + β\}(x) p\_\{2α + β\}((A E {-} B) x\^{}2) p\_\{3α + β\}((A\^{}2 F + C J {-} D) x\^{}3) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((A G {-} C) x\^{}3),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = 1,    E = 2 B,    C + D = F + C J,    F = G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.4.6.}\label{section-257}

Write now

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α p\_β(y) w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is, \(4\alpha + \beta\) not being a root,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(1) p\_β(y) p\_α({-}1) = p\_\{{-}α\}(1) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1).            (13)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transform the left member by (1):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(1) p\_β(y) p\_α({-}1) = p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}A y) p\_\{2α + β\}(B y) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}C y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}D y\^{}2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transform the right member of (13) successively by (8), (6) and (4):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{{-}α\}(1) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{2α + β\}(A y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}B y) p\_β(C y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(D y\^{}2)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}B y) p\_\{2α + β\}(A y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}A B H y\^{}2) p\_β(C y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(D y\^{}2)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_β(C y) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}B y) p\_\{2α + β\}(A y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((D {-} C J {-} A B H) y\^{}2)}
\NormalTok{   = p\_β(C y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}B y) p\_\{2α + β\}(A y) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((D {-} C J {-} A B H) y\^{}2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

So (13) rewrites:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(C y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}B y) p\_\{2α + β\}(A y) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}((D {-} C J {-} A B H) y\^{}2) =}
\NormalTok{   p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}({-}A y) p\_\{2α + β\}(B y) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}C y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}D y\^{}2),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C = 1,    A = B,    D {-} C J {-} A B H = {-}D.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Taking into account the results already obtained:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = B = C = 1,    E = 2,    F = G,    D + 1 = F + J,    2 D = H + J.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.4.7.}\label{section-258}

Write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_β p\_\{3α + β\}(x) w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{3α + 2β\}(x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(1) p\_\{3α + β\}(x) p\_β({-}1) = p\_\{{-}β\}(1) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(x) p\_\{{-}β\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transforming the left member by (4), the right by (7), one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + β\}(x) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}J x) = p\_\{3α + 2β\}(x) p\_\{3α + β\}({-}J x),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \(J = -1\).

\subsubsection{3.4.8.}\label{section-259}

Write finally

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α p\_\{α + β\}(y) w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = p\_\{2α + β\}(y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(1) p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_α({-}1) = p\_\{{-}α\}(1) p\_α({-}1) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_α(1) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Transforming the left member by (2), the right by (3), one obtains:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_\{2α + β\}({-}E y) p\_\{3α + β\}(F y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}G y\^{}2) =}
\NormalTok{    p\_\{{-}α\}(1) p\_\{2α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + β\}(H y) p\_\{{-}α\}({-}1).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is immediate to see that, if one makes \(p_{-\alpha}(-1)\) commute
with \(p_{3\alpha + \beta}(H y)\), then \(p_{2\alpha + \beta}(y)\), one
does not introduce in the right member any new terms in
\(p_{3\alpha + \beta}\). The latter therefore writes, denoting by empty
parentheses quantities whose exact value does not matter to us:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}( ) p\_\{2α + β\}( ) p\_β( ) p\_\{3α + β\}(H y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}( ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Comparing with the left member, one has at once \(F = H\), whence by the
previous results \(2 D = D + 1\), so \(D = 1\), and finally
\(F = G = H = 2 D - J = 3\), which completes the determination of the
coefficients \(A, \cdots, J\) and the proof of (iii).

\subsubsection{3.4.9.}\label{section-260}

Let us prove (i) finally, in the usual manner. One has successively:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α w\_β w\_α = w\_α w\_β w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} t\_α = w\_\{3α + β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} · t\_α,}
\NormalTok{w\_β (w\_α w\_β)\^{}2 = w\_β w\_\{3α + β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} · s\_β(t\_α) · t\_β = w\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} · t\_α t\_β · t\_β = w\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} · t\_α,}
\NormalTok{w\_α (w\_β w\_α)\^{}3 = w\_α w\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} = w\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\NormalTok{w\_β (w\_α w\_β)\^{}4 = w\_β w\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}\{{-}1\} w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\} · t\_β = w\_\{3α + β\} · t\_β,}
\NormalTok{w\_α (w\_β w\_α)\^{}5 = w\_α w\_\{3α + β\} w\_α\^{}\{{-}1\} · s\_α(t\_β) · t\_β = w\_β · t\_β t\_α · t\_α = w\_β\^{}\{{-}1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(w\_α w\_β)\^{}6 = (w\_β w\_α)\^{}6 = e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 3.4.10.} \emph{Condition (v) of 2.4 is composed of}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(A)   int(h\_α h\_β h\_α h\_β h\_α) v\_β = v\_β,}
\NormalTok{      int(h\_β h\_α h\_β h\_α h\_β) v\_α = v\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and, setting}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{v\_\{α + β\} = int(h\_β) v\_α,    v\_\{2α + β\} = int(h\_α h\_β) v\_α,}
\NormalTok{v\_\{3α + β\} = int(h\_α) v\_β\^{}\{{-}1\},    v\_\{3α + 2β\} = int(h\_β h\_α) v\_β\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the commutation relations:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(B)   v\_β v\_α = v\_α v\_β v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{2α + β\} v\_\{3α + β\} v\_\{3α + 2β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{α + β\} v\_α = v\_α v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{2α + β\}\^{}2 v\_\{3α + β\}\^{}3 v\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}3,}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{2α + β\} v\_α = v\_α v\_\{2α + β\} v\_\{3α + β\}\^{}3,}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + β\} v\_α = v\_α v\_\{3α + β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + 2β\} v\_α = v\_α v\_\{3α + 2β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{α + β\} v\_β = v\_β v\_\{α + β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{2α + β\} v\_β = v\_β v\_\{2α + β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + β\} v\_β = v\_β v\_\{3α + β\} v\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}\{{-}1\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + 2β\} v\_β = v\_β v\_\{3α + 2β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{2α + β\} v\_\{α + β\} = v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{2α + β\} v\_\{3α + 2β\}\^{}3,}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + β\} v\_\{α + β\} = v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{3α + β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + 2β\} v\_\{α + β\} = v\_\{α + β\} v\_\{3α + 2β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + β\} v\_\{2α + β\} = v\_\{2α + β\} v\_\{3α + β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + 2β\} v\_\{2α + β\} = v\_\{2α + β\} v\_\{3α + 2β\},}
\NormalTok{      v\_\{3α + 2β\} v\_\{3α + β\} = v\_\{3α + β\} v\_\{3α + 2β\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.5. Explicit form of the generators-and-relations
theorem}\label{explicit-form-of-the-generators-and-relations-theorem}

\textbf{Theorem 3.5.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned
\(S\)-group, \(T\) its maximal torus, \(\Delta\) its system of simple
roots, \(u_{\alpha} \in U_{\alpha}(S)^{\times}\) and
\(w_{\alpha} \in Norm_{G}(T)(S)\) the elements defined by the pinning
(\(\alpha \in \Delta\)). Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T : T → H,    f\_α : U\_α → H,    α ∈ Δ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be morphisms of groups, \(H\) being an \(S\)-sheaf in groups for
(fppf); let \(h_{\alpha} \in H(S)\), (\(\alpha \in \Delta\)) be sections
of \(H\), and set \(v_{\alpha} = f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha})\),
\(\alpha \in \Delta\). In order that there exist a morphism of groups}

\[
f : G \to H
\]

\emph{extending \(f_{T}\), \(f_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\) and
satisfying \(f(w_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\) (\(\alpha \in \Delta\)) (and
then necessarily unique), it is necessary and sufficient that the
following conditions be satisfied:}

\emph{(i) For every \(S' \to S\), every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), every
\(t \in T(S')\) and every \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(f\_T(t)) f\_α(x) = f\_α(int(t) x) = f\_α(x\^{}\{α(t)\}).            (1)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), every \(S' \to S\) and every
\(t \in T(S')\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(h\_α) f\_T(t) = f\_T(s\_α(t)) = f\_T(t · α\^{}* α(t)\^{}\{{-}1\}).            (2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) For every \(\alpha \in \Delta\),\footnote{N.D.E.: The
  relations (3₁) and (3₂) form the description of the normalizer of the
  torus, (3₁) being, like (4), in a group of rank 1, while (3₂) is in a
  group of rank 2.}}

\[
h^{2}_{\alpha} = f_{T}(\alpha^{*}(-1)),            (3_{1})
(h_{\alpha} v_{\alpha})^{3} = e.            (4)
\]

\emph{(iv) For all \(\alpha, \beta \in \Delta\), \(\alpha \neq \beta\),
such that \((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = 0\) (resp.
\((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = -1\), resp. \((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = -2\), resp.
\((\alpha^{*}, \beta) = -3\)):}

\emph{(a) the relation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(h\_α h\_β)\^{}2 = f\_T(α\^{}*({-}1) β\^{}*({-}1))     if (α\^{}*, β) = 0;}
\NormalTok{(h\_α h\_β)\^{}3 = e,                       if (α\^{}*, β) = {-}1;        (3₂)}
\NormalTok{(h\_α h\_β)\^{}4 = f\_T(α\^{}*({-}1)),            if (α\^{}*, β) = {-}2;}
\NormalTok{(h\_α h\_β)\^{}6 = e,                       if (α\^{}*, β) = {-}3.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(b) The relations (A) and (B) of 3.1.3 (resp. 3.2.8, resp. 3.3.7,
resp. 3.4.10).}

This follows at once from 2.3, 2.6 and the calculations done in each
particular case.

\textbf{Remark 3.5.2.} \emph{One may present the preceding results in a
slightly different way: one gives oneself morphisms, for
\(\alpha \in \Delta\),}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a\_α : T · U\_α → H,    b\_α : Norm\_\{Z\_α\}(T) → H,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and one sets}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h\_α = b\_α(w\_α),    v\_α = a\_α(u\_α);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{then the conditions to be verified are the following:}

\emph{(1) all the \(a_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\) and all the
\(b_{\alpha} (\alpha \in \Delta)\) have the same restriction to \(T\);}

\emph{(2) conditions (4) and (iv) of 3.5.1 above are satisfied.}

\subsubsection{3.5.3.}\label{section-261}

Various applications of this theorem will be given in the following
Exposé. Let us mention one here: Theorem 3.5.1 gives a description by
generators and relations of \(G\) in the category of \(S\)-sheaves for
(fppf); in other words, consider for each \(S' \to S\) the group
\(H(S')\) generated by \(T(S')\), \(U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(\alpha \in R\),
and \(w_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in R\), subjected to relations analogous
to (1), (2), (3₁), (4), (3₂), (A), (B); then \(G\) is none other than
the sheaf associated with the presheaf \(S' \mapsto H(S')\).

In particular, if \(S'\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed
field \(k\), one has \(G(S') = H(S')\) (an immediate consequence of the
Nullstellensatz in the form: ``a sieve over an algebraically closed
field, covering for (fppf), is trivial''), so that 3.5.1 yields at once
an explicit description by generators and relations of the ``abstract''
group \(G(k)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: For an arbitrary field \(k\) and \(G\)
  simply connected, R. Steinberg gave a presentation of the group
  \(G(k)\) in {[}St62{]}, Th. 3.2, see also {[}St67{]}, § 6, Th. 8.}

\subsection{4. Uniqueness of pinned groups: fundamental
theorem}\label{uniqueness-of-pinned-groups-fundamental-theorem}

\textbf{Theorem 4.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a nonempty scheme. The functor
\(R\) of 1.6 is fully faithful: let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two pinned
\(S\)-groups, \(p\)\footnote{N.D.E.: To avoid a notational problem later
  on, we have replaced \(q\) by \(p\), so that in what follows, \(q\)
  (resp. \(q_{1}\)) is an arbitrary power of \(p\).} an integer
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} such that \(x \mapsto x^{p}\) is an
endomorphism of \(G_{a, S}\), and \(h : R(G') \to R(G)\) a
\(p\)-morphism of pinned root data. There exists a unique morphism of
pinned groups}

\[
f : G \to G'
\]

\emph{such that \(R(f) = h\).}

The uniqueness is proved in 1.9. It suffices to prove existence. By
hypothesis, one has a bijection \(d : R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'\) and a
map \(q : R \to {p^{n} | n \in \mathbb{N}}\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(d(α)) = q(α) α    and    \^{}t h(α\^{}*) = q(α) d(α)\^{}*}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(\alpha \in R\). In particular, the semisimple ranks of \(G\)
and \(G'\) coincide.

\subsubsection{4.1.1.}\label{section-262}

Suppose \(rg_{ss}(G) = rg_{ss}(G') = 0\). Then \(G\) and \(G'\) are
tori: one has \(G = T = D_{S}(M)\), \(G' = T' = D_{S}(M')\) and \(h\) is
simply a morphism of ordinary groups \(h : M' \to M\). One then takes
\(f = D_{S}(h)\).

\subsubsection{4.1.2.}\label{section-263}

Suppose \(rg_{ss}(G) = rg_{ss}(G') = 1\). Consider then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T = D\_S(h) : T → T\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By hypothesis, one has a commutative diagram, where
\(\alpha' = d(\alpha)\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\} ──α\^{}*──→ T ──α──→ G\_\{m, S\}}
\NormalTok{   │              │            │}
\NormalTok{ q(α)            f\_T          q(α)}
\NormalTok{   │              │            │}
\NormalTok{   ↓              ↓            ↓}
\NormalTok{G\_\{m, S\} ──α\textquotesingle{}\^{}*──→ T\textquotesingle{} ──α\textquotesingle{}──→ G\_\{m, S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One then applies Exp. XX, 4.1.

\subsubsection{4.1.3.}\label{section-264}

Suppose \(rg_{ss}(G) = rg_{ss}(G') = 2\). Then, by Exp. XXI, 7.5.3, one
knows all the possibilities for \(h : R(G') \to R(G)\). Let us examine
them successively, verifying each time the conditions of 2.5.

Denote \(\Delta = {\alpha, \beta}\), \(\Delta' = {\alpha', \beta'}\) in
such a way that \(d(\alpha) = \alpha'\), \(d(\beta) = \beta'\).

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{4.1.4. \(G\) and \(G'\) of type
\(A_{1} \times A_{1}\)}{4.1.4. G and G\textquotesingle{} of type A\_\{1\} \textbackslash times A\_\{1\}}}\label{g-and-g-of-type-a_1-times-a_1}

One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(α\textquotesingle{}) = q α,    h(β\textquotesingle{}) = q\_1 β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us show that the conditions of 2.5 are satisfied: (ii) and (iii)
follow from 3.1.2 (ii) and (iii); let us prove (i).

One has\footnote{N.D.E.: We have spelled out what follows.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D\_S(h) t\_\{αβ\} = D\_S(h)(t\_α t\_β) = \^{}t h(α\^{}*)({-}1) · \^{}t h(β\^{}*)({-}1) = α\textquotesingle{}\^{}*(({-}1)\^{}q) · β\textquotesingle{}\^{}*(({-}1)\^{}\{q\_1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, the hypothesis that \(x \mapsto x^{p}\) is an endomorphism of
\(G_{a, S}\) (and \(S \neq \emptyset\)) entails that \(p = 1\) or that
\(S\) is of characteristic \(p\); in all cases \((-1)^{q} = -1\) (if
\(q\) is even, \(p = 2\) and \texttt{1\ =\ -1}). Consequently,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D\_S(h) t\_\{αβ\} = α\textquotesingle{}\^{}*({-}1) · β\textquotesingle{}\^{}*({-}1) = t\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} β\textquotesingle{}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This shows that condition 2.5 (i) is satisfied.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{4.1.5. \(G\) and \(G'\) of type
\texttt{A\_2}}{4.1.5. G and G\textquotesingle{} of type A\_2}}\label{g-and-g-of-type-a_2}

One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(α\textquotesingle{}) = q α,    h(β\textquotesingle{}) = q β.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set \(X_{\alpha + \beta} = Ad(w_{\beta}) X_{\alpha}\) and
\(X'_{\alpha' + \beta'} = Ad(w_{\beta'}) X_{\alpha'}\). Let us verify
the conditions of 2.5. For (i), one reasons as above, using 3.2.1 (i);
for (ii), it is immediate by 3.2.1 (ii); it remains to verify (iii). We
must check that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(z) ↦ p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(z\^{}q)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a morphism of groups. The only nontrivial commutation relation is
that of 3.2.1 (iii), which is written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x y),}
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}q) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}q y\^{}q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{4.1.6.}\label{section-265}

One reasons similarly for \(G\) and \(G'\) of type \texttt{B\_2} (resp.
\texttt{G\_2}), when the radicial exponents are equal, using 3.3.1
(resp. 3.4.1); it remains, therefore, to treat --- in order to complete
the case of groups of rank 2 --- the two exceptional cases of Exp. XXI,
7.5.3.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{4.1.7. \(G\) and \(G'\) of type
\texttt{B\_2}, \(S\) of characteristic 2, \(q(\alpha) = 2q\),
\(q(\beta) = q\)}{4.1.7. G and G\textquotesingle{} of type B\_2, S of characteristic 2, q(\textbackslash alpha) = 2q, q(\textbackslash beta) = q}}\label{g-and-g-of-type-b_2-s-of-characteristic-2-qalpha-2q-qbeta-q}

The positive roots are
\({\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta}\) and
\({\alpha', \beta', \alpha' + \beta', \alpha' + 2\beta'}\) (note that
the ``short'' simple roots are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta'\)). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(α\textquotesingle{}) = 2 q α,    h(β\textquotesingle{}) = q β,    h(α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}) = q(2α + β),    h(α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}) = 2 q(α + β),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d(α + β) = α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{},    q(α + β) = 2 q,}
\NormalTok{d(2α + β) = α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{},    q(2α + β) = q.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\_\{α + β\} = Ad(w\_β) X\_α,    X\_\{2α + β\} = Ad(w\_α) X\_β,}
\NormalTok{X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\},    X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us now verify the conditions of 2.5.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  Since \(S\) is of characteristic 2, one has \texttt{-1\ =\ 1} on
  \(S\), hence
  \(t_{\alpha \beta} = t_{\alpha} = \alpha^{*}(-1) = e = \beta'^{*}(-1) = t'_{\beta'} = t'_{\alpha' \beta'}\)
  (cf.~3.3.1 (i)).
\item
  One has by construction
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_β = X\_\{2α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(2α + β)\};}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_α = X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α + β)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 3.3.1 (ii) and the fact that \texttt{-1\ =\ 1} on \(S\), one has on
each side

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α + β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α + β)\};}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{2α + β\} = X\_β,    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(2α + β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(β)\};}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{α + β\} = X\_α,    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α + β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α)\};}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{2α + β\} = X\_\{2α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(2α + β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(2α + β)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  By 3.3.1 (iii), one sees that the only nontrivial commutation relation
  in \(U\) (resp. \(U'\)) is
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(x\^{}2 y),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

resp.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{} y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{} y\textquotesingle{}\^{}2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We must verify that the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(z) p\_\{2α + β\}(t) ↦ p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{2q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}(z\^{}\{2q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(t\^{}q)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a morphism of groups; one sees at once that this amounts to seeing
that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{2q\}) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{2q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}((x y)\^{}\{2q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}((x\^{}2 y)\^{}q),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is none other than the second relation above (setting
\(y' = x^{2q}\), \(x' = y^{q}\)).

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{4.1.8. \(G\) and \(G'\) of type
\texttt{G\_2}, \(S\) of characteristic 3, \(q(\alpha) = 3q\),
\(q(\beta) = q\)}{4.1.8. G and G\textquotesingle{} of type G\_2, S of characteristic 3, q(\textbackslash alpha) = 3q, q(\textbackslash beta) = q}}\label{g-and-g-of-type-g_2-s-of-characteristic-3-qalpha-3q-qbeta-q}

The positive roots are
\({\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + 2\beta}\)
on the one hand,
\({\alpha', \beta', \alpha' + \beta', \alpha' + 2\beta', \alpha' + 3\beta', 2\alpha' + 3\beta'}\)
on the other (as in the preceding case, the short simple roots are
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta'\)). One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h(α\textquotesingle{}) = 3 q α,    h(β\textquotesingle{}) = q β,    h(α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}) = q(3α + β),}
\NormalTok{h(α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}) = q(3α + 2β),    h(α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}) = 3 q(α + β),}
\NormalTok{h(2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}) = 3 q(2α + β),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which gives

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d(α + β) = α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{},    q(α + β) = 3 q,}
\NormalTok{d(2α + β) = 2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{},    q(2α + β) = 3 q,}
\NormalTok{d(3α + β) = α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{},    q(3α + β) = q,}
\NormalTok{d(3α + 2β) = α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{},    q(3α + 2β) = q.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\_\{α + β\} = Ad(w\_β) X\_α,    X\_\{2α + β\} = Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\},}
\NormalTok{X\_\{3α + β\} = {-}Ad(w\_α) X\_β,    X\_\{3α + 2β\} = Ad(w\_β) X\_\{3α + β\};}
\NormalTok{X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = {-}Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\},    X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\},}
\NormalTok{X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\},    X\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us now verify the conditions of 2.5.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  \(t_{\alpha \beta} = e\) and \(t'_{\alpha' \beta'} = e\) by 3.4.1 (i).
\item
  One has by construction
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_α = X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α + β)\};}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_β = {-}X\_\{3α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\} = {-}X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = {-}X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(3α + β)\};}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{3α + β\} = X\_\{3α + 2β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(3α + β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(3α + 2β)\};}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{α + β\} = X\_\{2α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α + β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\} = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(2α + β)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 3.4.1 (ii), one has on each side:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_α) X\_\{2α + β\} = {-}X\_\{α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(2α + β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\} = {-}X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\} = {-}X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(α + β)\};}
\NormalTok{       …                                          …}
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_β) X\_\{3α + 2β\} = {-}X\_\{3α + β\},    Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(3α + 2β)\} = Ad(w\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\} = {-}X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\} = {-}X\textquotesingle{}\_\{d(3α + β)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(The dots replace four verifications of the same kind.)

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  The only nontrivial commutation relations in \(U\) and \(U'\) are, by
  3.4.1 (iii) (and taking into account \texttt{3\ =\ 0} on \(S\)):
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_β(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(x\^{}2 y) p\_\{3α + β\}(x\^{}3 y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(x\^{}3 y\^{}2),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_α(x) = p\_α(x) p\_\{α + β\}(y) p\_\{2α + β\}({-}x y),}
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α + β\}(y) p\_β(x) = p\_β(x) p\_\{3α + β\}(y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}({-}x y);}

\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) =}
\NormalTok{    p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}({-}x\textquotesingle{} y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}({-}x\textquotesingle{}\^{}2 y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}({-}x\textquotesingle{}\^{}3 y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}({-}x\textquotesingle{}\^{}3 y\textquotesingle{}\^{}2),}
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{} y\textquotesingle{}),}
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\textquotesingle{}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\textquotesingle{} y\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We must verify that the morphism \(\phi : U \to U'\) defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{φ(p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_\{α + β\}(t) p\_\{2α + β\}(u) p\_\{3α + β\}(v) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(w))}
\NormalTok{  = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}(t\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}(u\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(v\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}(w\^{}q)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a morphism of groups. Now one verifies immediately that the three
last commutation relations are also written

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{3q\}) =}
\NormalTok{    p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}((x y)\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}((x\^{}2 y)\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}((x\^{}3 y)\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}((x\^{}3 y\^{}2)\^{}q),}
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{3q\}) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}\{3q\}) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{2α\textquotesingle{} + 3β\textquotesingle{}\}({-}(x y)\^{}\{3q\}),}
\NormalTok{p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}q) = p\textquotesingle{}\_\{β\textquotesingle{}\}(x\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + β\textquotesingle{}\}(y\^{}q) p\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} + 2β\textquotesingle{}\}({-}(x y)\^{}q);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which shows that \(\phi\) is indeed a morphism of groups and completes
the proof of 4.1.7.

\subsubsection{\texorpdfstring{4.1.9. Case where \(G\) and \(G'\) are of
semisimple rank
\texttt{\textgreater{}\ 2}}{4.1.9. Case where G and G\textquotesingle{} are of semisimple rank \textgreater{} 2}}\label{case-where-g-and-g-are-of-semisimple-rank-2}

For each root \(\alpha \in \Delta\), denote
\(\alpha' = d(\alpha) \in \Delta' = d(\Delta)\). For each
\((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\), consider the pinned groups
of semisimple rank \(\leqslant 2\), \(Z_{\alpha \beta}\) and
\(Z'_{\alpha' \beta'}\). The morphism of groups \(M' \to M\) underlying
\(h\) defines a \(p\)-morphism of root data

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h\_\{αβ\} : R(Z\_\{αβ\}) → R(Z\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} β\textquotesingle{}\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By virtue of the preceding results, there exists therefore a morphism of
pinned groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_\{αβ\} : Z\_\{αβ\} → Z\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{} β\textquotesingle{}\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \(R(f_{\alpha \beta}) = h_{\alpha \beta}\). Let us prove that
the \(f_{\alpha \beta}\) satisfy the gluing condition of 2.5; indeed
\(f_{\alpha \beta}|_{Z_{\alpha}}\) and \(f_{\alpha \alpha}\) are two
morphisms of pinned groups

\[
Z_{\alpha} \to Z'_{\alpha'}
\]

corresponding to the same morphism of pinned root data, and therefore
coincide by the uniqueness result already proved. By 2.5 there exists
therefore a morphism of groups

\[
f : G \to G'
\]

extending the \(f_{\alpha \beta}\). This is evidently a morphism of
pinned groups such that \(R(f) = h\), which completes the proof of
Theorem 4.1.

\subsection{5. Corollaries of the fundamental
theorem}\label{corollaries-of-the-fundamental-theorem}

The most important is:

\textbf{Corollary 5.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a nonempty scheme, \(G\) and
\(G'\) two pinned \(S\)-groups, \(h\) an isomorphism of pinned root
data}

\[
h : R(G') \xrightarrow{\sim} R(G).
\]

\emph{There exists a unique isomorphism of pinned \(S\)-groups}

\[
f : G \xrightarrow{\sim} G'
\]

\emph{such that \(R(f) = h\).}

Note that 5.1 also follows from 3.5.1 (the relations of 3.5.1 may be
written using only the datum of \(R(G)\)); note also that 5.1 follows
from the most elementary part of the proof of 4.1 (one does not need to
consider the ``exceptional isogenies'' of 4.1.7 and 4.1.8).

\textbf{Corollary 5.2 (``Uniqueness theorem'').} \emph{Let \(S\) be a
scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two splittable \(S\)-groups (Exp. XXII, 1.13).
If \(G\) and \(G'\) are of the same type (Exp. XXII, 2.6), they are
isomorphic.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two splittable \(S\)-groups. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic.}

\emph{(ii) \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic locally for the (fpqc)
topology.}

\emph{(iii) There exists an \(s \in S\) such that the \(s\)-groups
\(G_{s}\) and \(G'_{s}\) are of the same type.}

Indeed, one evidently has (i) ⇒ (ii) ⇒ (iii). On the other hand, (iii)
entails that \(R(G) = R(G_{s}) = R(G'_{s}) = R(G')\), hence that \(G\)
and \(G'\) satisfy the condition of 5.2.

\textbf{Corollary 5.4 (``Uniqueness of the Chevalley schemes'').}
\emph{Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two reductive groups over \(\mathbb{Z}\)
possessing split maximal tori.}\footnote{In fact, one may prove that
  every \(\mathbb{Z}\)-torus is split.{[}\^{}N.D.E-XXIII-14{]}}
\emph{The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic.}

\emph{(ii) There exists \(s \in \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) such
that \(G_{s}\) and \(G'_{s}\) are of the same type.}

\emph{(iii) \(G_{\mathbb{C}}\) and \(G'_{\mathbb{C}}\) are of the same
type.}

Indeed, \(G\) and \(G'\) are splittable by Exp. XXII, 2.2.

\textbf{Corollary 5.5 (``Existence of outer automorphisms'').} \emph{Let
\(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group, \(h\) an automorphism of
the pinned root datum \(R(G)\). There exists a unique automorphism \(u\)
of \(G\) respecting its pinning and such that \(R(u) = h\).}

Let us make the preceding corollary explicit.

\textbf{Corollary 5.5.bis.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a split
reductive \(S\)-group, \(R^{+}\) a system of positive roots of \(G\).}

\emph{Choose for each simple root \(\alpha\) an isomorphism of vector
groups \(p_{\alpha} : G_{a, S} \xrightarrow{\sim} U_{\alpha}\). Let
\(h\) be an automorphism of \(M\) permuting the positive roots and the
corresponding coroots: if \(\alpha \in R^{+}\), \(h(\alpha) \in R^{+}\)
and \(h^{\vee}(\alpha^{*}) = h(\alpha)^{*}\). There exists a unique
automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) inducing \(D_{S}(h)\) on \(T\) and such that
\(u \circ p_{\alpha} = p_{h(\alpha)}\) for every simple root
\(\alpha\).}

\textbf{Corollary 5.6.} \emph{Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two reductive
\(S\)-groups. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic locally for the (fpqc)
topology.}

\emph{(i bis) \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic locally for the étale
topology.}

\emph{(ii) For every \(s \in S\), \(G_{s}\) and \(G'_{s}\) are
isomorphic.}

\emph{(iii) The functions \(s \mapsto\) type of \(G_{s}\) and
\(s \mapsto\) type of \(G'_{s}\) are equal.}

Indeed (i bis) ⇒ (i) trivially, (i) ⇒ (ii) by the principle of finite
extension (EGA IV₃, 9.1.4), (ii) ⇒ (iii) trivially; it remains to prove
(iii) ⇒ (i bis). Now one may suppose \(G\) and \(G'\) splittable (Exp.
XXII, 2.3), in which case the assertion follows from 5.3.

\textbf{Corollary 5.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a reductive
\(S\)-group, \(G'\) an \(S\)-group that is affine, smooth, and with
connected fibers. Let \(s \in S\) be such that \(G_{s}\) and \(G'_{s}\)
are isomorphic; there exists then an étale \(S' \to S\) covering \(s\)
such that \(G_{S'}\) and \(G'_{S'}\) are isomorphic.}

Indeed, by Exp. XIX 2.5 and Exp. XXII 2.1, one may suppose \(G\) and
\(G'\) reductive splittable and one is reduced to 5.3.

In the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, one deduces from 5.6
and 5.7:

\textbf{Corollary 5.8.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field and \(G\) and \(G'\)
two reductive \(k\)-groups. The following conditions are
equivalent:}\footnote{N.D.E.: Another proof of this corollary, not using
  the reduction to the case of groups of rank 2, was given by M.
  Takeuchi ({[}Ta83{]}, Th. 4.6); see also {[}Ja87{]}, II 1.14.}

\emph{(i) \(G\) and \(G'\) are of the same type.}

\emph{(ii) \(G \otimes_{k} \bar{k}\) and \(G' \otimes_{k} \bar{k}\) are
isomorphic.}

\emph{(iii) There exists a finite separable extension \(K\) of \(k\)
such that \(G \otimes_{k} K\) and \(G' \otimes_{k} K\) are isomorphic.}

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a nonempty scheme and \(R\) a
root datum. The following conditions are equivalent:}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  This corollary is rendered superfluous by Exp. XXV, which shows the
  existence of a split group of type \(R\) over
  \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\), hence over any base \(S\). (In
  fact, after XXV 1.3 one finds a reference to the present corollary to
  ensure that the reductive \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group obtained is split, but
  this already follows from XXII 2.2; cf.~N.D.E. (3) of XXV.)}

\emph{(i) There exists a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(R\).}

\emph{(ii) There exists an \(S\)-group of type \(R\).}

\emph{(iii) There exists locally for (fpqc) a reductive \(S\)-group of
type \(R\).}

It is evidently a matter of proving (iii) ⇒ (i). To simplify the proof,
suppose that there exist a faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism
\(S' \to S\) and a reductive \(S'\)-group \(G'\) of type \(R\). One may
suppose \(G'\) splittable; fix a pinning \(E'\) of \(G'\); denote
\(R = R(G', E')\). The two pullbacks of
\texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ E\textquotesingle{})} to
\(S'' = S' \times_{S} S'\) are pinned groups \((G''_{1}, E''_{1})\),
\((G''_{2}, E''_{2})\); one has canonical isomorphisms
\(p_{i} : R(G''_{i}, E''_{i}) \xrightarrow{\sim} R\), whence an
isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p = p\_2\^{}\{{-}1\} ∘ p\_1 : R(G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_1, E\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_1) → R(G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_2, E\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_2).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By the uniqueness theorem, there exists a unique isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : (G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_1, E\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_1) ⥲ (G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_2, E\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\_2)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \(R(f) = p\). One has therefore on \(G'\) a gluing datum; this
is a descent datum.

Indeed, one must verify a compatibility condition between the pullbacks
of \(f\) on
\texttt{S\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}, but it
suffices to make this verification on the transforms of these arrows by
the functor \(R\), since the latter is fully faithful. Now \(p\) is
indeed a descent datum, by construction, which shows that \(f\) is one
too. Since \(G'\) is affine, this descent datum is effective; since the
pinning of \(G'\) is stable under the descent datum, one verifies easily
that there exists a pinned \(S\)-group \((G, E)\) which gives
\texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ E\textquotesingle{})} by base extension
and which is therefore of type \(R\).

\emph{N.B.} Naturally, in the language of fibered categories, the
preceding proof simplifies (and becomes intelligible).

\textbf{Corollary 5.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a nonempty scheme. Let \(R\)
be a pinned root datum such that there exists a reductive \(S\)-group of
type \(R\). Then there exists a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(R\), unique
up to a unique isomorphism.}

\textbf{Definition 5.11.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, we shall
denote by \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) the unique pinned \(S\)-group of type
\(R\), by \(T_{S}(R)\) its canonical maximal torus, by \(B_{S}(R)\) its
canonical Borel subgroup, etc.}

If one has a morphism \(S' \to S\) (\(S'\) nonempty), one may identify
\(\acute{E}p_{S'}(R)\) with \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R) \times_{S} S'\), etc. In
particular, if \(\acute{E}p_{\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})}(R)\)
exists (we shall see that this is always the case), one denotes it
\(\acute{E}p(R)\), and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ép\_S(R) = Ép(R) ×\_\{Spec(ℤ)\} S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One says that \(\acute{E}p(R)\) is the \emph{Chevalley group scheme of
type \(R\)}.

\subsubsection{5.12.}\label{section-266}

It therefore comes to the same thing to say that the \(S\)-sheaf in
groups \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(R\), or to say that it
is locally isomorphic (for the étale or (fpqc) topology) to
\(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\). Likewise, by virtue of the conjugation theorems,
it comes to the same thing to say that \((G, T)\) is a reductive
\(S\)-group of type \(R\) equipped with a maximal torus, or to say that
it is locally isomorphic to \((\acute{E}p_{S}(R), T_{S}(R))\); likewise
with Borel subgroups or Killing couples.

\subsection{6. Chevalley systems}\label{chevalley-systems}

The explicit calculations of No.~3 have important numerical
consequences. We first lay down the following definition.

\textbf{Definition 6.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a
split \(S\)-group. One calls} Chevalley system of \(G\) \emph{a family
\((X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in R}\) of elements}

\[
X_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}
\]

\emph{satisfying the following condition:}

\emph{(SC) for every pair \(\alpha, \beta \in R\),}

\[
Ad(w_{\alpha}(X_{\alpha})) X_{\beta} = \pm X_{s_{\alpha}(\beta)}.
\]

Recall (Exp. XX, 3.1) that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X\_α) = exp(X\_α) exp({-}X\_α\^{}\{{-}1\}) exp(X\_α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note that (SC) entails in particular \(X_{-\alpha} = \pm X_{\alpha}\)
for \(\alpha \in R\), by virtue of the relation (Exp. XX, 3.7)
\(Ad(w_{\alpha}(X_{\alpha})) X_{\alpha} = -X^{-1}_{\alpha}\).

\textbf{Proposition 6.2.} \emph{Every split group admits a Chevalley
system. More precisely, let
\((\Delta, (X'_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta})\) be a pinning (1.1) of
the split group \((G, T, M, R)\); there exists then a Chevalley system
\((X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in R}\) of \(G\) such that
\(X_{\alpha} = X'_{\alpha}\) for \(\alpha \in \Delta\).}

Let us first show that it suffices to verify condition (SC) for
\(\alpha \in \Delta\); for every \(\alpha \in R\), there exists a
sequence \({\alpha_{i}} \subset \Delta\) such that
\(\alpha = s_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{n}}(\alpha_{n+1})\), whence,
applying condition (SC) for each of the \(\alpha_{i}\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\_α = ± Ad(w\_\{α\_1\}(X\_\{α\_1\}) ⋯ w\_\{α\_n\}(X\_\{α\_n\})) X\_\{α\_\{n+1\}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 3.1.1 (iii),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_\{α\_1\}(X\_\{α\_1\}) ⋯ w\_\{α\_n\}(X\_\{α\_n\}) w\_\{α\_\{n+1\}\}(X\_\{α\_\{n+1\}\}) w\_\{α\_n\}(X\_\{α\_n\})\^{}\{{-}1\} ⋯ w\_\{α\_1\}(X\_\{α\_1\})\^{}\{{-}1\}}
\NormalTok{    = α\^{}*(±1) w\_α(X\_α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now, it suffices to note that
\(w_{\alpha_{i}}(X_{\alpha_{i}})^{-1} = \alpha^{*}_{i}(-1) w_{\alpha_{i}}(X_{\alpha_{i}})\)
and that for every pair of roots \((\beta, \gamma)\),
\(\beta(\gamma^{*}(-1)) = (-1)^{(\gamma^{*}, \beta)} = \pm 1\), which
entails that if (SC) is satisfied for the pairs \((\alpha_{i}, \gamma)\)
(\(\gamma \in R\)), it is so for every pair \((\alpha, \beta)\),
(\(\beta \in R\)).

Let us now construct a system \((X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in R}\) in the
following manner. For every \(\alpha \in R\), choose a sequence
\({\alpha_{i}} \subset \Delta\) as above, and define \(X_{\alpha}\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{X\_α = Ad(w\_\{α\_i\}(X\_\{α\_1\}) ⋯ w\_\{α\_n\}(X\_\{α\_n\})) X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\_\{n+1\}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To verify (SC), it suffices to prove:

\textbf{Lemma 6.3.} \emph{Let
\((G, T, M, R, \Delta, (X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta})\) be a pinned
\(S\)-group; let \(\alpha_{i} (0 \leqslant i \leqslant n + 1)\) be a
sequence of simple roots such that}

\[
int(s_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{n}})(\alpha_{n+1}) = \alpha_{0}.
\]

\emph{Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ad(w\_\{α\_1\} ⋯ w\_\{α\_n\}) X\_\{α\_\{n+1\}\} = ± X\_\{α\_0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Reasoning as in 2.3.4 with the help of Tits's lemma (Exp. XXI 5.6), one
is reduced to verifying lemma 6.3 in the two following cases:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \(G\) is of semisimple rank at most 2, or b)
  \(w_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots w_{\alpha_{n}}\) is a section of \(T\).
\end{enumerate}

In case a), note that 6.3 is a consequence of 6.2 and that 6.2 has been
verified in part (i) of 3.1.2 (resp. 3.2.1, resp. 3.3.1, resp. 3.4.1).

It therefore remains to prove 6.3 in case b), or, what amounts to the
same thing, that if \({\alpha_{i}}\) is a sequence of simple roots such
that \(s_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{n}} = id\), then
\(t = w_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots w_{\alpha_{n}}\) satisfies
\(\alpha(t) = \pm 1\) for every root \(\alpha \in R\). By virtue of the
structure of the Weyl group (Exp. XXI, 5.1), the word
\(s_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{n}}\) in the free group generated by
the \(s_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in \Delta\), is in the invariant subgroup
generated by the \((s_{\alpha} s_{\beta})^{n_{\alpha \beta}}\),
\((\alpha, \beta) \in \Delta \times \Delta\). One is therefore reduced
to the case where \(s_{\alpha_{1}} \cdots s_{\alpha_{n}}\) is of the
form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{s\_\{α\_1\} ⋯ s\_\{α\_i\} (s\_\{α\_\{i+1\}\} s\_\{α\_\{i+2\}\})\^{}\{n\_\{α\_\{i+1\} α\_\{i+2\}\}\} s\_\{α\_i\} ⋯ s\_\{α\_1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t = s\_\{α\_1\} ⋯ s\_\{α\_i\}(t\_\{α\_\{i+1\} α\_\{i+2\}\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one is reduced to verifying that for every pair of simple roots
\((\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2})\) and every root \(\beta \in R\),
\(\beta(t_{\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}}) = \pm 1\), which is trivial, in view
of the values of \(t_{\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}}\) calculated in No.~3 (part
(i) of 3.1.2, 3.2.1, 3.3.1, 3.4.1).

\textbf{Proposition 6.4.} \emph{Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a split
\(S\)-group, \((X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in R}\) a Chevalley system of
\(G\). Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two non-proportional roots;
suppose}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{long(α) ⩽ long(β),    i.e.    |(β\^{}*, α)| ⩽ |(α\^{}*, β)|.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Let \(q\) and \(p - 1\) be the integers \(\geqslant 0\) such that
the set of roots of the form \(\beta + k \alpha\), \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\),
is}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\{β {-} (p {-} 1) α, …, β, …, β + q α\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(cf.~Exp. XXI, 2.3.5; by loc. cit., one has therefore
\(-(\alpha^{*}, \beta) = q - p + 1\)). Then the commutation relation
between \(U_{\alpha}\) and \(U_{\beta}\) is given by the following table
(which exhausts the possible cases, since the length of the preceding
root chain is \(p + q - 1 \leqslant 3\)),}

\emph{where, for each \(\gamma \in R\), one writes
\(p_{\gamma}(x) = \exp(x X_{\gamma})\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(p, q)    p\_β(y) p\_α(x) p\_β({-}y) p\_α({-}x)}
\NormalTok{({-}, 0)     = e}
\NormalTok{(1, 1)     = p\_\{α + β\}(± x y)}
\NormalTok{(1, 2)     = p\_\{α + β\}(± x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(± x\^{}2 y)}
\NormalTok{(1, 3)     = p\_\{α + β\}(± x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(± x\^{}2 y) p\_\{3α + β\}(± x\^{}3 y) p\_\{3α + 2β\}(± x\^{}3 y\^{}2)}
\NormalTok{(2, 1)     = p\_\{α + β\}(± 2 x y)}
\NormalTok{(2, 2)     = p\_\{α + β\}(± 2 x y) p\_\{2α + β\}(± 3 x\^{}2 y) p\_\{α + 2β\}(± 3 x y\^{}2)}
\NormalTok{(3, 1)     = p\_\{α + β\}(± 3 x y).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} By virtue of Exp. XXI, 3.5.4, there exists a system of
simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\) satisfying: \(\alpha \in \Delta\), and
there exist \(\alpha' \in \Delta\) and \(a, b \in \mathbb{Q}_{+}\) such
that \(\beta = a \alpha + b \alpha'\). Consider the pinning
\((\Delta, (X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta})\) of \(G\). The commutation
relation to be verified is a relation between elements of
\(U_{\alpha \alpha'}\); one is therefore reduced to the explicit
calculations of No.~3, and one concludes at once by condition (SC).

\textbf{Corollary 6.5 (Chevalley's rule).} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme,
\((X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in R}\) a Chevalley system of the split
\(S\)-group \(G\). If \(\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta \in R\), then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[X\_α, X\_β] = ± p X\_\{α + β\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(p\) is the smallest integer \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}
such that \(\beta - p \alpha\) is not a root.}

Indeed, since the assertion is symmetric in \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\),
one may suppose \(long(\alpha) \leqslant long(\beta)\), and one is
reduced to 6.4.

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme such that
\(6 \cdot 1_{S} \neq 0\) and \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group. If
\(R'\) is a subset of \(R\) such that}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_\{R\textquotesingle{}\} = t ⊕ ⨁\_\{α ∈ R\textquotesingle{}\} g\_α            (*)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is a Lie subalgebra of \(g\), then \(R'\) is a closed subset of
\(R\) (Exp. XXI, 3.1.4).}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added the following proof. Note that it
  suffices that 2 and 3 be nonzero on \(S\); for example the result is
  valid for \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z})\).}
Indeed, let \((X_{\gamma})_{\gamma \in R^{+}}\) be a Chevalley system of
\(g\), and let \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\) be such that
\(\alpha + \beta \in R\). By 6.5 and 6.4,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[X\_α, X\_β] = ± p X\_\{α + β\},    with p ∈ \{1, 2, 3\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since neither 2 nor 3 are zero on \(S\), this entails, by (*), that
\(g_{R'}\) contains \(g_{\alpha + \beta}\), hence
\(\alpha + \beta \in R'\).\footnote{N.D.E.: On the other hand, let us
  point out that if \texttt{2\ =\ 0} on \(S\) and \(R\) is of type
  \(C_{n}\), then the set \(R'\) of short roots (which is a root system
  of type \(D_{n}\)) is not closed in \(R\), but is a part of type (R)
  of \(R\), symmetric (cf.~XXII 5.4.2 and 5.4.10), i.e.~it corresponds
  to a subgroup \(H_{R'}\) of type (R) of \(G\) with reductive fibers:
  this is in particular the case for the natural embedding (in
  characteristic 2) of \(SO(2n)\) into \(Sp(2n)\). Likewise, if
  \texttt{2\ =\ 0} on \(S\) and \(R\) is of type \texttt{F\_4} (resp. if
  \texttt{3\ =\ 0} on \(S\) and \(R\) is of type \texttt{G\_2}), the set
  \(R'\) of short roots (which is a root system of type \texttt{D\_4}
  (resp. \texttt{A\_2})) is not closed in \(R\), but corresponds to a
  subgroup \(H_{R'}\) of type (R) of \(G\), with reductive fibers.}

\subsubsection{6.7.}\label{section-267}

It is possible to make explicit the exact value of the various \(\pm\)
of this section, thanks to the study of the group \(Norm_{G}(T)\), and
more precisely of the ``extended Weyl group'':

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W\^{}* = N(ℤ),    where N = Norm\_\{Ép\_ℤ(R)\}(T\_ℤ(R))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(cf.~5.11), which is an extension of \(W(R)\) by an abelian group of
type \((2, 2, \cdots, 2)\), which is ``responsible for the
signs''.\footnote{Cf. J. Tits, \emph{Sur les constantes de structure et
  le théorème d'existence des algèbres de Lie semi-simples}, Publ. Math.
  I.H.É.S. \textbf{31} (1966), 21--58.} \footnote{N.D.E.: see also
  {[}Ti66{]}.}

\textbf{Remark 6.7.1.}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this remark.}
\emph{Note that, by point (i) of 3.1.2 and 3.n.1 (\(n = 2, 3, 4\)), the
elements \(w_{\alpha}\) and \(w_{\beta}\) of \(N(\mathbb{Z})\) satisfy
the ``braid relations'':}

\begin{Shaded}
