\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α w\_β ⋯ = w\_β w\_α ⋯    (n\_\{αβ\} factors in each term).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(See also {[}Ti66{]}, {[}BLie{]}, § IX.4, Ex. 12, and {[}Sp98{]},
9.3.2.)

\section{Exposé XXIV. Automorphisms of reductive
groups}\label{exposuxe9-xxiv.-automorphisms-of-reductive-groups}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Version of 13/10/2024.}

The first part of this Exposé (nos 1 to 5) is a direct consequence of
the existence, for a reductive group, of ``sufficiently many outer
automorphisms'', a result which is itself a consequence of the weakest
form of the isomorphism theorem for pinned groups. The second part (nos
6 and 7) presents two applications of the more precise results of the
preceding Exposé; in particular, no 7 uses the theorem of generators and
relations in its explicit form. Finally, we have given in an appendix
(no 8) some results on ``Galois'' cohomology used in the text.

Let us specify our cohomological notation: if \(S\) is a scheme and
\(G\) an \(S\)-group scheme, we write \(H^{1}(S, G)\) for the first
cohomology set of \(S\) with coefficients in \(G\), computed for the
(fpqc) topology; this is also the set of isomorphism classes of (fpqc)
principal homogeneous sheaves under \(G\). We write
\(H^{1}_{\acute{e}}t(S, G)\) for the corresponding set for the étale
topology; this is therefore the part of \(H^{1}(S, G)\) formed by
classes of homogeneous sheaves under \(G\) which are quasi-isotrivial (=
locally trivial for the étale topology). We write \(Fib(S, G)\) for the
part of \(H^{1}(S, G)\) formed by classes of representable sheaves
(principal homogeneous bundles). We thus have the inclusions

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹\_ét(S, G) ⊂ H¹(S, G),}
\NormalTok{Fib(S, G) ⊂ H¹(S, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If every principal homogeneous sheaf under \(G\) is representable (for
example if \(G\) is quasi-affine over \(S\), cf.~SGA 1, VIII 7.9), then
\(Fib(S, G) = H^{1}(S, G)\).

If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism for the (fpqc) topology, we write
\(H^{1}(S'/S, G)\) for the kernel of the canonical map
\(H^{1}(S, G) \to H^{1}(S', G_{S'})\). It is known that
\(H^{1}(S'/S, G)\) can be computed simplicially (TDTE I, § A.4), which
implies that when \(S' \to S\) is covering for the étale topology,
\(H^{1}(S'/S, G)\) is also the kernel of
\(H^{1}_{\acute{e}}t(S, G) \to H^{1}_{\acute{e}}t(S', G_{S'})\).

Finally, following Exp. VIII, 4.5, we call ``theorem 90'' the following
assertion: ``every principal homogeneous sheaf under \(G_{m, S}\) is
representable and locally trivial'', an assertion equivalent to
``\(H^{1}(S, G_{m, S}) = \operatorname{Pic}(S)\)'', or again to
``\(H^{1}(S, G_{m, S}) = 0\) for \(S\) local (or more generally
semi-local)''.

\subsection{1. The automorphism scheme of a reductive
group}\label{the-automorphism-scheme-of-a-reductive-group}

\subsubsection{1.0.}\label{section-268}

It is convenient first to make certain definitions of the preceding
Exposé more precise. Let \(S\) be a nonempty scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(R = (M, M*, R, R*, \Delta)\) a pinned reduced
root datum (Exp. XXIII 1.5). We call \emph{pinning of \(G\) of type
\(R\)}, or \emph{\(R\)-pinning of \(G\)}, the datum:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  of an isomorphism of \(D_{S}(M)\) onto a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\)
  (or, what amounts to the same, of a monomorphism \(D_{S}(M) \to G\)
  whose image is a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\)), identifying \(R\) with
  a root system of \(G\) relative to \(T\) (Exp. XIX, 3.6) and \(R*\)
  with the corresponding set of coroots,
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  for each \(\alpha \in \Delta\), of an
  \(X_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g_{\alpha})^{\times}\).
\end{enumerate}

For \(G\) to possess an \(R\)-pinning, it is necessary and sufficient
that it be splittable and of type \(R\) (Exp. XXII, 2.7).

If \(u : G \to G'\) is an isomorphism of \(S\)-reductive groups, to
every \(R\)-pinning \(E\) of \(G\) there corresponds by ``transport of
structure'' an \(R\)-pinning \(u(E)\) of \(G'\). If \(v : R' \to R\) is
an isomorphism of pinned root data, to every \(R'\)-pinning \(E\) of
\(G'\) there corresponds by transport of structure an \(R\)-pinning
\(v(E)\) of \(G\).

Let us call a \emph{pinned group} a triple \((G, R, E)\) where \(G\) is
an \(S\)-reductive group, \(R\) is a pinned reduced root datum, and
\(E\) is a pinning of \(G\) of type \(R\). We call an \emph{isomorphism
of the pinned group \((G, R, E)\) onto the pinned group
\texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ R\textquotesingle{},\ E\textquotesingle{})}}
a pair \((u, v)\) where \(u\) is an isomorphism \(u : G \to G'\) and
\(v\) is an isomorphism of pinned root data \(v : R' \to R\), such that
\(u(E) = v(E')\).\footnote{N.D.E.: Hence
  \(Lie(u)(X'_{v(\alpha)}) = X_{\alpha}\), for every \(\alpha \in R'\).}

\textbf{N. B.} If \(S\) is nonempty, \(v\) is uniquely determined by
\(u\), and we shall also say by abuse of language that \(u\) is an
isomorphism of pinned groups. In particular, if \((G, R, E)\) is a
pinned group, an automorphism of \((G, R, E)\) is therefore an
automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) such that there exists an automorphism \(v\)
of \(R\) with \(u(E) = v(E)\); it is therefore an automorphism of \(G\)
normalizing \(T\), inducing on \(T\) an automorphism of the form
\(D_{S}(h)\) where \(h\) is an automorphism of \(M\), and permuting
among themselves the elements \(X_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in \Delta\). (As
is easily seen, the preceding conditions moreover characterize the
automorphisms of \((G, R, E)\).)

One has an obvious contravariant functor

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Φ :  (G, R, E) ↦ R,   (u, v) ↦ v}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the principal result of the preceding Exposé (Exp. XXIII, 4.1) shows
us that this is a fully faithful functor (we shall moreover see in the
next Exposé that it is an equivalence of categories). It follows in
particular that the group of automorphisms of \((G, R, E)\) is
canonically isomorphic to the group of automorphisms of the pinned root
datum \(R\) (cf.~Exp. XXIII, 5.5).

\subsubsection{1.1.}\label{section-269}

Let \(S\) be a scheme; endow \((Sch)/S\) with the (fpqc) topology and
consider the \(S\)-group sheaf \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\), where
\(G\) is an \(S\)-group scheme. One has an exact sequence of \(S\)-group
sheaves

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → Centr(G) → G ─int→ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which defines a monomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{j : G / Centr(G) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The image sheaf of \(j\) is the sheaf of \emph{inner automorphisms} of
\(G\); for an automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) to be inner, it is necessary
and sufficient that there exist a covering family \({S_{i} \to S}\) and
for each \(i\) a \(g_{i} \in G(S_{i})\) such that
\(int(g_{i}) = u_{S_{i}}\). In this case, if \(v\) is another
automorphism of \(G\), one sees at once that \(int(v) u = v u v^{-1}\)
is the inner automorphism defined by the family \(g'_{i} = v(g_{i})\).
It follows that the image of \(j\) is normal in
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\). The quotient group sheaf, denoted
\(Autext(G)\), is the sheaf of \emph{outer automorphisms} of \(G\). One
thus has an exact sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → G / Centr(G) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G) → Autext(G) → 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The preceding definitions are all compatible with base change. They are
naturally valid in any site.

\subsubsection{1.2.}\label{section-270}

Let \(S\) be a scheme and \((G, R, E)\) a pinned \(S\)-reductive group.
Let \(E\) be the (abstract) group of automorphisms of the pinned root
datum \(R\), i.e.~the group of automorphisms of \(R\) normalizing
\(\Delta\). By Exp. XXIII, 5.5, one has a canonical monomorphism

\[
E \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)
\]

which associates to \(h \in E\) the unique automorphism \(u\) of the
pinned group \(G\) such that \(\Phi(u) = h\). This monomorphism
canonically defines a monomorphism of sheaves

\[
(*)    a : E_{S} \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G).
\]

For an automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) to be a section of the image sheaf of
\(a\), it is necessary and sufficient that the following conditions be
satisfied:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \(u\) normalizes \(T\). One then knows that \(u\) permutes the roots
  of \(G\) relative to \(T\). If \(\alpha \in R\), then
  \(u(\alpha) : t \mapsto \alpha(u^{-1}(t))\) is locally on \(S\) of the
  form \(t \mapsto \beta(t)\), with \(\beta \in R\). The second
  condition is then written as follows:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(\alpha \in \Delta\) and if \(U\) is an open set of \(S\) such
  that \(u(\alpha)_{U} \in R\), then \(u(\alpha)_{U} \in \Delta\) and
\end{enumerate}

\[
Lie(u_{U})(X_{\alpha})_{U} = (X_{u(\alpha)})_{U}.
\]

It follows at once from the definitions that the sections of
\(a(E_{S})\) normalize the subgroups of \(G\) defined by the pinning:
\(T\), \(B\), \(B^{-}\), \(U\), \(U^{-}\).

These definitions being set, one has:

\textbf{Theorem 1.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. Consider the canonical exact sequence of
\(S\)-group sheaves\footnote{N.D.E.: One recalls that
  \(ad(G) = G / Centr(G)\) denotes the adjoint group of \(G\), cf.~XXII
  4.3.6.}}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → ad(G) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G) ─p→ Autext(G) → 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\) is representable by a smooth
and separated \(S\)-scheme.}

\emph{(ii) \(Autext(G)\) is representable by a finitely generated
twisted constant \(S\)-scheme (Exp. X, 5.1).}

\emph{(iii) If \(G\) is splittable, the preceding exact sequence splits.
More precisely, for every pinning of \(G\), the morphism (cf.~1.2 (*))}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p ∘ a : E\_S → Autext(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an isomorphism.}

Let us first show how the theorem follows from the following lemma:

\textbf{Lemma 1.4.} \emph{Under the hypotheses of (iii),
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\) is the semi-direct product
\(a(E_{S}) \cdot ad(G)\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced here and in
  the sequel the notation \(int(G)\) by \(ad(G)\).}

The lemma immediately implies the theorem when \(G\) is splittable.
Since \(G\) is locally splittable for the étale topology (Exp. XXII,
2.3), hence also for the (fppf) topology, and since the latter is ``of
effective descent'' for the fibered category of twisted constant
morphisms (Exp. X, 5.5), one deduces (ii) in the general case (cf.~Exp.
IV, 4.6.8). To deduce (i), one notes that \(ad(G)\) is affine over
\(S\), hence the morphism \(p\) is affine when
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\) is representable, and one concludes by
descent of affine schemes.\footnote{N.D.E.: cf.~SGA 1, VIII 2.1.}

It therefore remains only to prove 1.4. For this, it suffices to prove:

\textbf{Lemma 1.5.} \emph{If \((R, E)\) and
\texttt{(R\textquotesingle{},\ E\textquotesingle{})} are two pinnings of
the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\), there exists a unique inner
automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) over \(S\) transforming one pinning into the
other (i.e.~such that there exists \(v : R' \xrightarrow{\sim} R\) with
\(u(E) = v(E')\), cf.~1.0).}

\paragraph{1.5.1. Uniqueness.}\label{uniqueness.}

It suffices to prove that if \(G\) is a pinned \(S\)-group and if
\(int(g)\) is an automorphism of pinned group (\(g \in G(S)\)), then
\(int(g) = id\). Now one has first \(int(g) T = T\), \(int(g) B = B\),
so \(g \in Norm_{G}(T)(S) \cap Norm_{G}(B)(S) = T(S)\) (cf.~for example
Exp. XXII, 5.6.1). It follows that \(int(g)\) normalizes each
\(U_{\alpha}\) and that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(int(g)) X\_α = Ad(g) X\_α = α(g) X\_α}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(\alpha \in \Delta\). One thus has \(\alpha(g) = 1\) for
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), so
\(g \in \bigcap_{\alpha \in \Delta} (Ker \alpha)(S) = Centr(G)(S)\)
(Exp. XXII, 4.1.8). QED

\paragraph{1.5.2. Existence.}\label{existence.}

It suffices to prove this locally for the (fpqc) topology. Let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(T, M, R, Δ, (X\_α)\_\{α ∈ Δ\})    and    (T\textquotesingle{}, M\textquotesingle{}, R\textquotesingle{}, Δ\textquotesingle{}, (X\textquotesingle{}\_\{α\textquotesingle{}\})\_\{α\textquotesingle{} ∈ Δ\textquotesingle{}\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be the two pinnings. By conjugacy of maximal tori, one may assume
\(T = T'\). Up to restricting \(S\), one may assume that the isomorphism
\(D_{S}(M) \simeq D_{S}(M')\) comes from an isomorphism \(M \simeq M'\)
carrying \(R\) onto \(R'\), and one is reduced to the situation
\(T = T'\), \(M = M'\), \(R = R'\). Since the systems of simple roots
are conjugate by the Weyl group (Exp. XXI, 3.3.7), one may also assume
\(\Delta = \Delta'\). There then exists for each \(\alpha \in \Delta\) a
scalar \(z_{\alpha} \in G_{m}(S)\) such that
\(X'_{\alpha} = z_{\alpha} X_{\alpha}\), and it suffices to construct
locally for (fpqc) a section \(t\) of \(T\) such that
\(\alpha(t) = z_{\alpha}\) for each \(\alpha \in \Delta\). But the
morphism \(T \to (G_{m, S})^{\Delta}\) with components
\({\alpha, \alpha \in \Delta}\) is the dual of an injection
\(\mathbb{Z}^{\Delta} \to M\), hence faithfully flat, which completes
the proof of 1.5.2 and so of 1.3.

\textbf{Corollary 1.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\) is affine (resp. of finite
type, resp. of finite presentation, resp. quasi-compact) over \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) \(Autext(G)\) is finite over \(S\).}

\emph{(iii) For every \(s \in S\), one has
\(rg_{red}(G_{s}) - rg_{ss}(G_{s}) \leqslant 1\).}

Indeed, since \(ad(G)\) is affine, flat and of finite presentation over
\(S\), the morphism \(p : \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G) \to Autext(G)\)
is affine, faithfully flat and of finite presentation.

If \(Autext(G)\) is finite over \(S\), it is affine over \(S\), hence so
is \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\), which proves (ii) ⇒ (i). If
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\) is quasi-compact over \(S\), it is of
finite presentation over \(S\) (being in any case locally of finite
presentation and separated over \(S\)); by Exp. V, 9.1, \(Autext(G)\) is
then of finite presentation over \(S\), hence finite, which proves (i) ⇒
(ii). Finally, to prove the equivalence of (ii) and (iii), one may
assume \(G\) split, and one is reduced to Exp. XXI, 6.7.8.

\textbf{Corollary 1.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. Then
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)^{0} \simeq ad(G)\).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) an \(S\)-group scheme smooth, affine and
with connected fibers over \(S\). Then the \(S\)-functor}

\[
Isom_{S-gr.}(G, H)
\]

\emph{is representable by a smooth and separated \(S\)-scheme (which is
affine over \(S\) if \(G\) is semisimple).}

Indeed, let \(U\) be the set of points \(s\) of \(S\) such that
\(H_{s}\) is reductive; this is open (Exp. XIX, 2.6); if \(S'\) is an
\(S\)-scheme, \(H_{S'}\) is reductive if and only if \(S' \to S\)
factors through \(U\). It follows that the canonical morphism
\(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, H) \to S\) factors through \(U\). One may therefore
assume \(S = U\) and one is reduced to:

\textbf{Corollary 1.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two \(S\)-reductive groups. Then}

\[
F = Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')
\]

\emph{is representable by a smooth and separated \(S\)-scheme (affine if
\(G\) or \(G'\) is semisimple). Moreover, \(S\) decomposes as a sum of
two open subschemes \texttt{S\_1} and \texttt{S\_2} such that
\(F_{S_{1}} = \emptyset\) and such that \(F_{S_{2}}\) is a principal
homogeneous bundle on the left (resp. right) under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S_{2}-gr.}(G'_{S_{2}})\) (resp.
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S_{2}-gr.}(G_{S_{2}})\)).}

Indeed, let \texttt{S\_2} be the set of points of \(S\) where \(G\) and
\(G'\) are of the same type, and let \texttt{S\_1} be its complement.

Since the type of a reductive group is a locally constant function,
\texttt{S\_1} and \texttt{S\_2} are open. It is clear that
\(F_{S_{1}} = \emptyset\), and one may assume \(S = S_{2}\). By Exp.
XXIII, 5.6, \(F\) is a principal homogeneous sheaf under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\), locally trivial for the étale
topology. It follows that \(F_{0} = F / ad(G)\) is a principal
homogeneous sheaf under \(Autext(G)\), locally trivial for the étale
topology, hence representable (Exp. X, 5.5). Since \(ad(G)\) is affine,
\(F\) is therefore also representable.

Let us remark that in the course of the proof, we have obtained:

\textbf{Corollary 1.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two \(S\)-reductive groups of the same type at each \(s \in S\). Then
\(ad(G)\) operates freely (on the right) in \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\), the
quotient sheaf}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}) = Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{}) / ad(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-scheme, which is a
principal homogeneous bundle under \(Autext(G)\) (and which is therefore
finite over \(S\) if \(G\) is semisimple). Moreover, the isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{}) ≃ Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G\textquotesingle{}, G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined by \(u \mapsto u^{-1}\) induces an isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}) ≃ Isomext(G\textquotesingle{}, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 1.11.} If \(Isomext(G, G')(S) \neq \emptyset\), one says
that \(G\) is an \emph{inner twisted form} of \(G'\); then \(G'\) is an
inner twisted form of \(G\); one can then reduce the structure group of
\(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\) to \(ad(G)\). More precisely, let
\(u \in Isomext(G, G')(S)\), considered as a section
\(u : S \to Isomext(G, G')\). Write

\[
Isomint_{u}(G, G')
\]

for the inverse image under the canonical morphism
\(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G') \to Isomext(G, G')\) of the closed subscheme of
\(Isomext(G, G')\) image of \(u\). The natural operation of \(ad(G)\) on
\(Isomint_{u}(G, G')\) endows this scheme with a structure of principal
homogeneous bundle; by extension of the structure group\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have corrected \(ad(G) \to Autext(G)\) to
  \(ad(G) \to \operatorname{Aut}(G)\).}
\(ad(G) \to \operatorname{Aut}(G)\), \(Isomint_{u}(G, G')\) recovers
\(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\).

By Hensel's lemma (Exp. XI, 1.11), 1.8 gives at once:

\textbf{Corollary 1.12.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a henselian local scheme,
\(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(G'\) a smooth affine \(S\)-group with
connected fibers, \(s\) the closed point of \(S\). If \(G_{s}\) and
\(G'_{s}\) are isomorphic \(\kappa(s)\)-algebraic groups, then \(G\) and
\(G'\) are isomorphic. More precisely, every \(\kappa(s)\)-isomorphism
\(G_{s} \simeq G'_{s}\) comes from an \(S\)-isomorphism
\(G \simeq G'\).}

Applying now 1.7 (resp. 1.12) to the scheme of dual numbers over a
field, one deduces from Exp. III, 2.10 (resp. 3.10) point (i) (resp.
(ii)) of the following corollary.

\textbf{Corollary 1.13.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field and \(G\) a
\(k\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) If \(G\) is adjoint, one has
\(H^{1}(G, Lie(G/k)) = 0\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected the
  original, which stated (i) without assuming \(G\) adjoint. Following
  the characterization of the \(H^{i}(G, -)\) as derived functors of
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{G}(k, -)\) (Exp. I, 5.3.1; see also {[}Ja87{]},
  I 4.16), one has \(H^{i}(G, V) = Ext^{i}_{G}(k, V)\) for every
  \(G\)-module \(V\); now if \(char(k) = p > 0\) and \(G = SL_{p, k}\),
  then \(Lie(GL_{p}/k)\) is a non-trivial extension of \(k\) by
  \(g = Lie(SL_{p}/k)\), so \(H^{1}(G, g) \neq 0\). See also the
  addition 1.15.1 below.}}

\emph{(ii) One has \(H^{2}(G, Lie(G/k)) = 0\).}

\textbf{Remark 1.14.} (i) The assertion concerning \(H^{1}\) was known
(Chevalley); the one concerning \(H^{2}\) had been proved in most cases
of the classification by Chevalley.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  In fact, the conjunction of 1.13 and the uniqueness theorem over an
  algebraically closed field is essentially equivalent to the uniqueness
  theorem. A direct proof of 1.13 would therefore give a way to deduce
  the general uniqueness theorem from Chevalley's uniqueness theorem
  over a field.
\end{enumerate}

The existence of reductive groups of all types over all schemes (Exp.
XXV) shows that the obstructions to lifting a \(k\)-reductive group
\(G\) over Artinian rings with residue field \(k\) (which by Exp. III,
3.8 are elements of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H³(G, Lie(G/k) ⊗ V) ≃ H³(G, Lie(G/k)) ⊗ V,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(V\) is a certain \(k\)-vector space (equipped with the trivial
action of \(G\))) are zero. This seems to suggest that
\(H^{3}(G, Lie(G/k)) = 0\). Here too, a direct proof of this fact (if it
is true) would doubtless give a way to deduce the general existence
theorem from the existence theorem over a field (Chevalley's Tôhoku).

\textbf{Corollary 1.15.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field,\footnote{N.D.E.: We
  have replaced ``scheme'' by ``field''.} \(G\) a \(k\)-reductive group.
Consider \(k\) as a trivial \(G\)-module. Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(G, k) = H²(G, k) = 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Because of the correction made in 1.13, we have given
  another proof in the case of \(H^{1}\). On the other hand, it follows
  from a theorem of G. Kempf that \(H^{i}(G, k) = 0\) for every
  \(i > 0\), cf.~{[}Ja87{]}, II 4.5 and 4.11.} Since
\(H^{i}(G_{\bar{k}}, \bar{k}) = H^{i}(G, k) \otimes \bar{k}\), one may
assume \(k\) algebraically closed. An element of \(H^{1}(G, k)\) is
nothing but a morphism of \(k\)-groups \(\phi : G \to G_{a, k}\). Then
\(\phi(G) = G / Ker(\phi)\) is a smooth, connected and reductive
subgroup (cf.~XIX 1.7) of \(G_{a, k}\), hence trivial. So
\(H^{1}(G, k) = 0\).

Consider now the \(k\)-reductive group \(H = G \times_{k} G_{m, k}\).
One has \(Lie(H/k) = Lie(G/k) \oplus k\), a decomposition stable under
\(H\). For any \(H\)-module \(V\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hⁱ(H, V) = Hⁱ(G, H⁰(G\_\{m, k\}, V))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(this follows from the characterization of \(H^{i}(H, -)\) as derived
functors of \(H^{0}(H, -) = H^{0}(G, H^{0}(G_{m, k}, -))\), and from the
fact that the functor \(H^{0}(G_{m, k}, -)\) is exact, cf.~Exp. I, 5.3.1
and 5.3.3). In particular, one has for every \(i\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hⁱ(H, Lie(H/k)) = Hⁱ(G, Lie(G/k)) ⊕ Hⁱ(G, k)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence \(H^{2}(G, k) = 0\) by applying 1.13 (ii) to the reductive group
\(H\).

\textbf{Corollary 1.15.1.} \footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this
  corollary, drawn from remarks of O. Gabber, which makes 1.13 (i) more
  precise.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field, \(G\) a \(k\)-reductive group,
\(Z\) its center and \(R = (M, M*, R, R*)\) the type of \(G\). Then one
has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(G, Lie(G/k)) ≃ Ext¹\_ℤ(M / Γ₀(R), k).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular, \(H^{1}(G, Lie(G/k)) = 0\) if and only if \(Z\) is
smooth over \(k\).}

Indeed, let \(g\) (resp. \(z\), resp. \(g_{ad}\)) be the Lie algebra of
\(G\) (resp. \(Z\), resp. \(G_{ad} = G/Z\)). It follows from 1.15 (and
from its proof) that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(G, g) = H¹(G\_ad, g) ≃ H¹(G\_ad, g/z).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set \(C = Coker(g \to g_{ad})\); one has an exact sequence

\[
0 \to g/z \to g_{ad} \to C \to 0.
\]

Since \(H^{1}(G_{ad}, g_{ad}) = 0\) (1.13) and
\(H^{0}(G_{ad}, g_{ad}) = 0\) (cf.~Exp. II, 5.2.3), one obtains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(G\_ad, g/z) ≃ H⁰(G\_ad, C).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To compute the right-hand term, one may assume \(k\) algebraically
closed. Let \((G, T, M, R)\) be a splitting of \(G\); then
\(Z = D_{k}(M / \Gamma_{0}(R))\) and \(C\) is identified with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Coker( Hom\_ℤ(M, k) → Hom\_ℤ(Γ₀(R), k) ) ≃ Ext¹\_ℤ(M / Γ₀(R), k),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

equipped with the trivial action of \(G_{ad}\). The corollary follows,
since \(Z\) is not smooth over \(k\) if and only if \(char(k) = p > 0\)
and \(M / \Gamma_{0}(R)\) has \(p\)-torsion (Exp. IX, 2.1).

\textbf{Definition 1.16.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. We call a} form of \(G\) over \(S\) \emph{an
\(S\)-group scheme \(G'\) locally isomorphic to \(G\) for the (fpqc)
topology (it amounts to the same to say (cf.~Exp. XXIII, 5.6) that
\(G'\) is locally isomorphic to \(G\) for the étale topology, or again
that \(G'\) is an \(S\)-reductive group of the same type as \(G\) at
every point of \(S\)).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.17.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) The functor}

\[
G' \mapsto Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')
\]

\emph{is an equivalence between the category of forms of \(G\) over
\(S\) and the category of principal homogeneous bundles under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism, forms of \(G\)
trivialized by \(S'\) and bundles trivialized by \(S'\) correspond.}

\emph{(iii) Every principal homogeneous sheaf under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\) is representable and quasi-isotrivial
(i.e.~locally trivial for the étale topology).}

The first assertion is formal in the category of sheaves (for (fpqc) for
example). On the other hand, every sheaf locally isomorphic to \(G\)
(for (fpqc)) is representable (since \(G\) is affine over \(S\)) and
locally isomorphic to \(G\) for the étale topology. Finally, for every
form \(G'\) of \(G\), the \(S\)-sheaf \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\) is
representable, by 1.8. The corollary follows at once.

\textbf{Corollary 1.18.} \emph{The set of isomorphism classes of forms
of the reductive group \(G\) over \(S\) is isomorphic to}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G)) = H¹\_ét(S, Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G)) = Fib(S, Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism, the subset formed by forms
trivialized by \(S'\) is isomorphic to
\(H^{1}(S'/S, \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G))\).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.19.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(R\) a pinned
reduced root datum such that \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\)\footnote{N.D.E.:
  cf.~XXIII, Definition 5.11.} exists (condition automatically
satisfied, cf.~Exp. XXV). Write}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A\_S(R) = Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Ép\_S(R)) = ad(Ép\_S(R)) · E(R)\_S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(i) The set of isomorphism classes of \(S\)-reductive groups of
type \(R\) (Exp. XXII, 2.7) is isomorphic (by Exp. XXIII, 5.12) to}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, A\_S(R)) = H¹\_ét(S, A\_S(R)) = Fib(S, A\_S(R)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) If \(S' \to S\) is a covering morphism, the subset formed by
the classes of groups splittable over \(S'\) is isomorphic to
\(H^{1}(S'/S, A_{S}(R))\).}

\textbf{Remark 1.20.} With the preceding notation, to every
\(S\)-reductive group of type \(R\) is canonically associated a right
principal homogeneous bundle under \(A_{S}(R)\):

\[
Isom_{S-gr.}(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), G) = P.
\]

Note that \(P\) is to be interpreted as the ``scheme of pinnings of
\(G\) of type \(R\)'' (cf.~1.0). Moreover \(P\) is also a principal
homogeneous bundle (on the left) under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\), a structure that appears at once in
the description above.

\textbf{Proposition 1.21.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a henselian local scheme,
\(s\) its closed point. The functor}

\[
G \mapsto G_{s}
\]

\emph{induces a bijection of the set of isomorphism classes of
\(S\)-reductive groups onto the set of isomorphism classes of
\(\kappa(s)\)-reductive groups.}

\emph{In particular, for every \(S\)-reductive group \(G\), there exists
a finite surjective étale morphism \(S' \to S\) such that \(G_{S'}\) is
splittable.}

Using the existence of the \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) (Exp. XXV), one is
reduced to proving that if one writes \(H = A_{S}(R)\), the canonical
map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Fib(S, H) → Fib(κ(s), H\_s)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective (and that every element of \(Fib(S, H)\) has the property
indicated above). Now, every finite part of \(H\) is contained in an
affine open set (it is indeed trivial for a constant group, and \(H\) is
affine above a constant group); one may therefore use the result proved
in the appendix (8.1).

\subsection{2. Automorphisms and
subgroups}\label{automorphisms-and-subgroups}

Let us introduce a notation: if \(H = \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\),
and if \(X\) is a subfunctor of \(G\), we write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, X) = Norm\_H(X),    Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, id\_X) = Centr\_H(X).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(Y\) is a second subfunctor of \(G\), one defines similarly
\texttt{Aut\_\{S-gr.\}(G,\ X,\ Y)\ =\ Aut\_\{S-gr.\}(G,\ X)\ ∩\ Aut\_\{S-gr.\}(G,\ Y)},
and if \(G'\) is a second \(S\)-group and \(X'\) a subfunctor of \(G'\),
one writes \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, X; G', X')\) for the subfunctor of
\(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\) defined by: for every \(S' \to S\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, X; G\textquotesingle{}, X\textquotesingle{})(S\textquotesingle{}) = \{ u ∈ Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{})(S\textquotesingle{}) | u(X\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}) = X\textquotesingle{}\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\} \}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one defines similarly \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, X, Y; G', X', Y')\),
etc.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have made explicit the preceding definitions
  (the original indicated ``One defines similarly
  \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, X, Y)\), \ldots,
  \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, X; G', X')\), \ldots{}'').}

\textbf{Proposition 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\) (resp. \(B\) a
Borel subgroup of \(G\), resp. \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of
\(G\)). Write \(T_{ad}\) (resp. \(B_{ad}\)) for the maximal torus (resp.
Borel subgroup) of \(ad(G)\) corresponding to \(T\) (resp. \(B\)):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B\_ad ≃ B / Centr(G) = B / Centr(B),}
\NormalTok{T\_ad ≃ T / Centr(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, T)\) (resp.
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B)\), resp.
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B, T)\)) is representable by a closed
subscheme of \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\), smooth over \(S\), and
the exact sequence of Theorem 1.3 induces exact sequences:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → Norm\_\{ad(G)\}(T\_ad) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) → Autext(G) → 1;}
\NormalTok{1 → B\_ad → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B) → Autext(G) → 1;}
\NormalTok{1 → T\_ad → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B, T) → Autext(G) → 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By descent of closed subschemes,\footnote{N.D.E.: cf.~SGA 1, VIII 1.9.}
one is at once reduced to the case where \(G\) is pinned and where
\(B \supset T\) is its canonical Killing couple (cf.~Exp. XXII, 5.5.5
(iv)). Since the group \(E\) of 1.2 normalizes \(B\) and \(T\), the
result follows at once from the normalization theorems in \(ad(G)\)
(Exp. XXII, 5.3.12 and 5.6.1).

Using now the conjugation theorems (cf.~Exp. XXIII, 5.12), and arguing
as in no 1, one deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 2.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two \(S\)-reductive groups of the same type at each point. Let
\(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) be a Killing couple of \(G\)
(resp. \(G'\)).}

\emph{(i) The \(S\)-functor \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, T; G', T')\) is
representable by a closed smooth subscheme of \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\)
which is principal homogeneous under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, T)\).}

\emph{Moreover, \(Norm_{ad(G)}(T_{ad})\) operates freely on this scheme,
and one has a canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T; G\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}) / Norm\_\{ad(G)\}(T\_ad) ≃ Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) The \(S\)-functor \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, B; G', B')\) is
representable by a closed smooth subscheme of \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\)
which is principal homogeneous under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B)\).}

\emph{Moreover, \(B_{ad}\) operates freely on this scheme and one has a
canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B; G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}) / B\_ad ≃ Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) The \(S\)-functor \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, B, T; G', B', T')\) is
representable by a closed smooth subscheme of \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\),
principal homogeneous under \(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B, T)\).}

\emph{Moreover, \(T_{ad}\) operates freely on this scheme and one has a
canonical isomorphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B, T; G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}) / T\_ad ≃ Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Arguing again as in no 1, one deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 2.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\). The
functor}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}) ↦ Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T; G\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{resp.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}) ↦ Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B; G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{resp.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}) ↦ Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B, T; G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an equivalence between the category of pairs
\texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ T\textquotesingle{})} (resp. of pairs
\texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ B\textquotesingle{})}, resp. of triples
\texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ B\textquotesingle{},\ T\textquotesingle{})}),
where \(G'\) is a form of \(G\) and \(T'\) a maximal torus of \(G'\)
(resp. \(B'\) a Borel subgroup of \(G'\), resp. \(B' \supset T'\) a
Killing couple of \(G'\)), and the category of principal homogeneous
bundles under the \(S\)-group \(H\), where
\(H = \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, T)\) (resp.
\(H = \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B)\), resp.
\(H = \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B, T)\)).}

\emph{Moreover, every principal homogeneous sheaf under \(H\) is
representable and quasi-isotrivial, so that one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, H) = H¹\_ét(S, H) = Fib(S, H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 2.4.} Under the conditions of 2.2, the morphism noted
set-theoretically \(u \mapsto u(T)\) (resp. \(u \mapsto u(B)\), resp.
\(u \mapsto (u(B), u(T))\)) induces an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{}) / Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) ≃ Tor(G\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{resp.    Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{}) / Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B) ≃ Bor(G\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{resp.    Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{}) / Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B, T) ≃ Kil(G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The proof is immediate: it suffices to do it locally for (fpqc), so one
may assume \(G \simeq G'\), and one is reduced to Exp. XXII, 5.8.3
(iii).

\textbf{Remark 2.5.} The preceding results are at once interpreted in
terms of restriction of the structure group: if \(G'\) is a form of
\(G\), corresponding to the principal bundle \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\), to
give a restriction of the structure group of this bundle to
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, T)\) amounts to giving a maximal torus
\(T'\) of \(G'\), the bijections suggested above being that of 2.4 on
the one hand, the map \(T' \mapsto Isom_{S-gr.}(G, T; G', T')\) on the
other. Similarly for Borel subgroups and Killing couples.

\textbf{Proposition 2.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two \(S\)-reductive groups of the same type at each point, \(T\) (resp.
\(T'\)) a maximal torus of \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)). Then \(T_{ad}\)
operates freely on \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, T; G', T')\), the quotient}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P = Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T; G\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}) / T\_ad}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is representable; it is a principal homogeneous bundle under}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A = Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) / T\_ad,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(A\) is representable by a twisted constant \(S\)-scheme,
extension of \(Autext(G)\) by
\(W_{ad(G)}(T_{ad}) = Norm_{ad(G)}(T_{ad}) / T_{ad}\). Moreover, if one
makes \(A\) operate on \(T\) in the obvious way, the bundle associated
to \(P\) is none other than \(T'\).\footnote{N.D.E.: Therefore, if \(P\)
  possesses a section, then \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic; in
  particular \texttt{T\_P} and \(T'_{P}\) are isomorphic. See the
  addition 4.5.1 where this remark is developed in the case where
  \(G = \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\).}}

The first part of the proposition follows at once from the preceding
results. To prove the second, one notes that there is an obvious
morphism \(P \times_{S} T \to T'\) (defined by \((u, t) \mapsto u(t)\));
to show that after passage to the quotient by \(A\) it induces an
isomorphism, one may once again assume \((G, T) \simeq (G', T')\), in
which case it is immediate.

In an entirely analogous way, one has:

\textbf{Proposition 2.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two \(S\)-reductive groups of the same type at each point,
\(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) a Killing couple of \(G\)
(resp. \(G'\)). If one makes
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B, T) / T_{ad} \simeq Autext(G)\)
operate in the obvious way on \(T\), the bundle associated to
\(Isomext(G, G')\) is none other than \(T'\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.8.} \emph{Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two
\(S\)-reductive groups that are inner twisted forms of each other; let
\(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) be a Killing couple of \(G\)
(resp. \(G'\)). Then \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  by 2.7, since \(Isomext(G, G')\) possesses a section (cf.~the
  preceding N.D.E.).}}

\textbf{Remark 2.9.} It is not true in general that \(B\) and \(B'\) are
isomorphic; they are however inner twisted forms of each other (cf.~no
5).

One can develop ``Isomint'' variants\footnote{N.D.E.: Recall that
  \(Isomint_{u}(G, G')\) is defined in 1.11.} of the preceding results.
Let us point out one:

\textbf{Proposition 2.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\)
two \(S\)-reductive groups of the same type at each point,
\(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) a Killing couple of \(G\)
(resp. \(G'\)). Let \(u \in Isomext(G, G')(S)\); consider}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isomint\_u(G, B, T; G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}) = Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B, T; G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{}) ∩ Isomint\_u(G, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{It is a smooth and affine \(S\)-scheme which is a principal
homogeneous bundle under \(T_{ad}\). In particular,
\(Isomint_{u}(G, B, T; G', B', T')(S) \neq \emptyset\) if and only if
the corresponding element of \(H^{1}(S, T_{ad})\) is zero.}

To conclude this section, let us prove two results which will be useful
later:

\textbf{Proposition 2.11.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). The obvious
morphism}

\[
T_{ad} \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, id_{T})
\]

\emph{is an isomorphism.}

This follows from the preceding statements; moreover, one has given a
direct proof in the course of the proof of 1.5.2.

\textbf{Corollary 2.12.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, there
exists an equivalence between the category of pairs
\texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ f)}, where \(G'\) is a form of \(G\) and
\(f\) is an isomorphism of \(T\) onto a maximal torus of \(G'\), and the
category of principal homogeneous bundles under \(T_{ad}\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.13.} \emph{If \(H^{1}(S, T_{ad}) = 0\), and if
\(G'\) is a form of \(G\) possessing a maximal torus isomorphic to
\(T\), then \(G'\) is isomorphic to \(G\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.14.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme such that
\(\operatorname{Pic}(S) = 0\), and \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group of
constant type. For \(G\) to be splittable, it is necessary and
sufficient that \(G\) possess a split maximal torus.}

Let \(G\) be a reductive group, \(rad(G)\) its radical (Exp. XXII,
4.3.9); since \(rad(G)\) is central and characteristic in \(G\), one has
a canonical morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{q : Autext(G) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(rad(G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 2.15.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group.
The following sequence is exact:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → ad(G) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, id\_\{rad(G)\}) ─p→ Autext(G) ─q→ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(rad(G))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and \(Ker(q) = Im(p)\) is an open and closed subscheme of
\(Autext(G)\), finite over \(S\).}

One may assume \(G\) split. The first assertion is immediate; the second
follows from Exp. XXI, 6.7.5 and 6.7.7.

Writing \(H = \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, id_{rad(G)})\), one deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 2.16.} \emph{There exists an equivalence between the
category of pairs \texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ f)}, where \(G'\) is a
form of \(G\) and \(f\) is an isomorphism of \(rad(G)\) onto the radical
of \(G'\), and the category of principal bundles under a certain
\(S\)-group scheme \(H\), where \(H\) is such that there exists an exact
sequence}

\[
1 \to ad(G) \to H \to F \to 1,
\]

\emph{where the \(S\)-group \(F\) is étale and finite over \(S\).}

\subsection{3. Dynkin scheme of a reductive group. Quasi-split
groups}\label{dynkin-scheme-of-a-reductive-group.-quasi-split-groups}

\subsubsection{3.1.}\label{section-271}

Recall (Exp. XXI, 7.4.1) that a \emph{Dynkin diagram} is a finite set
endowed with the structure defined by a set of pairs of distinct
elements (\emph{bonds}) and a map to \texttt{\{1,\ 2,\ 3\}}
(\emph{lengths}). To each pinned reduced root datum \(R\) is associated
a Dynkin diagram \(\Delta(R)\), whose underlying set is the set of
simple roots.

\subsubsection{3.2.}\label{section-272}

Let \(S\) be a scheme. An \(S\)-\emph{Dynkin scheme} is a finite twisted
constant \(S\)-scheme \(\Delta\), equipped with the structure defined by
a subscheme \(L\) of \(\Delta \times_{S} \Delta\) having empty
intersection with the diagonal, and by a morphism
\(\Delta \to {1, 2, 3}_{S}\). If \(S'\) is a connected\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have added the hypothesis that \(S'\) be connected.} \(S\)-scheme,
\(\Delta(S')\) is naturally endowed with a structure of Dynkin diagram.

One defines at once the following notions: isomorphism of two Dynkin
schemes, base change of a Dynkin scheme, constant Dynkin scheme
associated to a Dynkin diagram.

Every descent datum on a Dynkin scheme for the étale topology is
effective.

\subsubsection{3.3.}\label{section-273}

We propose to associate to each \(S\)-reductive group \(G\) an
\(S\)-Dynkin scheme. Suppose first that \(G\) is splittable over \(S\);
for every pinning \(E\) of \(G\), write \(\Delta(E)\) for the constant
Dynkin scheme associated to the pinned root datum defined by \(E\); if
\(E\) and \(E'\) are two pinnings of \(G\), there exists by 1.5 a unique
inner automorphism of \(G\) over \(S\) transforming \(E\) into \(E'\);
this automorphism of \(G\) defines an isomorphism
\(a_{EE'} : \Delta(E) \xrightarrow{\sim} \Delta(E')\); the \(a_{EE'}\)
evidently form a transitive system, so that one may identify the
\(\Delta(E)\) (i.e.~take the inductive limit); the result is a constant
Dynkin scheme denoted \(Dyn(G)\). If now \(G\) is an arbitrary
\(S\)-reductive group, there exists a covering family for the étale
topology \({S_{i} \to S}\) such that \(G_{S_{i}}\) is splittable.
Arguing as previously, one therefore has a canonical descent datum on
the \(Dyn(G_{S_{i}})\), allowing one to construct by descent an
\(S\)-Dynkin scheme \(Dyn(G)\).

\subsubsection{3.4.}\label{section-274}

This construction satisfies the following properties (which moreover
essentially characterize it):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  To each \(S\)-reductive group is associated a Dynkin scheme
  \(Dyn(G)\); to every isomorphism \(u : G \xrightarrow{\sim} G'\) is
  functorially associated an isomorphism
  \texttt{Dyn(u)\ :\ Dyn(G)\ ⥲\ Dyn(G\textquotesingle{})}.
\item
  If \(S'\) is an \(S\)-scheme and \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, one
  has
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Dyn(G ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}) ≃ Dyn(G) ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(E\) is a pinning of \(G\), defining the pinned root datum with
  Dynkin diagram \(\Delta\), one has
\end{enumerate}

\[
Dyn(G) \simeq \Delta_{S}.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(u\) is an inner automorphism of \(G\), \(Dyn(u)\) is the identity
  automorphism of \(Dyn(G)\).
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{3.5.}\label{section-275}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. It is clear that
the functor \(\operatorname{Aut}_{Dyn}(Dyn(G))\) of automorphisms of
\(Dyn(G)\) for the structure of Dynkin scheme is representable by a
finite twisted constant \(S\)-scheme. By 3.4 (i) and (ii), one has a
canonical morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G) → Aut\_\{Dyn\}(Dyn(G)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which, by (iv), factors through a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Autext(G) → Aut\_\{Dyn\}(Dyn(G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

More generally, if \(G\) and \(G'\) are two \(S\)-reductive groups, one
has a canonical morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}) → Isom\_\{Dyn\}(Dyn(G), Dyn(G\textquotesingle{}));}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

in particular, if \(G'\) is an inner twisted form of \(G\) (1.11), the
Dynkin schemes \(Dyn(G)\) and \(Dyn(G')\) are isomorphic.

\subsubsection{3.6.}\label{section-276}

If \(G\) is semisimple (resp. adjoint or simply connected), the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Autext(G) → Aut\_\{Dyn\}(Dyn(G))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism). Indeed, one may assume \(G\)
pinned and one is reduced to the corresponding result for pinned reduced
root data (cf.~Exp. XXI, 7.4.5).

One has an analogous result for \texttt{Isom}'s; whence it follows in
particular that two semisimple adjoint (resp. simply connected)
\(S\)-groups are inner twisted forms of each other if and only if their
Dynkin schemes are isomorphic.

\subsubsection{3.7.}\label{section-277}

One can give a different construction of the Dynkin scheme associated to
a reductive group. Let \(R\) be a pinned reduced root datum, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group of type \(R\); write \(\Delta(R)\) for the Dynkin
diagram defined by the root datum \(R\). One has (3.5) a canonical
morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A\_S(R) = Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Ép\_S(R)) → Aut\_\{Dyn\}(Δ(R)\_S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The \(S\)-reductive group \(G\) corresponds (1.17) to a bundle
\(Isom_{S-gr.}(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), G)\), principal homogeneous under
\(A_{S}(R)\). The bundle under
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{Dyn}(\Delta(R)_{S})\) associated corresponds to a
form on \(S\) of \(\Delta(R)_{S}\): this is \(Dyn(G)\); in other words,
this associated bundle is none other than
\texttt{Isom\_\{Dyn\}(Δ(R)\_S,\ Dyn(G))}. In this last form, the proof
is immediate.

\subsubsection{3.8. Dynkin scheme and Killing
couples.}\label{dynkin-scheme-and-killing-couples.}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(B \supset T\) a
Killing couple of \(G\). There exists a canonical morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i : Dyn(G) → Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T, G\_\{m, S\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which identifies \(Dyn(G)\) with the ``scheme of simple roots of \(B\)
relative to \(T\)''; this morphism is defined at once by descent from
the pinned case. Note moreover that the datum of \(T\) and of \(i\)
allows one to reconstruct \(B\) (``biunivocal correspondence between
systems of simple roots and systems of positive roots'').

It follows from the preceding description of \(D = Dyn(G)\) that there
exists a canonical root of \texttt{B\_D} with respect to \texttt{T\_D}:
this root \(\alpha_{D}\) is the image under \(i(D)\) of the identity
morphism of \(D\). One thereby deduces a canonical invertible
\texttt{O\_D}-module \(g_{D}\):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_D = (g ⊗\_\{O\_S\} O\_D)\^{}\{α\_D\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In the pinned case, one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D = ⨿\_\{α ∈ Δ\} S\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where each \(S_{\alpha}\) is a copy of \(S\), and \(g_{D}\) is then the
\texttt{O\_D}-module which induces \(g_{\alpha}\) on \(S_{\alpha}\), for
every \(\alpha \in \Delta\).

\subsubsection{3.9. Quasi-pinnings. Quasi-pinned
groups.}\label{quasi-pinnings.-quasi-pinned-groups.}

If \(G\) is an \(S\)-reductive group, we call \emph{quasi-pinning of
\(G\)} the datum:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  of a Killing couple \(B \supset T\) of \(G\),
\item
  of a section \(X \in \Gamma(Dyn(G), g_{D})^{\times}\).
\end{enumerate}

We say that an \(S\)-reductive group is \emph{quasi-splittable} if it
possesses a quasi-pinning. We call \emph{quasi-pinned group} a reductive
group equipped with a quasi-pinning.

Let \(B \supset T\) be a Killing couple of the \(S\)-reductive group
\(G\); then \(G\) is quasi-pinnable relative to this Killing couple if
and only if \(g_{D}\) possesses a non-zero section at every point,
i.e.~if the element of \(\operatorname{Pic}(Dyn(G))\) defined by
\(g_{D}\) is zero. Suppose in particular that \(S\) is semi-local; then
\(Dyn(G)\) is also semi-local, so \(\operatorname{Pic}(Dyn(G)) = 0\).
One deduces:

\textbf{Proposition 3.9.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme,
\(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. For \(G\) to be quasi-splittable, it is
necessary and sufficient that it possess a Borel subgroup.}

\footnote{N.D.E.: We have detailed the reference to Exp. XXII, 5.9.7.}
Indeed, \(S\) is affine so, by the first assertion of Exp. XXII, 5.9.7,
if \(G\) possesses a Borel subgroup \(B\), it also possesses a Killing
couple \(B \supset T\). Then, since \(\operatorname{Pic}(D) = 0\),
\(g_{D}\) possesses a section \(X\) nowhere zero.

Let still \(A\) be a semi-local ring and \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\);
remark now that for every \(S\)-reductive group \(G\) the morphism
\(Bor(G) \to S\) is surjective (since \(G_{s}\) possesses Borel
subgroups, for every \(s \in S\)) and smooth and projective (Exp. XXII,
5.8.3), so it possesses sections after a finite surjective étale
extension of the base.\footnote{N.D.E.: The original referred to EGA IV,
  § 24, which has not appeared. The point is to use ``Bertini's
  theorem''. Let us detail the argument, which was indicated to us by O.
  Gabber. Let \(X \to S\) be a surjective, smooth and projective
  morphism; replacing \(S\) by a connected component, one may assume
  that \(X/S\) has constant relative dimension \(d\) at every point
  (cf.~EGA IV\_4, 17.10.2). One may also assume that \(X\) is a closed
  subscheme of a projective space \(P^{n}_{S} = P(E)\), where \(E\) is a
  free \(A\)-module of rank \(n + 1\) (cf.~EGA II, 5.3.3). Let
  \(s_{1}, ..., s_{r}\) be the closed points of \(S\); by Bertini's
  theorem (see for example {[}Jou83{]}, I 6.10), there exists an open
  set \(U\) of the product \(P = P(E^{*})^{d}\), with non-empty fibers,
  such that for every point \(u = (f_{1}, ..., f_{d})\) of
  \(U_{s_{i}}\), the intersection of \(X_{\kappa(u)}\) with the \(d\)
  hyperplanes of \(P^{n}_{\kappa(u)}\) defined by \(u\) is étale over
  \(\kappa(u)\). Up to shrinking \(U\), one may assume that \(U\) is the
  complement in the affine space \(A^{nd}_{S}\) of the locus of zeros
  \(V(Q)\) of a certain polynomial \(Q\) of degree \(m > 0\). One then
  sees easily (by induction on the number of variables) that \(V(Q)\)
  cannot contain all rational points of \(A^{nd}_{\kappa(s_{i})}\) if
  \(|\kappa(s_{i})| > m\). Since the morphism
  \(A \to \prod_{i} \kappa(s_{i})\) is surjective, one can find a monic
  polynomial \(R \in A[X]\) of degree \(m\) whose image in
  \(\kappa(s_{i})[X]\) is irreducible if \(\kappa(s_{i})\) is finite,
  and possesses \(m\) distinct roots if \(\kappa(s_{i})\) is infinite.
  Put \(A' = A[X]/(R)\) and \(S' = \operatorname{Spec}(A')\); then
  \(S' \to S\) is étale, finite and surjective, and the residue field at
  each of its closed points \(s'_{1}, ..., s'_{t}\) is of cardinality
  \(\geqslant 2m\). Then \(U\) possesses a rational point \(u_{i}\) over
  each closed point of \(S'\), and since
  \(A' \to \prod_{i} \kappa(s_{i})\) is surjective, these lift to a
  section \(u\) of \(P_{S'}\). Write \(Z\) for the intersection of
  \(X_{S'}\) with the \(d\) hyperplanes of \(P^{n}_{S'}\) defined by
  \(u\), and \(V\) for the open set of \(Z\) formed by the points at
  which \(Z\) is étale over \(S'\). By EGA IV\_3, 11.3.8, \(V\) contains
  the fibers \(Z_{s'_{i}}\) for every \(i\); since \(\pi : Z \to S'\) is
  proper, it follows that the closed set \(\pi(Z - V)\) is empty, whence
  \(V = Z\). Then \(Z \to S'\) is surjective, étale and proper, hence
  finite, as is the composite \(Z \to S\), and this yields the desired
  section of \(X \to S\).} One deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 3.9.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\)
an \(S\)-reductive group. There exists an étale, finite and surjective
morphism \(S' \to S\) such that \(G_{S'}\) is quasi-splittable.}

\textbf{Remark 3.9.3.} Under the preceding conditions, let \(T\) be a
maximal torus of \(G\) (cf.~Exp. XIV, 3.20); then one may moreover
assume that \(G_{S'}\) is quasi-splittable relative to \(T_{S'}\): it
suffices to apply the preceding argument to the ``scheme of Borel
subgroups containing \(T\)'', which is finite and étale over \(S\) (Exp.
XXII, 5.5.5 (ii)).

\subsubsection{3.10.}\label{section-278}

Let \(E\) and \(E'\) be two quasi-pinnings of the \(S\)-reductive group
\(G\). There exists a unique inner automorphism of \(G\) transforming
\(E\) into \(E'\). Indeed, one is at once reduced to the split case,
where the assertion has already been proved (1.5; it suffices indeed to
note that for an inner automorphism of \(G\) it amounts to the same to
respect a pinning or the underlying quasi-pinning). One concludes as in
no 1 that a

quasi-pinning of the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\) defines a splitting
\(h\) of the exact sequence:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → ad(G) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G) ⇄\^{}\{h\}\_\{p\} Autext(G) → 1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the image of \(h\) being the subgroup of
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\) which leaves invariant the
quasi-pinning.

Similarly if \(G\) and \(G'\) are two quasi-pinned \(S\)-groups, one
defines in a natural way the subfunctor

\[
Isom_{S-gr. q-\acute{e}p.}(G, G')
\]

of \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\); the projection of \(Isom_{S-gr.}(G, G')\)
onto \(Isomext(G, G')\) induces an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(*)    Isom\_\{S{-}gr. q{-}ép.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{}) ⥲ Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Theorem 3.11.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(R\) a pinned
reduced root datum such that \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) exists (cf.~Exp.
XXV), \(E\) the group of its automorphisms. Consider the three following
categories:}

\emph{(i) The category \texttt{Rev} of principal Galois coverings of
\(S\) with group \(E\) (the morphisms are isomorphisms of
\(E\)-bundles).}

\emph{(ii) The category \texttt{Redext} whose objects are the
\(S\)-reductive groups of type \(R\) (Exp. XXII, 2.7), the morphisms
from \(G\) to \(G'\) being the elements of \(Isomext(G, G')(S)\).}

\emph{(iii) The category \texttt{Qép} of quasi-pinned \(S\)-reductive
groups of type \(R\) (the morphisms are the isomorphisms respecting the
quasi-pinnings).}

\emph{These three categories are equivalent: more precisely, one has a
diagram of functors, commutative up to functorial isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{       qép}
\NormalTok{Rev ───────→ Qép}
\NormalTok{   ╲          ╱}
\NormalTok{rev ╲        ╱ i}
\NormalTok{     ╲      ╱}
\NormalTok{       Redext}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

We shall describe below these three functors, leaving to the reader the
task of verifying the commutativity of the diagram.\footnote{N.D.E.: We
  have sketched in 3.11.4 the verification of the fact that the functors
  \(i\), \texttt{rev} and \texttt{qép} are fully faithful, and that the
  composite \(rev \circ i \circ q\acute{e}p\) is isomorphic to the
  identity functor of \texttt{Rev}.}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{3.11.1. The functor
\(i\).}{3.11.1. The functor i.}}\label{the-functor-i.}

It is the obvious functor: \(i(G) = G\), \(i(f) =\) image of \(f\) under
the isomorphism of 3.10 (*).

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{3.11.2. The functor
\texttt{qép}.}{3.11.2. The functor qép.}}\label{the-functor-quxe9p.}

Let \(S'\) be a principal Galois covering of \(S\) with group \(E\). Let
\((G, T, M, R, \Delta, (X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta})\) be a pinning
of \(G = \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) and \((X'_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta}\)
the corresponding pinning of \(G' = G_{S'} = \acute{E}p_{S'}(R)\). By
Exp. XXIII 5.5 bis, there exists a unique morphism of groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{θ : E → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Ép\_S(R)) = A(R)(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that, for every \(h \in E\), \(\theta(h)\) induces \(D_{S}(h)\) on
\(T\) and \(Lie(\theta(h))(X_{\alpha}) = X_{h(\alpha)}\) for every
\(\alpha \in \Delta\). Taking into account the action of \(E\) on
\(S'\), one thereby obtains an action of \(E\) on \(G'\), compatible
with the action of \(E\) on \(S'\) and respecting the canonical
quasi-pinning of \(G'\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have expanded the original
  in the foregoing, to show that the action of \(E\) on \(G'\) is
  obtained by combining the natural action of \(E\) on
  \(\acute{E}p_{S'}(R)\) and the given action on \(S'\). The canonical
  Killing couple of \(G'\) is preserved by this action, as is the
  quasi-pinning given by the element \(\tilde{X}'\) of
  \(\Gamma(\Delta_{S'}, Lie(G'/S')_{\Delta_{S'}})\), equal to
  \(X'_{\alpha}\) on the copy of \(S'\) indexed by \(\alpha\) (indeed,
  since \(E\) acts on \(\Delta_{S'}\) by permutation of the copies of
  \(S'\), one has indeed \(h(\tilde{X}') = \tilde{X}'\) for every
  \(h \in E\)).} Since \(S' \to S\) is covering for the (fpqc) topology,
it is an effective descent morphism for the fibered category of affine
morphisms, and one writes

\[
q\acute{e}p(S') = Q-\acute{E}p_{S'/S}(R)
\]

for the quasi-pinned \(S\)-group obtained by Galois descent.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  see, for example, TDTE I, p.~22, Example 1. One can also describe
  \(q\acute{e}p(S')\) as the twist of \(G = \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) by the
  \(E\)-torsor \(S'/S\), i.e.~the (fpqc) sheaf quotient of
  \(S' \times_{S} G\) by the right action of \(E\) defined by
  \((s', g) \cdot h = (s' h, h^{-1}(g))\). Since \(G\) is affine over
  \(S\) and since \(E\) acts on \(G\) by group automorphisms, this sheaf
  is representable by an \(S\)-group \(G^{\sharp}\), which is a
  ``twisted'' form of \(G\), and \(D^{\sharp} = Dyn(G^{\sharp})\) is the
  twist of the constant Dynkin scheme \(\Delta_{S}\) by the torsor
  \(S'/S\). Since \(E\) normalizes \(B\) and \(T\), one obtains likewise
  a pair \((B^{\sharp}, T^{\sharp})\) which is a Killing couple of
  \(G^{\sharp}\). On the other hand, let \(g = Lie(G/S)\) and
  \(g^{\sharp} = Lie(G^{\sharp}/S)\); for every \(U \to S\), the
  sections of \(g^{\sharp}\) on \(U\) are the \(E\)-equivariant
  \(S\)-morphisms \(U \times_{S} S' \to W(g)\). Since
  \(D^{\sharp} \times_{S} S'\) is \(E\)-isomorphic to
  \(\Delta \times S'\), equipped with the action
  \((\alpha, s') \cdot h = (h^{-1}(\alpha), s' h)\), one obtains that
  the morphism given by \((\alpha, s') \mapsto X_{\alpha}\) is a section
  of \(g^{\sharp}\) on \(D^{\sharp}\) which is a quasi-pinning, i.e.~a
  section nowhere zero of
  \((g^{\sharp} \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{D^{\sharp}})^{D^{\sharp}}\)
  (cf.~3.8).}

\paragraph{\texorpdfstring{3.11.3. The functor
\texttt{rev}.}{3.11.3. The functor rev.}}\label{the-functor-rev.}

Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group of type \(R\). One writes

\[
rev(G) = Isomext(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), G);
\]

this is a principal homogeneous bundle under \texttt{E\_S} (cf.~1.10 and
1.19), that is, an object of \texttt{Rev}.

\paragraph[3.11.4. ]{\texorpdfstring{3.11.4.
\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this number.}}{3.11.4. }}\label{n.d.e-xxiv-22}

It is clear, by the isomorphism 3.10 (*), that the functor \(i\) is
fully faithful. On the other hand, if \texttt{G\_0}, \(G\), \(G'\) are
\(S\)-reductive groups, the natural morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom(G\_0, G) ×\_S Isom(G, G\textquotesingle{}) → Isom(G\_0, G\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induces a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(⋆)    Isomext(G\_0, G) ×\_S Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{}) → Isomext(G\_0, G\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since, for every \(S' \to S\), if \(g_{0} \in G_{0}(S')\),
\(g \in G(S')\), \(u \in Isom(G_{0}, G)(S')\), and
\(v \in Isom(G, G')(S')\), one has the equality
\texttt{v\ ∘\ int(g)\ ∘\ u\ ∘\ int(g\_0)\ =\ v\ ∘\ u\ ∘\ int(u\^{}\{-1\}(g)\ g\_0)}.
Taking \(G_{0} = \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\), one obtains a map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isomext(G, G\textquotesingle{})(S) → Hom\_\{Rev\}( Isomext(Ép\_S(R), G), Isomext(Ép\_S(R), G\textquotesingle{}) )}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and to show that this is a bijection, one may assume by (fpqc) descent
that \(G\) and \(G'\) are pinned, in which case it is evident.

Similarly, if \texttt{S\_1}, \texttt{S\_2} are two objects of
\texttt{Rev} and if one writes \(S_{i} \times^{E} \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\)
for the \(S\)-group \(q\acute{e}p(S_{i})\) obtained by twisting
\(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) by the \(E\)-torsor \(S_{i}\) (cf.~N.D.E. (21)),
one has a natural map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{Rev\}(S\_1, S\_2) → Hom\_\{Qép\}(S\_1 ×\^{}E Ép\_S(R), S\_2 ×\^{}E Ép\_S(R)),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and to show that this is a bijection, one may assume by (fpqc) descent
that \texttt{S\_1} and \texttt{S\_2} are trivial \(E\)-bundles, in which
case it is evident.

Thus the three functors of the diagram are fully faithful. Moreover, for
every object \(S'\) of \texttt{Rev}, one has a natural morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S\textquotesingle{} → Isomext(Ép\_S(R), S\textquotesingle{} ×\^{}E Ép\_S(R))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and to see that this is an isomorphism, one may assume by (fpqc) descent
that \(S'\) is a trivial \(E\)-bundle, in which case it is evident.

One thus has an isomorphism of functors
\(Id_{Rev} \to rev \circ i \circ q\acute{e}p\). Since the functor
\texttt{rev} is fully faithful one obtains therefore, for every
\(S\)-reductive group \(H\) (not necessarily quasi-split), a bijection

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isomext(Q{-}Ép\_\{rev(H)/S\}(R), H)(S) ≃ Aut\_\{Rev\}(rev(H))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

functorial in \(H\). In particular, the identity morphism of \(rev(H)\)
corresponds to a ``canonical'' element \(u_{0}\) of
\(Isomext(Q-\acute{E}p_{rev(H)/S}(R), H)(S)\); moreover, every
\(u \in Isomext(Q-\acute{E}p_{rev(H)/S}(R), H)(S)\) corresponds to an
automorphism \(\phi_{u}\) of \(rev(H)\), and \(q\acute{e}p(\phi_{u})\)
is the unique automorphism of pinned \(S\)-group of
\(Q-\acute{E}p_{rev(H)/S}(R)\) such that
\(u_{0} \circ q\acute{e}p(\phi_{u}) = u\). We have thus proved theorem
3.11.

Let us develop one of the corollaries of 3.11:

\textbf{Corollary 3.12.} \emph{For every \(S\)-reductive group \(G\),
there exists a quasi-pinned \(S\)-group \(G_{q-\acute{e}p.}\) and an
``outer isomorphism'' \(u \in Isomext(G_{q-\acute{e}p.}, G)(S)\). The
pair \((G_{q-\acute{e}p.}, u)\) is unique up to a unique isomorphism.}

Indeed, one may assume \(G\) of constant type \(R\), and one takes
\(G_{q-\acute{e}p.} = Q-\acute{E}p_{rev(G)/S}(R)\).

\paragraph{3.12.1.}\label{section-279}

Note that the datum of the pair \((G_{q-\acute{e}p.}, u)\) allows one to
define canonically the \(S\)-scheme (cf.~1.11)

\[
Q = Isomint(G_{q-\acute{e}p.}, G),[{}^{N}.D.E-XXIV-23]
\]

which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(ad(G_{q-\acute{e}p.})\),
and whose datum ``is equivalent'' to that of the inner twisted form
\(G\) of \(G_{q-\acute{e}p.}\). Moreover, \(Q\) is none other than the
``scheme of quasi-pinnings of \(G\)'', a definition which accounts for
its structure of principal homogeneous bundle (on the left) under
\(ad(G)\) (3.10) --- compare with 1.20.

\textbf{Proposition 3.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a
semisimple adjoint (resp. simply connected) \(S\)-group, \(B \supset T\)
a Killing couple of \(G\), \(Dyn(G)\) the Dynkin \(S\)-scheme}

\emph{of \(G\). There exists a canonical isomorphism of \(S\)-group
schemes}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T ⥲ ∏\_\{Dyn(G)/S\} G\_\{m, Dyn(G)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(Recall (cf.~Exp. II, § 1) that the right-hand side is by
definition the \(S\)-functor which to \(S' \to S\) associates
\(G_{m}(Dyn(G) \times_{S} S')\), or, what amounts to the same,
\(G_{m}(Dyn(G_{S'}))\).)}

\emph{First proof.} Let us do it for simplicity in the adjoint case.
Consider the composite morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T → ∏\_\{D/S\} T\_D → ∏\_\{D/S\} G\_\{m, D\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the first morphism is the canonical morphism, the second is
\(\prod_{D/S} \alpha_{D}\) (we have written \(D = Dyn(G)\)). To verify
that this morphism is an isomorphism, one may assume \(G\) split; now,
in this case, this is none other than the morphism
\(T \to (G_{m, S})^{\Delta}\) with components \(\alpha\), for
\(\alpha \in \Delta\), and the latter is an isomorphism (Exp. XXII,
4.3.8).

\emph{Second proof.} By 2.8, 3.5 and 3.11, one may assume that
\(G = Q-\acute{E}p_{S'/S}(R)\), \(T\) being the canonical maximal torus.
On \(S'\), one has by Exp. XXII 4.3.8, an isomorphism
\(T_{S'} \xrightarrow{\sim} (G_{m, S'})^{\Delta}\), defined by the
simple roots (resp. the simple coroots). The group \(E\) operates on the
right-hand side by permutation of \(\Delta\). Now the bundle associated
to \(S'/S\) by \(E \to \operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)\) is \(Dyn(G)\) (3.7),
and one concludes at once.

Using Prop. 8.4 of the appendix, one deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 3.14.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, T) ⥲ H¹(Dyn(G), G\_m) ⥲ Pic(Dyn(G)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{In particular, \(H^{1}(S, T) = 0\) when \(S\) is semi-local.}

\textbf{Remark 3.15.} Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(B \supset T\) (resp. \(B' \supset T'\)) a
Killing couple of \(G\) (resp. \(G'\)), \(u \in Isomext(G, G')(S)\). Set
(cf.~2.10)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P = Isomint\_u(G, B, T; G\textquotesingle{}, B\textquotesingle{}, T\textquotesingle{});}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

this is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(T_{ad}\) (by
\((f, t) \mapsto f \circ int(t)\)).

Let on the other hand \(D = Dyn(G) = Dyn(G')\) (identified via \(u\)
(3.5)), and let \(L = Isom_{D}(g_{D}, g'_{D})\) be the principal
homogeneous bundle under \(G_{m, D}\) defined by the invertible
\texttt{O\_D}-module

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_D\}(g\_D, g\textquotesingle{}\_D) = g\textquotesingle{}\_D ⊗ (g\_D)\^{}∨.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Each \(f \in P(S')\) defines an isomorphism of
\(g_{D} \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'}\) onto \(g'_{D} \otimes_{O_{S}} O_{S'}\),
whence a canonical morphism

\[
P \to \prod_{D/S} L.
\]

This morphism is an isomorphism, compatible with the isomorphism of
operator groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_ad ⥲ ∏\_\{D/S\} G\_\{m, D\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined above. Indeed, it suffices to verify it in the case where the
two groups are pinned, where it is easy.

It follows in particular that in the isomorphism

\[
H^{1}(S, T_{ad}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Pic}(Dyn(G))
\]

of 3.14, the class of the bundle \(P\) is transformed into
\(c\ell(g'^{D}) - c\ell(g_{D})\). The bundle \(P\) is therefore trivial
if and only if \(g'^{D}\) and \(g_{D}\) are isomorphic.

If \((G, B, T)\) is quasi-splittable, for example if one takes for \(G\)
the group \(G'_{q-\acute{e}p.}\), with its canonical Killing couple, it
follows that the image of the class of \(P\) is none other than the
obstruction to the quasi-splitting of \(G'\) defined in 3.9.

\subsubsection{3.16. Symmetries}\label{symmetries}

\paragraph{3.16.1.}\label{section-280}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(B \supset T\) a
Killing couple of \(G\). Write \(D = Dyn(G)\). Recall (Exp. XXII, 5.9.1)
that there exists a unique Borel subgroup \(B^{-}\) of \(G\) such that
\(B \cap B^{-} = T\). If \(X \in \Gamma(D, g_{D})^{\times}\) defines a
quasi-pinning of \(G\) relative to \((B, T)\) (3.9), then
\(Y = -X^{-1} \in \Gamma(D, (g_{D})^{\vee})^{\times}\) defines a
quasi-pinning of \(G\) relative to \((B^{-}, T)\); one says that this is
the \emph{opposite quasi-pinning}.

If \(R\) is a pinned reduced root datum and if \(E\) is an \(R\)-pinning
of the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\), one defines an \(R\)-pinning
\(E^{-}\) said to be \emph{opposite to \(E\)} in the following way: one
keeps the same maximal torus \(T\), one takes the opposite of the
isomorphism \(D_{S}(M) \xrightarrow{\sim} T\), and one ``pins'' by
\(Y_{\alpha} = -X^{-1}_{\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, g^{-\alpha})^{\times}\),
for \(\alpha \in \Delta\). The quasi-pinning underlying \(E^{-}\) is the
quasi-pinning opposite to the quasi-pinning underlying \(E\).

\textbf{Remark.} In the notation of Exp. XIX, 3.1, if one sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_α(X\_α) = exp(X\_α) exp(−X\_α\^{}\{{-}1\}) exp(X\_α),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one has \(w_{\alpha}(X_{\alpha}) = w_{-\alpha}(Y_{\alpha})\) (loc. cit.,
3.1 (vi)).

\textbf{Proposition 3.16.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) Let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(G\); there exists a unique}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i\_T ∈ (Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) / T\_ad)(S) ⊂ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that \(i_{T}(t) = t^{-1}\) for every section \(t\) of \(T\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \((B, T)\) be a Killing couple of \(G\); there exists a
unique section}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_\{B, T\} ∈ (Norm\_G(T) / T)(S) = W\_G(T)(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that \(int(w_{B, T})(B) = B^{-}\) (with the obvious abuse of
language).}

\emph{(iii) Let \(Q = (B, T, X)\) be a quasi-pinning of \(G\),
\(Q^{-} = (B^{-}, T, Y)\) the opposite quasi-pinning; there exists a
unique inner automorphism of \(G\)}

\[
n_{Q} \in Norm_{ad(G)}(T_{ad})(S) \subset \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)
\]

\emph{such that \(n_{Q}(Q) = Q^{-}\), that is, \(n_{Q}(T) = T\),
\(n_{Q}(B) = B^{-}\), \(n_{Q}(X) = Y\).}

\emph{(iv) Let \((R, E)\) be a pinning of \(G\), \((R, E^{-})\) the
opposite pinning; there exists a unique automorphism of \(G\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u\_E ∈ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) ⊂ Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{such that \(u_{E}(E) = E^{-}\), i.e.~\(u_{E}(t) = t^{-1}\) for
every section \(t\) of \(T\), and \(Ad(u_{E}) X_{\alpha} = Y_{\alpha}\)
for every \(\alpha \in \Delta\).}

\emph{Proof.} (ii) follows from Exp. XXII, 5.5.5 (ii), then (iii)
follows from 3.10, and (iv) follows from Exp. XXIII, 4.1. Finally to
prove (i), one may assume \(G\) pinned. Existence follows from (iv) for
example, uniqueness from the fact that an automorphism of \(G\) inducing
the identity on \(T\) is given by a section of \(T_{ad}\) (2.11).

\textbf{Corollary 3.16.3.} \emph{One has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i\_T² = w\_\{B, T\}² = n\_Q² = u\_E² = e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Moreover, \(i_{T}\) (resp. \(u_{E}\)) is \(\neq e\) if
\(G \neq e\), and \(w_{B, T}\) (resp. \(n_{Q}\)) is \(\neq e\) if \(G\)
is not a torus.}

\textbf{Corollary 3.16.4.} \emph{In the situation of (iii) (resp. (iv)),
\(n_{Q}\) projects onto \(w_{B, T}\) (resp. \(u_{E}\) projects onto
\(i_{T}\)) by the canonical morphism}

\[
Norm_{ad(G)}(T_{ad}) \to W_{ad(G)}(T_{ad}) \simeq W_{G}(T),
\]

\emph{resp.}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) / T\_ad.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 3.16.5.} \emph{The preceding definitions are
compatible with base change, and are functorial under isomorphism (in an
obvious sense).}

\textbf{Proposition 3.16.6.} \emph{(i) One can define uniquely for each
reductive group \(G\) over a scheme \(S\) an element}

\[
s_{G} \in Autext(G)(S)
\]

\emph{in such a way that this construction is functorial in \(G\) under
isomorphism, is compatible with base change, and is such that whenever
\(T\) is a maximal torus of the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\), \(s_{G}\)
is the image of \(i_{T}\) under the canonical morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, T) / T\_ad → Autext(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) One has \(s^{2}_{G} = e\), and \(s_{G}\) is a central element
of \(Autext(G)\).}

\emph{(iii) Under the conditions of 3.16.2 (ii), if one identifies
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G, B, T) / T_{ad}\) with \(Autext(G)\)
(2.2), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_\{B, T\} i\_T = i\_T w\_\{B, T\} = s\_G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iv) Under the conditions of 3.16.2 (iv), if one identifies
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.-\acute{e}p}(G, R, E)\) with \(Autext(G)\)
(1.3 (iii)), one has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{n\_E u\_E = u\_E n\_E = s\_G.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Proof.} (i) is proved without difficulty by descent. On the other
hand, since \(i_{T}\) is evidently a central section of square \(e\) in
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(T)\), (ii) follows immediately; (iii) is a
consequence of (iv) by descent. Finally, under the conditions of (iv),
it is clear that \(n_{E} u_{E} = u_{E} n_{E}\) and that this
automorphism of \(G\) respects the pinning; modulo the identification
made, it is therefore equal to its image in \(Autext(G)\); but \(n_{E}\)
is inner and \(u_{E}\) projects onto \(s_{G}\).

\textbf{Remark 3.16.7.} (i) One determines \(s_{G}\) explicitly in each
case of the classification thanks to (iii): for each irreducible pinned
root datum it suffices to compose the symmetry through the origin with
the symmetry in the Weyl group (i.e.~the element \(w_{0}\) of the Weyl
group such that \(w_{0}(\Delta) = -\Delta\)). One finds the following
results: one has \(s_{G} = e\) except for \(A_{n}\) (\(n \geqslant 2\)),
\(D_{n}\) (\(n\) odd) and \texttt{E\_6}, in which case \(s_{G}\) is the
unique non-trivial ``outer automorphism''.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  The automorphism \(u_{E}\) is the one used to construct ``the compact
  real forms'' in the theory of semisimple Lie algebras.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Remark 3.16.8.} We defined in 3.16.1 an involution in the
\(S\)-scheme \(Q = Isomint(G_{q-\acute{e}p.}, G)\) of quasi-pinnings of
\(G\) (cf.~3.12.1); by transport of structure from \(G_{q-\acute{e}p.}\)
to \(G\), one sees at once that this involution is given by the action
of an element of \(ad(G_{q-\acute{e}p.})(S)\): the element \(n_{0}\)
defined (3.16.2 (iii)) by the canonical quasi-pinning of
\(G_{q-\acute{e}p.}\).

In the same way, one has defined an involution in the \(S\)-scheme

\[
P = Isom_{S-gr.}(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), G)
\]

of \(R\)-pinnings of \(G\) (cf.~1.20). Arguing as before, one sees that
this involution is given by the action of the automorphism \(u_{0}\) of
\(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) defined (3.16.2 (iv)) by the canonical pinning of
\(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\).

\subsection{4. Isotriviality of reductive groups and of principal
bundles under reductive
groups}\label{isotriviality-of-reductive-groups-and-of-principal-bundles-under-reductive-groups}

\subsubsection{4.1. Definitions. Isotriviality
theorem}\label{definitions.-isotriviality-theorem}

\textbf{Definition 4.1.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme, \(P\) a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\).
One says that \(P\) is} locally isotrivial \emph{(resp.} semi-locally
isotrivial*) if for every point \(s \in S\) (resp. every finite set
\(F\) of points of \(S\) contained in an affine open set) there exist an
open set \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) (resp. \(F\)) and a finite
surjective étale morphism \(S' \to U\) such that \(P_{S'}\) is trivial.*

\textbf{Definition 4.1.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group. One says that \(G\) is} locally isotrivial
\emph{(resp.} semi-locally isotrivial*) if for every point \(s \in S\)
(resp. every finite set \(F\) of points of \(S\) contained in an affine
open set) there exist an open set \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) (resp.
\(F\)) and a finite surjective étale morphism \(S' \to U\) such that
\(G_{S'}\) is splittable.*

\textbf{Remark 4.1.3.} (i) The equivalence of categories 4.1.1 of 1.17
respects by definition local (resp. semi-local) isotriviality.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item
  Add to the conditions of 4.1.1: \(G\) locally of finite presentation
  over \(S\). Then the principal bundle \(P\) (or the reductive group
  \(G\)) is locally isotrivial (resp. semi-locally isotrivial) if and
  only if for every \(S' \to S\), \(S'\) local (resp. semi-local),
  \(P_{S'}\) is isotrivial (or \(G_{S'}\) isotrivial), that is to say,
  if there exists \(S'' \to S'\) finite surjective étale such that
