  \(P_{S''}\) is trivial (or \(G_{S''}\) split).
\item
  In the case of tori, definition 4.1.2 coincides with that of Exp. IX,
  1.1.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{4.1.4.}\label{section-281}

Recall (Exp. XXII, 4.3 and 6.2) that for every reductive group \(G\), we
have introduced the groups \(rad(G)\), \(corad(G)\) and
\(d\acute{e}r(G)\). The groups \(rad(G)\) and \(corad(G)\) are tori,
which are split when \(G\) is split; moreover, there exists an isogeny
\(rad(G) \to corad(G)\). The \(S\)-group \(d\acute{e}r(G)\) is
semisimple, one has \(G / d\acute{e}r(G) = corad(G)\); it follows that
for every principal homogeneous bundle \(P\) under \(G\),
\(P / d\acute{e}r(G)\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under
\(corad(G)\). This said, one has:

\textbf{Theorem 4.1.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group of constant type.}

\emph{(i) The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(a) \(G\) is locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial.}

\emph{(b) The torus \(rad(G)\) is.}

\emph{(b') The torus \(corad(G)\) is.}

\emph{(c) The Galois covering of \(S\) associated to \(G\) (3.11) is.}

\emph{If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), these conditions are also
equivalent to}

\emph{(d) The torus \(T\) is locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial.}

\emph{(ii) Let \(P\) be a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\); for
\(P\) to be locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial, it is necessary and
sufficient that the \(corad(G)\)-principal bundle \(P / d\acute{e}r(G)\)
be so.}

\textbf{Corollary 4.1.6.} \emph{The conditions of (i) are satisfied when
\(G\) is semisimple or when \(S\) is locally noetherian and normal (or
more generally geometrically unibranch). The conditions of (ii) are
satisfied when \(G\) is locally (resp. semi-locally) isotrivial.}

For (i), the first assertion is trivial from (b), the second follows
from (c) and Exp. X, 5.14 and 5.15. For (ii), it suffices to note that
by virtue of theorem 90, a principal bundle under a split torus is
semi-locally isotrivial.

\subsubsection{4.2. Proof: the semisimple
case}\label{proof-the-semisimple-case}

Let us first prove, for later reference:

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\) (resp. \(B\) a
Borel subgroup, resp. \(B \supset T\) a Killing couple of \(G\)), \(P\)
a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\), \(G'\) the twisted form of
\(G\) associated to \(P\) (via the morphism
\(int : G \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(G)\)). One has canonical
isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P / Norm\_G(T) ⥲ Tor(G\textquotesingle{}),    P / B ⥲ Bor(G\textquotesingle{}),    P / T ⥲ Kil(G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By construction, \(G'\) is the quotient of \(P \times_{S} G\) by a
certain action of \(G\) (\(((p, g')) g = (pg, g^{-1} g' g)\)); one
therefore has a morphism \(P \times_{S} G \to G'\), that is, a morphism

\[
P \to \operatorname{Hom}_{S}(G, G'),
\]

which, as one sees at once, factors through a morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : P → Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, G\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(to verify this assertion, one may assume \(G = P\), in which case one
has \(G' = G\), \(f = int\)). The set-theoretic map
\(p \mapsto f(p)(T)\) defines a morphism

\[
P \to Tor(G').
\]

To verify that this morphism induces an isomorphism
\(P / Norm_{G}(T) \xrightarrow{\sim} Tor(G')\) as announced, one may
again assume \(P = G\) in which case one is reduced to Exp. XXII, 5.8.3
(iii). (In fact, \emph{loc. cit.} should be replaced by the statement
above.) One argues similarly for \texttt{Bor} and \texttt{Kil}.

\textbf{Proposition 4.2.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme,
\(G\) an \(S\)-semisimple group of constant type.}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is isotrivial.}

\emph{(ii) Every principal bundle under \(G\) is isotrivial.}

Let us prove (i). Up to making a finite surjective étale extension of
the base, one may, by 3.9.2, assume \(G\) quasi-split. But then \(G\) is
isotrivial by construction (3.11, the group \(E\) being finite). To
prove (ii), one may, by (i), assume \(G\) split; one is then reduced to:

\textbf{Lemma 4.2.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme. Every
principal bundle under a split reductive group is isotrivial.}

Indeed, with the notation of 4.2.1, where \(B \supset T\) denotes the
canonical Killing couple of the split \(G\), the \(S\)-scheme
\(Kil(G')\) possesses a section, after finite surjective étale extension
of the base, by 3.9.2. One may therefore reduce the structure group of
\(G\) to \(T\); but \(T\) is split, so \(H^{1}(S, T) = 0\) (theorem 90).

\textbf{Corollary 4.2.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and}

\[
1 \to G \to G' \to G'' \to 1
\]

\emph{an exact sequence of \(S\)-group schemes (for (fpqc)), \(G\) being
semisimple of constant type. Let \(P\) be a principal homogeneous bundle
under \(G'\), suppose the sheaf\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced
  ``bundle'' by ``sheaf'', and then \(G'\) by
  \texttt{G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}.} \(P / G\) associated
representable (for example
\texttt{G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} affine over \(S\)). For
\(P\) to be locally isotrivial (resp. semi-locally isotrivial), it is
necessary and sufficient that \(P / G\) be so (as bundle under
\texttt{G\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}).}

If \(P\) is trivial, \(P / G\) is too, which shows that the condition is
necessary. Conversely, suppose \(S\) local (resp. semi-local) and
\(P / G\) isotrivial, so trivialized by a finite surjective étale
extension \(S'\) of \(S\). Extending the base to \(S'\), one may reduce
the structure group of \(P_{S'}\) to \(G_{S'}\). But \(S'\) is still
semi-local and \(G_{S'}\) semisimple of constant type, so the obtained
bundle is isotrivial (4.2.2).

\subsubsection{4.3. Proof: general case.}\label{proof-general-case.}

Let us first note that 4.1.5 (ii) follows at once from the application
of 4.2.4 to the exact sequence

\[
1 \to d\acute{e}r(G) \to G \to corad(G) \to 1.
\]

Let us therefore prove (i). If \(G\) is split, \(rad(G)\) and
\(corad(G)\) are split, as is \(rev(G)\); so (a) implies (b), (b'), and
(c).

\paragraph{4.3.1.}\label{section-282}

One has (c) ⇒ (a). Let \(R\) be the type of \(G\); one has an exact
sequence

\[
1 \to ad(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)) \to A_{S}(R) \to E_{S} \to 1.
\]

Applying 4.2.4 to the bundle \(P = Isom_{S-gr.}(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), G)\)
and to the associated bundle \(rev(G) = P / ad(\acute{E}p_{S}(R))\), one
has (c) ⇒ (a).

\paragraph{4.3.2.}\label{section-283}

One has (b) ⇒ (a). It suffices to prove that if \(rad(G)\) is split,
\(G\) is semi-locally isotrivial. Now let \(G_{0} = \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\);
consider the category of pairs \texttt{(G\textquotesingle{},\ f)}, where
\(G'\) is a form of \texttt{G\_0} and \(f\) is an isomorphism of
\(rad(G_{0})\) onto \(rad(G)\).

One knows (2.16) that this category is equivalent to the category of
principal homogeneous bundles under a certain \(S\)-group \(H\)
extension of a finite twisted constant group by a semisimple group. It
suffices to prove that every principal bundle under \(H\) is
semi-locally isotrivial; this follows at once from 4.2.4.

\paragraph{4.3.3.}\label{section-284}

One has (b') ⇒ (a). One can argue as previously (it will moreover be the
same group \(H\) that arises). One can also see that (b) and (b') are
equivalent: a torus isogenous to a locally split torus is also locally
split (cf.~Exp. IX, 2.11 (iii)).

\paragraph{4.3.4.}\label{section-285}

One has (d) ⇒ (a). It suffices to prove that a group of constant type
possessing a split maximal torus is semi-locally isotrivial; this
follows at once from 2.14.

\paragraph{4.3.5.}\label{section-286}

One has (a) ⇒ (d). It suffices to prove that a maximal torus of a split
group is semi-locally isotrivial. More precisely:

\textbf{Lemma 4.3.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \texttt{T\_0} a split maximal torus of \(G\),
\(W_{0} = Norm_{G}(T_{0}) / T_{0}\) (this is a locally constant
\(S\)-group, constant if \(G\) is of constant type, by 2.14), \(T\) a
maximal torus of \(G\).}

\emph{There exists a morphism \(S' \to S\) which is principal
homogeneous under \texttt{W\_0} (hence étale finite and surjective, and
even principal Galois if \(G\) is of constant type) such that \(T_{S'}\)
is conjugate to \((T_{0})_{S'}\) by an element of \(G(S')\) (and so in
particular split).}

Indeed, one knows that \(Transp_{G}(T_{0}, T)\) is a principal
homogeneous bundle under \(Norm_{G}(T_{0})\) (cf.~for example Exp. XI,
5.4 bis). Set \(S' = Transp_{G}(T_{0}, T) / T_{0}\); this is a principal
homogeneous bundle under \texttt{W\_0}. Extending the base from \(S\) to
\(S'\), one can reduce the structure group of \(Transp_{G}(T_{0}, T)\)
to \texttt{T\_0}. Now \(S'\) is semi-local and \texttt{T\_0} split, so
\(Transp_{G}(T_{0}, T)\) possesses a section over \(S'\).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  by ``theorem 90''.} QED

\subsubsection{4.4. Use of the existence of maximal
tori}\label{use-of-the-existence-of-maximal-tori}

Using Grothendieck's existence theorem for maximal tori (Exp. XIV,
3.20), one can considerably sharpen the preceding results. Let us state
at once:

\textbf{Theorem 4.4.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(R\) a
pinned reduced root datum, \(W\) its Weyl group, \(E\) the group of its
automorphisms. (Recall that \(E\) operates naturally on \(W\) and that
the semi-direct product \(A = W \cdot E\) is identified with the group
of automorphisms of \(R\) non-pinned, cf.~Exp. XXI, 6.7.2).}

\emph{(i) Every principal homogeneous bundle under \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\)
is trivialized by a principal Galois covering \(S' \to S\) of group
\(W\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group of type \(R\); let
\(rev(G) = Isomext(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), G)\) be the associated Galois
covering of \(S\) with group \(E\). Let \texttt{W\_0} be the form of
\texttt{W\_S} associated to \(rev(G)\). There exists a morphism
\(S' \to S\), which is a principal homogeneous bundle under
\texttt{W\_0}, such that \(G_{S'}\) is quasi-splittable (i.e.~possesses
a Borel subgroup).}

\emph{(iii) Every \(S\)-reductive group of type \(R\) is split by a
principal Galois covering \(\tilde{S} \to S\) with group \(A\).}

Let us first state:

\textbf{Proposition 4.4.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(P\) a principal
homogeneous bundle under \(G\), \(G'\) the twisted form of \(G\)
associated to \(P\) (one then has, cf.~4.2.1, a canonical isomorphism
\(P / Norm_{G}(T) \xrightarrow{\sim} Tor(G')\)). Let \(T'\) be a maximal
torus of \(G'\), defining a composite morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{S → Tor(G\textquotesingle{}) ⥲ P / Norm\_G(T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Consider the canonical morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P → P/T → P / Norm\_G(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and take their inverse images by the preceding morphism:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{   P  →  P/T  →  P / Norm\_G(T)}
\NormalTok{   ↑      ↑           ↑}
\NormalTok{   H  →   S\textquotesingle{}  →       S.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Then \(S'\) (resp. \(H\)) is a principal homogeneous bundle over
\(S\) (resp. \(S'\)) under \(W_{G}(T)\) (resp. \(T_{S'}\)). Moreover, if
one makes \(W_{G}(T)\) operate on \(T\) in the obvious way, the bundle
associated to \(S'\) is isomorphic to \(T'\).}

The first two assertions are trivial, the last is proved like the
corresponding assertion of 2.6.

\textbf{Corollary 4.4.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\)
an \(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). Suppose one of
the two following conditions is satisfied:}

\emph{(i) \(T\) is split.}

\emph{(ii) \(T\) is contained in a Borel subgroup of \(G\), and \(G\) is
either adjoint, or simply connected.}

\emph{Let moreover \(P\) be a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\).
There exists an \(S\)-scheme \(S'\), which is a principal homogeneous
bundle under \(W_{G}(T)\), such that \(P_{S'}\) is trivial.}

Indeed, if \(G'\) is the form of \(G\) associated to \(P\), then \(G'\)
possesses a maximal torus \(T'\) (Exp. XIV, 3.20). Resuming the notation
of the preceding proposition, one sees that \(H^{1}(S', T_{S'}) = 0\)
(by theorem 90 for (i), by 3.14 for (ii)). The morphism \(H \to S'\)
possesses a section, so \(P_{S'}\) also possesses a section over \(S'\).
QED

Let us now prove the theorem. Assertion (i) is a particular case of the
preceding corollary (take \(G = \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\), endowed with its
canonical split torus). Let us prove (ii). One knows (3.12) that \(G\)
is an inner twisted form of

\[
G_{0} = Q-\acute{E}p_{rev(G)/S}(R).
\]

If \texttt{T\_0} is the canonical maximal torus of \texttt{G\_0},
\(W_{G_{0}}(T_{0})\) is the group \texttt{W\_0} described in the
statement. The form \(G\) of \texttt{G\_0} corresponds to a principal
homogeneous bundle \(P\) under \(ad(G_{0})\)
(\(P = Isomint(G_{0}, G)\)). The group \(W_{ad(G_{0})}(T^{ad}_{0})\) is
canonically isomorphic to \texttt{W\_0}, and one obtains the wanted
result by applying 4.4.3 to the situation
\((ad(G_{0}), T^{ad}_{0}, P)\), hypothesis (ii) of 4.4.3 being well
verified. Let us finally prove (iii). Resume the notation of (ii); one
has a diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{              rev(G)}
\NormalTok{              ↗     ↘}
\NormalTok{            E\_S      W\_0}
\NormalTok{              ↘     ↗}
\NormalTok{                S\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One knows that \(G_{S'}\) is isomorphic to \((G_{0})_{S'}\) and that
\((G_{0})_{rev(G)}\) is splittable. If one sets
\(\tilde{S} = S' \times_{S} rev(G)\), \(G_{\tilde{S}}\) is splittable,
and it only remains to verify that \(\tilde{S}\) is indeed a principal
Galois covering of \(S\) with group \(A\), which follows from the
following more general lemma (naturally valid in any site):

\textbf{Lemma 4.4.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(H\) two
\(S\)-group schemes, \(G \to \operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(H)\) an action
of \(G\) on \(H\), \(E\) a \(G\)-principal homogeneous bundle, \(F\) an
\texttt{H\_0}-principal homogeneous bundle, where \texttt{H\_0} is the
form of \(H\) associated to \(E\). Then \(E \times_{S} F\) is endowed
naturally with a structure of principal homogeneous bundle under the
semi-direct product \(H \cdot G\).}

Write \((e, g) \mapsto eg\) (resp. \((f, u) \mapsto f u\)) for the
action (on the right) of \(G\) on \(E\) (resp. of \texttt{H\_0} on
\(F\)). Write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p : E ×\_S H → H\_0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for the canonical projection (\texttt{H\_0} is by definition the
quotient of \(E \times_{S} H\) by \(G\) acting on it by the formula
\((e, h) g = (eg, g^{-1} h g)\)). Consider the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{r : E ×\_S F ×\_S H ×\_S G → E ×\_S F}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined set-theoretically by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{r(e, f, h, g) = (eg, f · p(e, h)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The morphism \(r\) indeed defines an action of the semi-direct product
\(H \cdot G\) on \(E \times_{S} F\). Indeed, one has set-theoretically

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{r(r(e, f, h, g), h\textquotesingle{}, g\textquotesingle{}) = (egg\textquotesingle{}, f p(e, h) p(eg, h\textquotesingle{}));}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p(e, h) p(eg, h\textquotesingle{}) = p(e, h) p(e, g h\textquotesingle{} g\^{}\{{-}1\}) = p(e, h g h\textquotesingle{} g\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{r(r(e, f, h, g), h\textquotesingle{}, g\textquotesingle{}) = r(e, f, h g h\textquotesingle{} g\^{}\{{-}1\}, g g\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which had to be proved.

To prove now that this law is indeed a law of principal homogeneous
bundle, one may assume that \(E\) and \(F\) are trivial, in which case
one sees at once that \(E \times_{S} F\) is also a trivial bundle.

\subsubsection[4.5. Isotriviality of maximal tori of semisimple
groups]{\texorpdfstring{4.5. Isotriviality of maximal tori of semisimple
groups\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added this no 4.5.}}{4.5. Isotriviality of maximal tori of semisimple groups}}\label{isotriviality-of-maximal-tori-of-semisimple-groupsn.d.e-xxiv-26}

Let us bring out here the following result, contained implicitly in 2.6
(cf.~the N.D.E. (13)) and which was mentioned at the end of Exp. IX 1.2.
Recall (XXIII 5.11) that, for every scheme \(S\) and every reduced root
datum \(R\), one writes \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R)\) for the unique pinned
\(S\)-group of type \(R\) (which exists by Exp. XXV) and \(T_{S}(R)\)
its canonical maximal torus.

\textbf{Proposition 4.5.1.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an \(S\)-semisimple group
of constant type \(R\); assume that \(G\) possesses a maximal torus
\(T\) (which is the case if \(S\) is semi-local, by XIV 3.20).}

\emph{(i) Then
\(P = Isom_{S-gr.}(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), T_{S}(R); G, T) / T_{S}(R)_{ad}\)
is a principal \(S\)-bundle under the finite group
\(\operatorname{Aut}(R)\), and \texttt{T\_P} is a split maximal torus of
\texttt{G\_P}. Consequently, \(T\) is isotrivial.}

\emph{(ii) Moreover, for every finite set \(F\) of points of \(P\)
contained in an affine open set, there exists an open set \(U\) of \(P\)
containing \(F\) such that \texttt{G\_U} is split.}

\emph{Proof.} The exact sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → T\_S(R)\_\{ad\} → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Ép\_S(R), T\_S(R)) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T\_S(R))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

induces for every \(S' \to S\) a morphism of bundles
\(P_{S'} \to Isom_{S'-gr.}(T_{S'}(R), T_{S'})\), so if \(P_{S'}\)
possesses a section, then \(T_{S'}(R)\) and \(T_{S'}\) are isomorphic.
This is in particular the case for \(S' = P\).

Note moreover that
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(\acute{E}p_{S}(R), T_{S}(R)) / T_{S}(R)_{ad}\)
is none other than the constant \(S\)-group
\(\operatorname{Aut}(R)_{S}\), and that \(P\) is identified with the
\(\operatorname{Aut}(R)_{S}\)-torsor \(Isom(R, \tilde{R}(G, T))\), where
\(\tilde{R}(G, T)\) denotes the twisted root datum associated to
\((G, T)\) (cf.~XXII 1.10).

Then (ii) follows from (i) and from 2.14, taking into account the fact
that the \(g_{\alpha}\) (\(\alpha\) ranging over the roots of \(R\)) are
free \texttt{O\_U}-modules of rank 1 on a sufficiently small affine open
set \(U\) containing \(F\).

\subsection{5. Canonical decomposition of an adjoint or simply connected
group}\label{canonical-decomposition-of-an-adjoint-or-simply-connected-group}

In this section, we shall use the results of no 1 to generalize to the
case of schemes a classical decomposition of adjoint (resp. simply
connected) groups. So as not to overburden the exposition indefinitely,
the proofs are sketched and the details are left to the reader; in fact
it is always a matter of absolutely standard proofs in the theory of
principal bundles: reduction of the structure group, twisting, etc.

\subsubsection{5.1.}\label{section-287}

Recall (Exp. XXI, 7.4) that a Dynkin diagram is a disjoint union of its
connected components, which are Dynkin diagrams. Moreover, every
non-empty connected Dynkin diagram corresponding to a root datum is
isomorphic to one of the standard diagrams (\(A_{n}\), \(B_{n}\),
\ldots, \texttt{G\_2}) which were exhibited in Exp. XXI, 7.4.6. In the
sequel, we shall be interested only in Dynkin diagrams whose connected
components are of one of the preceding types. Let \(T\) be the set of
these standard diagrams. For every Dynkin diagram \(D\), let
\(n(t) = n_{D}(t)\) be the number of connected components of \(D\)
isomorphic to \(t\), where \(t \in T\). The \emph{type} of \(D\) is by
definition \(\sum_{t \in T} n_{D}(t) \cdot t\).

A Dynkin diagram of type \(t\) is said to be \emph{simple of type
\(t\)}, a Dynkin diagram of type \(n \cdot t\) is said to be
\emph{isotypic of type \(t\)}. Let \texttt{D\_0} be the set of connected
components of \(D\) and let

\[
a : D_{0} \to T
\]

be the obvious map. The type of \(D\) is none other than
\(\sum_{x \in D_{0}} a(x)\).

\subsubsection{5.2.}\label{section-288}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(D\) an \(S\)-Dynkin scheme (verifying the
restrictive condition stated above). The cokernel of the pair of
morphisms \(L \Rightarrow D\) (\(L =\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have replaced
  \(R\) by \(L\), as in 3.2.} scheme of bonds of \(D\)) is written
\texttt{D\_0}. This is the ``scheme of connected components'' of \(D\)
(it

exists trivially when \(D\) is constant; the general case is deduced
from this by descent); it is a finite twisted constant \(S\)-scheme. One
has a canonical morphism

\[
a : D_{0} \to T_{S}.
\]

For \(t \in T\), set \(a^{-1}(t) = D_{0, t}\); this is a subscheme of
\texttt{D\_0}, whose inverse image in \(D\), written \(D_{t}\), is the
\emph{isotypic component of type \(t\)} of the Dynkin scheme \(D\). Each
\(D_{t}\) is a subscheme of \(D\), and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D = ⨿\_\{t ∈ T\} D\_t.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note that the degree of \(D_{0, t}\) at \(s \in S\) is \(n(s, t)\), if
the type of \(D\) at \(s\) is \(\sum_{t} n(s, t) \cdot t\).

\subsubsection{5.3.}\label{section-289}

In what follows, we shall consider only semisimple adjoint (resp. simply
connected) groups. To simplify the language, we shall state the results
for adjoint groups; all statements will remain valid if one substitutes
everywhere ``simply connected'' for ``adjoint''.

Recall that an adjoint reduced root datum is determined up to
isomorphism by the type of its Dynkin diagrams. We shall therefore say
that an adjoint root datum \(R\) (resp. a semisimple adjoint group
\(G\)) is \emph{of type \(\sum n(t) \cdot t\)} if its Dynkin diagrams
are (resp. if its type is given by an adjoint root datum of type
\(\sum n(t) \cdot t\)). We shall say that \(R\) or \(G\) is \emph{simple
of type \(t\)} (resp. \emph{isotypic of type \(t\)}) if its type is
\(t\) (resp. \(n \cdot t\), \(n > 0\)).

If \(G\) is a semisimple adjoint group, we shall use the symbols
\(Dyn_{0}(G)\) and \(Dyn_{0, t}(G)\) in the sense defined in 5.2.

\subsubsection{5.4.}\label{section-290}

Let \(t_{i}\), \texttt{i\ =\ 1,\ 2,\ ...,\ n}, be distinct elements of
\(T\), and let \(R_{i}\) be a pinned adjoint root datum isotypic of type
\(t_{i}\). Consider the product
\(R = R_{1} \times \cdot\cdot\cdot \times R_{n}\) (Exp. XXI, 6.4.1). Let
\(S\) be a scheme such that the different \(\acute{E}p_{S}(R_{i})\)
exist (cf.~Exp. XXV). One verifies at once that there exists a canonical
isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(*)    Ép\_S(R) = Ép\_S(R\_1) ×\_S ··· ×\_S Ép\_S(R\_n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Moreover, if \(E_{i}\) denotes the group of automorphisms of \(R_{i}\),
\(E\) the group of automorphisms of \(R\), \(D_{i}\) (resp. \(D\)) the
Dynkin diagram of \(R_{i}\) (resp. \(R\)), one has isomorphisms:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E\_i ≃ Aut(D\_i),    D = ⨿ D\_i,    E ≃ ∏ E\_i ≃ Aut(D).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Combining with (*) and 1.4, one sees that (*) induces an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A\_S(R) ≃ A\_S(R\_1) ×\_S ··· ×\_S A\_S(R\_n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Proposition 5.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-semisimple adjoint group. There exists a unique decomposition}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ≃ ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} G\_t,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(G_{t}\) is an \(S\)-semisimple adjoint group isotypic of
type \(t\). Moreover, the preceding decomposition induces isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Dyn\_t(G) ≃ Dyn(G\_t),    Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G) ≃ ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G\_t).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This has indeed been proved above when \(G\) is split. In the general
case, one may assume \(G\) of constant type \(R\). Using the preceding
decomposition of \(A_{S}(R)\) and 1.17, one deduces the wanted
decomposition of \(G\). The other results are then proved by descent.

\textbf{Remark 5.6.} More generally, if \(G\) and \(H\) are two
semisimple adjoint groups, one has canonical isomorphisms as follows
(the diagram is commutative):

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H)            ⥲    ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} Isom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G\_t, H\_t)}
\NormalTok{       ↓                                              ↓}
\NormalTok{Isomext(G, H)                  ⥲    ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} Isomext(G\_t, H\_t)}
\NormalTok{       ≀                                              ≀}
\NormalTok{       ↓                                              ↓}
\NormalTok{Isom\_\{Dyn\}(Dyn(G), Dyn(H))    ⥲    ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} Isom\_\{Dyn\}(Dyn(G\_t), Dyn(H\_t)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 5.7.} One can give an intrinsic characterization of
\(G_{t}\), which we state below without proof: it is the largest
reductive subgroup of \(G\) invariant (and moreover characteristic) and
isotypic of type \(t\).

The preceding proposition allows one to reduce the study of semisimple
adjoint groups to that of isotypic semisimple adjoint groups. It is this
study that we shall now undertake.

\subsubsection{5.8.}\label{section-291}

Let \(R\) be a pinned reduced adjoint simple root datum of type \(t\),
\(I\) a nonempty finite set, \(R^{I}\) the product root datum of copies
\(R_{i}\) of \(R\), for \(i \in I\). Write \(E\) for the group of
automorphisms of \(R\), which is identified with the group of
automorphisms of the Dynkin diagram \(D\) of \(R\). The Dynkin diagram
of \(R^{I}\) is identified with \(D^{I}\), which shows that one has an
exact sequence:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → Aut(D)\^{}I → Aut(D\^{}I) → Aut(I) → 1,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\operatorname{Aut}(I)\) denotes the group of permutations of
\(I\). It follows that the canonical isomorphism

\[
\acute{E}p_{S}(R)^{I} \simeq \acute{E}p_{S}(R^{I})
\]

induces an exact sequence

\[
1 \to A_{S}(R)^{I} \to A_{S}(R^{I}) \to \operatorname{Aut}(I_{S}) \to 1,
\]

the last group being the \(S\)-constant group associated to
\(\operatorname{Aut}(I)\). Note moreover that \(I\) is canonically
identified with the set of connected components of \(D^{I}\).

If \(G\) is an \(S\)-semisimple group of type \(R^{I}\), defining
(cf.~1.17) a principal homogeneous bundle \(P\) under \(A_{S}(R^{I})\),
the definition of \(Dyn(G)\) by descent (3.7), and that of
\(Dyn_{0}(G)\) (5.2), shows that the bundle associated to \(P\) by the
morphism \(A_{S}(R^{I}) \to \operatorname{Aut}(I_{S})\) is none other
than \(Isom_{S}(I_{S}, Dyn_{0}(G))\), corresponding to the form
\(Dyn_{0}(G)\) of \texttt{I\_S}. Using again the equivalence of
categories 1.17 and the preceding exact sequence, one deduces by a
formal argument that there exists a \(Dyn_{0}(G)\)-reductive group of
type \(R\), say \texttt{G\_0}, and an \(S\)-isomorphism
\(G \simeq \prod_{Dyn_{0}(G)/S} G_{0}\).

\textbf{Proposition 5.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-semisimple adjoint group isotypic of type \(t\). There exist a
\(Dyn_{0}(G)\)-semisimple adjoint group \texttt{G\_0} simple of type
\(t\), and an \(S\)-isomorphism (unique)}

\[
G \simeq \prod_{Dyn_{0}(G)/S} G_{0}.
\]

\emph{Moreover, this isomorphism induces an exact sequence}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → ∏\_\{Dyn\_0(G)/S\} Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G\_0) → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G) → Aut\_S(Dyn\_0(G)) → 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One may evidently assume \(G\) of constant type \(n \cdot t\). The first
assertion has already been proved (the uniqueness assertion is evident).
The second is then deduced from the split case by descent.

One can combine 5.5 and 5.9:

\textbf{Proposition 5.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-semisimple adjoint group, \(D = Dyn(G)\) its Dynkin scheme.}

\emph{(i) There exists a canonical decomposition}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{G ≃ ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} ∏\_\{D\_\{0, t\}/S\} G\_\{0, t\} ≃ ∏\_\{Dyn\_0(G)/S\} G\_0,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where each \(G_{0, t}\) is a \(Dyn_{0, t}(G)\)-simple adjoint
group of type \(t\) (resp. where \texttt{G\_0} is a
\(Dyn_{0}(G)\)-semisimple adjoint group whose type at
\(x \in Dyn_{0}(G)\) is \(a(x) \in T\) (the morphism
\(a : Dyn_{0}(G) \to T_{S}\) was defined in 5.2)).}

\emph{(ii) The preceding decompositions induce isomorphic exact
sequences (written vertically), where
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S, a}(D_{0})\) denotes the scheme of automorphisms
of \(Dyn_{0}(G)\) which commute with the morphism
\(a : Dyn_{0}(G) \to T_{S}\):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                  1                              1}
\NormalTok{                  ↓                              ↓}
\NormalTok{   ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} ∏\_\{D\_\{0, t\}/S\} Aut\_gr.(G\_\{0, t\}) ⥲ ∏\_\{Dyn\_0(G)/S\} Aut\_gr.(G\_0)}
\NormalTok{                  ↓                              ↓}
\NormalTok{        Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G)                    →     Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G)}
\NormalTok{                  ↓                              ↓}
\NormalTok{   ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} Aut\_S(Dyn\_\{0, t\}(G))           ⥲  Aut\_\{S, a\}(Dyn\_0(G))}
\NormalTok{                  ↓                              ↓}
\NormalTok{                  1                              1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Corollary 5.11.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, the three
following categories are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) the category of principal homogeneous bundles under \(G\).}

\emph{(ii) the category of principal homogeneous bundles under
\texttt{G\_0}.}

\emph{(iii) the product category, for \(t \in T\), of the categories of
principal homogeneous bundles under the \(G_{0, t}\).}

This is deduced formally from the preceding decompositions and from 8.4.

\textbf{Corollary 5.12.} \emph{One has canonical isomorphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Tor(G) ≃ ∏\_\{t ∈ T\} ∏\_\{D\_\{0, t\}/S\} Tor(G\_\{0, t\}) ≃ ∏\_\{Dyn\_0(G)/S\} Tor(G\_0),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{and similarly replacing \texttt{Tor} by \texttt{Bor} (resp.
\texttt{Kil}).}

Trivial starting from the split case.

\textbf{Remark 5.13.} The canonical morphism

\[
Dyn(G) \to Dyn_{0}(G)
\]

allows one to consider \(Dyn(G)\) as a \(Dyn_{0}(G)\)-Dynkin scheme; in
fact it is the Dynkin scheme \(Dyn(G_{0})\) of \texttt{G\_0}.

Similarly if \(T \subset B\) is a Killing couple of \(G\), corresponding
canonically to the Killing couple \(T_{0} \subset B_{0}\) of
\texttt{G\_0}, one verifies that the obstructions to the quasi-splitting
of \(G\) and \texttt{G\_0}, which lie (3.9) in
\texttt{Pic(Dyn(G))\ =\ Pic(Dyn(G\_0))} coincide. One deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 5.14.} \emph{The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(G\) is quasi-splittable,}

\emph{(ii) \texttt{G\_0} is quasi-splittable,}

\emph{(iii) each \(G_{0, t}\), \(t \in T\), is quasi-splittable.}

\subsection{6. Automorphisms of Borel subgroups of reductive
groups}\label{automorphisms-of-borel-subgroups-of-reductive-groups}

\textbf{Lemma 6.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a
split \(S\)-group, \(\Delta\) a system of simple roots of \(R\), and
\(B\) the corresponding Borel subgroup. Then \(B_{u}\) is generated as
(fppf) group sheaf by the \(U_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in \Delta\).}

Let \(H\) be the group subsheaf of \(B_{u}\) generated by the
\(U_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in \Delta\). Let us prove
\(H \supset U_{\beta}\) (\(\beta \in R^{+}\)) by induction on the
integer \(ord(\beta) = ord_{\Delta}(\beta) > 0\) (cf.~Exp. XXI, 3.2.15).
The assertion is verified by hypothesis for \(ord(\beta) = 1\). Suppose
then \(ord(\beta) > 1\) and \(U_{\gamma} \subset H\) as soon as
\(ord(\gamma) < ord(\beta)\). There exists \(\alpha \in \Delta\) such
that \(\beta - \alpha \in R^{+}\) (Exp. XXI, 3.1.1). Let \(p\) be the
largest integer such that \(\beta - p \alpha = \beta' \in R^{+}\). One
has \(U_{\alpha}, U_{\beta'} \subset H\), \(\beta' - \alpha \notin R\).
One is therefore reduced to proving:

\textbf{Lemma 6.2.} \emph{Resume the notation of Exp. XXIII, 6.4.
Suppose \(p = 1\), that is, \(\beta - \alpha\) not a root. If \(H\) is a
group subsheaf of \(B_{u}\) such that
\(U_{\alpha}, U_{\beta} \subset H\), then
\(U_{i\alpha + j\beta} \subset H\) whenever \(i\alpha + j\beta \in R\),
\(i > 0\), \(j > 0\).}

Let us distinguish four cases according to the value of
\(q = 0, 1, 2, 3\). In the sequel \(x\) and \(y\) denote two arbitrary
sections of \(G_{a, S'}\), \(S' \to S\).

If \(q = 0\), there is nothing to prove.

If \(q = 1\), one has
\(p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm x) = p_{\beta}(-y) p_{\alpha}(-x) p_{\beta}(y) p_{\alpha}(x) \in H(S')\),
so \(U_{\alpha+\beta} \subset H\).

If \(q = 2\), one similarly has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{α+β\}(±xy) p\_\{2α+β\}(±x²y) = p\_β(−y) p\_α(−x) p\_β(y) p\_α(x) ∈ H(S\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, up to changing certain signs,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(x, y) = p\_\{α+β\}(xy) p\_\{2α+β\}(x²y) ∈ H(S\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(p_{\alpha+\beta}\) and \(p_{2\alpha+\beta}\) commute, one then
has \(F(x, 1) F(1, -x) = p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^{2} - x)\).\footnote{N.D.E.:
  We have corrected \(F(-1, x)\) to \(F(1, -x)\).} If
\(a \in G_{a}(S)\), the equation \(X^{2} - X = a\) defines a free
surjective extension of \(S\) (this is
\(\operatorname{Spec} O_{S}[X]/(X^{2} - X - a)\)); one therefore has
\(p_{2\alpha+\beta}(a) \in H(S')\) so \(U_{2\alpha+\beta} \subset H\),
hence also \(U_{\alpha+\beta} \subset H\) (since \(F(1, a) \in H(S')\)).

If \(q = 3\), one similarly has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(x, y) = p\_\{α+β\}(xy) p\_\{2α+β\}(x²y) p\_\{3α+β\}(x³y) p\_\{3α+2β\}(x³y²) ∈ H(S\textquotesingle{});}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{3α+2β\}(±x) = F(1, 1)\^{}\{{-}1\} p\_β(−x) F(1, 1) p\_β(x) ∈ H(S\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one obtains that \(U_{3\alpha+2\beta} \subset H\) and so

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{K(x, y) = p\_\{α+β\}(xy) p\_\{2α+β\}(x²y) p\_\{3α+β\}(x³y) ∈ H(S\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Computing then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{K(x + y, 1) K(−x, 1) K(1, y)\^{}\{{-}1\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

modulo \(U_{3\alpha+2\beta}\), one finds

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_\{2α+β\}(2x² + y² + 2xy − y) p\_\{3α+β\}(y³ + 3xy² + 3x²y − y) ∈ H(S\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(a \in G_{a}(S)\), the ``equations''

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x² = −xy − y + 1 − a}
\NormalTok{y² = 3y − 2 + 3a}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

define a free surjective extension of \(S\); one then has
\(y^{3} + 3xy^{2} + 3x^{2}y - y = 0\) and the preceding expression gives
\(p_{2\alpha+\beta}(a) \in H(S')\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected
  \(p_{3\alpha+\beta}(a)\) to \(p_{2\alpha+\beta}(a)\), and detailed the
  end of the argument.} One has thus proved that \(H\) contains
\(U_{2\alpha+\beta}\) and \(U_{3\alpha+2\beta}\) and that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E(x, y) = p\_\{α+β\}(xy) p\_\{3α+β\}(x³y) ∈ H(S\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\) and \(p_{3\alpha+\beta}\) commute, one is
reduced to the preceding computation, i.e.
\(E(1, x) E(1, -x) = p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x^{3} - x)\), whence
\(U_{3\alpha+\beta} \subset H\), then \(U_{\alpha+\beta} \subset H\).

\textbf{Remark 6.2.1.} The preceding proof shows that one could have
replaced the hypothesis ``\(H\) contains \(U_{\alpha}\) and
\(U_{\beta}\)'' by ``\(H\) contains \(U_{\alpha}\) or \(U_{\beta}\), and
\(H\) is invariant under \(int(U_{\alpha})\) and \(int(U_{\beta})\)''.

\textbf{Theorem 6.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two
\(S\)-semisimple groups, \(B\) (resp. \(B'\)) a Borel subgroup of \(G\)
(resp. \(G'\)). Every isomorphism \(B \xrightarrow{\sim} B'\) is induced
by a unique isomorphism \(G \xrightarrow{\sim} G'\).}

The assertion is local for the étale topology and one may assume \(G\)
split: \(G = (G, T, M, R)\), \(B\) being defined by the system of
positive roots \(R^{+}\) of \(R\). The given isomorphism
\(u : B \xrightarrow{\sim} B'\) induces an isomorphism of \(T\) onto a
maximal torus \(T'\) of \(B'\), hence of \(G'\). The given isomorphism
\(T \simeq D_{S}(M)\) gives an isomorphism \(T' \simeq D_{S}(M)\) in
which the elements of \(R^{+}\) become the constant roots of \(B'\) with
respect to \(T'\), hence the elements of \(R\) the constant roots of
\(G'\) with respect to \(T'\). Since \(G\) and \(G'\) are semisimple,
the coroots are determined by duality (Exp. XXI, 1.2.5), which proves
that \texttt{(T\textquotesingle{},\ M,\ R)} is a splitting of \(G'\)
such that \(R(G) = R(G')\).

Applying Exp. XXIII, 5.1 (uniqueness theorem), one deduces that there
exists a unique isomorphism \(G \xrightarrow{\sim} G'\) coinciding with
\(u\) on \(T\) and the \(U_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha \in \Delta\). By 5.1,
the restriction of this isomorphism to \(B\) is \(u\). QED

\textbf{Remark 6.3.1.} (i) Using Exp. XXII, 4.1.9 and arguing as in
\emph{loc. cit.} 4.2.12, one can in the statement of the theorem replace
``isomorphism'' by ``isogeny'' (resp. ``central isogeny'').

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  The theorem is false for reductive groups. Take for example
  \(G = G' = SL_{2} \times G_{m}\) identified with the group of matrices
  below:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\{ ( a b 0 )}
\NormalTok{  ( c d 0 ) : ad − bc = 1, h invertible \};}
\NormalTok{  ( 0 0 h ) }
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

take for \(B = B'\) the Borel subgroup defined by \(c = 0\) and for
\(u\) the automorphism of \(B\) below:
\(u(a, b, d, h) = (a, b, d, ah)\).

\textbf{Corollary 6.4.} \emph{The functor \((G, B) \mapsto B\) from the
category formed by pairs \((G, B)\), where \(G\) is an \(S\)-semisimple
group and \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\), to the category of
\(S\)-group schemes (morphisms being isomorphisms) is fully faithful.}

\textbf{Corollary 6.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-semisimple group, \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\), \(B'\) an
\(S\)-group locally isomorphic to \(B\) for (fpqc). Then \(B'\) is
locally isomorphic to \(B\) for the local finite étale
topology\footnote{N.D.E.: denoted (étf) in Exp. IV 6.3. In other words,
  for every \(s \in S\) there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(s\)
  and a finite surjective étale morphism \(V \to U\) such that
  \(B' \times_{S} V \simeq B \times_{S} V\).} and there exists an
\(S\)-semisimple group \(G'\) of which \(B'\) is a Borel subgroup;
\(G'\) is unique up to a unique isomorphism inducing the identity on
\(B'\).}

\textbf{Corollary 6.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-semisimple group, \(B\) a Borel subgroup of \(G\). Then
\(\operatorname{Aut}_{S-gr.}(B)\) is representable by an affine and
smooth \(S\)-scheme, \(Autext(B)\) is representable by an étale and
finite \(S\)-scheme, and the obvious morphisms induce an isomorphism of
exact sequences}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → B\_ad → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, B) → Autext(G) → 1}
\NormalTok{        ≀         ≀                ≀}
\NormalTok{1 → B\_ad → Aut\_\{S{-}gr.\}(B) → Autext(B) → 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This follows at once from 2.1 and from the preceding results. The reader
is left the task of developing the analogues of the results of nos 1, 2,
3, 4 in the framework above.

\textbf{Remark 6.7.} If \(S\) is a scheme and \(B\) an \(S\)-group,
\(B\) can therefore be a Borel subgroup only of a unique semisimple
group, well determined by \(B\). It therefore remains to characterize
the \(S\)-groups \(B\) that are Borel subgroups of semisimple
groups.\footnote{N.D.E.: One can ask whether every smooth affine
  \(S\)-group, each of whose geometric fibers is a Borel subgroup of a
  semisimple group, is a Borel subgroup of a semisimple \(S\)-group. (We
  have suppressed the ``counter-example'' given in the original, for
  \(S =\) scheme of dual numbers over a field \(k\), which was
  erroneous, as M. Demazure pointed out to us.)}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{7. Representability of the functors
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\), for \(G\)
reductive}{7. Representability of the functors \textbackslash operatorname\{Hom\}\_\{S-gr.\}(G, H), for G reductive}}\label{representability-of-the-functors-operatornamehom_s-gr.g-h-for-g-reductive}

\subsubsection{7.1. The split case}\label{the-split-case}

\paragraph{7.1.1.}\label{section-292}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group, \(T\) its maximal
torus, \(\Delta\) the set of simple roots and, for
\(\alpha \in \Delta\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u\_α ∈ U\_α\^{}×(S),    w\_α ∈ Norm\_G(T)(S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the elements defined by the pinning.

Let on the other hand \(H\) be an \(S\)-group scheme; we are interested
in the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\), and more precisely
in the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{q : Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H) → Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T, H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let then

\[
f_{T} : T \to H
\]

be a morphism of \(S\)-groups; consider \(q^{-1}(f_{T}) = F\). This is
the functor defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F(S\textquotesingle{}) = \{ f ∈ Hom\_\{S\textquotesingle{}{-}gr.\}(G\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}, H\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}) | f = (f\_T)\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\} on T\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\} \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has a morphism of \(S\)-functors

\[
i : F \to H^{2n},
\]

where \(n = Card(\Delta)\), defined set-theoretically by
\(i(f) = (f(u_{\alpha}), f(w_{\alpha}))_{\alpha \in \Delta}\). By Exp.
XXIII, 1.9, \(i\) is moreover a monomorphism.

\textbf{Proposition 7.1.2.} \emph{If \(H\) is separated over \(S\),
\(F\) is representable and \(i\) is a closed immersion.}

The usual technique of relative representability\footnote{N.D.E.: See
  for example the proof of XXII 5.8.1.} shows us that it suffices to
prove that, given sections

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{v\_α, h\_α ∈ H(S),    for α ∈ Δ,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the \(S\)-schemes \(S'\) such that there exists an \(S'\)-homomorphism

\[
f : G_{S'} \to H_{S'}
\]

extending \((f_{T})_{S'}\) and verifying \(f(u_{\alpha}) = v_{\alpha}\),
\(f(w_{\alpha}) = h_{\alpha}\), are exactly those that factor through a
certain closed subscheme of \(S\). One may evidently assume \(S\)
affine.

To simplify the sequel, let us say that a morphism
\(Y \to X\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have corrected \(X \to Y\) to
  \(Y \to X\).} of affine schemes verifies condition (L) if \(Y\) is the
spectrum of an \(O(X)\)-algebra which is a free \(O(X)\)-module. It is
clear that if one restricts to the category of affine schemes, a
product, or a composite of morphisms verifying (L) verifies (L), and
that (L) is stable under base change.

\textbf{Lemma 7.1.3.} \emph{Suppose \(S\) affine, and let
\(\alpha \in \Delta\). Consider the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a : T ×\_S T → G\_\{a, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{defined set-theoretically by
\(a(t, t') = \alpha(t) + \alpha(t')\).}

\emph{(i) \(a\) is faithfully flat and of finite presentation.}

\emph{(ii) Let \(R\) be the fibered square of \(a\). The structure
morphism \(R \to S\) verifies (L).}

It is first clear that the morphism \(a\) is surjective, since
\(\alpha : T \to G_{m, S}\) is. It is trivial that \(a\) is of finite
presentation. Since \(\alpha\) verifies (L), it suffices, to prove (i)
and (ii), to show that the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u : G\_\{m, S\}² → G\_\{a, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

defined set-theoretically by \(u(x, y) = x + y\) verifies (L). In other
words, it suffices to verify that for every ring \(A\), the ring
\(A[X, Y, X^{-1}, Y^{-1}]\) is a free module over its subring
\(A[X + Y]\).\footnote{N.D.E.: We have simplified the proof of the
  original.} Now \texttt{A{[}X,\ Y{]}} is a free module with basis
\texttt{\{1,\ X\}} over the subring \(B = A[X + Y, XY]\) (one has
\(X^{2} - (X + Y) X + XY = 0\)), so
\(A[X^{\pm 1}, Y^{\pm 1}] = A[X, Y]_{XY}\) is free over
\(B_{XY} = A[X + Y, (XY)^{\pm 1}]\) with basis \texttt{\{1,\ X\}}, and
free over \(A[X + Y]\) with basis the elements \((XY)^{p}\) and
\(X(XY)^{p}\), for \(p \in \mathbb{Z}\).

\textbf{Lemma 7.1.4.} \emph{Let \(\alpha \in \Delta\), and let
\(b : T \times_{S} T \to H\) be the morphism defined set-theoretically
by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{b(t, t\textquotesingle{}) = int(f\_T(t)) v\_α · int(f\_T(t\textquotesingle{})) v\_α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{Let \(f_{\alpha} : U_{\alpha} \to H\) be an \(S\)-morphism. The
following conditions are equivalent:}\footnote{N.D.E.: In what follows,
  the group law of \(U_{\alpha}\) is written additively, that is, if one
  writes \(p_{\alpha} : G_{a, S} \xrightarrow{\sim} U_{\alpha}\) for the
  isomorphism such that \(p_{\alpha}(1) = u_{\alpha}\) and if
  \(x = p_{\alpha}(z)\), then \(\alpha(t) x\) (resp.
  \(a(t, t') u_{\alpha}\)) denotes \(p_{\alpha}(\alpha(t) z)\) (resp.
  \(p_{\alpha}(a(t, t')) = \alpha(t) u_{\alpha} + \alpha(t') u_{\alpha}\)).}

\emph{(i) \(f_{\alpha}\) is a morphism of groups; one has
\(f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha}) = v_{\alpha}\) and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T(t) f\_α(x) f\_T(t)\^{}\{{-}1\} = f\_α(α(t) x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for all \(t \in T(S')\), \(x \in U_{\alpha}(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

\emph{(ii) One has \(f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha}) = v_{\alpha}\) and the
relation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(a(t, t\textquotesingle{}) u\_α) = b(t, t\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for all \(t, t' \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\).}

If \(f_{\alpha}\) verifies (i), one has
\(f_{\alpha}(\alpha(t) u_{\alpha}) = int(f_{T}(t)) v_{\alpha}\), which
entails (ii) at once. Conversely, suppose (ii) verified and let us prove
the various conditions of (i); let us first prove the last. Since \(a\)
is covering for (fpqc), it suffices to prove that if
\(t, t', t'' \in T(S')\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T(t) f\_α(a(t\textquotesingle{}, t\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) u\_α) f\_T(t)\^{}\{{-}1\} = f\_α(α(t) a(t\textquotesingle{}, t\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) u\_α);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

now this also reads

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T(t) b(t\textquotesingle{}, t\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}) f\_T(t)\^{}\{{-}1\} = b(t t\textquotesingle{}, t t\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

an evident property from the definition of \(b\). It remains to prove
that \(f_{\alpha}\) is a morphism of groups. Now the preceding property
gives at once

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_α(α(t) u\_α) f\_α(α(t\textquotesingle{}) u\_α) = (f\_T(t) f\_α(u\_α) f\_T(t)\^{}\{{-}1\}) · (f\_T(t\textquotesingle{}) f\_α(u\_α) f\_T(t\textquotesingle{})\^{}\{{-}1\})}
\NormalTok{                              = b(t, t\textquotesingle{}) = f\_α(α(t) u\_α + α(t) α(t\textquotesingle{}) u\_α).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One therefore has \(f_{\alpha}(x + x') = f_{\alpha}(x) f_{\alpha}(x')\),
whenever \(x\) and \(x'\) are sections of the open subset
\(U^{\times}_{\alpha}\) of \(U_{\alpha}\), which is schematically dense;
one concludes then by Exp. XVIII, 1.4.

\paragraph{7.1.5.}\label{section-293}

Let us fix provisionally an \(\alpha \in \Delta\). The morphism \(a\) is
faithfully flat quasi-compact, so \(G_{a, S}\) is identified with the
quotient of \(T \times_{S} T\) by the equivalence relation \(R\) defined
by \(a\). Let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⇉\^{}\{i\_1\}\_\{i\_2\} T ×\_S T}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be this equivalence relation.

For the morphism \(b\) to factor through \(a\),\footnote{N.D.E.:
  i.e.~for condition (ii) of 7.1.4 to be satisfied.} it is necessary and
sufficient that \(b \circ i_{1} = b \circ i_{2}\); that is, if one
writes \(K\) for the kernel of the pair of morphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R ⇉\^{}\{b ∘ i\_1\}\_\{b ∘ i\_2\} H,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

it is necessary and sufficient that \(K = R\). Now \(H\) is assumed
separated over \(S\), so \(K\) is a closed subscheme of \(R\). Recall,
on the other hand, that \(R\) is essentially free over \(S\) (7.1.3).

\paragraph{7.1.6.}\label{section-294}

By the foregoing, if \(S'\) is an \(S\)-scheme, for there to exist over
\(S'\) an \(f_{\alpha}\) verifying the conditions of 7.1.4 (i) (and then
necessarily unique), it is necessary and sufficient that
\(K_{S'} = R_{S'}\), and that the morphism \(f_{\alpha}\) obtained
verify \(f_{\alpha}(u_{\alpha}) = v_{\alpha}\).

The first condition is equivalent to the fact that \(S' \to S\) factors
through a certain closed subscheme of \(S\) (Exp. VIII, 6.4\footnote{N.D.E.:
  see also the addition in Exp. VI\_B, 6.2.3.}); if one replaces \(S\)
by this closed subscheme, the second condition defines once again a
closed subscheme of \(S\) (equality of two sections of \(H\), now \(H\)
is assumed separated over \(S\)).

Up to replacing \(S\) by this closed subscheme, one may therefore assume
that there exists a morphism \(f_{\alpha} : U_{\alpha} \to H\) verifying
the conditions of 7.1.4 (i). Taking the intersection of the subschemes
of \(S\) obtained for each \(\alpha \in \Delta\), one may assume this
condition verified for every \(\alpha \in \Delta\).

\paragraph{7.1.7.}\label{section-295}

Similarly, consider for each \(\alpha \in \Delta\) the two morphisms of
\(S\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T ∘ int(w\_α), int(h\_α) ∘ f\_T : T → H.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(H\) is separated over \(S\) and \(T\) essentially free over
\(S\), the same reasoning as previously shows that, up to replacing
\(S\) by a closed subscheme, one may assume that for every
\(\alpha \in \Delta\) one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_T ∘ int(w\_α) = int(h\_α) ∘ f\_T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{7.1.8.}\label{section-296}

Using now the theorem of generators and relations (Exp. XXIII, 3.5), one
sees that there exists a homomorphism of groups \(f : G \to H\)
verifying the required conditions if and only if a certain finite set of
algebraic relations between the sections
\(h_{\alpha}, v_{\alpha}, f_{T}(\alpha^{*}(-1))\)
(\(\alpha \in \Delta\)) of \(H\) is satisfied:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R\_i( (h\_α)\_α, (v\_α)\_α, (f\_T(α\^{}*(−1)))\_α ) = e,    i = 1, ..., n.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(H\) is separated over \(S\), this defines once again a closed
subscheme of \(S\), and one is done.

\textbf{Corollary 7.1.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a split
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) its maximal torus, \(H\) an \(S\)-group
scheme separated over \(S\). Let further \(P\) be a property of
morphisms such that:}

\emph{(i) A closed immersion verifies \(P\).}

\emph{(ii) The composite of two morphisms verifying \(P\) also verifies
\(P\).}

\emph{(iii) \(P\) is stable under base change.}

\emph{(iv) The structure morphism \(H \to S\) verifies \(P\).}

\emph{Then the canonical morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H) → Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T, H)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is relatively representable by a separated morphism verifying
\(P\).}\footnote{N.D.E.: i.e.~for every
  \(S' \to \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, H)\), with \(S'\)
  representable, \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H) \times_{S} S'\) is
  representable and the morphism of \(S\)-schemes
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H) \times_{S} S' \to S'\) is separated
  and verifies \(P\).}

Indeed, one may assume \(G\) pinned; the structure morphism
\(H^{2n} \to S\) verifies \(P\) and one concludes by 7.1.2.

\textbf{Corollary 7.1.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) a split
\(S\)-reductive group, and \(H\) an \(S\)-group scheme smooth and with
affine fibers.\footnote{N.D.E.: We have suppressed the hypothesis that
  \(H\) be quasi-separated, which is superfluous.} Then the functor
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-scheme
locally of finite presentation and separated over \(S\).}

Indeed, since \(H\) is smooth over \(S\), one can consider its neutral
component \(H^{0}\), which has affine fibers, is smooth, separated and
of finite presentation over \(S\) (Exp. VI\_B, 3.10 and 5.5). Since
\(G\) has connected fibers, one may replace \(H\) by \(H^{0}\). Since
\(G\) and \(H\) are then of finite presentation, one may assume \(S\)
noetherian, and one applies 7.1.9 taking for \(P\) the property ``of
finite type''. But, by Exp. XV, 8.9, one knows that
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(T, H)\) is representable by a separated
\(S\)-scheme locally of finite type.

\textbf{Remark 7.1.11.} If \(H\) is affine over \(S\), one can replace
the reference to Exp. XV by Exp. XI, 4.2.

\subsubsection{7.2. General case}\label{general-case-2}

\textbf{Proposition 7.2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\). Let on the other
hand \(H\) be an \(S\)-group scheme, such that the structure morphism
\(H \to S\) verifies the following condition:}

\emph{(+) Each point \(s \in S\) possesses an open neighborhood \(U\)
such that the morphism \(H_{U} \to U\) is quasi-projective.}

\emph{Then the canonical morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H) → Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T, H)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is relatively representable by a morphism verifying (+).}

When \(G\) is splittable relative to \(T\), one applies 7.1.9 taking for
\(P\) the property (+) above. When \(G\) is locally isotrivial, for
example semisimple (4.2.2), one notes that the assertion of the theorem
is local for the local finite étale topology (indeed, the property of
being quasi-projective is local for the global finite étale topology and
ensures the effectiveness of descent for this topology, cf.~SGA 1, VIII,
7.7). Finally, in the general case, one uses the following lemma:

\textbf{Lemma 7.2.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(T\) a maximal torus of \(G\), \(G'\) the
derived group of \(G\) (Exp. XXII, 6.2), \(T' = T \cap G'\) the maximal
torus of \(G'\) corresponding to \(T\) (Exp. XXII, 6.2.8). Then the
diagram}

\[
G \leftarrow G'
\uparrow    \uparrow
T \leftarrow T'
\]

\emph{is an amalgamated sum in the category of \(S\)-group sheaves: that
is, for every \(S\)-group sheaf \(H\), the following square is
cartesian:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H)  →  Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G\textquotesingle{}, H)}
\NormalTok{        ↓                    ↓}
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T, H)  →  Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(T\textquotesingle{}, H).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, if \(rad(G)\) is the radical of \(G\), then
\(rad(G) \subset T\), so

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad(G) ∩ G\textquotesingle{} = rad(G) ∩ T\textquotesingle{} = K,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the product in \(G\) induces isogenies (Exp. XXII, 6.2)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{i : G\textquotesingle{} ×\_S rad(G) → G,    j : T\textquotesingle{} ×\_S rad(G) → T.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(f_{G'} : G' \to H\), \(f_{T} : T \to H\), and
\(f_{T'} : T' \to H\) be morphisms of \(S\)-groups such that
\(f_{G'}|_{T'} = f_{T}|_{T'} = f_{T'}\). Let us show that there exists a
unique morphism of \(S\)-groups \(f : G \to H\) inducing \(f_{G'}\) and
\(f_{T}\). Let \(f_{rad} = f_{T}|_{rad(G)}\)\footnote{N.D.E.: We have
  replaced \(f_{r}\) by \(f_{rad}\).} and let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\_1 = f\_\{G\textquotesingle{}\} · f\_\{rad\} : G\textquotesingle{} ×\_S rad(G) → H.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For \(f\) to exist (and it will evidently be unique), it is necessary
and sufficient that \(f_{1}\) induce the identity on the kernel of
\(i\), that is, that \(f_{G'}\) and \(f_{rad}\) coincide on \(K\); but
the existence of \(f_{T}\) shows by the same argument that \(f_{T'}\)
and \(f_{rad}\) coincide on \(K\). It only remains to note that
\(f_{G'}\) and \(f_{T'}\) evidently coincide on \(K \subset T'\).

Arguing now as in 7.1.10, one deduces from 7.2.1:

\textbf{Corollary 7.2.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) an \(S\)-group scheme smooth and
quasi-projective over \(S\) with affine fibers. Then
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-scheme
locally of finite presentation and separated over \(S\).}

\subsubsection{7.3. Phenomena specific to characteristic
0}\label{phenomena-specific-to-characteristic-0-1}

If \(G\) and \(H\) are two smooth \(S\)-groups, \(g\) and \(h\) their
Lie algebras, one has a canonical morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie : Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H) → Hom\_\{O\_S\textbackslash{}text\{{-}Lie alg.\}\}(g, h),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the right-hand side has an obvious definition.

\textbf{Proposition 7.3.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme of
characteristic 0 (i.e.~a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-scheme), \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(H\) an \(S\)-group scheme smooth and
quasi-projective over \(S\) with affine fibers.}

\emph{(i) \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\) is representable by a
smooth and separated \(S\)-scheme over \(S\).}

\emph{(ii) If \(G\) is semisimple, this scheme is affine and of finite
presentation over \(S\).}

\emph{(iii) If \(G\) is simply connected (Exp. XXII, 4.3.3), the
canonical morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie : Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H) → Hom\_\{O\_S\textbackslash{}text\{{-}Lie alg.\}\}(g, h)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is an isomorphism.}

\textbf{Lemma 7.3.2.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic 0,
\(G\) a \(k\)-reductive group, \(V\) a finite-dimensional \(k\)-vector
space, \(G \to GL(V)\) a linear representation of \(G\) in \(V\). One
has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H⁰(G, V) = H⁰(g, V),    Hⁱ(G, V) = 0,    for i \textgreater{} 0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The first equality is true in general for a smooth connected
group;\footnote{N.D.E.: Indeed, it is clear that
  \(V^{G} \subset V^{g}\). On the other hand, \(H = Centr_{G}(V^{g})\)
  is a closed subgroup of \(G\), smooth since \(char(k) = 0\); by Exp.
  II 5.3.1, one has \(Lie(H) = Centr_{g}(V^{g}) = g\), and since \(H\)
  is smooth and \(G\) connected this entails \(H = G\), whence
  \(V^{g} \subset V^{G}\) (see also {[}DG70{]}, § II.6, Prop. 2.1 (c)).}
in the case of a reductive group, one can prove it as follows: one may
assume \(k\) algebraically closed, hence \(G\) splittable, hence \(G\)
generated by subgroups isomorphic to \(G_{m, k}\),\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Indeed, the union of the maximal tori of \(G\) is dense in \(G\),
  cf.~\emph{Bible}, § 6.5, Th. 5 (= {[}Ch05{]}, § 6.6, Th. 6).} and it
suffices to verify the assertion for this group, which is easy.

From this first equality it follows that \(H^{0}(G, V)\) is an exact
functor in \(V\) when \(G\) is semisimple; \(g\) is indeed then a
semisimple Lie algebra and one applies {[}BLie{]}, § I.6, exercise 1
(b). The assertion remains true when \(G\) is reductive; indeed, if one
introduces the radical \(R\) of \(G\)\footnote{N.D.E.: Note that \(R\)
  is a torus.} and the quotient \(G/R\) which is semisimple, one has
\(H^{0}(G, V) = H^{0}(G/R, H^{0}(R, V))\), and \(H^{0}(G, -)\) is
composed of two exact functors. Applying then Exp. I, 5.3.1, one deduces
\(H^{i}(G, V) = 0\) for \(i > 0\).

\textbf{Remark 7.3.3.} Under the preceding conditions, if \(G\) is
semisimple, one has \(H^{1}(g, V) = H^{2}(g, V) = 0\), cf. {[}BLie{]},
\emph{loc. cit.} (b) and (d).

\paragraph{7.3.4.}\label{section-297}

Let us now prove the proposition. Already, by 7.2.3,
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\) is representable by an \(S\)-scheme
locally of finite presentation and separated over \(S\); to show that it
is smooth, it suffices to prove that it is infinitesimally smooth (Exp.
XI, 1.8),\footnote{N.D.E.: i.e.~that for every \(S\)-scheme \(S'\) local
  artinian, with closed point \(s'\), every morphism of
  \(\kappa(s')\)-groups \(G_{s'} \to H_{s'}\) lifts to a morphism of
  \(S'\)-groups \(G_{S'} \to H_{S'}\). By Exp. III 2.8, this follows
  from the vanishing of \(H^{2}(G_{s'}, V)\), where
  \(V = Lie(H_{s'}/\kappa(s'))\).} which follows from Exp. III, 2.8 (i)
by 7.3.2. We have thus proved (i).

Let us show that (ii) follows from (iii). It suffices first to prove
that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\) is affine over \(S\); it will
then be of finite presentation over \(S\), since it is smooth over \(S\)
by (i); in any case
\texttt{Hom\_\{O\_S\textbackslash{}text\{-Lie\ alg.\}\}(g,\ h)} is
representable by a closed subscheme of

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{O\_S\textbackslash{}text\{{-}mod.\}\}(g, h) ≃ W(g\^{}∨ ⊗\_\{O\_S\} h)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which is an affine \(S\)-scheme, and the desired conclusion appears when
\(G\) is simply connected.

In the general case, one may assume \(G\) split, so
\(G \simeq \acute{E}p_{S}(R)\); introducing the simply connected root
datum \(sc(R)\) (Exp. XXI, 6.5.5), and using the existence theorem (Exp.
XXV, 1.1), one constructs a simply connected \(S\)-group \(\tilde{G}\)
and a central isogeny \(\tilde{G} \to G\). The kernel \(K\) of this
isogeny is a finite diagonalizable \(S\)-group (so a twisted constant
\(S\)-group, \(S\) being of characteristic 0) and
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(K, H)\) is (trivially) representable by a
separated \(S\)-scheme (if \(K \simeq (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_{S}\),
then \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(K, H)\) is isomorphic to
\(Ker(H \to^{n} H)\)). One has an exact sequence of ``pointed
\(S\)-schemes'':

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G, H) →\^{}u Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(G̃, H) → Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(K, H),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so \(u\) is a closed immersion, hence
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, H)\) is affine over \(S\).

\paragraph{7.3.5.}\label{section-298}

Let us finally prove (iii). Arguing as in the proof of (i) and using
7.3.3, one can show that the \(S\)-scheme
\texttt{Hom\_\{O\_S\textbackslash{}text\{-Lie\ alg.\}\}(g,\ h)} is
smooth over \(S\). To prove (iii), one may therefore assume
\(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), where \(k\) is an algebraically closed
field of characteristic 0; it even suffices to prove that the morphism
\texttt{Lie} is bijective on \(k\)-valued points and that it induces a
bijection on tangent spaces at two corresponding points. Let us first
show that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{k{-}gr.\}(G, H) → Hom\_\{k\textbackslash{}text\{{-}Lie alg.\}\}(g, h)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective.

If \(u : G \to H\) is a morphism of \(k\)-groups, the graph of \(u\) is
a connected subgroup of \(G \times_{k} H\) which is determined by its
Lie algebra which is the graph of \(Lie(u)\); the map is therefore
injective. Conversely, if \(v : g \to h\) is a morphism of Lie algebras,
the graph \(k\) of \(v\) is a Lie subalgebra of \(g \times h\),
isomorphic to \(g\). In particular, since \(g\) is its own derived
algebra, the same is true of \(k\) and so, by a theorem of Chevalley
({[}Ch51{]}, § 14, Th. 15), \(k\) is the Lie algebra of a connected
subgroup \(K\) of \(G \times_{k} H\).\footnote{N.D.E.: see also
  {[}Bo91{]}, II 7.9. Moreover, we have added the sentence that follows.}
Moreover, since \(k \simeq g\) is semisimple, \(G\) is a semisimple
\(k\)-group. Since

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim(K) = dim(k) = dim(g) = dim(G)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and since \(K \cap H\) is finite (because its Lie algebra is zero), the
canonical morphism \(pr_{1} : K \to G\) is finite and dominant; since
\(G\) is connected, \(pr_{1}\) is surjective; it is therefore an
isogeny. Since \(G\) is simply connected and \(K\) semisimple then, by
Exp. XXI 6.2.7, \(pr_{1}\) is an isomorphism, so \(K\) is the graph of a
morphism of \(k\)-groups \(u : G \to H\) such that \(Lie(u) = v\).

Finally, let \(u : G \to H\) be a morphism of \(k\)-groups. The tangent
space to \(\operatorname{Hom}_{k-gr.}(G, H)\) at \(u\) is identified
with \(Z^{1}(G, h)\) (cf.~Exp. II, 4.2; \(G\) operates on \(h\) by
\(Ad_{H} \circ u\)); similarly, one can prove that the tangent space to
\texttt{Hom\_\{k\textbackslash{}text\{-Lie\ alg.\}\}(g,\ h)} at
\(Lie(u)\) is identified with \(Z^{1}(g, h)\). We must therefore prove
that the canonical map \(Z^{1}(G, h) \to Z^{1}(g, h)\) is bijective. Now
one has a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{0 → h\^{}G → h → Z¹(G, h) → H¹(G, h)}
\NormalTok{        ↓    ↓        ↓        ↓}
\NormalTok{0 → h\^{}g → h → Z¹(g, h) → H¹(g, h)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and by 7.3.2 and 7.3.3 one has \(h^{G} = h^{g}\) and
\(H^{1}(G, h) = 0 = H^{1}(g, h)\), whence the desired conclusion.

\textbf{Remark 7.3.6.} It is presumably the case that if \(S\) is a
locally noetherian scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-semisimple simply connected
group, \(H\) an \(S\)-group scheme smooth, \texttt{Ĝ} and \texttt{Ĥ}
their formal completions along the unit section, every homomorphism
\(\hat{G} \to \hat{H}\) comes from a unique homomorphism of \(G\) into
\(H\), which would generalize 7.3.1 (iii). When \(S\) is the spectrum of
a field \(k\) and \(H\) is affine and of finite type, this follows from
a theorem of Dieudonné ({[}Di57{]}, § 15, th. 4).\footnote{N.D.E.: See
  Exp. VII\_B for the definition of the formal groups \texttt{Ĝ} and
  \texttt{Ĥ}. Suppose that \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), where \(k\)
  is a field. By \emph{loc. cit.}, 2.2.1, to give a morphism of
  \(k\)-formal groups \(v : \hat{G} \to \hat{H}\) is equivalent to
  giving a morphism of \(k\)-Hopf algebras
  \(\phi : Dist(G) \to Dist(H)\), where \(Dist(G)\) denotes the algebra
  of distributions (at the origin) of \(G\), cf.~Exp. VII\_A, 2.1 or
  {[}DG70{]}, § II.4, 6.1 or {[}Ja87{]}, I 7.7 (it is called the
  ``hyperalgebra'' of \(G\) in {[}Di57{]} and {[}Ta75{]}). Theorem 4 of
  {[}Di57{]} (see also {[}Ta75{]}, 0.3.4 (f) and (g)) generalizes in
  this context the theorem of Chevalley used in 7.3.5; one thereby
  obtains that there exists a closed connected \(k\)-subgroup \(K\) of
  \(G \times H\) such that \(\hat{K}\) equals the graph of \(v\); since
  \(Dist(K) \to Dist(G)\) is an isomorphism, \(K \to G\) is a finite
  étale morphism. One then deduces that \(K\) is semisimple and then, by
  Exp. XXI 6.2.7, that \(K \to G\) is an isomorphism (since \(G\) is
  simply connected); see also {[}Ta75{]}, 1.8 and 2.2. More generally,
  \emph{loc. cit.} studies the \(k\)-groups \(G\) having the property
  (SC): every finite étale morphism of \(k\)-groups \(G' \to G\), with
  \(G'\) connected, is an isomorphism. Note finally that what precedes
  shows that every \(Dist(G)\)-module \(V\) of finite dimension is,
  uniquely, a \(G\)-module; for an extension to the case of a split
  reductive \(k\)-group \(G\) (or even of a Borel subgroup of \(G\)) see
  {[}Ja87{]}, II 1.20 (and the references therein).}

\subsubsection{7.4. An example}\label{an-example}

By way of example, we shall determine

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(SL\_\{2, S\}, SL\_\{2, S\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{7.4.1.}\label{section-299}

Recall (Exp. XX, no 5) that \(SL_{2, S}\) is the \(S\)-group scheme
formed by the matrices \(( a b ; c d)\) over \(S\) satisfying
\(ad - bc = 1\). A maximal torus \(T\) is defined by the monomorphism
\(\alpha^{*} : G_{m, S} \to SL_{2, S}\)

\[
\alpha^{*}(z) = ( z   0)
         ( 0  z^{-1}).
\]

A root of \(G\) with respect to \(T\) is defined by
\(\alpha(\alpha^{*}(z)) = z^{2}\), a corresponding monomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p : G\_\{a, S\} → SL\_\{2, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

being defined by

\[
p(x) = ( 1 x)
       ( 0 1).
\]

Finally, the representative of the Weyl group corresponding to
\(u = p(1)\) is

\[
w = (  0  1)
    ( -1  0).
\]

Recall on the other hand (Exp. XX, 6.2) that \(SL_{2, S}\) is generated
by \(T\), \(p(G_{a, S})\) and \(w\), subject to the relations

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\^{}*(z) p(x) α\^{}*(z\^{}\{{-}1\}) = p(z² x),}
\NormalTok{w α\^{}*(z) w\^{}\{{-}1\} = α\^{}*(z\^{}\{{-}1\}),}
\NormalTok{w² = α\^{}*(−1),}
\NormalTok{(w u)³ = 1.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{7.4.2.}\label{section-300}

Let \(f\) be an endomorphism of \(SL_{2, S}\). It defines first a
homomorphism \(f \circ \alpha^{*} : G_{m, S} \to SL_{2, S}\). The kernel
\(Ker(f \circ \alpha^{*})\) is a closed subgroup of \(G_{m, S}\), hence
is locally on \(S\) equal to a \(\mu_{n, S}\) (\(n \geqslant 1\)) or to
\(G_{m, S}\). Up to restricting \(S\), one may therefore assume that
there exists an \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and a monomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f\textquotesingle{} : G\_\{m, S\} → SL\_\{2, S\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

such that \(f \circ \alpha^{*}(z) = f'(z^{n})\).

By the conjugacy of monomorphisms \(G_{m, S} \to SL_{2, S}\), one can,
after an étale-covering extension of the base, find a section \(g\) of
\(G\) such that
\(f \circ \alpha^{*}(z) = int(g) \circ \alpha^{*}(z^{n})\). Transforming
\(f\) by \(int(g)\), one is therefore reduced to the case where there
exists an \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) such that
\(f \circ \alpha^{*}(z) = \alpha^{*}(z^{n})\).

\paragraph{7.4.3.}\label{section-301}

Consider now the morphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ∘ p : G\_\{a, S\} → SL\_\{2, S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It verifies the condition

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\^{}*(z\^{}n) (f ∘ p)(x) α\^{}*(z\^{}n)\^{}\{{-}1\} = (f ∘ p)(z² x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(n = 0\), it follows at once that \(f \circ p\) is invariant under
the homotheties of \(G_{a, S}\), hence constant. If \(n \neq 0\), one
can apply Exp. XXII, 4.1.9; \(x \mapsto x^{n}\) is an endomorphism of
\(G_{a, S}\), there exists a \(\lambda \in G_{m, S}\) such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ∘ p(x) = p(λ x\^{}n);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

this relation is moreover valid for \(n = 0\), taking \(\lambda = 1\).
Up to again extending \(S\), one can find a \(z \in G_{m, S}\) such that
\(z^{2} = \lambda\). Replacing \(f\) by \(int(\alpha^{*}(z)) \circ f\),
one is therefore reduced to the case where one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f ∘ α\^{}*(z) = α\^{}*(z\^{}n),    f ∘ p(x) = p(x\^{}n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{7.4.4.}\label{section-302}

Finally, one must have
\(f(w) \alpha^{*}(z^{n}) f(w)^{-1} = \alpha^{*}(z^{n})^{-1}\) and
\((f(w) u)^{3} = 1\). By Exp. XX, 3.8, this entails \(f(w) = w^{n}\).
Since \(G\) is generated by \(T\), \(p(G_{a, S})\) and \(w\), this
entails that for every \(( a b ; c d) \in G(S')\), \(S' \to S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f( a b ) = ( a\^{}n b\^{}n )}
\NormalTok{  ( c d )   ( c\^{}n d\^{}n ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\paragraph{7.4.5.}\label{section-303}

Summarizing the preceding discussion, one sees that locally on \(S\) for
the étale topology, one can find for every endomorphism \(f\) of
\(SL_{2, S}\) an (inner) automorphism \(\phi\) of \(SL_{2, S}\), and an
integer \(n \geqslant 0\) such that \(f = \phi \circ F_{n}\), where

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{F\_n( a b ) = ( a\^{}n b\^{}n )}
\NormalTok{   ( c d )   ( c\^{}n d\^{}n ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Note that if \(f = \phi \circ F_{n}\), the integer \(n\) is well
determined by a fiber \(f_{s}\) of \(f\), for example by \(Ker(f_{s})\).
It follows that \(n\) is a locally constant function on \(S\).

\paragraph{7.4.6.}\label{section-304}

One deduces at once that if \(f\) is an endomorphism of \(SL_{2, S}\),
then \(S\) decomposes canonically as a sum of open and closed subschemes
\texttt{S\_0}, \texttt{S\_1}, \(S_{p^{n}}\) (where \(p^{n}\) ranges over
the set of positive powers of prime numbers) such that:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  \(f_{S_{0}}\) is the zero morphism,
\item
  \(f_{S_{1}}\) is an isomorphism (= an inner automorphism),
\item
  \(S_{p^{n}}\) is of characteristic \(p\) and \(f_{S_{p^{n}}}\)
  decomposes uniquely in the form \(\phi \circ F^{n}_{p}\), where
  \(\phi\) is an inner automorphism and \(F_{p}\) the Frobenius
  endomorphism of \(SL_{2, F_{p}}\).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{7.4.7.}\label{section-305}

In other words,
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}-gr.}(SL_{2, \mathbb{Z}}, SL_{2, \mathbb{Z}})\)
is the sum scheme:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  of a scheme isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\),
\item
  of a scheme isomorphic to
  \(\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{Z}-gr.}(SL_{2, \mathbb{Z}}) \simeq ad(SL_{2, \mathbb{Z}})\),
\item
  for each prime number \(p\) and each integer \(n > 0\), of a scheme
  isomorphic to
  \(\operatorname{Aut}_{F_{p}-gr.}(SL_{2, F_{p}}) \simeq ad(SL_{2, F_{p}})\).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{7.4.8.}\label{section-306}

It follows in particular that

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{F_{p}-gr.}(SL_{2, F_{p}}, SL_{2, F_{p}})\) has
  an infinite number of connected components, and so is not
  quasi-compact.
\item
  If \(S\) is a scheme of unequal characteristics,
  \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(SL_{2, S}, SL_{2, S})\) is not flat over
  \(S\).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{8. Appendix: Cohomology of a smooth group
over a henselian ring. Cohomology and the functor
\(\prod\)}{8. Appendix: Cohomology of a smooth group over a henselian ring. Cohomology and the functor \textbackslash prod}}\label{appendix-cohomology-of-a-smooth-group-over-a-henselian-ring.-cohomology-and-the-functor-prod}

\textbf{Proposition 8.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a henselian local scheme,
\(s\) its closed point, \(G\) an \(S\)-group scheme smooth such that
every finite subset of \(G\) is contained in an affine open
set.\footnote{This last condition is in fact unnecessary (cf.~A.
  Grothendieck, \emph{Groupe de Brauer III}, in \emph{Dix Exposés sur la
  cohomologie des schémas}, North-Holland, 1968, theorem 11.7 and
  remarks 11.8.3).} Then}

\emph{(i) If \(P\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\), there
exists an \(S' \to S\) finite, surjective étale that trivializes \(P\).
One has \(Fib(S, G) \simeq H^{1}_{\acute{e}}t(S, G)\).}

\emph{(ii) For every finite surjective étale morphism \(S' \to S\), the
canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, G) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{} ⊗\_S κ(s) / κ(s), G\_s)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is bijective.}

\emph{(iii) The canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Fib(S, G) → Fib(κ(s), G\_s)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is bijective.}

\paragraph{8.1.2.}\label{section-307}

If \(K\) is a finite separable extension of \(\kappa(s)\), there exists
an \(S' \to S\) finite surjective étale such that
\(K \simeq S' \otimes_{S} \kappa(s)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: Note that \(S'\)
  is still local and henselian. Furthermore, we have kept the numbering
  of the original: there is no no 8.1.1.} If \(P\) is a principal
homogeneous bundle under \(G\), then \(P\) is smooth over \(S\), hence
\(P_{s}\) smooth over \(\kappa(s)\); there therefore exists a finite
separable extension \(K\) of \(\kappa(s)\) such that \texttt{P\_K}
possesses a section (cf.~EGA IV\_4, 17.15.10). Representing \(K\) as
said above, one sees that \(P_{S'}\) possesses a section by ``Hensel's
lemma'' (cf.~EGA IV\_4, 18.5.17), which proves the first part of (i).

Conversely, if \(P\) is a principal homogeneous sheaf under \(G\) for
the étale topology, there exists an \(S' \to S\) finite surjective étale
that trivializes \(P\) (indeed every covering family of a henselian
local scheme for the étale topology is dominated by a family reduced to
a morphism \(S' \to S\) of the wanted form).

By virtue of the descent hypothesis made on \(G\), \(P\) is
representable (SGA 1, VIII, 7.6), which completes the proof of (i), and
shows that (ii) entails (iii). It only remains to prove (ii).

\paragraph{8.1.3.}\label{section-308}

The map of (ii) is injective: let \(P\) and \(Q\) be two principal
homogeneous bundles under \(G\) trivialized by \(S'\). Consider the
\(S\)-group sheaf
\texttt{H\ =\ Isom\_\{G\textbackslash{}text\{-bundles\}\}(P,\ Q)}; since
\(H_{S'}\) is isomorphic to \(G_{S'}\), \(H\) is representable, by the
second hypothesis on \(G\), cf.~above. If
\(H(\kappa(s)) \neq \emptyset\), then \(H(S) \neq \emptyset\) by
Hensel's lemma, so \(P\) and \(Q\) are isomorphic.

\paragraph{8.1.4.}\label{section-309}

Let us finally prove that the map of (ii) is surjective, or equivalently
that the canonical map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Z¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, G) → Z¹(S\textquotesingle{} ⊗\_S κ(s) / κ(s), G\_s)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is surjective. Let \(Z^{1}\) be the \(S\)-functor defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Z¹(T) = Z¹(S\textquotesingle{} ×\_S T / T, G\_T);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the preceding map is identified with the map

\[
Z^{1}(S) \to Z^{1}(\kappa(s));
\]

by a further application of Hensel's lemma, it suffices to prove that
\(Z^{1}\) is representable by a smooth \(S\)-scheme.

\paragraph{8.1.5.}\label{section-310}

Let us prove that \(Z^{1}\) is representable by an \(S\)-scheme locally
of finite presentation. Let \(C_{i}\), \texttt{i\ =\ 0,\ 1,\ ...}, be
the \(S\)-functor defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\_i(T) = C\_i(S\textquotesingle{} ×\_S T / T, G\_T),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

that is

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\_i(T) = G((S\textquotesingle{} ×\_S T / T)\^{}\{i+1\}) = G((S\textquotesingle{}/S)\^{}\{i+1\} ×\_S T),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

or again

\[
C_{i} = \operatorname{Hom}_{S}((S'/S)^{i+1}, G).
\]

Since \(Z^{1}\) is obtained from \texttt{C\_1} and \texttt{C\_2} by
fibered products, it suffices to prove that \(C_{i}\), \(i = 1, 2\), is
representable by an \(S\)-scheme locally of finite presentation.

\paragraph{8.1.6.}\label{section-311}

If \(T \to S\) is a finite surjective étale morphism that decomposes
\(S'\), then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{C\_i ×\_S T = Hom\_T((S\textquotesingle{} ×\_S T / T)\^{}\{i+1\}, G\_T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is representable by a product of \(n\) copies of \texttt{G\_T}, where
\(n\) is the degree of \((S'/S)^{i+1}\). Applying once more the
hypothesis on \(G\), one deduces that \(C_{i}\) is indeed representable
by an \(S\)-scheme locally of finite presentation (SGA 1, VIII,
\emph{loc. cit.}).

\paragraph{8.1.7.}\label{section-312}

To prove that \(Z^{1}\) is smooth, we must now, by definition, prove
that if \(T\) is an affine \(S\)-scheme, \texttt{T\_0} the closed
subscheme defined by an ideal \(J\) of square zero, the canonical map

\[
Z^{1}(T) \to Z^{1}(T_{0})
\]
