is surjective. Since \(G\) is smooth, the canonical map
\(G(T) \to G(T_{0})\) is surjective,

and it suffices to prove that the canonical map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{} ×\_S T / T, G\_T) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{} ×\_S T\_0 / T\_0, G\_\{T\_0\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is bijective.

Changing notation slightly and generalizing the hypotheses, it now
suffices for us to prove:

\textbf{Lemma 8.1.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be two affine schemes,
\(S' \to S\) a faithfully flat morphism, \(J\) an ideal of square zero
on \(S\), \texttt{S\_0} the closed subscheme it defines, \(G\) a smooth
\(S\)-group. Set \(S'_{0} = S' \times_{S} S_{0}\),
\(G_{0} = G \times_{S} S_{0}\). The canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, G) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{}\_0/S\_0, G\_0)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is bijective.}

\textbf{Remark 8.1.9.} If one assumes \(G\) commutative, the same
assertion is valid for all \(H^{i}\), \(i > 0\), with an analogous
proof.

\emph{Proof.} Let \texttt{M\_0} be the quasi-coherent
\(O_{S_{0}}\)-module \(M_{0} = Lie(G_{0}/S_{0}) \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} J\).
For each \texttt{S\_0}-prescheme \texttt{T\_0}, set
\(M_{0}(T_{0}) = H^{0}(T_{0}, M_{0} \otimes_{O_{S_{0}}} O_{T_{0}})\),
and let

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M = ∏\_\{S\_0/S\} M\_0    and    Ḡ = ∏\_\{S\_0/S\} G\_0}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

be the \(S\)-group functors defined by \(M(T) = M_{0}(T_{0})\) and
\(\bar{G}(T) = G_{0}(T_{0})\), where \(T_{0} = T \times_{S} S_{0}\). By
Exp. III, 0.9 and (0.6.2), there exists for every affine \(S\)-scheme
\(T\) an exact sequence, functorial in \(T\):

\[
1 \to M(T) \to G(T) \to \bar{G}(T) \to 1.
\]

We have to study the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, G) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{}\_0/S\_0, G\_0) = H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, Ḡ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Suppose first \(G\) commutative. One then has an exact cohomology
sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, M) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, G) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, Ḡ) → H²(S\textquotesingle{}/S, M);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hⁱ(S\textquotesingle{}/S, M) = Hⁱ(S\textquotesingle{}\_0/S\_0, M\_0) = Hⁱ(S\textquotesingle{}\_0/S\_0, M\_0),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and one knows (TDTE I, B, Lemma 1.1) that
\(H^{i}(S'_{0}/S_{0}, M_{0}) = 0\) for \(i \neq 0\).

If now \(G\) is not commutative, we must use the exact sequence of
non-abelian cohomology. If \(u \in Z^{1}(S'/S, \bar{G})\), one knows
that the elements of \(H^{1}(S'/S, G)\) having the same image in
\(H^{1}(S'/S, \bar{G})\) as the class of \(u\) are in the image of the
corresponding coboundary map:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, M\_u) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, G),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(M_{u}\) is the \(S\)-functor \(M\) ``twisted by \(u\)''.
Similarly, if \(v\) is an element of \(Z^{1}(S'/S, \bar{G})\), there
exists a ``coboundary''

\[
\Delta(v) \in H^{2}(S'/S, M_{v}),
\]

where \(M_{v}\) is the \(S\)-functor \(M\) ``twisted by \(v\)'', such
that \(\Delta(v) = 0\) if and only if the class of \(v\) is in the image
of \(H^{1}(S'/S, G)\). It suffices to prove that one has
\(H^{1}(S'/S, M_{u}) = H^{2}(S'/S, M_{v}) = 0\).

Now recall (Exp. III 0.8) that the action of \(G\) on \(M\) defined by
the exact sequence is none other than that which is deduced functorially
from the adjoint representation of \texttt{G\_0}:

\[
ad : G_{0} \to \operatorname{Aut}_{O_{S_{0}}}(Lie(G_{0}/S_{0})).
\]

The element \(u\) (resp. \(v\)) therefore acts in
\(M_{S' \times_{S} S'}\) via an
\(S'_{0} \times_{S_{0}} S'_{0}\)-automorphism of \(Lie(G_{0}/S_{0})\).
Since \(u\) (resp. \(v\)) is a cocycle, this automorphism is a descent
datum; write \(L_{u}\) (resp. \(L_{v}\)) for the quasi-coherent
\(O_{S_{0}}\)-module obtained. One verifies at once that for
\(T \to S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M\_u(T) = H⁰(T\_0, L\_u ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_0\}\} J ⊗\_\{O\_\{S\_0\}\} O\_\{T\_0\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and the same relation replacing \(u\) by \(v\). One therefore has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{}/S, M\_u) = H¹(S\textquotesingle{}\_0/S\_0, L\_u ⊗ J),}
\NormalTok{H²(S\textquotesingle{}/S, M\_v) = H²(S\textquotesingle{}\_0/S\_0, L\_v ⊗ J),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and both are indeed zero by virtue of the result already used.

\textbf{Proposition 8.2.} \emph{Let \(C\) be a category possessing
fibered products, equipped with a topology coarser than the canonical
topology, \(S' \to S\) a morphism of \(C\), \(G'\) an \(S'\)-group
sheaf, \(G\) the \(S\)-group sheaf \(\prod_{S'/S} G'\). Let
\(H^{1}_{S}(S', G') \subset H^{1}(S', G')\) be the set of classes of
principal homogeneous sheaves under \(G'\) which are trivialized by a
sieve of \(S'\) obtained by base change from a suitable covering sieve
of \(S\). The canonical map \(H^{1}(S, G) \to H^{1}(S', G')\) defined by
the functor}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P ↦ P ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induces a bijection}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, G) ⥲ H¹\_S(S\textquotesingle{}, G\textquotesingle{});}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the inverse bijection is defined by the functor
\(P' \mapsto \prod_{S'/S} P'\).}

For every object \(X\) of \(C/S\), one has by definition a functorial
isomorphism in \(X\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Hom\_S(X, G) ⥲ Hom\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}(X ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One therefore has for each \(S\)-object \(T\) a functorial bijection in
\(T\)

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(T/S, G) ⥲ H¹(T\textquotesingle{}/S\textquotesingle{}, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Replacing now the unique morphism \(T \to S\) by an arbitrary covering
family of \(S\) and passing to the inductive limit, one deduces the
first part of the statement. The second part is deduced without
difficulty.

\textbf{Lemma 8.3.} \emph{Under the conditions of 8.2, the assertion
\(H^{1}_{S}(S', G') = H^{1}(S', G')\) is local on \(S\): suppose there
exists a covering family \({S_{i} \to S}\) such that for every \(i\),
one has
\(H^{1}_{S_{i}}(S' \times_{S} S_{i}, G') = H^{1}(S' \times_{S} S_{i}, G')\).
Then \(H^{1}_{S}(S', G') = H^{1}(S', G')\).}

Indeed, let \(P'\) be a principal homogeneous sheaf under \(G'\). Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P\textquotesingle{}\_i = P\textquotesingle{} ×\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\} (S\textquotesingle{} ×\_S S\_i);}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by hypothesis, there exists a covering family \({S_{ij} \to S_{i}}\)
such that for each \(j\), \(P' \times_{S'} (S' \times_{S} S_{ij})\)
possesses a section. But \({S_{ij} \to S}\) is a covering family of
\(S\), and \(P'\) is indeed trivialized by the covering family of \(S'\)
obtained from this one by base change.

\textbf{Proposition 8.4.} \emph{Let \(S' \to S\) be a finite étale
morphism of schemes. Let \(G'\) be an \(S'\)-group sheaf, \(G\) the
\(S\)-group sheaf \(\prod_{S'/S} G'\). For the étale (resp. local finite
étale, resp. (fpqc)) topology, the functors}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P    ↦   P ×\_S S\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{∏\_\{S\textquotesingle{}/S\} P\textquotesingle{}    ↤    P\textquotesingle{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{induce inverse bijections of each other:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, G) ≃ H¹(S\textquotesingle{}, G\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By 8.2, it suffices to show that \(H^{1}_{S}(S', G') = H^{1}(S', G')\).
By 8.3, it suffices to do this locally for the local finite étale
topology; one may therefore assume that \(S'\) is a finite direct sum of
copies of \(S\), say \texttt{I\_S}, where \(I\) is a suitable finite
set. Then \(G'\) is given by a family \((G_{i})_{i \in I}\) of sheaves
on \(S\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S\textquotesingle{}, G\textquotesingle{}) ≃ ∏\_\{i ∈ I\} H¹(S, G\_i).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

On the other hand

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H¹(S, G) ≃ ∏\_\{i ∈ I\} H¹(S, G\_i),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whence, by 8.2, \(H^{1}_{S}(S', G') = H^{1}(S', G')\). QED

\textbf{Remarks 8.5.} One can interpret 8.2 and 8.3 by the following
exact sequence (\(f\) is the given morphism \(S' \to S\))

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{1 → H¹(S, f\_*(G\textquotesingle{})) → H¹(S\textquotesingle{}, G\textquotesingle{}) → H⁰(S, R¹f\_*(G\textquotesingle{})).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In the commutative case, this exact sequence follows from the Leray
spectral sequence; it is still valid in the non-commutative case
(cf.~Giraud's thesis\footnote{N.D.E.: See § V 3.1.4 of {[}Gi71{]}.}).

In this form, one sees that the result is still valid if \(f\) is only
assumed finite, or simply integral, the topology being the étale
topology, because for every \(G'\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R¹f\_*(G\textquotesingle{}) = \textbackslash{}text\{final sheaf\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by SGA 4, VIII, 5.3.\footnote{N.D.E.: This reference also refers to § V
  3.1.4 of {[}Gi71{]}.}

On the other hand, this result becomes false if one takes a topology
such as (fpqc) or (fppf), even if \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\), \(k\)
algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p \neq 0\),
\(S' = \operatorname{Spec}(k[t]/t^{2})\), \(G' = \mu_{p}\) or
\(\alpha_{p}\).

Similarly, 8.2 becomes false, even for the étale topology, if one
suppresses in it the hypothesis that \(f\) is finite, as one sees by
taking for \(f\) an open immersion; for example if
\(S = \operatorname{Spec}(V)\), \(V\) a complete discrete valuation ring
with algebraically closed residue field, \(S'\) being the open subset
induced at the generic point, and \(G'\) the constant group
\((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})_{S'}\), with \(n\) prime to the residue
characteristic of \(V\), one has \(H^{1}(S, G) = 0\),
\(H^{1}(S', G') \neq 0\). Moreover, replacing \(S'\) by
\(S \coprod S'\), one deduces an analogous example, with \(S' \to S\)
étale surjective, hence covering for the topology considered.

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-10}

\section{Exposé XXV. The existence
theorem}\label{exposuxe9-xxv.-the-existence-theorem}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{N.D.E.: Version of 13/10/2024.} For the sake of completeness,
we give in this Exposé a proof of the existence theorem for split
groups. Like Chevalley's original proof (``Sur certains schémas de
groupes semi-simples'', \emph{Séminaire Bourbaki}, May 1961, no. 219),
it rests on the existence of complex semisimple algebraic groups of all
possible types. The principle of a more satisfactory proof, establishing
directly the existence of a simply connected split semisimple
\(\mathbb{Z}\)-group corresponding to a given Cartan matrix, was given
by Cartier (unpublished).\footnote{N.D.E.: Such a principle was also
  sketched by B. Kostant {[}Ko66{]}; a complete proof, using quantum
  groups, has been given recently by G. Lusztig {[}Lu09{]}.} Let us
point out, however, that the difficulty is not to give an explicit
construction of a group scheme, but to verify that the group thus
constructed really meets the required conditions, that is, essentially,
that its fibers are indeed smooth and reductive.

\subsection{1. Statement of the
theorem}\label{statement-of-the-theorem-4}

\textbf{Theorem 1.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a non-empty scheme. The
functor}

\[
G \mapsto R(G)
\]

\emph{is an equivalence of the category of pinned \(S\)-reductive groups
with the category of pinned reduced root data.}

By virtue of the uniqueness theorem (Exp. XXIII, 4.1), the preceding
statement is equivalent to:

\textbf{Corollary 1.2 (Existence of split groups).} \emph{For every
reduced root datum \(R\), there exists a split reductive
\(\mathbb{Z}\)-group \(G\) such that \(R(G) \simeq R\).}\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Let us also point out that the work {[}BT84{]} of F. Bruhat and J.
  Tits contains a variant of Chevalley's construction (\emph{loc. cit.},
  2.2.3--2.2.5 and § 3.2), which yields in particular a smooth affine
  \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group \(G\) with connected fibers, possessing a split
  maximal torus, and whose generic fiber is a reductive
  \(\mathbb{Q}\)-group of type \(R\); the fact that the geometric fibers
  of \(G\) are reductive follows from the study of the unipotent radical
  of a special fiber carried out in \emph{loc. cit.}, 4.6.12 and 4.6.15
  (valid for more general \(G\), associated with a valued root datum),
  but it is simpler to deduce it from the description of \(g = Lie(G)\),
  from Exp. XIX 1.12 (iii), and from the existence of the elements
  \(w_{\alpha}(X)\) of Exp. XX 3.1 (iv) (cf.~{[}BT84{]}, 3.2.1).}

In particular:

\textbf{Corollary 1.3.} \emph{Let \(k\) be a field. For every splittable
reductive \(k\)-group \(G_{k}\), there exists a reductive
\(\mathbb{Z}\)-group \(G\) such that
\(G \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k \simeq G_{k}\).}

Conversely, let us remark first that to prove 1.2 it suffices, by Exp.
XXII 4.3.1 and Exp. XXI 6.5.10, to consider the case where the root
datum \(R\) is simply connected (and even irreducible if one insists, by
Exp. XXI, 7.1.6).

On the other hand, under the conditions of 1.3, the group scheme \(G\)
is of constant type (since \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) is
connected), hence of type \(R(G_{k})\); by Exp. XXIII, 5.9, it follows
that the validity of 1.3 for a given group \(G_{k}\) entails the
existence of a split \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group of type
\(R(G_{k})\).\footnote{N.D.E.: In fact, Exp. XXIII, 5.9 is not necessary
  because the present Exposé constructs, for every semisimple
  \(\mathbb{Q}\)-group \(G_{\mathbb{Q}}\), a semisimple
  \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group \(G\) of the same type as \(G_{\mathbb{Q}}\) and
  equipped with a split maximal torus \(T\); hence, by Exp. XXII 2.2,
  \(G\) is split.}

To prove 1.2, and hence 1.1, it therefore suffices to prove 1.3 when
\(k\) is of characteristic zero (for example \(k = \mathbb{C}\)) and
\(G_{k}\) is simply connected (and in particular semisimple), as well
as:

\textbf{Proposition 1.4.} \emph{For every simply connected reduced root
datum \(R\), there exists a semisimple algebraic \(\mathbb{C}\)-group of
type \(R\).}

One may prove 1.4 in the following way. One knows first that there
exists a complex semisimple Lie algebra \(g\) of type \(R\), cf.~for
example N. Jacobson, \emph{Lie Algebras}, ch.~VII, Th. 5.\footnote{N.D.E.:
  Let \(\Delta\) be a base of \(R\) and \(\tilde{g}\) the complex Lie
  algebra generated by generators
  \((e_{\alpha}, f_{\alpha}, h_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in \Delta}\) subject to
  the relations \([h_{\alpha}, h_{\beta}] = 0\),
  \([e_{\alpha}, f_{\beta}] = h_{\alpha}\) if \(\beta = \alpha\) and
  \texttt{=\ 0} otherwise,
  \([h_{\alpha}, e_{\beta}] = (\alpha*, \beta) e_{\beta}\) and
  \([h_{\alpha}, f_{\beta}] = -(\alpha*, \beta) f_{\beta}\). In
  \emph{loc. cit.}, \(g\) is defined as the quotient of \(\tilde{g}\) by
  the intersection of the kernels of the finite-dimensional irreducible
  representations of \(\tilde{g}\); in {[}Se66{]}, § VI.5, Th. 9 (see
  also {[}BLie{]}, VIII, § 4.3, Th. 1) it is shown that \(g\) is the
  quotient of \(\tilde{g}\) by the relations
  \(ad(e_{\alpha})^{1-(\alpha*, \beta)}(e_{\beta}) = 0\) and
  \(ad(f_{\alpha})^{1-(\alpha*, \beta)}(f_{\beta}) = 0\). For an
  explicit description of the structure constants (in particular the
  choice of signs), see Exp. XXIII 6.5 and 6.7 as well as {[}Ti66{]}, §
  4, Th. 1 and (for types A, D, E) {[}Sp98{]}, 10.2.5.} Then
\(G = \operatorname{Aut}(g)^{0}\) is a semisimple algebraic
\(\mathbb{C}\)-group of type \(ad(R)\).\footnote{N.D.E.: One may suppose
  \(R\) irreducible, hence \(g\) simple. By a general argument, one
  knows that \(Lie(G)\) is the complex Lie algebra of derivations of
  \(g\) (cf.~{[}DG70{]}, § II.4, Prop. 2.3); but these are all inner
  (cf.~{[}BLie{]}, I § 6.1, Cor. 3 of Prop. 1), hence \(Lie(G) = g\);
  consequently \(G\) has no invariant subgroup of dimension
  \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}, hence \(G\) is semisimple. Its root system
  is then the same as that of \(g\); moreover, the center of \(G\) acts
  simultaneously trivially and faithfully on \(g\), hence is trivial,
  hence \(G\) is adjoint.} By \emph{Bible}, § 23.1, Prop. 1, one deduces
from this the existence of a semisimple \(\mathbb{C}\)-group of type
\(R\).

The rest of this Exposé is devoted to the proof of 1.3 for \(k\) of
characteristic zero and \(G_{k}\) semisimple. It will be carried out in
two stages: construction of a ``piece of \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group scheme''
(n° 2), and study of the group obtained by application of the ``theorem
of Weil'' (n° 3).

To avoid confusion, we shall not use in n° 2 the abbreviated notation
\(X_{k}\) to denote the \(k\)-scheme \(X \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\), where
\(X\) is a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-scheme.

\subsection{2. Existence theorem: construction of a piece of
group}\label{existence-theorem-construction-of-a-piece-of-group}

\subsubsection{2.1.}\label{section-313}

Let us choose, once and for all, a splitting of \(G_{k}\), denoted

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(G\_k, T\_k, M, R)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(cf.~Exp. XXII, 1.13), a system of simple roots \(\Delta\) of \(R\)
(defining the system of positive roots \(R^{+}\)), a Chevalley system
\((X_{\alpha,k})_{\alpha\in R}\) of \(G_{k}\) (Exp. XXIII, 6.1 and 6.2)
satisfying the following supplementary condition (cf.~XX 2.6): for every
\(\alpha \in R\), one has

\[
X_{\alpha,k} X_{-\alpha,k} = 1.
\]

Finally, let us choose on the subgroup of \(M\) generated by \(R\) a
total order relation compatible with the group structure, such that the
roots \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0} are the elements of \(R^{+}\). We then
denote the roots

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{−α\_n \textless{} −α\_\{n−1\} \textless{} ⋯ \textless{} −α\_1 \textless{} α\_1 \textless{} α\_2 \textless{} ⋯ \textless{} α\_n.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For \(\alpha \in R\), we denote by \(U_{\alpha,k}\) the vector group
corresponding to the root \(\alpha\), and by

\[
p_{\alpha,k} : \mathbb{G}_{a,k} \xrightarrow{\sim} U_{\alpha,k}
\]

the isomorphism of vector groups defined by \(X_{\alpha,k}\).

\subsubsection{2.2.}\label{section-314}

The splitting of \(G_{k}\) includes in particular an isomorphism of
\(k\)-groups

\[
T_{k} \simeq D_{k}(M).
\]

Put \(T = D(M)\); this is a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-torus, and the previous
isomorphism may be regarded as an isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T\_k ≃ T ⊗\_ℤ k.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One has

\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}-gr.}(T, \mathbb{G}_{m}) = M,
\]

and one will regard the elements of \(R \subset M\) as characters of
\(T\). Likewise, one will regard the elements of \(R*\) as morphisms of
\(\mathbb{Z}\)-groups \(\mathbb{G}_{m} \to T\).

\subsubsection{2.3.}\label{section-315}

For each \(\alpha \in R^{+}\), let \(\mathbb{G}_{a}(\alpha)\) be a copy
of the group \(\mathbb{G}_{a}\); consider the \(\mathbb{Z}\)-scheme

\[
U = \mathbb{G}_{a}(\alpha_{1}) \times \cdots \times \mathbb{G}_{a}(\alpha_{n}).
\]

If \(U_{k}\) denotes the unipotent part of the Borel group \(B_{k}\) of
\(G_{k}\) defined by \(R^{+}\), denote by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a : U ⊗\_ℤ k ⥲ U\_k}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the isomorphism of \(k\)-schemes defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(x\_1, …, x\_n) = p\_\{α\_1,k\}(x\_1) ⋯ p\_\{α\_n,k\}(x\_n).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{2.4.}\label{section-316}

The group law of \(U_{k}\) translates into relations of the form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(x\_1, …, x\_n) · a(y\_1, …, y\_n) = a(z\_1, …, z\_n),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where each \(z_{h}\) (\(h = 1, \cdots, n\)) is expressed as a polynomial

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{z\_h = x\_h + y\_h + Q\_h(x\_1, …, x\_\{h−1\}, y\_1, …, y\_\{h−1\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the coefficients of \(Q_{h}\) being integers (Exp. XXII, 5.5.8 and Exp.
XXIII, 6.4). Moreover
\(Q_{h}(x_{1}, \cdots, x_{h-1}, 0, \cdots, 0) = 0\).

Let us equip \(U\) with the composition law defined by the preceding
formulas (which are indeed ``defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\)''). Since this
law induces on \(U_{k}\) its group law, it is associative, and
\texttt{(0)} is a unit element (indeed, the two preceding assertions are
expressed by relations between the polynomials \(Q_{h}\), and
\(\mathbb{Z} \to k\) is injective). Let us show that this is a group
law: if \((x_{i})\) is a section of \(U\) (over some \(S\)), one
computes the inverse \((y_{i})\) of \((x_{i})\) by the recurrence
formulas

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y\_i = −x\_i − Q\_i(x\_1, …, x\_\{i−1\}, y\_1, …, y\_\{i−1\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

which are still ``defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\)''.

In summary, we have constructed on \(U\) a group law such that the
previous isomorphism \(a\) is an isomorphism of groups.

For each \(\alpha \in R^{+}\), consider the morphism

\[
p_{\alpha} : \mathbb{G}_{a} \to U
\]

defined by \(p_{\alpha}(x) = (x_{i})\) where

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{x\_i = x  if α\_i = α,}
\NormalTok{x\_i = 0  if α\_i ≠ α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is a closed immersion and a group homomorphism; we denote its image
by \(U_{\alpha}\). One has
\((x_{i}) = p_{\alpha_{1}}(x_{1}) \cdots p_{\alpha_{n}}(x_{n})\), which
proves that \(U\) is identified with the product

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U = U\_\{α\_1\} · U\_\{α\_2\} ⋯ U\_\{α\_n\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{2.5.}\label{section-317}

Let \(T = D(M)\) act on each \(U_{\alpha}\) through the character
\(\alpha\); one verifies at once that this defines an action of \(T\) on
the group \(U\), and one can construct the semi-direct product
\(B = T \cdot U\). One has a canonical isomorphism of \(k\)-groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{B ⊗\_ℤ k ⥲ B\_k.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If we now take any order on \(R^{+}\), the morphism

\[
\prod_{\alpha\in R^{+}} U_{\alpha} \to U
\]

defined by the product in \(U\) is still an isomorphism. Indeed, since
both sides are flat \(\mathbb{Z}\)-schemes of finite presentation, it
suffices to verify the assertion on geometric fibers; one is then
reduced to Lazard's theory (\emph{Bible}, § 13.1, Prop. 1): one
considers \(U\) as a group with operators \(T\), and one uses the fact
that the \(U_{\alpha}\) are pairwise non-isomorphic as groups with
operators (since the characters \(\alpha \in R^{+}\) of \(T\) are
pairwise distinct on each fiber).

\subsubsection{2.6.}\label{section-318}

Replacing \(R^{+}\) by \(R^{-} = -R^{+}\), one constructs similarly the
groups \(U^{-}\), \(B^{-}\), \(U_{\alpha}\) (\(\alpha \in R^{-}\)) and
the isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α : 𝔾\_a ⥲ U\_α,  α ∈ R⁻.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us finally introduce the product scheme

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω = U⁻ × T × U;}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one has a canonical isomorphism of \(k\)-schemes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Ω ⊗\_ℤ k ⥲ U⁻\_k ×\_k T\_k ×\_k U\_k ≃ Ω\_k,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(\Omega_{k}\) is the ``big cell'' of \(G_{k}\) (Exp. XXII,
4.1.2).

From now on, we identify \(\Omega \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) with
\(\Omega_{k}\) by the previous isomorphism; we regard \(U^{-}\), \(T\),
\(U\) as subschemes of \(\Omega\), through their unit sections. We
denote by \(e = ((0), e, (0))\) the ``unit section'' of \(\Omega\).

Our goal now is to put a piece-of-group law on \(\Omega\).

\textbf{Lemma 2.7.} \emph{Let \(\alpha \in \Delta\), and let
\(w_{\alpha,k}\) be the element of \(Norm_{G_{k}}(T_{k})(k)\) defined by
\(X_{\alpha,k}\) (recall that by definition}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_\{α,k\} = p\_\{−α,k\}(−1) p\_\{α,k\}(1) p\_\{−α,k\}(−1)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{There exist an open subset \(V_{\alpha}\) of \(\Omega\) containing
the section \(e\), and a morphism}

\[
h_{\alpha} : V_{\alpha} \to \Omega,
\]

\emph{satisfying the following conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(h_{\alpha}(e) = e\),}

\emph{(ii) \((h_{\alpha}) \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) coincides with the
restriction of \(int(w_{\alpha,k})\) to
\(V_{\alpha} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k \subset G_{k}\).}

\emph{(iii) One has \(T \subset V_{\alpha}\), and \(h_{\alpha}\) sends
\(T\) into \(T\). For every \(\beta \in R\), one has
\(U_{\beta} \subset V_{\alpha}\) and \(h_{\alpha}\) sends \(U_{\beta}\)
into \(U_{s_{\alpha}(\beta)}\).}

By virtue of the definition of a Chevalley system (Exp. XXIII, 6.1),
there exists for each \(\beta \in R\) an integer \(e_{\beta} = \pm 1\)
such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{int(w\_\{α,k\}) p\_\{β,k\}(x) = p\_\{s\_α(β),k\}(e\_β x)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

for every \(x \in \mathbb{G}_{a}(S)\), \(S \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\).

Let \(S\) be any scheme, and write an arbitrary element of \(\Omega(S)\)
in the form

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u = ( ∏\_\{β∈R⁻, β≠−α\} p\_β(x\_β) · p\_\{−α\}(x\_\{−α\}),  t,  p\_α(x\_α) · ∏\_\{β∈R⁺, β≠α\} p\_β(x\_β) ),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where one has chosen some (arbitrary) order on \(R^{-} - {-\alpha}\) and
\(R^{+} - {\alpha}\) (cf.~2.5).

One defines a morphism
\(d : \Omega \to \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{d(u) = α(t) + x\_α x\_\{−α\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let \(V_{\alpha}\) be the open subset \(\Omega_{d}\) (that is, the open
subset of \(\Omega\) defined by ``\(d(u)\) invertible''); it contains
\(e\), \(T\), and each \(U_{\beta}\), \(\beta \in R\). Let

\[
h_{\alpha} : V_{\alpha} \to \Omega
\]

be the morphism defined by \(h_{\alpha}(u) = (a(u), b(u), c(u))\) where

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(u) = ( ∏\_\{β∈R⁻, β≠−α\} p\_\{s\_α(β)\}(e\_β x\_β) ) · p\_\{−α\}(−x\_α d(u)⁻¹),}

\NormalTok{b(u) = t · α*(d(u)),}

\NormalTok{c(u) = p\_α(−x\_\{−α\} d(u)⁻¹) · ( ∏\_\{β∈R⁺, β≠α\} p\_\{s\_α(β)\}(e\_β x\_β) ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(s_{\alpha}\) permutes the positive roots (resp. negative roots)
distinct from \(\alpha\) (resp. \(-\alpha\)), \(c(u)\) (resp. \(a(u)\))
is a section of \(U\) (resp. \(U^{-}\)) and the previous morphism is
well-defined. It satisfies (i) and (iii) trivially. As for (ii), this
follows at once from the definition of the \(e_{\beta}\),
\(\beta \in R\), and from Exp. XX, 3.12.

\textbf{Lemma 2.8.} \emph{There exist open subsets \(V\) and \(V'\) of
\(\Omega\) and morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h : V → Ω,  h′ : V′ → Ω,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{satisfying the following conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(V\) and \(V'\) contain \(e\), and \(h(e) = h'(e) = e\).}

\emph{(ii) The morphism induced by
\(h' \circ h : h^{-1}(V') \to \Omega\) is the restriction of the
identity morphism.}

\emph{(iii) The \(k\)-morphisms \(h \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) and
\(h' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) are the restrictions to
\(V \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) and \(V' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) of
automorphisms of the group \(G_{k}\).}

\emph{(iv) \(V\) and \(V'\) contain \(U\), \(T\) and \(U^{-}\); \(h\)
and \(h'\) send \(U\) into \(U^{-}\), \(U^{-}\) into \(U\), and \(T\)
into \(T\).}

Let \(w^{0}\) be the element of the Weyl group of \(G_{k}\) that
transforms \(R^{+}\) into \(R^{-}\). Write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w⁰ = s\_\{α\_n\} ⋯ s\_\{α\_1\},  α\_i ∈ Δ}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(no relation to the numbering of 2.1). Put

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w\_0 = w\_\{α\_n,k\} ⋯ w\_\{α\_1,k\} ∈ Norm\_\{G\_k\}(T\_k)(k).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Define by recursion on \(i \leq n\) an open subset \(V_{i}\) of
\(\Omega\) and a morphism \(h_{i} : V_{i} \to \Omega\) by
\(V_{0} = \Omega\), \(h_{0} = id\), and, for \(i = 0, \cdots, n - 1\),

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{V\_\{i+1\} = h\_i⁻¹(V\_\{α\_\{i+1\}\}),  h\_\{i+1\} = h\_\{α\_\{i+1\}\} ∘ h\_i,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where the notations \(V_{\alpha_{j}}\) and \(h_{\alpha_{j}}\) are those
of 2.7.

Take \(V = V_{n}\) and \(h = h_{n}\). The conditions in (i), (iii) and
(iv) bearing on \(V\) and \(h\) are indeed verified; for (i) and (iii)
this follows at once from 2.8, for (iv) from the fact that
\(h \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) is the restriction of \(int(w_{0})\) to
\(V \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\).

Since \((w^{0})^{2} = 1\), one also has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{w⁰ = s\_\{α\_1\} ⋯ s\_\{α\_n\} = (s³\_\{α\_1\}) ⋯ (s³\_\{α\_n\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Setting

\[
w'_{0} = (w_{\alpha_{1},k})^{3} \cdots (w_{\alpha_{n},k})^{3},
\]

and carrying out the same construction as above, one deduces from it an
open subset \(V'\) and a morphism \(h'\) also satisfying (i), (iii),
(iv). Moreover, \(h' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) is the restriction of
\(int(w'_{0})\) to \(V' \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\). But for each simple
root \(\alpha \in \Delta\), one has \((w_{\alpha,k})^{4} = e\) (cf.~Exp.
XX, 3.1), hence \(w'_{0} \cdot w_{0} = e\), which shows that
\(h' \circ h\) induces the identity morphism on a non-empty open subset
of \(\Omega \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\). But since \(\Omega\) is smooth and
of finite presentation over \(\mathbb{Z}\),
\(\Omega \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} k\) is schematically dense in \(\Omega\),
which proves (ii).

\textbf{Proposition 2.9.} \emph{There exist an open subset \texttt{V\_1}
of \(\Omega \times \Omega\), an open subset \texttt{V\_2} of \(\Omega\),
and morphisms}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π : V\_1 → Ω,  σ : V\_2 → Ω,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{having the following properties:}

\emph{(i) If \(x \in \Omega(S)\), then \((e, x)\) and \((x, e)\) are
sections of \texttt{V\_1}, and}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π(e, x) = π(x, e) = x.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) \texttt{V\_2} contains \(e\) and \(\sigma(e) = e\).}

\emph{(iii) \(\pi_{k}\) and \(\sigma_{k}\) are the restrictions of the
morphisms \(G_{k} \times_{k} G_{k} \to G_{k}\) and \(G_{k} \to G_{k}\)
defined by the product (resp. the inverse).}

\emph{Proof.} Let \((v, t, u)\) and \((v', t', u')\) be two sections of
\(\Omega\). Then \(h(u)\) is a section of \(U^{-}\), \(h(v')\) is a
section of \(U\) by 2.8 (iv), and one can therefore regard
\((h(u), e, h(v'))\) as a section of \(\Omega\). Let \texttt{V\_1} be
the open subset of \(\Omega \times \Omega\) defined by the condition:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{((v, t, u), (v′, t′, u′)) ∈ V\_1(S) ⟺ (h(u), e, h(v′)) ∈ V′(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(notation of 2.8). If \(((v, t, u), (v', t', u'))\) is a section of
\texttt{V\_1}, then \(h'(h(u), e, h(v'))\) is defined; it is a section
of \(\Omega\) which one can decompose:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h′(h(u), e, h(v′)) = (v′′, t′′, u′′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One then sets

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π((v, t, u), (v′, t′, u′)) = (v · ᵗv′′ t⁻¹, t t′′ t′, t′⁻¹ u′′ t′ · u′).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The verification of (i) is immediate (by 2.8 (ii)). To verify the
condition in (iii) bearing on \(\pi\), one sees that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{h′(h(u), e, h(v′)) = u v′ = v′′ t′′ u′′}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

when \(u \in U(S)\), \(v \in U^{-}(S)\), \(S \to k\), by virtue of 2.8
(iii) and (ii). One constructs \(\sigma\) similarly: if \((v, t, u)\) is
a section of \(\Omega\), \(h(u^{-1})\) is a section of \(U^{-}\),

\(h(v^{-1})\) is a section of \(U\), \(h(t^{-1})\) is a section of
\(T\), so \((h(u^{-1}), h(t^{-1}), h(v^{-1}))\) is a section of
\(\Omega\) and one can define an open subset \texttt{V\_2} of \(\Omega\)
by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(v, t, u) ∈ V\_2(S) ⟺ (h(u⁻¹), h(t⁻¹), h(v⁻¹)) ∈ V′(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and a morphism \(\sigma : V_{2} \to \Omega\) by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{σ(v, t, u) = h′(h(u⁻¹), h(t⁻¹), h(v⁻¹)).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One verifies the conditions on \(\sigma\) as above.

\textbf{Corollary 2.10.} \emph{\(\pi\) is ``generically associative''
and \(\sigma\) is a ``generic inverse'': if \(x, y, z \in \Omega(S)\)
and if the expressions below are defined (which always happens over an
open subset of \(\Omega\) containing the unit section), one has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π(x, π(y, z)) = π(π(x, y), z),  π(x, σ(x)) = e = π(σ(x), x).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, the two sides of each of these formulas define morphisms between
smooth \(\mathbb{Z}\)-schemes of finite presentation, which coincide on
the generic fibers, by 2.10 (iii).

\textbf{Corollary 2.11.} \emph{Let \(\alpha \in R\). For all \(S\) and
all \(x, y \in \mathbb{G}_{a}(S)\) such that
\((p_{\alpha}(x), p_{-\alpha}(y)) \in V_{1}(S)\) and
\(1 + xy \in \mathbb{G}_{m}(S)\) (which defines an open subset of
\(\mathbb{G}^{2}_{a,S}\) containing the section \texttt{(0,\ 0)}), one
has:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{π(p\_α(x), p\_\{−α\}(y)) = ( p\_\{−α\}( y / (1 + xy) ), α*(1 + xy), p\_α( x / (1 + xy) ) ).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The proof is the same as before, by Exp. XX, 2.1.

\subsection{3. Existence theorem: end of the
proof}\label{existence-theorem-end-of-the-proof}

To simplify language, let us pose the following definition.

\textbf{Definition 3.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(G\) an
\(S\)-group scheme. One says that \(G\) is} admissible \emph{if there
exists an open immersion of \(S\)-schemes
\(i : \Omega_{S} = \Omega \times S \to G\) satisfying the following
conditions:}

\emph{(i) The diagram}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(V\_1)\_S ──i ×\_S i──▶ Ω\_S ×\_S Ω\_S ──i ×\_S i──▶ G ×\_S G}
\NormalTok{   │                                              │}
\NormalTok{   π                                              π\_G}
\NormalTok{   │                                              │}
\NormalTok{   ▼          ─────────── i\_S ───────────▶        ▼}
\NormalTok{  Ω\_S                                             G,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \(\pi_{G}\) denotes the multiplication morphism in \(G\), is
commutative.}

\emph{(ii) There exists a finite set of sections \(a_{j} \in \Omega(S)\)
such that the \(i(a_{j}) \cdot i(\Omega_{S})\) cover \(G\).}

By Weil's ``theorem'' (Exp. XVIII, 3.13 (iii) and (iv)), one has:

\textbf{Lemma 3.2.} \emph{If for every scheme \(S\) étale and of finite
type over \(\mathbb{Z}\), every admissible \(S\)-group is affine, then
there exists an admissible affine \(\mathbb{Z}\)-group.}

Now one has:

\textbf{Lemma 3.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme and \(G\) an admissible
\(S\)-group. Then \(G\) is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\),
with affine connected semisimple fibers.}

Since \(\Omega_{S}\) is smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\),
with connected fibers, the same holds for \(G\), by condition (ii). To
verify 3.3, one may therefore suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of a
field \(K\). Let us identify \(\Omega_{K}\) with its image in \(G\). It
is clear that \(\Omega_{K}\) is the product

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∏\_\{α∈R⁻\} U\_\{α,K\} · T\_K · ∏\_\{α∈R⁺\} U\_\{α,K\}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

of the subgroups \texttt{T\_K} and \(U_{\alpha,K}\) (\(\alpha \in R\))
of \(G\). The Lie algebra of \(G\) is therefore identified with the
direct sum

\[
Lie(T_{K}) \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha\in R} Lie(U_{\alpha,K}).
\]

Since the inner automorphism defined by a section of \texttt{T\_K} acts
on \(U_{\alpha,K}\), and therefore on \(Lie(U_{\alpha,K})\), through the
character

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α ∈ R ⊂ M ≃ Hom\_\{K{-}gr.\}(T\_K, 𝔾\_\{m,K\}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the previous decomposition of \(Lie(G)\) is exactly the decomposition
under the adjoint action of \(T\). The roots of \texttt{G\_K} with
respect to \texttt{T\_K} are therefore the \(\alpha \in R\). Apply Exp.
XIX, 1.13. Let \(T_{\alpha}\) be the maximal torus of
\(Ker(\alpha) \subset T_{K}\), and let
\(Z_{\alpha} = Centr_{G}(T_{\alpha})\); it suffices for us to prove that
each \(Z_{\alpha}\) is reductive. Now \(Z_{\alpha} \cap \Omega_{K}\) is
none other than

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{∏\_\{β∈R⁻, β|\_\{T\_α\} = e\} U\_\{β,K\} · T\_K · ∏\_\{β∈R⁺, β|\_\{T\_α\} = e\} U\_\{β,K\};}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but the roots vanishing on \(T_{\alpha}\) are the rational multiples of
\(\alpha\), hence \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\); this proves

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Z\_α ∩ Ω\_K = U\_\{−α,K\} · T\_K · U\_\{α,K\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To prove that \(Z_{\alpha}\) is reductive, it suffices, by Exp. XX 3.4,
to prove that \(U_{\alpha,K}\) and \(U_{-\alpha,K}\) do not commute,
which follows at once from 2.11.

It follows from 3.2 and 3.3 that the proof will be complete if we prove:

\textbf{Lemma 3.4.} \emph{If \(S\) is a locally noetherian scheme of
dimension \(\leq 1\), and if \(G\) is a smooth \(S\)-group of finite
type with affine connected semisimple fibers, then \(G\) is affine (and
therefore semisimple).}

\textbf{Nota.} In Exp. XVI, it was seen that 3.4 is true without
hypothesis on \(S\), but the proof is relatively delicate; since here we
need only the particular case 3.4, we give a direct proof of it.

Consider the Lie algebra \(g\) of \(G\), which is a locally free
\(\mathcal{O}_{S}\)-module, and the adjoint representation of \(G\)

\[
Ad : G \to GL_{\mathcal{O}_{S}}(g).
\]

To prove that \(G\) is affine over \(S\), it suffices to prove that the
morphism \texttt{Ad} is affine. Since \(G\) is smooth with connected
fibers, it is separated over \(S\) (VI\_B 5.5), so the morphism
\texttt{Ad} is separated. Using a result proved in the appendix (see
4.1), it suffices to prove that the morphism \texttt{Ad} is
quasi-finite. One is thus reduced to the case where \(S\) is the
spectrum of a field; in this case \(G\) is affine, hence semisimple, and
one is reduced to Exp. XXII 5.7.14.

\subsection{4. Appendix}\label{appendix}

We used in the course of the proof the following proposition:

\textbf{Proposition 4.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a locally noetherian scheme
of dimension \(\leq 1\), let \(G\) and \(H\) be two \(S\)-group schemes
of finite type, and \(f : G \to H\) a quasi-finite separated group
morphism. If \(G\) is flat over \(S\),\footnote{N.D.E.: We have added
  the flatness hypothesis, which had been omitted.} then \(f\) is
affine.}

We shall give the proof only in the case where \(G\) is smooth over
\(S\), a hypothesis which is indeed verified in the application we have
made of the proposition.

\subsubsection{4.2.}\label{section-319}

By EGA II, 1.6.4, one may suppose \(S\) reduced. By the usual techniques
of passage to the limit,\footnote{N.D.E.: cf.~EGA IV\_3, 8.10.5 (viii).}
one may suppose \(S\) local. If \(\dim(S) = 0\), the assertion is
trivial,\footnote{N.D.E.: Indeed, if \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(k)\)
  (\(k\) a field), then \(f\) is the composite of the projection
  \(p : G \to G/Ker(f)\) and a closed immersion \(i\), and since
  \(Ker(f)\) is finite over \(k\), \(p\) is finite (VI\_B 9.2).} suppose
\(\dim(S) = 1\). By faithfully flat descent, one may suppose that \(S\)
is complete with algebraically closed residue field. Replacing \(S\) by
its normalization \(\tilde{S}\) if necessary, one may (EGA II, 6.7.1 and
EGA 0\_IV 23.1.5) suppose \(S\) normal.\footnote{N.D.E.: Indeed, the
  irreducible components \(S_{1}, \cdots, S_{r}\) of \(S\) are complete
  integral noetherian local schemes, hence, by a theorem of Nagata
  (cf.~EGA 0\_IV, 23.1.5) the normalization \(\tilde{S}_{i}\) is finite
  over \(S_{i}\), and therefore \(\tilde{S}\) is finite over \(S\).
  Then, by a theorem of Chevalley (cf.~EGA II, 6.7.1), if
  \(f \times_{S} \tilde{S}\) is an affine morphism, then so is \(f\).}
One is therefore reduced to the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a
complete discrete valuation ring \(A\) with algebraically closed residue
field.

\subsubsection{4.3.}\label{section-320}

Let \(\eta\) (resp. \(s\)) be the generic (resp. closed) point of \(S\).
Consider the image \(f_{\eta}(G_{\eta})\) of \(G_{\eta}\) in
\(H_{\eta}\). It is a closed subgroup scheme of \(H_{\eta}\). Let \(H'\)
be the schematic closure in \(H\) of \(f_{\eta}(G_{\eta})\). Since
\(H' \to H\) is affine (it is a closed immersion), one may replace \(H\)
by \(H'\) and so suppose \(H\) flat over \(S\) and \(f_{\eta}\)
surjective. Since \(f_{\eta}\) is finite, and \(G\) and \(H\) are flat
over \(S\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{dim(G\_s) = dim(G\_η) = dim(H\_η) = dim(H\_s).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{4.4.}\label{section-321}

Let \(H^{0}_{s}, \cdots, H^{n}_{s}\) be the irreducible components of
\(H_{s}\), where \(H^{0}_{s}\) denotes the neutral component, and let
\(z_{0}, \cdots, z_{n}\) be their generic points. Since each local ring
\(\mathcal{O}_{H,z_{i}}\) is of dimension \(\leq 1\), the morphism
\(G \times_{H} \mathcal{O}_{H,z_{i}} \to \mathcal{O}_{H,z_{i}}\) is
affine because quasi-finite and separated (cf.~Exp. XVI, Lemma 4.2), so
\(G\) is affine over \(H\) in a neighborhood of \(z_{i}\). Denoting by
\(V\) the largest open subset of \(H\) such that \(G|_{V}\) is affine
over \(V\), it follows

that \(V\) contains all the \(z_{i}\),\footnote{N.D.E.: The following
  sentence has been added.} so contains at least one closed point
\(y_{i} \in H^{i}_{s}\) (and one has \(\kappa(y_{i}) = \kappa(s)\) since
\(\kappa(s)\) is algebraically closed).

On the other hand, \(V\) is obviously stable under the translation
defined by any element \(g \in G(S)\). But one has
\(\dim(G_{s}) = \dim(H_{s})\) and \(f_{s}\) is finite, so

\[
f(s) : G^{0}_{s}(s) \to H^{0}_{s}(s)
\]

is surjective. Since \(A\) is complete and \(G\) smooth over \(S\), the
canonical map \(G^{0}(S) \to G^{0}_{s}(s)\) is surjective; since
\(H^{0}_{s}(s)\) acts transitively on each \(H^{i}_{s}(s)\), it follows
that \(V \supset H_{s}(s)\), hence (since \(\kappa(s)\) is algebraically
closed) \(V \supset H_{s}\).\footnote{N.D.E.: When \(G\) is not assumed
  smooth over \(S\), one may proceed as follows. Let \(h_{0}\) be a
  rational point of \(H^{0}_{s}\) and \(g_{0}\) a rational point of
  \(G^{0}_{s}\) such that \(f(g_{0}) = h_{0}\). By VI\_B 5.6.1, there
  exists a commutative diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{                   g}
\NormalTok{          S′′ ────────▶ G}
\NormalTok{          │ ╲           │}
\NormalTok{          π   ╲ φ       │}
\NormalTok{          │     ╲       │}
\NormalTok{          ▼       ▼     ▼}
\NormalTok{          S′ ─── w ───▶ S}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

  where \(w\) is étale and surjective, \(\pi\) finite and surjective,
  and \(\phi^{-1}(s)\) is formed of a single point \(s''\) such that
  \(g(s'') = g_{0}\). Then the morphism \(G_{S''} \to H_{S''}\) is
  affine above a neighborhood of \(h_{0} y_{i}\), and the same holds for
  \(G_{S'} \to H_{S'}\) (EGA II, 6.7.1), and then for \(G \to H\) by
  faithfully flat descent (EGA IV\_2, 2.7.1 (xiii)). Hence
  \(h_{0} y_{i} \in V\), and it follows that \(V\) contains
  \(H_{s}(s)\), and therefore \(H_{s}\).}

Since one obviously has \(V \supset H_{\eta}\), since \(f_{\eta}\) is
finite, one therefore has \(V = H\). \emph{QED}.

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-11}

\section{Exposé XXVI. Parabolic subgroups of reductive
groups}\label{exposuxe9-xxvi.-parabolic-subgroups-of-reductive-groups}

\emph{by M. Demazure}

\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} Version of 13/10/2024.}

This Exposé studies the parabolic subgroups of an \(S\)-reductive group
\(G\). Its essential result is the conjugacy theorem (5.4). The
essential tool is the notion of \emph{transversal position} of two
parabolic subgroups, a notion studied systematically in §4. Another fact
plays an important role: the decomposition of the unipotent radical
\(rad^{u}(P)\) of a parabolic subgroup \(P\) as successive extensions of
vector groups (2.1)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} Since the Levi subgroups of
  \(P\) form a torsor under \(rad^{u}(P)\) (1.9), this entails, when
  \(S\) is semi-local, that \(P\) has a Levi subgroup and hence a
  maximal torus (2.4).}.

Various schemes associated with \(G\) are studied in §3; §6 deals with
the split subtori\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} The terminology ``trivial
  torus'' has been replaced by that of ``split torus''.} of \(G\) and
their relations with parabolic subgroups.

Finally, in §7, we briefly expound how, over a semi-local base, one
formulates the ``relative theory'' of reductive groups as presented over
fields in the article of A. Borel and J. Tits, \emph{Groupes réductifs},
Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS, no. 27. In that article, cited
{[}BT65{]} in what follows, the reader will moreover find, in the case
of a base field, other results that have not been touched on here.

\subsection{1. Recollections. Levi
subgroups}\label{recollections.-levi-subgroups}

\textbf{Definition 1.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a sub-\(S\)-group-scheme of \(G\). One says
that \(P\) is a} parabolic subgroup \emph{of \(G\) if}

\emph{(i) \(P\) is smooth over \(S\),}

\emph{(ii) for each \(s \in S\), the \(s\)-quotient-scheme
\(G_{s}/P_{s}\) is proper (i.e.~Bible, §6.4, Th. 4 (= {[}Ch05{]}, §6.5,
Th. 5), \(P_{s}\) contains a Borel subgroup of \(G_{s}\)).}

\textbf{Proposition 1.2} (Exp. XXII, 5.8.5). \emph{Let \(S\) be a
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of
\(G\). Then \(P\) is closed in \(G\), with connected fibers, and}

\[
P = Norm_{G}(P).
\]

\emph{Moreover, the quotient sheaf \(G/P\) is representable by an
\(S\)-scheme that is smooth and projective over \(S\).}

\textbf{Proposition 1.3} (Exp. XXII, 5.3.9 and 5.3.11). \emph{Let \(S\)
be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) and \(P'\) two
parabolic subgroups of \(G\). The following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(P\) and \(P'\) are conjugate in \(G\), locally for the étale
(resp. (fpqc)) topology.}

\emph{(ii) For each \(s \in S\), \(P_{s}\) and \(P_{s}'\) are conjugate
by an element of \(G(s)\).}

\emph{(iii) The strict transporter \(Transt_{G}(P, P')\) of \(P\) into
\(P'\) (defined by}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Transt\_G(P, P\textquotesingle{})(S\textquotesingle{}) = \{ g ∈ G(S\textquotesingle{}) | int(g) P\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\} = P\textquotesingle{}\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\} \}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{for every \(S' \to S\)) is a closed subscheme of \(G\), smooth and
of finite presentation over \(S\), which is a principal homogeneous
bundle on the right under \(P\) and on the left under \(P'\).}

\textbf{Proposition 1.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a nonempty scheme,
\((G, T, M, R)\) an \(S\)-split reductive group, \(R'\) a subset of
\(R\). The following conditions on \(R'\) are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) \(g_{R'} = t \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R'} g^{\alpha}\) is
the Lie algebra of a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\)
(necessarily unique, Exp. XXII, 5.3.5).}

\emph{(ii) \(R'\) is of type (R) (Exp. XXII, 5.4.2) and contains a
system of positive roots.}

\emph{(iii) \(R'\) is a closed subset of \(R\) and satisfies: if
\(\alpha \in R - R'\), then \(-\alpha \in R'\) (that is,
\(R = R' \cup (-R')\)).}

\emph{(iv) There exist a system of simple roots \(\Delta\), and a subset
\(A\) of \(\Delta\) such that \(R'\) is the union of the set of positive
roots and the set of negative roots that are linear combinations of the
elements of \(A\).}

\emph{(v) \(R'\) contains a system of simple roots of \(R\); moreover,
if \(\Delta \subset R'\) is a system of simple roots of \(R\) and one
sets}

\[
A = (-R') \cap \Delta,
\]

\emph{then \(R'\) is the union of the set of positive roots and the set
of negative roots that are linear combinations of the elements of
\(A\).}

One has (i) ⇔ (ii) by Exp. XXII, 5.4.5 (ii) and 5.5.1. One has (iii) ⇒
(ii) by Exp. XXI, 3.3.6 and Exp. XXII, 5.4.7. One trivially has (v) ⇒
(iv) ⇒ (iii). One has (iii) ⇒ (v) by Exp. XXI, 3.3.6 and 3.3.10.

It therefore remains to prove that (i) implies that \(R'\) is a closed
subset of \(R\). But this last assertion can be verified on any
geometric fiber; one may therefore assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of
an algebraically closed field.

Let \(P\) be the parabolic subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) whose Lie
algebra is \(g_{R'}\). Since the Borel subgroups of \(P\) are the Borel
subgroups of \(G\) contained in \(P\), it follows from Bible, §12.3, Th.
1, and from Exp. XXII, 5.4.5 (i), that if one denotes by \(U\) the
unipotent radical of \(P\), then \(T \cdot U\) is the subgroup of \(G\)
containing \(T\) whose Lie algebra is

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g\_\{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\} = t ⊕ ⨁\_\{α ∈ R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\} g\^{}α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is the intersection
of the systems of positive roots of \(R\) contained in \(R'\). In
particular, it follows that
\texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is closed and that
\(R'' \cap (-R'') = \emptyset\). On the other hand, the group
\(H = P/U\) is reductive, the canonical image \(\bar{T}\) of \(T\) is a
maximal torus of it (\(T \to \bar{T}\) is an isomorphism), and one has
an isomorphism of \(\bar{T}\)-modules, i.e.~of \(M\)-graded vector
spaces,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(H) ≃ t ⊕ ⨁\_\{α ∈ R\_s\} g\^{}α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(R_{s}\) is the complement of
\texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} in \(R'\). It follows
that \(R_{s}\) is naturally identified with the set of roots of \(H\)
relative to \(\bar{T}\), and in particular satisfies \(R_{s} = -R_{s}\).
One immediately deduces that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{} = \{ α ∈ R\textquotesingle{} | −α ∉ R\textquotesingle{} \},        R\_s = \{ α ∈ R\textquotesingle{} | −α ∈ R\textquotesingle{} \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us now show that \(R'\) is closed. Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R'\) such
that \(\alpha + \beta \in R\); let us prove that
\(\alpha + \beta \in R'\). If \(\alpha, \beta \in R''\), then
\(\alpha + \beta \in R''\) because
\texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is closed. If
\(\alpha \in R_{s}\), \(\beta \in R''\), and if
\(\alpha + \beta \notin R'\), then \(\alpha + \beta \in -R''\), and one
has \(-\alpha = -(\alpha + \beta) + \beta \in R''\) because
\texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is closed, which entails
\(-\alpha \in R'' \cap R_{s}\) and contradicts the fact that
\(R_{s} \cap R'' = \emptyset\). It therefore remains to study the case
where \(\alpha, \beta \in R_{s}\). If \(\alpha + \beta \notin R'\), then
\(\alpha + \beta \in -R''\). But, as \(\alpha + \beta \neq 0\), there
exists a system of positive roots of the root system \(R_{s}\)
containing \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), hence a Borel subgroup of
\(H = P/U\) containing the canonical image of \(U_{\alpha}\) and
\(U_{\beta}\). Its inverse image in \(P\) is a Borel subgroup containing
\(U_{\alpha}\), \(U_{\beta}\) and \(U\), hence \(U_{\alpha}\),
\(U_{\beta}\) and \(U_{-(\alpha+\beta)}\), which is impossible.

\textbf{Corollary 1.5.} \emph{A parabolic subgroup of a reductive group
is of type (RC) (Exp. XXII, 5.11.1).}

\textbf{Proposition 1.6} (Exp. XXII, 5.11.4). \emph{Let \(S\) be a
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a subgroup of \(G\) of
type (RC)}\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} ``Parabolic subgroup'' has been
  replaced by ``subgroup of type (RC)'', as in Exp. XXII, 5.11.4,
  because it will be useful later on (4.5.1, 6.17) to be able to apply
  this statement to \(P \cap P'\), when \texttt{P,\ P\textquotesingle{}}
  are two parabolic subgroups such that \(P \cap P'\) is of type (RC).}.

\emph{(i) \(P\) possesses a largest invariant sub-group-scheme that is
smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected unipotent
geometric fibers. It is a characteristic subgroup of \(P\), called the}
unipotent radical \emph{of \(P\), denoted \(rad^{u}(P)\). The quotient
sheaf \(P/rad^{u}(P)\) is representable by an \(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(ii) If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(P\), \(P\) possesses a
reductive subgroup \(L\) containing \(T\) such that:}

\emph{(a) Every reductive subgroup of \(P\) containing \(T\) is
contained in \(L\).}

\emph{(b) \(P\) is the semidirect product \(L \cdot rad^{u}(P)\),
i.e.~the canonical morphism \(L \to P/rad^{u}(P)\) is an isomorphism.}

\emph{Moreover, \(L\) is the unique subgroup (resp. reductive subgroup)
of \(P\) containing \(T\) and satisfying (b) (resp. (a)). Finally, one
has}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_P(L) = L,        Norm\_P(T) = Norm\_L(T).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{1.7.}\label{section-322}

A subgroup \(L\) of \(P\) satisfying condition (b) above is called a
\emph{Levi subgroup} of \(P\). It is a maximal reductive subgroup of
\(P\); indeed, it is reductive, since isomorphic to \(P/rad^{u}(P)\).
Let us show that it is maximal for this property. Let \(L'\) be a
reductive subgroup of \(P\) containing \(L\); to prove that \(L' = L\),
one may reason locally for the (fpqc) topology, and hence assume that
\(L\) has a maximal torus \(T\), and one is reduced to 1.6 (ii).

If \(L\) and \(L'\) are two Levi subgroups of \(P\), then \(L\) and
\(L'\) are conjugate in \(P\), locally for the (fpqc) topology. Indeed,
locally for this topology, one may assume that \(L\) (resp. \(L'\)) has
a maximal torus \(T\) (resp. \(T'\)); since \(T\) and \(T'\) are
conjugate in \(P\) locally for the (fpqc) topology, one may assume
\(T = T'\), and one then has \(L = L'\), by 1.6 (ii). But since
\(P = L \cdot rad^{u}(P)\) and \(Norm_{P}(L) = L\), one immediately
deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 1.8.} \emph{Let \(P\) be a subgroup of type
(RC)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} cf.~N.D.E. (3).} of the \(S\)-reductive
group \(G\). If \(L\) and \(L'\) are two Levi subgroups of \(P\), there
exists a unique \(u \in rad^{u}(P)(S)\) such that \(int(u) L = L'\).}

Let us denote by \(Lev(P)\) the functor of Levi subgroups of \(P\): for
\(S' \to S\), \(Lev(P)(S')\) is the set of Levi subgroups of \(P_{S'}\).
From 1.8 one deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 1.9.} \emph{Let \(P\) be a subgroup of type
(RC)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} cf.~N.D.E. (3).} of the \(S\)-reductive
group \(G\). Then \(Lev(P)\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under the
\(S\)-group \(rad^{u}(P)\), and in particular is representable by an
\(S\)-scheme that is smooth and affine over \(S\), with integral
geometric fibers.}

It follows immediately from 1.6:

\textbf{Corollary 1.10.} \emph{Let \(P\) be a subgroup of type
(RC)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} cf.~N.D.E. (3).} of the \(S\)-reductive
group \(G\). The functor \(Tor(P)\) of maximal tori of \(P\) is
representable by an \(S\)-scheme that is smooth and affine, the
``relation \(L \supset T\)'' defines a morphism}

\[
Tor(P) \longrightarrow Lev(P),
\]

\emph{the fiber of which over \(L \in Lev(P)(S)\) is identified with
\(Tor(L)\) (Exp. XXII, 5.8.3).}

The first assertion of 1.10 is a consequence of the other two and of
Exp. XXII, 5.8.3.

\textbf{Definition 1.11.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a nonempty scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\),
\(E = (T, M, R, \Delta, (X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta})\) a pinning of
\(G\). One says that \(E\) is} adapted \emph{to \(P\), or that \(E\) is
a} pinning of the pair \((G, P)\), \emph{if \(P \supset T\) and if the
Lie algebra of \(P\) is of the form
\(t \oplus \bigoplus_{\alpha \in R'} g^{\alpha}\), where \(R'\) is a
subset of \(R\) containing \(R^{+}\).}

In particular, if \(T \subset B\) is the Killing pair defined by the
pinning, one has \(T \subset B \subset P\).

Under the preceding conditions, one sets
\(\Delta(P) = \Delta \cap (-R')\); then, by Exp. XXII, 5.4.3, one has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α ∈ Δ(P)  ⇔  α ∈ Δ and U\_\{−α\} ⊂ P  ⇔  α ∈ Δ and U\_\{−α\} ∩ P ≠ e.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows immediately from 1.4 (v) and Exp. XXII, 5.11.3 and 5.10.6:

\textbf{Proposition 1.12.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\),
\((T, M, R, \Delta, (X_{\alpha})_{\alpha \in \Delta})\) a pinning of
\(G\) adapted to \(P\), \(\Delta(P)\) the subset of \(\Delta\) defined
above.}

\emph{(i) The unipotent radical \(rad^{u}(P)\) of \(P\) is none other
than}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_\{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\} = ∏\_\{α ∈ R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}\} U\_α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{where \texttt{R\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} is the set of
positive roots that, in their decomposition along \(\Delta\), involve at
least one element of \(\Delta - \Delta(P)\)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}
  \(\Delta(P)\) has been corrected to \(\Delta - \Delta(P)\).} with a
nonzero coefficient.}

\emph{(ii) The unique Levi subgroup \(L\) of \(P\) containing \(T\) is
none other than}

\[
Z_{\Delta(P)} = Centr_{G}(T_{\Delta(P)}),
\]

\emph{where \(T_{\Delta(P)}\) is the maximal torus of
\(\bigcap_{\alpha \in \Delta(P)} Ker(\alpha)\); moreover, one has
\(T_{\Delta(P)} = rad(L)\).}

\textbf{Corollary 1.13.} \emph{Every Levi subgroup \(L\) of the
parabolic subgroup \(P\) of the reductive group \(G\) is a} critical
subgroup \emph{of \(G\), i.e.~satisfies (Exp. XXII, 5.10.4):}

\[
L = Centr_{G}(rad(L)).
\]

This follows immediately from 1.12 and from the following lemma, which
is contained in 1.4 and Exp. XXII, 5.4.1:

\textbf{Lemma 1.14.} \emph{Locally for the étale topology, every pair
\((G, P)\), where \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of the reductive group
\(G\), may be pinned (1.11).}

Let us note:

\textbf{Proposition 1.15.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(E\) and
\(E'\) two pinnings of \(G\) adapted to \(P\). The unique inner
automorphism of \(G\) over \(S\) that transforms \(E\) into \(E'\) (Exp.
XXIV, 1.5) comes from \(P\), via the morphism}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P ⟶ P/Centr(P) = P/Centr(G) ⟶ G/Centr(G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, it suffices to reason as in Exp. XXIV, 1.5, using:

\textbf{Lemma 1.16} (Exp. XXII, 5.3.14 and 5.2.6). \emph{The maximal
tori (resp. Borel subgroups, resp. Killing pairs) of a parabolic
subgroup \(P\) of the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\) are conjugate in
\(P\), locally for the étale topology.}

\textbf{Proposition 1.17.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) and \(P'\) two parabolic subgroups of
\(G\), \(B\) a Borel subgroup contained in \(P\) and \(P'\). If \(P\)
and \(P'\) are conjugate in \(G\) locally for the étale topology, then
\(P = P'\).}

Indeed, one may assume that there exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that
\(int(g) P = P'\). Then \(B\) and \(int(g)^{-1} B\) are two Borel
subgroups of \(P\). Possibly after extending \(S\), by 1.16 one may
assume that there exists \(p \in P(S)\) such that
\(int(p) int(g^{-1}) B = B\). Then

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p g\^{}\{{-}1\} ∈ Norm\_G(B)(S) = B(S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and \(g \in B(S) \cdot p \subset P(S)\), hence \(P' = int(g) P = P\).

\textbf{Remark 1.18.} \emph{If \(P\) and \(P'\) are two parabolic
subgroups of \(G\) containing a common Borel subgroup, then
\(P \cap P'\) is again a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). Indeed, it is
smooth along the unit section (Exp. XXII, 5.4.5), and it contains a
Borel subgroup.}

\textbf{Proposition 1.19.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(G'\) its derived group (Exp. XXII, 6.2.1).}

\emph{(i) The maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P ↦ P\textquotesingle{} = P ∩ G\textquotesingle{}    and    P ↦ P\textquotesingle{} · rad(G) = Norm\_G(P\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are mutually inverse bijections between the set of parabolic
subgroups of \(G\) and the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G'\). One has
\(rad^{u}(P) = rad^{u}(P')\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) and
\(P' = P \cap G'\). The maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L ↦ L\textquotesingle{} = L ∩ G\textquotesingle{} = L ∩ P\textquotesingle{}}
\NormalTok{L\textquotesingle{} ↦ L\textquotesingle{} · rad(G) = Centr\_G(rad(L\textquotesingle{}))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are mutually inverse bijections between the set of Levi subgroups
of \(P\) and the set of Levi subgroups of \(P'\). Moreover, one has
\(rad(L') = (rad(L) \cap G')^{0}\).}

The proof (by reduction to the split case, for example) is
straightforward and is left to the reader, together with that,
immediate, of:

\textbf{Proposition 1.20.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(L\) a Levi
subgroup of \(P\). The maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Q ↦ Q ∩ L = Q\textquotesingle{},     Q\textquotesingle{} ↦ Q\textquotesingle{} · rad\^{}u(P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are mutually inverse bijections between the set of parabolic
subgroups of \(G\) contained in \(P\) and the set of parabolic subgroups
of \(L\). Moreover, the Levi subgroups of \(Q'\) are the Levi subgroups
of \(Q\) contained in \(L\).}

One may complete 1.6 as follows:

\textbf{Proposition 1.21.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).}

\emph{(i) \(P\) possesses a largest invariant subgroup that is smooth
and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected solvable geometric
fibers. It is a characteristic subgroup of \(P\), called the} radical
\emph{of \(P\), and denoted \(rad(P)\). The quotient sheaf \(P/rad(P)\)
is representable by an \(S\)-semisimple group.}

\emph{(ii) If \(L\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(rad(P)\) is the
semidirect product of \(rad^{u}(P)\) and \(rad(L)\); one has
\(rad(L) = L \cap rad(P)\), hence \(L = Centr_{G}(L \cap rad(P))\), and
\(P/rad(P) \simeq L/rad(L)\).}

Indeed, assertion (i) being local, one may assume that \(G\) has a Levi
subgroup \(L\), and one is reduced to proving that
\(R = rad^{u}(P) \cdot rad(L)\) has the properties announced in (i),
which is immediate. For (ii), it only remains to show that
\(rad(L) = L \cap rad(P)\), which follows immediately from the fact that
\(L \cap rad(P)\) is smooth and has connected fibers, \(L\) being the
centralizer of a torus\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} cf.~XIX 1.4.}.

\subsection{2. Structure of the unipotent radical of a parabolic
subgroup}\label{structure-of-the-unipotent-radical-of-a-parabolic-subgroup}

\textbf{Proposition 2.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\),
\(rad^{u}(P)\) its unipotent radical. There exists a sequence of
sub-group-schemes of \(rad^{u}(P)\)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad\^{}u(P) = U\_0 ⊃ U\_1 ⊃ U\_2 ⊃ · · · ⊃ U\_n ⊃ · · ·}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{possessing the following properties:}

\emph{(i) Each \(U_{i}\) is smooth, with connected fibers,
characteristic and closed in \(P\). The commutator of a section of
\(U_{i}\) and a section of \(U_{j}\) is a section of \(U_{i+j+1}\) (over
a varying \(S' \to S\)).}

\emph{(ii) For each \(i \geqslant 0\), there exists a locally free
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(E_{i}\) and an isomorphism of \(S\)-group
sheaves}

\[
U_{i} / U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\sim} W(E_{i}).
\]

\emph{Moreover, the automorphisms of \(P\) (over a varying \(S' \to S\))
act linearly on \(W(E_{i})\).}

\emph{(iii) For every \(s \in S\), one has \(U_{n,s} = e\) for
\(n > \dim(rad^{u}(P)_{s})\).}

\subsubsection{2.1.1.}\label{section-323}

Suppose first that the pair \((G, P)\) is pinnable. Let
\((T, M, R, \Delta, \cdots)\) be a pinning of \(G\) adapted to \(P\);
let \(\Delta(P)\) be the part of \(\Delta\) defined by \(P\). Let
\(\alpha_{1}, \cdots, \alpha_{p}\) be

the elements of \(\Delta(P)\), and \(\beta_{1}, \cdots, \beta_{q}\) the
elements of \(\Delta - \Delta(P)\). Every root \(\gamma \in R\) is
written uniquely as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{γ = a\_1 α\_1 + · · · + a\_p α\_p + b\_1 β\_1 + · · · + b\_q β\_q.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(γ) = b\_1 + · · · + b\_q. [\^{}N.D.E{-}XXVI{-}7]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It follows immediately from the definitions that the following
properties hold (cf.~1.12):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  \(U_{\gamma} \subset P \Leftrightarrow a(\gamma) \geqslant 0\).
\item
  \(U_{\gamma} \subset rad^{u}(P) \Leftrightarrow a(\gamma) > 0\).
\item
  \(a(n \gamma + m \gamma') = n a(\gamma) + m a(\gamma')\) for all
  \(n, m \in \mathbb{Z}\).
\end{enumerate}

For \(i > 0\), let \(R_{i}\) be the set of roots \(\gamma \in R\) such
that \(a(\gamma) > i\). Each \(R_{i}\) is a closed set of roots
satisfying \(R_{i} \cap (-R_{i}) = \emptyset\). Consider (Exp. XXII,
5.6.5) the \(S\)-group

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_i = U\_\{R\_i\} = ∏\_\{γ ∈ R\_i\} U\_γ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It is a closed sub-group-scheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), with
connected fibers.

Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\); consider the commutation relation of Exp.
XXII, 5.5.2

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{p\_α(x) p\_β(y) p\_α(−x) = p\_β(y) ∏\_\{n, m ∈ ℕ\^{}*\} p\_\{n α + m β\}(C\_\{n, m, α, β\} x\^{}n y\^{}m),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where each \(p_{\gamma}\) is an isomorphism of vector groups
\(G_{a, S} \xrightarrow{\sim} U_{\gamma}\). Let us first remark that if
\(a(\alpha) > i\) and \(a(\beta) > j\), one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{a(n α + m β) = n a(α) + m a(β) ⩾ n(i + 1) + m(j + 1) \textgreater{} i + j + 1}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

when \(n\) and \(m\) are \texttt{\textgreater{}\ 0}. It follows that the
commutator of a section of \(U_{\alpha}\) and a section of \(U_{\beta}\)
is a section of \(U_{i+j+1}\) (over a varying \(S' \to S\)), which
indeed entails \((U_{i}, U_{j}) \subset U_{i+j+1}\). For each
\(i \geqslant 0\), the quotient \(U_{i} / U_{i+1}\) is therefore
commutative; it is naturally identified with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U\_i / U\_\{i+1\} ≃ ∏\_\{a(γ) = i+1\} U\_γ ≃ W(E\_i),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(E_{i}\) is the direct sum of the \(g^{\gamma}\) for
\(a(\gamma) = i + 1\).

Let us return to the above commutation formula, and suppose
\(a(\alpha) \geqslant 0\), \(a(\beta) > i\). If
\(n, m \in \mathbb{N}^{*}\),

-- either \(a(n \alpha + m \beta) > i + 1\),

-- or \(a(n \alpha + m \beta) = i + 1\), in which case one necessarily
has \(m = 1\).

This proves first that \(int(p_{\alpha}(x))\) respects \(U_{i}\) (hence
also \(U_{i+1}\)), and then that, in the expression of
\(int(p_{\alpha}(x)) p_{\beta}(y)\), only terms of the form
\(p_{n \alpha + \beta}(C_{n, 1, \alpha, \beta} x^{n} y)\) occur modulo
\(U_{i+1}\), which are therefore linear in \(y\). It follows that the
inner automorphisms defined by sections of \(U_{\alpha}\) act linearly
on the quotient \(U_{i} / U_{i+1}\) identified with \(W(E_{i})\). As
this is also trivially true for the inner automorphisms defined by
sections of \(T\), and as \(P\) is generated by \(T\) and the
\(U_{\alpha}\), \(a(\alpha) \geqslant 0\), one deduces that:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  each \(U_{i}\) is invariant in \(P\),
\item
  the inner automorphisms defined by sections of \(P\) act linearly on
  \(U_{i} / U_{i+1} \simeq W(E_{i})\).
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{2.1.2.}\label{section-324}

Now let \((T', M', R', \Delta', \cdots)\) be a new pinning of \(G\)
adapted to \(P\).

By 1.15, there exists an inner automorphism of \(G\) coming from \(P\)
that transforms the old pinning into the new one. Possibly after
extending \(S\), one may assume that this inner automorphism is of the
form \(int(p)\), \(p \in P(S)\). If one takes up the preceding
constructions using the new pinning, it is clear that the groups
\(U'_{i}\) and the isomorphisms \(U'_{i} / U'_{i+1} \simeq W(E'_{i})\)
obtained are deduced from \(U_{i}\) and
\(U_{i} / U_{i+1} \simeq W(E_{i})\) by transport of structure via
\(int(p)\). It follows from remarks (i) and (ii) above that one
therefore has \(U'_{i} = U_{i}\), and that the two vector structures
constructed on \(U_{i} / U_{i+1} = U'_{i} / U'_{i+1}\) coincide.

This shows that the groups \(U_{i}\) and the vector structures on the
quotients \(U_{i} / U_{i+1}\) are independent of the pinning considered
(and in particular invariant under every automorphism of \(P\), as one
sees easily).

We have therefore proved the proposition when the pair \((G, P)\) is
pinnable (part (iii) is trivial, since by Exp. XXI 3.1.2, the set
\({ a(\gamma) | \gamma \in R}\) is an interval of \(\mathbb{Z}\), hence
one cannot have \(\dim(U_{i, s}) = \dim(U_{i+1, s})\) unless
\(U_{i, s} = e\)).

\subsubsection{2.1.3.}\label{section-325}

In the general case, there exists a covering family for the (fpqc)
topology \({ S_{j} \to S}\) such that each pair
\((G_{S_{j}}, P_{S_{j}})\) is pinnable (1.14). By the preceding, one has
descent data on the \(rad^{u}(P_{S_{j}})_{i}\), compatible with the
vector structures of the quotients, and one concludes by descent of
closed subschemes (resp. locally free modules)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}
  cf.~SGA 1, VIII 1.3, 1.9 and 1.10.}.

\textbf{Corollary 2.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). One has}

\[
H^{1}(S, rad^{u}(P)) = 0,
\]

\emph{i.e.~every principal homogeneous bundle under \(rad^{u}(P)\) is
trivial.}

Indeed, \(S\) decomposes as a sum of subschemes on each of which
\(rad^{u}(P)\) is of constant relative dimension. One may

therefore, by (iii), assume that there exists \(n\) such that
\(U_{n} = e\). Since
\(H^{1}(S, U_{i} / U_{i+1}) = H^{1}(S, W(E_{i})) = 0\) by TDTE I, B, 1.1
(or SGA 1, XI 5.1), one concludes at once.

\textbf{Corollary 2.3.} \emph{Under the preceding conditions, \(P\)
possesses a Levi subgroup \(L\). If \(L\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\),
the canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}1(S, L) ⟶ H\^{}1(S, P)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is bijective (cf.~the introduction of Exp. XXIV for the definition
of \(H^{1}(S, -)\)).}

The first assertion follows from 2.2 and 1.9. The canonical map
\(H^{1}(S, L) \to H^{1}(S, P)\) is surjective, because \(P\) is the
semidirect product \(L \cdot rad^{u}(P)\). To prove that it is
injective, it suffices to see that for every principal homogeneous
bundle \(Q\) under \(L\), one has \(H^{1}(S, rad^{u}(P)_{Q}) = 0\),
where the subscript \(Q\) denotes twisting by the \(L\)-bundle \(Q\).
This can be proved in two ways: one may take up the proof of 2.2, using
the fact that the vector structures on the \(U_{i} / U_{i+1}\) are
invariant under \(L\); one may also remark that \(rad^{u}(P)_{Q}\) is
identified with the unipotent radical of the parabolic subgroup
\texttt{P\_Q} of \texttt{G\_Q}, and apply 2.2 to \texttt{P\_Q}.

\textbf{Corollary 2.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). There exists
a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) contained in \(P\).}

Indeed, in view of 2.3, \(P\) has a Levi subgroup \(L\), and it suffices
to prove that \(L\) has a maximal torus, which follows from Exp. XIV,
3.20.

\textbf{Corollary 2.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be an affine scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). There exists
a locally free \texttt{O\_S}-module \(E\) such that \(rad^{u}(P)\) is
isomorphic as an \(S\)-scheme to \(W(E)\).}

Indeed, let us prove by induction on \(i\) that one has an isomorphism
of \(S\)-schemes

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad\^{}u(P) / U\_i ≃ W(E\_0 ⊕ E\_1 ⊕ · · · ⊕ E\_\{i−1\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is clear for \(i = 0\). Assume \(i > 0\); then
\(rad^{u}(P) / U_{i}\) is a principal homogeneous bundle with base
\(rad^{u}(P) / U_{i-1}\), under the group

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(U\_\{i−1\} / U\_i)\_\{rad\^{}u(P) / U\_\{i−1\}\} ≃ W(E\_\{i−1\} ⊗ O\_\{rad\^{}u(P) / U\_\{i−1\}\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Now the base is affine (e.g.~by the induction hypothesis), so this
bundle is trivial (TDTE I or SGA 1 XI, \emph{loc. cit.}), and there
exists an isomorphism of \(S\)-schemes
\(rad^{u}(P) / U_{i} \simeq (rad^{u}(P) / U_{i-1}) \times_{S} (U_{i-1} / U_{i})\),
which completes the proof.

\textbf{Corollary 2.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme,
\({s_{i}}\) the set of its closed points, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive
group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). The canonical map}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad\^{}u(P)(S) ⟶ ∏\_i rad\^{}u(P)(Spec κ(s\_i))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{is surjective.}

Indeed, if \(S = \operatorname{Spec}(A)\), \(\kappa(s_{i}) = A/p_{i}\),
and if \(E\) is given by the projective (hence flat) module \(E\), we
must prove that the map

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E ⟶ ∏\_i E ⊗\_A A/p\_i}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is surjective. It suffices to do this when \(E = A\), in which case it
is well known (cf.~Bourbaki, \emph{Alg. Comm.} Chap. II, §1, no. 2,
Proposition 5).

\textbf{Corollary 2.7.} \emph{Let \(k\) be an infinite field, \(G\) a
\(k\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\); then
\(rad^{u}(P)(k)\) is dense in \(rad^{u}(P)\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme,
\({s_{i}}\) the set of its closed points, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive
group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), and \(L_{i}\) a Levi
subgroup of \(P_{s_{i}}\) for each \(i\). There exists a Levi subgroup
\(L\) of \(P\) inducing \(L_{i}\) for each \(i\).}

Indeed, let \texttt{L\_0} be a Levi subgroup of \(P\) (2.3). For each
\(i\), let \(u_{i} \in rad^{u}(P)(\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(s_{i})))\)
be such that \(int(u_{i}) L_{0, s_{i}} = L_{i}\) (1.8); if
\(u \in rad^{u}(P)(S)\) induces \(u_{i}\) for each \(i\) (2.6), then
\(L = int(u) L_{0}\) answers the question.

\textbf{Corollary 2.9.} \emph{In the situation of 2.1, let moreover
\(H\) be a sub-group-scheme of \(G\), smooth and of finite presentation
over \(S\), with connected fibers, such that \(P \cap H\) contains
locally for the (fpqc) topology a maximal torus of \(G\). Then for each
\(i \geqslant 0\), there exists a locally direct factor submodule
\(F_{i}\) of \(E_{i}\) such that the isomorphism
\(U_{i} / U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\sim} W(E_{i})\) induces an isomorphism
of groups}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(U\_i ∩ H) / (U\_\{i+1\} ∩ H) ⥲ W(F\_i).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Indeed, \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) (Exp. XXII, 5.2.1). On
the other hand, the assertion to be proved is local for the (fpqc)
topology, and one may assume \(G\) split relative to a maximal torus of
\(P \cap H\); one may even reduce to the situation of 2.1.1, with \(H\)
defined by a subset \(R'\) of \(R\). Taking up the notation of
\emph{loc. cit.}, one sees by Exp. XXII, 5.6.7 (ii) that
\(U_{i} \cap H = \prod_{\alpha \in R_{i} \cap R'} U_{\alpha}\), hence
that \((U_{i} \cap H) / (U_{i+1} \cap H)\) is identified with
\(\prod_{\alpha \in R', a(\alpha) = i+1} U_{\alpha}\), which yields the
result.

\textbf{Corollary 2.10.} \emph{In the situation of 2.9, the conclusions
of 2.2, 2.5, 2.6, 2.7 are also valid when \(rad^{u}(P)\) is replaced by
\(rad^{u}(P) \cap H\).}

\textbf{Corollary 2.11.}\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} Corollary 2.11 has been
  added; it will be used in 4.5.1 and 6.17.} \emph{Let \(G\) be an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup, \(H\) a subgroup of
type (RC) of \(P\) such that \(rad^{u}(H) = rad^{u}(P) \cap H\). Then
statements 2.2 to 2.8 are also valid when \(P\) is replaced by \(H\).}

\subsection{3. Scheme of parabolic subgroups of a reductive
group}\label{scheme-of-parabolic-subgroups-of-a-reductive-group}

\subsubsection{3.1.}\label{section-326}

Let \(E\) be a finite twisted constant \(S\)-scheme (Exp. X, 5.1).
Consider the \(S\)-functor \(Of(E)\), where \(Of(E)(S')\) is the set of
open and closed subschemes of \(E_{S'}\) (or, equivalently, the set of
open and closed subsets of \(E_{S'}\)); then \(Of(E)\) is representable
by a finite twisted constant \(S\)-scheme. Indeed, if \(E = A_{S}\),
where \(A\) is a finite set, one has immediately
\(Of(E) \simeq P(A)_{S}\) (where \(P(A)\) denotes the power set of
\(A\)), and one concludes by descent of open and closed subschemes. One
trivially has:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Of(E\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}) = Of(E)\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\},        Of(E ×\_S E\textquotesingle{}) = Of(E) ×\_S Of(E\textquotesingle{}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{3.2.}\label{section-327}

Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. The functor
\(Par(G)\) of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) is defined by

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Par(G)(S\textquotesingle{}) = the set of parabolic subgroups of G\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

In particular, \(G \in Par(G)(S)\), \(Bor(G) \subset Par(G)\). We
propose to define a morphism

\[
t : Par(G) \longrightarrow Of(Dyn(G))
\]

possessing the following properties:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\tightlist
\item
  \(t\) is functorial in \(G\) (with respect to isomorphisms) and
  commutes with base change.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  If \((T, M, R, \Delta, \cdots)\) is a pinning of \(G\) adapted to the
  parabolic subgroup \(P\) (1.11), the canonical isomorphism
  \(Dyn(G) \simeq \Delta_{S}\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.4 (iii)) transforms
  \(t(P)\) into \(\Delta(P)_{S}\) (notations of 1.11, 1.12).
\end{enumerate}

Let first \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) and
\((T, M, R, \Delta, \cdots)\) a pinning of \(G\) adapted to \(P\). One
defines \(t(P)\) by (ii); the subscheme \(t(P)\) of \(Dyn(G)\) thus
constructed is independent of the pinning chosen. Indeed, if
\((T', M', R', \Delta', \cdots)\) is another pinning of \(G\) adapted to
\(P\), the unique inner automorphism of \(G\) transforming the first
pinning into the second comes from \(P\) (1.15); the canonical
isomorphism \(\Delta \xrightarrow{\sim} \Delta'\) therefore transforms
\(\Delta(P)\) into \(\Delta'(P)\), which entails the announced result.

If now one no longer assumes \((G, P)\) to be pinnable, it follows
immediately from 1.14 and the definition of \(Dyn(G)\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.3)
that one may define by descent an open and closed subscheme \(t(P)\) of
\(Dyn(G)\), unique, such that for every \(S' \to S\) for which
\((G, P)_{S'}\) is pinnable, one has \(t(P)_{S'} = t(P_{S'})\).

\textbf{Theorem 3.3.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group,}

\[
t : Par(G) \longrightarrow Of(Dyn(G))
\]

\emph{the morphism defined above.}

\emph{(i) For two parabolic subgroups \(P\) and \(P'\) of \(G\) to be
