\(U \times_{k} U'\) defined by the cartesian diagram

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{U ×\_k U\textquotesingle{} ─────→ G}
\NormalTok{   ↑               ↑}
\NormalTok{   │               │}
\NormalTok{   V ─────→ Gen(Q/P) ∩ Gen(Q/P\textquotesingle{});}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

since \(V(\bar{k}) \neq \emptyset\) by what was just seen, \(V\) is
dense in \(U \times_{k} U'\), hence has a section by 2.7.

If \(k\) is finite, \(P\) (resp. \(P'\)) has a Borel subgroup \(B\)
(resp. \(B'\)), by virtue of

Lang's theorem (cf.~5.1.5), since the schemes
\texttt{Bor(P)\ ≃\ Bor(P/rad\^{}u(P))} and
\texttt{Bor(Q)\ ≃\ Bor(Q/rad\^{}u(Q))} are smooth. If \texttt{B\_1} is a
Borel subgroup opposite to \(B\) (4.3.5 (i)), there exist
\(a \in B^{u}(k)\) and \(a_{1} \in B^{u}_{1}(k)\) such that
\(int(a a_{1}) B = B'\) (5.2); then
\(B_{0} = int(a a_{1}) B_{1} = int(a) B_{1}\) is opposite to \(B'\) and
to \(B\); if \texttt{Q\_0} is the unique parabolic subgroup of \(G\)
containing \texttt{B\_0} and of the same type as \(Q\) (3.8),
\texttt{Q\_0} is in transversal position relative to \(P\) and \(P'\)
(4.2.1 (vi)). On the other hand, by 5.2, \texttt{Q\_0} is written
\texttt{int(u\ u\textquotesingle{})\ Q} with \(u' \in U'(k)\),
\(u \in U(k)\), which is what was to be demonstrated.

\textbf{Corollary 5.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\).
There exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \texttt{int(g)\ P} is in
osculating position relative to \(Q\), i.e.~(4.4.2) that
\(int(g) P \cap Q\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).}

Indeed, by 4.3.5 (i), there exists a parabolic subgroup \(P'\) of \(G\)
opposite to \(P\). By 5.3, there exists a parabolic subgroup \(P'_{1}\)
of \(G\) of the same type as \(P'\), in transversal position relative to
\(P\) and \(Q\). If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(P'_{1} \cap Q\) (4.2.7
(ii)), and if \texttt{P\_1} is the opposite of \(P'_{1}\) relative to
\(T\), then \texttt{P\_1} and \(Q\) are in osculating position, by
4.4.5. On the other hand, \(P\) and \texttt{P\_1} being opposite to
\(P'_{1}\), there exists \(g \in rad^{u}(P'_{1})(S)\) such that
\(int(g) P = P_{1}\) (4.3.5 (i)). QED.

Let us remark, moreover, that for the same reason there exists
\(u \in rad^{u}(P)(S)\) such that \(int(u) P' = P'_{1}\), hence \(g\) is
written \texttt{int(u)\ u\textquotesingle{}} with
\(u' \in rad^{u}(P')(S)\), which gives
\(P_{1} = int(u u' u^{-1}) P = int(u u') P\) and re-proves 5.2 in
passing.

Statements 5.3 and 5.4 are the essential results of this section. Let us
first state some consequences of 5.4.

\textbf{Corollary 5.5.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) If \(P\) and \(Q\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) and if
\(t(P) \subset t(Q)\) (cf.~3.3), there exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that
\(int(g) P \subset Q\).}

\emph{(ii) Let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P\_1 ⊃ P\_2 ⊃ · · · · · · ⊃ P\_n    and    P\textquotesingle{}\_1 ⊃ P\textquotesingle{}\_2 ⊃ · · · · · · ⊃ P\textquotesingle{}\_n}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be two chains of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) such that
\(t(P_{i}) = t(P'_{i})\). There exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that
\(int(g) P_{i} = P'_{i}\) for each \(i\).}

\emph{(iii) Let
\texttt{P,\ Q,\ P\textquotesingle{},\ Q\textquotesingle{}} be four
parabolic subgroups of \(G\) such that \(t(P) = t(P')\) and
\(t(Q) = t(Q')\). If the pairs \texttt{(P,\ P\textquotesingle{})} and
\texttt{(Q,\ Q\textquotesingle{})} are in transversal (resp. osculating)
position, there exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(int(g) P = P'\) and
\(int(g) Q = Q'\).}

\emph{(iv) Let \(P\) and \(P'\) be two parabolic subgroups of the same
type, \(L\) (resp. \(L'\)) a Levi subgroup of \(P\) (resp. \(P'\)).
There exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(int(g) P = P'\) and
\(int(g) L = L'\).}

\emph{Proof:} (i) follows at once from 5.4; (ii) is proved by induction
on \(n\), the case \(n = 0\) being trivial; one may therefore assume
\(P_{i} = P'_{i}\) for \(i = 1, \cdots, n - 1\); by 5.2 there exists
\(g \in G(S)\) such that \(int(g) P_{n} = P'_{n}\); but then \(P_{n}\)
and \(int(g) P_{n}\) are contained in \(P_{n-1} = P'_{n-1}\), hence
\(g \in P_{n-1}(S)\) (4.4.4 (ii)) and \(int(g) P_{i} = P'_{i}\) for
\(i = 1, \cdots, n\).

On the other hand, (iv) follows at once from 5.2 and 1.8. Let us
demonstrate (iii) in the case of ``transversal position''; the assertion
is a consequence of (iv) when the types of \(P\) and \(Q\) are opposite
(4.3.3 (iii)); in the general case, by 4.2.7 (iii) and 4.4.6, one may
find parabolic subgroups \(P_{1}, P'_{1}, Q_{1}, Q'_{1}\) of
\texttt{P,\ P\textquotesingle{},\ Q,\ Q\textquotesingle{}} respectively,
such that \texttt{P\_1} and \(P'_{1}\) are opposite, as are
\texttt{Q\_1} and \(Q'_{1}\), and such that \(t(P_{1}) = t(P'_{1})\);
there therefore exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that
\(int(g) P_{1} = P'_{1}\), \(int(g) Q_{1} = Q'_{1}\), and one may assume
\(P_{1} = P'_{1}\) and \(Q_{1} = Q'_{1}\); but then \(P\) and \(P'\) are
in osculating position and of the same type, hence \(P = P'\) (4.4.4
(i)); for the same reason \(Q = Q'\).

It remains to demonstrate assertion (iii) in the case of ``osculating
position''. By the conjugacy theorem (5.2), one may assume \(P = P'\);
by the same theorem, one may find \(g \in G(S)\) such that
\(int(g) Q = Q'\); but then \(g \in P(S)\) by 4.4.4 (ii) and one has
\(int(g) P = P = P'\).

\textbf{Definition 5.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). One says
that \(P\) is} minimal \emph{if whenever \(Q\) is a parabolic subgroup
of \(G\) contained in \(P\), one has \(Q = P\).}

One should note that this is not in general a notion stable under
passage to fibers.

\textbf{Corollary 5.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) Let \(t, t' \in Of(Dyn(G))(S)\). If there exist in \(G\) a
parabolic subgroup of type \(t\) and a parabolic subgroup of type
\(t'\), there exists a parabolic subgroup of type \(t \cap t'\). In
particular, there exists a smallest element \(t_{\min}\) in the set of
\(t(P)\), \(P\) running through the set of parabolic subgroups of
\(G\).}

\emph{(ii) Every parabolic subgroup of \(G\) contains a minimal
parabolic subgroup. For a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) to be minimal, it
is necessary and sufficient that it be of type \(t_{\min}\). Two minimal
parabolic subgroups of \(G\) are conjugate by an element of \(G(S)\).}

This follows at once from 5.4 and 5.5 (i).

\textbf{Remark 5.8.} \emph{A parabolic subgroup opposite to a minimal
parabolic subgroup is also minimal; this entails
\(s(t_{\min}) = t_{\min}\).}

\textbf{Corollary 5.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). The
canonical morphism}

\[
G \longrightarrow G/P = X
\]

\emph{makes \(G\) an \(X\)-bundle locally trivial (in the sense of
Zariski) with group \texttt{P\_X}. If \(L\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\),
the canonical morphism (cf.~3.12)}

\[
G \longrightarrow G/L = Y
\]

\emph{makes \(G\) a \(Y\)-bundle locally trivial (in the sense of
Zariski) with group \texttt{L\_Y}.}

It suffices to prove that if one has a morphism \(S' \to S\), where
\(S'\) is local and a morphism \(S' \to X\) (resp. \(S' \to Y\)), it
lifts to a morphism \(S' \to G\). In other words, one may assume \(S\)
local, and one must show that the map \(G(S) \to X(S)\) (resp.
\(G(S) \to Y(S)\)) is surjective.

The first assertion was demonstrated in 5.2; let us demonstrate the
second. Let \(y \in Y(S)\); its canonical image in \(X(S)\) comes from a
\(g \in G(S)\); the projection \(y'\) of \(g\) in \(Y(S)\) therefore has
the same projection as \(y\) in \(X(S)\). There exists therefore a
unique \(u \in rad^{u}(P)(S)\) such that \(y' u = y\), and the
projection of \texttt{g\ u} in \(Y(S)\) is indeed \(y\).

\textbf{Corollary 5.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\)
an \(S\)-reductive group.}

\emph{(i) Let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(L\) a Levi
subgroup of \(P\). The canonical maps (cf.~3.21) induce bijections}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}1(S, L) ⥲ H\^{}1(S, P) ⥲ H\^{}1\_\{t(P)\}(S, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(ii) Let \(t, t' \in Of(Dyn(G))(S)\); one has (cf.~3.21)}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}1\_t(S, G) ∩ H\^{}1\_\{t\textquotesingle{}\}(S, G) = H\^{}1\_\{t ∩ t\textquotesingle{}\}(S, G).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iii) If \(P\) and \(Q\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) in
osculating position, the following canonical diagram is cartesian and
composed of injections:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{H\^{}1(S, P) ─────→ H\^{}1(S, G)}
\NormalTok{   ↑                  ↑}
\NormalTok{   │                  │}
\NormalTok{H\^{}1(S, P ∩ Q) ──→ H\^{}1(S, Q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us demonstrate (i). The map \(H^{1}(S, L) \to H^{1}(S, P)\) is
bijective by 2.3; the map \(H^{1}(S, P) \to H^{1}_{t(P)}(S, G)\) is
surjective (3.21); let us show that it is injective, i.e.~that the
canonical map \(H^{1}(S, P) \to H^{1}(S, G)\) is injective. Let \(Q\) be
a principal bundle under \(P\), \texttt{Q\_1} the associated principal
bundle under \(G\), \(P'\) and \(G'\) the corresponding twisted forms of
\(P\) and \(G\). It is clear that \(G'\) is an \(S\)-reductive group and
that \(P'\) is a parabolic

subgroup of it. The set of elements of \(H^{1}(S, P)\) that have the
same image as the class of \(Q\) in \(H^{1}(S, G)\) is naturally
identified with the kernel of the canonical map
\(H^{1}(S, P') \to H^{1}(S, G')\), and this, by the exact sequence of
cohomology, with the set of orbits of \texttt{G\textquotesingle{}(S)} in
\((G'/P')(S)\) (for these arguments of non-abelian cohomology, see
Giraud's thesis\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} See {[}Gi71{]}, §III.3.}). But
\texttt{G\textquotesingle{}(S)} acts transitively on \((G'/P')(S)\) by
5.2.

Let us demonstrate (ii): let \(Q\) be a principal homogeneous bundle
under \(G\) and \texttt{G\_Q} the corresponding twisted form of \(G\).
By definition (3.21), we must prove that \texttt{G\_Q} has a parabolic
subgroup of type \(t \cap t'\) if and only if it has parabolic subgroups
of type \(t\) and \(t'\), which is none other than the conjunction of
3.8 and 5.7 (i). Finally, (iii) follows at once from (i) and (ii).

Let us now state a consequence of 5.3.

\textbf{Corollary 5.11.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\)
an \(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). If
\(P \neq G\), there exist at least three distinct parabolic subgroups of
\(G\) of the same type as \(P\); in other words, \(P \neq G\) entails
\((G(S) : P(S)) \geqslant 3\).}

Indeed, let \(P'\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) opposite to \(P\)
(4.3.5 (i)). Since \(P \neq G\), one has \(rad^{u}(P') \neq e\) (by
4.3.2 for example). By 2.1, \(rad^{u}(P')(S) \neq e\); let then
\(u \in rad^{u}(P')(S)\), \(u \neq e\). Then \(int(u) P \neq P\), and by
5.3, there exists a \texttt{P\_1}, of the same type as \(P\), and
opposite to \(P\) and \texttt{int(u)\ P}; then \texttt{P\_1}, \(P\) and
\texttt{int(u)\ P} are three distinct parabolic subgroups of \(G\), of
the same type as \(P\).

\subsection{6. Parabolic subgroups and split
tori}\label{parabolic-subgroups-and-split-tori}

\textbf{Proposition 6.1.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(g = Lie(G/S)\), and \(Q\) a split subtorus of
\(G\). Write \(Q = D_{S}(M)\) and let}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = ⨁\_\{α ∈ M\} g\^{}α}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{be the decomposition of \(g\) under the action of \(Q\). Let
\texttt{M\_1} be a subset of \(M\) such that \(0 \in M_{1}\) and that
\(\alpha, \beta \in M_{1} \Rightarrow \alpha + \beta \in M_{1}\).}

\emph{(i) There exists a unique smooth subgroup \(H_{M_{1}}\) of \(G\),
with connected fibers, containing \(Centr_{G}(Q)\), and whose Lie
algebra is \(\bigoplus_{\alpha \in M_{1}} g^{\alpha}\).}

\emph{(ii) One has the following implications:}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M\_1 = \{0\}              ⟹  H\_\{M\_1\} = Centr\_G(Q),}
\NormalTok{M\_1 = −M\_1             ⟹  H\_\{M\_1\} is reductive,}
\NormalTok{M\_1 ∪ (−M\_1) = M       ⟹  H\_\{M\_1\} and H\_\{−M\_1\} are parabolic subgroups of G,}
\NormalTok{                          opposite, with common Levi subgroup H\_\{M\_1 ∩ −M\_1\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

To demonstrate (i) and (ii), which are local for the (fpqc) topology,
one may assume that \(Q\) is contained in a maximal

torus \(T\) of \(G\); one may furthermore split \(G\) relative to \(T\).
Assertion (i) then follows at once from Exp. XXII, 5.3.5, 5.4.5 and
5.4.7; the assertions of (ii) follow from Exp. XXII, 5.3.5, 5.10.1,
5.11.3 and, in this Exposé, 1.4 and 4.3.2.

\textbf{Corollary 6.2.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(Q\) a split subtorus of \(G\). There exists a
parabolic subgroup of \(G\) of which \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) is a Levi
subgroup.}

Indeed, writing \(Q = D_{S}(M)\), one chooses a total order structure on
the group \(M\), one calls \texttt{M\_1} the set of positive elements of
\(M\); the group \(H_{M_{1}}\) answers the question.

\textbf{Corollary 6.3.} \emph{If the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\) has a
non-central split subtorus, it has a proper parabolic subgroup
(i.e.~\(\neq G\)).}

By 5.9 and 5.10, one derives from 6.2:

\textbf{Corollary 6.4.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(Q\) a split subtorus of \(G\). The canonical
morphism \(G \to G / Centr_{G}(Q)\) is a locally trivial fibration.}

\emph{If \(S\) is semi-local, the map \(G(S) \to (G / Centr_{G}(Q))(S)\)
is surjective, and the map \(H^{1}(S, Centr_{G}(Q)) \to H^{1}(S, G)\) is
injective.}

\subsubsection{6.5.}\label{section-348}

Suppose \(S\) connected. If \(T\) is an \(S\)-torus and \(T'\) and
\texttt{T\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}} are two split subtori of
\(T\), their product \(T' \cdot T''\)\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}
  Multiplicative notation has been adopted, i.e.~``their sum
  \(T' + T''\)'' has been replaced by ``their product
  \(T' \cdot T''\)''.} is also a split subtorus of \(T\). Indeed,

it is identified with the quotient of \(T' \times_{S} T''\) by
\(T' \cap T''\), a quotient that is split by Exp. IX, 2.11. It follows
that \(T\) has a largest split subtorus; one denotes it \(T_{spl}\).

\textbf{Lemma 6.6.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected scheme, \(T\) an
isotrivial \(S\)-torus, \(T_{spl}\) its largest split subtorus. The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) There exists a homomorphism \(T \to G_{m, S}\) distinct from
\(e\).}

\emph{(ii) \(T_{spl} \neq e\).}

Since \(T\) is assumed isotrivial, there exist a finite group
\(\Gamma\), a connected principal Galois covering \(S' \to S\) of group
\(\Gamma\), and an isomorphism \(T_{S'} \simeq D_{S'}(M)\); \(M\) is
then endowed with a structure of \(\Gamma\)-module, and one has a
natural isomorphism
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S}(T, G_{m, S}) = H^{0}(\Gamma, M)\).

On the other hand, let \(V\) be the vector subspace of
\(M \otimes \mathbb{Q}\) generated by elements of the form \(g(m) - m\),
\(g \in \Gamma\), \(m \in M\). One verifies at once that
\((T_{spl})_{S'}\) is identified with \(D_{S'}(M / M \cap V)\).
Assertion (i) is therefore equivalent to \(H^{0}(\Gamma, M) \neq 0\), or
equivalently to \(H^{0}(\Gamma, M \otimes \mathbb{Q}) \neq 0\), whereas
assertion (ii) is equivalent to \(M \neq M \cap V\), or equivalently to
\(M \otimes \mathbb{Q} \neq V\). Now one has
\(M \otimes \mathbb{Q} = H^{0}(\Gamma, M \otimes \mathbb{Q}) \oplus V\),
as one verifies at once (consider the projector
\(M \otimes \mathbb{Q} \to H^{0}(\Gamma, M \otimes \mathbb{Q})\) that
sends \(x\) to the average of the transforms of \(x\) by \(\Gamma\)).

\textbf{Lemma 6.7.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a scheme, \(G\) an
\(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) such that
\(P \neq G\), \(L\) a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(Q\) its radical. There
exists a homomorphism \(Q \to G_{m, S}\) distinct from \(e\).}

Consider the unipotent radical \(U\) of \(P\); it is invariant under
\(int(P)\), hence under \(int(Q)\). Consider the invertible
\texttt{O\_S}-module \(det(Lie(U))\), the ``maximum exterior power'' of
the locally free \texttt{O\_S}-module \(Lie(U)\). The adjoint
representation defines a homomorphism of groups

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : Q ⟶ Aut(det(Lie(U))) = G\_\{m, S\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

If \(P \neq G\), then \(U \neq e\). Let us choose \(s \in S\) such that
\(U_{s} \neq e\). Splitting \(G_{s}\) relative to a maximal torus
containing \(Q_{s}\), one sees at once that \(f_{s} \neq e\).

\textbf{Proposition 6.8.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of
\(G\), \(L\) a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(Q\) its radical, \(Q_{spl}\)
the largest split subtorus of \(Q\) (i.e.~the largest central split
subtorus of \(L\)). Then}

\[
L = Centr_{G}(Q_{spl}).
\]

Set \(L' = Centr_{G}(Q_{spl})\); this is a reductive subgroup of \(G\)
containing \(L\); moreover, \(P' = P \cap L'\) is a parabolic subgroup
of \(L'\), of Levi subgroup \(L\) (1.20). If \(L' \neq L\), then
\(L' \not\subset P\) (since \(L\) is a maximal reductive subgroup of

\(P\), cf.~1.7), hence \(P' \neq L'\).

Let \texttt{G\_1} be the derived group of \(G\), and
\(P_{1} = P' \cap G_{1}\). By 1.19, \texttt{P\_1} is a parabolic
subgroup of the semisimple group \texttt{G\_1}, \(L_{1} = L \cap G_{1}\)
is a Levi subgroup of it, and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Q\_1 = rad(L\_1) = (rad(L) ∩ G\_1)\^{}0 = (Q ∩ G\_1)\^{}0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \texttt{L\_1} has a maximal torus \texttt{T\_1} (Exp. XIV, 3.20),
and the latter is isotrivial (Exp. XXIV, 4.1.5), \texttt{Q\_1}, being a
subtorus of \texttt{T\_1}, is also isotrivial (Exp. IX, 2.11); since
\(P_{1} \neq G_{1}\), one may apply 6.7 and 6.6, and one therefore has
\((Q_{1})_{spl} \neq e\), whence \((Q_{spl} \cap G_{1})^{0} \neq e\),
hence \(Q_{spl} \not\subset rad(L')\) (since \(rad(L') \cap G_{1}\) is
finite), which is contradictory with the definition of \(L'\).

\textbf{Corollary 6.9.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(Q\) a critical subtorus of
\(G\) (i.e.~such that \(rad(Centr_{G}(Q)) = Q\)). For \(Centr_{G}(Q)\)
to be a Levi subgroup of a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), it is necessary
and sufficient that \texttt{Centr\_G(Q)\ =\ Centr\_G(Q\_\{spl\})}, that
is, \texttt{Lie(G)\^{}Q\ =\ Lie(G)\^{}\{Q\_\{spl\}\}}.}

This follows from 6.2 and 6.8.

\textbf{Corollary 6.10.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(L\) a subgroup of \(G\). The
following conditions are equivalent:}

\emph{(i) There exists a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) of which \(L\) is a
Levi subgroup.}

\emph{(ii) There exists a split subtorus of \(G\) of which \(L\) is the
centralizer.}

\emph{(iii) There exists a homomorphism \(G_{m, S} \to G\) of which
\(L\) is the centralizer.}

Indeed, one has (i) ⇒ (ii) by 6.8, and (iii) ⇒ (i) by 6.1; it remains to
prove (ii) ⇒ (iii). Suppose then \(L = Centr_{G}(Q)\), with
\(Q = D_{S}(M)\); write \(g = Lie(G/S)\) and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{g = ⨁\_\{α ∈ M\} g\^{}α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and let \(R\) be the set of \(\alpha \in M - {0}\) such that
\(g^{\alpha} \neq 0\).

Since \(R\) is finite and does not contain \texttt{0}, there exists a
homomorphism \(u : M \to \mathbb{Z}\) such that \(u(\alpha) \neq 0\) for
each \(\alpha \in R\). By duality, \(u\) gives a homomorphism
\(G_{m, S} \to Q\), hence a homomorphism \(f : G_{m, S} \to G\). One has
\(Centr_{G}(f) \supset Centr_{G}(Q)\); these are two smooth subgroups of
\(G\), with connected fibers; their Lie algebras coincide (since both
are equal to \(g^{0}\)); they therefore coincide, by a customary
argument.

\textbf{Corollary 6.11.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. The maps}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L ↦ rad(L)\_\{spl\},        Q ↦ Centr\_G(Q)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{are mutually inverse bijections, which reverse the natural order
structures, between the set of subgroups \(L\) of \(G\) that are Levi
subgroups of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) and the set of split subtori
\(Q\) of \(G\) such that \texttt{rad(Centr\_G(Q))\_\{spl\}\ =\ Q}.}

\textbf{Corollary 6.12.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. Consider the following
assertions:}

\emph{(i) There exists a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) distinct from
\(G\).}

\emph{(ii) \(G\) has a non-central split subtorus.}

\emph{(ii bis) \(G\) has a non-central split subtorus of relative
dimension 1.}

\emph{(iii) There exists a homomorphism of groups \(G_{a, S} \to G\)
that is a closed immersion.}

\emph{Then one has (i) ⇔ (ii) ⇔ (ii bis) ⇒ (iii).}

The only new assertion is (i) ⇒ (iii). Let then \(P\) be a parabolic
subgroup of \(G\), distinct from \(G\). Then \(U = rad^{u}(P) \neq e\).
Consider the last non-trivial subgroup \(U_{n}\) of the composition
series of \(U\) (2.1). One has an isomorphism \(U_{n} \simeq W(E_{n})\),
where \(E_{n}\) is a locally free \texttt{O\_S}-module, hence
free\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} Since \(S\) is assumed semi-local and
  connected.}. Since \(E_{n} \neq 0\), there exists a locally
direct-factor monomorphism \(O_{S} \to E_{n}\), hence a closed immersion
\(G_{a, S} = W(O_{S}) \hookrightarrow W(E_{n}) \simeq U_{n}\), which
yields (iii) at once.

\textbf{Remark 6.12.1.} \emph{When \(S\) is the spectrum of a field of
characteristic 0, it follows from the Jacobson--Morozov theorem that
(iii) ⇒ (ii bis). The preceding four conditions are then equivalent
(``Godement's criterion'', cf.~{[}BT65{]}, 8.5).\footnote{This is more
  generally true when \(S\) is the spectrum of a perfect field
  (Tits).{[}\^{}N.D.E-XXVI-31{]}}}

\textbf{Definition 6.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. One says that \(G\) is}
anisotropic \emph{if \(G\) contains no split subtorus not reduced to
\(e\).}

\textbf{Corollary 6.14.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme. For the \(S\)-reductive group \(G\) to be anisotropic, it is
necessary and sufficient that it have no parabolic subgroup
\(P \neq G\), and that its radical be anisotropic.}

Using now 6.6, Exp. XXIV, 4.1.5, and Exp. XXII, 6.2, one deduces:

\textbf{Corollary 6.15.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an isotrivial \(S\)-reductive group (e.g.~\(G\)
semisimple, or \(S\) normal (Exp. X 5.16)). For \(G\) to be anisotropic,
it is necessary and sufficient that \(G\) have no parabolic subgroup
\(P \neq G\), and that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G, G_{m, S}) = e\).}

\textbf{Proposition 6.16.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group. The maximal split subtori of
\(G\) are the largest central split subtori of the Levi subgroups of the
minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\). Two such tori are conjugate by an
element of \(G(S)\).}

Let \(Q\) be a maximal split subtorus of \(G\).\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.}
  The following sentence has been spelled out.} Then, by 6.2,
\(L = Centr_{G}(Q)\) is a Levi subgroup of a parabolic subgroup \(P\) of
\(G\), and since \texttt{Q\ ⊂\ rad(Centr\_G(Q))\_\{spl\}}, the
maximality of \(Q\) entails \texttt{Q\ =\ rad(Centr\_G(Q))\_\{spl\}}. By
6.11, \(L\) is a minimal element of the set of Levi subgroups of
parabolic

subgroups of \(G\), hence \(P\) is a minimal parabolic subgroup of \(G\)
by 1.20. It then follows from 5.7 and 5.5 (iv) that two subtori such as
\(Q\) are conjugate by a section of \(G(S)\). The conjugacy of the \(Q\)
and of the pairs \((P, L)\) then entails the first assertion of 6.16.

\textbf{Corollary 6.17.} \emph{Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local
scheme, \(P\) and \(P'\) two minimal parabolic subgroups in standard
position (4.5.1.1). Then \(P \cap P'\) contains a common Levi subgroup
of \(P\) and \(P'\).}

Indeed, \(P \cap P'\) contains a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\), by 4.5.1
(v); let \(L\) be the unique Levi subgroup of \(P\) containing \(T\).
One has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rad(P) ∩ T = rad(P) ∩ L = rad(L)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

by 1.21, hence \(rad(P) \cap T\) contains \(rad(L)_{spl}\), which is a
maximal split subtorus of \(G\), hence is necessarily equal to
\(T_{spl}\). One therefore has \(L = Centr_{G}(T_{spl})\), and by
symmetry \(L\) is also a Levi subgroup of \(P'\).

\textbf{Remark 6.18.} \emph{It follows from 1.21 that the parabolic
subgroup \(P\) of \(G\) is minimal if and only if \(rad(P)\) contains a
maximal split subtorus of \(G\); then, by the proof of 6.17, if \(T\) is
a maximal torus of \(P\), \(T_{spl}\) is a maximal split torus of \(G\)
and of \(rad(P)\), and \(Centr_{G}(T_{spl})\) is a Levi subgroup of
\(P\). Moreover, every Levi subgroup of \(P\) is obtained in this way.}

\subsection{7. Relative root datum}\label{relative-root-datum}

In this section, \(S\) will denote a non-empty connected semi-local
scheme, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \(Q\) a maximal split subtorus
of \(G\), and \(L\) the centralizer of \(Q\) in \(G\),
i.e.~\(L = Centr_{G}(Q)\).

\subsubsection{7.1.}\label{section-349}

Since \(Q\) is the largest central split subtorus of \(L\), every
section of \(G(S)\) that normalizes \(L\) also normalizes \(Q\). One
therefore has (cf.~7.1.1)

\[
Norm_{G}(L)(S) = Norm_{G}(Q)(S).
\]

On the other hand, one saw in 6.4 that the map \(G(S) \to (G/L)(S)\) is
surjective. It follows that one has a canonical identification

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W\_G(Q)(S) = (Norm\_G(Q) / Centr\_G(Q))(S) ≃ Norm\_G(L)(S) / L(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

One will denote by \(M\) the group
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Q, G_{m, S})\), so that one has a canonical
isomorphism \(Q \simeq D_{S}(M)\). One will denote by \(W\) the group of
automorphisms of \(M\) defined by \(W_{G}(Q)(S)\). One therefore has
isomorphisms

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{W ≃ W\_G(Q)(S) ≃ Norm\_G(L)(S) / L(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{7.1.1.}\label{section-350}

One does not in general have \(Norm_{G}(L) = Norm_{G}(Q)\). Take, for
example, for \(S\) the spectrum of a field \(k\), having a quadratic
extension \(k'\), for \(G\) the unitary group
\(Q-\acute{E}p_{k'/k}(A_{2})\) (cf.~Exp. XXIV, 3.11.2).

Since the minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\) are its Borel subgroups,
their Levi subgroups are maximal tori, and one has
\((Norm_{G}(L)/L)(k) = S_{3}\).

On the other hand, since \(G\) is not split, the maximal split tori of
\(G\) are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\), hence isomorphic to
\(G_{m, k}\). Since \(Norm_{G}(Q)/L\) acts faithfully on \(Q\), one has
\((Norm_{G}(Q)/Q)(k) = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\).

\subsubsection{7.2.}\label{section-351}

If \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\) (one
exists by 6.2), \(P\) is necessarily minimal (cf.~6.18). By the
conjugacy of minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\) (5.7), of that of Levi
subgroups of a parabolic subgroup (1.8), and of the equalities
\(P = Norm_{G}(P)\) and \(Norm_{G}(L) \cap P = L\) (1.6), one obtains:
the set of (minimal) parabolic subgroups of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\)
is principal homogeneous under the group \(W\).

\subsubsection{7.3.}\label{section-352}

The Lie algebra of \(G\) decomposes under the action of \(Q\) as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(G) = Lie(L) ⊕ ⨁\_\{α ∈ R\} Lie(G)\^{}α,}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \(R\) is the set of non-zero characters of \(Q\) such that
\(Lie(G)^{\alpha} \neq 0\) (roots of \(G\) relative to \(Q\)).

Let us denote by \(M^{*}\) the group
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(G_{m, S}, Q)\), which is in duality with
\(M\) and on which \(W\) acts naturally by transport of structure.

\textbf{Theorem 7.4.} \emph{With the notations of 7.3, there exists a
unique map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^{*}\) from \(R\) to \(M^{*}\) that
defines on \((M, M^{*})\) a root datum (Exp. XXI, 1.1) whose Weyl group
is \(W\).}

\emph{Moreover, the parabolic subgroups \(P\) of \(G\) with Levi group
\(L\) and the systems of positive roots \(R^{+}\) of \(R\) correspond
bijectively via the relation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(P) = Lie(L) ⊕ ⨁\_\{α ∈ R\^{}+\} Lie(G)\^{}α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{7.4.1.}\label{section-353}

Suppose first that the existence of the map
\(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^{*}\) sought has been proved. By Exp. XXI,
3.4.10, \(s_{\alpha}\) is the unique element of \(W\) such that for
every \(m \in M\), \(s_{\alpha}(m) - m\) is a rational multiple of
\(\alpha\), which shows that \(s_{\alpha}\) is determined by \(\alpha\);
as one then has\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} \(\alpha^{*}(m)\) has been
  corrected to \(\alpha^{*}(m) \alpha\).}
\(\alpha^{*}(m) \alpha = m - s_{\alpha}(m)\), one sees that
\(\alpha^{*}\) is determined by \(\alpha\), which proves the uniqueness
of the map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^{*}\).

\subsubsection{7.4.2.}\label{section-354}

Let \(\alpha \in R\) and let \(L_{\alpha}\) (resp. \(H_{\alpha}\), resp.
\(H_{-\alpha}\)) be the unique smooth subgroup of \(G\) with connected
fibers containing \(L\) and such that (cf.~6.1 (i))

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(L\_α)   = Lie(L) ⊕ ⨁\_\{γ ∈ ℤα ∩ R\} Lie(G)\^{}γ,}
\NormalTok{Lie(H\_α)   = Lie(L) ⊕ ⨁\_\{γ ∈ ℕα ∩ R\} Lie(G)\^{}γ,}
\NormalTok{Lie(H\_\{−α\}) = Lie(L) ⊕ ⨁\_\{γ ∈ −ℕα ∩ R\} Lie(G)\^{}γ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\(L_{\alpha}\) is a reductive subgroup of \(G\), \(H_{\alpha}\) and
\(H_{-\alpha}\) are parabolic subgroups of it with Levi subgroup \(L\),
and \(H_{\alpha}\) and \(H_{-\alpha}\) are opposite relative to \(L\)
(cf.~6.1 (ii)).

By 7.2, there therefore exists
\(s_{\alpha} \in Norm_{L_{\alpha}}(Q)(S) / L(S) \subset W\) such that
\(s_{\alpha}(H_{\alpha}) = H_{-\alpha}\). One has
\(s_{\alpha}(\alpha) = -\alpha\) (because \(\alpha\) (resp. \(-\alpha\))
is the common divisor of the elements of \(R\) occurring in
\(H_{\alpha}\) (resp. \(H_{-\alpha}\))), and one has
\(s^{2}_{\alpha} = id\) (since \(s^{2}_{\alpha}(H_{\alpha})\) and
\(H_{\alpha}\) are both opposite to \(H_{-\alpha}\) relative to \(L\)).
One has therefore constructed an \(s_{\alpha} \in W\) satisfying the
following properties:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(x)     s\_α(α) = −α,    s\_α\^{}2 = id;}
\NormalTok{(xx)    s\_α can be represented by an element of L\_α(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let us moreover remark that \(s_{\alpha}\) is constructed canonically
from \(\alpha\), and in particular that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(xxx)    for every w ∈ W, one has w s\_α w\^{}\{−1\} = s\_\{w(α)\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{7.4.3.}\label{section-355}

We now propose to prove the assertion:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(xxxx)    for every m ∈ M, s\_α(m) − m ∈ ℤα.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Since \(S\) is connected, this assertion is local for the (fpqc)
topology. One may therefore assume that \(L_{\alpha} = G_{1}\) is
splittable relative to a maximal torus \texttt{T\_1} of \(L\). Let then
\((G_{1}, T_{1}, M_{1}, R_{1})\) be such a splitting. The monomorphism
\(Q \to T_{1}\) identifies \(M\) with a quotient of \texttt{M\_1}; let
\(p : M_{1} \to M\) be the canonical map.

The image of \texttt{R\_1} under \(p\) consists, possibly with the
inclusion of zero, of the roots of \texttt{G\_1} with respect to \(Q\)

(hence of the elements of \(R\) that are integer multiples of
\(\alpha\)); one therefore has \(p(R_{1}) \subset \mathbb{Z}\alpha\). By
(xx), there exists an element of \(Norm_{G_{1}}(L)(S)\) that induces
\(s_{\alpha}\) on \(Q\). By Exp. XXII, 5.10.10, there therefore exists a
section \(w \in (W_{1})_{S}(S)\) that induces \(s_{\alpha}\) on \(Q\)
(one denotes by \texttt{W\_1} the Weyl group of the root datum
\((M_{1}, R_{1}, \cdots)\)). Possibly after restricting \(S\), one may
therefore assume that there exists \(w \in W_{1}\) inducing
\(s_{\alpha}\) on \(Q\), hence satisfying
\(p(w(m_{1})) = s_{\alpha}(p(m_{1}))\) for every \(m_{1} \in M_{1}\).
But, by definition of \texttt{W\_1}, \(w\) is a product of reflections
with respect to elements of \texttt{R\_1}, hence \(w(m_{1}) - m_{1}\) is
a linear combination with integer coefficients of elements of
\texttt{R\_1}. It follows that \(s_{\alpha}(p(m_{1})) - p(m_{1})\) is a
linear combination with integer coefficients of the elements of
\(p(R_{1}) \subset \mathbb{Z}\alpha\), hence an integer multiple of
\(\alpha\), as was to be proved.

\subsubsection{7.4.4.}\label{section-356}

One may therefore define an element \(\alpha^{*} \in M^{*}\)
by\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} \(\alpha^{*}(m)\) has been corrected to
  \(\alpha^{*}(m) \alpha\).}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{α\^{}*(m) α = m − s\_α(m).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

By (x), one has \((\alpha^{*}, \alpha) = 2\); on the other hand, it
follows from (xxx) that for every pair
\((\alpha, \alpha') \in R \times R\), one has
\(s_{\alpha}(\alpha') \in R\) and
\(s_{\alpha}(\alpha'^{*}) = s_{\alpha}(\alpha')^{*}\), which proves
(cf.~Exp. XXI, 1.1) that the constructed map
\(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^{*}\) indeed defines a root datum on
\((M, M^{*})\).

\subsubsection{7.4.5.}\label{section-357}

Let \(W'\) be the Weyl group of this root datum (the group of
transformations of \(M\) generated by the \(s_{\alpha}\)); one has
\(W' \subset W\).

Let on the other hand \(\geqslant\) be a total order relation on the
free abelian group \(M\); set
\(R^{+} = { \alpha \in R | \alpha \geqslant 0}\). One knows that
\(R^{+}\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\). Let \(w \in W\),
represented by an \(n \in Norm_{G}(L)(S) = Norm_{G}(Q)(S)\). Set
\(P = H_{R^{+}}\)

(notation of 6.1); by \emph{loc. cit.}, \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of
\(G\) with Levi subgroup \(L\). One obviously has
\(int(n) P = H_{w(R^{+})}\). It then follows from 7.3 that
\(w(R^{+}) = R^{+}\) entails \(w = e\). As the group \(W'\) acts
transitively on the systems of positive roots of \(R\) (Exp. XXI, 3.3.7)
and the stabilizer in \(W\) of \(R^{+}\) is the identity, one concludes
immediately that \(W = W'\). One also concludes that \(W = W'\) acts in
a simply transitive way both on the set of systems of positive roots of
\(R\) and on the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) with Levi group
\(L\), which entails the last assertion of 7.4. QED.

\subsubsection{7.5.}\label{section-358}

If \(P\) and \texttt{P\_1} are two minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\),
with Levi subgroups \(L\) and \texttt{L\_1}, and if one denotes by \(Q\)
and \texttt{Q\_1} the maximal central split tori of \(L\) and
\texttt{L\_1}, then the pairs \((P, Q)\) and \((P_{1}, Q_{1})\) are
conjugate: there exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(int(g) P = P_{1}\)
and \(int(g) Q = Q_{1}\).

Indeed, \(P\) and \texttt{P\_1} are conjugate (5.7) and one may
therefore assume \(P = P_{1}\); then \(L\) and \texttt{L\_1} are
conjugate by a section of \(P(S)\) (1.8). Moreover, if \(g\) and \(g'\)
are two sections of \(G\) conjugating the pairs \((P, Q)\) and
\((P_{1}, Q_{1})\), then \(g'^{-1} g\) normalizes \(P\) and \(Q\), hence
\(P\) and \(L\); but

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Norm\_G(P) ∩ Norm\_G(L) = P ∩ Norm\_G(L) = L = Centr\_G(Q).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The isomorphism \(Q \xrightarrow{\sim} Q_{1}\) induced by \(int(g)\) is
therefore independent of \(g\).

Let \(R\) and \texttt{R\_1} be the root data defined thanks to 7.4 in
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Q, G_{m, S})\) and
\(\operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Q_{1}, G_{m, S})\), and let \(R^{+}\) and
\(R^{+}_{1}\) be the systems of positive roots corresponding to \(P\)
and \texttt{P\_1}. The canonical isomorphism
\(Q \xrightarrow{\sim} Q_{1}\) defined above transforms \((R, R^{+})\)
into \((R_{1}, R^{+}_{1})\). One immediately deduces that one may define
the \emph{pinned relative root datum}\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} Recall
  (Exp. XXIII 1.5) that a pinned root datum is a root datum endowed with
  the choice of a system of positive roots (or of simple roots).} of
\(G\) over \(S\), by identifying the various \((R, R^{+})\) by means of
the transitive system of isomorphisms described above.

From now on, we shall denote \((M, M^{*}, R, R^{*}, R^{+}) = R(G/S)\)
this pinned root datum; for each pair \(P \supset Q\) as above, one
therefore has a canonical isomorphism
\(M \xrightarrow{\sim} \operatorname{Hom}_{S-gr.}(Q, G_{m, S})\)
transforming \(R\) (resp. \(R^{+}\)) into the set of roots of \(G\)
(resp. of \(P\)) relative to \(Q\), and \(W(R)\) into \(W_{G}(Q)(S)\).

\subsubsection{7.6.}\label{section-359}

Let still \(Q\) be a maximal split torus of \(G\), \(P\) a (minimal)
parabolic subgroup of \(G\) with Levi group \(Centr_{G}(Q)\),
\((M, M^{*}, R, R^{*}, R^{+})\) the corresponding pinned root datum
(7.4), and \(\Delta\) the set of simple roots of \(R^{+}\). For every
\(A \subset \Delta\), let \(R_{A} \subset R\) be the set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R\_A = R\^{}+ ∪ (ℤA ∩ R\^{}−)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

consisting of positive roots and negative roots that are linear
combinations of elements of \(A\). It is a closed set (Exp. XXI, 3.1.4)
of roots, and every closed set containing \(R^{+}\) is uniquely of this
form (Exp. XXI, 3.3.10). By 6.1,

there exists a unique subgroup \texttt{P\_A} of \(G\), smooth and with
connected fibers, containing \(Centr_{G}(Q)\) and such that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(P\_A) = Lie(G)\^{}0 ⊕ ⨁\_\{α ∈ R\_A\} Lie(G)\^{}α.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

It then follows at once from 6.1, from the conjugacy of minimal
parabolics, and from the fact that the set of roots of a parabolic
subgroup of \(G\) containing \(Q\) is closed (which is deduced at once
from 1.4 by splitting), that:

\textbf{Proposition 7.7.} \emph{(i) The map \(A \mapsto P_{A}\) is a
bijection of the set of subsets of \(\Delta\) onto the set of parabolic
subgroups of \(G\) containing \(P\). This bijection preserves the
natural order relations of inclusion.}

\emph{(ii) Every parabolic subgroup of \(G\) is conjugate by a section
of \(G(S)\) to a unique \texttt{P\_A}.}

\subsubsection{7.8.}\label{section-360}

Let \(P \supset Q\) be as above. Consider the relative root datum (7.5)
of \(G\) over \(S\) and the canonical isomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : (M, M\^{}*, R, R\^{}*, R\^{}+) ⥲ (M, M\^{}*, R, R\^{}*, R\^{}+).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The set \(\Delta\) of simple roots of \(R^{+}\) is transformed into the
set \(\Delta\) of simple roots of \(R^{+}\), hence every subset \(A\) of
\(\Delta\) into a subset \(f(A) \subset \Delta\).

\textbf{Definition 7.9.0.}\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} The numbering 7.9.0
  has been added to highlight the definition of ``relative type''.}
\emph{Let \(H\) be an arbitrary parabolic subgroup of \(G\). By 7.7
(ii), it is conjugate to a unique \texttt{P\_A}. Let us denote
\(t_{r}(H) = f(A) \subset \Delta\). One verifies at once using the
conjugacy theorems that \(t_{r}(H)\) is independent of the choice of the
pair \(P \supset Q\). One says that it is the} relative type \emph{of
\(H\).}

\textbf{Proposition 7.9.} \emph{(i) The map \(H \mapsto t_{r}(H)\)
induces a bijection between the set of conjugacy classes (under
\(G(S)\)) of parabolic subgroups of \(G\), and the set of subsets of
\(\Delta\).}

\emph{(ii) Let \(H\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(P\) a minimal
parabolic subgroup contained in \(H\), \(Q\) the maximal central split
torus of a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(\Delta\) the set of simple roots of
\(P\) relative to \(Q\), and \(f : \Delta \xrightarrow{\sim} \Delta\)
the canonical isomorphism. Then, for every \(\alpha \in \Delta\), one
has the equivalence:}

\[
f(\alpha) \in t_{r}(H)  \Leftrightarrow  Lie(H)^{-\alpha} \neq 0
\]

\emph{and one has \(H = P_{A}\), where \(A = f^{-1}(t_{r}(H))\).}

\emph{(iii) If \(H\) and \(H'\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\)
containing \(P\), then (see 3.8.1 (ii) and 5.5 (i) for other equivalent
conditions):}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_r(H) ⊂ t\_r(H\textquotesingle{})  ⇔  t(H) ⊂ t(H\textquotesingle{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsubsection{7.10.}\label{section-361}

One can study the relative positions of two minimal parabolic subgroups;
the results are as follows (one refers to

4.5.2 for the notation \(t_{2}(P, P_{1})\)):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\arabic{enumi})}
\item
  If \(P, P_{1}, P', P'_{1}\) are four minimal parabolic subgroups of
  \(G\), then \(t_{2}(P, P_{1}) = t_{2}(P', P'_{1})\)
  (i.e.~\((P, P_{1})\) and \((P', P'_{1})\) are conjugate locally for
  (fpqc)) if and only if there exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that
  \(int(g) P = P'\) and \(int(g) P_{1} = P'_{1}\).
\item
  Let us fix in particular a minimal parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \(G\)
  of Levi subgroup \(L\), and let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(L\).
  Consider the scheme \(Par_{t_{\min}}(G; P)\) of minimal parabolic
  subgroups of \(G\) in standard position relative to \(P\). One has a
  morphism (cf.~4.5.5)
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{f : Par\_\{t\_\{min\}\}(G; P) ⟶ W\_P(T) \textbackslash{} W\_G(T) / W\_P(T)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

whose fibers are ``the orbits of \(P\) in \(Par_{t_{\min}}(G; P)\)''. By
(1), \(f\) therefore induces a monomorphism

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{P(S) \textbackslash{} Par\_\{t\_\{min\}\}(G; P)(S) ↪ (W\_P(T) \textbackslash{} W\_G(T) / W\_P(T))(S).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The image of this morphism is identified with \(W\); this is the Bruhat
theorem: each orbit of \(P(S)\) in \(Par_{t_{\min}}(G; P)(S)\) contains
one and only one parabolic subgroup of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\) (that
is, of the form \texttt{int(n)\ P}, where \(n \in Norm_{G}(L)\)).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  In other words, let \(E(S)\) be the set of \(g \in G(S)\) such that
  \texttt{int(g)\ P} and \(P\) are in mutual standard position. Then
  \(E(S)\) has a partition into double cosets modulo \(P(S)\) indexed by
  \(W\):
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E(S) = P(S) · W · P(S)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

(obvious notation). Setting \(U = rad^{u}(P)(S)\), one may also write

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{E(S) = U(S) · Norm\_G(L)(S) · U(S),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

thereby exhibiting a partition of \(E(S)\) into double cosets modulo
\(U(S)\), indexed by \(Norm_{G}(L)(S)\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\arabic{enumi})}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, then \(E(S) = G(S)\), and one
  recovers {[}BT65{]}, 5.15.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Counterexamples 7.11.} \emph{Let
\(S = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})\), \(G = SL_{2, S}\).
Let \(B\) be the standard Borel subgroup formed of matrices
\texttt{(a\ b;\ c\ d)} with \(c = 0\). Let \(g = ( 1; -2 1)\) ∈
G(S)\texttt{{[}scil.:}g = (1, 1; −2, 1)\texttt{{]};\ set}B' = int(g)
B\texttt{.\ Then}B(S) = B'(S)\texttt{,\ and}B ∩
B'\texttt{does\ not\ contain\ a\ maximal\ torus{[}\^{}N.D.E-XXVI-37{]}.\ This\ shows\ on\ the\ one\ hand\ that\ two\ distinct\ minimal\ parabolic\ subgroups\ may\ have\ the\ same\ group\ of\ sections,\ and\ on\ the\ other\ hand\ that\ there\ exists\ no\ general\ criterion\ allowing\ one\ to\ recognize\ whether\ two\ minimal\ parabolic\ subgroups}P\texttt{and}P'\texttt{are\ in\ standard\ position,\ using\ only\ the\ groups}P(S)\texttt{and}P'(S)\texttt{.\ In\ particular,\ the\ part}E(S)\texttt{of}G(S)\texttt{does\ not\ seem\ to\ be\ definable\ using\ only\ the\ situation}\{G(S),
P(S),
Norm\_G(L)(S)\}\texttt{(in\ the\ preceding\ case,\ this\ part\ is\ defined\ by}c
≠ 2`\footnote{\emph{N.D.E.} More generally, for every \(S\)-scheme
  \(S'\), \(E(S')\) is defined by the condition: ``\(c\) is zero or
  invertible''.}).}

\subsubsection{7.12.}\label{section-362}

One now proposes to study the variation of \(R(G/S)\) with \(S\). Let
then \(S'\) be an \(S\)-scheme, also semi-local connected and non-empty.
Let \(Q\) be a maximal split torus of \(G\); then \(Q_{S'}\) is a split
torus of \(G_{S'}\); let \(Q'\) be a maximal split torus of \(G_{S'}\)
containing \(Q_{S'}\). Set

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{M  = Hom\_\{S{-}gr.\}(Q, G\_\{m, S\}) ≃ Hom\_\{S\textquotesingle{}{-}gr.\}(Q\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}, G\_\{m, S\textquotesingle{}\}),}
\NormalTok{M\textquotesingle{} = Hom\_\{S\textquotesingle{}{-}gr.\}(Q\textquotesingle{}, G\_\{m, S\textquotesingle{}\}).}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The monomorphism \(Q_{S'} \to Q'\) induces an epimorphism
\(u : M' \to M\). Denote

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{L  = Centr\_G(Q),         L\textquotesingle{} = Centr\_\{G\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}\}(Q\textquotesingle{}),}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

one has \(L' \subset L_{S'}\).

If \(H\) is a subgroup of \(G\) containing \(L\), then \(H_{S'}\)
contains \(L'\), and one has

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Lie(H) = Lie(L) ⊕ ⨁\_\{α ∈ R\_H\} Lie(H)\^{}α,}
\NormalTok{Lie(H\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}) = Lie(L\textquotesingle{}) ⊕ ⨁\_\{α\textquotesingle{} ∈ R\textquotesingle{}\_\{H\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}\}\} Lie(H\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\})\^{}\{α\textquotesingle{}\},}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

where \texttt{R\_H} (resp. \(R'_{H_{S'}}\)) denotes the set of roots of
\(H\) (resp. \(H_{S'}\)) relative to \(Q\) (resp. \(Q'\)). One
immediately derives that

\[
R_{H} \subset u(R'_{H_{S'}}) \subset R_{H} \cup {0}.
\]

Taking \(H = G\), one sees first that
\(R \subset u(R') \subset R \cup {0}\); taking then for \(H\) a minimal
parabolic subgroup \(P\) of Levi subgroup \(L\), one sees that
\(R'_{H_{S'}}\) contains a system of positive roots of \(R'\), hence
(7.4) that there exists a minimal parabolic subgroup \(P'\) of
\(G_{S'}\) of Levi subgroup \(L'\) contained in \(P_{S'}\). One has
therefore constructed a diagram

\[
Q_{S'}   \subset   L_{S'}   \subset   P_{S'}
   \cap            \cup            \cup
   Q'    \subset   L'      \subset   P'.
\]

If \(R^{+}\) (resp. \(\Delta\)) is the system of positive roots (resp.
simple) of \(R\) defined by \(P\),

and if one defines similarly \(R'^{+}\) and \(\Delta'\), one easily
verifies that

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R\^{}+ ⊂ u(R\textquotesingle{}\^{}+) ⊂ R\^{}+ ∪ \{0\},        Δ ⊂ u(Δ\textquotesingle{}) ⊂ Δ ∪ \{0\}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Let now \(w \in W \simeq Norm_{G}(Q)(S) / Centr_{G}(Q)(S)\), and
\(n \in Norm_{G}(Q)(S)\) a representative of \(w\). One has
\(int(n) Q = Q\) hence \(int(n) L = L\), hence
\(int(n) L_{S'} = L_{S'}\). Then \(Q'\) and
\texttt{int(n)\ Q\textquotesingle{}} are two maximal split tori of
\(L_{S'}\), hence are conjugate by a section \(x \in L(S')\), and one
has \(int(n x) Q' = Q'\), hence \(n x \in Norm_{G_{S'}}(Q')(S')\). Let
\(w'\) be the image of \(n' = n x\) in
\(W' \simeq Norm_{G_{S'}}(Q')(S') / Centr_{G_{S'}}(Q')(S')\). It is
clear that the operation of \(w'\) on \(M'\) is compatible with the
projection \(u : M' \to M\) and that the induced operation on \(M\)
coincides with that defined by \(w\).

Using now the definition of relative root data and the conjugacy
theorems, one proves without difficulty:

\textbf{Theorem 7.13.} \emph{Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be two non-empty
connected semi-local schemes, \(S' \to S\) a morphism of \(S\)-schemes,
\(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group,}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{R(G/S) = (M, M\^{}*, R, R\^{}*, R\^{}+),      R(G\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}/S\textquotesingle{}) = (M\textquotesingle{}, M\textquotesingle{}\^{}*, R\textquotesingle{}, R\textquotesingle{}\^{}*, R\textquotesingle{}\^{}+)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{the pinned relative root data. There exists a canonical
homomorphism}

\[
u : M' \longrightarrow M
\]

\emph{satisfying the following conditions:}

\emph{(i) \(u\) is surjective.}

\emph{(ii) For every \(w \in W\), there exists an element \(w'\) of
\(W'\) compatible with \(u\) and which induces \(w\) on \(M\).}

\emph{(iii) For every subset \(X\) of \(M\), denote
\(X^{\wedge} = X \cap (M - {0})\). Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{u(R\textquotesingle{}\^{}+)\^{}∧ = R\^{}+,        u(Δ\textquotesingle{})\^{}∧ = Δ.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\emph{(iv) For every parabolic subgroup \(H\), consider
\(t_{r}(H) \subset \Delta\) and \(t_{r}(H_{S'}) \subset \Delta'\). Then}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{t\_r(H\_\{S\textquotesingle{}\}) = (u\^{}\{−1\}(t\_r(H) ∪ \{0\})) ∩ Δ\textquotesingle{} = \{ α\textquotesingle{} ∈ Δ\textquotesingle{} | u(α\textquotesingle{}) ∈ t\_r(H) or u(α\textquotesingle{}) = 0 \}.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\textbf{Remark 7.14.} \emph{If \(G\) is splittable over \(S\), its
maximal split tori are maximal tori, and the relative notions introduced
here then coincide with the absolute notions already introduced. The
preceding theorem therefore gives a description of the relative root
datum \(R(G/S)\) and of the relative type \(t_{r}\), via the absolute
root datum and the absolute type of the group \(G_{S'}\), \(S'\) being
chosen in such a way that \(G_{S'}\) is splittable (cf.~Exp. XXIV,
4.4.1). We refer to {[}BT65{]}, 6.12 et seq. for this description.}

\subsubsection{7.15.}\label{section-363}

Let \(S\) be a Henselian local scheme, \(s_{0}\) its closed point,
\texttt{S\_0} the spectrum of the residue field of \(s_{0}\), identified
with a closed subscheme of \(S\); for every object \(X\) above \(S\),
let us denote by \texttt{X\_0} the object above \texttt{S\_0} deduced
from \(X\) by base change. Let finally \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive
group. For every parabolic subgroup \(\bar{P}\) of \(G\),
\(\bar{P}_{0}\) is a parabolic subgroup of \texttt{G\_0}; conversely,
for every parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \texttt{G\_0}, there exists a
parabolic subgroup \(\bar{P}\) of \(G\) such that \(\bar{P}_{0} = P\)
(this follows from Hensel's lemma and from the fact that \(Par(G)\) is a
smooth \(S\)-scheme); in particular (cf.~5.7), a parabolic subgroup
\(\bar{P}\) of \(G\) is minimal if and only if \(\bar{P}_{0}\) is
minimal. Such a subgroup \(\bar{P}\) of \(G\) being chosen, an analogous
reasoning shows that the maximal split subtori of \(\bar{P}_{0}\) are of
the form \texttt{T\_0}, where \(T\) is a maximal split subtorus of
\(\bar{P}\). It follows without difficulty that the relative root data
of \(G\) over \(S\) and of \texttt{G\_0} over \texttt{S\_0} are
canonically isomorphic, so that the theory of parabolic subgroups of
\(G\) reduces to that of parabolic subgroups of \texttt{G\_0}.

Let us remark, moreover, that every \texttt{S\_0}-reductive group is of
the form \texttt{G\_0} (Exp. XXIV, Prop. 1.21), which conversely allows
one to reduce the study of parabolic subgroups of an
\texttt{S\_0}-reductive group to the corresponding study over \(S\).

\subsection{Footnotes}\label{footnotes-12}

\section{SGA 3: Group Schemes}\label{sga-3-group-schemes-1}

\emph{Séminaire de Géométrie Algébrique du Bois-Marie}, 1962--1964.

M. Demazure and A. Grothendieck, with collaborators J.-E. Bertin, P.
Gabriel, M. Raynaud, M. Artin, J.-P. Serre. 2011 SMF \emph{Documents
Mathématiques} re-edition by Demazure (Tomes I, II, III, with N.D.E.
footnotes).

\subsection{Abstract}\label{abstract}

This Séminaire develops the theory of group schemes over an arbitrary
base prescheme, in two complementary parts. Part I (Exposés I--VII\_B,
Tome I) lays foundations: schematic and categorical syntax, faithfully
flat quasi-compact descent, fibered categories and sheaves, the
construction of quotient schemes, generalities on algebraic groups and
group schemes, and the infinitesimal study of differential operators and
formal groups, including the correspondence between height-\texttt{1}
radicial group schemes and restricted \(p\)-Lie algebras. Part II
(Exposés VIII--XXVI, Tomes II and III) develops the structure theory:
groups of multiplicative type (VIII--XII); regular elements in algebraic
groups and Lie algebras (XIII--XIV); smoothness and maximal tori (XV);
groups of zero unipotent rank, unipotent algebraic groups, and
extensions (XVI--XVII); Weil's theorem on the construction of a group
from a rational law (XVIII); and, in Tome III, the structure theory of
reductive group schemes --- generalities (XIX), the rank-\texttt{1} case
(XX), root data (XXI), splitting and subgroup structure (XXII),
uniqueness of pinned groups (XXIII), automorphisms (XXIV), the existence
theorem (XXV), and parabolic subgroups (XXVI). The Séminaire generalizes
the Borel--Chevalley structure theory of affine algebraic groups to
arbitrary base preschemes, with Chevalley's ``Tôhoku'' groups over
\(\mathbb{Z}\) as a guiding example.

\subsection{Reference convention}\label{reference-convention}

Following the source's §7 convention (see the
\href{00-i-avertissement-introduction.md\#introduction}{Introduction}),
SGA 3 is cited as \texttt{(Exp.\ N,\ M.K)} where \(N\) is the Exposé
Roman numeral and \texttt{M.K} is the decimal numbering inside that
Exposé --- for example \texttt{(XII,\ 3.2)} for statement 3.2 of Exposé
XII. A bare \texttt{5.7.11} refers to the proposition of that name in
the same Exposé. The split Exposés are cited as \texttt{VI\_A},
\texttt{VI\_B}, \(VII_{A}\), \(VII_{B}\) (matching the source's typeset
subscript notation).

Cross-volume citations follow the source's abbreviations:
\texttt{EGA\ X,\ x.y.z} for the \emph{Éléments de Géométrie Algébrique},
\texttt{SGA\ n,\ X\ y.z} for other SGA volumes, \emph{Bible} for the
\emph{Séminaire Chevalley} 1956/58, and TDTE for Grothendieck's
\emph{Techniques de descente et théorèmes d'existence} (Bourbaki,
1959--62). See the \href{glossary.md}{glossary} for the full list.

\subsection{Editorial conventions}\label{editorial-conventions}

\begin{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Terminology.} SGA 3 retains the historical SGA/EGA distinction
  between \emph{prescheme} (\texttt{préschéma}) and \emph{scheme}
  (\texttt{schéma}, in the older sense of separated prescheme), matching
  SGA 1 and SGA 2 (Exposés I--XIII). The translation honors this
  throughout all 26 Exposés. As Grothendieck notes in the Introduction
  (§ 6), SGA 3 also deliberately replaces the usual hypothesis ``of
  finite type'' by ``of finite presentation''; the translation preserves
  this distinction.
\item
  \textbf{Editor footnotes (N.D.E.).} The 2011 SMF \emph{Documents
  Mathématiques} re-edition (M. Demazure, ed.) added footnotes recording
  corrections, updates, modern references, and the current status of
  questions raised in the original 1962--1964 seminar. In this
  translation, original footnotes from the Séminaire authors (Demazure,
  Grothendieck, Bertin, Gabriel, Raynaud, Artin, Serre) use slugs like
  \([{}^{I}-3-1]\), while editor footnotes use \([{}^{N}.D.E-I-3]\) so
  the two are visibly distinct.
\item
  \textbf{Page marks.} HTML comments
  \texttt{\textless{}!-\/-\ original\ page\ N\ -\/-\textgreater{}} mark
  the start of page \(N\) in the 2011 SMF re-edition, whose pagination
  is the reference for the errata sheets.
\item
  \textbf{Mathematics.} Mathematics is written with Unicode and wrapped
  in backticks where formatter mangling is a risk (most identifier-rich
  expressions). Displayed equations use fenced
  \texttt{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}text}
  blocks, optionally pinned with
  \texttt{\textless{}!-\/-\ label:\ eq:III.\textless{}Exp\textgreater{}.X.Y\ -\/-\textgreater{}}.
\item
  \textbf{Split Exposés (VI and VII).} Exposés VI and VII are split into
  A and B parts in the source. Filenames keep the split (\texttt{06A-},
  \texttt{06B-}, \texttt{07A-}, \texttt{07B-}); cross-references use
  \texttt{VI\_A}, \texttt{VI\_B}, \(VII_{A}\), \(VII_{B}\).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Provenance}\label{provenance}

This is a translation, not a critical edition. The authoritative text
remains the French 2011 SMF \emph{Documents Mathématiques} re-edition,
derived from the SLN 151, 152, 153 of 1970 as re-typeset by M. Demazure.
For any claim that matters mathematically, consult the source: this
English version exists to make the volume readable, not to replace it.

\subsection{Common OCR repairs}\label{common-ocr-repairs}

The 2011 SMF re-edition is modern LaTeX, so OCR is high quality. Most
math symbols survive. These items still recur:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Dropped sub/superscripts on big operators.} \(\Gamma\),
  \(H^{i}\), \(Ext^{i}\), \(R^{i} f_{*}\), \texttt{O\_X}, \texttt{Lie},
  \(T_{e} G\), \(\mu_{n}\), \(G_{m}\), \(G_{a}\), \(\alpha_{p}\),
  \(D(M)\), \(w\alpha(X)\), root operators \(U_{\alpha}\),
  \(T_{\alpha}\) may lose their indices. Recover from context.
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{Cb} instead of \texttt{Ĉ}.} Hat on category symbol
  drops. Restore.
\item
  \textbf{\((\ast)\) / \((\ast\ast)\) / \((\ast\ast\ast)\) for original
  footnote markers.} Render as \([{}^{<}exposé>-<sec>-<n>]\)
  slugs (\([{}^{I}-1-1]\), \([{}^{I}-1-2]\), \ldots).
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{(N)} for N.D.E. footnote markers} (small Arabic digit
  in parentheses). Render as \([{}^{N}.D.E-<exposé>-N]\)
  (\([{}^{N}.D.E-I-3]\), etc.) and translate the body of the note.
\item
  \textbf{\(\ddot{\imath}\) or \texttt{ı}} (dotless i with floating
  diacritic) --- restore to \texttt{ï}.
\item
  \textbf{Backslash escapes} surviving from LaTeX:
  \texttt{\textbackslash{}\&} → \texttt{\&}, \texttt{\textbackslash{}\#}
  → \texttt{\#}.
\item
  \textbf{Arrows.} \(-\to\) → \(\to\), \(7\to\) → \(\mapsto\), \(\sim=\)
  (often broken across lines) → \(\cong\),
  \texttt{\textbackslash{}sim\textbackslash{}n\textbackslash{}to} (OCR
  artefact) → \(\xrightarrow{\sim}\) or \(\to\) annotated
  \texttt{\textasciitilde{}}.
\item
  \textbf{Greek subscripts.} \(\pi 1\), \texttt{H0}, \texttt{G\ m} etc.
  should be \(\pi_{1}\), \(H^{0}\), \(G_{m}\) (with backticks).
\item
  \textbf{\texttt{◦} for opposite category} drops to \(o\) or
  \texttt{0}. Restore \({}^{\circ}\) or \({}^{\circ}\) (degree sign),
  matching local convention.
\item
  \textbf{VIB, VIIA, VIIB citations.} Render as \texttt{VI\_B},
  \(VII_{A}\), \(VII_{B}\). Preserve subscript via underscore.
\item
  \textbf{« » guillemets.} Translate to English quotes (\("\cdots"\))
  unless the source uses them to mark a Grothendieckian coinage, in
  which case keep them as quotation marks in the translation too.
\item
  \textbf{Hat across line break} for formal completions: \(Et( b / X)\)
  → \(\hat{E}t(\hat{X})\). Same as SGA 2.
\item
  \textbf{Math run-ons.} Restore displayed equations as fenced
  \texttt{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}text}
  blocks.
\item
  \textbf{Embedded N.D.E. footnotes.} Source convention is
  \((N) N.D.E. : <text>\) at page bottom. Recover the whole footnote
  (which may span lines) and translate as
  \([{}^{N}.D.E-<exposé>-N]\).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Style anchors (non-negotiable for cross-volume
consistency)}\label{style-anchors-non-negotiable-for-cross-volume-consistency}

Inherited from SGA 1 / SGA 2. Deviate only if the SGA 1/2 corpus is
itself inconsistent.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{File naming.} \texttt{00-i-errata.md},
  \texttt{00-i-avertissement-introduction.md},
  \texttt{00-ii-preface.md}, \texttt{00-iii-errata.md},
  \texttt{NN-\textless{}slug\textgreater{}.md} for each Exposé (using
  \texttt{06A}, \texttt{06B}, \texttt{07A}, \texttt{07B} for the split
  Exposés), \texttt{glossary.md}, \texttt{README.md},
  \texttt{zz-i-index-notations.md}, \texttt{zz-iii-index-notations.md},
  \texttt{zz-iii-index-terminologique.md}.
\item
  \textbf{Heading hierarchy.}
  \texttt{\#\ Exposé\ N.\ \textless{}English\ Title\textgreater{}} (with
  \texttt{\_A} / \texttt{\_B} suffix where applicable), then numbered
  \texttt{\#\#\ 1.\ \textless{}Section\ Title\textgreater{}}, then
  sub-sections
  \texttt{\#\#\#\ 1.1.\ \textless{}Subsection\textgreater{}}. The Exposé
  heading carries a
  \texttt{\textless{}!-\/-\ label:\ III.\textless{}Roman\textgreater{}\ -\/-\textgreater{}}
  comment on the next line.
\item
  \textbf{Statement blocks.} \texttt{**Proposition.**},
  \texttt{**Lemma.**}, \texttt{**Theorem.**}, \texttt{**Corollary.**},
  \texttt{**Definition.**}, \texttt{**Remark.**}, \texttt{**Example.**},
  \texttt{**Scholie.**} on their own line. Statement numbers go inline:
  \texttt{**Proposition\ 3.1.2.**\ *Statement…*}. The label
  \texttt{\textless{}!-\/-\ label:\ III.\textless{}Roman\textgreater{}.X.Y\ -\/-\textgreater{}}
  follows on the next line.
\item
  \textbf{Math.} Unicode math wrapped in backticks for inline. Displayed
  math in fenced
  \texttt{\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}\textasciigrave{}text}
  blocks. Numbered displayed equations get
  \texttt{\textless{}!-\/-\ label:\ eq:III.\textless{}Roman\textgreater{}.X.Y\ -\/-\textgreater{}}.
\item
  \textbf{Footnotes.} Markdown \([{}^{slug}]\) syntax. Original
  footnotes: \([{}^{<}exposé>-<sec>-<n>]\) (e.g.
  \([{}^{I}-1-1]\)). Editor footnotes:
  \([{}^{N}.D.E-<exposé>-<n>]\) (e.g.~\([{}^{N}.D.E-I-3]\)).
\item
  \textbf{Page marks.}
  \texttt{\textless{}!-\/-\ original\ page\ N\ -\/-\textgreater{}} at
  page boundaries (page numbers from the 2011 re-edition).
\item
  \textbf{Cross-references.} Source's own convention: \((VI_{B}, 5.3)\),
  \texttt{(EGA\ III,\ 4.1.5)}, \texttt{(SGA\ 1,\ IV\ 3.8)},
  \texttt{(Bible,\ XIV)}.
\item
  \textbf{Bibliographies.} Each Exposé's own bibliography section is
  preserved as \texttt{\#\#\ Bibliography}, entries as a numbered (or
  \texttt{{[}Key{]}}-keyed) list, journal titles in italics.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Cross-Exposé additions (discovered during
translation)}\label{cross-exposuxe9-additions-discovered-during-translation}

Each translated Exposé file ends with a fenced HTML-comment block titled
\texttt{LEDGER\ DELTA\ —\ Exposé\ \textless{}N\textgreater{}} recording
new terminology choices that the translator encountered beyond what this
glossary already covers. Those deltas are kept in place at the foot of
each Exposé rather than copied here, both to preserve the audit trail
and because consolidating the deltas (which span
\textasciitilde500--1,500 terms across the 26 Exposés) into a single
table would make the glossary harder to scan than the per-Exposé tables.
A future editorial pass may de-duplicate the most cross-cutting entries
(e.g.~\emph{dévissage}, the \texttt{prescheme}/\texttt{scheme} split,
Demazure's \emph{épinglage} → \emph{pinning}, Bertin's ``anti-affine''
envelope) into the tables above; until then, consult the deltas in the
Exposé files for the authoritative per-Exposé terminology choices.
